## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, AND ECONOMICAL LIBRARY, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III;**

A chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illuminated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; augmented with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers, and in which places of their works, commented on the texts of the individual books of Scripture.

An edition of the greatest accuracy, and easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and the number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and above all this collection itself: one, systematic, and chronological, bringing together for the first time in our library six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, gathered from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

**SECOND SERIES**, in which are published the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology was printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; the three hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for eighteen hundred. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are supplied in it only in Latin translation.

# In the year of the Lord 1112

Sigebert of Gembloux published the *Chronicle of Sigebert*.

Edited by D. Ludwig Conrad Bethmann.

(*In Pertz, German Historical Monuments, Writers, vol. V, p. 268.*)

[Col. 0009]

# Prolegomena

## Sigebert’s age, homeland, birth, deeds, and writings

## § I. Life

[Col. 0009A]

Sigebert [Note: [Col. 0009B] He almost always writes his name in this form. The following evidence concerning his life and writings is all that survives: *On Illustrious Men*, 172; the *Chronicle* under the year 1112; the *Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux* in Dachery II, 768; and the *Elevation of St. Guibert* in the *Acta Sanctorum*, May, vol. V, 266. We have supplied these passages in full. All the rest derive from them. Among more recent works, one is sufficient: V. D. Sigfrid Hirsch, *On the Life and Writings of Sigebert* (Berlin, 1841), a work of exceptionally learned diligence, especially in investigating sources; we gratefully acknowledge that we have learned much from it.], born in Belgica [Note: [Col. 0009B] This is highly probable, though the evidence is lacking. When he calls himself a Frank and a Gaul — in the preface: “the origin of our people, namely the kingdom of the Franks”; in *On Illustrious Men*, 84, he abbreviated the Gallican Psalter, “which we Gauls use”; compare 156: “and many, especially Germans, authorize such a manner of fasting” — he does not indicate France, but Gembloux, where he wrote. For in the *Life of Deoderic*, chapter 5, he places Metz in Belgica, and in the years 1020 and 1094 he calls Francia “Gaul.”] around the year 1030, entered the profession of the Rule of Saint Benedict at a very early age in the monastery of Gembloux, then governed by Abbot Olbert [Note: [Col. 0009B] This can be inferred only from his own account of Olbert in the *Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux*. His words there are: “Those whom he now protects by his grace, he formerly nourished here with such fatherly mercy.” It is not strictly necessary to think that these words refer to Sigebert himself, since they may equally well signify the entire flock of Gembloux. Yet what is related there about Olbert is of such a kind that no one could have written it who had not loved Olbert while he was alive and been present when the news of his funeral reached Gembloux.], a man distinguished for virtue and learning.

When Olbert died in 1048 and Macelin was elected abbot, Sigebert soon afterward moved to Metz [Note: [Col. 0010B] He himself says in *On Illustrious Men*, 172: “placed at Metz in my early youth.”], to St. Vincent, at the invitation of Fulcuin, Macelin’s brother, who called him there to direct the schools.

After performing this office for a long time and acquiring great renown through writing and teaching, so that many came from every direction to hear him, he nevertheless preferred, “like a most prudent bee, to return to the hives of his own monastery” [Note: [Col. 0010B] As he himself says of Abbot Olbert in the *Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux*.]; and, returning to Gembloux around the year 1071 [Note: [Col. 0010B] For he had already written at Gembloux the letter on married priests, published in 1075. The *Miracles of Saint Sigebert*, composed while he was still at Metz — if Sigebert is indeed its author, which there is no reason to deny — cannot have appeared before the seventh year after the translation of the saint, namely 1070.], which he loved above all, he devoted himself there to the same occupations as among the people of Metz.

Entirely devoted to prayer, reading, writing, and teaching, although he seemed especially suited to judging public affairs, he nevertheless always abstained from conducting such business, being concerned solely with the inner welfare of his monastery. For its sake he did not shrink from labor even in old age.

When the people of Gembloux desired the elevation of their founder, Guibert, Sigebert was one of those most active in the undertaking: a monk of ancient learning and reverence, “the eye of this church of ours at Gembloux,” which he watched over piously through his life, conduct, and religious fervor. He was all the more certain of Guibert’s grace of holiness because he had pursued the saint’s life, full of virtues, with much elegance of style.

Having received an evident opportunity to fulfill his desire through the manifest display of miracles, he began to negotiate with those who possessed the necessary authority concerning the elevation of the saint’s body. [Col. 0011A] Finally, after consulting the will of Lord Abbot Liethard and receiving his blessing, he himself undertook a mission to obtain from the bishop of Liège the authority required for the matter [Note: [Col. 0011C] *Elevation of St. Guibert*, in the *Acta Sanctorum*, May, vol. V, 266]. He carried it out with such skill, although then nearly eighty years old, that almost at the end of his life he at last saw the solemn celebration of the elevation in 1110 and himself celebrated it with readings and antiphons [Note: [Col. 0011C] *On Illustrious Men*, 172].

Two years later, on the third day before the Nones of October 1112 [Note: [Col. 0011C] Not in 1113, as Robert of Torigni reports. For Abbot Liethard had already died on the sixth day before the Nones of February 1113. Robert’s error arose because the copy of the *Chronicle* that he transcribed, from Beauvais, divides the year 1112 into two years.], he died.

How gracious a memory he left behind is testified by his disciple from Gembloux [Note: [Col. 0011C] In the *Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux*. We give it from an excellent Leipzig manuscript collated by Waitz.]:

> Lord Sigebert, praiseworthy and beloved among the learned of his age for the integrity of his morals and the variety of his knowledge, has no need of our praises, because his works praise him. When, in the time of his youth, under Abbot Macelin, he was made known to the people of Metz and lived for a long time in the monastery of St. Vincent the Martyr with Abbot Fulcuin, he was an open fountain of wisdom, not only for monks but also for clerics who flocked to him from every direction.
>
> His memory remains sweet to many of the people of Metz even today, and traces of his teaching still survive among them. What and how much he wrote there at their request, he himself shows in the *Book of Illustrious Men* that he composed.
>
> He was dearly loved not only by Christians but also by the Jews living in the same city, because he was skilled at distinguishing the Hebrew truth [Note: [Col. 0011C] That is, the text translated into Latin by Jerome from the Hebrew itself, not from the Septuagint. Compare the *Chronicle* under the years 382 and 395.] from the other editions, and in those matters that they stated according to the Hebrew truth he agreed with the assertions of the Jews.
>
> After a long time, and only with difficulty having obtained permission, he returned to the monastery of Gembloux. [Col. 0012A] He brought many things for the use and adornment of the church, acquired through the voluntary generosity of those whom he had instructed.
>
> The older men, those of higher rank and sharper judgment, who were in the city of Liège, used to visit him whenever some question arose, bringing it to him and discussing it with him. Chief among them was Lord Henry, archdeacon and dean of the church of St. Lambert. At his request Sigebert wrote for the people of Trier a book on the fasts of the Four Ember Seasons, as well as many things that he mentions in the *Book of Illustrious Men*.
>
> In the monastery of Gembloux he instructed me, who have written these things, and many far better men; he sent many of them before him, and, alas, left only a few behind him.
>
> Yet although he was a prudent man of great gravity, he was not austerely indiscriminate, but toward everyone, as circumstances required, he displayed a measured moderation. Reading and meditation upon the divine Scriptures occupied him above all, yet the daily celebration of Mass and devout prayer to God always took precedence.
>
> Worn down by long old age, when he had taken to his bed with a final illness, he lost nothing of the prudence innate in him. Since the brothers wished that, when he died, he should receive a place of burial within the monastery, he, as a man of higher counsel who preferred to be found humble in the sight of God rather than presumptuous, earnestly requested that he be buried in our cemetery with all the brothers.
>
> Thus he died on the third day before the Nones of October, in the time of Lord Abbot Liethard [Note: [Col. 0011C] The following verses concerning him occur next in the Leipzig manuscript:
>
> “Joined to the just, may Sigebert live for Christ!
>
> The world changes and passes, though it is thought to stand.
>
> A living man passes away, but by dying passes beyond.
>
> Alas! Death spares no human being; it is given to all.
>
> No age passes beyond the fixed limits appointed for anyone.
>
> If tears for this world could bring back the dead,
>
> how many, and what sort, and how spiritual,
>
> renowned in every field of learning and, alas, now rare,
>
> would be found to mourn the deserved loss of Sigebert.
>
> But because the illustrious are rare and cannot be recalled,
>
> withdrawn from the world, may they be joined to the heavenly citizens!
>
> May God always grant us consolation. Amen.”
>
> In the same manuscript, later, folio 56, the following is found:
>
> **Epitaph of Lord Sigebert**
>
> “Alas! Death, increase of mourning, cause of grief!
>
> Through you, how many does the world mourn, snatched away from it!
>
> Your darts strike us and fix wounds even in the heart;
>
> this wound is fixed in the mind, and there is no resisting it.
>
> Here, breaking through the hardened heart, anguish strikes,
>
> when death, separating brothers and changing everything
>
> in which love for dear ones and social affection burn,
>
> disrupts by changing and breaks with its hard thumb
>
> both natural affections and social ones.
>
> Let a man flourish like a flower in spring;
>
> let him heap possessions upon possessions, distress mind and body,
>
> anxiously filling cares that will rush down with him:
>
> one day makes the wretched man utterly pitiable.
>
> Let him be king, let him be prince, let the common people be poor;
>
> the law of death draws them all alike, though it distinguishes them very carefully.
>
> For there is a just distinction of the just lot.
>
> Earthly things please the earthly and those devoted to the earth.
>
> Contempt for vain things and sparing use make the just leaner
>
> and more ready,
>
> so that they may be upright in ascent, in heart and in deed.
>
> Let them strive to be admitted among the heavenly,
>
> and cast out utterly among the lowest,
>
> to attain the pious joys of the highest life.
>
> Let the whole guardianship of the heart be their contest.
>
> For the predator lays snares prepared for everyone,
>
> and his evil mind possesses so many and varied deceptions
>
> that no bodily sense is safe from them;
>
> the deceitful enemy struggles by force and trickery
>
> to diminish the merit of the just or subject them to himself.
>
> If he swallows unstable minds, he considers them worthless.
>
> Thanks to you, Christ! Through you the just overcome
>
> all the snares and ruin that he prepares.
>
> Calling back those who follow crooked paths, you join to yourself those who stand,
>
> and your hope helps ours, your abundant power fulfilling it,
>
> saving us through hope and leading us, grateful to you, to the goal.
>
> You were like the just in your great devotion to integrity,
>
> suited to conducting divine and worldly affairs;
>
> law of life and mirror of what is right, you were, Sigebert,
>
> to whom our speech pays its due in writing.
>
> You lived in harmony; may you live forever as our companion,
>
> and may the same fellowship belong to our dead.”
>
> “Our verses give you two verses about yourself” [Note: [Col. 0013D] That is, since in the manuscript each individual verse consists of two parts, separated by a certain space and distinguished by a larger letter, the initial letters at the beginnings of the verses spell:
>
> “Peter, holy one, your
>
> Godescalcus made these verses.”
>
> [Col. 0014D] In the middle of the verses:
>
> “Kindly keeper of heaven’s keys,
>
> I beg you, open it to him.”
>
> Amen.] ].

These are the traditions we possess concerning Sigebert’s life: few, indeed, but sufficient to make us recognize a man so distinguished by the purity of his life and the humanity of his spirit that wherever he lived he was dear to everyone; modestly retiring, so that he always avoided glory and honors [Note: [Col. 0013C] Throughout the whole *Chronicle* he does not speak even a word about his own affairs. Indeed, in two letters in the Gembloux manuscript he inscribed not his own name but merely “a certain person’s letter.”]; and, until his death, deeply grateful to his monastery and to Olbert, who had been a father and supporter to him as a boy, for whom he erected so beautiful a memorial in the *Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux* [Note: [Col. 0013C] He is also the only one among the abbots of Gembloux whom he mentions in the *Chronicle*.].

He was a monk of ancient reverence, pure in mind, and a most vigorous opponent among monks of avarice and evil license [Note: [Col. 0013C] *Life of St. Guibert*, 8: “the root of evils and the wicked stepmother of monks, namely the desire for private property.” *Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux*: “under the pretext of poverty, while each person looks after himself and, disregarding the integrity of common life, seeks individually to increase his household property, people lived with excessive license, which is wholly inappropriate to the souls of monks,” and much else in the same place. Whatever he received as gifts from his disciples at Metz, he transferred entirely to his monastery.]; serious without being irritable, benevolent toward all, Jews no less than Christians; firm in judgment without arrogance, considering matters alone and not persons; an intrepid defender of justice and truth; wherever he saw wrongdoing, he condemned it sincerely but without hateful bitterness, not condemning as a zealot but as one who knew human nature well [Note: [Col. 0013C] Compare the *Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux*, p. 762].

We see him as much less devoted to superstitions and prodigies than most of his contemporaries. He dared to think and speak freely about miracles, and beyond what was usual in his age [Note: [Col. 0013D] In the *Life of St. Guibert*: “At last the man of God, perfected in the grace of virtues—which is greater than if he had shone with the glory of miracles. For virtues are sometimes obscured by miracles, whereas miracles are commended by virtues alone.”].

He appears exceptionally weighty in intellect, thought, and speech in the letters that he wrote at Gembloux. His remarks there concerning the practice of explaining everything allegorically [Note: [Col. 0013D] *Letter on the Four Ember Fasts*: “We also take pleasure in allegorizing the number of the weeks that distinguish the seasonal fasts. But since, as Origen says, in the fields of allegory there is free license to wander, that freedom should have a limit in its progress. This allegory is pleasing, but not in such a way that it should be fixed as the certain rule of the fasts.”]; his remarks on the dangers threatening the Church and religion because fasts, celibacy, and many other practices pertaining only to the monastic order were gradually imposed upon the Christian faith itself as though they were to be observed by everyone [Note: [Col. 0013D] Compare the letter *On Married Priests*]; his practice of returning always to the Sacred Scriptures as the supreme norm of the Church after rejecting other authorities [Note: [Col. 0013D] *On the Four Ember Fasts*: “In this we follow these and other holy and learned men, not because they were holy and learned, but because they are proved to be defenders of the truth,” and so forth.]; his practice of reducing those most serious questions to the condition of life and of human nature, and appealing to the reason of his readers, rather than using sophistries or emotions, as many were then doing; his statement that authorities are unnecessary where these matters speak clearly; his warning that truth must be sought in everything and that one must not serve the letter [Note: [Col. 0014C] “Why do we cling so tightly to the dead letter that we stray from the life-giving spirit?”]; and his position that something is not true because authorities say it, but that authorities are to be believed because they say what is true [Note: [Col. 0014C] The same work]—all this reveals a spirit far superior to that age, and one worthy of a higher station than the modesty of Sigebert wished to occupy.

It is therefore no wonder that the leading men of the Church of Liège always referred to the monk of Gembloux whenever some important matter had to be undertaken, and published his judgment as the public opinion of their church.

In learning he was distinguished among the foremost of his time. The ancient authors, especially Horace, were read by him with profit, as his writings show, scattered with flowers gathered from them; among the Fathers of the Church he preferred Jerome and Augustine.

He tasted Greek, even if he did not thoroughly absorb it [Note: [Col. 0014C] Some dispute this. Yet I scarcely believe that he would have inserted with a certain predilection so many Greek words—such as, in the *Life of Deoderic*, in the Invocation, *Kyrie* (“Lord”), *Christe* (“Christ”), *theos* (“God”), *pantocraton* (“Almighty”), *archos* (“ruler”), *anarchos* (“without beginning”), and *gymnasio* (“exercise”); in chapter 5, *aorasia* (“invisibility”); chapter 9, *logio* (“oracle” or “saying”); chapter 10, *prolensim* [uncertain]; chapter 17, *neutericis* [uncertain]; in verse 25, *anatolen* (“east”), *disin* (“west”), *mesembrian* (“south”), *arcton* (“north”), *paranimphus* (“bridegroom’s friend”); in verse 1, *hidraulin* (“hydraulic organ”), in verse 72, *orizon* (“horizon”); and in the epitaph of Deoderic, chapter 22, *ebdenis* [uncertain]—into the work he composed when still quite young, and into this work alone, unless he had done so under the stimulus of youthful pleasure, which delights learners when they immediately make use of what they have recently acquired. This also explains why such expressions no longer occur in his other works, since the pleasure of novelty was absent. Nor was the use of Greek so rare in those regions at that time. Many manuscripts of St. Amand at Elnone, St. Lawrence at Liège, and St. Peter at Gembloux—manuscripts that I have seen still extant—contain Greek words and sentences, indeed entire pages. — The authors of literary histories alone make Sigebert an expert in Hebrew, relying on the single passage from the *Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux* cited above, although comparison with the passage in the *Chronicle* sufficiently shows that Jerome’s translation, not the Hebrew words themselves, is indicated there. Sigebert’s other arguments do not depend on Hebrew learning.]: in Latin he cultivated both prose and poetry—heroic [Note: [Col. 0014D] The *Ecclesiastes* and the *Passion of the Holy Thebans*], elegiac [Note: [Col. 0014D] Frequently in the *Life of Deoderic*], and Alcaic [Note: [Col. 0014D] The poem on Deoderic and the *Passion of St. Lucy*]—not without the aid of the Muse.

Yet he accommodated himself to the practice of his age by making even the middle word of each verse rhyme with the final word, including in Alcaic verse.

He was also so skilled in music, through the instruction and example of Olbert, [Col. 0015A] that he knew how to compose antiphons in musical modes [Note: [Col. 0015C] *On Illustrious Men*, 172: “In the art of music I rendered antiphons and responsories for Saints Machlovius and Guibert melodious.” That musical and geometrical studies, initiated by Olbert, flourished equally in the monastery under Sigebert’s leadership is attested by many manuscripts of Gembloux written in the eleventh and twelfth centuries and preserved in the Burgundy Library. In one of them, no. 10090, parchment quarto, copied at the end of the eleventh century, among many other things, on four and a half leaves, one reads:

> “A certain person’s statement concerning the nature of the tones. There are five musical consonances, of which the first and best known is that called the diapason. Nevertheless, all verses are sung in this manner: ‘Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.’”

> It is nowhere apparent who the author was. A seventeenth-century hand wrote “Sigebert’s” above the word “a certain person’s,” and this seems not implausible. For the letters that our Sigebert himself lists among his minor works likewise have written above them in the Gembloux manuscript, “A certain person’s letter.”]

Nevertheless, he devoted the greatest effort to chronology and history.

## § II. Writings

He himself lists his writings in the book *On Illustrious Men*, following the examples of Jerome and Gennadius, as follows:

**[EXCERPT.]**
Sigebert of Gembloux, a monk, wrote many small works. When stationed at Metz in his youth, in the church of Saint Vincent, to instruct boys, I wrote the Life of Deoderic, bishop and founder of the church and abbey; in it, by way of digression, I also celebrated that city in heroic verse [Note: [Col. 0015C] Below.]. I wrote the Passion of Saint Lucy, who rests there, in Alcaic verse [Note: [Col. 0015C] Not yet published; only specimens are found [Col. 0015D] in Mabillon, Annales IV, 372, and in Jacobs and Ukert, Merkwürdigkeiten der Gothaer Bibliothek II, 1, 140.]. When certain people criticized that prophecy of Saint Lucy—“I announce to you the peace granted to the Church of God, Diocletian having been expelled from his kingdom and Maximian having died today”—I replied carefully, having considered the chronology and the truth of the events [Note: [Col. 0015D] This unpublished letter is found in Gotha codex no. 61.]. Nevertheless, I also wrote a sermon in praise of that virgin, in which I arranged, in the proper chronological sequence, her translations from Sicily to the Italian city of Corfinium and from Corfinium to Metz, a city of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0015D] Edited by Meurisse in Historia episcoporum Mettensium, p. 329.].

I wrote the Life of King Sigebert, founder of the church and abbey of Saint Martin situated outside the city of Metz [Col. 0016A] [Note: [Col. 0015D] In Duchesne, SS. II, 591. Another version, published by Surius under 1 February, in Acta Sanctorum, February I, 227, and by Bouquet II, 597, has been proved by V. D. Hirsch to be an interpolated version of the former genuine text. The occasion for writing it seems to have been supplied by the translation of the saint carried out in 1063. Mosander and Henschenius also attribute to Sigebert the history of this translation, together with its miracles, written after 1070 (in Acta Sanctorum II); since this attribution rests on no testimony apart from Mosander, nothing nevertheless contradicts the opinion, which is highly plausible.].

After returning to the monastery of Gembloux, I wrote the Passion of our patrons, the Thebans, in heroic verse [Note: [Col. 0015D] The only manuscript of the poem, which had been considered lost, was shown to me by Geel at Leiden in the public library, 114, A. The poem is divided into three books: the first contains 892 verses, the second 900, and the third 1,130. The prologue of the first book recounts how the poet entered the temple of Philosophy and what splendid things he saw there, together with a poetic enumeration of the holy Fathers of the Church. The prologue [Col. 0016C] of the second book urges the poet, having left his bed on the first day, to continue on the journey he had undertaken; it adds some remarks on the praises of Aurora, friend of the Muses, and a beautiful description of evening time. The prologue of the third book concerns Diocletian’s persecution and how God preserved his Church. These details too I owe to Geel’s humanity, which I can never praise enough.].

I wrote the Life of Saint Guibert the confessor, founder of our church at Gembloux [Note: [Col. 0016C] In Surius under 23 May; Mabillon, Acta V, 301; Acta Sanctorum, May V, 259. It was written before Guibert became famous for miracles, which began to occur in 1099.], from which I excerpted the lessons in suitable order for his deposition. By the art of music I composed antiphons and responsories for Saints Maclovius and Guibert [Note: [Col. 0016C] No longer extant.].

I also wrote the Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux [Note: [Col. 0016C] Dachery, Spicilegium II, 759. Sigebert ended with the first years of Mascelin. What follows concerning Mascelin and Thietmar was added by another writer. The remainder was written by several people over the course of time, as the autograph Leipzig manuscript shows.]. I improved the Lives of Saints Maclovius [Note: [Col. 0016C] In Surius under 15 November. It was written at the command of Abbot Thietmar, who ruled from 1076 to 1099.] and Theodard [Note: [Col. 0016D] In Surius under 10 September; Acta Sanctorum, September III, 597.] in a more polished style.

I initially improved the Life of Saint Lambert in a polished style; later, at the request of Henry, archdeacon and dean of the church of Saint Lambert, I embellished it with comparisons drawn from the ancients, in accordance with the sequence of events. Nevertheless, some people prefer the earlier version, as being simple, and copy it more carefully. For it is clearer in meaning and more lucid in wording [Note: [Col. 0016D] Chapeaville published the earlier, simple version under the false name of Reinerus, Gesta pontificum Tungrensium I, 411; the other, ornamented version is in Acta Sanctorum, September V, 589. The ancients in question are Moses, Joshua, David, Constantine the Great, and Saint Benedict.].

At the request of the same man, I also replied, with powerful arguments from the Fathers, to the letter that Pope Hildebrand wrote to Herman, bishop of Metz, attacking royal authority [Note: [Col. 0016D] Hitherto unpublished and regarded as lost, I found it in Brussels in an excellent Gembloux manuscript of the early twelfth century, where it bears the title: “Sayings of a certain author concerning the discord between pope and king, criticized by examples from earlier times.” It begins: “We read in the Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs,” etc. It was written between 1076, when Hildebrand first wrote to Herman, and 1084, when Henry, called “king” in the letter, obtained the imperial crown.].

I wrote to Henry himself an apology against those who criticize the masses of married priests [Note: [Col. 0016D] It exists in the same Gembloux manuscript under the title: “Letter of a certain author against the slander of laymen directed at married presbyters.” Martène and Durand published it in Thesaurus I, 230, attributing it to Wenricus, although a hand from the beginning of the seventeenth century had already written the name “Sigebert” in the margin of the manuscript. Unaware of this, Hirsch recognized the truth by conjecture alone and proved it by arguments, pp. 196–211.].

At his request also, I replied to the letter of Pope Paschal, who ordered the church of Liège, just as that of Cambrai, to be destroyed by Robert, count of the Flemings [Col. 0017A] [Note: [Col. 0017C] Paschal’s letter was written in 1102 or 1103, and therefore at the same time as Sigebert’s reply. Hirsch lists eleven editions of it, in the following chronological order: Conciliorum collectio Coloniensis II, 809; Schardius, Dissertatio de jurisdictione imperii et ecclesiae; Centuriatores Magdeburgenses XII, p. 1110; Goldast, Apologia, p. 189; Conciliorum collectio Parisiensis XXVI, 701; Labbe, Concilia X, 630; Brown, appendix to Ortwin Gratius, Fasciculus rerum expetendarum et fugiendarum, p. 176; Hardouin, Concilia VI, 2, 769; Eccard, Corpus historiae medii aevi II, 238; Martène, Collectio amplissima I, 587; Mansi, Concilia XX, 986. Gervais translated it into French in 1697; into Dutch, if I am not mistaken, in our own time by van Asch van Wyk, councillor of Utrecht.].

Nevertheless, at his insistence, I replied to the people of Trier concerning the fast of the Ember Days (Quattuor Tempora). They observe the rules of a certain Berno, which, in their view, are well arranged according to allegory, and they differ from the custom of the people of Liège [Note: [Col. 0017C] There are two letters: one written immediately after the council of 1095, the other shortly afterward. Martène published them in Thesaurus I, 295 and 306, from a twelfth-century Gembloux manuscript, now Brussels no. 5476.].

I rendered Ecclesiastes in heroic verse, arranging it in a work of varied texture in three ways: literally, allegorically, and mythologically [Note: [Col. 0017C] Andreae [Col. 0017D] and Miraeus saw the unpublished poem at Gembloux; where it is now, we do not know.].

Imitating Eusebius Pamphilus, who was the first among the Greeks to arrange a Chronicle from the time of Abraham, I too ordered, from the point at which his work breaks off up to the fourth year, the whole sequence of times and events, as far as I could, with moderation of style. When I was carefully rereading Bede’s De temporibus and saw him censuring Dionysius, the compiler of the cycles, because, by incorrectly arranging the years of the Lord’s Passion, he seemed in every respect to conflict with the Gospel of John at the points determining Easter, I thought it worthwhile to remove, by going back farther, the whole cloud of error and to pour the light of truth into those who love truth.

For Marianus Scotus, a man far more eloquent than others of his age, had undertaken the same task. In weaving his Chronicle from the birth of Christ to the state of his own times, he had arranged the years of Christ, on one side, according to the authority of the Gospel, and, directly opposite, according to Dionysius, so that the diligent reader could see how far Dionysius deviated from the truth of the Gospel.

But when I considered that the supporters of Dionysius, once they had absorbed his teaching, were not easily brought to abandon it, I balanced the caution of my modest intellect with an even measure. Proceeding midway between them, I gathered all the years that had elapsed from the origin [Col. 0017C] of the world, or that would elapse in the future, inscribing the calculation according to Hebrew truth—namely, by lunar cycles, which close after nineteen years, and solar cycles, which close after twenty-eight years, whose multiplication produces the great cycle of 532 years.

I distinguished the years in lines on either side, together with Adam’s years, the epacts, the concurrents, the Easter limits, and the Sundays of Easter. I followed the same path as Dionysius, but not the same tracks. A diligent reader will easily discover this, if he is curious.

And because I divided the entire work into ten great cycles, each consisting of 532 years, I prefaced the book with this title, so that it might be called the Decennial. I also placed before it a prologue in the form of a dialogue, which I divided into three little volumes, indicating, through the persons of the questioner and the respondent, the purpose and usefulness of the work itself and the branch of philosophy to which it belongs—namely, physics.

I also appended useful rules [Col. 0018B] for finding years, dates, and indictions, according to the arrangements of the work itself [Note: [Col. 0017D] The book is unpublished; Miraeus gave its opening lines in his preface to Sigebert, from a now-lost Gembloux manuscript.].

Imitating Jerome and Gennadius as well, I wrote this final little book, On Illustrious Men, as far as I was able to investigate from the knowledge available to me [Note: [Col. 0017D] Published in Suffridus Petrus, Scriptores ecclesiastici, Cologne 1580; Miraeus, Bibliotheca ecclesiastica, Antwerp 1639; Fabricius, Bibliotheca ecclesiastica, Hamburg 1718. The works attributed to Sigebert by others in addition to these—sermons, letters, Lives of the Roman Pontiffs, the History of Jerusalem, the Life of Saint Lullus, the Chronicle of Saint Vincent of Metz, the Chronology of the Bishops of Metz, and the Passion of the Eleven Thousand Virgins—are refuted both by the profound silence of Sigebert, who elsewhere mentions even minor works, and by Hirsch, pp. 346–353, who has shown that they entirely lack supporting arguments.].

## Chronicle

Of these works, the Chronicle is first in fame but almost last in date. He did not compose it with a continuous pen, nor in such a way that, once the works preceding it had been completed, he immediately committed the events of his own time to writing as he learned of them. Rather, he seems to have written the whole work only during the final decade of his life.

For the years 956–1099 were written almost in a single course, neither before 1100 [Note: [Col. 0018C] This is shown above all by the Annals of Liège, which Sigebert did not append almost in their entirety to the Chronicle for the years 956–1099, but wove into it, so that it is sufficiently clear that this whole part of the work could not have been composed before 1100. Moreover, since the material for the years 1097–1099 came from a letter of the crusaders published only at the beginning of 1100, these years too must have been written in one course, and not before 1100. Only one passage seems to object: under the year 1068, Sigebert still appears unaware of Deoderic’s death, which we learn from Bernold occurred in 1073. But the name of the emperor prevents us from assuming that this passage was written at that time: from 1058 onward he consistently, and with a certain affectation, gives him the name Henry, showing that all this was composed only after 1083. Moreover, Marianus’s Chronicle, which Sigebert used extensively, could not have been available before 1082. The words under 1081—“whence the earth grieved” and “grieves”—and under 1085, “thus written concerning this,” cannot have been written in those very years.] nor after 1106 [Note: Under the year 1056, the words “for fifty years,” which Sigebert added only when preparing a second edition of the work, are attested not only by the Gembloux manuscript but also by manuscript A, where they are absent.]. Hence I believe that the earlier sections too were composed not long before that time.

He released it publicly [Col. 0018C] before 1105 [Note: Ekkehard copied it in that year, and Waltram in 1109.]. Later he went through the whole work again, corrected it, and enlarged it [Note: The additions made in the Gembloux manuscript by hands 1, β, γ, δ, and ε are absent from manuscript A. We have enclosed them in brackets so that it may be clear what belongs to the first recension and what to the second. [Col. 0019C] All the manuscripts of the second recension place the Chronicles of Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper before our author’s work. One might therefore easily believe that Sigebert himself had prefixed them to this second recension, since the Verdun manuscript shows that they were not yet present in the first. But in that case those Chronicles ought to have existed in the Gembloux manuscript, or at least in Anselm’s time, which F1 2, 4 forbids us to believe. It is certain that Sigebert wished to continue Eusebius and Jerome with his Chronicle; but it does not follow that he joined it so closely to them that they formed a single book. The preface already argues against this: it is extensive, as befits a distinct book appearing under its own auspices, and it does not refer to Eusebius even once. There is no foundation for the contrary opinion apart from the agreement of these manuscripts; but we do not need Sigebert to explain that agreement. Since we very often see scribes copy several works from different manuscripts into one, the monk of Affligem, B., from whom all those manuscripts derive, wished to have the whole history of the world contained in one volume for his monastery. He therefore prefixed to Sigebert the same manuscript of Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper that Sigebert had used; concerning it, see below, no. 52. If Sigebert himself had added it, he would certainly have omitted Prosper, since an author taking up the thread from the end of Jerome would have done so.].

He carried it down to the year 1111 [Note: He himself attests this in On Illustrious Men: “I ordered, as far as I could, with moderation of style, the whole sequence of times and events up to the year 1111.”]. But, overtaken by death, he did not himself publish this second recension. Anselm issued it immediately in 1112, adding a brief account of that year and of Sigebert’s death [Note: Every manuscript, without exception, contains the words concerning Sigebert’s death, which evidently must be attributed to Anselm. Since, in the Gembloux manuscript, they are written with exactly the same pen and ink as the rest of the narrative for 1112, that narrative too must be attributed to Anselm. This is already probable in itself and is made certain by Sigebert’s words extending only to the year 1111. Indeed, the appearance of the Gembloux manuscript could easily lead someone to believe that Anselm’s narrative begins earlier, at the words under 1111, “What, or how,” etc.; these are in another hand and do not fit well with what precedes. The beginning of the year 1111 itself already contains some features that might raise doubts about the author. It is written almost as though nothing had yet been said about Henry V, Gregory VII, or his quarrel with the emperor; compare the words “Henry the fifth of this name, king,” and “what was begun by Gregory the ninth pope of this name, who was called Hildebrand.” Henry, whom Sigebert had previously almost always called emperor, is now called king. Yet the very use of “emperor” shows that the years 1108–1110 were written after his coronation. It is therefore highly plausible that the account of the coronation too belongs to the same author, although this is not certain, since Sigebert’s words up to the year 1111 may be understood as referring both to the beginning and to the end of that year. We therefore leave this uncertain; but that the whole year 1112 belongs to Anselm, we seem justified in maintaining. The manuscripts of the second recension do indeed contradict this, since, although they do not contain Anselm’s continuation, they all present the year 1112. But they all also contain Sigebert’s death. If they could add the account of his death, which no one will deny was written by another, they could just as well add the whole year, which in the Gembloux manuscript is attached to what precedes by the same hand and without any intervening space. As for the Alnensis manuscript and B3*, which add after 1112, “Thus far Sigebert brought his Chronicle,” the authority of such subscriptions—made from the manuscripts that the scribes were copying—is no greater than that of the French continuator, F2, who maintains that Sigebert carried his Chronicle to 1148, or of Robert of Torigni, who says that it ends in 1100. Robert surely says this because he had decided to begin his own work in that year with the reign of Henry I, as Hirsch rightly observed. For he copied Sigebert word for word as far as 1112. In the same way, Ralph of Diceto and Baldwin of Ninove falsely indicate the ending of Robert’s work and of the Affligem continuator.].

Sigebert undertook it as an old man, thoroughly prepared by long and varied practice in writing and by his studies devoted to the calculation of times, and further assisted by a great supply of books for that period [Note: Olbertus, the founder of the Gembloux library, had already, according to Sigebert in the Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux, “collected more than 100 volumes of Sacred Scripture and 50 books of secular learning.” Many others had been added to that number in Sigebert’s own time, as is shown by the form of writing in the many Gembloux manuscripts that now adorn the Brussels library.].

In addition, he possessed long experience of life and knowledge of human affairs not prejudiced by monastic preconceptions; he had a mind passionately devoted to truth, judging events and people without anger or partiality. His was an age stirred by the gravest questions, of the kind that usually prepares writers and readers alike. In the midst of that turbulent age there was also the secure leisure of the monastery, where he could think what he wished and write what he thought, fearing nothing for himself, since both the church and the whole people of Liège held the same views.

Thus Sigebert seemed, more than anyone else, almost called to write history; and it is deeply regrettable that he composed nothing but rather barren annals. Two things above all led him in this direction: his love of chronological study above all else, and the example of Marianus, Bede, and Eusebius. Since, throughout the whole Middle Ages, many people who wrote history aimed to embrace the entire history of the world in a single volume, Sigebert too tried to accomplish this. He admired Eusebius and Jerome, while he did not approve the others to the same degree, and he carried their work down to his own time by the same method they had used.

He therefore wished his Chronicle to be nothing other than what we commonly call a synchronistic survey of universal history. He assigned the first place to the calculation of time. Thus the succession of popes and the succession of emperors and kings are read in full, while the narrative of events is added only in second place. In selecting events, he aimed to carry forward in one continuous thread the more serious affairs of the empire, the dangers and advances of the Church, and men distinguished by holiness and learning, while scattering the rest as if by way of incidental mention.

In narrating events, however, he strives for equal brevity throughout the entire Chronicle. He therefore treated the events of his own time with the same barrenness as the earliest centuries—for he did not wish to narrate, but to make notes. And, so that the uniformity of the synchronistic survey would not be disturbed if he gave a great deal about his own time in the manner of Lambert, Herman, and others, he preferred to patch together almost the entire work from other sources [Col. 0021A] [Note: As he himself says of Olbertus in the Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux.]. This manner of writing was not merely excused by the Middle Ages; it was considered highly useful and pursued as vigorously as possible.

## Sources

His sources were the following: Jerome [Note: Years 381, 382, 386, 406. In investigating the sources, I gratefully acknowledge how much I owe both to our Waitz and to the book of V. D. Hirsch.]; Augustine [Note: On Heresies, years 386 and 404.]; Orosius; Idatius; Prosper [Note: By this name he always means the Pithoean or Imperial Chronicle. On it, compare Waitz in our Annals VII, 230. He did not know Prosper’s genuine Chronicle. He therefore used a manuscript containing Eusebius, Jerome, and the Pithoean Chronicle. That such a manuscript already existed before Sigebert is shown by the old Bollandist manuscript; compare Acta Sanctorum, May VII, preface, 40. I have seen the same chronicle, following Eusebius and Jerome without Sigebert, in two fifteenth-century manuscripts of the Brussels Royal Library: 9486, where it is followed by Martinus Polonus, and 9486, where it is followed by Marianus. Waitz therefore rightly limited Scaliger’s claim that the Chronicle was found only in Sigebert’s manuscripts.]; Rufinus, Ecclesiastical History; Gennadius, On Ecclesiastical Writers; Cassiodorus, Tripartite History; Jordanes; Gregory’s Dialogues; the prologue to the Salian Law [Note: Year 422.]; Lives of many saints, including those of Jerome, Gregory the Great, Martin, Maurus, Remigius, Antidius, Amandus, Clodulf of Metz, Maclovius, Columbanus, Kilian, Wulfram, and Gertrude; Adrevald’s Translation of Saint Benedict; Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs; catalogues of pontiffs; Gregory of Tours; Fredegar with the continuations; Deeds of the Frankish Kings [Col. 0021B]; Bede; Paul the Deacon; Miscellaneous History; Flodoard’s History of Reims; Aimoin’s History of the Franks; Einhard’s Life of Charlemagne; Regino; the Annals of St-Vaast, Fulda, and Metz [Note: From these he also drew whatever words of the Bertinian, Fulda, and Regino annals are found in his work; he did not consult the annals themselves.]; the Annals of Lobbes [Note: He used them for the years 903–972; he did not use the earlier part.]; and above all the Annals of Liège [Note: At first he uses them more rarely, for the years 570, 630, 646, 661, 665, 735, 737, and 774; from then on he entirely abandons their traces until 956. From that point he incorporated them into the Chronicle almost in their entirety and in nearly the same words. Indeed, the years 1113–1146, with only very few exceptions, appear in the continuation of Anselm and the Gembloux continuation without even a change of wording. Yet anyone can see that this continuation cannot have derived from these annals. The Gembloux manuscript shows that it was written year by year, indeed month by month, as the events narrated occurred. Hence some will think that all the words of these annals found in Sigebert were copied into the annals only in the twelfth century, as we see happened in the Annals of Elnon, Marchiennes, and others. But both the manuscript itself and a comparison with the Annals of Laubach attest that everything before 1056 was copied in one continuous eleventh-century hand from older annals. Thus, up to this point, there can be no doubt that the Liège annals were Sigebert’s source. Furthermore, the years 1055–1098 were written by several eleventh-century hands at different times, generally contemporaneously with the events; there is no trace of the twelfth century in them, however closely one searches. These too, therefore, cannot have been taken from Sigebert. The situation is different in what follows. A single, previously unattested hand wrote the years 1099–1124 in one continuous course; the source’s description of the hand or ink (*nivium nimis humida*) is materially uncertain. Another hand then wrote the following material at the monastery of Fosses, likewise in a single continuous course, as far as 1137, where Anselm ends; then a new hand continues in one course to 1146, after which the surviving source fragment adds, “it afflicted many” (subject uncertain). Here the Gembloux continuation ends; the annals too cease for two years, and what follows displays almost as many hands as there are years. It is therefore evident that the Annals of Liège must be counted among Sigebert’s sources up to 1099, while the years 1099–1146 were copied almost word for word from him and from his Gembloux continuators on three occasions: first in 1024 by a Liège writer, then in 1137 and 1146 by two monks of Fosses.]; Auxilius, On the Formosian Disaster [Note: Years 900–903. Compare Sigebert, On Illustrious Men, 112.]; Liudprand; Widukind; Ruotger’s Life of Bruno; Lambert’s Life of Heribert; Peter Damian’s Life of Odilo; Sigebert [Col. 0022A] himself, in the Lives of Guibert and Deoderic and in the Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux; Rudolf Glaber [Note: Years 977, 992, 1001, and 1003.]; Folcuin’s Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes; Anselm’s Deeds of the Bishops of Liège [Note: He now reads and uses it in the Wolfenbüttel manuscript for the years 883, 903, 960, 972, and 1014.]; Alpertus [Note: On the Bishops of Metz, years 982–984; On Various Times, 997 and 1003–1020.]; Balderic [Note: He drew extensively from it for the years 959–1054.]; Marianus; Wibert’s Life of Leo IX; Humbert’s embassy [Note: In Baronius XI, 210. He read and copied it for the years 1053 and 1054 from the manuscript of Saint Lawrence of Liège, now Brussels 9706.]; John’s Translation of Saint Nicholas [Note: Year 1087.]; the letter on the death of Hildebrand [Note: Year 1085.]; the letters of the crusaders [Note: Years 1097–1099 in Dodechin.]; and the coronation of Warner, Henry IV, and Henry V [Note: He did not use the Bertinian or Blandinian Annals, Thietmar, Herman of Reichenau, or Lambert. The passages Hirsch cites from the latter for 1048, 1066, and 1077 were taken by Sigebert from the Annals of Liège; the passage for 1067 came from the Life of Conrad and from accounts by contemporaries, for it contains more than either that Life or Lambert. In 1073, our author does not at all tell the same story about the Russians as Lambert, nor do they agree on the year. In 1071 Sigebert has far more concerning the Theban martyrs than Lambert, since he was then nearby and wrote a poem about them. The material for 1056 and 1062 could indeed have come from Lambert, but it could equally well have come from another source. Compare the notes there.]. 

Sigebert used these sources with considerable freedom. He copied some word for word; of others he conveyed only the sense, contracted, expanded, or corrected them—and not always successfully. Sometimes he stitched one narrative together from several sources; sometimes he divided the continuous words of a single source among several years, diligently, though not always correctly, attempting to assign each item to its proper time.

Thus, although he wished to construct a patchwork, he made it sufficiently varied; nor can one at least object that he copied his sources one after another without selection or judgment. Rather, although he had read very widely, he often excerpted only a very small amount from a large book, sought elsewhere for other material that he could have found in the same place, and judged that it was more accurately presented elsewhere.

In general, we see that he lacked neither acuity in perceiving the truth, nor cautious hesitation in uncertain matters, nor critical judgment in selecting both the sources and the material he would take from them. This, however, is his one and only merit in almost everything preceding the year 1024. For the whole section from 381 to 1023, with only very few exceptions, was compiled from the sources listed above and is therefore of no use whatever to us.

From 1024 onward he still drew much from other sources, but he added so much and so substantial a quantity of his own that he can now himself be regarded as a source. From this one, rather small section of the Chronicle—its years 1024–1112—we may therefore properly form a judgment of Sigebert as a historical writer; the rest is not Sigebert’s.

## Sigebert’s Reliability

[Note: [Col. 0023D] See below the observations that we append, from Hartzheim, “What Should Be Thought of Sigebert of Gembloux’s Twofold Assertion” (Conc. Germ., vol. III, p. 234, section heading), under the years 1074 and 1085. Editor of the Patrologia.]

Three principal charges are brought against him: that he was a schismatic; that, carried away by excessive devotion to the imperial party, he knowingly narrated falsehoods, indeed invented them, while concealing the truth; and that he made many serious errors in writing about times and events.

As for the charge of schism, Catholic writers have already removed that stigma from him: Fleury [Note: Fleury, Historia ecclesiastica, book LXV, no. 40.], Martène [Note: Collectio amplissima I, 588, note.], and the Benedictine authors of the Literary History [Note: Histoire littéraire de la France IX, 537.].

No one who reads his books without a preconceived attitude will deny that he was entirely free from excessive party zeal. He indicates events on the basis of the events themselves, not of the persons involved. He censures wrongdoing committed by the emperor no less than wrongdoing committed by the pope [Note: Compare 1073–1084, “but these things—to act” in 1085. De viris illustribus III, 163: “whose companion’s words alone are sufficient for everyone to understand how grievous and hateful the emperor himself was to the Saxons.” Compare the same work, 160–161.], and thus, in a rare example, maintained himself entirely above the parties.

He indeed supported the emperor together with his entire diocese; but it is not Henry whom he favors, nor the person of the pope at whom he is angry. Rather, it is the divine right of kings that was undermined; rebellions and perjuries that were sanctioned; the harmony of kingdom and Church that was disturbed; the son’s reverence toward his father that was corrupted; and human confidence that was shaken.

When he censures these things, he is so far from being led astray by party zeal that, if he had touched on them less, he would then rightly have been called excessively partisan. The fact that he does not narrate many matters unfavorable to Henry cannot be criticized on that account, since his plan was only to touch briefly upon the principal events. For he did exactly the same on the opposing side.

Yet those who criticize him for passing over some matters concerning Henry also accuse him, on the other hand, because he did not conceal every misdeed of the popes in silence, although he reverently omitted many things that he read in his sources [Col. 0023D]. If at times he speaks somewhat more sharply about Gregory and Paschal, he did so at least in good faith, without being conscious of error; nor can we prove that what he says about them is false.

Everywhere, rather, we see a man who loves truth. Thus, although he had not yet touched upon Deoderic’s less honorable actions in the Life of Deoderic, he supplied them in the Chronicle. If anything is uncertain, he indicates it; he never knowingly narrated or invented falsehood [Note: The passage under 773, which Gretser attacks most vigorously, is not Sigebert’s but that of the Aquicinian interpolator; he merely incorporated the letter of 1085 and did not invent it.].

## Chronology

That he unknowingly committed many errors in events and dates cannot be denied. He devoted his principal effort to the calculation of times; but since he followed so many authors, whose chronological systems were either very different or nonexistent, he could not adequately avoid numerous and serious errors.

Much in his chronology is arbitrary, where he could not learn the date from his sources, or where events had to be assigned to a definite year although they had no definite date in themselves—miracles, the lives of famous men, and similar matters. Very often he assigns to events drawn from his sources a date different from the one found there, not always correctly and without paying sufficient attention to the fact that some authors begin the year at Easter and others at the Nativity of the Lord.

Nevertheless, he investigated everywhere and calculated from whatever reliable foundations he could obtain; nor did he try to conceal uncertainties. Thus, in these matters, his intention deserves praise, but his authority is almost nonexistent.

This must be said especially of his catalogue of popes. In establishing their succession, he follows the Deeds of the Pontiffs up to 873, although he often departs from them in the dates; from that year onward he used Marianus and catalogues of the popes. Since these differed greatly among themselves, Sigebert tried to reconcile them.

But he soon saw, and candidly admits [Note: Year 995.], that he was unequal to the task. When he noticed that, in the numbering itself, he had diverged too far from them, he immediately passed from the ninety-third to the hundredth number [Note: Year 824.]. Nor afterward did he sufficiently guard himself against errors.

Later scribes either copied these matters literally or corrected them according to their own opinions. It is therefore clear that, for a more accurate knowledge of the succession and dates of the popes, the authority and usefulness of Sigebert and of all his manuscripts are entirely nil.

The same must be said of his whole chronology, not only before 1024 but afterward as well.

## Style

His style in the Life of Deoderic and the other Lives is exuberantly youthful, adorned with little flowers of rhetoric, indeed with poetic verses and especially with the rarer expressions of Horace [Note: For example, scobere, that is, “to clean by scraping”; minare, that is, “to lead” or “to conduct.”]. It is filled also with Greek expressions, antitheses, comparisons, and metaphors, and swollen with reading of Sacred Scripture and the Fathers. It delights in poetic rhythm and in sentences whose endings answer one another two or three times in a similar sound. This manner of writing was characteristic of the eleventh century and the first part of the twelfth, and was extremely common.

In the letters there is the same concern for matching sound. The style is less flowery and free of unusual expressions, but weightier in dignity, livelier in its sentences, and animated by a certain natural eloquence, not without wit and rhetorical skill. In every respect it must be counted among the best of its age.

In the Chronicle [Col. 0025A] the style is plain and composed, as befits an old man, and almost never rises above itself. From his earlier ornamentation he retained only the matching sounds at the ends of sentences, until, in the book On Illustrious Men, he laid aside even this final ornament.

### Excerptors

As soon as the work appeared publicly, it attracted an astonishing amount of human attention; it was copied, excerpted, and continued extensively, and for the subsequent centuries it was of the greatest importance for the writing of history, both in content and in form. The first to use it was Ekkehard of Aura, already in the middle of 1105 and frequently thereafter; following him came the Saxon annalist and chronicler; then the author of the treatise *On Investiture*, commonly called Waltram of Naumburg, in 1109 [Note: On this work and the others, see Hirsch’s extremely thorough investigation, pp. 408–437. He copied word for word the entries for the years 791, 798, 801, 752, 420, 963, 1046, and 1047.]; then the Annals of Liège, in 1124 [Note: See note 56 above.]; Nicholas of Liège, in his *Life of Saint Lambert*, between 1124 and 1147; Hermann of Tournai [Note: Dachery, *Spicilegium* II, 903.]; Orderic Vitalis, before 1132; Rupert of Tuy, in his *History of Saint Lawrence of Liège*, before 1135; his continuator Reiner [Note: He used Sigebert, Anselm, and the Gembloux continuators.]; the continuator of Fulcoin, around 1160; the annotator of Adam of Bremen [Note: See *Archiv* VI, 821.]; the interpolator of the Lobbes Annals [Note: For it is evident that the years 448, 637, 646–660, 895, 958, 963, and 969 were added there, in another hand, from Sigebert.]; the Elnon Annals [Note: In addition to the continuous interpolating hand, several passages were added there from Sigebert by various hands.], and from these the Tournai Chronicle [79*]; the Marchiennes Annals [Note: Unpublished, extending to the year 1076, copied from the Liège Annals, and heavily interpolated in another twelfth-century hand from Sigebert for the years 1079–1107. Entire sections were copied from him.]; the Floreffe Annals [Note: Unpublished, extending to 1139, copied from the Liège Annals, with many additions later made at the end of the twelfth century from Sigebert.]; the Parc Annals [Note: Unpublished; for the most part excerpted from the Liège Annals and Sigebert.]; the Rheims Chronicle, in 1190 [Note: Labbe, *Bibliotheca manuscripta* I, 355.]; the Liège Chronicle, in 1192 [Note: Martène, *Thesaurus* III, 1403; it used Sigebert and Anselm.]; Lambert the Little, before 1195 [Note: He copied Sigebert, Anselm, the Gembloux continuators, and the Anchin Chronicle.]; Andrew of Marchiennes, in 1194 [Note: He used the Anchin manuscript.]; Ralph of Diceto, in 1199 [Note: He used Robert of Torigni.]; the author of the narrative *On the Holy War* [Note: Martène, *Collectio* V, 536.]; a monk of Egmond, in 1204; Nicholas of Amiens, in 1204 [Note: Born in 1147, as he himself says, he wrote a chronicle from the creation of the world to 1204, contained in eight books. Before 381 he compiled it entirely from Eusebius and Jerome; for 381–1155 he copied word for word from Sigebert’s Ursicamp manuscript; for 1156–1200 he excerpted from the Anchin B5 manuscript, adding absolutely nothing except ten brief notes for the years 418, 424, 434, 535, 633, 636, 648, 679, 684, and 706, from the *Miscellaneous History*, and eleven others, for the years 902, 1121, 1147, 1152, 1153, 1162, 1187, 1200, 1202, 1203, and 1204, concerning only popes and matters relating to Amiens and Gaul. He treated the material with such brevity that the years 1100–1204 occupy scarcely eight pages; and with such ignorance that, for example, he turned Sigebert’s words under 561, *in Scotia Brendanus claruit* (“Brendan was renowned in Scotland”), into *in historia Brendanus floruit a. 583* (“in history Brendan flourished in 583”), and wrote *in amicitiam incurrente* (“entering into friendship”) in place of *in Armeniam incurrente* (“invading Armenia”). The work, not worthy of publication, survives in a manuscript once belonging to Pithou and later to Christina, among the Vatican manuscripts, no. 444, from the fourteenth century. Its copy is the Paris manuscript among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 783, which we used. Brial published an excerpted continuation, XIV, 21.]; Robert, a monk of Saint-Marien at Auxerre, in 1210 [Note: He used the Ursicamp manuscript.], and the Tours Chronicle derived from him [Note: Martène, *Collectio* V, 917.], Gerard of Frachet, in 1264, and William of Nangis, in 1304; Helinand [Note: He used the Mortemer manuscript.]; Alberic of Trois-Fontaines, in 1241 [Note: He used the Affligem manuscript and Helinand.]; Giles of the Golden Valley, in 1247; Matthew Paris [Note: He used Roger of Wendover.]; Vincent of Beauvais [Note: He used the Ursicamp manuscript.]; Martin of Poland; the Annals of Saint-Médard at Soissons, in 1269 [Note: Dachery, *Spicilegium* II, 486.]; Baldwin of Ninove, in 1293 [Note: He used the Affligem manuscript.]; John of Ypres, in 1294; the Gallic Chronicle, in 1306 [Note: In the fourteenth-century Paris manuscript among the Saint-Germain French manuscripts, no. 659.]; Matthew of Westminster, in 1307; the Icelandic Annals, in 1328 [Note: See Waitz in our *Annals* VII, 690, who says that they derive from a certain manuscript of Robert of Torigni. On Theodoric, the author of the *History of Norway*, who already praises Sigebert, see Hirsch, p. 415.]; the author of the poem on Lohengrin, after 1356; Henry of Hervord, and, following him, Körner; the interpolator of Rodulf of St-Trond, in 1366 [Note: Unpublished, in the Brussels manuscript no. 18181.]; Peter of Thymo, in his *Chronicle of Brabant*, in 1429 [Note: Preserved unpublished in the archives of the city of Brussels; see *Archiv* VII, 707.]; and the Chronicle of Saint Bavo, shortly after 1497 [Note: See note 106 below].

In addition to these, Sigebert was used by Lambert Waterlos in his *Chronicle of Cambrai*, begun in 1152, who possessed a manuscript of Family B; by Bertimanus, author of the *Genealogy of the Counts of Flanders*, which Galopin published under the title *Flanders the Generous*, shortly after 1164; by Roger of Wendover in the *Flowers of History*, in 1235, who used a manuscript of Robert of Torigni; by James of Guise in the *Annals of Hainaut*, before 1398; by John Brando of Dunes, in 1431; and by Anianus in the *Chronicle of Aldenburg*, in 1448.

### Continuators

The procession of continuators—greater than that of any author except Martin of Poland—is led by Anselm, a pupil of Guirin of Gembloux, who became a master among the monks of Hautvillers and later among those of Lagny. After 1099 he returned to Gembloux, where from February 1113 he governed as abbot with great distinction until his death in 1136. He was esteemed by everyone for his love of learning and elegance of character; in talent he was inferior to Sigebert, wavering in judgment [Note: See the years 1130 and 1132 concerning the emperor Lothair. On Anselm, see *Acta Sanctorum*, June VII, 171; Delvenne, *Biographie des Pays-Bas*, Mons, 1829, I, 23.], and excessively preoccupied with miracles, portents, and storms; nevertheless, he transmitted much that is useful to us.

Having already begun in 1112 to continue Sigebert’s Chronicle [Note: See note 49* above.], he carried it forward to the end of 1135, with his pen running alongside the events themselves. For, as we see from his autograph manuscript, he committed events to writing immediately as they occurred, stopping his pen two or three times in a single year and taking it up again when new reports arrived; he supplied what he learned only later and corrected what he subsequently discovered to be false. Thus the book, proceeding in the very footsteps of the events, appears worthy of the highest confidence, especially in its assignment of events to their dates.

The author himself produced several successive versions of it. For we have seen that, from the year 1024 onward, the material supplied from it was used by the Liège Annals; in 1126 a monk of Saint-Amand copied it, and in 1131 a monk of Verdun transcribed it in full; in 1136 it served as the basis for a supplement to the Fosses Annals.

Anselm was immediately followed by the first Gembloux continuator, who wrote the year 1136 and the beginning of 1137; another, at different times and with ink much changed, added material for 1137 and continued to 1145 (the printed words *prudens lector*, “a prudent reader,” have uncertain syntax); from that point a third proceeded continuously to the end of 1148. The monks of Fosses therefore used the book again for their own Annals; our manuscripts F1, F2, F3, and F4 copied it in full; Reiner of Liège and the Liège Chronicle excerpted it. In addition to these, it was used together with Anselm and the Gembloux continuators by the Ursicamp continuator and his followers, Nicholas of Amiens and Vincent of Beauvais; by Andrew of Marchiennes; Lambert the Little; Alberic; Baldwin of Ninove; Iperius; and the Chronicle of Saint Bavo. The work was first published by Miraeus, and from his edition by Struve and Bouquet.

Furthermore, a Frenchman [Note: In chapter 7 he simply designates the king of the Franks, without adding his name, as “the most serene king,” and often calls him “the most Christian.”], a certain associate of Saint Bernard, believing that all this material had been written by Sigebert of “Gembloux” up to 1148, undertook to continue him, “passing over other matters and touching briefly upon those relating to pontifical history,” and narrating only “what he had recognized as true by sight and hearing.” But unless he himself declared that he was Sigebert’s continuator, no one would count him among them. His work is plainly different in purpose and form: it is divided not by years but by chapters, and deals almost entirely with the Council of Rheims, the expedition of Conrad and Louis, Arnold of Brescia, and other ecclesiastical affairs; all these matters are narrated at great length and on the basis of accurate knowledge [Note: Among other things, we read in chapter 40 that, as early as 1150, the bishop of Winchester transported to England ancient statues bought up in Rome to adorn his house.]. It is therefore regrettable that the single manuscript, F2, has preserved it for us only to the middle of 1150 [Col. 0028B]; it will be published in its proper place.

Already in 1112 or 1113, the monk of Anchin [B], having before him Sigebert’s Chronicle as the author had left it at his death, prepared for a second edition, with Anselm’s notice for the year 1112 appended at the end, copied it fairly accurately, except that he inserted certain additions of his own, especially concerning his monastery. He also appears to have prefixed Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper to Sigebert [Note: See note 49 above.]. This manuscript B was the source of all the others [Note: This is proved as follows. Although manuscripts B1, B2, B3*, B4*, B4**, and B5 differ greatly among themselves in readings and additions, they nevertheless reveal a common source because all append the continuations of Sigebert, Anselm, and the Gembloux continuators, and because they in turn continued these, each in a different manner but all using the same foundation, the Anchin continuation.

“Furthermore, C1, C2*, C3, C4*, C5, D, D1, D1*, D2, E, and E8h., though differing greatly among themselves, nevertheless have readings in which all, or at least several, agree—for example, under 767, *Scomnas*; under 882, *Hunnam*; under 928, *Gana*; under 939, *bellaria*; under 953, *Baginoensium*; omissions under 962 and 1012; additions under 1048, 1096, and 1099; and finally the continuations. These manuscripts too, therefore, claim a special source for themselves, which we conjecture to have been the Arras manuscript.

“Family B1, B2, B3, B4, and B5 differs from those manuscripts as much in its readings as, especially, in its continuations. Yet in the additions made to Sigebert under the years 651, 690, 773, 1076, 1979 [probably 1079], 1080, 1084, 1086, 1087, 1088, 1090, 1092, 1093, 1095, 1096, 1100, 1102, 1105, 1109, 1111, and 1112, and in the words omitted under 954, 958, 987, 1012, and 1106, the manuscripts of both families agree—sometimes all, sometimes several. Moreover, all prefix Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper to Sigebert, except C5, which has been so abridged that it cannot be cited here.

“This cannot be explained otherwise than by supposing that both families descended from a single source containing Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, and Sigebert, together with those additions common to both. Of these additions, those under 1079, 1080, 1086, 1087, 1088, 1090, 1093, 1096, 1100, 1102, 1109, and 1111 concern the monastery of Anchin; all except those under 1079, 1080, and 1096 were taken from the monastery’s still-unpublished Annals, whose primary copy is preserved at Douai. Those under 651, 690, 1084, and 1086 concern regions near it; those under 1076, 1092, 1095, and 1105 concern the bishops of Cambrai, to whom the monastery was subject. This primary manuscript B, then, must have been written at that monastery.

“Most of the additions mentioned above are also found in the other Anchin manuscript, B5; but they cannot have descended from it, since some of them are present in the older manuscripts C4*, D, and E. The fact that all these additions are not found in every manuscript is explained by the practice, observable throughout nearly all the manuscripts of Sigebert, by which scribes inserted the history of their own monastery and omitted that of others, according to their preference.

“We shall present these additions, gathered together in one place, after Sigebert.”

In 1148, the continuation of Anselm and the Gembloux continuators was added to the same manuscript, and thus B1 copied the whole work. Later it was continued at the monastery of Anchin itself, apparently at different times, with special attention to matters concerning Flanders and the Crusades, many of which were taken from the Blandijnberg Annals and a few from the Anchin Annals. We know this continuation only through four others built upon it [Note: In the continuations B2, B3*, B4*, and B5, which differ greatly among themselves, scattered passages occur that are identical in all of them; it is often sufficiently clear that other material has been inserted between these passages. They cannot have passed from one continuation into another—for then many more passages ought to be common to these continuations—but can be explained only by supposing that they had a common foundation.].

The first is that of the monk of Vaucelles [B2], who copied the whole book to 1163 [Col. 0029A], omitting some material and adding other material of his own. Shortly after 1497, the author of the Chronicle of Saint Bavo copied almost the whole of this, inserting much material from Lambert’s *Floridus*, the Blandijnberg Annals, the Saint Bavo Annals, the *Genealogy of the Counts of Flanders*, Martin of Poland, John of Thilrode, Giles of Roya, Adrian But, Trithemius, and others [Note: It is found in the manuscript formerly at Blandijnberg and now in Brussels, no. 14524, from which Brussels 16531 and Amiens 356 were copied. De Smet published it in full in *Corpus chronicon Flandriae* I, 455; Vandeputte published the first part, up to 772, in the *Annals of Saint Peter of Blandijnberg* (Ghent, 1842, quarto), from a sixteenth-century paper manuscript in the Ghent archives.

“This is precisely the same work—indeed, printed from the same manuscript—as that which Dom Brial published under the name *Auctarium Blandiniense*, XIV, 16, from a copy of an equally Blandijnberg manuscript, which he had in his possession and which de Bast calls *une tout autre production* (*Institution des communes*, Ghent, 1819, pp. 99, 112), communicated to him by D. Nelis. Nowhere does Dom Brial say that it was found there after Sigebert; in both his text and the Chronicle the ending is abrupt and the wording identical. Brial contains absolutely nothing that the Chronicle does not also contain; what the Chronicle has in addition to it consists only of a very few passages omitted by Brial, who himself implies that he did not publish everything. Therefore a continuation of Sigebert from Ghent never existed.”]

The second was a monk of Affligem [B3], who sprinkled Sigebert, Anselm, and the Gembloux continuators with certain additions concerning Affligem Abbey, drawn from the *History* and Annals of Affligem, and seventy-seven others from the Blandijnberg Annals. He then used the Anchin continuation up to 1156, so that he virtually buried it beneath the mass of his own additions; from 1157 to 1163 he proceeds solely on the basis of his own material. He wrote before 1189 [Note: For under 1154 he calls Henry king of the English “the one who now reigns,” and says that he died in 1189.], with his sympathies inclined toward the emperor Frederick; Miraeus omitted most of this. Alberic of Trois-Fontaines and Baldwin of Ninove used him. We know him only through a copy made at the beginning of the thirteenth century by a monk of Eiham [B3*]. Miraeus published it under the title *Affligem Supplement*, and Struve derived his edition from Miraeus.

The third, a monk of Hasnon [B4], copied the Anchin manuscript up to 1167, using the Blandijnberg Annals in ninety-six places. Apart from these, he added very little of his own, including three narratives concerning Hasnon Abbey [Note: Under the years 670, 1069, and 1150.], which show that he wrote there. Here and there he abridged Anselm, the Gembloux continuators, and the Anchin continuation; he added no continuation of his own. [Col. 0029C] We know him only through B4* and B4**, which were copied from it with great accuracy.

Within B4**, between 1296 and 1306, a monk R. of Marchiennes inserted many passages in the margin and between the lines. These were copied word for word from the Blandijnberg, Marchiennes, and Elnon Annals and from the Lives of Saints Amandus, Amatus, Rictrude, and Gertrude; they are of no value.

Finally, a monk of Anchin [B5], at the request of Simon, abbot from 1174 to 1201, copied the primary Anchin manuscript again, up to 1148, and then continued it in such a way as to expand considerably the continuation appended to it, using it as the foundation of his own; he added material of his own from there to the end of 1201, apparently at different times [Note: Compare the entry for 1190 concerning Emperor Frederick: “His body is still being guarded unburied”; the entry for 1192, which must have been written before the death of Henry in 1197, since it says “the future king”; the entry for 1194, “this year”; the entry for 1197; “a beautiful procession of seeds,” apparently; and in the same place, “we have by no means yet heard of a certain victory for our men.”

“Lambert the Little and Andrew of Marchiennes had already used the same source before 1195. In the preface to the work the author says only this about himself: ‘In the thirteenth year of Conrad, king of the Germans, and the fourteenth of Louis, king of the Franks, the seventh of that name, at the request of certain brothers of Anchin and later by the authority of Simon, abbot of that same church, a certain monk, a close associate of that same church and moderately learned, appended the following material to the end of the volume. He wrote what he had heard more than what he had seen, and left to the knowledge of posterity what he had heard from trustworthy informants.’”]

He took some material from the Anchin Annals, but most of it—especially the material concerning the Crusade—from the reports of those who had taken part in it.
