The author admires Emperor Frederick [Note: Yet not because of an unjust partisan bias; compare 1156, “he dismissed him unjustly”; 1161, “through the emperor’s violence”; 1162, “the schismatic Octavian”; and 1163, “the emperor’s oath, so rash.”], though Miraeus silently omitted it everywhere.

Another hand then added, in a single stroke, brief notices for 1201–1237, all but three of them copied word for word from the Anchin Annals [Note: In the sole manuscript B5 they survive only to the middle of 1225, since its final leaf has been lost. But in the B5* continuator built upon it, not only these notices are found, but also everything presented by the Anchin Annals for 1226–1237. Yet B5* did not use the Annals; it copied manuscript B5 literally (compare the identical error in both). Therefore the passages from the Annals found in it must also have existed in B5.]. This manuscript was copied by Lambert the Little; Andrew of Marchiennes; William, author of the Chronicle of Andres; Nicholas of Amiens; the monk of Clairmarais, who continued the *Genealogy of the Counts of Flanders* [Note: In Martène, *Thesaurus* III, 388.]; the interpolator of the Elnon Annals; and Iperius. Miraeus published it, and Struve derived his edition from Miraeus.

Having obtained the same manuscript, a monk of Saint-Winnoc at Bergues [B5*] copied from it accurately the years 1149–1201 and mixed into the years 1201–1237 much material relating especially to Flanders. The author appears to have lived at that time [Note: We infer that he wrote at Bergues, near Dunkirk, because he treats chiefly the history of that region; because he uses words with a French flavor, such as *saisivit* (“seized”); and because, after giving a full account of the translation of Saint Iduberga, he adds: “It took place in the time of Lord Incelmar, abbot of Bergues.”]. This continuation is now appearing for the first time [Note: We know it only through B5**, compiled by a monk of Blandijnberg from various books with such carelessness that he sometimes joined together, on the same line and without any distinction, authors who were as different as possible. Thus he appended to our manuscript, as though it were a single work, an entirely different compilation that he himself assembled for the years 1222–1228: he copied the Blandijnberg Annals word for word and inserted among them abridged Lives of the popes from Martin of Poland, together with a little material excerpted from Baldwin of Ninove and certain Brabantine annals.

“It is therefore not a compilation worthy of publication; we have mentioned it here only so that no one may believe it to be the continuation of the Bergues manuscript merely because it is appended to that manuscript in B5** and in its two copies.”]

William of Andres used this continuation, and Iperius used William.

Besides these, another manuscript must have descended from Anchin B, now lost, written in the diocese of Arras [C] [Note: The words of the continuation seem to suggest this: “Lambert, bishop of Arras, of blessed memory, died.” I would most gladly believe that this was our Laon manuscript C4, were it not for two objections. First, C4 was written from 1136 onward, whereas C3 seems already to have been written in 1127. Second, under 596, the false Laon reading *Theudelina* is found among the other manuscripts only in C4*. Nor can C3 have been its source, since it lacks certain passages found in the others, such as those under 1080, 1084, 1086, 1088, 1093, 1096, and 1111.].

At first it had no continuation; D and the sources of manuscripts D1 and D2 derive from it in this form. A few additions were then made to it. Thus, in 1127, the Tournai manuscript [C3] was copied from it; another hand subsequently added very brief notes for the years 1132–1174, and a third added entries for 1332, 1333, and 1334.

In 1136, a monk of Saint Vincent at Laon [C4] copied manuscript C, but from 917 onward omitted much and added a little, chiefly material concerning Laon [Note: These omissions and additions may perhaps be attributed to the monk of Corbie, since we know the nearly entirely lost Laon manuscript only through this copy. Yet several features show that the Corbie copyist worked with his pen but not with his intellect: in the continuation, which invited alteration and omission even more than the Chronicle did, he omitted nothing; of his eight additions, those concerning Laon are under 928, 1052, and 1104, as well as the entry under 1096, which must have been written at Saint Vincent.], and carried its continuation, enlarged especially with matters concerning Laon, first to 1136 and then, with his pen always keeping pace with events, to 1145.

Thus a monk of Corbie [C4*] accurately copied the whole work through 1154, adding nothing [Col. 0031B]. The now-lost manuscript of Val-Secret [Note: We know that this existed solely from the words: “Seek the following sequence of this work at Val-Secret,” which a hand from the middle of the twelfth century added after the Corbie manuscript. Its traces may perhaps be sought in the Premonstratensian continuation B1.] continued it.

At the beginning of 1155, a certain Premonstratensian monk built a new continuation for the years 1113–1155 upon the Laon continuation. In its earlier portion he sewed onto it large patches, mostly excerpted from the *Life of Norbert*; in the later portion he supplied much new and highly useful material. We possess it in one of our manuscripts, B1. We shall see below that it was again interpolated from Anselm by a monk of Ursicamp.

The Burbure manuscript [C5] also appears to have descended from manuscript C. After a greatly abridged Sigebert, it adds a brief continuation for 1114–1164, which agrees with the Laon continuation in its first three years; it then contains several passages that also passed into the Chronicle of Saint Bavo [Note: See note 106 above. These are the years 1122, 1126, 1133, 1134, 1135, and 1137.], as well as others found nowhere else.

All the manuscripts enumerated thus far sometimes add much to Sigebert and sometimes remove much, but they left his wording and the order of his sentences untouched. The first to dare to alter this was the monk of Beauvais [D], who copied manuscript C, with its continuation, sometime between 1138 and 1147 [Note: He himself, not another hand, writes under 1109: “His son Louis reigned after him for twenty-nine years,” something that he could not have written before 1138. Another hand subsequently added a continuation that already ends in 1147.].

He made ten new additions, chiefly concerning Beauvais; omitted thirty passages; and transposed sentences extensively, not merely within individual years but often from one year to another. From 939 onward he made an entirely different catalogue of the popes of his own devising. Thus this manuscript is truly the worst of all, yet by a remarkable fate it was more important for the writing of history than any of the others. For from it descended not only the following manuscripts but also every edition except that of Miraeus.

At first it had no continuation. Another hand added to it a very brief continuation for 1114–1147; a third enlarged it and carried it to 1163 [Note: First published by Labbe, *Bibliotheca manuscripta* I, 390; thereafter by Struve, p. 1015, and Bouquet XIII, 334.].

The entire manuscript, with many omissions, was copied at Saint Victor in Paris [D2]. In 1155, a monk of Mortemer [D1] accurately copied it after it had been enlarged by the earlier continuation [Note: Mortemer, in the diocese of Rouen, had adopted the Cistercian rule in 1137 from the monastery of Ursicamp, or Orchamp, in the diocese of Noyon.], and added seven brief notices. Two others inserted much material into it for the years 1114–1165; later continuators carried it to 1234 [Note: Published by Martène, *Thesaurus* III, 1437; excerpted by Bouquet XII, 781, and XVIII, 354.].

A Cistercian monk of Ursicamp [D1*] copied this manuscript, omitting the continuation. He inserted thirty-two additions from Geoffrey and the remainder from various excerpts, and compiled a new continuation for 1113–1155. Having obtained manuscript B1, he extensively interpolated its Premonstratensian continuation through 1128 with material from Anselm, which he was reading there; after that he copied it in full, making only fifteen additions throughout, which show that the author lived at Ursicamp.

This manuscript was followed by D1** and E8h., from which the first edition descended. Nicholas of Amiens, Vincent of Beauvais, Robert of Auxerre together with the Tours Chronicle, Gerard of Frachet, and William of Nangis likewise depend upon it.

Finally, and the most distinguished of the continuators, is ROBERT OF TORIGNI, who professed the Rule of St Benedict at Bec in 1128, was elected prior there in 1149, and, on 27 May 1154, was summoned to the abbey of Mont-Saint-Michel “of the Peril of the Sea,” which he administered with the highest distinction until his death on 25 May 1186; a man outstanding in the nobility of his family [Note: [Col. 0033B] Cf. the year 1180.], no less experienced in public affairs than in letters, highly esteemed by the king and queen [Note: [Col. 0033B] So much so that in 1161 he received their daughter Eleanor from the baptismal font, and in 1162 was entrusted with the custody of Pontorson. Earlier, in 1156, the same king, Henry II, had come to him at Mont-Saint-Michel, and again two years later with Louis VII. Pope Alexander also summoned him to Tours for the council of 1163; when it was over, Robert went to Rome and, returning from there, visited England.—For Robert’s life, see Robert himself throughout the Chronicle from 1154 onward; Labbé, *Bibliotheca manuscripta* I, 348; *Gallia Christiana* XI, 520; from these sources the authors of *Histoire littéraire* XIV, 363, Bouquet XIII, preface, 30, and Hirsch, p. 387, drew their material. Nearly everything Fabricius says is false.], an exceptionally devoted seeker out and collector of books [Note: [Col. 0033B] As Henry of Huntingdon calls him. Among other works, he was the first to bring Pliny into Normandy.], and, in the glory of learning, the leading Norman of his age. He encouraged others to write history and himself cultivated it in writing [Note: [Col. 0033B] Robert’s writings are these: *History of Henry I*, or the eighth book of William of Jumièges, covering 1135–1150.—Continuation of Sigebert, begun in 1150.—Letter to Gervase, from 1150–1154, published by Dachery after the works of Guilbert, p. 715.—*On the Change in the Order of Monks in Normandy*, 1154, in Dachery, p. 811.—*Annals of Mont-Saint-Michel*, from 1154 to 1159, inserted in his own hand into the monastery cartulary, now in the public library of Avranches, no. 80.—Prologue to Augustine’s *Flowers*, in Dachery, p. 716.—Prologue to Pliny, corrected by Robert himself; this book, sent to the monks of Saint-Germain two centuries ago, is now said to be in the royal library at Paris.—Letter to the abbot of Bec, 1182, in Bouquet XVIII, 333.—The works attributed to him beyond these lack evidence. The catalogue of abbots compiled in 1643, in Dachery, *Epistolae Lanfranci*, p. 351, says that Robert published 154 volumes and, as the *History of Saint Michael* reports, that a tower had decayed beneath rubble and rainwater (*impluvium*); an error appears to be present here: these 154 books are not works he himself composed, but books he collected.]. Among these, first place belongs to the *Chronicle* added to Sigebert. Since he especially wished to narrate the history of his own country, he joined this, in the medieval manner, to universal history in such a way that, having borrowed manuscript D from the bishop of Beauvais, he copied Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper from it without alteration, changed nothing and omitted nothing in Sigebert, but inserted the archbishops of Rouen and the history of the English and Normans, taking everything from the *Annals of Rouen*, Bec, and Mont-Saint-Michel, and from William of Poitiers, William of Jumièges, and Henry of Huntingdon. His continuation begins in the year 1100; at first it relies chiefly on Sigebert and Henry of Huntingdon, while after 1154 it is wholly Robert’s own work. He began writing it in 1150 [Note: [Col. 0033D] Compare the year 1117, which he is still arranging, thirty-two years after the events.] and carried it in a continuous account up to the year in which he initially decided to bring it to an end [Note: [Col. 0033D] In the preface he himself says: “I shall then, with God permitting and helping—without whom we can do nothing—undertake to collect [the material] up to the year 1150 . . . .” Thus E3a, E7b, and E8d read it, and the E manuscript had originally written it so; but in this manuscript Robert himself later changed the year to 1182.—When Ralph of Diceto says that Robert wrote it up to 1147, he does the same thing that he saw Robert do in Sigebert: he imagined that the year in which Robert intended to begin was the last year he wrote, although Robert’s Chronicle, exactly like his version of Sigebert, also excerpted material after 1147.]. But, as often happens, when he had reached that point and had no reason to stop writing, he continued to 1154, still at Bec; and at Mont-Saint-Michel as well he brought the work, begun at various times, to the end of his life. He published it several times, according as different people wished either to copy the whole work or to add what had recently been composed to what had already been copied. First he published it at the beginning of 1156 [Note: [Col. 0033D] For E2 ends here, as does the first hand in E and E8d.], then at the end of 1157 [Note: [Col. 0034B] E3a and E3b end here. Matthew Paris says that Robert wrote up to this point.], then in 1169 [Note: [Col. 0034B] E8a and E8b end here, as does the second hand in E8d; the abridged text ends in E8e and E8h, and doubtless also in E8c and E8d.], and finally in 1182, when he again decided to bring the work to an end [Note: [Col. 0034B] This is indicated both by the whole character of the material for this year and by Robert himself in his letter to the abbot of Bec, published from E6 by Brial, XVIII, 333. I believe that the letter has been interpolated in name only, not fabricated in its entirety; this is also shown by the fact that in the preface he changed the number 1150 to 1182. The hand also changes in E; E7a and E7b end here.—After examining the manuscript E6 itself, Pertz demonstrated that Robert’s work, which is read there on fols. 70–93, originally constituted a separate manuscript, written in the late twelfth century. On its first pages, left blank by the scribe, another hand, somewhat neater but likewise from the late twelfth century, wrote this letter, which Pertz transcribed from the manuscript as follows:

“Robert, abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel of the Peril of the Sea, to his dearest lord and father Roger, abbot of Bec by the grace of God: whatever a son owes a father and whatever a servant owes a lord.

“A certain young man came to us and requested on your behalf that I send you part of our chronicles, containing the period of eighty-two years, namely from the martyrdom of Saint Thomas the Martyr up to the present time. Wishing, however, to add a full measure to it, I have taken care to send you whatever I wrote after I departed from the church of Bec, covering a period of twenty-eight years. The remainder, which I composed before coming to Mont-Saint-Michel, is with you in the chronicles that I obtained from the bishop of Beauvais with great labor.

“Indeed, the book of the chronicles of Eusebius of Caesarea is highly useful for elucidating many questions concerning both the Old Law and the New, that is, the Gospel. He begins his chronicle in the forty-third year of King Ninus, in which Abraham was born, and carries it to the twentieth year of the emperor Constantine. Jerome translated this from Greek into Latin; to it Jerome himself added material of his own, from Constantine’s twentieth year to the death of Valens. Prosper follows, and carries his history up to the capture of Rome by Genseric, king of Africa. After him begins Sigebert of Gembloux, a monk, and he carries his history from the thirty-first year to the year 1100, in which year Henry I, king of the English, began to reign. I attempted to continue something in the sequence of his chronology, beginning with the day on which Henry I the Elder began to reign, and carried it to the year 1182. He himself narrates the history of nine kingdoms together; when six of these had fallen away, I continued only three, namely those of the Romans, the Franks, and the English; and, imitating him, I pursue these three kingdoms.

“Furthermore, I beseech Your Paternity, and the holy congregation over which God has placed you, to remember my dearest father and lord, Richard, bishop of Avranches, who died on 6 March.

“May Your Holiness be well and live long.”

Saint Mark’s Day is 25 April, and that Richard died in 1182 is attested by our author below under the year 1183 and confirmed by the necrology of Lucerne, used by the authors of *Gallia Christiana*. Everything else in this letter also fits this year, except for the one name, Roger, the abbot of Bec, to whom it is addressed. For, as Robert himself testifies below, this Roger had already died in the middle of 1180 and had Osbern as his successor. For this reason Hirsch, p. 394, doubts the entire letter. But since, apart from that point, there is absolutely nothing in it to arouse suspicion, and no reason appears why anyone should have fabricated such a letter, I would rather believe that the error lies in the name “Robert,” rather than with the scribe—for it is the scribe’s hand, not the author’s—or that the scribe, reading incorrectly, took *pro osb*, that is, “for Osbern,” or supplied the name on his own.]. But, changing his plan once again, he continued it to the end of 1183, corrected numerous passages in the earlier portions, added some material, and thus in 1184 presented a second recension of the entire work to King Henry [Note: [Col. 0036A] With his own hand he wrote the following words: “Robert . . . made a history . . . up to the present time, namely containing the years up to A.D. 1181. He presented this book to his dearest lord H., king of the English; it contains the history . . . of Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Sigebert, and his own.” He prefixed this to manuscript E in the same hand with which he closed the years 1182 and 1183, and wrote at the head of the preface: “up to the year 1184.” E8c and E8f end here, and in all probability E8d, E8e, and E8g also ended here. Thus E8c belongs to the second recension, as we know with certainty of E8b, E8e, E8f, E8h, and the second and third hands in E8d. E1–E7 follow the first recension; E contains both, the first in deleted words and the second in superscript additions.]. In the following year he again took up his pen, and only when he died in 1186 did he finally lay it down.

The work, already widely read while its author was alive, was excerpted by Ralph of Diceto, Roger of Wendover in 1235, Nicholas Trivet in 1307, Matthew of Westminster, the Chronicle of Bec, and an anonymous annalist [Note: [Col. 0037A] For the years 1087–1239 in E8b; Bouquet XII, 786, and XVIII, 343, published its beginning and end.], and remained in the hands of scribes, not without alterations. Only one monk, of SAVIGNY (E2), changed the actual wording, while also omitting much and adding other material of his own, especially concerning his monastery. The monks of JUMIÈGES (E4) and LÉRINS (E7b), leaving the style of the language untouched, nevertheless altered the complete text by adding and omitting material according to their own methods. A certain other scribe copied Robert’s second recension up to the words concerning the year 1169, where “they perished”; he neither enlarged nor altered it, but omitted especially what concerned the monasteries and the history of individual persons, thus abridging, above all, the years 1162–1168. E8a–E8h copied him, E8a and the second hand in E8d reproducing him exactly. E8b added a brief continuation [Note: [Col. 0037A] From 1169 to 1259, published by Duchesne, *Scriptores Normanni*, 977; Bouquet XII, 788, and XVIII, 345.]; E8c, E8e, and the third hand in E8d added Robert’s complete work from 1169 to 1182. Finally, the monk of SAINTE-MARIE-DE-VŒU [Note: [Col. 0038A] Or Vallis-Ascii, in the diocese of Rouen, of the Cistercian order, founded in 1157 from Mortemer.] (E8h) joined this continuation to the Ursicampine one in such a way that, after making an extremely accurate copy of manuscript D1*, he added Robert’s shorter text for 1155–1169 and the complete text for 1169–1186, with a few notes of his own monastery scattered here and there. In the same manuscript a monk of Jumièges appended a continuation for 1187–1210. Having obtained this book, William the Little in 1513 arranged for the first edition to be produced from it. Thus, since the Ursicampine manuscript had been glued together from the Beauvais text, the Laon and Gembloux continuations, a strange fate brought it about that the first edition, and the text accepted down to the present, became almost a cento stitched together from all the families [Note: [Col. 0039] Here are the families of manuscripts and continuations, whose interpolations we have indicated with the sign =. See the preceding page.].

## Manuscripts

We know that sixty-three manuscripts of Sigebert and the continuators existed; nineteen have already been lost, while forty-four survive. Of these, twelve had been used by nine editors before us; we have used thirty-three. The manuscripts of the Gembloux family are therefore as follows.

### 1) Manuscript formerly belonging to Saint Peter of Gembloux

This manuscript, after the destruction of that house, came into the hands of a bookseller and was recovered by D. Baude, who most generously communicated it to me in 1840. I collated it myself. It is now Brussels, Burgundian Library, no. 18239, from which it was again most generously sent to us for use in preparing the edition. It is very well preserved, on parchment, small folio, sixty-two leaves. The quires are unnumbered; the lines are drawn sometimes with a stylus and sometimes with lead; the script is from the beginning of the twelfth century, extremely simple, and there are no decorated letters apart from the title written in red. Lists of kingdoms appear at the top of each page, while the years of Christ are marked in the margin only by decades. Individual sentences are distinguished by wider spacing and a capital letter. The punctuation is exceptionally good and had to be retained almost everywhere. There are fourteen scribal errors throughout the entire manuscript.

Leaves 1–42, joined in five quires, were written by Sigebert himself in his autograph hand at four different times. It is the same hand in which he wrote the *Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux* in the Leipzig manuscript: beautiful, firm, and so accurate that it contains only eight very slight slips of the pen.

Leaves 1–2 (“It begins”—“Priam”) were written in a single stint, with forty-one lines per page. Leaves 3–6 (“Others”—the year 422) are in a different ink, in smaller letters, which gradually recover the earlier size; from this point to the end of leaf 42 there are forty-two lines per page, ruled on the inside. On leaf 6 the conclusion, covering the years 423–425, is in suddenly smaller letters. Leaves 7–42, covering 426–972, are in another ink, which does not change thereafter. Later, at various times, the author himself corrected, deleted, and added several things here and there; after the year 972 no trace of his hand appears.

Leaves 43–50, covering 973–1084 and constituting the sixth quire, were written by a second hand at the beginning of the twelfth century, very similar to Sigebert’s but more ornate in its capitals. The orthography differs somewhat. The letter *a*, which Sigebert always wrote with an accent, lacks the accent in this and all the subsequent hands. There are three slips of the pen; there are forty-one lines per page; the parchment is thicker and smoother. Three pages, containing the years 973–979 and 1077, together with Hildebrand—through the end of 1088—had already been darkened by a wash one or two centuries ago so that they could be read more easily.

Leaves 51–54, covering 1085–1111 “was rubbing away,” and constituting the seventh quire, were written by a third hand, the same hand that wrote the beautiful material for 1136–1137. It ends in the middle of a page, the remainder of which is blank.

The fourth hand wrote only the inserted leaf 55. It is entirely different and somewhat cramped. There are no kingdom lists; the abbreviations and orthography are different, with forms such as *karta*, *karissimus*, *dominus papa*, *Henricus*, and *monacus*. On the last half-page, a hand that we believe to be Anselm’s, sufficiently similar to the preceding one but not identical, and in somewhat darker ink, wrote continuously the year 1112 and Sigebert’s death. A different hand added shortly afterward “who—left.” Then, without leaving any space, the page concludes with the year 1113, written in Anselm’s hand but at another time.

Leaves 56–62 constitute the eighth quire. Its first leaf had already been cut out before 1115, but nothing is missing. These leaves contain the years 1114–1135. Anselm himself wrote them, with a greatly changed ink and style. He perhaps used one stroke of the pen for 1113 and 1115; thereafter he wrote 1115 and the addition to 1113, then 1116–1118, on three occasions. For 1119–1121 the third hand wrote again, but Anselm corrected it and himself wrote 1122. Then he wrote 1123 and part of 1117; then 1124 and 1125 on three occasions, 1126 twice, 1127 twice, 1128 six times, and 1129 twice.

In 1130, with the same pen, he changed his attitude: he praises Gregory, whom he had just censured, and censures Lothar, whom he had praised. In 1132 he again changed, shortly afterward, what he had initially written against Lothar. The hand nevertheless remains entirely the same, Anselm’s, through the end of 1135.

For 1136 the third hand wrote again; another hand erased the ending and made a different one. In 1137, after “Prudent,” the beautiful sixth hand (1η.) follows, taking up the pen six times. At 1145, after “Reims,” the seventh hand follows in a continuous passage up to “when they had elapsed,” where it ends at the bottom of the page, leaving the last page of the quire and of the manuscript blank.

In addition, many additions and corrections occur throughout the manuscript, which we distinguish as follows. After writing the work, Sigebert later corrected several passages in second revisions, in black ink; still other passages were added later, in third revisions, in dark-brown ink and a neat hand. All these readings occur in every manuscript, and therefore were made before the work was first published.

Apart from these, other hands—1β, γ, δ, and ε—exactly contemporary with Sigebert in age, though slightly different from him and from one another in style, abbreviations, and ink, added several things, partly in erasures and partly in the margin. After the year 972, when Sigebert’s hand ends, they do not occur again, except in the years 1003, 1012, and 1076. Manuscript A omits all of these and usually has in the erasures the material Sigebert had originally written there. Nothing of these additions is found in Ekkehard or Waltram either; all the remaining manuscripts, however, apart from A, contain these additions and corrections of 1β–ε everywhere. It is therefore clear that they were made neither before the first edition of 1105 nor after the second, prepared by Anselm in 1112, for the B manuscript, written in that year, already contains them. They must therefore belong to Sigebert, made at various times between 1106 and 1111 as he revised, enlarged, and corrected his work.

That they were written by others rather than by the author himself is not at all unusual, since we see the same thing in Anselm’s continuation for 1119–1121 and in other autograph manuscripts; the difference in dates explains it. Since a person’s hand and manner of writing can plainly change greatly over time, some of these passages may indeed have been written by Sigebert himself, though not all. A further question is whether all these additions really belong to Sigebert, or whether they were instead interpolated by Anselm before he published his teacher’s work in 1112. The excessive variation in hands and ink prevents us from believing the latter. We have enclosed all of them in brackets, so that the second recension may be distinguished from the first.

A third kind of addition is also found in our manuscript and must be distinguished as follows. Hand 1ζ, before 1145, added material under the years 761, 876, and 888. Hand 1η, a native of Liège and the same hand that wrote the years 1137–1145, inserted the abbots of Gembloux and matters especially relating to Liège into Sigebert under the years 465, 651, 694, 710, 711, 714, 735, 761, 849, 890, 964, 987, 991, 1012, 1036, 1041, 1048, 1072, and 1092. He left Anselm and the continuators untouched. Hand 1θ, of the same period, added some material from Florennes under the years 1010, 1015, and 1088. Hand 1ι, contemporary, added material under 1133, 1134, and 1135; and hand 1κ, also contemporary, under 1131 and 1148.

All these additions passed into only manuscripts F1, F2, F3, F4, and B3*. They therefore cannot have been made before 1132, the year in which A was written. Finally, another interpolating hand, almost contemporary, 1λ, appears under the years 1083, 1087, 1121, and 1130 and passes into only F3 and B3*. It therefore cannot have arisen before 1148.

Thus 1ζ–λ are truly interpolations foreign to Sigebert and Anselm, and for that reason we have placed them after Sigebert’s text, to be given under the name of the Gembloux supplement.

The Gembloux manuscript therefore presents, in a certain sense, three texts:

1. The primary text, as Sigebert himself first published it, represented by A: “1. Sigebert’s second revisions; third revisions.”
2. The second text, as Sigebert himself revised it and Anselm published it, represented by B–E, with additions 1β–ε.
3. The third text, as the monks of Gembloux produced it after 1131, represented by F1, F2, F3, and F4, with additions 1ζ–λ.

### A*) Manuscript of Alne

Now Middlehill no. 4632, parchment, folio; concerning it see Sander, *Bibliotheca Belgica* II, 261, and our *Annals* VIII, 767. According to Pertz, who examined it in 1844, it was written by two hands of the twelfth century. The first reaches the end of 1112; the second continues from that point and carries the pen continuously to the end of 1126.

It was copied fairly accurately from 1, apparently at the end of 1126 and before Anselm himself had erased certain things under the year 1119. It has nothing distinctive or peculiar, at least in Anselm. It ends near the end of 1126, with the words “they conquered” in the middle of the page.

Another hand of the late twelfth century appended:

“In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1187, Jerusalem was captured by the Saracens under Saladin, their king, because of the sins of its inhabitants and the discord of the princes of that land. On 11 February the sky appeared to burn, as it were, during the night.”

Another hand added:

“When was the city of Constantinople given to the Latins,
When did the empire pass from the Latin people?
Baldwin was there, a Fleming, while he was count.
It was the year of Christ twelve hundred and four.”

### A.) Manuscript of Saint Paul of Verdun

No. 36, parchment, folio, twelfth century, in two columns and without colors. Leaves 14–113 contain Sigebert with Anselm up to the year 1131, “of Mary,” where it ends in the middle of a page; nothing is missing.

In Sigebert it was copied from the first edition, while in Anselm it appears to have been copied from 1 itself. It is of the greatest importance because it alone preserved the primary text where it has already been erased in 1—for example under 535, 569, 578, 688, 763, 829; compare 532. It omits everything added by 1β–λ, but also omits several passages that were already in the primary text, such as 522, 659, 690, 954, 1067, 1099, 1126, 1127, 1129, and 1130, as well as the whole years 1092 and 1110. On the other hand, it added certain material of its own under 594, 900, 914, and 1106. We have indicated all these passages, together with all its other readings that could be of any importance. Our Waitz collated it and described it in our *Annals* VIII, 446.

### F1.) Manuscript formerly belonging to Pierre Pithou

Now Brussels no. 14782. Its first quire, which I found in the royal manuscript Paris 7193, is parchment, folio, written at the beginning of the twelfth or thirteenth century by one hand, in two columns, without lists of years or kingdoms. It contains nothing except what is found in 1, which it copied accurately with all the additions except 1λ and the years 1090, 1119, and 1136. It neither changed nor added anything, except under 1121 and 1144. I collated it myself.

### F1*.) Manuscript of the Paris Carmelites

Now royal manuscript 4993, parchment, quarto, early thirteenth century, copied from F1, from which it differs only slightly under the years 453 and 1042. I collated it myself but never recorded its readings.

### F2.) Manuscript formerly belonging to Bongars

Now Bern no. 367, parchment, quarto, thirteenth century. It contains the material found in 1 and a continuation that ends in the middle of chapter 45; after several blank leaves follows the second part of the *History of Jerusalem*. It is very close to F1. It has all the additions except 1λ, and adds material of its own under 597, 1141, 1142, 1144, and 1145. It distorts names in a remarkable fashion, for example “Nantici” and “Cartanus” for “Namuci” and “Cajetanus,” and is full of errors.

### F3.) Manuscript formerly belonging to Thou

Now royal Paris manuscript 4864, parchment, folio, fourteenth century, written by one hand. It contains Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper; then, after a blank leaf, the material found in 1. The final leaf and two others containing the years 631–652 are missing. It copied 1 with all its additions, but quite incompetently; after 1020 it adds certain material in the most absurd fashion. It omits some passages under 453, 714, 963, 1119, and 1134, but merely through carelessness. I collated it myself.

### F4.) Royal Paris manuscript 4994

Parchment, fifteenth century. It contains Sigebert with the Gembloux material up to 1148, according to Waitz, who examined it.

## 2. Manuscripts of the Aquicintine family

### [B.] Earlier Aquicintine manuscript

See above, column 28.

### B1.) Manuscript of Cambrai 863

From the library of the metropolitan church of Cambrai, received as the bequest of Valerius Duflos, canon and archdeacon of Brabant of that church, in 1610. It is parchment, large quarto, beautifully written by one hand in the twelfth century. It contains Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Sigebert, Anselm, and the Gembloux material, followed by another continuation covering 1113–1155, written by the same hand, which ends at the top of the final page of the quire.

The same hand then added two theological notes: “In the year 1146 Master Gilbert stirred up a heresy—but in the Son,” and the *Chronicle of Hugh*. Its form and appearance are like those of 1; the text is free from errors. Some passages are missing under 954, 958, 1099, 1105, 1106, 1120, 1123, 1127, 1128, 1130–1132, and 1136. Additions occur under 651, 773, 1076, 1079, 1084, 1086, 1090, 1092, 1093, 1094, 1096, 1100, 1105, 1109, 1130, 1134, 1135, and 1136. Other manuscripts of this family likewise add and omit all these passages. There is absolutely nothing peculiar to this manuscript anywhere, for the continuation too plainly appears to have been copied from another source. I collated it myself.

### [B2.] Manuscript of Saint Mary of Vaucelles

Later belonging to Ortelius, then to Livineius, and finally to the Antwerp Society of Jesus, where Kluit saw it and calls it “an elegant parchment folio manuscript written before 1239” in *Historia critica Hollandiae* I, 2, 61. The Bollandists, in *Acta Sanctorum*, May VII, preface, 40 (compare February III, 216, and March I, 265), say that it contains “Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Sigebert, and finally, among other things, certain names and the origin of the kings of the Franks up to 1250.” Now lost, it is known to us only from the additions which Miraeus excerpted from it and from the Chronicle of Saint Bavo, which copied almost the whole of it.

### [B3.] Manuscript of Affligem

Written before 1189 and now lost. The following manuscript derives from it.

### B3*.) Manuscript of Saint Savior of Eiham

As appears from a sixteenth-century inscription on the first page: “Here rests H. Gillis Knudde, provost of this monastery” (the words “of Eiham” were added in the seventeenth century), “and the monastery had been reformed in the same year, by the grace of God, by its restorer Godefridus de Braele, abbot.” It later belonged to Justus Lipsius and is now at Leiden among the Lipsian manuscripts.

It is a parchment folio, written by one beautiful hand at the beginning of the thirteenth century from the Affligem manuscript, so accurately that it did not even change its words “this,” “that,” and so forth, referring to the monastery of Affligem. It contains Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, a pilgrim’s account of Mount Sinai—“From Katerina . . . he crossed over,” comprising twenty lines—Sigebert, Anselm, the Gembloux material, and a continuation up to 1163, “he will find.”

Its Affligem source was not copied in its entirety from B. In Sigebert it copied a manuscript of the third Gembloux text, very similar to F2, with all the additions 1β–λ. It does not have the additions of the other manuscripts except under 597, where it has the same addition as F2, and it has its own additions under 1005, 1030, 1033, 1063, 1086, 1087, 1088, 1091, 1093, 1095, 1096, 1100, 1101, and 1105.

In Anselm and the Gembloux material, having abandoned this text, it comes closest to B4. It omits the same passages—quite a number, which we indicate everywhere—but B4 omits also 1129, 1139, and 1144, which are found here. It contains certain passages absent from B3*. It adds material under 1119, 1127, 1128, 1140, 1142, and 1146, and has only one passage peculiar to itself, under 1139.

In the continuation it is much fuller. Throughout the book, from the year 606 onward, the Affligem scribe inserted seventy-seven notes copied word for word from the *Annals of Blandinium*, sometimes the same ones as in B4*, sometimes others. We shall indicate only their years, since the wording is better taken directly from the source itself. I collated it myself.

### [B4.] Manuscript of Saints Peter and Paul of Hasnon

Still seen by Martène in *Voyage littéraire* II, 97, but now lost. It was the source of B4* and B4**.

### B4*.) Manuscript formerly belonging to the Society of Jesus at Bruges

Now Brussels 9070–9075, parchment, folio, fourteenth century, written by one hand. It contains Orosius, Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Sigebert, Anselm, and the Gembloux material, with a continuation to 1167, “his wife,” followed by Valerius Maximus.

It presents Sigebert’s second text. The omission of the years 1074 and 1080, and the fact that Hildebrand is everywhere called Gregory, prove that the Hasnon monk supported the papal side. Of the additions in B it copied only those under 651, 690, 1079, 1086, 1090, 1092, 1093, and 1105. It has additions of its own only under 610, 670, 1069, 1070, 1120, 1134, 1136, and 1149, concerning Hasnon and Affligem.

Between 859 and 1165 the Hasnon monk made ninety-six additions, copied word for word from the *Annals of Blandinium*, many of which are also found in B3*. Neither manuscript derived from the other; both derived from the Blandinian annals. It has a certain similarity with B3* under 1073, 1074, and 1111. In Anselm and the Gembloux material the two agree closely, and both add material under 1119, 1127, 1128, 1140, and 1146, although in these passages too each contains material missing from the other.

The continuation is much shorter than in B3* and B5*. Since the additional passages found in B3* are not also found in B5, and those found in B5 are not also found in B3*, while all the material found in B4* is found both in B3* and in B5, this appears to be the genuine Aquicintine continuation. It ends in the middle of both a page and a sentence; but the same hand adds Valerius Maximus. The end of manuscript B4 had therefore already been lost at that time. I collated it myself.

### B4**.) Manuscript of Saint Rictrude of Marchiennes

Now Douai no. 750, parchment, folio, written between 1296 and 1306 by R., a monk of Marchiennes.

First, in six quires, he copied from B4 Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Sigebert, Anselm, the Gembloux material, and the continuation to 1167, “he returns.” It resembles B4* so closely that one would call it a copy of that manuscript, unless it had passages found in other manuscripts that are absent from B4*, under 773, 954, 1076, and 1095, and unless it were much freer from errors.

Shortly afterward, as appears from the character of the writing, the same R. interpolated the manuscript as follows. He wrote a quire of ten leaves containing:

“Here begins a letter against those who say that chronicles are empty or useless. Since . . . .”

“Here begins the preface to the following work. Therefore, venerable predecessors and orthodox fathers . . . .” [from the preface of the *Annals of Saint-Vaast*].

“Gregory, Anselm, Sigebert, and the monks of Gembloux each arranged their histories of kingdoms and times. But since we did not possess the histories of all the aforementioned writers, finally, at the urging, or rather pious admonition, of Father P., by the grace of God the venerable minister of this church of Marchiennes, and also at the urging of certain brothers . . . I, Brother R., the least of all, in obedience to the abbot’s command, undertook to transcribe the histories of certain of those mentioned above, namely Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, and Sigebert of Gembloux. Since in these histories I found no chronicles . . . up to the first year of Abraham’s birth, for this reason I turned my pen back to those earlier times . . . .”

“Here ends the preface. From the best creator of all things, and so forth.”

There follows R.’s own work, which is nothing but a sequence of years, with brief notes taken from Sacred Scripture, Bede, Peter Comestor, and Vincent. He placed these ten leaves before the manuscript he had already written, and added thirty-six supplements to it, sometimes in the margin, sometimes between the lines, and sometimes on attached slips. All were excerpted from the following sources:

- The *Life of Saint Amandus*: 571, 609, 610, 626, 633, 648, 649, 661, and 677.
- The *Life of Rictrude*: 614, 645, 659, 687, and 701.
- The *Life of Vedastus*: 687.
- The *Life of Amatus*: 666, 685, and 690.
- The *Life of Gertrude*: 655.
- The *Annals of Marchiennes*: 633 and 653.
- The *Annals of Saint-Amand*: 614, 691, 698, 782, 828, 855, 862, 871, 907, 1041, and 1050–1089.
- Material concerning the monastery of Saint-Amand: 828, 974, and 1118.

He closes the continuation with the year 1167, “he returns,” to which he appended three notes from the Aquicintine continuation and the *Annals of Elnon*.

He appended Jacob of Vitry’s *History of Jerusalem* to the middle of chapter 90, together with a chronicle for the years 1187 and 1280, “he had received the cutting”—“they found him bound,” which is also read in D1, sewn in by another hand. I collated it myself.

### B 5.) Codex of Saint Salvator at Aquicinctum, now Douai, no. 756, parchment, large quarto

Written most beautifully by four hands at the end of the twelfth century, in single columns at first and in two columns from the year 902 onward. Of these hands, the first wrote Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, and Sigebert in a continuous script and ink, very similar in appearance to Codex 1. The second, proceeding along the middle of the line, added Anselm and the Gemblacensis material up to the year 1148, “he died,” where it ends with the fourth leaf of the gathering. The third wrote the continuation for the years 1149–1158 [Col. 0045D] in a new gathering, whose first page it left blank; it therefore intended to write a separate and distinct codex. The fourth, however, joined it to the earlier one in such a way that the latter’s final four leaves, containing nothing but the end of the year 1148, were removed; it transcribed that ending onto the page left blank by the third hand and carried the continuation itself forward to the year 1201. Its pen was not indeed as continuous as that of the three earlier hands, yet neither was it contemporaneous with the events. Everywhere it acted rather as a scribe than as an author. Thus, at the end, it added only a bifolium, since it saw that it did not need more to reach the year 1200. The years 1191–1200, which we have seen were composed by the author in separate years, the scribe wrote in a continuous script and with one ink [Col. 0046A]; afterward he added the year 1201. Everything following, beginning with “He died,” was added in a continuous script by another thirteenth-century hand, from the Annals of Aquicinctum. Since the end has been lost, the codex now ends with a gathering.

It presents Sigebert’s text in the second recension, accurately copied; there are no traces of the other hands. There are two erasures, at the years 773 and 1105. It omitted certain passages at the years 954, 958, 987, 1099, 1113, 1119, 1123, 1127, 1128, 1130, 1131, 1132, and 1136, and most of the material concerning Gemblacum and other monasteries, some of which must already have been absent from its source, B. It has additions at the years 1076, 1079, 1080, 1084, 1086–1096, 1100, 1102, 1105, 1109, 1111, and 1130, all from B.; it has no additions of its own. A foreign hand leaves only one trace in the whole codex, at the year 773. I collated it myself.

### [B5*.] Codex of Saint Winnoc at Bergues, now lost

We know only by conjecture that this codex existed. It was copied from B5 while the latter’s final leaf was still present. We do not know what form Sigebert’s text had in it. It copied the continuation fairly well, but inserted many things into its brief appendix for the years 1201–1237, as we see from its copy, B5**.

### B5**.) Codex of Saint Peter at Blandain, now Brussels 16531

Parchment, quarto, sixteenth century. I discussed it in our *Annals* VIII, pp. 541ff. On folios 161–263 it presents, without any title, the Aquicinctine continuation for the years 1149–1201, together with an appendix for 1201–1237 enlarged by many interpolations. It is apparent that these were made by a monk of Bergues and copied from him into B5**, with remarkable confusion of the chronology [Col. 0046C]. The Blandain scribe then joined to this continuation, as though it were a single work, Annals for the years 1205–1288, which are as far as possible unrelated to the Bergues continuation. I copied it myself.

### B5***.) Codex of Baluze, now Royal Paris, 5440

Paper, folio, sixteenth century, end. It contains nothing except a copy of the years 1149–1288 “from the codex of Saint Peter at Ghent,” which is our B5**. I collated it myself.

### B5****.) Royal Paris Codex among the remnants of Saint-Germain, 13

It was copied from B5*** in the year 1719. I inspected it myself.

## 3. Codices of the Arras family

### [C.] Codex perhaps from Arras

This codex must have been copied from B. before B. received the additions of Anselm [Col. 0046D] and the Gemblacensis material. It incorporated many of B.’s additions and omitted some; it made very few additions of its own. It greatly corrupted the names. Another hand subsequently added a continuation down to approximately the year 1127, traces of which we see in C3. 4*.

### C1.) Cambridge Codex, Corpus Christi College 51

Parchment, folio, late thirteenth century; in *Catalogue of Manuscripts in England* I, 3, no. 1333, 51. It contains Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, and Sigebert, whom it copied faithfully. The very few omissions had already been made by C. or B. It has additions at the years 651, 690, 773, 1048, 1076, 1079, 1080, 1084, 1086, 1087, 1088, 1090–1096, 1099, 1100, 1105, 1109, and 1111, all of which are also found in other witnesses. It has no additions of its own except at the years 640, 698 (“the commemoration [depositio] of our outstanding Father Bertin”), 807, and 820; these appear to show that the material was either written at Saint-Bertin or copied from a Bertinian source [Col. 0047A]. In 1074 a seventeenth-century hand scattered in some material concerning King William. Collated by Oehler.

### [C2.] Codex of Saint-Josse-sur-Mer, now lost

Its copy is:

### C2*.) Codex formerly Erickengris, later Colbert, now Royal 4867

Parchment, folio, fifteenth century, elegantly written and decorated with pictures; a good witness. It alone omits certain passages at the years 755, 758, 827, 975, and 987; others it omits together with other witnesses. In these matters it often agrees with one manuscript of family A. It has additions at the years 1079, 1080, 1084, 1086, 1092, 1095, 1096, 1099, 1100, 1105, and 1109, from B. and C.; it has no additions of its own except at 795 and 840, concerning Saint-Josse-sur-Mer. Collated by Kurtz.

### C3.) Codex of Saint Martin at Tournai, now Royal Paris 1793

Parchment, folio, twelfth century. Written by one hand, it contains certain works of Jerome, Eusebius, Jerome’s continuation, Prosper, Sigebert, and a very brief continuation for the years 1114–1127. This continuation is found in nearly the same words in C4 and partly in C5. The Tournai scribe therefore did not compose it, but copied it from its original, C., adding two notices of his own. A second hand later scattered notes for the years 1132–1172, and a third added notes for 1332–1334.

Its format and appearance are the same as those of 1. The text was accurately copied from C.; the names, already greatly corrupted in C., were read that way here and were not corrupted by this scribe. It omits the passages at the years 954, 958, 962, 1012, 1099, and 1105, and includes additions at the years 651, 690, 773, 1048, 1079, 1086, 1092, 1093, 1099, 1100, 1105, and 1109. It already found all these in C. in this form, although it did not receive all of C.’s additions [Col. 0047C]. It has nothing proper to itself. Collated by our Waitz.

### C4.) Codex of Saint Vincent, now in the Public Library of Laon

Parchment, folio, written in 1136. It contained Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, and Sigebert, copied from C., together with that codex’s continuation, which a monk of Laon enlarged and carried forward at various times to the year 1145. Since its end has been lost, it now ends in the year 596: “extends as far as.” V. C. Pertz examined it and described it in our *Annals* VII, 533.

### C4*.) Codex of Saint Peter at Corbie, now Leiden Public Library 30

Parchment, folio, in single columns, most beautifully written by one hand. On the first page that hand wrote: “This book of the monastery of Saint Peter at Corbie was written in the year 1154” [Col. 0047D].

It contains Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Sigebert, and the continuation for the years 1113–1145, all written with one pen, although it is evident that the continuation was composed at different times at Saint Vincent in Laon. From this codex, from the reading of both copies of *Theudelina* at 596, and from several additions concerning Laon, we see that the Corbie codex was copied from C4, accurately enough up to the year 942. Thereafter it abridged the material in a remarkable fashion, to the extent that it excerpted rather than copied all the years, leaving intact only the years 949, 964, 971, 978, 979, 981, 982, 985, 986, 990–996, 998, 999, 1006, 1011, 1016, 1017, 1019, 1022, 1027–1029, 1034, 1035, 1056, 1059, 1060, 1063, 1066, 1069, 1091, 1094, 1102. We mention this here once and will not indicate the omissions under each individual year [Col. 0048A].

It has additions at the years 651, 690, 1048, 1076, 1079, 1092, 1095, 1096, 1099, and 1105, shared with other witnesses. Its proper additions are only those at the years 928, 1052, 1053, 1096, and 1104, all of which it found already in C4. It adds nothing at all itself; I therefore believe that these abridgements had already been made by the Laon monk and were merely copied by the Corbie scribe.

Another hand, entirely contemporary, scattered marginal notes concerning the monastery of Corbie at the years 664, 807, 815, 821, 827, 828, and 1141. The same hand wrote at the end: “Seek the following sequence of this work at Val-Saint-Lambert.” A third hand, only slightly later, added a few items at the years 419, 662, 844, and 885. I collated it myself.

### C5.) Codex of Saint Mary near Bourbourg, now Boulogne

Parchment, quarto, late twelfth century. It presents nothing except Sigebert’s *Chronicle*, without a title and abridged, with the year numbers omitted [Col. 0048B]. The year 383 occupies two lines; the years 384–386, 388–393, 395, 406–412, 418–437, 452, and so forth are entirely absent. After the year 1100, however, it presents the author in full. It has additions at the years 1102, 1105, 1109, and 1111, all of which are also found in B5. After Sigebert, a brief continuation in the same hand follows down to the year 1164, “they completed.” I collated it myself.

## 4. Codices of the Beauvais family

### D.) Codex formerly Beauvais, later Loisel, now Paris, Notre-Dame Collection 94

Parchment, folio, with exactly the same appearance as 1. It contains Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, and Sigebert, copied by one beautiful hand between the years 1138 and 1147 [Col. 0048C] from C. The names are greatly corrupted—such as Symon, Hyspania, Watheo, Cheberth, Dando, Remerbuch, and Ausburg, for Sunno, Hasbania, Wache, Ecberth, Lando, Reinesburch, and Ansburg—and it has already taken from its source the additions at the years 651, 690, 773, 1048, 1076, 1079, 1084, 1099, 1100, and 1109.

But this scribe was the first to alter the text extensively and in a wholly arbitrary manner: he transposed sentences, added, omitted, and changed words; he made the catalogue of popes entirely different, omitting many things for the first time and adding others of his own, sometimes in the text and sometimes shortly afterward in the margin. These additions, chiefly concerning Beauvais, occur at the years 649, 731, 1015, 1024, 1051, 1067, 1069, 1078, and 1092.

Another contemporary hand added three additions at the years 1109, 1111, and 1112, together with a very brief continuation for the years 1114–1147 [Col. 0048D]. A third enlarged this continuation and carried it forward to the year 1163. On the final page of the codex, a sixteenth- or seventeenth-century hand wrote a few items concerning Beauvais. Collated by Waitz.

### D1.) Codex of Saint Mary of Mortemer, later Colbert, now Royal 4863

Parchment, quarto, mid-twelfth century. It contains Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, and Sigebert, together with the Beauvais continuation to the year 1147, copied from D. with the utmost accuracy in 1155. It neither omitted nor changed anything; it added only a few items at the years 1054, 1098, 1107, 1120, 1153, 1154, and 1155.

Two hands of the same date interpolated this continuation and carried it forward to the year 1165; thereafter many other hands, contemporary with the events, continued it to the year 1234. Later, annals written in the following century were sewn into the codex; these are the same as those found in B4**, [Col. 0049A] together with some other immaterial material. Collated by Waitz.

### [D1*.] Codex of Ursicamp

Written between 1155 and 1200. It contained Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, and Sigebert, copied word for word from D1, which it neither altered nor abridged, but interpolated in more than fifty places from Geoffrey and other sources. It then contained the continuation for the years 1115–1155, which all editions except that of Miraeus possess, taken from B1. In the earliest years it interpolated Anselm; from 1129 onward it copied B1 in full, making fifteen additions of its own.

We know this now-lost codex from its copies D1** and E8h. We shall give its additions collected together in one place; we shall not reproduce the entire continuation.

### D1**.) Codex of Dijon 322

Parchment, folio, copied by one hand at the end of the twelfth century from D1*. It did so with such fidelity that it neither added nor omitted even a word. Collated by Waitz; see him in our *Annals* VII, 534.

### D2.) Codex of Saint Victor at Paris 238

Parchment, folio, late twelfth century. It contains Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, and Sigebert, together with the Beauvais continuation, copied directly from D., splendidly but with very many omissions. It is therefore of no value. Inspected by our Waitz.

## 5. Codices of Robert of Torigni

### [E*.] Codex of Bec, Robert’s autograph, now lost

It contained Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, and Sigebert, copied from D. and interpolated by Robert, together with his continuation for the years 1100–1153 and his treatise *On the Change of the Monastic Order* [Col. 0049C]. It is indicated in the catalogue of the books of Bec and by Robert himself in the letter prefixed to E6:

“The remaining works which I made before coming to Mont-Saint-Michel are with you in the chronicles, which I obtained from the bishop of Beauvais with great labor.”

It is the source of codex E.

### E.) Codex of Saint Michael of Periculum Maris in Normandy, now Public Library of Avranches 86

Parchment, small folio. On leaves 1 and 2, prefixed to the codex only after the year 1184 and written by a late twelfth-century hand, are the *Titles of the Books Given by Philip, Bishop of Bayeux, to the Church of Bec*, and the *Titles of the Books in the Bec Armarium*.

Robert himself prefixed leaf 3 in the year 1184 as the title page of the codex, and wrote on its reverse:

“Contained in this volume are the following works: the Chronicle of Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea … Thereafter the same Jerome carried it forward … Then follow Prosper’s chronicles in the order of history, which contain seventy-seven years. Thereafter follows the chronography of Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, which he began with the year 381 from the Lord’s incarnation and carried forward to the year 1100 of the same era, in which year the first Henry, king of the English, began to reign.

From that year Robert, abbot of Saint Michael of Periculum Maris, made a history containing the deeds of the Romans, Franks, and English down to the present time—that is, containing the years up to A.D. 1184. This book he presented to his most dear lord Henry, king of the English; it contains this history and the other works noted on this page, namely those of Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, [Col. 0050A] Sigebert, and his own work, which is placed at the end.

Concerning the history of Orosius, which he composed on the *Ornament of the World*: ‘From Adam, the first man … and from the preaching of our Lord Jesus Christ, 351 years.’”

The codex itself consists of twenty-nine gatherings written by several hands. The first hand wrote Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, and Sigebert. Sigebert begins:

“Here begins the prologue of Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, to the chronography edited by him, which he began with the year 381 from the Lord’s incarnation and carried forward to the year 1100, in which year the first Henry, king of the English, began to reign. ‘Since we are about to speak …’”

It ends:

“he placed at Aquicinctum.”

“Here ends the chronicle of Sigebert, monk of Gembloux. Here begins the prologue of Robert to the works that follow concerning the description of times” [the words “up to the year 1184” were added in erasure by the same hand that wrote folio 3 and the material below for 1181–1184, namely Robert’s hand] [Col. 0050B]:

“On the chronography … of the incarnation.”

Then follows *On the Change of the Monastic Order*, concerning the abbots and abbeys of Normandy and their construction: “‘It pleases me …,’ etc.,” as in Dachery, p. 811. But the rubricator added in the margin:

“Here ends the prologue. You will find the continuation of the chronography below, on the twelfth leaf. For here, through the scribe’s fault, certain matters—although not unworthy of remembrance—have been inserted.”

The end of this treatise has been enlarged by erasure.

Then begins “The letter of Henry the archdeacon to Warinus concerning the kings of the Britons: ‘You ask … farewell.’” Also, concerning the same history: “‘Further … is found.’” From the same history, concerning the modern saints of England: “‘Who … shine forth.’”

Then begin Robert’s chronicles: “‘Henry,’ etc.”

This first beautiful hand of the middle of the twelfth century wrote continuously, without interruption, from the beginning of the codex through the year 1156, “he followed,” preserving exactly the same appearance and ink throughout. The lines were ruled in lead; the initial letters were red, green, and blue. The overall appearance is the same as in D. and 1.

In names it varies between *Hericus* and *Heiricus*; at first *Northmanni*, afterward always *Normanni*, rarely *Normani*; *Dunelme* and *Duneline*, indeed *Duveline*; almost always *Willmus*, rarely *Guillmus*, while *Guillermus* is written in full only once, by Robert himself, at the year 1183. *Dns*, when written in full, is always *donnus*; *ecclesiae* is used consistently at first, later *ecclesie*; apart from this word, everywhere *e* is used for *e*, *oe*, and *ae*. Slips of the pen are extremely rare. Erasures and corrections, whether by the scribe or by Robert, are rare in Sigebert.

The kings of the English and the archbishops of Rouen are sometimes found in the text and sometimes supplied in the margin [Col. 0050D] and between the lines; it is uncertain whether these additions were made by the scribe or by Robert. In Robert’s continuation, these marginal additions become much rarer and the erasures more frequent; all except those at the years 1128 and 1151 originated with the author.

Another hand begins at the year 1156, “About this time,” in a different ink, continuing along the same line, less firmly, and frequently changing its appearance and ink. A third begins in 1157, “the Hagarenes,” often changing its form while writing; it omits the green lines drawn in the margin up to this point throughout the codex. A fourth begins in 1161, “King Henry,” written at different times; toward the end of the line the green lines appear again. A fifth begins in 1167, “On the Nativity,” neat, with a different orthography; it distinguishes individual sentences not by capital letters but by the sign §, which the fourth hand had already used toward the end [Col. 0051A]. The first hand returns at 1168, “In the month of February,” in a new gathering, which it wrote in its entirety at a different time. A sixth begins in 1177, in a new gathering, very similar to the preceding one and perhaps the same hand, written on several occasions. A seventh begins in 1181, “In the preceding year.” An eighth begins with “Andronius” and again uses the sign §. The ninth is Robert’s own hand, which also wrote folio 3 of the codex. In a new gathering it writes “the most beloved lord” in one continuous script through the end of 1183; from there it gradually continues to “having been brought about by his death” at the end of a leaf in the third gathering. The fourth, fifth, and seventh gatherings have been lost; in the sixth and eighth, certain thirteenth-century notes concerning the monastery of Saint Michael are found.

We thus see that a new hand generally begins with a new gathering. But if we consider that even in those portions written by one hand the appearance varies greatly, sometimes suddenly and sometimes gradually; that passages which seem very different often appear, upon closer inspection, to have been written continuously; and that Robert’s hand displays the greatest variety in other codices of Saint Michael as well, it is more than probable that most of what we attribute to eight hands belongs to one person—indeed, to Robert himself.

It is certain that after the year 1156 the codex proceeds, for the most part, in agreement with the events narrated, and that all corrections in it were made by the author’s hand. These include those at the years 912, 1032, the preface to 1114, and 1118, 1128, 1130, 1135, 1142, 1145, 1146, 1149, 1151, 1154, 1155, 1156, 1181, and 1182, made only when, in 1184, he offered the second recension of the work to the king [Col. 0051C]. The remaining corrections, at 899, 1128, 1157, 1162, and 1164–1174, had already been made earlier.

Thus the codex of Saint Michael was copied from the Bec autograph E*. up to the year 1156; after 1156 it is itself an autograph. I collated it myself.

### E1.) London Codex among the Arundel Manuscripts 18

Formerly Gresham College 2917, 18. Parchment, fourteenth century. It contains Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, and Sigebert according to Robert’s recension, but proceeds only to the year 1100.

### E2.) Codex of the Holy Trinity at Savigny, later Colbert, now Royal 4862

Parchment, folio, thirteenth century, written by one exceptionally beautiful hand. It contains Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Sigebert, and Robert through the year 1156, “the Angevin district.” On the two following leaves it contains notices for 1213–1258, a history of the monastery for 1112–1243, and notes for 1212–1305. Then, by the first hand, follows Hugh’s *Chronicle*.

Above Sigebert’s text it states:

“What follows, up to the year 1113 from the Lord’s incarnation, was collected by Sigebert G., monk, and he does not bring it to a close at 1100, as Robert does, but immediately joins his continuation to it as though it were Sigebert’s work.”

After 1113 it places Robert’s abbreviated preface, in which it says again:

“He carried it forward to A.D. 1113.”

The first recension of Robert follows, but it abridged and altered the whole work so thoroughly that it can often scarcely be recognized. It omitted all Robert’s additions before 876 and many afterward, including those at 966, 971, 976, 989, 1006, 1027, 1040, 1041, 1073, 1077, 1078, and 1089, among others. It adds material of its own at 938, 1085, 1098, 1099, 1112, 1120, 1124, 1138, 1146, 1149, 1151, and 1152 [Col. 0052A]; these we shall assign to Robert. Collated by Waitz and myself.

### E3a.) Codex of the Church of Bayeux

Parchment, quarto, early thirteenth century, copied from E. by three hands. It contains Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Sigebert, and Robert to the end of the year 1157, “Ricarius.” Then follow Robert’s treatise *On the Change of the Monastic Order* and Hugh of Rouen’s letter. It contains no interpolations. I inspected it myself.

### E3b.) Codex of Saint Mary at Reading in England, now British Museum, Harleian 651

Parchment, folio, early twelfth century. It contains Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Sigebert, and Robert to the end of the year 1157. A seventeenth-century hand added the continuation through the end of 1168 from codex E8a. Inspected by Pertz in 1844.

### E4.) Codex of Saint Peter at Jumièges, now Rouen Y 87, 60

Parchment, quarto, thirteenth century; the same as that at Montfaucon, p. 1214. It contains Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Sigebert, and Robert’s first recension, which ends at the top of the page in the year 1159, with the words “Robert, bishop of Obsonium [Obsoniensis; place uncertain], died, and succeeded him …”

On the following pages are written the *Annals*, beginning “John—John the pope was born,” and ending, with their conclusion lost, in the year 874. They were edited by Labbe. I inspected it myself.

### E5.) Rouen Codex U 11, 7

Parchment, folio, fourteenth century. It contains Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper, followed by the statement: “What follows is taken from Sigebert’s chronicle,” consisting of nothing but fairly arbitrary excerpts through the year 1164. Then follows a *Chronicle* from Orosius through Heraclius and Sisebut: “A brief account of the times … he became renowned for his life and miracles.” I inspected it myself.

### E6.) Codex of Saint Michael of Periculum Maris, now British Museum, Cottonian Domitian 8

Parchment. After much other material, it contains Robert for the years 1153–1179, preceded by his letter, which Brial edited from this codex in XVIII, 333.

According to Pertz, who inspected the codex in 1844, folios 70–93, containing Robert, were joined to the rest of the codex only later; previously they formed a separate codex. The scribe left the first page blank, and a later, neat hand of the late twelfth century wrote on it the letter which we gave above from this codex.

Robert’s work begins on folio 70 verso, written by one continuous late-twelfth-century hand through “when,” where the leaf ends. The end of the codex has therefore been lost; I have no doubt that it extended to the middle of the year 1182. See *Archiv* VII, 75 [Col. 0052D].

### E7a.) Oxford Codex among the Bodleian Manuscripts 212

Parchment, folio, fifteenth century. It presents Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Sigebert, and Robert through the year 1182, “the monk of Bec,” together with the treatise *On the Change of the Monastic Order*. See *Archive* VII, 536.

### E7b.) Codex of Saint Taurinus at Évreux, later Bigot, now Royal 4861

Parchment, folio, thirteenth century. It contains Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Sigebert, and Robert through the year 1182, “the monk of Bec”; then the letter of Oliver, certain excerpts from Robert, William of Jumièges, and the Annals of Évreux from Christ to the year 1317, edited by Brial XVIII, 353.

It follows Robert’s first recension, but omits certain items, including those at the years 1142, 1145, 1146, 1135, 1159, and 1160. At the year 1162, “Frederick,” it begins a new gathering in two columns, still by the same hand, and from that point omits nothing. It makes additions at the years 1114, 1118, 1119, and 1181, and concerning the monastery of Lyre at 1146, 1147, 1152, and 1166. Collated by Waitz and myself.

### E8a.) British Museum Codex, Kings Library 13, C. 11

Parchment, folio, twelfth century. It contains Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Sigebert, and Robert through the year 1169, “they perished,” and is certainly of the same recension as what follows. Robert’s treatise *On the Change of the Monastic Order* follows. Inspected by Pertz in 1844. See *Archive* VII, 77.

### E8b.) Codex of Saint Victor at Paris 287, formerly 419

Paper, quarto, late fifteenth century. Among much other material, folios 120–168 contain Robert’s work from the year 1138, “Stephen … 1169, they perished,” of the second recension. Duchesne, *SS. Norm.* 977, and after him Bouquet XII, 788 and XVIII, 1345, edited it from this very codex, though less accurately.

The text is not altered in wording, but passages concerning monasteries or individual persons are omitted. It has a brief continuation for 1169–1259, perhaps written at the monastery of Vallomont. Folios 168–175, in the same hand, contain a *Chronicle*: “1087. William died … 1239. Edward, son of Henry, king of England,” edited by Bouquet XII, 786 and XVIII, 343. I inspected it myself.

### E8c.) Codex of the University of Cambridge 1153

Parchment, thirteenth century. It contains Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Sigebert, and Robert through the year 1183, “they pursue peace,” together with the treatise *On the Change of the Monastic Order*. See *Archive* VII, 536 [Col. 0053C].

### E8d.) Codex formerly of Louis M. … of Rouen, later Bigot, now Royal 4992

Parchment, small folio, thirteenth century. In gatherings 1–20 the first hand wrote a notice of the provinces, a calendar, Sigebert, and Robert through the end of 1155, of the first recension, with the treatise *On the Change of the Monastic Order* inserted immediately after the preface, as in E.

In gatherings 21 and 22, a second hand added the years 1156–1169, “they perished,” of the second recension, greatly abridged. In gatherings 23–25, a third hand wrote all the remaining material of the same recension through the year 1182, “many Latins,” with the final three leaves lost. The complete codex therefore undoubtedly ended, like E8c. I inspected it myself.

### E8e.) Royal Hanover Codex

Paper, late seventeenth century. Copied from a manuscript in the Bodleian Library, NE. B. 6. 9, folio 121a.

“Here begin the chronicles of Robert of Mont-Saint-Michel. Henry, son of the first William, etc.”

The Bodleian codex cannot be our E6; E6 ends already at the word “Bec,” whereas E8e continues later to “Poitiers.” It follows the second recension. The years 1139–1169 are read exactly as in E8b. I collated it myself.

### E8f.) Royal Madrid Codex X 81

Paper, folio, fifteenth century. On its first seventeen leaves it contains Sigebert together with Robert’s continuation through the words at the year 1182: “Henry III, son of Henry, died; while his father was alive he was king of England.” But it abridged both works, Robert’s especially, so severely that it can scarcely be counted among the codices. The prefaces of Sigebert and Robert, together with the letter to Warinus, are entirely absent; only excerpts of the remainder are read. It has no material of its own. Asconius and Valerius Flaccus, written by Poggio’s hand, follow in the codex. Our Knust inspected it and copied Robert’s continuation.

### E8g.) Vatican Codex of Queen Christina of Sweden 152, or 322

See *Acta Sanctorum*, March I, 455; Montfaucon, p. 17; Bouquet XIII, 300 and XVIII, 336, who used a copy at Saint-Germain among Durand’s miscellanies. It appears to come very close to E8h., but has additions at the years 1158, 1159, and 1160.

### [E8h.] Codex of Saint Mary of Voto, later of William the Little, now lost

It contained Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, [Col. 0054B] and Sigebert together with the Ursicamp continuation, copied from D1*. It then contained Robert’s text for the years 1154–1169, “they perished,” abridged exactly as in E8b; the years 1169–1186 were complete and belonged to the second recension, with a few additions at 1159, 1164, 1169, 1181, and 1182. Then followed the Jumièges continuation for 1187–1210. We know it only from the first edition.

## 6. Lost codices

**Saint Peter of Selincourt.** Parchment, quarto. Sigebert; chronology from Adam to Louis the Pious; a catalogue of popes and bishops of Thérouanne through the year 1160. See Montfaucon, 1197.

**Signy.** Concerning this, see Tissier, *Cistercian Library* VII, 100.

**Soissons.** Cited by Haenel, p. 441. I sought it in vain at Soissons, and likewise elsewhere.

**Arras.** Fifteenth century; according to Haenel, p. 33, it contained Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Sigebert, and Martin of Troppau.

**Saint-Ghislain.** According to Sander, *Bibliotheca Belgica* I, 246, it contained “the chronicle of Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, and Sigebert, as well as another very ancient work by an unknown author.”

**Stavelot.** See De Reiffenberg, *Philippe Mouskes*, preface, p. 17.

**Val-Saint-Lambert.** With the Laon continuation; see above, C4*.

**Saint Lawrence of Liège.** In the catalogue of the books of Saint Lawrence, written in the twelfth century in the codex of that monastery, now Brussels 9814, it is indicated as follows:

“Tripartite History of Sozomen, together with the chronicle of Sigebert, monk of Gembloux.”

**Ottobonianus.** See Montfaucon, p. 188.

## 7. Works falsely attributed to Sigebert

The Vienna Codex Eugen. 18 and Brussels 14855 are inscribed with Sigebert’s name falsely; they contain William of Nangis. The Trier Codex 1287 contains Robert of Auxerre. The Saint-Germain codex which Montfaucon cites among the Coislin manuscripts on p. 1121 is now Saint-Germain français 659, fourteenth century. As our Waitz points out, it is a chronicle written in the French language down to the year 1306, for which Sigebert was, among other authors, a foundation.

## Editions

We possess the following editions:

### a.) First edition

*Sigebert of Gembloux, monk, Chronicle from the year 381 to 1113, with insertions from the history of Geoffrey and additions of Robert, abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel, comprising the following 103 years, published for the first time through the efforts of the most reverend lord William the Little, doctor of both laws, canon of the royal chapel.*

It was offered for sale in the workshop of Henri Estienne, where it was printed [the abbreviated imprint in the source is difficult to expand with certainty], in quarto.

At the end:

“This chronicle of Sigebert, with not a few additions, was completed at Paris by Henri Estienne … at the expense of the same man and of Jean the Little, distinguished bookseller, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1513, on the first day of June.”

An edition prepared by Antonius Rufus from codex E8h., with D2 also used, but not sufficiently accurately. Nevertheless, forms such as *Alience*, *Falconius*, *Fanuel*, *Gigunix*, *Brogo*, *Penectesel*, and *Ramaldo* in place of *Nicholaus*, *Alienor*, *Malcomus*, *Manuel*, *Guingamp*, *Drogo*, *Penevesel*, and *Rainaldo* can scarcely be attributed to the codex. The editor seems knowingly to have changed, omitted, and added nothing, if one may judge from the fact that it agrees fairly well with D1** and E8b in the years 1025–1169.

### b.) Simon Schard, *Four Chronographers of German Affairs*

Frankfurt am Main, 1566, folio.

At the end:

“Printed at Frankfurt am Main by Georg Corvinus, Sigismund Feyerabend, and the heirs of Wigand Gallus, 1566.”

Some copies have on the title page “Paris, Jacques Dupuis, 1566”; others “Basel”; others “Lyons.” It is nevertheless the same book, with only a different title prefixed. In Sigebert’s case it contains nothing except the complete reprint of the first edition.

### c.) Margarinus de la Bigne, *Sacred Library of the Holy Fathers*

Paris, 1575, and a second edition, 1589, folio. It presents Sigebert, without the continuations, reprinted from the first edition, in volume VII, p. 1339.

### d.) *One Volume of Distinguished Ancient Writers of …*, from the library of Johann Pistorius

Frankfurt, from the heirs of A. Wechel, 1583, folio; and a second edition, Hanover, 1613, folio [Col. 0056A]. In Sigebert it is Schard reborn, with nothing added.

### e.) Laurentius de la Barre, *Christian History of the Ancient Fathers*

Paris, 1583, folio. He reproduced the first edition once again.
f.) *The Chronicle of Sigebert of Gembloux, a monk, compared with the autograph and the oldest manuscript codices; to it was added the chronicle of Anselm, abbot of Gembloux, with the continuations of Gembloux, Affligem, Vaucelles, and Anchin, edited by Aubert Miraeus.* Antwerp, H. Verdussen, 1608, small folio.

Miraeus was the first, and the only one, to publish our author in an authentic form. He reproduced the entire Gembloux codex accurately: he concealed nothing from it and altered nothing, although he distinguished its additions by the form of the letters, not always correctly [Col. 0056B].
