He inserted the additions of codices B2, 3*, and 5 in their proper places, but not all of them [Note: [Col. 0055C] Thus, from B3*, he omitted thirty-five items, while at the years 1084–1086 he attributed to it material that is by no means found there.]; elsewhere he presents material from other sources, without identifying them [Note: [Col. 0055C] A. 484, 529, 633, 644, 695, 701, 739, 784, 863, 881, 887, 934, 937, 953, 990, 1048, 1063, 1064, 1077, 1084, 1095, 1098, 1101, 1116, 1124, 1125, 1128, 1132, 1134, 1135, 1138, and everything that he printed in slanting type in the Anchin appendix.]; he himself seems to have composed some of these [Note: [Col. 0055D] A. 990: “Fulquinus m. e. c. d. m.” [abbreviated; expansion uncertain]; 1077: “Lamberti S. m. H. c. d.” [abbreviated; expansion uncertain]; and several others.].

Those who accuse him of having acted in bad faith in the case of Sigebert and the Gembloux materials are unjust; but in the case of Anselm [Note: [Col. 0055D] A. 1114: he omitted “with great and glorious renown”; 1127: “due”; 1133: “the greed of the Romans”; compare 1131.], and in the Anchin and Affligem materials, the accusation is entirely justified. For from the year 1155 onward he silently omits everything in which Frederick is praised [Note: [Col. 0055D] A. 1155: “the empire flourishes, and the lofty lord of all things is exalted”; 1157: “whom justice, courage, and generosity made praiseworthy and beloved by all good men”; 1158: “having employed his steadfastness”; ibid.: “pious and just”—“adorning affairs”; 1161: “For he feared”—“he himself was regarded as pious and beloved by all, so that the dukes and counts of William, king of Sicily, deserted their lord and went over to him”; and many other passages.], or his opponents are criticized [Note: [Col. 0055D] A. 1155: “stubbornly lusting after money”; ibid.: “the emperor, always rejecting their insatiable greed”; 1156: “so that he might destroy it and fraudulently seize his inheritance”; 1158: “who proved rebellious”; 1159: “they contend for the papacy” changed to “they aspire to the papacy”; ibid.: “with oaths violated”; ibid.: “admiring and abhorring their treachery beyond what can be believed”—“to be avenged.”]; indeed, he suppresses the very events when they carry this implication [Note: [Col. 0055D] A. 1156: “the emperor, having left his wife at the judgment and advice of the bishops and archbishops”; 1161: “at the advice of the princes.” Sometimes this produces an amusing result, as when at 1156 he omits “he first joined her in marriage.”]. Nor did he fear deleting such passages from the codex itself, not with a pen but with a knife [Note: [Col. 0055D] A. 1155, 1158, and already in Anselm at 1131: “Just as … affected” and “Although … requires.”].

For the years 1149–1164 he excerpted the Anchin chronicle only very briefly; thereafter he does give it in full, but censored in the same manner as B3*. He omits not only passages favorable to the emperor [Note: [Col. 0055D] A. 1169, 1172, 1173, 1180, 1181, 1191, 1194, 1196.], but also many others [Col. 0056C] [Note: [Col. 0055D] A. 1184, 1186, 1187, 1190, 1192, 1198.]; he makes the author say things different from what he actually wrote, often in a ridiculous fashion [Note: [Col. 0055D] Thus he always calls the nobles of Germany *primates*; he changes “fearing” into “seeing,” “the emperor’s loyal men” into “supporters,” “rebels” into “enemies,” “rebellion” into “disturbance,” “through the emperor’s piety” into “with the emperor’s agreement,” “pride” into “spiritedness,” “the cardinal carries out reluctantly” into “attempts to carry out”; “the duke of Saxony, having received bad advice from evil men, rebels against his lord, namely the emperor Frederick,” into “Henry, duke of Saxony, rebels against the emperor Frederick”; shortly afterward, “he disdained to come” into “he did not wish to come”; and “the assistance of his lord” into “his assistance.”]; indeed, he erased from the codex itself whatever displeased him [Note: [Col. 0055D] At 1131 he erased the same passages that he had erased in the Gembloux manuscript and in B3*; he also erased them in B5, adding in the margin: “This passage seems to require expurgation and to deserve censure.” At the year 1183 he wrote in the margin: “These things seem to require careful reading.”]—and thus he acted not as an editor but as a censor and falsifier.

He would have done the same with Sigebert as well, had he not known that, since this author had already been published so often, such a procedure would accomplish nothing [Col. 0057A] except arouse suspicion. The material he added to the Anchin continuation and distinguished in slanting type is not found in B5, and we do not know where he obtained it; this much is certain: it was not excerpted from any single codex, but gathered from many authors, with some portions composed by Miraeus himself.

g.) Struve, in the third edition of the *Pistorian Writers*, Regensburg, 1726, large folio, reprinted Sigebert together with the continuations of Ursicamp, Waulsort, and Gembloux from the first edition of Pistorius. But he inserted in their proper places everything that Miraeus possessed from B2, 3*, and 5; beneath the text he placed the more important variants of the Miraean reading, together with Miraeus’s own notes and his own. He then appended the continuations of Anselm, Gembloux, Affligem, and Anchin from Miraeus [Col. 0057B], and the Beauvais continuation from Labbe. By combining everything in this way, he confused it to some extent; he contributed nothing genuinely new except occasional, sometimes useful, brief notes.

h.) Dachery, in his edition of Guibert of Nogent, was the first to publish Robert of Torigni in full from codex E, using E4 as well. He rendered the names less accurately, omitted some passages here and there, and presents Robert’s additions to Sigebert only from the year 876 onward; even among these he forgot some. He added no notes.

i.) Bouquet and Brial, III, 332; V, 375; VI, 233; VII, 249; VIII, 308; X, 216; XI, 163; XIII, 256; XVIII, 334, provided excerpts only. In addition to the editions, they used here and there codices B5***, E2, 7b, 8b, and d.

[Col. 0057C] The principle of our edition was this: to present Sigebert’s text as the author himself established it for publication, while indicating its original form everywhere in the notes. We therefore took codex 1 as our foundation and reproduced it accurately. We incorporated into the text all additions written in Sigebert’s own hand before he first published the book, indicating everywhere in the notes what the author added in his second and third revisions.

We enclosed the additions 1β–ε, dictated by Sigebert after the year 1105 while he was preparing a second edition, in brackets—not because they were spurious, but so that it might be evident that they had been absent from the primary text. What had previously been written there, but had since been erased, we indicated beneath the text insofar as we could recognize it from A. [Col. 0058A]

The additions 1ζ–λ, which we know are not by Sigebert but were made by various people only after the year 1136, we removed from Sigebert’s text and collected together after it under the title *Appendix of Gembloux*. To report the complete range of variants from the remaining codices would have been both excessive and unnecessary, since we know that its origin is arbitrary and that its useless bulk would have obscured the necessary notes. We therefore thought it best to select only those variants that might have some importance for recognizing the primary text, distinguishing the families of codices, or tracing the history of the published text. Nor did we indicate the transpositions of codex D, which were invented only by the Beauvais scribe; anyone wishing to know them will learn them more effectively from the editions.

We have always scrupulously indicated omissions in the various codices, except in C4* and 5 [Col. 0058B], concerning which see what we said above. We have given all the additions of all the codices; but instead of inserting each one into Sigebert under its respective year—since he would thereby have been overwhelmed by such a mass—we collected them according to their authors, under the titles *Appendix of Anchin, Affligem, Vaucelles, Hasnon, Laon, Corbie, Beauvais, Mortemer, Ursicamp,* and *Robert of Torigni*, placing them before those continuations which were written by the same authors as the additions and drawn from the same sources. These are nothing other than additions of the same kind, gradually expanding at greater length, as Robert provides a particularly clear example.

Thus the reader immediately sees the provenance of each addition, its date, its source, and the degree of trust it deserves. Material belonging to the same author and the same monastery is not scattered; the history of the text is more clearly understood; and Sigebert’s chronicle is offered to readers in its pure form, just as it was composed.

We have also accurately reproduced the character and external form of the work, as codex 1 displays it and most of the other codices preserve it. The one exception is that Sigebert marked the years of Christ only by decades in the outer margin, whereas we have placed each year beside its entry. Beyond this, we judged that very considerable effort should be devoted to investigating the sources from which Sigebert and his continuators drew.

**L. C. Bethmann**

[Col. 0057]

## HERE BEGINS THE CHRONICLE OF Sigebert, MONK OF GEMBLOUX

[Col. 0057D] Since, with God’s help, we are going to say something about the contemporaneity of kingdoms, let us first say a little about the origin of the individual peoples, insofar as we shall be able to follow the footsteps of our ancestors, guided along the paths of histories. We shall place the kingdom of the Romans in the first line; that of the Persians in the second; that of the Franks in the third; that of the Vandals in the fourth; that of the English in the fifth; that of the Lombards in the sixth; that of the Visigoths in the seventh; that of the Ostrogoths in the eighth; and that of the Huns in the ninth.

I think nothing need be said about the kingdom of the Romans except what the prophet Daniel interpreted concerning the fourth kingdom: just as iron crushes, subdues, and shatters everything, so from its origin it had battered, subdued, and shattered almost all the kingdoms of the world; but at the end of time that kingdom, which had stood for so long and so firmly on its iron legs without any weariness, would at last begin to totter with a terrible crash from the lofty level of its domination, when the iron of its strength had been mixed with the clay of human weakness.

The Persians were the first to assail this kingdom. They had always been almost equal in standing to the Romans, but now, when the condition of the state was wavering, they did not fear to attack them openly; moreover, they were able to cut away part of their territory when, after Julian the Apostate had been killed and the Roman army miserably subjugated, they became excessively fortunate through the Romans’ misfortune. Thus that kingdom, which for so long had held almost all the peoples of the world as prey and under its domination, now, because Almighty God mixed for it a double measure in the cup from which he had poured for the others, lay exposed as prey and an object of mockery to almost every people. Those who once contended with other nations for glory could now scarcely provide adequately for their own safety.

For whatever peoples, either to reduce the size of their population at home or from a desire to exercise their own savagery, went into exile from their native land, attacked the Roman Empire, cut out from its vast body portions, as it were, for themselves, and established in them a place from which to rule. This will become clear in what follows.

As for the origin of the Persian kingdom, it does not seem useful at present to trace it back further, because the reader will sufficiently recall from the histories of the ancients how great was the antiquity of this kingdom and how extensive and powerful was the nobility of that antiquity. I shall note only this: although they had often abused victory over the Romans, now, after the recent killing of Julian, the defeat of the Roman army, the mutilation of the Roman Empire’s borders, and the settlement of peace by treaty for twenty-nine years according to their own pleasure, they bore their prosperity with little restraint. While their king Shapur acted with increasing arrogance, they were wholly hostile to Christians and Romans.

### (Deeds of the Kings of the Franks)

Let us make known to others, on the trustworthy account of our ancestors, the origin of our people, namely the kingdom of the Franks. After that famous destruction of the city of Troy, known to every age and nation, the surviving Trojans, having been defeated by the victorious Greeks, divided their course. One part went with Aeneas to Italy to establish the Roman Empire; another part, namely twelve thousand men, under Antenor, reached the neighboring regions of Pannonia beside the Maeotian marshes. There they built a city, which, in memory of themselves, they called Sicambria. They lived there for many years [Col. 0060A], grew into a great people, and, making frequent incursions into Roman territory, extended the traces of their ferocity as far as Gaul.

### (Miscellaneous History)

The Caesar Constans, son of Constantine the Great, found them so hostile to the Romans that he crushed them in war and, after finally subjecting them to the Roman Empire, compelled them to become somewhat gentler in their savagery. Some years later, when the Alans rebelled against the emperor Valentinian and the emperor was unable to defeat them completely because the impassable Maeotian marshes protected them, Valentinian proposed that, if any people could enter these marshes and crush the rebellious Alans, he would free that people from tribute for ten years.

Attracted by this agreement, the Trojans, trusting in their courage and prudence, entered the Maeotian marshes, which were inaccessible to the Romans, under the leadership of Priam, exterminated the people of the Alans, and thus satisfied Valentinian. Delighted by their valor, Valentinian called those who had first been called Trojans, then Antenorids, and later also Sicambri, “Franks” in the Attic language, a word which in Latin is interpreted as “ferocious.”

### (Fredegar)

Others say that the Franks were surnamed from a certain king of theirs, Frantio, who, being exceptionally brave in war, directed his journey into Europe after fighting with many peoples, settled between the Danube and the Rhine, and whose descendants grew there. Until that time they had refused to accept the yoke of anyone.

### (Prosper)

Whatever the origin of the name “Franks,” then, the historians, collecting whatever they could from the more remote past, report that this Priam ruled over them at the time of the earlier Valentinian. For, recalling from the very name of their king the nobility of that Priam under whom Troy was destroyed, they gloried in the belief that the beginnings of their people had sprung from him.

When the ten-year period had elapsed and the tax collectors demanded tribute from the Franks, the Franks, becoming insolent because of their earlier victory and presuming on their strength, dared not only to refuse the tribute but also to rebel against the Romans. The Romans assembled an army, fell upon the Franks, and, after defeating them, crushed them to the point of annihilation.

### (Bede)

The Britons, or Brittones, from whom the island of the Ocean was called Britain, lived under Roman rule from the time of Gaius Julius Caesar until the year of the Lord 413. In the time of Marcus Antoninus Verus, at the insistence of Lucius, king of the Britons, they received the mysteries of Christianity through the envoys of Pope Eleutherius; some of them advanced in it even to the crown of martyrdom.

When they were exhausted by the frequent and almost continual incursions of the Picts, and were themselves found weak and incapable of resisting their enemies, on the advice of their king Vortigern they invited the English people from the borders of Saxony and appointed them as their defenders against every attack of their enemies. After the English had protected them vigorously and bravely for some time, they were eventually enticed by the desire to rule and brought to this by the weakness of those whom they had undertaken to defend. The native Britons, subjected by so violent an injustice to the foreign English, yielded, as if defeated, to their law and name [Col. 0061A], and were never able to shake off their subjection to them [Note: [Col. 0061] In place of this passage, D1** and E8h have an interpolation concerning the Britons taken from Geoffrey of Monmouth; all editions except Miraeus’s derive it from them.].

### (Jordanes)

The Vandals, also originally from Scythia, were defeated by the Goths and began to invade the lands of others because they were unable to retain their own. After they had dwelt near the Danube for a long time, Giberich, king of the Goths, defeated them in war once again and expelled them from there. He forced them to abandon the settlements they seemed to possess by whatever means, submit themselves to the Roman Empire, and humbly ask Constantine the Great to grant them a place to live.

They obtained this request, and peacefully inhabited the Pannonias assigned to them by Constantine for sixty years. In the thirteenth year of Arcadius and of Honorius, summoned at the instigation of Stilicho, who was plotting rebellion against the state, they poured through Gaul, joining the Alans to themselves [Col. 0061B], and for some time ravaged it most miserably. The Goths drove them out from there as well—not with concern for the peace of Gaul, but to empty the country for their own plundering.

The Vandals attacked Spain and for a long time devastated now Spain, now Gaul; but they could not be safe there from the Goths either. Since the Goths were grievously disturbing Italy, Honorius, after deliberating with his advisers, granted the Goths Spain and Gaul, which he grieved had been seized from him by the Vandals and other peoples, with a binding confirmation.

When, therefore, the Goths hastened to drive the Vandals and other enemies from the territories assigned to them, and the Vandals, hemmed in on every side, were tormented by fear of the Goths, an unexpected and welcome opportunity for good fortune came to them because of the sins of the people. For when hostility arose through envy between the Roman commanders Boniface and Aetius, Boniface, having been worsted, did not wish to avenge the injury done to him except at the cost of harm and danger to the state. He crossed over to Spain and invited the Vandals to seize Libya and Africa. They hastened there and established their kingdom for a long time, disturbing both divine and human things without any regard for humanity or divinity.

### (Paul the Deacon)

We read of a definite origin for the Winili, who were later called Lombards in their native language because of their long beards, but we do not find a definite date for their origin. We read that kings ruled over them, and we have learned even their names, but we do not find the years of their reigns distinguished by periods of time.

They lived in Scandinavia, an island of Scythia. When they had multiplied so greatly that their land could no longer contain them, they decided to reduce their numbers by sending out one-third of the population, and they determined by lot who should depart. Accordingly, one-third of the Winili, as the lot had selected them, left the island of Scandinavia under the leaders Agio and Ibor. They wandered from place to place, uncertain and vagrant; and, often attacked in many wars, they defended their safety and freedom manfully, since the matter concerned their very lives.

After Agio and Ibor died, Agelmund was the first to rule over them, for twenty-three years. While he was conducting himself with excessive confidence, he was killed by the Bulgars together with many of his people. Lamissio ruled second; after him Lethu ruled third for forty years; Ildehoch was fourth; Gudeoc fifth, at the time when Odoacer ruled in Italy. The sixth king of the Lombards was Claffo, the seventh Tato, the eighth Waltarith, and the ninth Audoin, who led the Lombards into Pannonia. The tenth was Alboin, who, after leading the Lombards into Italy, established their kingdom there most firmly.

### (Jordanes)

From the history of Jordanes we have learned that the Goths, who among the ancients were called Getae and who later divided themselves and created two kingdoms, namely those of the Ostrogoths and Visigoths, had the following origin.

They first inhabited Scandia, an island of Scythia. Not content with possessing it, they departed from there with their king Berich. Roaming through the neighboring islands and lands of Scythia, they harassed the neighboring peoples with war and subdued the surrounding nations by the terror of their name. Later, under their fifth king Filimer, they advanced farther into Scythia and wandered for a long time, far and wide, as far as the nearer banks of the Danube and the lands of Thrace, Dacia, and Moesia.

There they coalesced into a great people for a long time, indeed for many centuries. By adding many peoples to themselves through their victories, they enlarged their name and strength. Strong in power and clever in intelligence, and educated even in the disciplines of philosophy, they cast off their native barbarism and surpassed the other barbarian peoples in humanity and good character.

In the time of the emperor Decius, after crossing the Danube with their king Gniva, they pressed heavily upon the Roman Empire. When Decius attacked them in war, they routed the Roman army and killed Decius himself together with his son Decius. Elated by this success, and often afterward gaining the upper hand over Roman commanders in battle, they were a terror to the entire Roman world.

While they still remained beyond the Danube, in the time of the emperor Valens they began to clash with one another in civil war. Athalaric, the leader of one party, prevailed over Fritigern, the leader of the other. Fritigern asked Valens for assistance and promised to become a Christian. Valens sent aid and, being himself an Arian, caused them to be led into the sect of the Arians.

In the thirteenth year of Valens, the Huns, who themselves were raging powerfully and savagely in Scythia, took advantage of the opportunity provided by the internal conflict among the Goths. They invaded their territory unexpectedly and, after defeating them in war, either subjugated them to themselves, tormented them in captivity, or expelled them from their homeland.

Thus the Goths, who had subjected many peoples to their service [Note: [Col. 0061] “Service” is written above “dominion” by the same hand in 1; nothing has been erased.], were themselves subjected to the dominion of the Huns. They greatly increased the Huns’ power, since all who had served the Goths obeyed the rule of the Huns through the Goths. In this way the Huns surpassed almost all the peoples of Scythia in dominion and strength.

Some of the defeated Goths crossed the Danube and entered the territories of the Roman Empire; they asked Valens to grant them land for settlement. After obtaining this request, they restrained themselves for a time from every insolent use of arms. At last, compelled by Roman greed and by want of property, they stirred up serious wars in the very heart of the empire.

The emperor Valens confronted them, but was defeated by them in battle and burned in the fire. By the just judgment of God, he brought great calamity upon the state and increased the enemies’ exultation. These Goths, therefore, who pressed upon the Roman Empire, called themselves Visigoths, that is, western Goths. For many years they troubled the western borders of the Romans as far as the most distant parts of Spain, where they later formed a kingdom.

The Goths who remained in their ancestral land beyond the Danube under the dominion of the Huns had petty kings of their own people, and called themselves Ostrogoths, that is, eastern Goths. Later, through their king Theoderic, they received from the emperor Zeno the gift of a kingdom in Italy and held it for many years.

Thus the Goths, as though violently brandishing the two horns of their head toward east and west, created two kingdoms from themselves: that of the Visigoths in Spain and that of the Ostrogoths in Italy.

### (Jordanes)

The barbarism of the Hunnic people, whose kingdom held supremacy throughout almost all Scythia, would make me keep silent about the kingdom of the Huns, were it not for that famous destruction of Gaul and Italy which compels me to speak—when through Attila, their king, God’s judgment spread far and wide. God unsheathed him like a sharpened and honed sword from the sheath of his indignation against sinful peoples.

I shall therefore briefly disclose what is read in the histories of the ancients concerning their origin. Filimer, king of the Goths, son of the great Gadaric, who held the rule of the Getae in the fifth place after their departure from the island of Scandia, entered the lands of Scythia with his people. There he discovered among his people certain magical women, whom they call *Alirunnae* in the Gothic language. Suspecting them, he drove them out from among his people and, having banished them far from his army, compelled them to wander in the wilderness.

### (Miscellaneous History XII)

When wild men, whom some call *fauns of the fig trees*, saw them wandering through the desert and mingled with them in sexual intercourse, they produced this most savage race. It first lived among the Maeotian marshes: a small, ugly, and puny sort of human being, known by no speech except one that conveyed an imitation of human language. Those whom they could scarcely overcome in war, they drove to flight by instilling excessive terror through the frightfulness of their appearance. They had the appearance of a dreadful blackness and, if it is permissible to say so, something like a misshapen lump rather than a face, with more spots than eyes. Their grim appearance revealed the confidence of their spirit.

On the first day of their birth they also rage against their male offspring. For they cut the cheeks of the males with iron, so that, before they receive the nourishment of milk [Col. 0064A], they are forced to endure the ordeal of a wound. Hence they grow old without beards and are beardless without attractiveness, because the face furrowed by iron removes, through scarring, the timely beauty of hair.

They are indeed small in stature, but clever, agile in their movements, and exceptionally ready for riding; broad-shouldered and prepared for bows and arrows; strong-necked and always holding their heads high in pride.

### (Jordanes; the source reads “JOBD.”)

These men, although possessing human form, live with the savagery of beasts. Born, therefore, from such a stock, the Huns were a source of horror and dread to all the neighboring peoples.

Their power was increased by their victory over the Goths, who lived beyond the banks of the Maeotian River and flourished in Scythia with the glory of exceptional power and courage. The Huns obtained this victory in the following way.

Hun hunters, following the tracks of a hind crossing the Maeotian marshes—marshes that they had previously thought impassable—carefully explored the Scythian region. They reported everything they had discovered to the Huns and encouraged them to cross. Under their guidance, the Huns crossed the marshes and, like a sudden whirlwind, descended upon the Scythian peoples. They subdued them all and drove the Goths themselves, who ruled over or surpassed the others, from their settlements.

After this fortunate success, the Huns, elevated above the other peoples of Scythia by their victory over the Goths, spent approximately eighty years working toward the upheaval and ruin of the world. From this victory of theirs until the death of Attila, we shall record their kingdom in this work.

Besides these, there were other peoples who tore apart the Roman Empire: the Gepids, Alans, Turks, Bulgars, and many others. All came out from the northern region, so that perhaps the prophet’s saying may be seen to have been spoken concerning this: “From the north evil shall be unleashed upon the whole earth.”

Let us therefore begin the fabric of our narrative from the year of the Lord 381. In that year, after the death of Valens, the younger Valentinian and Gratian, sons of the elder Valentinian, began to rule jointly and ruled for six years. From this year Shapur, who had long ruled the Persians, ruled for twenty-eight years. From this year the Britons were under Roman rule for thirty years [Note: [Col. 0063] Sigebert first wrote XXXta III, but the III seems to have been erased by him immediately after it was written, since he always places the same mark over the other numerals; it is absent here. Only A, F1, and F2 have XXX.]. From this year the Vandals, with their king Modigisilus, raged cruelly through Gaul for thirty-three years [Note: [Col. 0063] A, F1, and F2 have thirty-two.]. Over the Franks dwelling in Sicambria, Priam ruled [Note: [Col. 0063] In 1, an uncertain hand adds five years from this year, as does B3*; the others lack it.]. Others write that he perished in the war in which, as we have said, the Franks were severely battered by the army of the earlier Valentinian and compelled to leave Sicambria.

Fritigern, who had ruled over the Visigoths for some time, ruled for three years from this year. Winitharius was in charge of the Ostrogoths, who remained in their ancestral land under Hunnic dominion; from this year until the death of Attila, petty kings of their people ruled them for approximately eighty years.

Balamber ruled the Huns; after him, Mundzuch, the father of Attila; Octar and Rugila, his brothers; and Bleda and Attila, his brother, ruled from this year until the death of the emperor Marcian, for approximately eighty years.

In the year 4331 from Adam [Note: [Col. 0065] Thus initially in 1. A, B4*, C1, and C3 have 4332; 1 was later corrected to 5579; so too C2* and D.], according to Dionysius; but in the year of the Lord 381, according to Dionysius; in the 289th Olympiad, in the fourth year after the death of the impious Valens, they rule.

### (Prosper)

Theodosius, appointed master of the soldiers by Gratian, defeated many barbarian peoples with incredible speed and remarkable success and restored the exhausted state in the eastern regions.

### (Miscellaneous History, Cassiodorus, Idacius)

At that time Damasus was distinguished at Rome, in the thirteenth year of his papacy [Col. 0065B]; Didymus of Alexandria, who had been deprived of sight from his fourth year of age, yet, although ignorant of the elementary disciplines, was so remarkable in literary knowledge that he astonished even philosophers [Col. 0065B]; Jerome, wholly devoted to divine Scripture; Gregory of Nyssa; Gregory of Nazianzus; Martin, bishop of Tours; Ambrose of Milan; Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia; and in Egypt Pachomius, the abbot, and Meletius, bishop of Antioch, who was all the more renowned because Theodosius foresaw in a dream that Meletius would clothe him in the imperial purple cloak and crown him with the diadem.

## 382

2. 2. 2. 2. 2. 2. 2. 2.

### (Prosper)

Gratian strongly favors religion and, in every respect ready to serve the state, makes Theodosius his partner in the empire.

### (Jerome, *Life of Saint Paula*)

Paula, exceptionally noble among the distinguished matrons of Rome, renounces the world.

### (Jerome, Preface to the Psalms)

Jerome corrected the Psalter which was sung in all the churches according to the translators of the Septuagint. When it was again corrupted, he composed a new Psalter, which would differ little from the edition of the Septuagint translators and would agree closely with the Hebrew. To make this clear to everyone, he distinguished the Psalter by asterisks, that is, the star +, and by obeli, that is, the reclining bar ÷. He taught that the material contained under the asterisk + as far as the two dots .. was found in Hebrew but omitted by the Septuagint; whereas the material contained under the obelus ÷ as far as the two dots was not found in Hebrew but had been added by the Septuagint, following only Theodotion’s translation [Col. 0065D] [Note: [Col. 0065] “Following only Theodotion’s translation” was later erased by another hand, perhaps Anselm, and placed after “would agree”; F1 and F2 have it there, while A, B3*, and F3 lack it.].

Pope Damasus, at Jerome’s request, instituted the singing of this Psalter in the Gallican churches; for this reason it is called the Gallican Psalter. The Romans, retaining the Psalter according to the Septuagint for themselves, call theirs the Roman Psalter.

Since these two Psalters were insufficient for presenting testimonies concerning Christ against the Jews, who accept only what is found in Hebrew, Jerome added a third, called the Hebrew Psalter, because at the request [Col. 0066A] of the wise man Sophronius he translated it from the Hebrew truth into Latin word for word. Sophronius himself translated this Psalter and other works of Jerome from Latin into Greek.

### (Bede, Gennadius, Idacius)

Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, began in this year a cycle concerning the observance of Easter, arranged for one hundred years, which he called a *laterculus*; that is, from the first consulship of Theodosius.

### (Chronicle of the Pontiffs)

At Jerome’s request, Pope Damasus instituted the practice of saying in church at the end of the psalms, “Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit; as it was.” He also instituted the singing of psalms in the church night and day [Note: [Col. 0065] “Instituted … to be sung” is written over an erasure of half a line by Sigebert in his second revision. The following words, “But so that … reached,” were added by 1δ in the margin; they are absent from A alone and consequently were lacking from the first edition of 1105.].

[So that choirs divided into two parts might sing the psalms alternately, this had already been instituted in the church of Antioch in the time of the emperor Constantius by Flavian and Diodorus, men of approved life and learning; from there it spread even to the ends of the whole world.]

3. 3. 3. 3. 3. 3. 3. 3.

### (Prosper)

Maximus seizes imperial power in Britain through tyranny.

### (Idacius)

After Frithigern, Athanaric rules second among the Visigoths for one year. Having entered into an alliance with Theodosius and been invited by him to Constantinople, he died there on the fifteenth day after his arrival.

Basil of Caesarea, renowned for both philosophy and holiness, to whom God appeared and taught him, at his prayer, to consecrate the holy sacrifice in his own words; to whom it was revealed that the soldier and martyr Mercurius had killed the emperor Julian; who reconciled to Christ a young man who, out of love for a virgin procured for him by the devil, had denied Christ, publicly disputing with the devil; who obtained from God that Saint Ephrem the Syrian should speak Greek; who by prayer erased the written and sealed sins of a sinful woman [compare Jerome]—famous for these and many other deeds, when a Hebrew physician truly declared by examining his pulse that death was approaching him, postponed his death until the following day by prayer. Thus converting the physician and his household to Christ, he died happily.

Pope Damasus, maliciously accused of adultery, was cleared by forty-four bishops, while his accusers were expelled from the Church.

Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea, having turned to the heresy named after him, was condemned by Pope Damasus. He said that Christ at his birth assumed flesh alone and not a soul; or, if he assumed a soul, that he assumed not a rational soul but merely a life-giving soul; that the power of the divinity had taken the place of a soul for the assumed flesh; and that the flesh itself had not been assumed from Mary, but that the flesh and the Word were of one substance [Note: [Col. 0065] The passage from “Basil … were of one substance” is written over an erasure by Sigebert in his second revision.].

(PSEUD. DAM.) Pope Damasus decreed that archdeacons—who are also called chorepiscopi, that is, bishops of districts or villages—should presume nothing against bishops. For *chore* is Greek, meaning “village” or “district” in Latin. (ISID.) The Visigoths were without a king under Theodosius for thirteen years. (JORD.) Winitharius, king of the Ostrogoths, rebels against the Huns in Gothia for the sake of freedom. (PROSP.) Bishop Ambrose writes books on the Holy Spirit to the emperor Gratian. (CASS.) The body of Paul, bishop of Constantinople, who had been strangled by heretics in exile under Constantine, is brought back to Constantinople with honor by the emperor Theodosius.

385. R. 5. P. 5. F. 5. B. 5. W. 5. W. 1. O. 5. H. 5.

(BEDA.) In Gaul Saint Romanus of Blaye dies. Theodosius makes his son Arcadius Augustus. (PROSP.) Justina, the Arian mother of Valentinian, rages with detestable hatred against Ambrose and the whole holy Catholic Church. (G. r. F.) After Priam, Marcomir, son of Priam, and Sunno, son of Antenor, rule the Franks for thirty-six years. Under their leadership the Franks leave Sicambria and settle beside the Rhine in the towns of Germany. (JORD.) Winitharius defeats the Huns in battle.

386. 6. 6. 1. 6. 6 2. 6. 6.

(BEDA.) Maximus crosses into Gaul and kills the emperor Gratian at Lyon; but his brother Valentinian, under a pretended treaty of peace, he drives out of Italy for three years. Theodosius rules alone for eleven years. (JORD.) Balamber, king of the Huns, kills Winitharius in battle. After him Hunimund reigns as the second king among the Ostrogoths for two years. (BEDA.) The second universal synod, of 150 fathers, assembles at Constantinople by order of Theodosius and with the support of Pope Damasus. It condemns Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is God, and teaches that the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Father and the Son; it also gives the form of the creed which the entire confession of Latins and Greeks sings in the Church at solemn Masses. At this synod it was decreed that the bishop of Constantinople, as bishop of the new Rome, should have the privilege of rank after the Roman pontiff. (MARIAN.) Priscillian, a bishop in Spain who establishes the heresy named after him, disturbs the Church. (AUGUST., *On Heresies* 70.) He confused the persons of the Holy Trinity, saying that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit were the same person. He regarded the eating of meat as impure; he separated husbands from unwilling wives and wives from unwilling husbands; he attributed the creation of all flesh not to the good and true God but to evil angels; he said that souls were of the same nature and substance as God, and that they descended gradually through seven heavens and certain principalities to a kind of voluntary contest—not, however, one to be carried out on earth—and encountered an evil prince, by whom he said this world was made, and by whom they were sown through various bodies of flesh. He also said that human beings were bound to the stars by fate, and that our body was composed according to the twelve signs of the heavens: Aries in the head, Taurus in the neck, Gemini in the shoulders, Cancer in the chest, Leo in the hands, Virgo in the belly, Libra at the navel, Scorpio in the hips, Sagittarius in the male organ, Aquarius in the bladder, Capricorn in the shins, and Pisces in the soles of the feet. (IDACIUS. MARIAN.) Having been heard at councils of bishops concerning these matters, he went to Rome, where he was rejected by Saints Damasus and Ambrose. In Gaul as well, at the synod of Bordeaux, he was judged a heretic by Saint Martin [Note: “by Saints … Martin”: erased by Sigeb. himself, but in the same ink as the rest; therefore it was written immediately when the entire codex was being produced, not in a later correction.] and others. When he understood that he would be condemned, he appealed to the emperor Maximus. After being heard by him and expelled from the episcopate, he was killed at Trier by the prefect Evodius, together with many of his followers, the emperor having ordered that accomplices of this sect in Spain should be executed. The bishops Ithacius and Ursacius, the accusers of Priscillian, are deprived of communion with the Church by the bishops, who declared that it was unlawful for a person of any kind to be killed through the accusation of bishops; the emperor Maximus and certain bishops defended Ithacius and Ursacius. For this reason Saint Martin was harassed by Maximus, because he refused to communicate with the Ithacians. Nevertheless, he scarcely managed to obtain that the Priscillianists should not be put to death. (HIER., *Life of Saint Paula*.) Paula, having left Rome and established herself at Bethlehem, serves Christ there together with her daughter Eustochium; by her holy way of life she inspires many to emulate holiness.

387. 1. 7. 2. 7. 7. 3. 1. 7.

(PROSP.; G. pont.) Siricius presides as the thirty-seventh over the Roman Church. [Note: B, C, D, and E have “thirty-sixth,” and so on; cf. the year 399.] He decreed that a repentant heretic should be received into the Church through the laying on of the priest’s hand. He exiled the Manichaeans found at Rome. Bishop Ambrose was the first to introduce among the Latins the practice of singing antiphons in the Church, bringing it from the Greeks, among whom this practice had long been established through the institution of Ignatius, bishop of Antioch and a disciple of the apostles. Ignatius, carried up into heaven in a vision, saw and heard how the angels sang hymns to the Holy Trinity through the alternation of antiphons. (CASS.) The Franks destroy Quintinus and Heraclius, Roman commanders, together with almost all their forces, near Trier. (PROSP.) In Egypt John the anchorite shines forth in holiness and the spirit of prophecy.

The emperor Theodosius washes away, by an exemplary act of public penance, the monstrous crime he committed when he had seven thousand citizens at Thessalonica killed in revenge for the judges who had been killed in the revolt. 394. 8. 14. 9. 14. 14. 10. 4. 14.

(BEDA.) Jerome here ends his book of illustrious men; Gennadius begins from this point. (PROSP.) At Alexandria, by order of Theodosius, the temples of the idols are destroyed by Theophilus, the bishop. When the famous shrine of Serapis had been demolished, a martyr shrine is consecrated there, and the bones of John the Baptist are deposited in it; they had been transferred to Alexandria in the following manner. (RUFINIUS, *Ecclesiastical History*.) While the apostate Julian was ruling and raging against Christ, pagans broke open the tomb in the city of Samaria where John the Baptist had been buried, extracted his bones, and scattered them through the fields; then, gathering them again, they burned them in the fire and scattered the holy ashes, mixed with dust, through the air. But certain monks from Jerusalem mingled with the enraged pagans and collected as many bones as they could; they carried them to their abbot Philip at Jerusalem. Philip sent them to Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. (MARIAN.) Saint Patrick the Scot is sold in Ireland together with his sisters. There, while he was the king’s swineherd, he often enjoyed conversations with angels.

395. 9. 15. 10. 15. 15. 11. 5. 15.

Arsenius flourishes at Rome. Until his fortieth year he served honorably at the imperial court; then, from being a senator, he became a monk and for fifty-five years shone in the desert as an example of holiness, admirable to all. When Jerome was translating the sacred Scriptures of the Old Testament from the Hebrew original into Latin, the edition of the Septuagint interpreters, which had been held by all Greeks and Latins, began to be regarded as secondary. Although holy and learned men were distressed that this was being done contrary to the Church’s long-established custom, the authority of the Hebrew truth nevertheless prevailed once it became clear how far the Septuagint interpreters differed from it.

396. 10. 16. 11. 16. 16. 12. 6. 16.

(H. m.) At this time, in the Judean town of Emmaus, a fully formed child was born, divided from the navel upward, so that it had two chests and two heads, each with its own senses. One ate and drank, while the other did not eat; one slept, while the other remained awake. Sometimes they slept together, and yet they also played with each other; both cried, and they struck one another. They lived for nearly two years. One of them died, while the other survived for four days. (MARIAN.) The emperor Valentinian, driven to weariness of life by the excessive harshness of Arbogast, master of the soldiers, ended his life by hanging. Eugenius becomes a tyrant with the help of Arbogast. (BEDA.) The bodies of the prophets Habakkuk and Micah are revealed. Didymus the Blind dies at Alexandria in his eighty-fifth year.

397. 11. 17. 12. 17. 17. 13. 7. 17.

(PROSP.) Theodosius kills Eugenius and Arbogast in battle and himself dies not long afterward. After him his sons Arcadius and Honorius rule for thirteen years. (V. Ambr.) The bodies of the martyrs Nazarius and Celsus are discovered and raised at Milan by Ambrose.

398. 1. 18. 13. 18. 18. 14. 8. 18.

(PROSP.) Constantinople, fearing God’s anger, escapes after being moved to repentance by fire flashing terribly above a cloud. Rufinus, master of the eastern army, rebels and is killed by Stilicho, master of the western army. Gildo, count of Africa, rebels and withholds the customary payments from the Romans. Stilicho kills him not long afterward and restores Africa to its former status. (JORD.) The Visigoths, having broken their treaty with the Romans, make Alaric king over themselves; he reigns for eighteen years. [Note: “eighteen”: erased in 1; F2 and many others have fifteen.]

399. 2. 19. 14. 19. 19. 1. 9. 19.

(G. pont.; MARIAN.; CASS.) Anastasius presides as the thirty-seventh over the Roman Church. [Note: Thus in manuscript 1, corrected; the other manuscripts agree.] (MARIAN.) According to some, Saint Martin dies this year. (GENNAD.) At this time the following holy and learned men flourished in the Church: John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople, renowned for holiness and learning, but in his eloquence more severe and outspoken than was proper; Donatus, bishop of Epirus, who spat out an enormous dragon and killed it in its mouth, and which eight yokes of oxen could scarcely drag away to be burned; in Spain, the historian Orosius; and in Aquitaine, Severus, who wrote the life of Martin and many other works. In old age he was led astray by the Pelagians and maintained silence until his death, correcting through silence what he had sinned by speaking. (V. Servat.) In Gaul were Severinus of Cologne and also Servatius, the tenth bishop of Tongeren, a kinsman of our Lord Jesus Christ—not only because he did the will of God the Father, but also according to the flesh. (Gen. Servat.) He was born in Persia as the son of Emmius, whose father was Eliud, the brother of Elizabeth, who bore John the Baptist. Eliud’s and Elizabeth’s mother, Esmeria, was the sister of Anna, who bore Mary, the mother of the Lord.

(H. m.) From this time onward the Visigoths on one side and the Huns on the other make severe incursions into the Roman provinces. At Rome, during a gladiatorial show, the monk Telemachus rebukes the people who are engrossed in the spectacle and is stoned by them. Offended by this, the emperor Honorius abolished gladiatorial shows forever by his edict.

401. 4. 21. 16. 16. 21. 3. 11. 21.

The emperors, following the zeal of their father Theodosius, order the temples of idols to be destroyed throughout the Roman world. Jerome and Rufinus, the Aquileian presbyter, quarrel over questions concerning the Scriptures and compose against one another books of invective, written in language sufficiently polished but excessively biting.

402. 5. 22. 17. 22. 22. 4. 12. 22.

(PROSP.) Saint Martin dies this year at the age of eighty-one and after twenty-six years as a bishop, according to Prosper, who writes that he died in the fifth year of Arcadius and Honorius; (SEV.) rather, according to Severus, who writes in his life [Note: More probably in *Dialogue on the Virtues of Saint Martin* III, 13, Hirsch.] that he lived sixteen years after the death of Priscillian.

403. 6. 23. 18. 23. 23. 5. 13. 23.

(V. Ambr.) Ambrose of Milan dies; Bishop Paulinus of Nola describes his life for Bishop Augustine. (PROSP.; IDAC.) This Paulinus, later bishop of Nola, when he was master of countless estates, chose religion in an admirable example, selling everything and making himself free for it. His wife Terasia, who became his sister by renunciation of marriage, equaled him in the witness and merit of a blessed life. He offered himself into barbarian slavery in place of the captive son of a poor widow; but when his identity was divinely revealed, he restored many captives to freedom. (H. m.) At this time Sisinnius, Martyrius, and Alexander are martyred by pagans in Italy. When their bodies were being carried to Milan, a blind man was given sight through them. He said that he had been directed there in a vision by Bishop Ambrose, who told him that he had been appointed to share in the company of these martyrs. (H. m.) Wishing to disturb the peace between the imperial brothers, Stilicho had Alaric, king of the Goths, appointed master of the soldiers. [Note: Incorrectly; this happened twice, first by Arcadius and then by Attalus.]

404. 7. 24. 19. 24. 24. 6. 14. 24.

(G. Pont.) Innocent presides as the thirty-eighth over the Roman Church. [Note: Thus in 1, corrected from thirty-ninth; the others agree.] He decreed that the kiss of peace should be given at Mass; that a fast should be observed on Saturday; and that oil consecrated by the bishop for the use of the sick might be used not only by presbyters but also by all Christians, for anointing themselves and their dependents as need required. (PROSP.; AUG., *On Heresies* 88.) In Britain Pelagius attempts to defile Christ’s Church with detestable teaching, saying that a person can be saved by his own merits without the grace of God; that each person is guided toward righteousness by his own will; that infants are born without original sin and are as innocent as Adam was before the transgression; that they should not be baptized in order to be freed from sin, but in order to be admitted by adoption into the kingdom of God; and that even if they are not baptized, they nevertheless have eternal and blessed life outside the kingdom of God. He said that Adam alone was harmed by his sin, and that he died not because of the guilt he deserved but because of the condition of nature; he would have died even if he had not sinned. He also said that the prayers offered by the Church, whether for unbelievers or for believers, are ineffectual. Pope Innocent condemned him, Caelestius, and Julian, his associates. Jerome, Augustine, and others also attacked them as enemies of the faith with the weapons of truth. (CASS.) The Eastern churches too are gravely troubled by a question raised about God: whether God is corporeal and has a human form, or whether he is incorporeal and entirely unlike human form. Some of the simpler-minded assert that God is corporeal and has human form, while others refute this.

405. 8. 25. 20. 25. 25. 7. 15. 25.

At Rome the remarkable life of Alexis, the noblest of the Romans, is made known. On the first night of his marriage he left his bride and became a pilgrim for Christ for sixteen years. At last, at Edessa, a city of Syria, an image of the holy mother Mary revealed him; he fled from there as well and, against his will, reached the Roman harbor. His father received him as a poor man. [Cf. the *Annals of Liège.] There, recognized by no one, he lived for sixteen years. He wrote the course of his life on a sheet of paper and died. [Note: “described”: *descipto* in 1.] When his identity was revealed by a divine voice, he filled all Rome with astonishment and joy. (H. m.) John Chrysostom, having many priests hostile to him, as well as Eudoxia, the wife of the emperor Arcadius, is expelled from the episcopate and exiled. When the people riot on his behalf, he is recalled. He is exiled a second time; but when an earthquake severely shakes the imperial city, the citizens recall him. Abbot Pachomius, completing his life in virtue at the age of 110, dies.

406. R. 9. P. 26. F. 21. B. 26. W. 26. W. 8. O. 16. H. 26.

The emperor Arcadius transfers the bones of the prophet Samuel from Judea to Constantinople, with the crowds meeting them so joyfully that they seemed to see him alive. Paula dies at Bethlehem; Jerome writes her life. (*Life of Saint Augustine*.) Augustine philosophizes in the Church; the number of his books, treatises, and letters extends to more than 1,030, not counting many others.

407. 10. 27. 22. 27. 27. 9. 17. 27.

(PROSP.) Radagaisus the Scythian, coming from Scythia with 200,000 Goths, invades Italy. From this there arises a great roar of blasphemers against Christ, who blame the Christian age and exalt the prosperity of the pagans. Among them Symmachus the orator raged especially, even writing letters advocating idolatry and the restoration of the altar of Victory. (GENNAD.) Augustine, in his book *The City of God*, and Orosius, in his history, stopped the mouths of these barking men by thrusting into them the bone of truth. The poet Prudentius too refuted Symmachus’s blasphemies in a finely written little work in verse.

408. 11. 28. 23. 28. 28. 10. 18. 28.

(PROSP.—H. m.) After many cities had been devastated, Radagaisus, shut in by the Romans, perishes with all his men. Sdigerdis rules the Persians for thirty-four years. Augustine at Hippo in Africa and Jerome at Bethlehem in Judea argue with one another by letter, almost to the point of quarrel, about certain passages of Scripture, especially the passage in which Paul says that he resisted Peter to his face because Peter was blameworthy. Jerome had written that Paul rebuked Peter not genuinely but as a pretence; Augustine, on the contrary, said that he rebuked him genuinely, not as a pretence.

409. 12. 1. 24. 29. 29. 11. 19. 29.

(CASS.) John Chrysostom, forced by his enemies to resign the episcopate, is banished by Arcadius and dies there not long afterward. Pope Innocent and the western bishops suspend communion with the eastern bishops because of the wrong done to John. A storm of exceptionally heavy hail, descending upon Constantinople, threatens God’s anger for John’s death; the death of the empress Eudoxia follows.

410. 3. 2. 25. 30. 30. 12. 20. 30.

(H. m.) The eastern emperor Arcadius, fearing for his eight-year-old son Theodosius and appointing Sdigerdis, king of the Persians, as the boy’s guardian in his testament, dies. Sdigerdis kindly accepts guardianship of the boy and establishes the firmest peace with the Romans through Maruthas, bishop of Mesopotamia. Maruthas was held in the highest regard by both Persians and Romans. At Utica the earth gave a bellowing sound for seven days. (PROSP.—H. m.) Stilicho, aspiring to the empire for his son Eucherius, becomes destructive to the state, himself admitting some barbarian peoples into the kingdom and encouraging others by his support. Consequently their fury, especially that of the Vandals, blazed through Gaul with greater violence than usual. (Ibid.) After Arcadius’s death, Honorius rules for fourteen years with his cousin Theodosius.

411. 1. 3. 26. 31. 31. 13. 21. 31.

(*Life of Saint Antidius*.) Atticus of Constantinople flourishes as a bishop. The Vandals, under their leader Croscus, roam through Gaul and overthrow many cities and churches. At last Croscus is captured by Marianus, governor of Arles, dragged ignominiously through the cities he had conquered, and tortured to death. [Note: The earliest outline of this narrative is given by Gregory of Tours I, 32 and 34; its popular form by Idacius in Canisius, *Lectiones antiquae*, ed. Basnage II, 191; from this Aimoinus III, 1, the *Gesta Trevirorum*, and the eleventh-century *Life of Saint Antidius*, in *Acta Sanctorum*, June V, 43, expanded it. Sigebert took his account from the latter. Hirsch; cf. Loebell, *Gregory of Tours*, 411.] During this upheaval, among many others, the Sedunian martyrs Florentinus and Hilary, Desiderius of Langres with his archdeacon Vincentius, and Antidius, bishop of Besançon, are martyred. Of this Antidius it is read that once, on the Tuesday after Palm Sunday, as he was crossing the bridge over the River Doubs, he saw a troop of demons reporting their deeds to their prince. Among them was an Ethiopian carrying a sandal in his hand, as a sign that he had finally brought down the Roman bishop, whose sandal it was, after attacking him for seven years. Antidius called the Ethiopian to him, mounted upon him by the power of God and of the holy cross, and, carried by the demon, arrived at Rome on Thursday at the hour when the Office was celebrated. While the demon waited outside the doors, Antidius reported the matter to the pope and moved him, by denying that the sandal was his, to repentance. After celebrating Mass in his place and taking a portion of the chrism he himself had consecrated, he returned to his church, again carried by the demon, on Holy Saturday at the hour when the Office was celebrated. At Rome a woman of gigantic stature, born to parents of ordinary height, was a source of amazement to many. [Note: “At Rome … many”: added later by Sigeb.]

412. 2. 4. 27. 32. 32. 14. 22. 32.

(H. m.) Alaric, king of the Visigoths, ravaging through Italy, sends word to the emperor Honorius that he must either engage him in battle or grant the Goths a place to live in his kingdom. Honorius grants them Gaul, exposed on every side to the fury of the peoples.

413. 3. 5. 28. 33. 33. 15. 23. 33.

(JORD.) The Vandals, abandoning Gaul, which they had torn apart for so many years, out of fear of the Goths, occupy Spain together with the Alans and Suevi. They lived there for nearly thirty years. (Ibid.) After Alaric had made a treaty with Honorius and was advancing toward Gaul, which had been granted to him, Stilicho suddenly attacked him on the holy day of Easter. Victorious at the first assault, Stilicho was later disgracefully defeated by the Goths. [Note: This occurred on 29 March 403.] (H. m.) When Honorius learned that Stilicho was the instigator of such great evils and was plotting against his life, he killed him together with his son Eucherius. [Note: In the year 408.] (JORD.) Alaric breaks the treaty and returns to Italy. He captures Rome, burns many places in it, and afflicts many people, but restrains himself from bloodshed and slaughter and spares those who flee to the thresholds of the saints. [Note: 9 Kalends of September, 410.] On the third day he voluntarily leaves Rome, intending to sail to Sicily, but suffers shipwreck and dies soon afterward at the city of Consentia by a sudden death. Rome was captured on 9 Kalends of September, in the 1,164th year of its foundation. [Note: Sigeb. had written ICLXI II; but the L had already been erased. F3 has ICXIIII; A has “in the year M. C. forty-fourth”; all the others have ICLXIIII.] (H. m.) In those days, on the coast of Utica in Africa, a giant’s tooth was found so enormous that, if it were cut into pieces the size of our teeth, a hundred teeth could be made from it. [Note: “of its foundation … could be made”: Sigeb. added this in a later correction in the lower margin.] (GREG. TUR.) Meanwhile, when the Vandals again invaded Gaul, the Franks engaged them and killed their king Modigisilus together with 20,000 Vandals. The final destruction of the Vandals would probably have followed, had not their survivors been aided by Respendial, king of the Alans. (PROSP., BEDA.) At this time the strength of the Britons had been greatly weakened by the excessive invasions of enemies. Since they could obtain no aid from the Romans, who were everywhere hard-pressed by war, they withdrew from Roman rule and suffered greatly under many calamities for approximately sixty-seven years. After Modigisilus, his son Gunderic ruled the Vandals in Spain for sixteen years. Athauulfus was the third king of the Visigoths and reigned for three years. [The Franks, frequently invading Gaul, first plundered and then, in a second invasion, burned the city of Trier, which Treber, son of Ninus, king of the Assyrians, had founded after fleeing from the face of his stepmother Semiramis and named Treberim after himself. [Note: Thus in the first recension. The other manuscripts read: “The Franks, invading Gaul, first plunder and then, in a second invasion, burn the city of Trier, which is so called from its founder Trebeta, stepson of Semiramis, the wife of Ninus. After being driven from the kingdom following Ninus’s death, he founded this city above the River Moselle and named it Treberim after himself.” One manuscript, A, has this expanded account; Sigebert had therefore written it first.]]

414. R. 4. P. 6. F. 29. B. 1. W. 1. W. 1. O. 24. H. 34.

(H. m.) Athauulfus returns to Rome and strips it of what remained. Among others he also carries away Placidia, sister of the emperor Honorius, as a captive and takes her as his wife. (Ibid.) Because the emperor Honorius trusted in God with the devotion of an excellent religion, God freed him from the many tyrants rising against him on every side. (JORD.) In Britain there were Gratianus; in Gaul, Constantinus and his son Constans, made Caesar after being a monk; after them, also in Gaul, Gerontius and Maximus, Salustius, Jovinus, and Sebastianus; (IDAC.) in Africa, Heraclianus; and at Rome, Tertullus and that Attalus whom the Goths, after capturing Rome, created emperor in jest, making him appear for one day in imperial costume and on the following day serve them in a slave’s costume. This man, however, then aspiring to rule not in jest but in earnest—all of them, after usurping tyranny, perished in different places and at different times, captured or killed by the soldiers of Honorius.

415. 5. 7. 30. 2. 2. 2. 25. 35

(GENNAD.) Maximus, bishop of Turin, flourishes; he devoted himself elegantly to composing homilies and delivering them in the Church. Spain suffers severely from the sword of the Vandals, famine, pestilence, and the bites of beasts. (IDAC.) The Gallic city of Valencia is captured by the Goths. (PROSP.) At this time the heresy of the Predestinarians begins to spread. They are called Predestinarians because, disputing about predestination and divine grace, they asserted that the labor of good works benefits neither those who live piously, if they have been predestined by God to death, nor does it harm the impious that they live wickedly, if they have been predestined by God to life. This assertion both drew the good away from good works and provoked the wicked to wickedness. (Ibid.) This heresy is said to have originated from books of Augustine that were wrongly understood.

416. 6. 8. 31. 3. 3. 3. 26. 36.

(H. m.) The emperor Honorius, after suppressing the heretics in Africa, restores peace to the churches. After the Visigothic king Athauulfus is killed by his own men, Sigeric reigns for one year. (CASS.) A certain Jew, who had often been baptized for the sake of gain in many churches of heretics, came also to the church of the orthodox, intending to be baptized with the same purpose. When he was about to be baptized, the water in the font suddenly disappeared. Again and again water was brought and the font was filled, but again and again the water disappeared, displaying God’s power and the Jew’s faithlessness.

417. 7. 9. 32. 4. 4. 4. 27. 37.

(G. Pont.) Zosimus presides as the thirty-ninth over the Roman Church. [Note: Thus in 1, in an erasure; the other manuscripts agree.] He decreed that a candle should be blessed throughout the churches on Holy Saturday of Easter. (ISID.) After Sigeric is killed by the Visigoths, Wallia reigns for twenty-two years. [Note: It is uncertain where Sigebert obtained these twenty-two years for Wallia and, below, the years of Theodoric in 439, since Idacius assigns Wallia only two years and Isidore three. Jordanes, chapter 32, supports our reading.] (MARIAN.) Certain westerners, in the final year of the nineteen-year cycle, treating it as a common year rather than inserting an intercalary month and consequently celebrating Easter incorrectly, are recalled to the truth by a divine miracle. In one church in Italy, where every year on Holy Saturday, at the hour of baptism, water would miraculously flow and immediately return of itself, with no channel being visible at all, they celebrated Easter too early, namely on 8 Kalends of April. The water did not flow and, after they had waited through the entire day and night, disappointed them. On the lawful day of Easter, however, at the hour of baptism, the water flowed as usual and showed that Easter ought to be celebrated on 10 Kalends of May. (BEDA.) The bodies of the holy protomartyr Stephen, Nicodemus, Gamaliel, and Abibon are revealed to Lucian the presbyter. Bishop John transferred the body of the protomartyr Stephen from Caphargamala to Jerusalem. Several years later it was raised from there by the noblewoman Juliana, who, wishing to raise the body of her husband Alexander, buried beside the body of the protomartyr, lifted the body of the protomartyr instead of her husband’s body and carried it to Constantinople, glorified by the splendor of many miracles.

418. R. 8. P. 10. F. 33. B. 5. W. 5. W. 1. O. 28. H. 38.

(GENNAD.) The presbyter Orosius, returning from Jerome, to whom Augustine had sent him to learn about the question of the soul’s origin, (BEDA) carried the relics of the protomartyr Stephen to Africa together with the account of their discovery. As the grace of miracles accompanied this account, God made it wondrous everywhere. Augustine therefore wrote much about it, and Evodius wrote far more. (H. m.) Honorius, after making a treaty with the Goths, handed Aquitaine over to them. Wallia returned Placidia, captured by Athauulfus, to her brother Honorius. Honorius gave her in marriage to the count Constantius, by whom Placidia bore Valentinian, who later ruled after Honorius.

419. 9. 11. 34. 6. 6. 2. 29. 39.

(G. r. F.) After Sunno and Marcomir, the leaders of the Franks, had died, the Franks deliberated together that they too, like the other peoples, should have a single king. They therefore appointed Pharamund, son of the leader Marcomir, as their king; he reigned for eleven years.

420. 10. 12. 1. 7. 7. 3. 30. 40.

(G. pont.) Boniface presides as the fortieth over the Roman Church. When Eulalius was appointed against Boniface and the Church was divided on his account, both men were ordered by the emperor Honorius Augustus to leave the city. Eulalius was thus rejected, and by order of the emperor Boniface, because he had been ordained first, was restored to the apostolic see. [Note: The author of the treatise *On Investiture* copied this word for word in Goldast’s *Apologia*, p. 231.] He decreed that no woman or nun should touch or wash the consecrated altar cloth, or place incense; and that a slave or a person bound to a court or to any other service should not become a cleric.

421. 11. 13. 2. 8. 8. 4. 31. 41.

(*Life of Saint Jerome*.) Jerome, after completing his books over fifty-six years, dies at Bethlehem in the ninety-eighth year of his age. His body had been so weakened by his labors that he could not rise from his bed without grasping with his hands a rope hanging from a beam for this purpose. [Note: “Ninety-eighth” is corrected from eighty-ninth in 1; B3* and F1 have eighty-ninth; Sigebert’s first hand and the other manuscripts have ninety-eighth.]

422. 12. 14. 3. 9. 9. 5. 32. 42.

(*Salic Law*, *Deeds of the Kings of the Franks*.) The Franks began to use laws and dictated the Salic Law through four nobles of their people, chosen from among many and called by these names: Usogast, Bosogast, Salagast, and Widigast, in the villages of Germany called Salehaim, Bodohaim, and Windohaim. These four nobles, meeting for three sessions of legal proceedings and carefully considering the origins of cases, resolved to judge each matter through examination, as the Salic Law declares. (IDAC.) The Vandals, Alans, and Suevi, having divided the regions of Spain among themselves into three parts for settlement and having been divided into three kingdoms, clash in civil war.

423. 13. 15. 4. 10. 10. 6. 33. 43.

(PROSP.—H. m.) Honorius admits Constantius, the husband of his sister Placidia, to the imperial power; Constantius dies in the eighth month of his reign. When the Britons promised submission to the Roman Empire, Honorius sent them aid, and likewise sent aid to the Spaniards suffering from the war with the Vandals; but this was in vain.

[Col. 0078B] 424. 14, 16. 5, 11. 11. 7. 34. 44.

(PROSP.) Honorius dies after celebrating his thirtieth anniversary with the pomp of the captured tyrant Maximus at Ravenna. Theodosius rules both kingdoms for three years. (JORD.) Wallia, king of the Visigoths, pursues the Vandals in Spain and defeats them.

425. 1. 17. 6. 12. 12. 8. 35. 45.

(H. m.) John invites the Huns into the kingdom and, with their help, aims at tyranny. (JORD.) The Vandals invade Mauretania. At this time Bishop Theonistus is driven from his city of Philippi by heretics, together with his disciples Albanus, Ursus, Thabraham, and Tubraham. Of these, Albanus is martyred for Christ near Mainz in Gaul, while the others are martyred in different places in Italy. [Note: “At this time … are martyred”: in the margin, added by Sigeb. in a third correction; all the other manuscripts agree.]

[Col. 0078C] 426. 2. 18. 7. 13. 13. 9. 36. 46.

(G. pont.) Celestine presides over the Roman church as its forty-first bishop. He decreed that the 150 psalms of David should be sung before the sacrifice, antiphonally by everyone—something that had not previously been done, since only the Epistle of blessed Paul and the holy Gospel were recited. From this institution, excerpts from the psalms—introits, graduals, offertories before the sacrifice, and communions during Communion—began to be sung with musical modulation at Mass in the Roman church. (H. m.) Through Ardaburius, under an angel’s guidance, Theodosius overcomes the tyrant John. At Rome, between Aetius and Boniface, envy arising from their military glory gives birth to losses for the state.

[Col. 0078D] 427. 3. 19. 8. 14. 14. 10. 37. 47.

(H. m. PROSP.) Theodosius makes Valentinian, the son of his aunt Placidia by Constantius, emperor, and sends him with his mother Placidia to Rome to rule; and they ruled together for 24 years. Carthage was permitted to be surrounded by a wall. Cassian, expelled from the church of Constantinople by John Chrysostom and ordained presbyter at Massilia in Gaul, wrote much; among other works, he explains in books addressed to many people the lives of the fathers, their teachings, and their rules, which he had discovered in Egypt.

438. R. 1. P. 20. F. 9, B. 15. W. 15. W 11. O. 38. H. 48.

(Ib.) In Bithynia, a certain Timothy, deceiving many under the appearance of continence and religion, led them into the error of his heresy, saying that Christ, true God and true man, had indeed been born from the Virgin Mary; but he lied in saying that the divine nature had been changed into human nature. (JORD.) The Romans drive the Huns from Pannonia, which they had held for 50 years.

429. 2. 21. 10. 16. 16. 12. 39. 49.

(JORD.) Boniface incites Africa, over which he presided, to rebellion. Gunderic, king of the Vandals, after capturing Seville, impiously exalted himself and stretched out his hands in the church of that city; immediately, by God’s judgment, he was seized by a demon and died. (IDAC.) His brother Genseric succeeded him in the kingdom and ruled for 48 years. He is said to have apostatized from the Catholic faith into the Arian sect.

430. 3. 22. 11. 17. 1. 13. 40. 50.

(G. reg. Fr.) Clodius, son of Faramund, the long-haired king, rules over the Franks for 20 years. From this time the Franks began to have long-haired kings. Walamer, assuming the Ostrogothic kingdom, ruled for 31 years. His brother was Thiudemer, from whom Theoderic, king of Italy, was descended. (JORD.) Augustine arranged for Heraclius to be appointed his successor in the bishopric of Hippo [Note: [Col. 0079] A.—that is, H. H. s. s. f.—adds this; Sigebert adds it in the second recension; the reading of the rest is not specified.].

431. 4. 23. 1. 18. 2. 14. 1. 51.

[Col. 0079C] (G. reg. Fr.) Clodius invades Thuringia and lived for some time in Dispargum, a fortress of the Thuringians.

432. 5. 24. 2. 19. 3. 15. 2. 52.

(MARIAN.) Pope Celestine first sends Palladius as bishop to the Scots who believe in Christ. After him, the same Celestine sends to them Saint Patrick, a Briton by birth, son of Conches, the sister of Saint Martin of Tours. In baptism he was called Suchat; by Saint Germanus, Magonius; and by Celestine, Patrick. Ordained by him archbishop of the Scots, he converted the whole island of Ireland to Christ over 60 years, excelling in signs, holiness, and teaching. (CASS.) Nestorius, made bishop of Constantinople, becomes the author of the heresy that separates man from God in Christ, saying that a mere man, not God, was born from Mary and crucified by the Jews. (JORD.) King Wallia of the Goths prepares to drive from Spain as well the Vandals who had formerly withdrawn from Gaul through fear of Ataulf.

433. 6. 25. 3. 20. 4. 16. 3. 53.

(CASS.) The third universal synod, the first at Ephesus, of 200 bishops, was convened by order of the younger Augustus Theodosius. It condemned Nestorius, who asserted two persons in Christ, with a just anathema, showing that one person of our Lord Jesus Christ remains in two natures. (PROSP.) Nearly 20,000 soldiers fighting against the Vandals in Spain were killed. Genseric, fearing the hostility of the Goths and at the same time invited by Boniface, crossed over to Africa with the Vandals and all their families; invading and ravaging it, he inflicted great and prolonged calamity upon the Romans. (IDAC., CASS.) In Gaul, when Suptar, king of the Huns, was oppressing the Burgundians too severely, they placed their hope in the God of the Christians and asked to be baptized. Immediately engaging the Huns, although few, they killed many thousands of them and thus restrained their fury.

434. 7. 26. 4. 21. 5. 17. 4. 54.

(G. Pont.) Sixtus presides over the Roman church as its forty-second bishop. (PROSP.) The Romans engage the Vandals in Africa and are defeated. Boniface, after a conflict with Aetius, withdraws victorious but mortally wounded.

[Col. 0080B] 435. 8. 27. 5. 22. 6. 18. 5. 55.

(PROSP.) Germanus of Auxerre, Lupus of Troyes, Eucherius of Lyon, and Hilary of Arles shine as bishops in Gaul. Aetius goes to Rugila, king of the Huns, and with his aid returns to Roman territory. (G. pont.) Pope Sixtus is accused by Bassus and, by order of the emperor Valentinian, is cleared at Rome in a synodical judgment before 56 bishops; Bassus, however, condemned, is proscribed, and not long afterward, struck down by God, is honorably buried by the hands of Sixtus himself.

436. 9. 28. 6. 23. 7. 19. 6. 56.

(PROSP.) Aetius is restored to favor. Rugila, king of the Huns and an ally of the Romans, dies, and Bleda succeeds him.

[Col. 0080C] 437. 10. 29. 7. 24. 8. 20. 7. 1

(Ib.) Further Gaul, stirred to rebellion by the leader Bato, almost all the slaves of the Gauls conspired in the Bagaudae. From this year Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, began and in extreme brevity compiled a 95-year cycle concerning the calculation of Easter, within which he noted that all the variations in the observance of Easter were included.

438. 11. 30. 8. 25. 9. 21. 8. 2.

(CASS.) At this time Christianity was extended among the Persians. For Bishop Maruthas, serving as ambassador to them, freed King Yazdegerd’s son from a demon through prayer; by this his glory indeed increased, but a more grievous persecution of Christians broke out from the enemies of God. (H. m.) The empress Eudoxia, wife of Theodosius, hastened to Jerusalem in fulfillment of a vow and brought back from there, by God’s will, the relics of the protomartyr Stephen and the two chains that an angel had cast from the hands of the apostle Peter. Adding to them the chain with which Peter had also been bound at Rome, she made a triad; and thereafter, with the advice of the Roman pontiff, established at Rome the feast of Saint Peter called “At the Chains” on the Kalends of August. She did this especially to recall the people from the pomp of pagan superstition, since the city still celebrated on that day, according to pagan custom, the victory granted to Octavian Augustus over Antony and Cleopatra on the Kalends of August. (CASS.) The Devil deceived the Jews in the guise of a false prophet who claimed to be Moses, and, promising to lead them back to the Promised Land, brought them to cross the sea; there he caused many of them to perish in many ways. This event became the cause for many of those rescued from the danger to believe in Christ.

439. R. 12. P. 31. F. 9. B. 26. W. 10. W. 22. O. 9. H. 3.

(ISID.) King Wallia of the Goths, pursuing the Vandals out of hatred, also plans to persecute them in Africa. But prevented by death, he died; Theoderic succeeded him in the kingdom and ruled for 15 years [Note: [Col. 0081] XHH. B3*. C3. 4*. D.]. [Note: [Col. 0081D] Compare the year 417; Isidore has “33 years.”]

440. 13. 32. 10. 27. 11. 1. 10. 4.

(BEDA.) The Vandals ravage Africa, which they had invaded, in every manner. Amid this storm of tribulation, Saint Augustine departed to the Lord, in the thirteenth month of the siege of his city [Col. 0081B], in the seventy-third year of his age and the fortieth of his clerical or episcopal service. He wrote so much that no one could, throughout the whole of his lifetime, write all his books—or even read them.

441. 14. 33. 11. 28. 12. 2. 11. 5.

(G. pont.) Leo presides over the Roman church as its forty-third bishop. He was highly effective in delivering homilies. In the canon of the Mass he added the words “the holy sacrifice, the spotless offering.” [The following passage beginning “He” [Note: [Col. 0081] The continuation from “He” through “of the bishops” was written in the margin and erasure by 1δ.; it is absent from one copy, A.] Whenever some people asked him to give them relics of certain apostles or martyrs, he made a practice of celebrating Mass in honor of those apostles or martyrs at their bodies or memorials, whose relics were requested. He would then divide into pieces the altar cloth with which he had wrapped the consecrated body of the Lord and give it as the relics of the apostles or martyrs.
