If anyone doubted, he would pierce those cloths with a knife and draw blood from them, thus making clear to everyone that, at the consecration of Christ’s mysteries, the blood of the apostles or martyrs, shed for him, enters those cloths through divine power; and therefore it is right for them to be given as relics of the saints in whose honor they were consecrated.] (PROSP.) A memorable war broke out against the Burgundians, in which nearly the entire nation, together with its king, fell after being defeated by Aetius. (V. S. Germ.) The bodies of Priscus and the others who suffered with him at Auxerre are divinely revealed to Bishop Germanus.

442. 15. 34. 12. 29. 13. 3. 12. 6.

[Col. 0081D] After Yazdegerd’s death, his son Gauraranes rules the Persians for 38 years. When the leaders of the seditions in Gaul had been worn down and Bato captured, the Bagaudae uprising subsides.

443. 16. 1. 13. 30. 14. 4. 13. 7.

(ISID.) Guararanes dissolves the treaty with the Romans that his father had initiated and raids the Roman provinces. After the Romans granted Genseric a portion of Africa for settlement, peace was agreed between the Vandals and Romans—a peace more necessary than beneficial.

[Col. 0082A] 444. 17. 2. 14. 31. 15. 5. 14. 8.

(CASS.) The body of John Chrysostom, who had died in exile, is finally brought back to Constantinople through the insistence of Bishop Proclus and by order of the emperor Theodosius, who tearfully prayed that he might grant pardon to his father Arcadius and his mother Eudoxia, who had exiled him. Thus the dissension that still existed in the church over John’s condemnation came to an end. (H. m.) At Constantinople, during an earthquake in which the earth trembled for four months, a certain man was lifted into the air before everyone who was praying, by divine power. He was admonished by a divine voice that all should sing, after making litanies, “Holy God, holy and mighty, holy and immortal, have mercy on us,” adding nothing else. When this was done, the earthquake ceased. (Ib.) The Romans, under the leadership of Litorius, fight disastrously against the Visigoths.

[Col. 0082B] 445. 18. 3. 15. 32. 16. 6. 15. 9.

(G. r. F.) Clodius, king of the Franks, sending scouts from Dispargum fortress as far as the city of Cambrai, crossed the Rhine. Having crushed the many Roman inhabitants living on this side of the Rhine as far as the Loire River, he entered the Carbonaria Forest, took the city of Tournai, and from there hurried as far as the city of Cambrai. Staying there for a short time, he killed any Romans he found there; then, reaching the Somme River, he occupied everything. (FRED.) Theoderic, king of the Visigoths, occupies Spain.

446. 19. 4. 16. 33. 17. 7. 16. 10.

(H. m.) Gauraranes stirred up a persecution against Christians in Persia, which he harshly carried on for 30 years. Theodosius, although he had often defeated the Persians successfully, nevertheless wished to embrace peace so that the persecution of Christians might cease. (Prosp.---H. m.) Genseric seized Carthage by treachery and, bringing all Africa under his control, overthrew the power of the Roman kingdom in a lamentable disaster. (H. m., IDAC.) Regarding nothing as weighty or sacred, and hostile to everyone, especially the nobility and religion, he emptied out everything divine and human. He expelled the bishop and the entire clergy of the church of Carthage, made the holy places either dwellings for his own people or handed them over to Arians, and ordered Catholics to be persecuted everywhere. (BEDA.) Germanus of Auxerre and Lupus of Troyes are sent into Britain at the request of the Britons, to refute the Pelagian heresy that had sprung up there some years earlier and to establish the true faith by ecclesiastical authority. Meanwhile, while enemies according to custom were raiding the island, Germanus encouraged everyone to resist and himself became their leader. When the enemies were already drawn up for battle, he began with a loud cry of “Alleluia,” and when his men cried out with him, he turned the same enemies to flight and, winning a bloodless victory, rescued his homeland from the impending danger. (Ib.) The Britons, who for so many years had been exposed to plunder and the mockery of their enemies, invite the Angles from Germany. The Angles come to Britain and make it safe from its enemies; not long afterward they claim it for themselves. The Britons establish Ambrosius Aurelianus as their king, and under his leadership they fight against the Angles for 45 years with varying fortunes in war [Note: [Col. 0083] “45” was corrected by Sigebert, who had first written XLXV. C1, 2*, 3, D, and E have XLIIII. The words “Germanus ... fight” are absent from the first edition and undoubtedly already from D1*, 1**, E8h.].

447. R. 20. P. 5. F. 17. B. 1. W. 18. W. 8. O. 17. H. 11.

(H. m.) To Bleda, king of the Huns, who was ravaging the eastern empire with his brother Attila, Theodosius gives 6,000 pounds for his withdrawal, promising him an annual tribute of 1,000 pounds. (GREG. TUR. De gl. mart. 95.) At Ephesus, seven brothers were tortured for Christ by the emperor Decius. They shut themselves in a cave and, after praying, fell asleep there. About 192 years after their sleep, when the mouth of the cave that the emperor Decius had blocked was divinely opened, they rose from sleep and, affirming before the emperor Theodosius our belief in the resurrection—which was then greatly doubted—fell asleep again in Christ [Note: [Col. 0083] The passage from “At Ephesus” through “in Christ,” originally occupying one and a half lines, was expanded in the erasure by an uncertain hand. All copies except A have it. A reads: “At Ephesus seven sleepers, from the time of Decius, after 382 years of their sleep, rise from sleep; and, having affirmed our belief in the resurrection, which was then greatly doubted, they sleep again in Christ.” Thus Sigebert had first written it.].

448. 21. 6. 18. 2. 19. 9. 18. 12.

(G. r. F.) Merovech, son of Clodius, rules over the Franks for 10 years; from this very useful king the Franks are called Merovingians.

449. 22. 7. 1. 3. 20. 10. 19. 13.

(PROSP.) Bleda, king of the Huns, is killed through the treachery of his brother Attila. Succeeding him, Attila is wholly intent on the destruction of the world. (V. Rem.) Remigius of Reims is born [Note: [Col. 0083D] Not in this year, but in 457; compare Acta Sanctorum, October 1, 68.], his birth foretold by the monk Montanus through his name. When he was born, Montanus, who was blind, rubbed his eyes with the milk of his mother Cilinia and was given sight. (H. m.) Germanus of Auxerre, sent again to Britain with Bishop Severus of Trier, refutes the resurgent Pelagian heresy.

450. 23. 8. 2. 4. 21. 11. 20. 1.

(PROSP.) A new ruin once again rises in the East, since no fewer than seventy cities are devastated by the plundering of the Huns. (BEDA) Germanus of Auxerre, having gone to Italy, dies at Ravenna. His body is brought back to Auxerre amid great glory of miracles.

451. 24. 9. 3. 5. 22. 12. 21. 2.

(IDAC.) The emperor Theodosius died, and Martian succeeded him, ruling for 7 years [Note: [Col. 0083] B3*, C1, 2*, 3, 4*, and D have “6”], while Valentinian ruled with him for 5 years. (VICT. VIT.) As the Vandals’ persecution in Africa grew so fierce that they burned the divine books and made garments for themselves from sacred cloaks and vestments, Valerian, an eighty-year-old bishop, unwilling to hand over the divine sacraments to the profane, was excluded by King Genseric from the whole city [Col. 0084A] and from his own house. He spent the remainder of his life until death naked under the open sky. (PROSP.) Placidia, the mother of Valentinian, died at Rome.

452. 1. 10. 4. 6. 23. 13. 22. 3.

(BEDA.) At Pope Leo’s insistence and by order of the emperor Martian, the fourth universal synod was convened and held at Chalcedon, with 630 bishops. There it condemned Eutyches, the Constantinopolitan abbot, who declared that the Word of God and the flesh had one nature, and Dioscorus of Alexandria, formerly bishop and his defender, by the judgment of the fathers. It also again anathematized Nestorius, formerly bishop of Constantinople, long ago condemned at the synod of Ephesus, and condemned him with the other heretics. The same synod proclaimed that Christ God was born from the Virgin in such a way that we confess in him the substance of both the divine and human natures. It was decreed that Mary, the mother of the Lord, should be believed and called not only “Christ-bearer” (*Christotokos*) but also “God-bearer” (*Theotokos*), because of the blasphemies of Nestorius, who falsely said that she had borne not God but a mere man. Almost continuous earthquakes and many signs appeared in the sky. (IDAC.) In the evening the sky in the north became red like fire, with brighter lights intermingled within the fiery redness and shaped like stars. The moon was darkened, a comet appeared, and many other things occurred. Their significance was shown by the sequence of events that followed.

453. 2. 11. 5. 7. 24. 14. 23. 4.

(H. m.) Attila, king of the Huns, supported by Walamer, king of the Ostrogoths, Ardaric, king of the Gepids, and many northern nations subject to him, left Pannonia and invaded the Western Empire with 500,000 armed men. First, throughout all Gaul, God’s indignation raged so fiercely through them that no fortification at all could protect any city, fortress, or town from their fury. Finally, while they were besieging the city of Orléans, the Roman patrician Aetius hastened to the aid of Gaul, supported in turn by the military forces of Theoderic, king of the Visigoths, Merovech, king of the Franks, and other peoples. Battle was joined in the Catalaunian Plains and continued until nightfall. Aetius was indeed victorious and withdrew, but he did not destroy Attila completely. There 180,000 fighters were killed, among them Theoderic, king of the Visigoths. Attila, regaining hope after Aetius’s departure, returned to his homeland, intending to come back quickly after replenishing his army [Note: [Col. 0084D] It is established that these events occurred in the year 451.]. (Ib.) Thurismodus, son of Theoderic, assumed the Visigothic kingdom and ruled for 3 years. (V. Servat.) Nicasius, bishop of Reims, and his sister Eutropia were martyred by the Huns. Auctor, bishop of Metz, was captured; but when the Huns were struck blind, he was released together with the captives of his city. Servatius, bishop of Tongeren, had foreseen in the spirit long beforehand that this destruction threatened Gaul, and had learned from the apostle Peter at Rome that this judgment of God would be unavoidable. Therefore, leaving the city of Tongeren, which was destined to be overthrown, he transferred the episcopal see to Maastricht. (GREG. De gl. m. I, 13.) As the Arian heresy spread through Gaul, believing that the persons of the Holy Trinity were unequal and saying that the Son was lesser than the Father, and the Holy Spirit lesser than the Father and the Son, the Lord corrects the erring by a manifest miracle, showing that God in three persons is of one and equal substance and that unworthy people ought not to discuss divinity. For when the city of Bazas had been freed from the siege of the Huns by divine aid, and the bishop was celebrating Mass for the people in thanksgiving, he looked upward and saw above the altar what seemed to be three drops of equal size falling from the roof of the church, clearer than crystal. Flowing down together and being joined into one, they formed something like one most beautiful gem. When they had placed it in the middle of a golden, jewel-encrusted cross, other gems fell. When placed separately, it gave health to the sick; to those worshiping the image of the holy cross, it increased devotion, because it appeared bright to the devout and pure, but dark to the impious and unclean. (V. S. Urs.) More famous than all wars was the battle fought by the white-clad army of the eleven thousand holy virgins, under the leadership of the holy virgin Ursula. She was the only daughter of Nothus, a most noble and wealthy prince of the Britons. While she was not yet marriageable, she was sought in marriage by the son of a very savage tyrant. Seeing her father distressed by this—he feared God if he forced a daughter already devoted to God to marry, but feared the tyrant if he denied her to him—she was divinely inspired and advised her wavering father to agree with the tyrant, but on the condition that both he and the tyrant should provide ten virgins chosen for their birth, beauty, and age; that they should assign 1,000 virgins to each of them and to each of the ten; and that, after ships had been acquired to match their number—eleven ships—they should grant them a three-year respite for the practice of their virginity. She adopted this novel plan either to turn his mind away from her through the difficulty of the proposed condition or to use the opportunity to dedicate all her female contemporaries to God with her. After the agreement, ships and expenses having been provided for the virgins, they spent three years in preparations for war, to everyone’s amazement. At last, driven by the wind in a single day to the port of Gaul called Tiela, they landed at Cologne. From there, at the instruction of an angel, they traveled toward Rome, going by ship as far as Basel and proceeding on foot from Basel to Rome; then, following the same route, they returned to Cologne, which was surrounded on every side by the Huns. All of them were martyred by the Huns and triumphed in a new and wondrous manner, making Cologne more illustrious through their blood and burial [Note: [Col. 0085] The passage from “More famous than all wars” through “making Cologne more illustrious” was added by Sigebert on a stitched-in slip during his second revision, with a plus sign inserted in the text. But after this slip was lost, no trace of it remains in 1 except a few needle holes and a little thread. Miraeus still saw and published it. All the other codices have the passage except F3, which nevertheless displays the plus sign.].

454. R. 3. P. 12. F. 6. B. 8. W. 25. W. 1. O. 24. H. 5.

(H. m.) Attila attacked Italy and destroyed, plundered, or burned almost all its cities. Pope Leo came to him and obtained not only their safety but also his departure. When his men asked King Attila why he had been so compliant with Leo, he replied that he had not feared Leo himself but a certain venerable old man who, with a drawn sword, threatened him with death unless he fulfilled his will in everything.

455. 4. 13. 7. 9. 26. 2. 25. 6.

(JORD.) Attila attacked the Visigoths, but was defeated by Thurismodus and returned in disgrace. (H. m.) The Lord appeared in a dream to the emperor Martian and showed him that Attila’s bow had been broken. This was not without effect. That very night Attila, having become drunk at his wedding, was suffocated in bed when blood burst from his nostrils through apoplexy. His son Hernac ruled after him. The emperor Valentinian killed the patrician Aetius.

456. 5. 14. 8. 10. 27. 3. 26. 1.

(ISID.) Thurismodus, king of the Visigoths, is slain by his brothers Fritericus and Theoderic. His brother Theoderic succeeded him in the kingdom and ruled for 13 years. (H. m.) While Attila’s sons contended over the kingdom, the peoples subject to the Huns shook off the Hunnic yoke. (H. m.) The emperor Valentinian, plotting tyranny with Maximus, is killed by Transila, Aetius’s soldier.

457. 6. 15. 9. 11. 28. 1. 27. 2.

(V. Gen.) The virgin Genevieve of Paris shines throughout Gaul with great holiness. (H. m.) Maximus seizes the tyranny and violently abducts Eudoxia, Valentinian’s widow. She invites Genseric from Africa to rescue her from Maximus [Note: [Col. 0085] The words “Eudoxia ... rescue her” are absent from A.]. Genseric captures Rome and plunders everything; nevertheless, Leo the pope obtained from him that he refrain from fire, slaughter, and the torture of people. The tyrant Maximus is torn limb from limb by the people. For fourteen days Rome is stripped of its wealth. Genseric takes Eudoxia captive, together with her two daughters and a large number of people, and devastates the cities of Campania in every manner. (Ib.) In the midst of these events, Paulinus of Nola, offering himself as a substitute in barbarian slavery for the captive son of a widow, receives all the captives of his city [Note: [Col. 0085] This occurred around 414–417. The source of the error is already the *Historia Miscella*, which derived the story from Gregory the Great, *Dialogues* III.1; compare Hirsch, p. 65.]. Avitus is made emperor by the Romans. (IDAC.) Theoderic, king of the Visigoths, defeats the Suevi in Spain and, destroying their kingdom, extends his own as far as that point. (BEDA.) Some write that during the time of Martian John the Baptist revealed his head to two monks. (JORD.) Hellac, son of Attila, declared war on Ardaric, king of the Gepids, who had first rebelled against Hunnic servitude. Ardaric fought him, killed him together with 30,000 Huns, and inflicted a severe defeat upon the Huns. Thus, having recovered the liberty of his people and invaded their lands, he gave the other peoples an example of reclaiming freedom. (BEDA.) After Martian died, Leo succeeded him and ruled for 17 years [Note: [Col. 0087] C1, 2*, 3, and D have “16.”]. In regard to the Council of Chalcedon, he requested the individual opinions of each of the fathers; and because he learned that they were all one, he faithfully adhered to it. (H. m.) He made a treaty with Walamer, king of the Ostrogoths, and received his eight-year-old nephew Theoderic as a hostage. Up to this point Prosper brought his chronicle.

458. R. 1. P. 16. F. 10. B. 12. W 29 W. 2. O. 28. H. 3.

(G. r. F.) After Merovech, king of the Franks, died, his son Childeric ruled for 26 years. (JORD.) Hernac, son of Attila and king of the Huns, sought by war to reclaim the Ostrogoths as deserters from his rule and attacked Walamer. The Huns were defeated by him and forced to flee into the farthest regions of Scythia. (H. m.) After Avitus died, Majorian ruled for 4 years. Simeon, who stood enclosed on a column for 40 years [Note: [Col. 0087] “Simeon ... enclosed” was written in the margin and in the erasure by 1β.; previously there seems to have been only “Simeon, who.” The word “enclosed” is absent from A.], shone at Antioch with wondrous holiness. Among other things, he warned no one to swear by the name of God or any saint, indeed not even by the name of Simeon, promising that, if anyone perjured himself by him, he would ask God to grant that person impunity.

459. 2. 17. 1. 13. 30. 3. 29. 4.

(JORD.) The Ostrogoths, under the leadership of Thiudemer, defeat the Suevi in war and capture their king Hunimund, but send him back free.

460. 3. 18. 2. 14. 31. 4. 30. 5.

(H. m.) The Romans destroy Biorgus, king of the Alans, with his army in Venetia. (JORD.) Dintzic, son of Attila and king of the Huns, again challenges the Ostrogoths to war. The Huns were so completely defeated by them that thereafter the Ostrogoths were always a terror to them.

[Col. 0087D] 461. 4. 19. 3. 15. 32. 5. 31. 6.

(IDAC.) After Majorian was killed, Severus ruled for 4 years. (G. r. F.) Because Childeric behaved insolently and extravagantly, the Franks drive him from the kingdom. Giving half a gold coin to his friend Widiomar as a sign of his recall, should reconciliation ever occur, he hid for 8 years with Basinus, king of the Thuringians. The Franks, however, appoint the Roman commander Aegidius as their king. (JORD.) Hunimund, king of the Suevi, supported by the aid of the Sciri, attacks the Ostrogoths; in that war King Walamer is killed. His brother Thiudemer succeeds him and rules for 11 years. The Huns, their kingdom diminished both by the departure of subject peoples and by ill fortune in battle, continued to rule, but not with their former strength, until, much later, they were defeated by Charlemagne and perished together with their very name. From this point Attila’s sons ruled, and after them Zeliobes, for 50 years [Note: [Col. 0087] C1, 2*, 3, 4*, and D have “58.”]. (IDAC.) [At the city of Toulouse in Gaul, blood flowed from its center all day in a very broad stream; the Goths took this as an omen of their destruction [Note: [Col. 0087] The other copies add “1γ”; it is absent from A.].]

462. 5. 20. 4. 16. 33. 6. 1. 1.

(G. pont.) Hilary presides over the Roman church as its forty-fourth bishop. (BEDA.) At his command, Victorius composed the cycle of the Great Year. (JORD.) Thiudemer wages war against the Suevi and Sciri to their annihilation, in vengeance for his murdered brother.

463. 6. 21. 5. 17. 34. 7. 2. 2.

(H. m.) A certain painter wished to paint the Savior in the likeness of Jupiter, but his hands withered. When he confessed his guilt, Gennadius, bishop of Constantinople, healed him. (JORD.) Thiudemer, having crossed the Danube by the glacier road, also crushes the Suevi there.

464. 7. 22. 6. 18. 35. 8. 3. 3.

(H. m.) The prophet Elisha, who was filled with a double portion of Elijah’s spirit, excelled in life through many virtues. After his death, when a dead man accidentally thrown upon his body was revived merely by touching his body, and when for a long time he had shone through many miracles in Samaria, where he was buried—so that, among other things, demons roaring there with the voices of various wild beasts were driven from the bodies they had entered—he is transferred to Alexandria. (Ib.) Thiudemer rejoices that his son Theoderic is sent back to him by the emperor Leo.

465. 8. 23. 7. 19. 36. 9. 4. 4.

(H. m.) After Severus died, Anthemius ruled for [Col. 0088D] 4 years. (JORD.) Theoderic, an eighteen-year-old youth, crossed the Danube, attacked the Sarmatians, killed their king Babaz, and returned victorious to his father with the spoils of war [Note: [Col. 0087] Sigebert himself originally wrote this year and the following two years in this form. After they were erased in 1, a hand somewhat resembling 1η, but not actually 1η, wrote in their place: (GREG. TUR. II.14.) “The present year, which is the sixty-fourth from the passing of Saint Martin, is marked by the translation of his most revered body. For blessed Perpetuus, bishop of the city of Tours, since Martin, alive and even dead, shone with incomparable brilliance of miracles, built over him, in place of the former small chapel, a church of great magnificence, vaulting the whole structure upon the marvelous arrangement of 120 columns. He raised the holy body from the tomb on July 4, the annual day of his consecration as bishop, relying on angelic assistance, and transferred it to the place where it is now venerated; and on that same day he subsequently dedicated the church. Thus, because three festivals occur on one day—his episcopal ordination, the translation of his body, and the dedication of his basilica—Saint Martin is annually honored on July 4 with the most solemn devotion of the entire surrounding population. The place where his most sacred body rests, separated from the city of Tours by a short level stretch of intervening field toward the west, is called the New Fortress. There, in the aforesaid church, it has been fittingly placed beneath a canopy adorned with gold, silver, and gems, and is illuminated by such magnificence of miracles that throughout the entire Christian world it possesses apostolic glory.” “After Severus died, Anthemius ruled. Theoderic, having crossed the Danube, attacks the Sarmatians and kills their king Babaz.” The following year was not changed; in the third, the words “Genseric ... is defeated” were omitted. F1, F2, and F3 read exactly the same. All the others have the text we have given.].

[Col. 0089A] 466. R. 9. P. 24. F. 8. B. 20. W. 37. W. 10. O. 5. H. 5.

(H. m.) Servandus, plotting tyranny, is killed by Anthemius.

467. 10. 25. 9. 21. 38. 11. 6. 6.

(G. pont.) Simplicius presides over the Roman church as its forty-fifth bishop. He condemned Peter, bishop of Alexandria, accused of the Eutychian heresy. (H. m.) Romanus, plotting tyranny, is killed by Anthemius. King Genseric [Note: [Col. 0089] One copy adds “of the Vandals.”] attacks Italy and is defeated by the Romans in a naval battle.

468. 11. 26. 10. 22. 39. 12. 7. 7.

(H. m.) While Anthemius and his son-in-law, the patrician Ricimer, were contending at Rome over the empire, and while Olybrius had meanwhile been sent by the emperor Leo to rule, Ricimer killed Anthemius. (GREG. TUR.) Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, flourished. He instituted litanies before the Ascension, because earthquakes were overthrowing churches and houses in the city of Vienne, and because the fierceness of wolves and other wild beasts wandered throughout the city all year and devoured people. In addition, the king’s palace was consumed by heavenly fire on Holy Easter Day, adding much terror to the calamity. This rite of litanies spread from the church of Vienne to all the churches of Gaul.

469. 12. 27. 11. 23. 40. 13. 8. 8.

(H. m.) After Olybrius died in the seventh month of his reign, Glycerius ruled. (G. r. F.) While Aegidius was oppressing the Franks more severely than was just, Widiomar, perceiving that the Franks regretted the expulsion of Childeric, secretly recalled him by sending the divided gold coin as a signal and arranged for Aegidius to be expelled and Childeric restored to the kingdom. Basina, wife of Basinus, king of the Thuringians, left her husband and came to Childeric. He married her, and she bore him Louis. (ISID.) After Theoderic, king of the Visigoths, was slain by his brothers, Euric ruled for 19 years.

470. 13. 28. 12. 24. 41. 1. 9. 9.

(H. m.) The patrician Nepos, having expelled Glycerius and ordained him bishop of Salona, seizes the empire. (JORD.) Euric, king of the Visigoths, attempting to occupy Gaul, defeated in battle Riothimus, king of the Britons, who had come to the aid of the Romans for the defense of Gaul.

471. 14. 29. 13. 25. 42. 3. 10. 10.

(JORD.) Euric subjugated the defeated Burgundians. He also invaded the Gallic cities of Arverni, Arles, and Massilia, encouraged by Genseric’s plan to occupy the Roman provinces [Col. 0089D]—so that [the Ostrogoths would ravage the East and the Visigoths the West, while, with the emperors occupied elsewhere, he himself would rule securely in Africa. [Col. 0090A] (V. Rem.) Remigius becomes bishop of Reims. When the Saracens were raiding Egypt, at this time merchants from Venice transferred the body of Saint Mark the Evangelist from Alexandria to Venice [Note: [Col. 0089] “Saracens ... Venice” is in the erasure in 1γ and the other copies; it is absent from A.].]

472. 15. 30. 14. 26. 43. 3. 11. 11.

(H. m.) Orestes the patrician expels Nepos from the kingdom. Theudemer, king of the Ostrogoths, dies, and his son Theoderic is installed in the kingdom.

473. 16. 31. 15. 27. 44. 4. 1. 12.

(H. m.) When the emperor Leo died, Zeno ruled for 18 years [Note: [Col. 0089] XIX in C1, 2*, 3, and D]. Orestes established his son Augustulus as ruler and made a treaty with King Genseric. Meanwhile Odoacer set out for Italy with a great multitude of many peoples from the farthest borders of Pannonia. Passing through Noricum, he sought the blessing of Saint Severinus, whose name was then celebrated there, [Col. 0090B] and learned from him what was to come. After defeating Orestes, who had been besieged at Pavia, capturing and killing him, Odoacer subjected Italy to his own rule.

474. 1. 32. 16. 28. 45. 5. 2. 13.

(H. m.) Augustulus lays down the imperial power. Odoacer, seizing it, held it for 14 years without anyone disturbing him. The emperor Zeno appoints Theoderic, king of the Ostrogoths, ordinary consul—the first dignity after the imperial dignity—and places a golden equestrian statue of him before the palace.

475. 2. 33. 17. 29. 46. 6. 3. 14.

(G. r. F.) After the Vandals and Alans, and after the Goths and Huns, the Franks invade Gaul, not merely to make it their spoil, but so that it may become their permanent habitation. [Col. 0090C] After capturing Cologne, they put to flight in battle the commander Aegidius and kill many Romans.

476. 3. 34. 18. 30. 47. 7. 4. 15.

(Ib.) The Franks capture the city of Trier on the Moselle. (MARIAN.) The heresy of the Acephali arises: they attack the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon without naming their author; for this reason they were called Acephali, that is, “without a head.”

477. 4. 35. 19. 31. 48. 8. 5. 16.

(JORD.) Genseric, king of the Vandals, dies after arranging the succession to the kingdom among his sons, so that, when a brother died, the surviving brother would succeed without dispute from the sons. His son Huneric succeeds him and rules for 9 years [Note: [Col. 0089] VIII in C1, 2*, 3, and D]. (G. r. F.) Hilderic, king of the Franks, devastates the city of Orléans.

[Col. 0090D] 478. 5. 36. 20. 32. 1. 9. 6. 17.

(GREG. TUR.) Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, and all his clergy struggle bravely for Christ against the Arian heresy of the Vandals.

[Col. 0091A] 479. R. 6. P. 37. F. 21. B. 33. W. 2. W. 10. O. 7. H. 18.

(PAUL. DIAC.) Odoacer, king of Italy, defeats and kills Feletheus, king of the Rugians. Saint Severinus had foretold these events to Feletheus and his wife Gisa, since he was unable to restrain them from evil. (H. m.) In Africa, Huneric, king of the Vandals, tortured many orthodox Christians of different orders and ages—up to 4,975 of them—driving them into exile in various places, at various times, and subjecting them to various punishments until death. (PAUL. DIAC.) After the Rugians had been exterminated, the Lombards invaded Rugiland, that is, the homeland of the Rugians; at that time their fifth king, Gudeoc, ruled them. Since, therefore, we have mentioned the Lombards, we have not yet reached their period because of the obscure division of historical narrative. Let us now begin their narrative and gradually strive to ascend to a full and distinct history of them. As we said, after Ibor and Agio, their first king was Agelmundus, and the second Lamissio, so called because he was drawn out of a *lama*, that is, a “chasm.” For his mother, having given birth to seven at one delivery, threw them into a pool; and when King Agelmundus, passing by on a journey, stirred them with his spear, this child held his spear firmly. Brought up by him, he advanced so far in strength that he succeeded him in the kingdom and avenged his death upon the Bulgars. Lethu was the third, Hildeoc the fourth, and Gudeoc the fifth. From the time when they set out for Rugiland, through the following 40 years, the succession of their deeds was as follows. Under Gudeoc and his son Claffo, the sixth king, they lived in Rugiland. Under Tato, the seventh king, they lived in the fields of Asfeld; there, in the third year, after Tato killed Rodulf, king of the Heruli, and destroyed the Herulian kingdom, the power of the Lombards increased. Wacho killed Tato, and himself ruled as the eighth king; he left his son Walthari as successor to the kingdom.

480. 7. 38. 22. L. 1. 34. 3. 11. 8. 19.

(H. m.) Cuades rules the Persians for 42 years [Note: [Col. 0091] XLI in C1, 2*, 3, and D]. (G. r. F.) Audovachrius, commander of the Saxons, ravages Angers with a hostile fleet. (VICT. VIT.) At Carthage, Liberatus the abbot and six brothers are martyred by King Huneric in prison, in chains, by fire, and by bars.

481. 8. 1. 23. 2. 35. 4. 12. 9. 20.

[Col. 0091D] (G. r. F.) Aegidius, commander in Gaul, dies; his son Syagrius succeeds him. Audovachrius subdues Angers and other cities to himself and takes hostages. King Hilderic burns Angers and kills Paul, the count of the city. King Hilderic and Audovachrius, having formed an alliance, subjugate the Alemanni. (GREG. TUR.) During a famine in Burgundy, the senator Ectitius, while supporting four thousand poor people, heard a voice promising heavenly things.

482. 9. 2. 24. 3. 36. 5. 13. 10. 21.

(G. pont.) Felix presides as the forty-sixth over the Roman Church. He condemned Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, who assented to Peter of Alexandria, who had been condemned.

[Col. 0092A] 483. 10. 3. 25. 4. 37. 6. 14. 11. 22.

(H. m.) In Africa, Huneric, king of the Vandals, becoming more fiercely enraged than usual against the Church of God, summons all the bishops of Africa as if to a synod. After driving 444 Catholic bishops into flight and exile, he closed their churches or handed them over to the Arians, and afflicted the people with various punishments. He burned Letus, a bishop, to death. He also exiled Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, together with more than five hundred of his clergy, after torturing them in many ways.

484. 11. 4. 26. 5. 38. [lacuna]. 15. 12. 23.

(G. r. F.) After King Hilderic died, his son Ludowicus rules for thirty years. He married Rothild, daughter of Chilperic, king of the Burgundians, whom Gundebaud, his brother and king, had killed; and he had drowned his wife—that is, Rothild’s mother—by tying a stone around her neck.

485. 12. 5. 1. 6. 39. 8. 16. 13. 24.

(PROSP., app.) King Huneric of the Vandals, struck by God’s judgment, dies miserably, swarming with worms. After him Gunthamund rules for 9 years.

486. 13. 6. 2. 7. 40. 1. 17. 14. 25.

In Gaul, Remigius of Reims and his brother Principius, bishop of Soissons, are distinguished, as is Vedastus, later bishop of Arras; in Africa, Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe; in Italy, Germanus of Capua and Epiphanius of Pavia (cf. Gregory of Tours; the Annals of Liège).

[Col. 0092C] 487. 14. 7. 3. 8. 41. 2. 18. 15. 26.

(G. pont.) Gelasius presides as the forty-seventh over the Roman Church. He had the Manichaeans found at Rome deported into exile and burned their books. He composed treatises and hymns; among other things, he composed the prefaces and prayers of the sacraments in careful and polished language. (H. m.) The emperor Zeno grants the kingdom of Italy to Theoderic, king of the Ostrogoths. Theoderic defeats and kills in battle Trapsila, king of the Gepids, and Busan, king of the Bulgars. (PROSP., app.) Gunthamund recalls Bishop Eugenius from exile.

488. 15. 8. 4. 9. 42. 3. 19. 16. 27.

(ISID.) After Eoric, king of the Visigoths, died, his son Alaric ruled after him for 22 years [Note: [Col. 0091] XXI in B3*, C1, 3, 4*, and D]. (H. m.) After Theoderic had held the Ostrogothic kingdom for 16 years, he departed from Moesia and set out for Italy. He twice engaged Odoacer, king of Italy, twice put him to flight, and besieged him for three years after shutting him up at Pavia.

489. 16. 9. 5. 10. 43. 4. 1. 1[lacuna]. 28.

The apostle Barnabas, who had been burned for Christ at Salamis in Cyprus by the magician Bar-Jesus and by the Jews, caused his own body—which had still lain hidden in a crypt, concealed by John Mark, his cousin—to be found through his revelation. (Cf. Marianus.) The Gospel of Matthew was also found with it, written in Hebrew by Matthew’s own hand and buried there at the same time. Barnabas himself had always carried this Gospel with him, from the teaching of the apostles; wherever he found the sick, he placed it upon them, and through both Barnabas’s faith and Matthew’s merit they were all healed. (G. r. F.) Ludowicus, king of the Franks, engages Syagrius, commander of the Romans, at Soissons. Syagrius flees to Toulouse to Alaric; when Ludowicus demanded that he be handed over, Alaric returned him, and he was killed. Ludowicus transfers to the authority of the Franks whatever of Gaul had been under Roman rule.

490. R. 17. P. 10. F. 6. L. 11. A. 44. W. 5. W. 2. O. 18. H. 29.

(GREG. TUR.) Avitus, bishop of Vienne, flourished; he defended Gaul against the Arian heresy. He composed books in verse on the creation of the world. Sollemnis, bishop of Chartres, flourished; in preaching, he earnestly persisted in instructing the Franks in Christ. In the River Mineo in Spain, fish were caught on whose scales the date of the present year seemed to be inscribed. Hydatius, bishop of Lémica, a city of Spain, brought his chronicle—begun with the first consulship of Theodosius—down to this point. [Note: [Col. 0093D] Sigebert is mistaken; Hydatius ends in the year 467.] Gennadius, bishop, brought his book *On Illustrious Men* down to this point.

491. 18. 11. 7. 12. 45. 6. 3. 19. 30.

(G. pont.) Anastasius presides as the forty-eighth over the Roman Church. When he wished to restore Acacius, who had been condemned, many Romans refused communion with him. (BEDA, H. e.) The Britons, no longer able to endure the power of the Angles, yielded as the defeated to their authority and name. The first of the Anglian people was Elli, and the second Celin; each succeeded the other after his death, and they ruled among them for 70 years [Note: [Col. 0094D] Sigebert is mistaken in the chronology; cf. Hirsch, p. 62]. (MARIAN.) Saint Patrick, the second archbishop of Ireland, died in Christ in the 122nd year of his age. (ISID.) Odoacer, received by Theoderic into an alliance, is killed by him; Theoderic takes possession of Italy, lays aside his private dress, puts on royal attire, and rules in Italy for 36 years [Note: [Col. 0093] “thirty-two” in C3, corrected by D].

492. 19. 12. 8. 13. 1. 7. 4. 1. 31.

(H. m.) When the emperor Zeno died, Anastasius ruled for 25 years, or, as some wish, 27. Gunthamund, king in Africa, opened the Catholic churches that his uncle Huneric—or his grandfather Genseric—had closed, and, at the request of Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, recalled all the priests of God from exile. [Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, is struck down by divine will [Note: [Col. 0093D] so in the erasure of 1, apparently, and in the remaining witnesses; “Pope Anastasius was struck down by divine will” in A.] (cf. Marianus, Bede).]

493. 1. 13. 9. 14. 2. 8. 5. 2. 32.

(G. pont.) Symmachus presides as the forty-ninth over the Roman Church, with Laurentius ordained against him in a contest. This affair prolonged a grave schism in the Church for a long time, even to murders, until at last the power of King Theoderic, although he was an Arian, suppressed the dispute. He established this judgment of equity: that Symmachus should be pope because he had been ordained first and the larger party favored him. (GREG. dial.) Because of the fault arising from this dissension, Germanus, bishop of Capua, found the soul of the deacon Paschasius—who had stubbornly supported Laurentius, although otherwise a man of great holiness—in the baths, placed in purgatorial fire. (G. pont.) This Symmachus established that “Glory to God in the highest” should be sung at Mass every Sunday and on the feast days of martyrs. Pope Telesphorus, the seventh after Peter, had established that this hymn should be sung at Mass only on the night of the Nativity of the Lord, at Masses instituted by him for that night; and in it he added, to the angels’ words, what follows.

494. 2. 14. 10. 15. 3. 9. 6. 3. 33.

(PROSP., app.) After Gunthamund, king of the Vandals, died, his brother Trasamund ruled after him for 26 years.

495. 3. 15. 11. 16. 4. 1. 7. 4. 34.

(G. r. F.) King Ludowicus subjugates Thuringia to himself. (H. m.) King Theoderic wins over all the kings and princes of the neighboring peoples either by friendship or by marriage alliances, and, acting peacefully, builds royal residences in famous places. [At this time Launomarus of Chartres, founder of the monastery of Corbion, and Maximinus of Orléans, founder of the monastery of Micy, flourished; their disciples were the abbots Carileffus and Avitus [Note: [Col. 0093] “Launomarus…abbots” in 1 and the remaining witnesses; absent from A].]

496. 4. 16. 12. 17. 5. 2. 8. 5. 35.

(G. r. F.) Ludowicus extends the Frankish kingdom as far as the Seine. (G. pont.) Certain Romans, accusing Pope Symmachus by suborning false witnesses, secretly introduced Laurentius into the papacy. To settle this schism, King Theoderic appointed Bishop Peter, contrary to the canons, as visitor of the apostolic see.

497. 5. 17. 13. 18. 6. 3. 9. 6. 36.

(G. r. F.) Ludowicus enlarges the Frankish kingdom as far as the Loire. (G. pont.) Pope Symmachus clears himself of the charge brought against him in a council of 115 bishops. Peter and Laurentius were condemned, and Symmachus was restored to his see; but the dispute continued for a long time, even to slaughter and murder within and outside the Church.

498. 6. 18. 14. 19. 7. 4. 10. 7. 37.

(G. r. F.) King Ludowicus captures the fortress of Melun. (BEDA.) Trasamund, king of the Vandals in Africa, closed the Catholic churches and exiled 220 bishops; Pope Symmachus benevolently extended the hand of his generosity toward them. (ADO.) During this persecution, Bishop Fulgentius—renowned for holiness, wisdom, knowledge, style, and eloquence—endured much from the Arians for the true faith and was worn down by a long exile in Sardinia. (G. r. F.) Queen Rothild, an orthodox Christian, tried to draw King Ludowicus away from the error of paganism, but saw that her efforts were in vain.

[Col. 0095A] 499. R. 7. P. 19. F. 15. L. 20. A. 8. W. 5. W. 11. O. 8. H. 38.

(G. r. F.) King Ludowicus engages the Alemanni in battle. When his army was faltering there, he was compelled to bind himself by a vow to accept Christianity. After the king of the Alemanni had been killed and Alemannia reduced to tribute, he was baptized by Remigius, bishop of Reims; by his example and decree he led the Frankish people to the faith of Christ.

500. 8. 20. 16. 21. 9. 6. 12. 9. 39.

(V. S. Rem.) After King Ludowicus had granted many estates to the Church of Fémy, Remigius gave a large part of them to the Church of Laon and established the episcopal see there. He appointed Genebaud as its first bishop; when Genebaud had fallen into fornication with his former wife, but had been purified by seven years of penance and brought out of confinement by divine command, Remigius restored him to his see.

501. 9. 21. 17. 22. 10. 7. 13. 10. 40.

(G. r. F.) King Ludowicus engages Gundebaud, king of the Burgundians; after defeating him, he reduces Burgundy to tribute.

502. 10. 22. 18. 23. 11. 8. 14. 11. 41.

(H. m.) Symmachus the patrician brings distinction to the state, and with him his son-in-law Boethius, a man of consular rank, distinguished in both languages and learned in all the liberal arts, almost all of which he translated and expounded from Greek into Latin.

503. 11. 23. 19. 24. 12. 9. 15. 12. 42.

[Col. 0095C] (H. m.) In Africa, a certain Olympius, while blaspheming the Holy Trinity in the baths, was visibly burned when a fiery arrow came from heaven.

504. 12. 24. 20. 25. 13. 10. 16. 13. 43.

(H. m.) At Constantinople, while Deuterus, an Arian bishop, was baptizing a certain man named Barba, and, incorrectly distinguishing the Trinity, said, “I baptize you, Barba, in the name of the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit,” the water disappeared.

505. 13. 25. 21. 26. 14. 11. 17. 14. 44.

(H. m.) Alamundar, king of the Saracens, was baptized by orthodox Christians. When the Eutychians wished to lead him astray, he refuted them with the following fictitious argument. He said that he had received a letter stating that the archangel Michael had died. When they replied that this was impossible, because angels are of an impassible nature, he said: “How, then, according to you, was Christ crucified naked, unless he possessed two natures, since not even an angel died?”

506. 14. 26. 22. 27. 15. 12. 18. 15. 45.

(G. r. F.) The kings Ludowicus and Alaric form an alliance. (GREG. TUR.) Quintianus, bishop of Rodez, and Maxentius, abbot of Poitiers, flourish in Gaul.

[Col. 0096A] 507. 15. 27. 23. 28. 16. 13. 19. 16. 46.

(H. m.) Vitalianus, prompted by the people, rises against the emperor Anastasius, who was hated by God and men because of the Eutychian heresy.

508. 16. 28. 24. 29. 17. 14. 20. 17. 47.

(G. pont.) Hormisdas presides as the fiftieth over the Roman Church. He organized the clergy and instructed them in the psalms. Out of apostolic humanity, he absolved through his messengers the Greeks who had been stained by association with heretics. (G. r. F.) King Alaric, plotting an ambush against King Ludowicus, violates the treaty.

509. 17. 29. 25. 30. 18. 15. 21. 18. 48.

(G. r. F.) King Ludowicus, encouraged by signs of divine assistance, prepares for battle—when he was passing through Tours, he sent his horse to Saint Martin; unable to redeem it for one hundred solidi, he sent another hundred solidi and recovered it; believing that one who was so costly in a transaction would be good in assistance—and, moreover, having received from singing clerics an omen of victory in the words, “You have girded me with strength for battle,” he engages Alaric, king of the Visigoths. After killing him, he transferred to the Franks whatever the Visigoths possessed in Gaul, and, invading Toulouse, the seat of the Gothic kingdom, extended the Frankish kingdom as far as the Pyrenees. It is also said that the walls of the city of Angoulême collapsed before him. Amalric, Alaric’s son, fled to Spain and ruled there for 16 years. (FLODOARD.) After his father Gundebaud died, Sigismund ruled in Burgundy. [Gibrian the Scot, who journeyed through Gaul with his brothers and sisters, brought distinction to the city of Reims both by his life and by his death [Note: [Col. 0096C] 1γ, apparently, and the remaining witnesses; absent from A].] (Life of Saint Maurus.) Faustus, a disciple of Saint Benedict, who had been sent by him with Maurus to Gaul in this year, writes in the Life of Maurus that Saint Benedict flourished in the time of Justin the Elder and Hilderic, king of the Vandals; he adds that at that time King Theoderic killed the patrician Symmachus and Pope John. He also writes that Benedict died in this same year in which Maurus was traveling to Gaul, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, at about the third hour of the day; since this occurred that year on Holy Saturday, it shows that it was the first Easter. He likewise says that he himself came to Gaul in the time of King Theodebert, grandson of King Ludowicus. Since, therefore, he wrote what he had seen, let whoever can consider how this agrees with the sequence of histories, and let whoever considers it explain it [Note: [Col. 0095D] Sigebert rightly doubts this. But the chronological notions that create the difficulty do not come from Faustus; they were interpolated by Odo of Glanfeuil when he produced a new edition of that Life in the ninth century, which Sigebert regarded as the genuine Life. V. D. Hirsch explains the matter well in this way.]

510. 18. 30. 26. 31. 49. 16. 1. 19. 49.

(G. r. F.) King Ludowicus received from the emperor Anastasius letters patent concerning the consulship, a golden crown set with gems, and a purple tunic; from that day he was called consul and Augustus. The king himself sent to Saint Peter at Rome a golden crown set with gems, which is customarily called a kingdom.

[Col. 0097A] 511. R. 19. P. 31. F. 27. L. 32. A. 50. W. 20. W. 17. O. 2. H. 20.

(H. m.) King Theoderic, having sent his count Ibba against the Franks, killed thirty thousand of them in revenge for the death of Alaric, his son-in-law.

512. 20. 32. 28. 33. 21. 18. 3. 21. 51.

The first synod was held at Orléans by order of King Ludowicus; many provisions beneficial to the Church were decreed there. The virgin Genovefa of Paris, aged eighty, departed to the Lord.

513. 21. 33. 29. 34. 22. 19. 4. 22. 52.

(V. Arn.) Saint Arnulf, Saint Remigius’s son in baptism, flourished in Gaul. After many struggles in preaching Christ, he was martyred and buried in the Aquiline Forest of the Parisians by Scariberga, formerly his wife.

514. 22. 34. 30. 35. 23. 20. 5. 23. 53.

(G. r. F.) King Ludowicus dies after the Frankish kingdom had been extended throughout all Gaul and established both lawfully and peacefully. His son Lotharius, having divided the kingdom with his brothers Theoderic, Chlodomer, and Hildebert, ruled for 50 years [Note: [Col. 0097] LI in 1, apparently corrected, and in A; all the others have L]. His sister Rothild was taken as wife by Amalric, king of the Visigoths.

515. 23. 35. 1. 36. 24. 21. 6. 24. 54.

(G. r. F.) Sigismund, king of Burgundy, who had built the monastery of Agaunum, killed his son Sigeric, following the evil advice of his stepmother. He devoted himself to suitable penance and consecrated himself wholly to the martyrs of Agaunum; that he was worthy of pardon is demonstrated by the frequent grace of healings granted through him to many after his death, and by the cures given through him to those suffering from fevers. [At this time in Alexandria, many people of both sexes, seized by a demon, suddenly barked like dogs [Note: [Col. 0097] added in 1 and the remaining witnesses; absent from A].]

516. 24. 36. 2. 37. 25. 22. 7. 25. 55.

(GREG. TUR.) Theoderic, Lotharius’s brother, kills Chlochilaicus, king of the Danes, who was ravaging Gaul.

517. 25. 37. 3. 38. 26. 23. 8. 26. 56.

(BEDA.) The emperor Anastasius perished, struck by God with lightning; after him Justin the Elder ruled for 11 years. When Boethius, with the support of Symmachus, tried to defend the authority of the Roman senate against Theoderic, king of Italy, he was exiled by Theoderic and there composed his book *The Consolation of Philosophy*.

518. 1. 38. 4. 39. 27. 24. 9. 27. 57.

(G. r. F.) Theoderic, Lotharius’s brother, was invited by Ermenfrid, king of the Thuringians, to kill his brother Baderic, on the agreement that he would receive half of his kingdom; Theoderic kills King Baderic. (MAR.) The virgin of God, Brigid the Scot, dies in Scotland.

519. 2. 39. 5. 40. 28. 25. 10. 28. 58.

[Col. 0098A] (P. D.) John presides as the fifty-first over the Roman Church. When Wacho, king of the Lombards, died, his son Walthari ruled for 7 years.

520. 3. 40. 6. 1. 29. 26. 11. 29 [Note: [Col. 0097] XXVIII and thereafter in 1]. 59.

(G. r. F.) Chlodomer, Lotharius’s brother, and his brothers, prompted by their mother Rothild, rise against Sigismund and Godemar, sons of King Gundebaud, to avenge the killing of their grandmother and grandfather Chilperic. In the engagement, Sigismund is captured, while Godemar escapes by flight. (H. m.) When war arose between the Romans and Persians, Chuades, king of the Persians, killed Zeliobes, king of the Huns, who had come with twenty thousand men to assist him against the Romans, sending an army against him; he destroyed almost his entire army, suspecting that Zeliobes had received gifts from both sides—from him to fight against the Romans and from the Romans to fight against him. From this point I shall cease recording the kingdom of the Huns, because I read that all the kings of that people were called *khagans*, and I find no distinctive designation by which to distinguish them. (Ib.) Trasamund, king of the Vandals, binds his son Hilderic, by Eudoxia, daughter of the emperor Valentinian, who had been captured by Genseric, by an oath not to favor Catholics in his kingdom. After his father’s death, before assuming the kingdom, Hilderic ordered all Catholics to be recalled from exile and the churches to be restored to the bishops. Having thus received the kingdom, he ruled for eight years, seventy-four years having elapsed since his grandfather Genseric profaned the condition of the Church in Africa.

521. 4. 41. 7. 2. 30. 1. 12. 30.

[Col. 0098C] (Ib.) After Chuades, king of the Persians, died, Kabades ruled after him for 16 years. King Chlodomer, after killing King Sigismund together with his wife and sons, again engaged his brother Godemar and was killed by him. Boethius, worn down by a long exile, was killed by Theoderic, king of the Goths.

522. 5. 1. 8. 3. 31. 2. 13. 31.

(Life of Saint Maurus.) As Faustus writes, Saint Benedict truly flourished at this time, namely in the time of Justin the Elder and Hilderic, king of the Vandals. But neither the chronology of his life nor that of his death agrees with the cycle of Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0097D] Cf. the year 509]. (H. m.) Zathus, king of the Lazi, is baptized at Constantinople and received and rewarded by the emperor Justin [Note: [Col. 0097] “Zathus…rewarded” absent from A]. Symmachus, former consul, is killed by Theoderic, king of Italy.

523. 6. 2. 9. 4. 32. 3. 14. 32.

(BEDA.) Justin orders the Arians to be exterminated everywhere. To procure the revocation of this edict, Pope John was sent to Constantinople by Theoderic, king of Italy, an Arian and defender of the Arians. Before the city gate he restored sight to a blind man; after obtaining his request, he returned to Theoderic and was tortured by him in prison at Ravenna, where he died of hunger. (H. m.) Ninety days later [Col. 0099A] Theoderic suddenly died. A certain holy hermit saw him naked and barefoot, being thrust by Pope John and the patrician Symmachus into Vulcan’s cauldron. Athalaric, Theoderic’s grandson through his daughter, succeeded to the kingdom of Italy and the Ostrogoths and ruled for 8 years. (MAR.) Felix presides as the forty-ninth over the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0099] so in 1, F1, 3, and perhaps the first C1; but B4*, C1 corrected, C2*, 3, D, F2, and L have LII]. He was the great-great-grandfather of Pope Gregory.

524. R. 7. P. 3. F. 10. L. 5. 33. A. W. 4. W. 15. O. 1.

(GREG. TUR., III, 7.) King Theoderic, demanding fulfillment of the pact from King Ermenfrid, rises against him with his brother Lotharius. After Ermenfrid was routed from the battle following a great slaughter of his men, and died not long afterward, they subjugated all Thuringia to themselves. Among the captives was Radegund, daughter of Berthar, a king formerly killed by his brother Ermenfrid [Col. 0099B]; King Lotharius took her into his marriage.

525. 8. 4. 11. 6. 34. 5. 16. 2.

(G. r. F.) When Amalric, king of the Visigoths, treated his wife Rothild shamefully because she refused to participate with him in the Arian sect, he was killed in Spain by Childebert, Rothild’s brother. (ISID.) Theuda ruled after him for 17 years.

526. 9. 5. 12. 7. 35. 6. 1. 3.

(G. r. F.) King Lotharius, besieging Augustodunum, a city of Burgundy, with his brother Childebert, occupied all Burgundy after Godemar had been put to flight. (P. D.) After Walthari, king of the Lombards, died, Audoin, the ninth king, ruled for 17 years [Note: [Col. 0099] “17 years” absent from A]. (MAR.) The heresy of the Acephali is renounced. They say that the apostle Paul commanded in his letters that women should be made deacons because he mentions them after deacons; they are called Acephali, “without a head,” because the author of this error is unknown. (H. m.) Kabades, king of the Persians, grieving that his son Phatsuarsan had been led into the Manichaean sect, gathered all the Manichaeans together as if to reward them and sent an army against them, killing many thousands. (P. D.) When battle was joined between Thurismod, king of the Gepids, and Audoin, king of the Lombards, Alboin, Audoin’s son, killed Thurisind, son of Thurismod, and victory went to the Lombards. Thurismod, placing faith before anger and grief, later gave Alboin, who came to him under pledge of good faith, the armor of his son Thurisind, whom Alboin had killed.

527. 10. 6. 13. 1. 36. 7. 2. 4.

[Col. 0099D] (G. pont.) Boniface presides as the fifty-second over the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0099] so in all witnesses]. (BEDA.) Justin dies after appointing Justinian, his nephew through his sister, as his successor in the kingdom. This Justinian rules for 39 years. Through Belisarius he restrained the Persians from incursions into Roman territory. (P. D.) Audoin led the Lombards into Pannonia, where they lived for 42 years [Note: [Col. 0099] “Audoin…42” absent from D].

[Col. 0100A] 528. 1. 7. 14. 2. 37. 8. 3. 5.

(Annals of Liège, MARIAN.) Cassiodorus the senator, later a monk; Arator the poet; Priscian the grammarian; Victor of Capua, bishop, who, writing Easter cycles, refuted the errors of Victorius; Gregory of Langres; Nicetius of Trier; and Domitian of Tongeren flourish. (PROSP., app.) Gylemer, after killing Hilderic, rules over the Vandals for 4 years; he was of such cruelty that he spared not even his parents.

529. 2. 8. 15. 3. 38. 1. 4. 6.

(BEDA.) The body of the monk Antony is found through a divine revelation and brought to Alexandria.

530. 3. 9. 16. 4. 39. 2. 5. 7.

(G. pont.) John presides as the fifty-third over the Roman Church [Col. 0100B] [Note: [Col. 0099] Sigebert himself immediately corrected this from LIIII, which he had written earlier. LVIII corrected to LIIII in D]. The Franks wrest from Athalaric’s hands whatever his grandfather, King Theoderic of Italy, had held in Gaul. (VICT. VIT.) In Africa, certain orthodox bishops whose tongues had been completely cut out by the Vandals later spoke clearly and became a great miracle to many. One of them increased the miracle: when he turned to pride [Note: [Col. 0099] Anselm wrote above the line “or lust”: “lust” in F1, 2; “fornication” in A], he immediately lost the divine gift and became mute.

531. 4. 10. 17. 5. 40. 3. 6. 8.

(JORD.) After Athalaric, king of Italy and the Ostrogoths, died, his mother Amalasuntha associates with herself in the kingdom Theodahad, her father Theoderic’s nephew through his sister. (G. r. F.) Chlodoald, son of King Chlodomer, while his brothers had previously been wickedly killed by their uncle Lotharius [Col. 0100C], transferred worldly nobility to the nobility of divine service and became eminent in the clerical order through the example of his holiness. (Life of Vedastus.) Vedastus, the first bishop of Arras, is ordained by Saint Remigius.

532. 5. 11. 18. 6. 4. 7. 1. 41.

(cf. BEDA, MAR.) [This year the great year of 532 years from the nativity of Christ was completed. From this year also Dionysius the abbot begins his cycle of five nineteen-year cycles. Since the second year of this work ought, in the computation, to agree with the first year of Christ’s nativity, the thirty-fifth year of Dionysius’s cycle ought, in the computation, to agree with the thirty-third year of Christ’s nativity: namely, so that the sixteenth moon of April would fall on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, on a Thursday; Christ’s passion on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on a Friday; and the resurrection on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, on a Sunday. But since this does not occur, and instead the fourteenth moon of April falls that year on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, on a Monday, while Easter Sunday falls on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, it is rejected because it conflicts with evangelical truth [Note: [Col. 0099] The author had first expressed this in four lines. After erasing them, Anselm, apparently, expanded it as follows; the remaining witnesses except one A have this version: “Because in ancient times it had been assigned to the Alexandrian pontiff to announce each year the day on which Easter was to be celebrated to the Roman pontiff, and through him to the other churches of the West, which often either doubted or erred concerning the celebration of Easter, the Roman abbot Dionysius, no longer tolerating the error or ignorance of the Romans, begins from this year the cycle of the great year, namely 532 years. Although it is accepted by everyone, it is nevertheless rejected on this point: that, placing the Lord’s passion on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April and the resurrection on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, it seems to contradict evangelical truth.” Sigebert first wrote this, then later corrected it as given above.] (P. D.) The emperor Justinian abridged the books of Roman laws into a single volume, which is called the *Justinian*.

533. R. 6. P. 12. F. 19. L. 7. A. 42. W. 5. W. 8. O. 2.

(G. pont.) Agapitus presides as the fifty-fourth over the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0101] LV, corrected in D, and likewise thereafter]. (H. m.) Belisarius the patrician was sent by the emperor Justinian, by God’s command, to free Africa from the Vandals. Entering the city at night while carts belonging to peasants were coming in, he captured Carthage, received immeasurable sums of money, and brought Gylemer, reduced from flight to surrender, to the emperor at Constantinople. Thus the kingdom of the Vandals was destroyed; thus at last that Vandal fury, together with the name itself, was utterly extinguished. (Ib.) King Theodahad exiles Queen Amalasuntha, who had been entrusted to imperial protection [Col. 0101B]; not long afterward she was strangled in a bath by Theodahad’s contrivance, and he alone ruled over the Ostrogoths for one year. (G. pont.) Knowing that through this act he had incurred the emperor’s anger, he sent Pope Agapitus to Constantinople to obtain pardon for the deed. Agapitus found there that Anthemius, bishop of Constantinople, belonged to the Eutychian heresy. After excommunicating and exiling him, Agapitus had Mena appointed in his place. Agapitus died there, and his body was brought back to Rome. (P. D.) The emperor Justinian builds the Church of Holy Wisdom at Constantinople with incomparable workmanship [Note: [Col. 0101] “Justinian…builds” was added by Sigebert in a second revision].

534. 7. 13. 20. 8. 43. 9. 1.

(G. pont.) Silverius is installed as the fifty-fifth over the Roman Church by Theodahad. Belisarius is sent against Theodahad; Theodahad is killed by the Goths, and Witigis is installed in the kingdom. Belisarius destroys Naples; when the Goths flee, he enters Rome. Witigis besieges Rome; famine presses upon Italy. Witigis is captured and sent to the emperor. Because Silverius refused to restore Anthemius, he was exiled and died. (JORD.) Eldepadus, appointed king by the Ostrogoths, rules for one year. [(FLODOARD.) The abbot Theoderic, a disciple of Saint Remigius, and the abbot Theodulf, a disciple of that Theoderic, flourish in Francia [Note: [Col. 0101] added by an uncertain hand, perhaps Sigebert in a second revision, and by the remaining witnesses; absent from A].]

535. 8. 14. 21. 9. 44. 10. 1.

(G. p.) Vigilius presides as the fifty-sixth over the Roman Church. (H. m.) After Eldepadus was killed, Erarius rules for one year. (GREG., Dial.) In Gaul flourish [the uterine brothers, born on one and the same day and consecrated as bishops, Medardus to the see of Noyon and Gildardus to that of Rouen; and on one day released from the world and taken up by Christ; in Italy, the bishops Sabinus of Canusium, Cassius of Narni, Fulgentius of Utriculum, and Serbonius of Populonia [Note: [Col. 0101] in the erasure of 1δ, apparently; the remaining witnesses except A have this instead: “In Gaul Medardus, bishop, and Germanus of Paris flourish; in Italy, the bishops R. C., C. N., F. U., and Cerbonius of Populonia.” Thus Sigebert first published it].]

536. 9. 15. 22. 10. 45. 11. 1.

(H. m.) After Erarius was killed, Totila, also called Baduilla, reigns over the Ostrogoths for 11 years; he soon invades Italy and hears the following from Saint Benedict of Cassino concerning his future: “You do many evil things; you have done many; at last restrain yourself from wickedness. Indeed, you will cross the sea and enter Rome; you will reign for nine years and die in the tenth.” Some say that Saint Benedict himself died in this year.

537. 10. 16. 23. 11. 46. 12. 1.

(H. m.) Chosroes reigns among the Persians for 37 years. (G. r. F.) King Theoderic, brother of Lothar, died; his son Theudebert succeeded him. (Narrative concerning Theophilus.) [Note: The following was added by Sigebert himself on an attached slip.] At this time, in one of the cities of Cilicia, a certain Theophilus, the bishop’s steward, administered the secondary duties of ecclesiastical governance under the bishop with such prudence and usefulness that, when the bishop died, everyone acclaimed him as worthy of the episcopate. Content with the office of steward, he preferred that another be ordained bishop.

After he had been unjustly removed from the stewardship by that man, he fell into such impatience that, having hired a certain Hebrew magician, he sought through him help from the prince of demons to recover his dignity. Ordered by the demon to renounce Christ, the Son of God, and his mother Mary, together with the whole profession of Christianity; to confirm this renunciation in writing; to sign the document; and, once signed, to hand it over to him, Theophilus devoted himself to the demon’s service.

The next day, having recovered the honor of the stewardship, he soon came to his senses. For forty days he afflicted himself in every manner of penitence. First he reconciled himself with Mary, the pious Mother of God. When she appeared to him, he renounced the devil and professed Christ—the true Son of God and true God and man, born of the Virgin Mary—and the whole profession of Christianity; through her he also received the grace of her Son, Christ. As a sign of the forgiveness granted him, the Mother of Christ appeared again to him while he was sleeping and placed upon his breast the written document of renunciation that he had signed and given to the devil.

The next day, namely Sunday, Theophilus disclosed the whole course of events before the bishop and the entire church, moving everyone to amazement and to praise of God and of his mother Mary. He remained in the same place where the gracious Mother of Christ had appeared to him, and there, three days later, he died and was buried.

538. 11. 1. 24. 12. 47. 13. 2.

[Col. 0102D] (H. m.) Chosroes ravages the borders of the Romans. In Campania of Italy, King Totila, persecuting Benedict the Younger, renowned for holiness, on account of Christ, wished to burn him together with his cell; but when he was unable to do so, he threw him into a blazing furnace. The saint emerged from it the next day unharmed, and even his clothing was untouched.

[Col. 0103A] 539. R. 12. P. 2. F. 25. L. 13. A. 48. W. 14. O. 3.

(H. m.) Emperor Justinian killed two Bulgarian kings who were laying waste Thrace, together with many thousands of Bulgarians.

540. 13. 3. 26. 14. 49. 15. 4.

(H. m.) Chosroes captured Antioch. (G. r. F.) King Childebert rose up against his brother Lothar together with their nephew Theudebert; but because their mother Rothild acted earnestly before God to prevent civil war between the brothers, they were restrained by a dreadful storm. Since not even a sign of such terror appeared over Lothar, they returned to fraternal peace.

541. 14. 4. 27. 15. 50. 16. 5.

(H. m.) When Chosroes was now attacking the Romans for the fourth time, Belisarius compelled him to withdraw ineffectually. (GREGORY OF TOURS.) Various signs were seen in different places in Gaul. A comet appeared; on Easter Day the sky seemed to burn; real blood fell from a cloud onto people’s garments; and the house of a certain person appeared to have been spattered with blood from within. Various disasters followed, and illnesses, with pustules and blisters, afflicted the populations.

542. 15. 5. 28. 16. 51. 17. 6.

(H. m.) Belisarius [Note: Balisarius in 1 manuscript.] was sent back to Africa and destroyed Guintharith, who was reigning over what remained of the Vandals, together with his followers. (G. r. F.) The brothers Lothar and Childebert, having besieged Zaragoza in Spain, returned after the citizens prayed to God and carried around the tunic of the martyr Vincent; they received from the citizens, as a gift, the martyr’s stole, and acquired the greater part of Spain. (ISIDORE.) After Theuda, king of the Visigoths, was killed by his own men, Theudegisel reigned after him for 2 years. (Vita of Maurus.) Maurus, a disciple of Saint Benedict, shines in Gaul.

543. 16. 6. 29. 17. 1. 7.

(H. m.) Pope Vigilius, because he did not wish to recall Anthemius according to his promise, was sent ignominiously to Constantinople. King Totila of the Ostrogoths, after capturing Rome, lived for some time among the Romans like a father among his children, having been softened, as is believed, by the admonitions of Saint Benedict. (PAULUS DIACONUS.) After Audoin died, his son Alboin reigned over the Lombards in Pannonia for 24 years.

[Col. 0103D] 544. 17. 7. 30. 1. 53. [lacuna]. 8.

(GREGORY, Dialogues.) Herculanus, bishop of Perugia, was martyred by King Totila, his head having been cut off; after his death, however, his head was found joined to his body. (H. m.) Totila invaded Sicily. Narses, a eunuch and patrician of the Romans, was appointed and sent against Totila. (FRED.) After Theudegisel was killed by his own men while dining, Agilan reigned over the Visigoths for 9 years.

545. 18. 8. 31. 2. 54. 1. 0.

(H. m.) Narses formed an alliance with Alboin, king of the Lombards. [Col. 0104A] (Life of Remigius.) Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, died [Note: Rather, he died in the year 535; cf. Acta Sanctorum, October I, 68.].

546. 19. 9. 32. 3. 55. 2. 10.

(H. m.) Pope Vigilius was exiled. Narses, the patrician, with the Lombards assisting him, killed King Totila; after the Ostrogothic people had been destroyed to utter extermination, he completely overthrew the Ostrogothic kingdom. Thus the Gothic kingdom, which, as Jordanes says [Note: Sig. is mistaken—Jordanes, in fact, in De rebus Geticis, at the end, says that this was the one-thousand-three-hundredth year of the Gothic kingdom. HIRSCH.], had endured for approximately 2,400 years, came to an end among the Ostrogoths; but it remained intact among the Visigoths reigning in Spain. Teias, attempting to revive the Ostrogothic kingdom, reigned for 2 years.

547. 29. 10. 33. 4. 56. 3. 1.

(PAULUS DIACONUS.) When battle was joined between Cunimund, king of the Gepids, and Alboin, king of the Lombards, sixty thousand of them fell on both sides. Alboin killed Cunimund, made a drinking cup for himself from his skull, and took Cunimund’s captured daughter as his wife. When the Huns invaded the lands of the Gepids, the Gepid kingdom was completely destroyed.

548. 21. 11. 34. 5. 57. 4. 2.

(G. r. F.) King Theudebert did not cease disturbing Italy, both personally and through his general Bucellinus, with varying fortunes of war; he received either plunder or tribute from Italy and Sicily. King Teias was killed by Narses, and with him the remnants of the Goths were eradicated.

549. 22. 12. 35. 6. 58. 5.

(GREGORY OF TOURS.) Agericus, bishop of Verdun, shines in holiness. (P. D.) The patrician Narses defeated and captured Sinduald, king of the Britons, who had rebelled against him despite their former friendship, and hanged him.

550. 23. 13. 36. 7. 59. 6.

(G. r. F.) King Theudebert died, and his son Theudebald succeeded him. (GREGORY OF TOURS.) The flowers, grains, and fruits of the tree called the elder were transformed into the flowers, grains, and fruits of the vine [Note: “of the tree were transformed” was added by Sig. in his third revision.].

551. 24. 14. 37. 8. 60. 7.

The Fifth Ecumenical Synod was held at Constantinople. At it, the letter called Ibas, full of error, was condemned, and Theodore was shown to have fallen into the impiety of treachery by separating the person of the Mediator between God and human beings into two substances (cf. the Annals of Liège). Up to this point Bishop Jordanes composed his history.

[Col. 0104D] 552. 25. 15. 38. 9. 61. 8.

(G. pont.) Pelagius presides as the 57th bishop of the Roman church. Accused of the death of Pope Vigilius, he publicly satisfied the charge by swearing an oath while holding the holy Gospels and the cross. (GREGORY OF TOURS, On the Glory of the Martyrs, X.) At this time in the East, a certain boy, the son of Jews, was brought by Christian boys of his own age to receive the body and blood of Christ in the church of the holy mother of Christ Jesus. Because of this, his father threw him into a blazing furnace; Christians drew him out unharmed. He asserted that the woman depicted in that church, holding a child, had fanned the flames away from him with her cloak [Note: “This … had fanned away” was added by Sig. himself in his second revision.].

553. R. 26. P. 16. F. 39. L. 10. A. 62. W. 9.

(FRED.) When Agilan acted arrogantly toward his subjects, Athanagild, with the Romans assisting him, killed him and reigned for 22 years.

554. 27. 17. 40. 11. 63. 1.

(GREGORY OF TOURS.) Queen Rothild died. Winter became so harsh with snow and ice that birds and untamed wild animals could be caught by hand.

555. 28. 18. 41. 12. 64. 2.

(P. D.) The Frankish generals Bucellinus and Amingus were killed by Narses. (H. m.) Something resembling a spear appeared in the sky, extending from the north toward the west [Note: “Something resembling a spear … toward the west” was added by Sig. in his third revision.].

556. 29. 19. 42. 13. 65. 3.

(G. r. F.) King Theudebald died. Lothar, king of the Franks, subdued the Saxons who had rebelled against him and the Thuringians who were assisting them, in a severe battle and slaughter. (Annals of Liège.) Saint Medard, bishop of Noyon, died and was buried at Soissons.

557. 30. 20. 43. 14. 66. 4.

(GREGORY OF TOURS.) Queen Radegund, formerly the wife of King Lothar, having changed her clothing, shines with the nobility of holiness.

558. 31. 21. 44. 15. 67. 5.

(Life of Gregory the Great.) Gregory [son of the senator Gordianus [Note: “son of the senator” was added above the line in 1 manuscript, apparently; it is absent from the others and from A.]] grew up in Rome. After founding six monasteries in Sicily and a seventh in Rome in his own house, he became a monk from the office of urban prefect and shone in wisdom and knowledge, learning and holiness. (H. m.) A very terrible earthquake occurred for ten days [Note: “A very terrible earthquake occurred for ten days” was added by Sig. in his third revision.].

559. 32. 22. 45. 16. 68. 6.

(G. r. F.) After King Childebert died, the monarchy of the Frankish kingdom passed to his brother Lothar.

560. 33. 23. 46. 17. 69. 7.

At this time, a certain Jew secretly removed an image of Jesus the Savior from a church and pierced it with a weapon. Carrying it secretly to his house, he wished to burn it in flames; but when he saw himself stained with the image’s blood, he hid it in astonishment. Christians searched for it and, following the traces of blood, found and recovered it covered in blood; but they stoned the Jew. (P. D.) A disastrous epidemic of mortality occurred in Italy.

561. 34. 24. 47. 18. 70. 8.

(BEDE, Ecclesiastical History.) The third Æthelberht of the English reigns in Britain for 56 years. (Life of Saint Maclovus.) At this time Brendan shone in Scotland. Seeking the Fortunate Islands in a seven-year voyage, he saw many things worthy of a miracle. Macutes, also called Maclovus, was regularly educated by him and was his companion on that voyage; he shone in holiness and miracles in Britain. When the Britons grew hostile toward him, he passed to Gaul after cursing them, and under Leontius, bishop of the Santones, he shone for a long time through his miracles. After the Britons, afflicted by various disasters because of his curse, again received his blessing, he released and healed them [Note: “The Britons … he released and healed” was added by Sig. himself immediately afterward.].

562. 35. 25. 48. 19. 1. 9.

(H. m.) At Constantinople, certain men who plotted to kill the emperor were themselves killed. Belisarius, also accused of this crime, was acquitted by the emperor. (GREGORY OF TOURS.) In Gaul, a mountain above the Rhône River gave a bellowing sound for many days. At last it was torn away from the neighboring mountain and, together with churches and houses, people and animals, plunged into the Rhône [Note: “In Gaul … plunged into the Rhône” was added by Sig. in his third revision.].

563. 36. 26. 49. 20. 2. 10.

[Col. 0106B] (G. r. F.) King Lothar pursued his son Chramn, who had long rebelled against him and committed many evils in his kingdom, into Brittany. There he engaged in battle with Chonobrus, the auxiliary leader of the Britons; he killed Chonobrus, but had Chramn, once captured, burned with his wife and daughters.

564. 37. 27. 50. 21. 3. 11.

(MAR.) John presides as the 58th bishop of the Roman church. After Lothar, king of the Franks, died, his son Chilperic, having divided the kingdom with his brothers Heribert, Guntram, and Sigebert, reigned for 22 years.

565. 38. 28. 1. 22. 4. 12.

(BEDE.) After Emperor Justinian died, Justin the Younger reigned for 12 years. (P. D.) Many signs appeared in the sun and moon [Note: “Many signs appeared in the sun and moon” was added by Sig. in his third revision.].

566. 1. 29. 2. 23. 5. 13.

(P. D.) The patrician Narses was degraded from the patriciate at the accusation of the Romans. Because he was a eunuch, the empress Sophia taunted him, telling him to go to the women’s quarters and distribute wool to the girls. He replied that he would weave for her a web such as she would be unable to lay down while she lived, and he invited the Lombards to take possession of Italy. (BEDE, Ecclesiastical History.) Saint Columba, a presbyter who came from Scotland, was held in honor in Britain. [(Life of Maclovus.) Samson of Dol, archbishop, a kinsman of Saint Maclovus, and Samson’s successor Maclorius, who had crossed from transmarine Britain to this nearer Britain, shine in holiness and [Col. 0106D] teaching [Note: Added at the top of the page in 1 manuscript and in the others; absent from A.].]

567. 2. 30. 3. 24. 6. 14.

(G. r. F.) King Sigebert defeated the Huns, who were ravaging parts of the Frankish territories, in Thuringia. Meanwhile, his brother Chilperic invaded his borders and occupied the city of Reims. (P. D.) Fiery spears were seen in the sky, foretelling the Lombards’ invasion of Italy. [(GREGORY OF TOURS.) Saint Basolus, abbot, and Saint Sindulfus, presbyter and recluse, shine in Francia [Note: Added in 1 manuscript and the others; absent from A.].]

[Col. 0107A] 568. R. 3. P. 31. F. 4. L. 25. A. 7. W. 15.

(P. D.) King Alboin, taking with him the Saxons and other peoples and, by agreement, entrusting Pannonia to the Huns, friends of the Lombards, set out for Italy with all the Lombard families, and reigned there for 6 years. King Sigebert invaded the deserted lands of the Saxons and handed them over to the Suevi for settlement. New signs in the sky had foretold this novelty of evil long beforehand.

569. 4. 32. 5. 1. 8. 16.

(MAR.) The Armenians accepted the faith of Christ. (G. r. F.) King Sigebert opposed his brother Chilperic and occupied the seat of his kingdom at Soissons. He exiled his son Theudebert, who had been captured there; he defeated Chilperic in battle, drove him to flight, and freed his own borders from Chilperic’s arrogance. (G. Fr.) He himself married Bruma [Note: Sig. first wrote Brunichild; afterward he corrected it himself and added the words found in B. d. e. The others likewise have Brunichild; A. has Brunichild, but lacks “who was also called Brunichild.”], the daughter of Athanagild, king of the Visigoths, [who was also called Brunichild.]

570. 5. 33. 6. 2. 9. 17.

(Annals of Liège.) Saint Vedast died. (P. D.) Italy was overrun and devastated by the Lombards, with no one resisting; moreover, it was consumed by famine and pestilence.

571. 6. 34. 7. 3. 10. 18.

(GREGORY OF TOURS.) The Huns again engaged Sigebert in battle and, having nearly achieved victory by magical arts, withdrew; thereafter they remained allied with Sigebert throughout his life.

572. 7. 35. 8. 4. 11. 19.

(P. D.) Gregory was ordained bishop of Tours and was held in honor by everyone. After a three-year siege, the Lombards received Pavia by surrender and, possessing nearly all Italy except Rome and Ravenna, ruled there with power.

573. 8. 36. 9. 5. 12. 20.
