(H. m.) When battle was joined between the Romans and the Persians, victory went to the Romans. (GREGORY OF TOURS.) King Charibert died. The Spaniards and Franks disagreed over the celebration of Easter: the Spaniards celebrated Easter on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, but the Franks on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May. It became divinely clear that the Franks had celebrated correctly because the springs in Spain, which ordinarily are miraculously and spontaneously filled for baptism on Holy Saturday of Easter, were filled not on the Spaniards’ Easter but on the Franks’ [Note: “The Spaniards … were filled” was added in the margin by Sig. in his third revision.].

574. 9. 37. 10. 6. 13. 21.

[Col. 0107D] (P. D.) Among the Persians, Hormizd reigned for 18 years. Alboin, king of the Lombards, was killed by his arms-bearer through the treachery of his wife, whose father, Cunimund, king of the Gepids, he himself had once killed in battle and from whose skull he had made a drinking cup. One day, when he handed the cup to her, saying, “Drink with your father,” she, inflamed by feminine fury, had him killed in bed by his own arms-bearer. [Col. 0108A] Cleph was installed in the Lombard kingdom and reigned for 2 years.

575. 10. 1. 11. 1. 14. 22.

(G. pont.) Benedict presides as the 59th bishop of the Roman church. (Life of Gregory.) By him Gregory was permitted to depart to preach to the English; but when the people rioted, he was recalled and ordained the seventh deacon. (ISIDORE.) After Athanagild, king of the Visigoths, died, Leovigild reigned with his brother Liuva and afterward alone for 16 years. (P. D.) The poet Fortunatus came from Italy and shone in Gaul.

576. 11. 2. 12. 2. 15. 1.

(There.) After Cleph died, the Lombards were governed by dukes for 10 years. As famine pressed upon Rome, many Romans surrendered to the Lombards.

[Col. 0108B] 577. 12. 3. 13. 1. 16. 2.

(H. m.) After Emperor Justin died, Tiberius reigned for 6 years. He sent a supply of grain from Egypt and freed Rome from famine. (G. r. F.) Chilperic, king of the Franks, pressed his brother Sigebert excessively, both personally and through his son Theudebert, in something worse than civil war.

578. 1. 4. 14. 2. 17. 3.

(There.) King Sigebert engaged his brother Chilperic in battle, and Chilperic’s son Theudebert was killed there. When the Franks, hating Chilperic, wished to raise Sigebert as king over them, Sigebert was killed by two boys sent by Fredegund, Chilperic’s wife. [(FRED.) His wife Brunichild, governing the kingdom with her son Childebert—or with Childebert’s sons—was so intolerable to the Franks because of her arrogant conduct that it was reasonably believed that the Sibyl had prophesied about her: “Bruma will come,” she said, “from the regions of Spain; before her gaze peoples and the kings of peoples will perish. She herself will perish, torn apart by the hooves of horses.” Although she was so arrogant, she nevertheless honored the churches of God. She also founded many monasteries of saints and constructed buildings of astonishing workmanship, so that it was a wonder that she could have accomplished so much.] (G. r. F.) Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, died. (P. D.) The Lombard dukes indiscriminately destroyed cities and churches and brought under their rule what remained of Italy [Note: The words from “Fredegund … Italy,” with the two lines written by Sigebert erased, were expanded in this way by 1 manuscript and the others except A. In A the words enclosed in brackets are absent; the rest is read as we have given it, but at the end is added: “Childebert, son of Sigebert, received his father’s kingdom.” This, therefore, is what Sig. had first written.].

579. 2. 5. 15. 3. 18. 4.

[Col. 0108D] (H. m.) Because Tiberius was generous toward the poor, God aided his generosity by allowing him to discover many treasures. King Chilperic exiled Brunichild, Sigebert’s widow, together with her sons. (G. r. F.) Menas the solitary shines in Italy.

580. 3. 6. 16. 4. 19. 5.

King Hormizd of the Persians, invading the Roman provinces, was disgracefully defeated by the Romans and issued an edict that no Persian king should thereafter personally go out to battle. (GREGORY OF TOURS.) Fire was seen to run through the sky [Note: “Fire was seen to run through the sky” was added by Sig. in his second revision.].

581. R. 4. P. 7. F. 17. L. 5. A. 20. W. 6.

(G. pont.) Pelagius presides as the 60th bishop of the Roman church. While the Lombards were besieging Rome, he was ordained without the emperor’s command. He decreed that the daily preface of the sacraments at Mass should be changed, according to the ancient Roman order, to only nine prefaces: namely, for the Nativity of the Lord, the Epiphany, Easter, the Ascension, Pentecost, the Apostles, the Holy Trinity, the Holy Cross, and the Lenten fast. (BEDE.) From this point Gregory was sent to Constantinople as *apocrisiarius*; at the urging of Leander, bishop of Seville, he composed the books of the *Moralia on Job*. There, in the presence of Emperor Tiberius, he refuted Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, who was teaching falsely about the resurrection—that our body in the glory of that resurrection would be intangible, lighter than winds and subtle air—and, when Eutychius died not long afterward, Gregory completely extinguished his teaching. (P. D.) The Lombard dukes attacked Gaul, and, with varying fortunes of war, now the Franks and now the Lombards clashed with one another. Hospitius, a servant of God in Gaul, shone there; he had also foretold the coming of the Lombards.

582. 5. 8. 18. 6. 21. 7.

(GREGORY OF TOURS.) The Saxons, withdrawing from the Lombards in Italy and attempting to recover their lands in Germany, were late in abandoning the wars, after as many as twenty thousand of them had been killed by peoples sent there by Sigebert. (There.) Winochus the Briton came from Britain and shone in holiness in Gaul. Wolves entered the city of Bordeaux, fearing no one, and devoured the dogs [Note: “Wolves … devoured the dogs” was revised by Sig. in his second revision.].

583. 6. 9. 19. 7. 22. 8.

(H. m.) While Emperor Tiberius was invading Armenia, he died not long afterward; Maurice reigned for 21 years. (P. D.) Hermenegild, son of Leovigild, king of the Visigoths, married the daughter of King Sigebert. Through her he was converted to the orthodox faith and incurred the irrecoverable anger of his Arian father, Leovigild. (GREGORY OF TOURS.) At Tours true blood flowed from broken bread [Note: “At Tours … flowed from broken bread” was revised by Sig. in his second revision.].

[Col. 0109D] 584. 1. 10. 20. 8. 23. 9.

(H. m.) Chagan, king of the Avars, that is, of the Huns, broke peace with Emperor Maurice. (GREGORY OF TOURS.) The Persians ravaged Armenia with plunder, fires, and the captivity of bishops and peoples; yet they were entirely unable to burn the church of the forty-eight martyrs who suffered in Armenia under Licinius.

585. 2. 11. 21. 9. 24. 10.

(There.) Emperor Maurice acted vigorously against the Persians through his praetor. Antioch was overthrown by divine action in the following manner. A certain citizen of the city was so devoted to almsgiving and hospitality that he never ate on any day without a poor person or a guest. One day, as he went around the city until evening in search of a poor person or guest, he encountered an elderly man in white clothing standing with two companions in the middle of the city. He invited him to his lodging and received this reply:

“Could you not, man of God, save this city together with your Symeon, so that it would not be overthrown?”

After saying this, the old man shook the handkerchief that he held over one half of the city. Immediately that half, together with its dwellings and inhabitants, was overthrown. When he wished to shake the handkerchief over the other half of the city as well, he was scarcely persuaded by the many prayers of his two companions to spare the remaining half. Thus, after consoling the man who had witnessed these things by telling him that his house had been saved, he departed and appeared no more.

(P. D.) Guntram, king of the Franks, tired from hunting, was sleeping in the lap of his arms-bearer beside a stream. The arms-bearer saw a small animal emerge from the king’s mouth. When it wished to cross the stream but could not, the arms-bearer laid his sword across the stream and made a path for it to go and return. When it entered the king’s mouth again, the king awoke and, astonished, said that in a dream he had crossed an iron bridge and seen many treasures beneath a certain mountain. When he went to the place in accordance with the dream, he found great treasures, accepted them, and devoted them to the uses of the holy church [Note: “Guntram … devoted them” was added by Sig. in a correction, partly in erasure and partly in the lower margin.].

586. 3. 12. 22. 10. 25. 11.

[Col. 0110C] (P. D.) The Lombards appointed Authari as their king and, because of his rank, called him Flavius; from him all the Lombard kings were called Flavius. (FRED.) King Leovigild of the Visigoths, pursuing his son Hermenegild with hostile intent, condemned him to exile. (The same.) At this time Miro, king of Galicia, also died.

587. 4. 13. 23. 1. 26. 12.

(G. r. F.) King Chilperic of the Franks was killed at the instigation of his wife Fredegund. His four-month-old son Lothar was raised to the kingdom and reigned for 45 years.

588. 5. 14. 1. 2. 27. 13.

(P. D.) King Childebert received money from Emperor Maurice to drive the Lombards out of Italy. [Col. 0110D] But this was futile: at one time he returned as their ally; at another, having engaged them in battle, he was defeated by them; and at another, even if he was superior to them, the fortification of the cities prevented him from expelling them.

589. 6. 15. 2. 3. 28. 14.

(BEDE.) Leovigild, king of the Visigoths, killed his son Hermenegild with an axe in prison on the holy night of Easter because he refused to participate in the Arian communion. (FRED.) Childebert engaged Lothar’s army in battle and escaped defeated.

[Col. 0111A] 590. R. 7. P. 16. F. 3. L. 4. A. 29. W. 15.

(P. D.) Authari, king of the Lombards, married Theudelinda, daughter of Garibald, king of the Bavarians. Excessive rains caused floods, so that everyone said the waters of the Flood were overflowing again; and the disaster was so great that no one remembered a worse one since the beginning of the world. A great dragon, shaped like a massive beam, also descended through the Tiber into the sea together with an innumerable multitude of serpents. Sea creatures were suffocated by them and thrown onto the shore, where their decay corrupted the air.

591. 8. 17. 4. 5. 30. 16.

(H. m.) The Persians blinded King Hormizd; his son Chosroes killed him and fled to Emperor Maurice. With Maurice’s aid he defeated the Persians, received the Persian kingdom, and reigned for 39 years. (FRED.) After Leovigild, king of the Visigoths, died, his son Richared reigned for 15 years. (P. D.) After a flood occurred in Italy, almost beyond anyone’s belief, and great confusion followed, an indescribable mortality of human beings caused by an inguinal plague ensued; it first struck Pope Pelagius. Gregory was elected to the papacy. While awaiting the emperor’s approval, he instituted a sevenfold litany to appease God’s anger; as they proceeded, eighty people were struck by this plague, and at last God’s anger subsided.

592. 9. 1. 5. 6. 31. 1.

Gregory presides as the 60th bishop of the Roman church. Among his other works of piety, he obtained from God, through compassion and tears, the release from the punishments of hell of the soul of Trajan, formerly emperor of the Romans, although he was a pagan. Among the many things that he did and instituted for the benefit of the church, he methodically arranged and usefully compiled the antiphonary. He ordered the *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”) to be sung by the clergy at Mass and had the *Alleluia* said at Mass outside Quinquagesima. In the canon of the offering he added three words: “And dispose our days in your peace, and command that we be rescued from eternal damnation and numbered among the flock of your elect.” He also judged that the Lord’s Prayer should be recited over the offering after the canon.

(P. D.) After Authari, king of the Lombards, died, the Lombards, granting Queen Theudelinda the choice of selecting for herself a husband and a king for Italy, placed Agilulf in authority as king; he reigned for 25 years.

593. 10. 2. 6. 1. 32. 2.

[Col. 0111D] (GREGORY OF TOURS.) In Gaul, a certain man cutting wood in a forest was so tormented by flies that he became insane for two years. Then, adopting the appearance of a religious man, he presented himself as a false prophet, afterward as a magician, and then, even performing cures upon the sick, claimed to be Christ and ordered himself to be worshiped as Christ. Those who refused to worship him he attacked violently, together with the large crowd that followed him. Later he was killed by a certain faithful man, and his followers were scattered.

[Col. 0112A] King Richared of the Visigoths harassed the Roman borders. Up to this point Gregory of Tours arranged his history of the Franks.

[At this time Philtanus reigned on the island of Ireland, and Brendinus reigned in Scotland; Brendinus had a brother named Adelfius. From Adelfius’s daughter, called Gelgebes, Philtanus, king of Ireland, fathered Saint Fursey and his brothers Foillan and Ultan [Note: Added in the lower margin in 1 manuscript and the others; absent from A.].]

594. 11. 3. 7. 2. 33. 3.

(FRED.) The tunic of our Lord Jesus Christ was found in the city of Zaphat, not far from Jerusalem, through the confession of the Jew Simon, and was placed by the bishops Gregory of Antioch, Thomas of Jerusalem, and John of Constantinople in Jerusalem, at the place where Christ’s cross is venerated. Gaugericus, bishop of Cambrai, shines [Col. 0112B] [Note: A adds: “When neither anyone nor Pope Gregory himself could recall Severus, bishop of Aquileia, from the Arian heresy, the clergy and people of Aquileia, with Pope Gregory’s support, effected a division. The Arians at Aquileia adhered to Severus, while the orthodox established for themselves the seat of their bishopric at Grado. Thus, from one metropolitan church there came to be two metropolitans. Although after Severus’s death the church returned to unity of faith, it was never afterward able to be restored to the unity of its former union.”].

595. 12. 4. 8. 3. 34. 4.

(H. m.) At Constantinople a four-footed child was born, and another child having two heads; these prodigies foretold misfortune for the places in which they were born. (FRED.) King Richared of the Visigoths convened a synod of 62 bishops at Toledo. There he renounced and anathematized the Arian heresy and confirmed himself and the entire Visigothic people in the Catholic faith. (P. D.) Tassilo, appointed king of the Bavarians by Childebert, gained a triumph after defeating the Slavs.

596. 13. 5. 9. 4. 35. 5.

(P. D.) King Agilulf of the Lombards rose up against the Romans; but through the efforts of Queen Theudelinda, he soon afterward made a treaty with them. Pope Gregory sent this queen his books of the *Dialogues*. (FRED.) The sun diminished from morning until noon, down to one-third of its former size.

597. 14. 6. 10. 5. 36. 6.

(BEDE, Ecclesiastical History.) Pope Gregory sent Augustine with others to preach in England, as he himself had once intended to do. (FRED.) King Guntram, renowned for holiness, fell asleep in Christ; his kingdom passed to his nephew Childebert.

598. 15. 7. 11. 6. 37. 7.

King Richared of the Visigoths formed an alliance with the Frankish kings, and Childebert’s sister was given to him as wife. (BEDE, Ecclesiastical History.) Saint Columba, abbot and presbyter, teacher of the Scots and Picts, died. He left many monuments of holiness to his successors, except that, in rustic simplicity, he neither learned nor taught that Easter ought to be celebrated on the Lord’s Day. [Marculfus, abbot of Bayeux, shines in holiness in Gaul [Note: Added in 1 manuscript and the others except A.].]

599. 16. 8. 12. 7. 38. 8.

(BEDE.) Æthelberht, king of the English called the people of Kent, was baptized with his people when Augustine preached. Moreover, the people of the English called the Mercians, and the people of the Northumbrians—so called because they live on the northern side of the Humber River—had not yet heard the word of life under their kings Æthelfrith and Ælle.

600. R. 17. P. 9. F. 13. L. 8. A. 39. W. 9.

(BEDE, Ecclesiastical History.) Saint Goar came from Aquitaine and shines in Gaul. Augustine was consecrated bishop of the English by Etherius of Arles. (FRED.) King Childebert of the Franks died; his sons Theudebert and Theoderic succeeded him.

601. 18. 10. 14. 9. 40. 10.

The dispute between the Roman church and the arrogance of John, bishop of Constantinople, who usurped for himself the title of universal patriarch, began under Pope Pelagius and was thereafter vigorously pursued by Gregory. It could not cease before John himself died a sudden death. (P. D.) The Huns fought vigorously with the Franks in Thuringia. Queen Fredegund died. Agilulf formed an alliance with Theoderic. (H. m.) In the Nile River of Egypt, animals in human form were seen—namely, a man and a woman rising above the water as far as their waists. After people adjured them by God, they allowed themselves to be seen from morning until the ninth hour.

602. 19. 11. 15. 10. 41. 11.

(BEDE, Ecclesiastical History.) Augustine, bishop of the English, held a synod with the bishops of the Britons and Scots. Because he found the priests and monks opposed to justice—those whom he wished to have as partners in preaching—he terrified them with a prophecy of the calamity that would come upon them. (Life of Columba.) Saint Columbanus came from Ireland to Burgundy, where, with permission from King Theoderic, he began to build the monastery of Luxeuil.

603. 20. 12. 16. 11. 42. 12.

(H. m.) Emperor Maurice divinely learned beforehand that Phocas would kill him and his people; repenting of his wrongs, he earnestly asked that they be repaid to him here, through himself and through the servants of God. (G. r. F.) King Theoderic received his grandmother Brunichild, who had been expelled by the Austrasians.

604. 21. 13. 17. 12. 43. 13.

(H. m.) Emperor Maurice was killed by Phocas together with his wife and sons; Phocas reigned for 8 years. (BEDE, Ecclesiastical History.) The eastern English were converted to Christ, together with their king Sigebert, through the bishop Mellitus.

[Col. 0113D] 605. 1. 14. 18. 13. 44. 14.

(H. m.) When Maurice’s death became known, the Persians on one side and the Huns on the other ravaged the Roman provinces. (G. r. F.) Lothar and Theoderic clashed with one another in battle, in which more than thirty thousand are reported to have been killed; nevertheless, Theoderic gained the victory. In this battle an angel of the Lord was seen holding a drawn sword over the people.

606. 2. 15. 19. 14. 45. 15.

(GREGORY OF TOURS, *On the Glories of the Confessors*) Sabinianus presides as the sixty-second [pope] of the Roman Church. At this time, when a certain poor man was asking sailors for alms and received none, the shipmaster said: “Stop asking alms from us—we have nothing here except stones!” When the poor man replied, “Then let everything be turned into stones,” whatever was edible on the ship was changed into stones, while the color and form of the objects remained the same [Note: “[Col. 0113] Sabinianus … permanente”: Sig. in his second revision.] As famine grew worse at Rome, the Romans, disparaging Pope Gregory, who had already died, on the ground that he had dissipated the Church’s treasures through excessive generosity, wanted—since there was no living person against whom they could direct their anger—to erase his name from his books. Accordingly, when the Romans wished to burn the books of Pope Gregory, the deacon Peter opposed them, declaring that he had often seen the Holy Spirit, in the form of a dove, sitting above Gregory’s head while he was engaged in his work. Confirming this by an oath, he soon died as had been agreed, thereby giving credibility to his testimony. (FRED.) After Richaredus, Bettericus reigns among the Visigoths for seven years.

**607. 3. 16. 20. 15. 46. 1.**

(Vita Gregory) When Pope Sabinianus himself disparaged the generosity of his predecessor Gregory and under this pretext withdrew his hand from the needy, Gregory appeared to him in a vision and reproached him three times for the sin of stinginess and for this disparagement. When Sabinianus did not repent, Gregory reproached and threatened him horribly a fourth time and struck him on the head. Tormented by the pain, Sabinianus died soon afterward. (Gesta of the Pontiffs.) After him, Boniface presides as the sixty-third [pope] of the Roman Church [Note: “[Col. 0113] Sabinianus … quem”: Sig. in his third revision, in the margin; the remaining witnesses.] He obtained from the emperor Phocas that the Roman Church should be the head of all the churches, because the Church of Constantinople was writing that it was the first of all the churches. In a council of seventy-two bishops he decreed under anathema that no one, while the bishop of his city was alive, should dare to speak or form a party for himself; rather, on the third day after the bishop’s deposition, the clergy and people should freely elect a priest. (Gesta of the Franks.) The brothers and kings Theoderic and Theodebert subjugate the Basques to themselves [Note: “esset omnium … subjugant”: Sig. *curis secundis* in an erasure; he had previously written it somewhat more briefly].

**608. 4. 17. 21. 16. 47. 2.**

(FRED.) The body of Saint Victor of Thebes, who suffered martyrdom with Saint Ursus at Solodorum, is discovered. (P. D.) Secundus, a servant of God, shines forth in Italy. (FRED.) Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, is exiled by Theoderic. (BEDA, *Ecclesiastical History*.) Augustine, the first bishop of the English, dies, and Laurence is appointed in his place.

**609. 5. 18. 22. 17. 48. 3.**

(Gesta of the Pontiffs.) Boniface presides as the sixty-fourth [pope] of the Roman Church. (P. D.) He obtained the Pantheon at Rome from the emperor Phocas and converted it into a church of Saint Mary and the holy martyrs; on the Kalends of November he established there the solemnity of All Saints.

**610. 6. 19. 23. 18. 49. 4.**

(BEDA.) The Persians press heavily upon the Roman provinces. (P. D.) Agilulf, king of the Lombards, captures Mantua, Cremona, and certain fortresses of Italy.

**611. 7. 20. 24. 19. 50. 5.**

John, bishop of Alexandria, flourished; on account of his extraordinary generosity toward Christ, he earned the name “the Almsgiver.”

**612. R. 8. P. 21. F. 25. L. 20. A. 51. W. 6.**

(H. m.) Heraclius is elected emperor; after Phocas is killed and burned by fire, he reigns for thirty-one years. (FRED.) Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, is stoned to death and martyred by King Theoderic at the instigation of Brunichildis.

**613. 1. 22. 26. 21. 52. 7.**

(H. m.) The Persians do not cease their attacks against the Romans. (FRED.) After Bettericus, king of the Visigoths, dies, Sisebodus reigns for twenty-nine years [Note: “[Col. 0115] in loco raso”: Sig. enlarged the passage in a second revision]. The power and name of Saint John the Baptist are revealed through miracles at the Gallic city of Maurienne, which was divinely illuminated by relics of his body in the following manner. There was once a woman in that place who was exceedingly devoted to the holy Baptist and asked God to grant her something from his limbs. Persisting in this earnest prayer for three years, when anyone else might already have despaired, she placed her hope in God and swore that she would not eat until she received what she was asking for. Thus, after fasting for seven days, on the seventh day she finally saw a thumb of wondrous brightness appear above the altar and joyfully received God’s gift. When three bishops came to venerate it and wished to remove a portion from this holy relic, they were astonished to see three drops of blood fall from it onto the cloth placed beneath; each rejoiced that he had been deemed worthy of one drop [Note: “[Col. 0115] in loco raso”: Sig. enlarged the passage in a second revision].

**614. 2. 23. 27. 22. 53. 1.**

(MAR., *H. m.*; BURCH. XVII, 44.) Deusdedit presides as the sixty-fifth [pope] of the Roman Church. He instituted a second Mass among the clergy. He also decreed, in accordance with the regulations of his predecessors, that if any men or women had in any manner received their own children from the holy font, they should be separated from one another; or if a man took his spiritual co-mother, or a woman her spiritual co-father, in marriage—from the first gift of the Holy Spirit, which is the nourishment of consecrated salt, up to the seventh gift of the Holy Spirit—they should be separated; nevertheless, the woman should receive her marital dowry and, after the completion of a year, marry another man if she wished [Note: “He also … marry”: in the margin, Sig. in his third revision.] (FRED.) Saint Columbanus is expelled from Francia by King Theoderic at the instigation of his grandmother Brunichildis. Later, leaving his disciple Gallus in Alemannia, he built the monastery of Bobbio in Italy. (Vita of Amandus.) Saint Amandus of Elnone was becoming renowned throughout Gaul for miracles and preaching. Allowinus, also called Bavo, converted by him from a bandit and shut away as a solitary at Ghent, was likewise an example of holiness to everyone.

**615. 3. 24. 28. 23. 54. 2.**

(BEDA, *Ecclesiastical History*.) King Edilfrid of Northumbria destroys in battle Aedan, king of the Scots, together with nearly all his people [Note: “[Col. 0115D] Beda”: Bede says that this happened in 603]. This calamity befell the Scots in accordance with the prophecy of Bishop Augustine, who threatened that the Scots would be killed by the English because they had been reluctant to convert the English to life. The wrath of God also raged against the Scottish monks who had rebelled against Augustine. They had gone to this battle with their king according to their custom: while the king fought with weapons, they themselves fought by praying for him. Twelve hundred of them were killed by the English, with only fifty escaping by flight. Glodesindis of Metz flourished; fleeing from her betrothed, she devoted herself and her possessions to God, after a veil for her head had been sent to her by God through an angel.

**616. 4. 25. 29. 24. 55. 3.**

(H. m.) The Persians invade Syria and capture Damascus. (BEDA, *Ecclesiastical History*.) King Edilbert of Kent dies [Note: “[Col. 0116D] Beda”: Bede gives 613]; after him his son Ealdbald reigned for twenty-five years [Note: “[Col. 0115] XXIIII; Cl. 3, XXII; D, corrected from XXII.”] When Edilbert died, Raduald, king of the East Angles, became the fourth to receive that power of reigning over the English, so that the other kings of the English reigned at his command. After Edilfrid, king of Northumbria, was killed by King Raduald, Eduinus assumed the kingdom of Northumbria. (PAUL THE DEACON.) The Huns defeat the Lombards in Italy and lay waste Forum Julii after capturing it by treachery. (Vita of Lupus.) Saint Lupus, bishop of Sens, flourished; once, while he was consecrating the Eucharist, a gem descended from heaven from God into the chalice.

**617. 5. 26. 30. 25. 1. 4.**

(H. m.) Palestine is afflicted by war from the Persians. The holy city is also captured; as many as ninety thousand men are killed there, Zacharias the patriarch is taken captive, and the holy cross of the Lord itself is carried away. (Gesta of the Franks.) Between the brothers and kings Theoderic and Theodebert, at the instigation of their grandmother Brunichildis, a war more than civil arises. When battle is joined, after an immeasurable slaughter, Theodebert is captured. (BEDA, *Ecclesiastical History*.) Through Ealdbald and the sons of Siberctus, the English relapse into idolatry. (P. D.) After Agilulf, king of the Lombards, dies, his son Adaloald reigns for twelve years.

**618. 6. 27. 31. 1. 2. 5.**

(Gesta of the Pontiffs; MAR.) Boniface presides as the sixty-sixth [pope] of the Roman Church. (IVO, *Decree* VII, 22.) He decreed that no one should be dragged away violently from a church. He decreed that monks should exercise, in the office of the priestly rank, the power of binding and loosing [Note: “He decreed that monks should exercise, in the office of the priestly rank, the power of binding and loosing”: in an erasure, Sig. in his second revision; the remaining witnesses.] (FRED., BEDA, *Ecclesiastical History*.) King Theoderic of the Franks dies. King Ealdbald renounces idolatry. King Lothair kills the sons of King Theoderic, who had been captured in battle. He also had Queen Brunichildis, after being maimed in one foot and one arm, tied to the tail of an untamed mare and torn limb from limb, charging her with having caused ten kings to perish. Thus the monarchy of the Frankish kingdom returns to him. (Gesta of the Franks; Gesta of the Pontiffs.) The patrician Eleutherius, aspiring to the imperial power of the Romans, is killed at Rome. At this time there was a great earthquake in August; a disaster then followed among the people, namely an outbreak of scabies, so severe that no one could recognize his own dead. (A. of Liège.) John the Almsgiver dies. (H. m.) The Persians invade Egypt and capture Alexandria [Note: “Johannes … capiunt”: Sig. *curis secundis* in an erasure; the others].

**619. R. 7. P. 28. F. 32. L. 2. A. 3. W. 6.**

(H. m.) The Persians invade Libya and capture Carthage. (FRED.) King Lothair remits the tribute of twelve thousand solidi that the Lombards had paid to the Franks, since the Lombards had been made his perpetual allies. (BEDA, *Ecclesiastical History*.) Laurence, the second bishop of the English, dies.

**620. 8. 29. 33. 3. 4. 7.**

[Col. 0117B] (H. m.) Chosroes, king of the Persians, by no means permits peace to be made with the Romans. (BEDA.) Anastasius, a Persian converted from a magician into a Christian and monk, is captured by the Persians. After beatings, chains, and imprisonment, and after being hung for a long time by one hand, he is finally beheaded and martyred with seventy others. (Vita of Fara.) The virgin Fara of Christ flourished in Francia. Her brother Faro, who imitated her holiness, likewise flourished: from count he became a cleric, and from cleric bishop of Meaux [Note: “[Col. 0117] added by 1δ and the remaining witnesses; absent from A.”].

**621. 9. 30. 34. 4. 5. 8.**

(FRED.) King Sisebodus of the Visigoths acts vigorously against the Romans; he restores to Visigothic authority the province and other cities that had been wrested from the Franks.

**622. 10. 31. 35. 5. 6. 9.**

[Col. 0117C] (G. p., MAR.) Honorius presides as the sixty-seventh [pope] of the Roman Church. (Vita of Columbanus.) Saint Columbanus dies. His disciple Gallus flourishes in Alemannia.

**623. 11. 32. 36. 6. 7. 10.**

(H. m.) Chosroes, elated by success, rages beyond measure in the shedding of human blood, especially that of Christians. The emperor Heraclius forms an alliance with the Huns.

**624. 12. 33. 37. 7. 8. 11.**

(H. m.) As Heraclius set out to defeat the Persians, he took in his hands a manly image which human hands had not painted. Rather, in the icon, the Word that forms and orders all things brought forth a form without painting, as one born without seed. He attacked Persia and for six continuous years devastated it powerfully. (Vita of Columbanus.) Eustasius, abbot of Luxeuil, and Attila of Bobbio flourish after Columbanus.

**625. 13. 34. 38. 8. 9. 12.**

(FRED.) Pippin, son of Karloman, was exercising authority as mayor of the palace of King Lothair. Saint Arnulfus, son of Arnoldus, son of Ansbertus by Blithildis, daughter of the first King Lothair, assisted Pippin in administering the state. (BEDA, *Ecclesiastical History*.) Mellitus, the third bishop of the English, dies.

**626. 14. 35. 39. 9. 10. 13.**

(H. m.) The emperor Heraclius frequently routs the Persians in minor battles.

[Col. 0118A] **627. 15. 36. 40. 10. 11. 14.**

Austrigisilus of Bourges flourished in Gaul, and under him Sulpicius, Chunibertus of Cologne, and John of Tongeren. In Spain, Isidore of Seville was renowned both for holiness and for learning.

**628. 16. 37. 41. 11. 12. 15.**

(H. m.) Heraclius crushed the Persians in a great battle, in which he killed the Persian commander and nearly all the princes. Traversing Persia, he burned and overthrew the wondrous palaces of the Persians. (FRED.) Lothair entrusted his son Dagobert, raised to kingship, to Pippin and Arnulfus, to reign in Austrasia. (BEDA, *Ecclesiastical History*.) King Eduinus of Northumbria is baptized by Bishop Paulinus and, after Radoald, rules more powerfully than the other kings over the English.

**629. 17. 38. 42. 12. 13. 16.**

(H. m.) Syroes rebelled against his father Chosroes with the Persian princes. After confirming peace with the emperor Heraclius, he killed his father and his father’s sons, and reigned for one year. (Vita of Dagobert.) Dagobert, having incurred the anger of his father, King Lothair, because he had dishonored his father’s counselor by having him tonsured and shaved, fled to the church of Saint Dionysius at Paris. Since he could in no way be dragged out from there, he always held that place dear.

**630. 18. 39. 43. 13. 14. 17.**

(A. of Liège.) Saint Bavo dies. (H. m.) After Persia had been conquered and peace had been confirmed between the Romans and the Persians, Heraclius returned in glory. After King Syroes died, Adesir reigned after him. (P. D.) After Adaloald, king of the Lombards, died, Rotharith reigned after him for sixteen years. (BEDA, H. m.) King Erpualdus, who had apostatized from the faith of Christ with his father Radoald, renounces idolatry with his people at the urging of King Eduinus. (H. m.) At this time the leader of the Arabs, or Saracens, was Muhammad, a false prophet who, from an orphan and a pauper, was elevated to kingship through the illusions of his heresy. Born from the offspring of Ishmael, when he was poor and an orphan he joined himself to a certain exceedingly wealthy kinswoman of his named Chadiga, first as a hired servant and then as a bridegroom, and through her he became rich. Since she was distressed that he was afflicted with an epileptic illness, he said that this was not an illness but that he was seeing the archangel Gabriel at that moment, and that because he could not endure the sight of him he fell down, overcome in mind. He associated with Christians and Jews, confirming certain parts of his false prophecy from their Scriptures. He taught that those who kill an enemy, or who are killed by an enemy, enter paradise. He said that paradise consisted of bodily food and drink, and that there was there a river of wine, milk, and honey, intercourse with women—not those now present, but others to come after a long time—abundant pleasure, and many things of this kind. This is Muhammad, to whom the gentiles still offer the worship of deity. In the kingdom of the Saracens he appointed four commanders, who were called *amirei*. He himself was called *amiras*, or *protosimbolus*. (Gesta of the Franks.) King Dagobert engaged the Saxons in battle. His father, King Lothair, hastening to his aid, obtained victory after killing Bertaldus, the Saxon commander. Traversing all Saxony, he left no Saxon alive who exceeded the measure of his sword [Note: “[Col. 0119] what follows down to the year 652 has fallen out in F3.”].

**631. R. 19. P. 40. F. 44. L. 1. A. 15. W. 18.**

(H. m.) After conquering Persia, the emperor Heraclius brought Patriarch Zacharias back to Jerusalem with the population of captives. Carrying back the holy cross of the Lord, he wished to enter through the gate by which Jesus had gone out to undergo the cross, while dressed in imperial regalia; but the gate was closed by divine power. When, at the warning of an angel, he humbled himself, removed his shoes, and approached again, the gate opened of its own accord. Thus, after the cross had been brought back, he established an annual celebration of its Exaltation. Among the Persians, Ormisda reigns for ten years under the Saracens. (Gesta of the Franks.) After Lothair, the middle king of the Franks, died, his son Dagobert reigned after him for fourteen years [Note: “[Col. 0119] the entire year”: Sig. wrote it in an erasure in his second revision.]

**632. 20. 41. 1. 2. 16. 19.**

(H. m.) The Saracens, who until then had been under Persian rule, defeat the Persians in war and, reversing the former order, reduce them to their own dominion. From this point onward, instead of the kingdom of the Persians, the kingdom of the Saracens should be named. Muhammad, *amiras* of the Saracens, dies; after him Ebubeher rules for three years. (Ib.) An earthquake occurred, and for thirty days a sign in the form of a sword appeared in the sky, foretelling the impending power of the Saracens. (BEDA, *Ecclesiastical History*.) King Eduinus of Northumbria is killed by Penda and Ceduala, king of the Britons, and the faith of Christ in England is shaken.

**633. 21. 1. 2. 3. 17. 20.**

(G. p. MAR.) Severinus, the sixty-eighth [pope] of the Roman Church, and after him John, the sixty-ninth, preside. The emperor Heraclius, falling into the heresy of the Monothelites—that is, of those who believe in one operation in Christ—confounded Church and empire, while, against his wickedness, a disturbance of all things fought back. (H. m.) An unrelenting war arose between the Romans and the Saracens for this reason: when a eunuch of the emperor Heraclius was distributing rations to the soldiers, and among the others the Saracens serving under the emperor had also come to receive their ration, the eunuch indignantly said to them: “The emperor scarcely has enough rations to give the soldiers—how much less to these dogs!” Provoked by grief and shame, they incited the entire Saracen people to revolt. The Saracen commanders attacked the Romans, and three of the commanders were killed by the Romans, together with many others. (Vita of Amandus.) The infant Sigibert, son of King Dagobert, is baptized by Saint Amandus. When everyone was silent, the forty-day-old infant himself answered, “Amen,” and Amandus was ordained bishop of Tongeren.

[Col. 0120A] **634. 22. 2. 3. 4. 18. 21.**

(BEDA, *Ecclesiastical History*.) The Romans and Saracens clash with varying results. The successors of King Eduinus, having returned to idolatry, are soon killed by King Ceduala. [(FRED.) King Dagobert defeats the Slavs in war [Note: “[Col. 0119] added by 1β and the other seventy witnesses, except A.”].]

**635. 23. 3. 4. 5. 19. 22.**

(H. m.) Ebubeher, *amiras*, dies; after him Haumar rules for twelve years. While the Saracens were ravaging Syria, Heraclius transferred the holy cross of the Lord from Jerusalem to Constantinople. (BEDA, *Ecclesiastical History*.) Oswald, son of King Edilfrid, having assumed the kingdom of Northumbria after Eduinus, kills Ceduala, king of the Britons. Because he upheld the faith of Christ, he surpassed all the kings of Britain in eminence and brought under his authority peoples of four languages: Picts, Scots, Britons, and English. Bishop Aidan, one of Saint Columba’s disciples, came from Scotland and flourished among the English in holiness and learning. [(FRED.) King Dagobert defeats the Basques in war [Note: “[Col. 0119] added by 1β and the remaining witnesses, except A.”].]

**636. 24. 1. 5. 6. 20. 23.**

(Gesta of the Pontiffs.) Theodorus presides as the seventieth [pope] of the Roman Church. (H. m.) After capturing Damascus, the Saracens occupy Phoenicia and Egypt.

**637. 25. 2. 6. 7. 21. 24.**

[(AIMOIN., IV, 41.) At this time three brothers flourished in Francia: Ado, Rado, and Dado, who was also called Audoenus. Each demonstrated his devotion toward God by founding a monastery. Of these, Dado was the referendary of King Dagobert. A referendary was so called because public documents were referred to him, so that through him they could be confirmed with the king’s ring or seal. Eligius the goldsmith encouraged them toward this. He had long been renowned at the court of King Lothair and, through a gift of King Dagobert [Note: “[Col. 0119] 1γ and the remaining witnesses, except A, expanded the passage thus, partly in an erasure and partly at the bottom of the page; A has: ‘Eligius the goldsmith, long renowned at the court of King Lothair, while still a layman built Solignac through a gift of King Dagobert.’ Sig. first published it in that form.”], built the monastery of Solignac, where Saint Remaclus, coming from Aquitania, devoted himself to being trained under him in the service of Christ. Saint Aurea also flourished; Eligius placed her over the convent of virgins that he had built for himself at Paris. [Saint Dado built a monastery within the forest of Brie, which is called Resbacis; there he appointed Saint Aigulf as first abbot [Note: “[Col. 0119] added by 1γ and the remaining witnesses, except A.”].]]

**638. 26. 3. 7. 8. 22. 25.**

[Col. 0120D] (Vita of Amandus.) Saint Amandus, having set aside the bishopric of Tongeren, devoted himself to the ministry of the word. Under him Saint Landoald flourished. He instructed from childhood Lambert, son of Aprus, an illustrious man who would later become bishop and martyr, and led him into the way of God. (A. m.) The Saracens capture Jerusalem, which they had besieged for two years. Abbot Romaricus and Goericus, bishop of Metz, flourish.

[Col. 0121A] **639. R. 27. S. 4. F. 8. L. 9. A. 23. W. 26.**

(H. m.) The Saracens occupy Syria. The Jews in Spain become Christians. For Sisibutus, the most glorious king of the Goths, subjected to himself by warfare many provinces in Spain and cities of the Roman forces and converted the Jews in his kingdom to the faith of Christ.

**640. 28. 5. 9. 10. 24. 27.**

(*Life of Chlodulfus*.) Saint Arnulfus, from mayor of the palace becoming bishop of Metz, and from bishop becoming a solitary, falls asleep in Christ. His son Chlodulfus, later bishop of Metz, imitates his father’s holiness. His mother Doda, shut away at Trier, serves Christ. (Gesta of the Franks.) The Saracens capture Antioch. [Col. 0121B] (H. m.) King Dagobert sends his son Sigibert as king to the Austrasians, under the guardianship of Pippin and Bishop Chunibertus. (BEDA, *Ecclesiastical History*.) After Ealdbald, king of the English, dies, his son Earcombertus reigns after him for twenty-four years. He was the first in England to destroy the idols of the gods, extend the faith of Christ, and decree that the fast of Lent should be observed lawfully in England.

**641. 29. 6. 10. 11. 1. 28.**

(H. m.) After defeating the Persians once again in war and putting their king Ormisda to flight, the Saracens subjugate all Persia to themselves.

**642. 30. 7. 11. 12. 2. 29.**

(H. m.) The emperor Heraclius dies. His son Constantinus succeeds him and, in the fourth month of his reign, is poisoned and killed by his stepmother Martina and the patriarch Pyrrhus. Martina seizes the empire with her son Heraclona. (FRED.) After Sisebodus, king of the Visigoths, dies, Suitilan succeeds him and reigns for two years. (Ib.) Dagobert, with the Saxons assisting him against the Wends, grants them an annual tribute of five hundred cows.

**643. 1. 8. 12. 13. 3. 1.**

(H. m.) Heraclona, after his nose was cut off, and his mother Martina, after her tongue was cut out, are exiled. Constans, also called Constantinus, son of Constantinus, reigns for twenty-six years [Note: “Thus 1 (corrected from XXVII); D, XXVII; A, XXV; B4* and C3.”]. (BEDA, *Ecclesiastical History*.) King Oswald of Northumbria is killed by Penda, king of the Mercians; his son Oswi reigns after him for twenty-eight years. (FRED.) Dagobert subdues the Basques. Judacail, king of the Britons, purchases his favor for himself. [The virgin of Christ Reginulfa shines in holiness in Gaul [Note: “added by 1β and the remaining witnesses.”].]

**644. 1. 9. 13. 14. 4. 2.**

(H. m.) Haumar, *amiras*, builds a temple for himself at Jerusalem. Since the structure could in no way stand, at the Jews’ suggestion he orders the cross to be removed from above Mount Olivet; thus the structure of the temple was able to stand. (FRED.) In Spain, after Suintila had been rejected by the Visigoths on account of his cruelty, Sisenandus, raised to the kingship through Dagobert’s assistance, reigns for twenty years.

**645. 2. 10. 14. 15. 5. 1.**

King Dagobert of the Franks dies. It was revealed in a vision to a certain person that his soul had been seized for the judgment of God. When many saints were protesting against it because he had despoiled their churches, and the evil angels already wished to drag it away to the punishments of hell, it was freed from punishment through the intervention of Saint Dionysius, martyr of Paris, to whom Dagobert had been especially devoted. Chlodoveus, son of Dagobert, reigned after him for seventeen years, while his brother Sigibert was already reigning in Austrasia. [The mayor of the palace of this Chlodoveus [Col. 0122B] was Erchanoaldus [Note: “add. 1β.; rell. praeter A.”].]

**646. 3. 11. 1. 16. 6. 2.**

(P. D.) After Rotharith, king of the Lombards, dies, his son Rodoaldus reigns for five years. (A. of Liège.) Saint Remaclus is ordained bishop of Tongeren. [(Life of Saint Gertrude.) Modoaldus, brother of Itta and maternal uncle of Saint Gertrude, brings distinction to the archbishopric of Trier through his learning and holiness. His sister Severa, abbess in the same city, likewise does not fall short of her brother’s holiness [Note: “add 1. or Ans. or 1β.; rell. praeter A.”].]

**647. 4. 12. 2. 1. 7. 3.**

(H. m.) A certain Persian, pretending that he wished to worship Haumar, *amiras* of the Saracens, killed him by thrusting a sword into his belly. Hotmen succeeded him and ruled for ten years. (Gesta of the Franks.) Pippin, mayor of the palace, dies [Note: “Sig. is mistaken: he died around the year 610.”]. His son Grimoaldus exercises powerful authority at the court of King Sigibert.

**648. 5. 1. 3. 2. 8. 4.**

(H. m.) The Saracens occupy Africa. (BEDA.) Saint Furseus flourished in Ireland. Undertaking pilgrimage for Christ, he reached Gaul, [and, honorably received by King Chlodoveus, founded the monastery of Lagny [Note: “added by either Ans. or 1β, and by the remaining witnesses except A.”].] Not long afterward, his brothers Foillanus and Ultanus followed him with the same desire for pilgrimage and flourished throughout Gaul. Of these, Foillanus later founded the monastery of Fosses through the gift of the virgin Gertrude; there he also rests, crowned with martyrdom. (Gesta of the Pontiffs.) Martin presides as the seventy-first [pope] of the Roman Church. (FRED.) King Sigibert engages in battle with Radulfus, duke of the Thuringians.

[Col. 0122D] **649. 6. 2. 4. 3. 9. 5.**

Eligius flourished as bishop of Noyon, Audoenus, also called Dado, as bishop of Rouen, and Philibertus and Richarius as abbots of Ponthieu. Ansigisus, son of Saint Arnulfus, also flourished; Begga, the sister of Grimoaldus, had married him.

**650. 7. 3. 5. 4. 10. 6.**

(Vita of Gertrude.) Itta, having been left a widow, devoted herself and her possessions to God at the urging of Saint Amandus, founded the monastery of Nivelles, and placed over it her daughter Gertrude, a virgin worthy of God. Autbertus, bishop of Cambrai, flourished.

**651. R. 8. S. 4. F. 6. L. 5. A. 11.**

(P. D.) After Rodoaldus, king of the Lombards, is killed, Aripert reigns for nine years [Note: “VII. C3.”]. (Vita of Saint Remaclus.) King Sigibert, despairing of descendants, built twelve monasteries here and there for God, among which Stavelot and Malmedy were preeminent. In this work he was assisted by Grimoaldus, mayor of the palace, and Remaclus, bishop of Tongeren. Not long afterward Remaclus, wearied by the disturbances of secular life, assumed the monastic habit at Stavelot itself. In those days many of both sexes flourished in Gaul who, as a testimony to their holiness, devoted their efforts to building monasteries for God. Among these, in our vicinity, flourished Landelinus, also called Morosus, who had been brought back from banditry to Christ by Bishop Autbertus and founded the monastery of Lobbes; Gislenus of Celle; Madelgarius, a duke also called Vincentius of Hautmont and Soignies, and his wife Waldetrudis of Mons; and Waldetrudis’s sister Aldegundis of Maubeuge. Trudo of Hesbaye was also growing into a soldier of Christ. Besides these, many others from England or Scotland, traveling as pilgrims in Gaul, sowed the word of God and produced much fruit for God, namely Etto, Bertuinus, and Eloquius. (Translation of Saint Benedict.) The monastery of Floriacum is founded by the abbot Leodeboldus. Not long afterward, the body of Saint Benedict the abbot, brought from the fortress of Cassino by the monk Agiulfus, is transferred there. His sister Saint Scholastica’s body is transferred to Le Mans.

**652. 9. 5. 7. 1. 12. 8.**

(BEDA.) The emperor Constantinus, deceived by Paul of Constantinople, issued a *Typos* against the Catholic faith, declaring that neither one nor two wills or operations in Christ should be confessed—as though Christ were to be believed to have neither will nor operation. For this reason Pope Martin, having convened a synod of 105 bishops at Rome, anathematized the heretics Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, and also Paul, the instigator of the present persecution, who was harassing the Church by open and secret attacks. King Sigibert adopts Hildebert, the son of Grimoaldus the mayor of the palace, as his son and heir to the kingdom.

**653. 10. 6. 8. 2. 13. 9.**

Judochus, son of the king of the Britons, rejecting kingdom and world, lived as a pilgrim and hermit and rested in Christ in the district of Ponthieu [Note: “added by 1γ and the remaining witnesses.”]. (Gesta of the Pontiffs.) The emperor Constantinus, having sent an exarch to Italy, attacks the Church of God.

**654. 11. 7. 9. 3. 14. 10.**

(H. m.) Fire fell from heaven, and great fear came upon humanity. A very severe pestilence raged for three summer months. Everyone visibly saw a good angel and an evil angel circling the city at night; whenever, at the good angel’s command, the evil angel struck the door of a house with the spear he carried in his hand, so many people from that house died on the following day. [At this time Saint Foillanus of Fosses is martyred [Note: “added by either Ans. or 1δ, and by the remaining witnesses except A.”].]

**655. 12. 8. 10. 1. 15. 11.**

(H. m.) After capturing Rhodes, the Saracens overturned its famous Colossus; from its bronze nine hundred camels were loaded.

**656. 13. 9. 11. 5. 16. 12.**

The emperor Constantinus engages the Saracens in a naval battle and is disgracefully defeated. (Ib.) King Sigibert of the Austrasians dies, entrusting his son Dagobert, still extremely young, to the loyalty of Grimoaldus, so that he might be advanced to the kingdom with his assistance. (BEDA, *Ecclesiastical History*.) King Oswi of Northumbria, after making a vow to the God of heaven, engages King Penda of the Mercians with a small army. Amid the immense slaughter of the Mercians, he kills King Penda himself and causes the people of the Mercians to be converted to Christ. He also subjected the Picts to the kingdom of the English.

**657. 14. 10. 12. 6. 17. 13.**

(Gesta of the Pontiffs.) Olympius, an exarch sent by the emperor Constantinus to govern Italy and ordered to kill Pope Martin, since he could not accomplish this otherwise, arranged that during the solemn celebration of Mass, when the pope himself was handing him holy communion, his own guardsman should kill the pope. But at the hour of holy communion the guardsman could in no way see the pope. The exarch, however, was soon disgracefully defeated by the Saracens in Sicily and died even more disgracefully. (H. m.) After Hotmen, *amiras* of the Saracens, was killed, Muhavias, from being one of the commanders, became *amiras* and ruled for twenty-four years. (Gesta of the Franks.) Grimoaldus, mayor of the palace, had his lord Dagobert, son of Sigibert, tonsured and sent through Dido, bishop of Poitiers, to Scotland; he made his own son Hildebert king of the Austrasians.

**658. 15. 1. 13. 7. 18. 14.**

(Ib.) The Franks, grieving over Grimoaldus’s treachery toward Sigibert’s son, brought him, after his capture, to Paris for the judgment of Chlodoveus. Chlodoveus had him confined and consumed by a bitter death in prison; and he made his own younger son Hildricus king of the Austrasians. (Vita of Gertrude.) Itta, mother of Saint Gertrude, dies. (Vita of Lambert.) After Bishop Theodardus was martyred, Saint Lambertus, son of Count Aprus, brings glory to the bishopric of Tongeren through the splendor of his nobility and the grace of his holiness. At Arras, while the body of Saint Vedastus was being transferred by Bishop Vindicianus [Note: “[Col. 0123] Autherto B2. 5. Cl. 3. D., which is correct”], with Lambertus of Tongeren, Audomarus of Thérouanne, and other holy bishops and abbots present, Audomarus, who was blind from old age, was enlightened through the prayers of the bishops present and the merits of Saint Vedastus. Although he complained bitterly that he had been freed from blindness—a blindness he joyfully acknowledged had been inflicted upon him by God for his salvation—he was blinded again according to his own vow [Note: “[Col. 0125] prius breviora”: Sig. himself enlarged the previously shorter wording in an erasure in a second revision, together with the following year] (cf. Bald. I, 19).

**659. R. 16. S. 2. F. 14. L. 8. A. 19. W. 15.**

(Gesta of the Pontiffs.) After Pope Martin, exiled by order of Constantinus for confessing the faith and dying there, Eugenius presides as the seventy-second [pope] of the Roman Church. (H. m.) Constantinus subjugates Sclavia to himself [Note: “Sig. wrote the entire year in an erasure in his second revision; A has LXXI. R. e. p. (with C. S. s. s. absent).”].

**660. 17. 3. 15. 9. 20. 16.**

(H. m.) Muhavias, *amiras* of the Saracens, makes a treaty with the emperor Constantinus, so that the Saracens should pay tribute to the Romans—namely, one thousand *nomismata*, one slave, and one horse each day. King Chlodoveus, uncovering the body of Saint Dionysius of Paris, broke and carried away a bone of his arm, irreverently though eagerly; immediately afterward he fell into perpetual madness. (P. D.) After Aripert, king of the Lombards, dies, his sons Godebertus and Bertarith spend a year not so much arranging the kingdom as contending over it.

**661. 18. 4. 16. 1. 21. 17.**

(Gesta of the Pontiffs.) Vitalianus presides as the seventy-third [pope] of the Roman Church. (A. of Liège.) Saint Amandus of Elnone dies. (H. m.) The emperor Constantinus kills his brother Theodosius. (P. D.) Grimoaldus, duke of Turin, treacherously kills Godebertus, son of King Aripert, seizes his kingdom, marries Godebertus’s sister, and reigns for nine years. [(A. of Laubach; FLOD.) Saint Nivardus, archbishop of Reims, and his successor Reolus, as well as Bercharius the martyr, who was the first abbot of the monks of Autun, and Saint Berta, martyr and abbess, flourished in holiness in Francia [Note: “Thus 1γ, in an erasure of half a line and in the margin, as do the remaining witnesses except A; A has: ‘and he compelled his brother Pertarith to go into exile.’ Sig. first published it in that form.”].]

**662. 19. 5. 17. 1. 22. 18.**
(P. D.) Emperor Constantine invaded Italy and captured many cities of the Lombards; he besieged Beneventum, where King Grimoald severely defeated his army. (G. r. F.) King Chlodoveus of the Franks died, and his son Lotharius succeeded him and reigned for four years. His mayor of the palace after Erchauoald was Ebroinus. (V. Balth.) Queen Balthildis, Lotharius’s mother, built the monasteries of Corbie and Chelles for God. (P. D.) From this time onward, as the kings of the Franks degenerated from their customary strength and wisdom, the power of the kingdom was administered by the mayors of the palace, while the kings reigned in name alone. Their custom was to rule indeed according to their birth, but to do or arrange nothing, except irrationally to eat and drink, remain at home, preside before the whole people on the Kalends of May, give and receive greetings, accept and return services and gifts, and thus dwell with their household until the following May.

[Col. 0126A] **663. 20. 6. 1. 2. 23. 19.**

(Ib.) Emperor Constantine came to Rome; after stripping it of almost everything that served to adorn the city, he went to Sicily.

**664. 21. 7. 2. 3. 24. 20.**

Emperor Constantine attempted to transfer the imperial government to the city of Rome, but the people of Constantinople resisted him. (BEDA, H. e.) In England a major dispute arose between the Angles and the Scots concerning the observance of Easter, with the glorious King Oswi presiding; he also agreed with the Angles, who celebrated Easter according to Roman custom. (FRED.) After Sisenand, king of the Visigoths, died, Chintilan reigned for sixteen years. (V. Gertr.) Saint Gertrude of Nivelles died [Note: [Col. 0125] Hirsch proves that she died in 659, p. 64].

[Col. 0126B] **665. 22. 8. 3. 4. 25. 1.**

(A. Leod.) Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon, died. (BEDA, H. e.) Earconbert, king of the Angles, died, and his son Egbert reigned after him for nine years [Note: [Col. 0125] VIII. A. C1. 3. D.].

**666. 23. 9. 4. 5. 1. 2.**

(G. r. F.) King Lotharius of the Franks died. His brother Theodericus was raised to the kingship by Ebroinus, mayor of the palace.

**667. 24. 10. 1. 6. 2. 3.**

(Ib.) King Theodericus was rejected by the Franks because of Ebroinus’s insolence, and his brother Hildricus, who ruled in Austrasia, was summoned by everyone to reign. Thereafter Theodericus and Ebroinus were tonsured, and Theodericus was exiled at Paris to the monastery of Saint Dionysius, while Ebroinus was exiled to Luxeuil [Col. 0126C]. Hildricus’s mayor of the palace was Vulfoaldus. He founded the monastery of Saint Michael the Archangel in the diocese of Verdun, above the Meuse.

**668. 25. 11. 1. 7. 3. 4**

(BEDA.) Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Adrian were sent into England by Pope Vitalian.

**669. 26. 12. 2. 8. 4. 5.**

(H. m.) Emperor Constantine, also called Constans, hated by all his own people, was killed by his own men in a bath at Syracuse. A certain Mizius, who had plotted tyranny in Sicily, was soon put down. Constantine, the son of Constans, ruled as emperor for seventeen years.

**670. 1. 13. 3. 9. 5. 6.**

[Col. 0126D] (G. pont.) Adeodatus, the seventy-fourth, presided over the Roman Church. (BEDA, H. e.) After Oswi, king of Northumbria, died, his son Egfridus reigned for fifteen years. (P. D.) King Grimoald of the Lombards, on the ninth day after being bled, when, having taken a bow, he attempted to strike a dove, ruptured a vein in his arm; and when physicians applied poisonous medicines to him, he died. But Pertarith, son of King Ariperth, recalled from exile by divine providence and restored to the kingship by the Lombards, reigned for eighteen years [Note: [Col. 0127] XVII A. C1. 3. D. The following words, “At this time ... is illumined,” are added in the margin in Sig. cur. tertiis; the others]. At this time Saint Prejectus, an Arvernian citizen and bishop, flourished; he was also martyred by the leading men of that city in revenge for Hector, the patrician of Marseilles, who had been killed by King Hildricus of the Franks because of the injustices he had inflicted upon the Church of Arvernia. (BALD.) In the territory of Cambrai, the virgin of God Maxelendis, fleeing from her lover Harduinus because of her vow of virginity, was martyred by him. He was soon struck blind, but after three years he was restored to sight by her.

**671. R. 2. S. 14. F. 4. L. 1. A. 6. W. 7.**

(H. m.) Emperor Constantine, suspecting that his brothers might reign jointly with him, cut off their noses. (BEDA, H. e.) At this time a certain man in Britain rose from the dead and recounted many things that he had seen concerning places of punishment and the place of purgatorial fire.

**672. 3. 15. 5. 2. 7. 8.**

(BEDA.) The Saracens invaded Italy and, after plundering everything, returned to Alexandria. (V. S. Am.) Amatus, bishop of Sens, was long afflicted by King Theodericus through a harsh and irrevocable exile [Note: [Col. 0127] “Amatus ... was afflicted,” Sig. cur. tertiis; the others].

**673. 4. 16. 6. 3. 8. 9.**

(BEDA, H. e.) Egberth, king of the Angles, died; his brother Lothere succeeded him and reigned for twelve years. (H. m.) A rainbow appeared in the sky in March, and all flesh trembled, so that everyone said that the end had come [Note: [Col. 0127] “The fiery apparition ... was at hand,” Sig. cur. sec.; the others].

**674. 5. 17. 7. 4. 1. 10.**

[Col. 0127C] (BEDA, H. e.) Theodore held a synod in England and established many measures useful to the Church. This Theodore wrote a penitential book, distinguishing the manner of each offense with marvelous and careful discernment.

**675. 6. 18. 8. 5. 2. 11.**

(H. m.) A fleet of the Saracens arrived against Constantinople. After they had engaged the Christians fruitlessly for several years, on their return they perished, being drowned in large numbers.

**676. 7. 19. 9. 6. 3. 12.**

(V. S. Leod.) King Hildricus, by the frivolity of his conduct, aroused the hatred of the Franks against himself. Saint Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, was imprisoned by him at Luxeuil. (P. D.) In Italy there were rains and thunder such as no human age remembers, so that even people and livestock perished by lightning [Col. 0127D]. And unless the Lord had been appeased by the litanies that they recited daily, people would not have been able to thresh or store grain in the barns; indeed, the rains were so abundant that from them the legumes themselves sprouted again and reached maturity [Note: [Col. 0127] Here A. presents the words of Saint Audoenus, also called Dado, from R. e. o., from the year 690, where he omits them].

[Col. 0128A] **677. 8. 20. 10. 7. 4. 13.**

(G. pont.) Donus, the seventy-fourth, presided over the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0127] Sig. writes this here in error and continues in the same error below; B4*. 5. have seventy-five and continue accordingly; C1. 3., likewise, call Donus seventy-five, Agatho seventy-six, and Leo also seventy-six, so that from that point they again agree with Sigebertus; D., which had already preceded Sigebertus by one number from the year 530 onward, calls Donus seventy-six, Agatho seventy-seven, Leo again seventy-seven, and so forth]. (H. m.) When the Saracens and Arabs engaged the Roman army, thirty thousand Saracens were killed. (G. pont.) For three months, beginning in August, a star penetrating the heavens with its rays appeared in the eastern sky, from cockcrow until morning; a great mortality then followed in the East.

**678. 9. 21. 11. 8. 5. 14.**

(H. m.) The architect Kallinicus fled from Heliopolis in Syria to the Romans and invented the “sea fire.” Using it, the Romans burned the ships of the Saracens, setting them and their crews completely ablaze, and thus won the victory.

**679. 10. 22. 12. 9. 6. 15.**

[Col. 0128B] (G. pont.) Agatho, the seventy-fifth, presided over the Roman Church. (G. r. F.) The Frank Bodilo, whom Hildricus had ordered to be beaten while bound to a stake, ambushed Hildricus during a hunt and killed him together with his pregnant wife Blithildis. Theodericus was restored to the kingdom. Leudesius, son of Erchonoald, was made mayor of the palace on the advice of Bishop Leodegarius, who had been recalled from Luxeuil, and of the other nobles. (H. m.) Peace was confirmed between the Romans and the Saracens for thirty years, on the condition that the Saracens pay the Romans annually three thousand pounds of gold, fifty captive men, and fifty noble horses.

**680. 11. 23. 1. 10. 7. 16.**

(H. m.) The people of the Bulgars, who likewise came forth from Scythia and were raging everywhere, ravaged Thrace under their leader Bathaia [Col. 0128C]. When the army of Emperor Constantine encountered them, it was shamefully put to flight and severely beaten; and their raids gained such strength throughout the Roman state that the emperor, after making peace with them, was compelled to provide them with annual payments. (G. r. F.) Ebroinus, having emerged from Luxeuil, regained his strength, crushed his plotters, attacked King Theodericus, plundered his treasures and the Church, and killed Leudesius, the mayor of the palace. Pretending that a certain Chlodoveus was the son of King Lotharius, he made him king and compelled as many people as he could, by punishments, threats, and blandishments, to swear allegiance to him. (FRED.) After King Chintilan died, his son Tolgan, still a child, succeeded him in the kingdom of the Visigoths and reigned for four years. From this time the kingdom of the Bulgars should be recorded; their king was Bathaias [Col. 0128D]. (G. pont.) Pope Agatho received an imperial decree from the rulers, as he had requested, by which the amount customarily given for the ordination of a pontiff was reduced. It was nevertheless stipulated that, if an election should take place after his death, the elected man was not to be ordained unless a general decree had first been brought into the royal city according to ancient custom [Col. 0129A], and the ordination was to proceed with their knowledge and authorization.

**681. R. 12. S. 24. F. 2. L. 11. A. 8. W. 1. Bulg. 1.**

(BEDA.) The Sixth Ecumenical Council was convened at Constantinople. In it George, bishop of Constantinople, was recalled from the error of the Monothelites; Macarius of Antioch, however, and all who denied two wills and two operations in the one person of Christ, were anathematized. There were 289 bishops at this synod [Note: [Col. 0129D] Beda has 150].

**682. 13. 25. 3. 12. 9. 2. 2.**

(Cont. Fred.) Saint Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, was captured by Ebroinus and harshly tormented together with his brother Gerinus. Gerinus was soon afterward buried beneath stones [Col. 0129B]. (H. m.) Muhavias, emir of the Saracens, died; after him his son Gizid ruled for three years. (G. pont.) In Italy there was an extremely severe mortality among the people for three summer months.

**683. 14. 1. 4. 13. 10. 3. 3.**

(BEDA.) In England Queen Edildrudis flourished. Although she had been married to three men, she remained a virgin. After her death, her body was found incorrupt eleven years after her burial.

**684. 15. 2. 5. 14. 11. 4. 4.**

(G. pont.) Leo the Younger, the seventy-sixth, presided over the Roman Church. The Church of Ravenna, by imperial decree, was restored under the authority of the apostolic see, namely, so that whoever was elected bishop there would come to Rome [Col. 0129C] to be ordained. (BEDA, H. e.) King Egfridus severely ravaged the harmless people of Ireland. (Fred.) After Tolgan was rejected by the Visigoths because of the frivolity of his youth and tonsured as a cleric, Chintasindus reigned after him for twenty years.

**685. 16. 3. 6. 15. 12. 1. 5.**

(G. pont.) Benedictus, the seventy-seventh, presided over the Roman Church. (H. m.) After Gizid died, Marhuan ruled the Saracens for one year. (V. Lamb.) King Theodericus received Ebroinus back into favor, summoned a synod of bishops on his advice, and at it deprived many of them of their bishoprics on Ebroinus’s judgment; he also condemned some to irrevocable exile. Amid the stormy turmoil of this domestic persecution, Saint Lambertus too, removed from the bishopric of Maastricht, sought the harbor of monastic tranquility at the monastery of Stavelot, and there lived in retirement for seven years [Col. 0129D]. (V. Leod.) After Saint Leodegarius had long been tortured by Ebroinus—after hunger and the filth of prison, after the removal of his eyes, after the cutting off of the soles of his feet, after the cutting out of his tongue and lips—he finally completed his martyrdom by decapitation. (BEDA, H. e.) Ansigisus, the father of Pippin, was killed by Gunduinius, whom he himself had found, brought up, and received from the sacred font, and whom he had advanced to the highest military honors [Col. 0130A]. King Lohere of the Angles died, and King Egfridus of Northumbria was killed by the Picts. The Picts, Scots, and Britons pressed the Angles very hard and, having recovered the liberty that they had formerly lost through the Angles, invaded a large part of England. After Lohere, Edrich reigned for two years. After Egfridus, his brother Alfrid succeeded him and reigned for twenty years. (V. Kil.) Saint Chilian, a Scot and bishop of Würzburg, flourished.

**686. 17. 1. 7. 16. 1. 2. 6.**

(G. pont.) John, the seventy-eighth, presided over the Roman Church. (H. m.) After Emperor Constantine died, his son Justinian ruled for ten years. Habdalan ruled the Saracens for one year. Begga, the widow of Ansigisus, devoted herself and her possessions to God and founded the monastery of Andenne [Col. 0130B].

**687. 1. 1. 8. 17. 2. 3. 7.**

(G. pont.) Conon, the seventy-ninth, presided over the Roman Church. (H. m.) Habdimelich, emir, ruled the Saracens for twenty-two years. Peace was agreed between Justinian and Habdimelich, so that the Saracens would pay the Romans every day one thousand gold coins, one slave, and one horse. (G. r. Fr.) After Vulfoaldus, mayor of the palace, died, Pippin, son of Ansigisus, ruled in Austrasia together with Duke Martinus. Ebroinus engaged them in battle and won the victory; Martinus, fleeing, was killed by Ebroinus. (P. D.) After Pertarid, king of the Lombards, died, his son Cunipert reigned for twelve years. (BEDA, H. e.) After Edrich, king of the Angles, died, foreign kings ravaged and divided the kingdom of England for four years. Saint Cuthbert, bishop of the Angles, died.

**688. 2. 1. 9. 1. 1. 4. 8.**

(G. pont.) Sergius, the eightieth, presided over the Roman Church. He found in the treasury of Saint Peter a large portion of the Lord’s cross. The order of celebrating the Mass had by then already been fully arranged by the apostles and apostolic men. The Church recited the epistles and Gospels according to the tradition of the ancients; these were organized in a book called the *Comes*, which Jerome is said to have written for Constantine. Pope Alexander, the sixth pope, instituted the blessing and sprinkling of water, instituted the annual blessing of oil by the bishop, and ordered the old oil to be burned because of the newness of the sacrament. (BURCH., V, 3.) He inserted the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion into the consecration of the Eucharist, and just as blood and water flowed from the side of the crucified Jesus, so he instituted that water be mixed with wine in the consecration itself, decreeing that neither wine without water nor water without wine should be offered. The first Pope Sixtus, the seventh, instituted the hymn “Holy, holy, holy, Lord” [Note: [Col. 0129] For the passage “oil ... Sixtus,” in an erasure of one line he had first written “water”; in the margin, Sig. cur. tertiis; the rest (uncertain OCR)]; Pope Telesphorus, the eighth, instituted the fast of Lent seven weeks before Easter and added the angelic hymn “Glory to God in the highest.” Pope Damasus, the thirty-fifth, instituted that “I believe in one God” be sung on solemn days [Col. 0131A], and this was confirmed by decree of the Second Ecumenical Council, held at Constantinople by 150 bishops. Pope Celestine, the forty-first, instituted the antiphonal singing of the introits, graduals, offertories, and communions from the Psalms. Pope Gelasius, the forty-seventh, composed the collects and prefaces. Pope Gregory, the sixty-first, added “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”), “Christe eleison” (“Christ, have mercy”), and “Alleluia” (“Praise the Lord”) outside the period of the Quinquagesima, as well as the Lord’s Prayer, through which alone the apostles consecrated, after the canon of consecration. (G. pont.) To all these things Sergius added this final measure: that, during Communion, the clergy should sing “Lamb of God.” He also decreed that on the Annunciation of the Lord, on the festival called the Lord’s Presentation (*Hypapante*), and on the Nativity and Assumption of Saint Mary, litanies should be made. By divine revelation he transferred the body of the first Pope Leo [Col. 0131B]. (V. Leod.) The innocence and merit of Saint Leodegarius were demonstrated by many miracles. (H. m.) The emperor broke the peace agreed upon with the Saracens, inflicted evils upon them, and suffered worse evils from them. (G. r. F.) Ermenfridus killed Ebroinus, mayor of the palace of Neustria, who was oppressing the Franks insolently, and fled to Pippin. Waratho was appointed mayor of the palace in place of Ebroinus [Note: [Col. 0131] After this, one and a half lines were erased, beginning “Ansigisus ...” One copy, A., presents them as follows: “Ansigisus, the father of Pippin, was killed by Gunduinus. He himself had found him, raised him, and received him from the sacred font, and had advanced him to the highest military honors.” But these words were later erased; compare the year 685].

**689. R. 3. S. 2. F. 10. L. 2. A. 2. W. 5. B. 9.**

(H. m.) Justinian broke the peace made with the Bulgars and, engaging them, first defeated them, but afterward was ambushed by them and barely escaped. (Cont. Fred.) A battle was fought between Pippin and Gissemarus, the son of Waratho, near the fortress of Namur. Not long afterward Gissemarus was divinely punished, and Waratho also died; Bertarius, Waratho’s son-in-law, became mayor of the palace under King Theodericus.

**690. 4. 3. 11. 3. 3. 6. 10.**

(G. r. F.) Saint Audoenus, bishop of Rouen, died [Note: [Col. 0131] “Saint Audoenus, bishop of Rouen, died” is absent in A., where it is read under the year 676; C3; B3* and D. place it at the end of the year, and C4* in the following year]. (BEDA, H. e.) Archbishop Theodore of the Angles died. (Cont. Fred.) The Franks, hostile to Bertarius, sought to secure Pippin’s friendship through hostages and incited him against Bertarius’s authority.

**691. 5. 4. 12. 4. 4. 7. 11.**

King Theodericus, together with Bertarius, engaged Pippin and was defeated; Bertarius was killed by his own men. King Theodericus was captured by Pippin. Pippin subjected Neustria to himself and, ruling the entire kingdom alone under Theodericus, improved the state of affairs. He also restored Saint Lambertus to the bishopric of Maastricht [Col. 0131D]. (BEDA, H. e.) Saint Remaclus is said to have died this year. Wichtred, son of King Egbert, strengthened by religion and diligence, freed the people of the Angles from the oppression of foreigners and reigned over them for thirty-five years.

[Col. 0132A] **692. 6. 5. 13. 5. 1. 8. 12.**

(P. D.) Alahis, after putting Chunipert to flight, seized the kingdom of the Lombards; Chunipert engaged him in battle, killed him, and recovered the kingdom. (BEDA, H. e.) Willibrord, coming from England with twelve companions, flourished in holiness in Gaul. Saint Wandrigisilus, also called Wando, nephew of Ansigisus, mayor of the palace, through his brother Walchiso, flourished at this time; he built the monasteries of Fécamp and Fontenelle for God [Note: [Col. 0131] “In Gaul ... he built” is written in erasure in Sig. cur. tertiis].

**693. 7. 6. 14. 6. 2. 9. 13.**

(Cont. Fred.) King Theodericus of the Franks died. His son Chlodoveus reigned after him for four years. (H. m.) The Saracens severely defeated the Romans in a very great battle. (BEDA, H. e.) The priests Evaldus the White and Evaldus the Black, coming from England, were martyred in Gaul [Col. 0132B] and, by order of Pippin, were buried at Cologne.

**694. 8. 7. 1. 7. 3. 10. 14.**

(Ib.) Pippin defeated Rabbodus, duke of the Frisians, in battle and sent Willibrord to that people to preach. Arnual, a disciple of Chilian, bishop of Würzburg; Adamanus, abbot; Adhelmus; and Wilfrid, bishops, flourished in England [Note: [Col. 0131] After this, one line was erased. In 1ζ he added: “The people ... are converted,” which we shall give together with the other additions in 1ζ. One copy, A., supplies the erased line as follows: “Begga, the widow of Ansigisus, devoted herself and her possessions to God and founded the monastery of Andenne above the Meuse.” This, therefore, Sig. had first written, but suppressed in the second edition].

**695. 9. 8. 2. 8. 4. 11. 15.**

(G. pont.) Emperor Justinian attempted to invalidate the holy synod and unsuccessfully tried to expel Pope Sergius from the Church because he resisted him in this matter. (H. m.) An eclipse of the sun occurred at the third hour of the day, so that certain stars appeared clearly [Note: [Col. 0131] “An eclipse ... appeared” is added by Ans., apparently; all except A. omit it].

**696. 10. 9. 3. 9. 5. 12. 16.**

[Col. 0132C] (H. m.) Leo the patrician deprived Justinian of the kingdom, cut off his nose and tongue, and sent him into exile. Bede, a priest and monk flourishing in England, reached the thirtieth year of his age and spent the rest of his life usefully in reading, treating, and expounding Holy Scripture.

**697. 1. 10. 4. 10. 6. 13. 17.**

(G. r. F.) After Chlodoveus died, his brother Hildebertus reigned after him for sixteen years. (BEDA, H. e.) Willibrord, surnamed Clement by Pope Sergius and consecrated bishop to preach to the Frisian people, established his episcopal seat, by the gift of Prince Pippin, at a place called Vultaburch. It is now called Utrecht, a name composed from the name of the people, the Vultari, and *Trajectum*, as though “the town of the Vultari.” In the Gallic language *Trajectum* does not mean “town” [Col. 0132D]. (Vita Kil.) At the fortress of Würzburg in East Francia, Saint Chilian was secretly martyred with his disciples Colomannus and Tolmannus by Geilana, wife of Gozbert, ruler of the people of Würzburg. She feared being separated from her husband because Chilian reproved him for having married his own brother’s former wife. Their deaths remained hidden from everyone for a long time; but after Geilana and the martyrs’ executioners were seized by a demon, their confession made the matter known [Col. 0133A].

**698. R. 2. S. 11. F. 1. L. 11. A. 7. W. 14. B. 18.**

(BEDA.) Saint Ursmarus, through the intervention of Duke Hildulf, received from Prince Pippin the monastery of Lobbes to govern. The Synod of Aquileia, held there, hesitated to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council celebrated at Constantinople by Emperor Justinian and Pope Vigilius; Pope Sergius salutarily rebuked it and brought it back to agreement. (Vita S. L.) Saint Lambertus, daring to rebuke Prince Pippin because he had taken the concubine Alpais in addition to his lawful wife Plectrudis [Col. 0133B], was martyred at Liège by Dodo, Alpais’s brother, and buried at Maastricht; Saint Hubertus was appointed bishop in his place. (H. m.) Absimarus, also called Tiberius, after expelling Leo from the empire, cutting off his nose, and shutting him away in custody, ruled for seven years. (A. Leod.) Saint Begga, Pippin’s mother, departed to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0133] A. gives 689 according to the Annals of Liège; Hirsch, p. 64, proves that she died as early as 694 or 695].

**699. 1. 12. 2. 12. 8. 15. 19.**
