(Cont. Fred.) Drogo, son of Pippin and duke of the Campani, died. His brother Grimoaldus was appointed by his father Pippin as mayor of the palace in King Hildebert’s court, and the daughter of Rabbodus, duke of the Frisians, was betrothed to him. (P. D.) After Chunipert, king of the Lombards, died, his young son Liutpert succeeded to the kingdom, with Ansprandus as his guardian. (V. Lamb.) Dodo, the killer of Saint Lambertus, tortured by a most grievous illness, was consumed by worms and, because of the intolerable stench, was submerged in the river Meuse; all the accomplices in this crime were divinely punished within a year. The slayer of the holy martyr encountered his own brother, and one was killed by the other.

**700. 2. 13. 3. 1. 9. 16. 20.**

(H. m.) The Romans, ranging through Syria, killed two hundred thousand Saracens. (P. D.) Reginbertus, duke of the people of Turin, defeated Ansprandus, guardian of King Liutpert, in battle and reigned for one year. Therbellis ruled the Bulgars.

**701. 3. 14. 4. 1. 10. 17. 1.**

(P. D.) After Raginbertus died, his son Ariperth, having defeated Ansprandus in battle [Col. 0133D], captured and killed King Liutpert; he compelled Ansprandus to flee to Bavaria, allowed his younger son Liutprandus to flee to his father, and reigned for nine years. Chyntasindus, worn out by old age, abandoned the kingdom of the Visigoths, and his son Flavius Recinsuindus reigned after him.

**702. 4. 15. 5. 1. 11. 1. 2.**

(G. pont.) John, the eighty-first, presided over the Roman Church [Col. 0134A]. (H. m.) Justinian, fleeing from exile, took refuge with Cajanus, king of the Avars.

**703. 5. 16. 6. 2. 12. 2. 3.**

(BEDA, H. e.) Saint Benedict, abbot of the Angles, died. (H. m.) When Cajanus, corrupted by money from Emperor Leo, wished to betray Justinian to him, Justinian fled from him to Therbellis, king of the Bulgars.

**704. 6. 17. 7. 3. 13. 3. 4.**

(G. pont.) John, the eighty-second, presided over the Roman Church. (BEDA, H. e.) After Alfrid, king of the Northumbrians, died, Osred reigned for eleven years.

**705. 7. 18. 8. 4. 14. 4. 5.**

(H. m.) Justinian, with the assistance of Therbellis, king of the Bulgars [Col. 0134B], recovered the empire. In the middle of the circus he slaughtered Leo and Tiberius, usurpers of the empire; he blinded Callinicus, the patriarch, and sent him into exile; and he exercised such vengeance against his adversaries that almost every time he wiped away from his amputated nose a drop of rheum as it flowed down, he ordered one of those who had conspired against him to be slaughtered. Thus he ruled for a second time for seven years.

**706. 1. 19. 9. 5. 15. 5. 6.**

(G. pont.) Sysinnius, the eighty-third [Note: [Col. 0133] D. corrects “eighty-fourth” to “eighty-fifth” and continues accordingly], and Constantinus, the eighty-fourth, presided over the Roman Church. The Slavs ravaged Italy.

**707. 2. 20. 10. 6. 16. 6. 7.**

(BEDA, H. e.) The kings Choered and Opha of the Angles came to Rome, where they were tonsured as monks and served the King of kings.

**708. 3. 21. 11. 7. 17. 7. 8.**

(H. m.) Emperor Justinian broke the peace made with the Bulgars and, engaging them, barely escaped. (BEDA, H. e.) Abbot Adrian of the Angles died. The Picts and Scots accepted the Catholic rite of observing Easter.

**709. 4. 22. 12. 8. 18. 8. 9.**

(H. m.) Habdymelich, emir of the Saracens, died; after him Ulid ruled for seven years. (App. S. Mich.) While Childebert held the sole rule of the kingdom of the Franks, the archangel Michael appeared to Autbert, bishop of Avranches, and warned him once and again to found a church in the place in the sea that, because of its height, is called the Tomb, in his memory. He wished such veneration to be offered to him in the sea as is offered on Mount Garganus. Meanwhile a bull stolen secretly by a thief was tied up in that place. Therefore, warned a third time to lay the foundation in the place where he should find the bull tied, and to trace the circuit of the church according to the ground that he saw the bull had worn down with its feet, the bishop established a church in honor of the holy archangel. From that time onward, just as on Mount Garganus, so also in that place, which is now called “In the Peril of the Sea,” devotion to the archangel began to be practiced [Col. 0134D–0135A] [Note: [Col. 0135] “While Childebert ... began” is added in the margin by Anselmus, unless perhaps by Sig. cur. tertiis; the others].

**710. R. 5. S. 1. F. 13. L. 9. A. 19. W. 9. B. 10.**

(BEDA.) Emperor Justinian, having embraced the orthodox faith, invited Pope Constantine to Constantinople and honored him, both on his arrival and on his return, with glory worthy of an apostle. (V. Lamb.) Saint Hubertus, divinely admonished, transferred the body of Saint Lambertus from Maastricht to Liège amid the great glory of miracles, and transferred the episcopal seat to that same city. (P. D.) Ansprandus returned to Italy with the Bavarians and engaged Ariperth; when Ariperth fled and was drowned in a river, Ansprandus recovered the kingdom of the Lombards. After Ansprandus died three months later, his son Liutprandus reigned for thirty-two years.

[Col. 0135B] **711. 6. 2. 14. 1. 20. 10. 11.**

Saint Oda, wife of Boggis, duke of the Aquitanians, flourished in holiness in Gaul. She enriched the churches of God with her generosity and, at her death, rested in the diocese of Liège.

**712. 7. 3. 15. 2. 21. 11. 12.**

(H. m.) Philippicus, also called Bardanius, strangled Emperor Justinian and ruled after him for two years. (G. pont.) Pope Constantine and the Roman people refused to accept the name, letters, and image of Philippicus, the heretical emperor.

**713. 1. 4. 16. 3. 22. 12. 13.**

(Mett. [FRED.]) Saint Ursmarus, bishop and abbot of the monastery of Lobbes, died, and Saint Erminus succeeded him in its government [Col. 0135C]. Grimoaldus, mayor of the palace, while praying before the altar of Saint Lambertus at Liège, was killed by Raingarius, a follower of Rabbodus, duke of the Frisians. Theodoaldus, son of Drogo [Note: [Col. 0135] Incorrectly stated; “son of Grimoaldus,” as the Annals of Metz and the Continuation of Fredegar have], was appointed mayor of the palace by his grandfather Pippin.

**714. 2. 5. 17. 4. 23. 13. 14.**

(H. m.) Artemius, also called Anastasius, deprived Philippicus of the empire and his eyes, and ruled for two years. (G. pont.) Gregory, the eighty-fourth, presided over the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0135] Thus Sig., B4*, and C1. 3.; F1. has “eighty-sixth” and continues accordingly; D. corrects “eighty-sixth” to “eighty-seventh” and continues in the same way]. He decreed that during Lent, on the fifth day of the week, a fast and the celebration of Mass should take place in the Church, which had not been done previously. (P. D.) Petronax, a citizen of Brescia, moved by divine inspiration and encouraged by Pope Gregory, nobly rebuilt the monastery of Saint Benedict at Monte Cassino and gathered many under his rule to serve God according to the Rule [Col. 0135D], more than 110 years after it had been laid waste by the Lombards. (Cont. Fred.) Prince Pippin died and left as heir to his authority his son by Alpais, Charles, surnamed Tudites or Martellus. Plectrudis, Pippin’s widow, imprisoned her stepson Charles, whom she had captured, in the city of Cologne; and together with her grandson Theodoaldus she usurped the authority of mayor of the palace and the government of the kingdom.

[Col. 0136A] **715. 1. 6. 18. 5. 24. 14. 15.**

(Ib.) After Hildebert, king of the Franks, died, his son Chlodoveus reigned for four years. The Franks fought a mutually disastrous war against Theodoaldus; after defeating him, they appointed Raginfredus mayor of the palace and Chilpericus king. Charles was rescued from the custody of his stepmother by divine providence and soon attempted to wrest his authority from Raginfredus. First attacking Duke Rabbodus of the Frisians, who was supporting Raginfredus, he suffered heavy losses among his army. (A. Xant.) Saint Aegidius, coming from Greece, flourished in holiness in Provence.

**716. 2. 7. 1. 6. 25. 15. 16.**

(H. m.) Theodosius deposed Anastasius from the empire, ordained him a priest, and ruled for one year [Col. 0136B]. Since he had been sluggish and uneducated and a collector of public revenues, he was compelled by force by the army to assume the empire. (Ib.) Ulid, emir, died; after him Zuleymen ruled the Saracens for three years. (BEDA, H. e.) After Osred, king of Northumbria, was killed, Coenred reigned for four years. Ecberth, coming from Ireland, flourished in England in holiness and learning. Saint Germanus was transferred from Cyzicus to the episcopal see of Constantinople.

**717. 1. 1. 2. 7. 26. 16. 17**

(H. m.) Theodosius laid down the empire. After him Leo ruled for twenty-four years. (G. pont.) Pope Gregory consecrated Boniface, who had come from Britain, as bishop, and through him preached the word of God in Germany [Col. 0136C]. (Ib.) A very great and disastrous flood occurred at Rome. But when Pope Gregory appeased God with frequent litanies, it subsided after eight days.

**718. 1. 2. 3. 8. 27. 17. 18.**

(H. m.) Zuleymen, emir, together with his emirs and a fleet of almost three thousand ships, besieged Constantinople for three years. The Bulgars killed thirty thousand Saracens. (Cont. Fred.) Charles engaged Chilpericus and Raginfredus in the territory of Cambrai at Vinciacum on the Sunday before Easter, which fell on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April. Raginfredus was defeated and put to flight; Charles pursued them as far as Paris. (Vita S. Wlfr.) Duke Rabbodus of the Frisians was brought by the preaching of Bishop Vulfrannus to the point of being baptized. When he had dipped one foot in the font, he withdrew the other and asked: “Where are more of their ancestors, in hell or in paradise?” When he heard that more were in hell, he pulled out the foot he had dipped and said: “It is better that I follow the greater number than the smaller.” Thus deceived by a demon, who promised that he would give him incomparable goods three days later, he died a sudden and eternal death on that very third day [Col. 0136D].

[Col. 0137A] **719. R. 2. S. 3. F. 4. L. 9. A. 28. W. 18. B. 19.**

(H. m.) Zuleymen, emir, died. After him Haumar ruled the Saracens for two years. The people of Constantinople, steadfast in prayer and constant in battle, strongly resisted the Saracens. The Saracens perished without number from hunger, cold, war, and disease. After King Dagobert died, Lotharius reigned for two years. (BEDA, H. e.) After Coenred, Osrich ruled the Northumbrians for eleven years. (H. m.) While Constantine, son of Leo the emperor, was being baptized by the patriarch Germanus, he defecated in the holy font, giving a great omen that he would in the future be a scandal to the Church of God.

**720. 3. 1. 1. 10. 29. 19. 20.**

(Ib.) The Saracens, confounded, withdrew from the siege of Constantinople [Col. 0137B]. they themselves, together with their ships, being partly consumed by sea fire, partly sunk, and partly destroyed by a storm of fiery hail; and, of such a vast number of ships, scarcely five remained. Through this, God’s power was made known to all peoples. Within the city, however, 300,000 people died of plague. Haumar, persecuting Christians, made many of them martyrs of Christ. (Cont. Fred.) Hilpericus and Raginfredus enlisted Eudo, duke of Aquitaine, as an ally. Defeated by Charles in battle, they barely escaped by flight. Eudo, returning, took Chilpericus away with him. The Saracens crossed over from Africa into Spain under the leadership of Abdyrama, son of Muhavia, their emir, and claimed it for themselves. Thus the kingdom of the Visigoths and Suevi was destroyed [Col. 0137C] and reduced under the Saracens, after approximately 346 years had elapsed from the time when they were expelled from Scythia by the Huns; but approximately 256 years had elapsed from the time when, after the Vandals had withdrawn and the Suevi had been defeated, they began to reign in Spain. The kingdom of the third part of Spain, called that of the Galicians, which neither the Visigoths then nor the Saracens later were able to subdue, still flourishes unharmed and, protected by the faith of God, remains unconquerable.

**721. 4. 2. 2. 11. 30. 21.**

(H. m.) Haumar, emir, died; after him Gizid ruled the Saracens for four years. (Cont. Fred.) After King Lotharius died, Charles received Chilpericus from Eudo through envoys and made him his king. (BEDA.) The bones of Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, formerly transferred to Sardinia, were removed from Sardinia, which had now been devastated by the Saracens, and transferred to Pavia by King Liutprandus, who paid a great price.

**722. 5. 1. 1. 12. 31. 22**
(G. pont.) The emperor Leo often and earnestly labored to have Pope Gregory killed, but in vain, since the Italians and Lombards steadfastly resisted the emperor in defense of the pope. (A. Xantens.) In Campania of Italy, grain was burned, and barley and vegetables fell from heaven like rain. (A. Mett.) Charles, pursuing Raginfred, besieged Angers; after capturing it and defeating Raginfred, he granted it for habitation and assumed the rule of the whole kingdom. [Col. 0138A] (P. D.) King Liutprand besieged Ravenna; after capturing Classe, the city of the Ravennans, he destroyed it.

723. 6. 2. 2. 13. 32. 23.

(Cont. Fred.) Charles defeated the Saxons. Rigobert, bishop of Reims, was deposed from the episcopate by Charles [Note: [Col. 0137] Korolo in Sig.; B4* has Rigobertus—noluit (“Rigobert—did not wish”) at the end of the year.], his godson at baptism, because, when Charles was marching against Raginfred, Rigobert refused through fear of Raginfred to open the city of Reims to him. Eucherius likewise, bishop of Orléans, was deprived of his episcopate for a similar reason and exiled to Sarchinium, a village of Hasbania; he completed his life in holiness in the monastery of Saint Trudo.

724. 7. 3. 3. 14. 33. 24.

(H. m.) A certain Jewish sorcerer, promising Gizid that he would rule for forty years, persuaded him to order that the images of God and the saints be removed throughout his entire [Col. 0138B] kingdom. Deceived by the hope of a long reign, Gizid issued the edict, but soon died himself. After him Elvelith ruled the Saracens for twenty years. (A. Fuld.) Charles subdued the Bavarians by arms.

725. 8. 4. 4. 15. 34. 25.

(H. m.) The emperor Leo, deceived concerning the faith by a certain renegade named Beser, declared war against the images of Christ and his saints and ordered them everywhere to be removed and burned. For this error Pope Gregory rebuked him at length in writing, but in vain. Charles fought Lanfrid, duke of the Alamanni, and, after defeating him, subjected Alemannia to himself.

726. 9. 5. 5. 16. 35. 26.

[Col. 0138C] (Cont. Fred.) After Chilperic died, Charles made Theoderic king for himself; he reigned for fifteen years. Charles defeated the Saxons.

727. 10. 6. 1. 17. 36. 27.

The people of Constantinople rioted against the emperor Leo because of the deposition of the images of God; some were even martyred for this cause. (Cont. Fred.) Charles defeated the Suebi and Bavarians. (BEDA, H. e.) Wichtred, king of the Angles, died and left his son Ethelbert as heir to the kingdom. Cormesius ruled the Bulgarians.

728. 11. 7. 2. 18. 1. 1.

(Cont. Fred.) Charles crossed the Loire, drove Duke Eudo of Aquitaine—defeated in war—to flight, and harshly devastated Aquitaine.

[Col. 0138D] 729. 12. 8. 3. 19. 2 2.

(H. m.) Because Pope Gregory saw that the emperor Leo was incorrigible, he caused Rome, Italy, and all Hesperia to withdraw from his authority and prohibited the payment of taxes.

730. 13. 9. 4. 20. 3. 3.

(Cont. Fred.) Duke Eudo, inferior to Charles in every respect, invited the Saracens from Spain against him. (H. m.) Saint Germanus, having turned against the emperor Leo because of his impiety, was removed from the episcopal see. (BEDA, H. e.) Saint Ecgberht, priest of the English, died. (Cont. Fred.) The Saracens crossed the Garonne with all their families, as though intending to settle in Gaul; [Col. 0139A] they devastated everything and burned the churches of God. Charles, trusting in God’s help, joined battle with them and killed 375,000 of them [Note: [Col. 0139] CCCLXXXV (385) in C1, 3, D.] together with their king Abd al-Rahman, while losing 1,500 of his own men. Eudo, reconciled with Charles, also plundered the Saracen camps and crushed their remnants. (BEDA, H. e.) After Osric, king of Northumbria, died, Ceolwulf succeeded him.

731. R. 14. S. 10. F. 5. L. 21. A. 4. B. 4.

(H. m.) Gregory the eighty-fifth presided over the Roman Church; he too rebuked the emperor Leo for his error and turned the Roman people and the taxes of Hesperia away from him. (A. Xant.) In England, Bede, priest and monk, renowned for holiness and learning, died. (Cont. Fred.) After capturing Lyon and other cities, Charles subjected Burgundy to himself. Raginfred died.

732. 15. 11. 6. 22. 5. 5.

(H. m.) Constantine, the emperor’s son, married as his wife the daughter of Cagan, king of the Avars; after she was baptized, she maintained the true faith even when her husband apostatized. Charles fought Eudo in Wasconia and deprived him of both his principality and his life. King Liutprand took many cities and fortresses from the jurisdiction of the Roman pontiff. (P. D.; Cont. Bedae.) Ceolwulf, king of Northumbria, was captured, tonsured as a cleric, and afterward restored to the kingdom.

733. 16. 12. 7. 23. 6. 6.

(G. pont.) Pope Gregory gathered a synod of 905 bishops at Rome, confirmed the veneration of the holy images, and anathematized their violators by a general sentence. Charles, defeating Waifer and Hunald, the sons of Eudo, in battle, subjected Aquitaine to himself.

734. 17. 13. 8. 24. 7. 7.

(A. Fuld.) Charles invaded Frisia, killed Poppo, duke of the Frisians, with many others, and subjugated Frisia to himself.

735. 18. 14. 9. 25. 8. 8.

(A. Leod.) Saint Hubert died. (Cont. Fred.) Charles besieged Avignon, a city of Gaul captured by the Saracens through the treachery and cooperation of Maurontus, duke of Provence; after recovering it by force, he destroyed the Saracens to the last man. From this point I cease recording the kingdom of the English [Col. 0139D], because I do not possess the histories of the ancestors whom I shall follow [Note: [Col. 0139] E. cleverly altered this as follows: “I do not cease recording the kingdom of the English, because I possess the histories of the ancestors whom I shall follow,” and continues the years of the English kings.]

736. 19. 15. 10. 26 9.

(Ib.) While Athima, king of the Saracens, was being besieged by Charles inside the Gallic city of Narbonne, the Saracens came from Spain with another king, Amor, to bring him aid. When they engaged Charles, both kings were killed and the city was recovered by him; the Saracens were almost completely crushed. As Charles pursued those fleeing, the survivors were drowned in the depths.

[Col. 0140A] 737. 20. 16. 11. 27. 10.

(A. Leod.) Saint Erminus, bishop and abbot of Lobbes, died. (Cont. Fred.) Charles captured Nîmes, Agde, and other cities of the Gothic region that had been invaded by the Saracens, and destroyed them to their foundations.

738. 21. 17. 12. 28. 11.

(Ib.) After the Gallic city of Arles had been captured by the Saracens and everything around it demolished, Charles summoned King Liutprand of the Lombards to his aid, confronted them, and put them to flight through the terror of his name. Thus Charles, with God’s help, his own skill, and the courage of the Franks, deprived the Saracens—who had invaded almost all Asia, all Libya, and a large part of Europe—of every hope of invading Gaul. (P. D.) Transamundus, duke of Spoleto, rebelling against Liutprand, fled to the Romans.

739. 22. 18. 13. 29. 12.

(Cont. Fred.) Charles defeated Maurontus, duke of Provence, who had invited the Saracens, and subjected Provence to himself. (G. pont.) King Liutprand severely harassed Rome because it had given refuge to Transamundus.

740. 23. 19. 14. 30. 13.

(Cont. Fred.) Charles made the Saxons tributary to himself. (A. Mett.) Signs appeared in the sun, moon, and stars [Note: [Col. 0139] After this, a certain hand—not Sigebert’s—had written in the margin: “Anselm, an illustrious man, whose sister was . . . . . .” But after this was erased, 1δ. added it under the year 752; the remaining witnesses …]

741. 24. 20. 15. 31. 14.

(H. m.) After Theoderic, king of the Franks, Hilderic reigned for ten years. After the emperor Leo died, his son Constantine ruled for thirty-seven years. (Mett.) After pacifying and enlarging the Frankish kingdom, Charles, a warlike prince, died, leaving his sons Carloman and [Col. 0140C] Pippin as successors to his principate. (G. pont.)? Zacharias the eighty-sixth [Note: [Col. 0139] Eighty-fifth in A.] presided over the Roman Church. Since he found the republic disturbed by the Lombards, he immediately set everything in order through his goodwill and established peace with the Lombards for twenty years. He translated Gregory’s books of the Dialogues from Latin into Greek. (H. m.) Constantinople was severely afflicted by an earthquake for an entire year.

742. 1. 21. 1. 32. 15

(MAR.) Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, founded the monastery of Fulda in the Buchen Forest. (P. D.) King Liutprand of the Lombards died. The Lombards rejected Hildebrand, whom Liutprand himself had designated king, and Rachis ruled after him for seven years. [Col. 0140D] (Mett.) Prince Pippin confronted Hunald, duke of Aquitaine, who had rebelled against him; Carloman, meanwhile, devastated Alemannia. (H. m.) Artabasdus seized the imperial power against Constantine.

743. 2. 22. 2. 1. 16.

(Mett.) Ogdilo, duke of Bavaria, having abducted Pippin’s sister, rebelled against him; Pippin overcame him in battle, though at considerable cost. Carloman advanced into Saxony, captured the fortress of Hoscoburch, and received Theoderic the Saxon as a hostage for peace.

[Col. 0141A] 744. R. 3. S. 23. F. 3. L. 2. B. 17.

(H. m.) Elvelid, emir, died; Gyzid ruled the Saracens for one year. Constantine captured Artabasdus and put out his eyes and those of many of his friends. (A. Xantens.) Ash fell from heaven.

745. 4. 1. 4. 3. 18.

(H. m.) After Gyzid was killed, Hisces ruled the Saracens for one year. (Mett.) Pippin defeated Theodoald, son of Duke Gofrid. After the persecution that arose following the stoning of Stephen, the protomartyr, Maximinus, one of Christ’s seventy disciples, crossed into Gaul and brought Mary Magdalene with him. He also buried her after her death near the city of Aix, over which he presided. When Aix was devastated by the Saracens, Gerard, count of Burgundy, transferred Mary’s body to the monastery of Vézelay, which he had built [Col. 0141B] himself (cf. A. Xant.). Although some write that she rests at Ephesus, without any covering over her. (H. m.) Peter of Damascus, bishop, and Peter of Maiuma were martyred by the Saracens in Syria.

746. 5. 2. 5. 4. 19.

(Vita S. Kil.) The priest Athalongus, instructed by the blindness inflicted upon him to seek the bodies of the saints, recovered his sight when the bodies of Saint Kilian and his companions were found. When Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz, was informed of this by Athalongus, he decided that the fortress of Würzburg should be distinguished by the privilege of an episcopal see in honor of Kilian the martyr, who had been ordained bishop by Pope Conon to preach there and had received from God the place of his death and rest there. He ordained Saint Burchard as its first bishop. (H. m.) Marwan ruled the Saracens for six years. (Mett.) Carloman, brother of King Pippin, was tonsured as a monk at Rome by Pope Zacharias; first on Mount Soracte, in the monastery he had founded, and afterward at the monastery of Monte Cassino, he shone through a praiseworthy life.

747. 6. 1. 6. 5. 20.

(Mett.) Pippin pursued his brother Griphon, who had rebelled against him. (H. m.) The Saracens clashed in civil war.

748. 7. 2. 7. 6. 21

[Col. 0141D] (A. Lauriss.) Pippin captured Griphon in Saxony, together with his accomplices Tassilo, Lantfrid, and Suidiger, after defeating them in battle. He made Tassilo duke of Bavaria, while granting Griphon twelve counties in Neustria. This was not enough for Griphon, however, and he fled to Waifer [Col. 0142A] in Aquitaine. (H. m.) Pestilence and excessive mortality occurred among human beings in Calabria and Sicily. Small crosses, as though marked with oil, appeared on people’s clothing and on the veils of churches.

749. 8. 3. 8. 7. 22.

(G. pont.) When Rachis, king of the Lombards, attempted to trouble Rome after breaking the treaty, Pope Zacharias not only restrained him from evil but, through his prompting, caused him to come to Rome with his wife and sons and become a monk. His brother Aistulf succeeded him and reigned for seven years.

750. 9. 4. 9. 1. 23.

(A. Lauriss.) King Hilderic of the Franks was tonsured as a monk. Prince Pippin, by apostolic authority and through the election of the Franks, was anointed and consecrated king by Saint Boniface, [Col. 0142B] archbishop of Mainz, and reigned for eighteen years [approximately eighty-eight years after the mayors of the palace began to rule over the Frankish kings [Note: [Col. 0141] Added by a hand very similar to Sigebert’s; absent from the other witnesses except A.].

751. 10. 5. 1. 2. 24.

(Ib.) King Pippin fought the Saxons. Griphon, Pippin’s brother, was killed. [Remigius, brother of that same King Pippin and archbishop of Rouen, flourished in Gaul. King Pippin of Gaul improved the churches throughout Gaul in the Roman style of chant through his own efforts [Note: [Col. 0141] Written in the erasure of two lines by 1δ.; absent from the other witnesses except A.].]

752. 11. 6. 2. 3. 25.

(G. pont.) Stephen the eighty-seventh presided over the Roman Church. (H. m.) After Marwan the emir was killed, Muhammad ruled the Saracens for five years. When Aistulf, king of the Lombards, became so fiercely hostile to the Romans that he demanded tribute from every person, Pope Stephen was forced to come to Francia to seek the aid of King Pippin. On his journey, one night there appeared to him a great sign in the sky: namely, a fiery globe from the south, moving from the borders of Gaul toward the territory of the Lombards. (Lauriss.) The monk Carloman was also sent by Aistulf to his brother, King Pippin, to thwart the apostolic petition. (A. Mett.) Pope Stephen anointed Pippin king together with his sons Carloman and Charles, and through them blessed their descendants to inherit the royal succession forever; every foreigner was forbidden by apostolic anathema to invade it [Note: [Col. 0141D] Neither the Annals of Metz nor Regino contain this. The author of the treatise On Investiture, whom they call Waltram, who copied this passage, presents it as follows: “He anointed … confirming his brother’s line in royal and [Col. 0142D] imperial dignity.” Folcuin says the same thing in different words in the chartulary of Saint Bertin, p. 56, ed. Guérard.]. Anselm, an illustrious man [Col. 0142D] whose sister was the wife of King Aistulf, transferred the body of Pope Saint Sylvester to the monastery of Nonantola, which he had founded. [Note: [Col. 0141] In the erasure of two lines, 1δ.; absent from the other witnesses except A., which has: “King Pippin improved all the churches of Gaul through his own efforts with chants of Roman authority. The noble Anselm transferred the body of Pope Saint Sylvester from Rome to the monastery of Nonantola, which he had founded.” Thus Sigebert had originally published it.]

753. 12. 1. 3. 4. 26.

(Cont. Fred.) King Pippin attacked Italy; [Col. 0143A] Aistulf’s army was defeated by the Franks. Aistulf was compelled, at the command of the Franks, to make peace with the Romans. (Transl. S. B.) The monk Carloman attempted to remove the bones of Saint Benedict the abbot from the church at Fleury, where they had formerly been transferred, in order to return them to Monte Cassino. Through miracles shown by God and the resistance of the Franks, he was prevented from carrying out his plan. (H. m.) At this time a terrifying earthquake occurred. Some cities were completely overthrown, others partly destroyed, while still others moved from the mountains to the plains below, together with their walls and dwellings, remaining intact and unharmed for more than six miles. In Mesopotamia the earth also split open for a distance of two miles; another earth, less white and sandy, rose from its depths, and from it there emerged an unblemished mule-like animal [Col. 0143B] speaking with a human voice and announcing the invasion of a people from the desert against the Arabs.

754. R. 13. S. 2. F. 4. L. 5. B. 27.

(Mett.) The monk Carloman died at Vienne. (MAR.) Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, was martyred with his companions in Frisia by enemies of the faith; he was honorably buried in the monastery of Fulda, which he had founded in Thuringia.

755. 14. 3. 5. 6. 28.

(H. m.) The emperor Constantine gathered a synod of 330 bishops at Constantinople. After an edict was promulgated ordering the images of God and his saints to be removed, he greatly scandalized the Church of God and tyrannized the orthodox [Col. 0143C]. (Mett.) King Aistulf, having broken the peace treaty, besieged Rome. King Pippin, returning to Italy, besieged him shut inside Pavia and compelled him, against his will, to renew the peace treaty; he also made him restore to Saint Peter whatever belonged by right to him. Abbot Fulrad of Saint-Denis in Paris transferred the body of Saint Vitus the martyr from Rome to Paris.

756. 15. 4. 6. 7. 29.

(Lauriss.) Duke Tassilo was reconciled with his uncle, King Pippin. Aistulf, king of the Lombards, died by the judgment of God; Desiderius succeeded him and reigned for nineteen years.

757. 16. 5. 7. 1. 30.

(G. pont.) Paul the eighty-eighth presided over the Roman Church. (Lauriss.) Abdallah ruled the Saracens for [Col. 0143D] twenty-one years. Pippin forcefully broke into the Saxon fortifications and, after great slaughter, reduced them to tribute.

758. 17. 1. 8. 2. 31.

The body of Saint Petronilla, daughter of the apostle Peter, was transferred by Pope Paul. On her marble sarcophagus was read the following inscription, carved by the hand of the apostle Peter himself: [Col. 0144A] “To golden Petronilla, most beloved daughter.” (P. D. gesta ep. Mett.) Walpert, abbot in Italy, and Chrodegang, bishop of Metz and nephew of King Pippin through his sister Landrada, flourished in Gaul; Chrodegang founded the monastery of Gorze in the diocese of Metz. (Laur.) Waifer, son of Eudo and duke of Aquitaine, incurred Pippin’s anger by unjustly harassing Frankish affairs. When Pippin attacked Aquitaine, Waifer entered into a treaty of feigned peace.

759. 18. 2. 9. 3. 32.

(Mett.) While Abdallah was persecuting, the Church of God was troubled. When Waifer turned away from the peace treaty, King Pippin pressed him by devastating the district of Auvergne; he captured many fortresses and the city of Auvergne itself and carried away Bladinus, the city’s count, with many others. Saint Gengulf flourished in Burgundy and also shone with the glory of martyrdom [Col. 0144B].

760. 19. 3. 10. 4. 33.

(Mett.) Pippin captured the city of Bourges and fortified it after its capture. (H. m.) Telezas ruled the Bulgarians.

761. 20. 4. 11. 5. 1.

The head of John the Baptist was transferred to the city of Emesa. Chilping, count of Auvergne, and Amming, count of Poitiers, engaged Pippin’s troops and were killed with many others [Note: [Col. 0143] Sigebert had written it thus; but a hand very similar to that of 1δ. erased it and inserted: “The two counts Chilping … with many others, in the year 759.” It also expanded the year 761 in the erasure and margin as follows: “The head … endowed it,” to which 1η. added: “The same king … is called.” We shall publish these interpolations below together with the remaining additions of Gembloux. Manuscripts B3*, F1, F2, and F3 have what the interpolators wrote; all the others have what Sigebert wrote.]

762. 21. 5. 12. 6. 2.

(H. m.) Many were martyred by the emperor Constantine. Theletzis, having engaged the emperor Constantine, was defeated with great loss and disgrace to the Bulgarians; rejected by the Bulgarians for this reason, he was killed by them together with the leaders of the nation [Col. 0144C]. (A. Lauriss.) Duke Tassilo was completely alienated from King Pippin. Sabinus ruled the Bulgarians.] (H. m.) The Turks, bursting through the Caspian Gates, ravaged Armenia. When a pestilence had arisen in their homeland in ancient times, they tonsured themselves in the form of a cross at the Christians’ urging; and because the homeland’s salvation had been restored through this sign, they retained this custom of tonsure [Note: [Col. 0143] Added by 1γ.; absent from the other witnesses except A.; compare the following year.].] (Mett.) Waifer, losing confidence in his affairs, demolished the walls of the cities of Aquitaine to their foundations. Pippin rebuilt them and entrusted them, for the protection of his people, to loyal commanders.

763. 22. 6. 13. 7. 1.

(H. m.) A great frost lasted from the Kalends of October until February [Note: [Col. 0143] After this, more than half a line was erased. “The Turks, bursting through the Caspian Gates, ravage Armenia” was added by A. Sigebert had originally had this, but in the second edition he inserted it under the preceding year in expanded form.]. (Cont. Fred.) King Pippin devastated the region of Limoges with slaughter and fire. [Col. 0144D] (H. m.) Sabinus the Bulgar made a treaty with the Romans; rejected by his own people because of it, he fled to the emperor. A pagan Bulgar ruled the Bulgarians. (Ib.) Stars suddenly seemed to fall from heaven, terrifying everyone so greatly that they thought the end of the world was near.

764. 23. 7. 14. 8. 1.

(Lauriss.; Gesta epp. Mett.) Chrodegang, bishop, [Col. 0145A] transferred the bodies of the martyrs Gorgonius, Nabor, and Nazarius from Rome to Gaul. He placed Gorgonius at Gorze, Nabor at the monastery of Hyliriacum, and Nazarius at the monastery of Lorsch, which the illustrious count Canthuyr had founded and, in the preceding year, given to the church of Metz.

765. R. 24. S. 8. F. 15. L. 9. B. 2.

(Cont. Fred.) King Pippin devastated the Aquitanian cities of Agen, Périgueux, and Angoulême and subjected a large part of Aquitaine to himself. Chrodegang, archbishop of Metz, died. During the reign of the emperor Constantine and his wife Irene, in the Syrian city of Berytus, which lies under Antioch, the Jews found an image of Jesus our Savior in the house of a certain Jew. It had been left there by a Christian who had remained in that place. They treated it shamefully and inflicted upon the image all the insults that the Jews had inflicted upon Christ Jesus: they mocked it, spat in its face, struck it, reviled it abusively, pierced its hands and feet with nails, and offered it vinegar and gall. Finally, after opening its side with a lance, blood and water came out of it. Taking this in a small vessel, they tested whether the miracles they had heard Jesus perform were genuine by sprinkling all the sick gathered in their synagogue with this blood. Every one of them was healed of whatever illness afflicted him. At last the Jews were moved to remorse, all ran to Adeodatus, bishop of the city, and, after recounting the event, gave him the image together with the blood [Col. 0145C]. After they had been baptized, the bishop distributed the blood into vessels and sent it far and wide, preaching the mighty works of God; he charged everyone that every year, on the fifth day before the Ides of November, the passion of the Lord’s image should be celebrated (cf. A. Xant.).

766. 25. 9. 16. 10. 3.

(H. m.) The emperor Constantine and Abdallah the emir raged with equal madness against the orthodox and killed many of them for Christ. Moreover, Constantine, unable to endure the glory of the saints shining through miracles, ordered that their relics also be dug up everywhere and thrown into the deep. In the presence of King Pippin, a synod concerning the Holy Trinity and the images of the saints was held between the Greeks and the Romans. (Cont. [Col. 0145D] Fred.) King Pippin hanged Remistanus, brother of Eudo and therefore uncle of Waifer, who had defected from Waifer to Pippin and from Pippin to Waifer; Pippin’s men captured him in battle and suspended him from the gallows. (Ib.) Amyrmonon, king of the Saracens, sent envoys from Spain and, through gifts given and received, sought the favor and friendship of King Pippin.

767. 26. 10. 17. 11. 4.

(Lauriss.) Pippin crushed Aquitaine in a final destruction, captured Saintes, and carried away with him Waifer’s mother, sisters, and nieces, whom he had taken captive there. (G. pont.) After Pope Paul died at Rome, a certain Constantine, suddenly ordained a priest though previously a layman, seized the papacy through tyrannical ambition and became a great scandal to the Church of God. [Against him, Philip was made pope by certain Romans, but was deposed not long afterward [Note: [Col. 0145] Added by 1δ.; absent from the other witnesses except A.].]

768. 27. 11. 18. 12. 5.

(Cont. Fred.) The long conflict between Pippin and Waifer ended because Waifer was killed by his own men, who, weary of his wrongdoing, sought Pippin’s favor; not long afterward Pippin died. His son Charles, surnamed “the Great” because of his good fortune, shared the kingdom with his brother Carloman and ruled after him for forty-seven years. (G. pont.) After Constantine, the false pope, was expelled from the Church through the zeal of the faithful and deprived of his eyes, Stephen the eighty-ninth presided over the Roman Church. [Col. 0146B] He gathered at Rome a synod of bishops from both Gaul and Italy. At it, everything ordained by Constantine was annulled except baptism and chrism. The synod decreed that bishops consecrated by him should return to the rank they had held before that consecration and, if judged worthy, should be elected and consecrated again; priests and deacons consecrated by him were likewise to return to their former rank and, if worthy, to be consecrated again, but they were never to rise to a higher rank or order. Laymen whom he had ordained deacons or priests were to be completely degraded and remain in religious dress. Stephen also confirmed the veneration of the holy images and anathematized those who profaned them. He further decreed [Col. 0146C] that on every Sunday, at Mass, “Gloria in excelsis Deo” should be sung.

769. 28. 12. 1. 13. 6.

(Mett. [Laur.]) When Hunald was planning rebellion in Aquitaine, Charles advanced into Aquitaine and received all the Aquitanians and Wascones into submission. He took Hunald, who had fled to Lupus, duke of the Wascones, after Lupus sent him back to Charles with his wife; thus the Aquitanian war ended. Desiderius, king of the Lombards, entered Rome under the pretext of praying and blinded certain Roman nobles whom he had captured.

770. 29. 13. 2. 14. 7.

(H. m.) The emperor Constantine, wholly turned away from God, martyred the holy man Stephen by a bitter death after he had been confined for sixty years, although even pagans revered him. He compelled all his subjects to swear upon the wood of the holy cross that they would not venerate any image of God or his saints. He condemned those who invoked the Mother of God, those who kept vigils for God, those accustomed to live devoutly in churches, those who abstained from oaths and impurities, and those who kept the relics of the saints with them; he deprived them of their property and tortured them in every way. He burned the more reverent among them after smearing their beards with wax and pitch. He forced monks to take wives and nuns to take husbands. Many who avoided this earned martyrdom [Col. 0147A]. Never under the persecution of any pagan were more people martyred than under this man. Thelerigus ruled the Bulgarians.

771. R. 30 S. 14. F. 3. L. 15. B. 1.

(A. Lob.) Carloman, King Charles’s brother, died; his portion of the kingdom was united to Charles’s territories. His wife, together with her sons and Autharius the Frank, fled to Desiderius, king of Italy. Hunald, duke of Aquitaine, came to Rome as though intending to remain there. When he fled to the Lombards, he apostatized and soon afterward met a wretched end there, being buried under stones. (H. m.) The emperor Constantine prepared to fight the Bulgarians in a naval battle, but when nearly two thousand of his ships were wrecked by a north wind, he lost almost his entire army.

772. 31. 15. 4. 16. 2.

[Col. 0147B] (G. pont.) Adrian the ninetieth presided over the Roman Church. He labored exceedingly to restrain the frenzy of the heretics who condemned the images of God and the saints; after publishing a book against them, fortified by many scriptural citations, he weakened their errors and strengthened the true faith. In the offertories and the verses of the offertories, he doubled what had been doubled. (Mett. [Laur.]) King Charles devoted himself to the Saxon war, captured the Saxon fortress of Heresburg, and destroyed the shrine of Irminsul. When the army was suffering from thirst there, torrents of water suddenly poured out by divine will. Having obtained what he desired, Charles received hostages for peace from the Saxons.

773. 32. 16. 5. 17. 3.

[Col. 0147C] (Ib.) When Pope Adrian complained to King Charles about the many injustices of Desiderius, Charles advanced into Italy and besieged Desiderius shut inside Pavia [Note: [Col. 0147] See below, among the Aquicincian additions, the interpolation made for this year by an Aquicincian scribe. In the first erasure, which Hirsch presumes on p. 471, there is not even the slightest trace of an addition; therefore those who said that this interpolation was fabricated by Sigebert are mistaken.]

774. 33. 17. 6. 18. 4.

(Laur.) After breaking the peace treaty, the Saxons pressed upon the borders of the Franks with fire and slaughter; nevertheless, they could not burn the church at Fritzlar, which Saint Boniface had blessed and had foretold would never be consumed by fire. (JOH. Vita Gregor. M. II, 9.) King Charles, offended by the discordance of ecclesiastical chant between the Romans and the Gauls, and judging it more just to drink from a pure spring than from a muddied stream, sent two clerics to Rome to learn the authentic chant from the Romans and teach it to the Gauls. Through them the church of Metz first, and through it all Gaul, was recalled to the authority of Roman chant. (Mett. [Laur.]) During the siege, King Charles divided his army and captured many cities beyond the Po, including Verona. There Autharius the Frank, hiding with Carloman’s wife and sons, surrendered himself and them to the king. Adelgisus, son of King Desiderius, who had fled there, escaped and fled from there to Constantinople. (A. Leod.) As the siege of Pavia was made more severe by a deadly pestilence, the city opened to King Charles. [Col. 0148A] King Desiderius was captured with his wife, daughter, and all his leading men and sent into perpetual exile in Gaul by Agilfred, bishop of Liège. Whatever the Lombards had taken from the Romans over many years, Charles restored to them. After destroying the kingdom of the Lombards, he brought all Italy under the authority of the Frankish kingdom. Thus the defeated Lombards ceased to reign after 204 years, reckoned from the beginning of their rule in Italy. Returning to Saxony, King Charles engaged the Saxons with a threefold army, and victory came to him in every encounter.

775. 34. 18. 7. 5.

(H. m.) The emperor Constantine marched against the Bulgarians, but peace was agreed between them. Not long afterward, however, when the Bulgarians broke the treaty, the emperor attacked them unexpectedly and triumphantly defeated them. (Mett. [L.]) King Charles captured the Saxon fortress of Sigiburg; he fought them three times and, victorious, received hostages for peace from them.

776. 35. 19. 8. 6.

(H. m.) The emperor Constantine was struck by God with a plague of terrible fire and, crying out while still alive, “I have been delivered to unquenchable fire,” died miserably. After him his son Leo ruled for five years. Abdallah the emir also died; after him Mady ruled the Saracens for nine years. (Mett. [L.]) When certain people in Italy were planning rebellion, Charles returned to Italy, captured the city of Forum Julii, and ordered its duke Rothgaud, the instigator of the rebellion, to be beheaded. After capturing the city of Treviso as well, he inspired the others with terror through the majesty of his name. (Mett. [REG.]) While the Saxons were besieging the fortress of Heresburg, the glory of God appeared to everyone over the church: two shields, flaming with a bloody color, moved through the air as though in battle. Charles swept through Saxony like a storm, broke into its fortifications, and compelled them to surrender themselves and their country to him and, after giving hostages, to promise that they would become Christians.

777. 1. 1. 9. 7.

(Mett. [L.]) Winthichind, duke of the Saxons, fled to Northmannia. The baptized Saxons agreed that they would lose their freedom and all their possessions if they ever abandoned loyalty to Christ and the king.

[Col. 0148D] 778. 2. 2. 10. 8.

(Ib.) In Spain, Charles destroyed Zaragoza by devastation, besieged Pamplona, and, after capturing it and destroying its walls, subjected the Wascones and two Saracen princes to himself; he also received several cities into submission. At Winthichind’s urging, the Saxons devastated Francia; but, defeated by Charles, they saved themselves by flight. (H. m.) Thelericus the Bulgar fled to the emperor Leo; after having him baptized, the emperor made him a patrician. (Ib.) Chardamus ruled the Bulgarians.

[Col. 0149A] 779. R. 3. S. 3. F. 11. B. 1.

(Mett. [L.]) The emperor Leo invaded Syria. King Charles subjected the Westphalians in Saxony to himself. Hilterand, duke of Spoleto, submitted to King Charles and purchased his favor with many gifts.

780. 4. 4. 12. 2.

(Ib.) King Charles crossed the river Elbe; there the Bardengau people and the Nortliutae were baptized in his favor. Duke Tassilo of Bavaria rebelled against King Charles at the urging of his wife, who was the daughter of King Desiderius and was attempting through her husband to avenge her father’s exile. [Saint Sturm, first abbot of Fulda, died [Note: [Col. 0149] Added by 1δ.; absent from the other witnesses except A., which has it under the year 829; C2*.]. (cf. MAR.)]

781. 5. 5. 13. 3.

(H. m.) When the emperor Leo was consumed by desire for precious stones, he fell in love with the crown of the Great Church, took it, and wore it; carbuncles broke out on his head, and he was seized by a fever and died. After him his wife Irene ruled with her son Constantine for ten years. (Mett. [L.]) Mady the emir martyred many of both sexes for Christ. King Charles went to Rome for the sake of prayer, and there his sons were anointed kings: Pippin over Italy and Louis over Aquitaine. (Ib.) Duke Tassilo of Bavaria was reconciled to King Charles by Pope Adrian.

782. 1. 6. 14. 4.

(H. m.) At Constantinople someone found a golden stone and on it a man lying down, with this inscription: [Col. 0149C] “Christ will be born of the virgin Mary, and I believe in him. Under the emperors Constantine and Irene, O sun, you will see me again.” (Mett. [L.]) The Saxons rebelled and, defeated by Charles in war, handed over to him as many as 4,500 rebels and gave him hostages.

783. 2. 7. 15. 5.

(Ib.) The Saxons rebelled and, defeated by King Charles, were almost destroyed to the last man.

784. 3. 8. 16. 6.

(Ib.) The Saxons and Frisians rebelled and were defeated. The Westphalians were defeated by Charles, son of King Charles.

785. 4. 9. 17. 7.

(H. M.) Mady the emir died; after him Moses ruled the Saracens for two years. (Mett. [L.]) Charles devastated Saxony. Wintichindus and Albion, dukes of the Saxons, were reconciled to Charles and baptized, and the Saxon disturbances were suppressed.

786. 5. 1. 18. 8.

(Ib.) King Charles sent his seneschal Adulf against the Britons [Note: [Col. 0149] bittones in Sig.], and through him captured many Breton fortresses and their princes. (MAR.) The sign of the cross appeared on people’s clothing.

787. 6. 2. 19. 9.

(Mett. [L.]) Moses, the amir, died; after him his brother Aaron ruled the Saracens for 23 years. [Col. 0150A] King Charles came to Rome and advanced against Heregisus, duke of Benevento. Heregisus bought his pardon by giving gifts and hostages. War arose between the Franks and the Avars. (MAR.) Blood flowed from heaven and earth.

### 788. 7. 1. 20. 10.

(Mett. [L.]) Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, was judged guilty of treason against King Charles; therefore, after being tonsured by Charles, he was confined in a monastery together with his son Theodo. In Italy the Greeks and Romans fought. For the second time in Italy the Franks and Avars fought. For the third time the Avars and Bavarians fought. For the fourth time the Avars and Franks fought, and in all these encounters Charles rejoiced that victory had fallen to his men. (H. m.) At the insistence of Tarasius, patriarch of Constantinople, [Col. 0150B] and Pope Hadrian, a universal synod of 350 bishops was assembled at Nicaea. There the Catholic faith was confirmed by the subscription of all, in the presence of Irene and her son Constantine, and the heresy of those who execrated images of God was rejected forever. A powerful conspiracy was formed by the Austrasians against King Charles, under the leadership of Harderic. When it was discovered, many were either mutilated or exiled.

### 789. 8. 2. 21. 11.

(Mett. [REG.]) At Cologne on the Rhine Charles built and fortified two bridges and, entering Slavonia, subjected it to himself. [Note: [Col. 0149] “The Elbe”; see Regino and the Annals of Metz; cf. *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores II, 223, note.] (H. m.) Adelgisus, son of King Desiderius, who had fled to the Greeks after his father’s defeat, [Col. 0150C] came to Italy, encouraged by Greek aid, either to reclaim the kingdom or to exact vengeance. Having engaged the Franks in battle, he was captured by them and put to a bitter death.

### 790. 9. 3. 22. 12.

(EINH.) King Charles, wholly devoted to ecclesiastical propriety, carefully corrected the discipline of reading and singing (JOH., *Vita Gregorii Magni* II, 10). For, observing that the Gauls again differed from the Romans in singing, while the people of Metz diverged somewhat through the mere lightness of their nature, he corrected the discrepancy in the chant through singers whom Pope Hadrian once more sent to him from Rome. (EINH.) He was also concerned for the poor, not only in his own kingdom but even beyond the sea—in Egypt, Syria, Africa, and especially Jerusalem—relieving Christian poor people through the generosity of his almsgiving. For this reason above all he sought the friendship of overseas kings, so that there might be relief for the Christians living under them. (Ib.) Alcuin, born in Britain, the king Charles’s beloved teacher, excelled in literary knowledge in Gaul; it was chiefly under his instruction that the king himself learned all the liberal arts. He wrote many works, among them notably books on the Holy Trinity, written for the king himself. [He also corrected the sacred history at the king’s command. [Note: [Col. 0149] Added by 1δ.; absent from the others except A.]]

[Col. 0151A] ### 791. R. 10. S. 4. F. 23. B. 13.

(H. m.) Constantine deprived his mother Irene of the imperial power and ruled alone for six years. (Mett. [L.]) King Charles attacked the kingdom of the Avars by land and sea, leaving them hope of escape only in flight.

### 792. 1. 5. 24. 14.

(H. m.) The emperor Constantine met Chardamus of the Bulgarians and, shamefully defeated, was disgraced; Chardamus, having seized all the royal equipment, was enriched. Pepin, King Charles’s son by a concubine, deformed by a hump, was enticed by certain Frankish nobles with the promise of the kingdom and conspired against his father. Convicted, he was tonsured and shut up in the monastery of Prüm, where he served God until the end of his life. The other accomplices in the conspiracy were exiled, while a few were put to death.

[Col. 0151B] ### 793. 2. 6. 25. 15.

(Mett. [L.]) The Felician heresy was condemned and, in the presence of Pope Hadrian, renounced by Felix himself, its author. This heresy asserted that the Son of God was true God in the divine nature but merely titular in the human nature; likewise, that in the divine nature he was the true Son of God but in the human nature an adopted son, dividing the one person of God and man into two persons, namely, that of the true son and that of the adopted son. The Saxons wavered in faith and loyalty to the king.

### 794. 3. 7. 26. 16.

(H. m.) The emperor Constantine deprived many nobles whom he suspected of their eyes. (EINH.;---MARIANUS.) King Charles, educated not only in his native language but also in foreign languages, wrote down and committed to memory barbarian and very ancient [Col. 0151C] poems in which the wars and deeds of ancient kings were sung. He also began a grammar of the native language; he assigned names to the months of the year according to his own, that is, German, language; and he likewise called the twelve winds by their proper names, whereas previously only the four cardinal winds had been named.

### 795. 4. 8. 27. 17.

(Mett. [L]; EINH.) Terrified by Charles’s valor, the Saxons surrendered themselves to the faith of Christ and the king’s allegiance. King Charles, observing the Christian religion devoutly and reverently, honored the churches of God in every way and adorned them with sacred vessels and vestments, ordering that not even doorkeepers might minister in a church in ordinary clothing. He also built at Aachen [Col. 0151D] a basilica of extraordinary beauty, for whose construction he had columns and marble brought from Rome and Ravenna.

### 796. 5. 9. 28. 18.

(G. pont.) Leo, the 91st pope, presided over the Roman Church. He soon sent King Charles the key of the confession of Saint Peter together with the banner of the city of Rome. (Mett. [L.]) Witthan, king of the Obodrites, was killed by the Saxons.

### 797. 6. 10. 29. 19.

Heinricus, duke of the Friulians, after stripping Yringo, prince of the Avars, in Pannonia, sent his immeasurable treasure to King Charles. [Note: [Col. 0151D] He never existed; Regino created him because he did not understand the word *hring*, that is, “ring,” in the annals of Lorsch. From there he passed into the Annals of Metz, the source of Sigebert.] (Ib.) Thudun, prince of the Avars, surrendered himself and his homeland to King Charles and received the grace of baptism.

### 798. 7. 11. 30. 20.

(H. m.) The empress Irene, abusing her womanly grief over the empire taken from her, deprived her son Constantine of his eyes and imperial power and ruled alone for three years. Thatun the Spaniard, prefect of Barcelona, surrendered himself to King Charles and restored Barcelona, which had defected from him. (Mett. [L.]) King Charles defeated the Saxons in a severe battle. King Adelphon of Galicia sent many gifts to King Charles. (H. M.) The sun was darkened for seventeen days.

### 799. 1. 12. 31. 21.

(H. m.) The emperor Constantine died. In Spain, after Barcelona had been restored to the Saracens, it was besieged by Charles’s soldiers. The Romans captured Pope Leo while he was celebrating the solemnity of the Greater Litany and tore out his tongue and eyes. When his voice and sight had been divinely restored, they again plucked out his eyes and tongue by the roots. Freed from their hands, he fled as quickly as possible to Charles. (Mett. [L.]) Heinricus, duke of the Friulians, was killed by his own men.

### 800. 2. 13. 32. 22.

(Mett. [L.]) In the month of July there was frost twice, contrary to nature, hard and congealed by ice, but it harmed no crops. King Charles restored Pope Leo to the Roman see; he himself also hastened to Rome, examined the cases, legally condemned the guilty, and thus pacified all the disturbances of the Romans. (Ib.) The people of the Avars fell away from the faith. With the aid of the Franks, the Balearic Islands were defended against the Saracens. Through Widon, Charles’s duke, the Britons were defeated and received into submission. Gerold, duke of Bavaria, was killed in Pannonia when he engaged the Avars; concerning him it is read in the *Vision of Wetti* that he was numbered among the martyrs.

### 801. 3. 14. 33. 23.

The Romans, who had long since become estranged in spirit from the emperor of Constantinople, now, taking advantage of the opportunity because a woman was ruling them after blinding the emperor Constantine, her son, unanimously acclaimed imperial praises for King Charles, crowned him through the hand of Pope Leo, and called him Caesar and Augustus. They also applauded his son Pepin, who had been appointed king of Italy. (Mett. [L.]) Amymurlyn, king of the Persians, sent the emperor Charles an elephant and many gifts. Barcelona was captured. In Italy also the city of Theate was captured by the Franks. Saint Salvius, bishop, coming from Aquitaine to the royal estate of Valentia, was martyred by Winigard, son of Gerard, the administrator of that estate. After the emperor Charles the Great had been divinely warned three times to seek his body, he found it and buried it honorably, but punished his murderers severely; yet even after this God’s vengeance against them did not cease. Since the order of the kingdoms has been changed, the order of the titles must also be changed, because from now on the kingdoms of the Franks and Romans must be treated as one, while the kingdom of Constantinople must be distinguished from the Roman kingdom. Byzantium, a city of Thrace, was enlarged by the first Constantine into a new city and elevated as a royal city; all the glory of Roman dignity was transferred there, it was dedicated as the seat of the Roman Empire, and was called New Rome. After approximately 468 years had passed, when the Roman Empire had been divided from Constantinople, Charles, the first of the Franks to rule the Romans, ruled for fourteen years.

### 802. R. 1. F. 34. C. 4. S. 15. B. 24.

(Mett. [L.]) The Italian cities of Ostona and Luceria, which were hostile to Charles, were received into submission. The emperor Charles sent legates throughout his entire empire to administer judgment and justice to all [Col. 0153B] and established 23 legal chapters. [Note: [Col. 0153D] At Aachen. *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Leges I, 90.] The emperor Charles’s legates, returning from Aaron the amir, brought to Francia, among other gifts, the bones of Cyprian of Carthage, a martyr, and of Speratus, the first of the Scillitan martyrs, as well as the head of the martyr Pantaleon. (H. m.) Nicephorus sent Irene, deposed from the empire, into exile and ruled the Constantinopolitans for eight years.

### 803. 2. 35. 1. 16. 25.

(H. m.) The empress Irene died in exile. The emperor Nicephorus, engaging the Saracens, was utterly defeated. [Note: [Col. 0153] “N. i. S. c. p. v.” are lacking in C2*. D.] (Mett. [L.]) The emperor Charles transferred all the Saxons living beyond the Elbe to Francia and gave their districts to the Obodrites. (H. m.) [Col. 0153C] Aaron the amir advanced against the emperor Nicephorus with three hundred thousand men. Unable to withstand him, Nicephorus made a shameful treaty, agreeing to pay him annually thirty thousand nomismata, three nomismata as a poll tax for the emperor, and three for his son. Charles administered justice throughout the entire empire and established 29 legal chapters. [Note: [Col. 0154D] *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Leges I, 114; cf. Scriptores II, 225.]

### 804. 3. 36. 2. 17. 26.

(Mett. [L.]) Pope Leo came to the emperor Charles in Francia. (H. m.) After breaking his treaty with the Saracens, the emperor Nicephorus brought many misfortunes upon his empire. Godefrid, king of the Danes, having insolently abused his power against neighboring peoples, sought peace from the emperor Charles. The Avars, also called Huns, were subdued in a long war against the Franks and were so reduced in courage and power that those who had formerly been accustomed to attack others voluntarily were now unable even to defend themselves against others. For in this war all their glory and nobility perished, and whatever money and treasure they had amassed for so many centuries by conquering the world, all of it now fell to the victorious Franks; never had Francia been enriched by so great a quantity of spoils in any war.

### 805. 4. 37. 3. 18. 27.

The emperor Charles, although the emperors of Constantinople were indignant against him because of their envy of the imperial title bestowed upon him by the Romans, endured them with great patience and magnanimity; and because they regarded his power with suspicion, he reconciled them to himself by frequent embassies and made them his firmest allies. [Note: [Col. 0153] *crebris* (“frequent”), 1.] (Mett. [L.]) The Avars, unable to endure the attacks of the Slavs, obtained from the emperor Charles a place to live between Savaria and Carantania, and there they settled without the name of a kingdom, under Frankish authority. (Ib.) Charles, son of the emperor Charles, defeated the rebellious Bohemians and killed their duke Lethon.

### 806. 5. 38. 4. 19. 28.

(Ib.) Charles divided the kingdom among his sons and, having drawn up a testament, confirmed it by his own authority and that of Pope Leo. (Ib.) The Bohemians, aided by the Slavs, ravaged everywhere, but were bravely defeated by Charles, the emperor’s son.

### 807. 6. 39. 5. 20. 29.

(H. m.) Chumeyd the amir, sent by Aaron to destroy Lycia, reached Myra and tried to smash the shrine of Saint Nicholas; instead, he shattered another one. For this presumption he incurred God’s vengeance and, when an unavoidable storm followed, lost his entire fleet. The emperor Charles, through his deacon Paul, had the finest passages from the writings of the Catholic Fathers selected and compiled into readings suitable for each feast, to be read in the church throughout the cycle of the year. [Note: [Col. 0153] “Charles … had [this] done” was added in the margin by Sig., in the third correction; *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores II, 223.] (Mett. [L.]) The king of the Persians honored the emperor Charles with precious gifts through ambassadors. The Saracens ravaged Sardinia but were defeated by King Pepin of Italy. (H. m.) Chrumnus ruled the Bulgarians.

### 808. 7. 40. 6. 21. 1.

(Mett. [L.]) In Britain, Eardulf, king of the Northumbrians, was driven from his homeland and kingdom; but when he came to the emperor Charles, Charles restored him to his kingdom and homeland. (H. m.) Aaron the amir died; after him Muhammad ruled for five years.

### 809. 8. 41. 7. 1. 2.

(A. Leod.) Walcaudus assumed the bishopric of Liège and built the monastery of Andage in the Ardennes. (Mett. [L.]) King Pepin of Italy subjected Venice to himself by war and died not long afterward at Milan; [Col. 0154D] and the emperor Charles restored Venice to Nicephorus. The emperor Nicephorus embittered all his subjects with new and unjust laws and intensified God’s anger against himself. (Ib.) After Godefrid, king of the Danes, died, his son Heming sought peace from the emperor Charles.

### 810. 9. 42. 8. 2. 3.

(Mett. [L.]) Charles sent three armies into three parts of his kingdom: one beyond the Elbe, which defeated the Hilinones; one into Pannonia, which subdued the remnants of the Huns and the Slavs; and one against the Britons, which crushed their treachery. Victory came to him everywhere. (EINH.) Charles, the eldest son of the emperor, died. (MARIANUS) The emperor Charles made Christ heir of his possessions by testament. Having divided everything he possessed in mancipable property into three parts, he assigned one third to the poor and to those serving in the palace; he subdivided the other two parts into twenty-one portions and distributed them among the metropolitan bishops subject to him in equal number, so that each metropolitan church would retain one third of the portion assigned to it and divide two thirds among its suffragan bishops. The names of the archiepiscopal cities that were under Charles were: Rome, Ravenna, Milan, Forum Julii, also called Aquileia, Grado, Cologne, Mainz, Juvavum, also called Salzburg, Trier, Sens, Besançon, Lyon, [Col. 0155B] Vienne, Rouen, Reims, Arles, Darantasia, Embrun, Bordeaux, Tours, and Bourges. (H. m.) The emperor Nicephorus entered Bulgaria; and because he did not know how to restrain himself in victory, he was killed by the Bulgarians together with a large number of senators. His son Stauracius ruled after him for one year.

### 811. R. 10. F. 43. C. 1. S. 3. B. 4.

(H. m.) After Stauracius was deposed, Michael ruled after him for three years. (Mett. [L.]) Heming, king of the Danes, died. After him, two men contending with one another for the kingdom clashed in battle, in which nearly 11,000 Danes were killed. (EINH.) At Mainz, the bridge over the Rhine, five hundred paces long, which the emperor Charles had built of wood over ten years with immense labor and remarkable workmanship, so that it seemed capable of lasting forever, burned down in three hours so completely that not even a single splinter remained on the water.

### 812. 11. 44. 1. 4. 5.

(Mett. [L.]) The emperor Charles placed the imperial crown upon his son Louis and made Bernard, son of King Pepin, king of Italy. (Elev. Am.) In Francia, at the monastery of Elnon, Saint Amand was raised by Lothair, approximately 152 years after his burial. When his body was found still intact, his hair and fingernails, which appeared to have grown, were cut, and the teeth were extracted from his mouth with pincers; [Col. 0155D] blood then flowed from it, and is still preserved as a memorial for posterity.

### 813. 12. 45. 2. 5. 6.

(Mett. [L.]) The emperor Charles ordered councils to be held by the bishops throughout Gaul concerning the condition of the churches: one at Mainz, another at Reims, a third at Tours, a fourth at Chalon, and a fifth at Arles. (H. m.) Muhammad the amir engaged his brother Abdallah; defeated by him, he unwillingly allowed him to reign jointly with him. Through this war the Saracen kingdom was divided for several years. (Mett. [L.]) The emperor Michael, having engaged Chrumnus of Bulgaria, was defeated in battle and fled; in despair over his affairs, he became a monk and laid down the empire. After him Leo ruled for eight years.

[Col. 0156A] ### 814. 13. 46. 1. 1. 7.

(Mett. [L.]) The glorious emperor Charles, having enlarged and pacified his kingdom and empire and having ordered the condition of the Church in a holy and religious manner, died and was buried at Aachen in the seventy-second year of his life. Because of the greatness of his deeds he was surnamed “the Great”; Einhard wrote his life. After him his son Louis ruled for 26 years.

### 815. 1. 2. 2. 8.

(Mett. [L.]) Peace was established between the emperors Louis and Leo. Harald, king of the Danes, driven from his homeland and kingdom by the sons of Godefrid, came to the emperor Louis and implored aid in recovering them. Delighted by his success, Chrumnus attacked the people of Constantinople with excessive insolence and, through repeated incursions, roamed as far as the city gates.

### 816. 2. 3. 3. 9.

(G. pont.) Stephen, the 92nd pope, presided over the Roman Church. He soon came to Francia and crowned Louis emperor. (Mett. [L.]) The emperor Louis sent an army against the Danes and through it received hostages.

### 817. 3. 4. 4. 10.

(G. pont.) Paschal, the 93rd pope, presided over the Roman Church. (Mett. [L.]) The Basques rebelled against the emperor Louis, but, subdued by his army, quickly returned to their senses.

### 818. 4. 5. 5. 11.

(Ib.) Sclaomir, king of the Obodrites, defected from the emperor Louis and went over to the Danes.

[Col. 0156C] ### 819. 5. 6. 6. 12.

(Ib.) The emperor Louis subjected the Britons to himself. Their duke Murman, who had usurped the title of king, was killed by them. (Ib.) King Bernard of Italy was accused of conspiracy against the emperor and, judged guilty of treason, was first deprived of his kingdom and eyes, and thereafter of his life. (Ib.) Harald was sent back by Louis to the kingdom of the Danes.

### 820. 6. 7. 7. 13.

(Ib.) Sclaomir, king of the Obodrites, and Lupus, duke of the Basques, condemned to death, were exiled by the emperor Louis. (Cap. Aquisg.) At a general assembly held at Aachen, by arrangement of the emperor Louis, certain chapters were added by the bishops and abbots [Col. 0156D] for the use of regular monks; and, after many compilations from the Holy Scriptures had been made, rules were established for clerics and clerical women religious. Since the transmission of histories fails, the account of the Bulgarian and Saracen kingdoms also ceases.

### 821. 7. 8.

(G. pont.) Pope Paschal found the body of Saint Cecilia the virgin, she herself revealing its location, clothed in golden garments still soaked with her blood; he transferred her body, together with those of the saints Valerian, her husband, Tiburtius, and Maximus, and also of Pope Urban, into a church he had built for them. (Mett. [L.]) The emperor Louis confirmed by the oaths of his leading men the division of the kingdom that had been made among his sons. (Ib.) Leo, emperor of the Greeks, was killed in his palace [Col. 0157A] by a conspiracy of his leading men, especially Michael, count of the household troops; and Michael himself ruled for nine years.

### 822. F. 8. C. 1.

In Thuringia, a turf fifty feet long, fourteen feet wide, and one and a half feet high was cut and lifted from the earth without hands and carried more than 25 feet. In Saxony, the earth swelled up in the form of an embankment along a boundary for the length of one league.

### 823. R. et F. 9. 2.

(A. Leod.) The elevation of Saint Ursmar, confessor of Lobbes, was celebrated. [Note: [Col. 0157] “The elevation of Saint Ursmar, confessor of Lobbes, was celebrated” is absent from D.; C4* places it under the preceding year.] (Mett. [L.]) Drogo, brother of the emperor Louis, became bishop of Metz. (Ib.) Lothair, son of the emperor, was sent by his father to Italy; consecrated by Pope Paschal, he received the crown of the kingdom and the name of emperor and Augustus. (Ib.) At Rome certain nobles were killed because they appeared too ready to support the allegiance of the emperor Lothair. When this crime was also charged against Pope Paschal himself, the pope excused himself before the emperors and cleared himself by oath of the crime before the Roman people and the emperor’s legates, in the presence of a large number of bishops. (Ib.) An earthquake occurred; many villas and houses were burned by heavenly fire; human beings and animals were struck dead by lightning; crops were devastated by hail, and with the hail true stones of immense weight fell. These portents were followed by a great mortality among human beings. In the territory of Toul, at the village of Commerciacum, a twelve-year-old girl, after receiving Holy Communion from a priest at Easter, abstained first from bread for ten months, then from all food and drink for three years, and afterward returned to ordinary human life.

### 824. 10. 3.

(G. pont.) Eugenius, the hundredth [Note: [Col. 0157] So Sig. (again in error; cf. the year 817.) B4*, C1, 3, and 4* correct XCVI to XCVII and continue accordingly; B3* has XCIV and continues accordingly; C2* has XCV and continues accordingly.] pope, presided over the Roman Church. (Mett. [L.]) The bodies of Saint Severus, bishop of Ravenna, his wife Vincentia, and his daughter Innocentia were transferred to Mainz by Archbishop Otgar. (MAR.) In Gaul, before the summer solstice, when the air suddenly changed into a storm, a huge piece of ice fell with hail; it was fifteen feet long, six feet wide, and two feet thick. (Mett. [L.]) Among other gifts, the legates of the emperor Michael brought the emperor Louis books of Dionysius the Areopagite, written by him on the hierarchy, that is, the sacred order; at Louis’s own request they had been translated from Greek into Latin. These books were sent to Paris on the very feast of the holy martyr and were received with joy. The power of the holy martyr increased that joy by healing nineteen sick people there during that same night. (A. Leod.) Walcaudus, bishop of Liège, transferred the body of Saint Hubert [Col. 0158A] from Liège to the monastery of Andage. (A. Fuld.) Rabanus the sophist, second to none among the poets of his time, became abbot of Fulda. He discussed many matters from the Holy Scriptures and also composed a book on the praise of the Holy Cross, distinguished by a variety of figures and written in a difficult and wondrous poem; he sent it to Pope Sergius to be offered to Saint Peter.

### 825. 11. 4.

(Mett. [L.]) King Harald of the Danes was baptized at Mainz with his wife, sons, and his contingent of Danes; the emperor honored him with gifts and with part of Frisia, granted to him as a benefice. (Ib.) Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis and archchaplain of the sacred palace, sent to Rome and received from Pope Eugenius the body of Saint Sebastian the martyr, which he placed in the basilica of Saint Medard at Soissons. While it still lay unburied in the casket in which it had been brought, such an abundance of signs and miracles appeared in the name of that martyr that no mortal could either enumerate or recount them. Some are said to have been so astonishing that they exceed human credence, unless it were certain that God, for whom that martyr suffered, is able to do all things.

### 826. 12. 5.

(Ib.) The bodies of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, taken from Rome and transferred to Francia, were glorified by many miracles. The body of Pope Gregory is also said to have been transferred to the city of Soissons.

### 827. 13. 6.

[Col. 0158C] (G. pont.) Valentinus, the 101st pope, presided over the Roman Church. When he died after forty days of pontificate, Gregory, the fourth pope of that name and the 102nd pope of the Roman Church, presided; he was also called Leo IV. Rabanus published treatises on the Book of Wisdom and on Ecclesiasticus, addressed to Archbishop Otgar. Amularius wrote a book on ecclesiastical offices for the emperor Louis. (Praef. Ans.) Angelomus also published a treatise on the Book of Kings for the same emperor. Ansigisus, abbot of Lobbes, arranged in two little books the edicts of the emperor Charles the Great and of his son Louis concerning ecclesiastical law. He likewise arranged their edicts concerning secular law in two equally small books. [Note: [Col. 0157] “He likewise arranged …” is absent from D.]

[Col. 0158D] ### 828. 14. 7.

(Mett. [L.]) The Italian army of the emperor Louis, transported by fleet to Africa, engaged in battle and inflicted a great slaughter on the Africans. (Ib.) In Gascony, grain rained from heaven, resembling wheat but with shorter and rounder kernels. (MARIAN.) The bodies of Saints Valentinus and Genesius were transferred to the monastery of Reichenau.

### 829. 15. 8.

(Mett.) Agitation and conflict arose against the emperor Louis among his sons and leading men. This year, which is the year 4888 from the beginning of the world, the ninth great year from the beginning of the world ended; it consists of 532 years. [Note: After this, in 1, the following was erased: “Saint Sturm, first abbot of Fulda, died.” A alone adds the same; it is absent from the others. Cf. the year 780.]

### 830. R. et F. 16. C. 9.

At Constantinople Theophilus ruled for fifteen years. Pope Gregory, grieving that the suburb of the city of Rome around the church of the chief of the apostles, Peter, was being harassed by frequent Saracen incursions, resolved to build a new city there; encouraged by the counsel and assistance of the emperors, he began the new construction.

### 831. 17. 1.

(Transl. S. B.) The Saracens, raiding Sicily, also devastated the island of Lipari, where the body of the apostle Bartholomew rested. Long ago, because the pagans could not bear for it to be venerated by everyone on account of the excessive brilliance of its miracles, they had placed it in a leaden coffin and sunk it in the sea; from India it had been carried of its own accord as far as this island. Its bones, now scattered here and there by the Saracens and gathered by a monk to whom the saint himself revealed them, were transferred to Benevento. (Fuld.) The emperor Louis stripped some of those opposing him of their offices, exiled others, and deprived others of their possessions; by this he further embittered his sons and leading men against him.

### 832. 18. 2.

(Fuld.) Pope Gregory came to Gaul and acted against the emperor together with his sons. The emperor repudiated his wife Judith as though she were the cause of the troubles.

### 833. 19. 3.

(Fuld.) The emperor Louis, deserted and betrayed by his own men and reduced to the power of his sons, laid down his arms by the judgment of the bishops and was confined to perform penance. The sun and moon failed in an eclipse.

### 834. 20. 4.

(Fuld.) The emperor Louis, released, recovered his arms, empire, and wife, and compelled his son Lothair to return to Italy.

### 835. 21. 5.

At the warning of Pope Gregory and with all the bishops in agreement, the emperor Louis decreed that in Gaul and Germany the feast of All Saints should be celebrated on the Kalends of November, as the Romans celebrated it according to the institution of Pope Boniface. (WID.) At this time the relics of the martyr Vitus were transferred from Paris to Corvey in Saxony; therefore the Franks themselves testified that from that time the glory of the Franks had been transferred to the Saxons. (REGINO.) Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, was deposed; and many others who had conspired with him in the deposition of the emperor Louis were condemned and exiled.

### 836. 22. 6.

Pope Gregory solemnly dedicated the completed structure of the new city [Col. 0160A] and called it the Leonine City, either after Leo III, the third pope of that name, who had once laid the foundations of the work, or after himself, since he too was called Leo IV.

### 837. 23. 7.

(Fuld.) The Northmen gravely harassed Gaul, devastated Dorestad, and burned the town of Antwerp and the trading center of Witla, situated near the mouth of the Meuse; they received tribute from the Frisians. (G. pont.) Pope Gregory restored several cities of Italy, destroyed either by age or by hostile attacks, with new buildings or walls. [Note: [Col. 0159] “Pope Gregory … restored” is absent from D1**.] When the Saracens came as far as the Roman harbor to plunder, the Romans, at the insistence of Pope Leo and with the Neapolitans also assisting them, engaged them in battle and, with a severe whirlwind of winds divinely cooperating, nearly destroyed them after they had been defeated almost to annihilation. [Note: [Col. 0159] *u. adternetionem* in Sig. for *u. ad internecionem*.]

### 838. 24. 8.

(Fuld.) A comet appeared in the sign of Libra. The Northmen devastated the island of Walcheren and exacted tribute.

### 839. 25. 9.
