(Mett. [Fuld.]) The emperor Louis was reconciled with his son Lothair, who had come to him under pledge of faith, and granted him the dignity of the empire and the crown of the kingdom. A comet appeared in the sign of Aries, and for several days many fiery sparks, like stars, were seen running across the sky.

### 840. 26. 10.

(Mett. [F.]) The emperor Louis died, and Lothair, usurping the empire alone, ruled for fifteen years.

### 841. 1. 11.

(Mett. [REG.]) Charles and Louis, sons of the emperor, grieving that their brother Lothair had deprived them of their rightful share of the kingdom, prepared to rise against him.

### 842. 2. 12.

(Mett. [F. R.]) A comet appeared in the sign of Aquarius. While the three brothers were at odds over the division of the kingdom, battle was joined among them in the district of Auxerre, near the village of Fontenoy. So great a slaughter was inflicted on both sides that no age remembered such a massacre of men among the Frankish people; and their forces were so weakened there that they could no longer defend even their own boundaries against outsiders. Victory nevertheless came to Charles and Louis.

[Col. 0160D] ### 843. 3. 13.

(Mett. [F.]) Since the brothers had not yet ceased fighting, a discussion of peace was finally undertaken on the advice of the leading men, and forty nobles were chosen from the parties of each brother; meeting together, they were to divide the kingdom equally. Thus a truce was arranged until the following year. Meanwhile Louis, proceeding into Saxony, firmly suppressed a very powerful conspiracy of freemen who wished to overthrow their lords; the leaders of the faction were condemned to death.

[Col. 0161A] ### 844. R. et F. 4. C. 14.

(G. pont.) Sergius, the 103rd pope, presided over the Roman Church. To confirm his election, Louis, son of the emperor Lothair, was sent by his father and was anointed king of the Lombards by that same pope. (Mett. [F.]) The Moors occupied Benevento. [Note: [Col. 0161] “The Moors occupied Benevento” is absent from D.] After the kingdom had been described as divided into three parts, the brothers came together at the Gallic city of Verdun and made peace with one another; after giving and receiving oaths mutually, each returned to defend the part of the kingdom assigned to him. (Mett. [R.]) Charles received the western kingdoms, from the British Ocean to the River Meuse; from that time until now, the name Francia has remained in that region. Louis received the eastern kingdoms, namely all Germany as far as the waters of the Rhine, together with certain cities beyond the Rhine and their neighboring districts, because of the abundance of wine. Lothair, who was the eldest and was called emperor, held all the kingdoms of Italy together with Rome itself, as well as Provence and the central part of Francia between the Scheldt and the Rhine, which, its name having been changed, was called Lotharingia after him. After this division, therefore, Charles ruled in Francia for 34 years, and his brother Louis in Germany for 33.

### 845. R. 5. F. 1. C. 15.

(Mett. [F.]) King Louis of Germany subdued by war the Obodrites, who were attempting to defect from him, killing their king; he organized their land and people, divinely subjected to him, under his dukes. At Constantinople Michael and Theodora ruled for eleven years. [Note: [Col. 0161] In 1, the original reading was XIII or XIII, but it has now been altered by erasure to XI. A has XIIII.]

[Col. 0161C] ### 846. 6. 2. 1.

(Mett. [F.]) The Northmen gravely harassed Charles’s kingdom and came by ship as far as Paris. They fought three battles with the Frisians: they were defeated in the first and victorious in the other two. Charles fought unsuccessfully with the Britons. King Louis had fourteen dukes of the Bohemians baptized together with their people.

### 847. 7. 3. 2.

(G. pont.) Leo V, the fifth pope of that name and the 104th pope, presided over the Roman Church. He decreed that, while the sacred solemnities of Mass were being celebrated, no layman should dare to stand, sit, or enter in the presbytery, except the sacred people appointed for the ministry of the sacred office. He also decreed that the octave of the Assumption of Saint Mary should be celebrated in the Roman Church, which had not previously been done.

### 848. 8. 4. 3.

Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, appointed archbishop of Mainz, held a synod at Mainz by order of King Louis and decreed many things useful to the Church. (Mett. [F.]) A certain false prophetess, saying that the Day of Judgment was imminent, troubled Mainz, to the extent that she even won over some members of the sacred order. Corrected by the archbishop, she confessed that she had done this at the suggestion of a certain priest for the sake of profit.

### 849. 9. 5. 4.

(Ib.) The heretic Gottschalk is rationally, as many have thought, refuted by Rabanus the archbishop; nevertheless, he persisted in his error. (Transl. S. H.) The empress Saint Helena, buried by her son Constantine the Great, the first emperor of that name, in Rome in the church of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, in a purple mausoleum, was transferred to Francia by the monk Theogisus and is venerated with great reverence by the Franks in the diocese of Reims [Note: [Col. 0161] Sig. Cur. wrote the whole year in erasure in the third corrections; 1η adds: “buried in the monastery of Saint Peter, which is called Altum Vyleyr.” In place of these, A., after “diocese,” adds: “in Altuillari.”].

### 850. 10. 6. 5.

(Mett. [F.]) The Franks are severely defeated by the Bohemians in battle. [Col. 0162B] A malign spirit publicly declared through the mouth of a possessed man that he had presided over this war, and that he and his associates—namely, the spirits of pride and discord—had brought it about that the Franks turned their backs.

### 851. 11. 7. 6.

The relics of Saint Hermes the martyr are sent into Gaul by the emperor Lothar and honorably deposited at the monastery of Inda. (Ib.) A severe famine afflicted Germany, so that a father even wished to devour his own son; at that time Archbishop Rabanus showed great benevolence to the poor.

### 852. 12. 8. 7.

(Ib.) King Charles of the Franks captured the sons of his brother, King Pepin—Pepin and Charles—who were disturbing the kingdom, and, having had their heads tonsured as monks, thrust them into a monastery. [Col. 0162C]

### 853. 13. 9. 8.

(Mett. [R.]) The Northmen, entering the mouths of the Loire by way of the British Sea, attacked the city of Nantes, slaughtered the bishop while he was celebrating baptism on Holy Saturday, and killed the clergy and the people. From there they seized Angers, then Tours, and, like a storm, destroyed everything; they even burned the church of Saint Martin.

### 854. 14. 10. 9.

(G. pont.) Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, flourished in Francia; he wrote the Life of Saint Remigius. Benedict, the 105th to preside over the Roman Church, was installed. After he had been deposed through the conspiracy of certain wicked men, Anastasius seized the pontificate. But (Mett. [F.]) after Anastasius had been cast down and thrown into prison by envoys of the emperor Lothar, Benedict was honorably restored. The Northmen, who had grievously afflicted Francia for twenty years, returned to their homeland and were destroyed among themselves in an internecine war, so that no one remained of their royal line except a single boy [Note: [Col. 0161D] The famous passage concerning Pope Joan occurs in none of the manuscripts of Sigebert known to us, although the first edition presents it at this place. Unless it was inserted by the editor—which I doubt—it must have originated with a Votensis monk; but since manuscript E8h. is now lost, we have no certainty whatever on this matter. See what we shall say below concerning the Ursicampine Appendix.].

[Col. 0163A] ### 855. R. 15. F. 11. C. 10.

(Ib.) Earthquakes, unusual disturbances of the air, whirlwinds, storms, hail, and lightning bring many kinds of misfortune upon human beings. A certain man was even consumed by heavenly fire, while his clothing remained unharmed. (Ib.) The emperor Lothar, having divided the kingdom among his sons, renounced the world; after receiving the monastic habit at the monastery of Prüm, he soon thereafter fell asleep in the Lord. His son Louis, formerly anointed king by Pope Sergius, ruled for fifteen years. His brother Lothar, however, held Lotharingia [Note: [Col. 0163] Here A. presents the words: “At this time … Remigius …,” from the year 895, where it omits them.].

### 856. 1. 12. 11.

(Ib.) Rabanus, an archbishop of outstanding life and learning, died. The hermit Maginrad was martyred. (MAR.) At Constantinople Michael ruled alone [Col. 0163B] for twelve years [Note: [Col. 0163] Thirteen: C2*. 3. 4*. D.].

### 857. 2. 13. 12.

(G. pont.) Nicholas, the 106th to preside over the Roman Church, was installed; the emperor Louis strengthened his appointment by his presence. (Mett. [F.]) When a storm arose at Cologne and the people fled for refuge into the basilica of Saint Peter, lightning suddenly split and penetrated the basilica in the form of a fiery dragon, killing three men in different places but by a single stroke. It also left six others half-dead from the same blast.

### 858. 3. 14. 2.

(Ib.) The Franks complained to Louis, the brother of their king Charles, about Charles’s credulity and invited Louis to rule over them against Charles. He undertook this without deliberation and disgracefully crossed into another’s territory. (Ib.) In the diocese of Mainz a malign spirit gave clear evidence of its wickedness. At first, by throwing stones and pounding the walls of houses as though with hammers, then by speaking openly, exposing thefts, and sowing discord among neighbors, it harassed people. Finally it stirred everyone’s minds against one man, as though the others were suffering such things because of his sins. It burned up his crops after they had been gathered into one place; wherever he entered, the house was immediately consumed by fire, so that there was now no place left for him to stay except in the fields. Because of this, while the priests were performing litanies and sprinkling blessed water, the enemy, having wounded many by throwing stones, at last rested for a time. When the priests withdrew, the enemy, howling pitifully, finally named a certain priest and confessed that, when the blessed water was being sprinkled, he had hidden under that priest’s cloak as though he were his familiar companion; he accused him of having intercourse with the steward’s daughter. Thus it persisted for three years, until it consumed all the buildings there by fire.

### 859. 4. 15. 3.

(Ib.) The priest Probus died; his conduct and [Col. 0164A] learning had brought distinction to the church of Mainz. King Louis of Germany waged many battles vigorously against the Slavs; after capturing their prince, named Rastiz, he ordered his eyes to be put out because he had broken faith. (Ib.) While the princes of King Charles were quarreling among themselves, the Bretons, invading the abandoned land without assistance, came as far as Poitiers, devastating everything. King Charles pursued them as they returned, entered Brittany, and joined battle; the Franks were defeated, and the Bretons raged in their slaughter [Note: [Col. 0163D] A. 849. The Annals of Bertin report this under 860; Regino under 848; the Breton Chronicle under 848.].

### 860. 5. 16. 4.

(Ib.) When King Nomenoe of the Bretons was intent on devastating the kingdom of the Franks, Saint Maurilius, formerly [Col. 0164B] bishop of Angers, seemed to appear to him and stand by him. Struck on the head by him with a staff, he experienced the wrath of God in his death [Note: [Col. 0164D] A. 851. Annals of Bertin.]. (WIDUK. I, 16.) At this time Leutulf, duke of the Saxons, father of Duke Otto and grandfather of King Henry, transferred the body of Pope Innocent from Rome to Saxony [Note: [Col. 0164D] A. 844.].

### 861. 6. 17. 5.

(Mett. [R.]) Herispoe, son of Nomenoe, king of the Bretons, entered into alliance with King Charles and, after receiving gifts, submitted himself to his authority.

### 862. 7. 18. 6.

(Fuld.) King Lothar of Lotharingia, taking Waldrada, his concubine, over his wife Theutberga, with the consent of the archbishops Gunthar of Cologne and Theutgaud of Trier, brought great calamity upon himself. [Col. 0164C]

### 863. 8. 19. 7.

(Mett. [R.]) Hughbert, abbot and duke, brother of Queen Theutberga, rose up against Lothar on account of his sister’s repudiation. The archbishops Gunthar and Theutgaud, examined at Rome by Pope Nicholas concerning King Lothar’s adultery, were convicted both by the synodal acts they produced and by their own mouths; they were deposed from the episcopate and the sacred orders, anathematized, and granted only lay communion.

### 864. 9. 20. 8.

(Ib.) After the concubine Waldrada had been excommunicated by the apostolic legate, King Lothar, seeing that excommunication was also being threatened against him, took back his wife Theutberga. [Col. 0164D] But this did not help for long, because soon afterward he repudiated her and took back his concubine, nor could he thereafter be separated from her by any form of correction.

### 865. 10. 21. 9.

(ADON., Martyrol.) The bodies of the holy martyrs Eusebius and Pontianus, transferred to Gaul as a gift from Pope Nicholas, were honorably buried in monasteries dedicated to Saint Peter by the vow of religious men. (Mett. [R.]) The king of the Bulgarians was converted to Christianity with his people. Ministers of the sacred order were sent to him from the apostolic see, and, after he had also received assistance from King Louis, he was so firmly established in the faith that soon afterward, having appointed his elder son to the kingdom, he himself renounced the world and became a monk. But when his son, behaving like a youth, wished to return to pagan worship, the king resumed the military belt and royal dress, pursued his son, had his eyes put out, and thrust him into prison. Having installed his younger son in the kingdom, he took up the sacred habit again and persevered in it until the end of his life [Note: [Col. 0165] Here A. presents the words: “At this time … the monastery of Gimniacum,” from the year 895, where it omits them.].

### 866. R. 11. F. 22. C. 10.

(Ib.) After Herispoe was killed by his own men, his son Solomon ruled over the Bretons and entered into alliance with Charles, who was coming against him [Note: [Col. 0165D] A. 857. Annals of Bertin.]. (Ib.) The Northmen, returning to Gaul, devastated the territories of Nantes, Angers, Poitiers, and Tours. Duke Ramnulf of Aquitaine and the brave margrave Robert went out to meet them; but when the commanders themselves were killed while fighting recklessly, the rest were struck down in heaps by the Northmen like sheep by wolves.

### 867. 12. 23. 11.

(Ib.) When the Saracens were raiding the region of Benevento, the emperor Louis bravely confronted them. His brother Lothar hastened to his aid and fought many battles with them energetically, but his army was so heavily burdened by diseases caused by the unseasonable weather and by spider bites that he returned with great loss among his men.

### 868. 13. 24. 12.

(G. pont.) Adrian, the 107th to preside over the Roman Church, was installed. (Fuld.) A comet appeared with extraordinary clarity. Michael, emperor of the Greeks, had become so diminished in judgment and so deranged in mind that he ordered his attendants to be killed; yet, when he returned to himself, he demanded that they be brought back before him.

### 869. 14. 25. 13.

Basil, whom the emperor Michael had taken into his service when he was a poor man from the household of an abbot, and whom he had promoted to such great honors after making him chamberlain that he was called the emperor’s second self, was often ordered by the emperor, in his madness, to be killed. Fearing that he might be killed on such an occasion, Basil chose rather to kill the emperor himself than to be killed by him; and he ruled for seventeen years. [(Odo’s translation of the Life of Saint Maurus.) The body of Saint Maurus, who was a disciple of Saint Benedict, was transferred from Glanfeuil to Burgundy because of fear of the Normans and was moved to the monastery of Fosses, which Saint Babolene, a disciple of Saint Columbanus, built [Note: [Col. 0165] In erasure: 1γ; the others except A.].]

### 870. 15. 26. 1.

(Mett. [R.]) King Lothar went to Rome to Pope Adrian to offer his defense. When both he and the leading men of the kingdom were invited by the pope, as proof of their innocence, to undergo examination through the body and blood of the Lord, both he and all who rashly received the Lord’s body with him perished within that same year; Lothar himself died at Piacenza immediately on the return journey.

### 871. 16. 27. 2.

(Fuld.) A synod was held at Cologne for the dedication of a church by the three metropolitans of Lotharingia: Liutpert of Mainz, Bertulf of Trier, and Willibert of Cologne. Since the greater church, which is Saint Peter’s, was also to be dedicated by them, voices of malign spirits were heard during the preceding night, grieving and complaining among themselves that they were about to be driven from the dwellings they had possessed for a long time. (Mett. [R.]) King Charles of the Franks, after the death of his cousin Lothar, attempted to seize Lotharingia alone, but through the moderation and skill of his brother Louis, king of the Germans, he was brought to the point of dividing his cousin’s kingdom equally between them. (Fuld.) The army of Louis the German fought various wars against the Slavs with varying outcomes.

### 872. 17. 28. 3.

(Mett. [R.]) Domestic calamity afflicted King Charles of the Franks through his sons. For Charles himself seized and blinded Karloman, whom he had advanced in the clerical state as far as the office of deacon, because Karloman had turned to apostasy and, disturbing the kingdom by every kind of wrongdoing, had become another Julian. Moreover, when his other son Charles rashly wished to test the already tested courage of a certain soldier, Albwin, and engaged him alone in single combat, Albwin killed him, not knowing who he was. (Fuld.) The emperor Basil sent King Louis of Germany, among other gifts, a crystal of astonishing size, wonderfully adorned with gold and gems, together with a substantial piece of the holy cross.

### 873. 18. 29. 4.

(MAR.) John, the 108th to preside over the Roman Church, was installed. To him John, a deacon of the Roman Church, wrote a life of the first Pope Gregory, commendably published in four books. (Mett. [R.]) Adalgis, duke of the Beneventans, led astray by the Greeks, rebelled against the emperor Louis and caused many cities of Italy to defect from him. The emperor bravely resisted him and captured Benevento and Capua. But, persuaded by Adalgis’s stratagems to dismiss his army, he was so entrapped by him that he could not escape unless, compelled to make a disgraceful treaty, he swore to Adalgis that he would never in his lifetime enter the territory of Benevento. For this reason Adalgis was judged by the Roman senate guilty of treason and a public enemy, and, when war was decreed against him, fled to Corsica. (Fuld.) Charles the Younger, son of Louis king of the Germans, was grievously tormented by a demon in the presence of his father and his leading men; during the torment itself he confessed that this had happened to him because he was plotting a conspiracy against his father.

### 874. R. 19. F. 30. C. 5.

(Ib.) In Italy, at Brescia, blood is said to have rained from heaven for three days and nights. The Northmen, also demanding tribute from the kingdom of Louis king of the Germans, were severely cut down and defeated by his army. (Mett. [R.]) Innumerable locusts devastated Gaul. They were larger than ordinary locusts, had six sets of wings, six feet, and two teeth harder than stone. Flying in formations like battle lines, they sent leaders ahead with a few companions a day’s journey in advance to mark out places for the multitude that was to come. Arriving at the appointed place around the ninth hour and awaiting sunrise there, they covered the air for the space of a day, darkening the very brightness of the sun. With broad mouths and distended intestines, they ravaged every green thing in the grasses and trees, extending their day’s march over four or five miles. Reaching the British Sea in this pitiful spectacle, they were at last driven by the winds into the depths of the sea; but, cast back onto the shore by the ocean’s tide, they caused many to perish when the air was corrupted by their decay. (Fuld.) A severe famine followed and consumed many through starvation, so that nearly a third of the people perished.

[Col. 0167C] ### 875. 20. 31. 6.

(Ib.) The winter was harsher and longer than usual: snow and frost lasted from the Kalends of November until the spring equinox. (Ib.) Louis, king of the Germans, saw in a dream his father Louis, formerly emperor, adjuring him by the name of the Holy Trinity to rescue him from the torments in which he was being held, so that he might finally deserve to possess eternal rest. For this reason the son sent alms to various monasteries and earnestly aided his father. From this it was understood that, although the same emperor had done many things pleasing to God and human beings, he had nevertheless permitted more things contrary to God to be done in his kingdom. Among these, the more serious appeared to be that he did not resist the heresy of the Nicolaitans and did not take care to observe the admonitions of the archangel Gabriel, contained in twelve chapters, which Emarcus [Note: [Col. 0167] Thus Sig. corrupted the name Einhard, whom he read in the Annals of Fulda.] presented to him for reading and observance. (Mett. [R.]) The Northmen occupied the city of Angers with all their possessions, as though they intended to live there. King Charles, having summoned Solomon king of the Bretons, besieged it for many days. But when the Northmen had been brought to desperation, the king, against the wishes of his army, accepted money from them, permitted them to leave, and thereby gave them the opportunity to do worse things [Note: [Col. 0167D] A. 873. Regino.].

### 876. 21. 32. 7.

(Fuld.) A comet appeared more fiery than usual. A sudden and excessive inundation of waters occurred in June, so that in Saxony a certain village, far removed from torrents and rivers, was suddenly swallowed up completely, together with its people and animals, trees and buildings, church and altar, leaving no trace of habitation. (Mett. [R.]) The emperor Louis died in Italy. His uncle, King Charles of the Franks, went to Rome and, having won over Pope John and the Romans with gifts, was created emperor and ruled for three years. But Louis, his brother, immediately prepared war against him, because he had usurped his cousin’s empire alone and without consulting him. (Ib.) After the death of their king Solomon, the Bretons clashed among themselves in civil war over the right to rule; thus, against their will, they ceased their destruction of Gaul. (Fuld.) After acquiring the empire, the emperor Charles, puffed up beyond measure, despised Frankish customs and affected Greek splendor and unfamiliar dress. Clad in a long dalmatic and belted over it with a sash hanging down to his feet, with his head wrapped in a silk covering and a diadem placed upon it, he proceeded in this fashion. And although he was more timid than a hare and more ready to flee from enemies than to pursue them, he provoked his brother Louis, threatening that he would hire such great forces that, once the river had been drained by the horses, he himself would enter the kingdom of Germany through its dry bed.

### 877. 1. 33. 8.

The monk Heiric presented to the emperor Charles a splendidly written life of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, composed in heroic meter in six books. (Mett. [R.]) Louis, king of the Germans, died, leaving his three sons as heirs: Louis the Younger; Charles, who ruled not long afterward; and Karloman, father of the emperor Arnulf. The emperor Charles, rejoicing at his brother’s death and prepared to carry out against his brother’s sons the injustice he had conceived against his brother, attacked their kingdom with fifty thousand men and more and came as far as Cologne, while Louis’s sons occupied other places. Louis the Younger sent an embassy to his uncle and asked for terms of peace. When he could not obtain them, he bravely met him in battle, defeated him, and compelled him to flee with excessive loss to his army and great disgrace. (Fuld.) When a pestilence among livestock broke out in Germany, dogs gathered from every direction to feed upon the carcasses disappeared so completely that neither living nor dead could be found.

### 878. 2. 34. 9.

(Mett. [R.]) The emperor Charles went to Rome for the second time. He gave his niece, the daughter of the emperor Louis, in marriage to Boso, his wife’s brother, and, having granted him Provence, crowned him king, so that Boso might even appear to rule over kings. When the emperor Charles heard that his cousins Karloman and Charles were bringing an army against him, he was overcome with fear and prepared to return; on the way back, having been maliciously given a potion by a certain Jew named Sedechias, he died at Mantua. His son Louis, surnamed the Stammerer, ruled in Francia for two years, the second ruler after the division. Charles the Younger, son of Louis king of the Germans, meanwhile gained the empire with the support of certain Roman nobles; but Pope John was working to transfer the empire to Louis the Stammerer, son of the recently deceased emperor Charles.

### 879. R. 1. F. 1. C. 10.

(Fuld.) Pope John was injured by the Romans, to the point that he was even held in custody, because he did not favor Charles. Coming to Francia, he stayed with King Louis the Stammerer for nearly a year. More than five thousand Northmen were killed by the Franks in Gaul. At this time [Note: [Col. 0169D] Sigebert is greatly mistaken concerning the date. For in the necrology of Saint-Amand of Elnon, tenth century, now Valenciennes Library B. 5, 66, we read: “On the tenth day before the Kalends of October, the death of Milo, in the year of the Lord 872,” and: “On the eighth day before the Kalends of October, the ordination of Hubald as priest, in the year of the Lord 880.”] Milo, a monk of Saint-Amand, flourished; he published a metrical life of Saint Amand and wrote a book on sobriety to Charles the Bald. Under this Milo his nephew Hubald was also growing up. Distinguished in knowledge of the seven liberal arts, he excelled above all in music and composed chants for many saints with sweet and orderly melody.

### 880. 2. 2. 11.

(Fuld.) The sun was so darkened at the ninth hour of the day that stars appeared in the sky. (Mett. [R.]) King Louis the Stammerer of the Franks died, leaving his wife pregnant by him. While the Franks held various opinions concerning his kingdom—some judging that it belonged to the sons of Louis the Stammerer by his concubine, others agreeing that Boso, the petty ruler of Provence, should unjustly seize it, and others wishing to reunite it with the kingdom of Germany—a son was meanwhile born from Louis the Stammerer’s legitimate wife and was named Charles after his grandfather. The sons of Louis the Stammerer by his concubine, however, named Louis and Karloman, divided the kingdom of the Franks between themselves and ruled for four years [Note: [Col. 0169] Five: B3*. C1. 3. 4*. D.], while constantly persecuting Boso. (Ib.) In the Carbonarian Forest of Francia more than nine thousand Northmen were killed by the Franks.

### 881. 1. 1. 12.

After the emperor Charles’s brother Karloman died, and not long afterward his other brother Louis was carried off by an untimely death, Charles, after notable victories over his enemies, obtained the kingdom of Germany (Cf. ib.).

### 882. 2. 2. 13.

(Mett. [R.]) Charles was blessed as emperor at Rome by Pope John. (A. Vedast.) The Northmen, joined by Danes, roamed through Francia and Lotharingia and devastated with sword and fire Amiens, Arras, Corbie, Cambrai, Thérouanne, the territories of the Morini, Menapii, and Brabanti, and the entire land around the River Scheldt, including the monasteries of Saints Walaric and Richarius. (Mett. [R.]) From there they entered the River Waal and burned all Batavia, including the palace at Nijmegen. In the same year, the Northmen kings Godfrey and Sigifrid, encamped with an immeasurable multitude beside the Meuse at a place called Haslon [Note: [Col. 0170D] Cf. Mon. SS. I, 396.], burned Liège, Utrecht, Tongeren, Cologne, and Bonn [Note: [Col. 0169] “Hunna”: C3. 4*. D.], with the neighboring castles. At Aachen, after stabling their horses in the palace, they burned the town and palace; they also burned the monasteries of Stavelot, Malmedy, Inda, and Prüm. (Fuld. 881.) Ministers of the sacred order of both sexes hid wherever they could find a suitable refuge [Col. 0170B] and concealed the bodies and relics of the saints in safer places. (A. Ved., 879.) In addition to these evils, Hugh, son of King Lothar by the concubine Waldrada, tyrannized in Lotharingia, while the aforementioned Boso did so in Burgundy.

### 883. 3. 3. 14.

(Mett. [R.]) The Northmen burned the city of Trier and advanced as far as Metz, where they joined battle and defeated the Christians. In this battle Walo, bishop of Metz, was killed.

### 884. 4. 4. 15.

(Ib.) The emperor Charles, summoned by the Gauls and Germans to aid the kingdom, besieged the Northmen. King Godfrey entered into a treaty with him under which he was to receive the province of Frisia and Gisla, daughter of King Lothar, as his wife; he was baptized and received by the emperor from the sacred font. After also bestowing lavish gifts upon King Sigifrid, Charles made them withdraw from his kingdom. Soon returning to Francia, after many raids they demanded twelve thousand of refined silver as tribute from Karloman, king of the Franks; then, promising peace for twelve years, they returned to the sea. (FLOD.) At this time a certain Rudolph transferred the body of Pope and martyr Saint Callistus from Rome to Francia. Callistus had instituted the celebration of the fast of the four Ember seasons [Note: [Col. 0169] “At this time … instituted”: Sig., apparently in the third corrections; the others except A.].

### 885. 5. 5. 16.

(Mett. [R.]) After Karloman, king of the Franks, died—his brother Louis having already died the previous year—the Northmen returned to Francia, saying that they had agreed upon peace only with the king of the Franks, not with the Franks. Thus compelled, the Franks invited the emperor Charles to aid them and subjected Francia to him. He sent his army once and twice against the Northmen, who had encamped near Leuven, but accomplished nothing worthy of mention. Charles therefore also ruled in Francia for four years [Note: [Col. 0171] Five: C1. 3. 4*. D.]. Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, died.

### 886. R. 6. F. 1. C. 17.

(MAR.) Marinus, the 109th to preside over the Roman Church, was installed. At Constantinople, after the emperor Basil died, his son Leo ruled for eighteen years [Note: [Col. 0171] Sixteen: A.]. (Mett. [R.]) Hugh, son of King Lothar by the concubine Waldrada, hoping through rebellion to obtain his father’s kingdom of Lotharingia, persuaded Godfrey, king of the Northmen, whose wife was Hugh’s sister Gisla, by promising him half of the kingdom he desired, to ask the emperor to grant him imperial estates at his discretion. Hugh thought that by this means the emperor would be trapped from both sides: if he granted the request, the Northmen, enemies of the kingdom, would be admitted into the kingdom’s very heart; if he refused, Godfrey would appear to have a just cause for rebellion. When Duke Henry and Godfrey met by agreement in Batavia to discuss this matter at the emperor’s command, Godfrey was killed with his men during the negotiations. Not long afterward Hugh too was captured by Henry, blinded, and finally tonsured as a monk at Prüm.

### 887. 7. 2. 1.

(Ib.) The Normans, leaving Leuven, besieged Paris. Duke Henry led an army against them, but, riding carelessly, fell into a ditch that the Northmen had made and covered with rubbish, and was killed. (Ib.) Hugh, duke and abbot of extraordinary power and prudence, died.

### 888. 8. 3. 2.

[Col. 0171C] (MAR.) Agapitus, the 110th to preside over the Roman Church, was installed. He is not numbered in some books. (Mett. [R.]) Since the emperor Charles was unable to expel the Northmen, he finally made a treaty with them and granted them the regions beyond the Seine, whose inhabitants were rebelling against him. This part of Francia was named Normandy by the Northmen [Note: [Col. 0171] “Which part of Francia was named Normandy by the Northmen”: Sig. added this in the third corrections; but a hand very similar to 1δ, in the erased text, wrote “is called,” although it was their own region, though not as extensive as it is now. B3*. F1. 2. 3 have the same; the rest follow Sigebert.].

### 889. 9. 4. 3.

(MAR.) Adrian, the 111th to preside over the Roman Church, was installed. (Mett. [R.]) The emperor Charles, jealous of his wife because she behaved with Liutward, bishop of Vercelli, with greater familiarity than was proper, declared during a dispute that he had never had intercourse with her. She, boasting that she was a virgin, accepted repudiation and went to a monastery.

### 890. 10. 5. 4.

(Ib.) The emperor Charles, failing in body and mind, was rejected by the leading men of the kingdom, and Arnulf, son of King Karloman and his cousin, was elevated to the kingdom; he ruled for twelve years. Arnulf assigned to his uncle Charles, who was in need of even the necessities of life despite having been emperor, estates in Alemannia; Charles died the following year. (Ib.) The Roman Empire and the kingdom of the Franks were miserably torn apart. In Italy, Berengar and Wido contended for the kingdom. The Franks, however, neglecting Charles, the son of Louis the Stammerer, a boy scarcely ten years old, set Odo, son of the duke Robert, whom we said above had been killed by the Northmen, over themselves as king. Rudolph, having placed the crown upon his own head, was established as king of the Burgundians; that kingdom endured for a long time.

### 891. 1. 1. 5.

(MAR.) From this time Liutprand, deacon of the church of Pavia, begins his history. Basil, the 112th to preside over the Roman Church, was installed. He is not found in some books. (Mett. [R.]) Unable to conquer Paris, the Normans attacked Burgundy and besieged the city of Sens, but did not capture it. [Col. 0172B] (LIUDP.) In Italy, the Saracens seized a certain fortress called Fraxinetum and began to be a source of great destruction to Italy.

### 892. 2. 2. 6.

(Mett. [R.]) The Northmen returned from Sens toward Paris; repulsed from there, they burned the city of Troyes by way of the River Marne and devastated everything as far as the cities of Verdun and Toul. (LIUDP.) Wido twice defeated Berengar in battle and put him to flight. (A. Vedast. 888.) King Odo defeated the Danes in battle on the River Aisne.

### 893. 3. 3. 7.

(LIUDP.) King Arnulf, adding the duchy of the Bohemians to the duchy of Zwentibold, duke of the Moravians, thereby made the Bohemians hostile to himself and gave Zwentibold, through the increase of his power, an occasion to rebel against him. When he was not strong enough to defeat him, Arnulf opened the gates and admitted into the kingdom the people of the Hungarians, hostile to God; with their aid he defeated Zwentibold and made him tributary. [Saint Ulrich was born in Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0171] 1δ added this in erasure; the others except A. Under the following year C1 has it, and with D reads “Valdricus.”].]

### 894. 4. 4. 8.

(Mett. [R.]) The Northmen, again repulsed from Paris, attacked the territories of the Bretons. At first victorious, they were later defeated by the Bretons; twelve thousand of their men were killed in two battles. (Ib.) While King Odo was staying in Aquitaine at the advice of the Franks, the Franks recalled Charles, the twelve-year-old son of Louis the Stammerer, to his paternal kingdom and had him blessed as king at Reims by Archbishop Fulk; [Col. 0172D] a long conflict then arose between him and Odo.

### 895. 5. 5. 9.

(MAR.) Stephen, the 113th to preside over the Roman Church, was installed. (Mett. [R.]) Returning to Lotharingia, the Northmen fought the Christians near Liège and won. Sunderold, archbishop of Mainz, was martyred by the Northmen at Worms. When King Arnulf heard of the slaughter of his men, he hastened from Bavaria with a strong army to fight the Northmen. He attacked them on foot above the river called the Thilia [Note: [Col. 0173D] The Dyle in Brabant.] and inflicted such a massacre upon them that, from their innumerable multitude, scarcely anyone remained to carry adverse news to the fleet. The surviving Northmen, after crossing the Meuse, roamed through Ribuarian territory and the Ardennes, devastating them, and withdrew across the sea. At this time Berno flourished in Burgundy. Formerly a count, he became abbot of the monastery of Gigny, which he had founded himself; he also built, from a gift of Countess Ava, the monastery of Cluny as a cell of the monastery of Gigny. At this time Remigius of Auxerre also flourished, devoted to the exposition of divine and human writings [Note: [Col. 0173] “At this time … devoted”: Sig., apparently in the third corrections; the others except A., which already has it under 855 and 865.]. (Cf. Sig. On Illustrious Men.)

### 896. R. 6. F. 6. C. 10.

(Mett. [R.]) King Arnulf made his son Zwentibold, born of a concubine, king of the Lotharingians. [Col. 0173B] (Ann. Ved.) King Charles appealed to King Arnulf for aid against Odo. King Arnulf sent an army to his assistance, but it accomplished little. (Ib.) King Charles had Hundeo, king of the Northmen, baptized and received him from the sacred font.

### 897. 7. 7. 11.

(LIUDP.) When King Arnulf was summoned by the Italian Berengar to aid him against Wido, he sent his son Zwentibold with an army into Italy. But Guido, acting courageously and corrupting the army’s leading men with gifts, caused them to return ineffectual.

### 898. 8. 8. 12.

(Ib.) King Arnulf entered Lombardy with force and captured the city of Bergamo by arms. He hanged its count Ambrose by a noose before the city gate, and, having struck terror into the other cities, brought them all into his obedience. Odo, a musician, formerly a cleric of Tours, professed himself a monk under Abbot Berno [Note: [Col. 0173] “Odo … under Abbot Berno”: Sig., apparently in the third corrections; the others except A. At the beginning of the following year C4* has it.].

### 899. 9. 9. 13.

(Ann. Ved., 898.) King Odo of the Franks died, charging the leading men to receive Charles back into the kingdom. After Charles was received throughout the whole kingdom of the Franks, he ruled for twenty-six years. (Mett. [R.]) A synod was held at Tribur against laymen who were attempting to diminish episcopal authority; several decrees were issued concerning the condition of the holy Church [Note: [Col. 0173D] A. 895, Regino.].

### 900. 10. 1. 14.

(LIUDP.) Formosus, bishop of Porto, presides as the 114th bishop of the Roman Church, against the wishes of certain Romans who had wanted to make Sergius, a deacon of the Roman Church, pope, but had not prevailed. When this Formosus had at some point fallen under the suspicion of Pope John VIII, he abandoned the bishopric of Porto and fled through fear of him; and because, after being recalled by the pope, he refused to return, he was anathematized. Finally, coming to Gaul to make satisfaction to the pope, he was degraded even to the status of a layman [Note: These details appear to have been drawn from some continuation of the *Deeds of the Pontiffs*, as Hirsch attempts to prove, p. 76. He may also have taken something from a letter of John VIII, in Pagi’s notes to Baronius’s *Annals*, for the years 876, 883, and 891. On the matter, see also Köpke, *On Liutprand* (Berlin, 1842, 8vo), p. 78.], swearing that he would never again enter Rome or reclaim the bishopric of his city, and confirming by his own handwritten subscription that he would remain in lay communion. Later, restored to the episcopate by Marinus, John’s successor, contrary to the oath he had given, he not only entered Rome but also assumed the papacy of the Roman Church.

Because of this, amid great scandal, much dispute and controversy was carried on in the Church for many years: some judged that his consecration, and that of those ordained by him, ought to be invalid; others, by contrast, judging with sounder counsel that, whatever Formosus may have been, all his consecrations ought nevertheless to be considered valid, on account of the dignity of the priestly office and the faith of those who had been ordained—especially since Formosus himself had been absolved by Pope Marinus from the perjury of his oath.

Invited by this Formosus, King Arnulf came to Rome; but, being denied admission, he besieged Leonine Rome. When, by chance, Lepusculus was fleeing toward the city and the army was pursuing him with a great uproar, the Romans, in their fear, threw themselves from the wall and, by making heaps, provided the enemy with a place from which to climb the wall. Thus, after Rome had been captured, Arnulf had those who had injured the pope beheaded, and was blessed by the pope as emperor [Note: 896.].

(Mett. [R.]) Fulco, archbishop of Reims, is killed by Wenemar, a retainer of Baldwin, count of Flanders, because he had received from Charles the abbey of Saint Vedast of Arras as a benefice, which Baldwin had already occupied for several years, although no one had granted it to him.

### 901. 11. 2. 15.

(LIUDP.) King Guido, unable to endure Arnulf, the emperor who pursued him everywhere—for neither cities nor naturally fortified castles could withstand him while they sought safety by flight—the emperor having meanwhile besieged his wife [Note: 896.], she, already despairing of her affairs, gave him a deadly cup through one of the emperor’s household, whom she had corrupted with a large sum of money. After drinking it, he could not be roused for three days, being able, with his eyes open, neither to perceive nor to speak. This compelled him to retreat. Guido pursued him as he withdrew, but, struck down by the Lord, he died.

(MAR.) Boniface presides as the 115th bishop of the Roman Church.

### 902. 12. 3. 16.

(LIUDP.) The emperor Arnulf, weakened by a long illness—or, as some report, afflicted by tiny worms, called *pedunculi*, which swarmed throughout his body in such abundance that none of the physicians could lessen them—dies [Note: 899. Dcb. 8.]. His son Ludowicus succeeds him and reigns for ten years.

(MAR.) Stephen presides as the 116th bishop of the Roman Church for four months. He had first been ordained bishop of the Church of Anagni by Pope Formosus; he then persecuted Formosus, decreed that all his ordinations ought to be invalid, and did other things against him horrible to relate. For it is read [Note: And rightly so; see Baronius and the *Acts of the Saints*, May IV, 147.] that he himself—not Sergius—had Formosus’s body dragged from the tomb in a council, stripped of its papal vestments, and clothed in lay clothing; then, after two fingers of his right hand had been cut off, he had the body thrown into the Tiber.

(MAR.) Romanus presides as the 117th bishop of the Roman Church.

(LIUDP.) In Italy, Lambert, his son, reigns in Guido’s place against Berengarius.

### 903. R. 1. F. 4. C. 17.

(MAR. AUXIL.) Theodore presides as the 118th bishop of the Roman Church. Taking a position against Pope Stephen, he reconciled those ordained by Formosus, whom Stephen had forcibly degraded inside Rome and not outside it, although he had not dared to consecrate them again. After reconciling them, Pope Theodore returned the documents of renunciation and ordered them burned by fire [Note: We do not know from where Sigebert took this. See Mansi, *Councils* XVIII, 182.].

(MAR. AUXIL.) John presides as the 119th bishop of the Roman Church. Also to confirm the ordination of Formosus, which Stephen had deposed, he convened a synod of seventy-four bishops [Note: 898; concerning this synod, see Baronius XV, 529; Mansi XVIII, 221.] in the presence of the Frankish archbishops and the king at Ravenna. In their presence the synod that Stephen had held for the condemnation of Formosus was burned.

(LIUDP.) After Lambert, Guido’s son, dies, Berengarius gains possession of the kingdom.

(Ib.) The barbarian nation of the Hungarians, which had previously been kept at a distance by certain barriers and had not had permission to go out toward either the southern or the western region, was released by Arnulf after the barriers had been broken. While Arnulf lived, this had somewhat restrained their fury; now that he is dead, they spread through all Gaul, Germany, and Italy like a savage storm.

(Ann. Lob.) King Zuendebald is killed in battle by the Lotharingians. In this conspiracy and battle, whoever was wounded either did not escape death or was never able to recover.

(Ib.) After Francone, bishop of Liège, dies, Bishop Stephen is appointed in his place, a man distinguished for holiness and learning. He more elegantly composed for Archbishop Herimann a life and passion of Saint Lambert the martyr; (ANSELMUS) he also composed a nocturnal chant about the same martyr, a chant about the Holy Trinity, and one about the discovery of Stephen the protomartyr, in sweet and regular melody.

(A. Lob.) Count Conrad, father of the Conrad who reigned after Ludowicus, is killed in battle by Count Albert.

### 904. 2. 5. 18.

(MAR.) Benedict presides as the 120th bishop of the Roman Church. King Ludowicus is disastrously defeated in battle against the Hungarians. At Constantinople, after the death of Emperor Leo, his son Constantine and Alexander, Leo’s brother, rule for one year.

### 905. 3. 6. 1.

(Ib.) Leo presides as the 121st bishop of the Roman Church. Thirty days after his ordination, his priest Cristoforus seizes him and thrusts him into prison, then presides as the 122nd bishop through an invasion of the Roman Church. The Hungarians, elated by the previous year’s victory, reduce Ludowicus’s kingdom to tribute. (Cf. Mar.) At Constantinople, after the death of Emperor Alexander, Constantine reigns for thirty-nine years.

### 906. 4. 7. 1.

(LIUDPR.) The Hungarians reduce the defeated Greeks to tribute. Among the Greeks, Romanus, humble in birth but reputed for tested courage because he had killed a fierce lion, was appointed by Emperor Leo commander of the naval forces. Wishing to become guardian of the emperor Constantine, who was still a very young boy, he seized the guardian appointed for him by his father, together with all the leading officials of the palace, whom he had craftily summoned outside the city; he expelled them from the palace and honored those favorable to himself with court offices. Phocas, who had led the land army against Symeon, king of the Bulgarians, terrified by this news, fled from the battle and caused everyone else to flee; thus he increased the Bulgarians’ courage and strength to wage war more fiercely against the Greeks. Romanus himself captured him and deprived him of his eyes.

### 907. 5. 8. 2.

(MAR.) Sergius presides as the 123rd bishop of the Roman Church.

(LIUDP.) This is the deacon Sergius who had been rejected from the papacy because of Formosus. Formosus had made him a bishop, but he nevertheless withdrew to the Franks; with their help, he seized Cristoforus, the usurper, and thrust him into prison, then secretly entered Rome and usurped the papacy. By threats and terrors he compelled the Romans to regard all the ordinations of Formosus as invalid. In vengeance for his own rejection, he ordered Formosus—something forbidden even to say—to be dragged from his tomb, decapitated while ceremonially clothed in priestly garments, and thrown into the Tiber after three fingers had additionally been cut off. He unjustly degraded all whom Formosus had ordained and, even more unjustly, ordained them again. After Formosus had been found by fishermen and carried in a coffin to the basilica of the prince of the apostles, certain images of the saints were openly seen by everyone to have worshiped and reverently greeted him.

(Ib.) Among the Greeks, Romanus, having become the father-in-law of Basil, married the mother of the emperor Constantine so that he might act more securely, and betrothed his own daughter to Constantine.

(Ib.) The Hungarians make the defeated Bulgarians tributary to themselves.

### 908. R. 6. F. 9. [Note: VIII is an error for I, and the error continues in this way through the year 927.] C. 3.

(LIUDP.) Romanus, having obtained from the leading men that he should also receive the imperial garments and the diadem of the empire, no longer appeared to be the emperor’s guardian but the emperor above the emperor. He even had his son Christoforus raised to the imperial dignity and preferred him to the emperor Constantine in public precedence. But Christoforus died not long afterward.

### 909. 7. 10. 4.

(Ib.) While the Hungarians were ravaging Italy, King Berengarius engaged them in battle and was disastrously defeated. Romanus, emperor of the Greeks, appeased the Bulgarians, who were waging fierce war against the Greeks, by making a treaty with them.

### 910. 8. 11. 5.

(Ib.) Saracens from Africa, sent by their king into Italy to bring Apulia and Calabria, which were rebelling against the Roman Empire, under his rule by force of arms, after fiercely defeating the Apulians and Calabrians, turned toward Rome and occupied Mount Garigliano. There they constructed a fortification for themselves and waged war against many Italian cities.

Regino, abbot of Prüm, brought his chronicle, begun with the birth of the Lord, down to this year [Note: “Regino … brought down” is absent in D.] [Note: Ad. places this rather in the year 906.].

(Ib.) A certain Adelbert, one of the leading men of Austrasia, who had rebelled against King Ludowicus for seven years, was brought to the king by the deceit of Hatto, archbishop of Mainz, and beheaded.

### 911. 9. 12. 6.

(A. Lob.) The Hungarians ravage Germany.

(LIUDP.) Ludowicus, son of Boso by the daughter of Emperor Ludowicus, had been invited by the Italians from Burgundy to rule. Berengarius received him in battle and compelled him to swear that, if he were allowed to return, he would not come again into Italy.

### 912. 10. 13. 7.

(A. Lob.) King Ludowicus of Germany dies. Because of the insolence of tyrants in Italy and the great influx of evils, he did not deserve the imperial blessing. Conrad succeeds him and reigns for seven years; he too lacked the imperial blessing.

(Testa. Bern.) As Abbot Berno was dying, he appointed Odo, formerly a musician, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, on the condition that the Church of Cluny should annually pay the Church of Gigny a census of twelve denarii [Note: 926; see Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order* V, 88.] [Note: “Who himself … denarii” is written in an erasure half a line long in Sig., third revision; the others. One copy, C2*, entirely omits the words “Berno … denarii”; A. gives the same account only under the year 914: “Berno, abbot of Gigny, founder of the monastery of Cluny, appointed Odo, a musician and monk from the clergy of Tours, as abbot of Cluny after himself, on the condition that the Church of Cluny should annually pay the Church of Gigny twelve denarii.” It prefixes: “At this time the body of Saint Faith and martyr was transferred from the city of Agen to the monastery called Conques.” In the first copy there is no trace of erasure; hence these words seem to have been added by a monk of Verdun.].

### 913. 1. 14. 8.

Ludowicus, invited again by the Italians to rule, so quickly forgot his oath that he went into Italy against Berengarius; after expelling him, he usurped the kingdom of Italy.

### 914. 2. 15. 9.

(LIUDP.) The more powerful princes of the kingdom were plotting rebellion against King Conrad: namely Arnold of Bavaria, Burchard of Swabia, Everard of Francia, Gislebert of Lotharingia, and, more distinguished than all of them, Heinrich, duke of Saxony and Thuringia. By the king’s wisdom and strength they were brought back into his favor. Arnold alone fled to the Hungarians with his wife and children and remained there until the king’s death.

### 915. 3. 16. 10.

(Ib.) Ludowicus was captured at Verona and, after Berengarius had bribed the city’s guards with gold to admit him into the city, was deprived of his eyes.

(MAR.) The Hungarians, allied with Berengarius, ravage Alemannia and are heavily slaughtered by the Bavarians and Alemanni.

### 916. 4. 17. 11.

(A. Lob.) King Charles of the Franks received the kingdom of Lotharingia.

(LIUDP.) The Saracens, coming out from Fraxinetum and Mount Garigliano, occupy Calabria, Apulia, Beneventum, and also the cities of the Romans, to such an extent that the Romans held half of each city and the Saracens the other half; and they oppressed Italy most grievously.

### 917. 5. 18. 12.

(MAR.) Anastasius, the 124th, and after him Lando, the 125th, preside over the Roman Church.

(Ib.) The Hungarians, devastating all Alemannia, reach as far as Fulda.

### 918. 6. 19. 13.

(LIUDPR.) Romanus, emperor of the Greeks, arranged for his sons Stephen and Constantine to rule jointly with their lord, the emperor Constantine. The emperor Constantine himself earned his livelihood by the work of his hands, practicing painting beautifully.

(WID.) King Conrad solicits Hatto, bishop of Mainz, whose deceit had formerly brought about the death of Adelbert, to act also against Heinrich, duke of the Saxons, whose power made him suspect to the king. By the time the bishop had fashioned a golden chain to be placed around the neck of the duke while he dined with him, the plot had been exposed and frustrated. Three days later Hatto died from illness and anguish—or, as some say, from a stroke of lightning. His accomplices in the plot were also expelled from the country by the duke. When the king sent an army against Heinrich, the Saxons raged against it with such slaughter that the comedians were said to declaim: “Where could there be such a great hell as might contain so vast a multitude of the slain?”

(MAR.) The Hungarians proceed through Alemannia into Alsace and as far as Lotharingia.

### 919. 7. 20. 14.

(Ib.) John, bishop of Ravenna, presides as the 126th bishop of the Roman Church.

(WID.) As King Conrad was dying, he designated Heinrich, son of Otto, duke of the Saxons, as king before the princes of the kingdom. He therefore reigned for seventeen years.

### 920. R. 1. F. 21. C. 15.

(LIUDP.) King Heinrich marched into Bavaria with an army against Arnold, who had returned from the Hungarians, and by his courage and wisdom brought him back into his favor, additionally granting him the ordination of all the bishops of Bavaria.

(WID.) He also brought Burchard, duke of Alemannia, who had been deterred by war, over to himself.

(A. Lob.) Duke Rotbert, brother of King Odo, desiring the kingdom of the Franks against Charles, disturbed Francia; at his instigation nearly all the leading men of Francia opposed Charles.

### 921. 2. 22. 16.

(Ib.) After Stephen, bishop of Liège, died, Richarius, a catholic man, was ordained bishop by Charles through the authority of the Roman pope, Hilduin having been rejected. Hilduin had sought to obtain the bishopric by giving money to Duke Gislebert, in the hope that Gislebert would grant it to him.

(Vita Guib.) At this time our holy father Guicbert was renowned among the nobles of Lotharingia. He founded our monastery—that is, Gembloux [Note: “Our father,” “our,” and “that is,” here and everywhere in similar passages are omitted by A., C1, 4*, and D.]—and, distinguished by wealth, nobility, and power, laid aside the belt of worldly warfare and girded himself with the belt of holy religion in the monastic habit.

(V. Wenc.) Ziptineus, duke of Bohemia, converted to the faith of Christ, ruled in Bohemia justly and religiously; after him came his son Watizlaus, and after Watizlaus his son Wencezlaus, distinguished for justice and holiness. His brother Bolizlaus was excessively hostile to him.

### 922. 3. 23. 17.

(MAR. LIUDP.) While the Hungarians were ravaging Francia, Alsace, Alemannia, and Saxony, King Heinrich engaged them near the city of Merseburg. Vowing to God that, in order to gain victory, he would eradicate the simoniacal heresy from his kingdom, he destroyed them in an indescribable slaughter, almost to annihilation.

(WID.) King Heinrich granted pardon to any thieves, robbers, or assassins whom he saw to be strong-handed and fit for warfare; he gave them lands and weapons, formed them into a legion, and sent them to fight the barbarians, ordering them above all to spare only the townspeople.

(A. Lob.) King Charles of the Franks, fighting with the assistance of the Lotharingians near the city of Soissons against Rotbert, brother of King Odo, who was invading the Frankish kingdom against him, (WID.) killed him and many others, submitted himself and Francia to King Heinrich, and sent him, as a pledge of perpetual alliance and affection, the hand of the precious martyr Dionysius of Paris, encased in gold and gems.

### 923. 4. 24. 18.

(A. Lob.) Kings Heinrich and Charles formed an alliance at Bonn [Note: “hunnam” in C1, 3, 4*, and D; absent in B3*.]. Charles returned the kingdom of Lotharingia to King Heinrich, with the bishops and counts on both sides confirming the agreement by oath.

(MAR.) The blood of the crucified Lord came to Reichenau—perhaps that blood which flowed from an image of the Lord when, for the second time, the Lord suffered the earlier sufferings at the hands of the Jews in his image [Note: “The blood … suffered” is absent in D.].

(LIUDP.) The Africans, who through the fortification of Mount Garigliano were ravaging all Italy, were so crushed in battle by the forces of Pope John and the assistance of Romanus, emperor of the Greeks, that not even one survived who was not either slaughtered or captured. Many testified that the apostles of God, Peter and Paul, had been seen in that battle coming to the aid of the Christians.

### 924. 5. 25. 19.

(WID.) King Heinrich secured peace with the Hungarians for nine years.

(A. Lob.) King Charles of the Franks was captured by Count Heribert and thrust into custody at Péronne, because of the killing of Duke Rotbert, whom Charles had slain.

(LIUDP.) King Rodulf of the Burgundians was invited by the Italians to rule against Berengarius. After engaging Berengarius in battle and expelling him in victory, Rodulf held the kingdom of Italy for three years.

### 925. 6. 26. 20.

King Heinrich captured Brennaburch, a city of the Slavs, and imposed tribute on the defeated Slavs.

(WID.) While reviewing the agrarian soldiers, King Heinrich ordered that eight of them should remain in the countryside and the ninth in the city; the eight were to work in the fields both for themselves and for the ninth, while the ninth was to set aside in houses built by him for this purpose one-third of all their crops, so that none of them would lack anything in war and the cities would be full of supplies and men.

(LIUDP.) King Berengarius was impiously killed by the Italians. The Hungarians, traversing Italy under their leader Salardus, besieged and burned Pavia.

### 926. 7. 27. 21.

(A. Lob.) King Charles of the Franks died in exile and as a martyr while in Heribert’s custody. Rodulf reigned in Francia for two years.

(LIUDP.) Symeon the Bulgarian, who had become a monk from a philosopher and a soldier from a monk, ruled the Bulgarians and grievously crushed the Greeks. But Romanus, emperor of the Greeks, appeased his madness by making a treaty with him.

### 927. 8. 1. 22.

(WID.) After the death of King Charles, when the Lotharingians were unwilling to be subject to King Heinrich, a certain Lotharingian named Cristianus, feigning illness, deceitfully summoned Duke Gislebert to him, captured him, and sent him to the king so that through him he might bring Lotharingia under his authority. But when the king observed Gislebert’s ability and power, he betrothed his daughter Gerberga to him and once again placed him over Lotharingia.

(A. Lob.) Ludowicus, son of King Charles, fleeing those who were plotting against him, crossed the sea [into England. For his mother had been the daughter of the king of the English] [Note: Sig. had initially published: “fleeing, he crosses the sea. Rodulfus, etc.” Later, in the second revision, he inserted *per* before *mare* and, after erasing the words “Rodulfus … is appointed in his place,” wrote above the erasure “into England … is appointed in his place.” Thus Sig. expanded the passage while preparing the second edition. [Col. 0181] Hence all the others have the same reading except A., which follows Sigebert’s first edition. “Rodulfus … is appointed in his place” is absent in B4*, 4**.].

(LIUDP.) Rodulf is rejected by the Italians, and Count Hugo of Arles is appointed in his place as king.

### 928. R. 9. F. 2. C. 23.

(A. Lob.) Ludowicus returned to Francia and, although in distress, was nevertheless restored to the kingdom; he reigned for twenty-seven years.

(LIUDP.) King Hugo, with the counsel and valor of Count Samson, circumvented certain Italians whom he suspected and brought them under his authority.

(Ibid.) Ratherius, a monk of Lobbes, a man of extraordinary simplicity but renowned for his knowledge of the liberal arts, traveled to Italy with Hilduin, who had formerly sought the bishopric of Liège in Lotharingia, to King Hugo. Hugo appointed Ratherius bishop of Verona, while Hilduin was ordained archbishop of Milan.

(WID.) King Heinrich captured Grana [Note: “Gana” initially, but corrected; C1, 3, 4*, and D.] a city of Dalmatia, and imposed tribute on the Dalmatians.

### 929. 10. 1. 24.

(LIUDP.) King Heinrich extorted from Count Rodulf the lance of wondrous workmanship, sanctified by the nails of Jesus Christ crucified, which was said to have belonged to the first and great Emperor Constantine. The lance had been given to Rodulf, king of the Burgundians and of Italy, by Count Samson. Heinrich obtained it by prayers, threats, and gifts, adding also part of the province of the Swabians. He left it to his successors as a symbol and protection of the empire.

### 930. 11. 2. 25.

(Ibid.) Pope John was captured by the soldiers of Guido, the margrave, and thrust into custody; a pillow was placed over his mouth, and he was most cruelly strangled. Another John was appointed in his place, the brother of Alberic, who ruled Rome after expelling Hugo. Elsewhere it is read that Pope Leo presided at this point.

(MAR., WID.) Wencezlaus, prince of Bohemia, besieged by King Heinrich in the city of Prague, surrendered himself and the city to the king and paid the heavy tribute imposed upon Bohemia.

### 931. 2. 3. 26.

(MAR.) King Heinrich makes the kings of the Northmen and the Abrodites Christians.

(A. Laub.) Hubald, monk and philosopher of Saint-Amand in Elnone, died [Note: “Hubald … died” is absent in D.] [Note: 930, according to the Laubian Annals.].

(WID.) The Redarii, conspiring in numbers of up to two hundred thousand men, rebel against King Heinrich, seriously ravage his kingdom, and encourage neighboring peoples to revolt. But after being defeated in a severe battle by the king’s commanders Bernard and Tietmar, almost all are killed, or, while fleeing, drowned in the nearby sea. By this event the neighboring peoples are deterred from rebellion.

### 932. 13. 4. 27.

(LIUDP.) Arnold, duke of the Bavarians [Note: “Arnordus” in Sig.], came into Italy against King Hugo, was received by the Veronese, and, engaging Hugo, was defeated. Bishop Ratherius, expelled from his bishopric by King Hugo because he had favored the Bavarians, was exiled to Pavia, where he also brilliantly composed a book about his sufferings. He wrote many other things useful to readers.

### 933. 14. 5. 28.

(MAR.) Stephen presides as the 128th bishop of the Roman Church.

(LIUDP.) When the Beneventans were waging war against the Greeks, they castrated all the Greeks whom they captured.

### 934. 15. 6. 29.

(WID., MAR.) The Hungarians, demanding tribute from the Saxons, are killed or captured by King Heinrich’s army. After they had been destroyed almost to annihilation, the tribute they had demanded was paid out to the churches and the poor as an offering of thanksgiving to God. Otto, son of King Heinrich, married the daughter of Eathmund, king of the English.

### 935. 16. 7. 30.

(Ibid.) John presides as the 129th bishop of the Roman Church.

(LIUDP.) In the city of Genoa, a fountain of blood flowed forth most abundantly, perhaps foretelling the city’s impending ruin. In that same year the city was captured by Africans who came there with a fleet; all the citizens, except the children and women, were captured or killed, and the city was stripped even of its treasures.

(WID.) King Heinrich defeats the Danes, who were raiding the Frisians by piracy, and makes them tributary. He also has their king, Chiupa, baptized.

### 936. 17. 8. 31.

(MAR.) Leo presides as the 130th bishop of the Roman Church.

(LIUDP.) King Rodulf of Burgundy dies.

(Ibid.) Inger, king of the Russians, knowing that the Greek armies had been led away against the Saracens and dispersed to guard the islands, came with more than a thousand ships to attack Constantinople. He was already so confident of victory that he ordered the Greeks not to be killed but captured. Emperor Romanus, however, courageously confronted them with a small force and, having set Greek fire all around them, burned almost all of them together with their ships; only a few escaped. He ordered all the captives to be beheaded.

### 937. 18. 9. 32.

(WID.) Portents appeared this year. The sun was darkened in a clear sky; through the windows of houses it emitted rays as if bloody. The mountain where King Heinrich was later buried vomited flames in many places. The left hand of a certain man, amputated by iron, was restored to him while he slept almost a full year later; as a sign of the miracle, the place of its joining was marked by a line resembling blood.

King Heinrich dies. Although he had been glorious in conquering enemies, because he was peaceful he nevertheless made no effort to obtain the imperial blessing after the tyrants had been driven from Italy—tyrants who, like hired mercenaries succeeding one another, were tearing the empire apart. After him, his son Otto, by Mathilda, daughter of Theoderic, duke of the Saxons, ruled for thirty-six years [Note: XXXVII in Sig.’s first edition and A.; XXXVI already corrected in the first revision and in the others.].

[(WID.) Saint Odo, first abbot of Cluny, died; Ademarus succeeded him [Note: Added in the first revision and the others, except C2*, where the words are entirely absent, and A., which has only: “Odo, abbot of Cluny, died.” Nothing was erased in the first copy.].]

### 938. R. 1. F. 10. C. 33.

(LIUDP.) Everard, count of the palace, and Gislebert, duke of Lotharingia, rebel against Emperor Otto. Gislebert had the emperor’s sister Gerberga as his wife.

(MAR.) The Hungarians, after consuming many cities of Austrasia and Alemannia with fire and sword, crossed the Rhine at Worms, ravaged Gaul as far as the ocean, and returned through Italy.

(V. Wenc.) Wencezlaus, prince of Bohemia, a holy man, is martyred by his brother Bolizlaus, who had been led astray by ambition to seize the principate.

(WID.) In revenge for this, King Otto declared war on Bolizlaus, and a long conflict between them continued for fourteen years.

### 939. 2. 11. 34.

(LIUDP.) Everard and Gislebert captured Heinrich, the emperor’s brother, who had been besieged, and, detaching him from the emperor’s allegiance by their *pellatia* [uncertain; C1, 3, and 4* read *bellaria*, “delicacies”; absent in D.], attached him to their faction. They suggested to him that the kingdom belonged more properly to him, born during his father’s reign, than to Otto, who had been born before the reign.

(MAR.) The Hungarians are heavily slaughtered by the Saxons. Meanwhile Emperor Otto, returning from the Bavarians who were resisting him, exiled Everard; then, attacking the Bavarians again, he subjugated them all except one son of Arnold.

King Otto built the city of Magdeburg, which is also called Parthenopolis, that is, “city of virgins.”

(FULCU., c. 24.) Italy was afflicted by the heresy of the Anthropomorphites, that is, of those who said that God had a bodily form. Ratherius, bishop of Verona, opposed it both in words and in writing [Note: “Italy … opposed it” is found in Sig.’s third revision and in the others.].

### 940. 3. 12. 35.

(MAR.) Emperor Otto came into Lotharingia as far as Capremont.

(LIUDP.) Berengarius the Younger, grandson of the elder Berengarius through his daughter, fearing King Hugo, who was pursuing him because he aspired to the kingdom of Italy against him, fled to Herimann, duke of the Swabians, and through him to King Otto.

(WID.) King Otto defeated Bolizlaus in battle. But Bolizlaus, surrounding the men who were confident because of the victory, killed the king’s military commander and many others. The king ravaged Bohemia.

### 941. 4. 13. 36.

(MAR.) King Ludowicus of the Franks invaded Lotharingia and reached as far as Alsace, under the leadership of Everard and Gislebert.

(LIUDP.) King Hugo, having received Greek fire from the emperor of the Greeks, attacked Fraxinetum and captured it after burning the Saracens’ ships; he then drove them out.

(WID.) Tangmarus, brother of King Otto, went over from him to his enemies. Among his other misdeeds, he captured the king’s fortress of Heresburch. The king then surrounded him there, and Tangmarus perished, pierced by arrows inside the church.

### 942. 5. 14. 37.

(MAR.) Marinus presides as the 131st bishop of the Roman Church.

(V. Ud.) When Saint Udalricus came to Rome to visit him [Note: “Waldricus” in C4* and D.], he learned from Marinus that he would become bishop of Augsburg; this happened fifteen years later.

(LIUDP.) Gislebert and Everard, together with Heinrich, the emperor’s brother, were preparing war against the emperor near the Rhine. They encountered the emperor’s soldiers, and many engaged a few. Meanwhile the emperor had fallen prostrate in prayer on the other bank of the Rhine before the nails of the Lord fixed into his lance; the rebels were defeated and turned their backs, while Heinrich was wounded incurably in the arm.

(WID.) Dissension arose among the princes concerning the diversity of the law: whether, after fathers had died, the sons of sons who survived them ought to inherit, or whether, once their nephews had been disinherited, the inheritance ought to return to their paternal uncles. By the judgment of King Otto and all the princes, the determination of the truth was entrusted to trial by combat. Victory went to those who held that the sons of brothers ought to inherit together with their fathers.

### 943. 6. 15. 38.

(LIUDP.) King Otto besieged Brisach, a town of Alsace, which King Ludowicus held through the soldiers of Everard and Gislebert [Note: “By the soldiers of E. and G.” is absent in C4*, which from this point to the end of the chronicle omits so much that it now seems pointless to indicate each omission; we wished to record this once here.].

During this siege, at the persuasion of Frederick, bishop of Mainz, who had already defected in heart from the emperor, many deserted the emperor. This frightened the others, but the king alone remained undaunted. Meanwhile the king’s loyal men, namely Udo and Conrad, brother of Herimann, duke of the Swabians, unexpectedly attacked Everard and Gislebert near the Rhine while they were confidently intent on plundering the kingdom, and fought them fiercely. Everard was killed by the sword, while Gislebert was drowned in the waters of the Rhine; scarcely any of the others escaped without being either slaughtered or captured. At this news the king’s disloyal followers were broken in spirit, and Ludowicus withdrew from Alsace; the king and his loyal men rejoiced with him.

(WID.) King Ludowicus married Gerberga, Gislebert’s wife and, of course, the sister of Emperor Otto. The emperor betrothed Gislebert’s daughter, his own niece, to Duke Bertaldus of the Bavarians.

(LIUDP.; WID.) His duchy was given to Otto.

Ademarus, abbot of Cluny, appointed Maiolus as abbot in his place [Note: Added in the first revision and the others, except A. and C2*.].

### 944. 7. 16. 39.

(MAR.) Otto, duke of the Lotharingians, died. Conrad, King Otto’s son-in-law, succeeded him.

(LIUDP.) Emperors Stephen and Constantine, displeased that they were being restrained from youthful frivolity by their father’s just severity, set an ambush in the palace. While Constantine, son of Emperor Leo, knew nothing of it, they deposed their father from the palace throne, had his head tonsured, as is customary, and sent him to a nearby island where monks were engaged in philosophical study. But he suffered a dreadful eclipse [Note: “Eclysin” in Sig.] on the sixth day, at the third hour of the day. On that day in Spain, Addaram, king of the Saracens, was defeated in battle by the most Christian king of Galicia, Radamirus. In Italy a comet of extraordinary size appeared, foretelling the famine that followed.

(WID.) King Otto transferred the body of the martyr Innocent into the city of Magdeburg.

### 945. R. 8. F. 17. C. 1.

(MAR.) Emperor Otto subjugated all Lotharingia, with only Adalbero, bishop of Metz and brother of Duke Frederick, resisting him.

(LIUDP.) After the deposition of their father, Stephen and Constantine saw that Constantine, son of Emperor Leo, was preferred to them by everyone and that they themselves were scarcely even regarded as second in rank. While they were deliberating about doing to Constantine what they had done to their father, their plan was disclosed by Diabolinus, the instigator of the plot. When they had sat down to a banquet by prior arrangement and were deliberately disputing among themselves about precedence in seating, a signal was given by Constantine’s men. Both brothers were thrown from the throne and, with their heads tonsured, were sent to the same monastery to which they had sent their father, so that they might study philosophy with the monks. Thus, after the palace had been cleared of the usurping emperors, Constantine himself and his son Romanus, by the daughter of the emperor Romanus, ruled for seventeen years [Note: Thus Sig.; later corrected to XVI. C1, 3, and D (here corrected to XVI.) have XVIII; A. has XVII.].

(WID.) Count Gero bravely and repeatedly fought the barbarians, who were invading from every direction on the occasion of the civil war.

(BALD.) King Otto subjugated Burgundy.

(WID.) Count Hugo of Paris was excessively hostile to Ludowicus, king of the Franks.

[This Hugo was the son of the tyrant Rotbert, who was killed in the battle of Soissons by King Charles [Note: Added in the first revision and the others, except A.]. (Cf. Flodoard.)]

### 946. 9. 18. 2.

(MAR.) Agapitus presides as the 132nd pope of the Roman Church, and Benedict as the 133rd. [Note: “[and Benedict as the 133rd]” is absent in D.]

(WID.) Henry, the emperor’s brother, besieged by his brother in the city of Merseburg, threw down his arms, fell at his feet, and begged for mercy; he was confined in custody. (LIUDP.) [Col. 0185D] Archbishop Frederick was also expelled from Mainz by its citizens. King Otto captured or killed many who were plotting rebellion against him. (WID.) After Duke Bertold’s death, King Otto gave the duchy of Bavaria to his brother Henry, and thus restrained him from rebellion.

### 947. 10. 19. 3.

(LIUDP.) When King Hugh saw that Berengar, returning from Swabia to Italy, was being received by the Italians after they had abandoned Hugh, he entrusted his son Lothair to the loyalty of the Italians, so that at least he might reign jointly with Berengar. [Col. 0186A] Hugh himself returned to Arles, from which he had come.

### 948. 11. 20. 4.

(Ib.) After King Hugh’s death, his son Lothair reigned in Italy in name only; Berengar, king in fact and power, and accepted by everyone, exercised tyranny throughout Italy. (WID.) Henry, duke of Bavaria, captured Aquileia in Italy, twice defeated the Hungarians, crossed the Ticino, and returned with much booty. (V. Guib.) The immunity of our church—namely, of Gembloux—was confirmed this year by an imperial edict and strengthened by the impression of a ring. [Note: “of our church” and “namely” are absent in A, B1, 3*, 5, C1, 2*, 3. “The immunity … was confirmed” is absent in C4* and D.] Erluin, the first abbot of that place, elected by our holy father Guicbert, shone in holiness and religious fervor. (WID.) King Louis of the Franks, surrounded by his dukes, was captured by the Normans, [Col. 0186B] and, on Hugh’s advice, was sent to Lyon and handed over to public custody. His elder son, Carloman, was carried away by the Normans and died at Rouen.

### 949. 12. 21. 5.

(LIUDP.) When Taxis, king of the Hungarians, came into Italy, he received ten measures of coin from Berengar for his return. (WID.) King Otto advanced against France with thirty-two legions in order to liberate Louis. Louis was released from custody through fear of him. King Otto captured Lyon, shut Hugh up within Paris, and captured Reims. After expelling Hugh’s nephew, who had usurped the bishopric, he restored the legitimate bishop. He advanced powerfully as far as Rouen; after returning to Louis the castles and cities he had captured, [Col. 0186C] he returned to Saxony. [Note: “A. 946.”]

### 950. 13. 22. 6.

(MAR.) Very many great earthquakes occurred throughout Gaul and Germany. [Note: “Throughout Gaul … occurred” is absent in D.] (WID.) King Otto set out for Bohemia against Boleslaus; Boleslaus was reconciled to the king and ultimately submitted faithfully to him. When King Otto was preparing a second expedition into France, Hugh, unable to endure his power, met him beside the Cher River; and, after a peace agreement had been made according to the king’s will, he gave him his hand. [Note: “A. 947.”]

### 951. 14. 23. 7.

(MAR.) Mainz was besieged by the emperor Otto. [Note: “A. 953.”] (WID.) Archbishop Frederick was captured and thrown into custody, but not long afterward he was released through the king’s clemency. King Otto designated his son Liudolf, born of the daughter of the king of the English, as king after him by testament.

### 952. 15. 24. 8.

(WID.) Liudolf, the emperor Otto’s son, rebelled against his father at the instigation of Duke Conrad. He captured Reinsburg and turned many other cities and princes from his father to himself. The king besieged him after he had been shut up inside Mainz.

[Col. 0187A] ### 953. R. 16. F. 25. C. 9.

(Ib.) There was a battle on the Meuse between Conrad and Count Raginer of Hainaut. [Note: “Of Hainaut” appears as “of Baginensium” in C1, 3, D.] (V. Brun.) After Wicfrid’s death, the glorious Bruno, brother of the emperor Otto, assumed the archbishopric of Cologne.
