What sort of man he was before God and men, the reader may learn in his life, which Roger described brilliantly. Through Bruno’s efforts, the bodies of Saints Eliphius, Patroclus, Privatus, and Gregory were transferred from Rome to Cologne, together with Saint Peter’s staff. [Note: E. P. P. G. c. b. s. P. adds: “the bodies of Eliphius, Patroclus, Privatus, Gregory, with the staff of Saint Peter”; Sig. corrected this in the third revision; the other witnesses.]

### 954. 17. 26. 10.

(FULCUIN.) Ratherius, twice expelled from the bishopric of Verona, was ordained bishop of Liège by Archbishop Bruno, succeeding Farabert. (V. Guib.) [Col. 0187B] The immunity of our church—namely, of Gembloux—was also confirmed by apostolic authority by Pope Benedict, in the seventh year of his pontificate. [Note: “of our church” and “namely” are absent in A. “The immunity … of it” is absent in B1, 5, C1, 2*, 3, 4*, D.] (WID.) King Otto took as his second wife the widow of Louis, king of the Italians, and through her obtained Pavia.

### 955. 18. 27. 11.

(FULC.) After Liudolf had been restored to his father’s favor, Duke Conrad, a deserter from God and the emperor, went to the Hungarians and led them into Lotharingia as far as the Carbonaria Forest. But when God’s power was displayed against them at Lobbes, they were prevented from advancing farther and returned unharmed. (A. Lob.) After Louis, king of the Franks, died, his son Lothair, born of Gerberga, the emperor’s sister, reigned for thirty-two years. (WID.) Berengar, king of Italy, came into Germany to King Otto [Col. 0187C] and, placing his own hands and those of his son in the king’s hands, committed himself to him. (Ib.) The Bavarians fought successfully against the Slavs.

### 956. 19. 1. 12.

(Ib.) In Italy, during a violent thunderstorm, a stone of extraordinary size was hurled from the sky, presenting an immense marvel to those who saw it. Strong storms shook temples in many places. Priests of both orders perished from lightning strikes, and several terrifying portents, horrible to relate, appeared. (MAR.) After Frederick, archbishop of Mainz, died, William, the emperor Otto’s son, was substituted in his place. (A. Lob.; FULC.) After Ratherius was expelled from the bishopric of Liège, Baldric was substituted as bishop through the support of his uncle, Count Raginer of Mons.

[Col. 0187D] ### 957. 20. 2. 13.

(V. Brun.) Liudolf, the emperor Otto’s son, died in Italy. When the Hungarians were again ravaging Otto’s kingdom under the leadership of Duke Conrad, the emperor met them in battle. Conrad, repenting, fled from the Hungarians to the emperor and prayed to God that, as punishment for his treachery, he might be killed by the Hungarians in that very battle. (WID.) In that battle the Hungarians were defeated [Col. 0188A] and weakened to such an extent that afterward they did not dare even to mutter. They were so thoroughly crushed that scarcely any, or only a few, escaped. Conrad nevertheless fell there according to his vow. Three Hungarian princes were captured in the battle and died by hanging. (V. Brun.) Bruno, archbishop, who had also obtained the duchy of Lotharingia after Conrad, built the monastery of Saint Pantaleon at Cologne. (WID.) Henry, duke of Bavaria and King Otto’s brother, died; his son Henry succeeded him.

### 958. 21. 3. 14.

(A. Leod.) Erluin, the first abbot of Gembloux, was deprived of the light of his eyes. [Note: “Erluin, the first abbot of Gembloux, was deprived of the light of his eyes” is absent in B1, 5, C1, 2*, 3, 4*, D.] (V. Brun.) Archbishop Bruno caused many Normans, together with their princes, to be baptized. (WID.) The rebel Wichmann, fleeing from King Otto across the Elbe, brought the Slavs into his kingdom. The king fought them vigorously, killing their prince together with many others, and beheading seven hundred captives.

### 959. 22. 4. 15.

(MAR.) John presides as the 134th pope of the Roman Church. [Note: “John presides” is absent in D.] (FULCUIN.) Bruno, archbishop and archduke of Lotharingia, administering the affairs of his brother’s kingdom powerfully and diligently, summoned Count Raginer of Mons, called Longneck, to Valenciennes, captured him, and condemned him to irrevocable exile because he was disturbing the kingdom with wars—or, as is said more truthfully, because after the death of his kinsman Duke Gislebert he was presumptuously trying to seize by force what Gislebert had bestowed as a dowry upon his wife Gerberga, the emperor’s sister. (BALD., I, 94.) After Raginer’s possessions had been confiscated for the public treasury, his sons Raginer and Lambert fled to Lothair, king of the Franks. A prodigious event terrified many and restrained them from vices: signs of the cross appeared on the clothing of many, while the garments of others became dirty as if with leprosy. [Saint Gerard, founder of the monastery of Brogne, died. Note: This is added by 1β.; the other witnesses except A.]

### 960. 23. 5. 16.

(BALD.) At this time, through Otto’s efforts, the condition of the empire and the Church improved, and many monasteries and religious houses were either restored, enlarged, or built to the praise of God and the honor of the saints. (ANSELM.) Among them, Euraclus, who after Baldric became bishop [Col. 0188D] of Liège, built two monasteries in the city: one dedicated to Saint Paul the Apostle, and the other dedicated to Saint Martin the Bishop. [Note: “Among them … Saint Martin the Bishop” is absent in D.]

### 961. 24. 6. 17.

(MAR.) After the emperor Romanus died at Constantinople, Nicephorus reigned for ten years. (LIUDPR.) Saint Ulrich, [Note: “Waldricus” appears in B3*, C2*. “Saint Ulrich … in Gaul and Germany” is absent in D.] bishop of Augsburg, shines in holiness in Gaul and Germany. Since Gaul and Germany were now well pacified, the emperor Otto, intending also to pacify Italy—especially because Pope John and the other Italian bishops were urgently calling him for this purpose, so that he might free them from the hands of the tyrants Berengar and Adelbert—(A. Lob.) had his seven-year-old son Otto anointed king at Aachen on the holy day of Pentecost; (V. Brun.) after commending him to the archbishops, his brother Bruno and his son William, he set out for Italy.

### 962. R. 25. F. 7. C. 1.

(V. Guib.) Our holy father Guicbert, founder of our monastery—namely, of Gembloux—[Note: “Our holy father” and “our,” as well as “namely,” are absent in all witnesses except 1.] fell asleep in Christ at Gorze, where he served God because of his love for the fervent holy religion practiced there; and he who had abandoned everything received a hundredfold and eternal life. [Note: “And … received” is absent in C1, 3, 4*, D.] His body was brought back to [Col. 0189B] the monastery of Gembloux. [Note: C. v. e. r. e. a. c. G. adds: “His body was brought back to the monastery of Gembloux”; Sig. corrected this in the third revision; the other witnesses.]

### 963. 26. 8. 2.

(LIUDP.) After the emperor Otto had traversed Italy, and the tyrants of Italy had been so terrified by the majesty of his name that they hid in naturally fortified places or sought the protection of the Saracens, he was blessed as emperor at Rome by Pope John. The tyrants were renounced by Pope John and by the Romans. When Otto was returning to his homeland, Adelbert was recalled from Fraxinetum to Rome by Pope John; but when the emperor returned, they fled. After a council of bishops from all Italy had been assembled, John was accused of wicked crimes. Summoned for the third time, he delayed coming to offer his defense; eventually, after he had been condemned by everyone, Leo—still a layman—was substituted as pope by the election of all [Col. 0189C] and [Col. 0189D] the emperor’s consent. [Note: From a letter of Bernard of Hildesheim to Adalbert in Ussermann’s *Prodromus Germaniae sacrae* II, 208, where these words occur verbatim. HIRSCH.]

(BERNARD.) Thus Leo, presiding over the apostolic see, performed ordinations and the other acts that belonged to an apostolic office. Before long, when the Romans changed their allegiance toward the emperor, they received Pope John. He convened a synod, deposed Leo, and annulled his acts. It was publicly decreed by everyone that the synod held by Leo should not even be called a synod, but rather a brothel favoring adulterers. Therefore, all who had been condemned by his ordination were ordered to present their own indictment on a document containing these words: “My father had nothing for himself; he gave me nothing.” Thus deposed, they remained in those grades—if they had held any—that had not yet been conferred upon them by Leo. But if any were judged worthy to be ordained without having first received consecration, the same decree was imposed upon them as upon those condemned by Constantine the neophyte.

(LIUDP.) The Romans, bribed by Pope John, suddenly attacked the emperor while he was staying in Rome with only a few men. They were so thoroughly crushed by the emperor’s army [Col. 0190A] that, unless the emperor and Pope Leo had recalled the emperor’s soldiers from slaughter, the Romans would have been wiped out to the last man. After the Romans had been reconciled to the emperor through Pope Leo, Leo, sensing that snares were being prepared for him after the emperor’s departure, fled to the emperor. John, who had been pope, was enjoying himself with another man’s wife when he was struck by the devil at the appointed time and died without the Lord’s viaticum. Contrary to the oath they had sworn to the emperor—that they would never elect a pope without the consent of the emperor and his son Otto—the Romans established Benedict as pope. The emperor besieged Rome and afflicted the Romans so severely by slaughter and famine that they promised to receive Pope Leo. Benedict, rejected not only from the papacy but also from the priesthood, was stripped of his orders by Leo. [Col. 0190B]

[Note: The passage beginning “still a layman … so thoroughly crushed” was originally contained in two lines; in the third revision Sig. expanded it partly in an erasure and partly in the margin, while the other witnesses preserve it. A later hand attempted to restore the obscured passage but rather corrupted it. The words beginning “unless the emperor …” and ending “so thoroughly crushed” were cut away when all the Gembloux manuscripts received new bindings at the end of the seventeenth century. The words “that belonged to an apostolic office … so thoroughly crushed” are omitted by F3, which leaves a space. All the other witnesses have “which.”]

### 964. 27. 9. 3.

(Vita Deod.) After Adelbero, bishop of Metz, died, Deoderic, a cousin of the emperor Otto, was substituted as bishop. As the story goes, he examined the first letters of the names of all the bishops of Metz, which an angel of the Lord is said to have given to Saint Clement, the first bishop of Metz, and noticed that some were marked in gold and others in a cheaper metal according to their merits. When he also saw that the letter of his own name had been marked in silver, he is said to have declared that he would do such great good in the bishopric that the letter of his name ought deservedly to be marked in gold. [Col. 0190C] He displayed the beginning of this good intention in the monastery of the holy martyr and deacon Vincent, founded on the island of that city. (BALD. I, 99.) After the aged Arnulf, count of the Flemings, died, Lothair, king of the Franks, severely attacked and devastated Flanders. [Note: “Arnulf … devastated” is found in Sig.’s third revision; the other witnesses.]

### 965. 28. 10. 4.

(V. Brun.) The emperor Otto celebrated Pentecost at Aachen. [Note: Sig. is mistaken: it was at Cologne; see *Life of Bruno*, chapter 42.] His sisters came there from France, namely Gerberga, queen of the Franks and mother of King Lothair and Duke Charles, and Hathui, wife of Hugh, count of Paris; their son was Hugh, who later reigned in France. There the entire royal lineage was filled with such joyful mutual congratulation that throughout their whole lives scarcely any joy could have equaled this happiness. Otto [Col. 0190D] returned to Italy. Bruno, duke and archbishop, journeying into France to reconcile his nephews, King Lothair and Hugh’s sons, reached Compiègne; there, seized by fever, he returned to Reims. After assigning by testament to the churches of the saints whatever property he possessed, he died. His body was brought back to Cologne by Deoderic, bishop of Metz. [Note: After this, a line and a half was erased. The other witnesses have nothing there.]

### 966. R. 29. F. 11. C. 5

(MAR.) William, the emperor’s son and archbishop of Mainz, died. (WID.) At this time the Danes, who worshiped Christ Jesus and idols simultaneously, were disputing at a banquet with the cleric Poppo about the worship of God and the gods. The Danes asserted that Jesus Christ was indeed God, but that the gods were greater and older than he; Poppo, on the contrary, affirmed that Jesus Christ alone was the true God, one in substance and three in persons. King Harald of the Danes therefore ordered the cleric to prove the faith he had professed by a testimony of truth. When the cleric agreed, a piece of iron of immense weight, thoroughly heated, was placed in his hands for him to carry. After he had carried it to everyone’s satisfaction without any injury, the king completely rejected idolatry and turned himself and his people to the worship of the one true God. The cleric, moreover, was promoted to the bishopric.

### 967. 30. 12. 6.

(MAR.) John presides as the 136th pope of the Roman Church. [Note: “John presides” is absent in D.] (WID.) Wichmann, who had long been in rebellion against the emperor Otto, was killed by Misaca, a Slavic prince, friend and soldier of the emperor. (LIUDPR.) At this time the sons of Symeon, Peter and Bajanus, ruled the Bulgarians. Bajanus was so skilled in magic [Col. 0191C] that whenever he wished, he appeared able to become a wolf or any wild animal.

### 968. 31. 13. 7.

(A. Lob.) Otto the Younger, summoned by his father to Rome, was blessed as emperor by Pope John. (MAR.) By his power, the emperor Otto compelled the dukes of Benevento to submit to him. (WID.) The emperor Otto was the first to open, through his own initiative, veins of gold and silver in Saxony.

### 969. 32. 14. 8.

(V. Deod.) A certain count of the emperor Otto, who was close to him, was seized by the devil at Rome before everyone’s eyes, so that he tore his own flesh with his teeth. At the emperor’s command he was brought to Pope John, so that Saint Peter’s chain might be placed around his neck. When false clerics applied another chain to the raging man once and then twice, and no remedy resulted—for there was no power in it—at last the true chain of Saint Peter was brought and placed around the madman’s neck; the devil departed, foaming and crying out loudly. Deoderic of Metz seized the chain and declared that he would not release it unless his hand were cut off. At last, after the emperor had settled the dispute, he obtained from Pope John that the bishop might receive a ring cut from this chain.

(WID.) When the emperor Otto had sent part of his army to the Greeks to obtain a wife for his son Otto, the Greeks attacked them, plundered their camp, killed many, [Col. 0192A] captured many others, and sent them to Constantinople. To avenge this disgrace, the emperor Otto sent his more distinguished men into Calabria. They attacked the Greeks, killed many, dishonored many by cutting off their noses, and exacted tribute from the Greeks throughout Apulia and Calabria. When the people of Constantinople heard that their men had fought badly in Calabria, they rose up against their emperor Nicephorus.

### 970. 33. 15. 9.

(V. Deod.) Deoderic, bishop of Metz, bound to the emperor by blood, affection, and intimacy more closely than the others, served under him for three years during the Italian expedition and collected, by whatever means he could, many bodies and relics of saints from various places in Italy. First, from Marsica, Saint Elpidius the Confessor, whose companion Eutychius the emperor himself had already taken; from Amiternum, the martyr Euticetes, together with the relics of Maron and Victorinus, his companions; from Foligno, Felicianus, bishop and martyr; from Perugia, the martyr Asclepiodotus; from Spoleto, the martyr Serena, together with Gregory, the martyr of Spoleto; from Corduno, relics of Vincent, martyr and deacon, formerly carried from Spain to Capua by two monks and from Capua transported there; from Mevania, another Vincent, bishop and martyr; from Vicenza, Leontius, bishop and martyr; from Florence, the martyr Minias; from the city of Todi, Fortunatus, bishop and confessor; from Corfinium, Lucia of Syracuse, virgin and martyr, formerly transferred there from Syracuse by Duke Faroald of the Spoletans; from the Sabines, portions [Col. 0192C] of the bodies of the martyrs Protus and Hyacinth. Together with all these, and with a portion of the chain of Saint Peter the Apostle, some of his hair, the blood of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, and a fragment of the gridiron of Saint Lawrence the martyr—gifts presented to him by Pope John—as well as many other relics of the saints, Bishop Deoderic brought them into Gaul this year and placed them in the church of Saint Vincent the martyr, which he had built on the island of the city.

### 971. 34. 16. 10.

(MAR.) At Constantinople, the emperor Nicephorus, fearing that his sons would expel him from the empire because he was old, wanted to make them eunuchs. Their mother, the empress, since she could not otherwise free them, persuaded John to kill Nicephorus and reign. Accordingly, John secretly entered the palace with ropes, killed Nicephorus, and became emperor.

### 972. 35. 17. 1.

(A. Lob.) At Rome, the emperor Otto joined his co-emperor Otto in legitimate marriage to Theophanu, the niece of John of Constantinople, whom Pope John had crowned. (ANSELM.) Notger was ordained bishop of Liège. He surrounded the city with a wall, adorned it with buildings, renewed from its foundations the major church distinguished by the body of Saint Lambert, and founded the monastery of Saint John the Evangelist on the island. [Note: “Notger … founded” was written in the lower margin by Sig. in his third revision; the other witnesses. Here the quire ends. Everything up to this point was written by Sigebert’s hand. The next quire was written by a second hand.]

[Col. 0193A] ### 973 R. 36. F. 18. C. 2.

(MAR.) Stephen [Note: D has “Donus.”] presides as the 137th pope of the Roman Church. (BALD., I, 94.) The elder emperor Otto died. The monk Widukind wrote his life and also composed a history of the Saxons up to this year. Otto II reigned for ten years. (A. Leod.) Raginer and Lambert, the sons of Raginer Longneck, gradually recovering their strength, returned from France and fought a battle at Péronne with Warner and Rainald, who had occupied their father’s county. They killed them and many others, and, after fortifying the castle of Buxude above the River Haine, [Note: “La Haine.”] they ravaged Lotharingia. [Note: “Boussoit near Binche.”] Wenceslaus, prince of Bohemia, was martyred by his brother Boleslaus because of the latter’s desire to seize the principate. (V. Wenc.) He glorifies the city of Prague, where he rests, with many miracles.

### 974. 1. 19. 3.

(A. Leod.) Ratherius, concerning whom there is this monostich:

> Bishop of Verona, but three times an exile, Ratherius dies at Lobbes.

(BALD. I, 93.) His cousin Henry, duke of Bavaria, rebelled against the emperor Otto. The emperor Otto besieged the castle of Buxude, captured and destroyed it, and sent those captured there into exile. Yet Raginer did not desist from rebellion.

### 975. 2. 20. 4.

(A. Leod.) A great frost lasted from the Kalends of November until the spring equinox. (BALD. I, 94.) The emperor Otto subjugated Duke Henry. Majolus, abbot of Cluny, shone in holiness and religious devotion.

[Col. 0193C] ### 976. 3. 21. 5.

(MAR.) Saint Ulrich, [Note: “Waldricus” in D.] bishop of Augsburg, [Note: “Ansburgensis” in B3*, C2*, D.] died; what his life had been like was soon revealed by the glory of his miracles. (BALD. I, 100.) The emperor Otto set out against the Slavs. (Ib. 95.) The sons of Raginer Longneck, relying on the aid of the Franks and especially of Charles, later duke, engaged in battle with Counts Godefrid and Arnulf, who after Warner had invaded the county of Mons. They besieged Mont-Castel. After many had fallen on both sides in the conflict, the siege was lifted. The victory was uncertain, but the counts nevertheless received the palm of victory.

### 977. 4. 22. 6.

(V. Adalb.) Saint Wojciech of Prague, bishop, known by the name Adalbert, shone among the Wends in holiness and learning. [Col. 0193D] The people of the Liuticians returned to idolatry. [Note: “The people of the Liuticians returned to idolatry” is in an erasure in 1; it is absent in C2* and A, which instead has: “who, martyred among the Bruttians, is glorified by many miracles.” Sigebert initially published it in this form.] (BALD I, 100.) The duchy of Lotharingia was given to Charles, brother of Lothair, king of the Franks, and he was additionally induced by many benefits both to desist from his insolence and to oppose the actions of his brother Lothair. [Col. 0194A] (Ib.) The sons of Raginer, encouraged to act bravely for themselves by Frankish support and kinship—Raginer had married Hathui, the daughter of Hugh, later king, while Lambert had married Gerberga, the daughter of Duke Charles [Note: The source of this is unknown. There appears to be an error, since neither Hugh, born after 938, nor Charles, born in 945, could have had marriageable daughters at this time. HIRSCH.]—were restored to the land of their fathers.

### 978. 5. 23.

(BALD. I, 96.) After the kingdom had been pacified everywhere, while the emperor Otto was staying at Aachen, Lothair, king of the Franks, suddenly hastened to invade Lotharingia. The emperor withdrew because he was unprepared for battle, and the king returned home after extensive devastation. The emperor pursued him with an immeasurable army and, on the appointed day—namely, the Kalends of October—entered France. After traversing it until the Kalends of December, he devastated the territories of Reims, Laon, Soissons, and Paris with various forms of destruction, granting complete immunity only to God’s churches. On the return journey, however, he lost part of his baggage near the River Aisne. (ALPERT.) A certain recluse foretold concerning these events that all the instigators of this evil would die before seven years had passed. [Note: The words “concerning these events … would die,” which are not found in Balderic, were taken by Sigebert from a fragment of Balderic I, 93–97, which was inscribed in the eleventh century on a blank leaf of the Gembloux manuscript, now Brussels 5468; see *Archiv* VIII, 497. Alpertus tells the same story, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, IV, 697.]

### 979. 6. 24.

Fiery battle-lines were seen in the sky throughout the night before the fifth day before the Kalends of November. This year one thousand years are completed from the birth of Christ, according to the truth of the Gospel; according to Dionysius’s cycle, they were completed twenty-one years ago. Thus, in the year of the Lord’s Passion, [Col. 0194C] there is a contradiction of Gospel truth.

### 980. 7. 25.

(A. Leod.) The emperor Otto and King Lothair met on the River Cher [Note: “The Cher”] and were reconciled, exchanging oaths. King Lothair renounced his claim to Lotharingia. (BALD. I, 103.) The emperor Otto went to Italy. (Transl. S. L.) The bodies of Saints Landoald, Adrian, Amantius, and others were transferred from Wentreshoven, a village in Hasbania, to Ghent amid great glory of miracles. [Note: *Acta Sanctorum*, March III, 43.]

### 981. 8. 26.

(MAR.) Stephen presides as the 138th pope of the Roman Church. [Note: “Stephen presides” is absent in D.] The emperor Otto attempted to transfer Apulia and Calabria, provinces of Italy subject to the jurisdiction of the Greek kingdom, [Col. 0194D] to the Roman Empire, chiefly because of the kinship he had with the Greek emperor through his wife Theophanu.

[Col. 0195A] ### 982. R. 9. F. 27.

(ALPERT.) The Greeks, angered that the emperor Otto was invading the Greek provinces, enlisted the aid of the Saracens and engaged the emperor in battle in Calabria. In that battle nearly all the Roman forces were destroyed, almost to annihilation. The emperor, attempting to escape by swimming, was captured by sailors who did not know who he was. One of them, a Slavic merchant, recognized him but did not betray him. Through him the matter was reported to the empress and to Deoderic, bishop of Metz, who were awaiting the outcome at the city of Rossano; through the efforts of the Slav and the bishop, the emperor was with difficulty freed. When the sailors were eagerly awaiting the money brought to ransom him, the emperor mounted a horse and barely escaped. While everyone was disheartened by the disaster to the state, the empress alone, with feminine and Greek frivolity, taunted them because the Romans had been defeated by an army of her own nation; for this reason she began to be hated by the leading men.

### 983. 10. 28.

(Ib.) The emperor Otto, worn down by weariness and anguish of mind, died at Rome. The leading men disagreed about appointing his successor: some contended that the empire was owed to his son Otto, while others, out of hatred for the empress, wanted to transfer the empire from her son to Duke Henry, the son of Henry who had been the father of the first Otto. (BALD. I, 104.) This Henry treacherously seized the boy Otto himself and held him in custody. But the princes snatched the boy from Henry’s hands [Note: “And concerning the emperor … snatched” is abridged in C4* as: “the princes, his son Otto still a boy.”] and elevated him to the kingdom; he reigned for eighteen years.

[Col. 0195C] ### 984. 1. 29.

(Ib.) Lothair, king of the Franks, again striving to invade Lotharingia, captured the city of Verdun and Godefrid, its count. (ALPERT.) Deoderic, bishop of Metz, died; and, in accordance with the prophecy of the man of God, scarcely any of the leading men who escaped from the Calabrian battle survived long. Adelbero, a holy and noble man, son of Duke Frederick, assumed the bishopric of Metz.

### 985. 2. 30.

(BALD. I, 104.) King Lothair, seeing the emperor Otto prospering through the power of his soldiers, returned the city of Verdun and Count Godefrid.

### 986. 3. 31.

(A. Leod.) After Lothair, king of the Franks, died, his son Louis reigned in France for one year.

### 987. 4. 1.

(A. Leod.) After Louis, king of the Franks, died, the Franks wished to transfer the kingdom to Duke Charles, brother of King Lothair. While Charles deferred the matter to a council, Hugh usurped the kingdom of the Franks. He was the son [Col. 0196A] of Hugh of Paris by Hathui, sister of the first emperor Otto, and reigned for nine years. (G. abb. Gembl.) Herluin, the first abbot of our monastery—namely, of Gembloux—died, crucified by the martyrdom of prolonged and enduring blindness. [Note: “Herluin … died” is absent in C2*, 4*. “By the martyrdom of prolonged and enduring blindness” is absent in B5, C1, 3, D. “Our” and “namely” are absent in A, B1, 3*, 5, C1, 3, D.] [Note: “The fourth day before the Ides of August.”]

### 988. 5. 1.

Frequent and unusually great floods, lasting for a long time. Summer afterward was extremely hot and harmful to many, so that the crops were diminished. Duke Charles reclaimed the kingdom of the Franks, owed to him by paternal and ancestral succession, from Hugh, his nephew and king. Pressing him hard in war, he captured the city of Laon. King Hugh besieged Charles in Laon, but in the second month of the siege the besieged sallied forth and burned the camp of the besiegers. King Hugh himself, after many of his men had been killed, fled disgracefully and barely escaped. [Note: “The flood … to many” was written in the lower margin by 1η., after three lines had been erased. All the others have the same text.]

### 989. 6. 2.

(MAR.) Marinus presides as the 139th pope of the Roman Church. A great spring drought hindered the first sowing, and a severe famine followed. It is said that grain rained from the sky in Hasbania. Others also reported that small fish rained from the sky. [Note: “Marinus … presides” and “It is said … reported” are absent in D.] Excessive snow fell; afterward continuous rain prevented the autumn sowing altogether. Duke Charles stormed Montaigu; advancing as far as Soissons, he devastated the territory; from there he attacked Reims and returned to Laon with much booty.

### 990. 7. 3.

Duke Charles occupied Reims. He captured the archbishop whom King Hugh had appointed, together with some of the leading men, and exiled them to Laon.

### 991. 8. 4.

Duke Charles died. His son Otto succeeded him in the duchy of Lotharingia.

### 992. 9. 5.

(BALD. I, 110.) A synod of all France having been assembled at Reims, Arnulf, nephew of Duke Charles, whom Charles himself had appointed bishop of Reims [Note: False; it was Hugh.], was condemned and stripped of office by the judgment of all. Adelgarius, the priest who betrayed the city and opened its gates to Charles, was excommunicated irrevocably. (GERBERT.) Gerbert was substituted as bishop. But when certain men brought the matter into dispute, arguing that Arnulf could not be degraded without the knowledge and authority of the Roman pope, Gerbert, having been deposed, went to the emperor Otto. The emperor received him and first appointed him archbishop of Ravenna, and afterward made him Roman pope. Hence comes his monostich:

> Gerbert climbs from R. to R.; afterward, as pope, he flourishes in R.

[Col. 0197A] ### 993. R. 10. F. 6.

(Vita Od.) In Burgundy, Odilo, born in Auvergne and professed as a monk in the monastery of Cluny after having been a cleric at Brioude, was placed over that monastery after Majolus. He governed and advanced it for fifty-six years with extraordinary religious fervor. Distinguished above all by exceptional piety, he shone during his lifetime not only through examples of life but also through miracles. When he was reproached for seeming to be more merciful toward sinners than justice allowed, he replied: “If I must be condemned, I would rather be condemned for mercy than for harshness.” Otto was blessed as emperor. [Note: D gives “23 May 996.”]

### 994. 11. 7.

At this time the following men flourished in literary learning in Lotharingia: Heriger, abbot of Lobbes, and Adelbold, bishop of Utrecht; in France, Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, and Abbo, abbot of Fleury, who wrote a commentary on Victor’s computation.

### 995. 12. 8.

Gerbert, also called Sylvester, presides as the 140th pope of the Roman Church; he too excelled remarkably among those distinguished for literary learning. Some, passing over Sylvester, place Pope Agapitus at this point; this is believed not to have been done without reason. Since this Sylvester is said not to have entered through the door—for some even accuse him of necromancy—and since his death is also treated improperly, for he is said to have died after being struck by the devil, we leave the matter unresolved. He therefore appears to have been excluded from the number of the popes. [Col. 0197C] Hence, reader, I ask you: here and elsewhere, if any discrepancy concerning the names, years, or periods of the popes offends you, do not attribute it to me, for I write what I have heard or read, not what I have personally seen.

### 996. 13. 9.

(A. Leod.) After Hugh, king of the Franks, died, his son Robert reigned in France for thirty-five years.

### 997. 14. 1.

(Vita Her.) Heribert, ordained bishop of Cologne, shines with great holiness. (ALPERT. I, 11.) At this time Ansfrid was also renowned among the Gauls. Having been count of Brabant, famous no less for justice than for secular power, he laid aside the military belt, was tonsured as a cleric, and advanced so far that he was ordained bishop of the church of Utrecht.

[Col. 0197D] 998. 15. 2.

(MAR.) Agapitus, the 141st, presides over the Roman church [Note: [Col. 0197] “Agapitus … presides” is absent in D.]. (Vita Od.) At this time a certain religious man, returning from Jerusalem and having been refreshed for some time by the kindness of a recluse in Sicily, learned among other things from him that in that region there were places belching forth fiery flames. The inhabitants call these places the “Pots of Vulcan” [Note: [Col. 0197D] This is absent from Peter Damian’s *Life of Saint Odilo*, chapter 17. Sigebert added it from the entry for 532; cf. Glaber [Col. 0198D] Rodulfus II, 7. The source of all such narratives is Gregory, *Dialogues* IV, 30.]. In them the souls of the reprobate pay different punishments according to the quality of their merits, with demons assigned there to carry them out. He said that he had often heard their voices, anger, and terrors, and frequently also their wailings, as they lamented that the souls of the damned were snatched from their hands through the alms and prayers of the faithful—at this time especially through the prayers of the Cluniacs, who prayed unceasingly for the rest of the dead. When Abbot Odilo learned this from him, he established throughout all the monasteries subject to him that, just as the solemnity of All Saints is celebrated on the first day of November, so on the following day the memory of all those resting in Christ should be celebrated. This rite, spreading to many churches, caused the memory of the faithful departed to be solemnized.

999. 16. 3.

[Col. 0198B] (Glab. Rod. I, 4.) In Italy, Crescens, having seized the patriciate of the Romans, rebels against Emperor Otto.

1000. 17. 4.

(A. Leod.) In the thousandth year of Jesus Christ, according to Dionysius’s reckoning, many prodigies were seen. There was a very great earthquake; a comet appeared; on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January, around the ninth hour, the sky split open and, like a burning torch with a long trail, something descended toward the earth in the manner of lightning, with such brilliance that not only those who were in the fields but also those indoors were struck by the sudden burst of light. As this split in the sky gradually disappeared, there meanwhile appeared a shape resembling a serpent, with its head growing larger and with bluish feet.

1001. 18. 5.

[Col. 0198C] According to some, Octavianus, the 142nd, presides over the Roman church [Note: [Col. 0197] “Octavianus … presides” is absent in D.] (cf. Mar.). (GLAB. ROD. I, 4.) Emperor Otto attacked Crescens the patrician at Rome in war. Crescens was defeated and, dragged back after his flight, was captured, paraded while mounted backwards on a worthless beast, and, gradually mutilated limb by limb, was finally hanged outside the city.

1002. 19. 6.

While Emperor Otto was staying at Rome and dealing rather leniently with the Romans, considering how he might restore the rights of the kingdom and the church to their ancient condition, the Romans were thereby led to despise him. They suddenly conspired against him, and after killing some of his soldiers, besieged him in the palace. Through the efforts of Duke Henry of Bavaria and Hugh, margrave of Italy, he was scarcely extracted by means of a pretended agreement, and he left Rome with Pope Silvester. Since the wife of Crescens had lured the emperor into loving her with the hope of reigning, she, grieving over his departure, sent him poison. Consumed by it, he died in Italy while returning. The transalpine soldiers carried the dead emperor’s body, together with the imperial insignia, toward Gaul, but, harassed by repeated attacks from the Italians, fought their way through with their weapons. When the situation was already thought to be secure, however, Duke Henry of Bavaria, having wronged Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, from whose mouth everyone hung, violently wrested the royal insignia from him, as though they belonged to him by hereditary right. For he was the son of Duke Henry, who had been born from Henry, the brother of the first Emperor Otto. (MAR.) Duke Henry, having won over the minds of certain princes of the kingdom, was anointed king by Willigis, archbishop of Mainz, and ruled for twenty-two years.

1003. R. 1. F. 7.

(ALPERT. I, 5.) Emperor Henry quickly defeated the more powerful men of the kingdom who wished to stir up wars against him, and made tributaries of the pagan kings dwelling in inner Germany, who are called Wends [Winidi]. [(GLAB. ROD. III, 3.) Abbot Abbo of Fleury was martyred in Gascony [Note: [Col. 0199] “Abbo” is added by 1 δ and the others except A, C2*, and 4*.].]

1004. 2. 8.

Gerard, bishop of Cambrai [Note: [Col. 0199D] He did not become bishop until 1012.], and Adelbold, bishop of Utrecht, were held in high regard in the church and at court. Emperor Henry elevated the church of Bamberg to the dignity of an episcopal see and, since he had no children, made it heir to all his possessions. Therefore Theoderic, bishop of Metz, grieving that the dowry and patrimony of his sister, Empress Cunigund, were being assigned by the emperor to the church of Bamberg, rebelled.

1005. 3. 9.

(ALP. I, 6.) A comet of terrifying appearance, throwing flames here and there, was seen in the southern part of the sky. (BALD. III, 7.) After Duke Otto died, the duchy of Lotharingia was given to Count Godfrey, son of Godfrey of Ardennes [Note: [Col. 0199D] Balderic records these events at the urging of Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, and therefore after 1012.]. Chilperic wrote a book on the reckoning of the calendar in this year, as appears from his method for finding the years of the Lord by the indictions:

“If you wish,” he says, “to know how many years of Christ’s incarnation there are, multiply the sixty-six cycles of indictions that have elapsed since his incarnation by fifteen: the result is 990. Add twelve to this, because Christ was born in the third indiction. Add the indiction of the present year, namely three. Behold, you have in this year 1005 years of Christ” [Note: [Col. 0199D] Cf. Sigebert, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 145; Mabillon, *Annals*, p. 431.].

1006. 4. 10.

(ALP. I, 6.) Famine and mortality became so severe throughout the whole world that, through weariness of burying, those still drawing breath were buried together with the dead. (BALD. I, 114.) Emperor Henry besieged the fortress of Valenciennes, situated on the border of France and Lotharingia, which Count Baldwin of Flanders had invaded, while King Robert of the Franks and Richard, count of Normandy, came to his aid.

1007. 5. 11.

(Ib.) Because Emperor Henry had returned ineffectually from the siege of Valenciennes, he marched against Baldwin, invaded the fortress of Ghent, ravaged the land, and captured several leading men of Flanders. Terrified by this, Baldwin satisfied the emperor, returned Valenciennes, and, after giving hostages and swearing an oath of loyalty, surrendered to him. Later, compelled by a revolt among his own people, the emperor granted Valenciennes to Baldwin as a benefice, so that Baldwin might assist him against the rebellion of his subjects. Later he also added Walcheren [Walachras] to it [Note: [Col. 0199D] After 1012; cf. Bald. III, 2. Hirsch.].

1008. 6. 12.

(A. Leod.; G. abb. Gembl.) Balderic was ordained bishop of Liège. Burchard likewise became bishop of Worms; devoted to the Scriptures, he published that great volume of canons, compiled and excerpted from scriptural teachings everywhere, with the assistance in this work of his teacher, Abbot Olbert, a man learned in every respect.

1009. 7. 13.

(MAR.) Leo, the 143rd, presides over the Roman church. (A. Leod.) An eclipse of the sun occurred at the second hour of the day. (ALPERT. I, 8.) The Normans ravaging Frisia burned the town of Tiel. Emperor Henry besieged the city of Metz because Theoderic, his wife’s brother, had rebelled against him and usurped the bishopric of that city. For Duke Theoderic of Moselle, after his brother Albero had given the bishopric of Metz to his own son, while the boy was still a child, appointed Theoderic himself as his guardian. After excluding the boy from the city and usurping the bishopric, Theoderic also captured Duke Theoderic in war. When the city had been almost destroyed by the siege, peace was at last arranged.

1010. 8. 14.

(MAR.) Bishop Bruno was martyred. (ALP. I, 9.) The Normans returned to Frisia, and after killing many people, burned the town of Utrecht. At this time the people of Hungary, hitherto devoted to idolatry, were converted to the faith of Christ through Gisla, the emperor’s sister. Married to the king of Hungary, she persuaded the king through her persistent efforts [Note: [Col. 0199D] If this is not false, it is nevertheless highly doubtful; [Col. 0200D] cf. *Acta Sanctorum*, September I, 490. Gisla married Stephen already before 1003. Moreover, from the accounts of the miracles that began after the king’s elevation, celebrated in 1083, it appears that Sigebert composed this part of the chronicle no earlier than 1085.] to seek baptism for himself and for the entire Hungarian people. In baptism he was called Stephen; his merits are celebrated throughout Hungary with the glory of many miracles.

1011. 9. 15.

(BALD. III, 8.) In Lotharingia, near Mount Castrilocus, a little spring of water, very healthful to many, was turned into blood. A woman proved this by showing many people her face, washed with water from that spring and appearing bloodstained.

1012. R. 10. F. 16.

Olbert, abbot of our church—that is, the church of Gembloux—was ordained, a man who, in character, religion, and twofold learning, was either to be compared with or preferred to good and learned men [Note: [Col. 0201] “our” and “that is” are absent in A, B5, C1, 2*, 3, D, and F2. “A man … preferred” is absent in C1, 2*, 3, 4*, D, in which all the following material for this year is also absent.]. (ALPERT. II, 10.) Emperor Henry sent Duke Godfrey with an army into the territory of Brabant [to besiege the fortress of Leuven, but he returned unsuccessfully [Note: [Col. 0201] Added by 1 δ and the others except A.].]

1013. 11. 17.

(BALD. III, 17.) Emperor Henry, going to Italy to aid his men, whom the Greeks were oppressing while they ravaged the area around Benevento, Salerno, and Capua, captured the city of Troy [Note: [Col. 0201D] These events took place in 1022.]. (Ib., 5.) While Bishop Balderic was fortifying a castle in a village called Huguardes [Note: [Col. 0201D] Hougarde, near Tirlemont.], Count Lambert of Leuven attacked him. Since Lambert prevailed, and many of the bishop’s men were captured and killed, the bishop was struck by grave misfortune. (Ann. Leod.) A very great earthquake occurred around midday on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December.

1014. 12. 18.

(MAR.) King Henry was blessed as emperor. (ANSEL.) Bishop Balderic founded a monastery of the holy apostle James on the island of Liège, where Abbot Olbert was the first superior [Note: [Col. 0201D] Of Gembloux, 1021–1048.]. (BALD. III, 11.) Duke Godfrey defeated Count Gerard in war. Gerard had disturbed the kingdom in many ways; his son was killed along with many others in the battle, and Godfrey thus terrified his accomplices.

[Col. 0201C] 1015. 13. 19.

(BALD. III, 12.) At this time Saint Guictheht, also called Adalbert, bishop of Prague, was martyred among the Bructeri [Note: [Col. 0201] Anselm apparently wrote this in the erasure of one line, as did the others except A.]. Duke Godfrey ravaged the county of Mons. Raginer, pursuing him with his uncle Lambert of Leuven, engaged him in battle near Florennes. More than four hundred men were killed there, and Lambert himself fell. A remarkable event occurred there. (A. Leod.; BALD.) When Lambert already had hope of victory—for he wore a phylactery hanging from his neck to his chest, filled with relics of the saints, through whose protection he believed he would be safe in danger—the appointed end of his life approached. That phylactery came off his neck and leapt onto a mound in the field; and at once the previously invincible count was killed. One of the soldiers took the phylactery and hid it in his boot. But when his thigh and leg swelled up, he revealed what had happened and gave the phylactery to its lord, Hethelo [Note: [Col. 0201D] Balderic calls him Herimannus; Hezelo is the diminutive form.], the duke’s brother.

1016. 14. 20.

(V. Sim.) Symeon, born at Syracuse in Sicily and later a monk on Mount Sinai, flourished at this time. Coming to Jerusalem, he undertook a long pilgrimage for Christ; and when he came to Gaul with Poppo, archbishop of Trier, he was confined at Trier in the upper part of a tower. There, after many persecutions by human beings and many temptations by demons, he rested in a blessed end [Note: [Col. 0201D] D. 1 June 1035.]. The glory of frequent miracles made his merits known.

1017. 15. 21.

(MAR.) Benedict, the 144th, presides over the Roman church [Note: [Col. 0201] “Benedict … presides” is absent in D.]. (BALD. III, 19.) A comet, more remarkable than usual, appeared for four months in the form of a very large beam.

1018. 16. 22.

(A. Leod.; BALD.) Guolbodo succeeded Balderic in the bishopric of Liège. (ALPERT. II, 21.) In Frisia, Count Theoderic, son of Arnulf of Ghent, was waging war against the Frisians in vengeance for his father, who had been killed by them. The emperor sent Duke Godfrey to fight against him. When battle was joined, a voice suddenly arose—no one knew from where—crying, “Flee, flee!” Everyone fled; many men were killed by the few Frisians, but the duke was captured.

1019. 17. 23.

(Ib.) After obtaining from the emperor for the Frisians immunity from every injustice, Duke Godfrey was released from captivity [Col. 0202C] and died not long afterward [Note: [Col. 0202D] In 1023, according to the Blandin annals.]. His brother Gothelo was installed in the duchy.

1020. 18. 24.

(ALPERT. II, 14.) King Rudolf of Burgundy, provoked by the insolence of the Burgundians, considered giving the kingdom of Burgundy to Emperor Henry. But the feigned submission of the Burgundians turned him away from this intention. (MAR.) Pope Benedict came in Gaul [Note: [Col. 0202D] That is, in Franconia, as in 1094. They assembled at Bamberg on Easter.] to Emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 0201] After this, F3 immediately inserts in a continuous hand: “An account of a miracle performed in the region of the Saxons in the time of Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, etc.; King Pepin made a spring, etc.” The people of Gembloux added these items under the year 761; also, “Gregory’s statements on the nature of sacrifice,” etc. He was evidently reading them in the manuscript he was copying, inserted on a blank folio, which the scribe F3 mistakenly and ineptly incorporated here into Sigebert’s text.].

1021. 19. 25.

(Vita Her.) While celebrating Christmas at Cologne [Note: [Col. 0202D] 1020; for Sigebert begins the year at Christmas.], Emperor Henry appeased Archbishop Heribert, whom he had formerly treated unjustly, by a humble act of satisfaction. Reconciled with him, the archbishop predicted that he would soon die. Not long afterward he did die and began to shine with great virtues. Pilgrim succeeded him in the bishopric. (A. Leod.; Epit. Dur.) Durandus became bishop of Liège. This was like a drama in the theater of the world: a man born and raised in the most humble and poorest servile condition came to rule over his own carnal masters [Note: [Col. 0203D] Sigebert took this from the verse of the epitaph with which Stephen, abbot of Saint Lawrence, adorned Durandus’s tomb:

“Born and raised in the nest of a poor inheritance,  
By talent he rises above the highest nobles.  
Those whom he had taken as masters, he used as servants;  
What a great drama it was in the theater of the world!”  
Hirsch.].

1022. R. 20. F. 26.

(BALD. III, 36.) After a royal and synodal assembly had been held at Aachen for several days, such drought and harshness of weather broke out that many people collapsed from the excessive heat, and many animals also suddenly perished. The pavement and marble columns sweated with so much moisture that those who did not know the cause thought water had been sprinkled over them.

1023. 21. 27.

(Ib.) Emperor Henry and Robert, king of the Franks, met over the River Chiers at Mouzon [Col. 0203B] to discuss the condition of the church, the kingdom, and the empire. They agreed that, in order to confirm these matters, they should both meet the Roman pope at Pavia at a suitable time. The emperor gave such lavish gifts to the king and his men, and to many others who had gathered merely to admire the emperor’s majesty, that the emperor’s generosity could have been compared with the wealth of the kings of Persia or Arabia. An eclipse of the sun occurred at Easter.

1024. 22. 28.

When the princes consulted him about the succession to the kingdom, Emperor Henry designated Conrad, a man of royal lineage and outstanding freedom—for he had never submitted himself to anyone’s servitude—and died [Note: [Col. 0203D] This is highly doubtful. Cf. Stenzel, *Frankish Emperors* I, 9.]. Bishop Adelbold of Utrecht wrote his life [Col. 0203C]. The powerful Duke Cono, wishing to aspire to the empire, was rejected at the urging of Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, and certain leading men of the kingdom. Conrad was elevated to the empire and ruled for fifteen years.

1025. 1. 29.

John, bishop of Porto, brother of the recently deceased Pope Stephen [Note: [Col. 0203D] False. John IX was neither bishop of Porto nor Stephen’s brother, but rather the brother of Benedict VIII. Peter Damian, in *The Life of Saint Odilo*, chapter 2, says: “As soon as he [Benedict VIII] died, his own brother John succeeded him in the apostolic dignity.” After the aforementioned pope [Benedict] had departed from human affairs, he appeared in a night vision to John, bishop of Porto, and two others whose names are unknown to us, etc. A little later: “Immediately that same John, bishop of Porto, supported by letters of apostolic authority, reached Pavia with rapid steps.” Thus Sigebert could see that John IX and John, bishop of Porto, were two different persons. Moreover, John had already been elected in August 1024, not in 1025, as our author states.], presides as the 145th over the Roman church. (V. Odil.) Appearing to him, Pope Stephen, his brother [Note: [Col. 0204D] The *Life of Odilo* calls him Benedict VIII.], said that he was being tormented by infernal punishments but hoped that, through the intercession of Abbot Odilo, he might obtain pardon. For his sake Odilo labored for so long in every kind of prayer until it was revealed to him that his prayer for him had been heard. (A. Leod.) Raginard was ordained bishop of Liège. At Liège, on the public hill, he founded a monastery of Saint Lawrence and appointed Stephen, a man of holy memory, as its first abbot.

1026. 2. 30.

King Robert of the Franks resolved to invade Lotharingia but soon abandoned the attempt [Note: [Col. 0204D] 1025.]. When Duke Gothelo, who had been troubling Conrad’s kingdom out of private hatred [Note: [Col. 0204D] Conrad had waged war against his brother Godfrey.], and the other princes had been brought to unity in peace [Note: [Col. 0204D] At Aachen, according to Balderic III, 50. There Conrad celebrated Christmas in 1025.], prosperity increased for the king and tranquility for the kingdom.

1027. 3. 31.

(Ib.) King Conrad elevated his son Henry, still a child, to the kingship at Aachen [Note: [Col. 0204D] This happened only in the following year, 1028, on April 14; that year is also given by the Liège annals.]. At Easter he himself was consecrated emperor at Rome and suppressed the uprisings of certain Italians who opposed him. At this time ecclesiastical religion flourished through notable abbots: in France and Burgundy, through Odilo of Cluny, distinguished for piety, and William of Dijon, revered for severity; in Lotharingia, through Richard of Verdun, distinguished by devout seriousness and serious devotion, through Poppo of Stavelot, through Elias of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0203] “devout … Cologne” is absent in L.], through Olbert and Stephen of Liège, and through Berno of Reichenau.

1028. 4. 32.

At this time Guido of Arezzo, a man of great renown among musicians, flourished in Italy. In this respect he should even be preferred to philosophers: through his method, children learn unfamiliar melodies more easily than through a teacher’s voice or through the use of any instrument. By assigning six letters or syllables in measured sequence to the six notes that music alone regularly admits, and distinguishing these notes by the movements of the fingers of the left hand, he makes the elevations and descents of those six notes—extended and contracted across the full octave—present themselves clearly to the eyes and ears.

1029. 5. 33.

(Ib.) Emperor Conrad marched against the rebellious Slavs to subdue them [Note: [Col. 0204D] In the month of June.].

[Col. 0205A] 1030. R. 6. F. 34.

(Ib.) Emperor Conrad marched against the rebellious Hungarians to subdue them [Note: [Col. 0205] C4* omits this year; C1, 3, and D join it to the preceding year, numbering the following year 1030 and continuing in this way through our year 1036, which for them is 1035.].

1031. 7. 35.

After Robert, king of the Franks, died, his son Henry ruled in France for thirty years [Note: [Col. 0205] 1, corrected from another reading, and A have twenty-five.]. (BALD. III, 51.) At this time, by order of Emperor Conrad, a royal and synodal assembly was held at Tribur. Among other matters, the bishops wished to decree that, if the fast of the first month ever fell within the week in which the beginning of Lent occurs on Wednesday, the observance of both fasts should be completed through the fulfillment of a single office. But Gerard of Cambrai and the few who joined him [Note: [Col. 0205C] “and the few who joined him” is Sigebert’s own addition; cf. his letter on the Ember fast in Martène, *Thesaurus* I, 298. Hermann of Reichenau places this synod in 1035.] contradicted this decree of the majority and prevailed in having the fast of the first month celebrated in the other week, in which the office falls, according to the custom of the ancients.

1032. 8. 1.

(MAR.) Saint Bardo was ordained archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0205C] This happened on June 29, 1031; cf. the *Life of Saint Bardo*, chapter 11.]. Robert and Richard, who at this time had departed from Normandy for Apulia because of the overpopulation of their homeland, sought Apulia. Since the Italians were divided among themselves and offered assistance to one side against the other, they cleverly and forcefully defeated the Italians by exploiting this opportunity. By pressing their successes, they enlarged their reputation and prepared the way for future prosperity.

1033. 9. 2.

(BALD. III, 52.) An eclipse of the sun occurred around midday on the third day before the Kalends of July [Col. 0205C]. The bishops of France issued the following decree to be observed by the peoples subject to them. One of them said that letters had been brought to him from heaven instructing that peace should be renewed on earth. He entrusted the matter to the others and gave these commands to be conveyed to the peoples:

No one was to bear arms; no one was to reclaim what had been taken; and no one was to act as avenger of his own blood or that of any close relation, but he was to be compelled to forgive his attackers. They were to observe a fast of bread and water every Friday and abstain from meat and broth on Saturday. Content with this fast alone for the remission of all sins, they were to know that no other penance was to be imposed upon them, and they were to confirm by oath that they would observe these rules. Whoever refused was to be deprived of Christianity; and when he departed from the world, no one was to visit him or consign him to burial. They also issued many other intolerable commands, which seem burdensome to repeat.

When many people, eager for novelty, embraced this innovation more readily than was right, Gerard of Cambrai—the only Lotharingian whose parish belonged to the church of France—could not be induced by anyone’s urging to accept these measures. Instead, he refuted each article, saying that from the beginning the human race had been divided into three groups: those who pray, those who fight, and those who cultivate the land; and that one of two and two of one require mutual assistance. Therefore weapons ought to be borne, and acts of plunder ought to be restored by the authority of law and grace. The avenger of one who had been struck or killed should not be inflamed by compulsion, but should be reconciled with him according to the Gospel. A fast on Friday or Saturday should not be imposed upon everyone, because not everyone has the same capacity; nor should everyone be content with this one fast, because not everyone possesses the same capacity for repentance. To confirm these things by oath, or to increase the violation of an oath by perjury, was not useful. To excommunicate those who contradicted these measures, to deny visits to the sick or burial to the dead, was detestable. The authoritative decrees of the fathers were sufficient, together with the appropriate measure of penance imposed for neglecting them.

1034. 10. 3.

When Frederick, duke of Moselle, died [Note: [Col. 0206C] On the chronology, cf. Stenzel, *Frankish Emperors* II, 115, who nevertheless incorrectly assigns this to 1033.], leaving no male children to whom the duchy should belong, Duke Gothelo, having obtained from the emperor also the duchy of Moselle [Col. 0206C], ruled with greater power in Lotharingia.

1035. 11. 4.

Since the Burgundians did not cease their customary insolence against their king, King Rudolf handed over the kingdom of Burgundy to Emperor Conrad [Note: [Col. 0206C] In 1027, in the month of July. Rudolf died on September 6, 1032.]. The kings of that people had held it from the time of Emperor Arnulf for more than 130 years; thus Burgundy was once again reduced to the status of a province.

1036. 12. 5.

Odo of Champagne, demanding from Emperor Conrad, his nephew, the kingdom of King Rudolf, his uncle, begged that he might rule Burgundy under Conrad [Note: [Col. 0205] Here A, B3*, 4*, 4**, 5, C1, 2*, 3, 4*, D, and E begin a new year, writing XIV. VII; because C1, 2*, 3, 4*, D, and E had already joined the preceding year to 1030, they write XIII. VII. They continue in this manner. The same arrangement originally appeared in 1, and consequently in the year beginning “In the month of April,” the scribe himself had added in the margin the number MXL; in the year “Pope Leo,” ML; in the year “Frederick,” MLX; and so throughout Sigebert’s work. The years of the Lord are marked in the margin only by decades: before 972 in Sigebert’s own hand, and afterward by scribes. But 1 η, who began writing in 1137, erased these numbers XIII. VI before “Henry, king,” etc., and corrected the following ones so that they are given as we have them: those of the Romans through 1039, and those of the Franks through 1060. The same 1 η erased all the marginal years of the Lord and himself added one to each subsequent year, so that “the year of Emperor Henry” is now MXL, “the year of Saint Theobald” is ML, and so on through “the year of the eclipse of the sun,” MCXL. Since this arrangement alone is correct, we have also adopted it; but we have placed the numbers formerly written in 1 within parentheses.]. (A. Leod.) King Henry, son of Conrad, married the daughter of the king of the English [Note: [Col. 0207D] June 29, 1036.]. Waging war against the emperor, Odo invaded Lotharingia, attacked its fortresses, and besieged the city of the Leuci, called Toul, without restraining his fury in any way [Note: [Col. 0207D] 1037.].

1037. R. 13. (14.) F. 6. 7.)

(Ib.) Herimannus was ordained archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0207] “Herimannus was ordained archbishop” is absent in D and E.]. Odo besieged and captured the fortress of Bar. Duke Gothelo, indignant at the insolence of the Franks, met Odo with the Lotharingians. Battle was joined near Bar [Note: [Col. 0207D] November 15, 1037.], Odo was killed, and the Frankish army, battered by a heavy slaughter, was forced to flee from Lotharingia.

1038. 14. (15.) 7. (8.)

As the forces of the Normans in Apulia gradually increased through reinforcements from Normandy, they were encouraged to invade Apulia by their own valor and the weakness of the Italians. After capturing fortresses and cities either by deceit or by force, they gained power in Apulia and struck terror into the neighboring peoples through fear of their name. [Count Henry of Leuven was killed in his own house by a captive named Harmannus, and his son Otto succeeded him. When Otto was carried off by an untimely death, his uncle Balderic, also called Lambert, succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0207] Added by Anselm; the others except A omit it.].]

1039. (1040.) 15. (16.) 8. (9.)

(BALD. III, 55.) In the month of April, on the eighth day before the Ides, a fiery beam of astonishing size was seen in the sky between the southern and eastern regions. Moving above the sun, which was already declining toward sunset, it appeared to fall to earth; its traces could be seen for a long time. (Ib.) Emperor Conrad went to Italy to subdue those who were plotting rebellion [Note: [Col. 0207D] At the very end of 1036.]. Since all the Lombards had sworn an oath that they would not tolerate any lord who acted against them in a manner contrary to their wishes, he cast certain bishops into chains. When the bishop of Milan escaped by flight, the emperor burned the suburbs of Milan. On Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0207D] May 29, 1037.], while the emperor was being crowned at Mass in a small church beside the city, the thunder and lightning were so severe that some people lost their minds and some died. Bishop Bruno, who was celebrating Mass, and the emperor’s secretary, together with three others, said that during the solemnities of the Mass they had seen Saint Ambrose threatening the emperor in anger. The emperor left Italy [Note: [Col. 0207D] At the end of August 1038.]. An eclipse of the sun occurred on the day before the Ides of May, and the emperor died on the day before the Nones of June. After him his son Henry ruled for seventeen years.

1040. 1. 9. (10.)

(A. Leod.) Emperor Henry went to fight Odelric, duke of the Bohemians [Col. 0208A], but when the Bohemians resisted bravely, he returned without success.

1041. 2. 10. (11.)

(Ib.) With the aid of God obtained through the prayers of holy men, Emperor Henry avenged the misfortune of the previous year and subdued Odelric, duke of Bohemia.

1042. 3. 11. (12.)

When civil war broke out among the Hungarians, King Peter, expelled by them from the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0207D] 1041.], appealed to Emperor Henry for help. Henry powerfully supported him and ravaged Hungary. (ANSELM.) Guatho, from the clergy of Saint Lambert, a man distinguished by the spirit of wisdom and knowledge and by religious fervor, was ordained bishop of Liège.

[Col. 0208B] 1043. 4. 12. (13.)

At Constantinople, Constantine Monomachus ruled as emperor. (A. Leod.) Emperor Henry entered Hungary again. With a small force he put King Obbo to flight in battle and took the lance, the king’s insignia. He restored Peter, whom Obbo had expelled, to the kingdom of Hungary and made Hungary tributary to himself.

1044. 5. 13. (14.)

(Ib.) A severe famine devastated Gaul and Germany. Duke Gothelo died, and his son Godfrey, when the duchy of Moselle was denied to him [Note: [Col. 0207D] Deprived of his paternal right, according to the Liège annals. Sigebert is mistaken here and under 1048: Godfrey the Bearded had held the duchy of Moselle while his father was still alive; but now he also sought to obtain from the king, contrary to right, the other duchy owed to his brother—namely, Lower Lotharingia—as Hermann of Reichenau says under 1044; cf. Stenzel II, 117.], rebelled against the emperor after being refused the other duchy.

1045. 6. 14. (15.)

(Ib.) At the urging of certain faithful servants of God, Godfrey was induced to seek the restoration of the emperor’s favor. He was captured by the emperor and committed to custody [Note: [Col. 0208D] In July 1045.], but was released after giving his son as a hostage [Note: [Col. 0208D] At Aachen, in May 1046, according to Hermann of Reichenau.]. When the son died in captivity, Godfrey proceeded to rebel. Benedict, having invaded the Roman papacy by simony [Note: [Col. 0208D] 1033. The following account is not correctly narrated by our author; cf. Stenzel, *Frankish Emperors* I, 104 ff. Waltramus copied it word for word.], was uneducated in letters and had another pope consecrated alongside himself to carry out the duties of the ecclesiastical office by turns. When this displeased many people, a third was brought forward, who alone would fulfill the functions of the two.

1046. 7. 15. (16.)

The church of Saint Gertrude at Nivelles [Note: [Col. 0208D] Nivelles, in Hainaut.], which a few years earlier had been burned after negligence and carelessness had allowed the blood of the Lord to be spilled, was rebuilt anew and consecrated in the presence of Emperor Henry. Since one pope was disputing the papacy against two and two against one at Rome, King Henry went to Rome against them [Note: [Col. 0208D] He arrived there on December 23, 1046.]. After deposing them by canonical and imperial judgment, Suidiger, bishop of Bamberg, also called Clement, presided as the 146th over the Roman church [Col. 0209A], and Henry was blessed by him as emperor [Note: [Col. 0209D] December 25.]. The Romans swore that they would never elect a pope without his consent. (A. Leod.) At the instigation of Godfrey, Count Baldwin of Flanders [Note: [Col. 0209D] Baldwin V, of Lille.], rebelled against the emperor. When Theoderic, bishop of Metz, died, his cousin Adelbero succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0209] Adebbero in 1 and F3.], a man of great prudence and holiness.

1047. R. 8. F. 16. (17.)

(MAR.) Poppo, also called Damasus, presides as the 147th over the Roman church [Note: [Col. 0209D] Consecrated on July 17, 1048. Clement II had died on October 9, 1047.]. (A. Leod.) Godfrey burned the palace at Nijmegen and destroyed it beyond repair. He also burned the city of Claborum, called Verdun, together with the principal church of Saint Mary [Note: [Col. 0209D] October 24.]. [Col. 0209B] (ANSELM.) Franco, a teacher of the clergy of Liège, excelled both in literary learning and in moral integrity. He wrote to Archbishop Herimannus a book on the squaring of the circle, concerning which Aristotle says: “The squaring of the circle, if it is knowable, is not yet a science; but it is knowable.” (MAR.) So much snow fell in the west that it broke the forests.

1048. 9. 17. (18.)

Religious and illustrious men, distinguished by holiness, fall asleep in Christ: Odilo, abbot of Cluny [Note: [Col. 0209D] 1 January 1049], and Poppo of Stavelot [Note: [Col. 0209D] 16 June 1048]. (A. Leod.) Guatho, bishop of Liège [Note: [Col. 0209D] 8 July 1048], and Olbert, abbot of Gembloux, of holy memory [Note: [Col. 0209D] 14 July 1048]. Deoduin succeeds Guatho in the bishopric. Albert, who had received the duchy of the Mosellans, denied to Godefrid [Note: [Col. 0210D] Or rather, “taken away,” according to Hermann of Reichenau under the year 1047, who says that the emperor gave his duchy to a certain Adalbert; cf. Stenzel II, 118], is killed by Godefrid [Col. 0209C] [Note: [Col. 0210D] In the month of October]. (MAR.) Gerard of Alsace obtains his duchy, while Frederick obtains the other duchy [Note: [Col. 0209] “Men” through “obtains” are absent in D.]. (Wib. V. Leon.) Bruno, bishop of Toul, presides as the 148th pope of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0210D] Consecrated 12 February 1049]; he was called Leo, the ninth of that name. As he was traveling to Rome to take possession of the apostolic see, he heard the voices of angels singing: “The Lord says, I think thoughts of peace and not of affliction.” He composed chants for many saints and did and wrote many things useful to the Church. Once, when he encountered a poor leper before the doors of the papal residence, he carefully warmed him and placed him in his own bed; but when, after opening the door, he could not find him, he was astonished to realize that in the poor man he had received Christ.

[Col. 0209D] **1049. (1050.) 10. 18. (19.)**

Pope Leo, coming into Gaul in order to calm the disturbances in the empire stirred up by Baldwin and Godefrid, reconciled Godefrid with the emperor. (A. Leod.) But since Baldwin persisted more stubbornly, the emperor [Col. 0210A] led an army against him. At last Baldwin was brought to submission and, on the appointed day, made satisfaction to the emperor at Aachen [Note: [Col. 0210D] In the month of July]. (Vita Leon.) Pope Leo, after holding synods in Gaul and Germany, improved the condition of the Church [Note: [Col. 0209] B3' joins this entire year to the preceding one].

**1050. 11. 19. (20.)**

(V. Tietb.) At this time Saint Tietbald, not the least among the nobles of the Franks, was renowned. Having renounced the world and himself and followed Christ, he lived as a recluse in Vicenza, a city of Venetia, where in the twelfth year of his conversion he rested in a blessed death. How faithfully he had served God after receiving his calling was revealed by the abundance of miracles after his death. His bones, translated to Gaul, earned much veneration in many places. While Pope Leo was striving to drive the Normans from the borders of the Romans, he suffered great disaster, because he was captured along with many others [Col. 0210B] [Note: [Col. 0210D] 18 June 1052]; nevertheless, he refused to be released unless his companions were released as well. (MAR.) Bardo, bishop of Mainz, died [Note: [Col. 0210D] On 11 June 1051], and his holiness was made manifest through an abundance of miraculous grace.

**1051. 12. 20. (21.)**

(A. Leod.) Baldwin of Flanders, having invaded the county of the Hainaut people, rebels against the emperor. France is disturbed by Berengar of Tours, who maintained that the Eucharist which we receive at the altar is not truly the body and blood of Christ, but a figure of Christ’s body and blood. Accordingly, many people disputed extensively against him and on his behalf, both orally and in writing.

**1052. 13. 21. (22.)**

(V. Leon.) The king of Hungary dissents from the emperor Henry. To reconcile him, Pope Leo came to the emperor; but because friends of discord intervened, this was fruitless. Pope Leo, by apostolic authority and after holding a synod, decreed that Gerard, the fifth bishop of Toul before him, remarkable for the holiness of his life, should be solemnly numbered among the holy confessors in the Church.

**1053. 14. 22. (23.)**

(A. Leod.) Count Baldwin, invading the borders of Lorraine, burned the town of Huy. Godefrid rebelled again because, after marrying the wife of Marquis Boniface, he was excluded from Lombardy on the emperor’s orders. (HUMB.) As the Greeks were declining into a many-sided heresy, under the leadership of Michael, patriarch of Constantinople, and Leo of Acrida, archbishop of the Bulgarians, [Col. 0210D] Pope Leo, refuting their errors, wrote a book against them fortified by firm testimonies from Scripture. Nicetas also, a Constantinopolitan monk surnamed Pectoratus, wrote against the Romans [Col. 0211A] a book full of error and folly, entitled: *Concerning Unleavened Bread, the Sabbath, and the Marriages of Priests*.

**1054. R. 15. F. 23. (24.)**

(Ib.) Pope Leo, by a letter written to the emperor Constantine and winning his goodwill, sent his representatives—namely, Humbert, cardinal bishop of Silva Candida [Note: [Col. 0211D] That is, Humbert’s legation, in Baronius XI, 210; cf. p. 198. Our author read it in the codex of Saint Lawrence of Liège, now Brussels 9706, eleventh century], Peter, archbishop of Amalfi, and Frederick, the seventh deacon and chancellor—to Constantinople to refute the heresies of the Greeks. They were said to be like the Simonians, selling the gift of God; like the Valesians, castrating their guests and promoting them even to the episcopate; like the Arians, rebaptizing Latins baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity; like the Donatists, boasting that the orthodox Church existed only in Greece; like the Nicolaitans, allowing priests to marry; like the Severians, calling the law of Moses accursed; like the Pneumatomachi, cutting the confession of the Holy Spirit from the Creed; and like the Nazarenes, observing Judaism. They prohibited the baptism of infants dying before the eighth day after birth, the giving of Communion to women endangered in childbirth or during menstruation, and the baptism of women if they were pagans. They called the Latins “Azimites,” and, persecuting them excessively, closed their churches. They celebrated with leavened bread; in their children they anathematized the Roman Church and placed the Church of Constantinople above it.

After being kindly received by the emperor, they defeated the monk Nicetas before him so completely that he anathematized and burned the book he had written against the Romans. When the patriarch Michael refused to meet with them, they withdrew after placing a document of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia in the presence of the clergy and people. Michael falsified the document and, reading it to the people, summoned them—saying that the emperor had recalled them—to a synod in the emperor’s absence, so that they might be stoned by the people. When the emperor forbade this, Michael stirred up the people against him. But after Michael was convicted of falsifying the document of excommunication, he and all his supporters were removed from the emperor’s favor and palace.

Bishop Humbert of Silva Candida described these events and refuted the writings of the monk Nicetas and of Leo, archbishop of Acrida among the Bulgarians. These writings, translated from Latin into Greek, were accepted by the Greeks at the command of the emperor Constantine. (BALD. III, 68, 70.) The emperor Henry, having raised his five-year-old son Henry to the kingship at Aachen [Note: [Col. 0211D] 17 July], set out against Baldwin. As Baldwin fled, Henry crossed the Scheldt [Col. 0212A] and devastated everything; moreover, after the gates of Clusa [Note: [Col. 0211D] Ecluse, or Sluys] had been opened to him, he inflicted a great slaughter on his enemies. Advancing farther, he killed Count Lambert [Note: [Col. 0211D] Of Lens], a follower of Baldwin, together with many others. He also shut up many leading Flemings who had followed his army inside the city of Tournai and captured them after the siege. (MAR.) Pope Leo died [Note: [Col. 0211D] 19 April].

**1055. 16. 24. (25.)**

Gebhard, bishop of Eichstätt, also called Victor, presides as the 149th pope of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0212D] Consecrated 13 April]. Anno was appointed archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0212D] 3 March 1056]. While the emperor was established in Italy, his soldiers engaged the Slavs and Luticians in battle, and many were captured or killed. Baldwin of Flanders, together with Godefrid, besieged his uncle Duke Frederick [Col. 0212B] inside Antwerp, but when the Lotharingians came to his aid, he abandoned the attack. How greatly Pope Leo IX was esteemed before God became evident to all when God glorified him by displaying many miracles at his tomb in Rome.

**1056. 17. 25. (26.)**

Pope Victor, coming into Gaul, was received with glory by the emperor. (A. Leod.) While he was present, the emperor Henry died not long afterward [Note: [Col. 0212D] 5 October], and after him his son Henry ruled for fifty years [Note: [Col. 0211] The first copy originally read: “rules for [.....] years,” with the space for the number left blank and nothing erased. Later another contemporary hand entered “fifty” in this space, as all the other copies also have it. One copy, A, omits the words “fifty years,” showing that they did not yet exist in Sigebert’s first edition].

**1057. 1. 26. (27.)**

After a general assembly had been held at Cologne [Note: [Col. 0212D] In December 1056], Baldwin and Godefrid, through the mediation of Pope Victor, were restored to the king’s favor and to peace, and all the disturbances of war were quieted.

**1058. 2. 27. (28.)**

After the emperor Henry had captured certain castles in Frisia, the Frisians were restrained from rebellion. (MAR.) Paderborn, a city of Germany, was burned together with its principal church. In the monastery of the Scottish monks there was a certain monk named Paternus, who had long lived as a recluse and had often foretold this fire. Because he refused to leave on account of his chosen reclusion, he allowed himself to be burned.

**1059. (1060.) 3. 28. (29.)**

Frederick, son of Duke Gothelon, the seventh deacon of the Roman Church, formerly a cleric of Saint Lambert, because he was hated by the emperor Henry on account of his hatred for his brother [Col. 0212D] Duke Godefrid, became a monk at Monte Cassino after the embassy to Constantinople and later became abbot. By the election of the Romans, he presides as the 150th pope of the Roman Church, having changed his name to Stephen [Note: [Col. 0212D] He was elected abbot on 24 May 1057, pope on 2 August 1057, and died on 29 March 1058].

[Col. 0213A] In the district of Brabant near Tournai, multitudes of snakes gathered on both sides and engaged in a prodigious battle against one another. After many had been killed on both sides, the defeated party fled and hid in a hollow tree. The victorious party, pursuing them in the manner of conquerors, roared around the tree with hissing until the people set fire around it and all the snakes were burned.

**1060. R. 4. F. 92. (30.)**

(Cf. Mar.) Gerard, bishop of Florence, also called Nicholas, presides as the 151st pope of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0213C] Elected 28 December 1058]. (A. Leod.) Henry, king of the Franks, died [Note: [Col. 0213C] 29 June], and his son Philip ruled after him for forty-nine years [Note: [Col. 0213] It is no longer certain whether the number was written by the same hand as the rest or supplied later, since nearly two centuries ago the writing was retraced in ink so that it could be read more easily].

**1061. 5. 1.**

(MAR.) The chronicler Marianus [Note: [Col. 0213] Thus in 1, C1, and 3; D has *heronografus*] was renowned. Coming from Scotland into Gaul, he became a monk at Cologne; first he lived as a recluse at Fulda and afterward at Mainz.

**1062. 6. 2.**

In this year the bishop of Cologne, with the agreement of the leading men of the kingdom, who were indignant that the empire was not being governed manfully by the emperor Henry’s mother Agnes, violently and deliberately seized the boy and took him under his own protection, removing the administration of the empire from his mother. After giving an account of this matter before everyone, he regained the favor of his lord the emperor and, through the emperor’s son, returned to favor with the boy’s mother.
