But the empress, turning necessity into an act of will in order to close the mouths of those speaking evil about her [Note: [Col. 0213] “of those speaking” is written *lequentium* in 1], abandoned not only the dignity of the kingdom but also the burden of worldly affairs and went to Rome, to the threshold [Col. 0213C] of the apostles [Note: [Col. 0213C] In 1067, as can be gathered from Lambert under the year 1072. On 6 March 1067 she was still with her son at Regensburg; cf. Hund, *Metrop. Salisb.* I, 245]. There she remained until the end of her life [Note: [Col. 0213C] 14 December 1077], an example and a marvel to all in every good quality.

**1063. 7. 3.**

In this year the great cycle [Note: [Col. 0213] The words “of Dionysius” were erased afterward in 1] of 532 years ends. It contains twenty-eight nineteen-year cycles and is entirely useful for every reckoning of the paschal computation; from age to age it revolves within itself without error. [Col. 0214A] Yet it seems open to criticism in this respect: because the years of the Lord’s Incarnation were carelessly assigned to it, it disagrees with the truth of the Gospel concerning the year of the Lord’s Passion, asserting that the fourteenth moon of April fell on the first day of the week in that year. This is entirely false, because according to the testimony of the Gospel the fourteenth moon of April fell on the fifth day of the week that year, and on the sixth day, when the moon was fifteen [8 Kalends of April [Note: [Col. 0213] Added by 1δ and the others except A]], the Lord suffered.

A large army sets out from Gaul into Spain to fight the Saracens. But after the entire region had been ravaged by the Saracens, it returned ineffectively under the pressure of hunger.

**1064. 8. 4.**

(MAR.) The great cycle of 532 years, having been completed twice since the birth of Christ, begins for the third time. Alexander, bishop of Lucca, presides as the 153rd pope of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0213] Thus in 1 and the other copies; D has 160] [Note: [Col. 0214C] Consecrated 30 September 1061. Cadalus was elected at Basel on 28 October 1061]. [Col. 0214B] Against him, Cadalus, bishop of Parma, aspiring to the papacy, became a great scandal to the Church, because the prolonged dispute between them broke out even into killings [Note: [Col. 0213] After two and a half lines had been erased, Anselm wrote the following on the erasure:

“Lord Hermann, born of a noble Alemannic lineage, published his computus in this year and completed a most famous investigation into the natural course of the moon, examined with the greatest subtlety. From almost the beginning of his life he had been crippled from the kidneys downward and deprived throughout his life of the use of walking. Because he bore this scourge of God with the greatest patience and, moreover, gave thanks to God for it, he appeared, without human instruction in any liberal art, as a new philosopher gifted by God. He was exceedingly tranquil in character, rich in charity, kindly—something rare among learned men—friendly to everyone, solicitous in caring for the poor, and utterly pure in the chastity of virginity.”

The same words are read in B3*, 4*, 4**, F1, 2, and 3, and are written in another hand in the margin of B1; but they are absent from all the others. There can therefore be no doubt that they are not by Sigebert. In their place A has the following, which it omits below under 1067:

“But when a synod had been assembled at Mantua, through the mediation of Anno, archbishop of Cologne, Alexander, purging himself by oath of simony, was installed in the apostolic see, while Cadalus was rejected as a simoniac.”

Sigebert therefore first published this under the year 1064, but in a second revision transferred it to 1067. Moreover, in the codex of Saint Lawrence of Liège, now Brussels 10563, a fifteenth-century paper manuscript which among various little works also contains Hermann’s computus, the following is written above it:

“Epilogue on the life of Lord Hermann the Cripple. In the year of the Lord 1061, in the sixth year of the reign of Henry IV, Lord Hermann, of very noble lineage, and so forth as published above, down to ‘utterly pure in the chastity of virginity.’ I, Henry, an unworthy monk of the church of Würzburg founded by Dogebert, who saw and heard him, wrote this for those wishing to know. Is this the source of Anselm’s account?”]

**1065. 9. 5.**

(Ib.) After Duke Frederick died, Godefrid received the duchy [Note: [Col. 0214C] Lower Lorraine; cf. the years 1048 and 1070]. Herard, king of the English, died, and Harold succeeded him. Many who were traveling to Jerusalem in fulfillment of a vow to pray—up to seven thousand—were besieged by Arabs on Good Friday in a certain castle. They were killed or wounded in such a way that scarcely two thousand of the seven thousand and more returned.

**1066. 10. 6.**

(Ib.) A comet appeared throughout the entire Easter week. Harwich, king of the Northumbrians [Note: [Col. 0214C] Harold, also called Arbach, king of the Northmen, according to Marianus], came to England with nearly a thousand ships to become king and killed in the city of York more than a thousand laymen and one hundred English priests. King Harold of the English came against him with seven legions and killed him together with many others. Meanwhile William, count of the Normans, entered England with the Franks and, after joining battle with the English, killed Harold together with many thousands and ruled in England for twenty-six years.

[(V. Tietb.) Saint Tietbald died, living as a recluse in Vicenza, a city of Venetia [Note: [Col. 0215] Added by a beautiful hand, perhaps Anselm’s; the others except A, which already has it under the preceding year in this form, omit it: “Saint Tietbald the hermit and monk died.”]]

**1067. R. 11. F. 7. A. 1.**

(V. S. Conr.) Cuono, also called Conrad, primicerius of Cologne, sent by the emperor Henry to assume the archbishopric of Trier, was captured by Count Deoderic of Trier. Led into a forest by Deoderic’s followers, he was thrown three times from a cliff and, while still unharmed, pierced through with a sword. His body was covered with leaves in the forest. A peasant found it, carried it to a village, and buried it. Later it was transferred by Deoderic, bishop of Verdun, to the monastery of Tholey, where God immediately glorified it with many miracles [Col. 0215B] [Note: [Col. 0215D] He was killed in 1064 according to Marianus, and on 1 June 1066 according to the *Life of Saint Conrad* by the contemporary author Theoderic, a monk of Tholey, in *Acta Sanctorum*, June I, 127; our author excerpted all this from that work. What he relates under the following year concerning Deoderic, however, he did not take from the *Life*, Lambert, or any other surviving author. Marianus read: “The count himself, doing penance and going to Jerusalem, ended his life, and all his accomplices perished by an evil death.” In the *Life*, written before 1090, it reads: “Having suffered shipwreck, he encountered the violence of the sea.” Bernold likewise reports this. This opinion was therefore then very widespread and could not have been unknown to Sigebert, who had read and excerpted the *Life*. But considering that what happened in a shipwreck—something no one could have witnessed—could indeed be believed but could not be known, he wished, with commendable caution, to report nothing except what was certain: what became of him is still unknown].

While two men were contending for the papacy at Rome, a synod was assembled at Mantua [Note: [Col. 0216D] Cf. Stenzel, *Fränkische Kaiser*, II, 137; Giesebrecht, *Annales Altahenses*, in the appendix. The manuscripts show that Sigebert first assigned this synod to 1064 and then transferred it to 1067. We have already seen in many places that Sigebert has no authority whatsoever in assigning events to their correct dates; cf. 1092]. Through the mediation of Anno, archbishop of Cologne, Alexander, purging himself by oath of simony, was installed in the apostolic see, while Cadalus was rejected as a simoniac [Note: [Col. 0215] From “At Rome” through “was rejected” is absent in one copy, A. In 1 it is written in the same ink and by the same pen as the rest; nothing has been added in the margin there, nor has anything been erased].

**1068. 12. 8. 2.**

Count Deoderic of Trier, guilty before God and humanity of the martyrdom of Conrad, was exiled by the emperor. Having undertaken a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, what happened to him and to all who traveled in his company is still unknown. (MAR.) With the English harassed on one side by the Franks and on the other by the Scots, they were consumed by famine; many of them even ate human flesh.

[Col. 0215C] **1069. (1070.) 13. 9. 3.**

When the rivers had been locked by icy cold, the emperor Henry entered the land of the Luticians, struck them down with a tremendous slaughter, and devastated the land excessively.

**1070. 14. 10. 4.**

(A. Leod.) Gerard, duke of the Mosellans, died. Duke Godefrid also died [Note: [Col. 0216D] Of Lower Lorraine, on 24 December 1069]. His son Deoderic succeeded Gerard, and Godefrid the Hunchback, son of Godefrid, succeeded Godefrid. Although small in body, he was nevertheless outstanding in spirit. The Hungarians were planning a rebellion against their king Solomon, but they were restrained by fear of the emperor Henry, whose sister had married Solomon.

**1071. 15. 11. 5.**

In the church of Saint Paulinus the Confessor at Trier, the body of Saint Paulinus was discovered in an underground crypt. It had formerly been brought back from Phrygia, where he had lived in exile, and there suspended in iron chains by Bishop Felix [Note: [Col. 0215] Thus 1 punctuates the passage]. Many bodies of saints were also found beside it: on his right, namely, Palmatius, consul and patrician of Trier; on his left, Thyrsus, one of the leaders of the Theban Legion, who had been martyred in this city by Rictiovarus together with many Thebans; at his head, seven senators of the city—Maxentius, Constantius, Crescentius, Justinus, and the three brothers Leander, Alexander, and Sother; at his feet, Ormisda, Papirius, Constans, and Jovianus.

[Col. 0216B] Although many others were lying there, golden letters written on the wall marked only the names, time, and day of the Passion of these men and taught that they had all suffered under Rictiovarus. Duke Godefrid attacked the farther Frisians in war and almost annihilated them.

**1072. 16. 12. 6.**

After Baldwin the Younger, count of the Flemings, died [Note: [Col. 0215] B3* and 4* omit “B. i, F. c. d.” and place the rest of this year at the beginning of the preceding one; they place the words “Godefrid … annihilated” under the preceding year], his brother Robert, with the consent of the Flemings, seized Flanders against his cousin Arnulf. Arnulf met his uncle Robert together with Philip, king of the Franks. When battle was joined, Arnulf was killed, King Philip escaped by flight, and after many had been killed, Richildis, Arnulf’s mother, was captured on one side and Robert on the other. When each was released in exchange for the other, the war between them continued with varying fortunes.

**1073. 17. 13. 7.**

(MAR.) In this year, after two great years had elapsed from the fifteenth year of the emperor Tiberius, everything agrees according to the course of the sun and moon with the year in which Jesus Christ was baptized: that is, 6 January, the Sunday of the Epiphany; the beginning of his fast on Monday; and his temptation on 15 February, Friday.

(Ib.) Hildibrand, archdeacon of the Romans, also called Gregory, presides as the 153rd pope of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0216D] Elected 22 April, consecrated 29 June]. [Col. 0217A] Hermann of Liège became bishop of Metz. When two brothers, kings of the Rus’, were contending for the kingdom, one of them, driven from participation in the government, appealed to the emperor Henry, submitting himself and the kingdom of the Rus’ to him if he would restore him to the throne [Note: [Col. 0217C] Demetrius, at the beginning of the year 1075]. But this was fruitless, because the extremely serious dissension that had arisen in the Roman Empire urged him to protect his own interests rather than acquire those of another. For the Saxons, suffering many grave injuries and injustices at the hands of the emperor, rebelled against him; and the emperor devoted himself energetically to subduing them.

**1074. R. 18. F. 14. A. 8.**

(Cf. Sigebert’s letter *On Married Priests*, from Marinus.) Pope Gregory, having held a synod, anathematized the simoniacs, removed married priests from divine service, [Col. 0217B] and forbade laypeople to hear their Mass [Note: [Col. 0217] The remainder of this year is absent in C3* and 4*]. This was a novel measure and, as many thought, an ill-considered injury, contrary to the judgment of the holy Fathers [Note: [Col. 0217C] Sigebert is gravely mistaken both in fact and in law. He is mistaken in fact when he asserts that Pope Gregory VII believed the sacraments performed by excommunicated priests to be null and invalid, and that for this reason the pope forbade laypeople to attend the sacrifices of married priests whom he had excommunicated. Both the premise and the conclusion are false. This was already demonstrated in the eleventh century by Bernald of Constance, a priest, in his *Apologeticus*, written in support of Gregory VII’s prohibition, *On Not Attending the Sacrifices of the Excommunicated*. The prohibition was indeed issued by the pontiff in 1074 at a synod, with the purpose that married priests might be covered with salutary shame and brought to repentance for their incontinence, just as the purpose of every excommunication is the avoidance of all association with the excommunicated, according to the apostles Paul and John. The reason given by Sigebert, however, is either fabricated by him or borrowed from elsewhere and is utterly false, since no pontiff has ever judged the sacraments of an excommunicated person invalid. The Roman pontiffs have always considered baptism administered by a heretic—and indeed by a Jew or pagan—to be valid. Likewise, no one has ever denied that if a priest had fallen into heresy or schism, he could validly celebrate the Eucharist even while excommunicated. Baronius likewise demonstrated this briefly but clearly in the *Annales* under the year 1074, no. XL; it is unnecessary to adduce proofs of a certain fact. There was therefore nothing contrary to the judgment of the Fathers and nothing ill-considered in Gregory’s prohibition. HARTZHEIM, *Concilia Germaniae*, vol. III, p. 234].

Those Fathers had written that the sacraments performed in the Church—namely baptism, chrism, and the body and blood of Christ—are dispensed within God’s Church either by good or by wicked ministers, while the Holy Spirit secretly effects the efficacy of those same sacraments; because the Holy Spirit gives them life mystically, they are neither increased by the merits of good ministers nor diminished by the sins of wicked ones. Hence the saying: “This is he who baptizes.”

From this arose so grave a scandal that at no time of any heresy had the holy Church been divided by a more serious schism [Note: [Col. 0217D] It is a serious error to say that a schism arose from this prohibition. The schism arose in 1076, at the assembly of Worms, and at Brixen in 1080, where the king and thirty bishops set up as antipope against Gregory VII Guibert, archbishop of Ravenna, whom they had themselves previously recognized as pope. The cause that drove Henry to this schism was not the prohibition concerning clerical incontinence, which did not affect the king, but the prohibition against the simoniacal bestowal of Church dignities, which Henry, repenting of his invasion of churches, had promised in a written declaration in 1074 to avoid; Henry IV had promised to obey Gregory VII and the Church. When the king did not keep this promise, the pope summoned him to Rome to give an account; this summons was the final spur to breaking unity and imposing an antipope.

The scandals that follow from the rebellion of treacherous subjects after a just law has been promulgated ought not to deter the pope from his duty. Thus Christ our Lord, when he published or renewed the original decree concerning one husband and one wife, gravely offended the polygamous Jews, and the Pharisees were scandalized by their own wickedness, to such an extent that it was openly said that marriage was not expedient if this was the reason and obligation imposed on married people. Did Christ therefore yield to polygamy, which had been introduced through Mosaic toleration? So Gregory VII everywhere presses and inculcates the prohibition according to the decrees of the holy Fathers at the councils of Nicaea and elsewhere, which Bernald and others had long ago collected. ID., same work.]

Some acted for justice, others against justice; some did not avoid simony, while others concealed the stigma of greed beneath an honorable name, selling under the name of charity what they boasted of giving freely. As Eusebius says of the Montanists, under the name of offerings they accepted gifts with even greater artifice. Moreover, while only a few maintained continence, some merely pretended to it for the sake of profit and self-display, and many compounded incontinence with perjury or repeated adultery. In addition, taking advantage of this opportunity, laypeople rose up against the sacred orders and shook off all ecclesiastical subjection.

Laypeople profaned the sacred mysteries and argued about them; they baptized infants, using the filthy fluid from their ears instead of sacred oil and chrism; they regarded as of little importance receiving from married priests, at the end of life, the Lord’s viaticum and the Church’s customary funeral service; they burned the tithes assigned to priests; and, to understand the rest from a single example, laypeople often trampled underfoot the Lord’s body consecrated by married priests and voluntarily shed the Lord’s blood. Many other things contrary to right and law were done in the Church. On this occasion many false teachers arose in the Church and, through profane novelties, turned the people away from ecclesiastical discipline.

**1075. 19. 15. 9.**

(A. Leod.) The emperor Henry defeated the Saxons in a very severe battle [Note: [Col. 0218D] At the Unstrut, 9 June 1075], and, pressing them hard in a renewed campaign, forced all their leaders—bishops, dukes, counts, and the other powerful men—to surrender. The Hungarians rebelled against the emperor and subjected their king Solomon, driven from his kingdom, to prolonged imprisonment and torment. (Ib.) Deoduin, bishop of Liège, died, and Hienricus, noble in life and lineage, succeeded him. (MAR.) Anno, archbishop of Cologne, died [Col. 0218C] [Note: [Col. 0218D] 4 December 1075]. He had enlarged his diocese with properties and monasteries founded by him, among which the monastery of Siegburg was preeminent [Note: [Col. 0217] “Deoduin” through “Siegburg” are absent in D].

[Col. 0219A] **1076. R. 20. F. 16. A. 10.**

Pope Gregory inveighs entirely against the emperor Henry and turns as many people as he can away from him by word and writing. He also alienates from him the mind of his mother Agnes. (A. Leod.) A hired assassin kills Duke Godefrid in Frisia [Note: [Col. 0219] In the erasure of one line in 1δ, apparently; absent from all the others except A] [Note: [Col. 0219D] Other writers report that it happened at Antwerp].

In this year, the thirteenth year of the first nineteen-year cycle in Dionysius’s repeated great cycle, after two great years had elapsed since the Lord’s Passion, everything relating to the course of the sun and moon agrees with the year of the Lord’s Passion. From this it appears that Dionysius did not correctly attach the years of the Lord to his cycle. Since he began his cycle from the year of the Lord 532, he evidently intended Christ to have been born in the second year of the preceding great cycle. Consequently, since this year agrees with the year of the Lord’s Passion, it ought to have been not the thirteenth but the thirty-third year of the great cycle, because that was the year of the Lord’s Passion. Thus, by this consequence of the solar and lunar cycles, which agrees with the truth of the Gospel, Dionysius placed the birth of Christ twenty-one years later than he should have.

(Ib.) A great frost lasted from the Kalends of November until the spring equinox [Note: [Col. 0219] Another contemporary hand wrote above it, “in the middle of April.” B3*, C1, 2*, 3, and 4* read likewise. Afterward some material that had been inserted between this and the following year was erased. A presents it as follows: “Duke Godefrid was killed in Frisia by an assassin.”]

**1077. 21. 17. 11.**

(MAR.) The emperor Henry, having convened a council at Worms of twenty-four bishops and many leading men of the kingdom, ordered it to be decreed [Note: [Col. 0219D] 24 January 1076] that all the decrees and acts of Pope Hildibrand [Note: [Col. 0219] From this year onward B3* consistently calls him Gregory] were to be null. There almost everyone except a few renounced Hildibrand and judged that he should be deposed from the papacy.

(Ib.) Hildibrand [Col. 0219C], on the other hand, excommunicated the emperor Henry at Rome [Note: [Col. 0219D] In February 1076], under the pretext that the leading men of the kingdom might, as though for a just reason, oppose the excommunicated king. On Palm Sunday, around the sixth hour, a star appeared in a clear sky. When the Saxon princes who were subject to the emperor were released by those to whom they had been entrusted, the Saxons rebelled at the instigation of Pope Hildibrand. The pope himself met the emperor in Lombardy and falsely absolved him under the pretext of peace [Note: [Col. 0219D] 28 January 1077]. For all those who had previously renounced Hildibrand, heaping perjury upon perjury, renounced the emperor and established Duke Rudolf of Burgundy as their king [Note: [Col. 0219D] 15 March 1077]. The pope sent him a crown bearing the inscription: “The Rock gave [it] to Peter; Peter [gave] the diadem to Rudolf.”

(MAR.) Archbishop Siegfried of Mainz blessed him as king. When a revolt broke out at Mainz against them, Rudolf fled by night with the archbishop. Pope Hildibrand absolved all who opposed the emperor from disloyalty and perjury. Since the Alpine passes had everywhere been fortified against him, the emperor frustrated all their ambushes, came immediately through Aquileia to Regensburg [Note: [Col. 0219D] In the month of May], attacked Rudolf, forced him to flee, and in a renewed campaign devastated Swabia.

**1078. 22. 18. 12.**

(MAR.) The emperor Henry traversed Swabia, shattered its castles, and devastated everything, adding fear to his enemies, strength to his friends, and drawing back to himself many who, despairing of their fortunes, had defected from him. Bishop Hermann, confederate with Pope Hildibrand in spirit and therefore rebellious against the emperor, was expelled from the city of Metz.

**1079. (1080.) 23. 19. 13.**

(MAR.) At this time the Turks had gained power in the East over the Arabs and Saracens. Invading Armenia and Syria, they captured many cities and Antioch itself. (Ib.) At Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0219D] 12 May], after holding an assembly at Mainz, the emperor Henry decreed that Hildibrand should be deposed from the papacy. Setting out for Lombardy [Note: [Col. 0219D] Or rather, Brixen, 25 June 1080], he designated Guibert, archbishop of Ravenna, as pope in place of Hildibrand.

**1080. 24. 20. 14.**
Pope Hildebrand predicted, as though it had been divinely revealed to him, that in this year the false king would die. [Note: [Col. 0219D] Gregory VII himself wrote to the bishop of Trent (Eccard II, 176): “The feast of blessed Peter must not pass before it becomes most certainly clear to the knowledge of all that he has been most justly excommunicated.” Bonizo, wholly devoted to Gregory VII: “On the Monday after Easter, at St Peter’s, when he had excommunicated the king, he added: ‘Let it be known to all of you that, unless Henry comes to his senses by the feast of St Peter, he will be dead or deposed. And if this does not happen, no one ought thereafter to believe me.’” (Oefele, *SS. Boic.* I, 819.)] And indeed he predicted truly, but his conjecture concerning the false king deceived him, since he interpreted it, according to his own desire, as referring to King Henry. [Note: [Col. 0219] “Hildebrand—interpreted” is absent in B4* and 4**.] (Annals of Liège.) For King Henry engaged the Saxons in a severe battle, and in the encounter the false King Rudolf was killed, together with many princes of Saxony. [Note: [Col. 0220D] 15 October 1080.] (MAR.) Mainz experienced a great earthquake on the Kalends of December.

1081. 25. 21. 15.

(Ibid.) Mainz was for the most part consumed by fire. On the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the first hour of the night, there was a great earthquake accompanied by a grave roaring of the earth—perhaps portending the impending evil which resounded throughout the whole world, and through which the earth suffered and still suffers. (Annals of Liège.) For Emperor Henry set out for Italy to wage war against Pope Hildebrand; and the pope, having fortified towns and castles against him, prepared himself for rebellion and refused admission to Henry when he came hostilely toward Rome.

1082. R. 26. F. 22. A. 16.

Emperor Henry, having captured the towns and castles which stood against him for Hildebrand, besieged the Leonine City of Rome. (Ibid.) In Gaul [Note: [Col. 0221C] Rhenish Gaul.] Herman, a knight of Bishop Herman, having placed a crown upon his own head, [Note: [Col. 0221C] At Goslar, 26 December 1081. He had been elected on 9 August 1081.] exercised tyranny in Saxony after Rudolf. Marianus Scotus brought his chronicle, begun from Christ’s Nativity, down to this year, the fifty-sixth year of his life. He laboured greatly to correct the error concerning the years of the Lord found in the Dionysian cycle; this may readily be seen, since he sets down, on the one hand, the years of the Lord according to the Dionysian cycle, [Col. 0221B] and, on the other, according to the truth of the Gospel.

1083. 27. 23. 17.

(Ibid.) Emperor Henry, having captured the Leonine City of Rome, besieged Rome itself. A day having been agreed between the emperor and the pope for deciding the dispute between them, and peace not being reached because the pope dissembled, the Romans and many Italian bishops deserted the pope; fleeing, he withdrew to the Normans. [Note: [Col. 0221D] In 1084.]

1084. 28. 24. 18.

(Ibid.) The Romans received Emperor Henry into the city, [Note: [Col. 0221D] 21 March.] and by their judgment Pope Hildebrand was deprived of office. Guibert, archbishop of Ravenna, was enthroned in the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0221D] 24 March.] and named Clement. Those who supported the emperor contended that Hildebrand had justly been deposed as guilty of treason, because he had set up another king against the emperor and had assumed the audacity of rebellion. But those who held the contrary view protested that the universal pope could not be removed from the pontificate by a non-universal council, by the judgment of a few, by lay censure, or by imperial power; and [Col. 0222A] that, what was more serious, to install someone in the place of a living bishop was contrary to canonical authority; and other things of that kind. [Note: [Col. 0221] “Those who supported—kind” is absent in D.] King Henry was appointed patrician of the Romans; (Annals of Liège) and was consecrated emperor by Clement. [Note: [Col. 0221] Here the second hand ends in manuscript 1, with the quire which it wrote entire. The following half-quire was written by a third, very beautiful hand.] [Note: [Col. 0221D] 31 March.]

1085. 29. 25. 19.

Emperor Henry, having convened a royal and synodal assembly at Mainz, [Note: [Col. 0221D] 4 May 1085.] required all to approve Hildebrand’s deposition and Guibert’s ordination by subscribing to them. Some favoured this with hand and voice, but in heart still adhered to Hildebrand. Herman of Metz, though his bishopric had been adjudged away from him in his absence, was again expelled from the city. The emperor installed first one and then another hireling in the bishopric of Metz, but Christ’s sheep did not heed the voice of strangers. (Ibid.) [Col. 0222B] The emperor attacked the Saxons. [Note: [Col. 0221D] At the beginning of July.] They sought and obtained peace, agreeing that all those proscribed because of this rebellion should have their possessions restored. Since this was not done, they rebelled again [Note: [Col. 0221D] In September.], Count Egbert, the emperor’s kinsman, being more than anyone else their instigator. Walcher, a bishop in England from the clergy of St Lambert, was attacked without cause through the hatred of the English, and while celebrating Mass was martyred by them, like another Pope Stephen. Pope Hildebrand, living in exile at Salerno, died. [Note: [Col. 0221D] 25 May. The following letter is indeed false, though not invented by Sigebert himself; for it is also read in Florence of Worcester under the year 1084 (where the beginning, “We wish you to know, you who are concerned for ecclesiastical care,” is absent, and at the end is added, “with the archbishop of Mainz as witness”; and “not long after he died”; cf. *Mon. S. S.* V, 563). Florence therefore did not take it from our author. I believe it was known to both, not from some book, but in the manner in which we see many such things published and circulated in those times: namely, written into an empty space of a manuscript and thus preserved and propagated along with it. In this way we possess many papal decrees, various letters, laws, notices concerning holy wars, and so forth. In the same way the same letter is found written on the first page of a manuscript in the British Museum, Cotton Nero C. v, said already to be of the eleventh century; cf. *Archiv.* VII, 73.—This recantation [Col. 0222D] of the dying Gregory is as certainly fabricated as it is certain that his successor Victor III, who stood by him as he died, and Urban II testified that Gregory adhered to, and died with, his anathemas against Wibert, Henry, simoniacs, and incontinent clerics unless they repented; and as certainly as all historians report that these were his dying words: “I have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile.” The most illustrious Baronius believes that this penitence of St Gregory VII—whose miracles shone forth upon the world—was fabricated by Wibert or some adherent of Wibert in their little council (*Annals*, vol. XI, under the year 1084, no. 12). The opponents of St Gregory, excommunicated at the synod of Quedlinburg in 1085, were the pseudo-cardinals Hugh called Blanc or Albus, John, former bishop of Porto, and Peter, former chancellor, supporters of the antipope Guibert; Liemar of Bremen, Udo of Hildesheim, Otto of Constance, Burchard of Basel, Hutzmann [Col. 0223D] of Speyer, Wezilo, invader of Mainz, Siegfried of Augsburg, and Norbert of Chur were anathematized with burning candles, according to Berthold. These men were sufficiently cunning to attach a recantation to Gregory VII at the following little council of Mainz. HARTZHEIM, *Conc. Germ.* III, 234.]

I found the following written about him:

“We wish you to know, you who are solicitous for the care of the Church, that the lord apostolic Hildebrand, now at the end of his life, summoned to himself one of the twelve cardinals, whom he loved more than the others, and confessed to God, to St Peter, and to the whole [Col. 0222C] Church that he had greatly sinned in the pastoral charge entrusted to him for governance, and that, at the devil’s persuasion, he had stirred up hatred and anger against humankind. He said, moreover, that he had subsequently undertaken the sentence spread throughout the world for the increase of Christianity. Then at last he sent this aforesaid confessor to the emperor and to the whole Church, that he might request indulgence for him, [Col. 0223A] since he saw the end of his life approaching. And immediately he put on the angelic garment and remitted and dissolved the bonds of all his bans against the emperor and all the Christian people, living and dead, clerics and laypeople; and he ordered his own men to leave the house of Theodoric, and the emperor’s friends to come in.”

1086. R. 30. F. 26. A. 20.

The Saxons besieged the city of Würzburg in order to restore to his see its bishop, Albero, who had been expelled by the citizens. Emperor Henry attacked them. But his army, divinely terrified, gave way; more than four thousand of them fell, while only fourteen were killed on the Saxon side. [Note: [Col. 0223D] 11 August 1086.] An excessive inundation of waters caused damage and danger in many places. In Italy the flood was so great that rocks dissolved by the flow of the waters [Col. 0223B] destroyed many villages by their collapse. Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, who was also Victor, became pope against Clement; but weakened by dysentery, he died not long afterwards. [Note: [Col. 0223D] Elected 24 May 1086; died 16 September 1087.] Anselm, bishop of Lucca, Pope Hildebrand’s tireless collaborator, died in exile at Mantua. [Note: [Col. 0224D] 19 March.] He produced commentaries on Jeremiah and the Psalms, and in an eloquent book confirmed Hildebrand’s teaching; his holiness was demonstrated by miracles. Domestic birds—peacocks, hens, and geese—left their homes and became wild.

1087. 31. 27. 21.

Between the emperor and the Saxons battles were fought on more than one occasion, with varying outcomes. (Translation of St Nicholas.) In Italy, while the Venetians planned to remove the body of St Nicholas [Col. 0223C] from Myra in Lycia, devastated by the Turks, forty-seven citizens of Bari forestalled them. Coming from Antioch to Myra, they compelled the only four monks found there to show them the saint’s tomb. Having broken it open, they removed the saint’s bones, floating in a liquid of oil, complete in number, and brought them with glory to Bari. This translation occurred in the 745th year after the death of St Nicholas. [Note: [Col. 0224D] By John, archdeacon of Bari, in Mosander’s appendix to Surius, p. 399.] Fish die in the waters. [Note: [Col. 0223] After this, certain material had been written in manuscript 1 between this and the following year, but is now erased.]

1088. 32. 28. 22.

In Spain, Amful, king of Galicia, fought the Saracens bravely; he finally captured Toledo, their greatest city, after a siege of several years, and extended Christian worship there. Odo, formerly a monk of Cluny and bishop of Ostia, became pope against the emperor [Col. 0223D] and Guibert, and was named Urban. [Note: [Col. 0223] All the following material for this year is absent in B3* and C4*.] [Note: [Col. 0224D] 12 March.] Hence scandals grew in the Church and divisions in the kingdom, while one party dissented from another, while [Col. 0224A] kingdom and priesthood were at odds, while each excommunicated the other, while one despised the other’s excommunication because of prejudice either against the cause or against the person; and while each abused the authority of excommunication against the other more according to personal will than regard for justice, the authority of him who gave the power of binding and loosing was utterly despised (cf. Letter of Sigebert).

Indeed, to speak with the permission of all good men, this alone was a novelty—not to say a heresy—not yet emerged in the world: that the priests of him who “calls a king apostate” and “makes a hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people” should teach the people that they owe no subjection to evil kings; that, even if they have sworn an oath of fidelity to him, they nevertheless owe no fidelity, nor should those who act against the king be called perjurers; [Col. 0224B] indeed, that whoever obeys the king should be regarded as excommunicated, while whoever acts against the king should be absolved from the guilt of injustice and perjury.

1089. (1090.) 33. 29. 23.

(Annals of Liège.) At Cologne, Herman was ordained archbishop after Sigewin. [Note: [Col. 0224D] 25 July.] Godfrey, nephew through his sister of Godfrey the Hunchback, [Note: [Col. 0224D] Of Bouillon, son of Countess Ida.] was at last granted the duchy of Lotharingia. (Ibid.) A pestilential year, especially in the western part of Lotharingia: many, while the holy fire consumed their entrails and their limbs, eaten away and blackening like coals, either died miserably or, with hands and feet rotted away and amputated, were preserved for a life still more miserable; many others were tormented, twisted by contraction of the sinews.

[Col. 0224C] 1090. 34. 30. 24.

Emperor Henry returned to Italy to fight those opposed to him. [Note: [Col. 0224D] Mid-March.] The tyrant Herman, returning from Saxony to Lotharingia, laboured to stir up disturbances in the kingdom. While he carelessly approached the wall of a certain castle, he was struck on the head by a stone thrown from a tower and died. [Note: [Col. 0224D] Mid-September 1088, according to Bernold.] At Metz, the body of St Clement, the first bishop ordained there by the apostles, was found and elevated. Bishop Herman, received back into the city by the people of Metz with the emperor’s permission, lay down upon his bed after a generously celebrated meal and was found dead. [Note: [Col. 0223] “Herman—found dead” is absent in D.] [Note: [Col. 0224D] 4 May.] In Saxony Count Egbert, while pursuing the emperor’s faithful followers in war, was himself slain. Barrenness of the earth’s crops increased, and famine gradually crept in.

[Col. 0224D] 1091. 35. 31. 25.

(Ibid.) Emperor Henry captured the castles and fortifications of those opposing him in Italy; he also besieged and captured Mantua. [Col. 0225A] [Note: [Col. 0225D] 10 April.] Henry, bishop of Liège, of blessed memory, a lover of peace and religion, died, [Note: [Col. 0225D] 31 May.] and Otbert, from the clergy of that same church, succeeded him.

1092. R. 36. F. 32. A. 26.

William, king of the English, a man of exceptional strictness and severity, died. [Note: [Col. 0225D] In 1087.] His son William succeeded him. With nearly all the instigators of the Saxon war killed, the Saxons, weary of evils, made peace among themselves and ceased every movement of war. The Westphalians attacked Frisia and were nearly all killed by the Frisians. [Note: [Col. 0225] “Westphalians—killed” is absent in D. The whole year is absent in A.] [Note: [Col. 0225D] 21 July.]

1093. 37. 33. 1.

Conrad, son of Emperor Henry, joined his father’s opponents in Italy; and when many turned from the [Col. 0225B] father to the son, this matter greatly obscured the father’s earlier victories and weakened his power. On the Kalends of August, at the first hour of the night, a fiery dart was seen carried through the sky from south to north.

1094. 38. 34. 2.

(Annals of Liège.) In Gaul and Germany there was a severe mortality among people. In Italy, those who had gone over to the emperor from his enemies, when he returned to Gaul—[Note: [Col. 0225D] That is, Germany, as in 1020 and 1056.]—nearly all crossed back again to his enemies, and fortified against him the strongholds that he had captured.

1095. 39. 35. 3.

(Ibid.) The long-conceived famine became extremely severe, [Col. 0225C] and the year was calamitous, with many suffering hunger and the poor grievously harassing the wealthier through thefts and arson. In the middle of the night, on the fourth day before the Ides of September, there was an earthquake together with a violent whirlwind. The king of the English was troubled by his brothers with war in Normandy and England. In many parts of the world, on the day before the Nones of April at dawn, very many stars seemed to fall together from heaven to earth. When a certain man in France was astonished at seeing one especially large star fall to earth, he marked the place where it seemed to fall; when he poured water there, he was even more astonished to see smoke rise from it with the sound of boiling. Henry, count of Louvain, was slain. In the county of Namur we saw bread baked under ashes as if stained with blood. The king of the Hungarians died. [Note: [Col. 0225] “The king of the Hungarians died” is absent in B3* and C4*.] (Ibid.) Urban, [Col. 0225D] having held councils through Burgundy and France, renewed and confirmed Hildebrand’s decrees. He excommunicated Philip, king of the French, who, while his own wife was alive, had taken the wife of another living man.

1096. 40. 36. 4.

There was an eclipse of the moon on the third day before the Ides of February. Again, on the [Col. 0226A] seventh day before the Ides of August, there was an eclipse of the moon. (Ibid.) The peoples of the West, grieving that the holy places at Jerusalem were profaned by the heathen and that the Turks had already invaded a great part of the frontiers of Christians, were moved in innumerable numbers by one common inspiration. Encouraged by one another, with many signs shown to them, dukes, counts, powerful men, nobles and commoners, rich and poor, free persons and slaves, bishops, clerics, monks, old men and young, even boys and girls, all with one mind and with no one compelling them, flocked together from every direction: from Spain, Provence, Aquitaine, Brittany, Scotland, England, Normandy, France, Lotharingia, Burgundy, Germany, Lombardy, Apulia, and other kingdoms. Marked and armed with the power and sign of the holy cross, they prepared to avenge [Col. 0226B] the wrongs done to God upon the enemies of the Christian name. And the more prone each had formerly been to practise the warfare of the world, the readier he now became voluntarily to practise God’s warfare.

Meanwhile, peace having been firmly established everywhere, they first attacked the Jews in the cities in which they lived and compelled them to believe in Christ; those unwilling to believe they deprived of goods, slaughtered, or expelled from the cities. Some later returned to Judaism. Prominent in this war of God were Godfrey, duke of Lotharingia, and his brothers Eustace and Baldwin; Baldwin, count of Mons; Robert, count of Flanders; Stephen, count of Blois; Hugh, brother of the king of the French; Robert, count of Normandy; Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles; [Col. 0226C] and Bohemond, duke of Apulia.

1097. 41. 37. 5.

(Ibid.) A comet appeared in the west throughout the first week of October. Because of an excessive inundation of waters, autumn sowing was impeded, and barrenness of the earth’s crops followed. The army of God attacked the frontiers of the pagans and acted bravely. Their first battle was at the bridge of the river Pharphar, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March, where many Turks were killed. [Note: [Col. 0225D] This is false; cf. Hirsch, 130.] Their second battle was near Nicaea, on the third day before the Nones of March, [Note: [Col. 0226D] Sigebert is mistaken; it occurred in May—HIRSCH.] in which the pagans were likewise defeated. (Letter of the Crusaders. [Note: [Col. 0226D] Taken word for word from the letter of the crusaders to Pope Paschal, issued in 1100, in Dodechin under the year 1100; cf. Ekkehard under the year 1098.]) Thus, Nicaea having been captured, and Laodicea also captured, when there were more than three hundred thousand armed men in the Christian army, such an abundance of all supplies was available to them that a ram was sold for one coin and an ox scarcely for twelve.

[Col. 0226D] 1098. 42. 38. 6.

(Ibid.) During the siege of Antioch, Christians were so weakened by the scarcity of all provisions that scarcely one hundred good horses could be found in the entire army. Yet, although many withdrew in despair of their situation and many also returned home, when Antioch had been taken in the ninth month of the siege, the Christians were in turn besieged by the pagans and afflicted by such hunger that scarcely any could refrain from human flesh. But strengthened by God through the discovery of his lance, not seen since the time of the apostles, and with that lance going before them, the besieged attacked their besiegers on the fourth day before the Kalends of July and gained victory in this third battle. Their fourth battle was in Romania on the Kalends of July, and there the Turks were defeated. [Note: [Col. 0227D] “Their fourth battle—defeated” was added by Sigebert himself; but it is false. HIRSCH.] Having entrusted Antioch to Duke Bohemond, the Christians set out into Syria to avoid weariness and hunger, and especially because of the discord of the princes. Having captured the Saracen cities of Maʿarrat and Barra and many castles of the region, they were again afflicted there by such hunger that they were forced to eat the already stinking bodies of Saracens.

[Col. 0227B] (Annals of Liège.) Conrad, bishop of Utrecht, was killed in his own house by one of his men on the fourth weekday of Easter, after celebrating Mass. [Note: [Col. 0227] “Conrad—killed” is absent in D.] [Note: [Col. 0227D] 13 April 1099.] In many places, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, the sky seemed to burn at night; a severe pestilence among animals followed, and the crops were ruined by excessive rain and blight.

1099. (1100.) R. 43. F. 39. A. 7.

(Annals of Liège.) At Cologne, Frederick was ordained archbishop after Herman. [Note: [Col. 0227] “At Cologne—ordained archbishop” is absent in C4* and D.] [Note: [Col. 0227D] 23 August.] (Letter of the Crusaders.) The army of God, proceeding into the interior of Syria by divine command, was restored by God’s generous hand, because the citizens and inhabitants of the castles of that region sent ambassadors ahead with many gifts, ready also to hand over towns or cities to them. Having received assurances of safety from these people and imposed tribute upon [Col. 0227C] the cities, while many of those who had withdrawn were meanwhile returning to them at Tyre, the Christians at last reached Jerusalem.

After besieging it, and suffering from a lack of provisions and especially water, all, by common decree, walked around the city barefoot each day in prayer. Therefore, on the eighth day of this humiliation, and the thirty-ninth day of the siege, Jerusalem was taken, on the Ides of July, a Friday. In the Temple of Solomon and its portico, Christians joined battle with pagans in a fifth battle and slaughtered them with such fury that they rode in the blood of the slain up to their horses’ knees.

When arrangements had been made for those who were to hold Jerusalem, and the princes were already considering returning home, behold, the king of the Saracens came to Ascalon to fight [Col. 0227D] them, with one hundred thousand cavalry and four hundred thousand infantry. When the army of the Lord met them—having no more than five thousand cavalry and fifteen thousand infantry—God fought for his servants as they cried to him, and a cloud protected them from the sun’s heat. The Saracens, terrified by the Christians’ attack alone, all fled, casting down their weapons. In this sixth battle, fought on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, [Note: [Col. 0227D] Rather, the day before the Ides of August.] one hundred thousand pagans were killed; about two thousand were suffocated at the gate of Ascalon; the number of those who perished at sea and of those consumed amid the thorn-brakes of the forests is unknown. With Duke Godfrey chosen to rule among those remaining in Jerusalem, the other princes returned home.

Jerusalem was captured about 460 years after it had been taken a second time under Emperor Heraclius and possessed by the Saracens. [Note: [Col. 0227] “Jerusalem was captured—Saracens” is absent in A.] Saint Guibert, at the monastery of Gembloux which he founded, became illustrious through great miracles at his tomb. [Note: [Col. 0227] “Saint Guibert—miracles” is absent in A, B1, 5, C1, 2*, 3, 4, and D. In manuscript 1 it is written in the same hand as the rest.]

[Col. 0228B] 1100. R. 44. F. 40. A. 8. H. 1.

Guibert and Urban, who contended over the Roman papacy, ended their dispute by dying. [Note: [Col. 0227D] Urban II died on 29 July 1099; Guibert in September 1100.] Rainer, also called Paschal, became the 158th head of the Roman Church. [Note: [Col. 0228D] Elected 13 August 1099.] William, king of the English, died, and his brother Henry succeeded him in the kingdom. Godfrey, duke of the Lotharingians and prince of the Jerusalemites, died. [Note: [Col. 0228D] 15 July.] His brother Baldwin succeeded him in the principality. [Note: [Col. 0227] “He died, after whom his brother Baldwin ruled” in A.]

1101. 45. 41. 1. 1.

Conrad, son of Emperor Henry, still in rebellion against his father, died in Italy. [Note: [Col. 0228D] In July 1102.] Emperor Henry defeated Henry of Limburg, who opposed him, and, after capturing his castles, compelled him to surrender. But the emperor granted him even the duchy of Lotharingia, in return for a very great sum with which he purchased imperial favour. [Col. 0228C]

1102. 46. 42. 2. 2.

Since Robert, count of the Flemings, was troubling the city of Cambrai, Emperor Henry set out against him; but after capturing several of his castles, he was compelled to return because of the severity of the approaching winter.

1103. 47. 43. 3. 3.

Emperor Henry, having quieted the Saxon disturbances, established peace for four years. [Note: [Col. 0227] “Emperor Henry—established” is absent in D.] [Note: [Col. 0228D] At Mainz, 6 January; cf. *Mon. Legg.* II, 60.] At Liège, after a general assembly was held, Robert, count of Flanders, was received into the emperor’s favour. [Note: [Col. 0228D] 29 June.]

1104. 48. 44. 4. 4.

The Jerusalemites captured the city of Acre.

[Col. 0228D] 1105. 49. 45. 5. 5.

The Jerusalemites crushed an innumerable multitude of pagans in a glorious victory. The son of Emperor Henry turned away from his father [Note: [Col. 0228D] 12 December 1104.] and turned away from him all whom he could; [Col. 0229A] under the pretext of improving the commonwealth and restoring the Church, he rose against him. [Note: [Col. 0229] All the following material for this year is absent in B1, C1, 2*, 3, 4*, 5, and D; erased in B5; present in 1, A, B3*, 4*, 4**, F1, 2, 3.]

Extract from a letter sent to Emperor Henry by Werner, prince of Ancona:

“Certain clerics of the Roman Church, who were regarded as religious and wise, and who had been intimate adherents of Pope Hildebrand, Odard, and Rainer, abandoned their sect, which they had finally understood to be erroneous, and came to make satisfaction to the holy Church. The principal reason for this was that they knew with certainty that Pope Rainer was tainted by the Simoniac heresy. For Rainer was publicly accused of having sold, while he was abbot of St Lawrence, the priory of that same church to a monk for twenty solidi; and he could not deny it.

“He was also accused that, while seeking the papacy after Odard, he had promised by agreement and oath to Count Gregory of Tusculum, his son Theodulus, and Peter of Colonna, that he would give them one hundred pounds of Pavia coinage, an ounce (*uncia*) of confession, and three estates of the Roman Church—namely, Nympha, Zibera, and Aricia—if they consented to his election. And when elected, he gave, toward payment of this sum, the church’s golden chalice and a purple chasuble; Peter son of Leo and Albert son of Stephen paid the remainder of the sum for him; he also gave a pound of gold to the keeper of the archives.

“On this account the Romans withdrew from communion with him and, having held councils among themselves with bishops and cardinals, urged him voluntarily to clear himself of so great an accusation. When Rainer bore this indignantly, inflamed himself more toward rage than toward satisfaction, and threatened tortures and death against his accusers, the Romans declared him to be truly a heretic and schismatic and pronounced upon him a sentence of just condemnation.

“Among the Romans there stood out a certain Maginulf, an archpriest. Since he was of praiseworthy life, most highly learned in both branches of knowledge, and for a long time head of the Roman clergy, he was loved by all the Roman people as a father by his children. When he too, inflamed with zeal for God, publicly attested that Rainer was a heretic, almost all the Romans then cried out that Rainer, as a Simoniac, must be deposed, and Maginulf, as a witness to truth, installed in the apostolic see. But Maginulf, fleeing both the plots of men and the burden of apostolic honour, withdrew to a very strongly fortified place.

“Berto, however, the head [Col. 0229D] and commander of the Roman militia, came to him with an expedition of clergy and people, ostensibly to hear the word of life; he drew him out from there and brought him to Werner, prince of Ancona, in the city of Tivoli. Thus he was elected, [Col. 0230A] advanced to the apostolic see on the fourth day before the Nones of November [Note: [Col. 0229D] In 1100.] and called Sylvester IV. Meanwhile Pope Paschal crossed into Gaul, conducted synodal business, and, since the charge of simony unjustly brought against him by the Romans was not proved, retained the honour of apostolic dignity. But Maginulf, guilty of usurpation, was rejected by the Romans not long afterwards, and the fame of his name vanished.”

1106. R. 50. F. 46. A. 6. H. 6.

On the fourth day before the Nones of February a star was seen in the sky by day, from the third hour until the ninth, as though a cubit distant from the sun. On the second day before the Ides of February, at Bari in Italy, stars were seen in the sky by day, now as though rushing together, now as though falling to earth. For almost the whole month of February a comet appeared. [Note: [Col. 0229] “Fourth day before the Nones—appeared” is absent in D.]

How Henry, son of the emperor, rising against his father contrary to natural right and the sanction of the laws, treated him with indignity is shown by a letter, written in the father’s own voice, to Philip, king of the French. [Note: [Col. 0229] The following letter is absent in C2* and D.] [Note: [Col. 0229D] This letter was also published by Urstisius, *SS.* I, 396; Eccard, *Corpus historicum* II, 222; and, from Urstisius, by Baronius under the year 1106. Because of the similarity of subject, let us add what Martène published from a manuscript of Stavelot, *Collect.* 1, 609:

Verses of Emperor Henry to his son.

[Col. 0230D]

Since I am poor, no one is more despised than I.

Alas for me! What shall I do? Where shall I turn? Whom shall I trust?

Swabian and Saxon now yield falsely to you,

A faithless race indeed, through whom many have perished.

But if I am driven out, you too will be driven out, and error…

Worse than the first. My sweet son, beware!]: Most illustrious prince, and most faithful of all our friends in whom, after God, we place our hope: I have received you first and foremost [Note: [Col. 0229] MS 1 reads “precipium.”] among all, as the one to whom I judged it necessary to complain of and lament my calamities and all my miseries—indeed, to throw myself at your knees, if this were permitted without compromising the majesty of the Empire.

First, we judge it most grievous and intolerable not only for ourselves but for all who profess Christianity, that from that Apostolic See—from which, down to the memory of our own time, the saving fruit of consolation, sweetness, and the salvation of souls used to arise—there is now sent forth against us the scourge of persecution, excommunication, and every form of destruction; nor do they set any limit to their sentence, provided only that their undiscriminating will is satisfied. They have thus far abused the intemperance of this will against me so greatly that, without considering either God or what and how much evil may result from it, they attack me in every possible way, both personally and through their agents [Note: [Col. 0229] thus MS 1; the rest likewise.], although I have often offered obedience and all due submission to the Apostolic See, provided that the Apostolic See showed me the reverence and honor due to me, as it had shown to my predecessors. What they intend, however, I shall more suitably communicate to you in person, if God at some time grants us the opportunity for our desired conference.

Since, then, in this blazing persecution and hatred they saw that they were making little progress, they acted against the very law of nature. What I cannot say without the deepest anguish of heart and many tears—and what I tremble violently even to utter—is that they not only incited my son, my own most beloved Absalom, against me, but armed him with such fury that, first, in violation of the faith and oath [Col. 0231A] which, as a knight, he had sworn to his lord, he invaded my kingdom, deposed my bishops and abbots, and put my enemies and persecutors in their places; and finally—what I would most wish left unspoken, or, if it cannot be unspoken, would wish not believed—casting aside every natural affection, he aimed at my safety and soul, and cared nothing by what means, force or fraud, he might attain this height of his own peril and disgrace.

While I was in peace and in some security for my life, amid this great plotting of his wickedness, he summoned me, during the most holy days of the Lord’s Advent, to a place called Confluences, for a conference, as though a son were to deliberate with his father on their common welfare and honor. When I saw him, immediately, touched inwardly by paternal affection and the grief of my heart, I fell at his feet, [Col. 0231B] warning and entreating him by God, by faith, and by the salvation of his soul that, if I was to be scourged by God for my sins, he himself should seek no stain upon his own soul, honor, and name from me; for no decree of divine law has ever established that a son should be the avenger of his father’s fault.

But he, already finely—rather, most miserably—trained in wickedness, began to denounce this as though it were an abominable and accursed crime [Note: [Col. 0231] “and” and “accursed” are absent in C4*]; and he too fell at my feet, began to ask pardon for the past, and with tears promised that henceforward, as a knight to his lord and as a son to his father, he would obey me in all things with faithfulness and truth, if only I were willing to be reconciled with the Apostolic See. When I had most readily assented to this and promised to commit myself wholly to his deliberation and to the counsel of the princes in this matter, he promised that at the coming Nativity [Col. 0231C] he would lead me to Mainz; that there he would act as faithfully as possible for my honor and reconciliation; and that from there he would restore me to peace and security—upon that truth and faith by which God commands a father to be honored by his son and a son to be loved by his father.

Trusting this promise, which even a pagan must keep, I was making my way there, and my son had gone a little ahead of me, when certain of my faithful men met me and most truthfully declared that I had been deceived and betrayed under the false pledge of peace and faith. My son was summoned back; and, again most urgently admonished by me, he promised for a second time, under the invocation of the same faith and oath, that his soul would stand for my soul.

When we came to the place called Bingen, Friday before the Nativity had already arrived; the number of his armed men was now greatly increasing, and the fraud itself was beginning to be exposed. Then my son said to me: “Father, we must withdraw to the neighboring castle. For the bishop of Mainz will not admit you into his city while you are under ban; nor do I dare to place you, unreconciled and without peace, among your enemies. There you shall celebrate the Nativity with God’s honor and peace [Note: [Col. 0231] C1* has “celebrating”]; have with you whomever you please. Meanwhile I shall work as urgently and faithfully as I can for us both, because I regard your cause as my own.”

But I said: “My son, may God, witness and judge of our words and faith, be present between us today—God alone knows how I have raised you to full manhood and made you my heir, with how many of my labors and tribulations I have served your honor, and how many and how great enmities I have borne and still bear for your sake.” He again, now for the third time, under invocation of the same faith and oath, promised me that if an occasion of danger should arise, his head would stand for mine.

Thus, after he had shut me up in that same castle, the outcome of events made clear that he had spoken everything by mouth and heart [Note: [Col. 0231] “and” added by correction in MS 1.]. Of all my men, only four of us were confined; no one else could be admitted. Guards were assigned who were the bitterest enemies of my life. Blessed in all things is God, the mightiest King, who exalts and humbles whomever He wills [Note: [Col. 0231] D has “and”; C1* has “and humbling”].

Accordingly, on that most sacred day of His Nativity, when that Holy One of holy ones, the child, had been born for all His redeemed, that son was not given to me alone. For, not to mention the reproaches, insults, threats, and swords drawn against my neck unless I did all that was commanded; the hunger and thirst that I endured, and endured from those whom it was an outrage even to see and hear; and, still more grievous, not to mention that I had once been sufficiently fortunate: I shall never forget, never cease to complain to all Christians, that during those most holy days I was in that prison without any Christian communion whatever.

In those days of my penitence and tribulation, one of the princes, Wicbert, was sent to me by my son, saying that there was no hope for my life unless, without any opposition, I surrendered even the insignia of the kingdom [Col. 0232C], according to the will and command of the princes. But I, though the whole inhabited earth had been the boundary of my kingdom, was willing [Note: [Col. 0231] C1 and 4* have “unwilling.”] to exchange my kingdom for life. Since I understood that this had to be done and was so determined whether I wished it or not, I sent the crown, cross, lance [Note: [Col. 0231] Eccard has “crown, sceptre, mantle, lance”; Urstisius: “crown, sceptre, cross, lance”; compare Hirsch, p. 443], and sword to Mainz.

Then my son, having consulted with my enemies, went out, leaving there our faithful men and friends; and, as though he were to bring me there, he had me brought under a large escort and guard of armed men to the village called Ingelheim. There I found a great multitude of enemies gathered, nor did I find my son better disposed toward me than the rest. Because it seemed more firm and secure to them if they compelled me with my own hand to renounce the kingdom and all royal rights by the straw-ceremony, they all likewise threatened that, unless I did everything commanded, there could be no hope for my life.

Then I said: “Since the matter concerns life alone, than which I possess nothing more precious, I do whatever you command, so that at least while living I may offer penitence to God.” When I asked whether in this way at least I should be assured and secure of my life, the legate of that same Apostolic See who was present there—not to say, who had arranged all these things—answered that I could by no means be released unless I publicly confessed that I had unjustly persecuted Hildebrand, had unjustly installed Wicbert [Col. 0233A], and had hitherto pursued an unjust persecution against the Apostolic See and the whole Church.

Then, with the greatest contrition of spirit, prostrate on the ground, I began to beseech by God and by justice itself that a place and time might be given me in which, before all the princes, I might establish where I was innocent, clear myself by judgment, and then give from among the princes of the realm and my faithful men whatever hostages they wished. But that same legate refused me a day and place, saying that either everything had to be decided there, or there was no hope of my escape [Note: [Col. 0233] “there” absent in C1.].

At such a crisis of tribulation I asked whether, if I confessed everything commanded, my confession would obtain pardon and absolution, as was right. The same legate replied that it was not within his authority to absolve me. When I said in response: “Whoever dares receive one confessing must absolve the one confessed,” he said that, if I wished to be absolved, I should go to Rome to make satisfaction to the Apostolic See.

Thus stripped and abandoned—for by the same force and contrivance they had extorted from me castles, patrimonies, and whatever I had acquired in the kingdom—they left me in that same village. Having remained there for some time, and my son having directed, by the same scheme of his fraud, that I should wait for him, an embassy of certain of my faithful men came and warned me that, if I remained there even for a moment, I would either be carried from there into perpetual captivity or be beheaded in that very place. At this report, having then lost all confidence in life, I fled at once; in fleeing I came [Col. 0233C] to Cologne, stayed there some days, and afterward came [Col. 0234A] to Liège, where I found faithful men.

[Note: [Col. 0233] Adds: “By the counsel of these and the other faithful men of the kingdom, I have greater confidence and greater propriety in lamenting before you all these miseries of mine: greater confidence, indeed, because of the obligation of mutual kinship or ancient friendship; greater propriety because of the glorious name of so great a kingdom. And I ask you, by faith and friendship, to take thought in my great tribulations as though they were your own. Even if the bonds of faith and friendship did not exist between us, it nevertheless belongs to you and to all kings of the earth to avenge our injury and contempt, and to root from the face of the earth the example of such wicked treachery and violence, through the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.” These words, from “through the aid” to “Amen,” are also read in editions of this letter. It therefore seems that Sigebert first published them, whence A has them, but later deleted them, whence they are absent from the others. In MS 1 there is no trace of erasure.—The same letter is also found in a twelfth-century manuscript of St Mary at Villers, now in the city of Brussels, after treatises of St Bernard, copied from Sigebert, as the red rubric prefixed there shows: “Henry, son of Emperor Henry, rising against his father contrary to natural law and the sanction of laws.” The scribe transformed Sigebert’s following narrative into the end of the letter as follows: “I found faithful men. But while I was remaining at Liège, my son A. v. e. v. v. L. c. me p. s. 5. f. d. c. p. s. p. p. a. W. n. q. s. v. o. S. m. meis c. a. e. p. m. illius a p. r. etc.,” down to “he returned without glory.”]

While Emperor Henry was staying at Liège, his son came to Aachen; and, intending to march against his father to Liège on Thursday of the Lord’s Supper, he sent his men ahead to seize the bridge at Visé [Note: [Col. 0233C] Visé lies between Liège and Maastricht.], so that no one might oppose his approach. But when his father’s knights ran together to retake the bridge, the son’s knights were driven from it: some were captured, some drowned in the Meuse, and some killed; among them Count Bruno was also killed. Thus the son, advancing against his father, returned without glory.

While the people of Cologne kept faith with the emperor, and their archbishop incited the emperor’s son against his father, Cologne was besieged and attacked, but was not taken. Meanwhile Emperor Henry [Col. 0234B] died at Liège (7 August), and his namesake son succeeded him.

[Note: [Col. 0233] A presents the passage “Meanwhile—his son” as follows: “Emperor Henry, disinherited of the Empire and unreconciled to the Apostolic See, died at Liège on 7 August. At the very point of death he had commanded his royal son, who was besieging Cologne against him, that he should be buried at Speyer; and he sent him his ring through Burchard, bishop of Münster. But after he had meanwhile been buried in the church of St Lambert, divine service was prohibited in that church by apostolic authority, through Henry, bishop of Magdeburg and legate of the Apostolic See, until the body should be dug up and ejected from that church. It was transferred and reburied on 18 Kalends of September in an unconsecrated church outside the city, on Mount Cornelius, until it should deserve royal burial by apostolic absolution. After nine days had elapsed, envoys arrived to carry him to his son; he was dug up again and, amid the excessive devotion and attendance of the gathering populace, carried back into the city and again brought into the church of St Lambert, despite the opposition of the clergy. There certain poor clerics, hired for payment, celebrated a vigil of one night for him, while the church was vacant of divine service and the canons hid from the enraged people. On the following day, when the former tomb was loudly demanding that he be restored to it and those who, together with the aforementioned poor clerics, had kept watch around the body with drawn swords undertook to do this, they could scarcely be restrained by the counsel of certain elders. For they had become so inflamed by excessive devotion to him that all who had touched his bier believed themselves sanctified by him. Some even scraped the earth of his grave with their own fingernails and scattered it over their fields and houses as though for a blessing. Others laid old grain upon his bier, so that they might sow it mixed with new grain; for they hoped that in this way it would yield them a fertile harvest. At last, with the grief and opposition of the people, he was handed over to the envoys—for they cried that his absence would mean the peril and desolation of the city—and carried to his son, to be buried at Speyer as he had requested. The duke, etc.” We do not know whether Sigebert originally published these matters in this form and later suppressed them, or whether they should be regarded as an addition by the monk of Verdun.]

Duke Henry, who had gone over in spirit from the emperor to his son, armed the son against his father by his counsel, then returned from the son to the father and fought against the son’s party. Upon the emperor’s death he surrendered himself to the king’s son as guilty of treason against majesty [Note: [Col. 0233] so all manuscripts.], was captured by him and committed to custody, from which he escaped by his own resourcefulness. His duchy was given to Count Godfrey of Louvain.

**1107. R. 1. F. 47. A. 7. H. 7.**

Henry, the former duke, seeking to recover his duchy, occupied the town of Aachen against Duke Godfrey. But Duke Godfrey, unable to endure this, violently entered [Col. 0234C] the town of Aachen, frightened its citizens away from Henry’s support [Col. 0235A], and captured certain counts and many powerful and noble men. Henry himself barely escaped with his sons by flight; the duke judged it unworthy to capture Henry’s wife. He won over the counts and more distinguished men whom he had captured to his allegiance, on the condition that they serve under him as knights.

**1108. R. 2. F. 48. A. 8. H. 8.**

Emperor Henry marched against Robert of Flanders [Note: [Col. 0235C] At the end of October 1107; he returned in January 1108. Compare *Monumenta Legum*, II, 64.]; but, with a peace agreement more feigned than concluded on both sides, he returned almost without result. Bohemond, duke of Apulia, having gathered an army from every quarter, prepared to invade the Empire of Constantinople.

**1109. (1110.) 3. 49. 9. 9.**

In the diocese of Liège a sow gave birth to a piglet [Col. 0235B] with a human face. A four-footed chick was also born. Emperor Henry marched against the Hungarians [Note: [Col. 0235C] At the end of September 1108; he returned at the beginning of November.], but returned after making an agreement. Philip, king of the Franks, died [Note: [Col. 0236C] 29 July 1108.]. His son Louis succeeded him as king [Note: [Col. 0235] A has “succeeds his father”; B3* adds “for twenty-seven years”; B4* adds “for thirty-nine years”; B4* and D add “for twenty-nine years.”].

**1110. 4. 1. 10. 10.**

In June a comet appeared, directing its rays toward the south; many conjectured that this sign portended the future expedition of King Henry V toward Italy. Saint Wibert, founder of the monastery of Gembloux, where he also rests in burial, whom God had glorified far and wide for twelve years by many great signs of miracles, was elevated by the authority of the venerable Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, and with the assent of a general synod, by Lord Obert, bishop of Liège [Col. 0235C]. This elevation was celebrated with an innumerable concourse and marvelous joy of the people on 9 Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 0235] “Saint—October” absent in C4* and D; the entire year absent in A.].

**1111. 5. 2. 11. 11.**

Henry V, king of this name [Note: [Col. 0235] “king of this name” absent in D.], went to Rome in order to settle the discord between kingdom and priesthood. Begun by Pope Gregory VII [Col. 0236A]—whose name was Hildebrand—and inflamed by Gregory’s successors Victor and Urban, and above all by Paschal, it was a great scandal to the whole world.

(*Letter of Henry.*) The king wished to exercise the authority, custom, and documentary privileges of the emperors, who from Charlemagne—first of the kings of the Franks to rule the Romans—had ruled for more than three hundred years under sixty-three apostolic pontiffs: namely, that they lawfully conferred bishoprics and abbeys by ring and staff [Note: [Col. 0235] A has “pastoral staff.”] [Note: [Col. 0236C] “The king wished—staff,” and shortly afterward “He pressed—business” (p. 374, line 7), are taken from Henry’s encyclical, *Monumenta Legum* II, 70.].

Against this authority of their forebears, the popes decreed by synodal judgment that a bishopric or any ecclesiastical investiture could neither be nor ought to be conferred by a lay hand through staff or ring; and all who received a bishopric or another investiture belonging to ecclesiastical right [Col. 0236B] in this way were excommunicated. This was the principal reason why the king proceeded to Rome; and he forcefully crushed any Lombards who wished in any way to resist him.

[Note: [Col. 0235] Here in MS 1 the third hand ends, halfway down the final page of a quire, whose remaining portion was left blank. It is therefore clear that the whole quire was inserted after the following folios had already been written, and indeed inserted in place of several folios that had been cut out. There follows one folio in a fourth, wholly different and neat hand, very similar to Anselm’s but apparently not his. The first two lines have been deleted. The first was: “and he forcefully crushed any Lombards who wished in any way to resist him”; the second: “VI. III. XII. XII.” The third begins: “What or, etc.” Here the new year, marked VI. III. XII. XII., begins in A, B3*, and B4*, and thus continues thereafter. The same had been in MS 1, but it was corrected by the first corrector as we have given it. Everything following is abbreviated in D and E as follows: “In the reconciliation made between emperor and pope—for he had captured the pope himself with the bishops and cardinals—Henry was crowned emperor on Easter Day. After the Gospel had been read, the pope handed him before the altar of the apostles Peter and Paul, in the sight of all the princes, a privilege concerning the investiture of bishoprics or abbeys, both by ring and staff: that he might confer the investiture of staff and ring upon bishops or abbots of his realm freely elected without force or simony; after investiture, the bishop or abbot should receive canonical consecration from the bishop to whom it belonged. Confirmation of peace between apostolic pontiff and emperor, when in the celebration of Mass he handed him the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ: ‘Lord Emperor, we give you this body of the Lord, born of the Virgin Mary and suffering on the cross for us, as the holy and apostolic Church holds, in confirmation of true peace between me and you.’ Given on the Ides of April, fourth indiction.” Finally, C4*, omitting all this from “Against this authority of their forebears” to “fourth indiction,” has only: “A certain reconciliation was made between pope and emperor, who had captured the pope himself with bishops and cardinals.”]

What or how was agreed between pope and king, though much is said by many, we shall state only what we have read in a letter written by the king himself.

(*Letter of Henry.*) The pope pressed in every way to turn the king away from the power of conferring bishoprics or abbeys either by ring or by staff. When the king, through envoys, asked the pope how the kingdom could stand if all these things were taken from him, since his predecessors had granted and transferred nearly all royal rights to churches, the pope replied: “Let priests be content with the tithes and offerings of the Church; but let the king recover and retain for himself and his successors all [Col. 0236C] estates and royal rights which kings have bestowed upon churches.”

The king replied through envoys that he did not wish to inflict force and injustice upon churches. The pope promised, and affirmed with his supporters swearing on his behalf, that on the coming Sunday of Pentecost he would take away from bishops and churches, with justice and apostolic authority, all royal rights [Col. 0237A] and restore them to the kingdom: namely cities, duchies, marches, counties, mints, tolls, advocacies, all rights of centenarii or stewards, courts and villages with all their appurtenances that belonged to the kingdom, military service, and castles. He gave the king this agreement written in a charter, adding that he himself would not further trouble the king or kingdom, and would confirm it in a privilege under anathema, so that his successors might not presume to trouble him; that he would receive the king graciously and honorably, crown him emperor, and assist him by the aid of his office in holding the Empire. To ensure fulfillment of all these things, the pope gave hostages to the king. The king’s envoys, although they knew this could in no way be done, affirmed that if the pope fulfilled these things, the king too would renounce the investitures of churches, as the pope demanded [Col. 0237B].

(*Ibid.*) In this hope of promises, as the king made for Rome, Pope Paschal first sent men to meet him, then himself came with the leading Romans outside the city; they showed no reason for resistance. He had scarcely entered the city gates when his knights, wandering securely within the walls, were attacked: some wounded, others killed, and nearly all captured or despoiled. Yet the king, as though unmoved by a slight matter, proceeded in a calm spirit with procession to the doors of the church of the blessed apostle Peter. There, wishing to show that no disturbance of God’s churches proceeded from his will, he promulgated in the sight and hearing of all present this decree:
