“I, Henry Augustus, emperor, affirm to God and St Peter and all bishops and abbots and all churches: I do not wish in any way to take away anything which my predecessors, kings or emperors, granted or in any manner transferred to God.”

When this decree had been read and subscribed, he asked the pope to fulfill for him what was written in the charter of the agreement. The king likewise confirmed his agreement to the pope, four counts swearing that on the next Wednesday or Thursday the king would cause his princes to swear friendship and would give hostages, on the condition that, if the pope on the following Sunday fulfilled in every respect for the king what was written in the charter of his agreement. Therefore, as the king insisted that the pope confirm with justice and authority the agreement promised him concerning restoration of royal rights, all alike—his people and ours, namely bishops, abbots, and all children of the Church—resisted him to his face and denounced his decree as utter heresy. The pope wished, if it could be done without violating the peace of the Church, to issue this privilege:

“Let neither priests, abbots, nor clerics be occupied with secular affairs; nor let them attend the county court except to rescue the condemned; nor let them perform military service, which can scarcely or never be rendered without plunder, sacrilege, arson, and homicide; nor let ministers of the altar become ministers of the court; nor let them receive from kings things belonging to the kingdom. But all things belonging to the kingdom from the time of Charlemagne and the other emperors are decreed to be left to the king or emperor.” Under anathema he forbade any bishop [Col. 0238A] to seize things belonging to the kingdom. Under anathema he also forbade those who were to sit after him in the Apostolic See to dare trouble the king or his kingdom concerning this matter.

In the reconciliation made between pope and emperor—for the emperor had captured the pope himself with bishops and cardinals—the king’s oath was this:

“I, King Henry, will on the next Thursday or Friday release the lord pope, bishops, cardinals, and all captives and hostages; and I shall keep peace and security for the pope, his faithful men, and the Romans, both through myself and through my men, in their persons and possessions; and I shall obey him, saving the honor of the kingdom or Empire.”

About fourteen bishops and princes also swore this oath.

The oath on the pope’s side [Col. 0238B] was this:

“Lord Pope Paschal shall not trouble the lord king or his kingdom concerning the investiture of bishoprics or abbeys, nor concerning injury inflicted upon himself and his followers in persons or goods; nor shall he return any evil upon him or any person for this cause; and he shall never in any way pronounce anathema against the person of King Henry. Nor shall the lord pope fail to crown him, and by the aid of his office he shall assist him to hold the kingdom and Empire according to his ability. The pope shall fulfill this without fraud or evil intent.”

Fifteen bishops and cardinals confirmed the pope’s oath by swearing it.

When Henry had been crowned emperor, the pope, after the Gospel had been read, handed him before the altar of the apostles Peter and Paul, in the sight of all the princes [Col. 0238C], this privilege concerning the investiture of bishoprics or abbeys, both by ring and staff:

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ Henry, king of the Germans and, by the grace of almighty God, Augustus emperor of the Romans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Divine providence has established that your kingdom should be uniquely joined to the holy Roman Church. Your predecessors, by the grace of fuller virtue and prudence, attained the crown and Empire of the Roman city. To the dignity of that crown and Empire, moreover, divine majesty has advanced your person also, dearest son Henry, through the ministry of our priesthood. Therefore we also grant to your love, and confirm by the page of this present privilege, that prerogative of dignity which our predecessors granted to your predecessors, the Catholic emperors [Col. 0238D], and confirmed in pages of privileges: namely, that you may confer the investiture of staff and ring upon the bishops or abbots of your kingdom who have been freely elected without force and simony. After investiture, let him receive canonical consecration from the bishop to whom it belongs. But if anyone is elected by clergy and people without your consent, let no one consecrate him unless he is invested by you. Bishops and archbishops, moreover, are to have liberty canonically to consecrate bishops or abbots invested by you.

“For your predecessors so greatly enlarged the churches of their kingdom with benefactions from their royal rights that the kingdom itself ought especially to be strengthened by the support of bishops and abbots, and popular dissensions, which frequently occur in elections [Col. 0239A], ought to be restrained by royal majesty. Therefore your prudence and power ought to apply more diligent care, so that, by the Lord’s favor, the greatness of the Roman Church and the welfare of the others may be preserved through your benefactions and services.

“If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts in rash presumption to act against this page of our concession, let that person, unless he repents, be bound with the bond of anathema and suffer forfeiture of his honor and dignity. But may divine mercy preserve those who observe it, and grant that your person and power may rule happily for His honor and glory.”

Confirmation of peace between apostolic pontiff and emperor, when, in the celebration of Mass, he handed him the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ:

“Lord Emperor, we give you this body of the Lord, born of the Virgin Mary and suffering on the cross for us, as the holy and catholic Church holds, in confirmation of true peace and concord between me and you.”

Given on the Ides of April, fourth indiction.

[Note: [Col. 0239] Here in MS 1, halfway down the page, ends the hand which had written everything immediately preceding from “What or how.” Without any intervening space it immediately joins the following year, “God offended by sins,” etc., in a somewhat different hand, that of Anselm. All the other manuscripts likewise present these passages as connected; those lacking Anselm’s continuation—C1, C2*, C3, C4*, C5, and D—nevertheless end only with the death of Sigebert. Compare what we have noted above in the preface.]

## CONTINUATION OF ANSELM OF GEMBLOUX

[Col. 0239]

[Col. 0239B] **1112. R. 6. (7). F. 3. (4). A. 12. (13). H. 12. (13).**

[Note: [Col. 0239] Anselm originally had the numbers enclosed in brackets. But the first corrector amended them as we have given them; the others have the same, except the manuscript of Aulne and B3*, which agrees with Anselm through the year 1129 and is always one year ahead of us in the years of Christ, but from 1129 agrees with us.]

God being offended by human sins, many things happened this year. On Mont-Castrilocus, the church of St Waltrude, together with two other smaller churches and almost the whole town, burned [Note: [Col. 0239] MS 1, by correction, has “was burned.” “Many—burned” absent in D.]. The church of St Michael “of the Peril of the Sea” was struck by lightning and divinely burned [Note: [Col. 0239] MS 1, by correction, has “is burned.”], together with the buildings attached to it.

Gaudric, bishop of Laon, while attempting to recall the citizens of that city from their wrongly sworn commune-oath, was, dreadful to say, run through with a sword and killed by seditious men rushing to arms, on Thursday in Easter week, 7 Kalends of May, at the Greater Litany. In the tumultuous onrush of the confused crowd, the bishop’s house was also set on fire. Consequently the mother church itself of St Mary [Col. 0239C], and the church of St John the Baptist in the nuns’ abbey, together with all the neighboring dependent churches, were burned. The king of the Franks punished the authors of the sedition so severely that the example could deter both present and future persons from a similar crime.

[Note: [Col. 0239] Here B1, B2, B5, C1, C2*, C3, C4*, D, and E begin a new year marked VII. IV. XIII. XIII. In MS 1 only a new line begins, not at all a new year; nor does one begin in A, B3*, B4*, or B4**.]

In May, crops and trees scorched by holy fire proved false the hope of their fruit; certain woods moreover dried up. There followed a severe and prolonged sickness among men, with flux of the belly and mortality [Note: [Col. 0239] “Thus far Sigebert carried his chronicle,” add B3* and the manuscript of Aulne.].

Lord Sigebert, venerable monk of the monastery [Col. 0240B] of Gembloux, a man of incomparable genius in every branch of literary learning, recorder in this book of preceding times, died on 3 Nones of October, leaving us perpetual sorrow at his absence.

[Note: [Col. 0239] Thus A and Aulne; B4** has “and left his own perpetual sorrow at his absence”; B4* has “and left an everlasting memory of himself”; B1, B5, C1, C2*, C3, C5, and D have “and left us the most grievous sorrow of his absence”; absent in C4*. In MS 1 the entire year was written in one hand and with one pen; it originally ended at the word “died,” and nothing after that has been erased. But another hand later added: “He also left us the book *On Illustrious Men* and many useful memorials of his teaching and books.” The same is found in B3*, Aulne, F1, F2, and F3. Thereafter in manuscript 1, without intervening space, Anselm immediately continues on the same page; but all these things are absent from C1, C2*, C3, C4*, C5, and D.]

**1113. 7. (8.) 4. (5.) 13. (14.) 13. (14.)**
Lord Abbot Lietard died on 2 February; Anselm succeeded him as the eighth [abbot] in the monastery of Gembloux.  
[Note: “Lord—succeeds” is absent from B3* and Aln.]

On the Tuesday of Easter week, 8 April, the monastery of Prüm was burned, together with its workshops; the treasury and library of the church, by God’s providence, remained unharmed.  
[Note: “On the Tuesday—unharmed” is absent from B5.]

In the district of Brabant, on 23 April, near Tournai, so much snow fell that it even broke the forests. In August Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, went with Roger, count of Antioch, against the Turks. But when Roger had encamped with his army beside a certain river, the king advanced with his own men to reconnoitre the Turks’ arrival. The Turks, however, had occupied a certain hill, where they had placed ambushes in four locations, assigning four thousand horsemen to each ambush. The king was unexpectedly surrounded on every side by them and, after fifteen hundred of his men had been killed, escaped by a miserable flight.

When the people of Ascalon learned that King Baldwin was absent, they attacked Jerusalem with a large force. But, being unable to prevail against it, they demolished part of the church of St Stephen, situated outside the city where he was stoned, burned the crops, and thus returned without effecting anything. The Turks utterly destroyed the monastery of the monks situated on Mount Tabor; after killing the monks along with all the rest, they carried everything away for themselves. Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, married the widow of Roger, duke of Sicily.  
[Note: Adelaide of Montferrat.]

At Ravenna and Parma, cities of Italy, blood rained in the fields and within the walls, in June.  
[Note: “At Ravenna—June” was added by Anselm later, with the same ink and at the same time as the year 1115.]

1114. R. 8. (9.) F. 5. (6.) A. 14. (15.) H. 14. (15.)

Emperor Henry celebrated Christmas at Mainz with great splendour among his magnates and throughout the whole kingdom, and there married the daughter of Henry, king of the English.  
[Note: A. 1113. For Anselm begins the year at Christmas.]  
[Note: From this point the ink changes. The following year was written throughout in one continuous hand.]  
[Note: 7 January.]

1115. 9. (10.) 6. (7.) 15. (16.) 15. (16.)

[Col. 0241B] On the Ides of November, in the suburb of Antioch, the earth opened by night and swallowed many towers and adjoining houses with their inhabitants. A certain man, however—such is the nature of men—had moved away from those places with his wife and children; but, when returning, he was swallowed by the same earthquake in the very place where he had been. (Year 1112.)

Emperor Henry, when he thought that whatever he pleased was lawful, incurred the enmity of nearly the whole kingdom. For in previous years he had treacherously seized Chancellor Albert and certain other princes of the realm, and had consigned them to custody without hearing or judgment; he was therefore regarded with suspicion by others, who feared similar treatment. Hence Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, having also turned away from him, pursued him and his supporters with all his strength; he attacked the towns and castles arrayed against him, and devastated with sword and fire everything belonging to him.  
[Note: Already in the middle of the year 1114.]

Emperor Henry had promised that he would celebrate Easter at Aachen; therefore, among the other princes of the realm, Lord Otbert, bishop of Liège, was awaiting his arrival there. One of their number, Arnulf of Arslot, while rubbing his hands together, was seen—to the great wonder of all—to have blood flowing from his fingers, without any injury or sore. This occurrence, regarded as a great portent, signified the shedding of human blood because of the unworthy discord between the kingdom and its princes.  
[Note: From this point the ink changes.]

1116. 10. (11.) 7. (8.) 16. (17.) 16. (17.)

Emperor Henry withdrew into Italy because of the harsh disturbances in the kingdom, and especially to obtain the inheritance which rightly fell to him from his kinswoman, Margravine Matilda, who had recently died.  
[Note: 24 July 1115.]

1117. 11. (12.) 8. (9.) 17. (18.) 17. (18.)

In January, on the third Nones of that month, Wednesday, an earthquake occurred in certain places, though not everywhere, [Col. 0242A] at times milder and at times more violent; indeed, it is said that parts of some cities, together with churches, collapsed. The river Meuse also, beside the abbey called Susteren, seemed, as though suspended in the air, to have abandoned its bed.  
[Note: “Emperor Henry—abandoned” was written with one pen. The following passage, “This same year—terrified,” was written at another time but with the same pen continuously.]

This same year the city of Liège was struck by many afflictions. In May, on the night of the Finding of the Holy Cross, which then fell on the vigil of Ascension, while they were celebrating vespers in the greater church and singing the verse of the psalm, “Who is like the Lord our God?”, suddenly thunder together with an earthquake threw everyone to the ground. Lightning entered from the left side of the church and scattered no small pieces of plaster from the wall here and there; then, entering the tower, it split many portions of the beams. An intolerable stench followed, so that it could scarcely be dispelled even by a great quantity of aromatic substances.

Likewise, in June, on 7 June, about the ninth hour, a rain-cloud, suddenly swept down from the hill called Robert’s Mount, utterly overwhelmed and ruined the part of the city lying below it. It demolished many houses, destroyed an immense quantity of grain, killed a mother embracing two infants, one in each arm, and crushed eight other people in various places.

As vespers were being rung on Saturday, a certain woman, while washing a boy’s head, found her hands red with flowing blood.  
[Note: “As vespers—flowing blood” and “A certain monster—body” were apparently added by Anselm himself, with a note at the year 1038, when he was writing the year 1123; the ink and handwriting are the same. They are absent only from B4* and 4**. Note the play upon the sound.]

On 1 July, about the sixth hour, an exceedingly violent and dark whirlwind covered the city, and a cloud, suddenly torn apart, so damaged the entire roof of the greater church that it lay open to the rain, which flooded the whole pavement. Immediately lightning entered from the north side and killed a cleric reading from the pulpit behind the altar of Saints Cosmas and Damian, another praying before the crucifix, and a third coming out of the nearby church scriptorium at the very entrance to the church. Before the church doors, toward the bishop’s house, it also killed a layman.

On 9 July, from the third hour until the ninth, four whirlwinds from the four quarters of heaven circled the city; a wind also roared with great force and drenched the city with much rain.

On 3 August, at the first silence of night, while thunder was heard throughout the lands and lightning flashed repeatedly, and this happened again and a third time until dawn, the same whirlwind raged yet more violently against the city of Liège. Men sprang from their beds, filled the churches and chapels in sorrowful crowds, and devoted the whole night to supplications. At the first light of dawn, a fire with an immense flame encircled the city from the east, so great that everyone feared they would be burned by divine power. After this a great whirlwind burst forth [Col. 0243A] from the west and seemed to obscure the fire somewhat. Then the fire, as if victorious, blazed up again with flame; and, when the whirlwind returned, it hid itself a little. A third time the same fire blazed up, and a third time, nevertheless conquered by the whirlwind, it fell away. This spectacle greatly terrified the city from early morning until the third hour.

A certain monster was born at Namur, one whose equal has never, or rarely, been seen: namely, a two-headed infant. The people who saw it are witnesses. In sex and in its other limbs it had a single bodily structure. On 11 December, at midnight, with the stars shining in a clear sky, the moon, being thirteen days old, suffered an eclipse; its disk contracted and was suffused with many colours, especially blood-red, for nearly a whole hour.  
[Note: From this point the ink and character of the hand change.]

On 16 December, in the first hour of night, fiery battle-lines appeared in the sky from the north toward the east; then, scattered through the entire sky, they were a wonder and astonishment to observers for much of the night.

1118. R. 12. (13.) F. 9. (10.) A. 18. (19.) H. 18. (19.)

Baldwin, the second king of Jerusalem, brother of Godfrey, duke of Lorraine and first king of Jerusalem, died. They were sons of Count Eustace of Boulogne by Ida, sister of Godfrey the Hunchback, duke of Lorraine. When they had passed away, a third Baldwin reigned, son of Hugh, count of Rethel.

(18 January.) Pope Paschal died. John Gaetan succeeded him as the 159th pope, and named himself Gelasius. [Col. 0243C] But when Emperor Henry, then in Italy, made his way to Rome in order to choose a pope, John, fearing his presence, withdrew to Capua, already elected and ordained.  
[Note: 25 January.]  
[Note: First to Gaeta, where he was consecrated on 10 March.]

But the emperor, because he had not taken part in the election and had not consented to the ordination, caused a certain Spaniard named Burdin, a mere cleric, to be set over him through the efforts of certain Romans. (9 March.) John meanwhile crossed into Gaul, travelling through Burgundy and Gothia, the province called that of St Giles, and conducted synodal affairs.  
[Note: “Paschal—affairs” is placed under the preceding year in B3*, 4*, and 4**.]

(2 September.) Emperor Henry returned home from Italy to Lorraine and, according to the saying, “He who is feared by many must needs fear many,” invited the princes of the realm who had conspired against him to peace, now by threats, now by blandishments, [Col. 0243D] now by force, now by satisfaction.  
[Note: What follows to the end of the year 1121 was written by another hand—the same hand that wrote the years 1095–1111—but Anselm corrected it. “With the extinction—of Liège” is absent from B3*, 4*, and 4**, which instead contain certain material from the Annals of Blandain.]

Since the natural line of the counts of Flanders had entirely failed, Charles, nephew through the sister of Count Robert, son of the king of the Danes, was made count in their place.

1119. 13. (14.) 10. (11.) 19. (20.) 1.

(29 January.) John Gaetan, also called Pope Gelasius, died and was buried at Cluny. With the consent of all the bishops of both Germany and Gaul, together with the Romans, Lord Guy, archbishop of Vienne, was elected pope, designated to be called Calixtus, and blessed at Cluny as the 160th pope (1 February).  
[Note: Added later; absent from A.]

Later, in the middle of October, convening a synod at Reims, he consecrated many bishops in both kingdoms, among whom Lord Frederick was also anointed bishop of Liège. Meanwhile Emperor Henry came to Ivois; and while an embassy for reconciliation between kingdom and priesthood now went from king to pope, now in turn returned from pope to king, the light of peace was clouded by the disagreement of certain envious persons, and the emperor with his supporters was excommunicated (30 October).  
[Note: Juvigny, not far from Sedan.]  
[Note: After this Anselm himself had written in manuscript 1: “The monastery of Prüm, with all its appurtenances, burned, the treasury and library being preserved,” and several other things, now wholly erased, contained within the space of one line. But they were later erased; compare the year 1113. Only A and Aln. contain them; all the rest lack them.]

1120. 14. (15.) 11. (12.) 20. (21.) 2.

Lord Pope Calixtus, setting out for Rome, was received gloriously by the whole senate and populace and confirmed in the apostolic see as the 160th pope (3 January). Burdin, the false pope, was stationed at Sutri; after harassing and plundering pilgrims going to or returning from Rome, he was finally captured as a most contemptible apostate and had his head shaved as a monk.  
[Note: April 1121.]

The greater church of the bishopric of Münster, because its people had rejected their bishop, was burned together with the whole city by Bishop Theoderic himself and Lothair, duke of Saxony.  
[Note: “Leuder” in A.]  
[Note: “The greater—burned” was written by Anselm himself in an erasure; the rest of the witnesses have it.]

[Col. 0244C] 1121. 15. (16.) 12. (13.) 21. (22.) 6.

Lord Bishop Frederick died; at his tomb many signs, seen by very many people, are reported. In October Emperor Henry came to “Quintiliburch”; and magnates of the realm came from both sides, as did legates of the apostolic see, to treat of the controversy between the emperor and the kingdom, and also against the apostolic lord. But although they debated for a long time concerning the state of the realm, the investitures of churches, the inheritance of Siegfried, count palatine, and other matters, they returned more uncertain than they had come: partly favouring the king, partly postponing the case until the pope’s presence, and concealing their agreement.

An earthquake occurred in the second week of Advent, on Saturday at the third hour, 10 December, at times milder and at times more violent.  
[Note: Anselm himself added “An earthquake—occurred” later, at the same time as the words under the preceding two years, “The monastery,” etc., and “The greater [church],” etc. After this, three lines were erased. The first can no longer be read; the second was: “Emperor Henry celebrates the Lord’s Easter at Aachen. From there he hastens to Liège. H. . . . . . . to a certain . . . bur. t.” None of the remaining witnesses has this; but F1 and 2 instead add: “Baldwin, count of Hainaut, dies; his son Baldwin succeeds him.” Anselm himself subsequently wrote over the third line the first line of the following year. Thus we see that he made these three additions before the end of the following year.]  
[Note: Anselm is mistaken: he was at Würzburg; compare *Monumenta Legum* II, 74.]

[Col. 0245A] 1122. R. 16. (17.) F. 13. (14.) A. 21. (23.) H. 4.

The magnates of the realm, meeting with the bishops, brought Emperor Henry—God being favourable to him—to the most salutary resolution that the controversy concerning the investitures of churches between himself and the pope should finally be ended. Bruno, bishop of Speyer, and Arnulf, abbot of Fulda, were sent to Rome on the emperor’s behalf.

Meanwhile Emperor Henry celebrated the Lord’s Easter at Aachen (26 March), and then proceeded to Liège. There, after a complaint had been made to him about the insolences of a certain Godwin, he besieged, captured, burned, and destroyed his castle, called Monsfalconis, with the assistance of Duke Godfrey.  
[Note: Vauquemont.]

The church of Hainaut, together with all its appurtenances and the whole town, was burned in a revolt of its advocate; the treasury and library, however, were preserved. At Tours also, when contention arose between clergy and laity, the church of St Martin was wholly burned.

The apostolic lord, having seen and received the emperor’s embassy, himself weary of the excessively long-standing discord between them, willingly agreed. By the counsel both of the entire Roman senate and of all the Italian bishops, Lambert, bishop of Ostia, Saxo, cardinal of Monte Celio, and Gregory, another cardinal, were sent as papal legates to settle an affair of such importance.

In September, on the Nativity of St Mary, Emperor Henry came to Worms with the bishops and magnates of the realm; there the legates of the apostolic see met him. After the arguments had long been examined, as is customary in so great an assembly of magnates, the favour of their former friendship was at last restored between emperor and pope by God’s ordinance (23 September). Their agreement was as follows:  
[Note: *Monumenta Legum* II, 75; the manuscript of St Trond appears to derive from Anselm.]

“I, Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, grant to you, beloved son Henry, by God’s grace august emperor of the Romans, that elections of bishops and abbots in the German kingdom, which belong to that kingdom, shall take place in your presence without simony or any violence; so that, if any disagreement arises between the parties, you shall give assent and assistance to the sounder party by the counsel or judgment of the metropolitan and provincial bishops. The person elected shall receive the regalia from you by the sceptre, excepting all things known to belong to the Roman Church; and he shall perform what is rightfully due to you from these. In the other regions of the empire, however, the consecrated person shall receive the regalia from you by the sceptre within six months. In matters concerning which you make complaint to me and request help, I shall give you help according to the duty of my office. I grant you true peace, and also all who are or were on your side during this discord.”

Emperor Henry’s written reply:

“I, Henry, august emperor of the Romans, for the love of God and of the holy Roman Church and Lord Pope Calixtus, and for the salvation of my soul, surrender to God and to the holy apostles of God, Peter and Paul, and to the holy catholic Church, every investiture by ring and staff; and I grant that canonical election and free consecration shall take place in all the churches within my kingdom and empire. The possessions and regalia of blessed Peter which, from the beginning of this discord until the present day, whether in my father’s time or in mine, have been taken away and which I possess, I restore to the same holy Roman Church; those which I do not possess, I shall faithfully assist in having restored. The possessions also of all other churches, princes, and other persons, clergy and laity alike, which I possess, I shall restore according to the counsel of the princes and justice; those which I do not possess, I shall faithfully assist in having restored. And I grant true peace to Lord Pope Calixtus and the holy Roman Church and to all who are or were on his side; and in all matters in which the holy Roman Church requests help, I shall faithfully assist.”  
[Note: The entire year was written with one pen. From this point the character of the hand and the ink change.]

1123. 17. (18.) 14. (15.) 23. (24.) 5.

Lord Adelbero, chosen from the clergy of St Stephen at Metz, was ordained bishop of Liège. There is an ancient estate belonging to us, now called the Mount of St Guibert.  
[Note: A adds “at Gembloux.”]

There, under Christ’s auspices and with the consent of all the neighbours, it pleased us to build a new church. For long ago there had been a small wooden church there, enjoying the dignity of its privilege: namely, a baptismal font, burial rights, and tithes. But it had been neglected for about sixty years, more or less, so that scarcely any traces of a church remained there.

Therefore, in the year of the Lord 1123, on the Wednesday of Easter, we brought the body of our most holy patron Guibert there (18 April); by God’s favour, the influx of people of both sexes was estimated at twelve thousand. As we returned, it seemed good to us that the body of St Guibert should remain there; thereafter it shone with such brilliance of miracles that it is desired and frequented by peoples from every direction.  
[Note: The character of the hand changes. “Lord—frequented” is absent from B3*, 4*, and 4**. “An estate—frequented” is absent from B1 and 5.]

Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, was captured by the Saracens. Losing heart at this event, they gathered from every direction, sixty thousand being summoned together, in order to expel the Christians from their territories; and at Ascalon they deposited their baggage, namely their wives, children, [Col. 0246D] and provisions.

The Christians, hard pressed and having no hope except in God, proclaimed a fast for both sexes after the example of the Ninevites; even children, nursing infants, and all livestock were denied food. A day of battle was appointed. The Christians advanced, with horsemen and foot soldiers estimated at scarcely three thousand. [Col. 0247A] The leaders marched in front: namely, the patriarch, carrying Christ’s cross as a standard; Pontius, formerly abbot of Cluny, bearing the lance that pierced Christ’s side; and the bishop of Bethlehem, carrying in a pyx the milk of Holy Mary, perpetual virgin.

But the Saracens, spread abroad in every direction, surrounded the Christians in a circle from every side, so that no one could escape. While the Christians stood thus in battle array, they saw, with God aiding them, a brightness suddenly fall from the split air upon the pagans—not favourable, but very harmful—although the Saracens themselves did not see it. Immediately, deprived of the strength of all their powers, they were cut down as they fled everywhere, not only by men but even by boys and women. Seven thousand died in the battle; five thousand were drowned in the waters. But all the Christians returned unharmed, and cried aloud to the Lord on high the supreme and sweet song of victory.  
[Note: After this, one line erased. The pen changes.]

1124. R. 18. (19.) F. 15. (16.) A. 24. (25.) H. 6.

Emperor Henry celebrated Christmas at Aachen. The winter was harsher than usual, dreadful and oppressive through the repeated accumulation of falling snow. Many poor children and women died from the excessive cold. There was also a very great mortality among animals. In many fishponds fish perished, trapped beneath the ice. In Brabant innumerable eels, leaving the marshes because of the ice, fled and hid in haylofts—marvellous to relate—but there too died from the extreme cold and rotted.  
[Note: “In many—rotted” is absent from B3* and 4**.]

The winter was followed by an unseasonable state of the weather, now snow, now rain, now frost, alternating and very severe, until the middle of March. Thereafter, while the air continued bleak with long-lasting cold and rain, trees scarcely flowered even in May; scarcely at last did the grace of herbs and grasses revive in green growth.  
[Note: What follows to the middle of the next year was written in one hand and with one ink. Here also the sign + first occurs, to distinguish propositions; Anselm had never used it previously, but thereafter used it almost continually.]

But rain fell continually in every month and nearly destroyed the crops of the fields. For rye and oats greatly disappointed the hope of their yield. Many also were burned by the sacred fire.

Tyre, called *Sor* in the Hebrew language, a very great and ancient city of Phoenicia, situated in the heart of the sea, a colony of Sidonians, the commerce of the sea and mart of the whole world, celebrated in the prophecies of prophets and illustrious in poets’ songs—formerly indeed an island, but made part of the mainland when Nebuchadnezzar or Alexander, for its siege, had brought together many embankments across the narrow strait—having long ago been captured and partly carried into captivity by Nebuchadnezzar, and later utterly razed and destroyed to its foundations by Alexander, but, according to the prophets, rebuilt after seventy years and restored to its former condition, was in our own times, at the end of the world, besieged by Christians by land and sea, captured, and subjected to Christ’s rule.

(12 December.) Pope Calixtus, also called Guy, died. Lambert, also called Honorius, bishop of Ostia, succeeded him.

1125. 19. (20.) 16. (17.) 25. (26.) 7.

A most severe winter, lasting continuously for six weeks and very harmful. A grievous famine everywhere, with a great multitude of both sexes dying. In Hesbaye a low-born little woman gave birth to a monster with a doubly twin body, joined together with faces and bodies turned in opposite directions: in front, the form of a man, distinguished by the complete arrangement of body and limbs; behind, the face of a dog, likewise with the proper and complete form of body and limbs. In Brabant, in the village of Nerisca, another woman gave birth to four males in one delivery.  
[Note: The pen changes slightly.]

In the parish of Gembloux, while a householder was grinding a mixture of grains on the Lord’s Day, because of the scarcity caused by famine, for his household’s use, the flour suddenly burned through God’s just wrath, with a stinking blackness, as an example to posterity that they should presume nothing similar.

The church of St Dionysius, situated in the forest of Brocheroi, on 25 April, the feast of St Mark, at the first twilight of night, was utterly burned with all its appurtenances and the whole village; the treasury and archive chest, however, were preserved.  
[Note: Saint-Denis in Broqueroye, in the county of Mons.]

(29 March.) Emperor Henry celebrated the Lord’s Easter at Liège. Departing thence toward Aachen, he began to suffer from the illness called *dracunculus*, which was congenital to him; for this reason he remained there several days. He then came to Nijmegen.  
[Note: Nymwegen.]

Later, intending as it were to celebrate Pentecost, he came to Utrecht; but as his illness grew worse day by day, he finally lost life and kingdom on the Thursday in Pentecost week (23 May). His body, after the intestines had been removed and it had been sprinkled with salt, was brought back to Speyer.

Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, was released by the Saracens after a ransom had been given.  
[Note: The pen changes.]

(30 August.) In August, on the feast of St Bartholomew the apostle, the highest dignity of the magnates of the empire, or the most eminent glory of the Church—Eberhard and Romanus, legates of the apostolic see, and archbishops with bishops—assembled by agreement at Mainz and deliberated for themselves and for the whole Roman empire concerning the appointment of a king.  
[Note: “Or the most eminent—by agreement,” and shortly afterwards “with these same persons—coming,” are absent from B4**.]

Lothair, duke of Saxony, a wise and energetic man, devoted to ecclesiastical law, mighty in riches and victories, was chosen with the assent of all. In September he came to Aachen with the same legates, two archbishops, eight bishops, many abbots, and the most eminent chief men of the royal court. There, on Sunday, the Ides of September, he was blessed and anointed king by Frederick, archbishop of Cologne (13 September), while all the clergy and people acclaimed a festive song of victory.  
[Note: From this point the ink changes.]

1126. 1. 17. (18.) 26. (27.) 8.

A very severe winter; spring too was dangerous. King Lothair, marching against the Bohemians, suffered a great slaughter of his soldiers through the treachery of certain of his princes: namely, five hundred and forty were killed.  
[Note: The ink changes.]

In Syria this year the army of God fought the Saracens twice. In the first battle, two thousand five hundred pagans fell, and only fifteen Christians; in the second, however, the Christians did not gain a bloodless victory. Yet although a very large part of them perished, nevertheless, strengthened again by God’s help, they crushed and conquered countless enemies.

This year every crop was diseased, and the vines, together with all tree-fruit, were severely damaged.  
[Note: “This year—severely damaged” is absent from A and B5; Aln. ends at the word “conquered.” From this point the pen and ink change slightly.]

1127. R. 2. F. 18. (19.) A. 27. (28.) H. 9.

(Year 1126.) King Lothair celebrated Christmas at Cologne; but the archbishop, whether prevented by illness or through pretence, had withdrawn to Sigeberg. From there he came to Aachen at Epiphany (6 January). There the envoys of Charles, count of the Morini—namely the castellan of Ghent and the abbot of St Peter’s—came to him, announcing that their lord the count would render him due submission.  
[Note: Of Blandain.]

Nevertheless, the princes of Lorraine kept away from his presence. For new circumstances always change with a new power; and this was immediately apparent there. For the townsmen of Aachen and the king did not agree well, but treated one another rather injuriously. What relations existed between the king and Duke Frederick is not sufficiently known, because affairs are diminished or magnified according to the wishes of those who support or oppose them. This much is plain: they were falling into a serious breach.  
[Note: “Concerning the king—were falling” is absent from A. “There the envoys—were falling” is absent from B4*, 4**, and B3*, which also lacks what follows, “Anathema—had reduced.”]

[Col. 0249C] Anathema in the midst of the earth: a bold and shameful crime, to be punished in every age. For behold, Satan, released, wanders through the lands. Flanders and Burgundy, widely separated in the extent of their territories, conspire in the apostasy of the traitor Judas. Certain men, fearing condemnation for their crime, murder their lord Charles, count of the Morini, at Bruges, in a certain church, while he was singing psalms before the altar.  
[Note: St Donatian.]

One and the same Satan, on one and the same day, dared a similar crime in Burgundy. Certain accursed men, despairing of their salvation because they were guilty of treason, stabbed their lord William, count of Sedan, with swords in a certain church while he prayed before the altar. This occurred in the second week of Lent, Tuesday, 1 March. The murderers fled hither and thither, and perished by various injuries and an end sufficiently deserved by them.

The county of the Morini was granted by Louis, king of the French, to William, son of Robert, count of Normandy, brother of William, king of the English. Long before, when this Robert was returning from Jerusalem and could not repay borrowed money, his same brother William, king of the English, had expelled him from Normandy and subjected it to himself, while reducing his brother in England to honourable custody.

King Lothair celebrated Pentecost at “Babenbergen.”  
[Note: “The king—treachery” was written by the author himself in an erasure.]  
[Note: According to others, at Merseburg.]

There the duke of Bohemia arrived with many thousands of horsemen, made satisfaction to the lord king for his earlier treachery, and reconciled to himself, by the presentation of many splendid gifts, all those whose parents or friends he had killed.

The monastery of St Hubert in the Ardennes was burned, with all its appurtenances, on 7 July at the first silence of night; the treasury and archive chest, however, were preserved.  
[Note: “The monastery—archive chest” is absent from B1 and 5. From this point the ink changes.]

In the district of Lomme, in the village of Gerpinnes, a poor woman ground barley on the feast-night of St Michael and immediately made and baked unleavened bread from it. When she broke it to eat, she drew forth blood and water.  
[Note: Gerpinnes, near Charleroi.]

1128. 3. 19. (20.) 28. (29.) 10.

Lord Adelbero, bishop of Liège, died.  
[Note: The character of the hand changes. “D. A. e. L. died,” and immediately below, “Lord—bishop,” are absent from B3*, 4*, 4**, and 5.]

On Sunday, 28 January, thunder was heard about the ninth hour. Lord Alexander, archdeacon from the clergy of St Lambert, was consecrated bishop of Liège on 18 March.  
[Note: The pen changes.]

When, at the beginning of March, the clear air seemed cheerful, suddenly, in the middle of that month, it was all gathered into cloud and froze with cold; waters froze, the fields stiffened, and the elements were dissolved now by snow, now by frost, now by rains. A great mortality of sheep, lambs, [Col. 0250C] oxen, and cows followed. At last, by God’s mercy, all things returned to favour at the Greater Rogation.  
[Note: The pen changes.]

On 13 May, Monday, a great storm arose at Cologne; lightning also entered the greater church of St Peter and tore apart the right arm of the crucifix.  
[Note: The pen and ink change.]

When sedition and division arose between Count William and the Morini, through the efforts of Eustace and Daniel, leading men of Flanders, Theoderic, son of Theoderic, duke of Alsace, nephew through his sister Gertrude of Robert, count of Flanders, was summoned. But while Duke Godfrey of Leuven aided Count William, the armies of both met before the castle called Aalst. There Count William, engaging a certain knight in single combat, was pierced in the right arm by a lance and, when a *dracunculus* arose, died on the fifth day. The county of the Morini was granted to Theoderic by Louis, king of the French, because he was his kinsman through his maternal aunt Gertrude.  
[Note: The ink changes. “When sedition—Gertrude” is given thus by B3*, 4*, and 4**: “William, count of Flanders, together with Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, presses the castle of Aalst by siege; there, having received a very slight wound—or rather no wound but an incision—in his hand, he suddenly dies, supposedly after being badly dosed with a potion by a physician, though the cause is unknown. Theoderic succeeds him.”]

In the middle of September a very harmful frost occurred, in which vegetables and vines perished, and everything that could be pressed was turned sour. In Flanders many rivers became bloody, and likewise ditches.  
[Note: The pen changes.]

King Lothair encircled the city of Speyer in a long siege, but returned without success.

1129. R. 4. F. 20. (21.) A. 29. (30.) II. 11.

When January began with a thaw, such a flood of snow and rain swelled the rivers and fishponds that it washed away and hollowed out the nearby crops, overturned neighboring houses, and destroyed whatever was found in them. [Note: [Col. 0251] The hand changes.]

On the Tuesday of Easter week, a waxy sweat dripped from an ox belonging to a certain peasant as it ploughed, in the parish of Gembloux. [Note: [Col. 0251] The hand changes.]

A battle took place at Duras [Note: [Col. 0251D] Duras near Saint-Trond.] between Alexander, bishop of Liège, and Count Godfrey of Louvain, in which the slaughter was so great that 824 foot-soldiers on both sides together are said to have perished, apart from those who, fleeing, died wounded in the fields or woods; those who were drowned in the waters; and those who returned home and died at uncertain hours and days. Their total could not be calculated. Done on the seventh day before the Ides of August, Wednesday. [Note: [Col. 0251] “Done … Wednesday” was added later by Anselm.]

At Reims this year, at Easter, Louis king of the Franks raised his son to kingship after himself, in the presence of all the bishops and abbots of his realm. A very great pestilence afflicted oxen, cows, pigs, boars, stags, and goats. On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, there were flashes of lightning and thunder at the first silence of the night, in the first lunar phase, on Thursday. [Note: [Col. 0251] The script changes with the ink. Anselm himself wrote the following two pages, as far as the end of 1132, on an erasure; indeed, from “This year … with the whole town” at the beginning of the following year in one continuous hand, and the rest at several times.]

This year the scourge of divine fire spread astonishingly through Chartres, Paris, Soissons, Cambrai, Arras, [Col. 0251C] and many other places; but, more astonishingly, it was extinguished through Saint Mary, Mother of God. Young men, old men with the younger, even tender virgins, were burned upon their feet, hands, breasts, and—more grievously—upon their cheeks, and were swiftly extinguished. [Note: [Col. 0251] The following material as far as “could suffice” at the end of the year is absent from B4*. 4**., which contain only: “At Paris, in the church of the Blessed Virgin Mother, 103 are healed in one day.”]

At Paris there is a small church in honour of Saint Martin. A certain man afflicted by this illness had himself carried there. While he was spending the night there, crying out under the pressure of his sufferings, Saint Martin appeared at the first silence of the night and asked why he had entered his house. The man displayed the distress of his sickness and begged him to have mercy upon him. Saint Martin said to him:

“Know that in the court of the heavenly Judge a terrible and dreadful sentence has been pronounced: that this scourge of burning should rage through Gaul; and that the Mother of Mercy has obtained by her prayers that mercy should be shown to all who suffer from this disaster and call upon her. Therefore have yourself carried at Paris to the church of that holy Virgin Mother, and there you will be healed.”

The man replied: “You are called blessed by every mouth and a worker of miracles. It was in order to recover health through you that I entered your house.”

And Saint Martin said: “Without permission of the Virgin [Col. 0252A] Mother, who bore our God, who is a consuming fire, you cannot be healed.”

Saint Martin departed. Returning again, he ordered the man to go back to the Mother of Mercy. But he said: “Either I shall be healed through you, or I shall die here.”

And Saint Martin said: “The Lord Jesus Christ heals you through the prayers of his mother. And this shall be a sign to you: you will be the first; after you, six will be healed in this house. But all others who come will labour in vain.”

Saint Martin departed. The man, healed, proclaimed his healing. Many assembled; but from the great crowd only six were healed, as Saint Martin had foretold. At Paris they fled for refuge to the church of the Virgin Mother. One hundred and three were healed in a single day; two, whether by God’s command or permission, were not healed but died.

At Laon, on the feast of the Lord’s Ascension, [Col. 0252B] three died before the altar of the Ever-Virgin.

Let us pass to the city of Soissons. There, more especially than in all other places, the Mother of God made herself known to the peoples through miracles. There the dumb, blind, lame, and paralysed were healed; a dead man was restored to life.

We saw a dreadful thing. Divine fire had burned away the nose, lips, and chin of a poor woman; the stench filled those who smelled it, and horror filled those who saw it. Driven out of the house of the Virgin Mother, she returned to her own home. For her expulsion and sickness she grieved, groaned, and prayed, saying:

“Alas for me! The Mother of Mercy receives all and drives away none except me alone. O God, who for mercy’s sake became the son of a woman, heal me through the woman who is your mother, for the sake of your mercy.”

She prayed and was heard. On the night [Col. 0252C] leading into Saturday she recovered her health. Her flesh, nose, lips, and chin were restored; she recovered all that had been her own, whole and entire. You might have seen a noble miracle: that flesh became like the rest of her flesh, and, more wonderfully, at the joining of old and new flesh there appeared, as testimony, something like the mark of a very fine thread.

A certain young man, deaf and dumb, whom the abbess of the same church, where these things occurred, had reared from infancy for the love of God, was resting in the church at midday. He seemed to see an old man clothed in snowy garments, touching his ears and lips with his hand and saying: “Say: ‘God and holy Mary, have mercy upon me.’” He said this, was healed, gave thanks to God, and all the people magnified God.

A woman coming from the city of Reims [Col. 0252D] with her son to the house of the Holy Virgin, while seeking the salvation of her soul, lost her son; but she was consoled by God’s grace. For the boy, while playing in a chest, suddenly fell into a well ruined by age and died. As evening drew on, his mother sought her son; when she could not find him, she grieved and cried out. Neighbours ran together, and the city was disturbed. Someone [Col. 0253A] said that he had seen him playing with boys above the mouth of the well. They looked inside and saw him lying dead. He was pulled out and returned to his mother. Without delay she went to the church, followed by the whole city. Coming to the church, she laid him before the altar of the Virgin Mother and asked the Mother of Mercy to restore her son to her. At once she was heard by the Mother of Mercy: the boy rose; the child who had been dead lived. In testimony, the boy’s shirt was hung before the altar. The report flew into the ears of all; throughout Gaul the heart and tongue of every person trembled.

In Vermandois is a village called Fontaines, where miracles frequently occurred in the church of the Virgin Mother. Certain merchants and pilgrims, knowing the holiness of the place, firm in faith and devotion, were travelling there when they met [Col. 0253B] a matron, honoured as though she were a mother. She addressed them thus:

“I inform you that Mary, Virgin and Mother of the Lord, has judged the place at Soissons worthy of a more abundant affection. I advise you to come there.”

Since they paid little attention to the words they had heard, behold, the matron reappeared, repeated for a second time what she had first said, and departed. Astonished by so great a miracle, they made for Soissons. Upon arrival they saw the doors of the basilica shut fast; they prayed, were heard, and the doors of the basilica of the Virgin Mother were opened to them.

Therefore all those afflicted, when burned by the divine fire, fled to that noble church of the Virgin Mother. Though that church was full of sufferers, hear how gloriously they were healed in an instant. This most ancient and noble place contains within itself the under-garment of the holy Virgin Mother. One night, while all were groaning and sending forth the moaning of their hearts under excessive anguish together with grinding of teeth, they saw a splendid light, and with it the Mother of Mercy descending above the altar. The Mother and Virgin approached one of the sick and asked whether he wished to be healed; she understood his desired longing for health. She touched him, and he was healed. She commanded him to make this known in the same manner to all whom she had appeared. [Note: [Col. 0253] *nisa*, corrected from *jussa* in the manuscript.] They were touched and healed; the whole city rejoiced. The opening through which the light from light had entered remained as a sort of sign and is venerated by all.

At Chartres, where the shirt of the same Virgin is kept, an innumerable multitude was healed. What also shall I say of Cambrai? Cambrai is a most ancient and noble city, where there is a church [Col. 0253D] in honour of that Virgin Mother, endowed with her hair and blessed milk. There many sick persons were healed, whose number no one knows but God alone. At Arras, in the church dedicated to the Virgin Mother, so many and such great healings occurred [Col. 0254A] that every person would become speechless in trying to recount them. We have recorded these principal places; but if we wished to range through other places dedicated to her memory, where the wonderful power of the Lord healed all who fled there through inexpressible power, neither understanding nor reason could suffice for this.

Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, dies. [Note: [Col. 0253] “Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, dies in the year 1131” was supplied by Anselm, as is evident from the ink. It is absent from A.]

## 1130. R. 5. F. 21. (22.) A. 30. (31.) H. 12.

King Lothair at last captured the city of Speyer, besieged in turn every other year, on the third day before the Nones of January, Friday, having granted immunity. Lambert, also called Honorius, pope, died (14 February). The peace of the Roman Church was disrupted, while two men disputed over the apostolic see: one Gregory, the other Peter Leonis, a Roman by birth and a monk of Cluny.

Gregory [Col. 0254B] arrogated to himself the privilege of election from Pope Honorius while he was still alive, with the agreement of certain cardinals. Peter, glorying in the eminence of his blood, seized the house of Crescentius and raged through slaughter, robbery, and arson. The church of Saint Peter at Louvain was burned with the whole town. [Note: [Col. 0253] “The church … whole town” is absent from B1. 5. Here ends the ink with which Anselm had written all that precedes, from “This year the scourge of divine fire” to “with the whole town,” in one continuous hand. Anselm wrote what follows, from “Gregory” to “Saint Mary,” with another ink and pen.]

Gregory, fearing Peter’s power, fled from Saint-Paul and Spoleto, crossed the sea, and at last arrived at Saint-Gilles. [Note: [Col. 0253] Anselm first wrote: “fleeing through Tuscany and Lombardy and journeying round by Saint Michael in the passes, he came,” etc. But, having struck out “through … journeying,” he immediately wrote above it “from Saint … afterward,” as all the other witnesses also have.]

In October he then came into Burgundy, was received by Cluny, and was celebrated with the favour of all the Franks. Next, King Lothair of Germany, persuaded by the ambition of certain of his bishops, graciously honoured an embassy from France concerning Gregory and pledged himself to his election. At Perronne the church of Saint Fursey was entirely burned. [Note: [Col. 0253] “The church of Saint Fursey at Perronne was entirely burned” was later added by Anselm under 1131, when he was writing “Hugh … perished,” and under the preceding year “Baldwin king of Jerusalem dies.” It is absent from A and B1.]

Fulk, count of Anjou, [Col. 0254C] became king of Jerusalem. [Note: [Col. 0253] “Fulk, count of Anjou, became king of Jerusalem” was later supplied by Anselm with the same pen with which he completed this year. It is absent in A.]

## 1131. 6. 22. (23.) 31. (32.) 1. (13.)

Gregory, leaving France with a large retinue of bishops and abbots, crossed into Lotharingia and came to Liège on the third Sunday of Lent, which was the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. There he was venerated and honoured with gifts by King Lothair of Germany and many bishops and abbots, both Lotharingian and Trans-Rhenish. The whole city was fervent in service, occupied with greetings and feasting.

On Mid-Lent Sunday, Gregory, like the he-goat in Daniel, whose feet did not touch the earth, [Note: [Col. 0253] “like … earth” has been erased in manuscript 1, though it can still be read. It is absent from B3*. 4*. 4**., but is read in A, B1, F1, 2, 3. It was also present in B5; but Miraeus wrote in the margin: “This passage seems to require expurgation and censure,” and then either he himself or another erased “like … earth.”] ascended with carriages and wagons from the church of Saint Martin on the public hill, as though along Rome’s triumphal way, to the cathedral of Saint Lambert. He celebrated Mass, crowned the king and queen, and excommunicated married priests. Some estimated that thirty-two bishops and fifty-three abbots were present. Although the Lord says that he is present in the midst of two or three gathered in his name, [Col. 0255A] yet all their enactment needs neither pen nor parchment. [Note: [Col. 0255] “Although … parchment” has been erased in manuscript 1, though it can still be read; it is absent from B3*. 4*. 4**., but read in A, B1, F1, 2, 3. In B5 the same Miraeus wrote in the margin: “This passage seems to require censure,” and it was subsequently erased.]

The city of Utrecht was burned for the most part: namely, the bishop’s palace, the greater church of Saint Martin, another of Saint Boniface, and a third of Saint Mary. [Note: [Col. 0255] Here A ends; ink and pen change in manuscript 1. “The city … Saint Mary” is absent from B1. 5.]

Hugh Canna Avenae [Note: [Col. 0255] *campus avenae* in B3. 4**.] [Note: [Col. 0255D] Count of Saint-Pol.], after hostilities arose against the townspeople of Saint-Riquier [Note: [Col. 0255D] Saint-Riquier.] in the district of Ponthieu, entirely burned the whole town together with the church of Saint-Riquier. In that church some monks and an inestimable multitude of both sexes—an abomination to relate—perished together in the flames. [Note: [Col. 0255] After this, the ink changes in manuscript 1, and it originally began a new year, headed “VII. XXIIII. XXXIII. XIIII.” But this was erased, and “perished in the flames” was written over the erasure.]

Gregory, also called Pope Innocent, held a council at Reims after the feast of Saint Luke the Evangelist (18 October), with three hundred bishops and abbots, through the agency of Louis king of the Franks and his second-born son. [Col. 0255B] For the first-born, previously crowned, had then perhaps come to Paris and, as the report goes, was mocked by a demon in the form of a pig; while he wheeled his horse this way and that, he suddenly fell lifeless. Therefore his father, deeply grieved, arrived at Reims and brought with him his second-born son, obtaining from the pope that he be anointed, blessed, and crowned king. Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, died.

## 1132. R. 7. F. 23. (24.) A. 32. (33.) H. 2.

King Lothair celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Cologne. Infected with the poison of avarice, he annulled by his cunning the election of the holy church of Cologne. [Note: [Col. 0255] Thus Anselm wrote it. But later another hand, whose corrective work also appears in 1140, struck out “He … cunning” and wrote above it: “Here, amid the tumultuous sedition of many disputants, the election of the holy church of Cologne was long and repeatedly annulled.” This is the reading of B1, 3*, 4*, 4**, 5, F1, 2, 3.]

Again, coming to Cologne in the third week of Lent, he did nothing worthy of royal serenity. Then, coming to Aachen at Easter (10 April), he could establish nothing concerning the condition [Col. 0255C] of the realm; indeed, he postponed all complaints for later consideration. The city of Regensburg was almost entirely burned. [Note: [Col. 0255] “The city of Regensburg was almost entirely burned” was later added in manuscript 1; it is absent from B1. 5. After this, the script changes.]

Lord Bruno, from the clergy of Saint Peter’s at Cologne, became archbishop. King Lothair, having gathered his forces, went to Rome with Pope Innocent in September; but, through varying fortunes, he suffered many difficulties on the journey. [Note: [Col. 0255] From this point the script changes.]

## 1133. 8. 24. (25.) 33. (34.) 3.

On the fourth day before the Nones of August, at the twenty-seventh lunar day, an eclipse of the sun occurred at noon for almost half an hour, and stars were seen in the sky. [Note: [Col. 0255] The hand changes.]

King Lothair entered Old Rome on 30 April, restored Pope Innocent to the Lateran patriarchal palace, and was blessed by him as emperor [Col. 0255D] on 4 June. But, unable to recall Roman greed from [Col. 0256A] the division of factions, he ignored the matter and returned without effect. Peter, however, the false pope, ruled in the house of Crescentius; and each raged against the other with plunder, robbery, arson, and murder. [Note: [Col. 0255] The hand changes.]

In the town of Namur, [Note: [Col. 0256D] Namur.] as a butcher opened a slaughtered cow, a foetus with two heads appeared. [Note: [Col. 0255] The hand changes.] This year legumes and oats greatly belied the harvest’s expected yield. [Note: [Col. 0255] The hand changes.]

## 1134. 9. 25. (26.) 34. (35.) 4.

The community of the church of Malines, which is in Brabant, sends greetings to all the faithful.

On the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, a poisoned and rabid wolf, which had three living snakes inside its body, leaving its accustomed lairs, sought the countryside and destroyed an innumerable multitude of pigs, sheep, dogs, and cattle with its poisonous bite. Afterwards, attacking people with a violent onset, it grievously mauled more than twelve with its bite; four of them died a miserable death. Before dying, however, they could neither look at nor taste any liquid. At last, seized by four very brave men and disembowelled, it revealed through the snakes the evidence of its wickedness. [Note: [Col. 0255] From this point both pen and ink change.]

This year was very calamitous because of excessive drought, since oats, barley, and legumes greatly belied their expected yield. Theobald, count of Blois or Chartres, stands out in France above all the princes of Gaul by the great weight of his justice: gracious and familiar toward religious monks and clerics; defender of the Church; helper of the poor; comforter of the deserving; cautious and discerning in merchants’ transactions; [Col. 0256C] and punisher and avenger of the guilty and those who stray from right. [Note: [Col. 0255] The hand changes.]

On the Kalends of October, in the silent darkness of a stormy night, a great disturbance arose in the sea, so that it passed beyond its shores and yet settled back into itself. On the following night, at the first twilight, bursting beyond its bounds with all force, it destroyed everything round about—villages, castles, churches—so thoroughly that it utterly wiped out, people and livestock alike, three counties: Walcheren, Wales, and Bebrant. [Note: [Col. 0256D] See the Annals of Fosses, *SS*, vol. IV, p. 30.]

## 1135. 10. 26. (27.) 35. (36.) 5.

In [Note: [Col. 0255] The ink changes completely with the pen.] the city of Tournai, a lamb was born with one body, two heads, four ears, four eyes, [Col. 0256D] and eight feet. [Note: [Col. 0255] After this, a line and a half are erased. Then the ink changes.]

In the village called Braine [Col. 0257A] [Note: [Col. 0257A] Braine-le-Comte, between Halle and Mons.], in April a little child was born without neck or head, having little eyes in its shoulders. [Note: [Col. 0257] The hand changes.]

King Lothair [Col. 0258A] and Duke Frederick of Swabia make peace. [Note: [Col. 0257] Here Anselm’s hand ends. Without any interval or heading, on the same page there follows the same third hand which wrote the beginning of 1085–1111. It continues without interruption as far as “restore harmony.”]

## Continuation of Gembloux

[Col. 0257]

[Col. 0257B] ## 1136. R. 11. F. 27. (28.) A. 36. (37.) H. 6.

The monastery of Saint Vedast at Arras is burned, together with its cloister, workshops, and a great part of the town. No one in our age remembers so many villages, cities, castles, towns, or boroughs burned by accidental fire as are reported to have been consumed during this year.

[Lord Alexander, bishop of Liège, dies. [Note: [Col. 0257] Added between the lines by the seventh hand, the same one that wrote the end of the codex at Reims from 1145 onward; B1, 5, F1, 2, 3.]]

Anselm, the eighth abbot of the monastery of Gembloux, died. Although still alive and physically infirm, he was nevertheless energetic in devotion to God and the study of Scripture. [Note: [Col. 0257] “Although … energetic” is absent from B4**.] He continued this chronicle from the end of the chronicle written by the venerable Sigebert, monk of the church of Gembloux, down to this year, and left for the knowledge of posterity what he had seen or heard from trustworthy reporters.

We now learn from our own afflictions more than we read in books how destructive the evil of discord is for all. For when the monks and townspeople could not agree, nor the townspeople with the monks, on the election of an abbot to be appointed, the evil of discord proceeded so far that [Note: [Col. 0257] “The evil of discord … discord” is absent from B1. 5. “The evil of discord … ecclesiastical persons” is absent from B3*. 4*. 4**.] the duke of Louvain [Note: [Col. 0257D] Godfrey.] and the count of Namur, having broken the treaty of peace, fought one another as enemies for a long time. It was possible to see misery and the most violent plundering of all things; murders very frequently committed; villages burned with their inhabitants. Indeed, when the town of Gembloux, with its parish church, had been burned at great danger to its inhabitants, God’s mercy wonderfully checked the fire that was raging on every side and had already set ablaze the greater monastery adjoining it. The channel of the neighbouring river, having collected into a pool, was suddenly emptied of much of its stream, so that its sands were visible to those running about and resisting the enemy; and its water, poured over the monastery like rain, extinguished every fire by God’s power. Lest this seem unbelievable to anyone, many persons still attest it today, [Col. 0258B] not only laypeople but ecclesiastical persons.

[Lord Adelbero, taken from the clergy of Metz, is made bishop of Liège. [Note: [Col. 0257] Added in manuscript 1 by the fifth hand; B1, 5, F1, 2, 3. It is absent from B3*. 4*. 4**.]]

The monastery of Saint Dionysius at Brokorotht was burned, together with its cloister, all its dependencies, and the town; scarcely twelve years had elapsed since the former burning. [Note: [Col. 0257] “The monastery … elapsed” is absent from B1. 5; B3*. 4*. 4** place it at the beginning of the year after “a great part of the town.”]

Henry, king of the English, died (1 December 1135), a man of great kindness toward the poor and God’s churches, and therefore also of great generosity.

[Louis, king of the Franks, died [Note: [Col. 0257D] Finally, on the Kalends of August 1137.]; his son of the same name succeeded him. [Note: [Col. 0257] Added by the fifth hand. B1, 3*, 4*, 4**, 5, F2, 3; absent from F1.]]

King Lothair, having assembled a great army from his realm, set out for Rome a second time in September, wishing to restore to peaceful and united harmony the discord of the two contenders for the apostolic see. [Note: [Col. 0257] The third hand ends; the fifth begins.]

[Col. 0258C] After long deliberation over whom to raise to the royal name and honour, the English, when King Henry had died childless, appointed his cousin Stephen to reign in his place. Mons [Note: [Col. 0258D] Mons.] of Castrilocus, with the church of Saint Waudru and almost the whole town, was burned. [Note: [Col. 0257] “Mons … was burned” is absent from B1. 5.]

## 1137. 12. (11.) 1. (27.) 1. 7.

King Lothair, having remained in Italy for one year and five months with a military expedition, withdrew from entering the city of Rome because he could not restrain the battles and seditions of the two contenders for the apostolic see (May). In frequent armed encounters he wore down Roger, duke of Sicily, who was resisting him; he devastated Roger’s province with slaughter and fire, [Col. 0258D] yet did not compel him to surrender. Therefore, as the event of war was uncertain and the sword consumed neither side, King Lothair, overtaken by death on 3 December, ended the war with his life. Because of the attacks of enemies threatening on every side, he was carried away by his men not openly but, as it were, secretly, and was buried in Saxony.

[Arnulf, formerly a monk of Saint-Nicaise at Reims, is made abbot of Gembloux. [Note: [Col. 0257] Added between the lines by an uncertain hand; F1, 3. Absent from B1, 3*, 4*, 4**, 5.]]

[Col. 0259A] (In the year 1138, 25 January.) Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, died during the Italian expedition, in the sixth year of his episcopate. Peter Leonis, who had sought to retain the apostolic see by force, departed this life. Peace was restored to the churches of God and to Pope Gregory, and seditions and battles ceased. [Note: [Col. 0259] After this, a space of one line is left. The first hand begins, writing at various times down to the beginning of 1145. “Prudent … another commands” is absent from B3*. 4*. 4**.]

Prudent reader, I have something to say to you, desiring rather to be taught than to teach. Blessed Gregory says that it is inappropriate to pile into books matters that lack solid weight. For diligent readers they are not useful but tiresome. Following this example, from the many things that happen we write down a few, but the more important ones, so that there may be preserved, according to the law of a chronicle, a truth briefly arranged concerning events done, and so that useless, indiscriminately accumulated prolixity may be avoided. [Note: [Col. 0259] The ink changes.]

[Col. 0259B] But if you judge that we have omitted something worthy of record, know that it has been left to those devoted to writings; for not all of us can do everything, nor do all wish to do everything. And someone is praised for having said wisely and briefly:

> What should I give, what should I not give? You refuse what another commands.

## 1138. R. 1. F. 2. A. 2. H. 8.

The king [Note: [Col. 0259] The hand changes.] of the Danes, on hearing of the death of the king of the English, devastated the borders of England with every kind of cruelty, having a great fleet and both cavalry and infantry forces. He said that the kingdom of England was owed more properly to him than to King Stephen and the Normans [Col. 0259C] by hereditary right from his ancestors and through the proximity of the bordering sea, rather than from William the Bastard’s seizure.

The king of the English, judging it dangerous to engage on equal terms at the first onset with so fierce an enemy, delayed and watched for an opportunity. He easily overcame them in battle when they were scattered far and wide and intent upon plunder; having killed or captured many, he compelled the rest to return home in disgrace.

After King Lothair’s death, the princes of the German kingdom, unwilling to endure the rule over them of anyone outside the royal stock, established Conrad, a man of royal family, as king on 22 February. He was the nephew, through a sister, of King Henry V, the fourth emperor of that name. Duke Henry of Bavaria, because he had married the daughter of King Lothair and had already received children by her, took very badly Conrad’s elevation to the kingship and his own exclusion. [Col. 0259D] He turned away from Conrad’s friendship and loyalty all whom he could.

Hugh, appointed archbishop of Cologne after Bruno, died abroad while travelling to Rome for consecration, and Arnulf succeeded him. Godfrey of Louvain, duke of Lotharingia, a great glory of his homeland, a man who knew how in his time to adapt himself fittingly to the age and to honour, died.

[Col. 0260A] ## 1139. 2. 3. 3. 9.

Conrad III, king of that name, made Godfrey, son of Duke Godfrey, successor to his father’s dignity, chiefly because he had given him in marriage the sister of his own wife. Duke Henry of Bavaria, still hostile to King Conrad and not heeding that saying of worldly wisdom, “By endurance, whatever is wrong to correct becomes lighter” (Horace, *Odes* I.24), reached the end of life through the incurable disease of grief.

The leading men of the English nation, dissenting from their king, while one party variously supported another, afflicted the whole nation; and this was worse because it suffered citizens as enemies not outwardly but inwardly. Marshes and springs, which for several years had so failed through drought that they were thought unable to flow again, were seen to the astonishment of many not merely to flow, but to send out waters greater than usual. [Note: [Col. 0259] After this, both pen and ink change.]

## 1140. 3. 4. 4. 10.

An eclipse of the sun occurred on the fourth day before the Nones of April, when day was already drawing toward evening and the sky entirely clear. The sun seemed to be surrounded by Egyptian darkness, as by a black veil.

Discord arose between Albero, bishop of Liège, and Henry, count of Namur; and many evils occurred on both sides: plundering and fires, slaughter and murders. The cause of this discord was that the count of Namur unexpectedly attacked the town called Fosses—so called because the site itself gives it that name. After capturing or killing many and carrying off much plunder, he burned the whole town together with the monastery of Blessed Foillan and destroyed whatever stone buildings [Col. 0260C] were more prominent.

Henry, count of Limburg, grieving that he had been deprived of the ducal dignity which his father and grandfather had held, rebelled against Duke Godfrey, invaded the revenues of neighbouring estates belonging to him, and wherever he prevailed spared none of Godfrey’s friends. Duke Godfrey, deeply aggrieved at his insolence, besieged the town of Saint-Trond with a great army of cavalry and infantry, compelled the citizens to surrender, and took hostages for their promised loyalty. [Note: [Col. 0259] The same hand which corrected 1132 also struck out here “the citizens … loyalty” and wrote above it: “He came to besiege it; but when the townspeople forestalled the siege, he received them back into favour, accepting their reconciliation.” The same reading is found in B1, 5, F1, 2, 3, but not B3*. 4*. 4**.]

Then, advancing with the same army and entering the town of Aachen, he sat with great power for two days in the judicial seat, exacted the dues which it befitted the duke of Lotharingia to exact, bound the townspeople to his loyalty, and [Col. 0260D] deterred them from supporting Count Henry by a display of his power.

## 1141. 4. 5. 5. 11.

King Conrad forced certain magnates of his realm who resisted him to obey his authority, by besieging or taking their strongholds. Stephen, king of the English, insufficiently wary of the uncertain loyalties of princes adhering to him with feigned friendship, sought to overcome certain enemies; but, abandoned by his own men and intercepted by his enemies, he was captured and consigned to custody.

The scourge of divine fire burned many; but through the intercession of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and other saints, God’s mercy aided many suffering from this affliction.

The king of the Jerusalemites, with his army, supported by the assistance of Christians visiting the holy places where the feet of the Lord had stood, besieged the people of Ascalon by land and sea after cutting them off from every supply; he also captured some nearer camps of the enemy. [Note: [Col. 0261] B4* greatly abbreviates what follows.]

Adelbero II, bishop of Liège, grieving that the castle of Bouillon, which Bishop Otbert had acquired for the bishopric of Liège with a large sum of silver and all its dependencies, had now for seven years been violently held by the fraudulent seizure of Count Reginald, and unwilling that so great an honour and advantage be taken from God’s church, both for the present and the future, waited for an opportunity to reclaim justly what the Church had unjustly lost. But God, who had given him the desire for this, granted effect to his good will. Seeing his opportunity, he besieged the castle with a great multitude of cavalry and infantry. Trusting more in divine than human aid, he ordered the body of Blessed Lambert to be carried to the site of the siege, hoping that what he had begun would prosper and be hastened. Nor was he disappointed in his hope. Within a few days, with God’s help and that of Saint Lambert, he recovered the castle, which a long siege would scarcely have regained after much time and excessive labour by many people.

What remarkable miracles occurred there, [Col. 0261C] and what still occur at the body of Blessed Lambert, we leave to wiser people to assess or, if they please, record, since it is not the business of this work. [Note: [Col. 0261] Here F2 adds: “Louis king of the Franks, while still a youth, granted the church of Bourges liberty to elect whomever they wished as archbishop, except Peter, kinsman of Aimery the chancellor; and he swore publicly upon the holy Gospels that, during his lifetime, that man would not become archbishop. Nevertheless, he was elected, went to Rome, and was consecrated by Lord Innocent, who said that the king, being a boy, must be instructed and restrained lest he become accustomed to such actions; and he added that there is no true liberty where someone is excepted by a prince, unless he has shown before an ecclesiastical judge that that person ought not to be elected. Then it is reported that another king excluded the returning archbishop, but Count Theobald received him into his own land. All the churches obeyed him. The king was angered with Count Theobald for this and stirred up almost all the magnates to wage war against him together with the king.”]

## 1142. R. 5. F. 6. A. 6. H. 12.

The King of the English, released from the captivity in which he had been held under certain terms of peace, again rules the English people. [Note: [Col. 0261] This whole year was written by another hand, with a continuous pen.] [Note: [Col. 0261] Here F2 adds: “Count Radulf marries the queen’s sister, having put aside his own wife; the king procures a divorce through his bishops, the woman having been denied a hearing—and this in hostility toward Count Theobald.”]

The King of the Franks, repeatedly warning Theobald, count of Blois, both in person and through his envoys not violently to invade and retain what belonged to others, when his own possessions could more than sufficiently satisfy him, perceived that these warnings were heard with deaf ears; he therefore resolved to act by force, lest he be held in contempt. Finally, attacking with a great retinue his castle called Vitry, he either captured or killed the townspeople and soldiers who resisted him. When the town had been set ablaze, the fire grew so greatly that it also burned the very strongly fortified castle within it, at great peril to its inhabitants. Those captured, slain, or burned in this battle or fire were reckoned at fifteen hundred. In the region of Louvain honey fell from heaven like rain; many proved by seeing, tasting, and handling it that it was genuine honey. Godfrey the Younger, duke of Lotharingia, dies in the fourth year of his duchy. [Note: [Col. 0261] “Godfrey—dies” is absent from B3*, 4*, 4**.]
