King Conrad held a court at the town called Frankfurt, with a great assembly of the magnates of his kingdom (7 June), and, by their counsel and judgment, confirmed what required confirmation and corrected what required correction. Then, attacking with no large company certain rebellious Slavs who were troubling the realm, he found them not, as he had thought, unprepared; and so, as they resisted courageously, he withdrew for the time being. Not long afterward, however, he came upon them unexpectedly while they were off their guard: he captured or killed many of them; he drowned in the adjacent river many who had turned to flight; and he compelled the rest to surrender, redeeming his favor at a great price. In the parish of Gembloux there was born a monstrous boy, a marvel and terror to those who looked upon him.

1143. 6. 7. 7. 13.

The kingdom of the Franks suffers great disturbance from wars, through the discord of the king and the princes, among whom Theobald, count of Blois, was preeminent. The King of the English, his realm not yet pacified, wished to subdue the disobedient but could not, because nowhere did he find secure loyalty; and he grieved that his efforts did not prosper but were frustrated. [Note: [Col. 0261] The first hand returns here, continuing with the same pen as far as the word “destroyed” at the beginning of the following year.]

King Conrad grants to the son of Duke Godfrey the Younger, still a little boy, whatever benefice or dignity his ancestors had held from the emperor’s hand. The pagans neighboring the Christians of Jerusalem, wearied by their misfortunes and by the Christians’ repeated attacks, made a peace treaty with them; and they received from them, to cultivate under tribute, the lands which the Christians had taken from them and which lay uncultivated. Pope Gregory, also called Innocent, dies (24 September). Wido, also called Celestine, succeeds as pope.

1144. 7. 8. 8. 14.

The winter of this year was dangerous and destructive because of excessive rain and violent wind, so much so that it either wholly overthrew or in large part destroyed woods, churches, towers, and buildings thought to be most secure. Wido, also called Celestine, the 163rd ruler of the Roman Church, dies (9 March). Gerard, also called Lucius, succeeds as pope. A most severe famine afflicted many this year; scarcity of bread impoverished many. It is said, moreover, to have prevailed so greatly in the kingdom of the English that a very great multitude of both sexes perished of hunger. Not only the poor and those of moderate means, but also many thought to possess sufficient resources, were compelled by the harsh sword of famine to emigrate elsewhere, so that, if they could not entirely avoid the evil of want, they might at least lessen it. The ripening and harvesting of the wheat crop came later than usual; for, hindered by excessive rain, the reapers could scarcely reap on 8 Kalends of September [25 August], whereas we have sometimes seen them reap on 8 Kalends of August [25 July]. Fulk IV, king of Jerusalem, dies in the fifteenth year of his reign. His son Baldwin succeeds him.

The King of the Franks, knowing that disturbance of the head is disturbance of the limbs, agrees to make an alliance with Theobald, count of Blois, in order to calm the disorders of his kingdom. King Conrad, knowing on his own account, and through the admonitions of religious men, how much reverence is owed to the ecclesiastical order—to which God says, “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye”—used royal authority to compel those whom he knew, puffed up by the pride of secular power, to be acting insolently against bishops or other prelates of the holy Church, to desist from their insolence and make proper satisfaction to those whom they had offended. [Note: [Col. 0263] “Conrad—satisfaction” is absent from B4*.]

Vines and fruit-bearing trees did not yield their usual abundance, but were difficult in their produce and scanty and bitter in their fruits. [Note: [Col. 0263] After this F1 and F2 add: “Count Godfrey, brother of Count Baldwin, dies.”]

1145. R. 8. F. 9. A. 9. H. 1.

The kingdom of the Christians, which they acquired after exterminating the multitude of pagans possessing Jerusalem and its neighboring cities, reaches the fifty-first year of its beginning. Praise and glory belong to Christ, because Christians, with his help, possess the region in which Christ, through himself and through the apostles, inaugurated the Christian religion. [Note: [Col. 0263] “Kingdom—religion” is absent from B3*, 4*. After this F2 adds: “By the judgment of Pope Lucius, the archbishop of Tours obtained against the archbishop of Dol the subjection of the church of Dol, and deprived it of the use of the pallium which it had possessed for a very long time. Ashamed by this, the said archbishop of Dol did not dare return, but went to Roger, king of Sicily, who gave him the archbishopric of Capua.”]

Gerard, also called Lucius, pope, dies (25 February). Bernard, also called Eugenius, the 165th, succeeds him.

At Reims, in the monastery of Saint Remigius, Saint Gibrian the Scot shines by many miracles and is visited by a great concourse of people. [Note: [Col. 0263] From here follows the seventh hand, proceeding with the same pen and ink to the end of the codex.] Adelbero, bishop of Liège, dies. Henry, chosen from the clergy of Saint Lambert, the second bishop of this name, succeeds him. [Note: [Col. 0263] “Adelbero—succeeds” is absent from B3*, 4*.]

The city of Edessa, also called Roais, long possessed by Christians, is captured through Christian negligence and pagan treachery. All full-grown Christians found in it are slaughtered; youths of both sexes are sold as male and female slaves through the various provinces of the pagans. The Northmen, who had been subject to Henry, king of the English, holding his successor Stephen in little account, submit themselves to the rule of the count of Anjou. King Conrad celebrated Pentecost at Athernach, near Trier (3 June), and compelled certain rebels against him to surrender by attacking and defeating them.

1146. 9. 10. 10. 2.

The heresy of the Eunites springs up within Britain. Their leader was a man of perverse mind named Eon; although he was unlearned and could scarcely recognize even the letters of the alphabet, he nevertheless discoursed and disputed concerning the divine books with a polluted mouth. In wicked presumption, without sacred orders, he unworthily celebrated Masses, for the error and ruin of lost people; he even ordained bishops and archbishops for those who adhered to him. He also committed many other criminal acts contrary to the divine law. At last, filled with a diabolical spirit, he broke out into such madness that he said, and compelled others to believe, that he was the Son of God, asserting that he was the one through whom priests in church customarily conclude the general collect, saying, “Through the same our Lord.” But it is good to cover in silence the shameful and execrable acts which these heretics, called Eunites—that is, followers of Eon—perform in secret, lest they instill horror in weak hearers or even give rise to error.

The most grievous famine, long in preparation, prevailed so widely and so greatly that those who, from regard for God or compassionate feeling, stretched out a hand of mercy toward the swelling multitude of poor people could by no means support them without great burden. Famine also reduced many who had abounded in food and other necessities to begging. Western Christians, grieving over the destruction of the city of Edessa, also called Rohais, which the pagans had ravaged in the preceding year and had defiled there the practice of Christianity with every kind of filth, so much so that their ruler even made his bed upon the holy altar in the principal basilica and there lay with a prostitute, in insult and contempt of the highest God—[Note: [Col. 0263] “so much so—lay” is absent from B3*, 4*, 4**.]—moved, I say, by righteous grief at all these things, resolve unanimously and with equal agreement to set out to fight them. All were so ready and eager for this expedition that King Conrad of Germany and King Louis of France, encouraged by the exhortations of religious men [Note: [Col. 0263] B3*, 4*, 4** add: “and especially of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.”], likewise girded themselves for this campaign with willing hearts.

[Col. 0265A] 1147. R. 10. F. 11. A. 11. H. 3.

King Conrad raises his son Henry to kingship at Aachen (30 March), lest after his death the kingdom remain without a ruler and some disturbance of affairs arise. Many Christians, having set out over the English sea to fight the Saracens, at length crossed the sea and landed in Galicia at Saint James. Marching their army from there, they reached the most powerful city of the Saracens, called Ulixibona from the name of its founder. There they fought the Saracens with varying fortune in war; with God’s aid they gained victory, and, having killed or expelled the Saracens, peacefully possessed the city itself and all the surrounding region.

There was an eclipse of the sun about the third hour of the day, on 7 Kalends of November [26 October]. Before the sun’s light had yet been wholly restored, while eclipse-darkness still lay around, many saw a visible star in the sky. Others also said that they had seen divine majesty in the very disk of the sun, in the manner in which painters are accustomed to depict it in books. On the Nativity of the Lord, lightning struck a church at Jerusalem and knocked two large stones from a stone column near the Lord’s sepulchre. Passing thence to the place of the baptistery, it shattered into small pieces a hollow marble stone that held baptismal water. Then flying on to Mount Sion, it severely damaged a very beautiful tower of the basilica.

1148. 11. 12. 12. 4.

Kings Conrad and Louis, who had set out overseas in the preceding year with an innumerable army to fight the pagans, accomplished nothing successfully. Their army was worn down by such calamities—by famine, disease, and the sword of enemies—that scarcely a few returned home from so many thousands of that vast multitude. Although these things occurred by a hidden judgment of God, unknown to us, it is nevertheless certain that in that hostile territory they committed many crimes, many unlawful and shameful acts; and therefore, as God’s wrath rose against them, all their endeavor came to nothing. Nor will you readily find in histories or annals that from the beginning of Christianity to this time so great a multitude of God’s people perished so suddenly and miserably as has now occurred.

Pope Eugenius, having assembled a general synod at Reims, discussed and confirmed many matters concerning the condition of the Church. Among other things, he decreed that the enactments of his predecessor Pope Innocent should remain valid and unshaken, while whatever the antipope Peter Leonis had decreed or ordained should be regarded as void. He proclaimed this judgment: “We annul and judge void the ordinations made by the son of Peter Leonis and by other schismatics and heretics.” At this synod the aforesaid heretic Eon was brought and presented to the pope by a certain Catholic bishop of Brittany. Having then been examined and convicted before all concerning his perverse heresy, he retained his life and limbs at the request of the bishop who had brought him; nevertheless, by the pope’s command he was confined in custody, and there died not long afterward. It is said that as many as eleven hundred archbishops, bishops, and abbots attended this synod.

Terrors from heaven and storms beyond the usual measure occurred, sometimes more mildly, sometimes more severely. In March, on 8 Kalends of April [25 March], when day was already declining toward evening, there were most severe thunders, with immense lightning and driving rain. It did not then happen, as it usually does at other times, that the sound gradually reached human ears and then grew greater; rather, that crash of thunder burst out so suddenly and unexpectedly that it shook all who heard it with great fear and astonishment. Likewise, in July a great storm of thunder and lightning broke out in various places; but at the castle of Laon the force of the storm raged more fiercely than elsewhere. For, while the monks were singing Compline in the monastery of Saint Vincent, lightning struck the basilica and struck dead two monks standing in the choir; then flying to the high altar, it burned the linen cloths covering the altar. Yet a remarkable thing occurred there: the greater cloth, which surrounded the whole altar from above, could not burn although the other cloths were burning. It is said that many other things occurred in the same basilica from the lightning strike; but these are sufficient to make known how great is the terror of divine severity.

The city of Cambrai was largely consumed by fire, together with the principal church, the cloister, the bishop’s palace, and the monastery of Saint Aubert. [Note: [Col. 0265D] Here F3 ends, its final folio having been lost.] This year the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre in the same city was also burned, only a few years after its preceding conflagration.

# Supplement of Gembloux

[Col. 0265]

[Col. 0265D] Hand 1ζ, of the twelfth century, wrote after 1131 and before 1137. B3*, F1, F2, and F3 contain the same material.

771. The head of John the Baptist is transferred from Alexandria to Aquitaine as follows. A monk of praiseworthy life, named Felician, from the regions of Gaul, went with a few companions to Jerusalem for prayer. After fulfilling the offices of pious devotion, warned by an angelic communication, he made for Alexandria. There, as the same angel revealed it, he took up the head of John the Baptist from the place where Theophilus, bishop of that city, had formerly deposited it, and carried it into Aquitaine, into the territory of Angoulême. King Pippin was then staying there in the palace called Angériac; seeing that through Felician daily benefits came to the inhabitants and frequent victories over Aquitanian enemies to himself, he built a basilica of royal workmanship not far from the bank of the river Vulturnus, and, having constructed within it a ciborium of marvelous workmanship, deposited there with fitting adornment the head of the Forerunner. He also established a monastery of monks there and magnificently enriched it with royal estates. [Note: [Col. 0267] Partly in an erasure of two lines, the remainder in the margin. Then hand 1η added: “Turn the leaf to this sign θ, and it continues in the margin of the verso: θ The same, etc.,” as we shall give immediately under 1η.]

876. Duke Rollo entered Normandy with his men and ruled there for fifty-three years. From him is derived the genealogy of the dukes of Normandy and of the kings descended from them who subsequently ruled the English people.

Hand 1η, from Liège, which also wrote in 1137–1145. The same material is in B3* (which lacks 987, 991, 1012, 1037, 1042, 1048, 1072, and 1092), F1, F2 (which lacks 1042), and F3.

465. (Gregory of Tours.) The present year, the sixty-fourth from the passing of Saint Martin, is distinguished by the translation of his most reverend body. For, with that prerogative by which, while living, and even when dead, he shone with incomparable splendor of miracles, Saint Perpetuus, bishop of the city of Tours, built over him, in place of the earlier small shrine, a church of great magnificence, so that he vaulted the entire structure, supported by the marvelous arrangement of one hundred and twenty columns. Trusting in angelic assistance, he raised the holy body from the tomb and transferred it, on 4 Nones of July [4 July], namely the annual day of his consecration as bishop, to the place in which it is now venerated; and afterward dedicated the church itself on the same day. Thus it happens that, as three festivals coincide on one day—the ordination to the episcopate, the translation of the body, and the dedication of his basilica—Saint Martin is annually celebrated on 4 Nones of July with the most solemn devotion of all the people of the province. The place in which his most sacred body rests, separated from the city of Tours toward the west by a short stretch of level ground, is called Châteauneuf. There, in the aforesaid church, decently placed beneath a ciborium clothed with gold, silver, and gems, it is made illustrious by such a magnificence of miracles that it possesses apostolic glory throughout the whole world of Christianity. [Note: [Col. 0267] In an erasure.]

564. This Lothair built and endowed with royal generosity the monastery of Saint Medard in the city of Soissons, and chose there a place of burial. [Note: [Col. 0267] In the margin.]

592. He [Gregory] decreed that monks in the office of priestly rank should exercise the power of binding and loosing. [Note: [Col. 0267] In the margin.]

651. Saint Theodard succeeded him [Remaclus] in episcopal government. [Note: [Col. 0267] In the margin. Cf. the Annals of Lobbes.]

688. Innocent XXXVIII decreed that the kiss of peace should be given. [Note: [Col. 0267] Between the lines.]

694. (Life of Lambert.) The people of the Toxandri, who until that time had been devoted to the errors of idolatry, were converted to faith in Christ by the preaching of Saint Lambert, bishop of Maastricht. [Note: [Col. 0267] In an erasure of one line.]

710. From that time Liège was raised up and enlarged into a city. [Note: [Col. 0267] In the margin.]

711. (Saint Oda . . . died) in a village situated on the Meuse called Amay. [Note: [Col. 0267] Between the lines.]

735. (Saint Hubert died.) Florbert succeeds. [Note: [Col. 0267] In the margin.]

771. The same king [Pippin] made a reservoir spring, from which an aqueduct flowed underground through masonry structures into his palace from nearly two thousand [units] away. Dividing this water, he conducted it through iron and bronze into the basilica of Saint John the Baptist, so that beneath the ciborium it welled up through the hollow interior of a marble column; there the washing of holy baptism was performed in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and Saint John the Baptist, and the water then returned into the same reservoir. This monastery is called Angély. [Note: [Col. 0267] In the margin.]

849. (Concerning Saint Helena) deposited in the monastery of Saint Peter called Hautvilliers.

890. Bishop Franco acquired for the bishopric of Liège the abbey of Lobbes and the provostship of Fosses with their appurtenances.

958. (Erluinus, first abbot of Gembloux) by certain men hostile to holy religion. [Note: [Col. 0267] Between the lines.] (Read elsewhere in the passage.)

1042. (There.) Bishop Nihard dies.

1072. Abbot Mysac dies; Tietmar succeeds.

1092. Abbot Tietmar dies; Lietard succeeds.

1010. In the monastery of Florennes, monks were established in place of the clerics who had served there until that time.

1088. The monastery of Saint John at Florennes was burned in the sixty-second year of its consecration.

1133. Henry, king of the English, died in December, a man very generous to the poor and to the churches of God. [Note: [Col. 0269] Between the lines, but deleted in red ink.]

1134. In this year construction began on the hermitage of Mont-Dieu, on 10 Kalends of June [23 May].

1135. Louis, king of the Franks, died; his namesake son succeeded him. [Note: [Col. 0269] In an erasure.]

Hand 1κ, of the end of the twelfth century; the same material is in F1, F2, and F3.

1131. On the island of Scania in Denmark, eight bishops, together with their king’s son and many people, perished in a battle fought publicly on the second weekday of Pentecost.

1148. The Danes, Westphalians, and dukes of the Saxons agreed that, while others went to Jerusalem against the Saracens, they themselves would either utterly destroy the neighboring Slav people or compel them to become Christian. When the two sides had already come to arms, the Germans, having accepted money, sold out the Danes; withdrawing once battle had begun, they caused the swords of the Slavs to kill many thousands of Danes.

Hand 1λ, of the twelfth century; the same material occurs in B3*, 4* (excepting 1083 and 1087), F2 (excepting 1603 and 1130), and F3.

1083. Afflighem—attacks. [Note: [Col. 0269] See the Supplement of Afflighem.]

1087. This year Cnut, king of the Danes, is killed. Lord Fulgentius, the first abbot of the monastery of Afflighem, was elected this year on the feast of Saint Martin. [Note: [Col. 0269] See the Supplement of Afflighem.]

1121. Henry, king of the English, joined in marriage to himself Adelais, daughter of Duke Godfrey, and established her as queen in England. This king ruled his realm with great wisdom, restrained every movement of tyrants by remarkable ingenuity, and enriched churches with a generous hand. [Note: [Col. 0269] In the margin. What we have printed in slanting letters has been cut away.]

1142. (Concerning the monstrous boy) but he died shortly afterward. Godfrey the Younger, duke of Lotharingia, cut off by untimely death in the fourth year of his duchy, was consumed by a liver disease and buried at Louvain in the church. His namesake son succeeds, still in his first year of life. [Note: [Col. 0269] In the margin.]

1690. Saint Bernard, later the first abbot of Clairvaux, is born in Burgundy. [Note: [Col. 0269] Added by a thirteenth-century hand and by one F2 hand among the remaining hands.]

# Supplement of Anchin

[Col. 0269]

What was added to Sigebert at the monastery of Anchin, near Douai, can now be determined only by conjecture, since codex B has perished. For the additions in the remaining manuscripts, all of which we have seen above to derive from B, are in some cases found only in individual codices and must accordingly be assigned to those codices; in other cases they occur now in several, now in all, and these cannot be explained unless a common source is posited. We therefore give these latter additions here collected together. They must have been written in 1113, when codex B was copied, before Anselm had added anything to Sigebert beyond the year 1112. Another writer then, after 1148, added the continuation of Anselm, that of Gembloux, and one of his own. This too can be reconstructed only conjecturally. For B3* and B5 agree word for word in many places, and precisely the same material occurs in B4* and 4** without any addition. It is therefore more than likely that these also were present in B, the common source of these codices. We print them from B3*, B5*, and B4*, chiefly following the last, since it has refrained from interpolations. The continuator appears at first to have written only as far as the year 1155; for after this year the Afflighem continuation entirely abandons his traces. From then on we know him only from B4* and B5, but do not know his end, since B4* evidently laid down the pen in the middle of a sentence. The author not infrequently copied the Annals of Blandain.

651. (Landelin . . . founder of the monastery of Lobbes) of Aulne, Waulsort, and Crespin, where he rests in the body with his disciples Adelin and Domitian. [Note: [Col. 0269] Added by B1, 4*, 4**, 5, C1, 2*, 3, 4*, D, and E.]

685. Saint Amatus is exiled by King Theuderic at the counsel of Ebroin. [Note: [Col. 0269] Added by C1, 2*, 3, D, and E.]

690. Saint Amatus dies. [Note: [Col. 0269] Added by B4*, 4**, C1, 2*, 3, 4*.]

773. (Ivo’s *Panormia*.) Pope Adrian summoned Charles to Rome to defend the possessions of the Church. On his way, Charles besieged Pavia; leaving his army there, he reached Rome and celebrated Holy Easter there. Returning afterward, he captured Pavia; then he returned again to Rome, established a synod with Pope Adrian and 153 other religious bishops and abbots, at which Pope Adrian, with the whole synod, gave him the right to elect the pontiff and appoint the Apostolic See, together with the dignity of the patriciate. Moreover, he decreed that archbishops and bishops in each province should receive investiture from him, and that no bishop should be consecrated by anyone unless he were approved and invested by the king. He anathematized all who rebelled against this decree; unless they repented, their goods were to be confiscated. [Note: [Col. 0271] Added by B1, 2, 4**—in an erasure, in a hand slightly different but plainly contemporary—C1, 2*, 3, D, E. Hirsch, p. 42, rightly demonstrates that Charles was not at Rome in that year; but he errs in thinking that this passage had been admitted by Sigebert into his chronicle and later deleted by a certain monk. Sigebert never had it. See further *Monumenta Legum* II, 2, 160, note.]

1048. The venerable Hugh succeeds Odilo of Cluny. [Note: [Col. 0271] Added by C1, 2*, 3, 4*, D, and E.]

1076. Lietbert, bishop of Cambrai, dies; Gerard succeeds him. [Note: [Col. 0271] Added by B1, 2, C1, 2*, 3.] Baldwin the boy, brother of Arnold, who was slain at Dour, fought against the army of his uncle Robert and defeated him in battle. [Note: [Col. 0271] Added by B1, 2, 4**, 5, C1, 2*, 3, D, and E.] (The frost . . . until) the middle of April, its hardness lasting until the Kalends of April [1 April]. [Note: [Col. 0271] Added by C1, 2*, 3, 4*.]

1079. In this year the monastery of the Holy Savior was begun on the island called Anchin by the distinguished men Sicher and Walter. [Note: [Col. 0271] Added by B2, C1, 2*, D, E. B1, 4*, 4**, 5, and C3 have the same material, but these also add what follows, which the former lack.] Sicher had a wife named Matilda, noble indeed in birth but nobler in character. By repeatedly exhorting her husband, she urged him to undertake this work, especially because a certain holy man, Gordian by name, was said once to have lived there as a hermit. Thus it came about that these men, frequently conferring there, encouraged one another; and, after deliberation, they approached Anselm of Ribemont, a most noble man, and requested the island from him, since it was under his jurisdiction. Hearing their request, Anselm was greatly pleased and without delay freely granted what they asked.

Then, proceeding together by agreement, they approached Gerard, bishop of the city of Cambrai, to whose diocese the place then belonged. They explained their intention and, because they were his parishioners, asked him to assent to their vow. Upon hearing them, the venerable bishop willingly consented. Receiving the estate from Anselm’s hand, who held it from him as a benefice, he handed it over to them with the adjoining reed-bed. Having received it, they began to build a monastery there and endowed it as well as they could from their own allodial lands. Men devoted to God gathered there, dedicating themselves to Christ with their small possessions and desiring to be his little flock. The aforesaid bishop, caring for them, sent them two monks of upright life from the monastery of Hasnon to instruct them. To one of these, Alard by name, he entrusted their care and ordained him abbot.

Since the occasion has presented itself, it is pleasing briefly to disclose how great were his simplicity and goodness. If circumstances required him to travel somewhere, he did not choose the better horse for himself; indeed, he often guided the animal on which he rode with a halter instead of a bridle. When the monks sat in the cloister, he sat among them and behaved with sobriety like any one of them, conversing familiarly with them and forgetting that he was their lord. If anyone wished to show him reverence by kissing his hands or knees or in any other way, he forbade it with a certain rebuke, saying that he permitted them this custom, but declaring that those who would come after him would exact such reverence. Yet in reporting this we do not attack those who appropriately allow such acts to be done to them according to ecclesiastical custom.

Seeing that these brothers diligently applied themselves to their undertaking, the aforesaid bishop granted that church every liberty within his power, except that he retained in his own hand the staff of government, so that he might give it to the person canonically elected by the community. Moreover, he granted them certain altars and conferred countless benefits upon them. In the church of Saint Mary at Cambrai, over which the same Gerard presided as bishop, there was a venerable dean named Hugh. He encouraged both the bishop himself and other faithful men of both orders at Cambrai to be generous toward the aforesaid monastery. He too carried nearly all his substance there and first built the monastery, the brothers’ dwellings, and a guesthouse.

1080. At this time, by God’s permission, the monastery of Anchin was also burned through the carelessness of the brothers. [Note: [Col. 0271] Added by B2, 5, C1, 2*. B5 alone has what follows, “because—rest.”] For one of the brothers, carelessly carrying a light around his bed in the evening, suddenly set fire to the straw; immediately the nearby wall was scorched as the flame licked at the bedding, and from this the rest [cf. the Annals of Anchin].

1084. Baldwin, count of Mons, married Ida. [Note: [Col. 0271] Added by B1, 5, C1, 2*, D, E.]

1086. Countess Richildis dies. [Note: [Col. 0271] Added by B1, 2, 4*, 4**, 5, C1, 2*, 3.] (There.) This year the church of this monastery of Anchin was consecrated, in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and his mother Saint Mary, by Lord Gerard, bishop of Cambrai. The same bishop decreed that the feast of those saints whose relics had been brought here should be celebrated every year in this place. [Note: [Col. 0271] Added by B2, 5, C1, 2*, which lacks “this,” “in honor—Mary,” and “and decreed—place.”]

1087. Alard, first abbot of this church of Anchin, dies; (there) Alelmus from Normandy, of the monastery of Bec, succeeds him. [Note: [Col. 0271] Added by B5, C1, 2*.]

1088. Alelmus, second abbot of the monastery of Anchin, dies. (There.) Those suffering from fever experienced how great was his goodness: while sleeping at his tomb, they often laid aside their fever together with sleep. Haimericus, a monk from Arras learned in letters, succeeds him. [Note: [Col. 0271] Added by B5, C1.]

1090. At that time a monk named Gelduin came to Anchin. Formerly a monk of Laon and abbot of Saint Michael of Thiérache, he left his abbacy for love of God and became a recluse at Anchin. [Note: [Col. 0271] Added by B1, 4*, 4**, 5, C1, 2*, 3, D.]

1092. Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, dies (ibid.), [Col. 0273A] [“he loved our monastery greatly and strove to raise it in dignity. Hence it was ordained that at the morning Mass every day, if it is the Mass for the dead, the collect for him and his fellow bishops should be said in the second place” [Note: [Col. 0273] *qui—dicatur* is found in B5 alone.].] Walcher succeeds him [Note: [Col. 0273] added by B1, 2, 4*, 4**, 5, C1, 2*, 3, D, F3.]. In the suburb of Tournai, on the north side of the city, Odo of Orléans begins to build the monastery of Saint Martin, on 2 May, a Sunday. For, arriving there as agreed on that day, accompanied by a solemn procession led by Lord Radbod, bishop of that city, and by the clerics subject to him from the church of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, together with a very great multitude of people, he received the site from the same bishop, along with four brothers who were to serve God there with him under the canonical rule, wearing clerical dress. Odo, a native of Orléans, [Col. 0273B] then scholasticus at Tournai, was celebrated as inferior in fame to none on this side of the Alps for the art of dialectic and knowledge of the other liberal arts. Consequently clerics flocked to him from every quarter. One man, arriving from a foreign land, offered him a golden ring, upon which this one-line verse was inscribed: “A golden ring befits Odo of Orléans.” We have related these things so that it may be inferred from them how much honour he might have enjoyed in one of the royal churches, had he aspired to it; but he preferred to cleave to Christ in a place of poverty and want [Note: [Col. 0273] added by B1, 2, (which perhaps lacked *Ex condicto—indigentiae*), 4*, 4**, C3.].

1093. The church of Saint George of Hesdin is conveyed to the church of Anchin [Note: [Col. 0273] added by B4**; in the margin of B5; C1.]. As the fervour of religious devotion grew strong, Odo of Orléans, together with the other brothers established with him in this monastery of Saint Martin at Tournai, receives the monastic habit. And because the man’s fame, as we have said, had spread so widely, and so great a light could not remain long hidden under a bushel, by God’s ordering—who intended thereafter to exalt him more highly—the whole congregation, now grown more numerous by God’s bounty, unanimously and with one desire appointed Odo himself as its abbot, with the assent of the already mentioned Bishop Radbod. Divine grace so attended him that, although before his arrival the same place had lain deserted for almost three hundred years and had possessed no dependencies whatsoever, within twelve years he gathered there more than seventy monks, building sufficient workshops for them and acquiring so great an extent of fields and such resources [Col. 0273D] as more than sufficed for the necessary uses both of arriving guests and of the resident monks [Note: [Col. 0273] added by B1, 4*, 4**, C3.].

1095. Walcher having been expelled from the bishopric of Cambrai, Manasses succeeds him [Note: [Col. 0273] added by B1, 2, 4**, 5, C1, 2*, 3, 4*, D, E.].

1096. (They omit:) Certain Jews, led by zeal for maintaining [Col. 0274A] the law of their ancestral country, slaughter one another; others, pretending for a time to believe, later return to Judaism [Note: [Col. 0273] added by B3*, C1, 2*, 3, 4*, D, E.]. (Among the princes marked with the cross:) Anselm of Ribemont, founder of the church of Anchin [Note: [Col. 0273] added by B1, 5, C2*, 3, 4*.].

1099. While the Christians were vigorously defeating the Turks and claiming their cities and castles by warfare, it happened at a very strongly fortified castle named Arqa, situated eight days’ journey this side of Jerusalem, that many of them perished. Among them Anselm of Ribemont died after being struck on the head by a stone, repeating only these words three times after receiving the wound: “God, help me” [Note: [Col. 0273] added by B5? C1, 2*, 3, 4*, D.].

1100. Robert, count of Flanders, returning home from Jerusalem, brought with him the arm of Saint [Col. 0274B] George the martyr, which he sent to the church of Anchin [Note: [Col. 0273] added by B1, 2, 4**; in the margin of 5; C1, 2*, 3, D, E.] [and which was brought to Anchin by the venerable Haimeric, abbot of that place, on 20 June [Note: [Col. 0273] added by B1, 5, C1, 3.] (cf. Annals of Anchin).].

1102. (Annals of Anchin.) Haimeric, the third abbot of Anchin, dies; Gelduin succeeds him [Note: [Col. 0273] added by B5, C5.].

1105. Manasses, bishop of Cambrai, having assumed the monastic habit, Odo, first abbot of the church from the monastery of Saint Martin at Tournai, succeeds him in the bishopric [Note: [Col. 0273] added by B1, 2, 4*, 4**, 5, C1, 2*, 3, 4*, 5.].

1109. Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, also dies; and Hugh, abbot of Cluny; Pons succeeds him [Note: [Col. 0273] added by B1, 2, 5, C1, 3, 5, D.]. In this same year Gelduin, fourth abbot of Anchin, weary of the burden of government and preferring [Col. 0274C] the leisure of the enclosure he had formerly practised, relinquished the care of souls and again became a recluse at Saint-Bertin (cf. ibid.). Robert, a monk of the same monastery, succeeded him in pastoral care. I refrain from telling how he was elected, lest the account of our narrative offend anyone [Note: [Col. 0273] added by B2, 5, C1, 5.]. In this year many were afflicted with the sacred fire, their limbs blackening like coals [Note: [Col. 0273] added by B1, 2, 5, C1, 2*, 3, 5, D.].

1111. Robert, fifth abbot of the monastery of Anchin, distressed that the church entrusted to him was being harassed by the persecution of certain laymen, and also because this was imputed to him, took counsel and resigned the abbacy. Lord Alvisus succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0273] added by B2, 5, C1, 5.] [a monk of Saint-Bertin, later bishop of Arras [Note: [Col. 0273] added by C1, 5.] (cf. ibid.).].

[Col. 0274D] 1130. Lord Aibert, formerly a monk of the monastery of Crespin [Note: [Col. 0273D] Crespin, diocese of Cambrai.], flourished in Gaul as a recluse, with the approval and consent of Abbot Lambert: a man comparable in our time to no one, or to scarcely anyone at all. For twenty-four years he abstained from all bread, and for the same number from every drink, except two; a thing [Col. 0275A] marvellous to tell. Robert, archdeacon of Ostrevent, has illuminated his life in a careful style [Note: [Col. 0275] added by B1, 5.].

1131. When Lord Robert, bishop of Arras, died, Lord Alvisus, sixth abbot of the church of Anchin, succeeded him in the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0275] added by B2, 5.], a man of great religious devotion and exceptional strictness (cf. ibid.). Lord Gozwin is appointed in his place as seventh abbot in the church of Anchin [Note: [Col. 0275] added by B5.].

1134. At this time the chapel, begun long before by Lord Aibert, was completed by God’s will and help. Lietard, bishop of Cambrai, was invited to bless it, and with great rejoicing devoutly blessed it. For forty days it was so frequented, by God’s prompting, from almost every part of the kingdom that scarcely, or never before, [Note: [Col. 0275] I so conjecture; B1 has *ad*.] had anyone seen a mortal man like him [Col. 0275B]. At the same time, likewise, a church at Oscannum was consecrated by the bishop of Reims. The archbishop, bishops, and abbots of the province, supporting it, began to prevent the crowds from visiting Lord Aibert and to speak many slanders concerning him—matters which we thought it better to pass over in silence. Their opposition prevailed so far that, as a test, they sent to him Lord Absalon, abbot of Saint-Amand, and Parvinus, abbot of the Holy Sepulchre [Note: [Col. 0275D] at Cambrai.], to determine whether he was such and so great a man as the report concerning him, spread abroad, had struck the ears of all. Having discovered his holiness, they returned to those who had sent them, praising God in all things [Note: [Col. 0275] added by B1.].

1135. Lord Aibert, of pious memory, died and [Col. 0275C] left us perpetual sorrow at his absence, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1135, the twenty-fifth year of his enclosure, on holy Easter day [Note: [Col. 0275] added by B1.].

1149. R. 12. F. 13. A. 13. H. 5.

Conrad, king of the Germans, and Louis, king of the Franks, break camp and return from the journey to Jerusalem without any successful result: never had such misfortune befallen so great an army. (Annals of Blandain.) A very severe winter set in and prevailed for four months.

1150. 13. 14. 14. 6.

A conflict arose between Henry, bishop of Liège, and Henry, count of Namur. Therefore [Col. 0275D] armies having been assembled on both sides, they joined battle. The bishop proved superior and won the victory, though not without the slaughter of many.

1151. 14. 15. 15. 7.

The earth produced abundant crops; but, as flooding rains devastated everything from the feast of Saint John until the middle of August, they scarcely reached maturity. For wine and the other fruits failed in part; and what was gathered from the grapes turned sour.

[Col. 0276A] 1152. 15. 16. 16. 8.

(Annals of Blandain.) Emperor Conrad dies; his cousin Frederick succeeds him. In the church of Saint Nicholas, built in the town of Brussels, Saint Mary, Mother of Jesus Christ, performed many miracles. (Ibid.) The church of Saint-Bertin, with all its dependencies, was burned on the very feast of Saint-Bertin, while the solemnities of Matins were being celebrated.

1153. 1. 17. 17. 9.

A solar eclipse occurred on 26 January, the second feria; on 9 February, likewise the second feria, thunder was heard. (Ibid.) Pope Eugenius dies [Note: [Col. 0275D] D. 7 July.]; Conrad, the 158th pope, bishop of Santa Sabina, called Anastasius, vicar of his predecessor the lord pope, succeeds him [Col. 0276B]. Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, too—who had arisen like the morning star and was illuminating our order—departed to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0276D] D. 21 August.]. His life and teaching excelled so greatly that anything said in his praise falls short. A violent storm, making its course through our regions as though ploughing a furrow, in the course of one day consumed everything in its path as though with flames and left lamentable traces. (19 August.) Ascalon was captured by the army of the Lord at Jerusalem and occupied by our people, but only after much labour and a long war, during which the army had first suffered many dangers and grievous losses. For [Note: [Col. 0275] *Namque—possessa* is absent from B5.] in the days near the Purification of the Holy Mother of God, the king of Jerusalem set [Col. 0276C] out on campaign, surrounded the city with his army, and prolonged the siege until the feast of the Assumption of that most holy Virgin. On the day after that most sacred feast, he moved a tower with its engines up to the wall; and through underground engineering the wall was made to fall, affording our men a wide entrance. The first to break in with his troop was the provost and leader of that army, who served the Temple by profession of a brotherly fellowship. Reaching the city’s street surrounded by the ranks of his men, he held his ground there; hemmed in by the narrow streets, enclosed by walls, overshadowed by the roofs of houses, and surrounded by crowds converging from every direction, he was overwhelmed and cut down with all his company. Their heads were heaped into one pile, to be displayed to the king of Babylon [Col. 0276D] as a token of victory; their bodies were hung upon the wall, while the enemy taunted us and provoked God’s army with blasphemous words. At last our men, strengthened in the Lord, commending themselves to the Lord in most devout prayers and making vows to the Holy Mother of God, approached the wall on the third day. They brought up military implements, siege-engines, and ballistae, standing firm in faith. The Lord’s Cross went before the host in the patriarch’s hands. Then, by a manifest power of the Lord, all were struck with blindness, [Col. 0277A] so that, when the ballista hurled millstones with its force into their midst, none saw the stone coming in order to move from its path and evade its blow. Finally compelled, they surrender the city into the king’s hands; and from that time Ascalon became ours and was occupied by our people [Note: [Col. 0277] What follows is given from B4, 5, since from this point B3 wholly abandons all trace of this continuation.]: a city fortified by 150 very strong towers, with roofed upper chambers over its streets like vaulted crypts with panelled ceilings, and in some sense impregnable.

1154. R. 2. F. 18. A. 18. H. 10.

Pope Anastasius departed this life. Nicholas, previously called bishop of Albano, succeeds him; his name was changed, and he became Pope Adrian, the 159th (cf. Annals of Blandain). Henry was established as king in England; his grandfather was that great and famous king of England, [Col. 0277B] Henry. For his daughter, who was and was called empress because she had married the emperor, after the latter’s death was joined in marriage to the count of Anjou and bore this Henry and his brothers to him. While he was still an infant at his nurse’s breast, after the death of his grandfather King Henry he was taken to England and, following the election of all the princes and their sworn oaths, was confirmed in the kingdom. His kinsman Count Stephen was elected to govern the realm and rear him (cf. Annals of Blandain). Stephen, persuaded by the princes, seized and held the kingdom. On learning this, the empress entered England with an army; many severe battles were fought, and she performed many bold deeds. At last, after many years, when her son, [Col. 0277C] the young Henry, had grown up, and Stephen had died suddenly, by a death not sufficiently known, she established her son Henry in the kingdom.

1155. 3. 19. 1. 11.

Emperor Frederick, having set out in the preceding year, reached Rome in this year, worn down by many hardships on the journey and by various hostile opponents, all of whom he compelled to surrender and submit. But since he was by no means received by the Roman leaders, he entered Rome by armed force. Finding Pope Adrian friendly and favourable to him, he was confirmed and crowned with the imperial blessing in the church of Saint Peter. Meanwhile, his army, not ignorant of the enemy’s ambushes, surrounded the whole camp at Saint Peter’s church under arms, until, when all had been accomplished, it departed with the emperor. The Romans, having killed certain men left behind whom they had caught unawares, engaged with the emperor; but were soon turned to flight and driven to the channel of the Tiber. How many fell in the battle and how many were drowned in the river, I do not dare commit to writing. The emperor returns victorious. Godfrey the Younger, duke of Lotharingia, married the daughter of Henry, count of Limburg [Note: [Col. 0277D] Margaret.]; and thus, when all affairs had at last been settled in peace, the dispute long prolonged was ended on the condition that Godfrey should hold the duchy confirmed to him, the advocacy of Saint Trudo, and the castle of Rode [Note: [Col. 0277D] Rhode, near Waterloo.], and, receiving half of all that the same count possessed after his death, should become his successor by hereditary right [Note: [Col. 0277] What follows is given from B4, 5, since from this point B3 wholly abandons all trace of this continuation.].

1156. 4. 20. 2. 12.

Philip, son of Thierry, count of Flanders, marries Elizabeth, daughter of Ralph, count of Vermandois, at Beauvais (cf. Annals of Blandain).

1157. 5. 21. 3. 13.

(Annals of Blandain.) Thierry, count of Flanders, makes his third journey to Jerusalem with his wife Sibylla. After their departure, their son Philip leads an army to subdue the defiance of [Col. 0278B] Simon of Orzi, who refused to submit to him, and besieges and captures the castle of Inch.

1158. 6. 22. 4. 14.

Philip, count of Flanders and son of Thierry, leads a naval expedition against Thierry, count of Holland, and the pirates living under his protection. Having taken hostages, he returns victorious and burns Beveren [Note: [Col. 0277D] Near Antwerp.].

1159. 7. 23. 5. 15.

Thierry, count of Flanders, returns from Jerusalem for the third time.

1160. 8. 24. 6. 16.

(September 1159.) After the death of Pope Adrian, [Col. 0278C] a grave dissension arose in the Roman church over the papacy: Emperor Frederick and the easterners claimed Octavian, also called Victor, as pope for themselves, while the Italians claimed Roland, also called Alexander [Note: [Col. 0277] Thus B4*, 4**; B5 expanded this considerably.]. William Longsword, count of Boulogne, died without an heir. But Matthew, son of Thierry, count of Flanders, married the daughter of Stephen, king of the English, who had been abducted from the monastery [Note: [Col. 0278D] Romsey.] where she had been consecrated to God, and through her obtained the county of Boulogne. For this reason he was excommunicated by Samson, archbishop of Reims, and all his suffragan bishops; and he was severely harassed by a military siege from his father, Count Thierry, and his brother Philip.

1161. 9. 25. 7. 17.

(21 September.) Samson, archbishop of Reims, dies. [Col. 0278D] Henry, bishop of Beauvais and brother of Louis, king of the Franks, succeeds him. Bartholomew, archdeacon of the church of Reims, receives the bishopric of Beauvais. A severe famine. (1162.) Emperor Frederick conquered Milan and compelled it to surrender, after it had been besieged for five years.

1162. 10. 26. 8. 18.

Pope Alexander holds a council at Tours [Note: [Col. 0278D] A.D. 1163.]. (10 February.) Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, son of King Fulk, dies without [Col. 0279A] an heir. His brother Amalric, count of Jaffa, succeeds him.

1163. R. 11. F. 27. A. 9. H. 1. U. 1.

(Annals of Blandain.) Thierry, count of Flanders, makes his fourth journey to Jerusalem. Géza, king of Hungary, dies [Note: [Col. 0279B] D. 31 May 1161.]; his son Stephen succeeds him, having as wife the daughter of Henry, margrave of Austrasia, who was Emperor Conrad’s brother. Géza, brother of that Stephen, greatly troubles and harasses the kingdom of Hungary with the assistance of King Manuel, whose daughter he had married for this purpose.

1164. 12. 28. 10. 2. 2.

(1165.) [Annals of Blandain.] Philip, count of Flanders, goes with a great army of knights to Aachen, at Christmas [Note: [Col. 0280B] A.D. 1163.], to the court of Emperor Frederick, [Col. 0279B] from whom he received Cambrai and became his vassal; he also obtained great peace for the Flemings travelling to and from through the emperor’s territory. Returning from the court, he immediately sets out to meet his father, Count Thierry, returning from Jerusalem.

1165. 13. 29. 11. 3. 3.

(1166.) [Ibid.] Philip, count of Flanders, his brother Matthew, count of Boulogne, and Godfrey, duke of Louvain, launch an expedition with nearly seven thousand ships against Thierry, count of Holland. The count of Flanders held Thierry, who came to surrender with his men, in captivity for a long time. At Ghent a child was born with three heads and an animal’s tail on its neck. Likewise, in the village of Saint [Col. 0280A] Peter, a certain woman, pregnant for eleven months, gave birth to a monster shaped below like a quiver, above like a helmet, having two horns there. (Supplement of Anchin.) Lady Sibylla, countess of Flanders, of pious memory, died after serving for ten years at Saint Lazarus in Jerusalem.

1166. 14. 30. 12. 4. 4.

(1167.) War between Louis, king of the Franks, and Henry, king of the English, over the borders of their kingdoms. King Louis, with the aid of Philip, count of Flanders, puts the king of England to flight, and peace between them is secured until Easter of the following year. Lord Nicholas, bishop of Cambrai, dies; Peter, son of Thierry, count of Flanders, succeeds him. (1167.) Under the leadership of Rainald, archbishop of Cologne, [Col. 0280B] Christian, archbishop of Mainz, and Alexander, bishop of Liège, the eastern army of Emperor Frederick slaughtered fifteen thousand Romans and drove the rest as far as the Tiber. The aforesaid bishops, many others, and abbots died there of pestilence.

(1168.) Louis, king of the Franks, and Philip, count of Flanders, again undertake an expedition against Henry, king of England. Because the French begrudged and frequently disparaged Count Philip’s successes, he returned without praise. (1168.) When the duke of the Saxons, who in the same year had married the daughter of Henry, king of the English [Note: [Col. 0279] Thus B4* ends in the middle of the page. B4** now ends at *revertitur* (“he returned”).]. [lacuna]

## Supplement of Affligem

[Col. 0279]

[Col. 0279] A monk of Affligem (Affligem between Ghent and Brussels) copied Sigebert, Anselm, and the Gembloux writers, with the additions of Gembloux except for all those under the years 987, 991, 1012, 1037, 1042, 1048, 1072, 1090, 1092, and 1099. He himself added to these material from the Supplement of Anchin under 1096; from the annals of Blandain under 606, 610, 639, 640, 645, 658, 662, 664, 665, 674, 676, 678, 684, 695, 697, 698, 720, 763, 772, 806, 807, 812, 836, 851, 855, 870, 879–882, 885, 887, 891, 893, 896, 912, 913, 918, 928, 931, 932, 944, 949, 951, 960, 975, 1002, 1013, 1014, 1020, 1023, 1036, 1038, 1041, 1048, 1057, 1061, 1063, 1067, 1086, 1087, 1093, 1094, 1100, 1106, 1109–1111, 1118, and 1145; and then the entries which we shall give below. He composed his continuation in such a manner that for the years 1149–1155 he excerpted the Anchin continuation, inserting into it chiefly matters concerning Affligem from the History of that monastery; thereafter he proceeded in his own course. He wrote before 1189, as his words “this man who now reigns,” under 1154, show. Alberic of Trois-Fontaines and Baldwin of Ninove used him [Note: [Col. 0279C] Although the latter says, “The monk of Affligem carried his chronicle down to A.D. 1143, the twelfth of Pope Innocent and fifth of Conrad; he is plainly not merely to be compared with, but even preferred to, those who wrote before him, had he not been corrupted by the fault of copyists,” nevertheless he copied him word for word down to 1163 [Col. 0280C]. We have seen a very similar error above in Robert and Ralph at col. 33; from which we learn what weight should be assigned even to the most certain testimonies.]. Miraeus first published it, but whenever he found statements praising the emperor, he silently omitted them all. Struve second faithfully reproduced Miraeus’s text. We print it from the same sole manuscript used by Miraeus, B3*; since its Ename scribe interpolated nothing concerning his own monastery in the continuation, I should judge that the matters narrated under 1005, 1033, 1063, and 1139 concerning it were already written by the author of Affligem.

[Col. 0279C] 597. When this blessed Gregory was asked why the holy universal Church did not everywhere consecrate the Eucharist in one manner, he composed this letter, not very long but very useful:

“It is indeed customary for some to be troubled because in the Church some offer unleavened bread [Col. 0280C] and others leavened. For we know that the Church is divided into four orders: namely, those of the Romans, Alexandrians, Jerusalemites, and Antiochenes, which are called the general Churches; and although they hold one Catholic faith, they employ diverse mysteries of the offices. Thus the Roman Church offers unleavened bread, because the Lord assumed flesh without any admixture, as it is written: ‘The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us.’ Thus Christ’s body is made with unleavened bread. But the other aforesaid Churches offer leavened bread, because the Word of the Father was clothed in flesh and is true God and true man; just as leaven is mixed with flour, so the true body of our Lord Jesus Christ is made. Yet, both in the Roman Church and in the other above-named Churches, because of the inviolable faith, when we receive either unleavened or leavened bread, one body of our Lord Jesus Christ is made. But, as we have said, there is most certainly a divine sacrament involved, according to what we read in the Gospel: ‘That woman who, having taken [Col. 0281B] leaven, hid it in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened.’ The woman seems to me to be apostolic preaching, or the Church gathered from diverse parts. She takes leaven—that is, knowledge or understanding of the holy Scriptures—and hides it in three measures of flour, so that spirit, soul, and body, brought into unity, may not disagree with one another, but may obtain from the Father whatever they ask. Amen.”

1005. This Duke Godfrey was called “of Ename.” Ename was a town and very strongly fortified castle [Note: [Col. 0281D] Ename or Eenaeme, near Oudenaarde.], and the chief seat of the duchy of the kingdom of Lotharingia. Duke Godfrey married Matilda, daughter of Hermann, duke of Saxony, widow of Count Baldwin, son of Arnulf the Great, margrave. By her Godfrey fathered three sons: [Col. 0281C] Godfrey, Gozelo, and Hezelo. Count Hezelo, after the duke’s death, received and long held the castle of Ename together with the province of Brabant. He had a son named Hermann and a son named Berthild; while still young, they died and were buried in the church at Felseka. They later became renowned for many miraculous signs, but were secretly taken away by the monks of Verdun. He also gave another daughter in marriage to Reginar, count of Mons, together with the whole province of Brabant. Then, having arranged all his affairs as he wished, he left the castle and county in Reginar’s hands and became a monk at Verdun.

1007. At Ghent, the arrival of the body of Saint Livinus, [Col. 0281D] archbishop of Ireland and most devout martyr, on 17 August [Note: [Col. 0281] A somewhat later hand added this in the manuscript.].

1030. Count Baldwin, called the Bearded, gathered the bodies of the saints of his march—Bavo, Wandrille, Amandus, Vedastus, Bertin, Winnoc—with innumerable other holy relics. In the presence of Hugh, bishop of Noyon, with several other bishops and abbots, and with the leading men of all his realm assembled at Oudenaarde, he caused a peace sworn by all the people to be confirmed.

[Col. 0282A] 1033. In the days of Reginar Long-neck, the castle called Ename was treacherously surrendered and given to Baldwin the Bearded, who destroyed the castle to its foundations.

1063. In this year the monastery of Ename was built by Count Baldwin and Countess Athala.

1083. (History of Affligem.) By God’s help the monastery of Affligem took the following beginning. At the preaching of Wetheric, servant of God, who appeared like the morning star amid the cloud, to drive away the darkness of error, five knights were converted and wholly renounced their possessions. Among them was Gerard the Black, who seemed pre-eminent above the rest. Encouraged by his teacher’s counsel, he undertook with his companions to build up the place called Affligem—uncultivated, as its name suggests, in every respect, since it was fit only for gatherings [Col. 0282B] of robbers—and to construct a cloister there [Note: [Col. 0281] These items were added also by hand 1λ in the Gembloux manuscript (and thence to F3), as I suppose, from our very B3*.].

1086. (Ibid.) The founders of the monastery of Affligem, who, having abandoned everything, came so bare to build the cloister that they brought with them nothing but three loaves, half a cheese, and a few tools, after scarcely three years had passed secured the dedication of a church by Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, in honour of the apostles Peter and Paul. Countess Adela, with her two sons Henry and Godfrey, granted the same place freedom in order to build a monastery there. The aforesaid brothers associated with themselves monks from whom they might learn the monastic order. (Life of Arnulf.) Arnulf, bishop of the city of Soissons, became renowned as worthy of reverence for the spirit [Col. 0282C] of prophecy, purity of life, and miracles; by God’s appointment he was buried at Aldenburg [Note: [Col. 0281D] Oudenburg near Ostend; cf. the Ursicampine Continuation [Col. 0282D] under 1087.] in the church of Saint Peter.

1087. Lord Fulgentius, first abbot of this monastery, was elected this year on the feast of Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 0281] These items were added also by hand 1λ in the Gembloux manuscript (and thence to F3), as I suppose, from our very B3*.]. (History of Affligem.) Hugh, abbot of Cluny, is held to be distinguished by piety, outstanding in discernment, and renowned for holiness and religious devotion.

1088. (Ibid.) In this year Lord Fulgentius, first abbot of this monastery, was consecrated on the feast of Saint George.

1091. (Ibid.) The nobleman Heribrand, warned by Saint Peter in a divine revelation and seeing himself absolved from damnation, came to conversion at Affligem. On the thirtieth day he was immediately called by God. His five sons followed him, as did a brother of great name and power, Iggelbert; all were tonsured and transferred their earthly inheritances to heavenly treasures [Col. 0282D].

1093. Lanfranc, archbishop of the church of Canterbury, dies. Anselm succeeds him, outstanding in life and teaching, flower of bishops, light of his country, in all things an imitator of his master; he also wrote various works [Note: [Col. 0282D] Cf. the Ursicampine Continuation under 1097.].

[Col. 0283A] 1095. Henry, count of Louvain and the second of this name, is killed at Tournai. His brother Godfrey succeeds him.

1096. (History of Affligem.) Ida, countess of Boulogne, granted us the church in the village of Genappe, with the tithes and all its revenues, with the consent of her sons Duke Godfrey, Eustace, and Baldwin. Her son Duke Godfrey himself gave us five manses of land in the same village; to these she later added in augmentation certain adjoining parcels which plainly formed one whole.

1099. (Ibid.) Lord Abbot Fulgentius received the cell of Frasnes to govern.

1100. (Ibid.) Lord Abbot Fulgentius received the cell of Saint Andrew, situated near Bruges, [Col. 0283B] to govern.

1100. Anselm of Laon, teacher of teachers, is held in high renown. He laboured not only for himself: instructing many during his lifetime, after his death he made blessed those who came after, whom he enriched by his writings.

1105. The immunity of the church of Affligem is confirmed also by apostolic authority by Pope Paschal in the sixth year of his pontificate. Lord Abbot Fulgentius receives the place called Forest.

1119. Lord Abbot Fulgentius received the cell at Bornehem [Note: [Col. 0283D] Between Aalst and Antwerp.] to govern, the abbot handing it over and its canons becoming monks, because it could not be governed by them [Note: [Col. 0283] These are also found in B4*, 4**.].

1120. Lord Fulgentius, first abbot of Affligem, dies, [Col. 0283C] having adorned his times with the good fragrance of Christ until the end of his life. Lord Franco succeeds, appointed second abbot, truly praiseworthy in many respects. He founded the basilica of Affligem, adorned it with books and ornaments, enlarged its estates, and strengthened its religious observance [Note: [Col. 0283] These occur only in B4*, 4**, and are not read in B3*; but they plainly derive from no one other than the author of Affligem, and are therefore printed here.].

1122. Norbert flourished.

1126. Baldwin of Ghent, foremost among the foremost men of Flanders and Brabant, and prince of princes, renounced the world and was tonsured; after his death he was buried in the church of Affligem [Note: [Col. 0283] These are also found in B4*, 4**.].

1134. Lord Franco, second abbot of Affligem, dies; Albert succeeds [Note: [Col. 0283] These occur only in B4*, 4**, and are not read in B3*; but they plainly derive from no one other than the author of Affligem, and are therefore printed here.].

1136. Lord Albert, abbot of Affligem, lays down the burden of pastoral [Col. 0283D] care; Lord Peter succeeds [Note: [Col. 0283] These occur only in B4*, 4**, and are not read in B3*; but they plainly derive from no one other than the author of Affligem, and are therefore printed here.].

1139. The old church of Ename was demolished, and a new one was begun by Abbot Snellard. From this year began a famine lasting twelve years.

1140. Count Henry, son of Duke Godfrey, who had died in the preceding year, put aside the belt of knighthood and became a monk of Affligem. He received the mark of the heavenly warfare and, soon called by God, departed [Note: [Col. 0283] These are also found in B4*, 4**.].

[Col. 0284A] 1149. R. 12. F. 13. A. 13. H. 5.

(Supplement of Anchin.) Emperor Conrad and King Louis of France break camp and return from the journey to Jerusalem without any result: never had such misfortune befallen so great an army. A very severe winter set in and prevailed for four months.

1150. 13. 14. 14. 6.

(Supplement of Anchin.) A conflict arose between Henry, bishop of Liège, and Henry, count of Namur. The count indeed was intent upon establishing his domination; the bishop strove to free his own people from the count’s domination and heavy oppression. The count’s knights had gathered in a certain village called Hoylon. One of them, who seemed more powerful than the rest, laid hands upon the bishop in order to seize him; but [Col. 0284B] the bishop slipped away from him and, angered, vigorously urged his men to overthrow them. At last, through some mischance—I do not know what—the church was set on fire, and all who had taken refuge in it were burned and perished miserably. (Ibid.) At last, with armies assembled on both sides, they fought. The bishop proved superior. He put the count to flight and captured the more powerful among his men, but gained victory through the grievous slaughter of many.

1151. 14. 15. 15. 7.

(Supplement of Anchin.) The earth had abundant produce, but, as flooding rains devastated everything from the feast of Saint John until the middle of August, the crops scarcely reached maturity. For wine and the other fruits failed to a great extent, and what was gathered [Col. 0284C] from the grapes turned sour.

1152. 15. 16. 16. 8.

(Auct. Aquic.) Emperor Conrad closed his final day; Frederick, the sixtieth ruler of the Romans, his cousin, succeeded him, elected by the unanimous judgment of the princes. In the church of Saint Nicholas, built in the town of Brussels, Saint Mary, mother of Jesus Christ, performed such great miracles that nowhere, since the time of the apostles, have miracles so great and so frequent been heard of within so short a time. For when, with the consent of the abbot of Affligem and the counsel of the brethren, that shrine, to be adorned with gold and silver in honour of Saint Mary, had been brought from the church of Wavre [Note: [Col. 0284D] Wavre, not far from Waterloo.] together with the other relics contained there, [Col. 0284D] and reverently placed in the church of Saint Nicholas, immediately, through divine power working by the merits of the glorious Virgin, the blind received sight, the deaf hearing, the lame the power of walking; and so many sick persons, oppressed by various ailments, obtained their desired health from Easter week until the Nativity of Saint John.

If the brethren of the aforesaid church had committed these events individually to the faithful memory of posterity through the service of the pen, they would have written a substantial volume useful to later generations. This sweet savour quickly spread throughout the whole province [Col. 0285A]; not only from our own country, but also from very remote regions, there was a gathering of rich and poor. Believers of differing ages and of both sexes came with their offerings, and offered a sum of money not easily counted, to be divided in this manner: partly for the support of the poor, partly for the restoration of churches, and partly for the use of the brethren serving God in the churches of Affligem or Wavre. The abbot of Affligem and his brethren also came on foot as far as the town itself; there, clothed in albs and wearing copes, they arranged a procession of monks in a fitting and orderly manner. Thus, singing and praising God and His mother, they entered the church of Saint Nicholas amid great splendour and the applause of all the people, who are said to have gathered that day to the number of nearly thirty thousand [Col. 0285B]. The faithful testified that they had never seen, at any assembly ever held, whether by an emperor or at the command of the Roman pontiff, a procession so dignified and so well ordered.

Moreover, that glorious Lady bestowed upon her faithful during all that period a benefit which must not be passed over in silence, but indeed should be commended above the rest: through it, many wars already stirred up at the instigation of the Evil One, and disturbances, were soothed and brought to rest. For when many had come together from different places, of whom it was known that they were enemies of one another, immediately, without any exaction of money or any form of satisfaction such as is customary among secular persons in such affairs, [Col. 0285C] moved solely by fear of God and love for the most merciful Mother, they were reconciled in peace through the intervention of the faithful. When this time had ended, the shrine was carried back with the relics to the church named above; nevertheless, throughout that year the Mother of Mercy did not cease from the benefits she had begun on behalf of the sick. (Ibid.) The church of Saint Bertin, with all its appurtenances, was burned on the feast day of Saint Bertin itself, while the solemnities of Matins were being celebrated.

1153. R. 1. F. 17. A. 17. H. 9.

(Auct. Aquic.) An eclipse of the sun occurred on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, on the second weekday; on the fifth day before the Ides of February, likewise on the second weekday, thunder was heard. The townspeople of Brussels corrected this year the injury which in the preceding year they had inflicted upon the abbot and his brethren, being, as it were, people stiff-necked and obstinate in their opinion: namely, because they devoutly and humbly took Our Lady—so they call her [Note: [Col. 0285D] *Notre Dame*, “Our Lady.”]—from the church of Wavre, received her with honour, and in due time returned her peacefully and with joy. (Ibid.) Pope Eugenius closed his final day; Conrad, the 158th, bishop of Santa Sabina, called Anastasius, vicar of his predecessor the lord pope, succeeded him. The lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, who had arisen like the morning star and illuminated our order, also passed to the Lord; his life and teaching were so outstanding that whatever might be said in his praise would fall short [Col. 0286A]. Nor was it a small part of the wonder that in this year such barrenness lay upon our fields that the entire supply of our table scarcely sufficed for food for two or three months.

(Ibid.) A whirlwind of a most severe storm made its way through our territories, drawing, as it were, a furrow; in the course of one day it consumed everything like objects devoured by flames, and left mournful traces behind.

(Ibid.) Ascalon was captured by the army of the Lord which was at Jerusalem, and was occupied by our people; yet only after great labour and prolonged warfare, and after the army had first been afflicted by many dangers and heavy losses. For, in the days near the Purification of the holy Mother of God, the king of Jerusalem set his army in motion, besieged the gates, and encircled the city walls with his forces [Col. 0286B], continually threatening them with night watches and daytime warfare, prolonging the delay until the feast of the Assumption of that most holy Virgin, and persisting without weariness. On the day after that most sacred feast, therefore, he brought a tower with its engines up to the wall; and by underground engineering the wall was made to fall and afford our men a broad entrance.

Our men therefore rushed forward and broke in. The first to break through with his company was the provost and leader of that army, whose profession in the brotherhood’s association was military service to the Temple; surrounded by the ranks of his men, he reached as far as the city square and held his ground there. But, hemmed in by the narrow streets, enclosed by walls, overshadowed by the roofs of buildings, and surrounded by a crowd converging from every side, he was overwhelmed and [Col. 0286C] cut down with all his company. Their heads were piled into one heap, to be displayed to the king of Babylon as a sign of victory; their bodies were hung from the wall, while they reproached us and provoked the army of God with blasphemous words.

At length our men, strengthened in the Lord, told the king to fight bravely and not despair of God’s mercy, whose aid is especially accustomed to be present when human help is absent and not hoped for. Therefore, committing themselves to the Lord by what is the Christians’ particular safeguard—confession of sins, generous almsgiving, and most devout prayers—and making vows to the holy Mother of God, they approached the wall on the third day, brought up instruments of war, engines [Col. 0286D], and ballistae, and stood firm in faith. The Lord’s Cross, carried in the patriarch’s hands, went before the army, the surest pledge of victory, as it had always been in all our battles.

Then the Lord’s power was made manifest: it subdued blasphemous tongues, overthrew all the confidence of the proud, and scattered their counsels. A man who was present and remained in the army throughout the siege related to us what he saw. All were struck with blindness, so that when the ballista hurled millstones with its force into their midst, no one saw the approaching stone in order to move aside or avoid its blow. Why say more? They were compelled to confess the power of God which they had denied [Col. 0287A], and to acknowledge that He whom they had blasphemed was the faithful protector and helper of His own. Being unable to delay any longer, they surrendered the city into the king’s hands; and from that time Ascalon became ours and was occupied by our people.

This miracle seems one of the most astonishing of miracles: that a city fortified with one hundred and fifty exceedingly strong towers, and with upper chambers whose roofs stretched over its streets like a crypt covered with panelled ceilings, and thus in a manner impregnable, could at last be conquered—something nowhere recorded in the histories of the ancients.

1154. R. 2. F. 18. A. 18. H. 10.

(Auct. Aquic.) Pope Anastasius departed this life; Adrian, the 159th, formerly called Nicholas, bishop of Albano, succeeded him. Henry was established as king in England; his grandfather was that great and famous king of England, Henry [Col. 0287B]. For Henry’s daughter, who, having been married to the emperor, was called empress, and who after his death had been joined in marriage to the count of Anjou, bore by him this Henry, who now reigns [Note: [Col. 0287D] He died in 1189.], and his brothers. While he was still nursing at his nurse’s breast, after the death of his grandfather King Henry, he was carried to England in his cradle and there, by the election of all the princes and after oaths had been given, was confirmed in the kingdom.

Because he had to be kept under the hand of a guardian until his lawful age, his kinsman Count Stephen was elected to govern the kingdom and raise him. But Stephen, persuaded by the princes and inclining with too ready a favour to their flatteries, became a usurper and traitor, seized the kingdom, and held it. On learning this, his mother was raised and inflamed in spirit beyond a woman’s measure; without delay she entered England with an army. After engaging in many severe battles, she performed many daring exploits. At last, after very many years, when her son had now grown to young manhood and Stephen too had died suddenly, by a death not sufficiently known, she established her son Henry in the kingdom.

1155. 3. 19. 1. 11.

(Auct. Aquic.) Emperor Frederick, having set out in the preceding year, reached Rome in this year, worn down by many hardships on the journey and by various opponents offering hostile resistance. By both shrewdness and valour [Note: [Col. 0287] Miraeus erased the first six letters of this word in the manuscript; we have restored them from Alberic, whose reading V. D. Carl Grotefend had reached by conjecture.] he overcame them all and compelled them to surrender and submit [Col. 0287D]. He ordered the Roman princes to receive him peacefully and not refuse submission. Greedily seeking money, they stubbornly refused, saying that unless he accepted whatever terms they wished, he would find them not subjects but enemies.

The emperor, always rejecting their insatiable avarice, entered Rome by force of arms; finding Pope Adrian friendly and favourably disposed toward him, he was confirmed by a blessing and crowned in the church of Saint Peter. Meanwhile his army, not ignorant of the enemy’s plots, remained armed around the entire precinct of Saint Peter’s church [Col. 0288A], until all had been completed and it departed with the emperor. The Romans, their minds stirred by both shame and grief, having killed some who remained behind and whom they had caught unawares, joined battle with the emperor; but they were soon turned to flight and driven to the channel of the Tiber. How many fell in the battle, and how many were drowned in the river, I do not dare commit to writing. The emperor returned victorious. The empire flourishes, and the lord of affairs is exalted on high.

After we had suffered for many years from the barrenness of the land and scarcity of necessities, this year, with wheat wholly failing, in the utmost extremity we could scarcely devise, in our anxiety, what ought to be done. [Col. 0288B] Finally, however, it was decided that money should be borrowed on the credit of friends, and that we should buy what was necessary for food. We therefore sent our brethren into another region; they diligently carried out the task entrusted to them and, having retraced their journey, set out in a laden ship and reached the town called Oudenaarde. There is there a place where mills and sluices, receiving and releasing the passage of the waters, make the location so narrow and dangerous that our ship, in passing through, had to be held fast by very strong ropes tied to a post until it escaped and passed through that Charybdis. Thus, with so much caution and effort, the ship was brought—indeed, driven—toward that whirlpool and precipitous rush of roaring water; in the midst of the raging surge it was deprived of its safeguards. The fastenings came loose, the ropes broke [Col. 0288C], and every effort failed. Swept by the precipitous course of the violent stream, now thrown upward, now plunged into its depths, it was at last driven by the collision and violent shock of the waves against the nearest bridge and struck a firm, strong post supporting it. It broke the bridge, while itself suffering no loss, and passed through on a free and safe course. What shall we say to this? Let us give thanks to the Giver of all good things.

(Ibid.) Godfrey the younger, duke of Lorraine, took in marriage the daughter of Henry, count of Limburg. Thus, when all matters had at last been settled in peace, the dispute long prolonged was ended on this condition: Godfrey was to hold, without any opposition, the duchy confirmed to him, the advocatial lordship of Saint Trudo, and the castle of Rode; and, receiving after the count’s death one half of all that the same count possessed, he was to become successor by hereditary right. Arnold of Brescia, heretic and schismatic, disciple of Master Peter Abelard, was excommunicated by five apostolic pontiffs; finally, under Pope Adrian, he was hanged by a noose, his body was burned with fire, and its ashes were cast into the Tiber.

[Col. 0289A] 1156. R. 4. F. 20. A. 2. H. 12.

Emperor Frederick, by the judgment and counsel of bishops and archbishops, having put aside his wife, married the daughter of the count of Burgundy, named Renaud, from beyond the Saône. Her paternal uncle, Count William, had long kept her shut up under strict guard in a tower, so that he might destroy her and fraudulently seize her inheritance; but, through God’s mercy, she was freed from his hands and joined to the emperor in marriage.

Henry the younger, king of the English, turned against the king of France the large army and extensive military preparation which he had intended to lead into Ireland, in order to subject it to his dominion and, with the counsel of bishops and religious men, make his brother king of that island. He did this because he had married the French king’s abandoned wife [Col. 0289B], and sought, despite the king’s opposition, to possess her very great and extensive patrimony: namely, the duchy of Aquitaine and all dependent upon it.
