From this a grievous and lengthy conflict arose between them, so that in the regions of both kingdoms cities appeared to be destroyed, villages and towns burned, killings and violent plundering of every kind committed, and this evil, like a most grievous plague, spread intolerably from the Pyrenees almost to the borders of Flanders.

1157. 5. 21. 3. 13.

Theoderic, count of Flanders, now setting out for the third time with certain princes of his land, and taking also his wife, inflamed by a pious zeal of devotion, went to Jerusalem with four hundred knights and extensive military equipment [Col. 0289C]. His son Philip assumed the county; justice, courage, and generosity made him praiseworthy and beloved by all good people. He found it—namely Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0289D] That is, Jerusalem.]—at that time in such disturbance and desperation that they already feared they would be expelled from their borders, that the holy places would be left for the nations to profane, and that the whole land would be left for occupation.

For Noradin, son of Sanguinius, first breaking the treaty of peace and unexpectedly coming upon them, engaged and defeated them. A second time, fighting on the vigil of Pentecost, he captured and killed nearly six hundred proven soldiers in the army, some Templars and some knights of the king; the king himself barely escaped by flight, and he drove the rest into the castle of Belinas. Advancing without resistance through the land as far as the coast, he devastated much by slaughter. [Col. 0289D] The Lord, a helper in times of need and in tribulation, consoled those placed in such fear through the aforesaid count in this way. Trusting in God’s help and fortified by the sign of the holy Cross borne in the army, he joined the king and boldly engaged battle; he defeated Noradin and his men, humbled the defeated, and compelled the humbled to seek peace.

He captured and held, after overcoming it with great persistence and courage and stationing knights in it, the castle called Cavea, exceedingly troublesome to our men, through which they had lost nearly fifteen thousand of their own within seven years [Col. 0290A]. Then, coming to Antioch around the Nativity of the Lord, he acquired the two castles of Harenc and Femie and destroyed a third. Whatever its prince Raymond had lost through negligence and rash arrogance, when he was killed by the invading Turks together with the greater part of his army, Theoderic recovered by acting courageously. Going farther onward, he besieged Caesarea of Cappadocia and captured it on the fourth day; because he could not hold it, being too far from our forces, he destroyed it. Having prospered in all things, he returned to his people at Jerusalem with great glory and the joy of the Christians, and remained there for two years. His wife took the religious habit at Bethany.

Albert, margrave and count in Saxony, besieged and captured the castle of Brandenburg [Col. 0290B], in the land of the Slavs beyond the Elbe, through which the pagans severely afflicted the Christians; placing knights in it, he humbled the Slavs and thereby greatly extended Christian territory. Emperor Frederick moved his army a second time into Italy, intending more completely to subjugate it, with the duke of Bohemia and the other princes of his kingdom [Note: [Col. 0289D] This occurred only in June 1158; for in 1157 the emperor advanced no farther than Burgundy [Col. 0290D].].

The monastery of Gembloux, which about twenty years earlier had been set on fire [Note: [Col. 0290D] In 1136.] but extinguished, through God’s mercy and the intercession of the saints whose relics are contained in that church, by waters raised from the bed of the neighbouring river and poured over the monastery—now deprived of such protection, by God’s hidden judgment, was burned together with its cloister, the other workshops, and the entire town.

[Col. 0290C] 1158. 6. 22. 4. 14.

When Emperor Frederick was in Italy, having subdued cities and towns, the dukes, counts, and princes of the land came to him, partly through fear and partly through affection, and rendered him the submission and reverence owed to him (6 August), except for the Milanese, who proved rebellious toward him as they had toward his predecessors. Without any delay, employing his customary steadfastness, he besieged the city; although they had, it is said, sixty thousand armed men within, he nevertheless humbled them with great slaughter in the first and second engagements, and compelled them to surrender, giving two hundred of the city’s more noble inhabitants as hostages for peace and accepting whatever condition he imposed upon them.

After receiving these hostages and confirming the conditions by oath (8 September), he, as though secure, dismissed some of the army to their homes and some to winter quarters. He remained in Italy, called by all pious and just, and regarded as second after Charlemagne in justice and piety. Meanwhile, adorning his leisure with pious public works, he rebuilt the city of Lodi, which the Milanese had destroyed, transferring it to a safer site. He also renewed and fortified Como, which the same enemies of God and [Note: [Col. 0289] As it appears, Miraeus erased “of God and,” seeking also to erase from the manuscript the praises of Frederick; we have restored it from Alberic.] of himself [Col. 0291A] had almost destroyed.

1159. R. 7. F. 23. A. 5. H. 15.

(1 September.) Pope Adrian closed his final day. Chancellor Roland and Octavian, cardinal priest, contend for the papacy. About twenty years earlier, a most severe war had arisen between Godfrey the younger, duke of Leuven, and Walter surnamed Bertold. Godfrey was still a child lying in his cradle, while a mob of insurgents on both sides disturbed the peace. Hence great evil resulted, and like a contagion it seized the lands of both parties. Farmers, stripped of their goods, went forth as wretched exiles from their territories; the land, deserted by its inhabitants, remained uncultivated. One could see misery, burnings, murders, and violent plundering of every kind [Col. 0291B], for nearly twenty years, until in this year, in the fourth war, the ancient town of Grinbergen [Note: [Col. 0291D] Near Vilvoorde, toward the west.] fell—

> which had ruled for many years  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* II.363)

—and its great and famous castle, scarcely conquerable by human power, was, by God’s just judgment, burned and destroyed to its very foundations. This happened on the feast of Saint Remigius. Thus, deprived of every aid and abandoned by the count of Flanders, on whom alone he relied, he at last, though late, returned to peace with the duke.

The Milanese, violating their oaths, seized the castle in which the emperor had deposited his treasures, captured the knights guarding the castle, plundered the treasures, and, advancing farther, attacked his friends and allies. On hearing this, the emperor, marvelling beyond belief and horrified at their treachery, decreed that the injury done to God and to himself by the crime of faithlessness should be avenged with due retribution [Col. 0291C]. (In the year 1160.) Accordingly, he besieged the well-fortified castle of Crema [Note: [Col. 0292D] Crema.], in which their greatest confidence and strength lay; he captured the besieged place (26 January), destroyed it after taking it, permitted the knights found there to depart with their lives spared, and ordered everything belonging to the Milanese in the surrounding region to be ravaged.

1160. 8. 24. 6. 16.

Henry, king of the English, gave in marriage to Matthew, son of the count of Flanders, his niece, Stephen’s daughter, a nun and abbess consecrated in the cloister, contrary to the law, so that through her he might retain the county of Boulogne. Because the bride dedicated to God took not a bridegroom but an adulterer to the supreme King, the Enemy stirred up wars and disturbances between father and son, brother and brother [Col. 0291D].

Emperor Frederick, seeing that the Milanese behaved more insolently toward him because of the smallness of his army, sent throughout all the territories of his kingdom for men to come to his aid, and swore that he would not withdraw from the city until he had taken it. To ensure that this oath would remain valid, he designated, should he happen to die, two emperors: the son of his predecessor Conrad, and after him Henry, duke of Saxony.

1161. 9. 25. 7. 17.

A great army, called three times in the preceding year by the emperor, had assembled from all parts of the kingdom [Col. 0292A]. Greatly delighted by its arrival, and acting on the counsel of the princes, he immediately besieged Milan on every side and hemmed the inhabitants in so closely that they had no freedom to go out or come in, buy or sell. For out of reverence for the churches he feared to enter with armed force; and, in order to spare the soldiers who might be killed in battle, as often happens, he preferred to compel them to surrender under the torture of hunger.

Meanwhile, he attended daily to almsgiving for the poor, distributing the tenth part of all his revenues among them, believing that he could conquer better through alms to the poor than through the arms of soldiers. He was held pious and beloved by all, so that the dukes and counts of King William of Sicily abandoned their lord and joined him [Col. 0292B]. Baldwin V, king of Jerusalem, died; his brother Amalric succeeded him.

1162. 10. 26. 8. 18.

The Milanese, pressed by siege, hunger, want, and—what was more serious—sedition, sought mercy from the emperor through envoys. Provided only that their lives were spared, they promised to endure every condition proposed by him. Accordingly, on the Kalends of March, all came out in their companies: first the princes, then the nobles and knights, holding swords in their hands as though guilty of treason against majesty and traitors; then the mixed multitude, with ropes about their necks, in hair-shirts, their heads sprinkled with ashes, prostrated themselves at the emperor’s feet in the form of a cross [Col. 0292C].

The emperor, who had intended to kill them by various punishments as a warning to others, spared their lives and allowed them as many necessities as they could carry with them; he dispersed them throughout different regions, so that they were not permitted ever to return to the city. Then he ordered his men to enter the city and demolish the walls, towers, lofty and proud structures, and buildings—yet he spared three churches, those of Saint Mary, Saint Maurice, and Saint Ambrose, together with the clerics’ buildings, granting protection to their officials, houses, and property—and reserved the public treasury for himself.

The Plaisantines, Bolognese, and Brescian, allied with the Milanese against the emperor, frightened by their example, offered the same humble submission, prostrating themselves at the emperor’s feet as guilty of treason against majesty [Col. 0292D], and obtained pardon through his mercy.

A most grievous famine prevailed to such an extent that a modius of wheat was sold for thirty or more solidi of Leuven currency; and many thousands of people would have perished of hunger unless the Lord had looked upon the affliction of the poor people. For He who strikes and heals gave a good spirit to the hearts of His faithful; prompted by it, they extended a generous hand to the poor, supplied their want from their abundance, and sustained them by their generosity more lavishly than we had ever seen in our time.

Emperor Frederick, invited by the king of France so that, once the schism of the Roman Church had been removed, firm peace might be restored, convened a council in the territory of Besançon, at the town of Dole on the River Saône, on the feast of the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist. But at so great an assembly of kings, dukes, counts, archbishops, bishops, and abbots, the king of France was turned away from the emperor by the counsel and prompting of the men of Clairvaux; and all returned to their own lands without result, while the same discord, now even more severe, continued [Col. 0293A]. When the daughter of the king of France was betrothed to the son of the king of England, the conflict subsided and complete peace was agreed between them.

[Col. 0294A] 1163. R. 11. F. 27. A. 9. H. 1.

The bodies of the Three Magi were transferred by Rainald, elect of Cologne, from a church adjoining the city of Milan; amid the great joy and exultation of the whole province, they were brought into the city of Cologne and placed in the church of Saint Peter, in a wonderfully ordered procession such as had neither been seen nor heard of in all preceding centuries. Whoever wishes to know how they were transferred from their own regions to Constantinople, and from Constantinople to Milan, will find this in the church of Saint Peter at Cologne.

## Continuation of Aquicinctum

[Col. 0293]

We have already discussed this continuation, the most outstanding of all and at least contemporary with the events of its final decade, in column 29. We first give it entire from the excellent manuscript B5; yet, as we have seen above in column 45, it is not the author’s autograph.

[Col. 0293B] Brief epilogue. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, historian, wrote the beginning of this volume, setting forth in a truthful style for future readers the succession of kings and sequence of times from the birth of the patriarch Abraham to the twentieth year of the great emperor Constantine. He wrote in Greek; but blessed Jerome translated it into Latin. From Constantine’s twentieth year to the death of the emperor Valens, the same blessed Jerome arranged the narrative. From the first year of Gratian to the death of Valentinian the Younger, son of Placidia, Prosper, disciple of Saint Augustine, compiled it.

Thereafter Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, a man sufficiently learned, retracing matters more deeply, wrote from the first year of the first Theodosius to the seventh year of Emperor Henry V of that name. Thereafter Anselm, abbot of the aforesaid church of Gembloux, added what follows from Henry’s seventh year to the eleventh year of Emperor Lothair [Col. 0293C]. We do not know who wrote the rest, from Lothair’s eleventh year to the twelfth year of King Conrad. But from the thirteenth year of Conrad, king of the Germans, and the fourteenth year of Louis VII, king of the French, at the request of certain brethren of Anchin and afterwards under the authority of Simon, abbot of that same church [Note: [Col. 0293D] A.D. 1174–1201.], a monk of that church, a close associate, moderately learned, added the succeeding material down to the end of the volume. He wrote what he had heard rather than seen, and left for the knowledge of posterity what he heard from trustworthy reporters. For the learned men of our age think it beneath them to attend to these things and despise writing of this kind.

1149. R. 13. F. 14. A. 14. H. 6.

(Auct. Aquic.) In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1149, Conrad, king of the Germans, and Louis, king of the French, broke up their expedition and returned from the journey to Jerusalem without any successful outcome—never before had there been such misfortune for a Christian army in bodily matters. [Col. 0294B] Yet, through God’s mercy, the souls of many who were killed there by the Saracens and perished from hunger were saved.

Discord arose between Baldwin, count of Hainaut, and Sibylla, countess of Flanders; Flemish knights devastated the country in the district of Artois with fires and plundering. To make peace in this conflict Samson, the venerable archbishop of Rheims, came with some of his suffragan bishops; but because certain ill-disposed people disturbed the peace, he accomplished little. The church of Hasnon was then dedicated by the same archbishop. (Ibid.) A very severe winter grew intense and prevailed for four months.

1150. 14. 15. 15. 7.

Theoderic, count of Flanders, returned from Jerusalem [Col. 0294C]. Moved by the injury which Baldwin, count of Hainaut, had inflicted on his wife in the preceding year, he raised an army against him. But Baldwin, distrustful of his own strength, brought Henry, bishop of Liège, and Henry, count of Namur, against the Flemings. Since the Flemings resisted bravely in their usual manner, the count of Namur and bishop of Liège returned to their own lands dishonoured.

(Auct. Aquic.) A conflict arose between Henry, bishop of Liège, and Henry, count of Namur. Therefore, armies having assembled on both sides and engaged in battle, the bishop prevailed and gained the victory, though not without the slaughter of many.

1151. 15. 16. 16. 8.

Louis, king of the French, on the advice of the lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, repudiated his wife Aanor and lost the duchy of the province of Aquitaine [Col. 0294D]. For she was the daughter of the duke of Aquitaine. Aanor, formerly queen, married Henry, son of Geoffrey, count of Anjou, who afterwards reigned in England; thus this woman passed from one kingdom to another. By her he had four sons: King Henry, who died before his father; King Richard, who succeeded [Col. 0295A] his father; Geoffrey, count of Brittany; and John, called Lackland. He also had three daughters: one married the king of Spain, the next the king of Sicily, and the third the duke of Saxony.

By King Louis she had borne two daughters, of whom the first married Henry, count of Champagne, and the second Theobald, his brother, count of Blois. Louis, king of the French, took as his second wife Constance, daughter of the king of Spain, a very religious woman. By her he had two daughters: one married Henry the Young King, son of Henry, king of the English, and the other the son of the emperor of Constantinople. (Auct. Aquic.) The land bore abundant fruits, but, because a flood of rains devastated everything from the feast of Saint John until the middle of August, it scarcely brought them to maturity. Wine [Col. 0295B] and the other fruits partly failed, and what was gathered from the grapes turned sour. (Ibid.) In the city of Arras, after the lord Alvisus, bishop of blessed memory, who had died on the Jerusalem expedition [Note: [Col. 0295D] In 1147, according to the Annals of Anchin.], Godescalc was ordained the fourth bishop.

1152. R. 16. F. 17. A. 17. H. 9.

(Auct. Aq.) King Conrad closed his final day. The magnates and bishops of the kingdom, assembling together, elected (9 March) the illustrious Duke Frederick, son of Frederick, duke of Swabia. His maternal uncles were the aforesaid Emperor Conrad and Henry, duke of Austrasia, father of the queen of Hungary. (Ibid.) In the church of Saint Nicholas, built in the town of Brussels, Saint Mary, mother of Jesus Christ, performed many miracles [Col. 0295C]. The church of Saint Bertin was burned, with all its appurtenances and with a large part of the town, on Saint Bertin’s own feast day, while the solemnities of Matins were being celebrated.

1153. 1. 18. 18. 10.

(Auct. Aquic.) An eclipse of the sun occurred on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, on the second weekday. On the fifth day before the Ides of the same month, on the second weekday, thunder was heard. Pope Eugenius died; Conrad, the 166th pope, bishop of Sabina, called Anastasius, an old man and vicar of his predecessor the lord pope, succeeded him. The lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, who had arisen like the morning star and illuminated the monastic order, passed to the Lord. [Col. 0295D] His life and teaching were so outstanding that whatever might be said in his praise would fall short.

A whirlwind of a most severe storm made its way through the region, drawing, as it were, a furrow; in the course of one day it consumed everything like objects devoured by flames, leaving mournful traces. Ascalon was captured by the Lord’s army at Jerusalem and occupied by our people, yet only after great labour and prolonged warfare, and after our army had first been afflicted by many dangers and heavy losses. That city was fortified by one hundred and fifty exceedingly strong towers, and its streets were over-roofed by the upper chambers of buildings, like a crypt covered with panelled ceilings; it was in a manner impregnable.

Eustace, son of Stephen, king of England, died in England [Col. 0296A]. Constance, sister of Louis, king of the French, had married him. After Eustace’s death she was married a second time to the count of Saint-Gilles. Henry, son of the count of Anjou, fought King Stephen of England with varying success. Stephen, king of England, was reconciled with his kinsman Henry.

1154. 2. 19. 19. 11.

(Auct. Aquic.) Adrian, also called Nicholas, bishop of Albano for six years, is ordained the 167th bishop of the Roman Church. Stephen, king of England, suddenly dies from poison taken in food, as some assert (25 October); he is succeeded by his nephew Henry (ibid.), whose grandfather was that famous king Henry of England. For Henry’s daughter, who, having married the emperor, was called empress [Col. 0296B], after the emperor’s death married the count of Anjou and bore him the aforesaid Henry and his brothers. While he was still an infant at his nurse’s breast, after the death of his grandfather King Henry he was taken to England and, by the election of all the princes and after oaths had been given, was confirmed in the kingdom. His kinsman Count Stephen was also elected to govern the realm and raise the child. But Stephen, persuaded by the princes, seized and held the kingdom. On learning this, the empress entered England with an army and, aided by her brother Robert, count of Gloucester, undertook many bold acts after numerous serious battles had been fought. At last, after many years, when her son had now grown to manhood and Stephen had suddenly died, she established her son Henry as king [Col. 0296C]. William of Ypres, surnamed the Bastard, together with his knights, is expelled from England by King Henry because he had supported King Stephen. William, count of Boulogne, is restored to King Henry’s favour and peace, and every disturbance of war in England is calmed.

1155. 3. 20. 1. 12.

(Auct. Aquic.) Frederick the king, having set out for Rome in the preceding year, arrived there, worn down by many hardships on the journey and opposed hostilely by various persons; he compelled them all to submission and surrender. But since he was by no means received by the Roman leaders, he entered Rome by force of arms. Finding Pope Adrian friendly and well disposed toward him, he was confirmed and crowned with the imperial blessing in the church of St Peter [Col. 0296D]. Meanwhile his army surrounded the entire fortified precinct of the church of St Peter, until, all matters having been completed, it withdrew with the emperor. The Romans, having killed certain men left behind whom they had caught unawares, engaged the emperor; but soon turned to flight, they were driven to the channel of the Tiber. How many fell in the encounter, and how many were drowned in the river, I do not dare commit to writing. The emperor returns victorious.

Godfrey the Younger, duke of Lotharingia, took in marriage the daughter of Henry, count of Limburg. Thus, once all matters had finally been settled in peace, a dispute long continued was ended on the condition that Godfrey should possess the duchy of St Trudo, confirmed to him, and the castle of Rode; and that the same count, after Godfrey’s death, should receive and possess by hereditary right half of all that Godfrey held [Col. 0297A]. On the island of Anchin, the church of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, was dedicated by Godescalc, bishop of Arras, in July.

1156. R. 4. F. 21. A. 2. H. 13.

Emperor Frederick, with the consent of the archbishops and bishops of the German kingdom, unjustly dismissed his wife and thereby brought great calamity upon himself. The emperor himself married another wife, the beautiful virgin daughter of a certain duke of Burgundy.

(Auct. Aquic.) Philip, son of Thierry, count of Flanders, marries Elizabeth, daughter of Ralph, count of Vermandois [Col. 0297B], at Beauvais. Emperor Frederick is sharply rebuked by Pope Adrian and Roland, chancellor, over the divorce from his first wife. Taking this ill, he forbade the Roman cardinals entry into the cities and churches of his realm.

1157. 5. 22. 3. 14.

Pope Adrian and Emperor Frederick, hostility having arisen between them for various reasons, write letters to one another in exceedingly biting language.

Letter of Pope Adrian to Emperor Frederick:

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ Frederick, emperor of the Romans, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As the divine law promises length of life to those who honour their parents, so likewise it pronounces the sentence of death upon those who curse father and mother [Col. 0297C]. Moreover, we are taught by the voice of Truth that everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, we are not a little astonished at your prudence, since you appear not to show Blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church entrusted to him the reverence that you ought. For in the letter sent to us you place your own name before ours, thereby incurring the charge of insolence—if not arrogance.

What shall I say of the fidelity promised and sworn by you to Blessed Peter and to us, and of how you observe it? You demand homage and require fealty from those who are gods and all sons of the Most High—that is, from bishops; you join their consecrated hands to your own [Col. 0297D]; and, having openly become hostile to us, you close not only the churches but even the cities of your realm against cardinals sent from our side. Come to your senses, then—come to your senses, we counsel you. Since you deserved consecration and a crown from us, we fear for your nobility: while you grasp what has not been granted, you may lose what has been granted. Given at Palestrina, 24 June.

The emperor’s reply to the same:

Frederick, by the grace of God emperor of the Romans, ever august, to Adrian, supreme pontiff of the Catholic Church: may he adhere to all that Jesus began to do and to teach.

The law of justice restores to each person what is his own. We do not disparage our parents, to whom in this our kingdom we render due honour—namely, our forebears, from whom we received both the dignity and honour of the realm [Col. 0298A]. For before the age of Constantine, Sylvester is nowhere known to have possessed anything royal. But by Constantine’s pious grant peace was restored to the Church, liberty reinstated; and whatever your papacy is known to possess today as royal property, it holds by the generosity of princes. Accordingly, when we write to the Roman pontiff, we rightly and according to ancient custom place our name before yours.

Why should we not demand homage and feudal oaths from those who are gods by adoption and hold our royal rights? For he who is the true founder of us both, receiving nothing from a human king and conferring every good upon all, paid tribute to Caesar for himself and Peter, and gave you an example that you also should do likewise. He teaches you thus, saying: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart.” Therefore bishops must either surrender the royal rights to us, or, if they judge these useful to themselves, render to God what is God’s and to Caesar what is Caesar’s [Col. 0298B].

Your cardinals have indeed had churches closed against them, so that cities may not be opened to them; for we see in them not preachers but plunderers, not administrators of peace but robbers of money, not supporters of the world but devourers of money, insatiable beyond measure. When we see them such as the Church requires—bearing peace, enlightening the land, assisting the cause of the humble with justice—we shall not delay in supporting them with necessary stipends and provisions.

You also incur no slight charge against the humility that guards the virtues and against your own gentleness when you lay before secular persons questions of this kind, which contribute little to religion [Col. 0298C]. Let your fatherhood therefore take care lest, by recommending such things as we do not consider worthy, it place a stumbling-block before those who hasten, as toward an evening shadow, to lend their ears to your mouth. For we cannot refrain from answering what we have heard, since we see the detestable beast of pride already creeping even to the see of Blessed Peter. Ever providing well for ecclesiastical peace, fare well.

When these had been read, the pope attacked the emperor in every way and, by speech and writing, turned away from him all whom he could.

> [Note: [Col. 0297D] He imitates the words of Sigebert concerning Gregory VII, under the year 1076.]

The Italians rebel against the emperor, while he heads for Italy to subdue them. The Italians, having fortified their cities and castles, prepare to rebel; and they refuse admission to Milan to the emperor as he approaches it in hostility [Col. 0298D]. The emperor, however, having captured the fortifications opposed to him, besieges Milan.

(Ibid.) Thierry, count of Flanders, makes his third journey to Jerusalem with his wife Sibylla. After their departure, their son Philip leads an army to subdue the defiance of Simon of Oisy, who refused to submit to him; he besieges and captures the castle of Inchy. Hostility and conflict arise between Henry, king of England, and Louis, king of France.

1158. 6. 23. 4. 15.

Pope Adrian, after taking counsel with his cardinals, excommunicates Emperor Frederick, who, while his wife was alive, had brought in another wife, under the pretext that the magnates of the realm might oppose the excommunicated king on what appeared to be just grounds [Col. 0299A]. Pope Adrian and all the Roman cardinals except four invite William, king of Sicily, to rule Italy against Emperor Frederick, sending him through Chancellor Roland the banner of St Peter. This faction was not supported by Imerius, bishop of Tusculum; Octavian, cardinal-priest of the title of St Cecilia; Wido of Cremona; and John of St-Martin.

(Auct. Aquic.) Philip, count of Flanders, son of Thierry, leads a naval expedition against Thierry, count of Holland, and the pirates living under his protection. Having received hostages, he returns victorious and burns Beverwijk.

1159. R. 7. F. 24. A. 5. H. 16.

[Col. 0299B] Henry, king of England, after gaining the kingdom and becoming puffed up beyond measure, rebels against Louis, king of France, carrying out what he had long conceived in his mind. Having assembled an army, he crossed into Aquitaine and encircled the city of Toulouse with a siege. But the king of France, with his knights, entered the city in force before it could be besieged, and was received with great rejoicing by the count of St-Gilles and the citizens. Seeing this, and observing their concord and steadfastness, the king of England was distressed; fearing the king’s strength, he returned without effect.

(Auct. Aquic.) Thierry, count of Flanders, returns from Jerusalem for the third time. Countess Sibylla remained there; having assumed a religious habit at St Lazarus, she there rested in a holy end [Col. 0299C].

> [Note: [Col. 0299D] Year 1165 according to the Annals of Anchin and ours under the year 1165.]

1160. 8. 25. 6. 17.

After Pope Adrian’s death—

> [Note: [Col. 0299D] He died 1 September 1159.]

—Alexander, also Roland, chancellor of the Roman Church, is ordained pope, the 168th after Blessed Peter (cf. Auct. Aquic.). Against him Octavian, cardinal-priest of the title of St Cecilia, aspiring to the papacy, became a great scandal to the whole Church, because the lengthy contest between them even broke out into bloodshed. For Emperor Frederick, and the German bishops and princes, clothed Octavian with the mantle in the Lateran patriarchate and called him Victor. But the Italians, that is, the Lombards, consecrated Chancellor Roland outside Rome, at a place called the Cistern of Nero in the Sicilian district, and called him Alexander [Col. 0299D] (20 September 1159).

Alexander and Victor, contending for the papacy, each in rivalry send legates to France, to King Louis and the magnates of the realm. After their reports had been heard and examined in the city of Beauvais (July), the aforesaid king and all the bishops of his kingdom submitted to Pope Alexander. Emperor Frederick, however, and all the Germans obeyed Victor.

(Ibid.) William, son of Stephen king of England, count of Boulogne and steward of the king of England, dies without an heir. Matthew, son of Thierry, count of Flanders, takes as wife the daughter of Stephen [Col. 0300A], king of England, an abbess violently abducted from the monastery in which she had been consecrated to God, through the coercion of the king of England; through her he obtains the county of Boulogne. For this reason he was excommunicated by Samson, archbishop of Reims, and by all the bishops his suffragans; and he was grievously wronged by his father Thierry and his brother Philip on account of the castle of Lens, which he claimed against them by hereditary right. An embassy for reconciling the kingdom and priesthood now goes from Louis, king of France, to Frederick, emperor of the Romans, and now in turn returns from the emperor to the king.

1161. 9. 26. 7. 18.

(Auct. Aquic.) Emperor Frederick conquered the city of Milan, which had been besieged for five years, and compelled it to surrender [Col. 0300B].

> [Note: [Col. 0300D] He died 26 March 1162.]

The bodies of the three Magi, who came from the East to Bethlehem to worship the Lord, together with certain relics of saints resting in that same city, are transferred by Rainald, the emperor’s chancellor, and suitably deposited in the principal church of St Peter in the city of Cologne (year 1163).

(Ibid.) A severe famine. Samson, the venerable archbishop of Reims, died and was buried in the monastery of Igny.

> [Note: [Col. 0300D] Igny, diocese of Reims.]

He was succeeded by Henry, bishop of Beauvais and brother of Louis, king of France. Bartholomew, archdeacon of the church of Reims, succeeded in the bishopric of Beauvais. Louis, king of France, judging it unworthy that the state of the Church should be assailed by Emperor Frederick’s violence, sends to him Henry, count of Troyes [Col. 0300C], as envoy, to summon him to a mutual conference. They meet at the castle in Gaul called Dijon, where the holy martyr Benignus rests, intending to speak of the peace and unity of the holy and universal Church. But when the light of peace was disturbed by the disagreement of certain persons, they dealt with nothing worthy or useful, and each returned home (September 1162).

Octavian, also Victor, vigorously conducts synodal affairs throughout Emperor Frederick’s realm; Alexander, also Roland, fearing the emperor’s power, flees from Italy, crosses the sea, and comes to France (1162). He is gloriously received by King Louis and his magnates.

1162. 10. 27. 8. 19.

[Col. 0300D] (Auct. Aquic.) Pope Alexander, having convened a general council at Tours—

> [Note: [Col. 0300D] In the year 1163, in the octave of Pentecost.]

—excommunicated the schismatic Octavian, Rainald, archbishop-elect of Cologne, the archbishop of Mainz, and Hugh, abbot of Cluny, together with certain authors of the schism. At this council he discussed certain matters useful to the Church, renewed and confirmed the decrees of his predecessors, and declared void and invalid the ordinations performed by schismatics. Octavian likewise, holding a council in the city of Trier with German and Italian bishops adhering to him [Col. 0301A], anathematized Roland and his followers.

(Ibid.) Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, son of King Fulk, formerly count of Anjou, dies without an heir. He is succeeded by his brother Amalric, count of Jaffa.

1163. R. 11. F. 28. A. 9. H. 1.

(Auct. Aquic.) Thierry, count of Flanders, makes his fourth journey to Jerusalem. Géza, king of the Hungarians, dies; he is succeeded by his son Stephen, whose wife is the daughter of Henry, margrave of the Austrians, brother of Emperor Conrad. Géza, brother of this same Stephen, greatly disturbs and harasses the kingdom of Hungary with the assistance of Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, whose daughter he had therefore taken as wife.

[Col. 0301B] (20 April 1164.) Octavian, the pseudo-pope, dies and is buried in the city of Lucca. Wido of Cremona is elected by his followers and called Paschal. On the day of Pentecost, Emperor Frederick, having convoked a council of bishops and princes of his empire at Würzburg, repudiated Pope Alexander and submitted himself to Paschal. What was done at that council is attested by the letter of the emperor himself sent to the abbot of St Remaclus.

> [Note: [Col. 0301D] Cf. *Monumenta Legum* II, 155. It is, moreover, established that the Council of Würzburg and this letter belong to the year 1165 [Col. 0302D].]

Letter of Emperor Frederick to the Abbot of St Remaclus:

Frederick, by the grace of God emperor of the Romans and ever august, to his beloved and faithful N., abbot of St Remaclus: his favour and every good.

As your affection knows, we, together with all the princes, both secular and ecclesiastical, assembled magnificently at the court at Würzburg which we summoned for Pentecost. There, among other matters concerning the state of the holy Church, and especially concerning the affair of Lord Pope Paschal, which had been a doubt in the hearts of many, we, after consultation with all the princes and all clergy and laity present, faithfully and splendidly strengthened it [Col. 0301C]. Invoking also the grace of the Holy Spirit, we established and confirmed Lord Pope Paschal in this manner: we publicly swore with our own hand upon the relics of the saints that henceforth we would never receive the schismatic Roland as pope; and if he should die, neither would we ever receive his successor whom the opposing party might appoint.

But henceforth we shall acknowledge and uphold Lord Pope Paschal, as the universal and Catholic father, with obedience, honour, and reverence; and we shall never depart from him or from his party while he lives and we live [Col. 0301D]. If, however, it should happen that we depart this life, our successor, whom all the princes shall appoint, shall forever defend and maintain this honour of the empire and this our party under the same oath. All archbishops, bishops, and elects who were present, forty in number, each with his own hand beneath his stole, made and publicly confirmed this same oath upon the holy Gospels of God.

Moreover, to remove every doubt on our side, all the elects—the archbishop-elect of Cologne first, then the others—received holy orders at Würzburg on the Ember Saturday, with all devotion, to the praise of God and the honour of the empire [Col. 0302A]. Likewise all the secular princes—the duke of Saxony, Margrave Albert the Elder, the count palatine of the Rhine, the landgrave, and all the rest—swore the same thing upon the relics of the saints.

The honourable envoys of our friend the king of England, sent to us by him, likewise swore before our whole court upon the relics of the saints on the king’s behalf that the king himself, with his whole kingdom, would faithfully stand with our party; that he would uphold with us Lord Pope Paschal, whom we uphold; that he would support our party; and that he would no longer involve himself with the schismatic Roland or his party.

Therefore, having the fullest confidence in your affection and fidelity [Col. 0302B], we command you, urgently admonishing and ordering you, that you yourself, together with all the faithful of your church, swear and observe the aforesaid oath which we swore with our own hand before the princes and which the princes themselves swore and confirmed. On every Sunday and feast day, in the public Mass, as has been decreed by us and by the princes, you shall order a public prayer to be recited constantly, within and without, explicitly for Lord Pope Paschal.

It has therefore been decreed and established that all these oaths shall be completed within six weeks. If any cleric, monk, or layperson in our empire should in any way oppose this confirmation and our edict, know for certain that he is judged and condemned as a public enemy of God and the empire, without any hope of restoration [Col. 0302C], and deprived of every office, honour, and benefice.

We sent you letters of summons; and because, according to your wisdom, you would have been greatly necessary to us at court, we are very sorry that our letters did not reach you. Meanwhile await our presence in your region; for when we are nearer there, if you lack anything in justice, we shall fully provide it. Farewell.

All the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and princes of the whole realm subscribed to this emperor’s rash oath and made the same oath. Yet some of them adhered in their hearts to Pope Alexander. For this reason a grave scandal arose in the universal Church, and division increased in the kingdom [Col. 0302D], as one dissented from another and one was excommunicated by another. At that time the Church was divided, and Peter’s little ship was oppressed by the most violent waves.

1164. 12. 29. 10. 2.

(Year 1165.) Emperor Frederick celebrated Christmas at Aachen in his palace. All the magnates of the entire realm, ecclesiastical and secular alike, having been summoned by him, assembled at his court. Raising from its marble tomb the body of Lord Emperor Charlemagne, which rested in the basilica of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin, they placed it in a wooden shrine in the middle of that basilica [Col. 0303A].

(A. Aquic.) Philip, count of Flanders, was there with a great host of knights. Receiving Cambrai from the emperor, he became his man, and obtained broad peace for the Flemings travelling to and fro through the emperor’s lands. Returning from the court, he immediately went out to meet his father, Count Thierry, returning from Jerusalem.

> [Note: [Col. 0303D] This the earlier Continuator of Anchin had copied verbatim from the Annals of Blandain.]

Saladin, commander of the forces of Nūr al-Dīn, king of Damascus, enters Egypt with a great multitude of Turks and Saracens in order to subject it to himself. The sultan of Babylon—that is, the king of Egypt—therefore, distrusting his own strength and that of his followers, after taking counsel with his men sought Amalric, king of Jerusalem, as his helper, on condition that he would pay him an annual tribute and free Christians held captive throughout Egypt [Col. 0303B]. The king of Jerusalem agreed to these terms; entrusting the care of his kingdom to his kinsman Bohemond, prince of Antioch, he hastened with a strong army to help the king of Egypt.

When Nūr al-Dīn, king of Damascus, learned this, he gathered kings and peoples of the unbelievers from every quarter and besieged the castle of the prince of Antioch, called Harenc. The prince of Antioch, having assembled forces from all sides, left Antioch and arrived safely with his army as far as the castle. The Turks, abandoning the siege, halted not far from the castle amid narrow ground. On the following day the prince of Antioch pursued the Turks and fought them unsuccessfully, so that scarcely any escaped except those saved by the strength of their horses or by some chance occurrence. The prince was captured [Col. 0303C], and the count of Tripoli was also held, together with many others; some were taken prisoner, others mutilated.

Returning to the castle of Harenc, the Turks gained it with the utmost haste; and, pursuant to an agreement, they escorted the helpless multitude—women, children, and wounded persons alike—as far as Antioch. Amalric, king of Jerusalem, meanwhile, together with the sultan of Egypt, ravages with all his forces Saladin, who was overrunning Egypt. He shut Saladin up in the city of Bilbays and encircled him with a siege. Unable to withstand the king’s attack, Saladin sent messengers to him and surrendered himself to his allegiance. The king, after consultation, dismissed him and his followers; Saladin returned to Damascus.

After the king had returned to Jerusalem, the Saracen amirs, indignantly resenting that the sultan of Babylon had become tributary to Christians, massed together and attacked him with the aforesaid Saladin; they deprived him at once of life and kingdom [Col. 0303D]. Saladin, however, seized the kingdom of Egypt, which he had long coveted, and compelled the wife of the sultan whom he had killed—having forbidden her to mourn the loss of her husband—to enter into marriage with him. Nūr al-Dīn, king of Syria, dies not long afterward. The aforesaid Saladin killed the rightful successor to the kingdom and reigned in his place. Thus at that time East and West were afflicted by diverse calamities.

King Henry tyrannizes in England by taking away the rights of the churches of his realm. Thomas [Col. 0304A], archbishop of Canterbury, contending for the liberty of the Church, is exiled by him; crossing the English Channel, Thomas is received by Louis, king of France, with as much devotion as kindness. Godescalc, bishop of Arras, afflicted with an illness of the head, resigned his bishopric; he was succeeded by a certain Andrew, an abbot of the Cistercian order.

1165. R. 13. F. 30. A. 11. H. 3.

Pope Alexander, invited by the Romans against Emperor Frederick, leaves France and returns to Italy. On the feast day of Pope and Martyr St Clement (November), he himself celebrates Mass at St Peter’s in the Leonine City, Rome. Paschal, also Wido, the other pope, establishes his episcopal seat in the Italian city called Viterbo and, supported by the emperor’s power [Col. 0304B], harasses and plunders pilgrims and merchants from the land of France passing through Italy. Fearing this, many people, though unwilling, did him homage and honoured him with great gifts. Pope Alexander, mistrusting the Romans, withdrew to the people of Tusculum. Paschal, also Wido, taking with him [lacuna] of the emperor—

> [Note: [Col. 0304D] Something appears to be missing, E. P.]

—levelled to the ground the whole Cistern of Nero, where Pope Alexander had been consecrated.

(Auct. Aquic.) Philip, count of Flanders; his brother Matthew, count of Boulogne; and Godfrey, duke of Louvain, with nearly seven thousand ships, launch an expedition against Thierry, count of Holland. The count of Flanders kept Thierry, when he came with his followers to surrender, in captivity for a long time.

(Ibid.) At Ghent a child was born with three heads and an animal’s tail on its neck [Col. 0304C]. Likewise, in the village of St Peter, a certain woman, pregnant for eleven months, gave birth to a monster, shaped below like a quiver and above like a helmet, with two horns there.

> [Note: [Col. 0304D] The first source for these is the Annals of Blandain.]

(Ibid.) Lady Sibylla, countess of Flanders, of pious memory, died after serving for ten years at St Lazarus in Jerusalem.

1166. 14. 31. 12. 4.

Emperor Frederick sends an army into Italy to subdue the Romans who opposed him.

(Auct. Aquic.) War between Louis, king of France, and Henry, king of England, concerning the boundaries of their realms. With the help of Philip, count of Flanders, King Louis puts the king of England to flight, and peace between them is confirmed until Easter of the following year.

(Year 1167.) Under the leadership of Rainald, archbishop of Cologne; Christian, archbishop of Mainz; and Alexander, bishop of Liège, the eastern army of Emperor Frederick inflicted a slaughter of fifteen thousand Romans and drove the remainder as far as the Tiber [Col. 0304D]. The aforesaid bishops, except the archbishop of Mainz, and Duke Charles, son of Emperor Conrad, together with many others, died there of pestilence. The bones of Archbishop Rainald were brought back to Cologne and honourably buried in the church of St Peter. He was succeeded in the bishopric by his archdeacon Philip, son of Gozwin of Falkenberg.

Lord Gozwin, of pious memory, seventh abbot of Anchin, distinguished for charity and a lover of peace and religious life, departed this world on 9 October, about midnight, on Sunday, in the fourteenth indiction and the eleventh day of the moon (cf. *Annals of Anchin*). After he was buried in the church of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin, at the place where he had been accustomed to pray, amid the great lamentation of his sons, Alexander, prior of the same church, succeeded him as eighth abbot [Col. 0305A]. A great abundance of wine.

1167. R. 15. F. 32. A. 13. H. 5.

Emperor Frederick defeats the Italians in minor battles. But, strongly encouraged to defend the liberty of their homeland, they gather together from nearly all the cities of Italy situated between the Alps and Rome and splendidly rebuild the strongly fortified city of Milan in contempt of the emperor [Col. 0305B].

(Auct. Aquic.) Louis, king of France, and Philip, count of Flanders, again undertake an expedition against Henry, king of England. Because the French begrudged and repeatedly disparaged Philip’s successful achievements, he returned without praise.

(Ibid.) Nicholas, bishop of Cambrai, dies. Peter, son of Thierry, count of Flanders, is elected in his place. The church of St Bertin is severely harassed by Thierry, count of Flanders, through the cunning and persuasion of Robert, provost of Aire, the count’s chancellor.

> [Note: [Col. 0305D] “Born in the city of Chartres, Philip, count of Flanders, had made him extremely wealthy from a poor cleric, and very powerful in both Flanders and Vermandois. Although he held the provostships of nearly all the churches in Flanders, he always retained the title ‘provost of Aire,’” says Gilbert of Mons, p. 87, ed. De Chasteler.]

Thus Abbot Godescalc and the brethren of the same church, dismayed in spirit and deprived of human help, twice each day lay prostrate and cried out to God because of that affliction: namely, at Mass and at the end of Compline.

[Col. 0305C] 1168. 16. 33. 14. 6.

Count Thierry of Flanders dies in that village which he had taken from St Bertin through the violence of Provost Robert. He is succeeded in the county of Flanders by his son Philip. Before his father’s death, Philip had acquired through his wife the same county of Vermandois, due to him after the death of the young Count Ralph.

> [Note: [Col. 0306D] Elizabeth, Ralph’s eldest sister. Gilbert of Mons, p. 63, enumerates the entirety of Ralph’s inheritance.]

Baldwin, count of Hainaut, and Philip, count of Flanders, enter into alliance.

1169. 17. 34. 15. 7.

Emperor Frederick, intending to go and suppress the Italians, raises his still-boyish son Henry to the kingship at Aachen (15 August). A new disaster again arises among the Romans: engaging in civil war with the people of Tusculum, the Romans are almost destroyed to utter extinction [Col. 0305D]. For this reason great discord arose between Pope Alexander and the Romans. Pope Alexander, gathering military auxiliaries from every quarter, fought the Romans and the emperor’s adherents together with the Tusculans.

Emperor Frederick, however, sent his chancellor Christian, archbishop of Mainz, a wise and high-spirited man, into Italy with a strong army. Christian vigorously attacked the emperor’s rebels, destroyed their fortifications, captured cities, and subjected a large part of Italy to the emperor [Col. 0306A]. Baldwin the Younger, son of Baldwin, count of Hainaut, married Margaret, sister of Philip, count of Flanders.

> [Note: [Col. 0306D] In April; cf. Gilbert of Mons, p. 73.]

1170. 18. 35. 16. 8.

Henry, king of England, raises his son Henry to the kingship in England through the hands of the archbishop of York and his suffragans. From this arose hostility between Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, and the archbishop of York, because, according to the privileges granted to the church of Canterbury by the Roman pontiffs, the king of England ought to have been anointed by the archbishop of Canterbury [Col. 0306B]. Apart from other causes, this was especially the cause that brought martyrdom upon Blessed Thomas.

Louis, king of France, and Henry the elder, king of England, meet for a mutual conference. Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, was there with the magnates of both realms, and peace between him and the king of England was more glossed over than confirmed. Baldwin IV, count of Hainaut, dies on 8 November and is buried at Mons, in the church of St Waudru, by Alexander, abbot of Anchin.

> [Note: [Col. 0306D] On the seventh day after the feast of All Saints, in the year of the Lord 1171: Gilbert.]

His son Baldwin, the fifth count of that name, succeeds him. On that day a violent wind, mixed with rain, proved dangerous and destructive, so greatly that it overturned houses, towers, and buildings and uprooted forests. Among other things, it tore off the roof of the principal tower of St John the Baptist at Laon [Col. 0306C] and hurled it far from the church.

Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, having been injured by King Henry through a seven-year exile, at last returns to his see before Christmas, with the king’s permission.

1171. 19. 36. 17. 9.

Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all Britain, long afflicted by King Henry with injuries and the weariness of exile, on the fifth day after the Nativity of the Lord, at the ninth hour, in the principal church before a certain altar, had his head mutilated by the retainers of the aforesaid king and his brains poured out; he was crowned by the Lord among the company of precious martyrs (year 1170). At his tomb, wonderful and unheard-of miracles are performed by the Lord God through his merits [Col. 0306D]. Pope Alexander and all the bishops of France anathematize the murderers of the archbishop. Henry, king of England, is hated by all as a most vile apostate for the murder of Blessed Thomas.

Christian, chancellor of Emperor Frederick, proceeds to Tusculum to besiege Pope Alexander and the Tusculans, rebels against the emperor. Pope Alexander, fearing the chancellor already threatening at his very neck [Col. 0307A], dismayed in spirit, plans to flee the city. This intention became known to all; held in the city by their guard, he could not leave. Yet the citizens, adopting prudent counsel, appeased the chancellor with great services and honoured him with very great gifts of gold and silver, sending him away from their city to others.

1172. R. 20. F. 37. A. 18. H. 10.

In Italy, the peasant people of the marquis of Montferrat, together with certain knights, abandoning their lands and possessions with their wives and children, build a new city in opposition to Emperor Frederick, which they name Alessandria in honour of Pope Alexander. King Henry of England, carried beyond himself, seeking what had not been granted and aspiring to what was not his due, prepares ships and gathers knights from his kingdom, intending to subjugate the kingdom of Ireland [Col. 0307B] and, as he thought, to place a royal crown upon his own head. (A.D. 1171, Oct. 17.) Having therefore entered Ireland, when he perceived that the country people were quite ready to rebel, fearing both a shortage of bread, by which the country was afflicted, and the dangers of the winds on his return voyage, he withdrew in confusion to his own lands.

Pope Alexander sends legates into Normandy to King Henry: namely Autbert, cardinal-priest of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, and Theotimus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Vitalis. In their presence—[Note: At Avranches; Col. 0307D]—with the bishops and magnates of his realm standing by, the aforesaid king cleared himself, upon touching holy relics, of the murder of blessed Thomas; and, restoring at the cardinals’ discretion the churches of his kingdom and whatever was under his jurisdiction [Col. 0307C], he was absolved from the bond of anathema. This act greatly displeased Louis, king of the Franks, and all his magnates. The cardinals, however, who, having left Normandy, had intended to winter in France, the aforesaid king compelled, against their will, to return to Italy.

Pope Alexander, having heard of the miracles which God was working through his blessed martyr Thomas, decreed by apostolic authority that he should solemnly be held among the number of holy martyrs (A.D. 1173, Mar. 12). The murderers of blessed Thomas the archbishop, led by repentance, go to Pope Alexander and are punished with a severe sentence in the presence of all. Godescalc, formerly bishop of Arras, died.

[Col. 0307D] 1173. 21. 38. 19. 11.

Emperor Frederick and the marquis of Montferrat gather an army in order, in the following year, to conquer the Alexandrians and Italians who were acting tyrannically against them. A conspiracy against King Henry of England having arisen among his wife and sons, and also among certain of his magnates, his sons flee to Louis, king of France, seeking aid against their father. But King Louis—[Note: Col. 0307D]—taking with him Philip [Col. 0308A], count of Flanders, leads an expedition into Normandy.

Their army having been divided into two parts, Philip with his Flemings captured three strongholds with the utmost haste—[Note: Aumale and Briencourt, according to Gilbert and Robert of Monte; Col. 0307D.] Matthew, count of Boulogne, brother of Count Philip, was there mortally wounded by an arrow—[Note: Before Briencourt, according to Gilbert and Robert of Monte; Col. 0307D]—and died not long afterward; he was buried in the monastery of Saint Josse—[Note: In Ponthieu, between Saint-Valery and Boulogne; Col. 0308D.] The king of the Franks with his Frenchmen captured a certain castle with great difficulty; but, because those who were in the citadel of that castle resisted courageously, he could not take it. Thus the king, abandoning the siege of the castle, returned almost without effect.

King Henry of England deprived some of those opposing him of office, others of their goods, and thereby made even his friends more bitterly hostile to himself. Alexander [Col. 0308B], abbot of Anchin, gathered precious relics of very many saints from various places of churches, and fittingly placed them in a shrine prepared for this purpose with gold and silver. Andrew, bishop of Arras, died; Robert, provost of Aire, was elected in his place. Pope Alexander decreed that Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, should be honoured in the Church among the number of holy confessors. The winter was harsher than usual; unseasonable weather was added to winter. For, the air having become corrupted, in December people succumbed to various illnesses; many also died of the illness which physicians call catarrh and cough.

1174. 22. 39. 20. 12.

(Annals of Anchin.) Alexander, eighth abbot of the church of Anchin, died [Col. 0308C]. Simon, a monk of the same church, succeeded him as ninth abbot. Peter, bishop-elect of Cambrai, brother of Philip count of Flanders, with his brother’s consent abandoned the bishopric and clerical tonsure; in Whitsun week, on the Saturday called that of the Twelve Lessons, he girded himself with military arms. In the following year he took as wife the widow of the count of Nevers, and in that same year ended his life.

Robert, elect of Arras, through the influence and power of Count Philip, is elected bishop of Cambrai. In the bishopric of Arras, Frumald, archdeacon, is installed in Robert’s place, Robert himself striving for this result. After Pentecost, Emperor Frederick and the marquis of Montferrat, having entered Italy in force [Col. 0308D], surround new Alessandria with a siege—[Note: Incorrect: for the emperor was at Regensburg on 24 June, at Trivels Castle on 2 August, and still at Basel on 2 September. He pitched camp before Alessandria on 29 October; Col. 0308D.]

Louis, king of the Franks, Henry and Richard, sons of the king of England, together with Philip count of Flanders, again rise against the aforesaid king. Having set out for Normandy, they besiege the city of Rouen. A part of the Flemish army, at the prompting of Robert, elect of Cambrai, is sent across the sea to plunder England. Some were battered by a sea-storm, while others were bravely met and shamefully repulsed by English knights [Col. 0309A], and returned home in disgrace.

King Henry of England, seeing himself attacked by all, came to himself at last, attributed this to his sins, and, distrusting his own strength, sought divine help. Coming to Canterbury, he appeased blessed Thomas the archbishop—whom he had formerly treated unjustly—by humble and devout satisfaction, weeping most abundantly at his holy tomb. This, as we believe, brought him victory. For he immediately compelled the king of the Welsh, long rebellious against him, and certain of his enemies, to surrender within fifteen days, and also restrained the movements of some Englishmen hostile to him.

After this he returned to Normandy and entered the city of Rouen, besieged by the king of France, about [Col. 0309B] midnight. James of Avesnes, a wealthy and well-born knight, was subjected to insulting words by Robert, elect of Cambrai, during the siege of Rouen. The king of France and the count of Flanders returned from that siege without success; thus the sons who had come against their father returned without glory.

Robert, elect of Cambrai, is disgracefully killed at Condé by the servants of James of Avesnes—[Note: In autumn, according to Gilbert, p. 87; Col. 0309D.] Two archdeacons of Cambrai are elected to the bishopric through contention, namely Roger and Alard. But Roger having been rejected by Philip count of Flanders and the sounder party, Alard is installed. Each, desiring the bishopric, crosses the Alps and hastens in rivalry to Emperor Frederick in Italy. The emperor, having seen the persons [Col. 0309C], heard the account of the election, and seen the letters of Count Philip petitioning for Alard, and having taken counsel with the bishops present there, grants the bishopric to him.

Philip count of Flanders marches with an army against James of Avesnes for the killing of Robert, elect of Cambrai; but, checked through the intervention of Henry, archbishop of Reims, and with a peace agreement more feigned than settled by either side, he returns to Flanders. An excessively rainy winter severely wore down the army of Emperor Frederick besieging Alessandria.

1175. R. 23. F. 40. A. 21. H. 13.

(A.D. 1174, Sept.) King Henry of England and his sons are reconciled through the mediation of Louis, king of the Franks. Henry, archbishop of Reims, celebrated the Nativity of the Lord [Col. 0309D] at Anchin; then he went to Flanders, to the court of Count Philip. There James of Avesnes, having taken the oath prescribed by the judgment of the court concerning the death of Robert, elect of Cambrai, showed himself innocent.

On Holy Friday Philip count of Flanders, intending to set out for Jerusalem with many others, took the cross. A rainy and destructive summer delayed both the August harvest and the autumn vintage. Throughout Gaul and Germany a shortage of bread afflicted many. During this hardship [Col. 0310A], many monks and knights in this region of ours gave generous alms to the poor; among them the monks of Vaucelles stood out. Henry, archbishop of Reims and brother of Louis king of France, died. Around the Nativity of the Lord there was a great overflowing of rivers, so that the Seine, Aisne, and Oise, having burst their beds, inflicted great damage upon their inhabitants in a single night and killed many people as well.

1176. 24. 41. 22. 14.

Between Emperor Frederick and the Italians battle is frequently fought with varying outcome. Christian, the chancellor, is very concerned to restore peace between the emperor and the pope. King Henry of England, having sent messengers to Philip count of Flanders, detained him from his journey to Jerusalem this year by certain words or promises, I know not what [Col. 0310B].

James of Avesnes, sufficiently proud and insolent, rebels against his lord, the count of Hainaut. But Count Baldwin, taking his defiance badly, surrounds James’s castle of Condé with a siege, aided by Philip count of Flanders. James, distrusting his own forces, unwillingly surrendered the keys of the castle to the count. Having received the castle, the count levelled wall and tower to the ground—[Note: Gilbert gives a fuller account, p. 91; Col. 0309D.]

Peter, brother of Count Philip, died at Issoudun—[Note: “Hilseldunum”: Issoudun, in Berry. Robert of Monte says Peter died in 1177; Col. 0309D, 0310D.] Hostility having again arisen between Count Philip and James after the August harvest, the count of Flanders, taking with him the count of Hainaut, captured with the utmost haste two of James’s fortresses situated in the county of Vermandois [Col. 0310C]. One of them—[Note: Leschières; Col. 0310D]—he destroyed; the other—[Note: Guise; Col. 0310D]—he kept for himself. Thus, in Solomon’s words, “when the pestilent man is scourged, the country was more quiet.” There was a great abundance of bread and wine.

In the city of Cambrai and the castle of Saint-Quentin, at Ghent and Béthune, many churches and houses were burned. William, archbishop of Sens, brother of Elizabeth queen of France, is transferred from the church of Sens to the church of Reims. Amalric, king of Jerusalem, died; Baldwin, his son, succeeded him, incapacitated by age and illness.

1177. 25. 42. 23. 1.

Peace is established for five years between Emperor Frederick and the Italians. The Italians, submitting their swollen necks to the emperor, load him with great gifts of gold [Col. 0310D] and silver. (May.) While the emperor was staying in the city of Ravenna and Pope Alexander at Venice, embassies were sent back and forth more than once concerning the restoration of peace between them. Around Pentecost Philip count of Flanders set out for Jerusalem. William, son of the marquis of Montferrat, an outstanding young man who had married the daughter of Amalric king of the Jerusalemites, was killed by poison administered by knights from overseas.

### On the reconciliation of Empire and Priesthood

In this same year [Col. 0311A], on 24 July, great rejoicing took place in the universal Church, because the discord between Empire and Priesthood, which had been stirred up for twenty years and was a great scandal to the whole world, was, by God’s action, brought to peace on this day—[Note: Cf. *Monumenta Legum*, II, pp. 151 ff.; Col. 0311D.]

For Christian, archbishop of Mainz and chancellor, and the magnates of the realm together with the bishops, assembled and brought Emperor Frederick to Lord Pope Alexander at Venice, in the place called Rialto, barefoot and stripped of his royal adornments. With such humility did he fulfil what had been imposed upon him that without doubt it is to be believed to have been the work of Him of whom it is said: “The heart of the king is in the hand of God; wherever He wills, He shall turn it.” Indeed, how God-fearing, how obedient to the Church and to the lord [Col. 0311B] pope he made himself appear, he magnificently demonstrated by kissing the pope’s feet with tears and honouring him with royal gifts.

On the following day, namely the feast of Saint James the Apostle (25 July), the lord pope solemnly celebrated Mass with his cardinals and, having absolved the aforesaid emperor from the bond of anathema, communicated to him the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ as confirmation of unity and peace. The whole city rejoices and, honouring the emperor with gifts, devotes itself to banquets.

Pope Alexander, rejoicing in the peace received and in the honour bestowed upon him by God, sends letters to all the bishops of Gaul, containing the following account.

**Letter of Pope Alexander**

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers William [Col. 0311C], archbishop of Reims, legate of the Apostolic See, and his suffragans, and to his beloved sons the abbots established in the province of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, through the help, power, and favour of our dearest son in Christ, Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, and of his kingdom, we acknowledge that glorious and magnificent benefits have come to the most holy Roman Church and to us, it is fitting and consonant with reason that we should inform him and you, by whose aid we were powerfully helped in our necessities, of the prosperous and happy outcome of peace. For we hold as an undoubted truth that, after God, this same king together with his kingdom has worked for the honour and exaltation of the holy Church and has brought it great increase. And as we acknowledge this in word, so, by God’s action, we shall acknowledge it in deed and speech at every time.

Let it be known to your concern that our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, illustrious emperor of the Romans, by the inspiration of divine grace, having laid aside the error of vanity and turned to the way of truth, has returned reverently and devoutly, as was fitting, to obedience to the Church and to us. He has shown to blessed Peter in us that reverence and devotion which his predecessors customarily showed to our predecessors, and has promised that henceforth he will show it. On this account we give praise to the Most High, and consequently render abundant thanks to the king and kingdom [Col. 0312A], because in our tribulations and persecutions they did not abandon the Church and ourselves, but magnificently helped and defended us to the end.

Therefore we admonish and earnestly exhort your charity that, rejoicing with the Church and with us in our prosperity, you may persevere, as you have hitherto stood firm, in devotion to blessed Peter and to us; and that you may strive more eagerly to admonish and induce the king to remain in the same devotion with his kingdom.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, 27 July.

[Note: This letter is read in precisely the same words also in a twelfth-century Marchiennes manuscript, now among the Douai manuscripts, no. 302; Col. 0311D–0312D.]

On 24 July, Sunday, the very day on which peace was made between the emperor and the pope, the church of Marchiennes was dedicated in honour of the holy apostles Peter and Paul by William, archbishop of Reims, legate of the Apostolic See, and two bishops [Col. 0312B], his suffragans: namely Frumald of Arras and Everard of Tournai.

The summer was excessively dry and hot. The wheat harvest proved more abundant than usual. After the end of August, autumn was excessively rainy. The vintage of that season also was spoiled in many places. For the grapes, touched by a certain morning mist, rotted so completely that wine pressed from them caused great discomfort to those who drank it. Many people in this region of ours suffered from various fevers, and many died.

Louis king of the Franks and Henry the elder king of England form a splendid alliance. Henry count of Troyes, intending to go to Jerusalem with many others, takes the cross. Philip count of Flanders [Col. 0312C] is received with great honour by the princes and knights overseas. But a few days after he had arrived, hostility arose between him and the Templars over certain affairs of the kingdom. Leaving Palestine, he proceeds to Antioch in Syria at the invitation of the prince of that city. The beginning of winter was rather troublesome with frequent rains and gusts of wind.

The prince of Antioch and Philip count of Flanders, having assembled an abundant army from every quarter, besiege on all sides the castle of Harim, which had been violently taken from Christendom in previous years. When this was learned through messengers flying to and fro, Saladin, prince of Damascus, believing the city of Jerusalem to have been deprived of every military support, gathered the Turkish and Saracen commanders from Damascus and, intending—as his proud mind conceived—to take the city of Jerusalem [Col. 0312D] and utterly destroy all Christendom, arrived at Gaza with an innumerable multitude of archers and rustic troops added to his force.

Setting out from there towards Jerusalem, he encountered the king of that city and the Knights Templar, armed with the Lord’s cross and a small force of soldiers, but inspired by faith in Christ. Defeated, confounded, and put to shame by them, with almost all his men destroyed by sword or by the river flowing between, he returned to Damascus covered in the blood shed in the slaughter of his soldiers. This victorious battle was fought by the Christians [Col. 0313A] on Friday before the Nativity of Saint Andrew the Apostle, while Count Philip and the prince of Antioch with their armies were occupied in the siege of Harim.

On 30 November, in the night of the feast of Saint Andrew the Apostle, a violent wind coming from Africa was damaging in many places. Alard, bishop of Cambrai, died—[Note: 8 December, according to the necrology of Saint-Géry of Cambrai; Col. 0313D]—and was buried at Vaucelles. The election of a bishop, an appeal having been made to the Apostolic See, was deferred until the following year.

1178. R. 26. F. 43. A. 24. H. 2.

Around the end of January, when frost and snow melted, such a flooding of rivers broke out throughout all Gaul that it swept away fishpond sluices and mill structures in its rapid course, overturned houses, and killed many people. Roger, archdeacon of Cambrai [Col. 0313B], having received a gift from Emperor Frederick, is granted the bishopric of that city.

An eclipse of the moon took place on 5 March, Sunday, in the first hour of the night preceding Monday. On the same day Roger, bishop of Laon, being unable to withdraw the country people of his bishopric from the commune which they had wickedly sworn among themselves with the assent of King Louis, adopted evil counsel and assembled military auxiliaries from every side; on 6 March, that is, during Lent, he attacked them. Some were killed, many captured, and some, while fleeing, were killed in a certain river—[Note: Gilbert, p. 94, places this event in 1177; Col. 0314D.]

Philip count of Flanders, making little progress in the siege of Harim, broke camp around Easter and returned to Jerusalem to see the vision of the Holy Fire. Having therefore celebrated the Paschal solemnity there [Col. 0313C], and fearing the dangers of the sea, he returned home through Hesperia, Thrace, Pannonia, and Saxony.

The summer was dry and not overly hot until 3 July. Thereafter rains broke out and afflicted people until the very Kalends of January. For they could scarcely cut hay, harvest wheat, gather wine, or sow seed. An eclipse of the sun occurred on the Ides of September, before the sixth hour. Pope Alexander sends cardinal-subdeacons throughout nearly all Christendom to summon a council to be held in Lent of the following year.

Count Philip returned in October and was favourably received by his Flemings. Among them, the townspeople of Bruges offered him a monstrous fish [Col. 0313D], long before caught by fishermen and preserved with salt. It had a very large beak like that of a bird and, above its head, cartilage very like a sword.

1179. 27. 44. 25. 3.

In the second week of January abundant snow fell; a very severe and troublesome frost followed until the middle of February. The remaining days of that month, and March and April as well, were extremely cold, with a continuous east wind blowing. At the beginning of this year fodder for livestock was exceedingly expensive: what in past years had been bought [Col. 0314A] for three denarii was now sold for three solidi, namely hay and straw. A mortality among sheep and cattle followed.

### On the Council

(5 March.) Pope Alexander held a general council at Rome in the Lateran patriarchal palace, at which more than three hundred bishops attended, along with certain men from overseas. Some bishops from Greece also sent their legates there. An almost innumerable multitude of abbots was present as well. There the lord pope judged invalid the ordinations performed by the heresiarchs Octavian and Guy, and by John of Struma, who had followed them. Since the decrees of that council are many and are possessed by many people, it was not useful to write them out in the brevity of this chronicle.

[Col. 0314B] Simon, abbot of Anchin, on his return from that council stopped at Clairvaux and obtained relics of Lord Bernard, abbot of that monastery, which he had requested; he fittingly deposited them in the monastery of Anchin. The wheat harvest was thinner than usual; but oats and the seeds sown in the third month repaired the aforementioned losses.

Louis king of the Franks, taking with him Philip count of Flanders, crossed the sea and went to Canterbury, where he honoured the holy martyr Thomas with various gifts. Henry the elder king of England received him honourably. The autumn was exceptionally beautiful and warm until 3 October. Louis king of the Franks raises his son Philip to kingship at Reims, on the feast of All Saints. On the following Sunday William, archbishop of Reims [Col. 0314C], cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Sabina and legate of the Apostolic See, having summoned the bishops and all the clergy of Second Belgica, holds a council, consulting with his fellow bishops about matters necessary to himself or to the Church.

Once again the Roman Church is afflicted by the violence of schismatics. For after the reconciliation of Emperor Frederick with Pope Alexander, John of Struma, the presumptuous usurper of the apostolic name, distrusting his own strength and that of his followers, voluntarily fell at the feet of the lord pope. The lord pope, at the chancellor’s request, mercifully granted him pardon and made him provost of the church of Benevento.

But the schismatics, unable to endure the Church’s peace, again set up as antipope against Pope Alexander a certain cleric [Col. 0314D] descended from those whom the Romans call Frangipani; having changed his name, they called him Innocent III. A certain knight, brother of Octavian, who had advanced through contention against Alexander, supported him because of hatred for the pope, having handed over to him his tower or fortress, which he possessed as an exceptionally strong place near the city of Rome.

But the pope, more afflicted by this man’s violence than by the other schismatics, having taken counsel with his cardinals and restored peace with the cardinal-relatives of the aforesaid Octavian, bought the aforesaid fortress from the knight for a great price [Col. 0315A]. Thus, through the resourcefulness of Hugh the cardinal-deacon, himself among the noblest Romans, he captured the aforesaid fortress together with the repeatedly mentioned false pope. Brought to the feet of the lord pope, he was shut up permanently in a cage.

This year a great misfortune befell the Christians overseas: with almost all their soldiers killed or wounded, they lost the fortress of Jacob’s Ford. The duke of Saxony—[Note: Henry the Lion; Col. 0315D]—following evil counsel from evil men, rebels against his lord, Emperor Frederick.

1180. R. 28. F. 45. A. 26. H. 4.

Emperor Frederick, having assembled an army from every quarter in the preceding year, marches in hostility against the duke of Saxony. For this duke had in marriage a daughter of King Henry of England [Col. 0315B]; rebellious against the emperor, he was not merely insolent but proud. In the Italian expedition, most arduous and destructive, though three times summoned by the emperor himself, he had refused to come; nor had he sent either messenger or soldiers to help his lord.
