Therefore the emperor, moved beyond words, courageously subdues him by taking away his cities, castles, towns, and lands.

The citizens of Cologne, who themselves had been somewhat opposed to the emperor when he was setting out for Italy, hearing of the misfortune of the duke of Saxony and fearing the emperor, fortify their city with a ditch of extraordinary width and depth, and bring the waters of the Rhine around the circuit of that most noble city.

Christian, archbishop of Mainz and the emperor’s chancellor, while carrying out in Italy the business entrusted to him [Col. 0315C], is captured by the treachery of the son of the marquis of Montferrat. Philip, son of Louis king of France, marries Elizabeth, daughter of Baldwin count of Hainaut; she was the daughter of Margaret, sister of Philip count of Flanders. These nuptials were celebrated at Bapaume by Roger, bishop of Laon. Present were Counts Philip of Flanders, Baldwin of Hainaut, Henry of Namur, Clermont, Soissons, Ponthieu, and Saint-Pol.

Louis the elder king caused the queen to be crowned on Ascension Day, according to ancient custom, in the basilica of Saint Denis the Martyr, by the archbishop of Sens and his suffragans—[Note: “by” is absent from the manuscript; Col. 0315D.] This year, in this Gaul of ours, the earth produces wheat, barley [Col. 0315D], legumes, and a sufficient quantity of oats.

Henry count of Champagne, returning home from overseas through Asia Minor and Illyricum, suffered great loss through the ambushes of certain men: he lost not only his possessions, but also almost all his men, killed or captured. Louis VII, king of the Franks, disabled by paralysis for a year, at last lost both health and life in September. He had governed the kingdom of the Franks for forty-five years with fairly just moderation. His son Philip [Col. 0316A], the second king of that name, succeeded him.

Lord Simon, ninth abbot of Anchin, after consulting his brethren, dismantles the church of Saint Saviour in September, because so small a basilica was inadequate for the large community of Anchin. This had often been considered and discussed from the time of Lord Abbot Gozuin and his successor Alexander; but some alleged that it would disrupt the order, others the magnitude of the work and certain difficulties, while others were occupied with other matters, and the undertaking was delayed until the time of Abbot Simon.

At last, all united, with great heart and willing spirit, dismantle the old basilica, as has been said, intending to begin a new one in the following year. Therefore, after the Mass of the Holy Trinity had been celebrated most devoutly in the greater church [Col. 0316B], on 17 September they dismantled the high altar amid many tears, and deferred the beginning of the new church to the following year because of the approaching winter.

1181. 29. 1. 27. 5.

In the year of the Incarnate Word 1181, in the fourteenth indiction, with lunar year 13, concurrent 3, epact 3, and in the 103rd year from the first construction of that church, in March, on the second day of that month—that is, Monday of the second Sunday in Lent—the foundations of this new church of Anchin were laid.

After the Mass of the Holy Trinity had been celebrated, Abbot Simon, taking with him two abbots, John of Saint-Amand and Nicholas of Maroilles—[Note: Marcuilles; Col. 0315D]—proceeded to the place with saints’ relics [Col. 0316C], crosses, censers, and candles, the entire community wearing solemn copes. Baldwin, count of this district, was present there with a multitude of knights and other faithful of Christ. The count himself placed the first stone in the foundation with mortar, and there was great rejoicing in that church.

The day itself—something not to be passed over, but to be noted more carefully—was very bright and exceptionally beautiful, although all the preceding days of the month had been very rainy and cloudy. Henry, count of Troyes—[Note: Col. 0316D]—returned from overseas to his own lands in these days of Lent, and was received with great favour by his nephew the king of France and the other magnates of the realm.

Philip king of France and Philip count of Flanders, solicited by King Henry of England before Count Henry’s return [Col. 0316D] to lead an army with him against Emperor Frederick because of the disinheritance of the duke of Saxony, were dissuaded from such action by the advice of the aforesaid count. For Count Henry, being a wise man, said that it was neither useful nor just for the king to attack the emperor on account of injury to his duke, since neither he nor his father had ever been injured by the emperor.

At Selles, the estate of blessed Rictrude—[Note: of Marchiennes; Col. 0316D]—a lamb was born having two heads and seven feet. Within seven days of his return, Henry count of Troyes died at Troyes (17 March).

Hugh, formerly dean of Cambrai, who had been a great support to the church of Anchin at the beginning of its advancement, was removed from his own tomb, for the foundation of the new church was directing its course straight through it. A stone was found in his tomb bearing this inscription:

> Here is buried the body of Hugh, dean of the church of Saint Mary of Cambrai, who built the cloister with its portico of that church, and the chapel of Saint Gengulf. Moreover, to omit other things, for many years he abstained from flesh and did not lie upon a feather-bed, except perhaps in this monastery by command of the abbot. He built the cloister, portico, almonry, and chapel of blessed Mary, and conferred many other benefits upon the brethren [Col. 0317B]. On the feast of All Saints, after he had celebrated Mass, struck by a grave illness, he became a monk and died in good confession and true faith, in the year of the Lord 1093, on 6 November.

Emperor Frederick, warring against Henry his kinsman, duke of Saxony, subjugated to himself nearly all his castles and compelled him to flee to a certain island called Brunswich in the Saxon tongue. Henry king of England, grieving over the disinheritance of the duke of Saxony and of his own daughter, sends envoys to the emperor and promises gifts of gold and silver of great weight, if he will turn his mind away from oppressing the aforesaid duke.

But the emperor, with his innate and customary leonine constancy, despised gifts against his honour, closed his ears, and compelled the former duke, his rebellious subject [Col. 0317C], worn down by victorious battles, to surrender.

Pope Alexander, old and full of days, ended his life on an estate of the Roman Church about twenty miles from the city (30 August). When some foolish Romans heard of his death, they did not come out to meet him, as they ought, when he was borne to the city. Cursing him, and pelting with mud and stones the bier on which he was carried, they scarcely allowed him to be buried in the Lateran patriarchal palace.

Humbald, bishop of Ostia, older than Alexander in age, succeeded him. Changing his name, they called him Lucius III. He is the 169th head of the Roman Church.

Philip, the boy king of the Franks, and Philip count of Flanders, after the feast of All Saints [Col. 0317D], as winter approached—which in this year and this month was excessively rainy—fall into disagreement with one another, and with them all the leading men of France. The instigators of this evil are said to have been the count of Clermont—[Note: Ralph; Col. 0317D]—Ralph of Choisy—[Note: Choisy-sur-Bac, in the county of Vermandois; Col. 0317D]—and the sons of Robert surnamed Clement, counsellors of the king.

Thus the count first rises against the king, and the king in turn against the count. Burnings and plunderings are carried out; the despoiling of churches, the oppression of townspeople, and the ruin of the poor rage until Advent. At last, as the day of the Lord’s Nativity drew near [Col. 0318A], wise men negotiating with the king secured a truce in this war until the octave of Epiphany—[Note: Cf. Gilbert, p. 107; Col. 0318D.]

1182. R. 30. F. 2. A. 28. H. 6.

In the very days of the Lord’s Nativity, the Emperor Frederick sent envoys with a letter into France, advising the king to make peace with the count. If he would not do so, he should know for certain that Frederick would, to the extent of his power, bring aid to his own man, namely the Count of Flanders. After the octave of Epiphany, when the truce had expired, more knights than before were armed on both sides; plundering, slaughter, and arson were committed without any remedy. In the king’s battle-line the standard-bearers were the young King Henry of England and his brother Richard, Duke of Aquitaine, the Count of Clermont, and Ralph of Coucy. With the Count of Flanders were Baldwin, Count of Hainaut, Hugh, Count of Saint-Pol, James of Avesnes, and Hugh of Oisy, castellan of Cambrai. All Gaul, shaken by this tempest, bent this way and that; nor was there any place on this side of the Alps that escaped hearing the thunder of it. But as the days of holy Lent drew near, religious men running to and fro on both sides again obtained a truce until Easter.

On the third Sunday of Lent, Count Philip went to Liège for a conference with the young King Henry, son of the Emperor Frederick, and complained that he was being unjustly harassed by his lord, namely the King of France. King Henry, however, urged the count humbly to satisfy his lord, promising him on oath that his own assistance would not fail if the King of France refused to heed his counsel. Elizabeth, Countess of Flanders and Vermandois, after extreme sufferings and bodily infirmities, died on Good Friday (26 March). On the following day, with Count Philip present and amid the great tears of very many people, she was honourably buried in the church of the most blessed Mother of God, Mary, at Arras. After Easter, Henry the elder, King of England, crossed the sea and came into Normandy; for his sons, as we said above, King Henry and Duke Richard, were assisting the King of France against the Count of Flanders. The Duke of Burgundy and the Countess of Champagne [Note: Mary.], the king’s sister and formerly wife of Count Henry, allied with Count Philip and waged war against the king. But William, Archbishop of Reims, and Theobald, Count of Blois, the king’s uncles, laboured to restore peace.

Thus, when the truce between king and count had elapsed, peace was not expected but war. Unexpectedly, Henry the elder, King of England, Philip, King of France, and Philip, Count of Flanders, through the mediation of Henry, Bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See, met with archbishops, bishops, abbots, and the magnates of France between Crépy and the city of Senlis [Note: “They meet,” or something of that sort, is missing.]; and, with envoys of peace passing between them, a firm peace was firmly established among them. [Col. 0319A] [Note: Gislebert, p. 117, gives the terms.] Never in our age have we heard of so great a conflagration of war extinguished by so small a spark of peace.

Baldwin, King of Jerusalem, was suffering from the royal disease and weary of the heights of kingship. Meanwhile, the Templars and overseas knights repeatedly sent envoys, beseeching the kings of France and England to set the kingdom of Jerusalem in order, bring aid to the land, and carry out their purpose concerning the crown of that kingdom. Indeed, these same envoys were present at the aforesaid conference. Emperor Frederick celebrated the feast of Pentecost at Mainz with great splendour. Nearly all the leading men of the German kingdom were present at this imperial court; Count Philip of Flanders too was present with his barons, displaying himself, by his gifts, as more generous than all the princes of the realm, not without the amazement of many. There Henry, Duke of Saxony, was condemned to three years’ exile. Forced to leave the kingdom, he went with his wife to King Henry of England. At last, through the emperor’s mercy, he was allowed to possess certain revenues of his land for the maintenance of his exile.

Maurice, bishop of the city of Paris, a useful vessel and fruitful olive-tree in the house of God, flourishes among his fellow bishops in Gaul. Apart from those things which are inward, known to God alone, he shines outwardly in learning, preaching the word of God, distributing alms, and performing good works. He restored, at his own expense more than that of others, with an exceedingly fitting and costly work, the church of the most blessed Mother of God Mary, in which he sits as bishop. He widened the square before that church, between the two bridges, after purchasing at a great price from the citizens a site formerly occupied by many dwellings; he rebuilt the bishop’s residences; and he founded two abbeys, one for canons and the other for nuns. In church he is more assiduous than conspicuous. For I saw him on a certain non-solemn feast, while Vespers were being sung, not seated in the episcopal chair as is customary, but singing psalms and sitting in the choir with the others, surrounded by more than a hundred clerics. Henry, Bishop of Senlis, is likewise said to be an invincible lover of justice and a firm adherent of righteous severity.

The moon of August, both at its beginning and at its end, was exceedingly rainy and very cold, which caused great hardship in many places. For wet crops were stored in barns; hay, not yet cut or gathered, could scarcely be collected; and, what nearly all regretted more, the ripening and harvesting of wine came later. Four heretics were discovered in the city of Arras and imprisoned by Frumald, bishop of that city. One of them was called Adam the learned; another Ralph, a most eloquent layman; we do not know the names of the rest. [Col. 0320A] The bishop, already suffering from paralysis, reserved their judgment for the archbishop.

## 1183. R. 31. F. 3. A. 29. H. 7.

After the days of the Lord’s Nativity had passed, William, Archbishop of Reims, and Philip, Count of Flanders, met in the city of Arras to discuss their secret affairs. There, through a certain woman, the deceits of many heresies were uncovered in the count’s land. These heretics were supported by the authority of no heresiarch. Some call them Manichaeans, others Cataphrygians, and some Arians; Pope Alexander, however, calls them Pateruii. [Note: Read *Paterini*, i.e. *Peterenes*.] But whatever they may be, by confession from their own mouths they were convicted as most unclean heretics. Many were accused in the presence of the archbishop and the count: nobles and commoners, clerics, knights, peasants, virgins, widows, and married women. Then a decretal sentence was laid down by the archbishop and count: that those apprehended should be handed over to the flames, while their property should be surrendered to the priest and the secular ruler. [Note: The manuscript reads *sustantie*.]

Here the outstanding power of confession became apparent. For, as was truthfully established by those who were present, many previously guilty of heresy, through God’s merciful grace, escaped unharmed from the ordeal of hot iron and the danger of water. At the castle of Ypres twelve were brought to the ordeal of iron; but by the same power of confession all were saved. Frumald, Bishop of Arras, died [Note: 13 Kalends of May, according to the Necrology of Anchin.]; the aforesaid church was without a bishop for a full year.

After the death of Manuel, Emperor of Constantinople, his son, still quite a boy, succeeded him as emperor. During his father’s life he had married the daughter of Louis, King of the Franks. Following his father’s custom, he despised Greeks and loved Latins; he used their counsel and was sustained by their aid, and by clerical learning and lay justice. This was the cause of his destruction, as the following year will show.

Henry, the young King of England, and his brother Geoffrey, Count of Brittany, rose up against their brother Richard, Count of Aquitaine. When King Henry the elder, their father, heard of this, he was indignant that they had presumed to do such things without his consent, and sent a force of knights to assist his son Richard against his brothers. Fighting took place on both sides for many days, until the young King Henry, overtaken by untimely death, brought the war to an end (3 June). Amid many tears and the incomparable mourning of all—for he was loved exceedingly by everyone—he was carried to Le Mans and buried there. When his father heard this—for he had been present neither at the death nor at the burial—he had him brought from there to Rouen, with renewed and multiplied lamentation, and there, amid great groaning, buried him a second time with his fathers. In the city of Arras, Peter, abbot of Cîteaux, was elected bishop.

## 1184. 32. 4. 30. 8.

Emperor Frederick set out for Italy (September). [Col. 0321A] The Romans, despising Pope Lucius and scorning the clergy, devised an unheard-of outrage to insult the cardinals. Having happened to find certain clerics outside the city, they seized them and blinded them all except one. Setting them backwards upon the backs of asses, they gave them the names of cardinals. “This,” they said, “is the cardinal of St Mary Major; this one, of St Lawrence Outside the Walls; that one, of SS John and Paul; and you, of St George at the Golden Veil.” And so with the rest. Then they sent the spared man to the pope. When the pope beheld this, he groaned; striking with perpetual anathema those who had committed this crime, he left the city with his followers. Coming to Verona, he remained there until the day of his death. Some of the cardinals followed him; others, whose relatives had committed the aforementioned crime, remained in the city.

Philip, King of France, at the counsel of some of his barons who envied Philip, Count of Flanders, wished to dismiss his queen. But she turned to God and displayed such devotion, humility, and contrition towards the Mother of God in the city of Senlis that almost all who watched were moved to tears. Walking barefoot through the city streets, carrying candles in her hands, and lavishly distributing alms to all the needy, she entered the church of the blessed Mother of God. There she prayed for a long time; and on that very day she splendidly fed all the poor of the city, serving them herself. When the king and all his magnates heard this, they were moved to compassion and repentance, and abandoned their undertaking. Yet Count Philip now feared as enemies both the Archbishop of Reims and all those who had been accomplices in this counsel, whom he had formerly cherished as friends. For this reason and others, peace between the king and the count was disturbed.

After Pentecost the king and count met with their armies on the borders of their lands. The king’s army excelled in cavalry, while the count’s in bodies of very well-armed infantry. The count had brought with him, drawn upon a four-wheeled cart, a very tall standard bearing a dragon above it; the king and all France took this very ill. Nevertheless, through the mediation of Henry, King of England, the truce was extended from the approaching feast of St John until the following year. During this truce Baldwin, Count of Hainaut, was received into the king’s allegiance, at which Count Philip was greatly angered.

On the first of May, at about the sixth hour, a sign appeared in the sun. Its lower part was wholly darkened; in the middle it had something like a dim beam; all the remaining part was pale, so that all who saw it showed the same colour in their faces. This sign terrified many, because a certain Master Odo had predicted it, having sent letters to the Archbishop of Reims concerning the danger of the coming wind. Philip, Count of Flanders, and Baldwin, Count of Mons, met for mutual conference in a place called Mont-Saint-Remi. [Note: Or the Ward of St Remigius.] There Baldwin begged him to bring assistance against Henry, Duke of Louvain, who was disinheriting him; the count refused, and they parted in discord.

Baldwin, Count of Mons, marched with an army against Henry, Duke of Louvain, to the place called Lembeek. [Note: Lombeke near Ninove. On these events see Gislebert, pp. 131 ff.] But, not finding the duke unprepared and, as some assert, betrayed by his own men, he returned without effect. In August Philip, Count of Flanders, took a second wife, the daughter of Afonso, King of Portugal, named Theresa. [Note: Gislebert calls her Matilda; Ralph of Diceto, Beatrice.] Peter, Abbot of Cîteaux, was ordained bishop of Arras at Verona, in the church of the blessed martyr Zeno.

The Greeks, taking offence because their emperor placed Franks before them, deceitfully summoned his kinsman Andronicus, bidding him come and, as a wise man, support the emperor, who was a boy. Andronicus gladly received the envoys and, taking with him Saracens from Iconium, entered the city. The next day he entered the palace with a few men, adored and greeted the emperor; the emperor honoured him magnificently and entrusted himself to his protection. Andronicus received him into his good faith. Carefully surveying the court, he carried into action what he had long desired in his mind. For after a few days, entering the palace surrounded by armed soldiers, he killed all the Greeks, Franks, and English whom he found there. Finally, he seized the emperor himself and his mother and confined them in prison; shortly afterwards he had them taken to the sea and cruelly killed, innocent as they were, and killed all his household who remained in the city. Then, having placed the diadem upon himself, he ruled that most noble city not as an emperor but as a tyrant. Afterwards, treating these deeds as nothing, he contracted an unlawful marriage by taking the wife of his kinsman—the emperor, his lord—namely the daughter of the King of France.

Count Philip of Flanders repeatedly approached Baldwin, Count of Mons, through envoys, asking him to agree with him and with his advantageous purpose. But Baldwin would not consent. [Note: The manuscript reads *adquiescenti*.] In November Philip, Archbishop of Cologne, entered his land from the east; Philip, Count of Flanders, from the south; and the men of Douai and Pabule from the west; and they devastated it with fire and plunder. Baldwin, Count of Mons, gathering seven hundred armed men and wishing to invade the count’s land by force of arms, came armed with armed men to the village called Obercicourt; but, changing his plan, he returned and allowed the soldiers whom he had hired to depart. As the Lord’s Nativity approached, a truce was granted on both sides.

## 1185. R. 33. F. 5. A. 31. H. 9.

Many people in different places in France, Flanders, and [Col. 0323A] Hainaut, fearing the discord and war of princes, each surrounded his city, castle, or village with a wall and strengthened it with a ditch. When the truce between king and count was due to end and the Count of Flanders was preparing his expedition, Count Baldwin of Mons invaded by force the land of James of Avesnes and, mindful of an old injury, gave it to the flames. For James was said to have been the instigator of discord between the two counts. After the feast of St John, the truce having ended, the king and count led out armies of armed cavalry and infantry, which, stationed in the district of Amiens, awaited the outcome. At last, by God’s will as we believe, the count returned to the king’s favour before anyone was captured, wounded, or killed. Then he surrendered to the king certain castles of the county of Vermandois, among which Caix, Torote, Montdidier, Calmont, and the county of Amiens were prominent. There the Counts of Flanders and Hainaut were reconciled, but not yet firmly in heart. [Note: Gislebert narrates these matters more fully, p. 145.]

This year abounded in grain and wine. The French insulted Count Philip in the king’s presence at Compiègne, provoking him with foolish words. Going into Germany to King Henry, encouraged by his counsel and to be strengthened by his assistance if necessary, he returned cheerfully to Flanders.

Andronicus, tyrant and apostate of Constantinople—for long before he had renounced Christianity—was killed in the palace by a worthy knight of royal lineage, whom he was plotting deceitfully to kill. Encouraged by the aid of his relatives and of citizens who hated Andronicus, the knight killed the man who intended to kill him and, with their consent, ruled in his place. He confined the empress, namely the daughter of Louis, King of France, and ordered that she be served with due honour.

Pope Lucius died at Verona (24 November). He was buried in the church of Blessed Mary, in a marble tomb before the high altar. He was succeeded by Hubert, Archbishop of Milan, formerly archdeacon of Bourges, who, changing his name according to the custom of his predecessors, was called Urban III. According to the numbering of the chronicle written above, he presided over the Roman see as the 170th. [Note: The manuscript has “180th,” and so thereafter.]

## 1186. R. 34. F. 6. A. 32. H. 10.

Emperor Frederick celebrated the days of the Lord’s Nativity with his son King Henry at Pavia. In those days the emperor arranged his son’s marriage (27 January), betrothing to him the daughter of Roger, formerly the very wealthy King of Sicily and Duke of Apulia, a kinswoman of the King of France. For she was born of the daughter of the Count of Retest[a]. Count Philip of Flanders attended this wedding with very many leading men of the Roman Empire. On his way there he left France and travelled through Germany; but on returning he came through France, lest he become an object of suspicion to the King of France. When the king heard of his arrival, he sent trustworthy envoys to him, instructing him and designating a place where they might meet for a private conference. The king received him honourably, they conferred together, and a firm peace was firmly established between them.

Pope Urban and Emperor Frederick renewed their long-standing hatred in mutual opposition. There were many causes of dissension. The chief was that the Patriarch of Aquileia and certain bishops had participated, without the pope’s consent, in the coronation of King Henry on a solemn day in Italy. The pope suspended them all from divine office. Another cause was that on the Saturday of Pentecost he consecrated Formosus, canonically elected Archbishop of Trier, as cardinal-priest, and on the following day as archbishop, against the emperor’s will. For another had been improperly elected, whom the emperor supported. As these and other causes intervened between pope and emperor, peace in Italy was disturbed (January). Emperor Frederick compelled the Cremonese, who were rebelling against him, unwillingly to enter his service with the aid of the Milanese. Leaving his son Henry in the regions of Benevento, the emperor returned to Germany (in the year 1187, February).

Henry the king, son of the emperor, unexpectedly encountered a servant of Pope Urban carrying with him many coins of gold and silver. He took away the gold and silver and, in insult to the pope, cut off the man’s nose. Baldwin, Count of Hainaut, and his uncle Henry, Count of Namur, marched against Godfrey, Duke of Louvain, and burned his land. The excellent town of Gembloux, with the church of St Wibert, was then burned.

Philip, King of France, and Philip, Count of Flanders, assembling a great army from every quarter, marched in hostility, and justly so, against the Duke of Burgundy. For he was most unjust: although he received the merchants of king and count under his pledged protection, he handed them over to be despoiled by his robbers. Unable to withstand the strength of king and count, after losing certain castles he came to the king’s feet and surrendered himself.

On the day before the Kalends of July, a most violent whirlwind and severe storm, coming from the south-west and tending eastward, ruined crops and all planted fields in many places. For stones larger than hens’ eggs fell in various places; they killed livestock in the fields and birds on the waters, smashed the glass windows of churches and roof-tiles of houses. The straw left in the fields was so foul-smelling and useless that it was not even fit for beasts to eat. Geoffrey, Count of Brittany, son of King Henry of England, died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October. When the sun stood in Libra, we escaped by God’s grace the danger of a great wind that had been predicted beforehand. For no one knows what is to come except God, and he to whom God has deigned to reveal it. Nor, as we believe, is God’s wise ordering subject to any astrologer or necromancer of Toledo. [Note: He alludes to a prophecy read under the year 1179 in Robert of Torigni.]

The vintage in the districts of Beauvais and Noyon was almost entirely ruined by the aforesaid storm; and not only in those places, but also in Dry Gamantia [Note: A forest in the district of Arras. Humid Gamantia is its lower part towards the Sambre.] or Humid Gamantia, in the county of Ostrevant and in Hainaut. Wherever it passed, it left behind traces to be mourned and lamented.

## 1187. A year grievous to us. R. 35. F. 7. A. 33. H. 11.

In the year of the Lord 1187, the twenty-sixth of Emperor Frederick, the seventh of Philip, King of France, and the thirty-third of Henry, King of England, incomparable grief and unspeakable sorrow befell all Christendom. For after the death of Baldwin, King of Jerusalem, son of Amalric, Baldwin, a boy, succeeded him—his nephew through his sister, son of William, Marquis of Montferrat, whom we said above had been killed by poison. By counsel of the leading men of the whole province, the guardianship of the boy and the kingdom was entrusted to the Count of Tripoli. But the boy’s mother, who was quite cunning, extorted from the patriarch and the other princes of the kingdom the promise that, should the boy die an untimely death, the royal crown should be restored to her.

Baldwin, King of Jerusalem, died under the guardianship of the Count of Tripoli. His mother, the Countess of Jaffa, demanded from the patriarch, the knights of the Temple and Hospital, and the other leading men of the province the crown of the kingdom, which she claimed as her hereditary right. Having received it, she placed it upon the head of her husband Guy, Count of Jaffa. This Guy was an Aquitanian by birth, from the castle of Lusignan, and not of royal stock. [Note: Lusignan.] This act displeased many princes, especially the Count of Tripoli. When the aforesaid king demanded homage from that count, he refused it. Moreover, he invited against him Saladin, King of Babylon and prince of Damascus, and caused him to break the peace treaty which he had made with the Christians for two years.

Saladin rejoiced when he heard of their discord. Gathering an innumerable army of Turks and Saracens from every direction, he set up camp near Mount Tabor before August. King Guy, however, assembled an army of Christians very small in comparison with that of the pagans and pitched tents near the city of Nazareth. The Count of Tripoli, repenting of what he had done, came to the king and, seeing the Christian army unprepared and small, advised the king to withdraw for the time being and fortify the cities and castles of the whole kingdom. The king did not heed him at all. The count immediately departed with his men and fortified and guarded his own land. King Guy, moreover, had not yet spent two months in the kingdom.

A wretched battle was joined, greatly lamentable to all Christians. The bishop of Bethlehem bore the Lord’s cross. In that conflict the priest himself was killed, the Lord’s cross was taken by the pagans, and—alas!—the glory was removed from Israel, as is related of the Ark of the Lord. [Col. 0326A] The king was captured; all the princes were either killed or taken captive; and an innumerable multitude of common people was slain. Thus, with nearly all the land stripped of its defenders, Saladin moved through the country: he captured cities, kept castles for himself or destroyed them, overthrew monasteries, killed monks, priests, and clerics, dishonoured and killed nuns. The king, with the other captives and the Lord’s cross, was taken to Damascus. Armenians, Greeks, and Christians redeemed the Lord’s Sepulchre with its church and the Temple of the Lord from Saladin by paying a great price in gold.

These were the cities that remained to the Christians: Antioch in Syria, guarded through the strength of its prince and inhabitants; Tyre, a city of Phoenicia, retained through the enterprise of the son of the Marquis of Montferrat, brother of William whom we reported above to have been killed by poison; and Tripoli, preserved by its count and inhabitants. The Count of Tripoli, instigator of this evil, died.

Pope Urban left Verona, intending to go to Venice, and came to the city of Ferrara. There, on hearing the grievous news of the destruction of overseas Christendom, he fell ill (19 October). After his death and burial there, he was succeeded by his chancellor Autbert, who, changing his name, was called Gregory VIII, the 171st pope. [Note: The manuscript has “181st.”] Intending after his consecration to go to Rome, he died at Genoa on the journey itself (17 December), and after seventy days of his priesthood was buried there in the church of Blessed Mary. He was succeeded by Paul, Bishop of Palestrina, who, changing his name, was called Clement III, 172nd in the order of pontiffs. [Col. 0326C] [Note: The manuscript has “182nd.”] Richard, Duke of Aquitaine, son of Henry, King of England, was the first of all the princes of the French kingdom to take the cross, before Christmas, intending to avenge the wrong done to the Lord’s Sepulchre.

## 1188. 36. 8. 34. 1.

After the Lord’s Nativity, Philip, King of France, Henry, King of England, Henry, Bishop of Albano and Roman legate, and many others, bishops as well as dukes and counts, assembled on the borders of the two kingdoms. There they discussed various matters, especially the overseas Church. Both kings, together with many princes, bishops, and knights of their realms, noble and common, took the cross, intending to cross the sea. Richard, Duke of Aquitaine, rose against his lord the King of France. The king met him with all his strength and compelled him to surrender. When peace had been established between them, they led an army against Henry, King of England, and plundered and burned his castles; for he had always been rebellious against the kings of France (27 March).

On Mid-Lent Sunday, at Mainz, when a general court had assembled, Emperor Frederick, together with many bishops, the princes of all his realm, and an innumerable multitude of Germans, took the cross. Henry, Count of Namur, gave his only daughter, still an infant at the breast, to Henry, Count of Troyes, and with her granted him, after his own death, the whole county of his land. Baldwin, Count of Hainaut, his nephew through his sister, hearing and seeing this, was aggrieved because he greatly desired the same county and, to acquire it, had given much money both to Emperor Frederick and to the other members of the court.

When, before August, Henry, Count of Troyes, was unavoidably occupied in the war of the King of France and Count Henry was bedridden, Baldwin gathered an army from every quarter. Finding the castle of Namur, thought impregnable, stripped of soldiers and defenders, fortune smiled upon him and he captured it. In mid-August he advanced further and, surrounding the very strong castle of Bouvignes with a siege, captured it valiantly after fifteen days, and subjected to himself all the land of the county of Namur on this side of the Meuse. But after a few days Count Henry of Namur expelled the canons from the church of Floreffe, made it into a castle against Baldwin’s attack, and stationed knights there with their retainers. [Note: Gislebert narrates all these matters more fully, pp. 161–166, 170, 177–186.]

## 1189. R. 37. F. 9. A. 35. H. 2.

After Easter, Emperor Frederick set out with his army and, with great loss to his force, passed through Hungary, Thrace, and Greece, reaching as far as the renowned Syrian river Farfar. Our own knights—namely James of Avesnes, Hellin the seneschal, and many others of various rank and order—travelled through Apulia, crossed the sea, and besieged the city of Acre, which Holy Scripture calls Ptolemais.

At the same time William, the late King of Apulia, protector and defender of the overseas Christians, died without an heir. Having gathered all the princes of his realm, he designated as heir to the kingdom King Henry, son of Emperor Frederick, who had William’s aunt in marriage. They all promised him, by oath and pledged faith, that they would bow their necks to the said king. But after King William’s death, disregarding the faith and oath they had made, they created as their king a certain Tancred of royal stock.

Philip, King of France, taking with him Philip, Count of Flanders, and Richard, Count of Aquitaine, burned and destroyed the castles and towns of the realm of Henry, King of England. The King of England did not withstand them in battle, but, hearing of their approach, withdrew from place to place as though fleeing. At length he reached Le Mans. There the King of France and Count Richard pursued him. Hearing unexpectedly of their arrival, he was grieved beyond belief and fell ill. When he had come to the castle called Chinon, where part of his treasure was kept, he died as his sickness worsened. Carried to Fontevraud, that once rich and powerful man scarcely had the necessary funds for burial, and there he was buried in the monastery of nuns. He was succeeded by his son Richard, Count of Aquitaine.

Hugh, castellan of Cambrai, died. Elizabeth, Queen of France, a woman of considerable piety, departed to the Lord (15 March) and was buried, amid the excessive mourning of the French, in the church of Blessed Mary at Paris. The city of Arras, together with the church of St Vedast, was consumed by fire.

## 1190. 38. 10. 1.

[Col. 0328B] Around the feast of St John, Philip, King of France, and Richard, King of England, set out intending to cross the sea. The King of France made for the port of Genoa, while the King of England came to Marseille. On the day before the Kalends of August, the Christians besieging Acre, without consulting the leaders of the army, fought disastrously against Saladin, having been incited by Elbert, a priest and dean of Douai, as was reported to us by those who were present. Elbert himself was killed there, and many others; as many as six thousand perished.

While the King of France was waiting at Genoa for a favourable opportunity to cross, lightning struck from heaven five times in the same city on a certain day, greatly terrifying the king. At last, after all necessities had been prepared, he left the harbour and set sail on the feast of St Lawrence. Though they were sailing prosperously and had already crossed much of the sea, a contrary wind suddenly arose and compelled the king to turn back. Many ships were wrecked, horses lost, and the wooden engines which he was carrying to capture fortifications were destroyed. Many knights also were drowned and lost. Thus the King of France, frustrated in his attempt, remained at Messina, a city of Apulia, with the King of England, awaiting the crossing of the following year.

Count Philip of Flanders departed in mid-August [Note: Gislebert says that he set out in September.] and wintered in Italy. In that same year great sorrow befell our Christians. For the most pious Emperor Frederick, while swimming in the river Farfar near Antioch to bathe and cool himself, could not withstand the force of the water. Three times he was submerged in the depths of that water, and was drawn out with great effort by his knights. He survived for three days, speechless; having received the body of the Lord and holy anointing, he ended his last day (10 June). His body, embalmed with spices, is still kept unburied. His son Henry succeeded him in the kingdom. The army which remained in Syria was commanded by Conrad, Duke of Swabia, his son, a renowned knight.

Evrard, Bishop of Tournai, died. In the week preceding the Lord’s Nativity, a battle took place in Spain between the kings of the Spains and the Saracens. With God’s help, the Christians were victorious and killed an innumerable multitude of them.

## 1191. R. 1. F. 11. A. 2.

Many princes and bishops, and an innumerable multitude of common people who were besieging the city of Acre, died, both by natural death and by Saracen missiles: Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury; Roger, bishop of Cambrai; Frederick, duke of Swabia, a most valiant knight; Theobald, count of Blois, and his brother Stephen; likewise Helinus, seneschal of Flanders; and many others, whose names [Col. 0329B] we have not wished to write, because different reporters, bringing doubtful and uncertain accounts, have left us uncertain.

Philip, king of France; Richard, king of England; and Philip, count of Flanders, crossed the sea with their armies after March. Before crossing, Richard, king of England, married the daughter of the king of Navarre, rejecting the sister of the king of France, to whom he had been betrothed.

Pope Clement III died on 7 Kalends of April [26 March]. He was succeeded by Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in the Greek School, of most noble birth and advanced age, who was called Celestine III. He presided over the Roman Church as its 173rd pope. [Note: [Col. 0329D] 183rd, MS.]

Henry, king and son of Emperor Frederick, was crowned emperor by him at the Easter solemnity (15 April). In his elevation he endured many objections from both Romans and cardinals. At last, seeing the disturbance of the realms and the rebellion of the Apulians against him, he for the time being satisfied the cardinals, restoring to the pope many things which his predecessors had taken from the Church; and he handed over to the Romans the Tusculan fortress, which his father had taken from the pope. When the Romans received it, they gave their assent to the emperor’s coronation.

Philip, count of Flanders, was exceedingly generous during the siege of Acre, distributing his own resources to those in need, especially to knights who had exhausted their pay. If I had a thousand tongues, I could not describe the hardships of hunger, cold, and heat which the army of God endured during the four-year siege of the city.

The renowned Philip, count of Flanders, died on the Kalends of June [1 June], in the third month after his crossing, and was buried in the basilica of St Nicholas outside the wall of Acre. There also were buried more than fifty bishops, dukes, and counts. At his death the Christians felt incomparable grief, while the Saracens and Turks rejoiced.

An eclipse of the sun occurred on 9 Kalends of July [23 June], a Sunday, at the sixth hour, on the vigil of St John the Baptist; its brightness remained in the northern part, to the extent of one third of the moon.

After the feast of St John, Philip, king of France, and Richard, king of England, with their armies, leveled with the city wall, after great labor, the rampart which the Saracens had made extremely strong around the city; and they set up ten stone-throwing engines near the wall. The Saracens and Turks, unable to withstand their attack and despairing of retaining the city, surrendered it on 5 Kalends of July [27 June] to the king of France and the Christian army. The king accepted it on the condition that all might depart unharmed, provided that Saladin returned the Holy Cross and 2,600 Christian captives. But after the departure of the king of France, when the stated condition had been set aside, the king of England, who remained there, put 2,600 men to death by various tortures, retaining a few of the more noble prisoners through whom they hoped to recover the Holy Cross and certain captives.

Henry the emperor, fighting against Tancred, king of Apulia, besieged Naples (May). During this siege Philip, archbishop of Cologne, and many other dukes and counts died, and almost his whole army was consumed by the unhealthiness of the air. When the citizens of Salerno learned this, believing the emperor himself also to be dead, they who had formerly favored him seized the empress, because she was staying in that city, in order to regain Tancred’s favor, and committed her to honorable custody. The emperor, having lost his army and his wife, returned into inner Italy in sadness and grief.

At Cambrai John, archdeacon of that church and dean of Arras, was elected bishop.

[Col. 0330C] Richard, king of England, after the return of the king of France and the temporary repair of the ruined walls of Acre, divided his army into three divisions and moved toward Ascalon. The stretch of road between Acre and Ascalon was long. In the rear division, which protected those preceding it, many fell through Saladin’s ambushes and Turkish arrows. At last they reached Caesarea and rested there briefly. But as they traveled from Caesarea toward Jaffa, Saladin and his men met them on the Saturday vigil of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary. God’s power was wondrously displayed on that day. For Saladin, pursued by our men with his army, took flight; and near Arsuf our forces made such slaughter of the noble Saracens whom he had brought with him as he had not suffered in a single day during all the time of his rule. Of our men, however, none fell except James of Avesnes, an outstanding knight comparable to one of the Maccabees.

[Note: [Col. 0329] 1192. James of Avesnes, an outstanding knight comparable to one of the Maccabees, is martyred by the Saracens in battle. Annals of Anchin.]

In September a true report arrived of the death of Count Philip, who had ruled the county of Flanders vigorously for twenty-four years. All feared; all grieved, clergy and people alike. He was succeeded by Count Baldwin of Hainaut by hereditary right. For he had married Margaret, daughter of Count Thierry and sister of Philip; by her he had begotten Elizabeth, queen of France, and his sons Baldwin, Philip, and Henry.

Philip, king of France, came into France before the days of the Nativity of the Lord. But seeing his return home, certain knights who loved God too little, impatient of labor and conflict for Christ, and, like the sons of Ephraim on the day of battle, turning their backs to their enemies—not as knights, but as timid hares—returned to their homes, to their eternal disgrace. Not so James of Avesnes; not so. But because he persevered to the end, he will, as we believe, be saved and will triumph in heaven with the holy martyrs.

1192. R. 2. F. 12. A. 3.

Henry the emperor celebrated the days of the Nativity of the Lord at Worms with the great men of the realm. There, in the presence of the whole court, he confirmed the election of John, bishop-elect of Cambrai. Philip, king of France, likewise celebrated those days at Paris with his own men. Baldwin, count of Flanders, came to his court at the king’s command by letter. But the king received him neither courteously nor kindly. Seeing this, the count departed secretly from the city without greeting the king.

[Note: [Col. 0331D] Compare Gislebert, p. 230.]

On 18 Kalends of February [15 January], the fourth weekday, after sunset in the very twilight of night, many people saw a terrifying appearance of fire occupying the entire northern region of the sky. In many places in those regions there followed a visitation of divine fire. Therefore, in the bishopric of Tournai and in many places, a fast was proclaimed for the sixth weekday [Friday], except for all the sick and infants.

Baldwin the count, providing for himself and his land, sent Abbot Simon of Anchin and Daniel of Cambron to recover the king’s favor. At last, through the mediation of William, archbishop of Reims, and Peter, bishop of Arras, peace was made between king and count, to be confirmed at Péronne and Arras. In the seventh week before Easter, the king came to Péronne with his bishops and barons. There Count Baldwin appeared with his men; doing homage to the king, he possessed the eastern part of Flanders, while the king possessed the western part: Saint-Omer, Aire, Arras, Bapaume, the counties of Hesdin and Lens, the homage of Boulogne, Saint-Pol, Guînes, and Lins.

[Note: [Col. 0331D] Lille.]

The remainder fell to Baldwin. Philip the count had given all these aforementioned possessions to the king when he joined in lawful marriage to him his niece Elizabeth, daughter of his sister Margaret, countess of Hainaut.

[Note: [Col. 0331D] Gislebert, p. 233, tells the matter somewhat differently.]

While Marquis Conrad governed Tyre, the most noble city of Syrian Phoenicia, with just moderation, he was killed in the following way through the plot of a very powerful Christian prince, who envied his virtue and success. During the Easter days, on 3 Kalends of May [29 April], while the prince was sitting on horseback one day in that part of the city where the moneyers were and was attending to them, suddenly two men of that class whom historians call “Arsacids” approached him from either side, sent by the aforesaid treacherous prince. Fearing no one, in broad daylight and with a crowd of people standing by, they cruelly thrust into his sides the daggers improperly called “mercies,” and—alas!—killed the most noble prince. They were immediately killed by the people and, as was fitting, sent to Tartarus. The knight, worthy of worthy lamentation, was mourned; and such a prince was committed to burial in a tomb worthy of him.

Alas for grief! Illustrious princes and knights fall by the sword and die: Emperor Frederick; Frederick, duke of Swabia, his son; James of Avesnes; Helinus the seneschal; Philip, count of Flanders; Theobald of Chartres; Stephen of Blois; and innumerable others.

[Note: [Col. 0332D] Gislebert, p. 232, names more.]

And the refuse of knighthood, not worthy even to be named, which had taken up the cross of Christ, threw it down and fled back—not pursued by arrow, lance, or sword, but like a dog returning to its vomit and like a ravenous, insatiable wolf devouring with gaping mouth the goods of the Church and the small possessions of the poor of the Crucified One.

Richard, king of England, the duke of Burgundy, the other princes, and also the knights of the Temple and Hospital, after taking counsel together, established Henry, count of Champagne, as prince of all the Christianity beyond the sea, excepting the principality of Antioch; and they gave him the marquis’s wife in marriage. For she was born of royal stock: her mother was the daughter of King Amalric. To Guy, formerly king, the king of England gave the exceedingly rich island of Cyprus.

I follow an inverted order, but forgetfulness caused this. In the preceding year, when the king of France had crossed with his men to the city of Acre, the king of England sailed to the island of Cyprus. There a certain very powerful man was acting as tyrant against the emperor of Constantinople and had usurped the imperial title. The king of England landed against him from the sea with his men; defeating him bravely, he subjected the whole island to himself. He brought him prisoner, with his wife and children, along with stores of gold, silver, and other goods, and arrived at the army of the Lord, suffering from prolonged famine during the siege of Acre; with the wealth he had brought, he magnificently relieved their want. The king of England gave the daughter of this prince, whom he had brought with him in chains, to Guy, formerly king, together with the whole island of Cyprus.

But Count Henry, if God restores Jerusalem to us, was to become king. [Note: [Col. 0332D] These things were therefore written before Henry’s death, which the author himself recounts under the year 1197.] He possessed Tyre, Ascalon, Acre, Caesarea, Jaffa, and the other castles standing along the seacoast.

Tancred, tyrant of Apulia, sent envoys to Pope Celestine and the Romans, promising that he would restore to St Peter whatever the dukes of Apulia had taken from him in former times, if they would transfer to him the allegiance they held with Emperor Henry. When Pope Celestine heard this, he was greatly angered. In return he sent his own envoys—namely two cardinals—to Tancred, ordering him to release the empress from custody and restore her to the emperor; if he refused, he was to know for certain that he, along with the part of the province which favored him, would be struck with perpetual anathema.

After Ralph, bishop of Liège, who had taken the cross with Emperor Frederick, died on the journey in the preceding year, two men were elected contentiously in that church: Albert, brother of the duke of Louvain, and Albert, brother of the count of Rethel. Nevertheless, the more just, sounder, and larger party favored Albert of Louvain. But Emperor Henry, returning from the Apulian expedition, annulled both elections. Sending Lothair, the very wealthy provost of Bonn, to the city, he gave him the bishop’s palace, the villages, and castles of the bishopric, and ordered the clergy and people to obey him. All this, as some think, the emperor did on the advice of Baldwin, count of Hainaut.

[Note: [Col. 0333D] Not at all; for Baldwin labored much for his kinsman Albert of Rethel, to whom the emperor had promised the bishopric, but later, after receiving an excessive sum of money, he conferred it upon Lothair. Compare Gislebert, whom Baldwin sent to the emperor on Albert’s behalf, pp. 217, 221, 224, 228 ff., 235–246.]

For because of the duke’s pride and his inveterate hostile hatred toward him, he held the duke’s brother in enmity. Albert himself, the duke’s brother, seeing that injustice had been done to him, assumed the dress of a poor traveler out of fear of the emperor and came to the feet of Pope Celestine at the Lateran. When the pope had heard the grounds of the election and the agreement, he gave his letters to the elect, ordering the archbishop of Cologne to confer upon him the gift of consecration. Yet Lothair, the emperor’s elect, exercised episcopal jurisdiction throughout the churches, castles, and villages of that bishopric.

The waxing and waning moon of August was exceedingly rainy and stormy and very troublesome to reapers; nevertheless, the following moon of September was favorable, and thus the wheat harvest and vintage were moderately good. Richard, king of England—greedy and avaricious beyond human nature, hateful and rebellious toward all Christendom—having received a great price in gold from Saladin, destroyed Ascalon, the most famous city of the Christians. Tancred, tyrant of Apulia, compelled by Pope Celestine, released the empress from custody and returned her to the emperor.

[Col. 0333D] William, archbishop of Reims, having received letters from Pope Celestine, consecrated Albert, bishop-elect of Liège, as bishop at Reims in September. The archbishop of Cologne also excused himself from conducting his consecration and obtained by letter leave to confer upon him the gift of consecration. Emperor Henry, hearing that Albert, bishop-elect of Liège, had obtained from pope and Romans the grace of consecration contrary to his purpose, came to Liège in great anger (September), overthrew the houses of the clerics who adhered to him, and forbade that bishop entrance into his realm.

Tancred, tyrant of Apulia, died. When Pope Celestine heard of his death, he elevated Tancred’s son as king in Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily against Emperor Henry, whom he considered hostile because of Albert, bishop of Liège, and for other hidden causes.

An eclipse of the moon occurred on 11 Kalends of December [21 November], when the moon was twelve days old, at the eighth hour of the night; two parts of it were darkened, while the third part remained in brightness. On the following day Albert, bishop of Liège, having been led by certain traitors outside the city of Reims, was innocently killed—a just man by wicked traitors—with unheard-of cruelty. For Emperor Henry, who favored Lothair, whom he had intruded into the see of Liège, had expelled Albert from his realm. William, archbishop of Reims, and all the citizens of Reims, keeping him there, showed him great honor and reverence. He was buried amid the great tears of all in the principal church of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, where St Nicasius the archbishop had died for Christ.

Who the bishop’s killers were, and by whom they were sent, is unknown. [Note: [Col. 0334D] The duke of Louvain attributed it to the emperor.] Yet this is known: they came from Germany and fled there. Woe to them, because they went in the way of Cain, who killed his righteous brother Abel in the field after drawing him from his tent. These men, followers of Cain, cunningly led their father and lord out of the city of Reims so that they might more freely commit their crime; scarcely had the second month after his consecration elapsed when with a wicked sword they mutilated the head of the holy priest. Prudent reader, observe the unprecedented cunning of the traitors: on the day before they resolved to do this, they rendered him homage, lest he suspect them. Woe to the wicked betrayers, whose wickedness the heavens will reveal and against whom the earth will rise on the day of the Lord’s wrath, unless by the Lord’s aid they are converted.

Between Richard, king of England, and Saladin, and likewise between the Christians and Saracens overseas, a truce for three years was introduced and confirmed, on the grievous condition that our men should destroy the most noble city of Ascalon. Hugh, duke of Burgundy, died there; he was succeeded in the duchy of Burgundy by his son Odo. Many knights valiant in arms died overseas this year, some killed by Saracen swords and others by natural death. The survivors, except King Henry and his followers, made little progress there and returned home.

1193. R. 3. F. 13. A. 4.

In January the pilgrims from overseas returned to us, bringing no report concerning the recovery of the lost land that might gladden us or be worthy of writing down. Richard of holy memory, converted at Anchin, died and was buried in that same monastery. [Col. 0335A] This man showed remarkable abstinence from food and drink; he had no bed, or a hard one; his clothing was poor; and his compassion toward the poor and cloistered monks was exceptional.

[Note: [Col. 0335D] “Richard … exceptional” is found in the same words in the Annals of Anchin.]

Henry, duke of Louvain, and Henry his uncle, duke of the Ardennes, rose against the count of Hochstaden and his brother Lothair, whom Emperor Henry had intruded into the see of Liège, because of the murder of Albert, bishop of that city. They captured all his castles which he possessed around the Rhine, and destroyed and burned some of them. But the count and his brother fled to the emperor. Pope Celestine bound all the bishop’s murderers under perpetual anathema.

When Richard, king of England, was returning from overseas before the days of Lent, he considered certain regions suspect—Apulia, Calabria, Corsica, and Italy—because the murder of Marquis Conrad of Montferrat was, I know not whether justly, laid to his charge. Taking with him only a few companions so that he might more secretly reach his nephew, the duke of Saxony, he entered the land of the duke of Austria and was captured by that duke and committed to custody. For when this duke had been at the siege of Acre, the king of England had often subjected him to insulting words. The duke detained Richard with him for some time and afterward sent him to the emperor in Germany. The emperor took him under honorable guard wherever he went.

While Richard, king of England, was detained by the emperor, Philip, king of France, having gathered a large army from every part of the whole realm subject to him, went into Normandy after the Easter solemnity, in April, to lay it waste. He captured Gisors and many other castles of the Vexin territory. He surrounded Rouen, the metropolitan city of Normandy, with a siege; but as the citizens resisted bravely, stirred by the anger natural to him, he burned the stone-throwers and engines with which he had encircled the city, and returned ingloriously from the assault.

After Saladin died at Damascus, his sons succeeded him in the rule of Syria and Babylon [Egypt]. The churches of England and Normandy and the monasteries of monks were stripped of their treasures for the ransom of the king of England. Lothair, intruded at Liège, was deprived by Pope Celestine of every ecclesiastical prelacy because of the murder of Albert, bishop of the same city.

[Note: [Col. 0336D] Except the provostship at Koblenz.]

Emperor Henry, satisfying the relatives of the aforesaid bishop concerning his death, calmed the movement of the princes of the realm, who had risen against him because of this matter, on the condition that the duke of Louvain and of the Ardennes, Henry of Limburg, might, with the counsel of the chapter, choose whom they wished as bishop of Liège. Relying on imperial authority, they chose Simon, son of the duke of the Ardennes.

Philip the king married as his second wife Ingeborg, daughter of the king of Denmark, at Amiens on the vigil of the Assumption of St Mary. On the day of the Assumption itself, a Sunday, in the presence of William, archbishop of Reims; Peter of Arras; John of Cambrai; Theobald of Amiens; Lambert of Thérouanne; Stephen of Tournai; and the other suffragans of the archbishop, with many princes of France standing by, she was crowned with the royal diadem amid the joy and before the eyes of the entire city. But on the eighty-second day after this marriage, on the advice of certain persons, the king held a council with his archbishops, bishops, and barons at Compiègne. There certain bishops and knights arose and swore that there was consanguinity between the first queen and the second. Having accepted this oath, the king dismissed her without any delay or consultation.

From the Kalends of March [1 March] until the December moon, all the lunar months at their beginnings were exceedingly rainy, except October. On the night of the feast of St Martin there was an eclipse of the moon.

The following letter was brought from overseas to France:

> Brother Geoffrey, by God’s grace humble master of the holy house of the Hospital of Jerusalem, together with the whole chapter of that house, to his dearest and beloved brother in the Lord, William of Villeruns, preceptor overseas: greeting and brotherly love.
>
> Since we believe that you desire certain reports about what is being done in the land of the people of Jerusalem, we make known to you that, in the September just past, a certain man of the pagan people, noble by birth and famous in arms, named Mestoc, ended his life. Then the old lord of the Assyrians died; then the sultan of Iconium died; and after his death anger and discord arose among his sons. Then, in the first week of March, on the day called Wednesday, our persecutor Saladin died. At his death fear and disturbance came upon his people, and anger and dissension arose among his sons. Each of them—for one lives at Aleppo, another at Damascus, another at Babylon [Egypt]—disdains to be subject to his brother, but rather seeks the lordship of the other and of his land. Thus we know truly that since the loss of the land, Christ’s inheritance could not easily have been recovered. The land which Christendom holds under the truce remains almost entirely bereft of inhabitants.
>
> Done in the year of the Lord 1193, at the end of April.

[Col. 0336D] 1194. R. 4. F. 14. A. 5.

Richard, king of England, after a year’s captivity, was ransomed for a great and, so to speak, infinite price in silver. Emperor Henry honorably and graciously released him to England after peace had been established between them. Richard prepared ships in the harbor of Andover, crossed the sea, was received by his people with great favor, and fittingly restored to the throne of his kingdom. Those who had remained faithful to him he elevated with honors; the traitors he deprived of office, and some he even killed. Among them he flayed one who had been the seneschal of his brother John and on whose advice, it was said, John had deserted Richard and gone over to the king of France.

Because the days of Lent were approaching, a truce between him and Philip, king of France, was made until the octave of Pentecost. Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, gathering a large army during those Lenten days, went in hostility against Henry, duke of Louvain, and certain Flemings who had rebelled against him; but making little progress, he returned almost without result, and a truce was scarcely obtained until the middle of August.

Certain men coming from England into Normandy, provoking the men of the king of France with injuries, disturbed the peace of the land. For this reason the king of France, disturbed, did not wait for the truce until the octave of Pentecost as agreed. Instead, having gathered a great army from every side, he besieged around the Ascension of the Lord the very strongly fortified castle of the king of England called Verneuil.

[Note: [Col. 0337D] Verneuil.]

When Richard, king of England, heard this, he crossed the sea and came, not unprepared, to the siege of the castle with many knights and very brave men. The besieged, confident in both their numbers and valor and in the castle’s extremely strong defenses, resisted bravely, leaving the gates open in contempt for the French king’s army. While the king of France was sitting there, the king of England sent chosen knights to Évreux; through the treachery of the citizens, they killed all the men of the king of France who were guarding the castle of that city. For in the preceding year, while the king of England was held in Germany, the king of France had captured that city along with certain castles of Normandy.

When King Philip heard of the slaughter of his men, he became angry beyond what can be said. Abandoning the siege of Verneuil, he came with chosen knights to Évreux and utterly destroyed the entire city, together with the church of St Taurinus and other monasteries, on the solemnity of the Holy Spirit. The king of France had ordered the princes to keep the army at the siege of the castle; but once he had departed, none could restrain him.

Emperor Henry led an army against the Apulians who had rebelled against him (September).

At Arras a certain cleric and his sister were condemned to fire on a charge of homicide. A fire was lit on Baldwin’s Mount while an innumerable multitude of people stood by. Brother and sister were bound to the stake, and a great fire was kindled around them. The woman, invoking Holy Mary, Mother of God, with a loud cry from her heart, ineffable contrition, and confession with her mouth, and exhorting her brother to do the same, was delivered from the fire through the merits of the most blessed Mother of God Mary, while he died in the flames. A wonderful thing: neither her appearance nor speech was changed; not her hair nor a single strand was burned, nor did even the smell of burning remain upon her. When she was asked how she had been saved, she said that a most beautiful lady had been with her and drawn her from the fire. Thereafter she was brought back into the city to the church of Blessed Mary, her deliverer. Almost the whole city gathered, and in the presence of Lord Peter the bishop and the clergy, all raised praises; this great miracle, unheard of in our times, was authenticated by the aforesaid reverend bishop. This was done at Arras in this year, on the solemnity of the Holy Spirit.

Emperor Henry victoriously subjected to himself, without bloodshed, the Apulians, Sicilians, and Calabrians, formerly rebellious to him through Tancred’s violence, and also a certain part of Africa. Expelling its inhabitants, he almost entirely destroyed Palermo because through their faction the empress had been captured in the preceding year. He also seized and imprisoned the nobles of that region who had conspired against him and intended to kill him.

Margaret, countess of Flanders and Hainaut, died and was buried at Bruges in the church of St Donatian beside Count Charles. Her son Baldwin succeeded her in the county of Flanders. Thus the county returned to the rightful heir of Baldwin of Hainaut in the year of the Lord 1194. It had been possessed since 1072 by the successors of Count Robert of Callot, for 123 years.

[Note: [Col. 0337D] Read: Casletensis.]

The successors of this Robert were Robert his son; Baldwin his son; Charles his kinsman; William the Norman; Thierry; and his son Philip. All these arose from the line of Robert who, at Cassel, killed in battle his nephew Arnulf, son of his brother Baldwin of Hainaut, and thus seized the county of Flanders.

1195. R. 5. F. 15. A. 6.

January, February, and April were excessively rainy. On 5 Kalends of April [28 March], in the district of Cambrai, a storm with terrible thunder struck and so destroyed one village together with its church that scarcely small remains were left there.

Emperor Henry returned victoriously from Apulia in triumph (May), bringing with him in custody his wife, Tancred’s son, and the princes who had plotted against him. He also brought with him a great abundance of gold, silver, and other goods.

In July Saracens coming from Africa attacked the king of Spain whom they call “the Little One,” and his army, and inflicted great slaughter upon them. But on the next day the king of Spain, having regained strength through God’s grace, killed more than twenty thousand of them. In that battle the archbishop of St James died.

The election of Simon of Liège was annulled by Pope Celestine, and that of Albert was confirmed.

[Note: [Col. 0338D] Albert of Cuyck, who was elected at Namur in November 1194.]

Yet, to lessen Simon’s grief, the pope conferred upon him a certain cardinalate. Almost all the clerics who had come to Rome with him died, and he himself died there at the beginning of August. Albert, returning from Rome with confirmation of his election, came to Cîteaux and was detained there for a time because of illness. But a false rumor brought to Liège announced to the canons that he was dead. They immediately chose a distinguished canon, son of Philip of Montfaucon.

[Note: [Col. 0339D] Otto; but he submitted himself to Albert. Compare Gislebert, p. 265.]

Thus, after the murder at Reims of Albert, bishop of Liège, the church of Liège wavered in the election of a bishop.

The rain of August was very troublesome for reapers; that of September was burdensome for those gathering the vintage; and that of October was very unfavorable for sowers. On the sixth Ides of October [10 October], after midnight, a violent southwesterly wind overturned houses, destroyed towers, crushed many under falling houses, uprooted aged oaks and fruit trees, and caused great damage in many places.

Many men from the German kingdom—Lorrainers, Germans, and Saxons—at the urging of Emperor Henry took the cross (17 April): bishops, dukes, counts, knights, and an innumerable multitude of the remaining people. Philip, king of France, and Richard, king of England, after long discord at last returned to agreement.

Baldwin, marquis of Namur and count of Hainaut, died on 16 Kalends of January [17 December] and was buried with his fathers at Château-l’Abbaye.

[Note: [Col. 0339D] 12 Kalends of January [21 December], namely the eighth day before the feast of the Nativity of the Lord. Gislebert.]

But because the preceding part of this chronicle explains too little from what stock these counts of Hainaut sprang, we have considered it worthy to set this out briefly for readers. For they derive their origin from the imperial blood of the Romans and the royal blood of the Franks (*Genealogy of the Counts of Flanders*).

[Col. 0339C] Baldwin of Lille, count of Flanders, descended from the line of Charles the Bald, emperor of the Romans and king of the Franks, married Adela, daughter of Robert, king of the Franks. By her he begot Baldwin of Hainaut, count of Flanders and Hainaut, and his brother Robert of Cassel. Baldwin of Hainaut married Richilde, widow of Herman, count of Mons, who was of imperial blood and sister of St Leo IX, pope; by her he begot Arnulf, count of Flanders, whom his uncle Robert killed in the battle of Cassel, and Baldwin of Jerusalem, count of Hainaut, his brother.

Baldwin of Jerusalem married Ida, daughter of Emperor Henry IV, and by her begot Baldwin, from whom Robert, count of Flanders, took the castle of Douai. This Baldwin married Yolande, daughter of Gerard, count of Wassenberg, and by her begot Baldwin, who most effectively subdued the people of Valenciennes when they rebelled against him and increased the county by other useful acquisitions. He also married Ermensende, sister of Henry, count of Namur; by her he begot Baldwin the marquis, to whom fortunate successes also came often. He married Margaret, sister of Philip, count of Flanders; she bore him Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, and also Philip and Henry.

While his father was still alive, Baldwin married Mary, daughter of Henry [count of Champagne, whom he had begotten by a daughter of Louis VIII, king of the Franks.

1196. R. 6. F. 16. A. 7.

Henry the emperor, when winter had passed, again set out for Sicily and Apulia (August); and whatever needed correction in the kingdom was corrected by him. Ships and the other things necessary for the crossing were also prepared for the Germans who had taken up the cross in the preceding year. He placed over them the archbishop of Mainz, a most prudent man. Philip, king of the French, took as an additional wife to Queen Ingeborg the daughter of a certain German count.

> [Note: Col. 0340D: “Mary, daughter of the duke of Bohemia and Moravia.” MIR.]

Peace between Philip, king of the French, and Richard, king of England, was again disturbed. Therefore King Philip, having gathered a great army from every quarter, besieged the castle of the king of England in Normandy called Aumale; after six weeks he took and destroyed it. Many persons, especially young people, died of acute fever. Among them John, bishop of Cambrai, while setting out to join the king in Normandy, died at Amiens.

A most severe scarcity of bread afflicted and impoverished many this year. From the Apennine Mountains to the Ocean Sea, throughout all France and Germany, famine prevailed so greatly that a vast multitude of both sexes perished. Wheat was sold for forty or fifty solidi, though before this disaster it had cost four or five. Thus many who had been thought able to support themselves were compelled, under the dreadful pressure of famine, to emigrate elsewhere. In this way those who, for God’s sake, extended the hand of mercy to them could support the increasing multitude of the poor without great burden. People were forced to eat the flesh even of animals already putrefying, and unfamiliar roots of herbs. Not bread alone, but all other edible things, were sold at prices unheard of among us. Wolves, gathering together around the Alps on the roads and in villages, devoured many people without any fear. The harvest of wheat and the gathering of oats were extraordinarily scant, beyond human estimation.

1197. 7. 17. 8.

The months January, February, March, and April were normal and most pleasant for people this year. Nevertheless, the famine begun in preceding years found no relief, because the sparse harvest of provisions in the previous year could provide no alleviation. Even now thousands upon thousands are dying of hunger; indeed, many, constrained by this necessity, became robbers contrary to their customary way of life and were hanged by the noose. Yet the pleasant mildness of the spring season, and the apparently fine emergence of the crops, became no small consolation to those who waited.

Henry, bishop of Beauvais, was captured by the soldiers of Richard, king of England, and committed to harsh custody at Rouen. Peace between Philip, king of the French, and Baldwin, count of Flanders, was disturbed at the prompting of Richard, king of England. In July Count Baldwin, having assembled a plentiful army from every quarter, advanced against the king of the French through the districts of Tournai and Cambrai and took all the castles in that region. Then, moving toward the city of Arras, he besieged it from the east; but on the second day of the siege he suddenly withdrew.

When Philip, king of the French, heard this and took it ill, he gathered the bishops and abbots of his kingdom, together with a great multitude of cavalry and infantry, and marched against Baldwin. On the vigil of the Assumption of Blessed Mary he unexpectedly arrived at Douai; but, after receiving counsel advantageous to us, departed on that same day. Then, passing through the district of Laetia—

> [Note: Col. 0341D: “Or Laetica, by the river Lys, where the towns of Cassel and Aire are situated.”]

—he crossed the bridge at Aire over the river called the Lys and entered the count’s land to ravage it. But, having suffered certain misfortunes, he held a conference with the count outside Ypres; the business remaining unfinished, he returned to his own territory. Many who had feared his arrival laughed at his ineffectual departure. A truce for one year was sworn between the two kings.

The vintage throughout France—in the districts of Rheims, Laon, Soissons, Noyon, and Beauvais—was sparse and late. Consequently peasants who cultivated vineyards and had borrowed money against the future wine, being unable to repay it in wine, were forced to flee.

Henry the emperor died in Apulia (28 September). He was not of notable bodily stature; but his learning, greatness of spirit, justice, and prudence surpassed Absalom’s beauty. The world mourns his death: Syria, Sicily, Apulia, Calabria, Africa, Italy, Germany, Saxony, Bavaria, Swabia, Frisia, Austria, and Lotharingia. For all were troubled by his death. His little son was received by the Sicilians as king by paternal right; moreover Philip, brother of Emperor Henry, was appointed the boy’s guardian.

A lamentable misfortune occurred in the city of Acre. Henry, count of Champagne and prince of Christianity overseas, one day wished to open a window in the upper room of a certain house in that city; he fell through it to the ground and, his neck broken, alas, died in the sixth year of his principate. His death brought ineffable sorrow to Christians and great joy to Saracens. The Christian soldiers whom Emperor Henry had sent overseas before his death repeatedly fought the Turks; but we have not yet heard of any certain victory for our side.

1198. F. 18. A. 9.

A very mild winter: January, February, and March were calm and pleasant; April and May, however, were rainy and cold.

Celestine III, pope, died on 27 December, old and full of days. Lothair, cardinal deacon, a Roman by birth, called Innocent, became the third pope of that name, and, though young in age, presided as the 184th head of the Roman Church. Fulk, a venerable priest from the region of Paris, publicly preached throughout all France by apostolic authority.

> [Note: Col. 0342D: “The venerable priest Fulk preaches the word of God and heals many sick persons.” Annals of Anchin. Compare the *Annals of Anchin*.]

Although in his sermon he rebuked every vice, the full force of his preaching thundered especially against greedy and covetous usurers, negligent prelates, and incontinent priests.
