Almost the whole country was changed for the better through his preaching. He also converted a very great multitude of public women. He was powerful in working miracles: he gave sight to the blind, cured the lame, restored hearing to the deaf; and, what was more miraculous than all else, an innumerable multitude of people flocked from every direction to hear him as though he were an apostle.

After Emperor Henry’s death, the leading men of the German kingdom, uncertain whom to appoint king, elected Philip, duke of Swabia, brother of Emperor Henry—whom we have mentioned above as the boy’s guardian—as king: Swabians, Bavarians, Germans, Apulians, and Sicilians (5 March). But the Saxons and Lotharingians elevated Otto, count of Poitou, son of Henry, duke of Saxony, as king in the palace at Aachen. He was the son of the sister of Richard, king of England. By Richard’s counsel and assistance, and that of Count Baldwin of Flanders, with the consent of the archbishop of Cologne and the leading men of Lotharingia, Otto besieged the palace of Aachen against Waleran, son of the duke of Limburg, who held the town of Aachen for Philip, duke of Swabia, with a strong force of soldiers. In the sixth week of the siege, worn down by manifold hardships and receiving no aid from the man for whom they held the palace, they surrendered the castle to Otto with all honour preserved. Immediately the archbishop of Cologne, together with his suffragans, anointed him with holy oil and seated him upon the royal throne (12 July). For since the days of Charlemagne, the royal seat has been at Aachen, where Charlemagne himself rests. King Otto took as wife the daughter of Godfrey, count of Louvain and duke of Lotharingia.

Philip the duke and Otto the king, contending for the empire, could not cross the river Rhine, which divides Lotharingia from Saxony: Philip could not pass from east to west, nor Otto from west to east. Therefore I omit to prefix the title “King of the Romans,” that is, R., and the title “King of Jerusalem,” that is, H.; for after the death of Henry, son of Frederick, no one rules in Rome as emperor, and in the overseas regions, after the death of Henry, count of Champagne, no Christian rules as king.

After August, Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, having gathered a strong multitude both of mounted and foot soldiers, went into Flanders in order to restore to his county the castles which, as it seemed to him, belonged by right to himself but which the king held unjustly. The people of Aire, fearing his attack, received him peacefully and surrendered without delay. Then leading his army to Saint-Omer, he besieged the castle. Those under siege shut the gates and, by the count’s own agreement and counsel, sent messengers to the king in France. Receiving and expecting no assistance from him, they surrendered the castle to the count and, after six weeks, peacefully and honourably received him within it.

While Count Baldwin was besieging Saint-Omer, Richard, king of England, attended by a multitude of soldiers, attacked Philip, king of France, in the Vexin—

> [Note: Col. 0343D: “The Vexin, between the Andelle, the Oise, and the Seine.”]

—The king of the French came against him and, with his armour changed, fell into the river near Gisors. Barely drawn out from it, after some of his nobler knights had been captured, he escaped with great difficulty. Immediately gathering a plentiful army, he ravaged with fire and plundering the whole neighbouring land of Normandy. During this war, provisions, both for people and for livestock, were sold at a high price.

1199. F. 19. A. 10.

After the days of the Nativity of the Lord had passed, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, came into France as legate sent by Pope Innocent. He bore letters to Philip, king of the French, containing an apostolic command that he should lawfully restore to himself Queen Ingeborg, the venerable queen from whom he had been separated by a false oath of consanguinity. If he refused to comply, he was to be bound by anathema.

A council was held on the borders of the two kingdoms. The kings of France and England both assembled with a multitude of bishops, abbots, counts, priors, provosts, and an innumerable multitude of people of both orders. Much effort was made to establish peace between the kings and the count of Flanders, but it was not brought to effect. Still, a truce, to be maintained for five years, was obtained in words; it scarcely endured until Easter.

During Lent, a treasure was found in the Limousin, which the count of Limoges claimed for himself. Richard, king of England and supreme prince of that land, demanded the treasure from the count, but did not obtain it. Angered by this, the king besieged, himself armed and with an armed force, the count’s castle. There, wishing to strike a certain person with a crossbow bolt, the king himself was struck in the shoulder by that same crossbow; seven days later he died and was buried at Fontevraud with his father. His brother John succeeded him in the kingdom. John sluggishly pursued the war which his brother Richard had waged vigorously and powerfully against the king of France; finally making peace with the king, he released the bishop of Beauvais and other captives and sent them back to the king of France.

Peter of Corbeil was consecrated bishop of Cambrai. The harvest and vintage were moderately abundant. Cardinal Peter, remaining in France for ten months, carried out lukewarmly the business concerning the queen’s divorce entrusted to him.

Count Baldwin ravaged the land of the king of France with plundering and fire in the districts of Artois, Thérouanne, and Arida Gamantia. Philip, count of Namur, his brother, was captured with certain other knights; bound in irons, they were sent to the king in France. Mary, countess of Flanders, went to Paris to arrange peace between the king and the count. The king received her honourably and sent her home joyful and assured of peace, together with certain captives as pledges of peace. During Advent, Cardinal Peter held a council at Dijon, the castle of Burgundy, with ecclesiastical persons.

Every ordinance made there by them needs neither pen nor parchment.

1200. 20. 1.

Philip, king of France, and Baldwin, count of Flanders, met for a conference at Péronne during the very days of the Nativity of the Lord. There, through the resourcefulness of Countess Mary, they swore firm peace with one another; this peace was a great cause of joy both to France and to Flanders.

Cardinal Peter, passing through Burgundy, crossed the Apennine Mountains. There he issued the judgment which, by the pope’s command, he ought to have issued in France; and with unprecedented severity he placed the king and all his land under interdict. Certain bishops observed the sentence of interdict most fervently: the bishops of Paris, Senlis, Soissons, Amiens, Arras, and others of whom we have no knowledge. Pope Innocent extolled these bishops with remarkable praises in letters sent to them; those who defied the interdict he frightened with threatening words.

Philip, king of France, John, king of England, Baldwin, count of Flanders, and many other princes of the two kingdoms met for a mutual conference on the borders of France and Normandy. There Louis, the boy, son of the king of France, took as wife the daughter of the king of Spain; she was the daughter of the sister of John, king of England. There firm peace was confirmed among the kings and princes. For John, king of England, relinquished—

> [Note: Col. 0343D: That is, abandoned.]

—the castles of the Vexin, namely Gisors and others, over which war between the kings of the two kingdoms had been waged for many years. Octavian, bishop of Ostia, was sent to France as legate by Pope Innocent. The king of France received him honourably, verbally restored Queen Ingeborg to himself at the pope’s command, renounced the woman whom he had taken in addition, and thus obtained absolution for the land of the king of France from the interdict.

1201. 21. 2.

> [Note: Col. 0343: “The same hand added this year later, in slightly different ink. The same material, copied from ours, is found in manuscript Douai no. 840 and thence in Amiens no. 386.”]

The winter was neither mild nor excessively harsh, but moderate between the two. January, February, March, April, and May were pleasant and normal. In the middle of March, Cardinal Octavian, archbishops, and bishops assembled with Philip, king of France, in the city of Soissons, with an innumerable multitude of clergy and people, in order to conduct a certain and just judgment concerning the divorce of king and queen according to Pope Innocent’s command. But because John, cardinal of Saint Paul, a monk of our order, to whom this case had chiefly been entrusted by the Apostolic See, had not yet arrived, the conference was postponed until his arrival. When he came in May, the king, archbishops, and bishops received him with great joy in the aforesaid city of Soissons, in the church of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. Gifts were offered to him by the king, but that righteous man shook his hands free from the king’s gift.

They came together for the conference. The king appeared surrounded and armed by a multitude of advocates who would plead his case as he wished; but the queen came alone—alas—having no advocate but God. Since among so great a multitude no one dared, for fear of the king, to plead for her, an unknown poor cleric rose from the midst. With the permission of the king and cardinals, he explained the queen’s case so learnedly that the king himself, the cardinals, and all the bishops marvelled. It is said that neither afterwards nor before had he been seen by anyone in that city. The king, however, departed from the conference without awaiting the ecclesiastical judgment prescribed by the decrees of the holy Fathers. The cardinals and bishops also returned home, the case still undecided.

> [Note: Col. 0345: “Here this hand ends. What follows was written by another person at the beginning of the thirteenth century, continuously, without any change of handwriting or ink; moreover, the words *obiit—decimus* are on an erasure. Of these materials, what we have printed in smaller type was copied word for word from the Annals of Anchin, where the same material is found written in several contemporary hands.”]

(*Annals of Anchin.*) Lord Simon, our ninth abbot, died; Lord Adam, the tenth, succeeded him.

1203. The monks first entered the great church on Palm Sunday.

1204. Lord Adam, our tenth abbot, died; Lord William, the eleventh, succeeded him, later abbot of Saint-Amand. Having gone to Rome and returned thence, he became a monk of Clairvaux. When he became abbot of Saint-Amand, Lord Simon, the twelfth abbot, succeeded him. In his time he demolished many old workshops and constructed many new buildings, as well as costly, commendable, and fitting choir stalls. He also built a chapel in honour of the Blessed Virgin which, by its dignity and beauty, can hold the eyes of beholders in prolonged attention. He happily completed, with much labour and no small expense, the church begun by his uncle Simon, the ninth abbot, as may still be seen quite plainly. He adorned that church most diligently with two bell-towers and eleven bells.

> (Annals of Anchin.)

Moreover, he acquired many revenues. In this same year the city of Constantinople was captured by Count Baldwin, lord of Flanders and Hainaut; in that city, through God’s grace, he was elected and consecrated emperor and Augustus of the Romans.

1208. In this year William, our eleventh abbot, became abbot of Saint-Amand; Lord Simon, the twelfth abbot, of whom we have spoken above, succeeded him.

1212. Ferdinand of Portugal married Joan, countess of Flanders and Hainaut.

1213. In this year Lord Simon, the twelfth abbot, began to build the cloister. There was a great battle between Philip, king of France, and his party on one side, and Ferdinand, the Flemings, and Otto, emperor of Germany, on the other, at the bridge of Bouvines; but the French won the victory (27 July 1214). When Otto saw this, he withdrew with some of his followers. Ferdinand, however, and Renaud, count of Boulogne, who was with him, and Wilekin, count of Holland, were captured in that battle. Afterwards Ferdinand was redeemed from the king of France’s captivity at no small price through his illustrious wife Joan, countess of Flanders.

> [Note: Col. 0345: *illustram*, so the manuscript.]

The count of Boulogne died in a certain castle situated on the Seine, called Goulet, below Vernon.

> [Note: Col. 0345: “*sub unone*, manuscript.”]  
> [Note: Col. 0345D: “Year 1227. Most say that he was captured and died at Péronne.”]

1216. Louis, firstborn son of Philip, king of France, entered England and took certain castles; but in the following year he returned to France at the command of Pope Honorius.

1218. The monks of Anchin entered the new choir on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, in the presence of the venerable Everard, bishop of Amiens.

1219. Pope Honorius III granted Lord Simon, twelfth abbot of Anchin, and his successors the use of mitre and ring, with certain privileges and indulgences.

1222. In this year the foundations of the church of Blessed Mary were laid on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, Monday.

1223. Philip, illustrious king of France, died; his firstborn, Louis, succeeded him.

1224. In Lent of this year, a certain unknown man came and lived as a hermit in the forest of Glauchon near Mortagne.

> [Note: Col. 0346D: “In the region of Tournai.”]

At length he revealed to certain people that he himself was Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut and emperor of Constantinople. Hearing this, certain nobles believed his words, brought him honourably to Valenciennes, and, having adorned him there as befitted an emperor and count, conducted him through Flanders. Many Flemings did homage to him as count, and finally he entered Lille with a very great following and display.

When Louis, king of France, heard the report concerning him, he appointed him a day at Péronne, so that he might recognize the man who said that he was the king’s uncle and might render due homage to him for the county of Flanders, if he were count of Flanders, while coming and returning under safe-conduct. At last he came at the appointed hour and boldly appeared before King Louis and his council in the king’s palace. Examined under many questions, he gave no certain answer. He was thus convicted by many arguments of acting deceitfully and lying in every respect; he departed in shame. The aforesaid king had strictly commanded him to leave his territory without delay.

On the same day on which he took leave of the king, he came to Valenciennes both by day and night—

> [Note: Col. 0347: “Absent from the manuscript.”]

—from which place he secretly and stealthily fled. When this was heard, Joan, countess of Flanders, cautiously caused him to be sought; he was eventually found and brought to the said countess at Lille. There, by the judgment and counsel of her barons, he was condemned to be dragged by horses outside the town and hanged. Thus he ended his unhappy life.

1226.

> [Note: Col. 0347: “MCCXXV, manuscript.”]

King Louis set out against the Albigensians with many nobles, both bishops and princes: namely William of Joinville, archbishop of Rheims—

> [Note: Col. 0347B: “Joinville.”]

—. . . . .

> [Note: Col. 0347: “Here the name of some bishop has been erased.”]

—and Garin, bishop of Senlis—

> [Note: Col. 0347: “Thus corrected in the manuscript from *episcopis*, ‘bishops.’”]

—Philip, count of Boulogne, Guy, count of Saint-Pol, and many others, clerics as well as laymen. They besieged and took Avignon. But during the siege Count Guy of Saint-Pol was struck and killed by a stone from a mangonel. King Louis and many others, clerics as well as laymen, died by poison in that region; the king’s body was secretly and carefully brought to the church of Saint Denis in France and buried with royal honour.

> [Note: Col. 0347: “Here ends the final quire of the manuscript, which from the beginning contained only four leaves; therefore what is now lost does not appear to have been very extensive. We have supplied the material from the Annals of Anchin and from the Bergues continuation which is to follow immediately. That continuation copied it word for word from our manuscript, but did not use the Annals; therefore what occurs in that continuation and likewise in the Annals must also have been in B5. These are the passages enclosed above in brackets.”]

1227. (*Annals of Anchin.*) The church of Blessed Mary at Anchin was dedicated by the venerable Father Pons, bishop of Arras.

1234. (*Ibid.*) On the Ides of April died Lord Simon of pious memory, our twelfth abbot, a man very religious, honourable, and prudent, who governed the church of Anchin most vigorously for twenty-five years. Lord William, the thirteenth abbot, succeeded him, having been received as a monk by the aforesaid venerable father.

1137. (*Ibid.*) Joan, countess of Flanders, took as husband Thomas, brother of the count of Savoy.

## CONTINUATION OF BERGUES

[Col. 0347]

In the now-lost manuscript B5*, copied from B5, a monk of Saint-Winoc of Bergues scattered historical notes in the margins and between the lines of the continuation for the years 1201–1237 printed above, sometimes recounting matters he himself had seen, as under the year 1220. Immediately after these were written, William, abbot of Andres, inserted them verbatim into the chronicle of his monastery, except only for those passages indicated below the text.

> [Note: Col. 0347C: “Which, as he himself says, we have assembled into one compendium from the chronicles of Saint-Bertin and neighbouring churches”; D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, II.]

Iperius in turn copied them from William. In the sixteenth century a monk of Saint Peter’s at Ghent copied manuscript B5**, the Bergues manuscript, beginning with the year 1149. But with such ignorance did he combine the Bergues additions—undoubtedly inserted among the Anchin materials insofar as the intervening space allowed—with those materials into one whole, that the result was an extreme confusion of dates. Leaving that confusion untouched, we have everywhere indicated in the margin the correct years from the Chronicle of Andres.

> [Note: Col. 0347C: “We place them in the text, within brackets. Patrologia edition.”]

The same B5** appended to ours, without any distinction and as though it were one work, an entirely different composition for the years 1222–1228, compiled from the Annals of Blandain copied word for word, from Baldwin of Ninove, and from Martin of Poland, with only a very few materials inserted from elsewhere: an unworthy compilation to be published.

[1202] William, archbishop of Rheims, of pious memory, died.

[1204] In the year of the Lord 1202: “Lord Adam—of the Romans.”

> [Note: Col. 0348C: “Of the material which our author copied word for word from Anchin, we give here only the opening and closing words, printed in smaller type, since the complete text has already appeared on pp. 436–437.”]

[1208] In the year of the Lord 1203: “In this year William—of whom we have spoken above.”

[1203] Mary, wife of the aforesaid Count Baldwin and niece of the illustrious Philip, king of France, followed her husband. Having endured many severe perils of the sea, she finally reached Acre; there, worn down by a long illness, she breathed forth her spirit.

[1203] John, king of England, abandoning Normandy and Aquitaine with all their dependencies, fled as though to an asylum, swiftly crossed the sea, and came to England.

[1201] The Balvotins burned the house of Lady Matilda, queen of Portugal and countess of Flanders, at Furnes and reduced it to ashes. Angered by the affront inflicted upon her, she gathered a great army, sought those responsible, found them at the village of Houthem in the place called Holin, and besieged them.

[1212] In the year of the Lord 1204, Ferdinand of Portugal married Joan, countess of Flanders and Hainaut.

[1205] Baldwin, emperor of Constantinople, was captured by John surnamed Blake in a battle between them; thereafter he appeared to none of his own people.

[1205] Baldwin, count of Guînes, died on 2 January and was buried at Andres. The town of Bergues was besieged by the Blavotins. A few of the Isengrin party sallied out against them and immediately turned to flight. One of the Blavotins, named Gerard Fal, seeing his companions running before him and thinking they were enemies fleeing, killed seven of his own men. Afterwards the Isengrins, recovering strength and courage, gathered seven men together, whose leader was a certain knight named Christian of Prato, and put all the Blavotins to flight, numbering about six thousand men.

> [Note: Col. 0349: “The passage ‘The town was besieged—put them to flight’ is absent from the Chronicle of Andres.”]

[1213] In the year of the Lord 1205, Lord Simon, the twelfth abbot, began to build the cloister.

[1207] Lambert, bishop of Thérouanne, died; John, archdeacon and his nephew, succeeded him.

[1209] Because of the church of Canterbury, all England was placed under interdict; none celebrated divine offices except the Cistercians.

[1208] In the province of Saint-Gilles, the heresy of the Albigensians was discovered; its adherents wickedly murdered the venerable Peter, legate of the Apostolic See, because of his confession of Jesus Christ.

[1208] Philip, called *Suavus* (“the Swabian”)—

> [Note: Col. 0349: “*Suavis*, B5**.”]

—already made king of Germany and aspiring to the Roman Empire, perished when struck by the sword of one of his own men.

[1209] At the request of Renaud, count of Boulogne, Philip, king of France, entered the land of Arnold, count of Guînes. Having demolished the castle called Bonham and stationed guards in the other castles of that count, he returned to France.

[1213] “There was a great battle—he died at Goulet below Vernon.”

[1213] In the year of the Lord 1106: “Louis—France.”

[1211] Renaud, count of Boulogne, was expelled from his land by his lord Philip, king of the French.

[1212] The king of Morocco in Africa came by ship into the regions of Spain. Having resolved to attack the Christians, he immediately, as though assured of victory, ordered all the ships he had brought to be broken up.

[1212] The greater part of France, marked with Christ’s cross upon the breast, and an innumerable multitude from Flanders and Germany hurried to the province of Saint-Gilles to exterminate the unbelieving Albigensians.

[1212] In the following winter Ferdinand, son of the king of Portugal, married Joan, daughter of Lord Baldwin, emperor of Constantinople and count of Flanders and Hainaut.

[1218] In the year of the Lord 1207: “The monks—of the Lord.”

[1213] Philip, king of France, having assembled a great army and fleet, was thought by many to be about to cross to England. But he changed his plan, as it seemed, led his entire army into Flanders, received hostages from the principal towns—namely Ypres, Ghent, and Bruges—and returned to France. After his departure, Ferdinand, count of Flanders, recovered his towns. Subsequently Lord Louis, firstborn son of the king of France, burned and devastated for the most part the coastal town called Nieuwpoort and certain others, namely Bailleul and Steenvoorde; innumerable people of both sexes were captured there. Then, after a few days had passed, the count of Flanders took the city of Tournai. “Honorius—indulgences.”

[1219] In the territory of Saint-Pol, in August, such a flood of rain occurred that it destroyed a large part of the wall of that castle, while other villages, with all their houses, were submerged.

> [Note: Col. 0349: “The Chronicle of Andres does not contain ‘In the territory—submerged.’”]

[1214] John, king of England, came to Poitou with a great army. Having made an alliance with the Poitevins and recovered the castles, the lord king of France, greatly provoked, sent his firstborn son Louis and the marshal there with many knights to resist him. The king of France recalled his mercenaries from the Flemish castles. A few days later, Ferdinand, count of Flanders, entered the land of Arnold, count of Guînes, with a great army.

[1222] In the year of the Lord 1210 the foundations of the church of Blessed Mary were laid on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, Monday.

[1215] Frederick, king of Apulia, was crowned king at Aachen; there he took the cross, together with many bishops, dukes, and counts.

[1215] In the year of the Lord 1215, the holy universal synod was held at Rome, in the church of the Saviour called the Constantinian, in November, in the third indiction, in the eighteenth year of Pope Innocent’s pontificate. Four hundred and twelve bishops were also present, among whom were two of the principal patriarchs, namely those of Constantinople and Jerusalem. The patriarch of Antioch, detained by grave illness, could not come, but sent in his place the bishop of Antaradus as his vicar. The patriarch of Alexandria, being under the dominion of the Saracens, did what he could, sending his own brother, a deacon.

> [Note: Col. 0349: “The words *diaconum germanum suum* are absent from B5**; we added them from the Chronicle of Andres.”]

[1223] In the year of the Lord 1212, the illustrious Philip died; his firstborn, Louis, succeeded him.

[1216] Lord Louis, firstborn son of the lord king of France, according to his promise to the barons of England, crossed the sea with a great army and landed at Stenhore in England.

[1216] In the eighteenth year of his pontificate Innocent died on the third day of the month—

> [Note: Col. 0349: “Thus the manuscript; the passage is corrupt.”]

—that is, on 16 July, and was buried at Perugia. Honorius III, previously called Sinchius, succeeded him.

> [Note: Col. 0351: “*Cincius* in the Chronicle of Andres, which gives this material somewhat more briefly.”]

[1216] Henry, emperor of Constantinople, uncle of Louis, firstborn son of the king of France, paid the debt of death after being poisoned by his own wife.

[1216] John, king of England, called Lackland, breathed his last; his son Henry succeeded him.

[1224] In the year of the Lord 1213: “In Lent—he ended his life.”

[1225] In the year of the Lord 1214: “Louis—buried.”

[1227] In the year of the Lord 1215: “The church was dedicated—bishop.”

[1216] Peter, count of Auxerre, was consecrated emperor of Constantinople by Pope Honorius at Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls. He hastened to Constantinople and was treacherously captured in a tower by one of his own men, who had led him there to see it. The empress, his wife, escaped, though many of her people were killed.

[1218] Otto, emperor for a short time, died and was buried at Brunswick.

[1217] On the day before the Nones of March, Matilda, queen of Portugal, died; Philip, count of Flanders, had taken her as wife. Pons, bishop of Arras, died.

> [Note: Col. 0351: “The Chronicle of Andres does not contain ‘Pons, bishop of Arras, died.’”]

[1218] Simon, count of Montfort, died among the Albigensians by his own death; his son Alberic succeeded him, an illustrious man and Catholic in the faith of Christ.

[1231] In the year of the Lord 1217: “On the Ides of April—received as a monk.”

[1218] An innumerable multitude of crusaders hastened to Jerusalem by sea and land.

> [Note: Col. 0351: *mare*, “by sea,” B5**.]

With them the duke of Austria, a man Catholic in every respect, besieged the castle of Damietta, situated on the river Nile, which was called the key of Egypt and of the land of Jerusalem. Lord Alberic, archbishop of Rheims, returning from the land of Jerusalem, died at Pavia; the bishop of Langres succeeded him.

[1218] Lord Goswin, bishop of Tournai, of good memory, died.

> [Note: Col. 0351: “The Chronicle of Andres does not contain ‘Lord Goswin—died.’”]

[1219] Louis, firstborn son of the lord king of France, set out with a great army and an innumerable multitude against the Albigensians.

[1220] The city of Damietta on the Nile, long besieged by the Christians, was taken.

In the year of the Lord 1218, Louis, king of the Franks, took as his wife the daughter of the count of Provence. [Note: [Col. 0351] “Louis—Provence” is absent from the Chronicle of Andres.] [1220.] At the same time the church of Saint Giles was begun at the town. The glorious body of the glorious martyr of Christ Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, was elevated by Lord Stephen, archbishop of Canterbury, and Lord William, archbishop of Reims, with Henry, king of the English, still a boy, standing by [Note: [Col. 0351] Absent from B5**; supplied from the Andres chronicle.], and with very many bishops and abbots present, together with an innumerable multitude of clerics, knights, and others. [1220.] Frederick, called “the boy of Apulia,” was consecrated emperor of the Romans at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, by Pope Honorius. [1220.] Ralph, bishop of Arras, of good memory, died; Pons, archdeacon of Arras, succeeded him. [1220.] Arnold, count of Guînes, paid the debt he owed to death.

In the year of the Lord 1222, on the day after Saint Lawrence, at evening while the convent was dining, the air was disturbed among us; a density of darkness appeared, and the violence of the winds and crash of thunder filled us with great terror. The corruption of the air was so great that our waters were corrupted by it and fish died; trees and woods were as though consumed by fire; birds were killed; our vineyard was shorn nearly to the ground by the violence of hail and large stones; [Col. 0352B] the monastery’s glazed windows were shattered by the rushing winds, and some were even carried far away from the monastery. There was also such a stench that we had to close our nostrils because it was unbearable. [Note: [Col. 0351] “In the year—close” is absent from the Chronicle of Andres.] [1221.] The Saracens recovered the city of Damietta, which the Christians had possessed for some time. By command of Pope Gregory IX, Master Robert of the Order of Preachers came into the kingdom of France and the county of Flanders. He examined many persons of both sexes concerning the faith, consumed many unbelievers in avenging flames, and consigned many to perpetual imprisonment. [Note: [Col. 0351] These entries occur in B5**, but only after the personal entries, through a scribe’s error.] A glorious translation of Oswald, king and martyr, and of Ydberga [Note: [Col. 0351] *ydaberge* in B5*.], virgin and mother, formerly daughter of King Pippin, was performed by Lord Adam, bishop of Thérouanne, upon the mountain called Groneberch. [Col. 0352C] Their glorious relics were together deposited in a shrine fittingly made of gold and silver. Many venerable and illustrious persons attended this glorious translation: the aforesaid venerable Bishop Adam; Abbot John of Saint-Bertin; William, abbot of La Capelle; William of Andres; Roger, abbot of Saint John’s; John, abbot of Alciacum; William, provost of Watten; John, provost of Formeselles; Giles, provost of Lo; John, provost of Eversham; and very many other abbots and provosts; a great multitude of the ecclesiastical order; and the noble lady Joan, countess of Flanders and Hainaut, with a very large company of distinguished persons, [Col. 0352D] and an innumerable multitude of ordinary people. This translation took place in the time of Lord Ingelmar, abbot of Bergues.

In the year of the Lord 1211, John, son of Peter, count of Brittany, brother of Count Robert, took as wife the daughter of the count of Champagne. Therefore the king of France seized from the count of Champagne two of that count’s castles, namely Montereau in Fordione and Bray-sur-Seine. [Note: [Col. 0351] “By command of the supreme pontiff—Seine” is absent from the Chronicle of Andres.] [1232.] In that same spring, [Col. 0353A] new statutes concerning the reform of the Black Order were issued by Pope Gregory. [1222.] Lord Peter of Corbeil, archbishop of Sens, moderately well trained in literary learning, bade farewell to this world; Master Walter, surnamed Cornutus, succeeded him. Siwert, castellan of Bergues, a young man of good character and mature conduct, when he had prepared his hauberk, shield, and all his arms and was about to be made a knight, died on 2 May, lest malice should change his understanding. Robert, brother of King Louis, was made count of Arras and lord of Lens, Hesdin, and Saint-Omer; he took as wife the daughter of the duke of Brabant. In this year Henry, king of the English, took as wife the daughter of the count of [Col. 0354A] Provence, sister of the queen of the Franks. Geoffrey, bishop of Cambrai, died, and Master Givard of Laon, chancellor of Paris, succeeded him. [1237.] In the same year Baldwin, the young emperor of Constantinople, came to France and to Flanders, and the land that belonged to him by hereditary right was restored to him. [Note: [Col. 0353A] “Siwert—belonged” is absent from the Chronicle of Andres.] [1237.] Joan, countess of Flanders, took as husband Thomas, brother of the count of Savoy. [1223.] Philip, king of France, a Catholic man, an indomitable tamer of enemies, breathed his last, not without the great lamentation of Mother Church; he was borne to the monastery of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite and there buried with due honour.

## Hasnon Supplement

[Col. 0353]

The monk of Hasnon, copying Sigebert from manuscript B, received these additions from it for the years 651, 690, 773, 1076, 1079, 1086, 1090, 1092, 1093, 1095, 1100, and 1105; from the Affligem annals, for 1119, 1120, 1126, 1128, 1134, 1136, and 1140; and from the Gembloux annals, for 1142 and 1146. He further copied the Blandin annals for the years 859, 861–865, 869, 870, 878–882, 885, 887, 889, 891–893, 896, 898, 912, 913, 918, 922, 928, 931–933, 938, 941, 944, 945, 949, 951, 953, 959, 960, 962, 964, 973, 975, 979, 981, 989, 994, 995, 1002, 1009, 1013, 1014, 1020, 1023, 1030, 1032, 1035, 1036, 1038, 1041, 1044, 1045, 1048, 1057, 1058, 1061, 1063, 1067–1069, 1098, 1100, 1105–1111, 1114, 1118, 1133, 1137, 1145, 1159, 1161, and 1165. Besides these, it contains only the following, which we print from B4* and 4**.

[Col. 0353B] 610. The first foundation of the church of Marchiennes by Saint Amand and the first abbot of Saint Peter of Ghent. [Note: [Col. 0353] Absent from B4, where all entries for this year were added in the margin by a rubricator.]

670. (From Tomellus.) The monastery of Hasnon was founded by John, an illustrious man, and his equally illustrious sister Eulalia, in the year 670 of the Incarnate Word, while Pope Adeodatus presided over the Apostolic See, in the fourth year of King Theuderic, son of King Clovis and Queen Balthild. When the builder had put the finishing hand to the work, the venerable bishop Vindician of the church of Cambrai having been summoned, the place was dedicated to God and to the holy apostles Peter and Paul on 29 April. Then holy Zion, united to her Bridegroom, bore children of holy love, through whom she spread abroad the fragrance of virtues, so that she could joyfully say: [Col. 0353C] “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.”

1068. (Ibid.) The restoration of the monastery of Hasnon by Baldwin VI, margrave of the Flemings and at the same time count of Hainaut. Having expelled the secular canons, he distinguished the place with monastic observances and enriched it with more ample revenues, while Pope Alexander presided over the Apostolic See. When he had put the finishing hand to the work, the venerable bishops having been summoned, the place was dedicated to God and to the holy apostles Peter and Paul on 3 June. The dedication [Col. 0354B] of the church of Hasnon in honour of the apostles Peter and Paul, consecrated by three bishops—namely Lietbert, bishop of Cambrai; Rabodo, bishop of Noyon; and Rainer, bishop of Orléans—in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1070, indiction 8, epact 6, concurrent 4, cycle 4, while Pope Alexander presided over the Apostolic See; he had formerly been bishop at Lucca. Philip, son of Henry, reigned as king of the Franks, and Baldwin reigned as count of the Flemings and Hainaulters and restorer of that place. The saints present were: Saint Marcellus, pope, of Hautmont; [Note: [Col. 0353C] Hautmont, diocese of Cambrai.] Saint Omer of the people of Thérouanne; Saint Piat, martyr, of Seclin; [Note: [Col. 0353C] Seclin, near Lille.] Saint Ghislain of the monastery of Celle; Saint Salvius, martyr, of Valenciennes; Saint Vincent of Soignies; [Note: [Col. 0354C] Soignies, in Hainaut.] the Holy Innocents [Col. 0354C] of Condé; Saint Bertin, abbot; Saint Amatus of Douai; Saint Winoc, abbot; Saint Donatian of Bruges; Saint Wandrille, abbot; Saint Vedast of Arras; Saint Bavo; Saint Everard; Saint Amand of Elnone; Saint Eubert of Lille; Saint Landelin; Saint Hugh; Saint Aicadrius; Saint Rictrude; Saint Eusebia; Saint Aldegund; Saint Ragenfrid; Saint Regina; and Saint Waltrude. The names of the abbots who were present: Roland, first abbot of this place; Lambert; Adelard; Guederic; [Col. 0355A] Ursio; Walter; Gualdric; Remigius; Rainer; Rainard; Folcard; Siger; Heribert; Ermenger; and Walbert. The names of the abbesses: Fredesendis [Note: [Col. 0355B] *Fredesensis* in B4* and 4**.] and Gerberga.

1070. In the year of the Incarnate Word 1070, on 17 July, Baldwin VI, margrave of the Flemings and count of Hainaut, died. He gave arms to Philip, king of the Franks, son of Baldwin, likewise prince of the Flemings before him and guardian of that same King Philip, in the third year of Philip’s reign after [Note: [Col. 0355B] Supplied by the editor; absent from B4* and 4**.] his father’s death.

1149. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1149, indiction 12, epact 9, concurrent in the nineteen-year cycle 10, lunar key [Note: [Col. 0355B] A variable number used to find the beginnings of five movable feasts in Paschal cycles.] 18, the eighteenth lunar day, on 28 June, while Pope Eugenius presided and King [Col. 0355B] Louis reigned, the church of Hasnon was solemnly dedicated on Sunday in the octave of Pentecost. Throughout that day and night the air was wholly clear, although for nearly fifteen days it had been very rainy. The dedication was performed by Lord Samson, venerable bishop of the church of Reims, and his suffragans, distinguished men—Goscelin, bishop of Soissons; Nicholas, bishop of Cambrai; Milo, [Col. 0356A] bishop of Thérouanne; and Gerald, bishop of Tournai—in honour of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen. This was done in the time of Lord Fulk, the eighth abbot of that place. On the same day the altar of the Lord’s Cross in the middle of the basilica was consecrated by Lord Goscelin, bishop of Soissons; and, happily, the altar in honour of the blessed apostle Andrew in the oratory of Saint Mary Magdalene. Amen. Baldwin IV, count of Hainaut, attended with his barons. Many other honourable men were also present: Boso, archdeacon of the diocese of Reims; Hugh and Luke of Arras; John and Alard, archdeacons of Cambrai; Milo, archdeacon of Thérouanne; and very many abbots: of Saint-Theoderic, [Note: [Col. 0355B] Saint-Thierry-du-Mont-d’Or, diocese of Reims.] Saint-Médard; [Col. 0356B] of Homblières; [Note: [Col. 0355B] Homblières, diocese of Noyon.] Saint-Vincent; [Note: [Col. 0356B] Of Laon.] Mont-Saint-Martin; [Note: [Col. 0356B] Near Le Cateau, diocese of Cambrai.] the Holy Sepulchre; Saint-Aubert; Saint-Andrew; Saint-Humbert; [Note: [Col. 0356B] Of Maroilles.] Saint-Amand; Saint-Rictrude; Saint-Martin of Tournai; Saint-Landelin of the House of God called Clairfontaine; [Note: [Col. 0356B] Clairfontaine, diocese of Soissons.] Pratis; [Note: [Col. 0356B] Or Parcum Domini, near Louvain.] Géralmont; and Morimond. [Note: [Col. 0356B] Diocese of Langres.]

## Saint-Bertin Supplement

[Col. 0355]

Manuscript C1, besides additions from Anchin for the years 651, 685, 690, 777, 1048, 1076, 1079, 1080, 1084, 1086, 1087, 1088, 1090, 1092, 1093, 1095, 1096, 1099, 1100, 1105, 1109, and 1111, contains the following, drawn from certain annals of Saint-Bertin. As the Blandin annals which used them show, those annals were constructed upon certain annals of Saint Gall. This explains why the years 807 and 820 also occur in abbreviated form in Hermann of Reichenau.

640. The monastery of Sithiu was begun by Saint Bertin, in honour of Saint Peter.

698. The death of our eminent father Bertin, in the fifty-fourth year of his rule.

807. This year the moon was darkened three times, and the sun once.

820. The moon was eclipsed on 24 November.

## Saint-Josse Supplement

[Col. 0355]

Manuscript C2*, besides additions from Anchin for the years 651, 685, 690, 773, 1048, 1076, 1079, 1080, 1084, 1086, 1087, 1090, 1092, 1095, 1096, 1099, 1100, 1105, and 1109, has only the following:

795. Charlemagne founded the monastery [Note: [Col. 0355B] Charlemagne.] of the monks of Saint Josse, which is called “Above the Sea.” [Note: [Col. 0356B] Saint-Josse-sur-Mer, diocese of Amiens.]

840. During his reign in France, the elevation of Saint Josse, commonly called “Above the Sea,” took place.

## Continuation of Arras

[Col. 0355]

Above, at col. 28, we have endeavoured to prove that there existed a manuscript of Sigebert from which C1, C2, C3, C4, and C5 derived. That it had the same very brief continuation is clear from the fact that three other continuations—the Tournai, Laon, and Bourbourg continuations—[Col. 0357] agree almost word for word in their first years, though evidently none was copied from another. It therefore seems more than probable that the materials in which they agree were already in the common source C of those manuscripts C3, C4, and C5. That it was written before 1132 is apparent from the Tournai manuscript, in which all material through 1127 is written by one hand and the entry for 1132 immediately follows in another hand. The entry for 1115 may suggest that the manuscript was written in the diocese of Arras, but this is by no means certain. It was the source of the Tournai, Laon, and Bourbourg continuations. Moreover, very many of these entries occur in nearly the same words in both the Anchin and Blandin annals.

[Col. 0357A] 1114. A council was held at Beauvais.

1115. Lambert, bishop of Arras, of good memory, died.

1118. Pope Paschal died, and Gelasius succeeded him. There was an exceedingly violent wind on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord.

1119. Pope Gelasius died; Calixtus, also called Guy and formerly archbishop of Vienne, succeeded him; [Col. 0358A] he held a council at Reims.

1123. A council was held at Rome, at which peace between the pope and the emperor was confirmed.

1124. Pope Calixtus died, and Honorius succeeded him.

1127. Charles, count of Flanders, was killed at Bruges.

## Continuation of Tournai

[Col. 0357]

The Tournai manuscript C3 faithfully copied manuscript C, together with the additions it already contained for the years 651, 685, 690, 773, 1048, 1076, 1079, 1086, 1090, 1092, 1093, 1095, 1096, 1099, 1100, 1105, and 1109, and with its brief continuation, to which it itself added only a very few things for 1115–1127. Another person then added the years 1132–1179; a third added the remainder.

[Col. 0357B] 1114. (Continuation of Arras.) The council of Beauvais.

1115. (Ibid.) Lambert, bishop of Arras, of good memory, died, and Robert, born in the same city, succeeded him.

1117. (Ibid.) Pope Paschal II died, and Gelasius succeeded him.

1119. (Ibid.) Pope Gelasius died; Calixtus, also called Guy and formerly archbishop of Vienne, succeeded him; he held a council at Reims.

1123. (Ibid.) A council was held at Rome, at which peace between the pope and the emperor was confirmed.

1124. (Ibid.) Pope Calixtus died, and Honorius succeeded him.

1127. Lord Segard, second abbot of this monastery, [Note: [Col. 0357] A fifteenth-century hand corrected this to “monastery of Saint Martin of Tournai.”] a man of venerable life and greatly revered even by secular [Col. 0357C] authorities, died. (Ibid.) Charles, count of Flanders, was killed at Bruges, in the church of Saint Donatian, before the altar situated above the apse.

1132. The church of Saint Martin was dedicated by Lord Bishop Simon.

1136. Lord Abbot Walter, the fourth, succeeded Herman. At the same time there was a great drought and a great abundance of crops, and many died from the affliction of quartan fever.

1147. Louis, king of the Franks, went to Jerusalem with a large retinue, but returned having achieved nothing. A great snowstorm was followed by a violent inundation of waters. [In the year 1146.] At the same time the church of Tournai recovered its own bishop.

1149. A winter harsher than usual set in, [Col. 0358B] so severe that, more than three miles out from shore, a way was provided over the ice on the sea, and the swelling waves, solidified by frost, were seen in the likeness of towers. Before and after this frost, for many years there was a great scarcity of crops, so that at times at Tournai a sextary of wheat was sold for sixty shillings.

1153. Ascalon was captured.

1160. Lord Abbot Walter, the fourth, died, and Lord Abbot Ivo, the fifth, succeeded him.

1168. Count Thierry of Flanders died and left the county to his son Philip.

1171. Lord Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, was martyred by the retainers of Henry, king of England. The Lord does not cease to make known by virtues and miracles how great his virtue was. In the same year [Col. 0358C] Baldwin, count of Hainaut, died and was buried at Mons. His son Baldwin succeeded him. In the same year also the noble church of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin at Tournai was dedicated by the distinguished Lord Henry, [Note: [Col. 0357] “In the same year—Henry” occurs in an erased space.] archbishop of Reims, with several bishops assembled with him.

1172. A mild and windy winter, wearisome with storms and rains; and lightning and thunder in the middle of January. [Note: [Col. 0357] Another hand adds “Explicit”; some text written in red in the following column has been erased.]

1332. At this time the city of Tournai surrendered itself to the king of France, to whom it had previously been subject in no respect, through the hands of a certain knight called Lord John Doucasteler, in the cloister of Saint Martin at Tournai, [Col. 0358D] around the feast of Saint Martin in summer.

1333. On the Ides of May Lord William, called of Ventadour, a Cluniac monk and bishop [Col. 0359A] of Tournai, died. He presided for five years. Theotbald [Note: [Col. 0359] *Theolbaldus* in the manuscript.] of Sausoure succeeded him. He presided for nearly one year.

1334. He died. Lord Andrew of Florence, bishop of Arras, succeeded him. Lord William, archbishop of Reims, died. Lord John, Pope John XXII by divine providence, died on 5 December, indiction 2, epact 14, concurrent [Note: [Col. 0359] A space was left for the number.]. [Col. 0360A] He instituted the saying of the *Ave Maria* three times around the hour of Compline. He also composed the Hours of the Holy Cross. He composed a certain prayer, “Soul of Christ.” Whoever says it at Mass will obtain thirty days’ indulgence, namely twenty [Note: [Col. 0359] From an erasure.] for mortal sins and ten [Note: [Col. 0359] From an erasure.] for venial sins. He presided for eighteen years. Benedict XII succeeded him in the same year. [Note: [Col. 0359] Erased at the foot of the page: “In the year 1333 Lord William, bishop of Tournai, of good memory, died.”]

## Laon Supplement

[Col. 0359]

The Corbie manuscript C4*, besides additions from Anchin for the years 651, 690, 1048, 1076, 1095, 1096, 1099, and 1105, has only a few others and a continuation, which is plainly written at Laon in the monastery of Saint Vincent. Two other hands, of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, later wrote a few items here and there in the margin; we have separated these, which originated at the monastery of Corbie, from the Laon materials. The Laon continuation, taking up the Arras continuation at first, appears to have been written at different times. From 1154 the Premonstratensian continuator incorporated it entire into his work.

[Col. 0359B] 928. (Louis,) who was consecrated at Laon.

1052. Elinand became bishop of Laon.

1053. Pope Leo here consecrated the church of Saint Remigius at Reims.

1096. Elinand, of good memory, died. During his episcopate a certain woman from his town, called Civiacus, was convicted of strangling her son-in-law. As she was being dragged by the people to be burned for this crime, she obtained permission to pray in the church of Blessed Mary. There, deeply pierced in the innermost part of her heart, prostrate on the pavement, she confessed with many tears how she had committed that crime, and begged that the most merciful Mother of God would be present as her intercessor in so great a peril. She was then led to the place of punishment and, in a small structure in which she was to be burned, bound with firm bonds to a stake. [Col. 0359C] Fire was then set beneath her. When it had been consumed, it was rekindled again and again by her enemies; yet, with neither garment nor hair harmed, through the intervention of the Lord’s most merciful Mother she emerged untouched from the blaze, while all the people of the city of Laon rejoiced. A fuller account of this miracle is found written in a certain book in the church of Saint Vincent. Ingelran succeeded Elinand in the episcopate. [Note: [Col. 0359D] The same matters, but much more fully, occur in the Ursicampine Supplement.]

1104. Ingelran, bishop of Laon, died; Waldrick, chancellor of the king of England, succeeded him in the episcopate.

1113. Hugh, dean of Orléans, succeeded Waldrick [Col. 0359D] in the episcopate, living only seven months. Bartholomew succeeded Hugh. The mother church of Blessed Mary at Laon was consecrated anew.

1114. (Continuation of Arras.) The council of Beauvais was held by Conon, legate of the Roman See.

[Col. 0360B] 1115. (Ibid.) Lambert, bishop of Arras, of good memory, died.

1117. Master Anselm [Note: [Col. 0360D] Compare the Premonstratensian Continuation below, p. 448.] died on the Ides of July, a Sunday.

1118. (Ibid.) Pope Paschal II died, and Gelasius succeeded him. An earthquake occurred among us on 9 January, Wednesday. There was an exceedingly violent wind on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, lasting throughout the whole day and night.

1119. (Ibid.) Pope Gelasius died; Calixtus, also called Guy and formerly archbishop of Vienne, succeeded him; he held a council at Reims.

1121. In this year Abbot Siegfried was appointed to the church of Saint Vincent’s monastery at Laon.

1122. Lord Adalbero of the same church, [Col. 0360C] [Note: [Col. 0359] “Provost” seems to have dropped out.] a man of every honour and prudence, died. In the same year a second disturbance occurred at Laon. [Note: [Col. 0359] *communio* (“communion”) in the manuscript.]

1123. (Ibid.) A council was held at Rome, at which peace between the pope and emperor was confirmed.

1124. (Ibid.) Pope Calixtus died, and Honorius succeeded him. Henry, king of Lotharingia, having assembled as large a force of soldiers as he could, wished to enter the land of our king, who had likewise gathered an immeasurable multitude both of mounted soldiers and foot-soldiers. On hearing this, the king of Lotharingia desisted from his rash undertaking. This occurred on 14 August.

1127. (Continuation of Arras.) Charles, count of Flanders, was killed by treachery.

1128. Drogo was appointed the first abbot in the church of Saint John at Laon, after the nuns had been expelled, on 16 May, Wednesday.

1129. Abbot Siegfried died; Anselm succeeded. The boy Philip was anointed king on Easter Day, 14 April, with his father present.

1130. Thomas of Marle died on 8 November.

[Col. 0361A] 1131. While King Philip was leading his horse in the city of Paris, like a boy, a pig threw itself beneath the horse’s feet, causing the horse to fall upon him. Thus the boy was overtaken by a sudden and pitiable death on 13 October. The church of Saint Médard at Soissons was consecrated by Pope Innocent on 15 October. Louis, brother of the recently deceased Philip, still a boy, was consecrated king by Pope Innocent at Reims in a council on 25 October.

1132. The castle of La Fère [Note: [Col. 0361C] La Fère, located on the Oise, on the borders of Vermandois and Marle.] was besieged by Louis, king of the Franks, from 7 May until 9 July, but was not captured.

1133. An eclipse of the sun occurred on 2 August, Friday, at the fifth hour.

1134. Henry, king of England, died. His nephew Stephen, [Col. 0361B] his sister’s son, succeeded to the kingdom.

1135. An excessive wind on 28 October destroyed many towers and buildings. The sea overflowed its boundaries and unexpectedly submerged part of Flanders together with its inhabitants.

1136. In the year 1130, after the death of Pope Honorius, parties having formed, Gregory, who was called Innocent, and Peter of Leo were elected. But Innocent was confirmed in the office, and Peter was rejected. The dissension between them concerning the papacy, arising from that time, still endured into this year 1136. Because of this matter the emperor set out for Rome a second time in that same year 1136. In 1131, the second year of his pontificate, Innocent celebrated Mass at Laon in Saint Mary’s episcopal church on Palm Sunday, and on the following Monday in the church of Saint Vincent.

1137. There was a drought such as no one then living testified that he had seen or heard from his predecessors: springs and wells, and even some rivers, dried up. In the same year the count of Poitou went to Saint James in Galicia [Note: [Col. 0362C] Santiago de Compostela.] for prayer, and died on Holy Friday in the church of Saint James itself, before the altar, where he was also buried. Louis, the boy king of France, married his daughter at Bordeaux in solemn nuptials, in the presence of all the leading men of France, while his father King Louis was still living. Yet within almost the same month his father died in Paris [Col. 0362A] and was buried at Saint-Denis before the high altar, on 1 August. In this same year Emperor Lothair, after bringing Apulia into loyalty to the Roman Church, died while returning to his homeland. Conrad succeeded him.

1138. A dwelling for the servants of God is built at the place called Mont-Dieu [Note: [Col. 0362C] Carthusian Order.]. Those who live there observe the rule, gain the kingdom of heaven by prayers and fasts, and tame the rebellion of the flesh by the harshest hair-shirts. Lord Ebalus, monk of Saint Vincent at Laon, a man most eminent in every branch of learning, died.

1139. A violent storm arose on 2 July and lasted for almost four continuous nights, with thunder and very great lightning flashes.

[Col. 0362B] 1140. A quarrel arose between Louis, king of the Franks, and the Roman pope, and the Church was grievously troubled, for this reason: after the archbishop of Bourges died, a pastor consecrated by the pope was sent to that church, but, rejected by the king and certain others, was by no means admitted to the archbishopric.

1141. A violent wind arose on 19 January and lasted almost all day. With dreadful force it overthrew monasteries and houses, leveled ancient trees to the earth, and made manifest God’s wrath, deserved by human sins, against humankind. [Its force also weakened and displaced one of the towers of the church at Corbie; it collapsed, and its fall brought both damage and sorrow to the inhabitants. [Note: [Col. 0361] Added by another contemporary hand.]]

(1143 [Note: [Col. 0361] The number is absent.].) Pope Innocent died. Guy, also called Celestine, succeeded him.

(1144 [Note: [Col. 0361] The number is absent.].) Peace was restored [Note: [Col. 0361] *reditur* (“is returned”) in the manuscript.] to the churches of Gaul. Pope Celestine died. Lucius succeeded to the papacy. . . [Note: [Col. 0361] Thus in the manuscript.]

(1145 [Note: [Col. 0361] The number is absent.].) Eugenius replaced Lucius. The Romans reject his yoke; becoming exceedingly insolent through the audacity of their innate ferocity, they appoint for themselves a patrician to manage the affairs of the republic and act in the emperor’s stead during his absence.

[For the subsequent sequence of this work, consult Vallis Lucens. [Note: [Col. 0361] Added by the same hand as the entry for 1141.]]

## Corbie Supplement

[Col. 0361]

[Col. 0361D] 419. Here the Franks began to have kings, whereas before they had been accustomed to have two dukes or judges over themselves; and they established as their first king Pharamund, son of their duke Marcomer.

662. Here Lothair was the tenth king.

[Col. 0362D] 664. Theoderic, first abbot of Corbie, flourished.

807. Saint Adalard, ninth abbot of Corbie, cousin of Emperor Charles, flourished in Gaul.

815. The abbot of Corbie, with his brothers and sisters [Col. 0363A] and many nobles of the realm, was condemned to exile by Emperor Louis. In his place was installed the venerable tenth abbot, named Adalard. He was the first to begin building New Corbie.

821. Adalard, abbot of Corbie, and the other nobles of the realm were recalled from exile—except those whom death had deprived of life—and restored to their former honours.

827. Adalard, abbot of Corbie, was exceedingly renowned among the Franks.

[Col. 0364A] 828. Ratbert, surnamed Paschasius, disciple of Saint Adalard and investigator of all the divine Scriptures, flourished in Gaul.

844. Here Charles, after the division of the empire, was the first king of the Franks. Here Lothair, son of the pious Louis, son of Charlemagne, was the third emperor.

885. Here Charles was son of Louis, king of the Germans, who was son of the pious Emperor Louis.

## Premonstratensian Continuation

[Col. 0363]

We print from manuscript B1 the continuation which, built upon the Laon continuation, inserts almost nothing before 1126 except large passages stitched together from the Life of Norbert. In the following material it adds very many things drawn from elsewhere, which reveal a close relationship with the Valcellensis. After 1145 it perhaps took up the manuscript of Vallis Lucens; see above, col. 31. We do not know the author; it is nevertheless easy to see that he was a Premonstratensian of the diocese of Laon or Reims. He began writing no earlier than 1146, the year in which the Laon supplement ends. That the author did not carry the work beyond the beginning of 1155 is shown by the Ursicampine continuation, which adopted ours entire and was itself later excerpted by Nicholas of Amiens and Robert of Auxerre. The Valcellensis and Bourbourg continuations also appear to have used ours.

[Col. 0363B] After Ivo, who distinguished the church of Chartres by his life and teaching and who, among his other works, usefully compiled by his own industry the volume called Ivo’s *Decrees*, Geoffrey, venerable for the merit of his life and his wisdom, governed the church of Chartres. In the metropolitan church of Reims too, after the distinguished Manasses, when the usurper Gervase had been expelled, Ralph, surnamed the Green, succeeded. [Note: [Col. 0363D] In the year 1106.] (Continuation of Laon.) After Waldrick, bishop of Laon, had been wickedly murdered by citizens of his own city, Hugh, dean of the church of Orléans, was installed. When he died after seven months, the distinguished Bartholomew was promoted to the episcopate of the city of Laon. Through his diligence the episcopal church, which had been burned, was quickly repaired and consecrated anew; [Col. 0363C] the devastation of the city and province was relieved; and in many places where it had never previously existed, the fervour of religious life and worship of God was established, from where it was propagated into many distant and even overseas regions.

1114. R. 8. F. 5. A. 14. H. 4.

(Continuation of Laon.) A council was held in the city of Beauvais by Conon, legate of the Apostolic See.

1115. 9. 6. 15. 5.

(Ibid.) Lambert, bishop of Arras, of good memory, died; Robert succeeded him in the episcopate.

1116. 10. 7. 16. 6.

(Life of Norbert.) At this time Norbert, founder of the place and order of Prémontré, [Col. 0363D] a native of Lotharingia, distinguished and well known even to the highest princes by birth, riches, and eloquence, was set aflame by divine zeal. Setting aside worldly splendour, he was suddenly ordained, according to his wish, both deacon and [Col. 0364B] priest, and put on the tunic of Christ’s poverty. Devoting himself most fervently to preaching, carrying a bare cross for himself, bare himself he followed Christ. Having tested the manner of life of certain religious persons, he adopted a purpose of a stricter way and a severity unheard of in those times. For some time, walking barefoot in winter cold, he scattered the word of God and converted many from error.

1117. 11. 8. 17. 7.

(Continuation of Laon.) Anselm, the most renowned master of the city of Laon, eminent in literary learning and venerable for upright conduct and mature judgment, died. By profitable study and diligent labour, among his other works, he arranged in the Psalter marginal [Col. 0364C] and interlinear glosses from authoritative commentators in a polished abridgment.

1118. 12. 9. 18. 8.

(Ibid.) Pope Paschal died, and Gelasius, chancellor of the Roman Church, succeeded him in the pontificate. An earthquake occurred among us on 9 January, Wednesday. There was an exceedingly violent wind on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, lasting throughout the whole day and night. (Life of Norbert.) Pope Gelasius, having summoned a council at Reims, crossed the Alps and came into Gaul. The man of God Norbert came to him, walking barefoot as he was; he disclosed the purpose of his heart and received from him permission and authority to sow the word of God everywhere. Returning thence as far as Valenciennes, within the space of fifteen [Col. 0364D] days he lost to death the three companions whom alone he had; and there he received one in place of the three, namely Hugh, who succeeded him in the governance of the church of Prémontré.

[Col. 0365A] 1119. R. 13. F. 10. A. 19. H. 9.

(Continuation of Laon.) Pope Gelasius died at Cluny, and Guy, archbishop of Vienne, brother of Stephen count of Burgundy, was elected pope; and at his instance the council summoned by his predecessor was held at Reims. Baldwin, count of Flanders, nephew through his mother Clementia of Pope Calixtus, wishing forcibly to restore to Normandy William, son of Robert count of Normandy, whom Henry, king of England, his own brother, had taken captive, died of a wound to the head after occupying a great part of that same Normandy (cf. Annals of Blandinium). His cousin Charles, son of Canute king of the Danes, succeeded him in the principality.

1120. 14. 11. 20. 10.

[Col. 0365B] (Life of Norbert.) The man of God Norbert, especially commended to Pope Calixtus by Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, was offered the church of Saint Martin by the said bishop. But both because of its proximity to the city and because the clerics of that church shrank from his purpose and the austerity of his life, he left it. The bishop showed him various places in that province suitable for religious life; at last, by divine guidance, he settled at the place called Prémontré, where he began to lead a solitary religious life. During Lent he went out alone to gather companions; before Easter he returned with thirteen companions, and with them began at Prémontré to serve God according to the norm of canonical observance and the tenor of the Rule of Saint Augustine.

[Col. 0365C] 1121. 15. 12. 21. 11.

(Ibid.) At the church of Prémontré, while a certain brother was contemplating too deeply the ineffable Trinity, which is God, a demon stood beside him at Matins. It appeared to him bearing three heads, asserting that it was the Trinity and declaring that, because of the merit of his faith, he was worthy of a vision of the Trinity. But the brother, reflecting briefly, perceived not the whisper of a gentle breeze but the foul wind of a whirlwind; he recognized the enemy’s deceit and, reviling it, compelled it to depart. Nevertheless, it later deceived him by other means. When Lambert, bishop of Noyon, died, Simon, cousin of King Louis of the Franks, succeeded him.

1122. 16. 13. 22. 12.

[Col. 0365D] (Ibid.) While Norbert was preaching the word of God more insistently, at Nivigella a girl who had been tormented by a demon for a year was brought before him. As he repeatedly recited the Gospels and exorcisms over her, the demon mockingly uttered, through the girl’s mouth, the Song of Songs from beginning to end, then rendered the whole of it word for word in the Roman language, and afterwards in German. But as the servant of God pressed on more forcefully, the demon asked permission to enter a monk standing nearby; when it did not receive this, it replied that it would not depart that day, and throughout the day it contended fiercely with him before the people. The priest remained without food and continued the night in prayer. In the morning, while he celebrated the divine offices in the presence of the girl, as the demon chattered many things through her mouth, it fled in the midst of the solemn rites, leaving foul traces of stinking urine [Col. 0366A], and left behind the possessed vessel.

1123. 17. 14. 23. 13.

(Continuation of Laon.) After a council was held at Rome, peace between the kingdom and the priesthood was restored, and the right of episcopal investitures was wrested from the emperor.

(Life of Norbert.) When Norbert came to Cologne to seek relics of saints, having imposed a fast upon his followers and persisted in prayer, one of the eleven thousand virgins revealed her name and specifically indicated the place where she lay. On the following day she was solemnly raised up and was transferred by him, together with other relics of saints, to Prémontré. The next day, after spending the night in prayer at Saint Gereon’s, he ordered digging to be done in the middle of the church at daybreak, where no sign of a burial was visible [Col. 0366B], and found the body of Saint Gereon whole, without its brain, honourably and carefully laid away. This accorded with what was read of him: that part of his head, not the whole head, had been cut off. The clergy and people raised it with honour and reverence, and a portion of it was given to the man of God.

Returning thence to Prémontré, now having with him forty clerics and many laymen, he taught them to make profession according to apostolic institution and the canonical Rule of Saint Augustine. He carefully trained them in voluntary poverty, ready obedience, and the other instruments of spiritual warfare. Not long afterwards a certain count of Westphalia, Godfrey, came to him with his wife for the sake of conversion, and devoted three places in his allodial estate to divine worship through him: namely, the castle of Cappenberg, the place of Elostath, and Warlar [Col. 0366C]. Moved to compunction by his example, Count Theobald made himself a close friend of the man of God; thereafter, following his admonitions and counsel, he began to exercise much liberality and generosity toward the poor and all religious persons.

1124. 18. 15. 24. 14.

(Chronicle of Laon.) Pope Calixtus, of good memory, died, and Honorius succeeded him in the papacy.

(Life of Norbert.) As Father Norbert set out to visit him, he was honourably received and duly obtained what he requested; he learned by divine revelation that he would become bishop of Parthenopolis. On his return, while he was celebrating Mass at Würzburg on Easter Day amid a great crowd, a blind woman recovered her sight after he had received the mysteries and breathed upon her eyes [Col. 0366D]. Thereupon certain wealthy persons, moved to compunction, gave themselves and their possessions back to God; building a church there, they dedicated it to divine worship through the hand of the aforesaid father.

Returning thence to Prémontré, he caused one of his own men, Lord Walter, to be consecrated first abbot of the church of Saint Martin situated in the suburb of Laon. Through Walter’s diligence, with God cooperating, that church increased so greatly in a short time in both temporal and spiritual matters that it was already extending the renown of its good reputation and the offshoots of its holy planting into foreign and distant regions: namely, into Nervia, Flanders, England, Gascony, [Col. 0367A] Gothia, Spain, and Burgundy. We now see all these provinces sprinkled with a good fragrance through that same house. He also caused an abbot from among his brethren to be ordained at the church of Viviers. When, upon the brethren’s arrival there, an evil spirit attacked a certain man and tormented him for two days, he was cured through the man of God, the demon having been expelled.

He likewise undertook to organize a church in the castle of Antwerp for this reason. The townsmen of that castle had gradually fallen away from faith and good morals, having been deceived by a certain heretic, Tanchelm. Though a layman, this heretic was of excessive subtlety and sharper in speech even than many eloquent clerics. He said that ministers of holy orders, and the episcopal and priestly rank, were nothing; he denied that receiving the body and blood of Christ profited those who received them unto salvation. Wearing splendid apparel and garments embroidered with gold, with his hair twisted in a threefold cord, he enticed his followers—some three thousand armed men followed him—by persuasive words and lavish banquets; through them he cruelly attacked those who resisted him with slaughter. They believed in and reverenced him so greatly that they drank the water in which he had washed his body and carried it away as relics. Yet he was of such incontinence and impurity that he corrupted daughters in their mothers’ presence and betrothed women while their husbands looked on, asserting that this was a spiritual work. At last, after many errors and many killings, while sailing, he was struck in the head by a certain priest and died. Yet even after his death his error could not easily be rooted out [Col. 0367C]. Therefore the clerics of that place gave the church, with certain revenues, to Norbert to organize through the bishop’s hand, hoping that by his salutary teaching that heresy would be removed from their midst. And so it happened. For, moved to compunction by his preaching, men and women brought forth the Lord’s body, which they had stored in chests and holes for ten years and more; through his teaching they gradually returned to sound faith.

When Ralph, archbishop of Reims, died (23 July), Rainald succeeded to the episcopal office of the church of Reims. The Venetians, besieging Ascalon with a naval force, accepted an assessed payment of money from the people of Ascalon and withdrew; they then received Tyre, which had been besieged for some time, in surrender. [Col. 0367D] Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, was seized by the Saracens and, after a long captivity, was released upon payment of an assessed sum of money.

(Chronicle of Laon.) Emperor Henry, having assembled an innumerable multitude of troops, prepared to invade the borders of the kingdom of the Franks. But when Louis, king of the Franks, likewise hastened to meet him with an immense army, Henry abandoned his futile purpose on the advice of princes and bishops. This happened in August. Emperor Henry captured the castle of Montion and carried off as captive its count Rainald.

[Col. 0368A] 1125. R. 19. F. 16. A. 25. H. 15.

A most severe famine raged in Gaul. In it shone forth the generous munificence of Charles, illustrious margrave of Flanders, who supplied daily provisions to innumerable poor people in various places.

1126. 20. 17. 26. 16.

(Year 1125.) When Emperor Henry died, some princes, especially from Swabia and Alemannia, wished to raise his nephew Conrad to the kingdom; others advanced Lothair, duke of Saxony, a man of counsel and warlike ability, as king.

1127. 1. 18. 27. 17.

After the death of Bishop Lisiard [Note: [Col. 0367] Died 18 October 1126 according to *Gallia Christiana*; 1125 according to Bouquet.], Josselin, a man of counsel, became bishop of Soissons. At Cambrai [Col. 0368B], too, Hermann held the bishopric after Burchard. When he was expelled after three years, Lietard succeeded him; he himself, rejected after four years [Note: [Col. 0367D] Year 1137.], had Nicholas as successor.

(Life of Norbert.) After the archbishop of Parthenopolis had died, the clerics and citizens of that city assembled before Emperor Lothair at Speyer in order to elect an archbishop. At the prompting of Lord Gerard, legate of the Roman See, who happened to be present and later became Pope Lucius, and also of Albero, chief cleric of Metz, who later became archbishop of Trier, they elected as their shepherd Norbert, father of the church of Prémontré, who had happened to come there on certain business. With the king’s favourable assent, they promoted him to the priesthood of the aforesaid city.

Charles, count of Flanders, had made certain of his own men hate him through the enforcement of justice. During the days of Lent, while praying in the church to which he had come to hear Mass, with some of his nobles, he was killed by them [Col. 0368C]. The whole province, in zealous and unanimous concert, avenged this crime with such severity that an example of punishment so strict can scarcely be found. William, son of Robert, formerly count of Normandy, was installed in the principality by election of the princes and with the assent of Louis, king of the Franks. His uncle Henry, king of England, regarded him with suspicion, because, after disinheriting William, he held William’s father Robert captive; Henry stirred up the princes of Flanders to revolt against William. They summoned against him Thierry of Alsace, Charles’s cousin, and after William died from a wound two years later, advanced Thierry to the principality [Col. 0368D]. Fulk succeeded Baldwin in the kingdom of Jerusalem.

1128. 2. 19. 28. 18.

(Chronicle of Laon.) At Laon, in the church of Saint John, by counsel of the king and princes, the nuns, who were notoriously ill-reputed, were expelled and monks were put in their place. Drogo, venerable for religious life and eloquence, was appointed first abbot by Bishop Bartholomew; later Pope Innocent consecrated him cardinal bishop of Ostia at Rome (in 1136).

[Col. 0369A] 1129. R. 3. F. 20. A. 29. H. 1.

(Life of Norbert.) Archbishop Norbert removed the secular clerics from the church of Saint Mary at Magdeburg and installed brethren of his own order. He arranged that they should serve God there according to the tenor of the rule which he had established at Prémontré. At the church of Prémontré he also caused Lord Hugh, who had been his companion from the beginning of his poverty, to be appointed abbot as his successor. He likewise sent fathers appointed to govern the brethren to the churches of Antwerp and Floreffe.

(Chronicle of Laon.) Anselm, abbot and later bishop of Tournai, succeeded Seifrid at the church of Saint Vincent on the hill of Laon. Philip, the boy son of Louis king of the Franks, was anointed king at Reims on Easter Day, 18 Kalends of May, in his father’s presence [Col. 0369B].

1130. 4. 21. 30. 2.

(Ibid.) After Pope Honorius died, parties were formed, and Gregory and Peter of Leon were elected to the papacy; Gregory took the name Innocent, Peter that of Anacletus. But because Peter remained at Saint Peter’s, relying upon the power of his kindred, Innocent left Rome and went into Gaul. The Gallican Church adhering to him, he was confirmed in the papacy after councils had been held first at Reims and then at Pisa; Peter was anathematized by all the bishops of Gaul and Germany.

John, bishop of Thérouanne, of pious memory, died; Milo, abbot of Saint-Josse from the Premonstratensian order, succeeded him. When Robert, bishop of Arras, died, Abbot Alvisus was ordained bishop in his place [Col. 0369C].

(Chronicle of Laon.) Thomas of Marle, treacherously seizing merchants within his own safe-conduct, was attacked by King Louis with an army; wounded and captured by Ralph, count of Vermandois, he died at Laon.

1131. 5. 22. 31. 3.

(Ibid.) Pope Innocent celebrated the divine mysteries at Laon, in the church of Saint Mary, on Palm Sunday, and on the following Tuesday in the church of Saint Martin. Philip, the boy recently anointed king, was riding on horseback in the city of Paris when a pig happened to run beneath the horse’s feet; the horse threw him headlong, and his sudden and pitiable death brought mourning upon the Franks, 3 Ides of October [Col. 0369D]. The church of Saint Medard at Soissons was consecrated by Pope Innocent. After a council had been held at Reims, in the presence of Louis king of the Franks, his son Louis was consecrated king by Pope Innocent, 8 Kalends of November.

In these times the canonical order of the Premonstratensians and the monastic order of the Cistercians, like two olive trees before the Lord, supplied the world with the light of piety and the richness of devotion. Like fruitful vines, they spread the shoots of religious life in every direction; as the fragrance of their good reputation gradually spread through nearly all the bounds of the Christian world, they built new abbeys where the worship of God had not previously existed. [Col. 0370A] Hence brethren were even sent from Prémontré to Syria and Palestine, where they built several abbeys.

At about this time the Church presented a fair and beautiful face, adorned with the variety of different orders and professions. On one side Premonstratensians, on another Cistercians, elsewhere Cluniac monks, and likewise religious women and women devoted to God of diverse dress and profession, living regularly in continence and poverty under the yoke of obedience, stirred one another by the fervour of religion and competitively founded new monasteries in various places. With them the Carthusian monks too were gradually springing up. More continent than the rest, they set limits to the plague of avarice, under which we see very many labouring beneath the garb of religion: they established a fixed number of persons, animals, and possessions that they might in no way exceed. Each possessed an individual cell, and they met rarely, either for divine worship or for mutual consolation in charity; they chose more perfectly to die to the world and more diligently to live for God [Col. 0370B].

Among them Guigo, prior of the Charterhouse, flourished most eminently in religious life and wisdom. From the same house came Hugh, formerly prior, bishop of Grenoble and later metropolitan of Vienne, illustrious for the strictness of that religious observance. In addition, the knights of the Temple of Jerusalem and the brethren of the Hospital, living continently beneath religious dress, spread everywhere as they multiplied; whatever they could, from their own labour or the alms of the faithful, they sent to Jerusalem for the service of those fighting for God, and of the sick and all poor persons [Col. 0370C].

1132. 6. 23. 32. 4.

(Chronicle of Laon.) The castle of Fara was surrounded by siege by Louis king of the Franks from the Nones of May until 7 Ides of July, but was not captured. (Ibid.)
