An eclipse of the sun occurred 4 Nones of August, Friday, at the sixth hour [Note: [Col. 0369D] Laon and Burburg place it in the year 1133.].

1133. 7. 24. 33. 5.

(Life of Norbert.) Emperor Lothair prepared an expedition into Italy. Accompanied by bishops and archbishops, he conducted Pope Innocent to Rome; against Peter of Leon, who had fortified the monastery of Saint Peter, he powerfully established Innocent in the Lateran episcopal palace upon the papal throne. There Pope Innocent consecrated Lothair himself emperor [Col. 0370D].

1134. 8. 25. 34. 6.

(Ibid.) Archbishop Norbert, powerful in deed and word, founder of many monasteries and outstanding propagator of holy religious life, most equitable supporter of the Catholic Pope Innocent and most just denouncer of the schismatic Peter, returned with Emperor Lothair from the Italian expedition to his city. Not long afterwards he was seized by illness. Having suffered under it for four months, after wisely and faithfully administering his bishopric for eight years, he died in the presence of the brethren, having given his blessing. When a dispute arose over burial between the clerics of the major church and the brethren of Saint Mary [Col. 0371A], the matter was brought before the emperor; by his command Norbert was buried in the church of Saint Mary, with the sons and brethren whom he had begotten in Christ and brought up for Christ. His falling asleep in Christ occurred on 8 Ides of July.

1135. R. 9. F. 26. A. 35. H. 7.

(Chronicle of Laon.) Henry, king of England, died, a man of singular severity and discipline in the administration of his kingdom. Stephen, his nephew through his sister, succeeded him in the kingdom, but, deprived of a great part of the realm, he soon afterwards lost all Normandy. For Matilda, daughter of King Henry—first married to Emperor Henry and afterwards to Geoffrey, count of Anjou—with the help of Louis king of the Franks occupied the duchy of Normandy and brought great troubles and calamities upon Stephen in England itself [Col. 0371B]. She later captured him in war, but released him in exchange for her brother Count Robert, who had been captured by the queen of England. (Ibid.) There was an exceedingly violent wind on 5 Kalends of November, which threw down many towers and buildings.

1136. 10. 27. 1. 8.

(Ibid.) The sea overflowed its bounds and unexpectedly drowned part of Flanders with its inhabitants.

1137. 11. 28. 2. 9.

(Ibid.) There was such drought in France as no one then living testified that he had seen or heard from his predecessors: springs and wells, and even certain rivers, dried up. Emperor Lothair made a second expedition into Italy. William, count of Poitou, set out for Saint James in Galicia [Col. 0371C] for the sake of prayer; on Good Friday he died in the church of Saint James and was buried before the altar. As he was dying, he charged his nobles who were with him to give his elder daughter Eleanor in marriage to the younger Louis, king of the Franks, with the duchy of Aquitaine.

(Ibid.) The said Louis married her at Bordeaux, in the presence of the magnates of the kingdom, with the most solemn nuptials. Her father Louis died at Paris within nearly the same month and was buried before his body in the church of Saint Denis, on the Kalends of August, in the twenty-eighth year of his reign. Emperor Lothair, having brought Apulia into obedience to the Roman Church, died while returning to his homeland; Conrad, who had previously sought the empire, nephew through his sister of Emperor Henry [Col. 0371D], was elevated to the kingdom.

1138. 1. 1. 3. 10.

Drogo, bishop of Ostia, of good memory, a man distinguished in religious life and wisdom, died. Peter of Leon, who through schism had seized the primacy of the Roman See against Innocent and had for eight years now been a great scandal to the Church of God, died, struck by God’s judgment (25 January). Pope Innocent decreed that those ordained by him were to be degraded and not thereafter promoted to holy orders.

In these times a certain false emperor arose in the regions of Alemannia. After living in seclusion at Solothurn for several years, he emerged and falsely claimed to be Emperor Henry. Having attracted many to himself by deception, so that serious battles and killings occurred on his account—some accepting him, others openly declaring him a deceiver—his falsehood was at last exposed. He was tonsured as a monk at Cluny [Col. 0372A].

1139. 2. 2. 4. 11.

After the death of Rainald, archbishop of Reims [Note: [Col. 0371D] Year 1138, Ides of January.], the church of Reims lacked a bishop for almost two years. At length, in this year Samson, from the clergy of the church of Chartres, received the episcopal office of Reims.

At this time the Gallican Church flourished through men illustrious in religious life and wisdom: Milo, bishop of Thérouanne, outstanding in the virtue of humility; Alvisus of Arras, renowned for liberality, counsel, and eloquence; Godfrey of Langres; Hugh of Auxerre; Josselin of Soissons; Geoffrey of Châlons; and Alberic, archbishop of Bourges, most distinguished for learning and prudent counsel [Col. 0372B]. Among these and many other men then renowned for learning, Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, a man of most celebrated religious life, shone with the greatest distinction. As a most fervent preacher of God’s word and founder of innumerable monasteries, he daily inspired many souls toward the pursuit of religious life and the resolve of holy poverty.

(Chronicle of Laon.) A dwelling place for servants of God was built in the place called Mont-Dieu.

1140. 3. 3. 5. 12.

[Col. 0372C] Hugh of Saint Victor, canon of Paris, renowned for religious life and learning, and second to none of his age in mastery of the seven liberal arts, died [Note: [Col. 0371D] Died 11 February 1142; cf. Pagi and Mansi, on Baronius for the year 1140.]. Among the many works he wrote to good purpose, he also produced a highly necessary book on the sacraments, comprised in two volumes.

At Sens, in the presence of King Louis, a gathering of bishops and religious abbots was held against Peter Abelard, who was scandalizing the Church by a certain profane novelty of words or ideas. When summoned by them, as he was about to answer, fearing justice, he appealed to a hearing before the Apostolic See. Escaping in this way, he died not long afterwards at Saint-Marcel near Chalon. (Year 1142, 21 April.) The seed of hostility sprang up between King Louis and Count Theobald [Note: [Col. 0372D] of Blois.], because the count declined to accompany the king on the Aquitanian expedition [Col. 0372D].

1141. 4. 4. 6. 13.

Roger of Sicily, after occupying the principality of Calabria and Apulia, captured Pope Innocent in war. Having made some sort of peace with him, he obtained from him coronation as king; thus he was the first of Norman stock to assume for himself the title of king. Later he also occupied certain cities or provinces in Africa. The castle of Bouillon, which Count Rainald had unjustly held, was captured by the bishop of Liège [Col. 0373A].

(Chronicle of Laon.) When discord arose between the Roman pope and Louis king of the Franks, the Gallican Church was disturbed; the hostility which was thought to have been soothed between the king and the pope began to revive. The emperor of Constantinople, after besieging Antioch for some time, at last made peace with its prince and entered the city. But while engaged in hunting, as he drew his bow too vigorously, he wounded himself in the left hand with a poisoned arrow and died, having first captured several Turkish garrisons. After him his son Manuel assumed the empire.

1142. R. 5. F. 5. A. 7. H. 14.

Ralph, count of Vermandois, repudiated his wife and married Petronilla, sister of the queen. At the insistence of Count Theobald, Ivo, legate of the Roman See, was sent [Col. 0373B]; he excommunicated Count Ralph and suspended Bartholomew bishop of Laon, Simon bishop of Noyon, and Peter bishop of Senlis, who had effected that divorce.

1143. 6. 6. 8. 15.

(Ibid.) On 14 Kalends of February, a violent wind with terrible force overthrew monasteries and houses, levelling ancient trees with the ground. King Louis captured the castle of Vitry belonging to Count Theobald. Fire having been set, the church was burned, and in it thirteen hundred persons of different sexes and ages were consumed by fire. King Louis is said to have wept, moved by pity at this; and some consider that for this reason he undertook the Jerusalem pilgrimage [Col. 0373C]. He gave the castle to Odo of Champagne, nephew of Count Theobald, who wished on this occasion to recover through King Louis the inheritance taken from him by Theobald. Upon the death of the venerable Geoffrey, Guy became bishop of Châlons.

(Ibid.) Pope Innocent died, and Guy the castellan succeeded him, taking the name Celestine. Fulk, king of Jerusalem, also died. While hunting and pursuing a hare which suddenly appeared before him, the horse on which he rode threw him headlong and deprived him alike of life and kingdom. His son Baldwin then ruled with his mother. (Ibid.) Peace was restored between the pope and King Louis.

1144. 7. 7. 9. 1. S. 3.

[Col. 0373D] Pope Celestine, having discharged the office of the papacy for five and a half months, died (9 March), and Lucius succeeded him, having become pope from the office of Chancellor Gerard. Through the mediation of the abbot of Clairvaux, the hostility that had flared between King Louis and Count Theobald was soothed. Stephen, king of England, and the supporters of Matilda, daughter of King Henry, fought with varying fortune; that kingdom, which beyond others had for some time remained peaceful and prosperous, was miserably ravaged by sword, flame, and famine.

1145. 8. 8. 10. 2. 4.

Edessa, a city of Mesopotamia in which were the bodies of the apostles Thomas and Thaddaeus, and which had never been polluted by the filth of idolatry since it was first converted to Christianity, was besieged and captured by the Turks. Its bishop was beheaded, holy places were profaned, and many abominations too shameful to be mentioned were committed in them. Many thousands of every sex and age were massacred, tortured in various ways, carried away captive, and reduced to slavery [Col. 0374A]. Hence fear and grief increased among Christians, while pride and audacity increased among the enemies of Christ’s name. These indeed were the beginnings of evils.

Pope Lucius besieged in the Capitol the Roman senators who had risen against the Church; but disturbed thence by Jordan, son of Peter of Leon, and stricken with illness, he died within a year of his pontificate (25 February). Bernard, abbot of Saint Anastasius, succeeded him and was called Pope Eugenius [Col. 0374B]. The Romans raised Jordan as patrician and the senators against him and drove him from the city. He crossed the Alps into Gaul.

1146. 9. 9. 11. 3. 5.

Louis, king of the Franks, inflamed with zeal because Mesopotamia had been taken by the Turks—or, as others think, pricked by conscience over the burning of Vitry—received the sign of the cross at Vézelay and resolved to undertake an overseas pilgrimage with the princes of the kingdom and an innumerable multitude. The church of Tournai, which for about six hundred years, from the time of Saint Medard, had been under the bishop of Noyon without a priest of its own, began this year to have its own bishop: Anselm, abbot of Saint Vincent of Laon, consecrated at Rome by Pope Eugenius and sent to that city as bishop [Col. 0374C].

A most severe famine raged in Gaul. In it the generous munificence of Christ’s churches shone forth: they expended many thousands of measures to support the poor. At that time, in the diocese of Langres, at Mormant, where innumerable poor people were fed by daily alms, a certain man was discovered to have killed people and sold their cooked flesh; the poor hanged him from the gallows. Guy, bishop of Châlons, died.

1147. 10. 10. 12. 4. 6.

When King Conrad was at Frankfurt on the Purification of Saint Mary (2 February), the abbot of Clairvaux attached the sign of the cross to both the king and nearly all the princes of the kingdom [Col. 0374D], and the companions of the pilgrimage multiplied beyond count. God’s naval host, assembled from England, Flanders, and Lotharingia, departed on 2 Ides of April from the English port of Tredemunde [Note: [Col. 0373D] Dartmouth in Devonshire.] with about two hundred ships. On 4 Kalends of July, the vigil of the Apostles, it reached Lisbon [Note: [Col. 0374D] *Ulixbona*, Lisbon.] and, after a four-month siege, captured it by God’s power and their own exertions, through much slaughter and hardship. Though they numbered only thirteen thousand, they overcame two hundred thousand five hundred enemies; entering with hymns, they dedicated a church and appointed there a bishop and clerics. At the bodies of those killed there, three mute persons recovered the use of speech.

King Conrad undertook the pilgrimage in May with an innumerable multitude and incomparable strength. After crossing the Bosporus successfully, he unwisely turned aside to attack Iconium; when the produce of the land was consumed and provisions failed, his men afflicted by hunger turned back. As the Turks pursued them, he lost many thousands of his men [Col. 0375A]. Louis, king of the Franks, began the pilgrimage on 3 Kalends of June, at Pentecost. With countless thousands of his men, prepared for the expedition, he travelled through Hungary and, having crossed the Bosporus, was met by King Conrad. Many of Conrad’s men returned home because of want; Conrad, accompanied by few, was kindly received by the Franks and travelled with them for some time. But recalled from Thyatira by the emperor of the Greeks, he was conveyed to Jerusalem in the emperor’s ships. There was an eclipse of the sun [Col. 0375B] on 8 Kalends of November, a Sunday, from the second hour until the fifth.

1148. R. 11. F. 11. A. 13. H. 5. S. 7.

The Franks suffer very great losses in the deserts of Asia through the treachery and cunning of the Greeks and the frequent assaults of the Turks; and, tortured by extreme hunger, some feed upon the flesh of horses and asses. Thus, with much toil and loss, and with many perishing of hunger, they scarcely at last reached Seleucia, and from there made for Antioch and Palestine. Manuel, king of the Greeks, held in prison as captives the envoys of the king of Sicily, whom he had sent to him for the execution of a peace treaty. Therefore Roger, angered, dispatched a naval force and plundered Corinth together with certain other cities and castles [Col. 0375C] in Greece; and, taking an immeasurable quantity of cloaks and precious garments of various kinds, together with an abundance of gold and silver, he took several thousand Greeks captive. He also captured the island of Corfu [Note: [Col. 0375D] Corfu.], and built a strong garrison in its harbor. The Spaniards of the nearer provinces capture Almería, and in the following year Tortosa, notable cities of the Saracens. Alvisus, bishop of Arras, a man distinguished for integrity of life and learning, dies at Philippopolis [Note: [Col. 0375] 8 Ides of September according to the Necrology of Anchin; in 1147 according to the Annals of Anchin.]. Simon likewise, bishop of Noyon, ends his days at Seleucia. Amadeus, count of Maurienne, dies on the island of Cyprus. A council is held at Rheims by Pope Eugenius, in which a certain heretic from Brittany is brought forward and condemned. He claimed that he was neither a prophet nor any great personage, but, making a pun upon his own name—for he was called Eon [Col. 0375D]—he said that he was He who is to come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire; and he made some of his followers angels and others apostles, calling them by the proper names of angels or apostles. Condemned at the council and placed in the custody of the archbishop of Rheims, he died not long afterward, losing at once both life and remembrance. Much was also said and disputed against Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers, who by a certain novel subtlety of expression in his writings scandalized the Church. Accordingly, certain propositions which he did not dare, or was unable, to defend were condemned [Col. 0376A] and erased by himself.

At Laon, on 4 Non. July, after thunder had occurred, while the monks in the monastery of Saint Vincent were completing the course of the daytime office, two of them suddenly fell dead when struck by lightning; certain others, struck or terrified, scarcely recovered. The lightning also scorched the altar-cloth, penetrated the sanctuary, carried away part of the great cross and part of the cloister gate, and filled the whole house with horror. In other places too, people, buildings of men, or animals perished through lightning; and calamities more grievous than usual befell Christians, and were recorded. They also say that lightning struck at Jerusalem, in the Temple of the Lord or on the Mount of Olives, and that this was an omen of that misfortune.

In the territory of Geneva, a certain wolf unlike others in bodily size and ferocity of spirit [Col. 0376B] devoured men and deprived more than thirty persons, of different sexes and ages, of life. Wolves are known to have done likewise elsewhere in this year. Alfonso, count of Saint-Gilles, arrived in Palestine with a naval force; and, though great things were expected of him, he died at Caesarea in Palestine, wickedly poisoned, as they say, by the queen’s treachery. His young son entered a certain castle of his cousin, the count of Tripoli, but through that same man’s treachery was captured by the Turks together with his sister.

Damascus having been besieged for three days by the Franks, Germans, and Jerusalemites, and the outer walls which enclosed the gardens having already been taken, when the city was thought likely to be captured shortly, the siege was lifted, as they say, through the treachery of the princes of Palestine. [Col. 0376C] After the withdrawal had taken place, the king of France and the emperor, having again appointed a day for besieging Ascalon, met with their forces at Joppa. But because the Jerusalemites did not come as agreed, the emperor sailed to Constantinople; the king, as his men returned home, remained at Jerusalem for a year with a few companions. Roger, king of Sicily, sent a naval army to the coasts of Africa; and, after capturing the notable city called Africa, Sousse, Sfax, Kélibia, and several other forts, he sent back free to his own see the archbishop of Africa, who had come under servitude to Rome in order to be consecrated.

1149. 12. 12. 14. 6. 8.

Pope Eugenius, having returned to Italy, fights with varying success against the Romans. The emperors Conrad and Manuel [Col. 0376D] meet in Greece and prepare an expedition against Roger of Sicily. But their armies being broken up by hunger and unseasonable weather, Conrad returned to Germany as if intending to return again. Henry, brother of Louis, king of the Franks, despising worldly lineage, put on the monastic habit for Christ at Clairvaux and was advanced to the bishopric of the city of Beauvais. There was an eclipse of the moon on 11 Kal. April, about the ninth hour of the night, on the Saturday before Palm Sunday; and unseasonable winds followed for four continuous days. On the fourth day, however, there was a very great wind and an excessive inundation of rain. [Col. 0377A] On that day, in the territory of the Nervii near Ghent, a priest, after celebrating Mass, was struck by lightning and died; and in the territory of Rheims a certain cleric perished in the storm. Thunders, lightning-flashes, hailstorms, and tempests brought diverse misfortunes upon men in this year.

Louis, king of France, sailing from Palestine to return to his homeland, encountered Greek ships. While he was being taken by them to be presented to the emperor, who was besieging Corfu, George, commander of the ships of the king of Sicily, attacked them. For, after ravaging and plundering Greek provinces and approaching even the imperial city of Constantinople itself, he had shot golden arrows into the emperor’s palace and, having set fire to the suburbs, had violently carried away produce from the emperor’s gardens. Returning from there, he encountered the Greek ships, captured [Col. 0377B] them, rescued King Louis, but released the captives for the king’s sake. Meanwhile Manuel, after Corfu had surrendered, pursued the Sicilian ships with his own; and, after some ships had been captured, the king escaped by flight and was honorably received and escorted by King Roger and also by Pope Eugenius.

Raymond, prince of Antioch, a man terrible to all enemies of the Christian name, went out against the Turks on the Kalends of August. Many of his men were captured and slain in their ambush, and he himself was miserably killed. The Turks, carrying his head about, received into surrender nearly all the castles or cities that had been under his jurisdiction, except Antioch. When they were also grievously harassing that city, Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, went out against them into Syria; after routing them, on his return [Col. 0377C] he captured a Saracen fortification near Damascus and made the Damascenes tributary for three years. The Knights of the Temple rebuild Gaza, an ancient city of Palestine; fortifying it with towers, they severely harass the people of Ascalon.

1150. R. 13. F. 13. A. 15. H. 7. S. 9.

Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, in the thirty-eighth year of his episcopate, despising the worldly habit, assumes the monastic habit at Foigny [Note: [Col. 0377D] Foigny, diocese of Laon.]. Councils having been held throughout France, and Pope Eugenius also consenting that the abbot of Clairvaux should be sent to Jerusalem to exhort others, great discussion again arose concerning an overseas expedition; but the whole matter was annulled by the Cistercian monks.

[Col. 0377D] 1151. 14. 14. 16. 8. 10.

Men illustrious for religious devotion and prudence die: Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis [Note: [Col. 0377D] 1152, January 13.]; Rainald of Cîteaux; and Odo of Saint-Remi. Walter, abbot of Saint-Martin, becomes bishop at Laon; and Godescalc of Mont-Saint-Martin is made bishop at Arras. Bishops distinguished for character and learning die: Hugh of Auxerre and Joslenus of Soissons [Note: [Col. 0378D] 7 Kal. November according to the Necrology of Fimy; 25 October 1152 according to *Gallia Christiana*.]. Geoffrey, count of Anjou, after hostilities with King Louis, makes peace and dies within the space of one month. (A.D. 1152, January 8.) The noble and religious prince, Count Theobald, father of the poor, also dies. Many nobles likewise die in this year.

1152. 15. 15. 17. 9. 11.

(February 15.) Conrad, king of the Germans, dies. Although he had reigned for fifteen years, he never received the imperial blessing. His nephew Frederick, duke, succeeds him. Adalbero, archbishop of Trier, a man of great spirit and exceptional strictness, dies. There was an earthquake in parts of Italy. Louis, king of France, inflamed by a spirit of jealousy, repudiates his wife on a sworn allegation of consanguinity. Because Henry, duke of Normandy, marries her against his will, great hostility flares up between them. The queen of Jerusalem, having an excessively intimate relationship with the enemies of God, is opposed by her son, King Baldwin; [Col. 0378B] after besieging and capturing her strongholds, and being a second time prevented by her from entering the holy city, he finally enters by force. Besieging her in the citadel, he makes peace, leaves her Naples, and retains the rest of the kingdom for himself.

The Massamuti, whom some call Moabites, after usurping the kingdom of Mauretania and hanging its king on a gibbet, and after killing the king of Bougie also, invade his kingdom and threaten to invade Sicily itself, Apulia, and Rome as well. The illustrious man Ralph, count of Vermandois, dies. Pope Eugenius, peace having been made with the Romans, enters the City and for the first time dwells there with them in this year.

1153. 1. 16. 18. 10. 12.

King Frederick prepares an expedition into Italy. [Col. 0378C] (July 7.) Pope Eugenius dies, and Anastasius succeeds him. Louis, king of France, attacking the frontiers of Normandy with a very great army, receives the castle of Vernon in surrender. Meanwhile the duke of Normandy, acting vigorously in England against King Stephen, finally makes peace with him, on the condition that, while the king lives, he shall be second in England after him, and shall succeed on his death. The king of Jerusalem, having secured the integrity of his kingdom, at last captures Ascalon, the chief city of Palestine, after a long siege, not without grave loss and the slaughter of many of his men. Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, of venerable memory, after illustrious deeds, the gaining of many souls, and the founding of innumerable monasteries, rests in a blessed end. Theodoric, count of Flanders, recaptures the city of Cambrai after many citizens [Col. 0378D] had been taken prisoner. The religious man Walter, bishop of Laon, founder of many abbeys, passes to the Lord and is buried at Prémontré, where formerly, for Christ, he had assumed the habit of poverty. Walter, dean of Laon, succeeds him.

1154. 2. 17. 19. 11. 13.

Roger, king of Sicily, a useful and vigorous prince distinguished by his deeds, dies after notable victories over the Saracens and the occupation of their lands; nor does he leave behind him his son William, inferior to himself, as successor to his kingdom and victories. One of his own princes kills the king of Babylon; fleeing thence with an immeasurable quantity of treasure, he is killed by the Knights of the Temple, and, after his son is captured, all that wealthy and incomparable equipment falls to their use. William, king of Sicily, dispatching a naval army, ravages and plunders the city of Tinnis in Egypt; from there great riches of gold and silver and an abundant quantity of precious clothing are carried away. But on their return they encounter the fleet of the emperor of the Greeks; and although there were about 140 Greek ships, the Sicilians, fewer in number, defeat, plunder, and capture them, and an immeasurable abundance of varied wealth thus comes to the Sicilians. The Massamuti plunder a castle at Puteoli in Italy; the king of Sicily pursues them by sea through his men, captures and exterminates them. King Frederick crosses the Alps and acts vigorously in Italy (November); he destroys the castles of those [Col. 0379B] opposing him. Louis, king of France, receives Henry, duke of Normandy, into peace.

[Col. 0380A] Soon afterward, King Stephen having died, Henry enters England and, having secured the integrity of the kingdom, restores the ancient peace. Robert of Boves, a man full of every wickedness, inflamed with a spirit of jealousy, shut up in a house to be burned a certain one of his household with a little woman whom he suspected of having consented to him; after fire had been set and all combustible material consumed, the blaze did them no harm, but their own innocence preserved them sound and whole [Note: [Col. 0379B] Compare below, the Ursicampine continuation.]. (December.) Pope Anastasius dies, and Nicholas, bishop of Albano, becomes Pope Adrian. The moon suffered an eclipse on 11 Kal. January, in the latter parts of Gemini.

1155. R. 3. F. 18. A. 1. II. 12. S. 1.

In the regions of Burgundy, on 15 Kal. February, the third day of the week, [Col. 0380B] there were three earthquakes in one night, by which various buildings also are said to have been overthrown [Note: [Col. 0379] Thus the manuscript ends in the middle of a page. That the author truly laid down his pen here is shown by the interpolation of this Ursicampine continuation (D1*), which ends with the same words.].

## BURBACH CONTINUATION

[Col. 0379]

The manuscript of Blessed Mary near Burbach, C5, copied—or rather excerpted—manuscript C. From its additions it has only 1102, 1105, 1109, and 1111, material already found in B; it has nothing of its own except the following continuation, written in the same hand as the entire manuscript. The beginning of this continuation depends upon the Arras continuation. The years 1122, 1126, 1133, 1134, 1135, 1137, 1138, 1140, and 1145 are also found in the Chronicle of Saint Bavo, which, as we saw above at col. 29, was built upon the Vaucelles manuscript; whence it seems highly probable that the monk of Vaucelles had these same entries and perhaps drew them from ours.

[Col. 0379C] 1114. (Arras Continuation.) A council is held at Beauvais.

1118. (There.) Pope Paschal dies, and Gelasius succeeds him. A great wind arose on 12 Kal. January, overthrowing fortifications and bell-towers.

1119. Baldwin, count of Flanders, dies and is buried in the church of Saint-Bertin (cf. Preface). His nephew Charles, son of Cnut, king of the Danes, succeeds him. (Arras Continuation.) Pope Gelasius dies, and Calixtus succeeds him; he held a council at Rheims.

1122. In Flanders, at a village called Hovela, a child was born in the form of a fish, having neither arms nor thighs.

1124. (There.) The winter was exceedingly harsh.

1125. A most severe famine arose, beginning from the Kalends of [Col. 0379D] November and lasting until the new harvest. Pontius [Note: [Col. 0379D] The manuscript reads *Pontus*.], abbot of Cluny, died in prison and chains while in the custody of the Roman pontiff. A certain English boy, contracted from the loins downward, was raised upright at Saint-Omer through the merits of Saint Folcuin.

1126. A very great calamity came, which destroyed an innumerable multitude of both rich and poor.

1127. (There.) Charles, count of Flanders, is killed at Bruges; William, son of Robert, count of the Normans, succeeds him.

[Col. 0380C] 1128. Count William dies and is buried in the church of Saint-Bertin. Theodoric, son of Theodoric, duke of Alsace, succeeds him.

1129. An eclipse of the moon appeared on 4 Kal. November.

1130. Pope Honorius dies. A dispute over the papacy arises between Peter, son of Leo, and Gregory of Saint Angelo.

1131. In the district of Vermandois a child is born with three heads and the same number of hands. The village of Saint-Riquier, situated in the district of Ponthieu, is burned together with the church of that saint; more than two thousand people, women and children included, are reported to have been burned there by Hugh of Champ-Avoine, who besieged and burned that village with his knights.

1133. The sun was darkened on 4 Non. August, at the [Col. 0380D] sixth hour, so that stars appeared in the sky. At Bergues, in a village called Beirna, a lamb was born with two heads. At Bergues an infant was born with twelve fingers on its hands and as many on its feet, and with all its remaining limbs except a face. For it had neither head, nor eyes, nor nose, nor mouth; therefore it lived only one day.

1134. On 14 Kal. July thunder was heard, and unusual flashes of lightning appeared, so that some thought that the end of the world had come. [Col. 0381A] The city of Tripoli was besieged by the Babylonians; but, through God’s mercy, it was soon magnificently liberated by the king of Jerusalem, the patriarch, and their army, after twenty thousand Saracens had been slain and all their forces captured. The savage discord that had existed between the king of Jerusalem and the count of Tripoli was completely settled, and a joint siege of Ascalon was sworn. A council is held at Rheims, during the pontificate of Pope Innocent II.

1135. A great wind arose on 5 Kal. November, so violent that in various places it overthrew church towers and houses in cities. Henry, king of the English, dies. His nephew Stephen, count of Boulogne, succeeds him. Thunder was heard and flashes of lightning were seen on the Ides of December. A comet was seen in France [Col. 0381B].

1136. A certain priest named Heribert, convicted of heresy at Rheims, is degraded.

1137. Two boys are born, one in the district of Noyon, the other in the district of Lens, wearing a fleshly mitre as though it were linen, with fleshly tails hanging from their necks as though they were hair braided in the manner of knights who let their hair grow and braid it. Very many monasteries are burned in this year by divine judgment. Louis, king of France, dies; his son Louis succeeds him and takes as wife the daughter of the count of Poitou. Lothair, king of Germany, dies.

1138. Peter, son of Peter Leo, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mary across the Tiber, dies. [Col. 0381C] Rainald, archbishop of Rheims, dies. Thunder was heard on 8 Kal. July, the stroke of which was truly horrible, because unbearable to hear and therefore astonishing.

1139. Rome is reconciled to Pope Innocent. A general council is summoned at the Lateran. An eclipse of the sun occurs on 13 Kal. April, in the evening hour.

1140. Samson, dean of Chartres, becomes archbishop of Rheims. Stephen, king of England, and Baldwin, count of Hainaut, conspire with Hugh of Candavene against Theodoric, count of Flanders. He resisted them courageously, not without their severe loss, after their lands had been ravaged by fire, sword, the capture of men, the plundering of animals, and the destruction of castles [Note: [Col. 0381] I have supplied this word; it is absent from the manuscript.].

[Col. 0381D] 1142. A very harsh and prolonged winter, followed by such an extraordinary flood of waters that rivers, leaving their beds more than usual, overturned bridges, houses with their households, and nearby castles, and swept them away in their course.

1143. Pope Innocent II dies; Celestine succeeds him. On 14 Kal. February a violent wind arose from the right side of the northern quarter; it overthrew churches to their foundations, shattered and cast down bell-towers and towers of incalculable weight and great strength, uprooted trees, and destroyed castles and houses. [Col. 0382A] In their collapse it involved men, women, children, and livestock in death in several places. During the same week the sea also crossed its bounds and submerged a great deal of land.

1144. Pope Celestine dies, and Lucius II is set over the Roman Church.

1145. Pope Lucius dies; Eugenius III succeeds. A comet is seen.

1148. A council is held at Rheims by Pope Eugenius [Note: [Col. 0381] Here a leaf ends; the next begins with the year 1163. Thus a leaf containing the years 1149–1162 appears to have been lost.].

1163. Henry, king of England, exalting himself above what is called God or is worshipped, made savage and lifted up in pride, with the assent of Roger, archbishop of York, Gilbert, bishop of London, Hilary, bishop of Chichester, certain others, and indeed all his barons together, and urged on by his counsellor Richard, archdeacon of Poitiers, violently usurps for himself, contrary to right and law, every dignity and prerogative of ecclesiastical discipline. For this reason he banished from England Lord Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, a religious man worthy of glory and honor, who strongly opposed this apostasy and steadfastly exposed himself to death for justice and truth. Escaping secretly as best he could and crossing the sea, he arrived at the church of Saint-Bertin, where he was honorably received, as befitted so great a man. And rightly so: Saint Dunstan and Saint Anselm too, banished from England, had chosen this place as suitable for their pilgrimage [Col. 0382C].

In the district called Saint-Omer, in the parish of Saint Margaret, during the second week of Advent, an infant was born with two heads, four arms, and as many hands, having in its front parts a double nature, male and female, but in its rear parts only one organ of excretion.

1164. Such a thing occurred in the church of Sens. On Good Friday, an archdeacon of that city lay dead in the church, surrounded by four crosses, one of which, at his head, was more precious than the rest. When the appropriate time came for the offices of the day to be celebrated, Pope Alexander, who was then staying there, prepared with his clergy to perform the offices. Once they had begun, the air [Col. 0382D] began to be disturbed. When the readings had been read and the tracts proper to the day sung, and the Passion had also been begun, when they came to that place, “Crucify him, crucify him,” such a crash, together with a stroke of lightning, suddenly broke upon them that not one person in the whole church remained standing; all fell to the ground as though dead. The aforesaid precious cross too, as if sawn through the middle, fell into two pieces; one of them was found, while the other part wholly disappeared. After an hour the pope and his clergy recovered themselves and completed the office, sufficiently filled with pain and fear.

## VALCELLES CONTINUATION

[Col. 0383]

Since manuscript B2 has perished, from this continuation we can give only those things which Miraeus excerpted from it. Yet that there was much more is shown by the Chronicle of Saint Bavo, said above to have been constructed upon it at col. 29. There not only are many items from Miraeus found, but also many other matters which beyond doubt were taken from Vaucelles. But precisely what they are cannot certainly be said, since the compiler of Ghent used sources other than B2 as well. From the Burbach continuation certain entries are found there under the years 1122, 1126, 1136–1135, 1137–1140, 1144, and 1145; from the Anchin continuation, the years 1149–1152. Therefore the compiler of Ghent either collected all these from B5 and C5, or already found them in B2. I would more readily believe the latter, because under the year 1150 the Chronicle has certain things found not in B5 but in B1; and B1 evidently was available to the compiler of Vaucelles. But, leaving these uncertainties aside, one thing is certain: the Vaucelles manuscript did not possess an independent continuation. Rather, after copying manuscript B—or perhaps B5—down to the year 1163, it merely scattered additions taken from the Life of Norbert, the Prémontré continuation, perhaps the Burbach continuation as well, and elsewhere.

[Col. 0383A] 1114. (Prémontré Continuation.) A council was held at Beauvais under the presidency of Cono, bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Roman Church.

1115. (Life of Norbert.) The heretic Tanchelm, who had infected Antwerp, Walcheren, the surrounding islands, and maritime places in those regions with many heresies, is killed. Baldwin, count of Flanders, captured the castle of Encre after expelling Hugh of Candavene, who had usurped it, and gave it to his kinsman Charles. (Prémontré Continuation.) Lambert, bishop of Arras, dies. Peter the Hermit, returning from Syria, dies at Huy and is buried in the monastery which he had founded on the river Meuse. Clairvaux is founded; its first abbot was Saint Bernard.

1117. Baldwin, count of Flanders, because Hugh [Col. 0383B] of Candavene was ravaging his land wherever possible with robberies and arson, besieged the castle of Saint-Pol; but, through the mediation of Eustace, count of Boulogne, he was reconciled with Hugh and returned.

1119. (There.) Baldwin, count of Flanders, nephew of Pope Calixtus through his sister, dies. (Life of Norbert.) Cono, bishop of Palestrina and apostolic legate, holds a synod at Cologne and proclaims the excommunication of Emperor Henry. Norbert attended this synod, afterward founder of the Premonstratensian order, then recently converted and wearing a pilgrim’s dress.

1120. (There.) Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, and Norbert, abbot, found the church of Prémontré. As Norbert was returning from Cologne with relics of saints, Ermensendis, countess of Namur, offers him [Col. 0383C] a church in her village of Floreffe, in which to establish brethren.

1124. (There.) The canons of Antwerp, founded by Godfrey of Bouillon, duke of Lorraine and margrave of Antwerp, cede the church of Saint Michael to Norbert and his companions, and move thence to the church of Blessed Mary the Virgin.

1125. The monastery of Vicoigne near Valenciennes is begun; among Premonstratensian houses it is most beautiful.

1126. (There.) Godfrey, count of Cappenberg, having left the world to follow Christ with Norbert, founder among the Westphalians of the monasteries of Cappenberg, Varlar, and Elsey, dies.

1128. In this year the monastery of the Dunes [Note: [Col. 0383C] Ter Duinen, situated within the walls of the city of Bruges.] in Flanders began to be built by Lord Fulk, first abbot of that place.

1131. (Prémontré Continuation.) Milo, abbot of Saint-Josse-in-the-Wood, of the Premonstratensian order, is consecrated bishop of Thérouanne on the Kalends of March; the printed text includes an unexplained “45” before the date. In this year the monastery church of Saint Mary of Vaucelles [Note: [Col. 0383C] Vaucelles.] was begun in the territory of Cambrai. In the Golden Valley [Note: [Col. 0384C] Orval.] near Trier, Blessed Bernard places monks of his order.

1132. Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, passed away. Guigo, venerable [Col. 0384B] prior of the Carthusian house, by command of Pope Innocent, described his life, full of virtues, in an elegant style. A community of monks, with their abbot Ralph, a native of England, came to the place called Vaucelles on the Kalends of August. Blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, brought them there.

1133. The church of Saint Mary at Thérouanne was dedicated by four bishops: namely Milo, bishop of that city; Warin of Amiens; Simon of Noyon and Tournai; and Alvisus of Arras.

1137. (There.) William, duke of Aquitaine and count of Poitou, dying, left his daughter, whom he had as heir, betrothed to Louis, son of the king of France. The king’s son set out to marry her; meanwhile, his father the king having died, he was established in the kingdom, and [Col. 0384C] the kingdom of France and the duchy of Aquitaine were united. Abbot Fulk committed his house of the Dunes and the house of Clairmarais [Note: [Col. 0384C] Clairmarais, not far from Saint-Omer.], which he had begun at the same time, to the Cistercian order in the chapter at Clairvaux, under the hand of Lord Bernard, on the day of Saint Petronilla the Virgin.

1138. (There.) Rainald, archbishop of Rheims, dies. Fulk, abbot of the Dunes, resigns the office of abbot, and Lord Robert of Bruges is established abbot at the Dunes.

1140. (There.) Samson, provost of the church of Chartres, [Col. 0385A] is ordained archbishop of Rheims. At Tournai a young cleric named Henry saw many things in the Spirit. He also committed to human knowledge the life of Saint Eleutherius, bishop of Tournai, and prophesied many other things, both concerning the bishopric of that city and concerning other matters.

1141. (There.) Hugh, prior of the church of Saint Victor at Paris, dies, leaving many writings useful to Holy Church.

1145. A certain Turk named Sanguin captures Edessa, kills the Christians dwelling in that city, and profanes its churches.

1146. (There.) The church of Tournai, which for more than five hundred years had been entrusted to the bishops of the church of Noyon, receives from Pope Eugenius III a bishop of its own, named Anselm, Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, being among those who procured this.

1147. Part of the Christian army, sailing for Jerusalem, captured the Spanish city of Lisbon, by God’s power driving out the Saracens, and restored it to Christians. Emperor Conrad, with more than fifty thousand knights and an innumerable body of infantry, after crossing the sea called the Arm of Saint George, lost nearly his entire army through the treachery of the Greeks, the attacks of the Turks, and famine. Twelve monks, with Abbot Lawrence and five lay brothers, sent by Blessed Bernard from Clairvaux into Brabant, founded the monastery of Villers [Col. 0385C] (cf. Prémontré).

1148. Louis, king of the Franks, with nearly thirty thousand cavalry and a great multitude of infantry, after crossing the aforesaid sea, lost the greater part of his army through the treachery of Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, famine, and the pursuit of a hostile army; he came to Salamis and from there sailed for Antioch. The Cistercian monastery of Cambron [Note: [Col. 0385D] Cambron.] is founded in Hainaut. Cistercian monks are likewise established at Aulne [Note: [Col. 0385D] Aulne.] on the river Sambre by Blessed Bernard, at the request of Henry, bishop of Liège.

1149. In this year the church of the monastery of Saint Mary of Vaucelles was consecrated by Samson, archbishop of Rheims [Col. 0385D], on 7 Kal. June.

1151. Ralph, first abbot of this monastery of Vaucelles, departed from the world on 3 Kal. January. Richard succeeded him, likewise drawn from Clairvaux, mature in character and temperate in all things.

1153. Robert of Bruges, abbot of the Dunes in Flanders, was appointed Bernard’s successor at Clairvaux, having been chosen by Bernard himself. Then the house of the Dunes was without a shepherd for four months, until Albero, sent by Robert himself, succeeded him in its governance, which he held for two years. Peace was restored between Stephen, [Col. 0386A] king of the English, and Henry, count of Anjou, on the condition that, after Stephen’s death, Henry himself should succeed to the kingdom of England. He was the grandson through a daughter of Henry, king of England, and, claiming the kingdom of England by hereditary right, had inflicted many evils upon the land both personally and through his helpers, while he was duke of Normandy and Aquitaine. For he had married the daughter of William, duke of Aquitaine, whom King Louis of France had put aside on the pretext of consanguinity; through her he held that duchy. Bernard, bishop of Sidon, having died during the siege of Ascalon, Amalric, abbot of the regular canons in the place called Saint Habakkuk, or Saint Joseph of Arimathea, is substituted for him.

[Col. 0386B] 1154. Stephen, king of the English, dies; the aforesaid Henry succeeds without difficulty or opposition. Vicelinus, apostle of the Wends, dies.

1158. Lord Robert of Bruges, second abbot of the Dunes and of Clairvaux, departs from the world. He presided for twenty years: fifteen years and nearly five months over the Dunes, four years and eight months over Clairvaux. Lord Fastrad, abbot of Cambron in Hainaut, succeeds him in the governance.

1159. Milo, bishop of the Morini, formerly abbot of Saint-Josse-in-the-Wood of the Premonstratensian order, after ruling the see of the Morini for twenty-seven years, passes to the Lord. Milo II, his [Col. 0386C] archdeacon, an Englishman by birth and a regular canon of Saint Mary of the Wood, or of the Forest, succeeds him. The military Order of Calatrava begins in Spain.

1161. After the general chapter, Lambert, abbot of Cîteaux, resigns his office and gives up the abbey. The Cistercians make Lord Fastrad of Clairvaux their father, and those of Clairvaux receive Lord Geoffrey, abbot of Igny.

1162. In September Emperor Frederick, with Octavian, took up position near the river Saône, while King Louis was at Dijon. Many bishops, abbots, clerics, and laymen, both princes and common people, gathered on either side in order, if they could, to put an end to the schism in the Church [Col. 0386D]. They could not; rather, they departed from one another amid great discord and hostility. Therefore the chapter in that year was held not then at Cîteaux, but later, about the feast of Saint Martin, at a certain grange of Foigny [Note: [Col. 0386D] Foigny, diocese of Laon.].

1163. On 14 Kal. June Fastrad, abbot of Cîteaux, dies at Paris and is brought to Cîteaux before the Ascension. Lord Gislebert, abbot of Ourscamp, is appointed in his place after the Council of Tours.

## BEAUVAIS ADDITION

[Col. 0387]

A monk of Beauvais, copying Sigebert between the years 1138 and 1147, made the following additions of his own, besides the additions for the years 651, 685, 773, 1048, 1076, 1079, 1084, 1090, 1092, 1095, 1096, 1099, 1100, and 1109, which he already read in his source C. Another person afterward added three entries for 1109, 1111, and 1112, together with a continuation for 1113–1147, which a third carried down to the year 1163. Labbe published it from interpolated manuscript D2 in *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, I, 390; Struve published it from Labbe, p. 1015, and Bouquet, XIII, 334. We give it from D, with all the numerous chronological errors which it contains, indicating the true years in the margin.

[Col. 0387A] 649. E. N. A. q. e. D. R. shine [*clarent*], and likewise P. of the island of Herio and R. P., abbots, and Geremarus of Flavigny, as also the holy virgin Angadrisma near Beauvais. (The initial sigla are retained as printed.)

731. He ordained that, after the first commemoration of the saints in the canon of the Mass, the priest should say as follows: “And of those whose feast is celebrated today throughout the whole world before the sight of thy majesty, O Lord our God”; and he caused this institution to be inscribed on stone tablets in the oratory at Rome.

939. Stephen presides as the 128th bishop of the Roman Church.

956. Pope John presides as the 131st bishop of the Roman Church.

[Col. 0387B] —Leo indeed presides as the 133rd bishop of the Roman Church.

965. John presides as the 134th bishop of the Roman Church.

972. Pope Benedict presides as the 135th bishop of the Roman Church.

974. Boniface presides as the 137th bishop of the Roman Church.

975. Benedict presides as the 138th bishop of the Roman Church.

977. From this point onward, let there be silence concerning the empire of Constantinople.

984. John presides as the 139th bishop of the Roman church. — John presides as the 140th bishop of the Roman church.

986. John presides as the 141st bishop of the Roman church.

996. Gregory presides as the 142nd bishop of the Roman church.

998. John presides as the 143rd bishop of the Roman church [Col. 0387C] for ten months.

1003. John presides as the 145th bishop of the Roman church. — John presides as the 146th bishop of the Roman church.

1012. Benedict presides as the 148th bishop of the Roman church.

1015. The county of Beauvais is granted to Bishop Roger.  
[Note: [Col. 0387] Added later, but by the same hand.]

1024. At this time the distinguished Roger, bishop in the Gallic city of Beauvais, died. Among other benefactions, he gave to the church of St Peter, over which he presided, Ailly in Normandy [Note: [Col. 0387C] Ailly.] and Montiacum in the district of Vermandois. He also obtained the county of that same city from Odo, count of Champagne, giving him in exchange the castle of Sancerre [Note: [Col. 0387C] Sancerre.], situated in the territory of Bourges, which belonged to him by hereditary right.  
[Note: [Col. 0387] Erased; another hand corrected it to: “which is called Saint-Césaire.”]

1033. Benedict presides as the 150th bishop of the Roman church.

1051. “. . . . . it was disputed” among whom Lord Guy, abbot of the Cross of St Leutfrid [Note: [Col. 0387C] In Normandy, northward from Évreux.], composed an elegant book against him [Note: [Col. 0387C] Berengar. This book was published by Erasmus at Antwerp, 1530; by Vlimmerius at Louvain, 1561; and in the *Bibliothecae Patrum*, Cologne, vol. XII, and Lyons, vol. XVIII.] concerning the body and blood of Christ.

1067. In these times, when the city of Beauvais had been deprived of its bishop, Guy, dean and custos of the church of St Quentin of Vermandois and archdeacon of Laon, was appointed bishop of Beauvais [Col. 0388B] and consecrated by Gervasius, metropolitan of Rheims. Grieving deeply that he lacked the presence of the martyr Quentin, he built a church in his honour and memory not far from the walls of the city of Beauvais.

1069. Guy, bishop of Beauvais, dedicated the church, completed in two years, in honour of his patron, the martyr Quentin, on 4 October.

1078. From this time the canonical order began to flourish anew in the church of Blessed Quentin at Beauvais: first instituted in regular fashion by the apostles, and afterwards by the blessed bishop Augustine, under Master Ivo, venerable provost of that church and later bishop of Chartres.

1092. Lord Ivo, provost of St Quentin’s at Beauvais [Col. 0388C], having been consecrated by Pope Urban, becomes bishop of Chartres.  
[Note: [Col. 0387] In an erased place, but by the scribe of the manuscript himself.]

From this point, a second hand:

1109. The latest Easter fell on 25 April.

1111. Fire consumed nearly the whole suburb of the city of Beauvais.

1113. Very great barrenness of the land and vineyards. — After the death of the monk Sigebert, from this point we shall calculate the times of our own years.

1115. Lord Ivo, bishop of Chartres, died.  
[Note: [Col. 0388C] There is great dispute concerning the year and day of his death. Robert of Torigni, Matthew Paris, and the *Life of Robert of Arbrissel*, whom Pagi follows, place it in 1117. The calendar of St Quentin at Beauvais, cited by Pagi, has: “On the Kalends of January died Master Ivo, of venerable memory . . . in the year of Christ’s Incarnation 1116.” Since that calendar begins its years at Easter, this is our year 1117. The Premonstratensian continuator above, p. 447, gives the year 1113. The Martyrology of Chartres, according to Pagi, says that he died on the Ides of December, 1115. The calendar of St John of Chartres in the Valley, according to Pagi, has: “10 Kalends of January, in the year of the Incarnation 1115.” The necrology of St Mary of Chartres, now in the public library of Chartres, p. 26, which was copied at the beginning of the thirteenth century from a far older manuscript, has the following in a first hand of the early thirteenth century: “10 Kalends of January, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1115, Father Ivo died, bishop of this most holy see: a man of great religious devotion, most prudent in ecclesiastical and secular affairs, gentle in speech, remarkable for patience, eminent in chastity, and most learned both in sacred matters and in [Col. 0389D] philosophy. He bestowed upon the adornment of this church six good hangings, seven copes, three mitres, and three tapestries; he gave a missal, an epistolary, a Gospel-book, and one lectionary for Matins, and furnished them all with silver; he built a pulpit of marvellous beauty; he established schools. The episcopal house, which he had found poor and wooden, and reduced to servitude at the death or departure of bishops by certain evil customs introduced through the violence of the counts of Chartres, he rebuilt splendidly in stone from its foundation, [Col. 0390C] and rendered it free from servitude, together with everything belonging to it, movable and immovable. He confirmed that freedom by the guarantee of privileges of the Roman see, the king, and the count, which are kept in the archives of this church. He also acquired from the viscount a certain plot adjoining that house, to enlarge the house, and enclosed it with a wall; at Godan Bridge he built other houses for episcopal uses, and improved that same town in many respects. He converted the abbey of St John from secular to regular status, established and enlarged it. By his counsel and aid the hospital-monastery at Beaulieu was established. He converted all the junior benefices and precarial grants of this church to common use, and by both his own and apostolic privilege forbade their future distribution among individuals; by the same privileges he prohibited forced services, unjust exactions, and the improper incursions of servants through the provostships.”  
[Note: From this point, a wholly contemporary but different hand: “He gave this chapter the authority which he possessed to grant the [Col. 0390D] provostship of Ébrardville and its appurtenances; he caused the fixed charges for burial throughout the bishopric of this church to cease; when dying, he left one hundred measures of wine to augment the altar fund; and in many other matters he did much good for this church and its clergy.” Beneath are several figures of monks drawn in the earlier ink, raising their eyes and hands upward and seemingly invoking Ivo.]

[Col. 0389A] 1118. Gelasius presides as the 155th bishop of the Roman church.

1119. Calixtus presides as the 156th bishop of the Roman church.

1123 [1125]. Lothar succeeds Emperor Henry.

1125 [1124]. Honorius presides as the 167th bishop of the Roman church.

1129 [1130]. Innocent presides as the 168th bishop of the Roman church.

1133 [1138]. Upon Lothar’s death, Conrad succeeds him, nephew of the elder Henry.  
[Note: [Col. 0389C] Added by another hand.]

1136. The earliest Easter fell on 22 March in this year.

1137 [1136]. On the death of Henry, king of the English, Stephen, his nephew, succeeded him because he had no son [Col. 0389B].

1139 [1137]. Louis, king of the Franks, died. His son Louis succeeded to the kingdom; while still alive, the father had caused him to be consecrated by Pope Innocent at Rheims some years before.

1143. Celestine presides as the 169th bishop of the Roman church.

1144. Lucius presides as the 170th bishop of the Roman church.

1145. Eugenius, the 171st after him, becomes pope of Rome.

1147 [1147]. There was an eclipse of the sun on 28 October, [Col. 0390A] at the third hour, on Sunday. [1148.] A council at Rheims, presided over by Pope Eugenius.

From this point, a third hand:

1148 [1149]. Louis, king of the Franks, having undertaken the journey to Jerusalem, suffered Saracen ambushes and returned with great loss among his men. Odo, the second bishop of Beauvais, died.

1150. Henry, elder son of King Louis, becomes bishop of Beauvais.

1151. The roots of the crops having frozen in the ground, there was a very great scarcity of produce.

1152 [1153]. Anastasius, the 172nd pope, succeeds in the Roman church.

1153. Theobald, count of Troyes, died.

1154 [25 October 1155]. Stephen, king of the English [Col. 0390B], dies.

1155. Henry, son of Geoffrey, count of Anjou, succeeds him.

1156 [1154]. Adrian, the 173rd, becomes pope of Rome.

1159. Great contention between the king of the Franks and the king of the English over the city of Toulouse.

1160. An eclipse of the moon on 19 August.

1161 [1159]. Alexander, the 174th pope.

1163 [1161]. Samson, archbishop of Rheims, a man distinguished for learning and holiness, died.

## Supplement of Mortemer

[Col. 0389]

A monk of Mortemer (Mortemar, near Lyons, between Rouen and Gisors) copied manuscript D in 1155, with all its additions and continuation, adding only a few trifles of his own, which we place in brackets [Col. 0391]. A second, contemporary with the continuation, inserted many items, mostly taken from Anselm and the Gembloux writers, down to 1165; we have indicated these in italics. A third, about 1180, scattered in those items which we likewise distinguish in italics. The remaining entries were written by many hands at the same time as the events occurred. They have been published in Martène, *Thesaurus*, III, 1437, whence Bouquet took his text, XII, 781; XVIII, 354. We print them as our Waitz copied them from manuscript D1 itself.

[Col. 0391A] [1054. Battle at Mortemer.

[1056. (*Exordium Cisterciense*.)  
[Note: [Col. 0391D] That is, the *Exordium of the Cistercian Monastery*, by one of the founders—I would scarcely believe that it was St Stephen—printed in Tissier, *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, I, 1; Labbe, *Bibliotheca manuscripta*, I, 640.]

“In the bishopric of Langres there is known to be a monastery named Molesme, most renowned in reputation and conspicuous for its religious life. From its beginning divine mercy, within a short time, adorned it with great gifts of grace, ennobled it with distinguished men, and made it no less ample in possessions than illustrious in virtues. Yet because possessions and virtues are not wont to remain long in partnership, certain men of that holy congregation, clearly wise men who understood this more deeply, chose rather to be occupied in heavenly pursuits than entangled in earthly affairs. Hence lovers of virtue soon began to reflect upon the fruitful poverty of holy men. Observing at the same time that, although life was led there holily and honourably, [Col. 0391B] nevertheless the Rule which they had professed was observed less fully than their desire and purpose required, they spoke with one another about what moved each man, and together considered how they might fulfil the verse: ‘I will pay you my vows, which my lips have uttered.’ Why say more? Twenty-one monks, together with the father of that monastery, Robert of blessed memory, departed; by common counsel and common assent they strove to accomplish what they had conceived in one spirit. Therefore, after many labours and excessive difficulties—which all who wish to live devoutly in Christ must suffer—they at last attained their desire and came to Cîteaux, then a place of horror and vast solitude. Yet the soldiers of Christ, judging that the harshness of the site did not differ from the strict purpose which they had already conceived in mind, received it as a place truly prepared for them by God, as welcome as their purpose was dear. Thus, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098, strengthened by the counsel and authority of the venerable Hugh, archbishop of the church of Lyons and then legate of the apostolic see; of the religious Walter, bishop of Chalon; and also of the most illustrious prince Odo, duke of Burgundy, they began to establish the discovered wilderness as an abbey. The aforesaid Abbot Robert received pastoral care and staff from the bishop of that diocese, namely the bishop of Chalon, while the others established stability under him in the same place. But not long afterwards Abbot Robert himself, being demanded by the monks of Molesme, was restored to Molesme at the command of Pope Urban II, by the permission and consent of Walter, bishop of Chalon. Alberic, a religious and holy man, was appointed in his place. A peace settlement was retained between the two churches and confirmed by apostolic authority: henceforth neither was to receive a monk of the other to reside without regular commendation. When this had been done, the new monastery, through the concern and industry of its new father, and with God’s no slight co-operation, soon advanced in holy observance, became renowned in reputation, and increased in necessary resources.

[1107. (*Exordium Cisterciense*.) Battle at Tinchebray  
[Note: [Col. 0392D] Tinchebray, on the River Noireau, between Vire and Domfront.] between Count Robert and Henry of England. Alberic, abbot of Cîteaux, attained in the tenth year the prize of the heavenly calling for which he had not run in vain there for nine years. Lord Stephen succeeded him, an Englishman by birth, a most ardent lover and most faithful imitator of religion, poverty, and regular discipline. In his truly [Col. 0392B] blessed days the truth of what is written became manifest: ‘The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers.’ For the little flock lamented only that it was little; the poor of Christ feared only this—indeed, they feared almost to despair—that they could not leave heirs to their poverty. Their neighbours honoured the holiness of their life, but recoiled from its austerity; thus, though they approached them in devotion, they drew back from imitating them. But God, for whom it is easy to make great things from small and many from few, stirred the hearts of many, beyond expectation, to imitate them. Thus thirty persons lived together in the cell for testing novices: clerics and laymen alike, including men noble and powerful in worldly rank. From this heavenly visitation, so sudden and so joyful, the barren woman who did not bear children began at last, not without cause, to rejoice, because many children had been made for the desolate woman. Nor did God cease day by day to multiply the people for her and enlarge her joy, until, within about twenty years, that happy mother beheld around her table some twelve monasteries, from her own sons and from the sons of her sons, like shoots of olive trees. For she did not judge it unfitting to imitate the examples as well as embrace the institutions of the holy father Benedict. From the beginning, when the new plantation had begun to put forth new branches, the venerable Father Stephen, by a marvellously vigilant prudence of discernment, had provided a written rule [Col. 0392D] like a pruning tool, namely for cutting away shoots of schism which, if they grew up at some time, could choke the fruit that was to arise from mutual peace. Accordingly, he fittingly wished that document to be called the Charter of Charity, because its entire sequence breathes only the things of charity, [Col. 0393A] so that throughout it seems to pursue almost nothing else than: ‘Owe no one anything, except to love one another.’ That charter, arranged by the same father, confirmed by the aforesaid twenty abbots, and fortified by the authority of the apostolic seal, contains more fully what we have said; but here we shall touch briefly only upon its chief points.

“The abbot of Cîteaux and his brothers, not forgetful of their profession, set in order and unanimously resolved to observe in that place the Rule of Blessed Benedict. They rejected whatever conflicted with the Rule: frocks and pelisses, coarse cloth, hoods and drawers, combs and straw mattresses or bed-coverings, varied dishes in the refectory, fat, and everything else contrary to the purity of the Rule. Thus, making the strictness of the Rule the guiding principle of their whole life, they made themselves equal or conformed to the traces of the Rule both in ecclesiastical observances and in all others. Having put off the old man, they rejoiced to have put on the new. And because neither in the Rule nor in the life of St Benedict did they read that the same teacher had possessed churches, altars, offerings and burial rights, other people’s tithes, ovens, mills, villages, or serfs; nor that women had entered his monastery, nor that the dead had been buried there except his sister, they therefore renounced all these things, saying: ‘Where Blessed Father Benedict teaches that a monk should make himself separate from secular occupations, he clearly declares that such things ought not to have a place in the activities or hearts of monks, who must pursue the etymology of their name by fleeing these things.’

“They also said that tithes were distributed by the holy fathers, who were organs of the Holy Spirit and whose ordinances it is sacrilege to transgress, into four portions: one for the bishop, another for the priest, a third for guests coming to that church, widows, orphans, and poor persons having no other means of subsistence, and the fourth for restoring the church. Since in this reckoning they found no place for a monk who possessed his own lands and lived by working them himself and through his livestock, they refused to usurp such things unjustly as though they were another’s right. Behold: having despised the riches of this world, these new soldiers of Christ began, poor with poor Christ, to consider among themselves by what ingenuity, art, or labour they could maintain themselves and both rich and poor guests who came to them in this life, whom the Rule commands them to receive as Christ. They therefore determined that, with their bishop’s permission, they would receive bearded lay brothers, treating them in life and death, except for monastic profession, as themselves; and also hired labourers, because they did not think that without these people’s aid they could fully observe the Rule’s precepts day and night. They would also receive lands remote from human habitation; vineyards, meadows, woods, and waters for making mills, but for their own use and for fishing; and horses [Col. 0394A] and various livestock useful for human need. Wherever they established granges for agricultural work, they decreed that the aforesaid lay brothers, not monks, should govern those houses, because according to the Rule monks must dwell in their cloister. Since these holy men knew that Blessed Benedict had built monasteries not in cities, castles, or villages but in places removed from the throng of people, they promised to imitate him in this also. And just as he organized monasteries built for groups of twelve monks with a father added, they affirmed that they would do the same.”

1115. (Valcell.) The monastery of Clairvaux is founded under its first abbot, Bernard, a holy man.

[Col. 0394B] [1116. (Bellov.) Lord Ivo, bishop of Chartres, died.] (ANSELM.) In the suburb of Antioch, the earth opened at night and swallowed houses with their inhabitants.

1118. (Ibid.) An earthquake occurred so violent that it overthrew portions of certain cities.

[1119. (Bellov.) Gelasius presides as the 165th bishop of the Roman church.

[1120. (Ibid.) Calixtus presides as the 166th bishop of the Roman church. In this year Henry, king of the English, fought Louis, king of the Franks, between Andely and Noyon.  
[Note: [Col. 0393] Corrected from *nonieoium*.] In this battle King Louis himself fled, and nearly all the great men and nobles of France were captured.]

1122. (ANS.) An earthquake occurred during Advent, on 10 December.

[1123. (Bell.) Lothar succeeds Emperor Henry.] When a sedition arose at Tours between clergy and laity, the church of St Martin burned.

1124. (ANS.) Christians fight the Saracens between Jerusalem and Ascalon and are victorious.

[1125. (Bell. ANS.) Honorius presides as the 167th bishop of the Roman church.] Tyre was captured.

1126. (Ibid.) A most severe winter and a grievous famine. In Haspengouw a monster is born, a man in front and a dog behind.

1127. (Ibid.) Charles, count of Flanders, was killed at Bruges while praying in a church, through the treachery of certain of his great men.

[Col. 0394D] 1128. (Ibid.) Divine miracles shine forth at Soissons in the church of Blessed Mary the Virgin. Geoffrey, archbishop of Rouen, died. Hugh, abbot of Reading, succeeded him.

[1129. (Bell.) Innocent presides as the 168th bishop of the Roman church.] The monastery of Ourscamp was founded. The monastery at Beaumont was founded under its first abbot, Alexander, by the venerable Robert of Candos. It is now called Mortemer.  
[Note: [Col. 0393] “It is now called Mortemer” appears to have been written above the line later by the same hand.]

1131. (ANS.) A great synod is held at Rheims by Pope Innocent, and the younger Louis is blessed as king.

1132. (Ibid.) An eclipse of the sun on 2 August.

[Col. 0395A] [1133. (Bell.) On Lothar’s death Conrad, nephew of the elder Henry, succeeds.] Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, and Malachy, bishop of Ireland, are renowned for learning, holiness, and the glory of miracles.

1134. With King Henry’s consent, Abbot Alexander came with his entire convent into the forest of Lyons and built his monastery in the hermitage called Mortemer.

1135. King Henry died on 2 December; Stephen, his nephew, succeeded him on 25 December.

1137. Abbot Alexander joined the house of Mortemer to the Cistercian Order; Waleran, abbot of Ourscamp [Note: [Col. 0395D] Orcamp.], received it as a daughter-house and sent his monks there.

[1138. (Ibid.) Louis, king of the Franks, died. His son Louis, whom while still alive he had caused to be consecrated by Pope Innocent at Rheims some years before, [Col. 0395B] succeeds to the kingdom.] Abbot Alexander relinquished the abbacy; Adam, formerly prior of Ourscamp, succeeded him.

1141. England is ravaged by famine and the sword, while the princes of the land quarrel among themselves (cf. Gembloux).

[1143. (Bell.) Celestine presides as the 169th bishop of the Roman church.]

[1144. (Ibid.) Lucius succeeds him as the 170th.] A most violent wind overthrows many trees, towers, and houses. (Gembloux.) The city of Rouen was restored to Geoffrey, count of Anjou.

[1145. (Bell.) Eugenius, the 171st after him.] (GEMBLOUX.) A great famine grows severe in France.

[Col. 0395C] 1146. In England a boy, William, was crucified by Jews on Good Friday in the city of Norwich.  
[Note: [Col. 0395D] Norwich.]

[1147. (Bell.) There was an eclipse of the sun on 28 October, at the third hour, on Sunday.] King Louis undertakes the journey to Jerusalem with the French (cf. Gembloux).

1148. (Ibid.) A council at Rheims under Pope Eugenius.

1151. A continual and prolonged inundation of rain delayed and hindered the harvest.

1152. H., count of Anjou and duke of Normandy, later king of England, marries the former wife of King Louis; hence war arises between them.

[1153. (Bell.) Anastasius presides as the 172nd bishop of the Roman church.] The death of St Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux.

[Col. 0395D] [1154. Stephen, king of the English, dies. Adrian (ibid.), an Englishman, presides as the 173rd bishop of the Roman church. Lord Adam, second abbot of this monastery, died.] Stephen, prior of Ourscamp, succeeded him as third abbot.

[1155. Henry, nephew through a daughter of the elder Henry, succeeds to the kingdom.]

1156. The sign of the cross appeared in the moon. Alberic, a knight of Beauvais, suffered martyrdom for the Christian faith.

[Col. 0396A] 1157. Three were then seen, and in the middle was the sign of the cross.

1158. The daughter of Louis, king of the Franks, is given to the son of Henry, king of the English, and peace between them is confirmed.

1159. King Henry besieged Toulouse.  
[Note: [Col. 0395] Thus written by an uncertain hand after other material had been erased.] On the Nones of September three suns were seen in the western sky; but when two gradually disappeared, the day’s sun, which was in the middle, remained until sunset. Stephen died; Geoffrey of Étrépagny.  
[Note: [Col. 0395] “Stephen died; Geoffrey of Étrépagny” appears to have been written in 1163 by an uncertain hand and subsequently moved to this year.]  
[Note: [Col. 0396D] Étrépagny, in the county of Vermandois.]

1163. The third abbot of this place was recalled to govern the abbey of Ourscamp. Geoffrey succeeded him as fourth abbot.  
[Note: [Col. 0395] After other material had been erased.]

1165. Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, died. Rotrou, bishop of Évreux, succeeded him.  
[Note: [Col. 0395] From this point onward the hands vary continually.]

1166. From the arrival of the English in Great Britain, 813 years; from their baptism, 634; from the coming of the Normans, 100.

1169. King Henry caused his elder son Henry, son-in-law of Louis, king of the Franks, to be consecrated king by Roger, archbishop of York.

1171. At Canterbury, St Thomas, archbishop of that city, was martyred by four knights and passed to Christ.

1174. The city of Rouen was besieged by Louis, king of the Franks, the young King Henry, and the count of Flanders; all returned in confusion. Lord Geoffrey, fourth abbot of this place, died on the Kalends of September.  
[Note: [Col. 0395] By another hand.] Lord Richard, first abbot from Valssery, succeeded him as fifth.

[Col. 0396C] 1179. Lord Richard, the fifth abbot, departed from this house on 25 July. His successor came in the following year.

1180. On 3 August, the sixth abbot, Lord William, second from Valssery, came. Louis, king of the Franks, died. His son Philip, whom in the preceding year he had caused to be consecrated at Rheims on the Kalends of November, succeeded to the kingdom.

1181. Alexander, the 174th pope, died.

1182. Lucius, the 175th, succeeded him.

1183. Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen, died. Walter of Coutances succeeded him. Henry, the young king of the English, died.

1184. Ermelina, wife of Geoffrey of Étrépagny, died.

[Col. 0396D] 1186. Urban, the 176th pope. Geoffrey, count of Brittany, third son of King Henry, died.

1187. Jerusalem was captured by the Saracens, enemies of the Christian faith.

1189.  
[Note: [Col. 0395] Before “died,” another hand later added “2 Nones of July.”] Henry, king of the English, died on 3 Nones of September. Richard was crowned king of the English.

1190. Philip, king of the Franks, and Richard, king of the English, [Col. 0397A] undertake the journey to Jerusalem with an innumerable multitude of their people.

1191. The island of Cyprus was captured by King Richard, and afterwards Acre by the two kings. King Philip returned.

1192. King Philip enters Normandy and subjugates it to himself. King Richard, returning from Jerusalem, was captured and imprisoned by the duke of Austria, and afterwards handed over to Emperor Henry.

1194. King Richard returned to England after giving, or promising under hostages, more than two hundred thousand marks to the emperor and the other barons of the land for his liberation. Let no future reader be disturbed that nothing, or little, has here been written concerning the Roman emperors: while one contends against another to obtain the imperial sceptre, nothing worthy of memory is done, since everything is in confusion. After Pope Urban, three popes followed—Gregory, Clement, and Celestine—whose times are not described here.

1198. Pope Innocent.

1199. Richard, a most powerful king, perished after being struck by an arrow; his brother John succeeded him.

1200. On 9 February Lord William, abbot, died.

1203. The city of Rouen, together with all Normandy, was subjugated to Philip, king of France. King John withdrew into England, fearing that his barons would hand him over to the king of France.

[Col. 0397C] 1204. A most severe winter occurred, lasting three months and more. As a result, extreme mortality among animals, especially sheep and even wild birds, was caused by the severity of the cold, and famine followed. The city of Constantinople was captured by the count of Flanders, together with bishops, counts, noblemen, and most valiant men of France allied with him. Chosen emperor by common election there, he ruled nobly; after subjugating a great part of Greece, he was shortly afterwards killed by the Greeks. His brother was substituted for him upon the throne of the kingdom.

1207. Walter, archbishop of Rouen, died on 16 November. Master Robert, surnamed Pullen, succeeded him. [He lies at Mortemer.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] Added by a fifteenth-century hand.]

1209. Master Stephen of Langton, consecrated at Rome as archbishop to the title of the church of Canterbury, was opposed by King John, who wished to enthrone another; he banished the monks of Canterbury and the bishops of England. Because of this, once a sentence of excommunication had been pronounced against king and kingdom, the authority of the lord pope forbade even the Cistercian Order, together with the rest, solemnly to render the praises owed to God.

1210. Otto, nephew of Richard, formerly king of England, became emperor. At this time there was a certain false prophet [Col. 0398A] who said that Antichrist was already grown up and that the Day of Judgment was near.

1211. Count Simon de Montfort, with noble men from France and other kingdoms bringing him aid, attacked the heretics who were spreading in the province of Narbonne and were called Albigensians; making a great slaughter, he subjected a large part of their province to his power.

1212. In Spain the Christians fight the pagans; having gained victory, they kill many Saracens and compel the rest to flee. Count Reginald of Boulogne is stripped of all his land by Philip, king of France, and expelled from the kingdom, but received by Otto and John, king of England.
