King Philip of France, having assembled an army and a great fleet, plans to cross into England and seize it by arms; but meanwhile, when he suddenly enters Flanders and intends to subjugate it, the English arrive and violently carry off the king’s naval equipment [Col. 0398B], depriving him of the means of crossing.

1213. In Provence, near the castle called Muret, a battle worthy of eternal remembrance was fought. When Count Simon de Montfort, after making many slaughters of heretics, had subjected several cities and towns of Provence, the king of Aragon, the count of Toulouse, the count of Comminges [Note: [Col. 0397D] Comminges.], and the count of Foix [Note: [Col. 0398D] Foix.], having assembled a large army, besieged the aforesaid castle and began to attack it with siege-engines. The matter became known to Count Simon, who at once assembled very few men and boldly met the king of Aragon [Col. 0398C]. After the battle-lines had been drawn up, battle was joined on 12 September. The king of Aragon and many of his army fell; the rest escaped in flight and returned shamefully to their homes. Of Count Simon’s companions only one knight, with a few retainers, fell in that conflict. From the days of Judas Maccabaeus to the present time, we have never read anywhere of so great a multitude so marvellously conquered, cut down, and routed by so very few. At the same time, in the kingdom of France boys and girls, together with some youths and old people, carrying banners, candles, crosses, and censers, made processions and went singing through cities, villages, and castles, crying out in French: [Col. 0398D] “Lord God, exalt Christendom! Lord God, restore to us the True Cross!” They sang not only these words but many others, because the processions varied and each procession altered its chants as it pleased. This matter, unheard of in past ages, amazed many people and, as we believe, was a portent of the events that occurred in the following year. For the Roman legate entered the lands of Gaul and marked a vast multitude with the cross in the name of the Crucified; the number of this multitude is known to God alone. When Emperor Otto had been excommunicated by Pope Innocent, [Col. 0399A] the child of Apulia attempted to claim the Roman Empire for himself.

1214. Stephen, archbishop of Canterbury, and the other English bishops, monks, and clerics who had been held in exile for the church’s cause, were reconciled to the king through a cardinal; they were received by him into England and recovered their possessions. Thus the kingdom was absolved from the sentence of interdict and the king from the bond of excommunication. Tranquillity was restored to the churches with their bishops and to Christendom; country and possessions to the exiles; communion, with reconciliation, to the king; devotion to the people; and common joy to all Catholics at the restoration of peace to the church. Ferrand, count of Flanders, expelled from Flanders by Philip, king of France, sought out Otto, king of Germany, and John, king of England, and concluded an alliance [Col. 0399B] with them. Relying on their assistance, he returned to Flanders and powerfully wrested nearly all of it from the king of France, through the aid and exertions of distinguished men,  
[Note: [Col. 0399] Certain material deleted.] especially William, count of Salisbury, brother of the king of England, and Reginald, count of Boulogne. John, king of England, crossed by fleet into Aquitaine and, having reconciled many great men of the land to himself, restored a great part of the province to his own jurisdiction. Philip, king of France, therefore sent his son Louis against him, while he himself, having assembled an army, judged that he must meet the Flemings, whose strength had now grown too great. Accordingly, forces met on both sides within the borders of Flanders. After the battle-lines had been drawn up at the bridge of Bouvines, between Mortagne and Tournai, on 27 July, a Sunday [Col. 0399C], battle was joined. Some fell in the conflict, but at last the French won the palm of victory. In this Flemish battle, four counts—distinguished fighters—were captured from the field: the German “Cap-wearing Count” [Note: [Col. 0399D] That is, the *comes pileatus*, the Raugrave.], Ferrand of Flanders, William of Salisbury, Reginald of Boulogne, Otto’s seneschal, and about 150 other knights, both ordinary and distinguished. Afterwards King Philip moved his army against the king of England; but through the intervention of envoys, a five-year truce was confirmed between them. Thus King Philip returned to France and King John withdrew into England. During Advent, on 20 December, an earthquake occurred three times in one night. At the beginning of the day, on the Ides of January, a fiery globe larger than an ox and emitting a great light was seen in the air [Col. 0399D]. An eclipse of the moon occurred on 14 February.

1215. A general council is held at Rome by Pope Innocent. A grave dispute having arisen between the king of the English and the barons, England suffers beneath the sword and many calamities.

1216. Louis, son of Philip, king of the French, having allied himself with the magnates of England who were rebelling against their king, crossed into England with many ships and an armed army. Pope Innocent III died, and Honorius III succeeded him. John, king of the English, died. [Col. 0400A] He was succeeded by his son Henry, a boy of two years.

1217. A battle took place near the city of Lincoln between the king of England and the Northerners and many other powerful men, who were implacably hostile to that king. But God, having pity on the innocence of the boy king, granted him victory over his enemies before he was able to bear arms. Nor was this the only battle: a great naval engagement was also fought between the French and the English; and, divine power fighting on their side, the French youth, with all their naval equipment, were defeated by the English and carried off as spoil. There Eustace the Monk, an apostate, pirate, and most wicked robber, faithless to both kingdoms, was beheaded. At that time he was aiding the French, as was Robert [Col. 0400B] of Courtenay, commander of that fleet.

The very strong Egyptian city of Damietta was taken by the Christians, but soon recovered again by the Saracens. For the Saracens enclosed the Christian army together with its king and the other Christian nobles; and, no other way of escape being found, the Christians surrendered Damietta to the Saracens for their liberation. The Saracens in turn restored to the Christians, in exchange for recovering Damietta, the portion of the Holy Cross which they had held for nearly thirty-five years, together with all the Christian captives.

The boy of Apulia was raised to the imperial dignity by Pope Honorius. Louis, son of the king of France, after returning from England, again gathered an army and went to Toulouse, a most powerful city and at that time a refuge of the Albigensians [Col. 0400C] [Note: [Col. 0399] “Abigensians,” C.]; but accomplishing nothing there, Louis returned to the paternal territories of France.

1221 [Note: [Col. 0399] The year is uncertain.]. Stephen of Langton, archbishop of Canterbury, is restored to his own see and received peacefully by the boy King Henry.

1221. Robert Polain, archbishop of Rouen, died. He was succeeded by Theobald of Amiens, treasurer of the church of Rouen [and this Robert dedicated our church and was buried in our choir [Note: [Col. 0399] added by a fifteenth-century hand.]].

1222 [Note: [Col. 0399] “Abigensians,” C.]. The body of St Thomas of Canterbury is raised from the earth. St William, archbishop of Bourges, a monk of the Cistercian order, is canonized at Rome, in the fiftieth year after his martyrdom.

1223. Philip, most unconquered king of the French, who [Col. 0400D] had subjected to himself no small part of Aquitaine, Normandy, Flanders, and the greater part of Poitou, was removed from this life and died on 14 July. He never loved any traitor; rather, from all who came over to him he took castles and towns, and he utterly expelled them from his kingdom without hope of return. Having died at Mantes, he was buried at Saint-Denis, in the presence of twenty-two bishops, two cardinals, and the king of Jerusalem. His son Louis succeeded to the kingdom.

Before the death of King Philip, in the preceding year, a star was seen [Col. 0401A] near sunset in December, of very great size, burning like a torch, casting its rays upward and drawing them to a sharp point as into a cone. It seemed near the earth and was said to portend some prodigy. They called it a comet. Louis, son of King Philip, was anointed and crowned king at the city of Reims on 6 August.

1225 [Note: [Col. 0401] The year-number has been erased; perhaps it was 1224.]. Vitalis, abbot of Mortemer, died on 5 July. Osmund, prior of the same house, succeeded him.

1226 [Note: [Col. 0402] The number has been erased.]. Louis, king of the French, died on 7 November. His son Louis succeeded him. Osmund, abbot of Mortemer, died on 29 September. Lord Richard of Coutances succeeded him.

1227. Pope Honorius died; Gregory succeeded him.

[Col. 0402A] 1229. Theobald of Amiens, archbishop of Rouen, of pious memory, died on 25 September.

1231. He was succeeded by the venerable Maurice, afterwards archbishop of Rouen.

1234. On 12 January Maurice, archbishop of Rouen, of pious memory, died at Salicosa. The lord pope had transferred him from the see of Le Mans and appointed him to the church of Rouen. Burning with zeal and living for heaven, he spared no person on earth—not king, not prince, not tyrant, not rich man. He vehemently abhorred fornicating priests, cast them out of churches, and sent them to the Apostolic See to be absolved. Teachers of honourable life and good reputation he venerated and enriched with great benefactions. [Note: [Col. 0402] Some material at the foot of the page, perhaps illustrating the history of the year 1235, has been erased.]

## Supplement of Ursicampum

[Col. 0401]

Between 1155 and 1200, a monk of Ursicampum (Orcamp, diocese of Noyon) copied Sigebert from D1, together with all Sigebert’s additions and those of the Beauvais compiler. He himself added large patchworks copied word for word from Geoffrey of Monmouth, as well as certain other materials—those given here. He constructed a new continuation in the following fashion: copying the Premonstratensian continuation from B1, he interpolated it extensively from Anselm down to the year 1128; thereafter he presented it in its pure form, inserting throughout only those things of his own which we print here.

Nicholas of Amiens, Robert of Auxerre, and, through Robert, Gerard of Frachet and William of Nangis used it; so did Vincent of Beauvais. William le Petit edited it, and after him Schard, Pistorius, Struve, and Bouquet. Since the Ursicampum manuscript itself has perished, we give from its copy D1** only what the Ursicampum compiler added to his sources D1 and B1. It would have been useless to reprint the continuation in full, both because it is merely a compilation and because it has already appeared in print six times.

[Col. 0401C] (GEOFFREY.) Preface. “It recounts the ancient history of the Britons” — “they held the yoke.”

382. The city which Antoninus Pius founded with his son Aurelius, and called Sommonobria after the adjacent river, the emperor Gratian, having brought it under his authority, ordered to be called Amiens, from the circuit of its rivers, after its name had been changed. At that time the distinguished Faustinianus administered the Gallic prefecture. He fathered a son whom, out of love and remembrance of the blessed martyr Firmin, he named Firmin; in a later age Firmin became bishop of Amiens.

383. (Ibid.) “This Maximus” — “to exercise.”

386. (Ibid.) “A part of Gaul” — “is called.”

389. (Ibid.) “Of the Picts” — “Ireland.”

390. (Ibid.) “Another history” — “they should kill him.”

[Col. 0401D] 413. (Ibid.) “But after entering into” — “Uther Pendragon.”

414. (Ibid.) “It should be noted” — “they were striving.”

423. (BEDE, *Ecclesiastical History*.) “I think” — “sent by Honorius.”

424. (GEOFFREY.) “Constantine” — “emptied.”

431. (Ibid.) “After the killing” — “they obtained.”

434. (Ibid.) “In Britain” — “straps.”

436. (Ibid.) “The king of the Britons” — “his homeland.”

437. (Ibid.) “The son of Vortigern” — “Vortigern.”

439. (Ibid.) “King Vortigern” — “they obtained.”

445. (Ibid.) “King Vortigern” — “of this sort.”

446. (Ibid.) “At this point they place” — “may have been restored.”

[Col. 0402C] 147. (GREGORY OF TOURS, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*.) The names of the Seven Sleepers, which they received at baptism, are these: Malchus, Maximianus, Martinianus, Dionysius, John, Serapion, and Constantine. (GEOFFREY.) “Ambrosius” — “builds.”

457. (Ibid.) The tyrant Maximus is torn limb from limb by the people.

457. (Ibid.) “Over the island” — “named Anna.”

466. (Ibid.) “Uther Pendragon” — “to live.”

470. (Ibid.) “For if faith” — “having been overthrown.”

472. (Ibid.) “King Arthur” — “restored.”

(GREGORY OF TOURS, *Miracles of St Martin*.) “In these days St Perpetuus” — “and never appeared afterwards.”

473. (GEOFFREY.) “Arthur” — “they made.”

482. (Ibid.) “Arthur” — “to have returned.”

[Col. 0402D] 488. At this time the crypt of St Michael the Archangel was discovered on Mount Gargano; accordingly his memorial is celebrated each year with a solemn festival in the churches of God.

491. (GEOFFREY.) “At this point a certain man” — “is said.”

514. (Clovis — “dies”) and is buried at Paris in the basilica of the apostle St Peter, which he and Queen Clotild had built.

535. Moreover, St Medard transferred the episcopal see, formerly at Vermand, to Noyon because of the destruction of that place. After the death of St Eleutherius, bishop of Tournai, he also undertook the government of [Col. 0403A] the church of Tournai; after him his successors did likewise for many years, down to the time of Pope Eugenius III and finally Bishop Simon, who died in the year of the Lord 1148.

542. (Mixed History.) When a great mortality arose at Constantinople, the feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary was established. In Greek it is called Ὑπαντή (*Hypantē*), that is, “Meeting,” because on that day Symeon met the Lord when he was presented in the Temple; and so that mortality ceased. (GEOFFREY.) “Up to this time” — “may be compared with histories.”

549. (Ibid.) “But concerning this king” — “Vortiporius.”

556. St Medard of Noyon and Tournai died. At his passing heaven was opened, and divine lights shone before him for the space of two [Col. 0403B] hours. King Lothair caused his body to be transferred to the city of Soissons, promising that he would build a most fitting basilica over him and establish there a community of religious men. He indeed began the work, but his son Sigebert completed it.

561. (Ibid.) “Over the Britons” — “for many years.”

571. St Amand is born.

596. (PAUL THE DEACON.) “In these days the invading Lombards on Mount Cassino” — “carrying wine with them.”

604. (GEOFFREY.) “Through Augustine” — “the church.”

611. (Ibid.) “After Catheric” — “was done.”

616. (Ibid.) “The history further relates” — “he was compelled.”

[Col. 0403C] 632. (Ibid.) “Adunallo, king of the Britons” — “in the land.”

635. (Ibid.) “Here Bede says” — “built.”

675. (Ibid.) “By Cadwallon” — “they migrated.”

689. (Ibid.) “Cadwaladr” — “they were able.”

792. (Genealogy of Flanders.) At this time Lideric of Harlebeke, father of Ingerrand, ruled in Flanders. Ingerrand begot Andracus, father of Baldwin Iron-Arm, who married Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald.

843. (HUGH OF FLEURY.) “In these times Theodulf flourished” — “and, pitying him, ordered him to be released.” [Note: [Col. 0403] Under the year 854, the first edition and those which reproduced it contain the following: “854. It is said that this John was a woman, known only to one intimate companion, who embraced her; she became pregnant and gave birth while pope. Therefore some do not count her among the pontiffs, and for that reason she does not supply a number to the name.” But manuscript D1**, re-examined at this place at our request through M. Toussaint, librarian of Dijon, provides not even the slightest trace of those words; hence it appears that they were not in D1* either. They must therefore derive either from the Votic manuscript E8h or from the first editor; there is no third possibility. Yet the monk of Vaux, throughout Sigebert’s work, added absolutely nothing of his own; and in the continuation he added only a very few things, concerning solely his own monastery. Who could believe that a scribe otherwise most restrained in interpolating granted himself this one liberty? Thus no one remains except the first editor, whether he was Anthony Rufus or Henry Estienne. Whether he composed these words himself, or perhaps admitted into the text a marginal note added to manuscript E8h by another hand, we leave undecided.]

964. (Life of St Quentin [Note: [Col. 0403D] Compare *Gallia Christiana*, IX, 1080.].) At this time the church of St Quentin the martyr, situated on an island above the river Somme, became a monastery of a small number of monks. As time passed, however, the number of brethren increased and the income from its possessions grew, and it began also to be an abbey. In that place there still remain two wells. In one, the martyr’s head, and in [Col. 0404A] the other his body, had been found through angelic revelation by a venerable Roman matron named Eusebia. In reward for that service, through the same martyr she recovered the sight of her eyes, of which she had previously been deprived. This discovery took place in the fifty-fifth year after the martyr’s passion; he suffered martyrdom in the year of the Lord 332.

But after the aforesaid devout woman found the holy martyr’s body and placed it in the upper part of the eminent town which in antiquity was called Augusta of the Viromandui, after the lapse of many years no one knew where the martyr’s tomb was situated. Finally, while St Eligius was bishop of the church of Noyon, an inquiry having been made for the martyr’s body, a coffin was found in the bishop’s presence, buried deep [Col. 0404B] in the earth, in which that precious treasure was preserved. This second discovery took place under St Eligius in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 657, not without a great miracle of divine power. For when the blessed bishop, by night, with many lamps lit, found the sought coffin and pierced it with the digging tool he held in his hand, so great a fragrance of sweetest odour and such brightness of heavenly light suddenly streamed forth all around that those present were filled with marvellous scent, while those absent supposed that daylight had dawned.

1039. In Apulia there was a marble statue with a bronze circle around its head, on which was written: “At the rising of the sun on the Kalends of May, I shall have a golden head” [Col. 0404C] (cf. WILLIAM OF MALMESBURY, II.10). A certain Saracen, captured by Robert Guiscard, duke of the Normans, understood what this portended. At sunrise on the Kalends of May, having carefully marked the endpoint of the statue’s shadow, he found an immense treasure after digging up the ground there, and offered it to the duke for his own ransom.

1051. Lanfranc also, a man distinguished for holiness and learning, prior of the monastery of Bec and later, after being abbot of Caen, archbishop of Canterbury, disputed in dialogue against the error of Berengar.

1067. At this time Lanfranc, prior of the monastery of Bec, was eminent. To his exceptional teaching [Col. 0404D] Anselm came hastening from Burgundy—a man afterwards endowed with great virtue and wisdom—and succeeded him as prior under the distinguished man Herluin, the first abbot, [Col. 0405A] who founded the monastery of Bec from his own resources.

1080. Lanfranc, distinguished in learning and probity, flourishes in England, having been appointed archbishop of Canterbury after being abbot of Caen. At that time Anselm, eminent abbot of the monastery of Bec, flourished in Normandy and was very renowned for his holiness and wisdom. (Life of St Arnulf.) “At this same time in the monastery of St Medard” — “was consecrated bishop.”

1081. (Ibid.) “In the time of King Dagobert, the holy bishop Ursmar” — “a heavenly remedy was bestowed.”

1087. (Ibid.) “St Arnulf” — “had foretold, received.”

1094. While Helinand was bishop in the city of Laon, [Col. 0405B] a certain woman living nearby had a son-in-law handsome in youthful appearance. Out of love for her daughter she attended to him with great care; consequently a shameful suspicion concerning the woman and her son-in-law arose among the neighbouring people and greatly troubled her (cf. Laon). Unable to bear her reputation being defiled by such disgrace, she turned the cause of the injury against him and secretly arranged for him to be killed by two boys. Afterwards, moved to repentance for the homicide, she revealed her sin in confession to a priest. But after some time had passed, the priest quarrelled with her and reproached her to her face with the evil she had confessed. Hearing this, the relatives of the murdered man hurried to inform the viscount of Laon. [Col. 0405C] At the viscount’s command the woman was summoned and came; she did not conceal how she had killed the man. It was therefore judged that she ought to be burned. But first she was led to the church of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, where she recounted her sin in order before God and men, and thus faithfully commended herself to the merits and prayers of the most holy Virgin Mary.

Then, cast into the fire, she felt the burning not at all; rather, when the fire had been consumed, she remained unharmed through divine protecting grace. But the relatives of the slain man, attributing this occurrence not to divine power but to the weak material of the wood, kindled a fire around her again with stronger timber, yet achieved nothing. For when the miracle was repeated, God preserved her safe from the fire’s burning, to the praise of His [Col. 0405D] name and to the glory and honour of His Mother. Thus, emerging from the blaze unhurt not only in body but also in clothing and skin [Note: [Col. 0405D] “Skin” (*cute*) seems to be the required reading. Pertz.], she was led to the church of the Holy Mother of God amid the applause of all the people. After thanks had been rendered to God, she passed from this world a few days later, God so willing.

1095. (Ibid.) Helinand, bishop of Laon, of good memory, dies; Ingelrannus succeeds Helinand.

1097. When Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, died, [Col. 0406A] Anselm, abbot of Bec, already most renowned not only in Normandy but also in England for his holiness and learning, succeeded him in the episcopate. Although he had been received honourably by King William, the princes of the land, and an assembly of the whole church, he nevertheless later suffered many troubles and tribulations under that king in seeking to reform the condition of the church. For the kings of England had long maintained this unjust law: that they themselves should invest bishops elected to churches with the pastoral staff.

1099. Ansellus of Ribemont was a most prudent man, very useful to the army, and so devoted to the blessed martyr Quentin that every year, on the martyr’s feast-day, he had the solemnity celebrated before him by clergy gathered from every quarter, [Col. 0406B] and after the office was completed prepared for them an abundant table of refreshment.

1105. On the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord there was a great earthquake at Jerusalem. Two orbs, like the sun in appearance and light, shining with the likeness of every colour like the heavenly rainbow, appeared.

1112. Before these events, moreover, the same church of the Holy Mother of God at Laon had been violated by the treachery and murder of a most noble knight named Gerard, lord of the castle called Carisiacus. While he was at prayer before the holy image of Christ, men of the bishop, having formed a conspiracy, killed him. (GUIBERT, *On His Own Life*, III.11.) In those days there had been born in the same place a twin child [Col. 0406C] joined above the buttocks, having, that is, two heads and two bodies down to the loins, each with its arms. He was baptized and lived for three days.

1113. Bernard, an outstanding young man, illustrious in learning, conduct, and birth, and afterwards to be an example of great virtue, native of the Burgundian castle of Châtillon [Note: [Col. 0405D] Châtillon.], assumed the habit of religion at Cîteaux with his full brothers and many other companions, and lived there with wonderful religious fervour.

1114. This is Cono, one of those religious men who first led the eremitical life at Tronc-Bérenger [Note: [Col. 0405D] Or Arrouaise, now Aruaise, in Artois, where that order was founded by Heldemar, Cono, and Roger. See *Acta Sanctorum* for 13 January. Struve.], and who became founders of the Arrouaisian order, an order which flourishes and grows to this day.

[Col. 0406D] 1128. In this year many people of the district of Soissons, afflicted with the holy fire, assembled at the church of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, in the city of Soissons. There, waiting for a few days for the mercy of God and the aid of the Blessed Virgin, they obtained health through her merits and prayers, as the booklet of these miracles relates more fully. Thus, within fifteen days, one hundred and three persons named individually were quenched of this fire, and three crippled girls were restored to health. [Col. 0407A] Thereafter many other miracles took place there, among which two were more notable: one, the divinely restored nose and lip of a woman; another, concerning a boy who in a vision was caught up before God. He declared that he had seen our Lady the Virgin Mary pleading for the people’s salvation and that she had graciously received this answer from her Son: “Mother, you are the star of the sea; let it be as you wish.”

But while the Blessed Virgin complained concerning her house, which was poor and lowly, she heard again from her Son that money should be brought from beyond the sea and beyond the Rhine, from which a house might be built and appear splendid in the eyes of all who saw it. There are today as many witnesses to this vision, both in the magnificence of the work and in the abundance of the offerings, as there are persons willing to see them. The same boy also foretold shortly afterward that he would die; he survived scarcely one month. What was also especially astonishing about this boy was that he would recite all ancient history in verse, while he recounted the text of the Gospel and the deeds of the Lord as though he were reading in a book and repeating compositions dictated by others. When saying these things with closed eyes, he scarcely deigned to speak with laymen and illiterate persons, as though weary of their ignorance, he who heard such profound things within.

1129. (Continuation of Mortemer.) The monastery of Ursicampum was founded by the most noble bishop of Noyon, Lord Simon, son of Hugh the Great, brother of Count Ralph, and cousin of King Louis. A community of monks was brought from Clairvaux, and Lord Waleran was appointed its first abbot. He was the first of the more noble persons to make Clairvaux illustrious by his manner of life.

1131. Bishops of churches and secular princes most readily consented—or even voluntarily offered—lands, meadows, woods, and other things necessary for building monasteries. The church of St Mary in the bishop’s precinct and nearly the whole city of Noyon were consumed by fire, by a misfortune said to have been just, because many of them had dishonoured Pope Innocent with mocking words. Clairvaux produced two monasteries in one day, namely Longpont and Rievaulx, and a few months later Vaucelles.

1132. The holy man Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, died. Guigo, prior of the Charterhouse, wrote an account of his most religious life.

[Col. 0407D] 1135. The monastery of the Meadow (*de Prato*) was founded under its first abbot Peter: the first offshoot which Father Waleran produced from his own house.

1138. (Ibid.) At this time Alexander, of venerable life, the first abbot of Mortemer, gave himself and his house to the abbot of Ursicampum.

1140. The monastery of St Mary of Froidmont [Note: [Col. 0407D] “Cold Mountain,” diocese of Beauvais.] was founded by Waleran, first abbot of Ursicampum, of pious memory, under its chosen father Manasses.

1141. A dispute having arisen between the Roman pope and [Col. 0408A] Louis, king of the French, the Gallican church was disturbed. For when Alberic, archbishop of Bourges, died, Peter was sent, consecrated by Pope Innocent as pastor of that church. But King Louis rejected him because he had been ordained without the king’s consent, and he was by no means received into the city. Since Count Theobald appeared to support Peter’s side out of reverence for or in accordance with the pope’s will, the hostility which was thought to have been quieted began to break out again between the king and Theobald.

1142. Father Waleran, abbot of Ursicampum, died, founder of two abbeys [Note: [Col. 0407D] De Prato (“of the Meadow”) and Froidmont.], apart from the third [Note: [Col. 0408D] Mortemer.], which he adopted as his daughter.

1146. (Ibid.) At Norwich, a city of England, Jews crucified a certain Christian boy named [Col. 0408B] William. They buried him outside the city, and divine light, as they say, shining over him made this known. Thus he was found by the faithful and honourably placed in a church.

1148. Malachy, of holy memory, bishop of the Irish and legate of the Apostolic See, by God’s will came to the end of his life at Clairvaux. There he received the place of burial which he himself had chosen and foretold. He was succeeded by Christian, abbot of Mellifont, a man endowed with the greatest holiness. Christian had been archdeacon of that same holy man, and was the first abbot of the Cistercian order sent into Ireland by Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, of sacred memory.

1151. Perhaps the following event, which occurred that same year in the district of Soissons, signified this passing away of excellent men. When winter frost had hardened the ground severely, a turf of very great length and breadth was suddenly torn from the earth and carried far away to another place.

1154. Robert of Botua, a man full of every wickedness, entered his nephews’ castles and deceitfully exercised tyranny in the land (cf. Continuation of Prémontré). Inflamed also by a spirit of jealous rage, he ordered one of his quite faithful men, together with another man and a woman, to be shut in a small house to be burned. Yet, like the three youths of old, while the house burned and a flame fluttered above their heads like a bright cloud, they remained unharmed. [Col. 0408D] When the wicked servant to whom his master had entrusted this crime pursued them as they came out and, drawing his sword, wished to strike one of them, an invisible person suddenly seized him from behind by the hair of his head and hurled him headlong to earth with the horse on which he sat. He thereupon immediately vowed to go to St James. Those whom their own innocence had preserved likewise did not receive God’s grace in vain, but changed their lives for the better.

## Supplement of Nicholas of Amiens

[Col. 0409]

Around the year 1203 Nicholas of Amiens wrote, in eight books, a brief chronicle from the Creation of the World to 1203, compiled wholly word for word from Eusebius, Jerome, Sigebert, and Sigebert’s continuators of Ursicampum and Anchin. To these he added scattered material drawn from elsewhere, only that which we give here, from the royal Paris manuscript among the Latin Supplements, no. 783, an eighteenth-century copy of the manuscript once Pithou’s and then Christina’s, now Vatican manuscript 444, parchment, fourteenth century. From the same royal manuscript Dom Brial has already published excerpts for the years 1113–1204, XIV.21 and XVIII.701.

[Col. 0409A] 424. When he had often been rebuffed by a certain monk concerning what he was asking for, and was excommunicated by him, and the monk had fled, he said that he would not take food until he had been absolved by him. Although the bishop of that place declared him absolved, especially since not everyone has the power to excommunicate, the emperor nevertheless did not yield until he had been absolved by the one who had excommunicated him.

535. Having been accused by his people because, after celebrating Mass at dawn, he immediately took food—though illness drove him to do so—he was on his way to Rome and was thirsty in the desert through which he passed. He commanded wild hinds to stand still, and they stood until he had drunk their milk [Col. 0409B] and been refreshed. Then the poor man of Christ, having nothing with which to honour the pope, gave Vigilius birds suitable for food which he had seen flying, as he went on foot to Vigilius’s presence. Vigilius, recognizing the holy man’s sanctity, [lacuna].

633. After this man’s election, Roman soldiers invaded the Lateran church, carrying off all its gold and silver vessels. They divided one part among themselves and sent another part to the treasury. Mauritius the *cartularius*, and Isaac, patrician and exarch of all Italy, through whose agency these things were done, did not long enjoy impunity: Mauritius was afterward beheaded by Isaac, and Isaac was struck by God.

636. In this man’s time Pyrrhus, deposed from the see of Constantinople for heresy, came from Africa to Rome. Begging Pope Theodore for forgiveness of his error, he obtained it; but before leaving the city, he returned to his vomit and was excommunicated. Likewise Paul, heretical patriarch of the same see, was warned by envoys of Blessed Theodore to repent; when he did not comply, he was deposed.

648. He excommunicated Paul of Constantinople, who had taught the emperor Constantine to believe that there was no operation or will in Christ, in a council of one hundred and fifty bishops. Olympius was sent to govern Italy and promulgate that heresy there. When he accomplished nothing, he plotted the death of Pope Martin. [Col. 0409D] As Martin received communion in the church of St Mary at the Crib, Olympius waited for his sword-bearer, as they had arranged, to stab him; but God blinded the sword-bearer, who asked forgiveness for the treachery. Olympius too repented, returned to the faith, and confessed his fault. Afterwards others were sent by [Col. 0410A] the emperor to perpetrate the same crime; they carried Martin away to Cherson, where he later died. His body was eventually brought back to Rome and buried in the church of St Silvester.

679. In this man’s time the church of Ravenna, which had long separated itself from Rome, returned to it.

684. Under him the emperor granted that a Roman pope should be consecrated immediately after election, without seeking anyone’s consent.

786. When he once came to Constantinople, he was honourably received by Justinian and renewed the privileges of the imperial city. After he returned to Rome, Justinian was murdered by the heretic Philippicus, who seized the empire. Because of his heresy, he was not acknowledged as emperor at Rome; nor could Peter, whom he had sent to Ravenna to be duke of Italy and the Romans, be received by the Romans.

902. In these times Gormund, king of Africa and follower of the sect of Muhammad, gathered forces and crossed the sea to invade the kingdom of the English. Hysembert, who was plotting treason against his uncle Louis, fled to him and promised that with his assistance he would obtain France. Led by this vain hope, Gormund landed at Ponthieu with many ships full of warriors and ravaged the coast. While his army ranged outside the walls of Amiens and the citizens were weary from war, the matrons, indignantly bearing this, went out of the city with arms and compelled the enemies to flee to their camp. For this they earned the privilege that women should sit on the right in church. The king of the French subsequently defeated [Col. 0410C] those Saracens at Amiens, killing King Gormund and the traitor Hysembert with the sword.

1147. Nicholas of Amiens, who compiled this series of chronicles, is born.

1152. Theodoric, bishop of Amiens, had his cathedral church consecrated in honour of Blessed Mary and Blessed Firmin the martyr by Samson, archbishop of Reims, after summoning the neighbouring bishops.

1153. At Cansioles in the territory of Noyon, monks entered a little church and found a chalice carelessly placed in a small window, together with a cloth red with blood inside it. When the priest confessed his fault, they learned that, through negligence, he had customarily wiped the chalice with that cloth after consuming the sacrament.

1187. Gregory presides over the Roman church as its 171st pope. At once he sent legates through various regions to invite peoples to aid the Eastern church. Going to Ferrara and hastening to Rome, he came to Lucca, where he found the tomb of Octavian broken open and cast the bones outside the church. On the following day he came to Pisa and marked great men with the cross. Immediately struck by illness, Gregory VIII—who had eight processions on the road, sat for eight weeks, and suffered illness for eight days—ended his life, awaiting the eighth resurrection.

1200. At the same time Innocent, armed with a singular zeal for justice, condemned Philip, called king of the Germans, and the kings of Aragon, Spain, and Hungary, for various offences, by excommunication or interdict.

1202. When William of Reims was replaced, not by a successor in death but against his will in life, the clergy of Reims contended at Rome for a long time over a successor.

[Col. 0411B] 1203. Innocent, after a dispute arose between himself and the Romans, withdrew into Campania. The church of the Bulgarians, returning to unity, submitted itself to the Roman church and adopted the Latin usages in the sacrament of the altar and certain other matters. Their duke also swore fealty to the Roman pontiff, who, through the hand of his legate Leo, anointed and crowned him king.

The Franks, conveyed in a great fleet of Venetian ships to aid the Eastern Church, by Venetian guile—for they had entered into agreements with the Venetians, confirmed by oath [Note: [Col. 0411] “they undertake,” copy]—ravage the maritime regions of the Slavs. Then, at the request of Alexius, heir to the empire, they attack Constantinople together with them. They restore Alexius and his father Isaac, who had been expelled [Col. 0412A], after driving out the tyrant who had seized the empire. The ungrateful father turns his son, by an assembly of Greeks, away from affection for the Franks. But the son, compelled by necessity, again cultivates their friendship. In this disturbance, a certain man seizes the imperial crown and is slaughtered by the Greeks on the day of his coronation. Morculphus, secretary of Alexius and his father, kills them both, with the assent of the Constantinopolitans; permitting them the destruction of the Franks, he becomes an ill-fated emperor. He engages the Franks in frequent battles and is defeated in every one. The Franks, emboldened by unexpected daring, with Venetian naval assistance assault the city, scale the walls, and, entering the city, cut down the Greeks; they seize the fortifications, while Morculphus takes secret flight; for more than . . . [Note: [Col. 0411] “Something seems to have fallen out, although the copy gives no indication of anything of the kind.”] they harass the neighbouring peoples with arms. Their terror asserts . . . . [Col. 0412B] [Note: [Col. 0411] “consecrated,” copy] Having obtained cities and towers and almost the whole empire, they elect as emperor, on the counsel of the Doge of Venice, Baldwin, the illustrious Count of Flanders. He causes Latin clerics to be ordained in the cathedral churches, compelling the Greeks to obey them, and through them the Roman Church. A certain Venetian, elected patriarch, is consecrated at Rome by the hand of Innocent [Note: [Col. 0411] “consecrated,” copy].

The king of the Franks takes Normandy and Poitou, avenging the wicked transgressions of the king of the English [Note: [Col. 0411] “wicked,” copy].

Innocent anoints the prince of the Aragonese as king.

## CHRONICLE OF ROBERT OF MONT-SAINT-MICHEL

[Col. 0411]

Edited by Dr Ludwig Conrad Bethmann

[Note.]

Above, col. 31, we discussed the life and writings of Robert of Torigni, abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel. In 1150 he copied Sigebert from the Beauvais manuscript D, together with all that manuscript’s additions. What he himself added concerns England and the Normans only. He drew all his English material from Henry of Huntingdon, and his Norman material from William of Jumièges; from the *History of Henry*, added by Robert himself to William’s book [Note: [Col. 0411C] “Our author himself calls it the *History of Henry*; it is usually cited as the eighth book of William of Jumièges.”]; from Orderic Vitalis, Fulcher of Chartres, Milo’s *Life of Lanfranc* [Note: [Col. 0411C] “Written about 1150; in the *Acta Sanctorum*, 28 May, in Mabillon’s *Acta SS. Benedictinorum*, VI.2, and in Lanfranc’s works edited by D’Achery.”] and William [Note: [Col. 0411C] “Edited by D’Achery after Lanfranc’s works. I can scarcely believe that Robert already possessed the *Life of Abbot Boso*.”]; Eadmer’s *Life of Anselm* [Note: [Col. 0411C] “Written shortly after 1122; in the *Acta Sanctorum*, 2 April.”]; the miracles of St Wulfram [Note: [Col. 0411C] “D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, II, 286.”]; the passion of Saints Maximus and Venerandus; and the *Origins of the Cistercians* [Note: [Col. 0411C] “He also used this booklet in the treatise [Col. 0412C] *On the Change of the Order of Monks*.”]. Finally, he compiled the entire catalogue of the archbishops of Rouen from the Annals of Rouen [Note: [Col. 0412C] “In Labbe’s *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, I, 364; but they were published incompletely, with ‘the common matters omitted.’ They are indeed carried from Christ to 1344, but it is clear that they were composed much earlier and then continued at various times. Thus the scribe seems to have laid down his pen in 1145, and another only about 1173 to have taken it up again: the notices read between these years betray their seam sufficiently by their extreme brevity. They existed before 1110. For from them were then excerpted the Annals of Fontenelle (in Brussels manuscripts 7815 and 7821, from Christ to 1110, with a very brief continuation for 1127–1204 [Col. 0413B], written in another hand) and the Annals of Caen (in Duchesne, *Scriptores rerum Normannicarum*, p. 1015; in these likewise nothing is read after 1110 until 1120). Orderic too appears to have used them, and perhaps also the Acts of the Archbishops of Rouen, written at Saint-Ouen in the time of Gregory VII, in Mabillon’s *Annales veteres*. These four, therefore, although they contain very much also found in Robert, owe nothing to him, nor Robert to them.”], from which he also took a few other items.

The chronicle which he appended to Sigebert is, in its first forty years, almost nothing but a compilation from Henry of Huntingdon, William of Jumièges, the *History of Henry*, Sigebert, Fulcher of Chartres, Orderic Vitalis, the *Life of Lanfranc*, and the letter of the crusaders [Col. 0413] [Note: [Col. 0414B] “The year 1124.”]; thereafter it proceeds on its own course. In chronology he did not always follow his sources accurately; nor did he sufficiently guard against errors in matters done in his own time—indeed, matters occurring while he was writing and almost in his presence [Note: [Col. 0414B] “Cf. 1114, 1117, 1123, 1126, 1140, 1146 ff., 1180, 1181, 1182.”]—often confusing in one year events that had occurred in different years. Yet Robert’s good faith and devotion to truth are not at all to be doubted; and it is greatly to be regretted that a man of such learning and in such a position allowed himself, after Sigebert’s example, to become an annalist rather than a historian.

We know of three continuations: the unpublished Harleian continuation for 1158–1168 in manuscript E3b; the Jumièges continuation for 1187–1210, written in large part before 1209, which the first edition printed from E8h and which Schard, Pistorius, Struve, and Bouquet XVIII, 338 subsequently reproduced; and the Vallemont continuation for 1169–1239, printed from manuscript E8b by Duchesne, *Scriptores Normannici*, 1003, and Bouquet XVIII, 345. Since these continuations contribute absolutely nothing to German affairs, we did not judge that they should be printed again [Note: [Col. 0414B] “The chronicle for 1187–1268 read in D1, and in an expanded form in B4**, is not a continuation of Robert, with whom it has nothing whatsoever in common. Its author lived at Limoges, about 1250.”].—We listed Robert’s manuscripts above at col. 49. Antonius Rufus first printed him in 1513 in the first edition of Sigebert, but not entire: only 1154–1186, with the Jumièges continuation, from manuscript E8h, and the first part, as we have seen, greatly abridged. That edition abounds in shameful errors, and moreover caused great confusion for centuries by prefixing the Ursicampine continuation to ours and calling the two one work by one and the same author, Robert of Mont-Saint-Michel. Schard, Pistorius, and Struve reproduced it.

Then, in 1619, Duchesne, in the *Writers of Norman Affairs*, printed under the title *Chronicle of Normandy* an abbreviated part of Robert’s chronicle for 1138–1169, with the Vallemont continuation, from manuscript E8b. In 1651 D’Achery was the first to print Robert’s entire work, after the works of Guibert of Nogent, from manuscript E. Although he did not reproduce it accurately everywhere, the merit will always remain his that learned men were first able through him both to know which work of Robert’s was genuine and to use it. Then, in 1786, Brial, XIII, 283, printed excerpts from Robert according to D’Achery’s edition, correcting it here and there from E2, 7b, 8d, and 9 and illustrating it with quite useful notes; in XVIII, 338 he gave the Jumièges continuation from the first edition, and the Vallemont continuation from 1210 onward from manuscript E8b.

Finally, we here present Robert’s *Chronicle*, accurately reproduced from the largely autograph manuscript E, as the author himself corrected it in 1184. We have noted every error of the pen, which are few; and wherever hand or pen changes, we have always indicated it. From the remaining manuscripts we have used E2, 3a, 4, 5, 7b, 8b, d, e, f, h, so as to give all their additions and note what is lacking in them, excepting 2, 5, and 8f, which altered the text so arbitrarily that they can scarcely be regarded as manuscripts of Robert. Moreover, it seemed pointless to add variant readings from the others where the author’s own manuscript removes every doubt, unless there were erasures in E or a variation could contribute something toward identifying Robert’s different recensions. We have always indicated these matters. Passages Robert copied from other sources have been represented by their opening and closing words placed in the margin, lest omission of them compromise the Chronicle’s integrity. But since almost all the additions he scattered through Sigebert were taken word for word from other works, it sufficed, with the sources indicated in the margin, to give only their first and last words; the rest, however, we have given in full.

[Col. 0413A]

**385.** (386.—Annals of Rouen.) Peter is appointed seventh archbishop of Rouen.

**405.** (Ibid.) Victricius is appointed eighth archbishop of Rouen; Pope Innocent sent him a decretal letter.

**409.** Saint Evodius is appointed ninth archbishop of Rouen.

**417.** (Ibid.) Innocent is appointed tenth archbishop of Rouen.

**426.** (Ibid.) Evodius is appointed eleventh archbishop of Rouen.

**430.** (434.—Ibid.) Silvester is appointed twelfth archbishop of Rouen.

**441.** (442.—Ibid.) Malsonus is appointed [Col. 0413B] thirteenth archbishop of Rouen.

**451.** (Ibid.) Germanus is appointed fourteenth archbishop of Rouen.

**459.** Crescentius is appointed fifteenth archbishop of Rouen.

**473.** (Ibid.) Saint Gildard, sixteenth archbishop of Rouen, flourished; likewise Saint Remigius [Col. 0414A], bishop of Reims, and Saint Laudo, bishop of Coutances, consecrated by Gildard.

**499.** (Ibid.) Flavius is appointed seventeenth archbishop of Rouen.

**534.** (Ibid.) Praetextatus is appointed eighteenth archbishop of Rouen.

**569.** Saint Wandregisel was born.

**582.** (584.—Annals of Rouen.) Praetextatus, archbishop of Rouen, is murdered. Melantius succeeds him as nineteenth archbishop, though unworthily, because, as is said, he shared in the killing [Note: [Col. 0413] “Added later in the margin.”].

**593.** (596.—Ibid.) Hildulf is appointed twentieth archbishop of Rouen.

**596.** The passing of Saint Ebrulf, abbot [Note: [Col. 0413] “Added later in the margin.”].

**623.** (Ibid.) Saint Romanus, of wondrous holiness, becomes [Col. 0414B] twenty-first archbishop of Rouen.

**635.** (635.—Ibid.) On the death of Saint Romanus, Saint Audoenus is ordained twenty-second archbishop of Rouen [Note: [Col. 0413] “Added later in the margin.”].

**652.** The foundations of the church of Saint Wandregisel are laid [Note: [Col. 0413] “Added later in the margin.”] [Note: [Col. 0414B] “The *Deeds of the Abbots of Fontenelle*, ch. 6, say this was done in 645.”].

**677.** (680.—Ibid.) Saint Audoenus passes to the Lord; [Col. 0415A] Saint Ansbert succeeds him as twenty-third archbishop of Rouen.

**695.** (Ibid.) On Saint Ansbert’s death, Grippo succeeds as twenty-fourth archbishop of Rouen.

**719.** (Ibid.) Ravilandus is appointed twenty-fifth archbishop of Rouen.

**722.** (Ibid.) Saint Hugh flourished as twenty-sixth archbishop of Rouen; he also presided over the churches of Paris and Bayeux, and the abbeys of Jumièges and Fontenelle [Note: [Col. 0415] “Added later in the margin.”].

**730.** (Ibid.) Upon the death of Saint Hugh, Ratbert succeeds as twenty-seventh archbishop of Rouen.

**741.** (739.—Ibid.) Ragenfrid is appointed twenty-eighth archbishop of Rouen.

**755.** (754.—Ibid.) Remigius, uterine brother of King Pippin, is appointed twenty-ninth archbishop [Col. 0415B] of Rouen.

**761.** (Orderic Vitalis; Henry of Huntingdon IV.) On the death of Æthelberht, king of the English, Ecgfrith reigned.

**772.** (Annals of Rouen.) Mainard is appointed thirtieth archbishop of Rouen.

**780.** (Ibid.) Willermus is appointed [Note: [Col. 0415D] “The Annals of Rouen, Orderic, and the Acts of the Archbishops of Rouen call him Guillebert.”] thirty-first archbishop of Rouen.

**794.** (Henry of Huntingdon IV.) On the death of King Ecgfrith, Egfrid Pren reigned three years and was captured and carried off by Cenwulf.

**798.** (Ibid.) Cudred, king of the English, held the royal dignity for nine years.

**802.** Remigius, archbishop of Rouen, died; Lord Hugh succeeded him, son of Charles Augustus, [Col. 0415C] emperor and king of Francia.

## ROBERT’S PROLOGUE TO WHAT FOLLOWS, ON THE DESCRIPTION OF TIMES, UP TO THE YEAR 1184

[Note: [Col. 0421] “‘Up to the year MCLXXXIV’: the word *year* was written in an erasure by another hand, the same hand that wrote the years 1182–1184 below and composed the page prefixed to the manuscript, namely Robert’s own.”]

[Col. 0421]

[Col. 0421B] Since we are to speak in what follows of chronography, that is, the description of times, we shall first answer briefly those envious detractors who consider our labour useless; then we shall succinctly disclose, in this present prologue, the order of events to kindly disposed readers who expect it—indeed, demand it. Those who say, “What need is there to commit to letters the lives, deaths, and various fortunes of human beings, or to perpetuate in writing prodigies of heaven and earth or of the other elements?” should know that the good life and conduct of those who went before are set forth for the imitation of those who follow; while examples of evil people are described not that we may imitate them, but that they may be avoided.

Past prodigies and portents, which, when they appear, signify famine, mortality, or other scourges of heavenly vengeance imposed according to the deserts of humankind, [Col. 0421C] are therefore entrusted to writing and memory: so that, if similar things should occur, sinners who recall that they have incurred God’s anger in some respect may hasten at once to the remedies of repentance and confession, by which they will placate God. For this reason—though there are others—the lawgiver Moses sets forth in sacred history Abel’s innocence, Cain’s envy, Jacob’s simplicity, Esau’s guile, the wickedness of the eleven sons of Israel, the goodness of the twelfth, namely Joseph, and the punishment of five cities by consuming fire and sulphur: so that we may imitate the good, shudder at being followers of the wicked, and, fleeing the portentous burning of sin, escape its stench.

This is done not only by Moses, but by all expositors of Holy Scripture, in historical as well as moral books: they commend virtues, detest vices, and admonish us at once to fear and to love God. Therefore those must not be heard who say that books of chronicles, especially those issued by Catholics, should be neglected; for in them, as in other treatises, there is generally found an intention so useful.

Cyprian, bishop and martyr of Carthage, Eusebius of Caesarea, Jerome the presbyter, Sulpicius Severus, companion of Saint Martin, Prosper of Aquitaine, notary of Pope Saint Leo, [Col. 0422B] Gregory, bishop of Tours, and, to come to more recent men, Marianus Scotus, monk of Fulda, and Sigebert of Gembloux, were not ignorant of this and all published chronicles not without usefulness. Many others, religious and secular alike, did the same; I pass them over for brevity’s sake. Having spoken these words against opponents, let us disclose our purpose to kindly readers.

Preferring Sigebert of Gembloux to all modern chronographers and greatly admiring his industry, I shall attempt to continue something of his chronography’s sequence of times. For he, having copied according to most trustworthy exemplars the chronicles of Eusebius, which begin with Ninus, first king of the Assyrians—in the forty-third year of whose reign Abraham was born—and extend to the twentieth year of the reign of the most devout ruler Constantine; and having also appended the chronicles of Jerome, namely from the twentieth year of that ruler to the thirteenth of the Emperor Valens; and adding in sequence the chronicle of Prosper, that is, from the first year of Gratian to the fifth year of the emperors Valentinian and Marcian; finally appended work of his own. Yet he did not choose to begin where Prosper ended, but where he began: at the end of Jerome’s chronicles, namely in the year 381 of the Lord’s incarnation. He did this because, being a modern writer and a diligent investigator of many histories, he intended to add much that Prosper had not yet heard when he wrote these things.

He places at the head of the page of his book first the names of various kingdoms: namely, of the Romans, Persians, Franks, Britons, Vandals, Visigoths, Ostrogoths, [Col. 0422D] and Huns. Beneath the kingdoms he places the proper names of their kings; lower down, through the middle of the page, the years of the individual rulers; in the margin, the names of the Roman pontiffs and the years of the Lord corresponding directly to the years of the aforesaid kings. In mentioning the kingdom of the Britons, however, for nearly one hundred and twelve years he names no king of that island except Aurelius Ambrosius. Likewise, concerning the English, who succeeded the Britons, he mentions some necessary matters in their places, [Col. 0423A] but speaks only of those kings whom Bede, priest and doctor of the English, names in his history, although there were more kings among that people after Bede’s death than before it. Of the dukes of Normandy he says nothing or little. He did not do this negligently, but because he lacked these three histories.

I, however, since I possess these materials, do not despair of inserting into his chronicle, in suitable places and down to the year 1100 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the names and successions—and sometimes the more notable deeds—of those dukes, together with all the names of the archbishops of Rouen and some of the bishops of that province; and likewise of the kings of the English, of whom he makes no mention. I had proposed to do the same for the kings of the Britons, if only I could suitably include them within [Col. 0423B] the chronicle of Sigebert. But since Brutus, the great-grandson of Aeneas, from whom the island of Britain also takes its name, was the first to reign there, if I wished to set down in due order all the kings succeeding him, I would have to scatter the same names not only through Sigebert’s book, but also through the whole body of Jerome’s chronicle and through a large part of Eusebius’s *Chronography*. Yet, because it is unbecoming to add anything foreign to the writings of men of such authority—I mean Eusebius and Jerome—in order to satisfy the curious I shall append to this prologue a letter of Henry the archdeacon, in which he briefly enumerates [Col. 0424A] all the kings of the Britons from Brutus down to Cadwallon, who was the last of the powerful British kings and the father of Gadwalladr, whom Bede calls Cedwalla. As it is found in that letter, when this same Henry was travelling to Rome, and I provided him with access to a copy of the whole history of the Britons, he excerpted it at Bec.

Therefore, as has already been said, because the aforesaid Sigebert begins his chronicle with the year 381 of the Lord’s Incarnation and carried it down to the year 1100 of that same divine Incarnation, I shall henceforth, God permitting and helping—without whom we can do nothing—undertake to gather under the years of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0424B], down to the year 1182 [Note: [Col. 0423] Robert later corrected this in different ink; it had first been MCL, “1150,” which is also the reading of 3, 7b, and 8d.], those events which occurred in various provinces, especially in Normandy and England, and which have come to my knowledge. And I do this the more willingly because I wish to note in summary, year by year, the deeds of the first Henry, most vigorous king of the English and duke of the Normans, with whom I must begin. For this work I shall be aided both by the history which I recently composed concerning that king, now dead, and added to the *Deeds of the Dukes of Normandy*, and by the history of the aforesaid Archdeacon Henry, which he composed concerning the affairs of England, beginning with Julius Caesar and weaving the narrative in order down to the death of the aforesaid King Henry—that is, to the year 1135 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

[Col. 0423] **END OF THE PROLOGUE** [Note: [Col. 0423] Thus written in red, perhaps in Robert’s hand; it also adds: “You will find the continuation of the chronography hereafter on the twelfth folio. For here, through the copyist’s fault, certain things, though not unworthy of remembrance, are inserted”—namely, the little book *On the Change in the Order of Monks*, published by D’Achery, p. 811 ff. Manuscript 8b presents the same work here; 3 and 8a-c place it after the chronicle.]

**THE LETTER OF HENRY THE ARCHDEACON TO WARIN CONCERNING THE KINGS OF THE BRITONS BEGINS.**

[Col. 0423C] You ask me, Warin the Breton, courteous and witty man, why, in recounting the deeds of our country, I began with the times of Julius Caesar and omitted the most flourishing kingdoms which existed from Brutus down to Julius. I answer you, then, that although I sought knowledge of these times very often, both orally and in writing, I could not find it. So great is the ruin wrought by forgetfulness that, as time endures, it overshadows and extinguishes mortal glory.

Yet in this year, 1139 from the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 0423] “the thirty-ninth year,” E.], when I was travelling to Rome with Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, I found with amazement at Bec—where the same archbishop had been abbot—writings about the aforesaid matters. For there I met Robert of Torigni, a monk of that place, a man most diligent in seeking out and [Col. 0423D] collecting both sacred and secular books. When he questioned me [Col. 0424C] about the arrangement of the history of the kings of the English which I had published, and willingly heard what he asked of me, he offered me a book to read concerning the kings of the Britons who held our island before the English. I send you, dearest friend, excerpts from it—very briefly, as is fitting in a letter. “Aeneas—[you will find it].” Farewell.

Likewise, from the same history. For still greater elucidation of matters already stated and yet to be stated, we shall set down a certain part of the history of Henry the archdeacon, from which we have already excerpted the letter placed above. Thus he says in the first book of that history: “Britain was—[it is found].”

From the same history, concerning the modern saints of England: [Col. 0424D] “Who at Canterbury—[shine forth brilliantly].”

**ROBERT’S CHRONICLES BEGIN.**

[Col. 0423]

[Col. 0423D] **OF THE ROMANS. OF THE FRANKS. OF THE ENGLISH.**

(HUNT. VII.) Henry, son of the first William, king [Col. 0424D] of the English and duke of the Normans, after his brother, the second William, king of the English, had been killed and buried on the following day in the church of St Peter at Winchester, was elected king there. He gave the bishopric of Winchester to William Giffard. Going on to London, he was consecrated there by Maurice, bishop of London, after promising a desirable improvement of the laws and customs. On hearing this, Archbishop Anselm returned to England and gave in marriage to the new king Henry Matilda, a noble maiden, daughter of Malcolm king of the Scots and Queen Margaret.

(H. HENR.) A book written about the lives of both queens, mother and daughter, describes in plain language how great was their sanctity and learning. By her King Henry had one son, named William, and one daughter, who resembled her mother not only in name but also in virtue. [Col. 0425B] When this maiden was scarcely five years old, Henry IV, august emperor of the Romans, sought her in marriage through honourable envoys and took her as his wife.

(HUNT. VII.) After Jerusalem had been captured, as we have said, and after a great battle had later been victoriously fought against the army of the emir of Babylon, Duke Robert returned to Normandy in August and was received with joy by all the people. Thomas, archbishop of York, a man of flourishing intellect and intimate of the Muses, ceased to appear among men. Gerard, cantor of Rouen, succeeded him.

**1101. Henry 45. Philip 41. Henry I.**

(Ibid.) King Henry of the English, having held his court at Westminster at Christmas and at Winchester at Easter, found the magnates of England stirred against him because his brother Robert was arriving with an army. The king therefore sent a naval force out to sea to fight against his brother’s arrival; but some of them submitted to Robert as he came. When Robert landed at Portsmouth before the Kalends of August, and the king marched against him with very great forces, the magnates on both sides, unwilling to endure a war between brothers, established a treaty of peace between them on these terms: Robert was to receive every year 3,000 marks of silver from England; and whichever of the two lived longer was to be heir of the other if the other died without a son. Twelve of the foremost nobles on either side swore to this agreement. Robert then remained peacefully until the feast of St Michael in his brother’s kingdom, and [Col. 0425D] returned to his own lands.

Ranulf, the wicked bishop of Durham, whom King Henry had put in chains, after escaping from prison had secretly gone into Normandy, encouraging Duke Robert against his brother by his counsel and exhortation.

(SIGEB.) Conrad, son of Emperor Henry and still in rebellion against his father, died in Italy. Emperor Henry defeated Henry of Limburg, who opposed him; after storming his castles he compelled him to surrender. But, when Henry redeemed the emperor’s favour for a large sum, the emperor also gave him the duchy of Lotharingia; and thus they were reconciled.

(FULCHER.) The city of Caesarea was captured by the Christians.

**1102. 46. 42. 2.**

(HUNT. VII.) King Henry of the English, acting lawfully against him, exiled a most wicked and treacherous count, Robert of Bellême. He first besieged the castle of Arundel; and since it was extremely difficult to take, he built castles before it, then went and besieged Bridge until the castle was surrendered to him. Robert of Bellême then departed groaning into Normandy.

In the same year, at the feast of St Michael, Archbishop Anselm held a council at London, in which he forbade English priests to have wives—a thing not previously forbidden.

(Ibid.) This seemed most pure to some, dangerous to others: lest, while they sought a purity beyond their strength, they might fall into horrible impurity, to the utter disgrace of the Christian name. At that council many abbots who had acquired abbeys as God did not will lost them as God did will.

(SIGEB.) While Robert, count of Flanders, was besieging the city of Cambrai, Emperor Henry marched against him; after storming some of his castles, he was compelled by the severity of the approaching winter to return.

(FULCHER.) Stephen, count of Blois, was killed on 18 July at Ramla. Hugh the Great also died at Tarsus, and his son Ralph succeeded him.

**1103. 47. 43. 3.**

(HUNT. VII.) Duke Robert of the Normans came to England; owing to various intervening considerations and the king’s cautious prudence, the king forgave him the 3,000 marks which he owed him annually. In the same year blood was seen to bubble up from the ground in Berkshire near Hampstead.

(SIGEB.) Robert, count of Flanders, was received into the emperor’s favour.

(FULCHER.) The city of Acre was captured by the Christians. In antiquity it was called Ptolemais; some think it to be Accaron, but it is not. The latter is Philistine; the former is called Ptolemais. Accaron is a Philistine city near Ascalon; Acre, that is Ptolemais, has Mount Carmel on its south. Bohemond entrusted the principality of Antioch to his nephew Tancred, then sailed to Apulia and afterwards came to France. Ebremar succeeded Daibert, the first patriarch of Jerusalem.

**1104. 48. 44. 4.**

(HUNT.) King Henry of the English and his brother Robert, duke of the Normans, quarrelled through intervening causes. The king therefore sent soldiers into Normandy. Received by the duke’s traitors, they inflicted no small devastation upon the countships through plundering and burning. William, count of Mortain, disinherited in England for treachery, departed from the king into Normandy; a most valiant man of resolute spirit and ardent activity, he declared and waged against the royal troops a war full of calamity. Around the sun at noon there appeared four circles of white colour, a sign of what was to come.

**1105. 49. 45. 5.**

(Ibid.) King Henry of the English went into Normandy to fight against his brother. He acquired Caen with money, Bayeux by arms and with the help [Col. 0427A] of Fulk, count of Anjou. He also took several other castles, and nearly all the magnates of Normandy submitted to the king. After these deeds, he returned to England in August.

(SIGEB.) The Jerusalemites crush an innumerable multitude of pagans in glorious victory. The son of Emperor Henry, turning away from his father, turns away from him all whom he can, and rises against him under the pretext of improving the commonwealth and restoring the Church.

**1106. Henry 50. Philip 46. Henry I 6.**

(HUNT. VII.) Robert, duke of the Normans, came to his brother King Henry at Northampton, amicably asking that what had been taken from him be restored with brotherly goodwill. But since God did not approve their reconciliation [Col. 0427B], the angry duke went to Normandy, and the king followed him before August. When the king had besieged the castle of Tinchebray, the duke of the Normans came, with Robert of Bellême, the count of Mortain, and all his supporters. The king, however, had with him all the magnates of Normandy and the strength of England, Anjou, and Brittany, not without foresight.

Then, when the horns had sounded with their harsh blast, the duke of Normandy, with few men, most boldly attacked many. Accustomed to the wars of Jerusalem, he fiercely and terribly drove back the royal line, boldly acting as a man of admirable and long-proved valour. William, count of Mortain, too, advanced by throwing the English battle-line into disorder from place to place.

[Col. 0427C] Then the mounted line of the Bretons—while the king, the duke, and the other battle-lines were on foot, so that they might fight more steadfastly—rushed upon the duke’s line from the opposite side, which suddenly lost heart. The duke’s people, overwhelmed by sheer mass within a very small space, were broken up and defeated. A marvellous thing! He upon whom his father had pronounced a curse, and who had refused the kingdom of Jerusalem, could not endure.

Robert of Bellême, seeing this at once, looked to his own flight. Thus the most valiant duke of the Normans and the count of Mortain were captured. And the Lord repaid Duke Robert in kind: although he had rendered himself glorious in the actions at Jerusalem, he had refused the kingdom of Jerusalem when it was offered to him, choosing rather to devote himself to ease and idleness in Normandy than to labour for the Lord of kings in the holy city. Therefore [Col. 0427D] the Lord condemned him to perpetual idleness and everlasting imprisonment. A comet had appeared in that same year as a sign of this event. On Maundy Thursday two full moons were also seen, one in the east and the other in the west.

(ORD. VIT. VII, 659.) In this year was fulfilled what King William, on the day before he died, had said to his younger son Henry, of whom we are now speaking. When that most powerful king had his notaries draw up before him a record of his treasures to be given to churches and the poor, and sent great gifts in supplication to the clergy of Mantes, so that the churches he had burned might thereby be restored; when he assigned the duchy of Normandy, although absent, to Robert, his firstborn, and the kingdom of England to William Rufus—on which account he also sent Lanfranc the archbishop, through the latter, a letter concerning the installation of that king—Henry said to his father with tears: “And what do you give me, father?”

The king said to him: “I give you five thousand pounds of silver from my treasury.”

Henry replied: “What shall I do with treasure if I have no place to live?”

His father answered: “Be patient, son, and be strengthened in the Lord. Endure peaceably while your elder brothers go before you. Robert will have Normandy, and William the monarchy of all England. But in your time you shall have all the honour which I have acquired, and you shall surpass your brothers in riches and power.”

(SIGEB.) On 2 February a star was seen in the sky by day, emitting from itself a long ray from the third hour until the ninth, apparently about a cubit distant from the sun. How unworthily Henry, son of the emperor, rose against his father contrary to the law of nature and the right of laws is shown in a letter written in his father’s own words to Philip, king of France.

While Emperor Henry remained at Liège, his son came to Aachen; intending to proceed to Liège against his father, on the Thursday of the Lord’s Supper he sent his men ahead to seize the bridge at Visé, lest anyone oppose his arrival. But when his father’s soldiers rushed to recover the bridge, the son’s soldiers were driven from it: some were captured, some plunged into the Meuse, and some killed; among the latter Count Bruno was killed. Thus the son came against his father and returned without glory.

While the people of Cologne remained faithful to the emperor, their archbishop encouraged the emperor’s son against his father. Cologne was besieged and assaulted, but not taken. Emperor Henry then died at Liège, and his son Henry succeeded him. He later married Matilda, the noble maiden, scarcely five years old, daughter of King Henry of the English.

Duke Henry, who had passed in allegiance from the emperor to his son, armed him against his father by his counsel, and then, returning from the son to the father, fought against the son’s party: after the emperor’s death, he surrendered himself to the king’s son as accused [Note: [Col. 0427] E reads rerum (“matters”)] of treason. He was captured by him and committed to custody. He escaped from it through his own resourcefulness; his duchy, however, was given to Godfrey, count of Louvain.

**1107. 1. 47. 7.**

[Col. 0428D] (HUNT. VII.) King Henry of the English, having destroyed or subdued his enemies and arranged Normandy as he wished, returned to England and cast his distinguished brother the duke, together with the count of Mortain, into the darkness of prison. Victorious, and then for the first time a strong king, he held his Easter court at Windsor, where the magnates of England and Normandy attended together in fear and trembling. For formerly, both while he was young and after he became king, he had been held in great contempt. But the Lord, who judges far otherwise than the sons of men, who exalts the humble and brings down the mighty, cast down Robert, most renowned in everyone’s favour, and willed that the fame of despised Henry should shine throughout the world.

The Almighty Lord freely gave him three gifts—wisdom, victory, and wealth. Prospering in all things through these, he surpassed all his predecessors. The fame of his goodness and magnanimity spread among nearly all peoples. Maurice, founder of the church of London, died; and Edgar, king of the Scots, died. His brother Alexander succeeded him with King Henry’s consent.

(SIGEB.) Bohemond returned from Gaul to Apulia with a great army and began to ravage the land of Alexius, emperor of the Greeks. Henry, the former duke, seeking to recover his duchy, seized the town of Aachen against Duke Godfrey. Godfrey, unable to bear this, violently broke into Aachen, terrified the townsmen away from their support of Henry the former duke, and captured several powerful counts and many nobles. Henry himself escaped with his sons only with difficulty by flight. The duke considered it unworthy to capture Henry’s wife. Having won over the counts and more distinguished men whom he had captured on the condition that they serve under him, he brought them to his allegiance.

**1108. Henry 2. Philip 48. Henry I 8.**

(HUNT. VII.) When Philip, king of France, died, King Henry of the English crossed into Normandy and began a very great war against Louis, Philip’s son and the new king of France. After Gerard, archbishop of York, died, Thomas later succeeded him.

(SIGEB.) Emperor Henry marched against [Col. 0429C] Robert of Flanders, and, with a treaty of peace more feigned than concluded on both sides, returned almost without effect. Bohemond, duke of Apulia, having gathered an army from every quarter, prepared to invade the empire of Constantinople.

**1109. 3. 49. 9.**

(HUNT. VII.) Envoys of Henry, emperor of the Romans, outstanding in physical stature and splendour of dress, were sent to seek the daughter of King Henry of the English in marriage for their lord. King Henry therefore held a court at London more splendid than any he had ever held and, at Pentecost, received the oaths demanded by the emperor’s envoys.

(GEMM. VI, 9.) The lord Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, of venerable memory, died on 21 April, Wednesday before Maundy Thursday. That year the latest Easter occurred, namely 25 April. This reverend man wrote several works worthy of remembrance, which we have taken care to append below.

While he was still prior in the monastery of Bec, he wrote three treatises: first, *On Truth*; second, *On Freedom of Choice*; third, *On the Fall of the Devil*. He also wrote a fourth, entitled *On the Grammarian*, in which he replies to a pupil whom he introduces as disputing with him, and proposes and resolves many dialectical [Note: [Col. 0429] “dialectical,” E.] questions.

He also made a fifth little book, called the *Monologion*. For in it he speaks only by himself and with himself; setting aside every authority of divine Scripture, he seeks and finds through reason alone that God exists, [Col. 0430A] and by invincible reasoning proves and affirms that what true faith believes concerning God cannot be otherwise.

He likewise composed a sixth book, small indeed, but great in the weight of its thoughts and its most subtle contemplation, which he entitled the *Proslogion*. In that work he addresses either himself or God. He wrote also a seventh book of letters to various persons, answering their various concerns or directing the conduct of matters which concerned himself. He made an eighth work *On the Incarnation of the Word*. Written in epistolary style, he dedicated and sent it to Urban, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church.

He published a ninth book, entitled *Why God Became Man*. The tenth was *On the Virginal Conception*. The eleventh, *On Contemplative Prayers*, is called *Meditations* by very many; [Col. 0430B] in these it is readily apparent to readers how great a sweetness of heavenly things filled his mind. The twelfth and final treatise was *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*. For at the Council of Bari he had refuted the Greeks, who denied that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son; taking the subject from this, he composed this book at the request of Hildebert [Note: [Col. 0429] “Ildebert,” E.], bishop of Le Mans. If you seek something concerning his nation, life, and character, you will find it somewhat earlier.

(SIGEB.) In the parish of Liège a sow gave birth to a piglet with a human face. A four-footed chick was also born. Emperor Henry marched against the Hungarians, but returned after making a treaty. The lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny, died, and Pons succeeded him. This year many were afflicted by the holy fire, their limbs blackening like coals. Philip, king of France, died; his son Louis reigned after him for twenty-nine years.

**1110. 4. Louis 1. 10.**

(HUNT. VII.) The daughter of King Henry of the English, named Matilda, was given to Emperor Henry, to state it briefly, as was fitting. The same King Henry of the English levied three shillings from every hide of England. When he held his Pentecost court at the new Windsor which he had built, he disinherited those who had harmed him: namely Philip of Braose, William Malet, and William Baynard.

Helias, count of Maine, who held it under King Henry, died. But Fulk, count of Anjou and father of Geoffrey, took Maine with Helias’s daughter [Col. 0430D] and held it against King Henry. A comet appeared in an unusual manner. Having risen in the east and ascended into the firmament, it appeared to move backward.

(A. ROTH. 1109.) William died, and Geoffrey, dean of Le Mans, succeeded him as the forty-ninth archbishop of Rouen.
