(FULCHER.) King Baldwin of Jerusalem captured the cities of Beirut and Sidon. Gibelin became the third patriarch of Jerusalem.

(SIGEB.) In June a comet appeared, directing its rays to the south. Many maintained that this sign portended King Henry’s forthcoming expedition toward Italy.

[Col. 0431A] **1111. Henry 5. Louis 2. Henry I 11.**

(HUNT. VII.) King Henry of the English and duke of the Normans, proceeding into Normandy against Fulk, count of Anjou, who held Maine against his will, steadily inflicted the laws of war upon him with iron and fire. Robert, count of Flanders, died; he had taken a most illustrious part in the journey to Jerusalem, and his memory will therefore not pass away for ever. Baldwin his son succeeded him as count, a young man altogether vigorous in arms.

(SIGEB.) Emperor Henry went to Rome to settle the discord between empire and priesthood. Begun by St Gregory VII, Roman pope, also called Hildebrand, and stirred up by his successors Victor and Urban, and above all by Paschal, it was a great scandal to the whole world. The king, wishing to employ the authority, custom, and authoritative privileges of the emperors—who, from Charlemagne, the first of the Frankish kings to rule the Romans, had ruled for more than three hundred years under sixty-three apostolic pontiffs—lawfully bestowed bishoprics and abbeys by ring and staff.

Against this authority of their predecessors, the popes ruled by synodal judgment that no bishopric or other ecclesiastical investiture could or ought to be granted by ring or staff from a lay hand. Whoever received a bishopric or another investiture belonging to ecclesiastical right in this manner was excommunicated. It was chiefly for this reason [Col. 0431C] that the emperor was making for Rome. If any Lombards wished in any way to resist him, he crushed them by force.

In the reconciliation made between the emperor and the pope—for he had captured the pope himself together with bishops and cardinals—on Easter Day, after Henry had been crowned emperor and the Gospel had been read, Pope Paschal, also called Rainier, delivered to him before the altar of the apostles Peter and Paul, in the sight of all the princes, a privilege concerning the investiture of bishoprics or abbeys by ring as well as by staff: namely, that he might confer investiture by staff and ring upon bishops or abbots of his kingdom, freely elected without violence or simony; after investiture, however, the recipient was to receive canonical consecration from the bishop to whom confirmation belonged.

[Col. 0431D] As a confirmation of peace between the apostolic pontiff and the emperor, while celebrating Mass and giving him the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, he said: “Lord Emperor, we give you this body of the Lord, born of the Virgin Mary and having suffered on the cross for us, as the holy and apostolic Church maintains, as confirmation of true peace between me and you.” Given on 13 April, in the fourth indiction.

**1112. 6. 3. 12.**

(FULCHER.) Tancred, a most valiant knight, died. He enlarged and extended the principality of Antioch so greatly that none of his successors could retain what he had acquired. Roger, son of Richard and his kinsman, succeeded him.

(SIGEB.) Because God was offended by human sins, the church of St Michael “of the peril of the sea” was struck by lightning and burned, by divine agency, together with all its buildings.

(HUNT. VII.) King Henry of the English exiled [Col. 0432B] from Normandy the count of Évreux and William Crispin, and captured Robert of Bellême, of whom we have spoken above.

(SIGEB.) Bishop Waldric of Laon, attempting to call the citizens of that city back from the fellowship of an oath wrongly sworn, was, alas to relate, run through with a sword and killed by rioters rushing to arms, on Thursday in Easter week, 25 April, in the major litany. In the tumultuous onset of the disorderly crowd, the bishop’s house was set on fire; from it the mother church of St Mary, the church of St John the Baptist in the abbey of nuns, and all the neighbouring dependent churches were also burned.

The king of France punished the instigators of the sedition so severely that the example could deter both present and future persons from a like crime. [Note: [Col. 0431] After this, manuscript 2 adds: “At this time Master William of Champeaux, formerly archdeacon of Paris, a very learned man, assumed the habit of a regular canon. With some of his pupils, outside the city of Paris at a place where there was a chapel of St Victor the martyr, he began to build a monastery of clerics. When he had been raised to the bishopric of Châlons, the venerable Gilduin, his foremost pupil, became abbot there. Under his rule many noble clerics, trained in secular and sacred learning, gathered to live in that place. Among them Master Hugh of Lorraine flourished especially in learning and humble religious devotion; he produced many books. This year also saw the beginning of Savigny.”

All of this, except the final words, “This year also saw the beginning of Savigny,” has been taken word for word from our Robert’s book *On the Change in the Order of Monks in Normandy*. The following, quoted in the preface to the Rouen edition of the works of St Hugh, 1648, from a certain anonymous writer of Jumièges, agrees with it word for word: “Under Gilduin’s rule many noble clerics, trained in secular and sacred learning, gathered to live in this place. Among them Hugh of Lorraine, so called from the border of Saxony, flourished especially in learning and humble religious devotion. He produced many books, which need not be mentioned because they are commonly available.” Anyone can see that these are words of that Robertian treatise, except “so called from the border of Saxony,” words devoid of sense, which this anonymous writer of Jumièges seems to have added himself. Thus this anonymous writer can scarcely be counted among the testimonies concerning the homeland of St Hugh, among which all who have written on the matter have included him, most recently Liebner in *Hugo von St. Victor*, Leipzig, 1832, p. 18.]

**1113. 7. 4. 13.**

(HUNT. VII.) In the following year, though not in the present one, Henry, king of the English, gave the archbishopric of Canterbury to Ralph, bishop of Rochester. Then, after Thomas, archbishop of York, died, Thurstan succeeded him. A great dispute arose between the archbishops Ralph and Thurstan because the archbishop of York was unwilling, as customary, to submit to that of Canterbury. The case was often argued before the king and often before the apostolic pontiff, but it had not yet been decided.

King Henry of the English led an army into Wales, and the Welsh were made subject to him according to the greatness of his pleasure. A great comet appeared at the end of May. The king then crossed into Normandy.

[Col. 0432D] (ANS. GEMBL.) In May rye-crops and trees, scorched by the holy [Col. 0433A] fire, disappointed hopes of their fruit; certain woods besides were dried up. There followed a severe and prolonged sickness among people, with diarrhoea and mortality.

(HUNT. VII.) In this year King Henry of the English, returning to England, put Robert of Bellême into perpetual imprisonment at Wareham.

(ANSELM.) The venerable Sigebert, monk of the monastery of Gembloux, died on 5 October. A man of incomparable talent in every branch of letters, the recorder in this book of earlier times, he left his followers most grievous sorrow at his absence.

**1114. Henry 8. Louis 5. Henry I 14.**

(Year 1107.) After the death of Richard, son of Richard, son of Count Gilbert, a monk of Bec who was the last [Col. 0433B] abbot on the island of Ely, King Henry established Hervey as its first bishop (in 1108). One county, Cambridgeshire, was taken from the bishop of Lincoln and subjected to this new bishop. Eight counties, or provinces, still remained to the bishop of Lincoln: Lincolnshire, Leicestershire, Northamptonshire, Huntingdonshire, Herefordshire, Bedfordshire, Buckinghamshire, and Oxfordshire. [Note: [Col. 0433D] For the date, compare Eadmer, *Historia Novorum*, pp. 95 and 209, editions c-d of Selden in folio, [uncertain OCR] in the *Acta Sanctorum*, 21 April.]

(ORD. VIT. XII, 840.) After the death in Normandy of Gilbert, bishop of Évreux, a religious man, Ouen, a man of great holiness, succeeded him. [Note: [Col. 0434D] Orderic reports this as occurring in 1112.]

(FULCHER.) In an earthquake part of the city of Mamistra fell, as did two castles not far from Antioch, Mariscum and Triphalech. [Note: [Col. 0433] Here 5, 7b, and 8d add: “Alexius, emperor of Constantinople, died, and his son John succeeded him.” Manuscript 2 presents the same under the following year.]

**1115. 9. 6. 15.**

[Col. 0433C] (HUNT. VII.) King Henry of the English made all the magnates of the realm swear the fidelity owed to their lord to his son William, and returned to England.

(FULCHER.) Mamistra was devastated by a greater earthquake. In the same year, after Arnulf, the fourth patriarch, had been deposed by an apostolic legate, the patriarch himself went to Rome and was restored by Pope Paschal, from whom he received the pallium.

**1116. 10. 7. 16.**
(HUNT. VII.) Henry, king of the English, was present at Christmas at the dedication of the church of St Alban, which Robert, the venerable bishop of Lincoln, dedicated at the request of Richard, the illustrious abbot of that place. King Offa of Mercia, a devout man, had formerly translated the body of that martyr into the earlier monastery which he had built there and richly endowed. [Col. 0433D] [Note: [Col. 0434D] A.D. 793.] Paul, a monk of Caen, whom Archbishop Lanfranc had appointed abbot, rebuilt that monastery on a grander scale. His successor Richard had it dedicated by Robert, bishop of Lincoln, in the presence of King Henry. Geoffrey, their successor, translated the body of the aforesaid martyr into a shrine marvellously resplendent with [Col. 0434A] gold, silver, and gems, in the presence of Alexander, bishop of Lincoln, in the twenty-ninth year of King Henry.

This is the Offa who granted to the vicar of St Peter, the pontiff of the Roman city, a fixed payment called Rome-scot, from every household of his realm for ever. At that time, moreover, priests in England were so free from avarice that they would not accept lands for building monasteries unless compelled; kings were such lovers of religion that they either devoutly built very great monasteries or beneficially withdrew from the world. Thus did the kings of Wessex, Cædwalla and Ine. The former, having ruled powerfully for two years, left his earthly kingdom, went to Rome, was baptized there, and died in his baptismal white garments in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord [Col. 0434B] 688. The latter, having reigned for thirty-six years after Cædwalla, left his kingdom to his kinsman Æthelard, sought Rome, and there died as a pilgrim for the love of God.

Two successive kings of Mercia followed them: Æthelred and his successor, his kinsman Coenred. For in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 700, Æthelred, son of Penda, became a monk in the twenty-ninth year of his reign and was buried at Bardney. His successor Coenred, after reigning five years, went to Rome, became a monk there, and remained there until his death. With him Offa, son of Sighere, king of the East Saxons—who would have been king had he remained—went to Rome with equal devotion and embraced monastic life. Ceolwulf also, king of Northumbria, to whom Bede wrote his history of the English, [Col. 0434C] became a monk after reigning eight years, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 738, namely the third year after Bede’s death. His kinsman Eadberht, who succeeded him, likewise became a monk in the twenty-first year of his reign. Eight kings succeeded him in the same kingdom; all were betrayed, expelled, or slain by treacherous provincials.

Likewise Sigeberht, king of the East Angles, who honourably received St Fursey when he came from Ireland—and by whose gift and assistance that saint established a monastery in the stronghold of Cnobheresburg, later enlarged by King Anna and five nobles—this Sigeberht, I say, became a monk and left his kingdom to his kinsman Ecgric. Many years later they compelled him to go out against King Penda. Yet in battle he carried nothing in his hand but a staff, [Col. 0434D] and there he was slain with King Ecgric and the army. Sebbi also, king of the East Saxons, having devoutly taken the monastic habit, was buried in the church of St Paul in London. Thus these eight kings voluntarily gave up their kingdoms for Christ.

And, to return to the matter from which I have digressed: perhaps the monastery of St Alban is free and exempt from the levy of the aforesaid payment called Rome-scot because that same king, Offa, both first built the monastery and assigned the payment to the Roman Church. King Cnut of all England and Denmark, going to Rome in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1030, later granted this payment to the holy Roman Church from the whole kingdom of England; whereas Offa had previously given it only from his own kingdom, that is, from the part of England called Mercia. [Col. 0435A]

(HUNT. VII.) When King Henry crossed the sea to Normandy at Easter, a very great quarrel arose between him and Louis, king of the French. Its cause was this: Count Theobald of Blois, King Henry of England’s nephew, had taken up arms against his lord, the king of the French. King Henry sent his dukes and soldiery to aid him and afflicted the king severely.

**1117. Henry 11. Louis 8. Henry I 17.**

(Ibid.) A most grievous trouble arose for Henry, king of the English. Louis, king of the French, Baldwin, count of Flanders, and Fulk, count of Anjou, swore that they would take Normandy from King Henry and give it to William, son of Robert, duke of Normandy. Many of King Henry’s nobles also deserted him, to his very great loss. Yet he was not without foresight: he had as his allies the aforesaid Count Theobald, his nephew, and Conan, count of the Bretons. [Col. 0435C]

Accordingly, the king of the French and the duke of Flanders entered Normandy with an army. But after they had been there one night, fearing the arrival of King Henry with Englishmen, Normans, and Bretons, they returned home without battle. In the same year England was oppressed by very frequent gelds and various exactions for the king’s necessity. There were thunder and hail on the Kalends of December, and in the same month the sky appeared red, as though it were burning. On Christmas Eve there arose a violent wind, uprooting woods and destroying houses. The moon also suffered an eclipse. There was likewise a very great earthquake in Lombardy, destroying churches, towers, houses, and people.

Lord Pons, abbot of Cluny, wishing to correct to the last detail the excesses in food and dress of certain [Col. 0435D] monks who conducted the external business of that monastery, they rose against him. As their hostility grew, they accused him before Pope Paschal [Note: [Col. 0435D] Robert is mistaken: it was Calixtus II, in 1121, or rather 1123; see Duchesne, *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, pp. 462 and 1623.] of certain very grave charges, although false. When he disdained to answer them, saying that he cared neither for their accusation nor for the abbacy—for he trusted both in a good conscience and in his lineage, being the son of the count of Melgueil—he left the abbacy against the pope’s will and went to Jerusalem. [Col. 0436A]

But they, persisting in their malice, elected as abbot Hugh, prior of Marcigny. When he died within the first year of his rule, they elected a young man of notable nobility named Peter. How the aforesaid Pons, returning from Jerusalem, wished again to preside over the abbey which he had renounced, and how, when a schism had arisen in that monastery, much human blood was shed, it is shameful to tell. Yet the governance of the monastery of Cluny remained with the venerable Peter, who still directs it, thirty-two years having elapsed since then. Pons, however, finally died in the monastery called La Cava. [Note: [Col. 0436D] La Cava.]

There also died this year [Note: [Col. 0436D] In the year 1115.] Ivo, bishop of Chartres, a religious man of great learning. When young, [Col. 0436B] he heard Master Lanfranc, prior of Bec, lecturing on secular and sacred literature in that famous school which he maintained at Bec. Many men distinguished both by secular nobility and moral worth gathered there, men who later attained the highest summit of ecclesiastical rank and religious life. Afterwards Ivo himself for some time presided over the community of regular canons of St Quentin at Beauvais. Finally, becoming bishop, he governed the church of Chartres courageously and devoutly for almost twenty-three years. He left many monuments of his diligence, piety, and wisdom: namely, by building the monastery of the canons of St John of the Valley [Note: [Col. 0436D] Near Chartres.], where he too was buried; by building the episcopal residences; by freeing that bishopric from the evil customs and exactions of the count of Chartres; [Col. 0436C] and by writing many useful works.

**1118. 12. 9. 18.**

(HUNT. VII.) The long warfare of Henry and Louis, the kings, and of their nobles grievously harassed both kings, until Baldwin, the most valiant count of Flanders, was fatally wounded in a military uprising at Eu in Normandy and withdrew to his own lands. Moreover Robert, count of Meulan, the wisest in secular affairs of all those living in Jerusalem, and King Henry’s intimate counsellor, lost the light of this world. His sons succeeded him: Waleran became count of Meulan in Normandy, and Robert became count of Leicester in England.

(A. Roth.) Matilda the second, queen of the English, the venerable wife of King Henry and mother of the empress, died. [Col. 0436D] If we wished to recount individually the abundant generosity of her goodness and the many forms of her moral excellence, the day would fail us. Yet among her other good works, many churches in England, Normandy, and other provinces still shine with her benefactions. She was buried in Westminster. [Note: [Col. 0435D] “that is, in the church at Westminster”: Robert corrected this in an erasure. It is absent in 7b and 8d, which have: “May He have mercy on her, from whom are all things.”]

(FULCHER.) Pope Paschal also died in January of the same year, and Gelasius, the 165th pope, succeeded him. Alexius, emperor of Constantinople, also died, [Col. 0437A] and John succeeded him. Arnulf, patriarch of Jerusalem, died as well, together with very many other great men in the world. Baldwin, the first king of Jerusalem, also died in April. He was a most daring knight, who stormed and captured these cities: Acre, Caesarea, Beirut, Sidon, Tripoli, Arsuf; and he subjected to himself the lands of the Arabs as far as the Red Sea. He reigned eighteen years, and Baldwin the second, his kinsman, count of Edessa, succeeded him.

**1119. Henry 13. Louis 10. Henry I 19.**

(HUNT. VII.) In the fifty-second year since the Normans obtained England, and the nineteenth year of his reign, King Henry fought gloriously against the king of the French. The French king had placed in command [Col. 0437B] an army of nobles led by William, son of Robert, duke and brother of King Henry. He himself was in the following division with the greatest forces. King Henry had placed his nobles in the first line; in the second he himself was mounted with his own household; and in the third he stationed his sons with the strongest troops, on foot.

Thus the first French line immediately drove back and scattered the Norman nobles’ division with their horses. Then, striking the line in which King Henry was, it scattered that too. The royal lines therefore met each other, and battle was fought most fiercely on both sides. When the spears were broken, the matter was decided with swords. Meanwhile William Crispin, a high-spirited knight, struck King Henry’s [Col. 0437C] head twice with his sword. Though his hauberk was impenetrable, the force of the blow nevertheless affected the king’s head somewhat, so that blood burst forth. Stirred by fierceness of spirit, the king struck his assailant back so hard that, although his helmet was impenetrable, the force of the blow threw down both knight and horse. He was at once captured before the royal feet.

The infantry division in which King Henry’s sons were stationed had not yet struck, but rose up opposite, ready immediately to strike. When the French saw this, they melted in unexpected terror and turned their backs. King Henry remained victorious on the field until the captured leading men of the enemy were placed before his feet. Returning to Rouen, amid the sounds of trumpets and the chants of the clergy, he blessed God and the Lord of Hosts. In the same [Col. 0437D] year Pope Gelasius died—formerly called John of Gaeta [Col. 0438A]—and was buried at Cluny. Guy, archbishop of Vienne, succeeded him and was called Calixtus, the 166th pope. Baldwin, count of Flanders, died from the wound he had received in Normandy. His kinsman Charles succeeded him, son of Cnut the Holy, king of the Danes.

(FULCHER.) In the same year Roger, prince of Antioch, with seven thousand of his men, was slaughtered by the Turks near the town of Archasium. Thus King Baldwin, upon the death of the prince of Antioch, became king with another kingdom added—or, to speak less grandly, a prince.

**1120. 14. 11. 20.**

(HUNT. VII.) Henry, king of the English, having subdued and pacified everything in Gaul, returned joyfully to England. But during the very sea-crossing, by the divine judgment of God, though hidden, the king’s two sons William and Richard, and the king’s daughter and niece [Note: [Col. 0437D] “are created.” William was by his wife; Richard by a concubine; his daughter by a concubine, wife of the count of Perche; and his niece, wife of the count of Chester; “and many” is also found in manuscript 2.] together with many nobles, stewards, and chamberlains, were shipwrecked on the feast-day of St Catherine. [Col. 0438B]

> Thus, while the sea, surmounting the furthest planks, crawls over all,
>
> It drowns the king’s offspring and kills the honour of the world.

[Note: [Col. 0437D] We add this poem, unpublished so far as I know, which is found among other poems of Marbod of Rennes, Hildebert, and others in Brussels manuscript 8883, twelfth century.

> England weeps for drowned knights, for the drowned fosterling of the king;
>
> Much nobility perishes.
>
> The merry life of young men, the mature life of the living,
>
> The chastity of maidens: one wave kills so many at once.
>
> Here is drowned the sole son of one king,
>
> The kingdom’s sole hope: grievous is the mourning on both sides.
>
> No friend wept over him, nor closed his eyes;
>
> He is carried with pomp, yet is not buried in earth. [Col. 0438D]
>
> A fish’s belly is his tomb instead of marble; the murmur of water,
>
> The stench of the sea, was his perfume.
>
> Unworthy death strikes one worthy to live longer. When I recall
>
> That death with myself, nothing helps but weeping.
>
> Death is common to all; Death spares no dignity;
>
> Death is life to the devout, perpetual punishment to the wicked.
>
> We shall go without delay, but at an hour we do not know;
>
> For life is brief, fleeting, perishable, slight.
>
> Behold, we know well enough that we cannot escape;
>
> But what shall be the end? A worm, and then ashes.
>
> This strong knight shone greatly among his lords.
>
> Yet, now dead, may he rest in peace. Amen.]

**1121. 15. 12. 21.**

Henry, king of the English, was at Christmas at Brampton with Theobald, count of Blois, his nephew. Afterwards, at Windsor, he married Adeliza, daughter of the duke of Louvain, for the sake of her goodness and beauty. When the king was at Easter at Berkeley, he was crowned with his new queen at London at Pentecost. In summer, while he was marching with [Col. 0438C] an army into Wales, the Welsh humbly came to meet him and were reconciled with him according to the greatness of his desire.

**1122. 16. 13. 22.**

(HUNT. VII.) Henry was at Christmas at Norwich, Easter at Northampton, and Pentecost at Windsor; then at London and Kent. Afterwards he went into Northumberland to Durham. Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury, and John, bishop of Bath, died.

**1123. 17. 14. 23.**

(Ibid.) Henry, king of the English, was at Christmas at Dunstable and then went to Berkhamsted. From there the king went to Woodstock, a remarkable place where he had created a dwelling-place [Col. 0438D] for men and beasts. There [Col. 0439A] Robert, bishop of Lincoln, closed his last day. Hence:

> Robert, glory of bishops, whom surviving fame
>
> Shall grant to be perpetuated, dies not to perish.
>
> On the eleventh of deceitful January he left the dreams of the world,
>
> And, awakening, lives in the true everlasting way.

Afterwards, at the feast of the Purification, the king gave the archbishopric of Canterbury to William de Corbeil, formerly prior at Chich. At Easter, at Winchester, he gave the bishopric of Lincoln to Alexander, a venerable man and nephew of Roger, bishop of Salisbury. The king also gave the bishopric of Bath to Geoffrey, the queen’s chancellor. About Pentecost he crossed the sea.

In the same year Hugh de Montfort had completed an exceedingly strong castle in that place. When the king demanded it, Hugh refused to surrender it at his wife’s urging; she was the sister of Waleran, count of Meulan, who had already left the king after the quarrel became open. The king besieged and captured that castle. [Col. 0439B] (Ibid.) He then besieged Pont-Audemer and captured the count’s castle. Then he took Brionne [Note: [Col. 0439D] Brionne.], though not so easily. The king stationed his nobles with a great multitude of knights in several places in Normandy. This war severely afflicted the country.

(Ibid.) Pope Calixtus held a council at Reims [Note: [Col. 0439D] A.D. 1119.], attended by Louis, king of the French. Later in the same year, in November, the same pope came to Normandy to speak with Henry, king of the English. The great king and the great priest spoke together in the castle of Gisors. Calixtus had succeeded Gelasius; before becoming pope, Gelasius was called John of Gaeta, had been Pope Paschal’s chancellor, and many learned letters had flowed from his mouth. [Col. 0439C]

King Henry built around the tower at Rouen—which Richard, the first duke of the Normans, had built as a palace for himself—a high, broad wall with battlements, and within that wall he provided buildings suitable for a royal residence. He added to the tower itself the battlements that it lacked. In this tower is a window called Conan’s Leap, because from it Henry had caused a very wealthy traitor to the city of Rouen, named Conan, to be thrown down. Conan wished to hand the city over to the men of William, king of the English [Note: [Col. 0439D] A.D. 1090; see Orderic Vitalis, p. 690.]; but he was forestalled by the loyal followers of Duke Robert, [Col. 0439D] especially by Robert’s brother Henry, who then supported the duke’s party and consequently punished Conan with a fitting death.

Henry also built a high tower in Caen castle, and raised the wall of that castle, which his father had built, to a greater height. But he left untouched the wall around the Bourg, as it had been made by his father, King William. He likewise marvellously strengthened with tower and walls the castle called Arques [Note: [Col. 0439D] Arques.]; and he did the same at Gisors, Falaise, Argentan [Note: [Col. 0439D] Argentan.], Exmes [Note: [Col. 0439D] Hiemes.], Domfront [Note: [Col. 0439D] Domfront.], Ambrières [Note: [Col. 0440D] Ambrières, between Domfront and Mayenne.], the castle of Vire, and Vaure [Note: [Col. 0440D] Vaure.]. He likewise built the tower of Vernon. On the eve of St Martin there was a great thunderstorm and hail of extraordinary size.

(FULCHER.) Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, was captured by a certain emir Balak, who in the preceding year had also captured Joscelin of Turbessel, count of Edessa, and his kinsman Waleran.

**1124. Henry 18. Louis 15. Henry I 24.**

[Note: [Col. 0439D] At the beginning of this year manuscript 2 adds: “The church of Savigny was dedicated on the Kalends of June in honour of the Holy Trinity, having been begun by Abbot Vitalis and completed as far as the rear choir, then finished by Abbot Geoffrey. Five bishops attended this dedication: Turgis, bishop of Avranches; Richard, bishop of Coutances; Richard, bishop of Bayeux; John, bishop of Sées; and Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans.”]

(HUNT. VII.) Henry, king of the English, was happily [Col. 0440B] glorified. For William de Tancarville, his chamberlain, fighting with several other barons in set battle, captured Waleran, count of Meulan, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April—then still quite young, yet a knight strong in arms—together with his brother-in-law Hugh de Montfort, Hugh son of Gervase, and many other men of great valour and famous name, in the valley near Bourgthéroulde [Note: [Col. 0440D] The borough of Turold, now Bourgthéroulde, near Rouen.], on the road to the fortification of the castle of Vatteville. King Henry was then at Caen; on hearing the news he could not believe it until he saw them with his own eyes. They were therefore handed over to the king and put in prison, and so that great division and destruction of the country came to an end.

(FULCHER.) Tyre was captured, which modern people call Sagitta. Sidon, its neighbouring city, is now called Sur by its inhabitants, and is a metropolis. When Tyre had been taken, a quarrel arose concerning it between the patriarchs of Jerusalem and Antioch. The patriarch of Antioch asserted that in ancient times Tyre had been subject to his church; the patriarch of Jerusalem relied upon the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. If you wish to hear or read about the offices and privileges of these patriarchs of Jerusalem and Antioch, and the settlement of this dispute, consult the first year or thereabouts after Jerusalem was captured by the Christians. [Col. 0440C]

(Ep. Cruc. [Note: [Col. 0440D] That is, the *Epistle of the Crusaders*, published in *Monumenta SS.*, III, 14. Robert altered the order of words but retained almost all the words themselves.]) Antioch is a most beautiful and strongly fortified city, most wealthy in abundant revenues. Within it are four fairly high mountains, and upon one of them, namely the highest, stands a castle overlooking the whole city. [Col. 0440D] The city below is suitably built and surrounded by a double wall. The inner wall is spacious and rises into the air, built and joined of large squared stones. In the structure of this wall [Col. 0441A] are four hundred and fifty towers, with beautiful and elegant walls and defensive battlements. The outer wall is not so high, but is nonetheless admirably handsome. The city contains three hundred and forty churches. Owing to its great primacy it has a patriarch, to whose patriarchate 153 bishops are subject. To the east it is enclosed by four mountains. To the west a river called Pharfar flows past the city walls. Eighty-five kings raised, embellished, and ennobled it in founding it; the greatest and first among them was Antiochus, from whose name Antioch is called.

(V. Wilh.) Lord William of pious memory, the third abbot of the church of Bec, died: a glorious man of honourable life. In the twenty-fifth year of his age he became a monk of the aforesaid place; after spending fifteen years in private monastic life, he succeeded the venerable Anselm in governing that abbey. Having governed it vigorously for thirty years and a half, less six days, he departed from the world at about the seventieth year of his age and almost the forty-sixth of his monastic profession, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May. [Col. 0441B] We have resolved that his epitaph should not be passed over in silence:

> Beneath this tomb is covered William, the third abbot,
>
> Who was outstanding, wise, and devout;
>
> Sighing for heaven and leaving all worldly things,
>
> Bare of possessions, he followed Christ with devoted mind.
>
> His talent, excellence of character, and splendour of birth
>
> Made him dear and venerable to all.
>
> [Col. 0441C] He bore an appearance and life worthy of command;
>
> He always maintained purity of heart and body.
>
> For thirty-three years he increased and ruled Bec,
>
> A gentle lord to subjects, stern toward the proud.
>
> When he had reached his seventy-sixth year,
>
> Bringing his life to its end, he rested in peace.
>
> Then the Ram loses the bright companionship of Phoebus,
>
> And the sixteenth day of April was dawning.
>
> May God grant him to ascend the eternal kingdom,
>
> That he may reign for ever among the angelic hosts.

The devout Boso succeeded him, exceptionally learned in the New and Old Testaments, a man admirable in knowledge and incomparable in teaching (cf. H. Henr.). Divine power had moreover bestowed upon him such grace that no one, however sad and in need of counsel, came to him [Col. 0441D] without immediately departing from him joyful and advised. Beloved by God and pleasing to men, he was very intimate with Henry, king of the English, because the king had found in him true religion, remarkable holiness, and incomparable counsel. Though he was burdened by almost continual illness, through the Lord—or rather, as we believe, God acting for him—he nevertheless abundantly supplied everything necessary, as need required, to his community and to visitors.

(HUNT. VII.) In the same year Theulf, bishop of Worcester, and Ernulf, bishop of Rochester, died.

**1125. Henry 19. Louis 16. Henry I 25.**

(Ibid.) Henry, king of the English, was in Normandy, [Col. 0442A] and there gave the bishopric of Worcester to Simon, the queen’s clerk. He also gave the bishopric of Chichester to Sifrid, abbot of Glastonbury. William, archbishop of Canterbury, gave the bishopric of Rochester to John, his archdeacon. At Easter John of Crema, a Roman cardinal, came down to England and, travelling through bishoprics and abbeys not without great gifts, held a solemn council at London at the Nativity of St Mary.

Emperor Henry died, who had married Matilda, daughter of Henry, king of the English. It is worth hearing how severe Henry, king of the English, was toward wrongdoers. He had almost all the moneyers of all England mutilated and the right hands that had committed the crime cut off, because they had secretly debased the coinage. This was the dearest year of all in England: a horse-load of grain sold for six shillings. Lothair succeeded Emperor Henry.

After the death of Alexander, king of the Scots, his brother David succeeded him, a man of great holiness and piety. He married the daughter of the count of Galloway and Judith, the king’s cousin; and he held the two counties of Northampton and Huntingdon, which Count Simon of Senlis had possessed with the aforesaid woman. She bore him a son named Henry and two daughters, Claricia and Hodierna. [Col. 0442B]

**1126. Lothair 1. 17. 26.**

(Ibid.) Henry, king of the English, remained in Normandy at Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost. Having confirmed agreements with the princes of France such as befitted a most glorious king, he returned to England about the feast of St Michael. [Col. 0442C]

(H. Henr.) He brought with him his daughter, the Empress Matilda, widowed, as was said above, from so great a man. Though they wished gladly to keep her as their lady in that country, she refused.

(HUNT. VII.) Robert, bishop of Chester, died. Pope Calixtus died [Note: [Col. 0441D] 24 December 1124.]; Odo, bishop of Ostia, succeeded him and was called Honorius, the 167th pope.

**1127. 2. 18. 27.**

(HUNT. VII.) Henry, king of the English, held his court at Christmas at Windsor, then went to London. In Lent and at Easter he was at Woodstock, where a messenger told him: “Charles, count of Flanders, most beloved by you, has been murdered by his nobles in a monstrous act of treachery in the church at Bruges. The king of the French has given Flanders to William, your nephew and enemy. Now greatly strengthened, he has punished all Charles’s traitors with various torments.” [Col. 0442D]

Troubled by these matters, the king held a council at Rogationtide in London; and William, archbishop of Canterbury, likewise held one in the same town at Westminster. (H. Henr. 25.) When the king was at Winchester at Pentecost, he sent his daughter, the Empress, into Normandy, betrothed to Geoffrey, son of Fulk, count of Anjou and later king of Jerusalem: a woman powerful in character, kindly to all, generous in alms, a friend of religion, of honourable life, and a lover of the Church, by the abundance of whose benefactions the church of Bec shines in no small measure. By her Geoffrey himself fathered three sons, Henry, Geoffrey [Note: [Col. 0443] “Graufridum,” E.], and William. [Col. 0443A]

(HUNT.) In August the king came to Normandy after his daughter. Richard, bishop of London, had died; the king gave his bishopric to Gilbert Universalis, a most learned man. Richard, bishop of Hereford, also died.

**1128. Lothair 3. Louis 19. Henry I 28.**

(Ibid.) Henry, the wisest king, remaining in Normandy, entered France in hostility because the king of the French supported his nephew and enemy. [Col. 0443B] Remaining at Espartly for eight days, as safely as though he were in his own kingdom, he compelled King Louis not to send assistance to the count of Flanders. This accomplished, King Henry returned to Normandy.

A certain Duke Thierry came from Germany, laying claim to Flanders and having certain Flemish nobles with him; this was at King Henry’s instigation. Count William of Flanders came against him with his battle-lines drawn up. A fierce battle followed. Count William, though his men were few, alone made up their numbers by valour beyond estimation. Covered in enemy blood, he cleft the hostile columns with his lightning sword. The enemies were terrified by the strength [Col. 0443C] of his youthful arm and given to flight. But while the victorious count was besieging an enemy castle, which was to surrender the next day, he died, by God’s will, from a small wound in the hand. This most noble young man gained eternal fame in a short lifetime. Hence:

> That peerless man fell, whose back no arrow knew,
>
> Whose feet could not know flight.
>
> He was nothing but lightning whenever the occasion demanded;
>
> And if not lightning, he was like lightning.

Hugh of Payns, master of the knights of the Temple of Jerusalem, came to England and took many with him to Jerusalem, including Fulk, count of Anjou, the future king. Ralph Flambard, bishop of Durham, and William Giffard, bishop of Winchester, died. (A. Roth.) Geoffrey, archbishop of Rouen, died [Col. 0443D] in December. Thierry of Alsace succeeded William as count of Flanders.

[Note: [Col. 0443] Here another hand—the same one as at the year 1151, not Robert’s—adds: James, cleric of Venice, translated certain books of Aristotle from Greek into Latin and commented upon them: namely, the *Topics*, the *Prior* and *Posterior Analytics*, and the *Sophistical Refutations*, although an older translation of the same books already existed. This is absent in 2, 7b, and 8d.]

**1129. 4. 19. 29.**

(HUNT. VII.) Henry, king of the English, fortunate in almost every good thing, having pacified all matters in France, Flanders, Normandy, Brittany, Maine, and Anjou, returned joyfully to England. He held a great council at London on the Kalends of August concerning the prohibition of priests’ wives. [Col. 0444A] Present at that council were William, archbishop of Canterbury; Thurstan, archbishop of York; Alexander, bishop of Lincoln; Roger of Salisbury; Gilbert of London; John of Rochester; Sifrid of Selsey; Geoffrey of Bath; Simon of Worcester; Everard of Norwich; Bernard of St Davids; and Hervey, first bishop of Ely. For the bishops of Winchester, Durham, Chester, and Hereford had died.

Those whom Hugh of Payns, mentioned above, had taken with him to Jerusalem fared badly. The inhabitants of the Holy Land had offended God by various crimes. As is written in the books of Moses and Kings, crimes do not long go unpunished in those places. On the eve of St Nicholas, many Christians were defeated by a few pagans, although previously the opposite had customarily occurred. During the siege of Damascus, when a great part of the Christians had gone out to seek provisions, the pagans marvelled that many and very strong Christians were fleeing like women; pursuing them, they killed countless numbers. [Col. 0444B] God Himself pursued in that night with a storm of snow and cold those who had sought safety in flight among the mountains, so that scarcely anyone escaped.

In the same year Louis, king of the French, had his son Philip raised to the kingship.

(Gem. VII, 30.) I shall recount, perhaps to the reader’s pleasure, the successions in Apulia. The first ruler over the Normans in Apulia, while they were still newcomers and mercenaries of Waimar, duke of Salerno, was Tustin, surnamed Scistellus. When he died from the poison of a serpent that he himself had killed, Ranulf succeeded him in the principate; he founded the city of Aversa. His son Richard, prince of Capua, succeeded him. When Richard died, he left the same principate to his son Jordan; Jordan in turn left it to his son, the younger Richard. [Col. 0444C]

After some time Drogo of Hauteville, son of Tancred of Hauteville, became prince of the Normans in Apulia. Count Wazo of Naples killed him by treachery in the church of St Lawrence. His brother Humphrey succeeded him and subjected all Apulia to the Normans. At his death he entrusted his son Abelard, together with the duchy of Apulia, to his brother Robert, surnamed Guiscard for his cunning. Robert surpassed his brothers—all dukes or counts—in courage and intelligence. [Col. 0444D] For he subjected Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily to himself; and, having crossed the sea, he invaded the greater part of Greece and Africa. He did many good things and restored many bishoprics and abbeys.

(Ibid. 43.) Having set aside his first wife, a Norman woman, because of consanguinity, by whom he had had a son named Bohemond, Robert married the eldest daughter of Guaimar, prince of Salerno, with the support of Gisulf, brother of that girl. Her younger [Col. 0445A] sister married Jordan, prince of Capua. At Robert’s death, his son Roger, born of his second wife, succeeded to the duchy of Apulia; by that wife Robert had begotten three sons and five daughters. When that Roger and his sons after him had failed, his cousin Roger, son of Roger, count of Sicily, brother of Robert Guiscard, alone possessed both Apulia and Sicily. He was made king in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1130, because of the dispute between the two popes then elected at Rome. Anacletus, who was in Rome, granted him permission to be adorned with the royal diadem.

Let him who desires to hear marvels listen: there came into Normandy from distant regions an innumerable multitude of birds. Flying in flocks and occupying immense stretches of air, [Col. 0445B] they fought one another horribly, perhaps foreshadowing the countless evils that would come after King Henry’s death.

**1130. Lothair 5. Louis 20. Henry I 30.**
Honorius the pope died. He was succeeded by Gregory, cardinal-priest [Note: [Col. 0445] Thus at first in E., and thence in 7b, 8d. Later corrected—by an unknown hand—to *deacon*. Thus 8e] of the Roman Church, called Pope Innocent II. At the same time another cardinal, namely Peter Leonis, was elected—or rather thrust in—through the sedition of the raging populace and the violence of his own kin; he was called Anacletus by the people. Both lived for nearly eight years. Anacletus remained in the city because of his brothers, powerful men who held the lordship of the Castle of Crescentius. [Col. 0445C] Innocent, however, crossed to the regions beyond the mountains. Hence that one-line verse:

> Peter holds Rome; Gregory, the whole world.

(HUNT. VII.) Henry, king of the English, was at Winchester for Christmas and at Woodstock for Easter. There Geoffrey de Clinton was accused and falsely defamed for treason against the king. At Rogationtide he was at Canterbury for the dedication of the new church. In September he crossed into Normandy, and was at Bec for the Nativity of St Mary; he brought with him Hugh, newly elected archbishop of Rouen, formerly abbot of Reading. Hugh was consecrated as the fiftieth archbishop of Rouen on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, a Sunday, by Richard, bishop of Bayeux, together with his fellow bishops, in the church of St Ouen. [Col. 0445D] [Note: [Col. 0445] The following, as far as “the torch of the year,” Robert himself wrote in an erasure; it is absent from 2. In its place 4, 7b, and 8d have: “In the same year Arageis, earl of Moray, entered Scotland with Malcolm, the illegitimate son of Alexander, brother of King David, who had reigned before him, and with five thousand armed men; he wished to subject the whole region to himself. King David was then attending the court of the king of England; but Edward, his cousin and commander of the army, met him with an army, killed Earl Arageis, overthrew, captured, and put his troops to flight. Then he entered Moray, deprived of defender and lord; and henceforth, with God’s help, the entire extensive duchy of that region was subjected through Edward to the devout David.”]

After Aragois, earl of Moray, had been killed, David, king of Scotland, thereafter possessed that earldom. Gratian, bishop of Chiusi, compiled very useful decrees from decrees, canons, [Note: [Col. 0445] *singers* in E.] doctors, and Roman laws, sufficient for deciding all [Col. 0446A] ecclesiastical causes commonly brought before the Roman court and other ecclesiastical courts. Master Omnibonus, bishop of Verona, formerly his pupil, later abridged these. After Bohemond, prince of Antioch, had been killed, Raymond, brother of William, count of Poitou, married his wife and became prince of Antioch.

### 1131. 6. 21. 31.

(HUNT. VII.) After Christmas Henry, king of the English, received Pope Innocent at Chartres, refusing to submit to Anacletus. (H. Henr. 30.) After Easter that pope came to Rouen and was honourably received by King Henry; by Henry’s aid he was received throughout all Gaul. (HUNT. VII.) Later, in summer, King Henry returned to England, bringing his daughter with him. [Col. 0446B] Thus at the Nativity of St Mary a great assembly was held at Northampton. All the English magnates having gathered, it was decided that his daughter should be restored to her husband, the count of Anjou, who demanded her. When the king’s daughter was subsequently sent to her husband, she was received with a splendour worthy of so great a woman.

After Easter Reginald, abbot of Ramsey, founder of the new church, died. At the beginning of winter Hervey, first bishop of Ely, died. In the same year, in October, Philip, son of the king of the French and already made king, was riding a spirited horse in play when a pig crossed his path. The horse’s feet struck it as it ran; the new king was killed and, his neck broken, expired. Behold an unprecedented [Col. 0446C] event, worthy of astonishment! Behold how great a height was so lightly and so quickly reduced to nothing! In the same month Pope Innocent consecrated Philip’s brother Louis, a child of quite tender age, king at Reims, while the pope was holding a council there on the feast of Crispin and Crispinian, a Sunday. Loving God and the Church, he lived a most honourable life.

### 1132. 7. 22. 32.

(Ib.) King Henry was at Dunstable for Christmas and at Woodstock for Easter. After Easter an assembly was held at London, where several matters were discussed, especially the dispute between the bishop of St David’s and the bishop of Glamorgan concerning the boundaries of their dioceses. Baldwin II, third king of Jerusalem, died; he was succeeded by Fulk, count of Anjou, who had married the daughter of the aforesaid Baldwin, [Note: [Col. 0445D] Melisende.] and by her begot two sons, Baldwin and Amalric.

A learned cleric, grievously distressed by pain, [Note: [Col. 0445D] Note the verses; our author appears to have excerpted them from a longer poem.] weeping and lamenting day and night like a woman in labour, one [Col. 0447A] night, through pain neither awake nor asleep, saw the Virgin, Mother of the Lord, standing beside him. Because he had invoked her, she was present with him, clothed in white garments appropriate to virgins. > Stretching out her hand, she made wholly sound him who had always been distressed by the more pressing pain.

### 1133. Lothair 8. Louis 23. Henry I 33.

(HUNT. VII.) Henry, king of the English, was ill at Windsor for Christmas. At the beginning of Lent an assembly met in London concerning the bishops of St David’s and Glamorgan, and concerning the dispute between the archbishop and the bishop of Lincoln. At Easter the king was at Oxford, in the new hall. At Rogationtide another assembly was held at Winchester concerning the aforesaid matters. [Col. 0447B] After Pentecost the king gave the bishopric of Ely to Nigel, and that of Durham [Note: [Col. 0447D] *Dumelmie* in E.] to Geoffrey the chancellor. A little earlier he had given Winchester to Henry, abbot of Glastonbury, [Note: [Col. 0447D] Glastonbury.] his nephew, who nevertheless held the abbey together with the bishopric until his death; Hereford to Robert de Bethune, a Fleming and a religious man; and Chester to Roger, archdeacon of Lincoln, nephew of Geoffrey de Clinton.

His predecessor had been Robert surnamed “Peccatum” (“Sin”); an earlier predecessor was Robert the Norman of Limesey. More intent upon secular than divine affairs, he obtained Coventry monastery from King Henry and established there the chief see of the Mercians. That bishopric therefore has [Col. 0447C] to this day three seats: Lichfield, Chester, and Coventry.

(V. Lanf. 12.) In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1075, in the ninth year of William, king of the English, a council was assembled in London under the presidency of Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury and primate of the whole island of Britain. Sitting with him were venerable men: Thomas, archbishop of York; the other bishops and abbots of that island; and many persons of the religious order. There many beneficial ordinances were established for clergy and laity alike. By royal generosity and synodal authority permission was also granted to three bishops to transfer their sees from villages to cities: namely, to Herman, from Sherborne to Salisbury; to Stigand, from Selsey to Chichester; [Col. 0447D] and to Peter, from Lichfield to Chester.

The cases of some who still lived in villages or hamlets were deferred until the king could be heard: namely, Remigius of Dorchester, Giso of Hermeacensis, and Hefalt of Wells. By the king’s generosity and Lanfranc’s persuasion, the first was later transferred to Lincoln, the second to Bath, and the third to Thetford. Elfat, formerly chaplain to King William, was succeeded at Thetford by William de Beaufeu, a man of noble birth and chancellor of that king. When he died shortly afterwards, Herbert, a high-spirited [Col. 0448A] and very learned man, succeeded him by the gift of William Rufus. He had been a monk and prior of Fécamp, then, after his father, abbot of Ramsey, and finally bishop of Thetford. He bought for much money a great part of the town of Norwich; after houses had been uprooted and the site levelled over a vast area, he built, in an excellent place above the River Wensum, a most beautiful church in honour of the supreme Trinity, in memory of the monastery of which he had been a monk. He also added very large buildings necessary for the use of monks, whom he established there to serve God in that church, which he made the mother church and principal see of the bishopric of Norfolk.

(HUNT. VII.) King Henry also created a new bishopric at Carlisle, on the borders of England and Scotland, and made its first bishop [Col. 0448B] Æthelwold, prior of the regular canons of St Oswald, to whom he was accustomed to confess his sins. This bishop established regular canons in the church of his see. (A. Roth.) The sun underwent an eclipse on 4 Non. August [2 August]. On the same day King Henry crossed the sea into Normandy, never to return; many murmured that this was because of the sign that had occurred. At this time too a silver vein had been discovered near Carlisle, and the prospectors who sought it in the bowels of the earth paid King Henry five hundred pounds annually. In March Henry of Le Mans was born, first-born son of Count Geoffrey and the Empress Matilda.

### 1134. 9. 24. 34.

[Col. 0448C] Geoffrey, second son of Geoffrey of Anjou, was born at Rouen in May, at Pentecost. His mother, the Empress Matilda, was made ill by the difficulty of the birth, even to the point of despair. (H. Henr. 28.) Here her wisdom was shown by clear indications. For with a hand as generous as it was devout, she distributed her treasures among orphans, widows, other poor persons, and especially churches and monasteries. Above all other monasteries she enriched Bec with a more abundant blessing of gold, silver, precious stones, and manifold church ornaments. (Ib. 29.) She also asked her father that she might be buried there. When he at first refused, saying that it was more fitting for her to be buried at Rouen, where her ancestors—Rollo [Col. 0448D] and his son William, I mean—rested, she said that her soul would never be happy unless her wish in this matter alone were fulfilled. Her father granted what she asked; but by the Lord’s will she was restored to health.

(HUNT. VII.) Throughout this year King Henry remained in Normandy, rejoicing in his grandsons Henry and Geoffrey. In the same year King Henry gave the bishopric of Bayeux to Richard, son of Robert, count of Gloucester, and the bishopric of Avranches to Richard de Beaufeu. Robert, duke of the Normans, eldest son of King William who had subdued [Col. 0449A] England, died and was buried at Gloucester.

### 1135. Lothair 10. Louis 25. Henry I 35.

The moon underwent an eclipse on 4 Non. January [2 January]. (A. Roth.) A violent and terrible wind arose, greatly terrifying human minds, throwing down towers and houses and uprooting woods, on the vigil of the apostles Simon and Jude [Note: [Col. 0449D] 27 October], perhaps portending the death of the great prince Henry and the ruin of the whole country.

(HUNT. VII.) Throughout this year King Henry remained continuously in Normandy and often planned to return to England, never to come back again; but his daughter detained him through the various quarrels arising for several reasons between the king and the count of Anjou, namely through the contrivances of his daughter. These provocations stirred the king to anger and bitterness of spirit; some said that they were the natural cause of his decline, and later of his death. Thus, having returned from hunting at Saint-Denis in the Forest of Lyons, [Col. 0449B] the king ate lampreys, which always harmed him and which he always loved. Though his physician forbade him to eat them, the king did not submit to sound advice, as the saying goes:

> We strive for what is forbidden and ever desire what is denied.

This eating, therefore, bringing on most pernicious humours and violently provoking similar ones, lethally chilled his aged body and caused sudden and extreme disturbance. Nature resisted this by raising an acute fever, to dissolve the onslaught [Col. 0449C] of the gravest matter. But when he could no longer resist by any strength, the great king died on the first day of December, having reigned thirty-five years and four months.

(H. Henr. 33.)

> How little power accomplishes, how great wealth amounts to nothing,  
> King Henry proves. While living, the king had been  
> a friend of peace; indeed, richer than all others,  
> he had ruled the western people whom he had set above all.  
> Father of his people, king and protector of the weak—  
> while that good man falls, the wicked rage, oppress, and burn.  
> Let England mourn on this side, Normandy’s people weep on that.  
> Henry, when you die, peace dies; now grief belongs to both.  
> When a harsh fever, on the first night of December,  
> stripped the world bare, it multiplied the world’s evils.

[Col. 0449D]

> Outstanding in judgement, wealth, access, and fitting severity;  
> wondrous—more than can be told—in strength, long-suffering toward the guilty;  
> excellent, rich, not difficult of approach, reverenced:  
> here lies King Henry, once peace and the glory of the world.

(Ib. 31.) The names of the castles which King Henry newly built in their entirety in Normandy, on the border of that province, are these: Drincourt, Neufchâtel-sur-Epte, Verneuil, Nonancourt, Bonne-Moulins, [Col. 0450A] Mont-Colmie, Pont-Urson, the castle of Saint-Denis in the Lyons, Le Vaudreuil [Note: [Col. 0450D] Vaudreuil. BOUQ.], the towers of Évreux, the towers of Alençon, and the towers of Coutances. [Note: [Col. 0449] “the tower of St John near Mont-Saint-Michel and several others which we mentioned above” are added by 4, 7b, and 8d. In those witnesses the following words, “He made—many,” are absent. Robert corrected “He made—the matter of the canons” in an erasure about 1185.]

(Ib.) For in Normandy and England he founded many monasteries: Reading monastery; the monastery of regular canons at Cirencester; the monastery of Le Pré near Rouen; and the monastery of Mortemer. He also performed many other works of piety, which we have enumerated more fully in the book of his life.

(HUNT. VIII.) After King Henry died at Saint-Denis in the Forest of Lyons, on 4 Non. December [2 December], his body was brought to the city of Rouen by the archbishop, bishops, counts, and barons, many of whom had assembled. In the church of St Mary it was opened; his heart, tongue, [Col. 0450B] and entrails were buried before the altar in the monastery of Le Pré. The remainder of the body, liberally sprinkled with salt, was wrapped in hides and carried to Caen. It was placed beside his father’s tomb in the monastery of St Stephen, until those conducting his funeral could secure suitable passage across the sea. Within twelve days of Christmas, therefore, it was buried in Reading Abbey, dedicated to St Mary, which he himself had built from its foundations and enriched with ornaments and estates.

Stephen, his nephew and already king, attended his funeral, as did William, archbishop of Canterbury, and other magnates of the realm. For Stephen, while in his county of Boulogne, immediately upon hearing of his uncle’s death, crossed most swiftly into England; he was a man of great energy [Col. 0450C] and boldness. Although he had sworn an oath of fealty for the English kingdom to King Henry’s daughter, nevertheless [Note: [Col. 0449] Before and after *nevertheless*, something has been erased in E.; 7b, 8d: “nevertheless, relying on the strength and prudence of the kingdom”; 2 and Henry of Huntingdon: “nevertheless, relying on the strength and impudence of the kingdom.”] he seized the crown by his audacity.

William, archbishop of Canterbury, who had first sworn the oath to the king’s daughter, blessed him as king and did not live a year afterwards. Roger the Great, bishop of Salisbury, who had been second to do the same and had surpassed all others in this, bestowed the crown on him and the strength of his support. Hence later, by God’s just judgement, he was seized and tortured by the very man whom he had made king, and met a pitiable destruction. But why delay? It is plain what became of all who had taken the oath, bishops and earls alike.

(H. Henr.) Upon hearing of [Col. 0450D] King Henry’s death, the count of Anjou and his wife Matilda, daughter of that king, obtained without any difficulty the castles of Normandy: Domfront, Argentan, Exmes, Ambrières, Gorron, and Mont-Colmie. The count granted the three last named for the time being to Juhel of Mayenne, on condition that he faithfully assist him in acquiring the inheritance of his wife and sons. For Juhel said [Col. 0451A] that those towns lay in his own territory. All the strongholds of William Talvas, count of Ponthieu, which he held in Normandy and which King Henry had held in his hand before his death, were also restored to the aforesaid count; Henry had expelled William from them.

For this reason there had been some discord between the king, the count, and the empress before the king’s death, because he was unwilling to restore William’s fief. There was another and greater cause of their discord: the king refused to render fealty, when it was demanded, to his daughter and her husband for all the strongholds of Normandy and England. They demanded this for their sons, who were King Henry’s lawful heirs. Count Geoffrey, however, graciously restored [Col. 0451B] those same strongholds to William.

After the king’s death, as stated above, the Norman magnates immediately sent for Count Theobald, so that he might come and take Normandy. He accordingly came to Rouen and afterwards to Les Andelys on the Saturday of the Ember fast in the tenth month [Note: [Col. 0451D] December. BOUQ.]. The next day, while he and Robert, count of Gloucester, were in conference, a messenger came from England saying that his brother Stephen was already king. On hearing this, the count of Gloucester surrendered Falaise Castle, which he held, after first carrying away a great part of King Henry’s treasure, recently brought from England.

### 1136. Lothair 11. Louis 26. Stephen 1.

(HUNT. VIII.) King Stephen led a great army [Col. 0451C] into Scotland, and King David made peace with him. Yet he did not do him homage, because he had been the first of the laymen to swear to the empress; but Henry, David’s son, did homage to King Stephen. At Rogationtide, when it was reported that the king was dead, Hugh Bigod seized Norwich Castle and surrendered it to the king. Likewise the king took Badington Castle because its lord Robert had revolted from him. Then he besieged Exeter, held by Baldwin de Redvers. When the castle was surrendered, the king took the Isle of Wight from Baldwin and exiled him from England. In August, at Argentan, William, third son of Count Geoffrey, was born.

(H. Henr.) On the vigil of Epiphany a very great wind arose. William, archbishop of Canterbury, died, and [Col. 0451D] the archbishopric of Canterbury remained vacant for some time. Meanwhile many evils multiplied, not only in England but also in Normandy and many other places.

(H. Henr. 42.) The lord Boso, of pious memory, fourth abbot of Bec monastery, died: a man of great authority, renowned throughout the world, distinguished for wisdom, prudence, and especially the spirit of counsel. About the twenty-third year of his age he became a monk at Bec under St Anselm, abbot of that place. For twenty-six years he was a monk without office; then he was prior under Lord William, abbot and successor of the aforesaid Anselm, [Col. 0452A] for nine years. Elected by the whole community to succeed him as abbot, he ruled that abbey for twelve years and twelve days. He died on the night of the Nativity of St John the Baptist, that is, 8 Kalends of July [24 June], in the seventy-first year of his age and the forty-seventh of his monastic profession. [Note: [Col. 0451D] Compare the *Life of Boso* by Milo, after D’Achery’s edition of Lanfranc’s works.] A few days later Lord Theobald, then prior, a noble and worthy man, was elected abbot (H. Henr.).

> His struggle with the flesh ended, Boso, a man of Israel,  
> rested as abbot on the day when Zechariah’s son arose—  
> he than whom none greater is found  
> among all born of women.  
> By God’s mercy, on so glad a festival day,  
> may he enter paradise’s rest.  
> Abbot of Bec, whose speech was a sword,  
> [Col. 0452B] cutting away vice, by which destruction is dealt;  
> great Father Boso, a lion to the proud, a lamb to the meek,  
> sweet to the people, becomes ashes in this tomb;  
> he becomes ashes in this grave, he who, while he could live,  
> was by virtue both serpent and dove.  
> Therefore, seeing these verses, lest he be plunged in black Styx,  
> pour forth a prayer to the King, whom we believe  
> to be death’s death, and by whom every faithful person climbs to heaven;  
> may He, God who is there, mercifully grant him to be with Himself.

Count Theobald, nephew of King Henry, led by Robert, count of Leicester, besieged the bridge of St Peter and took it from Roger of Tosny (June). (H. Henr.) In the same year several leading men of England died: William, archbishop of Canterbury; [Col. 0452C] John, bishop of Rochester; William, bishop of Exeter; Richard son of Gilbert; Robert son of Richard, his uncle; Richard son of Baldwin, his cousin; and the second William de Warenne, count of Surrey. In September Geoffrey, count of Anjou, led a very great army into Normandy as far as Les Andelys, when that town was burned. On his return he took Le Sap [Note: [Col. 0452D] Le Sap, between the streams Touques and Charentonne.]. In the same week Waleran, count of Meulan, captured Roger of Tosny at Acquigny while he was engaged in plundering and burning.

### 1137. 12. 27. 2.

In Lent Stephen, king of the English, crossed into Normandy and besieged and captured Lisieux, which Raoul the chamberlain held. He then besieged [Col. 0452D] Grandselve. He also conferred at Évreux with his brother Count Theobald and covenanted to pay him two thousand marks of silver each year, because Count Theobald resented that Stephen, who was younger, had taken the crown which, as he said, was due to himself. When Grandselve fortress had been surrendered, King Stephen made peace with the king of France. His son Eustace did homage to him for that part of Normandy adjoining the kingdom of France.

Thereafter, when Stephen wished to enter the territory of the count of Anjou, a great disturbance arose in his army at Livarot [Col. 0453A] over a single cask of wine, which a Fleming had taken from a squire, Hugh of Gournay. Thus great dissension arose between the Normans and the Flemings. The king therefore returned with his undertaking unfinished. Soon afterwards the count of Anjou led an army much larger than the one he had brought in the previous year. Yet, through messengers going between him and King Stephen, the duke again granted a truce for three years, on condition that the king should give him two thousand marks of silver annually; he immediately received the sum due for the first year. This truce lasted one year on both sides, that is, until the feast of St John in the following year. These matters completed, King Stephen returned to England at Advent.

[Col. 0453B] (1 August.) Louis the elder, king of the French, died, and was succeeded by his son Louis, who married Eleanor, daughter of the duke of Aquitaine; by her he begot two daughters. (3 December.) In the same year Lothair, emperor of the Romans, died. He was succeeded by Conrad, nephew of Henry IV, husband of the empress, who had ruled before Lothair. On the Kalends of August [1 August], when King Louis died, the monastery of Corbie was burned that night. In the same year such drought occurred that ponds and many rivers dried up; in many places the earth burned for a very long time; very many trees in woods and thickets withered and died; and they burned with no one setting them alight.

Theobald, elect of the church of Bec, a man of great worth and [Col. 0453C] learning, was blessed as abbot of that church at Rouen by Lord Hugh, the archbishop, with the willing agreement of the whole convent.

### 1138. Conrad 1. Louis 1. Stephen 3.

(HUNT. VIII.) Stephen [Note: [Col. 0453] Here 8b begins.] king of the English besieged Bedford at Christmas. When it had surrendered, he moved his army into Scotland. For David, king of the Scots, who had sworn to the daughter of King Henry, acted most abominably through his men under a pretext of holiness. They ripped open pregnant women and tore out their prematurely delivered unborn children; they mutilated priests upon altars and perpetrated many other evils. Whatever the Scots touched was filled with horror. There were women’s cries, old men’s wailing, dying men’s groans, and the despair of the living.

[Col. 0453D] King Stephen therefore rose up and burned and destroyed the southern parts of King David’s realm, David himself not daring to engage him. After Easter the wicked rage of traitors flared up. One Talebot held Hereford Castle in Wales against the king; the king recovered it through siege. Robert, earl of Gloucester, held Bristol and Sled against him; Ralph Lovel, Cary Castle; Painel, Ludlow Castle; William of Mohun, Dunster Castle; Robert of Nichol, Warham Castle; Eustace son of John, Malmesbury; and William son of Alan, Shrewsbury. [Col. 0454A] The king took the latter by force of arms and hanged some of those captured. Hearing this, Walkelin of Dover surrendered Dover Castle to the queen, who was besieging him.

While the king was occupied in the southern parts of England, David, king of the Scots, led an innumerable army into England. The magnates of northern England resisted him bravely, at the exhortation and command of Thurstan, archbishop of York, having set up the *standard*, that is, the royal ensign, at Northallerton. It is reported that twelve thousand Scots were killed there, besides those found and slain in fields and woods. The rest, with very little bloodshed, won a happy triumph. The leaders in this battle were William, earl of Albemarle, William Peverel of Nottingham, Walter Espec, and Ilbert de Lacy, whose brother alone among all the knights was killed there. When the outcome of this battle was reported to King Stephen, [Col. 0454B] he and all present rendered the greatest thanks to God. This battle was fought in August.

At Advent Alberic, legate of the Roman Church and bishop of Ostia, held a council at London. There, through the efforts of King Stephen and the queen, Theobald, abbot of Bec church, a most venerable man, became archbishop of Canterbury, two and a half years after becoming abbot. By his counsel the abbey of Bec remained without an abbot, under Richard de Beaufeu the prior, from Christmas or a little before until Pentecost, namely until Theobald himself should return from Rome.

[Col. 0454C] In the same year, in October, Geoffrey, count of Anjou, besieged Falaise for fifteen days with a great army; Robert, count of Gloucester, was with him, having made peace with him around the preceding Easter. In the same year the people of Exmes and Bayeux were subjected to him. [Note: [Col. 0453] “Geoffrey, second abbot of Savigny, died,” added in the margin of 2 by another hand of the thirteenth century.]

### 1139. 2. 2. 4.

(Ib.) Stephen, king of the English, [Note: [Col. 0453] 8b joins this year to the preceding one.] after Christmas captured Sled Castle by siege. Afterwards he went into Scotland, where, while he pursued the business of war with Mars and Vulcan as his commanders, the king of Scotland was compelled to make peace with him. Taking Henry, son of the king of the Scots, with him into England, he captured Ludlow, where Henry himself was nearly captured after being dragged from his horse by an iron hook; but the king splendidly pulled him back from the enemy. [Col. 0454D] Having completed this undertaking, he went to Oxford.

There an affair appeared, notorious for its infamy and unprecedented in every respect. The king forcibly seized in his court Roger, bishop of Salisbury, and his nephew Alexander, bishop of Lincoln, although they refused nothing that was right. He put Bishop Alexander in prison there, and took the bishop of Salisbury with him to the latter’s castle called Devizes, than which none within the bounds of Europe was more splendid. By starving him, and by putting a noose around the neck of his son, who had been chancellor, so that he might be hanged, he extorted the castle from him in this fashion, not sufficiently remembering [Col. 0455A] the benefits which that man had bestowed on him above all others at the beginning of his reign. Likewise he took Sherborne, which yielded little to Devizes in beauty. Taking the bishop’s treasures, he used them to purchase Constance, sister of Louis, king of France, for his son Eustace. On returning, the king acted similarly toward Bishop Alexander until they surrendered the most pleasant castle of Newark. Likewise Sleaford Castle was surrendered to him.

Then, quite shortly afterwards, the daughter of King Henry, who had been empress of Germany and to whom England had been bound by oath, and Robert, earl of Gloucester, her brother, crossed into England in August. They had been invited by William of Albini, who had married Eliz, formerly queen, who possessed the castle and earldom [Col. 0455B] of Arundel, which King Henry had given her as dower. They landed at Arundel, because they then had no other harbour. From there Count Robert, with ten knights and ten mounted archers, hurried through the midst of King Stephen’s land to Wallingford, and thence to Gloucester. He announced the empress’s arrival to Brian, son of the count, and to Miles of Gloucester. He had left her, with his wife and the other baggage, in Arundel Castle, where King Stephen besieged her, but afterwards permitted her to depart under an agreement for Bristol.

The aforesaid Roger, bishop of Salisbury, died, worn out by sorrow [Note: [Col. 0455] *memore* in E.] as well as old age. Pope Innocent held a council at Rome, attended by Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury.

[Col. 0455C] Lord Lethard, a man of great holiness and learning, born of the stock of Bec, was elected and appointed abbot of Bec church by the unanimous whole community. He was excellently educated in both Testaments, strong in counsel, gracious in speech, restrained in words, discerning in discipline, slow to rejoice in earthly things, always rejoicing in eternal things, loving the good and correcting the wicked. For the circumstances of the time he governed the flock entrusted to him most well, although in his time the country was troubled by continual storm. [Note: [Col. 0455] *memore* in E.]

### (Year 1140.)

Stephen [Note: [Col. 0455] “by the unanimous whole community—was troubled” is absent from 8b. After this, 2, 4, 7b, 8d, and Henry of Huntingdon begin a new year and count the following “King Stephen besieged the city of Lincoln,” etc., as 1141: 4. 4. 6., and so thereafter; this alone is correct. But E., with 8b, continues here in the same year and numbers the following “King Stephen besieged the city of Lincoln,” etc., as 1140: 3. 3. 5., and so on; from 1153 E6 agrees with them in the entry “Louis, king of the French,” etc. Although this is false, since the author himself, when examining manuscript E., did not correct the error, we too judged it should be left untouched, merely placing the correct numbers in the margin.] expelled Nigel, bishop of Ely, from his bishopric, because he was nephew of the bishop of Salisbury and had incurred from him hostility toward that bishop’s lineage. It is needless to say where he was at Christmas or Easter, for by then [Col. 0455D] the solemn courts and royal splendours inherited from ancient succession had entirely disappeared; the immense abundance of treasure had perished; there was no peace in the land; slaughter, burning, and plunder devastated everything; everywhere were cries, lamentation, and horror. [Note: [Col. 0455] “Stephen—everywhere” is absent from 7b.]

Amalric, count of Évreux, died and was succeeded by his brother Simon. [Col. 0456A] Raoul the chamberlain died and was succeeded by his son William. Henry, count of Eu, died and was succeeded by his son John. Thurstan, archbishop of York, died and was succeeded by William, treasurer of the same church. Audoin, bishop of Évreux, died in England and was succeeded by Rotrou, a religious man, adorned with good character and beloved by all, son of Henry, count of Warwick. Geoffrey, count of Anjou, besieged and afterwards destroyed Fontenay Castle in the district of Exmes, a fortress exceptionally strong both by art and by nature, because Robert Marmion, lord of that castle, held Falaise against him. Henry [Note: [Col. 0455D] Of Sully.] became abbot of Fécamp; he was nephew of King Stephen.

### 1140. Conrad 3. Louis 3. Stephen 5.

[Col. 0456B] (Year 1141.) [ibid.] King Stephen besieged the city of Lincoln shortly before Christmas; Ranulf, count of Chester, had seized its fortifications by stratagem. The king remained there until the Purification of St Mary. Then the aforesaid Ranulf brought with him Robert, son of King Henry, his ally, together with many magnates and most powerful knights, to raise the king’s siege. When this most powerful and daring count had scarcely crossed an almost impassable marsh, he attacked the king in battle that same day, after the battle-lines had been drawn up. He himself, a man of admirable courage, had formed the first line with his own men; the second consisted of those whom King Stephen had disinherited; the third, of the great duke Robert and his men.

Meanwhile King Stephen, tossed by waves of anxious care, heard Mass on so great a feast day (2 February). As, according to custom, he offered God a candle worthy of a king and placed it in the hands of Bishop Alexander, it broke. This was for the king a sign of contrition. The pyx also, containing the body of the Lord, fell upon the altar when its fastening broke, in the bishop’s presence. This too was for the king a sign of downfall. Therefore the most resolute king advanced and confidently arranged his battle-lines. On foot, he stationed the whole mass of armoured men closely around himself, their horses having been removed; he directed the counts, with their men, to fight on horseback in two battle-lines. But those mounted lines proved very small indeed, for the false and factional counts had brought only a few men with them. The royal battle-line, however, was exceedingly large, marked by only one banner—namely that of the king himself.

The beginning of the battle. The line of the disinherited men, which advanced first, struck the royal line—in which were Count Alan, the man of Meulan, Hugh count of East Anglia, Count Simon, and the man of Warenne—with such force that it was immediately scattered, as it were in the twinkling of an eye, and its division broke into three parts. [Col. 0457A] Some of them were killed, others captured, others fled. The line commanded by the count of Aumale and William of Ypres attacked the Welshmen advancing on the flank and put them to flight. But the line of the count of Chester attacked the aforesaid force, and it was scattered in a moment, like the first line. Thus all the king’s cavalry fled, including William of Ypres, a man of consular rank and great valour. Others who did not obey flight were captured.

A wondrous thing, exceedingly marvellous to many! Though King Stephen, roaring like a lion, remained alone on the field, no one dared approach him. Gnashing his teeth, foaming at the mouth like a boar, and striking down the foremost enemies with repeated blows of a certain double-headed axe, he was greatly admired by all. Oh, if there had been a hundred like him, they would have defended the field longer! Alone as he was, he scarcely yielded as prey.
