Thus Stephen, king of the English, was captured on the day of the Purification of St Mary, and was led miserably into Lincoln, devastated by the enemy. God’s judgement upon the king having thus been accomplished, he was brought to the Empress and placed under guard in the tower of Bristol.

Then the Empress was received as lady by all the English people, except the people of Kent, where the queen and William of Ypres resisted her with all their strength. The Empress was first received by the Roman legate, the bishop of Winchester, and soon afterwards by the Londoners. Yet, whether through the prompting of treacherous men or by God’s will, she was expelled by the Londoners; and she then ordered the king to be put in fetters. A few days later, having gathered forces with her uncle, the king of Scots, and her brother Robert, she besieged the tower of the bishop of Winchester. But the bishop sent for the queen, William of Ypres, and the other magnates of England. Thus a great army arose on each side. At length the London army arrived; and, numerous as they were, those opposing the Empress compelled her to withdraw. Many were captured, including Robert, brother of the Empress, in whose tower the king was held; only by Robert’s capture could the king be released. Both were set free. Thus the king, miserably captured by God’s justice, was miserably delivered by God’s mercy (November). Robert had been captured on the day of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross.

That same year, [Col. 0457D] in the octave of Easter, John, bishop of Lisieux, submitted to Geoffrey, count of Anjou, and surrendered to him the city which he had held against him for some time. All the powerful men of the county of Lisieux likewise submitted to him. Around Pentecost the aforesaid Bishop John died. He greatly enriched the episcopal see with buildings and ornaments. He also enclosed with walls the city whose walls Bishop Humbert had demolished in order to build the church. He was succeeded by his nephew Arnulf, archdeacon of Sées, a very shrewd, eloquent, and learned man.

Waleran, count of Meulan, who surpassed all the magnates of Normandy in strongholds, revenues, and kinsmen, made peace with Geoffrey, count of Anjou; and Montfort Castle, which he had possessed since the death of King Henry, was granted to him. Therefore all the men of the district of Rouen also submitted to the noble prince—not the citizens of the city, but those living on this side of the river Seine as far as the river Risle. Falaise too was surrendered to Geoffrey, count of Anjou. The chapter-house of Bec was begun, both through the counsel and with the aid of Robert of Neubourg.

1141. [1142.] Conrad 4. Louis 4. Stephen 6.

Robert, count of Gloucester, crossed to Normandy in summer, taking with him hostages—the sons, namely, of the counts and magnates of England who favoured the Empress. They asked that Count Geoffrey [Col. 0458B] retain them and prepare to cross over for the subjugation of the kingdom of England. For a time the count refused, since he feared rebellion among the Angevins and his other men. He nevertheless entrusted to him his eldest son Henry, that Robert might take him with him. Without delay, in Count Robert’s presence, he besieged and took Aulnay.

> [Note: Col. 0457D: Aulnay, between Caen and Vire.]

After gathering a larger army, he proceeded to Mortain, which was surrendered to him, along with Tinchebray, Cérences, and Tillières: four castles belonging to the count of Mortain himself. Thereupon the men of Avranches and those of the Cotentin submitted to the same duke.

Louis, king of the Franks, afflicted Count Theobald and ravaged his land, especially in Champagne, where he burned the excellent castle of Vitry. A very great multitude of people of every sex and age were burned there. Pope Innocent then placed the king’s own land under interdict because he would not receive the archbishop of Bourges. He later did receive him, and the pope absolved him from the oath which he had made without good reason. The church of Beaumont is given to the church of Bec. (HUNT. VIII.)

Stephen, king of the English, built a castle near Winchester. Then an immense multitude of enemies unexpectedly descended. When the royal soldiers had begun their manoeuvres of encirclement and could not resist, the enemies forced the king to flee; many of his men were captured. William Martel, the king’s steward, was also captured, and for his ransom gave up the notable castle of Sherborne.

[Col. 0458D] That same year, after the feast of St Michael, the king besieged the Empress at Oxford until Advent. During that period, shortly before Christmas, the Empress departed by night across the frozen Thames, clothed in white garments, deceiving the eyes of the besiegers by the reflected light and likeness of the snow. She went to Wallingford, and Oxford was at last surrendered to the king. John, emperor of Constantinople, died after drawing a bow with a poisoned arrow so forcefully that he mortally wounded his hand. He was succeeded by his son Manuel.

1142. [1143.] 5. 5. 7.

Richard, bishop of Bayeux, died; he was succeeded by [Col. 0459A] Philip of Harcourt. Richard, bishop of Avranches, also died, and was succeeded by Richard, dean of the same church. That same year the count of Anjou besieged Cherbourg until it was surrendered to him. Verneuil and the valley of the Risle were also surrendered. Walter Giffard, count, and the other men of Caux likewise obtained his peace.

In September of that same year Pope Innocent died (24 September), and was succeeded by Guy of Castello, cardinal of the holy Roman Church, called Celestine, the 159th pope.

> [Note: Col. 0459: After this word *Marie* has been erased.]

He reigned five months and five days.

> [Note: Col. 0459D: Rather, twelve, for he died on 9 March 1144.]

(HUNT. VIII.) King Stephen attended a council in London in mid-Lent. Because no honour was shown by plunderers either to clerics or to the church of God, and because clerics and laymen alike were seized and ransomed, the bishop of Winchester, legate of the city of Rome, held at London a council necessary for the clergy in those circumstances. It decreed that no one who had violently laid hands upon a cleric could be absolved by anyone except the pope himself, and in his presence. Thus a little calm scarcely dawned upon the clergy.

That same year King Stephen seized Geoffrey de Mandeville in his court at St Albans. Therefore, in order that the king might release him, he surrendered to him the Tower of London, Walden Castle, and that of Pleshy. Deprived of possessions, Geoffrey invaded Ramsey Abbey and, expelling the monks, introduced plunderers. He was a man of the highest courage, but of still greater obstinacy against God.

[Col. 0459C] The bishop of Winchester and afterwards the archbishop of Canterbury set out for Rome to negotiate concerning the legation, Pope Innocent now being dead. Hugh, canon of St Victor at Paris, a man of pious memory, died—a religious man, very learned in both secular and sacred letters—leaving many books as a monument to his learning.

> [Note: Col. 0459: “Hugh died … learning” is written in an erasure by another hand, perhaps Robert’s. Witnesses 7b and 8d lack it, and instead have: “Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, married the niece of Conrad, emperor of the Romans, namely the sister of Frederick, who succeeded the same Conrad.”]

1143. [1144.] Conrad 6. Louis 6. Stephen 8.

(HUNT. VIII.) King Stephen besieged Lincoln. When the count of Chester was building a fortification against the castle which he held by force, nearly eighty of his workmen were suffocated by the enemy. The undertaking therefore left unfinished, the king departed in confusion. Geoffrey, count of Mandeville, harassed the king most vigorously and shone with great glory in all things.

In August, however, God’s splendour displayed a miracle worthy of His justice. He punished two men with the same penalty for the same sin: having torn monks away, they had turned churches of God into castles. Robert Marmion, a warlike man, had wickedly done this at the church of Coventry. Geoffrey had committed the same crime at Ramsey church, as we have said. Robert Marmion, therefore, rising against his enemies, was killed alone among the ranks of his own men before the monastery itself, [Col. 0460A] and, excommunicated, is consumed in everlasting death. Likewise Count Geoffrey, alone amid the dense battle-lines of his own men, was struck by an arrow shot by a most contemptible foot-soldier. Though he laughed at the wound, he later died from it, excommunicated. Behold: the same vengeance for the same crime, worthy to be proclaimed to all the saints in praise of God.

While that church was held as a castle, blood welled up from the walls of the church and cloister, manifesting divine indignation and foretelling the destruction of the wicked. Arnulf, son of the count, who after his father’s death held the church as a castle, was captured and exiled. The leader of the knights fell from his horse and expired with his brains spilled out. Rainier, leader of the foot-soldiers, accustomed to break into and burn churches, at last crossed the sea; but his ship became motionless. After the lot was cast three times and fell upon him, he was sent away in a boat with his wife and money; they immediately perished. The ship, however, once more sailed peacefully over the waters.

(A. Roth.) Geoffrey, count of Anjou, having gathered a great army after the feast of St Hilary, crossed the Seine at Vernon. Having pitched camp at Holy Trinity on the hill of Rouen, he was solemnly received by the citizens of Rouen on the following day, the feast of Saints Fabian and Sebastian (19 January). Yet at his very entrance, and throughout the day until after None, there was an exceedingly violent wind, uprooting woods and casting down houses.

When the city had been surrendered, the men of the count of Warenne, who supported King Stephen, refused to surrender the tower. Geoffrey, Count Waleran of Meulan, and the other princes of Normandy who had now made peace with the duke therefore besieged it. Though many engines were made, they could not take it because of the site and strength of the fortress. During this siege Rotrou, count of Perche, died, leaving two small sons, Rotrou and Geoffrey.

> [Note: Col. 0460D: “And Stephen,” BOUQ.]

Later Louis, king of the Franks, gave his widow to his brother Robert. At last, when provisions failed for those besieged within Rouen Castle, they surrendered themselves and the tower to Geoffrey, formerly count of Anjou and henceforth duke of the Normans. In the preceding year a part of that same tower had collapsed, namely the side through which Duke Geoffrey entered the city when it was surrendered to him, and where he set his engines to take the tower.

[Col. 0460D] After arranging what was necessary in the tower and city, the energetic duke pressed onward. Having gathered an exceedingly large mounted army—not only his own men but also friends and lords, for the count of Flanders, his brother-in-law, had come with 1,400 knights, and Louis, king of the Franks, had come with his forces—he attacked the castle of Driencourt, still held in resistance against him by the mercenaries of the count of Warenne. Seeing that they could not resist him, they surrendered the aforesaid castle, though unwillingly. Hugh of Gournay also surrendered the castle of Lyons, fearing that the count would destroy all his land.

Thus, peace having been made throughout Normandy except at Arques Castle, which William the Fleming, a monk, still held in loyalty to King Stephen, though Duke Geoffrey’s men besieged it without interruption, each returned home. John, bishop of Sées, died; he was succeeded by Gerard, a canon of the same church, a cheerful and very learned man. This John did a thing worthy of remembrance in the time of King Henry. He caused the secular canons of his church to live according to rule and according to the institution of St Augustine, providing suitable offices and a cloister. John of Lisieux, his uncle, and Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, wished to attempt the same in their churches, but failed in the very attempt.

In March Pope Celestine died (9 March). He was succeeded by Gerard, a citizen of Bologna, regular canon, chancellor of the Roman church, and cardinal of the title of the Church of the Holy Cross, or Jerusalem, which is the same church. He was afterwards called Lucius II, the 170th pope, and reigned one year.

1144. [1145.] Conrad 7. Louis 7. Stephen 9.

[Col. 0461C] (HUNT.) Stephen, king of the English, was initially occupied with campaigns concerning Hugh Bigod. But in summer Count Robert and the whole party of the king’s enemies had built a castle at Faringdon. The king, however, swiftly gathered his forces, hurried there, and brought a formidable and numerous London army. They assailed the castle every day while Count Robert and his supporters waited not far from the king’s army with larger forces; yet, with most glorious courage and not without great shedding of blood, they took it. Then at last fortune began to turn more favourably toward the king and to raise him aloft.

Alexander, bishop of Lincoln, again went to Rome. Returning in the following year with the pope’s favour, he was received joyfully by his own people. In summer Arques Castle was surrendered to Duke Geoffrey, after William the Fleming monk who commanded it had been accidentally killed in the tower by an arrow.

> [Note: Col. 0461D: Arques.]

That same year (3 January), through treachery, the Christians lost the city of Edessa in the principality of Antioch. In antiquity it was called Rages, but by modern people Rohais; it fell into the power of the Saracens, who killed the Christians they found there. Joscelin the younger of Turbessel, count of that city, was then absent.

That same year people first began at Chartres [Col. 0462A] to draw carts laden with stones, wood, provisions, and other goods on their own shoulders for the work of the church, whose towers were then being built. Whoever did not see these things will never see their like again. Not only there, but throughout almost all France and Normandy and in many other places: everywhere humility and affliction, everywhere repentance and forgiveness of evils, everywhere mourning and contrition. You might see women and men dragging themselves on their knees through deep marshes, being beaten with whips, frequent miracles happening everywhere, and songs and rejoicings offered to God.

There survives concerning this previously unheard-of matter a letter of Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, to Theodoric, bishop of Amiens, who had inquired about it. You would say that the prophecy was being fulfilled: “The spirit of life was in the wheels” (Ezekiel 1:20). Duke Geoffrey repaired the bridge of Rouen, making it very strong.

Pope Lucius died in March (25 February); he was succeeded by Bernard, abbot of the monastery of St Anastasius outside the walls of Rome. Pope Innocent, who had been the fourth pope before this man, had recently made it an abbey of the order of the monks of Cîteaux; and Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, when he sent a community there, had set this man over it, especially because the Roman pope, some time before this man entered monastic life, had promoted him to holy orders. He was a man from beyond the mountains, a citizen of Pisa. He was ordained in the first week of March and called Eugenius, the 171st pope.

The chancel of Bec monastery church was begun on the day before the Kalends of August, in the presence of the lord Letard, abbot of pious memory.

> [Note: Col. 0461D: “The chancel was begun … abbot” is absent from witness 8b.]

1145. [1146.] 8. 8. 10.

(HUNT. VIII.) King Stephen, gathering a large army, built an impregnable castle situated opposite Wallingford. Ranulf, count of Chester, now joined to the king by peace, was present there with great forces. Afterwards, when the count himself came peacefully to the king’s court at Northampton, the king seized him without any such fear on his part and cast him into prison, until he surrendered the most famous castle of Lincoln, which he had deceitfully taken from him, and whatever other castles were under his dominion. Thus the count, released from prison, was restored to free choice.

Seeing the miracles occurring in religious places, the varied affliction joined with humility as the carts came, hearing also the complaint of Christians returning from the holy places concerning the incursion of the pagans, and hearing the preaching of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, a man of authority not to be despised, to whom Pope Eugenius had entrusted this office: Louis, king of the Franks, Conrad, emperor of the Germans, Frederick his nephew, duke of Swabia, Waleran, count of Meulan, William, count of Warenne, his brother, Theodoric of Auseis, [Note: Col. 0462D: that is, Alsace or Ellesath,] [Col. 0463A] count of Flanders, and many other men of great authority and rank—Frenchmen, Normans, Englishmen, and innumerable others from other lands, not only knights and laymen but bishops, clerics, and monks—took the cross upon their shoulders and prepared for the journey to Jerusalem. The king of the Franks, his brother Robert, Geoffrey count of Meulan, and many others took the cross at Vézelay on Palm Sunday.

The church of Tournai began to have its own bishop, having been subject to the bishop of Noyon since the time of St Eligius. Duke Geoffrey fittingly restored the roofs of the tower and castle of Rouen which had been damaged during the siege. King Roger of Sicily took the province of Tripoli in Africa from the pagans.

A single toad was found enclosed within a hollow stone in the wall of the city of Le Mans. When it had been killed, toads thereafter appeared within the city walls, though they had never previously been seen there.

> [Note: Col. 0463: Robert himself later wrote, in place of the erased passage “A toad was found … had been seen”: “Richard of Lingèvres, an excellent knight, was in this expedition and was of great service. He had recently gone there from the county of Bayeux and received as a gift from King Roger the county of the island of Andros, which that same king had recently taken from the emperor of Constantinople.” Witnesses 2, 7b, and 8d contain this version and lack “A toad was found … had been seen.”]

There was an eclipse of the sun on the fifth day before the Kalends of November.

> [Note: Col. 0463C: Rather, on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, 1147. BOUQ.]

1146. [1147.] Conrad 9. Louis 9. Stephen 11.

(ibid.) King Stephen at Christmas was invested with the royal diadem in the city of Lincoln, into which no king had dared enter because certain superstitious persons forbade it. This shows how great was King Stephen’s boldness and his spirit’s freedom from fear of dangers.

> [Note: Col. 0463: Omitting the following passage, “Henry … received the order,” witness 2 adds here: “This year Lord Serlo, abbot of Savigny, gave himself, with all abbeys belonging to him, to the Cistercian Order. He did this into the hands of Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, in the presence of the venerable Pope Eugenius and all the abbots of the Cistercian chapter.” Another hand adds in the margin: “The prior rank of all other abbots after the lord abbot of Cîteaux and the first four abbots was granted to him and his successors. From that time it was secured that, without any interruption, one abbot of Savigny was among the definitors every year. The abbot of Savigny held this position in the year of the Lord 1243, that is, for ninety-six continuous years. Nor is it surprising that Savigny Abbey was thus honoured by consent of the chapter: by its conversion, it greatly honoured the Cistercian Order in the Lord, then poor in resources, increasing it by a multitude of abbeys, when, through zeal for religion, it abandoned its own customs and its customary general chapter at Savigny, in order humbly and in holy service to receive the institutions of the Cistercian Order. Therefore both the future abbot of Savigny and the whole congregation must take care lest the church of Savigny be deprived of these rights, to its grave prejudice; nor can conspiracy on this account be alleged against them in any way. For it is one thing to defend the fault of an individual and another to defend the cause and right of one’s own church, a duty imposed by the profession which a man makes when he is blessed as abbot.”]

Henry, son of Duke Geoffrey and the Empress, came from England into Normandy.

> [Note: Col. 0463: Omitting all that follows for this year, witness 7b has: “Lord Hildiernus, ninth abbot of St Mary of Lyre, died, of pious memory.”]

He was received by the community of Bec in solemn procession [Col. 0463C] on Ascension Day. The dispute between the monks of Bec and the canons of Oxford concerning the church of Beaumont was settled at Paris in the presence of Pope Eugenius. That same year regular canons were placed in the church of St Geneviève at Paris by Pope Eugenius’s authority, because the secular canons had injured the pope’s men during a procession. These canons had as their first abbot Henry, prior of the church of St Victor, from which church they received their order.

Louis, king of the Franks, Queen Eleanor, and their companions, mentioned above, departed from Paris for the Jerusalem expedition in the presence of Pope Eugenius. It is not our purpose to recount what tribulations and miseries they suffered on that journey, while passing through the land of the emperor of Constantinople: famine, pestilence, and attacks by pagans. For since the expedition was for the most part undertaken from plunder of the poor and despoiling of churches, and no punishment was inflicted upon those who behaved dishonourably, scarcely anything prosperous or worthy of memory was accomplished in that pilgrimage.

After Raymond, prince of Antioch, had been killed by the Saracens, his wife remained with his young son Bohemond III and his daughter Constance.

> [Note: Col. 0463: “After Raymond … Constance” was later added by another hand, perhaps Robert’s. It is absent from witnesses 2 and 7b.]

1147. [1148.] 10. 10. 12.

The Christians reached the holy places at Jerusalem, whatever their exertions, and around August, having besieged Damascus and made little progress because of the treachery of the Jerusalemites, they hastened to return. Things had gone better for Christian princes in Spain in the preceding year. The emperor of Spain, whose imperial capital is Toledo, aided by Pisans and Genoese, captured from the pagans the most noble city of Almería. The king of Galicia, relying on the help of Normans, Englishmen, and many others travelling to Jerusalem with a naval force, took the city of Lisbon from the Hagarites in [1147], just as in the preceding year he had taken from them another city, Santarém.

> [Note: Col. 0463C: Santarém.]

The count of Barcelona also took the city of Tortosa in the same year.

That same year, after Ascelin, bishop of Rochester, died, Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, appointed his brother Walter, archdeacon of Canterbury, to that church. Roger, bishop of Chester, also died on the Jerusalem journey, and was succeeded by Walter, prior of Christ Church, Canterbury.

> [Note: Col. 0464C: In 1149, according to Gervase of Canterbury.]

Henry Murdac, a Cistercian monk, became [Col. 0465A] archbishop of York. In [1148], Pope Eugenius convened a council at Reims during Lent. Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, came there secretly and contrary to King Stephen’s prohibition; he was therefore favourably received by the pope. On the death of Robert, bishop of Hereford, Gilbert, abbot of Gloucester, succeeded him. In [1146], William of St Barbara, dean of York, had in the preceding year become bishop of Durham.

1148. Conrad 11. Louis 11. Stephen 13.

Around Advent Duke Geoffrey besieged and destroyed, in the county of Lisieux, the castle of Robert Bertran Fag. [uncertain abbreviation]. Wonderful and astonishing were the deeds of Eudo, the false prophet and heretic. Condemned at the council of Reims and confined in the archbishop’s tower, he perished as wickedly as he had begun. It is better to be silent than to speak of his incantations, fantasies, deeds, and words.

> [Note: Col. 0465D: Compare above, cols. 265, 375.]

Raynald of Châtillon became prince of Antioch, having married the wife of Prince Raymond.

> [Note: Col. 0465: “Ainaldus [thus manuscript E] … prince” was added in manuscript E by Robert himself; it is absent from 8d.]

1149. 12. 12. 14.

The lord Letard, sixth abbot of Bec church, died, of holy memory. This venerable man, a native of Bec, received monastic life under the venerable Lord Abbot William. Living vigorously in it, an old man yet a virgin, he finished the course of his praiseworthy life on the sixth day before the Nones of July, Saturday within the octave of the Apostles Peter and Paul, at about the tenth hour of the day, in the sixty-fifth year of his age and the fiftieth of his monastic profession. He governed the abbey entrusted to him prudently, being a son of religion and afterwards its father and loving protector, for ten years and twenty-three days.

> To the homeland for which you uttered so many sighs,  
> Father Letard, freed from the flesh, you depart from here.  
> Sixth among the fathers, because yourself made perfect,  
> You receive abundant rewards with your fathers.  
> July hastened from the sixth before the Nones toward the Ides,  
> And you, when seven parts had been given, reap the eighth.

> [Note: Col. 0465: Robert wrote “You receive … reap the eighth” in an erasure. After this, 7b and 8d add:]
>
> The grain of wheat remaining sound upon the clod  
> Cannot grow until it has decayed.  
> Thus, unless our flesh is touched by the bitterness of death,  
> Though it has run the course, it receives no prize.  
> Therefore it is made known that it is unfitting to mourn  
> [Col. 0466C] If one who was a stranger seeks his homeland.  
> May merciful God preserve this man from eternal Avernus,  
> And grant him a kingdom filled with heavenly light.  
> May the Virgin, Mother of God, intercede, lest the dark spirit crush him;  
> May he obtain the kingdom of light for which he prays.]

This holy man was succeeded by Lord Roger, the second prior, excellently learned in both Testaments and suitably furnished with clerical and secular learning. He was elected unanimously by the whole community during the same octave of the Apostles Peter and Paul. Blessed at Saint-Wandrille on the feast day of St James the Apostle by the venerable Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, he was installed in his seat before the same community of Bec. From that time he diligently watched, day and night and to the best of his ability, over the flock entrusted to him.

> [Note: Col. 0465: “This venerable man … watched” is absent from 8b.]

Master Vacarius, a Lombard by origin, an honourable man learned in law, taught pupils Roman law in England in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1149. Since many, rich and poor alike, flocked to him for study, he compiled for the poor nine books excerpted from the *Code* and the *Digest*. They suffice for deciding all legal disputes customarily dealt with in the schools, if one knows them perfectly.

> [Note: Col. 0465: “Master … perfectly” written by Robert in an erasure.]
>
> [Note: Col. 0465D: Compare Savigny, *Geschichte des Römischen Rechts*, IV, ch. 36, p. 351.]

That same year, after Easter, Lord Bernard, abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel and monk of Bec, died; [Col. 0466B] he had greatly improved that monastery both within and without.

> [Note: Col. 0465: “monk … improved” is absent from 8b.]

Duke Geoffrey besieged Montreuil-Bellay in Poitou, built three stone castles there, and maintained the siege for three years, until Berlay, lord of the castle, surrendered himself to the count.

> [Note: Col. 0465D: Montreuil-Bellay.]
>
> [Note: Col. 0465D: Gerard de Berlai.]

The count then completely demolished the tower and castle. In the same year (March), a terrible whirlwind arose, overthrowing houses and breaking trees and brushwood; demons, it is asserted, fought in it in the forms of foul animals. On the feast of Pentecost David, king of Scots, girded with knightly arms Henry, eldest son of Duke Geoffrey and of his niece the Empress Matilda, who had crossed from Normandy to England in the preceding year.

> [Note: Col. 0466D: “In the year of grace 1149, in the middle of May,” says Gervase of Canterbury. “That [uncertain: *pio*] of the month of January,” says Gervase of Canterbury; nevertheless, there is no doubt that Henry received arms in 1149.]

That same year, around August, [Col. 0466C] Louis, king of the Franks, returned from Jerusalem. There was an exceptionally severe winter lasting three uninterrupted months, so dreadful that some people were injured in their limbs because of the excessive pain of the cold. Spring cultivation was largely left undone, and great famine consequently followed. Corbie monastery was burned again.

> [Note: Col. 0465: “Henry, lord of Fougères, died, having become a monk in the church of Savigny,” added by witness 2.]

1150. [1151.] 13. 13. 15.

The Count Theobald of Blois conferred knightly arms upon Geoffrey, son of Duke Geoffrey. After Duke Geoffrey had destroyed the castle of Montreuil, having besieged three stone castles for three years—a thing unheard of since Julius Caesar—and had also captured the lord of the castle of Bellai, despite even the will and prohibition of King Louis, King Louis and Geoffrey, Duke of Normandy, became enemies of one another. [Col. 0467A] Already in the preceding year [Note: In the year of grace 1150, … at the beginning of January, says Gervase of Canterbury.] Henry, the duke’s son, had returned from England, and his father had granted him his inheritance on his mother’s side, namely the duchy of Normandy. Discord having thus arisen between king and count, the king came with a great host, and Eustace, son of King Stephen, came with him into Normandy before the castle of Arques. Henry, Duke of the Normans, was there opposite him with a remarkable army of Normans, Angevins, and Bretons; but the commanders of his army, who were more mature than he both in counsel and in age, did not allow him to engage with the king, his lord, unless he could press him more severely in some respect than he had done before.

A little earlier in the same year, this duke had besieged the castle of Tillières, [Col. 0467B] but had withdrawn without accomplishing his purpose because of the king’s arrival; he had nevertheless burned the houses within the walls as far as the tower and the small castle around it. Geoffrey, Count of Anjou, took the castle of Le Neubourg from Robert, Count of Perche, which John, son of William Talvas, had lost through treachery in the preceding year. Therefore King Louis, angered, and Robert his brother, having assembled a huge army, came as far as Sées, the city of William Talvas, and burned it. Again King Louis, gathering an army from all his forces, in August had it led to the bank of the Seine, between Meulan and Mantes [Note: Mantes.]. Nor were Geoffrey, Count of Anjou, and his son Henry, Duke of Normandy, less prompt in marshalling their troops; they took up their position on the [Col. 0467C] border of the duchy of Normandy, intending to defend it.

Meanwhile, I believe by divine providence, which saw that the affair could not be ended without much shedding of human blood if the two armies met from opposite sides, King Louis was struck by a sharp fever in the city of Paris and confined to bed (26 August). For this reason, wise and religious men intervened, and a truce was given and accepted by both sides until the king recovered. When he had recovered, the serenity of peace shone forth through God’s mercy: Gerald of Berlai, over whom the discord had chiefly arisen, was restored, and the king received the homage of Duke Henry for the duchy of Normandy. When, therefore, both father and son had departed joyfully from Paris, and Duke Henry had ordered all the [Col. 0467D] nobles of Normandy to assemble at Lisieux on the approaching feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, in order to consult with them concerning his journey to England, his father, having been afflicted by a severe fever for many days at the castle of Le Lude [Note: Saint-Germain-en-Laye.], entered upon the way of all flesh on the seventh Ides of September, a man of great worth and energy, to be mourned without measure by his people. He alone among all mortals was buried within the walls of the city of Le Mans; for he was laid to rest in the church of Saint Julian, before the Crucifix.

[Col. 0468A]

May God grant him ascent to the eternal kingdom,  
That he may reign forever with the angelic hosts.

Before his death, he granted the county of Anjou to Henry, Duke of Normandy, his eldest son; to Geoffrey, his second son, he gave four castles. In the same year Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, died (13 January 1152), having greatly enlarged that monastery in ornaments, possessions, and buildings. He was succeeded by Odo, a monk of the same house, who in the preceding year had been made abbot of the church of Compiègne, when the king had placed the monks of Saint-Denis there.

Algar, bishop of Coutances, a very religious man, also died. He had installed regular canons in the church of Saint Lô at Coutances, in the church of Saint Lô at Rouen, [Col. 0468B] and in the church of Cherbourg. Richard, dean of Bayeux, succeeded him. An almost unheard-of famine in the preceding season, pestilence, and the sacred fire grievously afflicted humankind, especially the poorer people. At Advent the rivers overflowed beyond their usual bounds, carrying away even stone bridges and neighbouring houses. An earthquake occurred on the night of the feast of Saint Nicholas. Henry, Duke of Normandy, was received peacefully by the Angevins, who swore fealty to him; and thus he became Duke of the Normans and Count of the Angevins.

1151. [1152.] Conrad 14. Louis 14. Stephen 16.

(January.) The venerable Count Theobald of Blois died, nephew of King Henry and brother of Stephen, [Col. 0468C] King of the English, a prince of great holiness and generosity toward the poor. His three sons succeeded him. Henry, the eldest, received the counties of Troyes and Champagne, and whatever his father had possessed beyond the Seine; Theobald, the second son, the counties of Chartres and Blois and the district of Dunois; Stephen, the third son, the honour of Sancerre [Note: Sancerre. Bouquet.] in the district of Bourges.

(15 March.) In the same year Conrad, Emperor of the Romans, died. He had succeeded Lothair and was nephew of Henry IV, husband of the empress. He was never crowned at Rome; therefore he is not properly called emperor, but king of the Germans. He was succeeded by his nephew Frederick, Duke of Swabia.

[1152.] A quarrel having arisen between Louis, King of the French, and his wife, religious persons having been assembled in Lent [Col. 0468D] at Beaugency, they were separated by the authority of Christendom after an oath had been given before archbishops and bishops that they were related by blood.

(18 March.) After the close of Easter, Henry, Duke of Normandy and Count of Anjou, having assembled the counts of Normandy and other leading men at Lisieux, consulted with them concerning his journey to England. For his uncle Reginald, Count of Cornwall, had come in Lent on his behalf. About Pentecost, Henry, Duke of Normandy, whether by sudden [Col. 0469A] or premeditated counsel, married Eleanor, Countess of Poitou, whom King Louis had shortly before dismissed on account of consanguinity. When he heard this, King Louis was angered against the duke. For he had had two daughters by her, and therefore did not wish her to bear sons by anyone, lest his aforesaid daughters be disinherited.

After the feast of Saint John, while Duke Henry was at Barfleur [Note: Barfleur, not far from Cherbourg.] and intended to cross to England with an armed force, Louis, King of the French, Eustace son of Stephen, King of the English, Robert, Count of Perche, Henry, Count of Champagne, son of Count Theobald, and also Geoffrey, brother of the Duke of Normandy, assembled together in order to take from him Normandy and the county of Anjou [Col. 0469B] and the duchy of Aquitaine, which he had acquired with his wife—indeed, all his land—which these five had also divided among themselves.

When this became known, and he heard likewise of the siege of Neufmarché [Note: Between Gournay and Gisors.], where all the aforesaid princes had assembled except his brother Geoffrey, who was expected to attack with all his power in the county of Anjou, Duke Henry left Barfleur on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, intending, according to his ability, to relieve the besieged castle. That very night, an excessive flash of light appeared, and afterwards something like a huge dragon was seen moving through the sky from west to east. Meanwhile, while the duke was assembling a great army of chosen knights and foot-soldiers, the castle was surrendered through the treachery of its defenders, as though it had been taken by force. And [Col. 0469C] Duke Henry, whom almost all the Normans expected soon to lose all his land, conducted himself wisely, defended his own manfully against all, and was praised even by his enemies.

Toward the end of August, after stationing knights to guard Normandy, he himself went into the county of Anjou and so harassed his brother Geoffrey that he came to terms with him. Then, after a truce had been made between himself and the king, he prepared to cross to England; in this matter his boldness may be admired.

In the same year a certain man was told in dreams to cut off his hands and feet, and thus he would be saved. While doing this, he died. Michael, monk of Le Bec, was made abbot of Préaux on the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle [Note: “Michael … Apostle” is lacking in 8b.]. Pope Eugenius sent John, cardinal-priest of the Roman [Col. 0470A] Church, surnamed Paparo, as legate to Ireland [Note: A.D. 1150.], with four pallia. He gave one to the bishop of Dublin and the other three to three other bishops of the same island, placing five additional bishops under each of those who received pallia. This was done contrary to ancient custom and to the dignity of the church of Canterbury, from which the bishops of Ireland had been accustomed to seek and receive the blessing of consecration.

(3 March.) In the same year Matilda, wife of Stephen, King of the English, died. [Note: Here manuscript 2 adds: “In this year it was decreed in the Cistercian chapter that they should build no new abbey without fuller deliberation, because the number of abbeys of that order which had been founded had reached nearly five hundred. After the chapter of this year, Lord Serlo, abbot of Savigny, remained at Clairvaux, wishing to relinquish the care of his abbey, thinking thereby to provide both for himself and for the church. Since he had desired and sought this for so long—as a lover of holiness and quiet, wishing to flee disturbances and empty exaltations—Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, thought fit to consent to his request, provided the monks of Savigny agreed. He therefore sent his prior Philip, who persuaded them to yield and elect another abbot. But they said that they wished to take counsel concerning this from the abbots who had gone out from that house and were on this side of the sea. The abbots thus assembled took counsel and declared that they did not wish to let Lord Serlo go. Yet, because they doubted his return, they chose two other venerable persons, in order that they might have one of them; but both refused. Bernard, therefore, not wishing the monks of Savigny to be wholly deserted, sent Lord Serlo back to them to preserve the house until he himself should come there, and to provide both for them and for the house.” Manuscript 7b adds: “After Vincent, abbot of Châtillon, had been deposed, Sylvester, monk of Lyre, a man of venerable simplicity, was appointed in his place.”]

John, monk of Sées, became the second bishop of the Isle of Man, which lies between England and Ireland, but is nearer England than Ireland; hence its bishop is subject to the archbishop of York. The first [Col. 0470B] bishop there had been Wimund, a monk of Savigny; but because of his cruelty he was expelled and deprived of his eyes. William, bishop of Durham, died. Ralph of Péronne, Count of Vermandois, also died, leaving a small son named Hugh and one daughter under the guardianship of his nephew Galeran, Count of Meulan. He had begotten these children by his younger wife, daughter of William, Duke of Aquitaine. King Louis of the French had married his eldest daughter, by whom he had begotten two daughters. Henry, son of David, King of the Scots, likewise died. The younger William of Roumare also died while his father William was still living, leaving two sons born of the sister of William, Count of Aumale.

[1151.] In the preceding year the vintage was [Col. 0470C] scanty and very late; hence the wine was exceedingly dear and harsh in taste [Note: Compare above, col. 275.]. But in this year the vintage was timely, though wine was dearer than in the preceding year. Therefore taverns selling ale and mead came into common use even in France, something which in our memory had not been heard of in past times [Note: “In this year … heard of” is lacking in 8b.].

Geoffrey Arthur, who had translated the history of the kings of the Britons from British into Latin, became bishop of Saint Asaph in North Wales. Thus there are today four bishoprics in Wales and seventeen in England. In eight of them monks occupy episcopal sees—something which you will find either nowhere or rarely in other provinces; but it is found in England because the first preachers of the English, namely Augustine, [Col. 0471A] Mellitus, Justus, and Laurence, were monks. In the other eight episcopal sees are secular canons; in one, regular canons.

In the same year John the Roman, who had been a monk from childhood at Saint Sabas and later abbot of Saint Mary on the Roman Capitol, and who, after leaving that abbey, had become a monk of Le Bec, went to Rome. Returning thence, he brought with him the head of the blessed martyr Felix, companion of Saint Audactus, and freely gave it to the church of Le Bec.

As the pernicious doctrine of the heretic Henry was spreading, especially in Gascony, the Lord stirred the spirit of a young girl in that province to refute the same heresy. For three days in every week she lay without voice, consciousness, or even [Col. 0471B] breath; afterwards, returning to herself, she said that blessed Mary prayed for the Christian people and that blessed Peter had taught her the orthodox faith. Thereafter she discoursed wisely and orthodoxly concerning our faith; and, especially by refuting Henry’s heresy, she brought back into the bosom of holy mother Church many whom he had deceived.

(16 July.) After the fortress of Neufmarché had been surrendered, as stated above, to Louis, King of the French, that king withdrew his army as far as Chaumont [Note: Chaumont, near Gisors.]. But Henry, Duke of Normandy, having gathered no small force of chosen knights and foot-soldiers, encamped beside the river Andelle. Remaining there for some time, he ravaged that part of the Vexin which lies [Col. 0471C] between the rivers Andelle and Epte and belongs to the duchy of Normandy. But Geoffrey, Count of Anjou, after the death of Henry, King of the English, had granted it temporarily to Louis, King of the French, just as he had granted many other portions of the demesne lands of the duchy of Normandy to certain magnates of the same province, so as to make them readier in this way to assist him in bringing the aforesaid county under his rule.

Therefore the duke daily sent raiders into it to seek provisions for the men and beasts of his army. There he also destroyed and burned the castle of Bacqueville, and burned two other castles, Chitry and Étrépagny. While the French, who had pitched camp on the other side of the river Epte, were informed of this by the smoke but gave no assistance [Col. 0471D] to their men, he took by assault and burned the fortress of Hugh of Gournay, which they call La Ferté [Note: La Ferté.], except for the tower situated on a high hill. For Hugh denied the aforesaid duke the service owed to him and supported his enemies outside the castle of Gournay.

In the middle of August, Louis, King of the French, had his army cross the Seine at Meulan. On hearing this, the duke also led his forces over the bridge at Vernon, and with some swift-moving knights hastened at speed toward [Col. 0472A] Verneuil, where he had heard from scouts that the king was rushing. Suddenly William of Pacy sent him word to return to Pacy [Note: Pacy, on the river Eure.], to which the king was coming with a very great army. The duke, energetic and, as usual, unhesitating in coming to the aid of his own, turned his horse’s head and returned with his companions in such haste that before they reached Pacy, many of their horses were left dead or nearly dead on the road. Hearing of the duke’s arrival, the king, employing more prudent counsel, did not wish to enter his land, but returned to Mantes the same day.

The duke, summoned by Gilbert of Tillières, burned the castle of Breuil, belonging to Hugh of Neufchâtel, and another fortress called Malculfiville, situated in the district of Dreux. Returning thence into Normandy and harassing [Col. 0472B] Richer of Laigle, who was giving aid to his enemies, he compelled him to give hostages for keeping the peace, and he consigned to fire the fortress of Beaumont-le-Roger, where Richer received robbers and excommunicated persons. Toward the end of August, after stationing knights to guard Normandy, he went into the county of Anjou and besieged the fortress of Montsoreau. By pressing its defenders with an unremitting siege, he captured William, lord of that castle, who supported his brother’s party, together with many other knights. Forced by this misfortune and many others, his brother Geoffrey was reconciled with him.

Meanwhile, the King of the French, taking advantage of the duke’s absence, chiefly at the instigation of Count Robert his brother—who had married the widow of Rotrou, [Col. 0472C] Count of Mortagne, and to whom the king had given the castle in the district of Dreux [Note: Dreux.], a portion of the borough of Tillières, and a certain village belonging to the castle of Verneuil—consigned a portion of the borough of Tillières to ravenous flames. He also surrounded the castle of Nanteuil-la-Forêt with military equipment, but did it no harm. A few days later, after a truce had been made between king and duke, the duke prepared to cross the sea; but before he crossed, the king caused the truce to be restored. Nevertheless, without abandoning his intention to cross, the duke waited near the shipyards for a wind suitable for the passage; in this his worth and boldness may be observed.

In the Cistercian chapter it was decreed that no new abbey should henceforth be founded, because the number of abbeys of that order had increased to nearly [Col. 0472D] five hundred. After the death of Conrad, Emperor of the Romans, as stated above, his nephew Frederick succeeded him. Pope Eugenius had the book of Peter of Damascus translated from Greek into Latin [Note: “Eugenius [had the work] of Damascene…”: another hand in manuscript E adds the same matter as under the year 1128. It is lacking in 7b and 8d, and indeed also in 8b.].

1152. [1153.] Frederick 1. Louis 15. Stephen 17.

Henry, Duke of the Normans, crossed into England within the octave of Epiphany with thirty-six ships. An eclipse of the sun took place on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, at about the eighth hour; the moon was in its twenty-seventh day. The Duke of the Normans, besieging the very strongly fortified castle [Col. 0473A] of Malmesbury and King Stephen’s men within it, compelled them to surrender, although the king himself was nearby with several thousand armed men.

(January.) Gilbert [Note: de Clare, son of Richard de Bienfaite.] son of Richard died and was buried at Clare, in the cell which his grandfather Gilbert had given to the monks of Le Bec. His brother Roger succeeded him. After the octave of Easter, Louis, King of the French, came early in the morning from Mantes to Vernon with a great army and burned the borough lying outside the walls and a very fine village, fertile in vineyards, called Longueville. For Richard, son of William of Vernon, had provoked his anger by daring to plunder merchants under the king’s safe-conduct.

Gundreda, Countess of Warwick, [Col. 0473B] expelled King Stephen’s guards from the fortress of the city of Warwick and handed that fortress over to Henry, Duke of Normandy. When Roger, Count of Warwick, died, his son Henry succeeded him, born of Gundreda, uterine sister of Geoffrey, Count of Meulan. When Simon, Count of Huntingdon, also died, his son Simon succeeded him, whom he had begotten by the daughter of Robert, Count of Leicester. David, King of Scotland, a very religious man, also died, and his two grandsons succeeded him, whom his son Henry, who had died in the preceding year, had begotten by the daughter of William, Count of Warenne, namely the uterine sister of Geoffrey, Count of Meulan. The elder of these, Malcolm, obtained the kingdom of Scotland; his brother William, the county of Lothian. [Note: Here manuscript 2 adds: “In the present year after Pentecost, Lord Goswin, abbot of Cîteaux, came to Savigny and took Lord Serlo back with him. Lord Richard of Courcy, a monk of that church, was elected abbot of Savigny. From youth he had grown in prudence and integrity in that abbey and had long served there as prior; and shortly afterwards Goswin, the fifth abbot of Cîteaux, died, and Abbot Lambert succeeded him.”]

In July, on the seventh Ides [Col. 0473C] of that month, Pope Eugenius III, of venerable memory, entered upon the way of all flesh: a very religious man, generous in almsgiving, just in judgments, gracious and pleasant to all alike, poor and rich. At his tomb, which was honourably made for him in the church of Saint Peter, miracles appeared immediately after his death.

(9 July.) He was succeeded by Conrad, bishop of Sabina, who, by ancient custom, was vicar for episcopal business in the city of the apostolic see only while the pope was absent, by reason of the dignity of his place. A Roman by birth, elderly, and distinguished in authority among the Romans, he was thereafter called Anastasius IV, the 172nd pope.

[Col. 0473D] Henry, Duke of the Normans, besieged the castle of Crowmarsh, which King Stephen had built not far from Wallingford, in order to prevent the duke’s knights who were in the aforesaid castle from crossing the bridge over the Thames. When Crowmarsh Castle had for the most part been taken and King Stephen approached it with no great military force in order, according to the agreement, to assist his men, the fearless duke, without raising the siege, [Col. 0474A] drew up battle-lines opposite the king, prepared to fight. But religious persons intervened and held private negotiations with the leading men in the duke’s army; the matter was brought to this conclusion: after a five-day truce had been granted, King Stephen was to destroy his own besieged castle, taking out only his eighty surviving knights. For the duke had already captured twenty knights in a wooden tower, apart from sixty archers whom he had caused to be beheaded.

When the duke learned this condition, although it would have brought him great honour, he was greatly displeased. Yet, complaining only in this respect of the disloyalty of his own men, who had confirmed that agreement on the pledge of their faith, he accepted the aforesaid settlement lest he invalidate their pledge. The siege which had been arranged near Wallingford was accordingly lifted, [Col. 0474B] and King Stephen demolished Crowmarsh. For in the preceding year the household of Duke Henry, dwelling at Wallingford, had destroyed not only the castle of Broughton, which had long attacked them, but also the fortress which King Stephen, against right and justice, had erected near Reading Abbey.

Thereupon Duke Henry, with three hundred knights, met William of Gercy, constable of Oxford, Richard de Lucy, William Martel, and their companions as they came into his land; he drove them as far as Oxford and captured twenty of their knights. But the countless booty gathered from the surrounding countryside by the light-armed troops and other lightly equipped men who had pursued them, [Col. 0474C] he ordered restored to those to whom it belonged, saying that he had come not to plunder but to free the poor people from the rapacity of the powerful.

The Duke of Normandy captured the very strongly fortified and wealthy castle which was the chief place of a certain county, namely Stamford. Toward the end of July Louis, King of the French, gathering an immense army from all his forces, besieged Vernon Castle for nearly fifteen days. Since he made no progress either by repeated assaults or by various engines, and since the Count of the Morini, whom the moderns call the Flemings, and in whose numerous troops the king placed his chief trust, wished to depart, the king, lest he withdraw ingloriously without accomplishing anything at all, made secret agreements and promises with Richard of Vernon. At least his banner [Col. 0474D] was to be raised on the tower, and the tower was to be entrusted for safekeeping to Goel, son of Baldric, who was bound to both the king and Richard by the benefice of a knight’s fee. In September the King of the French came with a few men and, as though secretly, burned a certain part of the borough of Verneuil.

When William of Pacy died childless, Pacy Castle was restored to Robert, son of Robert, Count of Leicester, [Col. 0475A] because it belonged to the honour of Breteuil [Note: Breteuil, between Évreux and Moulins.], of which he was the lawful heir through his mother. A quarrel arose between Simon, Count of Évreux, and the sons of Ascelin Goel, namely William Lupel and Roger the Bald. As it grew stronger, the aforesaid count ravaged almost all their land, except for the strongholds [Note: That is, except for the castles.].

On the Nones of August, after a great thunderclap about sunset, lightning struck at Le Bec the top of the chimney of a chamber built above the running water. Splitting that chimney, it threw down half of it while the remaining half stood [Note: “On the Nones … stood” is lacking in 8b.]. A certain religious woman from the province of Lorraine, possessing a spirit of prophecy, sent to the Cistercian chapter letters that were very obscure and [Col. 0475B] spoke, as it were, under a covering; yet it could be perceived in them that she censured somewhat the lukewarmness of the order and the coldness of charity. She had predicted to Pope Eugenius that about the eighth year of his priesthood he would have peace and would reach the end of his life.

Baldwin III, King of Jerusalem, with God’s grace going before him, besieged the city of Ascalon for a long time and at last captured it, giving it to his brother Amalric, Count of Jaffa. Roger, King of Sicily, through his admirals captured Tunis [Note: Tunis.], a very great city in Africa. When Richard, bishop of Avranches, died on his journey to Rome, whither he had gone because of the dispute between two elects to the abbacy of Mont-Saint-Michel, Herbert, chaplain to the Duke of Normandy, was made bishop [Col. 0475C] of that see.

(10 August.) In August, about the octave of Saint Lawrence, Eustace, son of Stephen, King of the English, died because, as some say, he had plundered the land of Saint Edmund, king and martyr, on the feast of Saint Lawrence itself. In the same octave a son was born to Henry, Duke of Normandy, by his wife Eleanor, Countess of Poitou. The boy was called William, a name almost proper to the counts of Poitou and dukes of Aquitaine. The venerable Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, a man of remarkable religious devotion and effective learning, paid the debt of human life by dying on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, leaving very many monuments of his wisdom, especially in his commentaries on the Song of Songs. He was succeeded by Robert the Fleming, who was [Col. 0475D] abbot of the Dunes. Henry Murdac, archbishop of York and a Cistercian monk, likewise died.

Stephen, King of the English, and Henry, Duke of Normandy, his kinsman, were reconciled on the eighth Ides of November, with justice from heaven looking down, in the following manner. First, in an assembly of bishops, counts, and other nobles, the king acknowledged the hereditary right which Duke Henry possessed to the kingdom of England. [Col. 0476A] And the duke graciously granted that the king should hold the kingdom throughout his life, if he wished, provided that at once the king, bishops, and other powerful men should confirm by oath that after the king’s death, if the duke survived him, he would hold the kingdom peacefully and without opposition.

It was also sworn that possessions seized by usurpers should be restored to their ancient and lawful possessors, who had held them in the time of Henry, the excellent king; likewise that the castles built after the death of the aforesaid king should be destroyed, their number having increased to a total of 375 [Note: The number has been erased in manuscript E.]. Ranulf, Count of Chester, died, leaving his son Hugh as successor to his honour, born of the daughter of Robert, Count of Gloucester. Robert of Montfort captured his uncle [Col. 0476B] Galeran, Count of Meulan, at a prearranged meeting not far from the borough of Bernay. When Orbec Castle, in which that count was held, had been besieged by Count Galeran’s men, the count was finally set free after first surrendering to his aforesaid nephew the tower of Montfort.

1153. [1154.] Frederick 2. Louis 16. Stephen 18.

Louis, King of the French, married the daughter of Alfonso, King of Spain. The capital of this king’s realm is Toledo; because he rules over the lesser kings of Aragon and Galicia, they call him Emperor of Spain. Galeran, Count of Meulan, while besieging Montfort Castle, was disgracefully driven off by his nephew [Col. 0476C] Robert, after two castles which he himself had built near Montfort were destroyed.

Roger, King of Sicily, died on the fourth day before the Kalends of March. His son William succeeded him; before his death, his father had elevated him as king and partner in the kingdom. He married the daughter of García, King of Navarre, namely the sister of Sancho the Younger, and had by her his eldest son, named Roger. After the death, as stated above, of Henry, archbishop of York, Pope Anastasius restored William to the same see, gave him the pallium, and at Rome consecrated in his presence Hugh de Puiset, bishop of Durham and nephew of Stephen, King of the English. Pope Eugenius, Anastasius’s predecessor, had deposed this William.

Around Easter, Henry, Duke of Normandy, crossed the sea into [Col. 0476D] Normandy and began gradually and prudently to recall into his own right the demesne lands which his father, under the pressure of necessity, had temporarily granted to the leading men of Normandy. Then he went into Aquitaine and suppressed the rebellion of certain persons. William, archbishop of York, having returned to England, died while celebrating the divine mysteries, having, as they say, drunk poison from the chalice itself. Roger of Pont l’Évêque, archdeacon of Canterbury, succeeded him. [Note: After this, another hand in manuscript E, perhaps Robert’s, inserted between this line and the next the numbers III. XVII. XIX. MCLIV, and wrote the following word “Mense” (“In the month”) in an erasure. These numbers are lacking in all the others, which alone is correct. Hence, omitting these, the chronology of manuscript E, disturbed from the year 1140 onward, is restored. What follows, from “In the month” to “Constantine,” is lacking in 8b. Moreover, manuscript E6 begins at the words “Louis, King of the Fr…”.]

[Col. 0477A] In May, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, the fifth weekday within the octave of Pentecost, the monastery of Saint Michael of the Peril of the Sea, after the tribulation which it had suffered almost continually for five years, by God’s mercy took some breath of relief when Robert of Torigni, cloister-prior of the monastery of Le Bec, was unanimously elected by the entire convent. In the same month, Duke Henry, returning from Aquitaine, graciously gave his assent at Rouen on the feast-day of Saint John the Baptist to the aforesaid election, which Archbishop Hugh of Rouen, a man of supreme piety and ability, together with the empress, the duke’s mother, had most willingly confirmed earlier while present.

In the following month, on the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene, the aforesaid [Col. 0477B] elect was blessed as abbot at Saint-Philibert of Montfort by Herbert, bishop of Avranches, and Gerard of Sées, in the presence of Abbots Roger of Le Bec, Michael of Préaux, and Hugh of Saint-Sauveur at Coutances.

In August, Louis, King of the French, and Henry, Duke of Normandy, made peace in the following terms. The king restored to him two castles, Vernon and Neufmarché; and the duke gave him two thousand marks of silver to repair the damage which the king had suffered in capturing, fortifying, and holding the same strongholds.

Reginald of Châtillon became prince of Antioch, having married Constance, widow of Prince Raymond, whom the Turks had killed in the same year in which Louis, King of the French, returned from Jerusalem. Acting bravely against those Turks, [Col. 0477C] he took from them three castles which had belonged to the Christians.

About the Kalends of October, Henry, Duke of Normandy, having recovered by God’s mercy from the adverse illness by which he had been dangerously afflicted, went with an army into the Vexin at the summons of the King of the French and made peace between the king and Joscelin Crispin. Returning thence, he besieged Tillières for nearly fifteen days, beginning three castles there. After the castle had been surrendered and peace made with Richard, son of the count, who had held that fortified place, he received reliable news of the death of Stephen, King of the English. After speaking with his mother the empress, and summoning his brothers Geoffrey and William, as well as the bishops and nobles of Normandy, he came to Barfleur and there waited for one month [Col. 0477D] for a favourable wind to cross the sea.

For Stephen, King of the English, had died on the eighth day before the Kalends of November. His body was buried in the monastery of Faversham [Note: Faversham.], which his wife Matilda had built, and where she herself and her eldest son Eustace were buried. Meanwhile there was complete peace in England, through fear and love of Duke Henry, whom all men did not doubt would come and become king.

[Col. 0478A] On the sixth day before the Kalends of December Pope Anastasius of Rome died; he was succeeded by Nicholas, bishop of Albano, namely the 173rd pope, called Adrian IV, a religious man and English by birth. He had previously been abbot of the Regular Canons of Saint-Ruf in Provence, but had been made bishop of Albano by his predecessor Eugenius. [Note: “[called bishop of Albano]” is absent from 8b. Robert’s work begins here in the first edition.] Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers, also died, a religious man of extensive learning, who expounded the Psalms and the Epistles of Paul brilliantly. Louis, king of the Franks, went on pilgrimage to Saint James of Galicia, and was graciously received in Spain by the emperor of Spain, his father-in-law. Henry, duke of the Normans, crossed into England on the seventh day before the Ides of December, and was received with great rejoicing by clergy and laity.

[Col. 0478B] On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, the Sunday before the Nativity of the Lord, at Westminster, he was chosen by all and anointed king by Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury. All the bishops of the kingdom of England were also present: Roger, archbishop of York; Richard, bishop of London; Henry of Winchester; Robert of Lincoln; Walter of Chester; Gilbert of Hereford; Robert of Bath; John of Winchester; Robert of Exeter; Hilary of Chichester; Jocelin of Salisbury; Walter of Rochester; Nigel of Ely; William of Norwich; Hugh of Durham; and Æthelwold of Carlisle. There were also present from Normandy the venerable Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, a religious man who feared God;

[Col. 0478C] and the bishops Philip of Bayeux, Arnulf of Lisieux, and Herbert of Avranches. The earls of that kingdom were present, as were Thierry, count of Flanders, from the kingdom of France, and many others. An eclipse of the moon occurred on Sunday [Note: Rather, say Tuesday, 21 December. Bouquet.] before Christmas.

1155. Frederick 3. Louis 18. Henry 2.

King Henry began to restore to his own jurisdiction the cities, castles, and towns belonging to the crown of the kingdom, destroying newly built castles, expelling especially the Flemings from the realm, and deposing certain nominal [Note: *Imaginaire*: “imaginary,” nominal.] and pseudo-earls, to whom King Stephen had distributed almost everything belonging to the fisc with insufficient caution. An earthquake occurred on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February,

[Col. 0478D] [Note: Thus corrected from Marcy; this is the reading of 7b and 8d.] especially in Burgundy, so severe that it was felt three times during the night of the feast of Saint Prisca the Virgin at Cluny. A certain abandoned castle, situated not far from Cluny, was swallowed into an abyss, and the space in which the castle had stood was filled with water of immeasurable depth. In London, on the day before the Kalends of March, Monday, a son was born to Henry king of the English by his wife Queen

[Col. 0479A] Eleanor, and he was called Henry. Henry king of the English disinherited William Peverel of Nottingham because of the poison administered to Ranulf, earl of Chester. It is said that many persons were accomplices and privy to this crime. This year earthquakes occurred frequently throughout the whole of Lent in Burgundy and Lombardy. On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, Thursday, we also felt an earthquake at Mont-Saint-Michel before sunrise. On the death of Robert, bishop of Exeter, Robert, dean of Salisbury, succeeded him. Baldwin de Redvers died, and his son Richard succeeded him. [Note: “Baldwin died—his son” is absent from 8b.] On the Sunday after the octave of Easter, namely the fourth day before the Ides of April, King Henry at Wallingford caused the magnates of the English

[Col. 0479B] kingdom to swear fealty to his eldest son William for the kingdom of England; and, if the same boy should die prematurely, to his brother Henry. When the disagreement between Henry king of the English and Roger son of Miles of Gloucester concerning the tower of Gloucester had been settled, Hugh de Mortimer, a most arrogant man, self-confident, fortified his castles against the king. King Henry immediately besieged all his castles, namely Bridgnorth, Wigmore, and Cleobury; the last of these he captured shortly afterwards and destroyed. On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the first hour of the night, an eclipse of the moon occurred. In July, on the Nones of that month, Hugh de Mortimer made peace with King Henry and surrendered the castles of Bridgnorth and Wigmore. Garnier,

[Col. 0479C] abbot of Marmoutier, died and was succeeded by Robert, a Breton by birth. On the death of Roger son of Miles of Gloucester, earl of Hereford, his brother Walter succeeded to his paternal inheritance only; for King Henry retained the earldom of Hereford and the city of Gloucester in his own hand. Frederick, king of the Germans, went to Rome and, despite the opposition of the Romans, was received by Pope Adrian and consecrated emperor by him in the church of Saint Peter. But when he wished to advance farther, namely into Apulia—for he and Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, who had married Frederick’s sister, had agreed through their envoys that, coming from different directions, they would overthrow the kingdom of Apulia and its king William—he immediately changed his intention and returned to his own country.

[Col. 0479D] Yet war did not fail King William of Apulia. For Count Robert of Basseville, his kinsman, and Richard de Ling., count of Andria, thinking the king dead when he was not—for he had been ill, but later recovered—ravaged the kingdom of Apulia grievously. [Note: Thus corrected in E. Previously: “who had as wife a kinswoman.”] About the feast of Saint Michael, King Henry of the English, having held a council at Winchester, discussed with his magnates the conquest of

[Col. 0480A] the kingdom of Ireland and its grant to his brother William. Because this did not please his mother the Empress, the expedition was postponed for a time. Henry, bishop of Winchester, secretly sent his treasure ahead through the abbot of Cluny and departed England without the king’s permission, as it were clandestinely. Therefore King Henry overthrew all his castles. [Note: Here the first hand in 8d, which has written everything thus far, ends.]

1156. Frederick 5. Louis 19. Henry 2.

King Henry, intending to cross the sea, embarked at Dover and landed at Wissant. At the Purification of Saint Mary he was at Rouen; in the following week he conferred with Louis, king of the Franks, on the border of Normandy and France. Returning thence to Rouen, Thierry, count of the Flemings,

[Col. 0480B] his wife, the king’s aunt, and his brother Geoffrey came to him. But since Geoffrey would not accept what was offered him by the king, he withdrew into Anjou, and King Henry immediately followed him. [Note: Here the first hand in E ends. The hand that follows seems to be Robert’s own. Manuscript 2 also ends at the words “into Anjou”; another hand adds: “and so constrained him that he compelled him to make peace with him, leaving him none of the castles which he held except the city of Nantes; nevertheless, he promised to give him money each year.”]

About this time, after a considerable flooding of the Tiber, there was found at Rome, on an island in that river, in an ancient little church, in a certain sarcophagus, the body of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle, wholly intact except for the skin, which remained at Benevento when Emperor Otto, after capturing that city, transferred the body of the aforesaid apostle to Rome, as two bronze tablets demonstrate, inscribed with Greek and Latin letters, which were found with the apostle’s body. The body of Paulinus, bishop of Nola, was also found in the same church.

[Col. 0480C] Geoffrey, brother of Henry king of the English, expelled Hoël, count of Brittany, and captured the city of Nantes with the consent of its citizens. William, king of Sicily, utterly destroyed the city of Bari except for the church of Saint Nicholas, because its citizens, favouring the Greeks, had wickedly conspired against him. The same king also defeated the Greeks by land and sea, was enriched with their spoils, and restored to his own jurisdiction the castles and cities which he had lost. He also disinherited Count Robert de Basseville, his kinsman, because he had revolted from him. Nevertheless, he made peace with Pope Adrian, granting him the consecrations of the bishops of his kingdom and duchy, as the Roman Church had held them in ancient times; concerning this there had been discord between

[Col. 0480D] his father King Roger and the Roman pontiffs Innocent and Eugenius. That apostolic lord in turn granted him the kingdom of Sicily, the duchy of Apulia, and the principality of Capua. [Note: After this point in E the ink changes slightly; it is the same hand, but one that soon declines into a less cultivated style.]

During the octave of Pentecost Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, Rotrou, bishop of Évreux, and the bishops Richard of Coutances and Herbert of Avranches raised the body of Saint Firmatus at Mortain. When the archbishop thereafter came to Mont-Saint-Michel for prayer and to visit us, and had cheered us for four days by his pleasant exhortation and conversation,

[Col. 0481A] he had the altar of the Crucified consecrated by Herbert, bishop of Avranches, on Friday; on the following Saturday he himself consecrated the newly rebuilt altar of Blessed Mary in the northern crypt. In this altar we placed relics of the garments—as we believe—of our Lady herself, which we had found there in a lead casket in the old altar. [Note: “which we had found” is absent from 8b and 8h.]

In the district of Paris, the cloak of our Saviour was discovered by divine revelation at the monastery of Argenteuil, seamless and reddish in colour. As the letters found with it indicated, his glorious mother had made it for him while he was still

[Col. 0481B] a child. On the third day before the Kalends of June, Wednesday, the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension, about noon, for almost half an hour a circle of very great breadth, fiery and azure in colour, appeared around the sun. William, eldest son of Henry king of the English, died and was buried at Reading at the feet of Henry, his kingly great-grandfather. Æthelwold, the first bishop of Carlisle, likewise died. Gilbert de Gant also died. And the young Simon, son of Count Simon, being without land, received from King Henry his only daughter together with her honour. [Note: “And Simon—her honour” was added later in E, but in the same hand. It is also in 8b, 8d, and 8h; absent from 7b.] Henry king of the English captured the castles of Mirebeau and Chinon after a long siege. Loudun, however, was surrendered to him when his brother Geoffrey made peace with him, on this condition: that the king should give him every

[Col. 0481C] year one thousand pounds of English money and two thousand pounds of Angevin money. Thus, with God’s favour, the discord that had long endured between them was settled in July. On the death of Alan, bishop of Rennes, Stephen, abbot of Saint-Florent, a religious, learned, and eloquent man, succeeded him. [Note: “religious and” has been erased; absent from 8d and 8h.] Ingelbaud, archbishop of Tours, also died, and Gotho the Breton, bishop of Saint-Brieuc, succeeded him. Conan, count of Richmond, coming from England into Lesser Brittany, besieged and captured the city of Rennes, having driven out his stepfather Eudo the viscount. This year lightning and storms occurred frequently in Normandy in July. Thus in many places the harvest was ruined and people died from lightning strikes. There followed an abundance

[Col. 0481D] of rain, beginning in mid-August, which hindered both the gathering of the harvest and the subsequent sowing of seed. Because of the continual flooding rains, which lasted a long time, many towers, churches, and ancient walls collapsed in Normandy and England. Ralph de Fougères captured Eudo, viscount of Porhoët, in a battle; and

[Col. 0482A] for this reason the greater part of the Bretons accepted Count Conan as duke of Brittany, except John of Dol, who still resisted Conan and his supporters to the extent of his strength. Frederick, emperor of the Germans, married the daughter of William, count of Mâcon, [Note: Mâcon. But Robert is mistaken: Beatrice was the daughter of Renaud III, count of Burgundy, William’s brother.] and with her acquired the city of Besançon and many others which her father had held from the duke of Burgundy. Nevertheless, part of that honour remained with Count Renaud, the girl’s uncle. [Note: “married the daughter—girl” was added later in E, but in the same hand. It is also present in 8b and 8h; but “Frederick—girl” is absent from 7b.]

1157. Frederick 6. Louis 20. Henry 3.

The venerable Peter, abbot of Cluny, entered upon the way of all flesh on the eighth day before the Kalends of January. [Note: A.D. 1156, since Robert begins the year at Christmas.] William, king of Sicily, in a naval expedition conducted through his admirals captured the metropolitan city of Sibilia, situated

[Col. 0482B] between Africa and Babylon. This city is the capital of the kingdom of the island of Gerp; the king settled Christian inhabitants there and appointed an archbishop over them. On the Saturday within the octave of Easter, at a place in the territory of Avranches called Landa Aronis, about midday an immense whirlwind seemed to rise out of the earth; it enveloped and swept away everything nearby. Finally, as the whirlwind rose aloft, there stood beneath it, as it were, a column of red and azure colour; in this column arrows and lances seemed to be thrust and could be heard striking, though those watching could not see who wielded them. In the whirlwind standing above the column appeared, as it were, different kinds of birds flying about within it. A mortality among the people of that village immediately followed, and among the dead was the lord

[Col. 0482C] of the village. Nor was there mortality only in that village; it raged this year in many places of Normandy and neighbouring regions. The cloister monks of Cluny, in a tumultuous election—or rather an intrusion—elected as abbot a certain half-layman, Robert the Fat, kinsman of the count of Flanders, because of his family connection, despite the protests of the more mature and honourable persons who had been taken from that monastery for pastoral care. Gerard, bishop of Sées, died.

After the octave of Easter Henry king of the English crossed at Barfleur into England, and Malcolm king of the Scots surrendered to him everything that he held from his lordship: namely, the city of Carlisle, the Castle of the Maidens

[Col. 0482D] [Note: “of the Maidens” is erased in E; absent from 8d and 8h; present in 7b.], Bamburgh, Newcastle upon Tyne, and the earldom of Lothian. The king restored to him the earldom of Huntingdon. Likewise William, son of King Stephen, who was count of the city of Coutances—that is, of Mortain—and in England earl of Surrey, that is, of Warenne, by reason of the daughter of the third William de Warenne whom he had married, surrendered to him Pevensey and Norwich

[Col. 0483A] and everything that he held of his crown, and all his own fortifications both in Normandy and in England. The king caused him to hold everything that his father Stephen had held in the year and day in which King Henry, William’s grandfather, was alive and dead. Hugh Bigod surrendered his castles to the king. On the death of Louis, first abbot of Saint-Georges of Boscherville [Note: Saint-Georges de Boscherville, near Rouen.], Victor, a monk of Saint-Victor, succeeded him. Roger d’Aquila, a religious man who feared God, a Cluniac monk, became abbot of Saint-Ouen at Rouen, Freherius resigning because of illness. [Note: “on the death—illness” is absent from 8b and 8h.] Thierry, count of Flanders, and his wife, aunt of Henry king of the English, went to Jerusalem and placed their son Philip and

[Col. 0483B] all that was theirs in Henry king of the English’s hand. Around the feast of Saint John the Baptist, King Henry prepared a very great expedition, so that every two knights in all England were to equip a third, in order to subdue the Welsh by land and sea.
