[Note: From this point in E a different hand begins, and the ink changes.] The Almoravids again took by siege the city of Almería in Spain, along with certain castles, which they had lost to the Christians, putting to flight Alfonso, emperor of Spain. The emperor’s death followed from grief and shame at this flight, and discord arose among his sons. Robert, abbot of Cluny, was deposed and died, together with his companions, on the return from Rome; Hugh, prior of Claustrum, became abbot of Cluny. [Note: “Robert deposed—of Cluny” is absent from 8b, though not from 8h.]

When the truce between Baldwin, king of

[Col. 0483C] Jerusalem, and Nur al-Din son of Zangi, king of Aleppo, had been broken over a Saracen booty which King Baldwin had imprudently seized, the pagans besieged the city of Abilene, anciently called Caesarea Philippi, and destroyed all the villages except the principal fortress. But at length, on the arrival of the life-giving Cross and the Christian army, the pagans withdrew for a time; then they returned and found King Baldwin unprepared, since he had already dismissed the forces of his army and expected anything rather than an ambush. After many of the Templars, who alone remained with him,

[Col. 0484A] had been slaughtered, the king himself could scarcely be persuaded to withdraw. An earthquake followed this disaster of the Christians, especially in the lands overseas. The fleet of the admiral of Babylon also besieged Acre for one month, although in the preceding year the king of Jerusalem had received tribute both from Babylon and from Damascus. Amalric, count of Jaffa, brother of King Baldwin, married the daughter of Joscelin of Turbessel, formerly—before the Hagarenes captured it—count of Edessa, which modern people now call Rohais. Henry king of the English, having subdued the Welsh at will and restored to his barons the lands and fortifications which the Welsh had taken from them in King Stephen’s time, cut down woods and opened roads, fortified the castle of Rhuddlan and gave it to Hugh de Beauchamp;

[Col. 0484B] he also built another castle, namely Basingwerk, and between these two castles one house for the Knights Templar. In September a son was born to Henry king of the English and called Richard. [Note: Manuscripts 3a and 3b end here.]

1158. Frederick 7. Louis 21. Henry 4.

Frederick, emperor of the Germans, after Easter [Note: He was still at Augsburg on 14 June.] crossed the Alps, besieged the most noble city of Milan, and, after a long siege, when the city had surrendered and hostages had been given (8 September), advanced further in order, if possible, to crush William king of Sicily. On the death of Sancho, king of Spain, his son succeeded him, born of the daughter of García, king of Navarre. Geoffrey, archbishop of Bordeaux, also died,

[Col. 0484C] a religious man and an outstanding sower of God’s word. Theobald, bishop of Paris, likewise died. On the feast of Saint John the Baptist, Henry king of the English girded with military arms at Carlisle William, son of King Stephen, count of Mortain and of Warenne—the latter earldom he held through the daughter of William, count of Warenne, whom he had married. This William had died on the Jerusalem expedition. [Note: After this 8b adds: “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1157, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, a community with its abbot Richard de Bloseville left Mortemer, sent by Lord Stephen, then abbot of Mortemer, and came to this place called Le Bosc, situated in the territory of Rouen. For by many prayers Matilda the Empress, daughter of Henry the Great, king of England, and mother of the illustrious Henry, king of England, obtained from the aforesaid Stephen, abbot of Mortemer, that a community should be sent thence to build an abbey of the Cistercian Order, to the praise and honour of God, Blessed Mary, and all the saints.”

“What follows under this year in Robert, manuscript 8g expanded as follows, according to Bouquet: ‘In the year 1158 Geoffrey, second son of the Empress, brother of the king of the English and count of the Bretons, entered the way of all flesh on the seventh day before the Kalends of August; he was buried with great honour in the same city of Nantes, of which he had been count. Henry king of the English, having subdued Wales and made it wholly tributary, crossed into Normandy on the vigil of the Assumption of Saint Mary. Soon after he came to Rouen, he held a conference with the king of the Franks, namely on Thursday, the second day before the Kalends of September, between Gisors and Neufmarché, with the prelates of Holy Church and the barons of both provinces present. Therefore, Justice looking down from heaven, Louis king of the Franks, before the aforesaid persons, gave his first-born daughter by his second wife, named Constance, a little more than half a year old, to Henry, second son of the king of the English, who was nearly three years old, with all the Vexin and its fortifications, which had formerly belonged to the king of the English. Yet the king of the Franks retained custody of that land and all its fortifications until the girl reached marriageable age, subject to this arrangement: if the son of the king of the English should die before the consummation of marriage with the girl, the second, third, or other sons should marry her, receiving from the king of the English, under the name of a dower, in England the city of Lincoln

[Col. 0485] and one thousand pounds, and the service of three hundred knights; in Normandy, the city of Avranches, two castles, and one thousand pounds, and the service of two hundred knights. The bishops of both parties stood surety for this agreement. In September Henry king of the English went to Paris in order to bring into Normandy the king’s daughter whom he had accepted for his son. When Louis king of the Franks came to meet him with great honour and a retinue, he received him in the royal palace at Paris, furnished as befitted so great a king, with great rejoicing by all. That day they dined together late, in a manner wonderful to all, with affection and reciprocal manifestations of affection. On the following day the king of the Franks escorted him with his daughter as far as Mantes, generously supplying all necessities, both at the English king’s arrival and departure. In the same month a fourth son, named Geoffrey, was born in England to the king of the English. In the same month Henry king of the English invaded the Bretons with a great army. Greatly alarmed by his arrival, they surrendered to him their chief city of Nantes, of which the king’s brother had been count, and all submitted themselves to his lordship. Having begun the castle of Pontorson, two miles from Saint Michael’s, King Henry with a great army besieged Thouars, an impregnable castle on the border of Poitou and Anjou. In three days the castle was taken as far as the tower, and the tower surrendered; its count was expelled. In November, when the king of the Franks was setting out to pray at Saint Michael’s after danger at sea, the king of the English met him and received him with the greatest honour at Pacy, at Évreux, and at Neubourg, so that he might see his daughter, who was being brought up there. Then both kings were received at Bec in solemn procession, in which there were three bishops and many other persons; they rested there that night, the king of France in the greater hall and the king of England in another. For the king of England had decreed that the king of the Franks should always lodge in the more distinguished accommodation. At this place the king of the Franks said that he could love no one as much as the king of the English. Wonderful to relate! Who had ever heard that the kings of England and France were joined in such affection? When they departed, the king of the English provided an escort for the king of the Franks through his cities and castles as far as Saint Michael’s, and through Rouen as far as France, providing him abundantly with necessities throughout the journey. In the same month, at the king of the Franks’ intercession, the sons of Count Theobald made peace with the king of the English; previously they had been enemies of one another.’”]

(26 July) On the death in July of Geoffrey, count of Nantes, brother of Henry king of the English, King Henry crossed into

[Col. 0485A] Normandy in August. Having conferred with Louis king of the Franks on the river Epte about peace and arranging a marriage between his son Henry and Margaret, daughter of the king of the Franks, and after oaths had been exchanged on both sides, the king of England came to Argentan. On the feast of the Nativity of Blessed Mary he ordered the army of all Normandy to assemble there, so that they might be at Avranches on the feast of Saint Michael, to march against Conan, duke of Brittany, unless he surrendered to the king the city of Nantes, which he had seized. Thereupon, summoned by the king of the Franks, he came with a few men to Paris and was received with inestimable honour by King Louis, Queen Constance, and the magnates of the realm. The Franks rejoiced and celebrated both the peace of the two kings and the arrival

[Col. 0485B] of so great a guest. He conducted himself magnificently and generously toward all, especially toward the churches and Christ’s poor. In no church did he wish to be received with a procession, although he was pressed by the king of the Franks—indeed, by almost everyone—with prayers and entreaties to permit it. Returning thence, he brought the daughter of the king of France with him and entrusted her for guarding and upbringing to his faithful Robert of Neubourg.

In September, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, a son was born to Henry king of the English and was called Geoffrey. On the feast of Saint Michael, Conan, count of Rennes, and his Bretons came with him to Avranches and surrendered to the king the city of Nantes with the whole county of Medie, worth, it is said, sixty thousand solidi of Angevin

[Col. 0485C] money. From there the king came to Mont-Saint-Michel and, having heard Mass at the high altar, ate with his barons in the monks’ refectory. Abbot Robert obtained this from him only with great difficulty and many entreaties. Afterwards, in the abbot’s new chamber, [Note: “ate—the abbot’s chamber” is absent from 8b and 8h.] he granted the churches of Pontorson to Saint Michael and to the abbot and monks of that place, in the presence of Abbot Robert, Prior Ranulf, the monk Maner, Gervase, clerk of Chancellor Thomas, and Adam, scribe of Abbot Robert.

[Col. 0486A] On that same day he went to Pontorson, distributed assignments there among his officials, and arranged how that castle should be rebuilt. Departing thence with an armed force, he went to receive the city of Nantes. Once he had received it and arranged it as he pleased, after a few intervening days, with an innumerable army he besieged the castle of Thouars on Tuesday and captured it on Friday of the same week. A little later he went to meet Louis king of the Franks, who was coming to Mont-Saint-Michel to pray after danger at sea. From the moment Louis entered the duchy of Normandy, Henry escorted him and provided for him most fittingly at his own expense. Robert of Saint Pancras, monk of Saint Michael of the Mount, became abbot of Cerne.

[Col. 0486B] [Note: “Robert—Cerne” is absent from 8b and 8h.] On the feast of Saint Clement, a Sunday, both kings came to the Mount of the blessed archangel. Clergy and people alike went in great rejoicing to meet the king of the Franks. In the procession itself, apart from the community of monks, clergy, and an innumerable populace, there were two high prelates, one an archbishop and the other a bishop, and five abbots. Having heard Mass, they returned to Avranches. The king escorted Louis and accompanied both him and his party as far as the borders of his duchy, bestowing innumerable royal gifts upon them.

In December King Henry and Count Theobald of Blois, his kinsman, made an agreement as follows. Count Theobald surrendered to the king two castles, Amboise

[Col. 0486C] and Fréteval. And Count Rotrou of Mortain, his brother-in-law—for Odo, duke of Burgundy, had married one of Theobald’s sisters; the aforesaid Count Rotrou, more commonly called count of Perche, another; and William Gouet a third—this Rotrou, I say, surrendered to King Henry two castles, Moulins and Bonne-Moulin, which were dependencies of the duke of Normandy. But after King Henry’s death, Count Rotrou, [Note: *Rotocus* in E.] father of this Rotrou, had occupied them. King Henry, however, granted

[Col. 0487A] to this same Rotrou the castle of Bellême, and he did homage to the king for it. In the same year Abbot Robert of Saint Michael, while improving certain antiquated ornaments in the shrine of Saint Aubert the bishop with gold and silver, found within it the bones of that saint, except for the head, which is kept separately in the same church in a silver vessel. He also found with the body letters testifying to this fact and a tablet of green marble. [Note: Here two lines have been erased in E. “In the same year—body” is absent from 8b, 8d, and 8h.] The body of the blessed confessor and bishop Aubert was again placed in the same shrine, secured by three bands, together with the marble and the old document and a new one, which states in what year of the Lord’s Incarnation, and by which abbot, that body was then reinterred.

In the same year the bodies of the Three Magi,

[Col. 0488A] who worshipped our Saviour as an infant in Bethlehem, were discovered in an old chapel near the city of Milan; because Frederick, emperor of the Germans, was coming to besiege that city, they were raised and placed in the city out of fear of him. Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, captured from the pagans Caesarea the Great in Palestine, situated not far from Antioch. He also captured the castle of Harenc and entrusted it to Rainald of Saint-Valery.

1159. Frederick 8. Louis 22. Henry 5.

King Henry celebrated the feast of the Nativity with Queen Eleanor at Cherbourg, to which she had shortly before crossed over into Normandy.

[Note: [Col. 0487A] Cherbourg.]

[Note: [Col. 0487] Manuscript 8g, according to Bouquet, gives this year as follows: “In the year 1159 Henry, king of the English, held his court at Christmas at Cherbourg, as befitted so great a king, with a great company of princes. About the octave of Epiphany Theobald, bishop of Paris, formerly prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, the pious father paid the dues of death, and the bishopric was vacant for a little while. After the abbot of Saint-Évroult had been deposed, Robert of Blangy, a monk of Bec, was appointed abbot of that place in the first week of Septuagesima. At the beginning of Lent Henry, king of the English, went with his magnates as far as the city of Poitiers, intending to take counsel on bringing under his rule the lordship of the city of Toulouse, which the dukes of Poitou had formerly possessed by hereditary right. But the count of Saint-Gilles, who had married Constance, sister of the king of the French, and had had three children by her, relied upon the many fortifications of the city of Toulouse and on the aid of the king of the French, and refused obedience. Therefore, after a council on this matter had been held by both kings at the city of Tours, without their wills agreeing, Henry, king of the English, ordered the forces of England and Normandy, Maine and Anjou, Aquitaine, Gascony, and Brittany to assemble at Poitiers for the feast of Saint John the Baptist. He took an immense sum of money from all the bishoprics and abbeys of the aforesaid provinces, so that he might maintain so great an army around the aforesaid city until the feast of All Saints. On the day before the Nones of May [6 May] the city of Rouen was burned. Henry, king of the English, was at Bec with a great army of his magnates for the feast of the Ascension of the Lord, for the solemn procession and Mass; after remaining there for three days, he departed for Rouen. On the eighth, seventh, and sixth days before the Ides of June [6, 7, and 8 June], a conference was held at Héricourt between the king of the French and the king of the English, with the bishops and barons of both parties, concerning the agreements which they had previously made regarding the marriage of their children, and concerning the army of the king of the English which was to go to Toulouse. There they did not reach agreement, because the king of the French would not permit him to take Toulouse, on account of his sister and nephews. A kind of robbers, unheard of in former times, troubled England under the appearance of religion: posing as monks, they came upon travellers while they were in the windings of roads and woods; after making a signal to their companions, they killed them and plundered their money and goods. Malcolm, king of Scotland, crossed into Normandy with forty-five ships on 15 June [17 Kalends of July]; when he reached Poitiers, where the army of the king of the English was assembling, he was honourably received by that king. After the feast of Saint John the Baptist Henry, king of the English, advanced his army from Poitiers until they drew near the city of Toulouse. It is beyond our humble capacity to set forth the size, wealth, and ferocity of that army. Master Peter Lombard, a man of great learning and remarkable above the Parisian masters, was elected bishop of Paris and consecrated about the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul. About the same octave Louis, king of the French, held a conference with the king of the English near Toulouse, concerning the securing of peace with the count of Saint-Gilles. But since no peace was obtained, hostility and discord over a peace so long maintained arose between them; to the harm of the whole country, they parted from one another. The king of the French therefore entered Toulouse, which had been granted to him and to his nephews, and remained there continually with its count for as long as the king of the English stayed in the province. The king of the English, however, acting on the counsel of his princes, refused to besiege the king; but, besieging the surrounding castles, he quickly took them, grievously ravaged the whole province, and took Mont-Royal and the city of Cahors with its dependent territory. After his departure he left a great multitude of armed men in that province to guard it and the other castles he had taken; the leader of these was the king’s chancellor. When the discord between the two kings was heard of, Frenchmen and Normans fought grievously on the frontier of France and Normandy. Then Count Theobald, who was aiding the king of the English, did homage to him and, by the king’s command, returned into France, increasing the grief of the French. On 1 August Robert of Neubourg, justiciar over all Normandy, a man of great prudence and goodness, afflicted by illness, became a monk of the church of Bec, first generously distributing to the poor all his considerable private possessions. [lacuna] On 30 August [3 Kalends of September] Robert of Neubourg died. Having been a monk of Bec for nearly five weeks, he had in a short time, by God’s power and under a blessed beginning, been enriched with admirable abstinence, religious devotion, and every virtue; he left to all the leading men of the church an example of good life. Formerly rich, he had now become the poorest of Christians. On 1 September Pope Adrian entered the path of all flesh; he was succeeded by Roland, chancellor of the Roman Church, who is called Alexander, while some of the clergy elected Octavian, cardinal-priest, who is called Victor. [lacuna] About the feast of Saint Michael, the king of the English, following the counsel of his princes, returned home with his army and fortified Étrépagny near Gisors, which the king of France had earlier destroyed. When, as has been said, the king of the English withdrew from the aforesaid province, the king of the French immediately returned home and took much money from the churches and from his land. Meanwhile all the churches of both countries earnestly offered prayers to the Lord that He might restore both kings to their former peace. Hearing, therefore, that the king of the English had fortified the aforesaid castle, the king of the French, fearing for his own interests, hastened there with his army. Meanwhile, as evils multiplied in the land, about the feast of Saint Martin the count of Évreux handed over to the king of the English all his castles situated in France; the king placed his own garrisons in them, as Simon of Anet had done. Silvester, abbot of Châtillon, then departed this world, and was succeeded by Gilbert, a monk of Évreux. As the coming of the Lord drew near, the two kings, at the request of the great men of the country, made a truce until the octave of Pentecost. On the Sunday before Christmas Frogerius, archdeacon and almoner of the king of the English, was ordained bishop of Sées. This year, because of the flooding rains, which fell almost continuously from the feast of Saint John the Baptist until the feast of Saint Michael, the Seine and other waters overflowed their channels beyond measure and caused great damage to the surrounding population.”]

Henry, king of the English, and Raymond, count of Barcelona, entered into a treaty of friendship at the castle of Blaye, confirmed by oaths, on these terms: Richard, the king’s son, was at the appropriate time to marry the count’s daughter, and the king, after the marriage had been solemnized, was to grant them the duchy of Aquitaine.

[Note: [Col. 0489D] Blaye, on the Garonne.]

For this Raymond was a very powerful and wealthy man: through the inheritance of his wife he possessed the kingdom of Aragon, and through his paternal inheritance the county of the city of Barcelona.

[Note: [Col. 0489D] This must have been written while Raymond was alive, though our author says below, under the year 1162, that he had died.]

To return briefly to earlier events: Sancho, king of Aragon, had three sons, who succeeded him in turn: Sancho, Alfonso, and Ramiro. When the two eldest had succeeded one another and died without children, Ramiro, though a monk and already an old man, was removed from his monastery with the permission of the Roman pontiff and made king, lest that kingdom be seized by outsiders. In order that he might have an heir, Matilda, mother of William, viscount of Thouars, was joined to him; by her he had one daughter, whom the aforesaid Count Raymond married. From her was born this girl, whom, as we have said, was to be joined in marriage to the king’s son; her firstborn son was to become king of Aragon. Although the count himself possessed the kingdom of Aragon and could have become king if he wished, he wholly declined it, reserving the kingdom for his son, to whom it fell through his maternal descent.

In this year also, as in the preceding one, Frederick, emperor of the Germans, besieged the city of Milan, because the Milanese had rebelled against him. He threw down the towers of Pavia and Piacenza and brought almost all Lombardy under his will.

In the middle of Lent the king ordered an army to be raised from all Normandy, England, Aquitaine, and the other provinces subject to him, because Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, would not surrender to him the city of Toulouse, which the king claimed as the inheritance of his wife, Queen Eleanor. Robert, count of Mortain, uterine brother of King William who conquered the kingdom of England, had one son, William, who succeeded him and was captured in battle at Tinchebray by Henry I, king of the English; and three daughters. One married Andrew of Vitré, another Guy of Laval, and the third the count of Toulouse, William,

[Note: [Col. 0489D] William.]

brother of Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, who bore himself bravely in the Jerusalem expedition. The count of Toulouse had by her only one daughter. After the death of that girl’s father, William, count of Poitou and duke of Aquitaine, married her together with her inheritance—namely the city of Toulouse and the county of Toulouse. By her this same William begot a son called William, who succeeded him and was father of Eleanor, queen of the English.

If anyone asks how the count of Saint-Gilles later came to possess the city of Toulouse, let him know that the aforesaid William, count of Poitou, pledged that city to Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, his wife’s paternal uncle, for money which William had spent on the Jerusalem expedition.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] False: Raymond had already been travelling as a crusader for five years when William set out for Palestine in 1101. BOUQ.]

Accordingly, in the book concerning that expedition Raymond is called now count of Saint-Gilles, now count of Toulouse. After his death his son Alfonso possessed the same city; he died at Jerusalem at the time when Louis, king of the French, had gone there for the sake of prayer. Likewise, his son Raymond succeeded him; he married Constance, sister of the aforesaid Louis, king of the French, the widow of Count Eustace, son of Stephen, king of the English.

Therefore King Henry, about to undertake the aforesaid expedition and considering the length and difficulty of the route, did not wish to burden peasant soldiers or the multitude of townsmen and rustics. In Normandy he took sixty Angevin shillings from the fee of every hauberk, and from all the rest of his possessions in Normandy, England, and his other lands whatever seemed fit to him. He took with him his chief barons, but few in number, and countless paid soldiers. To this expedition, along with the other men from beyond the sea, came Malcolm, king of Scotland; there King Henry girded him with the belt of knighthood. The expedition lasted nearly three months. Although King Henry took the city of Cahors and the greater part of the duchy of Toulouse was subject to him by force or fear, he would not besiege Toulouse, out of regard for Louis, king of the French. Louis had fortified the city against Henry, king of England, and remained there day and night, wishing to bring aid to Raymond, his brother-in-law. Hence serious enmities arose between him and the king of the English, when Henry saw that the king of France was harming him, though he had placed great trust in his aid.

King Henry therefore sent back Count Theobald, who supported him, to harass the kingdom of France. But Henry, bishop of Beauvais, and Count Robert, lord of the castle of Dreux, brothers of the king of the French, resisted him and afflicted some places on the border of the duchy of Normandy by fire and plunder; the Normans retaliated in kind. Robert of Blangy, monk of Bec, became abbot of Saint-Évroult.

[Note: [Col. 0491] “Robert … Saint-Évroult” is absent in 8b and 8h.]

In July Robert of Neubourg, steward and justiciar of all Normandy, struck by illness, laid down the camel’s hump—that is, his countless riches—distributing them among churches, monasteries, and the poor. At last, taking the monastic habit at the monastery of Bec, which he loved above all others, he spent one month there in fruitful penitence. On 30 August [3 Kalends of September] he departed this life and was buried in the chapter house of Bec, which he had splendidly built at his own expense.

After the death of the venerable Milo, bishop of Thérouanne, Milo, archdeacon of the same church and a regular canon like his predecessor, was elected. When Samson, archbishop of Reims, wished to consecrate him, the clergy of the city of Boulogne—who had long been under the bishop of Thérouanne—wishing henceforth to have a bishop of their own as they had in ancient times, prohibited the archbishop, under apostolic appeal, from consecrating him except merely to the title of the church of Thérouanne. Rejecting this condition, the aforesaid bishop-elect went to Rome against those clergy while still unconsecrated, and there he was consecrated.

Master Bernard the Breton, chancellor of the church of Chartres, became bishop of Cornwall in Lesser Brittany. Master Peter Lombard also obtained the bishopric of Paris, with the acquiescence of Philip, dean of that church and brother of the king of France; he is said to have granted his own election to Peter.

On 1 September, after the death of Pope Adrian, two men were elected and consecrated: Roland, chancellor and cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mark, a religious man, called Alexander III, namely the 174th pope; and Octavian, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, called Victor III. The latter seized the papacy through his power and his noble relatives. Frogerius, the king’s almoner, became bishop of Sées. Walter, bishop of Chester, died. Robert, bishop of Exeter, also died,

[Note: [Col. 0491] Here manuscript 4 ends, at the words: “The bishop of Obsoniensis succeeded him,” at the top of the page.]

a religious man who feared God. Thierry, count of Flanders, returned from Jerusalem, but his wife Mabiria [Sibylla] remained with the abbess of Saint Lazarus at Bethany against her husband’s will.

[Note: [Col. 0491] Sibylla.]

In October Henry, king of the English, having fortified the city of Cahors and entrusted it to his chancellor Thomas, and having stationed guards and auxiliaries in suitable places, returned to Normandy, trusting in the aid of Raymond Berengar, count of Barcelona, Trencavel, count of Nîmes, William of Montpellier, and his other faithful men. From there he proceeded with a strong force into the territory of Beauvais and destroyed the very strongly fortified castle of Gerberoy, except for a certain stronghold; fire and smoke kept the king’s men from taking it. He burned and destroyed many villages. Simon, count of Évreux, surrendered to Henry, king of the English, his strongholds in France: Rochefort, Montfort, Épernon, and the rest. This greatly harmed the king of the French, who could not travel freely from Paris to Orléans or Étampes because of the Normans whom King Henry had placed in the castles of the count of Évreux. For this reason a truce was made between the two kings from December until the octave of Pentecost. On the return from the Toulouse expedition, in October, William, count of Mortain, died childless; Henry, the king, retained the county in his own hand.

## 1160. Frederick 9. Louis 23. Henry 6.

King Henry celebrated the Nativity with Queen Eleanor at Falaise; afterwards the queen crossed to England. On 1 January an earthquake occurred in the district of Coutances, at the castle of Saint-Lô, about the first hour.

[Note: [Col. 0491] Saint-Lô.]

Hardouin, dean of Le Mans, became archbishop of Bordeaux, although his predecessor had scarcely lived a year and a half. The Empress Matilda, struck by illness, generously distributed her wealth to churches, monasteries, and the poor, acting on the counsel of her son Henry, king of the English; she preferred the monastery of Bec above all others, as she had done during another illness.

After the church of Bayeux was burned by fire, Bishop Philip again laboured vigorously in restoring it. In May peace was made between Henry, king of England, and Louis, king of France; the former agreements were renewed and confirmed, and those who had aided either side were reconciled. Matthew, son of the count of Flanders, in an unheard-of precedent married the abbess of Romsey, Mary, daughter of King Stephen, and seized with her the county of Boulogne.

[Note: [Col. 0491] Mary.]

In July Henry, king of the English, assembled all the bishops, abbots, and barons of Normandy at Neufmarché, and Louis, king of the French, assembled his men at Beauvais. There the reception of Pope Alexander and the rejection of Victor were discussed; they agreed to Alexander and rejected Victor. In September Herbert, bishop of Avranches, died and was buried in the church of Blessed Mary at Bec, like his predecessor Richard of Beaufou. In the aforesaid month Queen Eleanor of England crossed to Normandy at the king’s command, bringing with her her son Henry and her daughter Matilda. On 16 October Philip, brother of Louis, king of France, dean of Saint-Martin at Tours, died.

[Note: [Col. 0491] After this, one line has been erased in E.]

Constance, queen of France, died in childbirth, leaving alive the daughter whose birth caused her death.

In October the king of England and the king of France met and confirmed their treaty of mutual peace. Henry, son of Henry, king of the English, did homage to the king of France for the duchy of Normandy, which belongs to the kingdom of France. A few days later Louis, king of the French, married the daughter of the elder Count Theobald. Soon afterwards Margaret, daughter of Louis, king of France, was betrothed at Neubourg to Henry, son of Henry, king of the English. King Henry then took the three very strongly fortified castles of Gisors, Neaufles, and Neufchâtel, situated on the river Epte on the frontier between Normandy and France; for he and the king of the French had agreed that, once their children’s marriage had been contracted, Henry should possess those fortresses which belong to the duchy of Normandy.

When the king of France heard this, he and his brothers-in-law—Henry, Theobald, and Stephen—took it badly. The three counts then united their forces and began fortifying the stronghold of Chaumont, which belonged to the fief of the castle of Blois, in order to harry the Touraine from there. But since that castle belonged to the holding of Hugh, son of Sulpicius of Amboise, who held it from Count Theobald—while he held the chief seat of his honour, namely Amboise, from King Henry—King Henry, upon hearing the news, hurried there without waiting for his companions, wishing to prevent construction of that castle. If it were completed, they would be able to range more freely through his land. When Count Theobald heard of the king of England’s approach, he departed from Chaumont, leaving it fortified and garrisoned. King Henry besieged the aforesaid castle and immediately took it; there were thirty-five knights and eighty servants in it. He restored the stronghold to Hugh of Amboise, who opposed Count Theobald to the best of his ability because Sulpicius, Hugh’s father, had been wickedly killed in the count’s prison. Thereupon King Henry fortified the towers of Amboise and Fréteval, stationed guards, and celebrated the Nativity with Queen Eleanor at Le Mans.

[Note: [Col. 0493] From this point in E there is a new hand, apparently Robert’s.]

## 1161. Frederick 10. Louis 24. Henry 7.

King Henry took into his own hand the fortifications of the count of Meulan and of his other barons in Normandy, and entrusted them to his faithful men. On the frontier of the duchy of Normandy he improved or rebuilt almost all his castles, especially Gisors. He made a park and royal residence around planted stakes at Chivilley near Rouen. He built a remarkable leper-house near Caen. He likewise renovated the hall and chambers before the tower at Rouen. And not only in Normandy, but also in the kingdom of England, the duchy of Aquitaine, the county of Anjou, Maine, and Touraine, he either built new castles and royal residences or repaired old ones. He also built a castle in the village called Amandiville, on the river Vire.

Achard, abbot of Saint-Victor at Paris, became bishop of Avranches. William the Englishman, prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, became abbot of the church of Ramsey in England.

[Note: [Col. 0493] “William … England” is absent in 8b and 8h.]

At the beginning of Lent, at Le Mans, Hugh, archbishop of Dol, weakened by blindness, surrendered the archbishopric in the presence of Henry, king of the English, and two legates of the Roman Church, Henry of Pisa and William of Pavia. He had held it for almost six years and had laboured greatly for its restoration. In his place Roger of Humez, archdeacon of Bayeux, was elected there. Bartholomew, archdeacon of Exeter, became bishop of Exeter. Richard Peccatum, archdeacon of Chester, became bishop of that church. Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, died on the second weekday of Easter.

After Easter, Henry, king of the English, and Louis, king of the French, first in the Vexin and afterwards in the Dunois district near Orléans, were incited to discord by Count Theobald. Having gathered their armies to defend their respective lands, they came almost into close conflict. After a truce had been made, following the feast of Saint John, Henry, king of the English, went to Aquitaine. Among other exploits, he besieged Châtillon above the city of Agen, a castle fortified by nature and art, and took it within one week, on the feast of Saint Lawrence, to the amazement and terror of the Gascons.

[Note: [Col. 0493] Le Dunois, near Orléans.]

Queen Eleanor gave birth to a daughter at Domfront. Henry, cardinal-priest and legate of the Roman Church, baptized her; Achard, bishop of Avranches, Robert, abbot of Saint Michael of the Peril of the Sea, and many others received her from the font. She was named Eleanor after her mother. Maurice, archdeacon of Paris, became bishop of that church. After the death of Juhel of Mayenne, his son Geoffrey succeeded him; he married the daughter of the count of Meulan.

[Note: [Col. 0493] “Maurice … Meulan” is absent in 8b and 8h.]

## 1162. 11. 25. 8.

King Henry celebrated the Nativity at Bayeux. In January Geoffrey of Mayenne surrendered to Henry, king of the English, three castles which his father had held after the death of the elder King Henry: Gorron, Ambrières, and Neufchâtel on the river Colmont. In the same month Aquilin of Fougères was removed from the castle of Pontorson, because the people of Avranches complained that he burdened their lands with excessive exactions and injuries. King Henry entrusted that castle for a time to Robert, abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel.

[Note: [Col. 0493] “In January … Mont[-Saint-Michel]” is absent in 8b and 8h.]

After the death of Samson, archbishop of Reims, Henry, brother of the king of France and bishop of Beauvais, succeeded him. Bartholomew, archdeacon of Reims, became bishop of Beauvais.

[Note: [Col. 0493] Samson.]

[Note: [Col. 0495] At this point, as the page ends in E, the hand changes its style; nevertheless it remains the same hand.]

On the first Sunday of Lent King Henry assembled the bishops, abbots, and barons of all Normandy at Rouen. Lodging a complaint against the bishops, their officials, and his vicomtes, he ordered that a council be held at Bonneville. Bonneville is in the district of Caux near the Seine, a royal residence much loved and frequented by the lords of Normandy. Julius Caesar, from whose name it is called Julia, founded it after destroying the city of Caletes, from whose ancient name the whole region lying between the Seine and the sea is still called. Richard I, duke of Normandy, and his son Richard II were raised from their tombs at Fécamp, where they had lain separately, and placed more honourably behind the altar of the Holy Trinity. Henry, king of the English, and the bishops of Normandy attended this translation, and he gave that church the wood of Les Hogs.

Count Robert of Basseville rebelled in Apulia against William, king of Sicily, his kinsman. Having gathered many allies, he won over the greater part of the coastal cities. Frederick, emperor of the Germans, took and destroyed the city of Milan, which he had besieged for three years and which was afflicted by famine, on 26 March; only the cathedral and certain other buildings were spared.

While the discord between kingdom and priesthood continued because of the schism of Octavian, whom Frederick, king of the Romans, had with him in Italy, Pope Alexander of Rome, trusting in Louis, king of the French, and Henry, king of the English—who always devoutly support and venerate the Roman Church—came by sea to the lands this side of the Alps around Easter. He was received with due honour at Montpellier in Provence.

Richard de Reviers, lord of the Isle of Wight, died in England, leaving a young son named Baldwin by the daughter of Reginald, count of Cornwall. Stephen, surnamed Burgundian, abbot of Saint Michael of Chiusa and a monk of Cluny, became abbot of Cluny, after Abbot Hugh had gone over to the party of the emperor and Octavian.

[Note: [Col. 0495] “Richard … Octavian” is absent in 8b and 8h.]

After the death of Hardouin, archbishop of Bordeaux, at Montpellier, while he was staying there at the court of the lord pope, the bishop of Lectoure succeeded him.

[Note: [Col. 0495] Lectoure, subject to the archbishopric of Auch.]

The peoples this side of the Alps, especially in Aquitaine, suffered from famine and mortality. Reginald of Châtillon, prince of Antioch, rashly entering the land of the Hagarenes, was captured after many of his men had been killed or taken captive. Thomas, chancellor of the king of the English, became archbishop of Canterbury.

[Note: [Col. 0495] “Thomas … Canterbury” is absent in 8b and 8h.]

Ralph of Tosny died, leaving a young son by the daughter of Robert, count of Leicester. In July, in Lesser Brittany, namely at Retz, blood rained, flowed from the banks of a spring there, and even issued from bread. In the same month John of Dol died and left his land and daughter under the protection of Ralph of Fougères; but the king of the English took the tower from his hand.

[Note: [Col. 0495] “In the same month … his hand” is absent in 8b and 8h.]

William, king of Sicily, crossed from Sicily into Apulia with a great army; having put Robert of Basseville and his accomplices to flight, he recovered the cities and castles which had revolted from him. John, treasurer of York, a cheerful and generous man and exceptionally learned, became bishop of Poitiers. After the death of Matthew, bishop of Angers, Geoffrey of Sées succeeded him, dean of that church and clerk of the king of the English.

[Note: [Col. 0495] “John … king of the English” is absent in 8b and 8h.]

Lupus, king of Valencia and Murcia, though a gentile and a Hagarene, sent Henry, king of the English, enormous gifts of gold, silk, other wares, horses, and camels, expecting great gifts himself in return. Raymond Berengar, count of Barcelona, a man lamented by all good people, died, leaving his son Alfonso, who became king of Aragon; that kingdom had fallen to him through his mother’s lineage.

Frederick, emperor of the Germans, and Louis, king of the French, were to meet on the river Saône, anciently called the Arar, to negotiate peace in September. But Frederick suddenly changed his mind because of the schism of Octavian, whose party he supported, and they returned home with the matter unresolved. Soon afterwards Louis, king of the French, and Henry, king of the English, met on the Loire at Cociacum and received Pope Alexander of Rome with fitting honour. Performing the office of grooms, they went on foot at his right and left, holding the bridle of his horse, and conducted him to the tent prepared for him. Through his mediation, with God’s favour, firm peace was restored between them.

Richard, bishop of London, died.

[Note: [Col. 0495] “Richard, bishop of London, died” is absent in 8b and 8h.]

Henry, having ordered and settled affairs and his castles in Normandy, Aquitaine, Anjou, and also Gascony, came to Barfleur at Advent, wishing, if possible, to cross before Christmas. But the wind prevented him, and he celebrated the Nativity with Queen Eleanor at Cherbourg. Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, married Constance, daughter of Bohemond II. Bohemond III, brother of the aforesaid girl, became prince, while his stepfather Raynald remained in captivity.

[Note: [Col. 0495] “Manuel … Raynald” was added later, but by the same hand. All the other witnesses contain it.]

## 1163. Frederick 12. Louis 26. Henry 9.

In January King Henry crossed to England, he and the queen, and was received with great rejoicing by nearly all the leading men of the land, who were awaiting him on the shore. For his son Henry had already gone before, and, as in Normandy, so also in England received the homages and fealties of the barons and knights. Upon the death of the archbishop of Lyons [Note: Col. 0497D: Heraclius. BOUQ.], the clergy and people, with the concurrence of Emperor Frederick, elected William, son of Count Theobald the Elder; Pope Alexander likewise confirmed this. That city, however, which lies on this side of the Rhône belongs to the kingdom of France; but because Guigo [Note: Col. 0497: G. has E.] the Dauphin and the counts of Forcalquier had deceitfully taken it from the aforesaid archbishop in the preceding year, and he had been unable to recover it through the king of France, that archbishop therefore transferred himself to the emperor, who restored the said city to him; and thereafter he held it from the emperor. [Note: Col. 0497: “the archbishop of Lyons … held it” are lacking in 8b and 8h.] [Note: Col. 0497D: What Bouquet XIII, p. 307, note, adduces makes Robert’s narrative doubtful; cf. below, under 1175.]

Rotrou, bishop of Évreux, and Rainald of Saint-Valery caused a survey to be made in Normandy by royal command, through the dioceses, of the lawful revenues and customary dues belonging to the king and barons. Philip, bishop of Bayeux, died in February. He was a prudent and shrewd man in increasing and recovering the possessions of that church, and accomplished much there; but the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. He had given himself to the monastery of Bec to become a monk, but “his way is not in man’s power.” For death overtook him, and he could not fulfill what he had intended; yet he had already given it one hundred and forty volumes of books. [Note: Col. 0497: Here, at the end of a folio, the handwriting changes in E. “He … given” is lacking in 8b and 8h.] [Note: Col. 0498D: Ravaisson published their catalogue, inscribed on the first folio of manuscript E, in his *Rapport au ministre*, Paris, 1841.]

The war of Robert of Montfort with Henry of Essex arose from the latter’s flight from battle against the Welsh. In it the same Henry was defeated; disinherited, he became a monk at Reading. The Welsh were subjected to King Henry at his pleasure. Malcolm, king of Scotland, did homage to Henry, son of the king of the English, and gave hostages to the king: namely, his younger brother and certain sons of his barons, for keeping the peace and concerning his castles, which the king wished to possess.

A certain boy, as is believed with the connivance of the monks, killed the abbot of Saint-Maximin at Orléans; and Pope Alexander and Louis, king of the French, expelled nearly all the monks from there, dispersed them among various abbeys, and installed there an abbot from Marmoutier. Likewise, in the preceding year, when the abbot of Lagny, riding out, had found someone who had wronged him and threatened to seize and ruin him, that man shot an arrow and struck the abbot through the eye into the brain, killing him. He was succeeded by Hugh, the natural son of Count Theobald the Elder. He had formerly been a monk at Tiron [Note: Col. 0498D: Tiron or Tironium, in the diocese of Chartres]; and in the time of King Stephen, his uncle, he was for some time abbot of Holme in England. Leaving that abbey, he became abbot of Cerisy. Leaving that again, he came to France to his nephews Henry and Theobald; and so, as we have said, became abbot of Lagny.

Gilbert, bishop of Hereford, upon the death of Richard, bishop of London, was translated to that see; and Master Robert of Melun, an Englishman by birth and advanced in years, was made bishop of Hereford. Roger, son of Robert, count of Gloucester, was elected to the bishopric of Worcester. [Note: Col. 0497: “A certain boy … Worcester” is lacking in 8b and 8h.]

In March Baldwin III, king of Jerusalem, died, a man to be lamented in every respect; and his brother Amalric succeeded him. To this Baldwin it was granted by divine mercy that he should take Ascalon, expel the Hagarenes, and devote it to divine service—something granted to no king before him: not to David for his holiness, nor to Solomon for his wisdom and riches, nor to Hezekiah for his righteousness, nor to any other.

On the octave of Pentecost Pope Alexander held a council at Tours, at which he excommunicated Octavian with the other schismatics and his accomplices. At that council two bishops—one consecrated by the hand of the archbishop of Tarragona, his metropolitan, the other by the archbishop of Toledo, primate of all Spain—were expelled from the church of Pamplona, to whose title both had been consecrated, and a third was substituted. The two, however, retained episcopal rank, and it was granted that, if vacant churches called them, they should become their bishops. [Note: Col. 0497: Here, at the end of a page, the handwriting changes slightly. “At that council … the martyr Nabor” is lacking in 8b and 8h.]

[Col. 0498C] **1164. Frederick 13. Louis 27. Henry 10.**

Count Thierry of Flanders went to Jerusalem for the third time. His eldest son Philip succeeded him, and, having married one of the other daughters of Ralph the Elder, count of Vermandois, and after his wife’s younger brother Ralph, count of Valois, had been struck by an elephant, he became through his wife lord of two counties, namely Vermandois and Montdidier.

Rainald, archbishop-elect of Cologne and chancellor of Frederick, emperor of the Germans, transferred the bodies of the Three Magi from Milan to Cologne. Since their bodies had been preserved with balsam and other spices, they remained outwardly intact as regards skin and hair. The first, as one who asserted that he had seen them told me, appeared, insofar as could be judged from face and hair, to be fifteen years old; the second thirty; and the third forty. Blessed Eustorgius, by the gift of a certain emperor, had transferred them from Constantinople to Milan, together with a certain table upon which they had been placed, in a small vehicle which two cows drew by divine power and will. The same Rainald also transferred from there the body of Saint Valeria, mother of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, and the head of the martyr Nabor.

At Rouen, on 30 January, William, brother of King Henry, died; he was buried in the church of Saint Mary. About the octave of Easter King Henry had the church of Saint Mary at Reading dedicated, and for three days maintained the community of monks and guests royally, also bestowing upon that church no small endowment. Hamelin, Henry’s natural brother, married the countess of Warenne, widow of William, count of Mortain, son of King Stephen. She was the daughter of William III, count of Warenne, who went to Jerusalem with Louis, king of France, and died there, leaving only the aforesaid countess surviving.

[Col. 0499B] In the district of Beauvais Saint Giles appeared in a nocturnal vision to a certain commoner, together with some persons of honorable appearance. He foretold that, when the man drew the first furrow with his plough on the following day, he would find a small iron cross, and commanded him to carry it to his church. The peasant then asked whether he should take it to Saint Giles in Provence. Saint Giles answered: “No, but to Saint Giles in the Cotentin, where my body is.” When this had been done, many miracles occurred there.

At the city of Lucca the schismatic Octavian died, called Victor by antiphrasis—that is, by an ironically contrary name; and he was succeeded, continuing in the same error, by Guy of Crema, called Paschal IV. Count Theobald of Chartres became betrothed to the daughter of Louis, king of France, and the king granted him the stewardship of France, which the count of Anjou had held in ancient times, and in our own day Ralph of Parron performed it on his behalf; accordingly, when doing him homage, he honored him as lord. But his elder brother Henry, count of Troyes, again took the daughter of King Louis whom he had earlier put away.

Frederick the emperor, after he had subdued Lombardy at his pleasure—where there are twenty-five cities, among them three archbishoprics, Milan, Ravenna, and Genoa—and had restored the royal fisc in that realm to a sum of fifty thousand marks, and re-established peace there alike for natives and foreigners, again faced rebellion from Verona and certain other cities. [Note: Col. 0499: Thus E. “But his brother Henry … rebellion” was later corrected in an erasure by the same hand.]

[Col. 0499D] The Welsh, not keeping faith with King Henry, harassed the neighboring lands by plundering, under a certain petty king of theirs called Rhys, and another man of the same depravity named Oeno, uncle of the aforesaid Rhys. Walter Giffard, count of Rochingham, died without an heir, and his county in England and land in Normandy reverted to the lordship of the king. [Note: Col. 0499: “Walter … king” is lacking in 8b and 8h.]

Richard du Hommet, constable of King Henry, having summoned the barons of Normandy and Brittany, took in August the castle of Combourg in Brittany into the king’s hand. Ralph de Fougères had held it after the death of John of Dol. In the same month blood rained at Rethel, in the diocese of Dol. Robert, the religious bishop of Chartres, died. [Note: Col. 0499: “Robert, bishop of Chartres … died” is lacking in 8b and 8h.] Hugh, the venerable archbishop of Rouen, died on 12 October. A man of great learning, he produced many pleasant works and was generous to widows, orphans, and other poor persons. He governed the church of Rouen honorably and courageously for nearly thirty years. [Note: Col. 0499: After this the handwriting and ink change in E. Added in 8h: “The illustrious Count Waleran of Meulan died. He bestowed many benefactions upon the church of Blessed Mary of Le Vœu, situated in the district of Caux, in lands, woods, vineyards, and revenues.”]

Amalric, king of Jerusalem, having been hired by the emir of Babylon, marched with an army to assist him in freeing a city of his called Barbastam, which Saladin, seneschal of Nūr al-Dīn, held against him after deceitfully seizing it. The city was therefore besieged for some time, at last captured, and restored to the emir. Friendship between them was confirmed, many captives restored, and the tribute doubled—for the emir had previously paid the king thirty thousand gold pieces annually—and the king returned home. But meanwhile Nūr al-Dīn had inflicted great damage on the Christians. Having captured their castle called Harim, taken Bohemond the Younger, prince of Antioch, and slain many persons, Habilina, that is, Belinas, was subsequently overrun by the Saracens.

**1165. Frederick 14. Louis 28. Henry 11.**

Henry, king of England, crossed to Normandy in Lent and spoke with the king of France at Gisors on the octave of Easter. Returning from there to Rouen, he received his cousin Count Philip of Flanders royally. Likewise there came to him envoys of Frederick, emperor of the Germans: Rainald, archbishop of Cologne and the emperor’s chancellor, and many other men of great power. They requested on the emperor’s behalf that he give one of his daughters to Henry, duke of Bavaria, and another to his own son, although he was still a little boy. Oaths having therefore been demanded and given, the king later sent his own envoys to Germany to receive from the emperor and his magnates the same oaths concerning the agreements made between them.

Rotrou, bishop of Évreux, became archbishop of Rouen. Henry, dean of Salisbury, was elected to the bishopric of Bayeux. Upon the death of Roger, abbot of Saint-Wandrille, a religious man, Anfrid, sacristan of the same monastery, succeeded him. [Note: Col. 0499: “Henry, dean … succeeded him” is lacking in 8b and 8h.]

Queen Eleanor of England, summoned by the king, came to Normandy, bringing with her her son Richard and her daughter Matilda. When the king returned to England and proceeded against the Welsh with great military equipment, the queen remained in the lands on this side of the sea. Pope Alexander of Rome, leaving Sens, where he had stayed for almost two years, came by sea to Montpellier and proceeded to the land of William, king of Sicily, although the plots of the German emperor’s pirates did not fail to threaten him at sea. William, brother of Count Theobald, was elected to govern the church of Chartres; the pope granted him a dispensation because of his youth, so that his consecration might be deferred for five years. [Note: Col. 0501: “William … his consecration” is lacking in 8b and 8h.]

In August a son was born to Louis, king of France, by his wife, and was called Philip. In October Queen Eleanor gave birth at Angers to a daughter, who was called Joanna at baptism. Robert, abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel, ordered the relics of Saint Lawrence to be placed in a finely made silver-and-gold arm reliquary: namely, the arm-bone called the *eschinum*, and four other smaller bones of the same martyr. Previously he had placed in a certain cup, gilded inside and out, the head of Innocent, companion of Saint Maurice. The aforesaid relics, together with part of the body of the martyr Saint Agapitus—namely, flesh with four ribs—Abbot Suppo of Mont-Saint-Michel brought from the monastery of Saint Benignus at Fruttuaria, where he had formerly been abbot, to the monastery of Saint Michael, by prayer and payment. The monastery of Fruttuaria is in Lombardy, in the diocese of Vercelli. [Note: Col. 0501: “Robert … Vercelli” is lacking in 8b and 8h.]

Malcolm, king of Scotland, a devout young man, died. His brother William succeeded him. Lightning struck the church of Saint Michael, in the tower and elsewhere, yet by God’s mercy did no harm. Robert, abbot of Marmoutier, died, and Robert of Blois succeeded him. [Note: Col. 0501D: Marmoutier-lès-Tours.] [Note: Col. 0501: “Lightning … Robert of Blois” was later added by the same hand; it is lacking in 8b and 8h.]

[Col. 0501C] **1166. Frederick 15. Louis 29. Henry 12.**

King Henry, having fortified the borders between the English and Welsh and stationed castles and soldiers, crossed the sea to Normandy in Lent. He then discussed with the king of France matters conducive to peace. Hearing also that the king of France had ordained that from his treasures and revenues, and likewise from those of all men, clergy and laity alike, within his dominion, for five years [Note: Col. 0501: “four years,” 8d], one penny from every twenty shillings should be sent annually to Jerusalem for the defense of Christendom, this high-minded king ordered the revenue of the first year throughout all his dominion to be doubled, while in subsequent years payment was to remain at one penny for each twenty shillings.

Waleran, count of Meulan, became a monk at Préaux and died. His son Robert succeeded him, born of the sister of Simon, count of Évreux. [Note: Col. 0501: After this the scribe himself erased three words in E. “Waleran … Cornish” is lacking in 8b and 8h.] The same Robert married the daughter of Rainald, count of Cornwall. William, king of Sicily, also died, and his son William succeeded him.

William Talvas, count of Sées, his son John, and again John, his grandson, son of his eldest son Guy, count of Ponthieu, granted King Henry the castle of Alençon and the Rock of Mâberie, with their appurtenances. Perhaps they lost these fortresses because they and their forebears had long maintained evil customs there, which King Henry immediately ordered to be improved. In September Stephen, bishop of Rennes, died. Robert, bishop of Bath, also died in England. [Note: Col. 0501: At the end of the page the handwriting changes in E, though only slightly. “In September … bishop” is lacking in 8b and 8h.]

Since the magnates of the county of Maine and the Breton region had, before the king crossed the sea, been insufficiently obedient to the queen’s commands and, it was said, bound themselves by oath to defend one another collectively if any one of them were oppressed, the king dealt with them and their castles as he pleased. Gathering armies from almost all his power on this side of the sea, he besieged, captured, and utterly destroyed the castle of Fougères. Then, after arranging the marriage of his son Geoffrey to Constance, daughter of Count Conan of Brittany and Richmond, Count Conan granted the king, as though for the use of his son, the whole duchy of Brittany, except the county of Guingamp, which had come to him through his grandfather Count Stephen. The king received homage from nearly all the barons of Brittany at Thouars. From there he came to Rennes, and by that city, which is the head of Brittany, took possession of the entire duchy. Since he had never seen Combourg or Dol after they came into his hands, he viewed them while passing through. Coming to Mont-Saint-Michel for prayer, he lodged that night at Genêts. [Note: Col. 0501: The ink changes.]

There came to him William, king of Scotland, and the bishop of the Isles of Man and of thirty-one others lying between Scotland, Ireland, and England. The king of the Isles holds these thirty-two islands from the king of Norway on this tribute: whenever a new king is installed, the king of the Isles gives him ten marks of gold, and owes him nothing for the rest of his life unless another king is again installed in Norway. The aforesaid bishop came to the king of England as envoy of this king of the Isles. For the said king is related to the king of England on the side of Empress Matilda, his mother. [Note: Col. 0501: From this point the ink and handwriting are wholly changed, and the spelling also frequently differs from that preceding.]

**1167. 16. 30. 13.**

At Christmas King Henry was at Poitiers, and his son Henry came to him from England. Before Lent the king came to Rouen; and, on the death of Roger, abbot of Saint-Ouen, a man of the highest religious devotion, he gave that abbey to Aimery, cellarer of Bec. Shortly before this Robert, bishop of Hereford, and Robert, bishop of Lincoln, had died in England. [Note: Col. 0501: “Before Lent … bishops” is lacking in 8b and 8h.]

In Lent the king of the English spoke with the count of Saint-Gilles at Mont-Magne. After Easter he led an army of knights into the Auvergne and devastated the land of Count William. The latter had pledged his word, in the presence of the lord king, to submit to justice in relation to his nephew, the younger count of Auvergne, whom he had disinherited; but this man, long hardened in evil days, broke faith, went over to the king of France, and sowed discord between them.

A great quarrel also arose between Henry, king of the English, and Louis, king of France, at the prompting of Jocelin, archbishop of Tours, concerning the collection of money intended for Jerusalem. This money had been assembled at Tours; the king of England wished to send it through his own messengers, since it had been raised in his county, while the king of France wished to send it through his own, because the church of Tours was his. The city of Tours was burned together with its principal church.

Amalric, king of Jerusalem, summoned by the emir of Babylon, with whom he was allied, besieged Alexandria, capital of Egypt, captured it, and restored it to the emir. The emir covenanted to pay him from that city an annual tribute of fifty thousand bezants, apart from the fifty-seven thousand which he received from Babylon. The same king also married a niece of Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, with immeasurable treasures.

About Pentecost Frederick, emperor of the Germans, having sent out his armies, killed many Romans, though he was himself to receive like treatment from them. About July he personally besieged and captured the Leonine City of Rome, destroying certain things near the church of Saint Peter, namely the portico and some other structures. He also brought the antipope Guy of Crema to Rome, and had him crown his wife empress on 1 August. Divine vengeance immediately followed. For Charles, son of Conrad, who had ruled before Frederick and was Frederick’s cousin, died; [Note: Col. 0503: After this, three words have been erased.] and Rainald, archbishop of Cologne and his chancellor, by whose counsel he committed many evils, [Note: Col. 0503: After this, several words have been erased.] and the bishop of Liège, and many others, bishops and consuls alike, similarly perished. It is said that, as the pestilence raged, twenty-five thousand men of his army died. The twenty-five cities of Lombardy rebuilt Milan and withdrew from the emperor, except Pavia and Vercelli. [Note: Col. 0503: “About Pentecost … Vercelli” is lacking in 8b and 8h.]

On the octave of Pentecost the king of the English and the king of France met in the Vexin to discuss peace. But the principal men of the French realm inflamed the mild disposition of King Louis, and nothing came of it. Each therefore assembled an immense army from all his power, and both fortified their castles. When the king of France had burned some small villages in the borderland between Mantes and Pacy, King Henry, angered though he greatly respected King Louis, burned the castle of the Bald Mount, a very strongly fortified and rich castle in which the king of France had assembled supplies and provisions for war, as well as many villages around it. On hearing this, the king of France took it grievously. Gathering his forces, he burned the broad estates that Saint-Ouen held in the Vexin, namely Vaux-de-Noyers and other villages; also the excellent borough of Andely, belonging directly to Blessed Mary and the archbishop of Rouen. He also ravaged certain possessions belonging to the church of the Holy Trinity at Rouen.

But swift vengeance was not lacking. For that same day, as many of his army returned to camp, they expired through thirst, the heat of the sun, dust, and terror. The same had happened long before to his father [Note: Col. 0503D: A.D. 1119.]: when he was about to engage Henry the Elder, king of the English, in battle and was defeated, he had lodged on the previous night in the same village; and the French—said, on the testimony of Valentinian, Roman emperor, to be so called from ferocity—had made the church of Blessed Mary at Andely a stable for their horses. Hence some of them were captured and others escaped by flight.

In August truces were made and sworn between Kings Henry and Louis until Easter. King Henry then went into Brittany and subjected to himself all the Bretons, including those of Léon. For Guihomar, son of Hervé, viscount of Léon, whose daughter Count Guy had married, submitted to the king after giving hostages, unnerved by fear when he saw his very strong castle burned and captured, and various other places either captured or surrendered. While the king was still staying in Brittany, he received news of the death of his mother, Empress Matilda. She died at Rouen on 10 September and was buried at Bec. Her dutiful son distributed immense treasures to churches, monasteries, lepers, and other poor persons for her soul. The empress had founded the monastery of Le Vœu in the district of Caux near Julia Bona, and placed Cistercian monks there. She also founded houses of canons, one near Caesar’s Borough and another in the forest of Goffer. At the stone hill above the Seine near Rouen, which she herself had begun, she left a large sum of money.

Richard, abbot of Saint-Pierre-sur-Dives, died, [Note: Col. 0503D: Diocese of Sées.] and was succeeded by Rannier, a monk of Caen. Michael, abbot of Préaux, also died—he was a monk of Bec—and Henry, monk of Bec and steward of guests, was substituted for him. [Note: Col. 0504D: Préaux, diocese of Lisieux.] [Note: Col. 0503: “Richard … guests” is lacking in 8b and 8h.] Jocelin, archbishop of Tours, was reconciled with the king of the English. The venerable Hugh, abbot of Cerisy, paid the debt of human life by dying; he had governed that monastery for nearly fifty years. Martin, a monk of the same place, succeeded him. [Note: Col. 0504D: Cerisy, diocese of Bayeux.] [Note: Col. 0505: “The venerable … place” is lacking in 8b and 8h.]

Queen Eleanor crossed to England, taking her daughter Matilda with her. On the eve of Christmas two fiery-colored stars appeared in the west, one large and the other small. They were as if joined together; afterward they separated by a great distance and ceased to appear. John, son of the king of the English, was born. [Note: Col. 0505: “John, son of the king of the English,” added by another hand; it is also present in the other witnesses.]

**1168. Frederick 17. Louis 31. Henry 14.**

At Christmas King Henry was at Argentan and held a great court there in his new hall. Matilda, daughter of King Henry, was taken to Germany, with boundless money and a very great retinue, to her betrothed Henry, duke of Saxony [Note: Col. 0505: Thus E.] and Bavaria. He held one of these duchies from his father, the other from his mother. His father was Duke Henry, born of the daughter of Emperor Lothair, who had ruled before Conrad. This Henry, namely the younger one who married the daughter of the king of the English, won so much territory from the pagans—that is, the Slavs and Wends—that he established three bishoprics there.

Count Thierry of Flanders died. [Note: Col. 0505: This word is written in E on an erasure of more than half a line.] His son Philip succeeded him, having long already governed that county while his father repeatedly undertook the Jerusalem journey. Stephen de Fougères, chaplain of King Henry, became bishop of Rennes. The monastery of Fécamp was burned. [Note: Col. 0505: At the end of the quire this handwriting ends. The first hand of the manuscript returns.]

In February there occurred a remarkable event in the district of Maine, at the castle of Fresnay, the castle of Roscelin, viscount of Maine. He had married Matilda, natural daughter of Henry I, king of the English, maternal aunt of Henry II, king of the English. By her he begot Richard, who succeeded him, and William, to whom Henry II, king of the English, gave in Brittany the daughter of Roland de Reux together with her land. At this fortress the river Sarthe, which flows past it, dried up for nearly an hour and a half, so that men wearing shoes could cross with dry feet, whereas formerly even horses could scarcely ford it without swimming. The same occurred in London with the river Thames in the time of Henry I, king of the English. On 16 February there was an earthquake, and a ball of fire was seen moving through the air. [Note: Col. 0505: “Stephen … through the air” is lacking in 8b and 8h.]

The Poitevins and Aquitanians, for the most part—that is, the count of La Marche, the count of Angoulême, Aimery of Lusignan, Robert and his brother Hugh of Sillé, and many others—wished to rebel against the king. Devoting themselves to arson and the plundering of the poor, they ravaged the surrounding country. On hearing this the king flew promptly to the scene. Resisting their madness, he captured the very strongly fortified castle of Lusignan, fortified it after capture, and destroyed their towns and fortified places. Having supplied his castles with soldiers and necessary provisions, he left the queen there with Count Patrick of Salisbury, uncle of Rotrou, count of Perche. On the octave of Easter he came between Pacy and Mantes in Normandy to speak with the king of France and demand satisfaction from him for his injuries. For the Poitevins had come to the king of France and given him their hostages against the king of the English, whose own men they were. Thus, when there was heated argument on both sides and the king of France would not restore the hostages he had unjustly received, a truce was given until the octave of Saint John.

About the octave of Easter, through Poitevin treachery, Count Patrick was killed and buried at Saint-Hilaire. He was succeeded by his son, born of the daughter of William, count of Ponthieu, mother of the countess of Warenne. Before the truce had been granted, the king of the English had summoned Eudes, viscount of Porhoët, who was then called count under the shadowy title, and upon whom he had bestowed such great benefits, to come to his service and aid. Eudes refused, as did certain other Bretons allied with him: Oliver, son of Oliver de Dinan, and his cousin Roland. The king, therefore, rightly angered against them, beginning with the head—that is, Eudes—ravaged and burned his land. First he destroyed the principal castle that Eudes held, that of Josselin. He also took from him the county of Broërec, whose chief city is Vannes, which the king seized into his own hand. Julius Caesar highly extols that city’s port in the book he wrote on the Gallic War. [Note: Col. 0505D: III.8. Today Vannes.] He also took from him half of Cornouaille. [Note: Col. 0505D: Cornouaille.]

He likewise besieged the castle of Hédé; after capturing it, he fortified it. Having devastated Eudes’s land and reduced it to his pleasure, he approached the territory of the men of Dinan, fortified the castle of Hédé, which Geoffrey of Montfort had surrendered to him, and destroyed Tinténiac. He then besieged for several days the very strong fortification of Bécherel belonging to Roland de Dinan, brought up siege engines, captured and fortified it. He would have besieged the castle of Lehon [Note: Col. 0506D: Between Dol and Dinan.], in which Roland especially trusted because it was most strongly fortified by nature and art, had not the short time remaining before he had to go to his conference with the king of France pressed him.

Having therefore delivered Roland’s land to plunder and fire, he did the same beyond the river Rance as on this side of it. Crossing the river and descending by Lehon, he flooded some places but spared the monks of Lehon. Circling Dinan, he destroyed some places and left others untouched. He did the same in the district of Alet. On the octave of Saint John they came to La Ferté-Bernard, where peace between the kings was discussed, but they departed without accomplishing anything. For the Bretons, like the Poitevins, had given hostages to the king of France and accepted an agreement under oath that the king of France would not make peace with the king of England without them. Hence the Bretons themselves, with the connivance of certain men of Maine through whose land they passed secretly, attended the conference.

After the borders were fortified, warfare continued on both sides until Advent. King Henry, acting cautiously, made peace with his kinsman Matthew, count of Boulogne, promising to give him annually the greater part of the money in return for withdrawing his claim [Note: Col. 0507D: That is, his demand.] to the county of Mortain. For Matthew had married a daughter of King Stephen, who had been count of Mortain. [Note: Col. 0507: “For Matthew had married … Mortain” is lacking in 8b, but absent in 8h.]

When Matthew came with many well-equipped knights to aid the king of the English, his lord and kinsman, John, count of Ponthieu, would not permit him passage through his land. Forced by necessity, he therefore came to the king by sea. On hearing this, the king, at Matthew’s request, entered John’s land with military equipment. Delivering the district of Vimeu to Vulcan, he burned forty villages and more, and fulfilled his will. [Note: Col. 0508D: Le Vimeu, between the mouths of the Authie and the Somme.]

The king of France secretly came to a fortress in Normandy called Chênebrun, burned it, and captured four knights there. When he learned this, the king of the English pursued him and captured many knights, among them the seneschal of Philip, count of Flanders. He also gave over to fire and flames the castle of Hugh of Neufchâtel, called Bruyères, so that its name might be justified by its burning. He did the same to Neufchâtel through his knights, though he himself was absent. Likewise the land of the count of Perche was for the most part devastated, at the count’s own instigation. [Note: Col. 0507: The following, “The king of England did many things … Alexander,” and “The Lombards … Lombardy,” is lacking in 8b and 8h.] The king of England did many other things in this war which we did not hear, or, if we heard them, do not recall.

Robert, count of Leicester, died, leaving his son Robert, who received with his wife the inheritance of Grandmesnil. Hervé of Lehon also died in Brittany, and his son Guihomar succeeded him. Likewise Guy of Crema, the antipope, died at Rome, and a certain pseudo-cleric called Calixtus succeeded him in the schism. When the archbishop of Sens also departed this life, William, bishop-elect of Chartres, succeeded him, though Pope Alexander granted him the bishopric of Chartres for two years. Henry, duke of Saxony and Bavaria, son-in-law of King Henry of England, came to the king’s court, was honored by him with great gifts, and returned to his own lands. The Lombards built a city not far from Vercelli, calling it Alexandria in honor of Pope Alexander, drawing inhabitants from each of the cities of Lombardy.

[Col. 0508A] **1169. Frederick 18. Louis 32. Henry 15.**
King Henry spent Christmas at Argentan. Bernard, bishop of Nantes, died. [Note: [Col. 0507] “Bishop of Nantes died” is absent in 8b, 8h.] On the Epiphany of the Lord, the king of France and the king of England made peace. Henry, son of Henry king of the English, did homage to the king of France, his father-in-law, for the county of Anjou and the duchy of Brittany, which the king granted to his same son-in-law. For he had previously done homage to him for Normandy; and the king of France granted him that he should be seneschal of France, an office belonging to the Angevin fief. Richard, son of Henry king of the English, did homage to the king of France for the duchy of Aquitaine. William Malet captured Robert of Sillé. [Note: [Col. 0507] “William Malet captured Robert of Sillé” is absent in 8b, 8h.] At the Purification of Blessed Mary, Henry, son of the king of the English, was at Paris, [Col. 0508B] and served the king of France at table as seneschal of France.

This seneschalship—or, as it was anciently called, the stewardship of the royal household—Robert, king of France, gave to Geoffrey Grisegonelle, count of Anjou, because of the assistance which he gave him against Otto, emperor of Germany. He also gave him all that he possessed in the bishopric of Angers. Later, when Geoffrey, count of Perche, and David, count of Maine, were rebels against that same Robert king of France, the aforesaid king of France, with Geoffrey Grisegonelle bringing him aid, besieged and captured the stronghold of Mortagne. And because David, count of the Manceaux, when summoned by the king to come to him, scorned to do so, the king gave Geoffrey Grisegonelle that man’s homage, the city itself, and all that he possessed in the [Col. 0508C] bishopric of Le Mans.

Henry, son of Henry king of the English, did homage to Philip, son of Louis king of France. Henry, king of England, conferred with Louis, king of France, at Saint-Germain-en-Laye. Geoffrey, son of the king of the English, did homage to his brother Henry for the duchy of Brittany, at their father’s command. Upon the death of Hasculf of Soligny, his son Gilbert succeeded him. Richard of Hara also died, leaving three daughters. [Note: [Col. 0507] “Upon the death … three daughters” is absent in 8b, 8h.]

In Lent King Henry went into Gascony; after destroying or fortifying many castles which were opposed to him, he made peace with the counts of Angoulême and of La Marche, and with many others of less notable name.
