Geoffrey, son of the king of the English, [Col. 0508D] came to Rennes in the month of May; and Stephen, bishop of Rennes, Autbert, bishop of Alet, Robert, abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel, and other religious persons received him with the highest reverence in the church of Saint Peter. There he received the homages of the barons of Brittany.

King Henry made deep and broad ditches between France and Normandy to keep off robbers. Likewise, in the district of Anjou along the Loire, in order to restrain the water which was ravaging crops and [Col. 0509A] meadows, he caused certain barriers, called *torsiae*, to be made for nearly thirty miles, and had dwellings built there for the men who were to maintain the barriers. He also freed them from military service and from many other obligations belonging to the fisc. [Note: [Col. 0509] “Likewise … belonging to the fisc,” in an erasure enlarged in this manner by Robert. Present in 7b; absent in 8b and 8h, together with the following “Hilary … abbots.”]

Hilary, bishop of Chester, and Nigel, bishop of Ely, died; as did Peter, abbot of Jumièges, Richard, abbot of Bernay, and Silvester, abbot of Redon. In August, when almost all had been pacified in Poitou and Gascony, King Henry came into Normandy, and the summoned Bretons hastened to him. The city of Catania in Sicily was shaken and overthrown by an earthquake, and many perished there. [Note: [Col. 0509] Here end 8a, 8b, the second hand in 8d, and the sixth, abbreviated hand in 8e; perhaps also in 8c and 8g. In 8b follows a brief continuation by the monk of Valmont. “The church of Fécamp was burned on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, on the fourth weekday after the octave of Pentecost” is added by 8d and 8h.]

King Henry built a very strong castle and a very large borough near the hedge of Malaffre, which [Col. 0509B] was called Belvoir. When Roger Malebranche deceitfully captured the city of Béziers, which its citizens had held against him, he put all alike—men and women—to death, either by hanging or another torture, and handed the city over to new inhabitants to be settled. For those citizens had cruelly killed their lord William [Note: [Col. 0509D] Correct: Raymond. BOUQ.], Trencavel, Roger Malebranche’s father, together with his young son, in a certain church.

King Henry made mills and fisheries at Angers on the river Mayenne. When William Goet died on the journey to Jerusalem, and Count Theobald wished to take into his own hand Montmirail and the other strongholds which had belonged to William Goet—of which Hervé of Ivoy, who had married the eldest daughter of William Goet, born of one of Count Theobald’s sisters, was enfeoffed [Note: [Col. 0509D] “Enfeoffed.”]—the aforesaid Hervé, seeing that he could not resist Count Theobald, since the king of France too was assisting Count Theobald’s party as his brother-in-law, through the intervention of a large sum of money and certain agreements, handed over to Henry king of the English Montmirail and another castle, namely Saint-Aignan in Berry. Thus discord was renewed between the king and the count.

## 1170. Frederick 19. Louis 33. Henry 16.

At Christmas King Henry was in Brittany at Nantes. Robert, archdeacon of Nantes, was made bishop of Nantes with the king’s consent, [Col. 0509D] after Bernard, his uncle. In Lent the sea overflowed its bounds, and in many places crops sown near it perished, swallowed up by the waves. Through a flood in England, the bones of a certain giant were uncovered; the length of his body, it is reported, was thirty feet.

In the same Lent King Henry crossed the sea into England, though [Col. 0510A] not without danger. Gilbert of Avranches having been drowned in the sea, Fulk Paynel, who had married his eldest sister, succeeded him. Sheriffs throughout England who had oppressed the people with exactions and robberies were punished by the king. After Pentecost King Henry, having summoned his son Henry into England, had him crowned king at London, at Westminster, with great rejoicing of clergy and people. Roger, archbishop of York, anointed him; for Thomas of Canterbury had remained beyond the sea, in Gaul, for almost a continuous six years.

The following bishops were present at this consecration: Gilbert of London, Jocelin of Salisbury, Walter of Rochester, Richard of Chester, Bartholomew of Exeter, and Hugh of Durham. Roger of Worcester was staying in Normandy; [Col. 0510B] Henry of Winchester and William of Norwich, prevented by illness, were absent. For Adelulf, bishop of Carlisle; Robert, bishop of Hereford; Robert, bishop of Bath; Robert, bishop of Lincoln; Hilary, bishop of Chichester; and Nigel, bishop of Ely, had fallen asleep in the Lord, and their sees were still vacant. From Normandy there were present Henry, bishop of Bayeux, and Froger, bishop of Sées, who had come with him into England.

Some take it ill that the archbishop of York anointed Henry the younger king. But let them know that the first William, who subdued England by arms, was anointed and consecrated by Aldred, the most devout man, archbishop of York, while the archbishop of Canterbury remained within the island of Britain—namely Stigand, [Col. 0510C] excommunicated by the pope.

Margaret, daughter of the king of France and wife of the younger King Henry, crossed into England; yet she was not then crowned, because the king had already been crowned and the bishops had departed. John, count of Eu, died, and his son Henry succeeded him, whom he had begotten by the daughter of William d’Aubigny [Note: [Col. 0510D] Helisende. BOUQ.], who is called count of Arundel. This man married Queen Alice, widow of Henry the elder, king of the English; by her he begot his eldest son William, Geoffrey, and this countess, wife of John of Eu, of whom the account speaks.

On the feast-day of the apostles Peter and Paul a terrible earthquake occurred in the lands overseas. By it the city of Tripoli fell, as did part [Col. 0510D] of Damascus and a great part of Antioch. The Hagarenes also did not escape this affliction: Aleppo, which is the capital of the kingdom of Nūr al-Dīn, and certain other cities of the Saracens did not escape this disaster.

After William, count of Nevers, died overseas, Matthew, brother of Philip, count of Flanders, and count of Boulogne, married his wife [Note: [Col. 0510D] Eleanor. BOUQ.], namely the sister of [Col. 0511A] the countess of Flanders. Thus these two brothers married two sisters, daughters of Ralph, count of Vermandois, nieces through their sister of Queen Eleanor of England; they acted cunningly in keeping the land of Ralph of Péronne through either brother. Matthew had previously had the daughter of King Stephen; after having two daughters by her, he returned to the religious life, which he had reluctantly left. [Note: [Col. 0511D] Mary had been abbess of Romsey before Matthew married her in 1160.]

About August King Henry returned to Normandy, leaving the younger Henry in England. King Henry made peace between Count Theobald and Hervé of Ivoy. In September King Henry fell ill, nearly to death, at La Motte-de-Gér [Note: [Col. 0511D] Near Domfront.]; but, through divine mercy and the supplication of God’s servants, to whom he humbly [Col. 0511B] commended himself, once his adverse sickness had been quieted, he recovered his health.

Giles, archdeacon of Rouen, was elected to the bishopric of Évreux; Richard, archdeacon of Coutances, to that of Avranches. Eleanor, daughter of Henry king of the English, was taken to Spain and solemnly betrothed to Emperor Alfonso. That part of Spain called Castile is the kingdom of this emperor. The capital of this realm is the city of Toledo. Two kings opposed the aforesaid king because of his tender age—for he had not yet completed fifteen years—Ferdinand of Galicia, his paternal uncle, and Alfonso of Navarre, his maternal uncle.

After Robert, son of Robert, count of Gloucester, died, Amaury, eldest son of Simon, count of Évreux, by the command and will of Henry king of England, [Col. 0511C] married the eldest daughter of Robert, count of Gloucester. The same king had previously also given to his kinsman Hugh, count of Chester, the daughter of the count of Évreux, his own kinswoman on his father’s side. The city of Le Mans was consumed by fire. The cell of Saint Victeur was also burned, but with God’s help was restored in better condition.

Henry king of the English went in prayer to Rocamadour [Note: [Col. 0511D] Rochamadour.], a place in the district of Cahors surrounded by mountains and fearful wilderness. Some say that Saint Amator, servant of Blessed Mary, was once the Lord’s bearer and nurse; and that, when the most holy Mother of the Lord had been assumed into the heavenly dwellings, Amator, forewarned by her, crossed over into Gaul [Col. 0511D] and long led a hermit’s life in the aforesaid place.

When he died and was buried at the entrance of the oratory of Blessed Mary, that place was long unknown, except that common report said that the body of Blessed Amator rested there, though it was unknown where it was. In the year from the Lord’s incarnation 1166, a native [Col. 0512A] of that region, approaching his end, perhaps by divine inspiration commanded his household to bury a clod of earth from his body at the entrance of the oratory. The ground having therefore been dug up, the body of Blessed Amator was found intact. Set in the church beside the altar, they show it intact to pilgrims; and there many unheard-of miracles are performed through Blessed Mary.

Therefore, as we have said, when King Henry came to this place in prayer, because he was approaching the land of his enemies, he assembled a multitude of armed men, both horsemen and foot soldiers, and went protected for prayer as though for battle, harming no one and generously providing alms for all, especially for the poor. Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, crossed into England. Stephen, count of Sancerre, brother [Col. 0512B] of Count Theobald, went to Jerusalem, carrying with him money which Louis, king of France, had caused to be collected for the aid of the church of Jerusalem. Odo [Note: [Col. 0512D] Corrected: Hugh. BOUQ.], duke of Burgundy and his nephew, went with him.

## 1171. Frederick 20. Louis 34. Henry 17.

At Christmas King Henry was at Bur, near Bayeux.

> The year one thousand one hundred and seventy-one  
> was the first in which Thomas, the primate, fell by the sword.  
> It was the fifth day of Christmas; the flower of the world  
> is plucked from the world, and begins to be the fruit of heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0511] These verses are absent in 7b.]

The Hagarenes came from Africa into Spain with many thousands of armed men. Hamo, bishop of Léon [Note: [Col. 0512D] Saint-Pol-de-Léon, in Finistère], was cruelly killed, as they say, through the counsel of Guihomar, [Col. 0512C] his brother, viscount of Léon, and of the younger Guihomar, his nephew. Conan, duke of Brittany, died, and all Brittany, the county of Guingamp, and the honour [Note: [Col. 0512D] A fief or more distinguished manor.] of Richmond passed, through the daughter of Count Conan—who had been betrothed to Geoffrey, son of King Henry—to Geoffrey. Haimeric, abbot of Saint-Ouen, died.

King Henry came in Lent to Pontorson and remained there for almost fifteen days. He did the same during Rogationtide and at Pentecost, when Guihomar came to him and surrendered himself and his castles, terrified by the multitude of knights and other armed men whom the king had sent against him to compel him, unless he obeyed the king’s will. In the following year Saint Thomas was canonized by Pope Alexander. [Note: [Col. 0511] “In the following year … Alexander” is in an erasure, by another hand. Added in the margin: “Canonized, that is, enrolled in the catalogue of saints. And it was ordered that his birthday should be celebrated as a feast-day by all, especially by the English.” The same wording occurs in 7b and 8d, and in 8h as well, except for the words “canonized, i.e. enrolled in the catalogue of saints.”]

The castle of Pontorson [Col. 0512D] was burned. The city of Norwich was likewise burned, together with the episcopal church and the workshops of the monks. Humbert, count of Maurienne, sent the abbot of Saint Michael of the Cluse to Henry king of England to arrange a marriage between John, the king’s son, and his own daughter, offering him all [Col. 0513A] his land. For that count was the son of Count Amadeus and exceedingly rich in the possession of cities and castles; nor can anyone enter Italy except through his land.

Theobald, count of Chartres, delivered to the fire several Jews who lived at Blois. For, having crucified a certain child at the feast of Easter in insult to Christians, they afterwards placed him in a sack and threw him into the river Loire. When he was found, Theobald, having convicted them of the crime, as we have said above, delivered them to the fire, except those who accepted the Christian faith.

They also did this to Saint William in England at Norwich, in the time of King Stephen; when he had been buried in the episcopal church, many miracles [Col. 0513B] took place at his tomb. The same thing was done to another at Gloucester in the time of Henry II, king. And in France, at the castle called Pontoise, impious Jews did likewise to Saint Richard; brought to Paris and buried in a church, he shines forth through many miracles. And frequently, as is said, they do this at Easter-time if they find an opportunity.

William Talvas, count of Ponthieu, died, and his nephew John, the son of his eldest son Guy, succeeded him in the county of Ponthieu. In the land which he held from the king of the English in Normandy and in the district of Le Mans, however, his son John, count, succeeded him. This man married the daughter of Count Elias, brother of Count Geoffrey of Anjou and duke of Normandy.

[Col. 0513C] King Henry the elder caused an inquiry to be made throughout Normandy into the lands of which King Henry, his grandfather, had been seised on the day he died. He also caused inquiry to be made as to what lands, woods, and other demesnes barons and other men had occupied after the death of King Henry, his grandfather; and in this way he almost doubled the revenues of the duchy of Normandy. Rhys, king of the Welsh, made peace with Henry king of the English. His uncle King Owen had died in the preceding year, and Owen’s sons were subject to King Henry. Margaret, wife of the younger King Henry, crossed into Normandy.

In July the king assembled his barons at Argentan; and while his expedition to Ireland was being discussed there, the envoys of Count Richard came to him, saying on the count’s behalf that he would hand over [Col. 0513D] to him the city of Dublin, Waterford, and his other strongholds, which he possessed by right of his wife, who had been the daughter of the king of Dublin, now dead. When the king heard this message, he ordered the count to surrender to him his land in England and Normandy and the open country in Ireland which he had acquired with his wife; and he granted him that he should be constable or seneschal of all Ireland.

The venerable Henry, bishop of Winchester and abbot of Glastonbury, died. He did many good things for the church [Col. 0514A] of Winchester in ornaments of gold and silver and silk vestments. He also distributed his wealth with a generous hand to churches and the poor. To increase his virtues, for some time before his death he had been deprived of bodily sight. In August the king crossed into England; and, having gathered both knights and the supplies necessary for so great an expedition, on the vigil of Saint Luke the Evangelist he crossed into Ireland (17 October). How successfully he crossed, landed, and was received is shown by the letters which he sent to King Henry, his son.

## 1172. Frederick 21. Louis 35. Henry 18.

At Christmas the younger King Henry was at Bur near Bayeux; and because he was then for the first time holding court in [Col. 0514B] Normandy, he wished the feast to be celebrated magnificently. Bishops, abbots, counts, and barons were present, and he bestowed many gifts on many people.

And, to show the multitude of those who attended: when William of Saint-Jean, governor of Normandy, and William fitz Hamo, seneschal of Brittany, who had come with Geoffrey, duke of Brittany, his lord [Note: [Col. 0513] Three words after this have been erased.], were dining in a certain chamber, they forbade any knight to dine in that chamber unless he was called William. After the others had been driven out of the chamber, 117 knights remained, all called William, apart from many others of the same name who dined in the hall with the king. [Note: [Col. 0513] Here the hand changes.]

Henry, duke of Saxons and Bavarians, son-in-law of Henry king of the English, [Col. 0514C] went to Jerusalem with a large retinue of knights. He would have undertaken great things there, and perhaps completed what he undertook, had the king and the Templars not opposed him. Yet he generously distributed among the poor and the churches of the Holy Land the treasures which he had carried with him.

After Easter, when he was in Ireland, the king heard that two legates, Albert and Theodinus, had been sent to him by Lord Pope Alexander concerning the case of Thomas, formerly archbishop of Canterbury, of pious memory. He came with the utmost speed from Ireland into England and from England into Normandy; having sent honourable persons before him to them, he conferred with them first at Savigny, then at Avranches, and thirdly at Caen, where that case was settled, as the public letters made on the matter testify, which are preserved by many persons who had assembled there. [Col. 0514D] [Note: [Col. 0513D] Boucq. prints them in XIII, 135.]

King Henry conferred with the king of France and sent his younger king into England so that Margaret, daughter of the king of France and his wife, might be consecrated queen. By counsel of the king of France, Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen, and Giles, bishop of Évreux, anointed her and crowned the king and his wife.

Around the feast of Saint Michael the king assembled the bishops of Normandy and Brittany, and he and the legates came to Avranches to discuss ecclesiastical affairs; but little was achieved because of the king’s illness. On account of this meeting many honourable persons came as far as the Mount to us, [Col. 0515A] among them the most devout men Lord Stephen, abbot of Cluny, and Lord Benedict, abbot of the Cluse. Reciprocally we extended their fellowship to ourselves and ours to them, as their letters held by us and ours carried away by them testify.

William, abbot of Vézelay, of pious memory, had done the same for us in the chapter-house at Vézelay. With these three churches—Cluny, the Cluse, and Vézelay—we have a special fellowship, greatly pleasing to us and to them. Around the feast of Saint Martin the younger king came from England with his wife, and they conferred with the king of France: he at Gisors, she [Col. 0515B] at Chaumont; the king received them most joyfully as his own children.

## 1173. Frederick 22. Louis 36. Henry 19.

King Henry and Queen Eleanor celebrated Christmas royally at Chinon. The younger king, however, celebrated the same feast with his wife Margaret at Bonneville. From there he followed his father into the district of Anjou, intending to remain in those parts until the Purification of Blessed Mary, when the king was to confer with the king of Aragon, the count of Maurienne, and the count of Saint-Gilles concerning Toulouse. [Note: [Col. 0515] This hand ends; the preceding hand returns.]

William, abbot of Reading, was made archbishop of Bordeaux. The count of Saint-Gilles [Note: [Col. 0515] Raymond. BOUQ.] made peace with the king of England concerning Toulouse, having done homage to him and to [Col. 0515C] Richard, his son and duke of Aquitaine. He promised to give him forty horses of great value yearly; and, if necessary, he would provide one hundred knights each year for forty days of service.

In Lent, because the elder King Henry had removed Asculf of Saint-Hilaire and other young knights from the counsel and household service of his son, the latter became angry, withdrew from his father, came to Argentan, and departed thence by night for the king of France, without the knowledge of the attendants whom his father had assigned to his service. Count Robert of Beaumont followed him, leaving his castles without guards; King Henry seized them. Hugh, count of Chester, returning from Saint-Jacques-de-Compostelle, also followed him; as did William Patric the elder, his three sons, and many others of lesser rank, whose houses, coppices, and woods the king devastated. [Col. 0515D] Likewise Queen Eleanor and her sons Richard, count of Poitou, and Geoffrey, count of Brittany, became estranged from him.

On the Wednesday before the Lord’s Supper, the prior of Canterbury and other honourable persons came to Sainte-Barbe in the bishopric of Lisieux, to King Henry and the Roman legates Albert and Theodinus; and [Col. 0516A] they elected Roger, abbot of Bec, to the archbishopric of Canterbury. But he pleaded his infirmity and would not consent to their election. Returning thence to England, they summoned the bishops and other religious persons and elected their own monk Richard, prior of Dover, as archbishop.

Richard, archdeacon of Poitou, was elected to the bishopric of Winchester; Geoffrey, the natural son of King Henry and archdeacon of Lincoln, to Lincoln; Geoffrey Ridel, archdeacon of Canterbury, to Ely; Robert Foliot, archdeacon of Lincoln, to Hereford; Ragnerius [Note: [Col. 0515] The manuscript reads *Rag.*], a Lombard and archdeacon of Salisbury, to Bath; and Jocelin, dean of Chichester, to Chichester.

But when the day had been appointed on which [Col. 0516B] the archbishop-elect of Canterbury should be consecrated and should in turn consecrate the other elects, in a general assembly of bishops and others who had gathered, the prior of Canterbury produced letters of the younger King Henry, in which he said that they were not to be consecrated; and if anyone laid hands on them, he summoned him to the hearing of Lord Pope Alexander. Thus the affair remained unfinished, and each departed to his own place. The prior of Winchester was made abbot of Glastonbury.

After Easter Bernard of La Ferté and his castle went over to the younger king. So also did Waleran of Ivry, Jocelin Crispin, Gilbert of Tuileries, Robert of Montfort, Ralph of Fay, Geoffrey of Lizon, Hugh of Sainte-Maure and his son, and William, chamberlain of Tankerville, [Col. 0516C] coming from England.

Philip, count of Flanders, captured the castle of Aumale [Note: [Col. 0515] Albemarle. BOUQ.], and in it Count William, lord of that castle, and Count Simon [Note: [Col. 0515] Of Évreux. BOUQ.]. Thereupon Henry, count of Eu, submitted himself and his castles to the younger king and the count of Flanders. After the feast of Saint John, Louis, king of France, having assembled his barons from all his kingdom, besieged the castle of Verneuil for almost a month. In that army, as some said, there were seven thousand knights, apart from the rest of the multitude. Hugh de Lacy and Hugh de Beauchamp, constables of that castle, their subordinate knights, and the burgesses resisted them bravely.

The younger King Henry, Philip, count of Flanders, [Col. 0516D] and Matthew, his brother and count of Boulogne, besieged the new castle called Drincourt with a great army. Doun Bardolf and his brother Thomas commanded the castle. Seeing that they could not resist the repeated assaults and the undermining of the walls, they secured a truce and went to their lord, the king of England, reporting that they could not withstand the power of the enemy. The king therefore allowed them to surrender the castle to the count of Flanders.

Matthew, count of Boulogne, brother of Philip, [Col. 0517A] count of Flanders, died from a wound received in the siege of Drincourt. Consequently his grieving brother, the count of Flanders, girded with knightly arms his brother Peter, who had been elected to the bishopric of Cambrai. On the third Ides of August, the most devout man Lord Stephen, abbot of Cluny, entered upon the way of all flesh. [Note: [Col. 0517D] This agrees with the Chronicle of Saint Stephen of Nevers in Martène, *Thesaurus*, III, 1387. The others say that he died in 1174, after voluntarily resigning in 1173.] Ralph, prior of La Charité [Note: [Col. 0517D] La Charité-sur-Loire, district of Auxerre.], cousin of Count Theobald, succeeded him. Roger, count of Clare, also died; his son Gilbert succeeded him and married the daughter of William [Note: [Col. 0517D] E has “G.;” 8h has “William.”], count of Gloucester.

King Henry, having assembled a great army of both cavalry and infantry, came to Breteuil, wishing [Col. 0517B] to bring aid to his men besieged at Verneuil by Louis king of France. When the king of France heard this, he followed the counsel of wise men and withdrew from the castle, leaving behind a large portion of his baggage and provisions.

King Henry summoned the barons of Brittany and exacted from them an oath of fealty. While the others observed it in some fashion, Ralph of Fougères [Note: [Col. 0518D] Fougères.] acted faithlessly: summoned by the king, he refused to obey, but began rebuilding the castle of Fougères, which the king himself had previously destroyed. When Hasculf of Saint-Hilaire, William Patric, and his three sons heard this, they rejoiced and came to him by byways. The count of Chester [Note: [Col. 0518D] Hugh. BOUQ.] and Count Eudo [Note: [Col. 0518D] Of Porhoët. B.] also followed them.

When Henry king of the English sent his Brabançons to ravage [Col. 0517C] Ralph of Fougères’s land, and they had done so to a great extent, a large number of those carrying provisions to the army, having neither commander nor protector, were killed between Saint-James and Fougères by Ralph of Fougères’s knights. Ralph of Fougères committed the castle of Saint-James to the flames, and likewise the castle of Tilly [Note: [Col. 0518D] Tilly. B.].

King Henry came secretly to Fougères to intercept Ralph; hearing of his arrival, Ralph sought safety in flight. Nevertheless the king’s men took such great booty as scarcely anyone of our time had seen. For Ralph of Fougères had ordered the people of all his land to take their horses, cattle, sheep, and all their property into [Col. 0517D] his forest; but before they could enter the forest’s hiding places, they were intercepted by the enemy and lost all that was theirs.

Ralph of Fougères, having won over by money and entreaties the guards who ought to have kept the castle of Combourg and the city of Dol for the king of England, captured those fortifications. When the king heard this, he sent his Brabançons and certain of his knights to their aid, should they need it. [Col. 0518A] The count of Chester, Ralph of Fougères, Hasculf of Saint-Hilaire, William Patric, and all the knights of Ralph of Fougères’s land, with a great multitude of foot soldiers, met them. Almost in a moment they were scattered; the knights fled, and many common people were killed.

But the count of Chester, Ralph of Fougères, and sixty knights with them, unable to escape because their enemies had blocked the road of flight, shut themselves up in the tower, except for Hasculf of Saint-Hilaire, William Patric, and certain others, who were captured and taken to Pontorson. Thus the tower of Dol was besieged by the Brabançons, the king’s knights, and the people of Avranches.

When Count Eudo came from France, he was unwilling to remain with Ralph of Fougères; instead he went into Porhoët, [Col. 0518B] fortified Jocelin’s castle, and captured the castle of Ploërmel.

In the following action may be seen the courage, industry, and swiftness of Henry king of England. He heard the news of the siege of the tower of Dol while he was at Rouen, on the night before Wednesday. On Wednesday itself, when daylight had already come, he departed from Rouen and arrived at Dol on the following day about the third hour, and besieged the tower. When he had prepared engines to capture it, those shut within, providing for themselves, surrendered the tower and themselves to the king’s will. The king then sent them through his fortresses, to be kept there under guard. Some, after receiving hostages, he retained with himself under free custody.

Robert, count of Leicester, wishing to disturb the kingdom of England, crossed with his wife, Hugh of New [Col. 0518C] Castle, his cousin, and many knights into England. But he, his wife, and Hugh of New Castle were intercepted and captured by the king’s faithful men near Saint Edmund’s, and were committed to custody. Many Flemings were killed there, and many others captured and killed; perhaps because they had practiced robbery in the land of Saint Edmund, king and martyr, which no one was permitted to do with impunity.

Ralph of Fougères gave the king of England his sons Ivel and William as hostages for himself. But he in no way consented to surrender himself to the king’s power; rather, fleeing through the woods, he remained hidden. Geoffrey of Pontorson, Bon, abbot of Ruzé, and other disinherited men of Maine and the district of Anjou, together with Ralph of La Haye, a Norman, [Col. 0518D] harassed the king’s land from the woods, lacking fortified castles. For the king’s Brabançons had destroyed the castle of La Guerche [Note: [Col. 0518D] La Guerche. B.], just as they had previously ruined Fougères and Ralph’s other fortifications.

Robert of Vitré died, and his son Andrew, born of the sister of Roland of Dinan, succeeded him. Since Roland himself lacked any other heir, he made his other nephew Alan heir to all [Col. 0519A] his land in the king’s presence.

## 1174. Frederick 23. Louis 37. Henry 20.

King Henry spent Christmas in the district of Bayeux, at Bur. William, bishop of Tréguier [Note: [Col. 0519] Tréguier. BOUQUET.], died; Ivo the Breton, archpriest of Tours, succeeded him. In the place of Haimo, bishop of Léon, an archdeacon of the same church was also elected—not canonically, but simoniacally. Although he enjoyed the favour both of clergy and people, he did not obtain consecration, because of the death of Joscius, archbishop of Tours. In Joscius’s place the clergy of Tours elected Bartholomew, dean of that church, an energetic young man of noble birth.

[Col. 0519B] William Patric the younger died at Paris, and his father William Patric also died; his son Ingelran Patric succeeded him and married the daughter of Richard, son of the count. The abbot of Saint-Florent died [Note: [Col. 0519] of Saumur.], and Ralph the Norman succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0519] “William Patric—Norman” is written on an erasure, in the same hand.]. Likewise Nutritus the recluse, a man of honourable life and great religious devotion, paid the debt of human life. At his tomb, as some say—which is beside the church of Saint Mary of Ardevon—God is glorified in the healing of the sick. In the preceding year Hamo of Landecop, a monk of Savigny, also died; because of his religious devotion and good works toward the poor, he was dear to God and humankind. The archbishop of Tarentaise [Note: [Col. 0519] Peter, BOUQUET.], formerly a monk of the Cistercian order, through whom in our time God is praised in the working of miracles, [Col. 0519C] came to the king of France, sent by the lord pope together with Alexander, abbot of Cîteaux, to restore peace between Henry, king of England, and his son the Young King. But, through the hindrance of human sins, he made little progress.

Around Easter Richard, elect of Canterbury, who had gone to Rome in the preceding year, was consecrated by Pope Alexander at Anagni. The archbishop of Tarentaise consecrated Raginerus [Note: [Col. 0519] E has “Rag.”], elect of Bath, his companion. Two queens were brought into England.

About the same time Louis, king of France, assembled at Paris all the barons of his realm who obeyed him, and held secret counsel with them concerning his undertaking. Thus the count of Flanders, [Col. 0519D] Count Theobald, the count of Clermont, and many others swore that around the feast of Saint John they would cross the sea with the Young King and, to the best of their ability, subject that kingdom to him. Those who remained behind swore that they would march with an army through Normandy, seize whatever castles they could, lay waste the country, or surround Rouen with a siege. This they did, with little success.

King Henry the elder, however, having many of the barons of France indebted to him, and having made them his intimates by great services [Col. 0520A] and gifts, learned this through them. He fortified his castles on the Norman frontier near France with arms, soldiers, and provisions. He also removed certain castle-wardens, lest by admitting his enemies and holding out for a long time they should commit some treachery against him. Then, having spoken with the barons of Normandy, he admonished and beseeched them to act manfully and remember that their forebears had often shamefully driven the French from their borders. Then, taking with him few—indeed almost none—of the Norman barons, he crossed into England with his Brabançons.

It should be noted with what humility he visited the tomb of the blessed martyr Thomas. When he saw Canterbury church, he dismounted from his horse and, clothed in a woollen garment and [Col. 0520B] barefoot, walked all the way to it through marshes and sharp stones, with the utmost devotion. In prayer at the tomb of the glorious martyr he was so devout and tearful that those who saw him were moved to tears. He had arrived there on Friday and, fasting, kept vigil there throughout the night. In the morning, proceeding to the chapter-house of the monks, he submitted himself to their scourges, imitating the Redeemer, who gave his back to the lash. But He did so for our sins; this man, for his own.

On the same day on which he departed from the holy place, William, king of Scotland, was captured at Alnwick by the barons of Yorkshire. That king, with Roger de Mowbray and his other accomplices, had throughout the summer ravaged the northern parts of England extending toward Scotland. On the following Wednesday [Col. 0520C] the king heard the news of this great joy. Delighted by so great a report, Henry made peace with Count Hugh Bigod; and, having placed King William of Scotland and Earl Roger of Leicester in secure custody, crossed with his earls into Normandy, leaving England at peace—a peace which in thirty days he had recovered when it was almost lost.

On arriving at Rouen, he sent his Welsh marchers beyond the Seine to plunder in the woods the provisions being brought to the French army. The French, fearing the king on one side and the Welsh on the other, came to the king to discuss peace. The king, therefore, delighted, fixed the Nativity of Saint Mary at Gisors as the time for peace to be restored between them. When that date had passed, [Col. 0520D] they met from both sides, but accomplished nothing except to set another date around the feast of Saint Michael, between Tours and Amboise. There, with God’s favour, peace came about: the king’s three sons humbly submitted to their father, and the king of France and the count of Flanders restored to the king of England the strongholds they had seized in Normandy. I ascribe this peace to Our Lady, the Mother of Jesus Christ, because on the vigil of her Assumption the whole army withdrew from the siege, and the citizens of Rouen [Col. 0521A] celebrated a joyful day in her church, as they ought, having been delivered from the siege.

After the feast of Saint John, Amalric, king of Jerusalem, died, and his son Baldwin IV succeeded him. Loradin, king of Aleppo, also died, and his son succeeded him, born of the sister of the count of Saint-Gilles, whom he had taken captive on the Jerusalem expedition. She and her son, having accepted a truce for seven years, promised to give a very great sum of gold to the king of Jerusalem. Saraguntat, Loradin’s nephew, killed Amulanius of Babylon and became ruler of Babylon and Alexandria.

When Drogo, abbot of Holy Trinity, died, William of Esperville, a monk of [Col. 0521B] Bec and prior of Évreux, succeeded him. When Robert, abbot of Cormeilles, also died, Hardewin, monk of Bec and prior of Saint Theodemir [Note: [Col. 0521] added above by the same hand: “or Himerius.” This is found in 8h.], succeeded him.

1175. Frederick 24. Louis 38. Henry 21.

King Henry spent Christmas at Argentan. Frederick, emperor of the Germans, coming into Italy with his wife, children, and a very great army [Note: [Col. 0521D] October 1174.], besieged Alessandria until Easter [Note: [Col. 0521D] That is, from 29 October 1174.], achieving nothing but suffering many losses. Warin of Gélardon, abbot of Pontigny, became archbishop of Bourges, just as the abbot who had governed that monastery before him [Note: [Col. 0522D] Guichard, BOUQUET; cf. above, year 1163.] had become archbishop of Lyons.

Around Easter the Young King was reconciled with [Col. 0521C] his father, after receiving from him and his brothers the oath that he demanded. Then the king sent his son Duke Richard into Aquitaine, and his son Geoffrey, count of Brittany, into Brittany, assigning Roland of Dinan to him as administrator of his land. Frederick, emperor of the Germans, withdrew from Alessandria, and negotiations took place for restoring peace between the lord pope and himself. But the emperor would not agree to peace while Alessandria stood, and the Lombards would not overthrow it; thus peace remained unsettled. He still stays at Pavia, unable either to advance or return.

Geoffrey, duke of Brittany, restored to his own authority what Count Eudo held of his lordship: namely Vannes, Ploërmel, Auray, and half of Cornouaille. After Easter [Col. 0521D] King Henry and his son the Young King crossed into England. Because clerics and laymen, barons and knights, had taken from his deer without his permission, he squeezed much silver out of them.

The king of Scotland was reconciled with the king of England in this manner. He did homage and swore fealty to him for all his land, as to his proper lord; and he granted that all the bishops of that land, ten in number, together with abbots, earls, and barons, should do the same. [Col. 0522A] The bishops and abbots, however, did not perform homage; but they bound themselves by oath to observe this, and to be subject to the church and archbishop of York, and to go there for consecration whenever necessary. Moreover King William delivered his fortresses—Roxburgh, the Castle of Maidens, and a third [Note: [Col. 0521] After this word E leaves a space for a name to be entered; “the Castle of Maidens, i.e. Edinburgh, and the third, i.e. Berwick,” 7b.]—to the king of England, who placed his own guards in them; the king of Scotland was also to supply their necessities. Further, the king of England would grant honours, bishoprics, abbeys, and other dignities in Scotland—or, rather, they would be granted by his counsel.

The prior of Canterbury became abbot of Battle; Peter, prior of Montacute, became abbot of Hyde; the prior of Bermondsey, abbot of Abingdon; and the prior of Winchester, abbot of Westminster. We are silent concerning certain lesser abbots. John of Oxford, [Col. 0522B] dean of Salisbury, was elected bishop of Norwich. Reginald, earl of Cornwall, natural son of the former King Henry, died and was buried at Reading. King Henry retained in his own hand the earldom of Cornwall and all the land which Reginald had held in England, Normandy, and Wales, for the use of his younger son John, except for a small portion which he gave to the earl’s daughters.

Robert, abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel, the writer of these times, while travelling in England obtained from the lord king a charter and seal confirming all alms bestowed on the church of the Mount, which had been given to that church up to the present time and would be given in the future [Note: [Col. 0521] The script changes, though the hand is still the same.]. Richard, son of the earl of Gloucester, died, and his son Philip succeeded him, born of the sister of Robert de Montfort. [Col. 0522C] Henry, brother of Louis king of France and archbishop of Reims, also died. Likewise the count of Nevers [Note: [Col. 0522D] Guy, BOUQUET.].

And, what is grievous—and should be passed over except for remembrance of a righteous man—Gerard, abbot of Clairvaux, was attacked three times by night with a knife by a false monk of the same order and mortally wounded. Yet during the three days that he survived, he was granted to receive confession, penance, and the sacraments of Christ’s body [Note: [Col. 0521] The script changes, not the writer.]. Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, convened a great council in England, in the city of London. The old dispute over the primacy of Britain still continued between him and Roger, archbishop of York. Likewise Bartholomew, archbishop of Tours, held a council [Col. 0522D] at Rennes with the bishops of Brittany. Hugh Peter-Leon, legate of the Roman see, crossed into England [Note: [Col. 0521] After this the script changes.].

1176. 25. 39. 22.

Snow and frost lasted from Christmas until the Purification of the Blessed Mary. Richer of Laigle died, and his son Richer succeeded him. Richard, earl of Striguil, son of Earl Gilbert, died, [Col. 0523A] leaving a little son by the daughter of the king of Dublin. He had acquired certain towns in Ireland, namely Dublin, Waterford, and others; when Henry, king of the English, went to that island, he took them into his own hand. The Irish promised King Henry tribute from the whole island: from each house, a cowhide or twelve silver pence. On the vigil of Easter, around midday, a violent wind arose, scattering houses and uprooting woods [Note: [Col. 0523] Here the quire and the hand end.].

1177. Frederick 26. Louis 40. Henry 23.

In Whitsun week the Lombards, especially the Milanese, defeated the army of Frederick, emperor of the Germans, who was then staying in the city of Pavia. He himself barely escaped by flight. William, [Col. 0523B] brother of Count Theobald, archbishop of Sens and bishop of Chartres, was translated to the archbishopric of Reims. At Sens, Guy by name, provost of Auxerre and archbishop of Sens, succeeded him. At Chartres, John of Salisbury, an honourable and wise man, succeeded him; he had formerly been clerk to Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, and afterwards to Saint Thomas the martyr, Theobald’s successor.

When the bishop of Beauvais died [Note: [Col. 0523D] Bartholomew, who died on 17 May 1175, BOUQUET.], Philip, son of Count Robert, brother of the king of France, succeeded him. William, king of Sicily, of the duchy of Apulia, and of the principality of Capua, requested Joan, daughter of Henry king of the English, in marriage through honourable envoys, and received her. Roger, abbot of Jumièges, a monk of Bec, died. Ralph, abbot [Col. 0523C] of Saumur, also died, and Manerius, sacrist of that place, succeeded him. William of Courcy also died, leaving a little son by the daughter of Richer of Laigle. William of Albini, whom they called earl of Arundel, likewise died, leaving four sons: William of Albini, the firstborn, and three others born of Queen Adeliza, wife of Henry, the first king of the English. This William married the widow of Roger, earl of Clare, daughter of James of Saint-Hilary, with all the land that James had held in England.

Philip, count of Flanders, having taken up the cross of the Lord, went to Jerusalem with a great company of knights. Hasculf of Saint-Hilary went to Jerusalem and died abroad. Peter, brother of Philip, count of Flanders, having married the countess of Nevers [Note: [Col. 0523D] Matilda, daughter of Raymond, count of Burgundy; first married to Odo II of Issoudun and then to Guy, count of Nevers. BOUQUET.], [Col. 0523D] who had been the wife of the lord of Issoudun castle [Note: [Col. 0523D] Issoudun, in Berry.], died [Note: [Col. 0524D] In 1176, according to the continuator of Sigebert of Gembloux, Aquicinctus.]. Perhaps this was because he had abandoned spiritual knighthood—that is, the clerical estate—since, having been elected to the bishopric of Cambrai, he forsook spiritual knighthood and became a secular knight. By this countess he begot one daughter.

Count Robert, son of Count Robert, brother of Louis king of France, married that countess [Col. 0524A] with the same county [Note: [Col. 0524D] False: the county was inherited by William, son of Matilda and Guy. BOUQUET.]; thus she became four-times married. Robert, abbot of Marmoutier, a venerable man, died, and Peter, a monk of that house, succeeded him. After Ralph, abbot of Cluny and cousin of Count Theobald, was deposed [Note: [Col. 0524D] Others say that he voluntarily resigned already in 1176.], Walter, prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, succeeded him; and the former abbot again became prior of La Charité. Robert of Blangy, an honourable and religious man, monk of Bec and abbot of Saint-Evroul, likewise died. Osbert, abbot of Lyre, also paid the debt of human life; his younger brother Walter succeeded him, just as he himself had succeeded his elder brother William. It is difficult or impossible to find three brothers succeeding one another [Col. 0524B] in the government of any church.

Earl Hugh Bigod died, and his son Roger succeeded him. Roger of Crypta, a monk of Holy Trinity, Canterbury, became abbot of Saint Augustine’s, after Clarenbald, the elect of that monastery, was expelled because he would not receive benediction from Saint Thomas; for this reason it was withheld from him. On Maundy Thursday Saint William was killed by Jews at Paris, who were burned by fire. Benedict, prior of Canterbury, became abbot of Burgh. In summer and autumn there was an extreme drought; consequently the sowing of the land, the harvest, and the hay for the most part failed, and the gathering of crops and vintage came earlier than usual.

On 24 July the lord Pope Alexander and Frederick, Roman emperor, were reconciled in the city of [Col. 0524C] Venice, in the house of that city’s patriarch. In August Henry the elder, king of the English, and his son Geoffrey, duke of the Bretons, crossed into Normandy with a very great retinue. The Young King Henry and Richard, duke of Aquitaine, his sons, met them with many barons, with great joy and honour. King Henry, taking with him his sons Henry the younger and Richard duke of Aquitaine, and assembling his barons at Vaux-Saint-Rémy, spoke with the king of France concerning matters of peace and concerning taking up the cross for the service of God. Then the lord king sent his son, the count of Brittany, with the other Bretons, to crush the pride of Guihomar of Léon.

Maurice, bishop of Paris, has for a long time laboured greatly [Col. 0524D] and effectively in building the church of that city; its head is now complete, except for the principal roof covering. If that work is completed, no work this side of the mountains will be found which can suitably be compared with it. On the death of Waleran, son of William Lupellus, the tower of Ivry came into the lord king’s hand—a possession which he had greatly [Col. 0525A] desired, though neither his father nor his grandfather had held it.

King Henry went into the district of Bourges and took into his own hand the castle of Ralph of Déols, because it was held of him, together with the only daughter of the lord of that castle and all her inheritance, which some say is worth as much as the revenue of all Normandy. The barons who guarded Issoudun castle, with all its appurtenances, offered it to him because Odo, lord of that castle, had recently died leaving a little son, and because it belonged to the county of Anjou. He refused to receive it because he had no heir, whom the duke of Burgundy, being his kinsman, had secretly carried off. [Col. 0525B] The viscount of the same castle likewise surrendered to him Turonium, a castle exceptionally well fortified both by art and by nature. King Henry also bought the entire land of the count of La Marche for six thousand marks of silver; according to the king himself, it was worth twenty thousand marks of silver.

The bishop of Limoges [Note: [Col. 0525D] Gerald, BOUQUET.], who was count of that city, died after living blind for ten years. Richard, duke of Aquitaine, took from the viscount of that castle [Note: [Col. 0525D] Adémar, BOUQUET.] the castle situated near that city, in whose monastery Saint Martial rests; and rightly so, because he assisted the party of the count of Angoulême [Note: [Col. 0526D] William, BOUQUET.], who was harassing the duke. Ruaud, bishop of Vannes, a religious man and monk of Cîteaux, died. Guihomar of Léon came to the lord king, [Col. 0525C] promising to carry out his will concerning all his land. Iarnagem of La Roche surrendered that castle to the lord king and to Count Geoffrey, his son.

As there had been an extreme drought in summer, so there was an extreme flooding of waters in winter. This year, around the feast of Saint John, many people were drowned in rivers. Many ships also perished at sea, among them one which carried Geoffrey, provost of Beverley, nephew of Roger, archbishop of York, chancellor of the Young King, and many other nobles; it sank near Saint-Valery. Moreover, as some say, almost thirty ships or more perished which were bringing wine from Poitou.

On the feast of Saint Martin the canons of Dol elected as archbishop Roland, dean [Col. 0525D] of Avranches, a religious and learned man. Present at this election were Henry, bishop of Bayeux, Richard, bishop of Avranches, Robert abbot of the Mount, and many religious men. On the night of Saint Andrew a violent wind arose; and on the feast itself and on the preceding vigil, a very great light appeared in the morning, moving from east to west. On that day Christians fought pagans at Saint-Georges de Ramla.

Saladin, who had married the wife of the now-dead Noradin, believed that he could capture the city of Jerusalem, deprived of defenders, [Col. 0526A] because the count of Flanders had led almost all the Christian knights to the siege of Harem. Nevertheless, the king of Jerusalem, the patriarch, and other religious men, having few knights and sergeants, by the power of the holy cross defeated an innumerable army of pagans. The length of this cross—from earth to heaven—appeared to the pagans, as they themselves declared. In this victory the Christians were enriched with gold and silver, horses, arms, and provisions.

1178. Frederick 27. Louis 41. Henry 25.

King Henry the elder held his court at Christmas at Angers. His sons, the Young King Henry, Richard duke of Aquitaine, and Geoffrey duke of Brittany, were there with him; and scarcely at any feast had he so many knights with him, except at his own coronation [Col. 0526B] or the coronation of his son the Young King. Stephen, bishop of Rennes, an honourable and learned man, died.

A remarkable vision befell him, which the bishop himself disclosed before his death to a monk familiar to us. A certain person appeared to him and, with a soft whistle, spoke these verses:

> Cease rashly to play; strive swiftly to rise from the dust.

He had written many pleasant things in rhythmic verse and prose to amuse and win the applause of men; and because the merciful One knew that he was soon to die, He warned him to abstain from such things and do penance. He also wrote the Life of Saint Firmatus, bishop, and the Life of Saint Vitalis, first abbot of Savigny. He also wrote for me fifty verses on old age, in the last of which [Col. 0526C] he placed one clause of the verses cited above. At his death the Mother of Mercy also appeared to him, whom he had always devoutly served.

Geoffrey, bishop of Angers, died. In mid-Lent, on 29 March, the church of Bec was dedicated by Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen, and the bishops Henry of Bayeux, Richard of Avranches, and Giles of Évreux. The kings of the English, father and son, and John, the king’s younger son, attended this dedication. The elder king gave as the church’s dowry one hundred Angevin pounds annually from his mills at Robec [Note: [Col. 0526D] A stream at Rouen.]. Robert of Argences, cellarer of Jumièges, became abbot of that church. Walter, subcellarer of Saint-Wandrille, became abbot of that monastery. Ralph of Sainte-Colombe, a monk [Col. 0526D] of that house, became abbot of Saint-Evroul. Jordan Tessun died, and his son Ralph succeeded him; he did homage to the abbot of the Mount at the Mount for the castles of La Roche and La Colombe.

William, king of Sicily, had a charter drawn up for his wife Queen Joan concerning her dower; part of it is set down here:

> William, by God’s favouring clemency king of Sicily, of the duchy of Apulia, and of the principality of Capua: by this present writing we give and grant in dower to Joan, our dearest wife, daughter of the magnificent Henry, king of the English, the city of Monte Sant’Angelo, the city of Siponto, and the city [Col. 0527A] of Vieste, with all their rightful holdings and appurtenances. For her maintenance we grant her, from the holdings of Count Geoffrey, Alesine, Peschizam, Bizum, Caprile, Baranum, and Silizum, and all else which that count is known to hold from the honour of the said county of Monte Sant’Angelo. Likewise for her maintenance we grant Caudelarium, San Clerico, Castello Pagano, Bisentinum, and Cognanum. We further grant that the monastery of Saint John of Lama and the monastery of Saint Mary of Pulsano, with all the holdings which these monasteries possess from the honour of the aforesaid county of Monte Sant’Angelo, shall belong to the tenure of her said dower. For the remembrance and inviolable confirmation [Col. 0527B] of this our gift and grant, we have ordered this present privilege to be written by the hand of Alexander our notary, strengthened with a golden bull impressed with a die, and adorned with our seal.

The witnesses to this charter and the king’s seal may be found at the beginning of Origen’s book on Numbers [Note: [Col. 0527D] Namely, in the library of Mont-Saint-Michel.].

Louis, king of France, and Henry, king of England, met for a conference not far from Nonancourt. There they discussed peace and firm concord between themselves, taking up the cross, and their journey to Jerusalem. They agreed that if either king should die during that expedition—may God avert it—the survivor should possess as his own all the other’s treasure, men, and movable goods, and complete the journey both for himself and for the deceased.

The heretics called Agennais, and many others, assembled near Toulouse, [Col. 0527C] holding erroneous views concerning the sacrament of the altar, marriage, and other sacraments. Peter, the Roman legate, and many other religious persons assembled with the aforesaid kings to refute them, but made little progress. Robert de Montfort died, and his son Hugh succeeded him, born of the sister of Ralph of Fougères. The city of Chartres and the monastery of Saint Peter in the Valley were burned; by God’s mercy, however, the church of Saint Mary and the clerks’ cloister survived.

1179. Frederick 28. Louis 42. Henry 26.

Philip, count of Flanders, returned from Jerusalem. (October 1178.) Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, sent honourable envoys to the king of France [Col. 0527D] requesting that he give his daughter to Manuel’s son; the king consented. Pope Alexander sent Octavian, subdeacon of the Roman Church, to the province of Rouen to summon the archbishop, his suffragans, and the abbots of that province. Likewise he sent other subdeacons east and west, south and north, to assemble at the general council to be held in Rome in the coming Lent.

The bishop of Tréguier [Note: [Col. 0527D] Ivo, BOUQUET.], while travelling to Rome, was robbed of all his possessions and horses and beaten so severely that he died within eight [Col. 0528A] days. Geoffrey Lois, son of a burgess of Guingamp of the same name, was elected in his place. Henry the elder, king of the English, crossed into England around the fair of Montmartin. Ralph, brother of the viscount of Beaumont and a first cousin of Henry, king of the English, was elected bishop of Angers. A solar eclipse occurred on 13 September. The abbot of Grestain died (in 1178), and William of Exeter, monk of Bec, succeeded him. Richard, bishop of Coutances, died [Note: [Col. 0527D] On 18 November according to the necrologies; but it is uncertain, [Col. 0528D] whether this was in this year or in 1178, BOUQUET.].

In the same year Robert, abbot of Marmoutier, died and Peter, a monk of that house, succeeded him. He died after scarcely a year in the government of the abbey, and Hervé of [Col. 0528B] Villiers-le-Bel, a monk of that house, succeeded him. The winter became exceedingly severe: snow lasted almost until the Purification of Saint Mary, having begun within eight days after Christmas. There was a very great flood, especially around the city of Le Mans, overthrowing bridges, houses, and mills and killing many people. This also occurred at Angers and in many other places.

Geoffrey, son of King Henry and duke of Brittany, acted vigorously. He so subdued Guihomar, viscount of Léon, who neither feared God nor respected man, and his sons, that he took all their castles and land into his own hand. He permitted the elder Guihomar only two parishes, until the next Christmas, when he and his wife were to go to Jerusalem [Col. 0528C] and perhaps not return. To the younger Guihomar he granted eleven parishes from his father’s land, retaining with himself the latter’s brother Hervé as a member of his household.

Richard, duke of Aquitaine, Geoffrey’s brother, acted likewise against Geoffrey of Rançon. He besieged, captured, and destroyed the castle of Talmont, which seemed impregnable, fortified by both art and nature, and likewise four other castles belonging to him. He did the same to the lord of Pons, destroying his castle of Pons; that lord had been allied with Geoffrey. After the destruction of Talmont, Count Richard, son of King Henry, went to England to Saint Thomas and to see his father. Certain Basques, Navarrese, and Brabançons [Col. 0528D] came to Bordeaux and ravaged the suburbs of that city with fire and plunder.

William, count of Meulan, having married the daughter of William, count of Aumale, became count of Aumale. Richard de Lucy renounced the world and royal affairs, and his nephew Richard, son of his son Geoffrey, succeeded him. When the daughter of the king of France [Note: [Col. 0528D] Agnes.] was being taken to marry the son of the emperor of Constantinople, she lodged at Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire. When one of her servants tried to accelerate the fire by pouring on oil, flame came out through the [Col. 0529A] openings of the chimney and fell upon its roof; by this accident the whole abbey was burned.

When the king of France wished to crown his son Philip, he fixed Reims as the place and the Assumption of the Blessed Mary as the date. After all that was necessary for such a business had been assembled, and all the barons of the entire kingdom of France summoned to meet at that place, the youth to be crowned turned aside on the way with his companions to hunt in a wood. Having lost all his companions, he remained wandering in the forest for one night. At last, having found a man making charcoal for smiths’ use, he was brought by him back to his companions. From solitude and fear, however, he contracted such an illness that [Col. 0529B] his coronation was then postponed.

His father, angered and intending to pray for himself and his son, went to the shrine of Saint Thomas in England, who had shown him much kindness when he was an exile in Gaul. For the love and honour of God and Saint Thomas, that king gave to the monks continually serving God in Canterbury church one hundred measures of wine, to be received by the aforesaid monks every year. With what honour, what joy, and what manifold generosity of gifts King Henry received him is not for us to describe.

This year Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, avenged himself upon Soliman of Iconium, who in the preceding year had put him to flight, captured many of his knights, and moreover taken from him the Lord’s cross. Emperor Manuel drove him away, captured many [Col. 0529C] of his knights, and Soliman himself abandoned the city of Iconium empty.

The judgment of a certain astrologer concerning future plagues:

> From the present year, 1179 of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in seven years, in the month of September, in the twelfth indiction, with the sun in Libra, there will be, if the Lord wills, a conjunction of all the planets in Libra and the tail of Scorpio. In this there is a remarkable signification of a change in changeable things. For there will follow a remarkable earthquake; places customarily liable to destruction will be destroyed, through Saturn and Mars remaining in the airy signs; and there will be mortality and disease.  
>
> The same conjunction also indicates a strong wind, blackening the air, making it dark, and infected with poisons. In [Col. 0529D] the wind a terrible voice will be heard, terrifying human hearts; it will take dust from sandy regions and cover with sand the nearby cities on the plain, first the eastern cities—Mecca, Baghdad, and Babylon—and all cities near sandy places. Indeed, none will escape without being covered by sand and earth.  
>
> The signs of this event are these, and those preceding it. In the same year, before the planets meet in [Col. 0530A] Libra, there will be an eclipse of the sun, by which its whole body will be darkened; and at the preceding opposition the moon will suffer a total eclipse. The eclipse of the sun will be fiery in colour and misshapen, indicating that a great war is to come, with the shedding of blood, near a river, in the land of the East and likewise of the West. Then discord will arise among Jews and Saracens until they wholly abandon their synagogues and *manummeriae* [meaning uncertain]; and their sect will be annihilated by God’s command. Therefore let it be known to you that, when you see the eclipse, you should depart from the land with all your people.  
>
> [Note: [Col. 0529] From this point the appearance of the hand changes only slightly, not the hand itself. E6 ends at the foot of the folio with the words “you should depart with,” the following text being omitted.]

1180. Frederick 29. Louis 43. Henry 27.

[1179, 5 March.] On the council which Pope Alexander III held at Rome. Pope Alexander III held a general council at Rome in mid-Lent. Its decrees, which were enacted there by him and his fellow bishops, are held among us. Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, gave his daughter, born of his former wife, to Rainerius, son of William, marquis of Montferrat. When she declared that she would never marry anyone unless he were a king, the emperor, delighted, had himself crowned, together with his wife and his son Alexius as junior emperor, with his wife, daughter of the king of France. Likewise, he had Rainerius, son of the marquis of Montferrat, crowned with the daughter whom he had given him; and he granted him the honour of Thessalonica, the greatest authority in his realm after the city of Constantinople.

[1179.] Conrad, brother of that same Rainerius, captured and imprisoned Christian, archbishop of Mainz and chancellor of the emperor of Germany. The king of Morocco, in whose power lies all Africa, as well as the Saracens who are in Spain, was sending his daughter to be taken in marriage by a certain Saracen king. The fleet and galleys of the king of Sicily found her and brought her to their lord. Therefore the king, rejoicing, made peace with her father and restored her; and her father restored to the king of Sicily two cities, namely Africa and Sibylia, which the Saracens had taken from William, king of Sicily, father of this king.

[1179.] The king of Jerusalem, a holy and honourable prince, being scourged by God—for God chastens every son whom He receives—and assisted by Christendom overseas, built a very strongly fortified castle, both by art and by nature, over the Jordan river, called Jacob’s Ford, where Jacob wrestled with the angel. It was delightful for the beauty of its woods, meadows, fish, and mills, and near the cities of Baniyas and Damascus. Since the Hagarene people have passage through this ford into the land of the Christians, they hate it exceedingly.

Roger, bishop of Worcester, died at Tours, a man honourable in birth and character; for his father, Robert, earl of Gloucester, was son of Henry I, king of England; his mother was daughter of Robert of Bellême; and Robert, son of Haimo, lord of Thorigny, was his grandfather.

> [Note: Col. 0529D. The year is 1179 according to Benedict of Peterborough.]

Giles, bishop of Évreux, died.

> [Note: Col. 0531D. The year is 1180 according to Benedict of Peterborough; 8 September 1179, from the necrology of St Leufroy, cited by *Gallia Christiana*, XI, 579.]

Roger, abbot of Bec, died, a religious, honourable, learned, and God-fearing man. None of his predecessors, except St Herluin, the first abbot, did as much at the monastery of Bec as he did. For almost the whole church was built and dedicated in his time; no church in all Normandy equalled its beauty. He built guest chambers with fireplaces, one above another, for receiving guests and persons. He also built an infirmary of extraordinary beauty and size. He improved the dormitory in its walls, glazing, and roofing. He made an aqueduct by which he brought from afar a most beautiful spring, distributed through the monastic offices; he also made a most beautiful basin to receive the water and built a roof over it. He paid a very great sum of money to Robert, count of Meulan, for the market which he established in the town of Bec. During his tenure twelve abbots from the church of Bec were appointed to govern churches, of whom I who write this was the second. He governed the monastery of Bec for thirty years, lacking ten days; Osbern, prior of Beaumont, a monk of the same house, succeeded him.

> [Note: Col. 0531D. The Chronicle of Bec has “thirty years,” and therefore places Roger’s death under 1179. This is false; compare above, under 1149.]

These three aforesaid men—the bishop of Worcester, the bishop of Évreux, and the abbot of Bec—passed to their fate, hindered by gout.

[1179, 1 November.] Philip, son of Louis, king of France, was crowned king at Reims by William, archbishop of Reims, his maternal uncle, and his suffragans, on the feast of All Saints. The elder king of England sent him great gifts in gold and silver and English game. The younger king of England attended this solemnity with a great company of knights, bringing with him at his father’s command so much that he accepted hospitality from no one, either at the feast itself or on the journey.

When the venerable Giselbert, abbot of Troarn, died, Durand of Cuverville, monk of the same place, succeeded him.

> [Note: Col. 0531D. Troarn, diocese of Bayeux.]

Robert, prior of St Peter-sur-Dives, succeeded Robert, abbot of Fontenay.

> [Note: Col. 0531D. Fontenay, diocese of Bayeux.]

Walter, abbot of Cluny, died. Though he lived only a short time in the governance of that church—namely, a year and a half—he freed it from a debt of four thousand marks, with which it had been burdened.

> [Note: Col. 0531D. Here Robert plainly errs in chronology. If Walter assumed the abbacy in 1177, as Robert himself said above, he must have died by the end of 1178 or the beginning of 1179. This agrees well with our words at the beginning of the following year. But the Chronicle of St Stephen of Nevers, in Martène, *Thesaurus*, III, 1387, says that Walter died on 6 September 1177, and that William had already died in 1180, not only in 1181 as Robert has it. A charter issued in 1180 to his successor, Abbot Theobald, proves this; see the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 1439; compare *Gallia Christiana*, IV, 1142. The Chronicle of Cluny must be used most cautiously for arranging dates.]

William, a monk of the same place and formerly abbot of Ramsey in England, succeeded him. He performed a remarkable deed: from his own treasures, which he had accumulated, and from the thousand marks which Henry, king of England, had given him, he removed for the greater part the remaining debt of the church of Cluny, amounting to fourteen thousand marks. He did another remarkable thing: he deposed the prior of Stallo, who used to lead forty horses in his retinue, and ordered him to be content with three mounts. He did yet another remarkable thing: he entirely abolished the one hundred and forty provisions which the burgesses had customarily received from the gifts of abbots.

When the Christians engaged Salahadin, many died on either side, but more Christians; and the master of the Temple was captured. When Salahadin wished to ransom him in exchange for his nephew, whom the Christians held captive, the master of the Temple refused, saying that it was not the custom of the Templars for any ransom to be given for them beyond a belt and a knife. Thus he died in captivity.

Another disaster befell our people. Salahadin, with an innumerable army, besieged the castle of Jacob’s Ford, captured it by engines and force, and sawed in two through their sides the Templars who were inside; he beheaded others of lower rank. Salahadin nevertheless offered to rebuild and fortify the castle and restore it to the Christians if they would return his nephew, mentioned above; whether this was done, we do not yet know.

1181. Frederick 30. Louis 44. Henry 28.

Henry, king of England, held his court in England at Christmas at Nottingham.

> [Note: Col. 0532D. Benedict of Peterborough assigns this to 1180—that is, 25 December 1179.]

William, abbot of Cluny, died at La Charité on the day after Epiphany, a man to be mourned for the good which he did for his church; but he lived only a short time, almost two years.

> [Note: Col. 0532D. Compare the preceding note.]

[1180, 28 December.] Richard, abbot of St Ouen, died; Samson, a venerable man and prior of St Stephen at Caen, succeeded him. Richard du Hommet, the king’s constable, after living religiously for one year and a half in the abbey of Aulnay, which he himself had built, died, leaving his sons William, Emmorain, and Jordan as heirs of his land.

> [Note: Col. 0531–0533. Here manuscript 8h adds: “In the year of the Incarnate Word 1181, the twenty-second of the episcopate of Pope Alexander, the sixteenth of Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen, on 5 March, the church of St Mary of Vœu, situated in the territory of Rouen, was dedicated in honour of the same Mother of God, Mary, by Lord Henry, bishop of Bayeux, with Bishops Richard of Avranches and Reginald of Bath in attendance, and with the illustrious Henry, king of England, son of the Empress Matilda, present, in the twenty-seventh year of his reign.”]

[1180.] Louis, king of France, having fallen into a most serious illness, Philip, his son and junior king, led by some counsel unknown to me, bound himself by oath that he would marry, at the proper place and time, the daughter of Baldwin, count of Hainaut, born of the sister of the count of Flanders.

> [Note: Col. 0533D. Elizabeth.]

The count himself granted him that after his death he should inherit the county of Flanders, although that count had male heirs by the aforesaid sister, countess of Hainaut. The king did this without the counsel of his mother the queen or of his uncles—William, archbishop of Reims; Henry, count of Troyes; Theobald of Chartres; Stephen of Sancerre—and his other friends. Therefore they, disturbed, sought the aid of Henry, the elder king of England, against his nephew Philip, the junior king of France.

Baldwin, abbot of Ford, a Cistercian monk, a man of great religious devotion and learning, was elected to the bishopric of Worcester. Robert, abbot of Glastonbury, died. John, bishop of Chichester, also died; Seffrid, a canon of that church, succeeded him.

Before Easter Henry the elder king crossed to Normandy and held his court at Le Mans at Easter. William, abbot of Caen, died, and Peter the sacristan, a monk of the same place, succeeded him.

> [Note: Col. 0533D. In 1179, according to the Chronicle of St Stephen at Caen.]

[1180.] On the day of the Lord’s Ascension, Philip, junior king of France, had his wife consecrated queen; he and she were crowned by the archbishop of Sens. The archbishop of Reims, who had crowned him king, was thereby more angered. Guarin of Girard, archbishop of Bourges, formerly abbot of Pontigny, died.

[1181.] John, bishop of Chartres, died. He had written the passion of St Thomas, archbishop and martyr of Canterbury, for he had lived with him in exile.

> [Note: Col. 0533. The ink changes in E.]

Theobald, prior of Crépy, a monk of Cluny, succeeded William as abbot of Cluny. Ingelram du Hommet, son of Richard du Hommet, died; his son Richard, born of the daughter of William de Similly, succeeded him.

> [Note: Col. 0533. In an erasure.]

My dearest Geoffrey of Montfort in Brittany, a man to be mourned, died; his son, born of the daughter of Rualent de Saie, succeeded him. Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, gave his sister to a most excellent knight, brother of Geoffrey of Lusignan; she had previously been the wife of William, son of the marquis of Montferrat. By her he had a son, who is kept and raised to receive the kingdom of Jerusalem, if he lives.

[1180, 18 September.] Louis, king of France, a religious and God-fearing man, died and was buried in a monastery of the Cistercian order which he had built.

> [Note: Col. 0534D. Barbeau, on the Seine.]

His son Philip succeeded him, as was already stated above. Geoffrey, natural son of Henry, the elder king of England, having relinquished the church of Lincoln to which he had been elected, became chancellor of his father the king.

[1180.] Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, died; his son Alexius, born of the sister of Raymond, prince of Antioch, succeeded him. He married the daughter of Louis, king of France. Mansamuz, king of the Almohads, who almost rules all Africa, began rebuilding ancient Carthage, aided by all the Hagarene people inhabiting that land. Soliman of Iconium died; he greatly loved Christians and did them many good services, and his brother succeeded him.

> [Note: Col. 0533. After this, two lines have been erased. Manuscript 7b adds: “Henry, count of Troyes, died, and his son Henry, born of the daughter of Louis, king of France, succeeded him.”]

On the woman who dies on Wednesday and rises again on Saturday. There was a very wealthy burgess in a place called Rocamadour.

> [Note: Col. 0534D. Rochamadour.]

The monks of the church of St Mary and St Amator had borrowed money from him, giving him, as a pledge, the church’s hangings. When the feast of Mary, Mother of God and Virgin, approached, the monks asked the burgess to lend them the hangings in his possession for the adornment of the church, intending to restore them to him after the celebration of so great a solemnity. But he, having the ear of his heart stopped up, was moved by no entreaty; rather, swelling with anger, he answered that the hangings were around the bed of his wife, who had recently borne him a child, and could not in any way be removed.

Why say more? The feast day passed, and the aforesaid church did not have its festal adornment. On the following night, Blessed Mary, Mother of our Lord, appeared in a dream to the wife of the aforesaid burgess and said:

“Your husband has committed a great sin, and his excessive impiety cannot go unpunished. On the third day your child will breathe out his spirit; and your husband, paying his debt to death, will on the eighth day exchange this temporal happiness for eternal punishments. But you shall go to my church which is in Bethlehem, and, after seeing there three tombs—of which the two outer ones are not empty—you shall choose the middle one for your grave. Meanwhile, every Wednesday about the ninth hour your spirit shall fail within you, and much blood shall run from your mouth and nostrils; until the ninth hour on Saturday you shall remain as if dead. At the ninth hour on Saturday, when your spirit returns, you shall pass both your hands over your face, and immediately your former colour and strength shall return to you.”

Blessed Mary spoke these words and departed. The woman, terrified, awoke; reflecting on her dream, she committed it to memory with great anxiety. At daybreak the next day, she began to tell her husband the dream in order. The wretch placed no faith in her words; nor, even when he saw the child’s spirit fail, did he think of doing penance. Rather, overtaken by death on the eighth day, according to the vision shown beforehand, he fell into the punishment of Gehenna.

The woman was troubled by the death of both, and, understanding that all had happened to her just as it had been revealed in the dream, hurried to Rome and disclosed the matter to the supreme pontiff. She further asserted firmly that in the fifth year thereafter a great famine would arise; that, through corruption of the air, an innumerable multitude of people would die; and that a severe punishment would strike the Roman clergy unless they repented of the practice of deceit, under which they had laboured from many past times down to the present day.

The lord pope, wishing to know more clearly whether the woman’s words rested on truth, entrusted her to twelve noble matrons, ordering them, when she fell asleep into death, to thrust hot awls into the soles of her feet and to stain their garments with the blood running from her mouth. O wonderful thing! On Wednesday, as she had predicted, at the ninth hour the woman grew pale and died, so that no vital breath remained in her, and abundant blood began to flow from her nostrils. But the matrons, not forgetful of the lord pope’s commands, thrust hot awls into the woman’s feet, yet she did not move for this reason. Moreover, they dyed their garments with her blood; but on Saturday, when the spirit of life returned to the woman, no trace anywhere appeared of the staining made by the blood.

> [Note: Col. 0535. After this the ink changes, though the hand remains altogether the same.]

1182. Frederick 31. Philip 1. Henry 29.

Henry, the elder king of England, held his court at Christmas at Angers.

> [Note: Col. 0535D. Benedict of Peterborough has: “at Winchester.”]

Ralph de Venneville, archdeacon of Rouen, resigned the king’s chancellorship, and the king gave him lands of great revenue. [1181—Benedict of Peterborough.] Geoffrey, son of the king, elected bishop of Lincoln, became the king’s chancellor and relinquished his election to Lincoln; and the king gave him large revenues in England, Normandy, and Anjou. John, son of Luke, a clerk of the king, was elected bishop of Évreux. [1182—the same source.] Guihenoc, archdeacon of Rennes, was elected to the bishopric of Vannes. The abbot of St Remigius at Reims was likewise elected to the bishopric of Chartres.

> [Note: Col. 0535D–0536A. Peter; but already in October 1181 the bishop confirmed a charter. BOUQ.]

Henry, count of Troyes, died, and his son Henry, born of the daughter of Louis, king of France, succeeded him.

> [Note: Col. 0536D. 17 March 1181. BOUQ.]

Simon, count of Évreux, died, and his son Amalric succeeded him in the county of Évreux in Normandy.
