Around Easter Eleanor, daughter of the king of England and wife of Alfonso, king of Castile, bore a son, who was called Sancho; she had previously also borne a daughter. The prioress of Fonte-Saint-Martin, a religious woman of high birth, being sister of the abbot of Savigny, who was nephew of Simon, count of Évreux, became abbess of Holy Trinity at Caen.

> [Note: Col. 0536D. Matilda. BOUQ.]

[1181—Benedict.] Near the end of July Henry, the elder king, crossed into England. Geoffrey, duke of Brittany, son of King Henry, betrothed his wife, daughter of Conan, count of Brittany.

At the Easter solemnity, at the castle called Mont-Aureux, a certain notorious woman, when she received the body of the Lord and Saviour in her mouth, did not swallow it, but carried it away and placed it in her chest wrapped in a linen cloth.

> [Note: Col. 0536D. Montoire, near Vendôme.]

When a young man, her lover, opened that chest, he found the host of the Lord’s body transformed into the appearance of flesh and blood. This also happened in a certain village belonging to the abbot of St Peter of Chartres, to a certain priest while he held the Lord’s body in his hands at Mass. A similar miracle occurred again in the diocese of Chartres in the time of Robert, bishop of Brittany: a certain peasant put the Lord’s body in the hood of his cloak and kept it there until his death; then it was found there in the form of flesh. The same miracle happened to a little woman in Flanders, who, after putting it in her chest, later found it in the appearance of flesh.

Likewise, at the city of Angers, while a certain priest was singing Mass, a little boy was present and saw a most beautiful little child in the hand of the priest consecrating the Lord’s body. Immediately the child went out of the church, crying to all whom he met: “Come and see the wonders of God!” Yet those entering the church saw nothing except the form of bread. This also happened to a most holy priest near Fécamp, while he sang Mass on the day of the dedication of the church of Holy Trinity at Fécamp. Sending his deacon, he summoned the bishops who had assembled for the dedication. They came; and the priest carried in his hands, in the chalice, that which was clothed as it had been, and they placed it upon the altar. The Lord’s mercy does these things to confirm in us faith in His sacraments, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

The mother of the sultan of Iconium, when she was near death, revealed to her son what she had always concealed: namely, that she was a Christian. She begged him to believe in Christ, who is Lord and king of all ages, and to love Christians. He promised to do this, but said that he did not dare openly to believe in the Saviour because of the pagans. His mother said to him:

“Son, when I am dead, make for me a lofty and beautiful tomb like a pyramid, and place upon it the sign of Christ’s cross.”

He replied that he could not do this by daylight. “Do it by night,” his mother said. This was done. On the next day, when the Hagarene people saw that sign, they were indignant against the prince and wished to kill him. Then one of them, raised by machines, attempted to take down the cross; but by God’s will he fell and died. Likewise, another was killed on another occasion. On the third day, when many thousands of people had assembled to pull down that structure, among whom was one particularly eager to do so, lightning and flashes came; he was killed first, and many thousands perished by divine fire. Then an angel of the Lord appeared and set a most radiant sign of the cross upon that pyramid. From this many believed in Christ, and they still venerate and worship that cross.

> [Note: Col. 0537. The ink and character of the hand change in E.]

Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, after governing the same church for forty years and labouring in the construction of the church and most beautiful buildings, resigned his bishopric and went to Paris, intending to spend the remainder of his days at St Victor in the most beautiful buildings which he had constructed there for his own use. Ralph de Venneville, archdeacon of Rouen and former royal chancellor, was elected to the aforesaid bishopric.

> [Note: Col. 0537. A different hand begins.]

(30 August.) In the preceding year, 1181, Pope Alexander III died; few of his predecessors in the past hundred years attained his learning. For he was a most eminent teacher in sacred Scripture, outstanding in decrees, canons, and Roman law. He solved and elucidated many very difficult and serious questions in decrees and laws. God also gave him this grace: although there had been one hundred and seventy-four Roman pontiffs from St Peter to him, only three preceded him in the number of years during which they presided over the Roman church: St Peter sat for twenty-five years; Sylvester I for twenty-three; Adrian I for the same number; Alexander himself for twenty-two.

He also held a council at Tours in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1163, at which he anathematized Octavian and his accomplices; we were present at that council. Likewise he held another council at Rome in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1180. Many ecclesiastical and secular persons assembled there. Among them came a citizen of Pisa named Burgundio, learned in both Greek and Latin eloquence. He brought the Gospel of St John, translated by himself from Greek into Latin, which John Chrysostom had expounded in homiletic discourse.

> [Note: Col. 0537. Thus E.]

He also declared that he had already translated a large part of the book of Genesis. He further said that John Chrysostom had expounded the whole Old and New Testament in Greek. The aforesaid Pope Alexander endured for almost twenty years three schismatics who had succeeded one another in the schism—namely Octavian, Guido, and Calixtus. When they failed, he ended his life in the peace of the Church. Hubert, bishop of Ostia, called Lucius, the 175th bishop of Rome, succeeded him.

The bishop of Ostia, according to ancient custom, ordains and consecrates the Roman pontiff. This custom arose because, after St Sixtus and St Lawrence his deacon had been martyred, St Justin the priest, with the Roman clergy, chose Dionysius as Roman pontiff, and Maximus, bishop of Ostia, consecrated him. From this custom onward the bishop of Ostia ordains and consecrates the Roman pontiff, and possesses the pallium solely for matters pertaining to the ordination and consecration of the Roman pontiff. Pope Eugenius joined the bishopric of Velletri to that of Ostia, thus making two into one. He did likewise with the bishopric of Porto, to which he joined the bishopric of St Rufina, making two into one.

[1181.] Roger, bishop of York, died, a learned man and industrious in increasing earthly possessions. He greatly enlarged, with revenues, both the cathedral church and the episcopal buildings—not only at York but in all his manors—and adorned them by rebuilding, so that the archbishopric of York was almost made equal to the archbishopric of Canterbury.

> [Note: Col. 0537. E reads “axit” for “auxit.”]

He left behind much wealth which did him no good. Philip, bishop of Rennes, formerly first abbot of Clermont, died. By revelation, he tore down the head of the church of Rennes to its foundations; in its demolition he found much money, with which he began to rebuild the head of the aforesaid church in a better design. Humphrey de Bohun, commander in the army with the younger King Henry, died. That army the aforesaid king had led into France to aid the party of Philip, king of France, against the count of Flanders. Henry, abbot of Préaux, and William, abbot of St Michael beyond the Sea, monks of Bec, died.

> [Note: Col. 0537–0538D. “Obiit” [“died”] was first written, but the same hand later corrected it and added the words “Henry, abbot of Préaux; and William, abbot of St Michael beyond the Sea,” which are also read in 8d and 8h. Manuscript 7a adds: “Henry, abbot of Préaux, monk of Bec.” Here manuscripts 7a and 7b end; nothing has been lost.]

In the year of the Lord 1181, on the third Ides (13 July), at the ninth hour of the day, there was an eclipse of the sun. Almost a third part of the sun was obscured, and from the beginning of the eclipse to its end there elapsed one equal hour and thirty-eight minutes. In the same year there was an eclipse of the moon on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January [22 December], namely on Tuesday night following, at the third hour of the night; slightly less than half was obscured, and the darkness lasted nearly two hours.

In the year of the Lord 1175:

> [Note: Col. 0537D. Corrected to 1176. BOUQ.]

an eclipse was twice seen in the moon: first at the Greater Litany, at the first hour of the night, after the day of Mark the Evangelist itself; second, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November [19 October], on the following night, at about the third hour of the night. In the year of the Lord 1178:

> [Note: Col. 0539. E has MCLXVIII [1168].]

we saw an eclipse in the moon on 5 March, on the following night, at the first hour of the night.

> [Note: Col. 0539. Thus E.]

In the same year there was an eclipse in the moon on 29 August; and in the same year and month, in the sun, on 13 September, around noon, when almost all was obscured. In 1179 also, the moon was seen to be eclipsed on 18 August, after the eighth hour of Sunday night. In 1180 there was an eclipse of the sun on 28 January, Tuesday.

[1182.] In March, Henry the elder king crossed to Normandy with a great quantity of gold and silver, ready to aid the king of France in making peace between him and the count of Flanders, as he did. Mabel, countess of Flanders, died without children.

> [Note: Col. 0539D. Elizabeth.]
>
> [Note: Col. 0539. The hand and orthography change.]

Andronicus, uncle of Alexius, emperor of Constantinople, angered because he had married the daughter of the king of France and kept many Latins as intimate companions, wished, since he himself was Greek, to expel them from his empire. Therefore, having enlisted the sultan of Iconium and many Saracens, they entered the city by treachery. He killed many Latins, and many Saracens were killed by Latins. Yet, by God’s will, peace was confirmed between them.

> [Note: Col. 0539. Here manuscript 8d ends, its final leaves having been lost.]

John, bishop of Poitiers, a man of great learning and eloquence, elected to the bishopric of Narbonne, having gone to Rome for the aforesaid blessing, with Pope Lucius’s assent was elected by the clergy of the First Lyonnaise as archbishop of Lyons. That see holds primacy over three archbishoprics. For the First Lyonnaise—that is, Lyons—is upon the Rhône; the Second Lyonnaise is upon the Seine, that is, Rouen; the Third Lyonnaise is upon the Loire, that is, Tours; the Fourth Lyonnaise, that is, Sens, is upon the Yonne.

> [Note: Col. 0539. Here manuscript 8e ends.]

[1182.] In this year there were two or three earthquakes around the feast of St Michael. In the same year a great discord arose between the king and his sons over the castle of Clairvaux, which was held of the Angevins; Richard, count of Poitou, had secretly fortified it, and the discord between father and sons still endures for the same cause. Henry the elder king sent an army into Brittany; they besieged and captured the tower of Rennes and, after it had been burned, rebuilt and fortified it. Afterwards the count of Brittany burned a great part of that city and the abbey of St Gregory, and burned Bécherel, castle of Roland de Dinan.

We heard from certain persons that Joanna, wife of William, king of Sicily, daughter of Henry, king of England, bore him a firstborn son, whom they called Bohemond. When he returned from baptism, his father invested him, by the golden sceptre which he held in his hand, with the duchy of Apulia. Since I have begun to speak of the daughters of my lord the king of England, I ought not to omit the king of Castile, whom they call Alfonso the little king, because his uncle Ferdinand still lives; if he died, the aforesaid Alfonso would be king of all Spain.

> [Note: Col. 0539. At the end of the quire in E, the following was written by another hand, continuously through the end of the year 1183. Thereafter, with the appearance of the hand slightly changed, exactly the same hand continues to the end of the manuscript.]

This Alfonso, by God’s grace and his own valour, married my dearest lady and baptismal daughter, Eleanor, daughter of the king of England. By her counsel and aid many good things befell him. First he captured the city of Cuenca, mother-city of extensive lands; and, as some say, he captured and fortified part of Córdoba, and two cities of King Lupus, Valencia and Murcia.

> [Note: Col. 0539. Thus E.]

He did many other good things which did not come to our knowledge. The third of the king’s daughters, namely Matilda the firstborn, married Henry, duke of the Saxons, Bavarians, and Swabians. No man has such great possessions as he, unless he is an emperor or king. For he has forty cities and sixty-seven castles, apart from many villages. Yet, although he was related by blood to Frederick, emperor of the Romans, when certain hostilities arose between them, the emperor of that realm, by the counsel of the archbishops and bishops of Germany, who hold almost all the cities under their power, exiled him. Therefore he came to Normandy, to Henry the king, his father-in-law, with his wife and children; and the king incurred very great expenses on his behalf, namely fifty Angevin pounds each day. With God’s help he will yet recover his land through the enterprise, strength, and wealth of the king of England.

1182. Frederick 30. Philip 1. Henry 27.

King Henry held his court at Caen and forbade any of the barons to hold a court, ordering them to come to his. The aforesaid duke of Saxony came there, and over one thousand knights assembled there. John, bishop of Chartres, died, and Peter, formerly abbot of St Remigius at Reims, succeeded him. Walter, bishop of Rochester, brother of Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, died; Waleran, archdeacon of Bayeux, succeeded him. Our father Richard, bishop of Avranches, died, a man of great learning, both secular and sacred, praiseworthy for upright morals, a virgin from the womb. Fulk Paynel died, and his son William succeeded him. Richard, abbot of Montbourg, died, and Robert, prior and monk of the same place, succeeded him. John Comyn, clerk of the king of England, became archbishop of Dublin in Ireland. Peter, bishop of Chartres, died; Rainald de Mâcon, treasurer of St Martin at Tours and nephew of Count Theobald, was elected in his place. Walter of Coutances became bishop of Lincoln and was consecrated by Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, at Angers, in the chapel of the lord king and in his presence.

[1183.] Henry the Third, our dearest lord, the young king, son of Henry the Second, most excellent and most illustrious king of the English, died at the castle of Martel [Note: [Col. 0541] “c. M.” written over an erasure. Here MS 8f ends.], on the third Ides of June, on the feast of the blessed apostle Barnabas. He was a man to be mourned in every respect, not only because he was the son of our dearest lord Henry the Second, most excellent king of the English, but also because he was most handsome in appearance, honourable in conduct, lavish in gifts, above all those whom we have seen in our age who had not yet been assigned a land [Col. 0541B]—although his father gave him fifteen thousand pounds of Angevin currency and more each year. Yet this was too little to satisfy the breadth of his heart. In the exercise of arms he was so great that he had no equal; princes, counts, and even kings feared him.

As he approached his end, because through the counsel of wicked men he had, by war for almost a year, offended God, holy Church, and his father, he received penance from a most holy bishop and many others. At the last he sent word to his father by letters that he should make amends on his behalf for what he had done against God and holy Church, and should have mercy upon his mother, the queen of the English, his wife, sister of Philip king of the French, and his knights and servants, to whom he had promised much but, prevented by death, could give nothing [Col. 0541C].

Before his death he had directed that his body should be buried in the church of Blessed Mary at Rouen, where his first ancestors lie: namely Rollo and his son William Longsword, dukes of the Normans, and also his uncle Count William, a man to be mourned in every respect. But when Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, many other ecclesiastical persons, many men of consular rank, and men of the highest distinction were escorting his funeral, they came to Le Mans and placed his body in the church of Saint Julian. On the following day the people of Le Mans, especially the citizens, buried him in that same place, against the will and appeal of those escorting his body. When his father heard of this, angered not only [Col. 0541D] because they had buried his son’s body there against his will, but much more because they had withdrawn from the siege of the castle of Limoges without his permission—not to say without his consent—he ordered the body to be dug up and carried to the church at Rouen. There it was honourably entombed, as befitted so great a man, on the left side of the altar of Blessed Mary, by the archbishops of Rouen and Canterbury, the bishops of Normandy, abbots, and other religious persons.

The venerable Albert, bishop of Alet, died; modern people call him bishop of Saint-Malo, though the city of his bishopric was anciently called Alet. Master Gerard, surnamed “the Maiden,” a man of great learning [Col. 0542A] and integrity, was elected to the bishopric of Chester, which bishopric has three sees: Chester, Coventry, and Lichfield. Henry, brother of Giles of Solereio and nephew of the abbot of Fécamp, was elected to the archbishopric of Bourges.

Again Andronicus expelled from Constantinople his nephew Alexius, the young emperor, and at last drowned in the sea both him and his mother and sister. When these had been removed from the world by death, Andronicus, who had tyrannically seized the empire, commanded his eldest son Manuel to take as wife the wife of the dead Emperor Alexius, sister of Philip king of the French, and to share with him the dignity of empire. When that honourable man refused, he cast him into chains, took her himself, contracted an incestuous [Col. 0542B] marriage—if it should be called a marriage—and had his younger son Kalojohannes crowned with him.

When Latins were being killed through the cruelty of this Andronicus, a certain cardinal of the Roman Church, named John, whom the Roman pontiff had sent to Constantinople at the request of Emperor Manuel—who was a religious man and wished through that cardinal’s preaching to restore the Greek Church to the institutions and submission of the Roman Church—this John, I say, when the Latins were being killed, was in his lodging. Certain religious men came to urge him to leave, lest he be killed. On hearing this, he said: “Far be it that this should happen. I stand here for the unity of the Church and the command of my lord Pope Alexander.” Then the faithless Greeks rushed upon him [Col. 0542C] and killed him. They tied a dog to him so that the dog’s tail was in his mouth, dragged him through the streets of the city, and, after digging a pit, burned him there. Afterwards religious men took his body from the pit and buried it most honourably, where miracles frequently occur.

Christian, archbishop of Mainz, died. He conducted himself not according to the manner of clerics but after the manner of a tyrant, leading armies and Brabançons. He did much evil to the Roman Church, to the men of Saint Peter, and to certain cities of Lombardy which opposed his lord, the emperor of Germany.

[1183.] Our dearest lord Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen, died. William, count of Gloucester, died without heirs except for three daughters: one is countess of Évreux; [Col. 0542D] another is the wife of William, count of Clare; the third is in the hand of God and of the lord king, who will give her to whom he wishes. William, dean of Bayeux, was elected to the bishopric of Coutances. William, dean of the canons of Saint Peter of the Court, which is the king’s chapel at the city of Le Mans, was elected to the bishopric of Avranches.

1183. Frederick 31. Philip 2. Henry 29.

King Henry held his court at Caen. Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, died. Gerard also died, bishop of Chester, a man of great piety and learning.

[1182.] In the preceding year [Col. 0543A], our Lady Saint Mary, Mother of Mercy, appeared to a certain carpenter working timber in a forest. She offered him a seal bearing the image of herself and of her son, our Saviour, with this inscription: “Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, grant us peace.” She commanded him to carry the seal to the bishop of Le Puy, so that he might preach in his province and throughout the surrounding regions that all who wished to keep peace with holy Church and her children should make such seals and wear them as a sign of peace; should make small white hoods as a display of peace and innocence; should, after taking an oath, maintain peace; and should destroy the enemies of peace. This was done. For many bishops, consuls, men of consular rank, [Col. 0543B] persons of middling condition, and poor people, adhering to this association, keep the peace and pursue its enemies. [Note: [Col. 0543] Here MS 8c ends.] William de Vecie died. William of Lancaster, a man of great honour and possessions, died. [Note: [Col. 0543] After this, two lines have been erased in E. The hand changes to a larger script and continues thus to the end.]

1184. Frederick 32. Philip 3. Henry 30.

King Henry held his court at Le Mans. Our lord Walter, bishop of Lincoln, became archbishop of Rouen. Pope Lucius, at the beginning of the fast—that is, on Ash Wednesday—ordained several cardinals, among them Master Melior as cardinal priest, and also made him his chamberlain; and the bishop-elect of Dol as cardinal deacon; and Master Ralph Niger, our dearest friend, a man of great integrity, learning, and piety.

Frederick, emperor [Col. 0543C] of the Romans, had one of his sons ordained king of Germany—not the eldest, but the second. [Note: [Col. 0543D] Robert is less accurate: for King Henry had already been crowned on 15 August 1169; but in this year, 1184, he first took up arms at Mainz, at Pentecost.] Henry, king of the English, by his wisdom and wealth acquired the sister of the king of Portugal in Spain, to become the wife of his kinsman Philip, count of Flanders. She accordingly came to the count of Flanders with an abundance of gold and silver (August). Her father, though very old, was still living. [Note: [Col. 0543D] Afonso Henriques, who died in 1185.] In his youth, aided by Englishmen and Normans, he captured from the Hagarenes the city of Olisipo, commonly called Lisbon. To this city he transferred from Valencia the body of Saint Vincent, levite and martyr, as some say; but the monk Aimo, in his account of the translation of this holy martyr’s body in the time of Emperor Charles, tells it differently [Col. 0543D]. With papal permission he made that same city an archbishopric, subjecting to it six other cities which he had acquired.

Baldwin, bishop of Worcester, was consecrated archbishop of Canterbury. Waleran, bishop of Rochester and chaplain of the archbishop [Col. 0544A] of Canterbury, died; Gilbert, archdeacon of Lisieux, succeeded him. John de Neelfa, archdeacon of Lisieux, was elected to the bishopric of Chester. [Note: [Col. 0543] “John … Chester” are lacking in MS 8h.] Peter Girald became bishop of Saint-Malo.

1185. 33. 4. 31.

A great conflict arose between Philip, king of the French, and Philip, count of Flanders, over the county of Vermandois. But the king of the French gathered an immense army from all his resources and compelled the count to do his will. Froger, bishop of Sées, died; he greatly improved mother Church and all his domain. He also left immense riches in gold and silver, which would do him no good. Robert, [Col. 0544B] elect of Montebourg, died [Note: [Col. 0544D] Montebourg, diocese of Coutances.], and William, a monk of that place, succeeded him.

John, the younger son of the king of the English, whom they call Lackland, although he possesses many extensive estates and many counties, crossed into Ireland and, God permitting, will be king in that country. Robert, bishop of Nantes, a man of great integrity and our friend, died while returning from Jerusalem. Geoffrey, bishop of Cornwall, died. The abbot of Pontigny became bishop of Arras. Theobald, abbot of Cluny, became cardinal bishop of Ostia; the son of the count of Clermont succeeded him. He had first been abbot of a certain Cistercian abbey; thence he was transferred to the abbey of Flavigny; then, when certain causes had arisen, he became [Col. 0544C] abbot of Saint Lucian the Martyr, first bishop of the city of Beauvais; and thence, as we have said, he became abbot of Cluny.

Again there was great agitation and dispute between Philip, king of the French, and Philip, count of Flanders. For the count of Flanders, ashamed because he had done the king’s will concerning the county of Vermandois, filled with anger and indignation, turned to the king of Germany, son of Frederick emperor of the Romans, so that he might aid him; and he performed homage to him for the county of Flanders. Hence great trouble arose throughout the whole kingdom of France.

In the preceding year Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, died, a man honourable, devout, and powerful against the Saracens, though afflicted with elephantiasis. Nor is this surprising, [Col. 0544D] for God chastises every son whom he receives. His nephew Henry succeeded him, [Note: [Col. 0544D] Robert is mistaken: it was Baldwin V, son of Sibylla, who died in 1186.] born of his sister, whose father was William, son of the count of Montferrat, himself born of a niece of Frederick emperor of the Romans. Afterwards the count of Jaffa [Note: [Col. 0544D] Guy of Lusignan] married the mother of the aforesaid King Henry, and [Col. 0545A] protects that young king and his kingdom until he reaches full age.

Bartholomew, the venerable bishop of Exeter, died. Jocelin, bishop of Salisbury, died. (24 November.) Pope Lucius of Rome died; Humbert, archbishop of Milan, succeeded him, called Urban the Third. [Note: [Col. 0545] After this, three lines have been erased in E. MS 8h adds “pope of Rome.”]

Lord Walter, archbishop of Rouen, obtained from our lord Henry, king of the English, that the abbey of Saint Helier, on the island of Jersey, founded on the same island by William son of Hamery, should, by the counsel and aid of the lord king, be joined to the abbey of Notre-Dame du Vœu near Cherbourg, which the Empress, mother of King Henry, had built. [Note: [Col. 0545] “H. f.”, that is, written over an erasure.] The former was three times richer, both in Normandy [Col. 0545B] and in England, than the abbey of the Vœu. Both, moreover, were of the order of regular canons. Thus the abbey of the Vœu became mother and head, possessing in perpetuity the abbey on the island and all that belonged to it.

The aforesaid archbishop of Rouen made his own chaplain abbot in that abbey; he was a canon of the same order. A certain constable of the lord King Henry, named Osbern de Hosa, who guarded the castle of Cherbourg with the district belonging to it, by command of the lord King Henry built at [Col. 0546A] that abbey of the Vœu a most beautiful residence containing suitable workshops for his own use. There, after his service under the lord king, he lived quite honourably for the rest of his life.

Eight days before his death he became [Note: [Col. 0545] Here E ends at the bottom of the third leaf of a quire; the fourth and fifth leaves, which contained the end of the work, are now lost. Yet MS 8h shows that only very little perished with those leaves, for it supplies the passages enclosed here in brackets. There can be no doubt that these are Robert’s. It also appears that the work ends with the words “Bishop Robert,” and that what follows in MS 8h for the years 1187–1210 was added by another contemporary author, apparently from Jumièges.] [a canon and, with the lord king’s permission, gave that abbey thirty-two marks of gold. He also gave the aforesaid abbey one hundred pounds of Le Mans currency for increasing its possessions, and sixty marks of silver in plate and as much again in vessels.

The aforesaid archbishop transferred Master William Hubaud, abbot of Grestain and monk of Bec, to the abbey of Saint-Martin of Pontoise, although the abbey of Grestain was three times richer than that one. But because of the kinship or close association which he had [Col. 0546B] with him, and because they were fellow-countrymen, he wished to have him near himself.

1186. Frederick 34. Philip 5. Henry 32.

Lord King Henry held his court at Christmas at Domfront. Henry of Bracqueville, prior of Touques, became abbot of Sées. At the city of Paris, in a certain monastery of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, there are thirty-two hairs of Saint Mary, the arm of Saint Andrew the apostle, and the head of Saint Denis the martyr, bishop of that city.]

## ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS

[Col. 0545]

## NOTICE ON THE BOOK ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS

*Hist. litt. de la France*, vol. IX, p. 543.)

[Col. 0545] A very celebrated work of Sigebert is his treatise *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, or, as he himself calls it, *On Illustrious Men*. The author conceived its plan on the model and in imitation of Saint Jerome and Gennadius, priest of Marseilles, who had composed similar works. He worked on it at different times, as he did on his *Chronicle*, and did not complete it until 1111. He accordingly included writers of his own time who had come to his knowledge. There are altogether as many as one hundred and seventy-one, including himself; for, following the example of Saint Jerome and Gennadius, who had done the same and whom he had proposed to imitate, he did not omit himself. His own entry is the most extensive, the most detailed, and consequently the most interesting. This had to be so, both because he had written much and because he was better informed about matters concerning himself than those concerning others. He says very little about his person, but enters into great detail concerning his writings.

However estimable this treatise—or rather catalogue of writers—may be, because it has preserved for us knowledge of several persons and of an even greater number of works whose existence would have been concealed from us without this aid, it nevertheless has defects, and of more than one kind. Not only is the author too brief in what he tells us concerning most of his writers, but he has also very often neglected even to characterize their persons and the productions of their pens. One readily sees that his purpose was to observe chronological order; but he was anything but exact in following it. His errors on this point are sometimes enormous. For example, he places (chs. 119, 120), among writers of the ninth century, Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, and Lawrence of Novara, who flourished in the first years of the sixth century. The patrician Dynamius (ch. 114), who belongs to the end of the same century or the very beginning of the next, is relegated among authors of the tenth century. Conversely, Ralph Glaber (ch. 50), who belongs only to the eleventh, is placed between Saint Gregory, bishop of Tours, and Saint Isidore of Seville, who belong to the sixth. These examples suffice to show Sigebert’s chronological inaccuracy. As for his lack of criticism, it is pardonable in an author writing in an age when that discipline was exceedingly rare.

We have three editions of his treatise *On Illustrious Men*. The first was due to the work of Suffridus Petrus, who published it in 1580 at Cologne, with Maternus Cholin (*Bib. Maj. Mon.*). The volume is octavo. The editor joined to this treatise those of Saint Jerome, Gennadius, Saint Isidore, Honorius of Autun, and Henry of Ghent on the same subject (*Bibl. S. Vinc. Cent.*). In 1639 Aubertus Miraeus produced another edition, with the same bibliographers, to whom he added Saint Ildefonsus. This edition was made at Antwerp, with Jacques Mesius, in a small folio volume. Finally, Fabricius (*ibid.*) published a final edition in which he included the preceding bibliographers and several others. This collection, forming a large folio volume, in which Sigebert’s text is accompanied by the scholia with which Miraeus had adorned it in his edition, was printed in 1718 at Hamburg by Christian Liebezeit and Theodor Christoph Felginer under the title *Ecclesiastical Library*.

[Col. 0547]

## SIGEBERT’S BOOK ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca ecclesiastica*, p. 93.)

[Col. 0547A] **CHAPTER I.** Marcellus, son of Marcus, prefect of the city of Rome, became, from being a disciple of Simon Magus, a disciple of the blessed apostle Peter. At the request of Christians who had not been present, he faithfully recorded the conflict of the apostles Peter and Paul with Simon Magus, at which he had continually been present, and permitted it to be read in Churches of God, near and far. To Saints Nereus and Achilleus, exiled for Christ on the island of Pontia, he wrote concerning the miraculous deeds of the blessed Peter and Paul and concerning the magical arts of Simon Magus. He wrote on the death of Saint Petronilla the virgin, daughter of the blessed apostle Peter. He wrote on the passion of Saint Felicula, virgin and martyr. He wrote on the passion of Saint Nicomedes, priest and martyr.

[Col. 0547B] **CHAPTER II.** John, also called Mark, from being a servant of the priest of Jupiter became a servant of the apostle Paul. He wrote the passion of the apostle Barnabas.

**CHAPTER III.** Polycrates wrote the passion of Saint Timothy the apostle [Note: [Col. 0547B] The *Passion of Saint Timothy*, under the name of Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, was published long ago by Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples. It mentions Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons; from this it may be inferred that it cannot be attributed to Polycrates, who succeeded Timothy after Onesimus. Certainly neither Eusebius in his *Ecclesiastical History* nor Jerome, ch. 45 of the *Catalogue*, where they discuss Polycrates, mentions this writing.], and many other things.

**CHAPTER IV.** Dionysius, born and educated at Athens, named Areopagite from the Athenian hill called the Areios Pagos, and converted to faith in Christ by the apostle Paul, acquired an extensive reputation by writing much. It is exceedingly remarkable that he was omitted by Jerome and Gennadius from their *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, especially since Jerome, although without naming him, mentions [Col. 0548A] his work, while Gregory in a homily on the Gospel mentions both his work and his name.

He wrote to Timothy, bishop of the Ephesians, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, that is, on the orders of angels; to the same, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*; to the same, *On Divine Names* and *On Symbolic Theology*; and to the same, *On Mystical Theology*. He wrote to Gaius, *How God Is Known or Seen through a Certain Ignorance*; to Polycarp, *How Opponents of Truth Are to Be Avoided*. He wrote a letter to Apollophanes, his fellow philosopher and contemporary, recalling that, when he himself was with him in Heliopolis, a city of Egypt, he had seen the world darkened by an eclipse of the sun on Friday, at the sixth hour of the day, when Jesus Christ hung on the cross; Dionysius himself was then thirty years old. He wrote to Theophilus concerning the order of ecclesiastical ranks and the excellence of priests. He wrote to the apostle John, exiled on the island of Patmos, foretelling that he would return to Asia. He also wrote other things to others, though brief, yet mystical and divine. The volume of his writings is called the *Hierarchy*. He was martyred under Emperor Domitian in the city of Gaul founded by Isius and named from Isius Paris. [Note: [Col. 0547B] See Honorius of Autun, book I, ch. 16.]

**CHAPTER V.** Linus, the first pope after Peter, wrote in Greek an account of the martyrdom of Peter and Paul, who suffered on one day, and sent it to the Eastern Churches. [Note: [Col. 0548B] Under the name of Pope Linus, the *Library of the Ancient Fathers* contains two little books on the *Acts* or martyrdom of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. But the narrative which now survives is wholly fabricated and contains many errors, as Baronius in his treatment of the events of the year 69, Bellarmine in the *Catalogue* and book II of *On the Roman Pontiff*, ch. 9, Possevinus in the *Sacred Apparatus*, and Claudius Espensaeus in book VI of *On Continence*, ch. 11, teach. See Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 15.]

[Col. 0549A] **CHAPTER VI.** Bishop Sedulius [Note: [Col. 0549B] Isidore in his *Catalogue*, ch. 7, calls Coelius Sedulius a priest, not a bishop. He wrote in verse four books of *Divine Wonders*, or the *Paschal Work*, which has been published, with the scholia of Antonio de Nebrija, at Basel in 1541 and among the Christian poets. The *Collections* under Sedulius’s name on all the Epistles of Saint Paul, published at Basel in 1528 and 1534—if indeed they are his—appear to have been corrupted by some Pelagian, as I have noted on Isidore. After Sedulius’s death, Asterius, Roman consul in 449, edited verses collected from Sedulius’s papers and dedicated them to Macedonius, as is clear from Asterius’s own epigram. Sirmond, in notes on Ennodius, shows from complete copies of Gennadius that Sedulius died while Theodosius the Younger, to whom he dedicated his work, and Valentinian were reigning.] wrote for the priest Macedonius books *On the Miracles of the Old and New Testaments*, which, after recasting them in metrical form, he entitled the *Paschal Song*. In dactylic verse he also rendered all the works of the Lord. He flourished in the time of Constans and Constantius, sons of Constantine the First, emperor.

**CHAPTER VII.** Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, wrote a *Life of Basil*, bishop of Caesarea. [Note: [Col. 0549C] On Amphilochius, see Jerome, ch. 133.]

**CHAPTER VIII.** Ulfilas, bishop of the Goths, invented Gothic letters; and although he was an Arian, he nevertheless performed a useful work, because by means of these letters he translated the divine Scriptures into the Gothic language. He lived in the time of Emperor Valens. [Note: [Col. 0549C] On him, Trithemius.]

[Col. 0549B] **CHAPTER IX.** Theodoret, bishop of the city called Cyrrhus from Cyrus, its founder and king of the Persians [Note: [Col. 0549C] Some call the city of Euphratesian Syria over which Theodoret presided Cyrrhus, as do Pliny, Ptolemy, and Stephanus; others call it Cyrus, as is frequently read in Theodoret himself, Procopius’s *Buildings*, and Hierocles’s *Synecdemus*. See Gennadius, ch. 89.], wrote *On the True Incarnation of the Lord* against Eutyches, who denied true flesh to Christ Jesus. He also wrote an *Ecclesiastical History*, continuing from the end of the *Ecclesiastical History* written by Eusebius of Caesarea and, after him, by the priest Rufinus.

[Col. 0550A] **CHAPTER X.** Socrates [Note: [Col. 0549C] Socrates, pupil in grammar of Ammonius and Helladius and an advocate at Constantinople, wrote seven books of *Ecclesiastical History*, embracing one hundred and forty years, from Constantine [Col. 0549D] the Great to the age of Theodosius the Younger. It has been published in Latin with Eusebius of Caesarea—whose *Ecclesiastical History* it immediately follows—in the translation of John Christophorson. Photius, *Library*, codex 26, judges that he has neither a particularly brilliant style nor accuracy in doctrine. Nicephorus certainly reported that he was a Novatian and impure in intention. Bellarmine and others made the same observation. Franciscus Torrensis, or Turrianus, accuses him of lying in more than one place.] wrote a history from the time of Constantine the First, emperor, to the reign of Theodosius the Younger.

**CHAPTER XI.** Sozomen, following the course of the same period, wrote a history. [Note: [Col. 0549D] Hermias Sozomenus Salaminius, long engaged in legal business at Constantinople, wrote nine books of *Ecclesiastical History*, extending from the consulship of Crispus and his father Constantine to the reign of Theodosius the Younger, to whom he dedicated this history. In his letter to Theodosius he himself explains the subject of each book. He differs from Socrates in certain matters and has a superior style, as Photius judges in codex 30. But the Apostolic See, as Gregory the Great says in book VI, epistle 95, refuses to receive Sozomen’s history, because it contains many falsehoods; it praises Theodore of Mopsuestia too highly and asserts that, up to the day of his death, he was a great doctor of the Church. What is said here of Theodore of Mopsuestia is not now found in Sozomen but in Theodoret. Yet it is probable that Sozomen wrote this in the books which have perished. For he states in the preface that he brought his history down to the seventeenth consulship of Theodosius the Younger, that is, to the year of Christ 439, so that a history of nearly twenty years is missing. Baronius also observed this in his notes on the *Martyrology* for 23 December. Bellarmine observes in the *Catalogue* that Sozomen, like Socrates, favoured Novatian errors. John Christophorson translated both from Greek and published them in Latin with Eusebius at Cologne and Louvain. Sozomen has also been published separately in Greek at Paris by Robert Estienne.]

**CHAPTER XII.** Epiphanius, scholasticus [Note: [Col. 0550C] At Cassiodorus’s request, as Cassiodorus himself reports in ch. 17 of *On Divine Readings*, Epiphanius scholasticus translated from Greek into Latin the ecclesiastical histories of Theodoret, Socrates, and Sozomen. From Epiphanius’s translation Cassiodorus compiled the *Tripartite History*.], combining the three histories of Theodoret, Socrates, and Sozomen into one history, added the *Tripartite History* to the ecclesiastical library.

**CHAPTER XIII.** Macer wrote in metrical style a book *On the Powers of Herbs*.

**CHAPTER XIV.** Paulinus, bishop of Nola, wrote, addressed to Bishop Augustine, a *Life of Ambrose*, bishop of Milan. He also wrote in verse a *Life of Felix of Nola*. [Note: [Col. 0550C] Gennadius, ch. 48.]

[Col. 0550B] **CHAPTER XV.** Bishop Evodius wrote a book *On Miracles Displayed in Africa through the Newly Discovered Relics of Stephen the Protomartyr*, which Orosius, Augustine’s disciple, brought to Africa. [Note: [Col. 0550C] Evodius, bishop of Uzalis in Africa, to whom letters of Saint Augustine survive, was one of the five African bishops whose letter to Pope Innocent I we possess. He committed to writing the miracles performed at the relics of Saint Stephen, which Orosius first brought from Palestine to the West. See Augustine, *City of God*, book XXII, ch. 8.]

**CHAPTER XVI.** Possidius, bishop of Calama, wrote a *Life of Augustine*, bishop of Hippo. [Note: [Col. 0550D] See Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 8.]

**CHAPTER XVII.** Paschasius [Note: [Col. 0550D] This is that Paschasius to whom the priest Eugippius sent the *Life of Saint Severinus, Apostle of the Norici*, written by himself, and submitted it to his judgment. Name, time, place, and sacred office show this, as Baronius relates under the year 496. The same Paschasius replied to him; Baronius prints that letter in the same place. Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, ch. 40, reports that this Paschasius died “in the time of Symmachus, bishop of the Apostolic See,” and that his very sound and eloquent books on the Holy Spirit survive. Symmachus held office from the year [Col. 0551B] 499 to 514. A different Paschasius was the deacon Paschasius of Dumium in Gallaecia, who dedicated his book *On the Lives of the Fathers*—the seventh in Plantin’s edition of 162—to Martin, abbot of Dumium, mentioned by Isidore in ch. 22. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book V, ch. 37, places the death of this Martin in the fifth year of King Childebert the Younger, to which Baronius assigns the year of Christ 583.] deacon of the holy [Col. 0551A] Roman Church, composed books on the Holy Spirit in an eloquent and faithful style. Because he stubbornly supported Laurentius against Pope Symmachus in the irregular appointment of Laurentius, Germanus, bishop of Capua, saw his soul after his death placed in the baths in purgatorial fire.

**CHAPTER XVIII.** Idatius, bishop of the Spanish city of Lémica, composed a chronicle beginning with the first consulship of the Emperor Theodosius.

**CHAPTER XIX.** Martin, bishop of Galicia, wrote a book *On the Four Virtues* for Theudemir [otherwise Miro], king of Galicia, and entitled the little book *A Rule of Honourable Life*. [Note: [Col. 0551C] Isidore in ch. 22 of the *Catalogue*, Sigebert in this chapter and below in ch. 118, mention this Martin of Dumium, or Galicia. He was first abbot and bishop of Dumium—he also built the monastery of Dumium in Gallaecia—and afterwards bishop of Braga in Lusitania.]

**CHAPTER XX.** Victor [Note: [Col. 0551C] Saint Victor, bishop of Capua in Italy, wrote *On the Paschal Cycle* around the year of Christ 540, during Justinian’s reign, as Bede, *On the Six Ages*, and *On the Reckoning of Time*, ch. 48; Ado of Vienne in the *Chronicle*; and likewise Marianus Scotus report. Victor’s cycle was received and approved at the Fourth Synod of Orléans, held in 541. Victor also wrote the preface to the *Harmony*, or concordance, of Tatian of Alexandria, who made one Gospel out of the four Gospels. [Col. 0551D] But Baronius, in his treatment of the events of 174, and Bellarmine following him, rightly observe that Victor of Capua was mistaken in the name. That Harmony is not by Tatian but by Ammonius of Alexandria, mentioned by Jerome in ch. 55 of the *Catalogue*.], bishop of Capua, elegantly [Col. 0551B] compiled a Gospel made out of the four Gospels, called the *Diapente*. He found it without an author’s name; and, seeing that it was confused because it lacked the numbered canons, he clarified it by adding the numbers of the canons through which Eusebius of Caesarea distinguished the four Gospels, thereby displaying without the confusion of error their common passages while showing and restoring to each its own distinctive material. He also wrote a book *On Easter*, refuting the error of Victorius, who, when ordered by Pope Hilary to write Paschal cycles, taught that Easter ought to be celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 455, whereas in that year it ought more correctly to have been celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of May.

## Chapter XXI

Eustathius [Note: [Col. 0551D] Eustathius, a most eloquent man, is praised in this place by Cassiodorus, Bede, and Sigebert. He translated into Latin from Greek the nine sermons of St Basil the Great on the beginning of Genesis, and dedicated them to his sister Syncletica, a deaconess. They survive with the works of St Basil, printed at Antwerp, Paris, and elsewhere in 1616. Cassiodorus says of him in chapter 1 of *On Divine Readings*: “Basil elucidated the beginnings of Genesis in the Attic tongue; Eustathius, a most eloquent man, translated him into Latin in such a manner that he seems to have matched the genius of that most learned man by the strength of his own eloquence. He extended to the creation of man in nine books.” Junilius, bishop of Africa—or rather Bede—in the preface to his Commentary on Genesis, says likewise: “Many have said much concerning the beginning of the book of [Col. 0552B] Genesis, but especially Basil of Caesarea, whom the interpreter Eustathius made Latin from Greek.” Sedulius mentions the sister-deaconess Syncletica, to whom Eustathius wrote, in the preface to his Paschal work, in these words: “Who would not wish and strive to win the judgment of the outstanding Syncletica, sacred virgin and servant of Christ, [Col. 0552C] who advanced the nobility of proud blood to glory by such humility that she deserves to become an athlete in the senate of the heavenly country? She drank so deeply, thirsting, from the Scriptures of ecclesiastical doctrine that, if the permission of her sex had not been lacking, she could have taught how manly a mind may dwell in the limbs of a female body.”] translated Basil of Caesarea’s *Hexaemeron* from Greek into Latin.

## Chapter XXII

Avitus [Note: [Col. 0552C] Alcimus Ecdicius Avitus, bishop of Vienne in Gaul, had a brother, Apollinaris, bishop of Valence, to whom he dedicated his poems. His dedicatory letter, drawn from a manuscript of Saint-Victor at Paris, is quoted by Sirmond in his notes on Ennodius. From that letter we learn that Avitus also published homilies. Indeed, only one remains, on the Rogations instituted by Mamertus, his predecessor. But fragments of several others are preserved among the remains of a very ancient book kept at Paris by Jacques-Auguste de Thou. One concerns the conversion of the lord Sigefric, delivered at Lyons on the day after his sister was received from the Arian heresy; another was preached in the basilica of the saints of Agaunum, [Col. 0552D] at the renewal of its monastery; a third at the restoration of the baptistery in the city of Vienne; a fourth in the basilica of St Peter founded by Sanctus, bishop of Tarentaise; a fifth at the dedication of a basilica at Geneva which enemies had burned; and others whose very titles awaken an immense longing for them, as do the rest of Avitus’s works listed by Isidore and Ado of Vienne. See Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 23.] bishop of Vienne, wrote one book of Homilies; six books, composed in verse, *On the Beginning of the World and Various Other Conditions*; and nine books of Letters. He flourished in the time of the emperor Zeno, under Gundobad, king of the Burgundians.

## Chapter XXIII

The priest Godelbertus, imitating this pursuit, ran elegantly in heroic verse through the histories and allegories of Holy Scripture, from the beginning of the world to the Virgin’s childbirth [Note: [Col. 0552D] Trithemius on him.].

## Chapter XXIV

Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, wrote five cycles of nineteen-year cycles, making ninety-five years, in which the first and last limit of Easter is found; yet even in this the whole variation of Easter is not confined [Note: [Col. 0552D] See Gennadius, ch. 57.].

## Chapter XXV

Paschasinus [otherwise Paschasius] [Note: [Col. 0552D] Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum in Sicily, recently restored from captivity among the Vandals, wrote in the year 443 to Pope Leo I a Paschal letter, published in a corrected text by Aegidius Bucherius, ch. 1 of his Commentary on Victorius of Aquitaine, at the Moretus press, 1633. He also wrote a Letter on the Condemnation of Dioscorus, published in vol. II of Binius’s *Councils* at Cologne.], [Col. 0553A] a deacon, wrote to Pope Leo against the error of certain persons who, in the year of the Lord 455, thinking it an ordinary year when it was embolismic, erred in celebrating Easter.

## Chapter XXVI

Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, likewise wrote to Pope Leo, who was uncertain about celebrating Easter in that year, which, although embolismic, was thought by some to be ordinary.

## Chapter XXVII

Dionysius, a Roman abbot [Note: [Col. 0553D] Dionysius Exiguus, a Roman abbot, in the consulship of Probus—that is, in the year of Christ 525—constructed his Paschal cycle. Omitting the profane calculation of years, he was the first to begin numbering from the Incarnation of Christ. This era or epoch, first devised by Dionysius, was gradually adopted throughout the Christian world, especially about the year 730. Previously years had been designated solely by the names of consuls, emperors, or kings of France. Dionysius was also the first to collect the sacred canons from decrees of councils into one body; Martin of Braga, Cresconius, Burchard, and others later imitated him. Dionysius’s work was first printed at Mainz in 1525 and later at Paris in 1609, under the title *Ancient Code of Canons of the Roman Church*, with Dionysius’s dedicatory letter to Stephen, bishop of Salona. When Charlemagne was at Rome, a copy of this Dionysian code was presented to him by Pope Adrian in the year 787, [Col. 0554D] as Sirmond recounts at length in vol. II of the *Councils of Gaul*. The same code is mentioned by Pope Nicholas in ch. *Si Romanorum*, distinction 19. Read Cassiodorus, *Institutions*, ch. 23.], surnamed Exiguus, distinguished by his twofold learning in Greek and Latin, translated from Greek into Latin the writings of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, to Pope Leo concerning the celebration of Easter in the year of the Lord 355. He also translated from Greek into Latin Gregory of Nyssa’s book *On the Creation of Man*, and the Life of Abbot Pachomius. He himself also wrote [Col. 0553B], after Cyril, a cycle of five cycles, beginning with the year 532 from the birth of Jesus Christ, which is the final year of the great cycle of 532 years, once completed from Christ’s birth.

Here it should be noted that, if the birth of Christ had been correctly placed by the calculators, the thirty-third or thirty-fourth year of the first great cycle ought to have agreed, in the reckoning of computation, with the truth of the Gospel and the authority of the Fathers, which says that Christ suffered in the thirty-second or thirty-third year of his age, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [25 March], on the sixth weekday, and that he rose again on the sixth day before the Kalends of April [27 March], on the first weekday. Since this was not so placed in the first great cycle, because Dionysius did not attend to the tenor of the years of the first great cycle, he too assigned the years of Christ in his own cycle, which, as I said, [Col. 0553C] he began with the repetition of the second great cycle; and he branded his forehead with the cautery of another’s error and falsehood, while he is blamed because the thirty-third or thirty-fourth year of his work does not agree with Gospel truth in the reckoning of computation. Hence it is evident that Christ’s birth was placed by the calculators twenty-one or twenty-two years later than it ought to have been.

## Chapter XXVIII

Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe [Note: [Col. 0554D] St Fulgentius went to Rome in the year in which Theoderic, king of the Goths, is recorded by Cassiodorus to have entered the same city, namely the year of Christ 500. In 504 he became bishop of Ruspe; he was banished to Sardinia with others by King Thrasamund; and finally, after Thrasamund’s death, peace having been restored to the African churches in 522 by Hilderic, son of Huneric, he returned to Africa. Molanus attributes the books of *Mythologies* to Fulgentius the Grammarian, Placiades. See Isidore, ch. 14. Ferrandus the deacon, praised in the next chapter, was this Fulgentius’s disciple.], distinguished in Greek and Latin and by his twofold learning, wrote much. He flourished in the homiletic manner of speech. He wrote books to Euthymius *On the Remission of Sins*. In one book he answered questions proposed to him by the deacon Ferrandus. He wrote books which [Col. 0554A] he entitled by letters: namely, the book *On Adam, or A*; *On Abel, or B*; *On Cain, or C*; and the rest according to the sequence of the letters.

If this is the same Fulgentius who wrote three books of *Mythologies* to Catus, priest of Carthage, then every reader may indeed be astonished at the sharpness of his intellect, who transferred the whole series of fables, expounded according to philosophy, either to the order of things or to the moral life of humankind. He wrote to the same Catus a book *On Obscure Expressions*. He also wrote three books *On Predestination* to Monimus; one book against the eleven objections of King Thrasamund; one book *On the Mystery of the Mediator*; one book *On the Immeasurability of the Son of God*; one book *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s [Col. 0554B] Passion*; and one book of letters to his friends. Lest I seem to mingle human matters with divine, I shall not mention among sacred books this man’s remarkable work, in which, referring the whole work of Virgil to physical theory, he sought the metal of gold in a clayey mass, as it were, and smelted it after finding it.

## Chapter XXIX

The deacon Ferrandus, mentioned above, wrote to Count Reginus a book *On the Seven Rules of Innocence*, and some other works.

## Chapter XXX

Gennadius, bishop [Note: [Col. 0554D] He was not a bishop.], after Jerome composed a *Book of Illustrious Men*, which he compiled from the fourteenth year of the reign of Theodosius the Elder to the time of the emperor Zeno, over about a hundred years. He also translated from Greek into Latin, retaining the same simplicity, the books of the monk Evagrius, written in simple language for the benefit of monks. [Col. 0554C] He also corrected certain books of the same author which translators had corrupted in rendering them faultily into Latin, and restored them to the author’s truth.

## Chapter XXXI

Benedict of Cassino, father of monks, born at Nursia in the Italian province, despising literary studies, sought the eremitic life; and, having advanced to the highest summit of monastic progress, wrote, in accordance with the life he lived, a Rule for monks, lucid in expression and especially excellent in discernment. Simplicius, his disciple, made public his master’s work, which had been kept hidden [Note: [Col. 0554D] See Honorius, book XXX.].

## Chapter XXXII

Faustus, disciple of St Benedict, sent by [Col. 0555A] Benedict himself to Gaul together with Maurus, Benedict’s monk, wrote the Life of that monk Maurus [Note: [Col. 0555C] It is found in Surius, 15 January.].

## Chapter XXXIII

Marcus the poet, an intimate of Benedict of Cassino, made an abridged heroic-verse selection from the Life of Benedict written by Gregory, and added a few things [Note: [Col. 0555C] This poem of Marcus was printed at Rome in 1590 with the third book of poems by Prosper Martinengo.].

## Chapter XXXIV

Orentius wrote a *Commonitory* for the faithful in heroic verse, to delight the reader by sweet brevity [Note: [Col. 0555C] See Gennadius, ch. 9.].

## Chapter XXXV

Jordanes [Note: [Col. 0555C] Jornandes, or Jordanes, formerly a notary of the Goths and bishop of Ravenna in 552, made from Cassiodorus’s twelve books an epitome of Gothic history. This book appeared at Paris in a more correct text from the manuscript of Pierre Pithou, together with the works of Cassiodorus. He also wrote *On the Deeds of the Romans* and of other peoples.], bishop of the Goths, wrote a History: in its first book recounting the deeds of the Romans, and in the second the origin and deeds of the Goths, down to the end of their kingdom.

## Chapter XXXVI

John, under the person of himself and his friend Basil, wrote a dialogue on the honour and burden of the priesthood, and on how great is the dignity, power, and weight [Col. 0555B] of priests.

## Chapter XXXVII

Boethius, a man of consular rank, is to be compared with—or preferred to—both secular and ecclesiastical philosophers, because he makes it uncertain whether he was more illustrious among secular or ecclesiastical writers. Let secular writers praise him because he translated and expounded from Greek the *Isagoge*, *On Interpretation* (*Perihermeneias*), and the *Categories*; because he expounded Cicero’s *Topics*; because he wrote the *Ante-Predicaments*, books *On Topical Differences*, *On the Kinship of Dialectic and Rhetoric*, *On the Distinction of Rhetorical Commonplaces*, *On the Common Predication of Power and Possibility*, books *On Categorical and Hypothetical Syllogisms*, and many other works; and because he wrote arithmetic and music for Latin readers. We ecclesiastics praise [Col. 0555C] him because he wrote the book *On the Holy Trinity*; because, exiled by Theoderic, king of the Goths and Italians, for wishing to defend the liberty of the Roman [Col. 0556A] city, he wrote the book *On the Consolation of Philosophy*. He was killed by that same King Theoderic [Note: [Col. 0555C] See Honorius of Autun, III.22.].

## Chapter XXXVIII

Arator [Note: [Col. 0555C] Arator was a Ligurian by birth, educated in Liguria itself, and practised as an advocate. He also creditably performed an embassy for the Dalmatians to Theoderic, king of the Goths; Athalaric testifies to this in Cassiodorus, *Variae*, book VIII, letter 12, in which he grants Arator the rank of count of the domestics. An ancient note prefixed to Arator’s books in most copies tells us that he was also adorned with the rank of count of the private estates before, leaving the court, he devoted himself to the Church. In the manuscript at Reims belonging to the monks of St Remigius, it begins thus: “With the help of blessed Lord Peter, this codex was presented by the illustrious Arator—formerly count of the domestics, formerly count of the private estates, a religious man, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church and apostolic see—to the holy and apostolic man, Pope Vigilius; received by him on the eighth day before the Ides of April,” and what follows.

Parthenius Ennodius had formerly been Arator’s master in composing sacred poetry, that is, in turning the Muse toward divine subjects. Therefore, after rendering the Acts of the Apostles in hexameter verse and offering his work, as stated, to Pope Vigilius, he sent it to Gaul to Parthenius, so that it might there be published through his agency. [Col. 0556C] On this matter the same manuscript at Reims contains Arator’s excellent epistle to Parthenius in elegiac verse, which Sirmond published at the end of his notes on Ennodius as previously unprinted. The two books of verse in which he treated the Acts of the Apostles are extant in the *Library of the Fathers* and elsewhere.] subdeacon of the Roman Church, published the Acts of the Apostles in heroic verse and presented them to Pope Vigilius of Rome.

## Chapter XXXIX

Abbot Eugippius [Note: [Col. 0556C] Rosweyde judges in the prolegomena to the *Lives of the Fathers* that two Eugippii, both abbots and flourishing in the glory of learning, lived in one and the same century. The earlier Eugippius, abbot of Lucullanum in Italy, praised by Isidore in ch. 13, wrote the Life of St Severinus the monk and flourished after the consulship of Importunus or Opportunus—that is, after the year of Christ 509. For, in the letter prefixed to his Life of St Severinus, [Col. 0556D] he says that he was writing two years after the consulship of Importunus, that is, in 511. The other Eugippius, the African abbot praised by Sigebert in this chapter, flourished in the time of Pope Pelagius II and Tiberius Caesar at Constantinople, that is, around the year 580; he is praised by Cassiodorus, *On Divine Readings*, ch. 23. “This man, for the sacred virgin Proba, as Cassiodorus calls her, selected questions and opinions from the works of St Augustine on various subjects and collected them into a single body, arranged in 338 chapters.” This work, divided into two volumes of the *Treasures of St Augustine*, as its title states, was printed at Basel in 1542 and Venice in 1543; but Bellarmine rightly warns in his Catalogue that one must beware the snares of heretics who brought this work to light. John Molanus, doctor of theology at Louvain, however, makes the two into one Eugippius.] at the urging of Renducis, bishop of Naples, selected from the books of Augustine, bishop of Hippo, and gave a codex of great usefulness to the virgin Proba; through the hands of the same Bishop Renducis he presented it to the Church of Naples. He lived in the time of Pelagius II and the emperor Tiberius Constantine.

## Chapter XL

Cassiodorus, consul and senator, later monk and abbot, made a commentary on the Psalms and divided the whole body of the work into three parts, namely into groups of [Col. 0556B] fifty Psalms. He wrote two books of *Institutions*, on how divine and human readings should be understood; and he compiled a book *On Etymologies* and another book by a priest on figures of speech. He wrote a book of titles, which he wished to be called a *Memorial* collected from Holy Scripture, so that those who dislike reading lengthy works might run through it briefly. He made concise expositions of the Apostolic Epistles, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Apocalypse. He also arranged a Catalogue of Roman Consuls. He translated Epiphanius Scholasticus from Greek into Latin; Epiphanius had combined the three histories of Theodoret, Socrates, and Sozomen into one *Tripartite History*. Finally, in the ninety-third year of his life, at his brethren’s request, he wrote *On [Col. 0556C] Orthography*, collecting its rules from twelve grammatical authorities; and one book *On the Soul* [Note: [Col. 0556D] See Honorius IV.21.].

## Chapter XLI

Gregory, a Roman by birth, formerly urban praetor, then monk and abbot, seventh deacon of the Roman Church, apocrisiarius, and pope of the Roman Church, wrote much. At the request of Leander, bishop of Seville, he expounded the book of Job in three ways—historically, allegorically, and morally—and, dividing the books into six books, completed this remarkable work in thirty-five books. He expounded in homiletic discourse the first and last parts of the prophet Ezekiel, which were more obscure. He wrote forty-two homilies on the Gospel to Bishop Marianus. At the beginning of his papacy he wrote to John, bishop of Ravenna, the book of the *Pastoral Rule*. He sent to Theudelinda, queen of the Lombards, as a gift the book of *Dialogues*, which he had with his deacon Peter concerning the miracles of saints of his time. He left to posterity as many books of Letters as the years [Col. 0557B] he lived in the papacy, namely thirteen and a half.

He also wrote other works which the Romans burned after his death; indeed, they would have burned all his works had not Peter, his deacon, intervened and confirmed on oath that he had seen the Holy Spirit, like a dove, seated above the head of Gregory as he composed, inserting its beak into his mouth. Peter did this on the condition that, if he died immediately after taking the oath, the Romans would desist from burning Gregory’s books; but if he did not die, he himself would also lend his hand to the burners of the books. Thus Peter expired amid the words of his oath, and the madness of the Romans ceased. This writing made Gregory as illustrious as did his compiling of the Antiphonary in the regular modulation of music and his establishment of schools [Col. 0557C] of singers in the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0557D] See Isidore, ch. 27, and Ildefonsus, ch. 1.].

## Chapter XLII

Anastasius, bishop of Antioch, translated Gregory’s book *Pastoral Rule* into Greek and furnished the eastern churches with a venerable work [Note: [Col. 0557D] St Anastasius the Sinaite, bishop of Antioch and martyr, died in the year 598. He was called the Sinaite because he had lived as a monk on Mount Sinai before being appointed over the Church of Antioch. He wrote various works, among which the *Library of the Ancient Fathers* contains two books of *Anagogical Contemplations on the Hexaemeron*, five books *On the Doctrines of the Faith*, translated by Godfrey Tilmann, several Orations, and Answers to Various Questions. His *Guide of the Way against the Acephali*, translated by Gretser, was printed at Ingolstadt in 1606. He also wrote various Sermons, some of which Achilles Statius rendered into Latin. The same Anastasius translated into Greek the *Pastoral* of Pope St Gregory. Baronius testifies in his notes on the Martyrology for 21 April that this translation is preserved in the library of the aforesaid Achilles Statius, among the priests of the Roman Oratory. There you will also find more concerning this Anastasius of ours and another bishop of Antioch and martyr bearing the same name; among other matters, Baronius notes that Nicephorus erred in book XVIII, ch. 24, by ascribing the name “Sinaite” and the writings mentioned above to the later Anastasius. In the Register of Pope Gregory I, moreover, several letters addressed to this Sinaite of ours survive. Further material may be found in Canisius, vol. III of *Ancient Readings*.].

## Chapter XLIII

Paterius [Note: [Col. 0558D] That Paterius served under Pope Celestine I on an embassy to the Irish is clear from the *Miscellanies* of Gerard Vossius, vol. V of the *Library of the Fathers*. See Honorius IV.5.], notary and second secretary of the Roman Church, collecting all the testimonies of Holy Scripture by which Gregory elucidated the obscurities of his exposition, published three books: two on the testimonies of the Old Testament and one on the testimonies of the New Testament; and he entitled the codex itself the *Book of Testimonies*.

## Chapter XLIV

[Col. 0558A] Claudius, abbot of the city of Classe, dictated many things from his own understanding concerning Proverbs, the Song of Songs, the Heptateuch, the prophets, and the books of Kings—things which he had heard Gregory expound, but which Gregory, because of illness and occupations, had not written down—lest they perish, so that at a suitable time they might be dictated in a more corrected form. When Gregory learned that these had been altered very harmfully, he diligently collected them again and corrected them appropriately.

## Chapter XLV

Fortunatus [Note: [Col. 0558D] Fifteen books of Poems and Letters by Venantius Honorius Clementianus Fortunatus, an Italian priest and bishop of Poitiers who lived under King Childebert, with sacred, historical, and geographical notes by Christopher Brouwer, priest of the Society of Jesus, were published at Mainz in 1603 and 1616.], an Italian by birth and educated in the liberal arts, was healed of eye pain through the power of Martin, bishop of Tours. For this reason he came to Tours; proceeding to Poitiers, he was first ordained priest there and then consecrated bishop. He wrote his *Hodoeporicon* in verse; [Col. 0558B] he wrote four books in verse *On the Life of St Martin*, many other works, and especially hymns for particular feast-days. He composed verses for individual friends in a sweet and eloquent style.

## Chapter XLVI

Justinian the Great, illustrious in the dignity of imperial majesty, seems to have been more illustrious than other emperors because he also gained a place among ecclesiastical writers. For he corrected with remarkable brevity the laws of the Romans, whose prolixity was excessive and whose discordance useless. He compressed into twelve books all the constitutions of the emperors, which had certainly been contained in many volumes, and caused that volume to be called the *Code of Justinian*. Again, he reduced within fifty books the laws of the individual magistrates or judges, which had extended to almost [Col. 0558C] two thousand books, and called the same code by the name *Digest* or *Pandects*. He also newly set forth four books of *Institutes*, in which the text of all the laws is briefly comprehended. He likewise gathered into one volume the new laws which he himself had established [Note: [Col. 0558D] See Isidore, ch. 18.].

## Chapter XLVII

Bishop Sixtus wrote a book *On the Perfect Life of Man*.

## Chapter XLVIII

Bishop Osius wrote a book *On the Observance of the Lord’s Discipline* [Note: [Col. 0558D] Trithemius on him.].

## Chapter XLIX

Gregory, bishop of Tours, [Col. 0559A] a man of great nobility and simplicity, wrote much in a simple style. He wrote two books *On the Life or Commemoration of Certain Confessors*. He wrote one book *On the Miracles of the Saints*; one book *On the Miracles of Julian, Martyr of Brioude* [otherwise Bruatensis]; four books *On the Miracles of St Martin Manifested in His Own Time*. He first abridged the History of the Franks in a small short book, and later arranged it more fully in nine [ten] books. He also wrote a Chronicle of ecclesiastical history [Note: [Col. 0559D] See Honorius III.33.].

## Chapter L

Rodolphus wrote a History of the Franks from his own time.

## Chapter LI

Isidore, bishop of Cordoba, wrote to Orosius four books on the books of Kings [Note: [Col. 0559D] Isidore, ch. 9.].

## Chapter LII

Proba, wife of Adelphus, expressed most fully in a cento from Virgil [Col. 0559B] the creation of the world and the Gospels: the subject matter being composed according to Virgilian verses, and the verses arranged according to the subject matter [Note: [Col. 0559D] Isidore, ch. 5.].

## Chapter LIII

Pomponius, from the same poet, among the other recreations of his style, composed a *Tityrus* in honour of Christ, and likewise an *Aeneid*.

## Chapter LIV

Julianus Pomerius wrote *On the Resurrection of the Dead* [Note: [Col. 0559D] Gennadius, ch. 98.].

## Chapter LV

The younger Isidore, bishop of Seville, wrote much. He wrote to Bishop Braulio twenty books of *Etymologies*. He wrote a book of *Prologues*; *On the Books of the Old and New Testament Which the Catholic Church Receives into the Canon*; *On Ecclesiastical Offices* to Fulgentius; *On the Birth, Life, and Death of the Holy [Col. 0559C] Fathers Praised in the Scriptures*; *On the Meanings of Names* to Orosius; and *On the Nature of Things* to Sisebut. He wrote a book *On Differences of Words*, a book *On the Properties of Things*, a book of sermons, and a book *On Ecclesiastical Doctrines*. He wrote the *Synonyms*, in which two persons are introduced: one of a lamenting human being, the other of Reason offering admonition. He also wrote the *Lament of the Penitent*, arranged alphabetically and with a prayer appended. He wrote one book *On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices* and one *On the Mysteries of the Saviour*. He went through the whole Old Testament, expounding it simply. [Col. 0560A] He also wrote other works suited to secular literature, which it does not concern us to mention.

## Chapter LVI

Julian, bishop of Toledo in Spain, wrote to Idalius, bishop of Barcelona, a book which he entitled *Prognosticon*, that is, *Foreknowledge of the Future Age*.

## Chapter LVII

Leontius, bishop of Neapolis on the island of Cyprus, wrote the Life of John, bishop of Alexandria, who was surnamed the Almsgiver because of his outstanding mercy toward the poor [Note: [Col. 0559D] Read Baronius’s Notes on the Martyrology for 23 January.].

## Chapter LVIII

Audoenus [Note: [Col. 0559D] St Audoenus died in the sixth year of Theoderic, king of the Franks—that is, in 672 or 673, not the sixteenth year, as is corruptly read in Surius under 24 August. He wrote in three books the Life of St Eligius, bishop and his contemporary, which Surius published mutilated. Would that someone might bring forth the complete text from manuscripts! He also wrote a Life of St Remigius, which exists in manuscript among the Swiss in the library of St Gall.], also called Dado, bishop of Rouen, wrote to Robert, bishop of Paris, the Life of Eligius, bishop of Noyon, in two books, explaining the miracles performed through him both during his life and after his death; in a third book [Col. 0560B] he recapitulated his whole life rhetorically and in clauses.

## Chapter LIX

Leo, the second pope of that name, adequately learned in Greek and Latin, translated from Greek into Latin the Sixth Synod, which was held at Constantinople in the time of Pope Agatho, his predecessor. In it were condemned those who proclaimed only one will and operation in the Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0559D] It is extant in the volumes of the Councils.].

## Chapter LX

Columbanus, abbot of Luxeuil [Note: [Col. 0559D] St Columbanus, first abbot in Ireland, afterward at Luxeuil in Burgundy, and finally at Bobbio in Italy, wrote among other works a Rule and penitential Canons. The Rule is extant in the *Florilegium of the Saints of Ireland*; its preface, published by Stengel in the *Corona Lucida*, should be prefixed to it. Moreover, the Rule of St Columbanus was stoutly defended against the slanders of Agrestinus by St Eustasius, abbot of Luxeuil, and approved at the Council of Mâcon in 627, as Jonas the monk teaches in the Life of St Eustasius and Sirmond in vol. I of the *Councils of Gaul*. The Irish Franciscan brethren living at Louvain are preparing for the press all the works of St Columbanus that can be found, as well as those of other Irish writers.], born in Ireland, the island of the Scots, and journeying into Gaul for Christ, was endowed with such a treasure of wisdom that, while still a young man, he wrote a Psalter in polished language and published many other works, [Col. 0560C] some worthy for singing and others useful for teaching.

## Chapter LXI

Jonas [Note: [Col. 0560D] Jonas, an Irishman or Scot, first monk and afterward abbot of Luxeuil in Burgundy, wrote the Lives of Saints Columbanus, Attala, Bertulf, and Eustasius, published by Surius. He succeeded Attala in the governance of the monastery of Luxeuil. Another Jonas, distinct from this one, was a monk of Fontenelle; he wrote the Life of St Wulfram, bishop of Sens, dedicated it to Bainus, bishop of Thérouanne, and it was published by Surius under 20 March.] wrote the Life of Abbot Columbanus and the Lives of Attala and Eustasius, who were disciples and successors of Columbanus.

## Chapter LXII

Abbot Benedict [Note: [Col. 0560D] Benedict, an abbot of the Benedictine order, flourished in the time of Louis the Pious and wrote the *Concord of Rules*, which Hugo Menard published at Paris in 1638, with notes by himself.] wrote for monks a book which he called the *Concord of Rules*, comparing the Rules of many Fathers with the Rule of St Benedict of Cassino, so that no Rule of the Fathers might differ from Benedict’s Rule—indeed, so that Benedict’s Rule might agree with the rules of all the Fathers.

## Chapter LXIII

Theodore, archbishop of the Scots, sent to Scotland by Pope Vitalian, wrote a Penitential Book, distinguishing the manner and [Col. 0561A] duration of penitence according to the manner of sinning.

## Chapter LXIV

Adamnan [Note: [Col. 0561D] Adamnan, otherwise Adamnanus or Adomnanus, an Irishman or Scot and abbot of the monastery of Hy, founded by St Columbanus, compiled his book *On the Places of the Holy Land* from the written account of Arculf, a Gallic bishop returned from Syria, as Bede reports in *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, ch. 16. His three books *On the Life of St Columbanus the Elder, or Columba the priest*—who flourished in 560—are found in Canisius, vol. I of *Ancient Reading*.], priest and abbot of the Scots, distinguished by literary learning, wrote a book *On the Holy Places of the Birth, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension of Jesus Christ*, and on the monuments of the holy Fathers.

## Chapter LXV

John Scotus, sufficiently capable in expounding divine and human writings, made commentaries on Matthew. He wrote a book *On Human Offices* and other works possessed by others.

## Chapter LXVI

Aldhelm, abbot of the Scots, at the command of a synod of his people, wrote a book against the error of the Britons, who either celebrated Easter at an improper time or did many other things contrary to peace and ecclesiastical custom; through it he brought many back to the [Col. 0561B] harmony of the Catholic Church.
