He also wrote a book *On Virginity*, which, following Sedulius’s example, he composed in a double work, that is, in prose and verse [Note: [Col. 0562D] Bellarmine, *Catalogue*, on him.].

## Chapter LXVII

Ceolfrith, abbot of the Scots, wrote a useful letter to the king of the Picts, who consulted him concerning the lawful observance of Easter and the tonsure of clerics. By it he satisfied the king, and the king restored his people to the concord of the Church.

### Chapter LXVIII

Bede, a monk by nation an Englishman, reveals in his own words who and whence he was, and what and how much he wrote. “When I was,” he says, “seven years old, I was entrusted by the care of my relatives to the most reverend Abbot Benedict for education, and afterwards to Ceolfrith; and, spending thereafter the whole time of my life in residence in the same monastery [Col. 0561C], I devoted all my effort to the study of Scripture. Amid the observance of regular discipline, I made it my delight always either to learn, to teach, or to write. In the nineteenth year of my life I received the diaconate; in my thirtieth, the rank of priest. From that time until the fifty-eighth year of my age, I took care briefly to annotate the writings of the venerable Fathers, and also always to add material in accordance with their sense and interpretation. The sum of these works is as follows:

“Four books on the beginning of Genesis as far as the birth of Isaac and the casting out of Ishmael; three books on the tabernacle and its vessels, and the garments of the priests; four books on the first part of Samuel as far as Saul’s death; two books of allegorical exposition On the Building of the Temple, like the rest [Col. 0561D]; likewise, thirty questions on the books of Kings; three books on the Proverbs of Solomon; six books on the Song of Songs; chapter-divisions on Isaiah and Daniel, the Twelve Prophets, and part of Jeremiah, excerpted from the treatise of blessed Jerome; three books on Ezra and Nehemiah; one book on the song of Habakkuk; one book of allegorical explanation, concerning Christ and the Church, on the book of the blessed Father Tobit.

“Likewise, chapter-headings for readings on [Col. 0562A] the Pentateuch of Moses, Joshua, Judges; on the books of Kings and Chronicles; on the book of the blessed father Job; on Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs; on the prophet Isaiah, and also Ezra and Nehemiah. Four books on the Gospel of Mark; six books on the Gospel of Luke; two books of Gospel homilies. On the Apostle, whatever I found expounded in the smaller works of Saint Augustine, I took care to write out in full in order; two books on the Acts of the Apostles; one book on each of the seven catholic epistles; three books on the Apocalypse of Saint John; likewise chapter-headings for readings on the whole New Testament; likewise books of letters to various persons, among which are: one On the Six Ages of the World; one On the Resting-Places of the Children of Israel; one on the saying of Isaiah, ‘And they shall be shut up there in prison, and after many days they shall be visited’ [Isa. 24:22]; one On the Calculation of the Leap Year; and one On the Equinox, according to Anatolius.

“Likewise, concerning the histories of saints: I rendered into prose the book on the Life and Passion of Saint Felix the Confessor from the metrical work of Paulinus. I corrected, as far as I could, according to its meaning, the book on the Life and Passion of Saint Anastasius, badly translated from Greek and still worse emended by some incompetent person. I described the Life of the holy Father Cuthbert, monk and bishop alike, first in heroic metre and afterwards in plain prose; the history, in two little books, of the abbots Benedict, Ceolfrith, and Huetbert [variant: Huatbert; Churbert] of this monastery, in which I rejoice to serve heavenly mercy; the Ecclesiastical History of our island and people in five books [Col. 0562C].

“A martyrology for the feast-days of the holy martyrs, in which I took care diligently to note, concerning all whom I could find, not only on what day, but also by what kind of contest, or under what judge, they conquered the world; a book of hymns in various metres or rhythms; a book of epigrams in heroic or elegiac metre; one book On the Nature of Things, and one On Times.”

Likewise, one larger book On Times; a book On Orthography, arranged in alphabetical order; likewise a book On the Art of Metre, with another little treatise appended, On Figures or Tropes—that is, on the figures and modes of expression in which Holy Scripture is composed. He also made a cento-commentary on the Song of Songs, collecting statements from the various works of Pope Gregory [Col. 0562D].

He died in the year 734 of the Lord’s Incarnation, when Leo ruled the Romans, Charles Martel the Franks under King Theuderic, and Edilbert the English.

### Chapter LXIX

Paul, deacon of the Church of Naples, translated from Greek into Latin the Life of Saint Mary of Egypt.

> [Note: Paul, deacon of the Church of Naples, translated the Life of Saint Mary of Egypt, which Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem, had written in Greek [Col. 0563B]. It is extant under 9 April in Surius. Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, later rendered this Life into verse, as Henry of Ghent reports in chapter 8 of his Catalogue.]

### Chapter LXX

Anianus, a distinguished man, at the command of Athalaric the king, published one volume concerning the laws of the Emperor Theodosius [Col. 0563A]; and, at the urging of Bishop Orontius, translated John Chrysostom’s book on Matthew from Greek into Latin.

> [Note: As also his sermons in praise of Saint Paul. All these are extant in the Latin edition of Chrysostom.]

### Chapter LXXI

Walafrid [Strabo] the abbot composed the Life and Miracles of Saint Gall the abbot, first in prose and then in verse.

> [Note: Walafrid Strabo, so called because of an eye defect, abbot of Reichenau—the “rich” or “greater” island—or, according to others, abbot of Saint Gall in Switzerland, wrote a useful book, On the Beginnings and Growth of Ecclesiastical Matters. It was printed with other writers on the same subject at Cologne in 1568, Rome in 1590, and elsewhere [Col. 0563C]. He also wrote the Lives of the holy abbots Gall and Othmar, published by Surius on 16 October and 16 November. He died in the year 840. Those who make two persons out of Walafrid and Strabo are mistaken.]

### Chapter LXXII

Christian [Druthmar], coming from Aquitaine into Gaul, made his name known by writing. For he expounded the Gospel of Matthew, promising also to treat the other Gospels.

> [Note: Christian Druthmar, a monk of the Benedictine order, wrote for the monks of Stavelot and Malmedy an Exposition on the Gospel of Saint Matthew, printed at Haguenau in 1530. He is thought to have lived around the year of Christ 840.]

### Chapter LXXIII

Bishop Verus described in eloquent language the Life of Eutropius, bishop of the Gallic city of Orange, illustrious in virtues and miracles.

> [Note: Verus, bishop of Orange—Arausio or Arausica—in Gaul, wrote the deeds of Saint Eutropius, his predecessor, enrolled in the Roman Martyrology under 27 May.]

### Chapter LXXIV

Gregory, the second Roman pope of that name, when questioned at Constantinople by the Emperor Justinian concerning certain chapters, answered every question with an excellent reply and issued written works. He also replied to the synodal letter which John, bishop of Constantinople, sent to Rome. Therefore, a steadfast defender of ecclesiastical doctrines and a most vigorous assailant of their opponents, he wrote against the Emperor Leo, who, deceived by a certain apostate from the faith named Beser, ordered images of God and His saints everywhere to be removed and burned [Col. 0564A].

> [Note: Pope Gregory II most vehemently resisted the impiety of Leo the Isaurian, emperor at Constantinople, and sent Saint Boniface into Germany to preach the teaching of the Gospel. Pope Hadrian thus says of him in his letter to Charlemagne, On Images: “The younger Lord Pope Gregory, presiding with seventy-nine most holy bishops before the confession-shrine of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and jointly confirming the testimonies of many holy Fathers, decreed that sacred images should be venerated and adored” [Col. 0563D]. He died in the year 731. He wrote numerous and very learned letters to that same Boniface; to Charles Martel; to the Thuringians, Saxons, and other peoples of Germany; to Saint Germanus, bishop of Constantinople; to Leo the Isaurian; and to others. They are read in the volumes of the Councils and in Baronius’s Annals.]

### Chapter LXXV

John, monk and priest of Damascus in Syria, renowned for life and learning, surnamed Chrysorrhoas (“Golden-Stream”), encouraged by the writings of Pope Gregory in which he attacked the impiety of the Emperor Leo, himself too wrote in Greek for Greeks against the Emperor Leo.

> [Note: Saint John of Damascus, a priest and Syrian by nation, a man of great learning and holiness—whom the Iconoclasts contemptuously called Manzur—wrote, in the time of Leo the Isaurian, emperor at Constantinople, Orations in Defence of Sacred Images against that Leo, about the year of salvation 731 [Col. 0564B]. Yet he survived long afterward and suffered much from the Emperor Constantine Copronymus in defence of Catholic doctrine. He also wrote four books On the Orthodox Faith, in which he was the first, as Bellarmine wisely observed, to comprehend all theology in a sound order. Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, commonly called the Master of the Sentences, and the other so-called scholastic doctors later imitated him [Col. 0564C]. Jacques Billius, abbot of Prunay, collected his works into one body, rendered a great part into Latin, and published them at Paris in 1577. Add to these the Damascene’s book Against the Acephali and another Against the Nestorians, published by Canisius in volume IV of his Ancient Readings.
>
> “John of Damascus, surnamed Manzur, was himself a most celebrated man, second to none of his age who were distinguished in learning. His writings are very numerous, especially philosophical works; selected Parallels on Holy Scripture; canons of hymns in iambic verse and in prose. At the same time Cosmas of Jerusalem flourished, a most ingenious man, altogether breathing that sweet musical modulation. The hymn-canons of John and Cosmas have admitted, and will admit, no comparison with the writings of others for as long as our life continues; but, as they have hitherto been incomparable, so they will be forever [Col. 0564D], as long as human beings live.” Thus Suidas in his Lexicon concerning the Damascene and Cosmas of Jerusalem.
>
> As to the History of Barlaam and Josaphat, there are those who think that the Damascene was not its author, although Billius, Rosweyde, and others have thought so. Rader, in his Introduction to John Climacus, or the Sinaite, judges it to be the offspring of “John, a monk of the monastery of Saint Sabas,” as is read in a manuscript catalogue of the Heidelberg Library. I have nothing definite to maintain; this I know: John of Damascus too, having left the forum and the crowds of the world, was a monk in the lavra of Saint Sabas.]

### Chapter LXXVI

Gregory III likewise wrote admonitory letters to the emperors Leo and Constantine, through whom a severe persecution had been stirred up against the images of God and His saints. Supporters of the emperors seized these writings from their bearers and tore them up. Gregory again sent writings to the emperors, and again they were taken from the bearers [Col. 0564B] and torn up. Since, therefore, the emperors refused to receive these admonitory writings of apostolic authority, Pope Gregory issued many writings against them to many persons.

> [Note: He died in the year of Christ 741.]

### Chapter LXXVII

Pope Zacharias translated the books of Dialogues of Pope Gregory I from Latin into Greek, and by their reading enlightened many persons ignorant of the Latin language.

> [Note: See Isidore, chapter 27; Honorius III, 32. He died in 752.]

### Chapter LXXVIII

Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, nephew through the sister of King Pippin, ennobling the nobility of his lineage by the zeal of holy religion, wrote a Rule which he gave specifically to the clergy of the Church of Metz to observe.

### Chapter LXXIX

Pope Hadrian abridged the books of letters of Pope Gregory I, selecting all that was more useful and reducing thirteen books to two. He also wrote to the emperors Leo the Younger and his son Constantine on behalf of the veneration of the images of God and His saints. He wrote to the Emperor Charles a book of apostolic authority, rebuking the error of those who wished to weaken certain chapters promulgated by the Second Council of Nicaea, by the authority of 350 bishops who anathematized the heresy of those who abhor images of God and His saints [Col. 0565B].

> [Note: These works are extant in the volumes of the Councils. He died in 796.]

### Chapter LXXX

Paul, a monk of the monastery of Monte Cassino [Col. 0565C], an Italian by nation, was summoned by the Emperor Charlemagne because of his learning. He wrote the Life of Pope Gregory I; he wrote the deeds of the bishops of Metz; he wrote the miracles of Saint Arnulf, who, first mayor of the palace to the king of the Franks and afterwards bishop of Metz, sought the eremitic life. He also wrote in eloquent and plain language the History of the Winili, who were later called Lombards.

> [Note: Paul, son of Warnefrid and Theodolinda, surnamed Winfrid, was by nation a Lombard. First a deacon of Aquileia, then chancellor of Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards, he was carried off among the noble captives by Charlemagne after his king’s defeat. Because of his prudence and varied learning, he was held in great honour for some time. Later, on some unknown suspicion, he was exiled to the island of Diomede; from there he fled to Arichis, prince of Benevento and son-in-law of King Desiderius. When Arichis died, he assumed the monastic habit at Monte Cassino.
>
> Besides the Lives of the holy Pope Gregory I and Arnulf of Metz mentioned by Sigebert, he also wrote the deeds of Saint Cyprian, bishop and martyr of Carthage—a little book which Pamelius prefixed to Cyprian’s works—and the Lives of Saints Benedict, Maurus, and the virgin Scholastica. These latter three were published at Rome in 1590 with poems by Prosper Martinengo. Arnold Wion published Paul’s verses on the virgin Scholastica in his Tree of Life under 10 February [Col. 0565D]. The Deeds of the Bishops of Metz, here mentioned by Sigebert, are extant in the Corpus of French History.
>
> The Historia Miscella also owes much to this Paul. Its first eleven books are the same as the ten books of Eutropius, except that Paul occasionally adds something of his own. Paul then continues Eutropius, and the following five books are his. The remaining books, namely the seventeenth and those following, were added by Landulf Sagax, chiefly from George Theophanes, or from Anastasius the Librarian, who translated Theophanes.]

### Chapter LXXXI

The Emperor Charles, through the hand of this his deacon Paul [Col. 0566A], selected the best passages from the writings of the Catholic Fathers and caused readings suitable for every feast throughout the yearly cycle to be compiled for reading in church, in two volumes.

> [Note: In 814 Charlemagne, emperor and king of the Franks, died at Aachen on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the seventy-first year of his age, the forty-seventh of his reign, and the fourteenth of his empire; he was buried there. He esteemed and supported learned men, among them Alcuin, Paul of Friuli, Einhard, and Usuard [Col. 0566C]; and was himself variously learned and educated, as the epitaph which he wrote in verse for Pope Hadrian abundantly demonstrates. Ansegisus, abbot of Lobbes, in 827 published in four books the capitularies or edicts of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, which he had arranged; Peter Pithou saw to their publication at Paris in 1588, and they were reprinted there in 1603. Ansegisus of Lobbes, moreover, was earlier than that Ansegisus who was only created archbishop of Sens in 801. The Codex Carolinus, published by Gretser in Germany, is also extant.]

### Chapter LXXXII

Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis at Paris, wrote to the Emperor Louis a Life of Dionysius himself in both styles—that is, prose and verse.

> [Note: Hilduin, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Denis, situated two miles from Paris, composed the Life of Saint Dionysius, bishop of Paris, in prose and verse. Matthew Galenus first published the prose at Cologne in 1563 with his Areopagitica, and Surius later published it under 9 October. Four metrical books are preserved in manuscript at the monastery of Gembloux. Rabanus Maurus dedicated his Commentary on the Four Books of Kings to Hilduin [Col. 0566D].]

### Chapter LXXXIII

Alcuin, or Albinus, born in Britain and summoned thence by the Emperor Charles, was so dear to him in intimate friendship that he was called the emperor’s darling. The emperor himself strove, especially through Alcuin’s instruction, to be initiated into all the liberal arts. Alcuin wrote much. He wrote a dialogue on [Col. 0566B] Genesis; a book to Count Wido On Virtues and Vices; and a handbook on certain psalms. He composed treatises on the Gospel of John. He wrote books On the Holy Trinity for the emperor himself; he answered questions proposed to him by Fredegisus. He wrote a Prognosticon on the age to come. He wrote to the virgin Eulalia On the Nature or Immortality of the Soul. At the emperor’s command he corrected the sacred Bible and wrote several other works.

> [Note: Besides the works here mentioned by Sigebert, Alcuin also wrote four books On Images, as Roger of Hoveden indicates in his account of the year 792; but they were falsely published under the name of the Emperor Charlemagne. Eliphilus—that is, John Tilius, bishop of Meaux—first published them in print at Paris. See under Honorius IV, 2.]

### Chapter LXXXIV

Einhard wrote the Life of the Emperor Charles all the more truthfully because he was more intimately attached to him. Imitating Bede, who abridged the Hebrew Psalter by extracting from it every verse containing words of prayer [Col. 0567A], he too abridged the Gallican Psalter, which we Gauls use, extracting from it every verse that contains words of prayer.

> [Note: Einhard—called Einardus by Sigebert—chancellor of the Emperor Charlemagne and abbot of Blandinium and Saint Bavo in the city of Ghent, imitating Suetonius, wrote in elegant style the Life of Charlemagne, frequently published at Cologne and elsewhere. He wrote four books On the Translation and Miracles of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, whose sacred relics he brought into Belgium, published by Surius; and a rhythmical or iambic poem on the same saints, likewise published by Surius. A manuscript Chronicle of Ghent says concerning Einhard: “In the year 826, the venerable man Einhard, very intimate with the most pious Emperor Louis, became abbot of the monastery of Ghent; he described in lucid style the famous deeds and acts of the glorious Emperor Charlemagne” [Col. 0567C]. Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, also mentions this work in a letter to Einhard. He died in 844.]

### Chapter LXXXV

Husuard the monk, prompted by the zeal of Jerome and Bede, who had partly noted the annually recurring feasts of saints, but especially encouraged by the zeal and command of the great Emperor Charles—who disliked the fact that Jerome and Bede, studying too much brevity, had passed over many necessary matters and left very many calendar days untouched—endeavoured for Charles’s sake to complete their unfinished work. Recording the feasts of saints on each individual day of the calendar, he produced a complete Martyrology.

> [Note: John Molanus, professor of theology at Louvain, first illustrated the Martyrology of Husuard, commonly called Usuard, a Gallic monk, with notes and additions; it is in everyone’s hands. Molanus discusses him and the other ancient martyrologies at length in his letter to the reader, as does Baronius in the prolegomena to the Roman Martyrology.]

### Chapter LXXXVI

Angelomus the monk, at the command of Drogo, bishop of Metz and son of the Emperor Charles, composed treatises on the four books of Kings.

> [Note: Angelomus, a monk of Luxeuil in the county of Burgundy, not of Lisieux, at the command of Drogo, bishop of Metz—who was the son of the Emperor Charlemagne—compiled from the commentaries of the ancient Fathers *Stromata* on the four books of Kings and on the Song of Songs; printed at Cologne in 1530 and at Rome by Manutius in 1565.]

### Chapter LXXXVII

Attularius [variant: Amularius] the monk wrote a brief little book On Ecclesiastical Offices. Later, writing on the same subject to the Emperor Louis, he set forth more fully in four books the order and reasons of ecclesiastical offices, and wrote one book On the Mysteries of the Mass.

### Chapter LXXXVIII

Bellator the priest expounded the Book of Wisdom of Solomon in seven books.

### Chapter LXXXIX

Rabanus, also called Maurus or Magnetius, formerly abbot of Fulda and afterwards archbishop of Mainz, wrote a book On the Praise of the Holy Cross, decorated with marvellous variety, which he sent to Rome to be offered to Saint Peter. He wrote for Archbishop Otgar a book on the books of the Wisdom of Solomon. He wrote on the first book of Maccabees, on Ezra [Col. 0568A], on Judith, one book On the Mysteries of the Mass, and one book On the Blessings of the Patriarchs. He wrote for Abbot Hilduin on the four books of Kings; one book On Questions of the Canons for Bishop Heribald; one book on the same subject for his fellow bishop Reginbald; and other works.

> [Note: Honorius IV, 4.]

### Chapter XC

Bishop Freculf wrote for Elisachar a history from the creation of the world to the birth of Christ. He did not neglect to resolve the difficulty of intervening questions; by inserting secular histories among sacred history, and fitting together the contemporaneity of kingdoms, he completed this work in seven books.

> [Note: Freculf, formerly a monk of Fulda and bishop of Lisieux in Normandy, wrote a Chronicle from the creation of the world to the time of Charlemagne. He dedicated the latter part to Judith, wife of the Emperor Louis the Pious. Conversely, Rabanus Maurus dedicated his commentary on Genesis to Freculf. He flourished in 840.]

### Chapter XCI

Ambrose Autpert wrote a book On Avarice; he also wrote ten books [Col. 0568B] on the Apocalypse, and several other works.

> [Note: Ambrose Autpert, alternatively Ansbert, a monk, flourished in the year 890 and wrote commentaries on the Apocalypse, the Psalms, and the Song of Songs, printed in folio at Cologne in 1536.]

### Chapter XCII

Florus expounded the Epistles of Paul in their entirety. He said nothing of his own, but turned over all the books of Augustine; collecting passages of the Pauline Epistles expounded by Augustine in different places, he restored the expounded passages to the order of the Epistles, noting the individual books of Augustine in which these passages had been expounded. Thus, by a new and remarkable industry, from another’s labour he produced a large volume of his own work.

> [Note: Florus, mentioned by Sigebert in this chapter, is, unless I am mistaken, the man who expounded Saint Paul’s Epistles from statements of Saint Augustine gathered here and there, and who defended Augustine’s teaching On Predestination against John Erigena, to be mentioned below in chapter 94 [Col. 0568C]. A different Florus from this one seems to have enlarged Bede’s Martyrology, later expanded by Usuard. This man is commonly called Master Florus and, if we believe Trithemius, was a Benedictine monk at Saint-Trond in the diocese of Liège. The Exposition of the Mass read in the Library of the Ancient Fathers also seems to be the work of this Master Florus. Petavius mentions Master Florus, deacon of Lyons, who wrote in the name of the Church of Lyons against Hincmar, bishop of Reims, about the year 848 [Col. 0568D].]

### Chapter XCIII

Lupus Servatus composed a book On Three Questions: that is, on free will; on the predestination of the good and the evil; and on a certain superfluous valuation or [Col. 0568C] redemption by Christ’s blood extending to the salvation of the ungodly. For a certain disturbance of faith arose concerning this matter in the year of the Lord 849.

> [Note: Lupus Servatus, abbot of Ferrières in the diocese of Sens and pupil of Rabanus Maurus, besides the Questions mentioned here, wrote a book of Letters, published at Paris by Masson in 1588, and a Life of Saint Wigbert, abbot of Fritzlar, published at Mainz by Buse in 1602. He died in 852.]

### Chapter XCIV

John Erigena [manuscripts of Gembloux and Affligem: *Eurigena*], at the command of Charles, son of the Emperor Louis, translated the books of Dionysius the Areopagite into Latin [Col. 0569A].

> [Note: Pope Nicholas writes thus about John Erigena in a letter to Charles the Bald: “It has been reported to our apostolic office that a certain man named John, a Scot by race, has recently translated into Latin the work of blessed Dionysius the Areopagite which he wrote in the Greek tongue, On the Divine Names and the Celestial Orders. According to custom, it ought to have been sent to us and approved by our judgment, especially since the same John, although he is said to possess much learning, is reported by frequent rumour to have held unsound views on certain matters in the past.”]

### Chapter XCV

Bertram [manuscripts of Gembloux and Groenendaal: Ratramnus] wrote a book On the Body and Blood of the Lord, and a book On Predestination for Charles.

> [Note: Bertram wrote a book On the Body and Blood of the Lord, printed at Cologne in 1532, at Basle in the *Micropresbytericum*, and elsewhere, but condemned by the Tridentine censors. So Molanus in his manuscript *Sacred Library*. Heretics first published it in print [[Col. 0569] The first Cologne edition of Bertram was prepared by Roman Catholics], and seem to have inserted whatever is read there that is either obscure or apparently ill-sounding. Certainly, in very many places he affirms Christ’s true presence after consecration and teaches transubstantiation, so that even the interpolator himself does not conceal this toward the end, saying that many things do not cohere and that what precedes contradicts what follows. Among others, Bartholomew Peter of Lintrensis, doctor of theology at Douai, observed this [Col. 0569D]. Paschasius Radbertus wrote against Bertram.]

### Chapter XCVI

The Emperors Michael and Theophilus wrote to Louis, king of the Franks, a most useful book concerning the veneration of images.

### Chapter XCVII

Paschasius Ratbertus, abbot of Corbie, wrote for Abbot Placidus a book On the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of Christ.

> [Note: Honorius IV, 10.]

### Chapter XCVIII

Almannus, monk of Hautvillers, wrote the Life of Saint Nivard, archbishop of Reims; the Life of Sindulf; the Life of Queen Helena; and [Col. 0569B] an account of her translation from Rome to the monastery of Hautvillers. Since in his time Francia was being devastated by the Normans, he bewailed the desolation of Francia and of his monastery, after the example of the prophet Jeremiah, in a fourfold alphabetic poem.

### Chapter XCIX

Hincmar, formerly a monk of Saint-Denis at Paris and afterwards archbishop of Reims, wrote the Life of Saint Remigius of Reims: first briefly composed, then enlarged from a short work into a book of great size, and then abridged from the large book by the industry of Fortunatus, bishop and poet. This Life, I say, Hincmar wrote, adding both what he found in the histories of earlier writers concerning Saint Remigius’s birth, life, or death, and what he gathered from scattered documents. According to the law of history, he omitted neither the matters learned from common report [Col. 0569C] nor Remigius’s testament. He wrote a reply to the Church of Ravenna in the person of the Emperor Charlemagne.

> [Note: John Buse published Hincmar’s letters, with other of his smaller works, at Mainz in 1620; John Cordesius did so at Paris in 1615. Sirmond published the description of the estate of Noviliacum, which Hincmar had obtained from Charles the Bald, together with Flodoard. Hincmar’s Life of Saint Remigius is read in Surius under 1 October. He died in 882, as Flodoard reports, book III, chapter 30.]

### Chapter C

Adrevald, also called Adalbert, monk of Fleury, wrote a History of the Miracles shown throughout Gaul by the merits of Saint Benedict of Monte Cassino, from the time when his body was translated from Monte Cassino to the monastery of Fleury until the time of Odo, king of the Franks.

### Chapter CI

Aimoin, monk of Fleury, completed the History of the Miracles of Saint Benedict begun by Adrevald, carrying it from the time of King Odo to the time of Robert, king of the Franks. He also wrote a History of the Franks and distinguished the geographical situation of the Gauls.

> [Note: Aimoin, or Aimon, was a monk of the renowned monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, by the walls of the city of Paris. Among other works, he wrote five books On the Deeds of the Franks, revised through the efforts of Jacques Breul, a monk of the same place, and published at Paris in 1603. The same books are extant in Freher’s Corpus of French History.]

### Chapter CII

Pope Nicholas collected into one volume letters of apostolic authority written by himself to various persons [Col. 0570B].

> [Note: They are extant in the volumes of the Councils.]

### Chapter CIII

At Pope Nicholas’s command, Anastasius translated into Latin the Life of John the Almsgiver, written in Greek by Bishop Leontius.

> [Note: Anastasius, librarian of the Holy Roman Church, rendered into Latin from Greek the Lives of Saints John the Almsgiver, Demetrius the Martyr, and others; the Chronicle of George Theophanes; and many other works. He also wrote a History of the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs. Having received it from Marcus Welser, John Buse collated it with manuscripts and arranged for its publication at Mainz in 1602. The Collections of the same Anastasius, which he compiled from Greek writings translated into Latin for the benefit of John, the Roman deacon mentioned by Sigebert below in chapter 106, while the latter was planning an ecclesiastical history, were published at Paris by Sirmond in 1620 [Col. 0570D].]

### Chapter CIV

Eric the monk described brilliantly in six little books, in metrical style, the Life of Germanus, bishop of Auxerre.

> [Note: They were published at Paris in 1543.]

### Chapter CV

Milo, monk of Saint-Amand, renowned for literary learning, wrote in metrical style the Life of Saint Amandus. He also wrote in verse for King Charles a book On Sobriety.

> [Note: Milo, monk of Elnone at Saint-Amand in Pabula, of the Benedictine order, uncle and teacher of Hucbald of Elnone, a most learned man, wrote the Life of Saint Amandus, bishop of Maastricht on the Meuse and founder of the monastery of Elnone, in verse and prose. Surius published it under 7 February. Verses written to the priest Haymo in four books, beginning, “The venerable feasts of our patron were drawing near,” are preserved in manuscript at Elnone, at Saint-Bertin in Saint-Omer, and elsewhere. The book On Sobriety for the Emperor Charles the Bald; a twofold hexameter poem On the Holy Cross, most ingeniously composed in the form of a sphere; and likewise a hexameter poem On the Conflict of Spring and Winter, are all preserved in manuscript at Elnone, at Saint-Amand in the diocese of Tournai. He died in 871.]

### Chapter CVI

John, deacon of the Roman Church, wrote in elegant style for John, seventh pope of that name, four books On the Life [Col. 0570C] of Pope Gregory I. At the request of Gauderic, bishop of Velletri, he also wrote the deeds of Pope Clement.

> [Note: John the Roman deacon was intimate with Anastasius, librarian of the Holy Roman Church, praised above in chapter 103. For the benefit of this deacon John, while he was planning an ecclesiastical history, Anastasius translated very many Greek works into Latin [Col. 0571C]. Of these, Jacques Sirmond, theologian of the Society of Jesus, published not a few at Paris in 1620.]

### Chapter CVII

Hucbald, monk of Saint-Amand, was so outstanding in his mastery of the liberal arts that he was compared with philosophers. He wrote the lives of many saints; and because he excelled in musical art, he composed the chants of many saints in sweet and regulated melody. He also wrote a book On the Art of Music, so arranging the strings of the monochord by letters of the alphabet that anyone might by them learn an unfamiliar chant without another’s instruction. He also wrote for the Emperor Charles the Bald a book of three hundred verses, in praise of bald men, every word of which begins with a single letter, namely C, as:

> **Carmina Clarisonae Calvis Cantate Camoenae.**  
> “Sing, clear-sounding Muses, songs for the bald.”

> [Note: Hucbald—also Hugbald or Hubald—of the Benedictine order, monk of Elnone at Saint-Amand, was “nephew of Milo, a monk there, distinguished in learning, famous for his writings, and also outstanding as a musician, who composed the chants of many saints,” to use the words of the manuscript Chronicle of Elnone [Col. 0571D]. He wrote the Life of Saint Lebuin, patron of Deventer, for Alberic, bishop of Utrecht; the Life of Saint Rictrude, abbess of Marchiennes; and the Life of Saint Aldegund, abbess and foundress of Maubeuge in Hainaut. These histories are extant in Surius’s volumes. He also wrote the Life of Saint Madelberta, abbess of Maubeuge, read in manuscript at the monastery of Saint-Ghislain in Hainaut; and the History of Saint Cilinia, mother of blessed Remigius, apostle of the Franks. His 136-verse poem In Praise of Bald Men, in which every verse begins with C, written for Charles the Bald, is in everyone’s hands. He died in the year 930.]

### Chapter CVIII

Abbot Notger wrote a book On Musical Notes and the Modes of Harmonies, so that anyone might see and understand [Col. 0571B] how the intervals of harmonies differ from one another.

> [Note: Honorius, book IV, chapter 9, also mentions Abbot Notger. He seems to be the same as the abbot Notger praised here by Sigebert. If the title “abbot” is removed, this may seem to designate Notger or Nother, surnamed Balbulus, monk of the celebrated monastery of Saint Gall in Switzerland, in the diocese of Constance, who died in 912 and wrote a Martyrology, published by Canisius in volume VI of his Ancient Readings [Col. 0572C].]

### Chapter CIX

Enchiriades, under the persons of a questioning disciple and an answering master, wrote a dialogue On the Theory of Music, and in three books explained the manifold rules of music.

### Chapter CX

Aurelian, cleric of the Church of Reims, wrote for Bernard, chief cantor and later bishop, On the Rules of Modulations—which they call tones or tenors—and on their names.

CAP. CXI. Regino, abbot of Prüm [Note: [Col. 0572C] Regino, abbot of Prüm in the diocese of Trier, wrote a Chronicle from the first year of Christ down to the year 910; this, with an appendix of fifty-seven years, was published at Frankfurt in 1566 [Col. 0572D]. Moreover, to fill the gaps and supply other matters lacking in the common edition of Regino, the fragment of the Frankish Annals, from the year 741 to the year 793, published by Canisius in volume III of *Ancient Readings*, will be useful.], wrote for Albero I, bishop of Metz, a Chronicle containing the principal deeds of the Franks, which he carried from Christ’s birth down to the year 908 after Christ’s birth.

[Col. 0571C] CAP. CXII. Auxilius wrote a dialogue, under the persons of an accuser and a defender, fortified with divine and canonical examples, against the internal discord of the Roman Church—namely, concerning the ordinations, disordinations, and superordinations of Roman pontiffs, and the disordinations and superordinations of those ordained by them.

[Col. 0572A] CAP. CXIII. Bishop Maximus wrote a book *On Ecclesiastical Ministries* and on the dress of clerics.

CAP. CXIV. Dinamius, an illustrious man and patrician, wrote a Life, full of virtues, of St. Marius, who was abbot of the monastery of Bobacum [Note: [Col. 0572D] The patrician Dinamius wrote the Life of St. Maximus, first abbot of Lérins and later bishop of Riez, and dedicated it to Urbicus, who had succeeded Faustus in the see of Riez. It appears in the Surian collection for 27 November and in the *Chronology of Lérins*. Whether St. Maximus ought to be read here in Sigebert, I have nothing to assert. Of Marius of Bobacum I have so far read nothing.].

CAP. CXV. Pelagius, deacon of the Roman Church, translated from Greek into Latin sixteen books *On the Life and Teaching, and on the Perfection, of the Holy Fathers*: one book *On the Progress of Monks*; one *On Stillness*; one *On Compunction*; one *On Continence*; one *Against Fornication*; one, *That a Monk Ought to Possess Nothing*; one, *That Nothing Ought to Be Done for Display*; one *On Patience and Fortitude*; one, *That No One Ought to Be Judged*; one, *That One Ought to Live Soberly*; [Col. 0572B] one, *That One Ought to Pray Continually and Soberly*; one *On Humility*; one *On Penitence*; one *On Charity*; and one *On Providence or Contemplation* [Note: [Col. 0572D] Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, final chapter.].

CAP. CXVI. John the subdeacon translated from Greek into Latin one book *On the Life and Teaching of the Fathers* [Note: [Col. 0572D] See Jerome, in the place cited.].

CAP. CXVII. Bishop Martin, through the hand of Paschasius the deacon, translated many questions and answers of the holy Egyptian Fathers at the monastery of Dumium [Note: [Col. 0572D] See Jerome, in the place cited.].

CAP. CXVIII. Smaragdus wrote a book *On Avoiding Vices and Maintaining Virtues*, which he entitled *The Diadem of Monks*, because, as a diadem shines with gems, so this book shines with virtues. He also wrote on [Col. 0572C] the Rule of St. Benedict, and several other works [Note: [Col. 0572D] Honorius, IV.6.].

CAP. CXIX. Caesarius, abbot of Lérins, wrote and delivered homilies suited to the life of monks [Note: [Col. 0572D] Gennadius, ch. 86.].

CAP. CXX. Laurence [Note: [Col. 0572D] This Laurence, priest and teacher of Gaudentius, [Col. 0573C] the first bishop of Novara, flourished about the year 363. See *Acta Eruditorum*, vol. II of the supplement, pp. 525–526.] “Honey-Tongued” wrote a book *On the Two Times*: that is, one from Adam to Christ, the other from Christ to the end [Col. 0573A] of the age. He also delivered homilies in a voice as though of honey; hence he was surnamed “Honey-Tongued.”

CAP. CXXI. Bishop Boniface wrote, in metrical style, a book on virtues and vices.

CAP. CXXII. Halitgar, bishop of Cambrai [Note: [Col. 0573C] Halitgar, or Halitchar, bishop of Cambrai and Arras, an apostolic man and born for public affairs, was sent by Emperor Charlemagne to Constantinople to Emperor Michael, and was received by him kindly and honourably. At the request of Ebbo, archbishop of Rheims, he wrote a *Penitential*, as also five books on vices, virtues, and the order of penitents; all these works are found in Canisius, volume V of *Ancient Readings*. He died at Cambrai in 832 and was buried on Mount St. Eligius, where there is now to be seen an abbey of regular canons in the diocese of Arras.], wrote for Ebbo, bishop of Rheims, a *Penitential Book* in accordance with the decrees of the canons.

CAP. CXXIII. Remigius, monk of Auxerre, renowned for expounding secular writings, made himself still more notably known by usefully expounding the divine Scriptures as well. For he expounded the Canon of the Mass, showing what had been placed or added in it, and by whom. He expounded the Song of Songs. He wrote a book [Col. 0573B] *On the Divine Offices*; he wrote *On the Individual Feasts of the Saints*; he answered Gualo, bishop of Autun, when he asked concerning two questions. One concerned the dispute of Michael the archangel with the devil over the body of Moses, which is read in the Epistle of the Apostle Jude. The other concerned the Lord’s reply to Job from the whirlwind: “Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you: he will eat grass like an ox; and can you draw out Leviathan with a hook?” He wrote other works too [Note: [Col. 0573C] Bellarmine discusses him in the *Catalogue*.].

CAP. CXXIV. Odo [Note: [Col. 0573D] St. Odo, the first abbot of Cluny, entered in the Roman Martyrology on 18 November, flourished in the year 920. He wrote two treatises on St. Martin, bishop of Tours, printed at Paris in 1511 with Sulpicius Severus. Consult the Library of Cluny, edited by André du Chesne.]—formerly chief cantor at Tours, then a monk and first abbot of Cluny—displayed elegant talent in writing and delivering homilies, and especially in composing chants in honour of the saints.

CAP. CXXV. Stephen [Note: [Col. 0573D] Stephen, made bishop of Liège in 903, died in 920. John Chapeaville published the Acts of St. Lambert, more carefully composed by him, from a manuscript codex in 1612, in volume I of *Matters Concerning Liège*.], formerly a cleric of Metz and then [Col. 0573C] bishop of Liège, rewrote in a more polished style for Herman, archbishop of Cologne, the Life and Passion of St. Lambert, which had been written rather crudely by the cleric Godescalc; [Col. 0574A] and he composed a nocturnal chant in honour of the same martyr. He also composed, in an authentic and sweet melody, a song on the Holy Trinity and a chant on the finding of Stephen the protomartyr. He also wrote for Robert, bishop of Metz, a capitular book, in which he distinctly assembled capitula, responsories, verses, and collects for each hour of night and day throughout the entire year.

CAP. CXXVI. Liutprand [also Liudprand], deacon of the church of Pavia, wrote in an elegant and varied style, for Recemund, bishop of the Church of Elvira in Spain, a History *On the Deeds of the Kings and Emperors of His Own Time*, which he entitled *Antapodosis*, that is, *Retribution* [Note: [Col. 0573D] Bellarmine discusses him in the *Catalogue*, and Pennotto, book I, *On Regular Canons*, ch. 52.].

[Col. 0574B] CAP. CXXVII. Ratherius [Note: [Col. 0573D] Ratherius was a monk of Lobbes, or Laubes, in the territory of Liège but in the diocese of Cambrai. Having gone to Italy with Hilduin, abbot of Lobbes, to King Hugh, he was made bishop at Verona, while Hilduin was made bishop at Milan. In the fourth year thereafter Hugh expelled him because he favoured Arnold, duke of the Bavarians. An exile at Pavia, he wrote to the Roman pontiff about his sufferings and hardships endured in the bishopric. At the same time the heresy of the Anthropomorphites troubled Italy, and he fought it both in speech and in writing. Moreover, while in exile he wrote six books of *Agonisticon*, or *Prefaces*, and a Life of St. Ursmar, abbot of Lobbes, which appears, though mutilated, in Surius for 18 April; the complete text is read at Lobbes. Yet Folcuin states in the Chronicle of Lobbes that the booklet was indeed corrected and enlarged by Ratherius but written by Anso. He also wrote *On the Art of Grammar*, which book he entitled *Sparadorsum* [Col. 0574D] (as may be inferred from Folcuin), in the German manner of speaking, because it preserves boys’ backs from whips. Otto, king of Germany, was then ruling Italy. He entrusted his brother Bruno to the instruction of Ratherius, the foremost among the palace philosophers, as Folcuin himself calls him. Bruno, afterwards chosen bishop of Cologne, advanced Ratherius to the see of Liège, and later restored him to the see of Verona when he was oppressed by the hatred of factional men. About this time he wrote, concerning his second exile, *Phrenesis*, because he was rejected as a madman; likewise “*The Plumb-Line and the Sirma*; a Synodal Letter to the Diocesan Priests; an Account of His Life; a Roman Itinerary; Sermons on Easter, the Lord’s Supper, the Ascension, Pentecost, and other matters.” Thus Folcuin. Trithemius adds, besides Sigebert, that he wrote one book on the body and blood of the Lord and one book of *Confessions*. His *Chronography* is read in manuscript at Gembloux. But “wearied,” [Col. 0575B] Folcuin’s words are, “by the insolence of the citizens of Verona, and at the same time regarding their inborn faithlessness with suspicion, he was considering a return.” Therefore he sent to the [Col. 0575C] abbot a book which he entitled *The Conflict of Two*, saying in it that he wavered whether he ought to return or not. Having returned to Belgium, he spent what remained of his life in the monastery of Aulne and died at Namur in 974.

> Bishop of Verona, but Ratherius was three times an exile.  
> His body was taken to Lobbes and buried in the church of St. Ursmar.],

formerly monk of Lobbes and bishop of Verona, a man of remarkable simplicity, wrote the Life of St. Ursmar of Lobbes. Twice expelled from the bishopric of Verona, he wrote a book in which, with rather witty urbanity, he laments his sufferings, interweaving many things concerning his case that may please and benefit readers. Afterwards made bishop of the Church of Liège, and expelled from it, he wrote a book which he entitled *Phrenesis*. He wrote a book which he entitled, as it seemed to him, *Ineffectual Chatter*. He wrote a book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* and *On God’s Predestination*. He wrote against the heresy of the Anthropomorphites—that is, of those who say that God has a bodily and human form—which heresy then grievously troubled Italy. He wrote *Agonisticon*, [Col. 0574C] that is, six books of *Prefaces*, one book of *Confessions*, and other works.

[Col. 0575A] CAP. CXXVIII. Wandalbert wrote a Martyrology in metrical style [Note: [Col. 0575C] Wandalbert, a monk of Prüm, flourished in the age of Emperor Lothair. He composed a Martyrology in heroic verse, which many judge to be the work I have read in the first volume of Bede under the title *Bede’s Ephemeris*. He wrote the Life and Miracles of St. Goar, published by Surius for 6 July.].

CAP. CXXIX. Widukind [Note: [Col. 0575C] Widukind, also Witichind, a Saxon by nation and monk of Saxon or Westphalian Corvey, wrote three books *On Saxon Affairs*, in which he records the deeds of Emperors Henry I and Otto I. [Col. 0575D] They were printed at Basel in 1532, Frankfurt in 1577, and elsewhere. He ends with the death of Otto I—that is, with the events of the year 903—at which time he also flourished.], monk of Saxon Corvey, wrote a History of the Saxons down to the death of Emperor Otto I; and for Matilda, daughter of Emperor Otto, he wrote the Life of that emperor. He wrote in verse the Passion of the virgin Thecla, and in a varied style he wrote the Life of Paul the First Hermit.

CAP. CXXX. Roger wrote the Life of Bruno [Note: [Col. 0575D] Bruno, full brother of Emperor Otto I and disciple of Ratherius praised in the preceding chapter, was archbishop of Cologne and, having been proclaimed by his brother Otto duke of all Lotharingia—that is, both Upper or Mosellan and Lower or Ripuarian Lotharingia—died in 965. His Life, published by Surius on 12 October, was written by Roger or Rotger, a Benedictine monk of St. Pantaleon at Cologne, who was Bruno’s contemporary. Read our Belgian calendar on 12 October.] of Cologne, who was archbishop, duke, and brother of Emperor Otto.

CAP. CXXXI. Flodoard [Note: [Col. 0575D] Flodoard—called Flauvaldus by Peter Pithou and commonly by others—was a priest and canon of the Church of Rheims, afterwards a monk and abbot of the monastery of St. Remigius in the city of Rheims. In four books he composed the *Deeds of the Bishops of Rheims*, or *History of the Church of Rheims*, extending to the year of Christ 948; it was published at Paris in 1611 by Jacques Sirmond and at Douai in 1615 [Col. 0576B] by George Colvener with notes. He also wrote a truly golden Chronicle of events from the year 919 to the year 966, in which year he died. Peter Pithou first published that Chronicle at Paris in 1588 among the Twelve Contemporary Writers of Frankish Affairs, and the Frankfurt editors published it again in 1594. Henry Bunderius, Dominican of Ghent, living in 1555, enumerates in his *Index of Manuscript Books in Belgium and Neighbouring Provinces* other works of Flodoard, not yet seen by me, in approximately these words: “Flodoard the priest wrote, in verse, fifteen books *On the Italian Triumphs of Martyrs and Confessors*, manuscript at Trier in the cathedral; *On the Triumphs of Christ and the Saints of Palestine*, in verse, three books, manuscript in the same place; thirdly, *On the Triumphs of Christ Accomplished at Antioch*, in verse, two books, manuscript in the same place.” If these writings still survive, would that someone might bring them to light!—We have fulfilled the wish. EDITORS.], monk of Rheims, wrote the *Deeds of the Bishops of Rheims*. He began his narrative with the founding of that city itself, which [Col. 0575B] first acquired the name Cordurus from the character of its citizens, who were hard of heart in war. Later the soldiers of Remus, fleeing from the face of Romulus, his brother, took refuge there; and they called it Remus, or Rheims, after the name of their leader Remus. This writer is worthily numbered among writers because, departing from his work in order to commemorate holy martyrs and confessors resting in churches adjoining or subject to the Church of Rheims, [Col. 0576A] he made known their Lives or Passions to readers.

CAP. CXXXII. Bishop Aldhelm [Note: [Col. 0576C] That the Adelmus mentioned in this chapter is the same man whom Sigebert reported above in chapter 66—Anthelmus in Bellarmine, Aldhelmus in Pitseus—may be inferred from what Pitseus himself relates in his book *On the Writers of England*. He was first an abbot and afterwards a bishop among his own people; most learned in verse and prose, in Latin and Greek, according to the verse:

> Aldhelm sang odes in a thousand lines.

> 

> Among other works he wrote a book against the errors of the Britons and Scots, *On the Celebration of Easter*, by which book he brought many back to sounder judgment, as Bede relates in book V of his *Ecclesiastical History of England*. He also wrote one book *On Virginity* in prose, published at Paris by Sonnius in 1576; one book *On the Praise of Virgins* in heroic verse, published at Ingolstadt by Canisius in 1608; *On the Deeds of the Saints*; a thousand verses of Riddles; and many other works which lie in manuscript in the libraries of England. He died in the year of salvation 709. Thus, approximately, Pitseus. His Life appears in Surius for 28 May. Bellarmine also treats the same man in the *Catalogue*, at the beginning of the eighth century, by whom—as also by Pitseus—he is called a saint.]—imitating Symphosius [Symposium], who, expressing through personification the qualities of individual things, wrote a book of Riddles in verse—likewise expressed the qualities of things and wrote a book of Riddles, completing it in a thousand verses, as he himself indicates in the initial letters of his prologue:

> Aldhelm sang odes in a thousand lines.

CAP. CXXXIII. Thomas wrote for his lord Hilduin a book of Riddles, brief indeed but full of truth and elegance. In it, through personification, he introduces Mother Wisdom and her seven daughters, the seven liberal arts, expressing [Col. 0576B] the whole character proper to themselves.

CAP. CXXXIV. Theodulus, an Italian by nation and learned in Greek and Latin, while studying at Athens heard pagans disputing with Christians. Gathering their arguments, he returned and set them into an allegorical eclogue [Note: [Col. 0576D] See Trithemius, ch. 185], introducing two persons in dispute and a third judging between the statements of the two. He calls the first Pseustis, named from falsehood, who puts forward human and fabulous matters; the second Alithia, [Col. 0577A] who sets against them divine and true matters; and the third Phronesis, named from prudence, through whom doubtful matters are examined. *Theodulus* means “servant of God.” The title of this book is *The Eclogue of Theodulus*. He died prematurely while living under clerical rule, and therefore did not revise his book.

CAP. CXXXV. Haymo [Note: [Col. 0577B] Haymo, an Anglo-Saxon and bishop of Halberstadt, besides commentaries on books of both Testaments, wrote an *Epitome of Sacred History*, published at Cologne in 1573 and Rome in 1564, with notes by Peter Galesini.] expounded the whole of the Apostle Paul, the Apocalypse, Isaiah, the Song of Songs, and other books; but not all of his works reached everyone.

CAP. CXXXVI. Folcuin [Note: [Col. 0577B] Folcuin, or Fulcuin, abbot of Lobbes, wrote the *Chronicle of Lobbes*, or *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, which survives in manuscript at Lobbes, at Tournai in the college of the Society of Jesus, at Gembloux, at Liège, and elsewhere. He died in 990.], abbot of Lobbes, wrote the *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, introducing by digression many matters useful to readers.

CAP. CXXXVII. Heriger, abbot of Lobbes [Note: [Col. 0577B] Heriger, or Hariger, abbot of Lobbes, died in 1107 and was buried before the altar sacred to St. Thomas in the church of St. Ursmar, which he had built. He wrote a History, or *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*. It survives in manuscript in an old parchment codex at St. Martin’s in Liège, together with the preface of Notger, bishop of Liège, to Werenfrid, abbot of Stavelot, in which these words are read: “I have collected, down to our own times, not only the periods and deeds of St. Remaclus but also those of the other pontiffs of our see, insofar as they could be gathered from anywhere.” Hence it has come about that some ascribe Heriger’s work to Notger. But because that history is attributed to Notger neither by Sigebert nor by Trithemius, nor is it mentioned by Anselm of Liège in his letter to Anno, archbishop of Cologne, nor by Giles, monk of Aulne, in his letter to Abbot Mauricius, I am led to believe that Heriger was the author of that history. Moreover, in the manuscript codex at Aulne Heriger’s name is expressly prefixed to the preface, while Notger’s appears nowhere. Heriger’s History was published at Liège in 1613 through the care of John Chapeaville. He also wrote, in verse, a Life of St. Ursmar, manuscript at Gembloux; and, in two books, the Life of St. Landoald and the account of his translation. That Heriger, too, and not Bishop Notger—whom Molanus ascribes them to in his notes on Usuard for 19 March—was the author of those books is established from an old manuscript Chronicle of Ghent [Col. 0577D], where the following is read under the year 981: “The miracles of St. Landoald and his companions, truthfully made public, were collected at the command of the outstanding pontiff Notger, and were described by Heriger, his teacher and master of music, briefly indeed but with sufficiently discerning and lucid language; and, confirmed by the authority of the bishop himself and the impression of his seal, they were faithfully sent to Wommar, abbot of the monastery of Ghent, and to all the brethren.” Elsewhere, however, the same chronicler of Ghent—under the year 972—seems to make Notger the author of that history, compiled both from ancient books once burned by Northmen and Danes and from the testimony of trustworthy elders. Heriger also left [Col. 0578B] a *Dialogue on the Discord of the Church*, with Adelbold and Heriger as interlocutors; it survives in manuscript at Gembloux.], distinguished in literary learning, wrote the *Deeds of the Bishops [Col. 0577B] of Liège*. In praiseworthy metrical style he wrote the Life of St. Ursmar. He wrote to Hugh a letter [Col. 0578A] concerning certain questions; under his own person and that of Bishop Adelbold he wrote a dialogue on the discord of the Church, on the coming of the Lord. He also gathered against Ratbert [Note: [Col. 0578B] Bertram or Berengar seems to be intended here. Or certainly Sigebert has suffered a lapse of memory.] many writings of Catholic Fathers on the body and blood of the Lord.

CAP. CXXXVIII. Adelbold [Note: [Col. 0578B] Adelbold, a Frisian by nation and noble at home, became bishop of Utrecht after being a cleric of Lobbes. Among other works he wrote, in two books, the Life of Emperor St. Henry, published by Surius. He died in 1027.], formerly a cleric of Lobbes [Note: [Col. 0578B] Therefore, before his episcopate Adelbold was not a monk but a cleric of Lobbes. Students of ecclesiastical antiquity should note that in former times not only monks but also clerics resided at Lobbes, as likewise among those of St. Vedast and St. Amand. The college of clerics or canons of Lobbes certainly had its seat in the church of St. Ursmar, now a parish church, [Col. 0578C] until the year of Christ 1409, when it moved from there to Binche, a town of Hainaut two miles distant from Lobbes. See our notes on the *Form of the Institution of Canons*, written by the Fathers of the Council of Aachen in 816 and published in print at Antwerp in 1638.], became bishop of Utrecht. He wrote the Life of Emperor Henry II and left many monuments of himself to posterity in both kinds of learning.

CAP. CXXXIX. Abbo [Note: [Col. 0578C] Abbo, also Albo, abbot of Fleury in the diocese of Orléans, wrote for Dunstan, bishop of Canterbury, the Life of St. Eadmund or Edmund, king and martyr of the English, published by Surius for 20 November. He also wrote in hexameter verse, for Gozlin, bishop of Paris, two little books *On the Siege of Paris by the Northmen* in the year 886 [ [Col. 0577] These are by another Abbo, monk of St-Germain-des-Prés. See *Patrology*, vol. CXXXII, col. 722.], which Peter Pithou published among the Twelve Contemporary Frankish Writers. He also made an Epitome of the Lives of Ninety-One Roman Pontiffs, from the book of Anastasius, librarian of the Holy Roman Church. It was printed together with the History of the same [Col. 0578D] Anastasius at Mainz in 1602, through the efforts of John Busaeus.], abbot of Fleury, showed how much he could accomplish in both branches of knowledge when he commented on the computus of Victorius. He died a martyr.

CAP. CXL. Aribo [Note: [Col. 0578D] Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, wrote a commentary on the fifteen Psalms of Ascents, as they are called; he died in the year 1030 or the one immediately following. He was distinct from another Aribo, bishop of Freising, who committed to writing the Lives of St. Corbinian and St. Emmeram, bishops of Freising.], archbishop of Mainz, commented on the fifteen Psalms of Ascents.

[Col. 0578B] CAP. CXLI. Burchard [Note: [Col. 0578D] Burchard, bishop of Worms and a Hessian by birth, was a monk of Lobbes and disciple of Olbert, later abbot of Gembloux, when, “with the collaboration,” says Sigebert in his Chronicle under the year 1008, “of his master Abbot Olbert, a man most learned in every respect, he produced a great volume of Canons,” in twenty books, printed at Cologne in 1538, Paris in 1549, and elsewhere [Col. 0579C]. He died in 1025. Burchard was later emulated by Ivo of Chartres and Gratian.], bishop of the city of the Vangiones, called Worms, composed with great diligence the great volume of canons [Col. 0579A] named *Burchard* after him. He authorized it with the testimonies of all authentic councils, the decrees of Roman pontiffs, and the opinions of nearly all Catholic Fathers; from it the decrees of all councils are still authorized.

CAP. CXLII. Olbert [Note: [Col. 0579C] Olbert, fourth abbot of Gembloux and first abbot of St. James among the people of Liège, was born in the village of Lede, on the border of the district of the Sambre. From childhood he was educated in the monastery of Lobbes under the discipline of Abbot Heriger; then he went to Paris, to the monastery of St. Germanus, and devoted himself to study and to the holy religious observance flourishing there. He also heard Fulbert, bishop of Chartres. Finally, he himself instructed Burchard—later bishop of Worms—in sacred letters at Lobbes. He died at Liège in 1148 and was buried in the church of St. James. He wrote a History of the Old and New Testament and several Lives of saints, among them a Life of St. Veronus the confessor, at the request of Count Rainer of Hainaut; it survives in manuscript at Mons among the Franciscans, in the Annals of Jacques de Guyse, and elsewhere.], formerly a monk of Lobbes and abbot of Gembloux, eminent for devotion to human and ecclesiastical learning and for religious zeal, made his name eternal by writing the Lives of holy Fathers and composing chants in honour of saints; and especially because Burchard, bishop of Worms, was brought by his instruction to devote himself to the usefulness of ecclesiastical life, and by Olbert’s effort, voice, [Col. 0579B] and hand, to publish for the common benefit of all that great volume of canons.

CAP. CXLIII. Albert, monk of Metz, wrote for a bishop a History of the deeds of his own time; though brief, it is useful.

CAP. CXLIV. Guido, monk of Arezzo [Note: [Col. 0579D] Guido, monk of Arezzo, in the year 1022 initiated a new and more concise system of music, having invented the six notes which we use today, as Baronius calculates in the *Annals*. But Sigebert, in his Chronicle under the year 1028, reports it there. In this same eleventh century lived Ralph Glaber, listed above by Sigebert in chapter 50 among writers of the sixth century, for what reason I do not know. Glaber was first a monk of St. Germanus at Auxerre and afterwards at Cluny; in five books he wrote for Odilo, abbot of Cluny, a History of the Franks from the year 900—or rather 1000—to the year 1045, in which year he was still living. Glaber, moreover, together with Helgaud, Suger, Rigord, William the Breton, William of Nangis, and other writers on Frankish affairs under the Capetian line of kings, [Col. 0580C] was first brought to light in the Frankfurt edition of 1596 from the library of Peter Pithou.], became renowned in the Church after nearly all musicians. He is to be preferred to his predecessors in this: by his method even boys and girls learn or are taught unfamiliar chants more easily than through a teacher’s voice or through the sight [or use] of some instrument, provided that the six letters or syllables are applied in musical sequence to the six notes which music alone admits, and that these notes are distinguished by the bendings of the fingers of the left hand through the whole diapason; thus the attentive [Col. 0579C] and relaxed raisings and lowerings of the same notes present themselves to eyes and ears.

[Col. 0580A] CAP. CXLV. Chilperic wrote, with commendable subtlety, a book on the method of computation, in the year 1006 [Note: [Col. 0580C] Sigebert discusses the same man in his Chronicle under the year 1005.].

CAP. CXLVI. Egebert [Note: [Col. 0580C] This same Egebert—Eckebert in Trithemius—unless I am mistaken, wrote the Life of St. Amor, confessor of Aquitaine, who rests at Belisia near the city of Tongeren in the diocese of Liège. It survives in manuscript in the monastery of St. Laurence outside the walls of Liège and elsewhere.], a cleric of Liège, wrote in metrical style a book *On Rustic Riddles*, at first brief; but, expanding the course of his argument, he wrote a second and larger book in verse on the same subject.

CAP. CXLVII. Leo of Acrida, archbishop of the Bulgarians, wrote a short booklet through which he spread so much deadly poison that all Greece would have perished from it, unless the force of that poison had been extinguished by the antidote of Roman authority and apostolic faith [Note: [Col. 0580C] Consult Baronius in the *Annals*.].

CAP. CXLVIII. Nicetas [Note: [Col. 0580C] Nicetas Pectoratus, priest and monk of the Studite monastery in the city of Constantinople, wrote a booklet against the Latins *On Unleavened Bread, Saturday Fasts, and the Marriages of Priests*. Canisius published it in volume VI of *Ancient Readings*, together with a letter written by Michael, patriarch of Constantinople, on the same subject, adding the antidote—that is, Cardinal Humbert’s reply to both booklets [Col. 0580D].], monk of Constantinople, surnamed Pectoratus, wrote a book [Col. 0580B] addressed to the Romans, which he entitled *On Unleavened Bread, the Sabbath, and the Marriages of Priests*, defending the Greeks, who offered sacrifice with leavened bread, who observed the Sabbath with the Jews, and who approved the marriage of priests.

CAP. CXLIX. Leo [Note: [Col. 0580D] St. Leo, formerly bishop of Toul in Lotharingia and supreme pontiff, the ninth of that name, wrote to Michael of Constantinople and Leo of Acrida, bishops, an outstanding booklet—or rather letter—against Greek errors. He also wrote various letters to Constantine Monomachus, emperor of the Greeks, and to many others; they are read in the volumes of Councils and in Baronius’s *Annals*, XI. His homilies and sermons were published at Louvain in 1565 and Cologne in 1598. He died in 1054, as Lambert of Aschaffenburg and Baronius calculate, or in the immediately following year, as Wibert relates in his Life of Leo.], formerly bishop of the city of the Leuci, called Toul, and ninth Roman pope of that name, wrote a letter to Emperor Constantine Monomachus, warning him not to allow so many heresies to gain strength in his empire. For the Greeks, like Simonists, sold the gift of God; like Valesians, they promoted even their castrated guests to the episcopate; like Nicolaitans, they permitted marriages to priests; like Donatists, they boasted that the orthodox Church existed in Greece alone; like Severians, they said that the Law of Moses was accursed; like Pneumatomachians, they cut the profession of the [Col. 0580C] Holy Spirit from the Creed; like Nazarenes, they observed Judaism; they forbade infants dying before the eighth day after birth to be baptized; and they forbade women endangered in childbirth or menstruation to receive communion, or, if they were pagans, to be baptized. They rebaptized Latins baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity; and, while themselves sacrificing with leavened bread, they called the Latins “Azymites,” and, closing their churches, persecuted them. Seeking to uproot from Greece such numerous and great heresies, Pope Leo also wrote to Michael, patriarch of Constantinople, reproving him for all these matters and, besides the rest, because he called himself universal patriarch, preferred the Church of Constantinople to the Roman Church, and anathematized the latter in her children. On these matters he also wrote useful letters to all the primatial bishops of Africa, Numidia, Egypt, and Italy [Col. 0581B]. He also wrote on these matters for the Greeks a book in an elegant style, overthrowing their errors with evangelical and canonical testimonies and establishing the faith of the Catholic Church. But if anyone considers the chants composed by him in honour of saints, he will deservedly compare him with Pope Gregory I.

CAP. CL. Humbert [Note: [Col. 0581D] Humbert, Benedictine monk of Toul, was brought to Rome by Pope Leo IX on account of his learning and made cardinal-bishop of Silva Candida. Sent by the same pope to Constantinople in 1054 as legate with Frederick, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church—afterwards Pope Stephen IX—and Peter, bishop of Amalfi, he wrote one book *Against the Calumnies of Michael of Constantinople and Leo of Acrida, Bishops*, and another *Against Nicetas Pectoratus*. These two books appear in Baronius’s appendix to volume XI of the *Annals*, in the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, and in Canisius, volume VI of *Ancient Readings*.], monk of Toul, was brought to Rome by Pope Leo because of his knowledge of letters and ordained cardinal-bishop there. Sent by the same pope to Constantinople to refute Greek heresies, he refuted the writings of Leo of Acrida, archbishop of the Bulgarians. He also refuted the writings of Nicetas Pectoratus and defeated him in the presence of Emperor Constantine to such an extent that [Col. 0581C] Nicetas himself anathematized his own book and cast it into the fire with his own hand. And everything that Humbert said or did there he wrote down, as though in dialogue, under the persons of a Roman and a Constantinopolitan.

CAP. CLI. Paul, whom the legates of the Roman Church used as interpreter at Constantinople, translated from Latin into Greek, with the assistance of his son Smaragdus, everything that Bishop Humbert disputed there or wrote. All these things, by command of Emperor Constantine [Col. 0582A] Monomachus, were deposited in the archive of the Church of Constantinople.

CAP. CLII. Anselm, monk of Rheims, wrote an Itinerary of Pope Leo IX from Rome into Gaul, chiefly in order to make known how great was the authority with which he held synods at Rheims and in other cities; with what subtlety and justice he examined ecclesiastical cases; with what discernment he corrected offenders; and how the power of God cooperated with him. This appeared clearly enough in one case at the Synod of Rheims, when the bishop of Freising acted contumaciously against apostolic authority and suddenly, before the eyes of all, was struck dumb.

### CHAPTER CLIII

Almannus [Note: Adelmannus; in Sigebert, Almanus: formerly scholasticus of Liège, later bishop of Brixen in Italy; once a pupil of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, together with Berengar, archdeacon of Angers. Against that same Berengar he wrote a very learned letter, *On the Truth of Christ’s Body and Blood in the Eucharist*, published at Louvain in 1561 by Johann Ulimmer with Lanfranc and other ancient writers on the same subject, and likewise at Paris and Cologne in the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*], the Grammarian, formerly a cleric of Liège and bishop of Brixen, wrote to Berengar, cleric of Tours, a letter accusing him of having torn himself away from the unity of the Catholic Church by teaching, in speech and writing, that the body and blood of Christ, which are daily offered upon the altar throughout the whole world, are not Christ’s true body and true blood, but a figure and likeness of his body and blood.

On the same matter he wrote a letter to Paul, primicerius of Metz, urging him also to call back their common friend Berengar from this depraved intention.

### CHAPTER CLIV

Berengar [Note: Berengar, archdeacon of Angers, more than once abjured his heresy concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist, and died repentant on the feast of the Epiphany in the year 1088, at the age of ninety. He was buried in the church of St. Cosmas near Tours. Claude Robert reports this in his *Gallia Christiana*, where he treats of the bishops of Angers. Against Berengar wrote Adelmann of Brixen, praised shortly before; Lanfranc of Canterbury; Alger of Corbie; Guitmund of Aversa; and Deodwin, bishop of Liège; their works survive in the *Library of the Ancient Fathers* and elsewhere. Hugh, bishop of Langres, whose work has not, so far as I know, been published, may be added to them. Deodwin was made bishop of Liège in 1048 and ceased to live in 1075. Baronius, however, errs in his account of the year 1035, as do the editor of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers* and others who attribute to Durand, bishop of Liège, the letter written by Deodwin against Berengar. Durand is known to have died in 1025, and thus before Berengar’s heresy was publicly promulgated. The error arose from the single letter D., the initial of both names. Berengar began to spread his heresy about the year of Christ 1035], a man outstanding in the liberal arts and especially in dialectical skill, wrote in a pompous style against Almannus the grammarian and bishop, refusing to acknowledge the benevolence of his correcting friend, but defending his own opinion concerning the mysteries of Christ.

Since many wrote to or against him on this matter, he himself wrote to or against them; and, while abusing dialectical sophisms against the simplicity of apostolic faith, he seems neither to excuse himself nor to edify others, because he obscures what is clear more than he clarifies what is obscure.

### CHAPTER CLV

Lanfranc, dialectician and archbishop of Canterbury, expounded the Apostle Paul; and wherever an opportunity in the passages arose, he sets forth, assumes, and concludes according to the rules of dialectic.

He wrote the praises, triumphs, and deeds of William, count of the Normans, who was the first to seize the kingdom of the English. He wrote invective letters against Berengar of Tours, refuting his writings concerning the body and blood of Jesus Christ. This Berengar was so thoroughly convicted at Rome by Pope Nicholas in a council of ninety-three bishops that he himself kindled the fire with his own hands and burned his writings, swearing that he would no longer say, teach, or write such things.

Yet because, disregarding his oath, he later wrote against the aforesaid synod, against Catholic truth, against the judgment of all the Churches, and specifically against Humbert, cardinal bishop of Rome, Lanfranc answered him; and, alternately placing his own name and Berengar’s, he distinguished their respective arguments. [Note: Honorius IV, 14, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.]

### CHAPTER CLVI

Berno [Note: Berno, formerly a monk of Prüm and abbot of Reichenau, wrote a book *On the Office of the Mass*, or on matters pertaining to the Mass, together with other works on the same subjects, printed at Cologne in 1568, at Rome, and in the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*. In chapter 2 of that book he relates that he was present at the coronation of Emperor Henry II by Benedict VIII in 1014. He also wrote the *Life of St. Ulrich*, bishop of Augsburg, published by Surius under 4 July. He died in 1048], abbot of Reichenau, was eminent in human and divine learning. I pass over what he wrote on human learning, among which stands out his pre-eminent work in musical art on the rules of symphonies and tones; and the fact that, in measuring the monochord, beyond Boethius’s rule—but with the assent of Guido, who is inferior to Boethius—he placed one tone beneath the *tetrachordum hypaton*, and, contrary to the usage of the ancients, usefully inserted the *synemmenon* within that very *tetrachordum hypaton*.

But I shall not pass over what he wrote concerning the fasts of the Four Seasons, concerning whose observance there is disagreement among many. Some, taking account of the times, select days in February, May, or September for the fast of Wednesday and Friday, and end the fast when Saturday falls on the Kalends. Others, without regard to the times, do not fast unless the Wednesday and Friday of the fast, together with Saturday itself, fall in March, June, or October. Many, especially the Germans, authorize such a rite of fasting on the authority of these writings of Berno.

### CHAPTER CLVII

Arnulf the monk, selecting the more suitable maxims from Solomon’s Proverbs, wrote and arranged both their literal and allegorical sense with metrical elegance.

### CHAPTER CLVIII

Marbod [Note: Marbod, bishop of Rennes in Armorican Brittany, was made bishop in 1096; after twenty-seven years he became a monk at St. Albin at Angers, and died in 1123. His letter to R., bishop of Angers, is found in volume II of the *Library of the Fathers*. Hildebert mentions Marbod in letters 80 and 200, as does Geoffrey of Vendôme, book II, letter 2], bishop of Rennes, expounded the *Song of Songs* in full with metrical elegance, embellishing both letter and allegory.

He wrote the Passion of St. Lawrence in verse. [Note: On Eucherius, see Gennadius, chapter 16.] He wrote in verse the Passion of the Thebans, following, as it were step by step, the thought of Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, who had written it in polished prose to Bishop Silvius.

### CHAPTER CLIX

Marianus Scotus [Note: Marianus Scotus wrote three books of Chronicles from the beginning of the world down to the year of Christ 1083; Dodechinus, abbot of St. Disibod, continued them down to the year 1200. It is pleasing to hear Marianus himself speaking of himself in his Chronicle:

“In the year 1028, I, wretched Marianus, was born in sins. In 1052, I, Marianus, left the world. In 1056, I, Marianus, having become a pilgrim for the heavenly kingdom, left my homeland and became a monk at Cologne on Thursday, the Kalends of August. In 1058, the city of Paderborn, with two monasteries, was consumed by fire on the Friday before Palm Sunday. In the monastery there was one named Paternus, a Scottish monk enclosed for many years, who also foretold the conflagration; and, seeking martyrdom in his cell, was burned there. On the Monday after the octave of Easter, leaving Cologne for prayer, I visited that place because of the good things told of his tomb; and thus I came to Fulda with the abbot of Fulda.

“In 1059, I, unworthy Marianus, was ordained priest with Sigfrid, abbot of Fulda, at Würzburg in mid-Lent, on the third Ides of March; and on the Friday after the Ascension, the second Ides of May, I was enclosed at Fulda for ten years. In 1043, Annuchadus, a Scot and recluse, died on the third Kalends of February in the monastery of Fulda. Lights were seen above his tomb and psalmody was heard. I, Marianus Scotus, enclosed for ten years, standing over his feet, daily sang Masses over him.

“In 1069, I, wretched Marianus, by command of the bishop of Mainz and the abbot of Fulda, on the Friday before Palm Sunday, the Nones of April, after ten years of my enclosure, was released from my cell at Fulda, came to Mainz, and was enclosed there for a second time on the feast of the Seven Brothers. In 1086 Marianus Scotus and recluse,” says Dodechinus, his continuator, “died and was buried at St. Martin’s.”], journeying through Gaul for Christ and becoming a monk at Mainz, was enclosed for many years. He wrote a Chronicle from Christ’s birth to the year 1082, demonstrating with remarkable subtlety the error of earlier chronographers, who placed Christ’s birth in such a way that, in their computation, the year of his Passion does not agree with Gospel truth.

Therefore, adding twenty-three years to the year in which earlier writers state that Christ was born, he set in the margin of the page, alternately on one side the years of evangelical truth and on the other the years of the earlier false computation, so that truth and falsehood may be distinguished not only by understanding but also by sight.

### CHAPTER CLX

Henry, formerly scholasticus of Trier and bishop of Vercelli, wrote under the person of Theoderic, bishop of Verdun, to Hildebrand, or Pope Gregory, a book *On the Discord between Kingdom and Priesthood*. He did not rebuke him, but entreated him as an elder and a father; and, with friendly persuasion and, as it were, the feeling of one grieved, he laid before him everything that widespread talk alleged he had done and said against the law of the statutes and the sanctity of religion. [Note: Consult Baronius.]

### CHAPTER CLXI

Anselm [Note: St. Anselm, a native of Mantua, was made bishop of Lucca by Alexander II. Later, when he had withdrawn into a monastery, Gregory VII recalled him to the episcopate. Renowned for holiness of life and miracles, he passed to the world above in 1086. He wrote two books against Guibert, the antipope, defending Gregory VII, the lawful Roman pontiff; these are found in Canisius, volume VI of the *Ancient Readings*. His letters are read in volumes of Councils and elsewhere.
