He rests at Mantua and is entered in the Roman Martyrology on 18 March], bishop of Lucca, a man renowned for literary learning, wrote on the prophet Jeremiah. He composed treatises on the Psalms. An untiring collaborator of Pope Gregory, he wrote for him against Guibert, whom Emperor Henry had placed above him. In a book adorned with testimonies of Scripture, he confirmed the teaching of Gregory VII.

### CHAPTER CLXII

Peter Damian, the seventh levite of the Roman Church, wrote the *Life of Odilo*, the fourth abbot of Cluny. Homilies composed by him in an eloquent style are also found. [Note: Honorius IV, 11, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.]

### CHAPTER CLXIII

Anselm [Note: Anselm, canon in the cathedral basilica of St. Lambert at Liège, wrote for Anno, archbishop of Cologne, the *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*, from the times of Bishop Theodard, who immediately succeeded St. Remaclus, down to his own time—that is, to the death of Bishop Wazo, which fell in 1048. Anselm’s history, together with other works on the same subject, was published at Liège in 1612 through the work of John Chapeaville, vicar-general of Liège. Chapeaville appended to Anselm four ancient authors who proclaimed the life and miracles of St. Lambert: Godescalc, canon of Liège; Stephen, bishop of Liège, mentioned above by Sigebert in chapter 125; Nicholas, canon of Liège; and Renerus, monk of St. Lawrence near Liège. Of these, Godescalc flourished in 770; Bishop Stephen died in 920; Nicholas flourished in 1120; and Renerus lived about 1130], a cleric of Liège, wrote the *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège* and in that book gave a full account of the life of Bishop Wazo, truthfully known to him.

### CHAPTER CLXIV

Franco, scholasticus of Liège, renowned for piety and for learning in both kinds of letters, made known to posterity how great his capacity was in writing. Let lovers of secular learning assess his learning from the book he wrote to Herman, archbishop of Cologne, *On the Squaring of the Circle*, concerning which Aristotle says: “The squaring of the circle, if it is knowable, is certainly not yet knowledge.”

For the sake of that knowable thing, secular philosophers may compare him with others, or even prefer him to them. We praise him because he devoted himself to divine Scripture and wrote several works, including one book *On the Method of Computation* and other works possessed by others. [Note: He was living in 1060.]

### CHAPTER CLXV

Bernard, a monk of Saxon stock, wrote to Harduin, archbishop of Magdeburg, a book against Henry, fourth emperor of that name, in a style indeed eloquent but bitter. Its words alone suffice for everyone to understand how grievous and hateful that emperor was to the Saxons.

### CHAPTER CLXVI

Gunter, monk of St. Amand, wrote the martyrdom of St. Cyriacus in metrical style. [Note: Consult our Belgian Fasti under 16 June.]

### CHAPTER CLXVII

Ivo, bishop of Chartres, wrote to Hugh, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, a letter not very long but strongly supported by canonical and Catholic testimonies, concerning the dissension of kingdom and priesthood and the unprecedented decrees of the Roman Church.

He also wrote very useful letters to various friends and compiled an outstanding volume of canons. [Note: Consult Bellarmine in the *Catalogue* and Baronius in the *Annals*. Francis Juret published Ivo’s letters at Paris with notes.]

### CHAPTER CLXVIII

Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, wrote a book *On the Holy Spirit* against certain Greeks who denied that the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son.

He also wrote the book entitled *Why God Became Man*; another, *On Meditating upon the Essence of Divinity*, which he entitled *Monologion*; and another likewise on the same matter, which he entitled *Proslogion*. In the first is found an example of meditation upon the rationale of faith; in the second, faith seeking understanding. He wrote another book, *On the Incarnation of the Word*, addressed to Pope Urban; another, *On Original Sin and Virgin Conception*; another, *On Truth*; another, *On Free Will*; another, *On the Fall of the Devil*; and another, smaller than the rest, *On the Bread of Sacrifice against the Greeks*.

He also wrote a rather large volume of meditations or prayers, and another book very useful for introducing students to dialectic, beginning: “On Grammar,” and so forth. Those who enjoyed acquaintance with him or his presence say that he wrote many other works as well. [Note: Honorius IV, 15.]

### CHAPTER CLXIX

Bernard, a cleric of Utrecht, commented on the *Eclogues* of Theodulus and elucidated sacred histories and secular fables through allegorical exposition. [Note: See above, chapter 154.]

### CHAPTER CLXX

Theoderic [Note: Theoderic, formerly a monk of Ghent, then abbot of St. Trudo in the diocese of Liège, wrote the Lives of Saints Bavo, Trudo, Rumold, and Landrada, abbess of Bilzen, published by Surius; likewise the Life of St. Amalberga, virgin of Temse, which survives in manuscript in my possession and elsewhere], monk and abbot of St. Trudo, improved the Lives of Saints Bavo, Trudo, and Rumold in a more polished style; and with elegant talent wrote many things in verse, briefly indeed, but commendably.

### CHAPTER CLXXI

Sigebert [Note: Sigebert, monk of Gembloux in Brabant, of the Order of St. Benedict, taught many and wrote many works during his early life at Metz, in the monastery of St. Vincent. He was intimate with Fulcuin, abbot of Lobbes. Having returned to Gembloux, he finally died at an advanced age on the third Nones of October, 1112, and was buried among his brethren.

The reader should note that Sigebert lived in times when Church and Christian commonwealth were greatly disturbed by the conflict between the Roman pontiffs Gregory VII, Urban II, and Paschal II on the one side, and Emperor Henry IV on the other. Consequently Sigebert, following the emperor’s side, was more hostile than was right to the pontiffs. Hence what he wrote against Gregory and Paschal, along with other works, was forbidden reading. Sigebert was refuted by Anselm in his eighth letter, addressed to Abbot William; by Baronius in the *Annals*; and by Bellarmine in the *Catalogue* and in his books of *Controversies*. See also the Prolegomena prefixed by me to Sigebert’s Chronicle, collated with the autograph and printed at Antwerp by the press of Verdussen in 1608. That edition alone is genuine, because free of the trifles and rubbish of Geoffrey of Monmouth, or of Asaph, which are scattered through all other editions], monk of Gembloux:

“While stationed at Metz in my early years, in the church of St. Vincent, I wrote many small works for the instruction of boys. I wrote the Life of Bishop Theoderic, founder of that church and abbey; in it, by way of digression, I celebrated the praise of that city in heroic verse. I wrote the Passion of St. Lucy, who rests there, in Alcaic metre. When some found fault with that prophecy of St. Lucy—‘I announce to you that peace has been granted to the Church of God, Diocletian has been expelled from his kingdom, and Maximian has died today’—I answered them after carefully considering the chronology and the truth of the facts.

“I likewise wrote a sermon in praise of that virgin, in which I set forth in ordered chronological sequence her translations from Sicily to Corfinium, a city of Italy, and from Corfinium to Metz, a city of Gaul. I wrote the Life of King Sigebert, founder of the church and abbey of St. Martin outside the city of Metz.

“After returning to the monastery of Gembloux, I wrote in heroic verse the Passion of the Thebans, our patrons. I wrote the Life of St. Guibert the Confessor, founder of our church at Gembloux; from it I extracted readings in proper order for his feast of deposition. In musical art I fashioned antiphons and responsories for Saints Malo and Guibert. I also wrote the *Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux* and improved in a more polished style the Lives of Saints Malo and Theodard.

“Having first improved the Life of St. Lambert in an especially polished style, I later, at the request of Henry, archdeacon and dean of the church of St. Lambert, adorned it with comparisons drawn from the ancients, following the sequence of events. Yet some prefer and copy more carefully the earlier version, because it is simpler: it is clearer in meaning and more lucid in words.

“At the request also of the aforesaid man, I answered with strong arguments from the Fathers the letter of Pope Hildebrand written to Herman, bishop of Metz, in disparagement of royal authority. I wrote an apology to Henry himself against those who impugn the Masses of married priests. At his request also I answered the letter of Pope Paschal, who declared that the church of Liège, no less than that of Cambrai, was to be destroyed by Robert, count of Flanders.

“Likewise, at his request, I answered the people of Trier concerning the fast of the Four Seasons. They observe the rules of a certain Berno, rules which, according to allegory, seem to them well composed, and they differ from the custom of the people of Liège.

“I rendered Ecclesiastes in heroic verse and expounded it in a threefold miscellaneous work: literally, allegorically, and mythologically. I imitated Eusebius Pamphilus, who was the first among the Greeks to arrange a Chronicle from Abraham’s time. I too arranged, from the point where he left off down to the year 1111, the whole succession of times and events, with such moderation of style as I could command.

“While carefully rereading Bede’s *On Times*, I saw that he censured Dionysius, composer of the cycles, for error, because, by wrongly arranging the years of the Lord’s Passion, he appeared in every respect to contradict John’s Gospel in the Paschal limits. Therefore I judged it fitting, by going further back, to dispel every cloud of error and pour the light of truth upon lovers of truth.

“Marianus Scotus, indeed, a man very eloquent for his age, had undertaken this same task. In weaving his Chronicle from Christ’s birth to the state of his own time, he arranged Christ’s years on one side according to the faith of the Gospel, and on the other according to Dionysius, so that a careful reader might see how far Dionysius strayed from Gospel truth.

“But I, considering that adherents of Dionysius, once they have absorbed his system, do not easily depart from it, weighed the precaution of my little intellect in an even balance. Proceeding between these positions, I gathered together, with their method set down, all the years elapsed from the origin of the world or yet to elapse, according to the Hebrew truth: namely, by lunar cycles, completed in nineteen years, and solar cycles, completed in twenty-eight years; multiplied together, these constitute the great cycle of 532 years. I set out in lines, on either side, the years of Adam, the concurrent epacts, the Paschal limits, and the Sundays of Easter, following the same road as Dionysius, though not in the same tracks. A careful reader will easily discover this if he is inquisitive.

“Because I divided the whole work into ten great cycles, each consisting of 532 years, I gave the book the title *Nineteen-Year Cycle* (*Decemnovennalis*). I also prefixed a prologue in dialogue form, divided into three small volumes, indicating, under the persons of questioner and respondent, the purpose and usefulness of the work and the branch of philosophy to which it belongs, namely physics. I also added useful rules for finding years, limits, and indictions according to its arrangements.

“Imitating Jerome and Gennadius, I wrote this final little book, *On Illustrious Men*, insofar as the knowledge gained by my researches was able to discover.”

## SIGEBERT’S *DEEDS OF THE ABBOTS OF GEMBLOUX* AND *LIFE OF WICBERT*

(Edited by Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. VIII, p. 504.)

## NOTICE

Sigebert, after returning from Metz to his monastery [Note: *Book on Illustrious Men* and *Deeds*, chapter 41], apparently between the years 1060 and 1070 [Note: Namely, before the death of Abbot Mysach in 1071], composed the *Life of Wicbert*, founder of the church of Gembloux, and the *Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux*.

In this undertaking, intending to satisfy his pious and grateful disposition toward the founders and Fathers of the monastery, he committed to memory not only what he himself, as a former pupil of Olbert, had experienced firsthand or learned from elders, but also consulted the ancient records of the monastery, especially the charters witnessing to events [Note: Compare *Deeds*, chapter 20] granted to the abbey of Gembloux by emperors, Roman pontiffs, bishops of Liège, and persons of lesser rank, and preserved in its archive. To give his work greater authority, he incorporated these documents into the book.

He arranged his narrative so that one recognizes a man distinguished by abundant learning and thoroughly conversant with historians [Note: He had by then read Folcuin’s *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*—chapter 13 of the *Life of Wicbert*; chapters 13 and 14 of the *Deeds*—Liutprand, the *Life of Chrodegang*, and the *Life of John of Gorze]; one readily perceives the sequence of events and approves the simple, clear, elegant style.

Both works seem to have been composed at nearly the same time, since in the autograph manuscript the *Life of Wicbert* is followed on the same page by the *Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux*, written in the same hand. The author’s chief purpose in both was to recount the deeds of Abbots Erluin and Olbert.

Regarding Erluin, he declares that he follows an earlier book by the monk Richarius, who lived at Gembloux under Erluin and composed his life in verse for Notger, bishop of Liège. Since part of that book had perished when its leaves were scattered and severed, Sigebert used Richarius’s own words and pieced the remaining fragments together in prose.

The principal part of the book must therefore be considered the Life of Olbert, a man pre-eminent in virtue and learning [Note: *Deeds*, chapter 63]. Sigebert entered the monastery while Olbert was abbot, shaped himself according to his example and instructions, and remained attached to him until his death.

He added only a few remarks concerning Olbert’s successor, Abbot Mysach, who was still living when he wrote the *Deeds*, and he stopped at Mysach’s life; nor did he resume his pen after Mysach’s death. The appearance of the book itself shows this [Note: Folio 39r.], and proves that another writer, a monk of Gembloux, appended the remainder [Note: Chapter 48 and what follows] of Mysach’s Life and the deeds of the following abbots. [Note: That the Lives of Thietmar, Liethard, and Anselm proceeded from the same author is shown not only by the writer’s hand but by his own statements in chapters 59 and 68; contrary to this, chapter 63 attributes Olbert’s Life to Sigebert.]

Since this writer did not wish his own name to disappear entirely, we clearly understand that he was Godescalc. [Note: I had first suspected that Anselm, Sigebert’s continuator in the Chronicle also, was the author; but after reading the manuscript, it is now possible to state the matter with certainty.] As we learn from himself, he was Sigebert’s pupil, “one of the few whom he left behind, after having sent many before him,” and he took up his deceased teacher’s work in such a way that he resolved to add the deeds of Mysach, Thietmar, Liethard, and Anselm.

Accordingly, he first wrote the remainder of Mysach’s Life and the Life of Thietmar; a little later he added the Life of Liethard. Then he appended Liethard’s final acts from chapter 65 onward at almost the same time as he undertook to write the Life of Anselm, who died in 1136. The remainder concerning Anselm, with which he completed the whole work, was not added much later. I therefore judge that the entire work of Godescalc was written within approximately the years 1130–1140.

The epitaph of Lord Sigebert contains, in an initial-letter distich, the name of its author. Following his teacher’s example, Godescalc wrote what he himself had experienced or could derive from authentic documents. For this reason he deserves no less praise than Sigebert, although no memorial of him survives apart from this book, and he comes to life again today only through it.

An excellent manuscript of the book survives.

1) A parchment codex, in small folio or elongated octavo, of 78 leaves. At the beginning one leaf, formerly the first, together with the leaf attached to it—that is, formerly placed between leaves 6 and 7—has perished; at the end several leaves have fallen out, so that only the larger fragment of the original codex survives. Nearly all are quaternions [Note: [Col. 0593C] Leaves 1–6; 7–15, with a leaf cut out between leaves 13 and 14; 16–23; 34–41; 42 ff.; 50 ff.; 62 ff.; 70 ff.], but they bear neither number nor letter signatures, except for the quinions of leaves 7–15 and 24–33, and the duernion of leaves 58–61, containing the little Panegyric. The last leaf, 78, has at its end the title: “HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE OF THE WORK FOLLOWING,” which proves that the work which formerly followed [Note: [Col. 0593C] Perhaps the Life of Theodard.] has been lost. On the first page traces may be seen of a certain charter, written in a twelfth-century hand [Note: [Col. 0593C] It was given to a certain William with his wife and son Hillin.], and a title [Note: [Col. 0593C] “Life of Saint Guibert, published by the reverend doctor Sigebert, monk of the monastery of Gembloux.”] written in the fourteenth century reveals that the earlier portions had already been cut away from the codex at that time.

On leaves 1r–13r are the Life of Wicbert; on leaves 13r–39r, the Deeds of the Abbots, written in Sigebert’s hand [Note: [Col. 0593C] Such as is reproduced in SS., vol. IV, plate I (the corrector’s hand in the Life of Bruno), and vol. VI, plates III and IV.]; Godescalc’s continuation occupies leaves 39r–57r. The Panegyric, for which there seems to be no obstacle to assigning it to the same author, fills leaves 58–61. Leaves 62–78 contain the Life of Maclovius, written by Sigebert at the request of Abbot Thietmar [Note: [Col. 0593D] Since it was composed at roughly the same time as the Life of Wicbert and the Deeds of the Abbots, we conclude Sigebert’s writings here. “HERE BEGINS SIGEBERT’S LETTER TO ABBOT THIETMAR. The Life of the most devout confessor of Christ, Maclovius, who was also called Macutes, had carefully been written in accordance with the truth of ancient history; but because it was arranged without sufficient order, described without sufficient elegance, and moreover excessively confused by barbarisms and solecisms, it lay so deeply covered by the long neglect of oblivion and carelessness that, as though worthy of no one’s hearing, it had already passed from everyone’s memory. But, considering that precious metal does not wholly lose its value, although it lies buried in earth’s rubble or discoloured by the roughness of rust, it pleased your fatherhood, O venerable Father Thietmar, to command my insignificance, after examining the text of the history, to improve it, as far as I could, from the gross accumulation of its faults [Col. 0594C] by some small refinement of language. Since I could not resist the command, I carried out the work laid upon me—not indeed as I wished, but as I was able in the weakness of my ability. For, after the manner of a rustic smith who, by blowing bellows and striking with hammers, draws dross from the raw mass of precious metal, so that it may be rendered readier for the hand of the skilled craftsman, I display to others the brightness of the material, so that anyone wishing to exercise the force of his craftsmanship may find material prepared for his use. Therefore I shall do what seems easy to do: namely, remove superfluities, correct faults, restore order to confused matters; but I shall by no means depart from the truth of the history, so that I may be said to have done nothing new, since I shall seem only to have renewed the old by polishing and rubbing it.” Chapters 7, 8, and 9 contain matters worthy of record: namely, that Maclovius, disciple of Abbot Brendan, sailed with him and nearly one hundred and eighty men in search of the Island of Felicity, and that at last, after seven years spent in wandering, they returned to their homeland [Col. 0594D].].

In the margin beside the final chapters of the Life of Wicbert have been written the numbers I, IIa, IIIa, IIIIa, Va, VIa, VIIa, VIIIa, namely the readings which Sigebert states that he selected in suitable order for Wicbert’s deposition feast [Note: [Col. 0594D] On Illustrious Men.]. Corrections and erasures made by the author’s hand attest the care bestowed upon the book; conversely, recent annotations and corrections testify that the book was handled or read perhaps in the seventeenth century [Col. 0594B].

The codex, long kept at Gembloux and thought to have perished in the fire in which the monastery and its library burned in the seventeenth century, came up for auction at The Hague in 1714 [Note: [Col. 0594D] Listed in the catalogue of Christ. Van Lom and Rutger Albers, p. 128, no. 660; they declared it written in Sigebert’s hand, though Uffenbach would not permit himself to be convinced of this (leaf 1, note in his hand).]. Bought by Uffenbach, it subsequently entered the library of the Leipzig senate, where I examined it in 1825. Now, through the favour of the most distinguished senate, and through the good offices of the eminent Mr Naumann, librarian, it was sent to me, and I transcribed it. Thus the authentic Life of Wicbert and, for the first time, the complete Deeds now appear. Until now, only extracts of the latter, marred by almost unbelievable faults, had been read in Dacherius’s *Spicilegium* [Note: [Col. 0594D] Vol. VI, p. 505 ff., and vol. II, pp. 759–769, folio. The editor never saw the codex, but obtained only those extracts; he was not even certain of the author, whom he thought to be one person, and therefore denied that he was Sigebert. The corruption of the text may already be judged on p. 790 from the torn-apart distichs. Half the book is also missing. The apograph used by Dacherius is now preserved in the Royal Library at Paris, Résidu de Saint-Germain 90, no. 4, 3; see *Archiv*, VIII, 315.].

Since it is possible to examine the autographs of Sigebert and Godescalc, I have produced the edition with the greatest care according to their standard, except that I supplied a few accidental omissions—for example, the accent customarily, though very rarely omitted, added to the preposition *a* by both Sigebert and Godescalc [Note: [Col. 0594D] As in Sigebert’s Chronicle.]. Both authors shorten the word *praeter*, writing *oter*, *praeter*, and *preter*. In other respects they differ from one another [Col. 0595A]: Sigebert consistently writes *Gemmelacum*, *-cunque*, *unquam*, *sed*; Godescalc, *Gemblacum*, *-cumque*, *umquam*, *s*. In Godescalc one may already find *lincolam* used for joining the separated parts of a word, a sign first employed in the twelfth century. Besides, it is worth noting that Sigebert variously spells the same name *Guibertus*, *Guicbertus*, *Wicbertus*, and *Wichbertus*, which I have thought necessary to preserve everywhere.

1*) Copies of our codex are found in the library at Amiens, no. 357, paper, sixteenth century, and at Brussels, no. 10292, paper, sixteenth century. See our *Annals*, vol. IX, pp. 398, 534.

Of the Life of Wicbert, first badly edited by Surius [Note: [Col. 0595B] 23 May.], then corrected and enlarged by Lambecius [Note: [Col. 0595B] *Commentaries*, II.] through the aid of a paper codex of the Imperial Library in Vienna, with some matters concerning Gembloux; and published in 1685 by Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0595B] In *Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict*, fifth century, p. 299.] without new aids, and by Henschenius [Note: [Col. 0595B] *Acta Sanctorum*, May VI, p. 260.] using the codices of Korsendonk, Utrecht, and Trier, I have further employed the following aids:

[Col. 0595B] 2) The codex of the Imperial Library at Vienna, among the ecclesiastical historians, no. 106, now no. 490: parchment, large octavo, twelfth century. I examined it in 1843, and now our Wattenbach has transcribed it with all possible diligence. Formerly, perhaps in the fifteenth century, it belonged to Saint Maximin’s at Trier. It contains the Life of Wicbert, carefully written but without chapter summaries; then a little work on his elevation, Sigebert’s prologue to the miracles of Saint Wicbert, a vision of the same Sigebert together with Wicbert’s miracles, Guibert the Younger’s account of the burning of the monastery of Gembloux, and, following the text on the earlier conflagration, the passage from Sigebert of Gembloux’s continuation as printed in our [Col. 0596A] sixth volume of the *Scriptores*, p. 385 (above, col. 239). On leaf 19 follows Sigebert’s Life of Saint Maclovius [Note: [Col. 0595B] Bound today in the same cover is another thirteenth-century codex, containing the Life of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris.]. The Miracles, worthy to be published for the first time by means of this book, appear to agree with it.

2b) The Korsendonk codex, used by Henschenius to correct Surius’s text, omitted the letter of Erluin appended to the Life of Wicbert; after the history of the elevation, it adds only chapter 3 of the Miracles by way of appendix. It is now untraced.

3) Vienna, Ecclesiastical History no. 128, now 3469, formerly the Ambras codex, presented by the monks of Gembloux to Emperor Maximilian I [Note: [Col. 0595B] According to the epigram published by Lambecius, Kollar, *Analecta*, vol. I, p. 933.]: paper, quarto, written about 1500, first brought to notice by Lambecius [Note: [Col. 0596B] Kollar printed certain portions from it, *Annals*, I.]. It contains the Life of Wicbert, omitting Erluin’s letter; extracts concerning the elevation [Note: [Col. 0596B] P. 917.]; the diplomas of Otto I and Benedict VII [Note: [Col. 0596B] P. 920.]; and, on leaf 21, the account of the burning [Note: [Col. 0596B] P. 926.], together with, on leaf 24, a note [Note: [Col. 0596B] P. 931.] from the continuation of Sigebert of Gembloux. Our Wattenbach has made the book available for our use.

[Col. 0596B] To it is added:

3b) The Utrecht codex, which abridges the history of the elevation. It was in Henschenius’s hands but is now untraced.

4) The codex of Saint Maximin at Trier, used by Henschenius, provided the Life of Wicbert without Erluin’s letter. It is now in the city library of Trier, no. 1151, vol. II, of the great parchment legendary, thirteenth century; cf. our *Annals*, VIII, 600.

5) The codex used by Surius for his edition [Note: [Col. 0596B] Other codices containing the Life of Wicbert by Hersfeld or by Guibert the Younger, and indicated in our *Annals*, do not concern our purpose.] is now untraced, to no disadvantage to our edition, which must without doubt rest on the autograph. Therefore we have said that readings of the remaining codices derived from it should be cited only rarely.

# DEEDS OF THE ABBOTS OF GEMBLOUX

[Col. 0595]

HERE BEGINS THE LITTLE BOOK ON THE DEEDS OF THE ABBOTS OF GEMBLOUX.

[Col. 0595C] 1. Richarius, Erluin’s monk, wrote in verse the Life of Erluin, the first abbot of Gembloux, addressed to Notger, bishop of Liège; but we do not know how it happened that, after the sheets were scattered and cut apart, it disappeared from everyone’s memory. Therefore we, gathering together as it were the pieces of a torn garment and sewing together whatever we have found written about him wherever it may be, have made it cohere, at least, as the structure of one little body. Therefore, lest the beginning of our account appear to waver through the uncertainty of some conjecture, let the words of Richarius himself be laid as a firm foundation [Note: [Col. 0595] Here remains the remnant of the cut-out leaf; but what it contained is not clear, unless one supposes that the first page was blank and the other was filled with the title of the book and the preface now found on leaf 13r. Since this seems by no means probable, I incline rather to hold that, while the book was being made, a single piece of parchment lacking its other side was used.].

[Col. 0596C] 2. The venerable Erluin, then, instructed in literary learning through the teaching of his own father, when he saw that nothing of profit was being done in the present world, began his still unformed desire to burn within him; he strove, laying aside the trappings of a slippery life, voluntarily to join the phalanx of cenobites. Indeed, together with Lord Wichpert, a servant of God, he vigorously undertook the building of the walls of the monastery of Gembloux; and by Wichpert’s assistance, as is clearer than daylight, there was gathered no small company of monks and boys living together in the Lord. For he proved welcome to all, distinguished in charity, [Col. 0597A] fervour, and cheerfulness, toward visitors and crowds of the poor. He knew how to render due recompense according to merits, to unfold the depths of mysteries to the simple, and to be shrewd in resolving and advancing arguments. Vigorous and steadfast against the storms of the malicious, unwilling to abase his spirit amid adversity, sober amid the prosperity of peace. Love and fear abounded among his subjects; doctrine gave fragrance among his pupils. Yet he whom no adversities could move, although shaken and tossed by bitter troubles, strove continually to climb by the steps of virtues to the realms of heaven. For he knew that calm circumstances do not make a person happy; rather, a mind conscious of its own rectitude shines more brightly the more it is worn down. The more the pleasures of this unstable world flourish in their springtime [Note: [Col. 0597] *ern.* corrected from *ern.* by a recent hand.] and draw themselves out in wide-ranging courses [Col. 0597B], the more they enter the inner chambers of Tartarean night; and, when the light is taken away, they fall into deadly, destructive ruin.

Indeed, though the above-mentioned and most praiseworthy patron was shut within the enclosure of the monastery and hidden from the world, yet, flourishing in heaven like a star pouring forth brilliance, powerful alike in word and deed, he shone everywhere. To monks and to gatherings of clerics he showed with all his strength, though celibate, the pattern of a life borne above the stars; and he exhorted in many ways those called from the vale of night to the fellowship of the heavenly Jerusalem, that they might strive to climb the paths of light by the steps of virtues. Crowned with the flowers of such pursuits, sowing the seeds of everlasting life in human hearts, and instructing innumerable companies of people by his own example, he taught them to despise the world’s harmful things and to embrace the saving purpose of life.

3. The aforesaid writer, in the very preface of his account, set forth these rudiments of the life and conversion of Abbot Erluin by anticipation; at the opening of his text he also immediately indicated the time when Erluin flourished, and confirmed the virtue of his deeds more openly by repeating it. He began thus:

> For a time he was in King Otto’s court,  
> A mirror to those on earth, a light and image of God.  
>   
> But when, devoted, he received the teachings of faith,  
> He strove to follow the Lord with a sincere heart.  
>   
> How patient, how gentle, how greatly kind  
> He continually was—who could recount it?  
>   
> [Col. 0597D] Living peaceably, he softened furious hearts,  
> Calling them from savagery to the ways of peace.  
>   
> Gentle in speech, modest with remarkable gravity,  
> He was neither harsh, fierce, nor violent.  
>   
> To all he was mild, gracious, devout, and kind—  
> Pleasing, sweet-spoken, compassionate, and good.  
>   
> Whomever he saw unhappy, sad, or grieving,  
> He aided with a father’s affection,  
>   
> Soothing sorrowing hearts by gentle speech.  
> He checked anguish [Note: [Col. 0597] At first, perhaps *expressit*, “pressed out”?], and bestowed glad joys.  
>   
> [Col. 0598A] How sparing he was in drink and food  
> The approved life of this holy man shows.  
>   
> He held hunger in check with food so scant  
> That it was restrained rather than satisfied;  
>   
> A little water removed the heat of thirst,  
> Not so much extinguishing it as leaving it cooled.  
>   
> Singing this upon his lips and turning it over in his heart:  
> That man does not truly live by bread alone.  
>   
> Rather the mind is fed by the power of the word, from which  
> Life receives the joys of everlasting light.  
>   
> Accustomed often to pass sleepless nights, he struck  
> Heaven’s stars with devout tears.  
>   
> With wakeful care he fitted strong reins,  
> Compelling his subdued limbs to yield to the spirit,  
>   
> So that purity of heart and the heat from above might [Col. 0598B]  
> Drive away the flames produced by the fire of the flesh.  
>   
> And so that his mind might remain continually suspended upon heaven,  
> And, though set upon earth, might already be above its heights,  
>   
> He kept meditation on the heavenly word upon his lips,  
> Hungering for justice, thirsting for justice.

4. Not merely initiated into these principles of life, but trained even to perfection, he lived as praiseworthily as possible in the habit of the clerical order [Note: [Col. 0597] *Laudabilis* corrected, as in the text.]. But because the Lord himself is the portion of inheritance for clerics, according to the name of those chosen into the Lord’s lot [Note: [Col. 0597D] That is, κλῆρος, “lot; clerical order.”], he earnestly sought that the lines of inheritance might fall to him in pleasant places. Therefore, advancing from virtue to virtue, he ascended from the degree of the canonical rule to the height of monastic life. There he lived no differently from [Col. 0598C] the life which he taught others to live; by his own example he drew them to take up the yoke of the same purpose, knowing, according to the Lord’s saying, that whoever breaks the Lord’s commandments and teaches others to break them shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5:19). Accordingly, being great in the kingdom of heaven through both doing and teaching good—that is, in the present Church—he was rightly called great. So highly commended everywhere by the manifold uprightness of his character, he was held worthy of reverence by all, and in every respect worthy of imitation by those who sought the fear of God.

Many, too, whom secular power adorned judged him worthy of their friendship, because in him reverence for holiness stood out, prudence in counsel flourished, and singular grace for winning souls to God had been divinely bestowed on him. To this, among other things, divine providence [Col. 0598D] also added the friendship of Wichpert, most noble in the world and most devout before God. Bound together by the indivisible bond of mutual charity, they wished one thing and refused one thing in the Lord; and where there was such a devout inspiration of unanimity, no conspiracy of opposition could enter at all.

But Erluin certainly believed that much was lacking to him, since he alone had withdrawn his foot from worldly vanity, while the other half of his soul—namely, the most devout Wicbert—still remained fixed in the mire of the worldly deep. Therefore, desiring truly and perpetually to enjoy the aforesaid friend Wichpert in the Lord, he burned with all his heart’s desire that he might win him for the Lord; and he eagerly sought to turn to the salvation of Wichpert’s soul all the grace of friendship which he could wield so effectively in his friend’s mind. Nor did he cease until, seizing with a strong hand the man more tightly embedded in the pit of worldly misery and the mud of secular power, he drew him out and put a new hymn of divine praise in his mouth. Thereafter he was a vigorous instructor to him in carrying out the whole course of his life, a faithful and prudent counsellor, and a ready helper when circumstances required. At his urging, Wichpert built a basilica for God, Saint Peter, and Saint Exuperius; he built workshops suitable to the cloisters of monastic religion [Note: [Col. 0599] The *s* has now been erased.]; [Col. 0599B] he assigned his possessions to God by hereditary right; he gathered there brothers fit for the continual service of God; and he obediently ordered himself, his household, and all his possessions according to God’s will.

Recognizing, therefore, that this man had been sent by God in his own time to win souls, and having well experienced that all his paths were directed by the Lord, the aforesaid Wichpert gave unceasing thanks to the Godhead for the heavenly aid bestowed upon him. Thus guided by saving counsel, he submitted himself wholly to Erluin’s instruction and chose and set him over himself and the community of his brothers as abbot, so that, laying aside every burden of worldly concern, he himself might attend more securely and intently to the purpose of the contemplative life.

5. Thus Erluin, the man memorable for his life [Note: [Col. 0599] Elluinus in the codex.], accepting not the honour but the burden of monastic government, began to labour with still greater fervour in the pursuits of regular discipline, because he knew that he would render account to God not only for himself, but also for the reckoning of those subject to him. It is unnecessary to speak at length in setting forth the condition of his life, since it is certain that he did nothing except what was pleasing in the sight of the true Judge. Nor is there doubt that one who pleased God so freely [Note: [Col. 0599] *Gratuito* corrected to *gratuite* in the codex.] through the eye of good intention also pleased God’s lovers through the zeal of good action; and one loved and revered by the good was, unsurprisingly, suspect and opposed to God’s adversaries [Note: [Col. 0599] *Contrarius*, “opposed,” in the codex.].

Therefore, caring inwardly for the salvation of souls and outwardly attending to the needs of bodies, he provided, as a prudent [Col. 0599D] and faithful householder, for the welfare of both the inner and outer person. Knowing that the insolence of secular power is accustomed to oppose ecclesiastical peace, he caused all that blessed Wichpert had assigned by legal testament to the Church of God committed to him to be confirmed in perpetuity by the sanction of imperial and apostolic authority. It will not be burdensome to insert those charters here, so that we may commend them firmly to the memory of posterity. The imperial charter is as follows:

6. In the name of the Lord God and eternal Saviour. [Col. 0600A] Otto, by favour of divine clemency king of the Lotharingians and Franks. Whatever is done by venerable and God-fearing men of the German peoples under the rule of our empire and the providential direction of God’s religion, we judge should be confirmed by our decrees, so that by our guarantee and protection it may be defended against the assaults of attackers [Note: [Col. 0599] *In* added in the margin.].

Therefore let the assembly of the faithful know that a certain Wichpert, withdrawing from the secular tumults of this life and despising transitory things in order to exchange them for eternal ones, turned to the rule of monastic life, considering with sincere affection of mind how, according to the means available to him, the service of the divine majesty might be increased by his own efforts. He immediately began to build a basilica at the place called Gembloux, in honour of the holy Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ. When his grandmother, named Gisla, saw her most dear grandson Wichpert aforesaid inflamed with the fervour of such desire, she conveyed to the same grandson by legal transfer hereditary properties for the support of building that monastery of Gembloux—properties which her husband, named Rothingus, had given her as a marriage portion—in the counties of Lomme and Darnau: namely, the estate of Gembloux with all belonging to it; likewise, in the same district, the estate called Bufiols with its appurtenances; and in the estate of Asnatgia, whatever he held by right, or those whose names we have endeavoured to record here: Robert, Angerus, Fulcold, Emmo, and Hericindis, except half a *mansus* which he gave to his sister for the salvation of his soul. And in the same district, the estate called Salvenerias with its appurtenances; one *mansus* which he bought, called Ruoz; and another fiscal *mansus* at the place called Vilers, formerly attached to the altar of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles.

Likewise, in the district of Asbain [Note: [Col. 0599D] Hasbania.], near the estate of Herines, one *mansus*, which Rothingus and his wife bought. Finally, when the most devout Gisla aforesaid saw with pious regard the rule of monastic life being multiplied, inflamed by divine ardour of true faith, she gave to her most beloved grandson, the oft-mentioned Wichpert, under the same gift, all that her aforesaid husband Rothingus had legally given as a marriage portion in the county of Wastenac: namely, the estates Naslei, Corbeis, Avoncurt, and Curceles; one *mansus* attached to the estate called Romenei; the estate called Molins; the wood called Boisotgis; [Col. 0600D] and the estates Ailant and Urei; one *mansus* in the estate of Ailant; one mill on the river Fontlaine in the county of Laon; and a certain oven in the city called Sens, paying annually thirty solidi in coin. Also the estates of Herhard and Caderaita. Likewise, in the county of Étampes, the estate called Maisons and the estate of Algeldi.

After these things, as the mercy of divine inspiration increased more and more in the oft-mentioned Gisla, seeing the company of monks multiplied and devoting herself to divine service, she gave also, in addition to what we have already noted, from her own inheritance in the county of Meaux, at the estate called Masuic, a certain portion of land and a share in ships, paying annually five solidi in denarii. In the same county, the estate called Biettine, in which there are a church, our half-share, a demesne *mansus*, a mill, a *camba*, and fishing rights. In the county of Reims, the estate called Molivort with its appurtenances; and, in a certain estate in the same county called Bergam, an excellent vineyard on the river Rim.

Meanwhile the aforesaid lord Wichpert, making legal transfers from the property inherited from his father and mother, gave whatever rights he seemed to possess outside the community of his brothers, in the name of God, our Saviour, and Saint Peter, key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, to the brothers living under regular discipline in the same place of Gembloux, whom God’s mercy had gathered there: namely, in the county of Brabant, at the place Melin, a church, a demesne *mansus* with its appurtenances, a *camba*, a mill, and Arnulf’s cultivated land; ten *mansi* of Lietzinis, which his mother alone, with her brother Oilbold, legally conveyed to her most dear son Wichpert; an island in the same estate; and, in the same district, half the estate of Putiau and half of Beurene. In the county of Darnau, he gave half the estate called Curtils, half the estate called Walaham, and half of Wasmont in the district of Asbain.

Indeed, in this matter he had as teacher and patron a certain venerable man, Erluin, [Col. 0601C] who himself changed the canonical rule under which he lived to the monastic life. The aforesaid Wichpert, after the church and cloister buildings which they had constructed together had been built, chose this man outright as his abbot, and entrusted himself and all the monks whom he had summoned to his governance, trusting himself to Erluin rather than to himself.

Therefore, because we ought to assist good men so that they may be able to be defended by our protection, by royal magnificence and the force of our authority we confirm whatever he bestowed upon that church at Gembloux, and whatever may thereafter, with God’s assent, be granted through the generosity of venerable men. No faithless person or any of his heirs may dare in any rashness to infringe it; rather, it shall remain always unshaken [Note: [Col. 0601] *Maneat*, “may remain,” corrected to *permaneat*, “may remain permanently.”]. Let them have the power, as they have requested of us, to elect a regular abbot and an advocate, either in that place or wherever seems better to them, who shall hold the properties given there under our law or under the protection of our counts. By the same authority of my command they are granted the power to build a castle, so that the pledges of the saints deposited there in worthy honour may be protected against false Christians or pagans [Col. 0602A], and those serving God may be protected from every adversity. No king succeeding us shall ever dare to demand from that place any service except the duties of prayers; released from every burden of subjection [Note: [Col. 0601] *Honore*, “honour,” corrected to *onere*, “burden.”], it shall be established in the perpetual protection of kings.

Nor shall any bishop, in whose diocese the place is situated, exercise any power against the abbot’s will; nor hold a synod; nor perform any act whatever, except only to ordain monks of that abbot. After the abbot’s death [Note: [Col. 0601] *Mortem* corrected to *mortemque*, “and after death.”], when summoned, the bishop shall, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and with the counsel of the monks and other neighbouring persons who fear God, bless the abbot chosen by command of the king; and, receiving no payment for any service except the established allowance of bread from Saint Saviour, he shall return [Col. 0602B] to the condition of his own see. And because the monastery lies under our dominion, we permit the abbot to appoint from among his own people whatever chancellor he wishes. Likewise, [we grant] a market, the striking of coinage, and material [Note: [Col. 0601] A recent hand adds: “for making [it].”]. Nor shall any count or royal envoy exercise any authority within the circuit of that abbey without the permission of the abbot and advocate. The same place shall be free from every toll; they shall pay no tax in city, castle, estate, upon waters, at bridges, or anywhere in our empire. And in times to come that place shall be protected by the rule and defence of kings, so that both we and succeeding kings may be protected by their prayer.

Furthermore, so that this may remain valid and unshaken in succeeding times, we have ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring and confirmed it below with our hand.

The sign of Lord Otto, most serene king. Brun, chancellor, in place of Archchaplain Fridurik, have recognized it.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October. Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 946, indiction 1 [Note: [Col. 0601] In another hand in an erased place.], the eleventh year of Lord Otto. Done at Liège. (S. R.) [Note: [Col. 0601] The diploma is written in such a manner that the original seems to have been before the writer’s eyes. The monogram and recognition sign are written in red.].

7. The charter of apostolic authority is as follows:

+ Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God [Note: [Col. 0601] “IN PERPETUITY” was first written and then erased.], to the religious and venerable abbot [Note: [Col. 0601] Thus in the codex.] of the monastery of the holy Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, and Saint Peter, newly established there, and to his successors in perpetuity. Since it is incumbent upon us, with great solicitude, to keep watch over all the churches of God and devout places [Note: [Col. 0601] Marked for deletion.], lest they suffer loss through any necessity, but rather receive the resources of their proper benefit, it is fitting for us, with the whole integrity of our pastoral mind, especially to secure the integrity and stability of such venerable places and diligently to confer there assistance for their benefit. Thus, what we know we have bestowed upon venerable places for the honour of the holy name and for the praise and glory of the divine majesty of our almighty God [Col. 0603A] may be acceptable to him, and from his most abundant mercy a worthy reward for such a pious work may be bestowed upon us in the heavenly citadels.

Therefore, because you have requested of us that, for love of almighty God and of Lord Otto, most excellent emperor and our beloved son, we should grant and confirm to you the aforesaid monastery, built in honour of the holy Saviour and Saint Peter, with all movable and immovable property which seems to lie beneath and belong to that monastery—both *mansi* and also castles, estates, and hamlets, both those now present and those which shall be until the end—situated in the place called Gembloux: we grant and confirm it by apostolic authority, so that no abbot from another monastery shall be appointed there. Rather, the servants of God living according to the Rule of Saint Benedict shall have authority to elect an abbot from their own congregation. The abbot shall be adorned with the privileges and insignia of the Apostolic See, so that, established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authorship we serve, he shall not be subjected to the jurisdictions of any other church.

Accordingly, we forbid a bishop of any church to possess any jurisdictional authority in the aforesaid monastery, except that he may have permission only to confer blessing. We decree by apostolic censure and by the authority of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, under the attestation of divine judgment and by strong and most severe prohibitions of anathema, that no successor of ours among the popes [Col. 0603C], nor any other person, great or small, shall ever presume to remove or alienate anything from the goods or possessions belonging to that monastery. If anyone—though we do not believe it—whether a great or small person, should in wicked audacity attempt to act against this our apostolic privilege, let him know that he is bound in the bond of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and condemned with all the impious to the eternal punishment of fire. But whoever observes this command shall abundantly obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from the most merciful Lord God.

Written by the hand of Boniface, notary, regional official, and scriniary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of March, indiction eleven. Fare well. + Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, through the hand of Stephen, bishop and librarian [Col. 0603D] of the holy Apostolic See, in the ninth year of the pontificate of our most holy lord Pope Benedict VII, in the sixteenth year of the reign of our lord Otto, great and peaceable emperor crowned by God, in the above-written month and indiction eleven (A.D. 988).

8. The aforesaid founder of the monastery of Gembloux bought half of the church in the estate of Biettine. He had conveyed the other half, which had been his own, to our church, as is evident from the text of this charter:

+ Let everyone possessed of the fear of God know that Lord Wichpert, devoted to God, having relinquished secular things [Col. 0604A] in exchange for eternal ones, did what was pleasing to God. At the command of his most illustrious abbot Erluin, to whose rule he had entrusted the whole place, he obtained for an ecclesiastical price, in the district of Meaux, the half of the church which he did not hold [Note: [Col. 0603] Applied by a recent hand, as are several other words.]. For that aforesaid church was held jointly by our house and a certain nobleman, Lambert. Having received the price, as we have said above, this man consecrated to God conveyed the payment and sought the remaining part of the church, in the presence of Lambert’s son Ansfrid. For Lambert himself handed it over to the advocate, and so confirmed it that it could in no way be altered for ever. And lest this transfer should ever be set aside, Lambert himself affixed his sign to the charter drawn up concerning it.

9. Charter concerning the estate in the village of Dorp, which a certain Fulquinus gave to Saint Peter and caused the transaction itself to be committed to writing for the remembrance of posterity.

Whoever possesses well the goods acquired in the present age possesses best of all when, from earthly and perishable things, he purchases eternal ones for himself. Therefore I, Fulquinus, in God’s name, with the counsel and encouragement of the most gracious Bishop Farabert, for the salvation of the soul of Bishop Richarius of blessed memory, and likewise of Farabert himself; moreover for the salvation of my own soul, and of my sons and brothers, and also for the benefit of Oila’s salvation, give and grant in perpetuity to the church of the holy Mother of God Mary, of blessed Peter the Apostle, prince of the apostles, and of Saint Exuperius, at the place called Gembloux, over which the distinguished Abbot Elluinus is known to preside [Note: [Col. 0603] thus c.], [Col. 0604C] a certain estate of my right in the district of Brabant, in the place called Dorp: together with half a church, one *camba*, sixteen manses, and a certain man named Iser; and with all appurtenances there, houses and buildings, fields, lands both cultivated and uncultivated, woods, meadows, common pastures and rights of way, waters and watercourses, movables and immovables, dependencies, livestock—all things, and everything whatsoever in that place appears to be our possession or lordship, property surveyed and unsurveyed, entire and complete, whether from allod [Note: [Col. 0603] “allodium” written above, or “alod” c.] or from purchase or from any other acquisition—which is known to have come to us there.

From our right and lordship we now give, hand over, and confirm forever in every respect to the aforesaid monastery, by this charter of donation, or by the rod and *andelagum*, for the use of the saints [Col. 0604D] mentioned above, from the present day onward. This is on the condition that the superiors of the aforesaid monastery shall from this day have, hold, and possess it, and shall have full and most secure power in every respect, Christ granting it, to do whatever they wish with it.

And if anyone hereafter—which I do not believe will happen—if I myself, God forbid, or any of my heirs, or any outside person, should presume to oppose or challenge this charter of donation and should not withdraw from doing so, let him be excommunicated and cut off from the thresholds of the holy Church of God [Col. 0605A]; and let him moreover render account for it on the day of dreadful judgment. To the person against whom he brings the suit, let him be compelled to pay one hundred ounces of gold and three hundred pounds of silver; and let him by no means be able to vindicate what he claims. But may this present donation, confirmed by my hand and, at my request, by the hands of worthy men whose names or signs are entered below, and supported by stipulation, remain unshaken for a long time.

The mark of Goderannus, advocate. The mark of Fulquinus and of the others. King Otto. Duke Cuno. Bishop Farabertus. Aletrannus, chancellor.

10. An agreement was reached between the venerable Abbot Erluinus and a certain Ermenfridus concerning an exchange of possessions. How it was made is shown by the charter drawn up concerning it.

[Col. 0605B] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity and of the Savior of the whole world. Whatever is seen to be diminished while something else is received in increase causes no loss, but rather brings great benefit to the soul. It pleased the venerable abbot of the holy church of Gembloux, named Erluinus, and a certain faithful servant of Christ called Ermenfridus, to exchange certain properties with one another; and so they did.

Therefore let it be known to all faithful members of the holy Church of God that the aforesaid Abbot Erluinus gave, with firm security, to the aforesaid faithful servant of Christ, Ermenfridus, a certain church in the village called Agioniscurta, in exchange for a village lying in the county of Asbania, called by its inhabitants Steria-monticula. From [Col. 0605C] this village he conveyed to Saint Peter, prince of all the apostles, and to Saint Exuperius, glorious martyr, in the aforesaid monastery of Gembloux, under most reliable witnesses, four manses in exchange for the aforesaid church, one for the salvation of his soul, and three in return for eight pounds of silver, with all things belonging to the same place: namely servants, cultivated lands, woods, lands cultivated and uncultivated, meadows, waters, and watercourses.

This exchange was made by the aforesaid Abbot Erluinus and his spiritual kinsman Ermenfridus, together with Ermenfridus’s wife Reinsede, on this condition: if anyone, at the devil’s prompting, should ever wish to destroy this charter of our exchange, let him be anathematized with every curse and excommunicated, unless before sunset he returns to repentance and groans over the fault of his evil intent. Done in the village of Namur, on the third Ides of April, in the year 961 of the Lord’s incarnation, in the fourth indiction, in the reign of the most pious King Otto. King Otto. Duke Cuno. Bishop Farabertus. Count Rotbertus. Aletrannus, chancellor.

11. At that time Bruno, archbishop and uterine brother of King Otto, was guardian of the kingdom of the Lotharingians. There was no duke; but in the duke’s place ruled an antichrist, hostile to God and to good men: namely Cuno, persecutor of the highest King in his own king, Otto, whom he had chosen. Nor is it at all surprising that he persecuted a human king, since he did not fear to oppose the heavenly King at Gembloux, taking from Him [Col. 0606A] a certain village called Sotheia. Having plundered it, he gave it to Boso, adding to the measure of his crime two men of the aforesaid place, namely Franco and Hubold. After carrying off the goods, they took no small booty: oxen and cows, one hundred pigs, besides goats and sheep, bees, and a sufficient quantity of land, the number of which is entirely unknown.

While this matter was underway, the venerable Abbot Erluinus, ruler of those dwelling in the aforesaid place, sought the mercy of the most serene king at his residence called Franconefort; and what he had wickedly lost, he recovered through lawful and royal command. Yet he was never able to recover the booty seized by hostile men. At that time Baldricus held the pastoral government of the church of Tongeren [Note: [Col. 0605D] Thus c., in place of *Tungrensis*.], [Col. 0606B] while Ansfridus, kinsman of our lord Wichpertus, exercised the office of advocate in the frequently mentioned place of Gembloux.

12. Concerning this village of Sotheia, the same venerable Abbot Erluinus made a grant with Goderannus, as the subscription of this charter shows:

May Christ everywhere preserve, by divine power, those whom true love keeps joined and united.

Therefore, whoever desires lawfully to enjoy intact and unblemished the fruits of sweetness and love arising from the benefit given him by God should strive, according to his ability, to increase that very benefit. For giving and receiving, as the testimonies of Scripture prove, are known to be most pleasing and most pacifying. Knowing this truth to be certain, the venerable Erluinus, [Col. 0606C] abbot of the monastery of Gembloux, and a distinguished man, Goderannus, advocate of the aforesaid place, determined between themselves to confer certain properties by way of grant; and they did so, united by no slight bond of affection.

At the request of the nobleman Goderannus, the aforesaid abbot gave him the village called Soteia in the county of Darnau, with all that belonged to it: namely the demesne holding, a church free from land-service and subject nowhere, a mill, and a *camba*. This church renders each year two offerings—that is, two sextaries of wine, two capons, and one modius of oats. The mill renders twenty modii, in grain and malt; and the *camba*, over a full year, [Col. 0606D] one hundred eminae of ale. There are also sixty-seven bonuaria of arable land, a considerable extent of meadow, fishing rights in the waters and their courses, woodland sufficient to fatten two hundred pigs, with outlets and returns, and the household belonging to the aforesaid place, forty-two persons in all, some of whom are bound to every sort of service. But if they are permitted to withdraw themselves from this condition of servitude, each must pay twelve denarii annually. This is the grant of the most excellent and God-worthy Abbot Erluinus.

In return, the distinguished Goderannus gave twenty bonuaria of arable land, likewise woodland sufficient to fatten three hundred pigs, and everything belonging to it within and without. [Col. 0607A] This exchange by grant was made on the condition that, so long as the aforesaid distinguished Goderannus lives, he shall hold and possess what he gave and what he received under the third hand: namely, that of his wife Adelendis and of one son only, Ermenfridus. After the death of these three, both portions shall pass to the place mentioned above, which shall hold them by right forever. Moreover, lest this grant be in any way disturbed or broken by any of these persons, it has been confirmed by the testimony of worthy men.

Done in the monastery of Gembloux, in the year 964 of the Lord’s incarnation, the eleventh indiction, and the second year of the reign of Lord Otto.

[Col. 0607B] 13. But let us return to the purpose of the work and briefly set forth what sorts and how great persecutions the religious man Erluinus endured, though he too was prepared to undergo martyrdom for the love of God. Abbot Fulquinus did not pass this over in silence in the little book which he wrote on the deeds of the abbots of Lobbes. Yet anyone who carefully examines the purpose with which he wrote will clearly understand that he did indeed recount the truth of what happened, but interpreted the cause of the event more from emotion than from fact.

14. This Erluinus, worthy of the friendship of all good men, as one usefully capable of gaining it and faithfully diligent in preserving it, was joined in a singular friendship with Count Raginerus, who because of the length [Col. 0607C] of his body was surnamed Longicollus, “Long-neck.” Distinguished in noble birth and power, he then ruled over the people of Hainaut [Note: [Col. 0607] *no* deleted.]. He was the uncle of Baldricus, first bishop of Liège; and because by his power he supported his nephew the bishop in all things, he received the abbey of Lobbes as a benefice.

It was astonishing that a man who, through the tyranny of secular power, was feared throughout the empire willingly obeyed the wholesome counsels of the venerable Erluinus and, when he heard him, did many things, so that the prophecy of Isaiah might fittingly be applied to him: “The lion shall eat straw like the ox; and the child from the breast shall delight himself over the hole of the asp; and the weaned child [Note: [Col. 0607] *no* deleted.] shall put his hand into the den of the basilisk” (Isa. 11:7) [Note: [Col. 0607] *jam ablatatus* written later by another hand.].

I say it was astonishing that a powerful count, who [Col. 0607D] frightened everyone by his strength like a lion, ate the straw of God’s word from the hand of Christ’s poor man; and that he who, like an asp and a basilisk, was accustomed to lay all things waste, let this man—who was a child in malice and had been weaned from the milk of worldly sweetness—put his hand into his den, that is, into the conscience of his heart. Therefore, although the seed of God’s word fell in his heart as on rock or among thorns, it happened, according to the Lord’s saying, that he received it indeed with joy; but because he had no root of love, though he believed for a time [Note: [Col. 0607] one letter erased and altered here.] and withdrew in the time of temptation, the seed was choked by the cares and riches of the world and bore [Col. 0608A] no fruit—though the farmer did not lose the fruit of his labor.

15. Therefore, although, as has been said, he raged with such madness, he nevertheless submitted himself to the holy man and permitted him to establish the observance of holy religion throughout his dominion. Thus he entrusted to him the monastery of Saint Vincent at the place called Soignies, where the rule of clerical order ought to have flourished, so that he might establish there the order of monastic life. But the undertaking remained unfulfilled because of the unfavorableness of circumstance and time.

He also entrusted to his hands the provostship of the abbey of Lobbes, so that the more closely Erluinus was attached to him, the more faithfully he might serve him; and the more religious he was, the more attentively he might govern according to rule the brothers of that place. Because this had been done against the brothers’ wishes, it greatly displeased their united body. Through the indulgence of former superiors, corrupted by unlawful license, many of them also boasting of secular noble birth, and accustomed to judge everything by personal favor rather than the holiness of religion [Note: [Col. 0607] *asucti* c.], [Col. 0608B] they bitterly resented having a man of humble condition and from another place set over them. It seemed grievous and intolerable to them to be so suddenly recalled by him from the strength of their own habits to the norm of regular life.

Certainly, if the fitness of things is considered, it will not seem very surprising that brothers who, through the relaxation of pastoral care, had departed from regular discipline for so many years could be brought back to upright living only with such difficulty. No, I say, it is not surprising that the dissoluteness of leniency had made them unbridled, when for more than ninety years no fatherly oversight of regular abbots [Col. 0608C] had kept watch over them. Instead, hirelings who were not shepherds and whose own sheep they were not had scattered the Lord’s fold. Seeking their own interests rather than God’s, they held all things for sale; and by selling doves in God’s church—that is, the graces of the Holy Spirit—they made God’s house a den of thieves.

This evil is believed to have rebounded upon the heads of those who, as evil shepherds, fattened on the milk of God’s sheep and clothed in their wool, scorned to drive wolves from Christ’s fold and, like dumb dogs unable to bark, allowed the souls subject to them to perish. For who would not curse it? Who, I say, would not abhor it: that such negligence, not to say greed, possessed the minds of bishops [Col. 0608D] that from the year of the Lord 863—when Hubert, duke hateful to God and brother of Queen Tietberga, expelled Abbot Hartpert and seized the abbey of Lobbes—until the year of the Lord 955, when Baldricus expelled Ratherius and received the episcopal throne of the church of Liège, that place, hitherto distinguished by the honor of such great nobility and religion, continued without the governance of an abbot?

For after the aforesaid Hubert, abbot and duke, perished in battle by God’s just judgment, Franco, who succeeded him in the administration and was himself afterward made bishop, obtained from the generosity of Emperor Arnulf that the abbey of Lobbes should be subject to the jurisdiction of the bishopric of Liège. After him came Stephen, then Richarius, after him Uhogo and Farabertus. All of these, I say, unwilling to forgo the great revenues of the abbey, annually gave and took back for a price the provostships which, under the name and obligation of obedience, they ought to have entrusted to religious and God-fearing men, as though they were rustic bailiwicks [Note: [Col. 0609] *vilic.* corrected.]. [Col. 0609A] They had thrown divine and human things into utter confusion there; they had made sacred and profane things indiscriminately intermingle. And, in a miserable fashion, they scorned to see what they thought profit for themselves turned into the ruin of souls. For where the pursuit of money was proposed as the first duty, you know well that virtue was placed after money. (Horace.) Where virtue was held in no honor, what hope of good could there be?

Thus, since the brothers would not return to the right path of correction, they opposed the will of the aforesaid man in every way and in all things. They cried out and complained that their goods were being prodigally squandered by him and that the substance of the monastery was being immoderately exhausted on the feasts of secular persons, above all in the service of Count Raginerus. Under this pretext they concealed their own fault, forgetting that saying by which Saint Benedict gives us regular instruction: “Before all things, let not the evil of murmuring appear in any word or sign.”

But the man of God, taught to possess his soul in patience, protected by the shield of humility and patience, endured every burden of adversity. Yet the greatness and character of what he suffered may be understood from the writings of Abbot Fulquinus. It happened, at the approach of vintage time, [Col. 0609C] while the brothers were complaining about him and plotting some sorrowful, I know not what, that Erluinus came upon them. They beat him with such a slaughter of clubs that he was thought altogether dead. But when he perceived that they had departed, catching his breath a little and blinking his eyes, he withdrew himself. Not long afterward, when no one expected it, he set out with the help of Bernard the advocate for the monastery’s village called Hercliacum.

After this, he obtained by entreaties that Count Raginerus and Bishop Baldricus should celebrate the Nativity of the Lord at Lobbes; and this he achieved. To all the brothers this seemed wholly blameworthy: they found it intolerable that their resources should be so lavishly expended on these men’s provisions and that holy places should be frequented indiscriminately by secular persons. When the holy celebration of the days of the Nativity had been fully observed [Col. 0609D] and the visitors had departed, the brothers complained together that their own resources were diminished and taken away. They then took courage and made for the village of Fontaines, which the Sambre washes; from there they carried off whatever wine was found.

Erluinus had then gone to the village of Bermeriacas. The brothers pursued him there with the whole household and a very great multitude of people. There again they raged against him with such a beating that it was remarkable he escaped death. Yet the power of Count Raginerus and the perseverance in God of the steadfast man did not therefore fail. Thinking that the unsound brothers would abandon their begun rebellion [Col. 0610A] if, after the care of souls had been entrusted to the venerable man under the title of abbot, they saw him acting in the monastery as Christ’s representative, he took counsel with Bishop Baldricus and with the bishop of the diocese of Cambrai. He had previously honored Erluinus with the title of chief provost, and he did not fear to entrust him with the care and oversight of the abbey.

The event turned out otherwise than he expected. From the very source from which he believed he would extinguish the flames of hatred and hostility [Note: [Col. 0609] *se* erased.], he fed greater and more dangerous sparks of evil. At last, when he had been promoted to the position of abbot, he scattered in various places all but a few whom he had removed from the monastery. In their estimation he did this because he held them suspect and did not have sufficient confidence in the safety of his life. But in truth he did it so that, gradually accustomed in other places [Col. 0610B] to the yoke of regular discipline, they might in some measure abandon the vanity of their habitual frivolity.

Yet neither fear of God could subdue them nor his own love attach them to him. Those who remained in the place, realizing that nothing was left for their sloth and their long-accustomed license, angered by the bitterness of this very despair, did not even fear to plot his death. To avoid prolonging the account, three of them, whose vanity of noble birth, strength of youth, and the ready support of relatives had supplied a more daring boldness, attacked the dormitory by night, at great and very grave peril to their order and profession. They dragged him out and, having pulled him beyond the enclosure of the cloister, treated him inhumanly: they deprived him of his eyes and cut away part of his tongue, though they did not deprive him of the capacity and use of speech. This was done on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the year 957 of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 0609] The Gembloux continuation writes the year 958, but our source deserves greater trust.].

Thus martyred, he understood too late that no hope of good remained for him among them, and at last he yielded. For he was placed in a ship so weakened and blind; he was carried away to Gembloux. Yet the labor of this righteous man was not altogether fruitless. The good fragrance of Christ—which was to some a fragrance of death unto death, to others a fragrance of life unto life—spread abroad the force of his kindness and fortitude. For after the brothers’ incorrigible frivolity had openly shown how dangerous it was for brothers to live without an abbot’s governance, they were thereafter permitted to live under an abbot. Their frivolity was restrained, the state of holy religion was reformed [Col. 0610D], and their property, which had been squandered through the greed and ambition of superiors, was more orderly established for the common benefit of the brothers.

16. Let us here consider briefly the congruity of events and compare one matter with another. This man of whom we speak both did something similar to our lawgiver, Saint Benedict, and suffered something similar. Therefore, we believe that, if it is permissible to compare small things with great, he will have something similar to Benedict also in the reward of his labors, since he was Benedict’s zealous imitator.

Saint Benedict, the model [Note: [Col. 0609] *mplar* corrected.] of our life, [Col. 0611A] once undertook to govern brothers of a monastery. When they strayed from the regular way and he could not draw them back to the path of righteousness, he tolerated them as long as he could and worked as earnestly as possible to correct them. But when he perceived that their festering ulcers could be healed by no soothing remedy and that, on the contrary, they were so inflamed even to madness that they did not fear to plot the physician’s death, he let them go and permitted them to follow their own course; living by himself, he sought where he might devote himself to more fruitful labor.

So too this man of ours patiently endured as long as he could the brothers committed to his charge, whom he saw united against him in evil, even at cost and danger to himself. But when he perceived that they even despised the death of their own souls, provided only they could kill him, he consulted his own safety, though late, and spared them somewhat [Col. 0611B] when, lest he should perish under another attack from them, he withdrew himself from their hands. They tried to cover the reproach of infamy by secretly administering a cup of poison to Saint Benedict; the shameless liberty of these men sought no cover for an open crime. Let us leave these matters undecided, to be judged by others.

17. Returning to the monastery of Gembloux, the servant of God had learned by experience that through many tribulations the kingdom of God is prepared for the faithful. He devoted himself all the more earnestly to contemplation and religious devotion because almost nothing outwardly pleased him any longer or could in any degree move him by the world’s allurements. Nor did he think it greatly to be lamented that he had to lack those eyes [Col. 0611C] in which even gnats and bedbugs glory, since his inward man found perfect delight in those eyes by which pure hearts contemplate God.

18. The bitterness of these misfortunes was increased soon afterward by the fate of Count Raginerus, who, bound to him in heartfelt friendship, had been accustomed to be a shield against the assaults of his enemies. Because Raginerus had become intolerable to the whole empire through the excess of his tyranny, Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, who managed the second place ably and wisely in the empire of his brother Otto, summoned him to Valenciennes, where by the unanimous judgment of all he was declared an enemy of the commonwealth, and caused him to be carried away into irrevocable exile.

Perhaps men of understanding who consider the matter more deeply may find it credible [Col. 0611D] that this happened to him by God’s disposition, through the merits of the holy man Erluinus, lest it should be without consequence that a friend of this world had in some fashion believed himself a friend of God. He resembled those of whom the Evangelist says concerning believers in Christ: “They loved the glory of men more than the glory of God” (John 12:43).

Since the saying of James is true—“The continual prayer of a righteous man avails much” (James 5:16)—who would doubt that the prayer of this righteous man could obtain from God that, in the punishments of this life, He should render to him the return for sin, whose will he had here upheld in his desires? For He who says through the prophet Nahum, “A double affliction shall not arise” (Nahum 1:9), easily finds this way of mercy: hedging the sinner’s path with the thorns of tribulation [Col. 0612A], He draws him by unwilling necessity to voluntary repentance.

We have learned something similar about Emperor Maurice (from Fredegar). Though he always hated judgment and justice, which are the foundation of a righteous throne, at about the eleventh hour of his life he was drawn back from the leisure of carnal life by God’s hidden judgment. Through the intervention of holy men, and especially of the most pious Pope Gregory, he obtained this: that, even late, he might here work the fruit of repentance, since God counted it as repentance to him that he was cruelly slaughtered with his whole household.

19. Not long afterward, an occasion brought upon these things a heavy accumulation of incomparable grief: namely, the deposition of the venerable and God-worthy Lord Wicpertus, which was a miserable upheaval of our affairs. For a violent wind rushed from the region of the desert—that is, a wind of tribulation burst forth from the unfruitful breast of enemies—and shook the four corners of our house, which surely could never [Note: [Col. 0611] *nunquam* c.] have stood against so great a tempest unless it had been founded upon the rock.

Heribrandus [Note: [Col. 0611] some words written above, but later erased.], a man eminent in power and noble birth and especially illustrious through his relationship to our pious father Wicpertus—for he was the husband of Reinuidis, Wicpertus’s sister—at last openly displayed the malice which he had conceived while Lord Wicpertus lived but had postponed out of reverence for him.
