Without any regard for justice, disregarding the authority of the imperial confirmation and setting aside the apostolic censure of anathema, [Col. 0612C] he violently seized the abbey, insolently plundered church property, and cried out that whatever the pious founder of our place had conferred upon us belonged by hereditary right more to himself than to the church.

All things were thrown into confusion. Everything that had formerly seemed secure and tranquil was made dangerous and uncertain by the whirlwind of sudden storm. There was no one to act for God, no one to favor the cause of justice. All had conspired as one; all afflicted Christ’s poor, or consented to those afflicting them. Induced by his example, the other brothers and nephews of our pious father, who were preeminent through manifold nobility throughout all Lotharingia, each in places convenient to himself either seized or plundered the property of our church, leaving nothing to the church’s men.

[Col. 0612D] 20. A principal figure among them was Rotbertus, the most powerful count of Namur. Though he surpassed all in power, he not only brought no help to the brothers crushed by the weight of tribulations; rather, seizing an opportunity from the circumstances of the time, he began to abuse them with all his power. He violently and unjustly took from the church and attached to his own interest the immunity of the county, which an authoritative charter declares had been conferred upon our church by royal authority.

Moreover, if anyone wished to collect from separate documents and combine into one account the daily plunderings and robberies of our property throughout the surrounding region, the seizures of estates, the most miserable oppression of the brothers, the many killings and captures of churchmen, the weakness or faithlessness of the advocates, and the nature and number of petitions sent day after day to the ears of princes concerning all these matters—petitions which amounted to nothing but beating the air—he would seem to undertake the task of an entire book. [Col. 0613A] And it is superfluous to labor without hope of result, because to enumerate losses is nothing other than to renew grief over what has been lost.

Yet this persistent importunity of the complaints did not cease until, after many years, Emperor Otto ordered Duke Otto, after hearing the case between the church and the invaders of the church, to restore the church’s condition by dividing the properties equally between them. This division was agreed between Heribrandus Bratuspans and the church; but from the other usurpers the church received nothing. Raginardus, brother of Lord Wicpertus, gave Saint Peter whatever allodial property he had in Gandrinul.

21. But the little flock of the brothers, in whom it pleased God the Father to give them the kingdom, sought to possess nothing of their own on earth. Knowing that nothing is lacking to those who fear God, and being deprived of human help on every side, they deemed it good to flee to Him alone who is the faithful helper of orphans. For, established under the pious shepherd Erluinus, they guarded themselves in the Lord’s fold lest they in any degree suffer the wolf’s bites. They were content to live however scantily, provided they could bless the Lord at all times and God’s praise might always be in their mouths.

[Col. 0613C] The man of God Erluinus himself, unwilling to have here an abiding city, where he saw so manifold and contrary a calamity of evils pressing upon him, sought for himself and his people the future dwelling not made by hands but eternal. Understanding that he could find it by nothing better than harmony in fraternal unanimity, he devoted his mind in every way to accomplishing the work of peace. For he prudently completed a work pleasing to God and useful for winning souls, begun by Lord Wicpertus of pious memory: he gathered together that fellowship of fraternity by which he bound in one bond of peace and love almost all God-fearing persons throughout Lotharingia and Francia, so that all might think one thing in Christ, love one thing, will one thing, refuse one thing; so that among them there might be nothing perverse, nothing dishonorable, nothing contracted through diabolical rivalry, nothing hateful or divided through opposition; so that they might truly be called the peacemaking children of God and, confessing their sins to one another and praying for one another, might be saved by alms, fasts, spiritual psalms, hymns, and the practices instituted for this purpose beyond the due measure of daily service.

22. Living such a life, Erluinus, a man of great renown, was for many years afterward an example of good living to all. But after the dross of his sins had been refined to purity in the furnace of prolonged tribulation, at last, tested like gold, he was drawn from the furnace of the flesh. He finally attained the prize of the heavenly calling for which he had so long desired, and in God’s kingdom received the double cup of martyrdom and confession. Departing from this world on the fourth Ides of August, [Col. 0614A] he was buried in the church of Saint Peter, faithfully and effectually, as we believe, pleading with the ears of the Almighty for the whole household of Saint Peter.

## Concerning Abbot Heriwardus

23. Bereft of their father, the men of Gembloux resolved to go to the king’s court to obtain a shepherd appointed over them. Yet they thought this ought not to be done without the counsel of the bishop of the diocese. At that time Notkerus presided over the people of Tongeren; he was very eminent in wisdom and noble birth. Not refusing counsel to those who sought it, he began to explain to them as eloquently as he could how unprofitable it was for poor men to be subject to kings; how arduous and difficult it was for Christ’s humble servants to approach the royal throne; and how unsuitable it was for men withdrawn from the world to serve lay persons.

They themselves, he said, had for a long time sufficiently experienced [Col. 0614B] how little counsel or help they had received from imperial majesty in time of need, when all men had taken all things from them without regard for imperial reverence and with no one opposing or defending them. For the king’s heart is turned away from helping them either by distance of lands or by the multiplicity of more pressing cares that always rest upon the royal side; and poverty itself is held to disgrace the pride of courtiers. He knew well enough how familiar rapacity is to palace hounds, how native voracity is to them.

But if they wished to give their assent to his counsel, he thought it would be very beneficial for them to permit themselves to be subject to the right of the bishop of Liège. Thus all oppression would be absent from them; indeed, ready defense against all would be present to them. He would easily obtain this from royal generosity, if only the brothers gave him voluntary submission.

As the bishop set out these and other considerations of the same sort, the brothers in unanimous agreement assented to him. Therefore, by common counsel, they chose Heriwardus, a religious and energetic man, and caused him to be established over them as abbot by the hand of the bishop of Liège. Heriwardus was brother of the often-mentioned Abbot Erluinus. He had been a monk of the monastery of Saint Michael the Archangel of Peril of the Sea, but had long lived with his brother at Gembloux, drawn there by pure desire for the holy religion flourishing there.

Bishop Notkerus, pleased that the brothers’ unanimity so obediently supported his wish, thought it fitting to repay them in kind. Therefore, besides other things which he bestowed upon them, he gave to the church of Gembloux the village called Templus, from which an annual revenue of one hundred solidi arises; and in the village of Namur, a small vineyard with land belonging to its cultivation. This Heriwardus bought a certain wood from a man named Rado, and from a certain Wicpertus an estate with its household in the village of Walaham; concerning this he caused the following charter to be drawn up:

+ Whoever are bound together by the unity of charity, raised alike upon the two wings of virtues, will be able to penetrate the heavenly mysteries above; and one part does not refuse the other such benefits as are fitting. Accordingly, as though compelled by this consideration, a certain man noble by birth, named Rado, together with his wife Engelrada, who was privy to the matter, came by common counsel, attended by their sons and the men of their kindred, to the monastery of the holy [Col. 0615A] Saviour and of Saint Peter, adorned with relics by Lord Wicpert, servant of God, and Erluin, venerable patron of the same place. Then, jointly declaring their intention to Lord Abbot Heriward, it was mutually agreed and approved that he should convey to the present house an exceptionally good wood, partly for the sake of divine mercy, but especially in return for gifts; with the consent, indeed, of Lord Abbot, of the brethren dwelling there, and of faithful men of both orders, and by legal authority he conveyed to the Holy Saviour an excellent wood, containing nearly a hundred *bonnaria*, above the river commonly called Dions. And it is immediately known that one hundred solidi, in coin, namely in gold and silver, and horses, were granted by us to both parties, according to their wish. Concerning this [Col. 0615B] conveyance a charter was afterwards drawn up, under the testimony of faithful men of both orders, by whose hands the conveyance was also completed. But if anyone—which may God forbid—should presume to raise any challenge against this charter, unless he correct himself concerning it, let him feel the Holy Saviour as his avenger; and let him also pay to us, against whom he has brought suit, thirty ounces of gold and a weight of silver, and let him by no means presume to recover what he claims. But in order that this present charter may remain firm and stable for ever, it is to be fortified by a stipulation and remain unshaken through long time. Moreover, let those present and absent know that Lord Abbot Heriward, together with the brethren, bought for the same price in money whatever Wichpert had hitherto possessed in the village commonly called Walaham [Col. 0615C], together with the well-known household, to hold in perpetuity.

After approximately three years had thus passed in his administration, Abbot Heriward paid the debt of human nature; and on 3 May he was gathered to his people and received burial in the church of Saint Peter.

## CONCERNING ERLUIN THE YOUNGER, ABBOT

24. (A.D. 991.) Erluin, kinsman of the former Erluin, was chosen third to the headship of the monastery of Gembloux, and was ordained abbot on the tenth day before the Kalends of January [23 December]. As regards the world, he sprang from freeborn parents, for Erluin, then bishop of Cambrai, was his maternal uncle; but as regards God, he had been thoroughly trained in the monastery of Gorze in the rule and discipline of monastic life—would that he had been as capable of vigorously carrying it out as he was adequately instructed in it! In his time, a certain Arnold, a nobleman, restored to Saint Peter that part of the estate of Gembloux which had come to him by right of his wife Richeldis. For Heribrand, who was the first invader of our possessions, begot Hubert, commonly called Hubezo, by Renuida, sister of Lord Wichpert, and two daughters, Richeldis and another whose name has been lost. Now of the half of the estate of Gembloux which, as we said above, Heribrand had unjustly claimed, a third part had fallen to each of these three in the division. This was the third part which had come to Arnold through the right of his wife Richeldis [Col. 0616A]; moved by love of God, he lawfully conveyed it to Saint Peter, and through the hands of Abbot Erluin the following instrument was drawn up:

+ To all the faithful of God’s holy Church, namely those now living and those to come, dwelling far and wide, we desire with the whole affection of our heart that it be made known that, in the days of the abbot called Erluin, who has newly taken charge of the monastery called Gembloux, a kinsman of the former patron bearing the same name, a man born of noble stock named Arnold, and his wife called Richeldis [Note: [Col. 0615D] *Richildis* corrected to *Richeldis* in c.], walking together in the divine commandments and mindful of godly fear and love, resolved by a counsel alike divinely inspired that, for the salvation of their souls, they should convey by lawful donation to God almighty, Saviour of all, and to Saint Peter, key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0616B], together with the other relics of saints which are presently venerated among us, the possession of all the inheritance that they hold within the abbey under our jurisdiction. Therefore, by the divinely inspired goodwill of both, on a certain day, namely the feast of the blessed bishop Medard, agreeing in common counsel and with faithful witnesses of both parties assembled, they lawfully conveyed to God our Saviour, in whose honour the aforesaid place was founded, and to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, everything which they are seen to possess within the abbey under our jurisdiction, as stated above; on the condition, namely, that they should enjoy its usufruct for their lifetime, but after the end of their common life it should be subject to the lordship of our monastery.

This is the portion of the whole possession: whatever is known to be held jointly in male and female slaves, together with the mill and brewery; further, in fields, tilled lands, cultivated and uncultivated ground, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, rights of way, that share of toll which accrues to them, and the other things subject to the aforesaid possession.

25. Under this Erluin the rigour of regular discipline began to soften, and the fervour of holy observance gradually to grow cold, because he did not possess much strength of righteous severity. For, as has often been said, ecclesiastical property had been dissipated on every side, and their revenues and allowances reduced; thus their domestic resources were greatly diminished. Accordingly, under the pretext of poverty, while each person looked to his own interests and, setting aside the honourable character of common life, sought privately to enlarge his own household resources, they lived with more licence than was right—something wholly harmful to monks’ souls. Thus from the sanctuary of God, whence previously a delightful fragrance had gone forth from the holy conduct of its inhabitants, there now spread an evil report, which, when it reaches secular ears, is sometimes more merciless in defaming our life. Therefore Erluin the younger, after spending more than twenty-three years under the name of pastoral office, died on the seventh day before the Kalends of June [26 May] (A.D. 1012), and deserved burial in the church of Saint Peter beside his predecessor Heriward.

## CONCERNING ABBOT OLPERT

[Col. 0617A]

26. But the merciful Lord quickly opened the eyes of His mercy and, through the intercession, as we believe, of His servant Wichpert, provided His house with a worthy steward. Truly, I say, the mercy of heaven distilled upon us when they chose Olpert to be appointed our fourth abbot. A few preliminary words must be said about him. He was born in the village called Lederna, on the border of the district of Sambre, of parents not lowly as regards the world, but religious as regards God. From boyhood he was regularly brought up in the monastery of Lobbes in monastic discipline and most thoroughly instructed in literary studies; the development of his natural ability showed what sort of man he would become. When he had drunk from the mouth of Heriger, abbot of Lobbes, the most learned man of his time [Col. 0617B], something of the sevenfold flavour of the liberal arts, he could not quench his thirst for study. Therefore, wherever he heard that anyone excelled others remarkably in knowledge of the arts, he at once flew there; and the more he thirsted, the more eagerly he drew some delightful draught from each man’s breast. At Paris he also devoted himself for some time both to study and to the holy religious life flourishing there at Saint Germanus [Note: [Col. 0617] *sanctum Germanum* corrected to *sancti Germani* in c.]. He studied for three years in the city of Troyes, where in a pleasing exchange he learned much from others and wisely taught others. Nor did he evade the instruction of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, whom all France proclaimed eminent in mastery of the liberal arts. But after he had, like a most prudent bee ranging through flowering fields, been filled with the clear nectar of learning, he returned to the hive of his monastery; and there he lived religiously as a student, and studiously as a religious.

27. At that time a certain Burchard had been appointed bishop in the city of Worms, a man not unworthy of episcopal honour, and, in the fervour of his youth, fittingly devoted to literary studies. He confidently charged Baldric the younger, bishop of Tongeren—who had been his companion and friend in the king’s palace—to send him someone endowed with literary learning, by whose help and instruction he might progress in knowledge of the Scriptures. Careful inquiry was made as to who was worthy to be sent to so great a man; in the end none was found more suitable than Olpert. With everyone holding him in good esteem, he was sent to the city [Col. 0617D] of the Vangiones. Received honourably by the bishop, he gained great favour and intimacy with him. The noble and powerful bishop did not disdain to submit himself in the role of disciple; the humble and foreign monk did not fear to render a teacher’s service to so great a man. And indeed it was necessary that he should be polished to the fingernail by the art of manifold learning, since his praise and reputation depended upon the subtle judgment of so wise a pupil. How much a man of such authority advanced through Olpert’s teaching may be judged from his deeds; for it is sufficiently established [Col. 0618A] that in that age he shone uniquely in learning in the Scriptures. This may be adequately proved by the fact that, while Olpert dictated and taught, he compiled that great volume of canons, a work exceedingly useful to holy Church, and, as though gathering flowers of every kind from the meadow of Scripture, placed high in the Church a crown more precious than gold and topaz. When the bishop perceived that his wishes had been fulfilled, he offered his teacher the choice whether he preferred to remain with him in honour and friendship or to return to his own people. He chose to return home, because God was pleased thus to provide for us. Therefore he was sent back with thanksgiving to Bishop Baldric; the eminence of his learning and religious life was praised, and, lest he be deprived of the return due for his labour, he was most earnestly commended to him [Note: [Col. 0617] *vicem* corrected to *vice*].

[Col. 0618B]

28. Since the house of Gembloux lacked a shepherd, Bishop Baldric deliberated anxiously with his men about who was worthy to undertake the care of this pastoral office. The unanimous judgment was that this place suited Olpert, adorned with a twofold learning, above all others. Accordingly, summoned by the bishop with his abbot Ingobrand, he was chosen, by the judgment of God and all good men, for the governance of the church; and by the hands of Abbot Ingobrand and Archdeacon Godescalc he was sent there. When the men of Gembloux heard that an abbot was being sent them without their consultation, in foolish rusticity they wished to resist episcopal authority—indeed, God’s appointment—refusing to offer any submission to one whose election, they grieved, had been made without their own will and counsel [Col. 0618C]. Foolish and blind men, who did not understand that God was providing for them better than they hoped. The remainder of that day, with night approaching, was spent in this obstinate rebellion. At morning, softened by the counsel of distinguished men acting as the bishop’s envoys, they ceased, though unwillingly, from their rash undertaking, and at last, only with difficulty persuaded, submitted their hands to the abbot chosen for them by the God of their salvation [Note: [Col. 0617] thus the manuscript]. This was done on the eighth day before the Ides of August [6 August] in the year of the Lord 1012; he was consecrated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October [21 September].

29. Having thus obtained the pastoral charge, he laboured diligently to fulfil in deeds the title of abbot. At the beginning he encountered great difficulty in restoring affairs—for outwardly the household estate was grievously impoverished, while inwardly great irreligion was appalling—yet one would scarcely believe, even when told, how soon and how easily the prosperity he desired smiled upon him [Note: [Col. 0617] *facili* corrected to *facile* in c.]. For, in order wisely to correct their undisciplined habits, he hedged in with the thorns of regular discipline the crooked paths upon which they had been accustomed to wander unlawfully; then he showed them the paths of uprightness on which they ought to walk toward life. Taught that the Shepherd of shepherds threatens those pastors who feed themselves rather than God’s flock, who rule them with harshness and power, and recall them from the byway of error with no fatherly affection, nor rescue from evil those who suffer, he bound up what was weak, strengthened what was broken, sought what was perishing, and, after the example of the Gospel Samaritan, poured upon their wounds the wine of severity and the oil of mercy [Note: [Col. 0619] *tes* corrected from *e* in c.]. Nor did hope deceive him. For he did not cease until, having taken up the winnowing fan of discretion, the mother of virtues, he had shaken the chaff of vices from the Lord’s threshing-floor and stored the purified grain of virtues in God’s granary, that is, in the hearts of the faithful. Nor did this seem enough to his good intention, always pressing forward. Knowing that idleness is the enemy of the soul, he also taught his men, now sufficiently imbued with holy religion, diligently to pursue literary studies [Col. 0619B], so that, while they traced with eyes and minds the footprints of the Fathers along the paths of Scripture, they might know beyond doubt to avoid the path of errors and might suffer no obstacles in following the path of truth.

30. Thus, while besides the matters that were outward, his daily concern pressed upon him, namely his unceasing care for the souls entrusted to him, the power of almighty God cooperated with his good will in both respects. For once the force of divine fear and the fervour of religion were rekindled inwardly, abundant household wealth immediately overflowed outwardly from the fruitful outcome of affairs. Therefore the God-devoted man Olpert, encouraged by good hope, began more urgently to press forward his undertakings. Seeing that the monastery with its workshops was ill-suited for monastic habitation—which displeased him because of its smallness, its complete lack of beauty, and above all because its excessive age seemed to threaten imminent ruin—he trusted in God, rich in mercy, and in the seventh year of his rule began to lay the foundations of a new church.

31. Seeing him advance day by day, Christ’s faithful encouraged him by willingly coming to his aid. Bishop Baldric, rejoicing that he had not been disappointed in his good estimate of the abbot whom he had chosen, devoted himself wholly to affection for him; and he conveyed to the church of Gembloux the church at Bavenchin, the new little church at Heis, and a tithe at Bernunfait [Col. 0619D] [or, according to a twelfth-century addition in c., at Sombresia].

32. At the same time (A.D. 1015, 12 September), battle having been joined at Florennes between Count Lambert, son of Regnier Long-Neck, and Duke Godfrey, Lambert was there cut down by swords and met his death. His most noble wife Gerberga, moved to contrition by her husband’s sins, sought the absolution and rest of his soul through the remedies of almsgiving; she wished that the church of Gembloux also, of which he himself had been count and defender, should continually discharge offices of prayer owed for his soul. Therefore, having adopted salutary counsel and with the support of her son Count Henry, she conveyed to the house of Gembloux her own estate called Tortosa, in the parish of Basciu. Since the count himself held in the village called Eyneis, within the parish of Gembloux, several *mansi* by the right of a benefice granted from the royal hand, a further equitable exchange was arranged: he received Tortosa and transferred it to the right of his benefice; while he caused Eyneis to be enrolled among the property of the church of Gembloux. This was more suitable to both parties because of proximity. Lest any descendant dare to overturn it, it was confirmed by the authority of the royal hand, as the text of this charter shows:

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. Henry [Col. 0620B], by the grace of God august emperor of the Romans, to all who wish to live piously in Christ. We wish all present and future persons to know of a grant made by our dignity which, at the petitions of certain of our faithful men, we have bestowed upon certain churches. The community of the church of Gembloux, situated in the district of Darnau, namely in the parish of the church of Liège, with its advocate present, made a certain exchange of land with Henry, advocate of the abbey of Nivelles, which exchange was made in the following manner. The community of the church of Gembloux gave to the church of Nivelles five *mansi* situated in the village called Basciu; and the aforesaid advocate of the church of Nivelles restored to it an equal number from his benefice, granted him by me, situated in the parish [Col. 0620C] of Gembloux. Concerning this exchange Wolbodo, bishop of the church of Liège, approached our imperial dignity and devoutly asked that it might obtain inviolable validity through us. I readily granted his request, since I had found him most faithful to me in all things and, on the testimony of many, had recognized the exchange as useful to both churches. We therefore confirm this act, performed with the consent of the faithful of both churches, and by imperial decree establish that it shall remain inviolable and unalterable for ever. And in order that this our authority and decree of consent may henceforth remain inviolate, we ordered this document to be drawn up and authenticated with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry, most invincible august emperor of the Romans. Gonterius, chancellor, noted this in place of Erchanbald, archchaplain. (L. [Note: [Col. 0619] the monogram of Emperor Henry II is present.] [Col. 0620D] M.) Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of December [26 November], in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1018, in the seventeenth year of the reign of Lord Henry II and the fifth of his empire. Enacted at Liège.

33. Abbot Olpert, rejoicing that through the help of good men God was granting a good outcome to his labour, directed his attention to increasing the brethren’s allowances, which were very meagre. Knowing that monks should live by the labour of their hands, after the example of the Fathers and Apostles, he worked continuously with the brethren, as the necessity of poverty required and the will of obedience urged; and, in suitable places of the aforesaid estate [Col. 0621A], he made dams [Note: [Col. 0621] corrected from *iis*] and constructed fishponds to receive fish, which he foresaw would be quite useful for the brethren’s needs.

34. Wolbodo, Baldric’s successor (A.D. 1018), being entirely devoted to the pursuit of holy religion, gladly welcomed Olpert’s more religious way of life, honoured him with his side and his ear, and encouraged him by his favour to aim at better things. Accordingly, the first thing he did was to confirm by the authority of his own stipulation what his predecessor had bestowed upon the church of Gembloux for the latter’s sake; moreover, he granted that church the liberty of immunity and committed the following matters to posterity for preservation by the witness of this charter:

Wolbodo, by the disposing mercy of God bishop of the holy church of Liège [Col. 0621B], to all who wish to live piously in Christ. We know that every one of Christ’s faithful must labour by every means to deserve the favour of the saints. For we are shaken by the waves alike of our own frailty, of the devil, and of this world, so that we cannot stand unless supported by their patronage. Therefore I resolved to seek, in whatever manner I could, the patronage of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, Saint Exuperius the martyr, and the other saints, and I determined to make this known to all, both present and future. My predecessor Baldric, himself touched by divine fervour, gave to the church of Gembloux a certain church situated on our estate at Bavechin, dedicated in honour of the saints mentioned above. He also gave the tithes of certain clearings which some men were making in the forest called Sombresia [Note: [Col. 0621] *sombresiae* and the following *et* added later] and Heis, belonging to that same church of Gembloux, and which no one of our predecessors had assigned to any parish. He bestowed these upon the aforesaid church under the testimony of suitable witnesses, but, prevented by death, did not make a charter of conveyance. Wishing, in making such a charter, to make me a participant in his almsgiving, I record the aforesaid gift under the firm attestation of this document. I add another gift on our own behalf, which I wish all to know. At our prompting the abbot and community of the aforesaid place have built a new church; beside it, abandoning the old one because it was small and about to collapse, they are taking care to transfer the cloister and everything else. But when these things have been done, they fear that future bishops may demand from the old church the dues of visitation [Col. 0621D], on the grounds, namely, that the monastery has ceased to be that church. Having carefully investigated the reason for this with many persons, I discovered that no dues of visitation had been given from the church of Gembloux to my predecessors from the time when that abbey was made subject, by the king’s munificence, to the see of the church of Liège. We decree that this mercy of my predecessors be preserved in future: namely, that, with only episcopal ordination reserved, they shall demand no obligation of visitation from the church of Gembloux. In accordance with the ordinances of the holy canons, let them allow the monks to lead a good and tranquil life, that they may devote themselves to prayer throughout their lives both for us [Col. 0622A] and for them. I, Wolbodo, bishop in name but not in deed, have subscribed and confirmed.

35. Bishop Baldric, often named above, entering into a profitable transaction for himself with God, the rewarder of all, chose to purchase from Him eternal things with perishable ones. Therefore, adopting Him as heir of his patrimony, he founded on an island at Liège a monastery in honour of James, the Lord’s brother, and assigned to it a portion of his temporal substance, which had fallen to him from the great wealth of his noble parents. But carried off by untimely death, he could not fully satisfy his wishes in this matter. Since the oversight of this place had as yet been assigned to no one, it belonged to the hand of the bishop alone. Therefore Wolbodo, Baldric’s successor [Col. 0622B], piously concerned and having taken counsel with his household, decided to entrust that place to the hands of the most prudent Abbot Olpert. Olpert for a long time resisted and humbly declined it, but at last, with difficulty, accepted obediently and carried it out wisely. For after building a cloister with its workshops as the opportunity of the time allowed, gathering men from here and there who were well directed according to the norm of regular discipline—and especially men trained according to the discipline of Abbot Richard, who was then everywhere renowned for the fervour of holy religion—he was the first there to establish the profession of monastic life. So long as he lived, he governed that place most vigorously to the praise of God and men.

36. No less persistently did he press forward with the undertaking of the church of Gembloux, striving to expend for the benefit of ecclesiastical affairs whatever he could extract from himself by every sort of labour [Col. 0622C]. Divine grace supplied the desired result to this ready ardour of good intention. For, as great success of prosperity smiled upon him, he saw the completion of the work he had begun sooner than he hoped: within nearly three years the church with its furnishings was built, the cloister also constructed with its workshops, and—what he desired most—there now flourished there in full the pursuit of holy religion and a not insignificant exercise of literary learning. He himself granted almost no rest either to mental concern or bodily labour, ever striving to complete the work. When everything had been prepared according to his wish [Col. 0622D], he caused the dedication of that church to be celebrated, amid the great rejoicing of all the neighbouring people, by Durand, venerable bishop of Liège, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August [25 July] in the year of the Lord 1022. Not long afterwards he caused the oratory of Saint Paul, situated within the cloister, to be dedicated by Durand’s successor Reginard on the sixth day before the Kalends of June [27 May]; with Reginard he deserved to hold a very great place in friendship. Later, after constructing a double oratory—the lower one in honour of John the Baptist and John the Evangelist, the upper one in honour of Michael the Archangel and Stephen the Protomartyr—he caused it to be solemnly dedicated by the same Reginard on the second day before the Ides [Col. 0623A] of August [12 August]. He also caused the bodies of Wichpert, the venerable and God-worthy founder of our house, and of his three predecessors—Erluin, Heriward, and the second Erluin—to be reverently transferred into this crypt.

37. This same faithful and prudent steward, knowing that to those who seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness the necessities of the body also ought to be added in due time, laboured with every urgency in his power, wherever God favoured him, to acquire estates, so that, since their outward needs were adequately supplied according to the resources of the place, they might serve God more peacefully and readily without the impediment of murmuring. Once the household estate had been arranged more systematically than before, so that the brothers’ established allowances could now be provided without constraint or delay, he strove to expend whatever surplus accrued for the benefit of posterity [Col. 0623B], knowing that whatever he gave beyond what was required he would receive back from God, the true Samaritan, who guards Israel. Nor was his labour in vain; for he laboured until he had considerably increased, and, so to speak, almost doubled the property of the church, which he had found extremely meagre. Either he faithfully bought, for a price, whatever he could obtain from whatever quarter, or he secured that, through the devotion of the faithful favouring his labour for their salvation, it should be conveyed to our church. Since the possessions thus scraped together in different places, from different persons, and by various arrangements [Note: [Col. 0623] *corrosa* corrected in another hand to *corrasa* in c.] are indeed numerous but small in size and not very great in estimated revenue, we cannot enumerate them all individually.

38. Also in his time, Hubetho, son of Heribrand and nephew of Lord Wichpert through his sister Renuida [Col. 0623C], moved by love of piety and justice and supported by his most noble wife Gudetha, restored to our church the portion which had fallen to him from the half violently and unjustly plundered from us by his father Heribrand. He was prompted by the example of his sister Richeldis, who, as we said above, had brought her own portion back to the rightful possession of the church of Gembloux. The sons of this same Hubetho, namely Hubert and Tietwin, also conveyed to our church a third part of the village of Puceu.

39. The same Lord Abbot Olpert gave an allod at Masau and Biettinis and received in exchange the village called Ferolt—an exchange not sufficiently advantageous to us in the estimation of the properties, but, as it seemed useful to him alone, advantageous because of proximity alone. Previously, indeed, through an equitable exchange made by his predecessors, when a certain part of that same allod had been given to the church of Susteren, the village called Mainil had been added to the property of our church.

40. What shall I say of the time when the excessive dearness of grain devastated all Gaul—how much favour he accumulated for himself with God by making alms, and how much glory he acquired among men by increasing the Church’s resources? Like another Joseph, touched by the grace of foresight, he had filled his granaries from the abundance of grain in preceding years, from which, by God’s providence, he prepared to relieve in season the want of his poor. While many others, led by the spirit of greed [Col. 0624A], turned the need of others to their own advantage—setting aside mercy toward the poor, they either hoarded their own goods more tightly or sold them more dearly—he wished neither to keep his goods through stinginess nor to sell them to others through avarice. Instead, becoming God’s creditor, he began to be a praiseworthy usurer. For, unwilling to sow sparingly lest he also reap sparingly, he sowed in blessings so that he might reap eternal life in blessings. And because God loves a cheerful giver (II Corinthians 9:7), he performed the work of almsgiving neither from sorrow nor from necessity, but displayed the compassion of a most merciful heart through the cheerfulness of his countenance. Besides those who, coming and going at every hour, shared in his bounty, he maintained not a few dependants of the church, as was fitting, from the storehouse of mother Church [Col. 0624B], appointing them without delay a daily stipend of sustenance. This might seem a miracle to all: though he was so lavish in almsgiving, so fatherly generous in relieving the poverty of other communities, so liberally ready to comfort even his noble neighbours in such a crisis, and though he assisted his own people—the people of the church—with compassion by seasonably remitting the customary rents of land, he never treated Christ’s flock, devoted to divine service in the solitude of the cloister, with less mercy. Rather, as sufficiency came to him from heaven, he served those who served God with every feeling of humanity.

41. Nor should it be omitted to state how great was his zeal for adorning the church. Though it is said, “What does gold do in a saint?” he had no means, in external things, of showing the desire of his heart toward God except by generously expending upon God’s worship those things which mortals deem foremost. That this has some value no one doubts: whether so that in time of need it may relieve the want of the poor or of those serving God; or so that a greater benefit for ecclesiastical use may fittingly be procured from it; or because coarse-minded people, judging everything more from their own disposition than from the truth of things, regard almost nothing as worthy of worship and reverence unless they see it adorned with things that they themselves love temporarily. Therefore, avoiding in either direction the fault of avarice, he hastened to spend upon the ornaments of the church whatever he could prudently gather from any source [Note: [Col. 0623] *unde : : unde* corrected to *undeunde*]. It is not difficult to give a summary of them here, since they are daily visible to the eyes. He made a silver panel before the altar of Saint Peter, fittingly embossed in relief; two other silver panels of smaller size; an altar frontal for the altar of Saint Exuperius the martyr; two cast silver candlesticks; one gold chalice and six silver ones; two gilt silver censers; four gold crosses and one silver cross; two silver fans; one gold Gospel-book, three silver ones; one silver Epistle-book; two silver reliquary caskets; eighteen copes [Col. 0625A] of silk cloth; twelve chasubles; two dalmatics; four subdeacons’ vestments; albs, stoles, tapestries, and other things which, although counted among incidental matters, were acquired by his diligence and zeal, or were bestowed upon the church by God’s faithful in gratitude for his love. Though these things are not so numerous in estimated value and in comparison with others’ riches, they are yet many, great, and precious in view of his good intention; for God, the rewarder of good deeds, judges not by how much but by the motive and quality of mind with which an offering is made to Him.

42. And because, together with the pursuit of religion, he caused the pursuit of literary learning also to flourish, so that they should not lack the means of practising this art as well, he supplied them with an abundance of books. For he did not permit their minds or hands to grow dull through idleness; rather, he wisely provided for their advancement by exercising them in the labour of writing and advancing their minds to better things through frequent meditation on the Scriptures. Therefore, directing his mind like another Philadelphus toward building, to the extent of his means, a complete library, he copied in one volume a history containing the Old and New Testaments [Note: [Col. 0625] corrected in c.; perhaps the reading was *conscripsit*, “he composed”]. And [Note: [Col. 0625] the same scribe continues in different ink; he had written *transscripsit*, “copied”] he collected more than a hundred volumes of sacred Scripture and fifty books of secular learning. It is indeed remarkable that one man, amid such slender resources, could acquire so much, unless one recalls that those who fear God lack nothing.

[Col. 0625C] **43.** As I recall the learning, talent, and labor of so great a man, I am wholly astonished that the power of both kinds of learning shone forth so exceptionally in him. [Note: [Col. 0625] *clarierit* corrected to *claruerit* in manuscript c.] For, though reared from childhood in the solitude of the cloister, he showed himself so capable and prudent in arranging worldly affairs that scarcely any secular person would have seemed preferable to him. Conversely, while he confined himself to the strictness of monastic life, amid the bustle of ecclesiastical administration he accomplished in hours snatched from work what scarcely another man devoted to God in the quiet of monastic solitude could achieve at leisure. Nor without cause did the fame of his name spread everywhere, since from his teaching so sweet a fragrance grew far and wide.

Besides those whom he nurtured under his own authority in learning and religious life, he advanced many persons of the clerical order, [Col. 0625D] and even some courtiers, through his instruction; their outstanding integrity or rank afterward brought great benefit and honor to Holy Church. Moreover, his praiseworthy memory still lives in the churches of God in this respect also: in certain places he composed clearly and elegantly the Lives of several [Note: [Col. 0625] *aliquas* immediately corrected to *aliquorum* in manuscript c.] saints; and, concerning their deeds, he most sweetly arranged chants in praise of God according to the rules of musical discipline, in which he was highly skilled. Among these works, at the request of Count Raginer he composed the Life of Saint Veron the Confessor; [Col. 0626A] he also composed a chant about him, as well as antiphons for the morning praises at the passing of Saint Waldedrude. Count Raginer himself and his wife Hathuidis granted to our church all the estate they possessed at Dion.

**44.** Living so praiseworthy and useful a life, after he had completed thirty-seven years of his prelacy, he felt himself summoned by God to the prize of the heavenly calling (A.D. 1048). And, following the example of the Lord Jesus, who, being about to pass to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world loved them unto the end, he likewise loved unto the end his sons, whom he had begotten for God in the bosom of maternal tenderness and reared with the affection of paternal concern.

Since he presided over two monasteries and, for that reason, had customarily changed his residence in turn under the constant pressure of governing, he was then staying for some time in the monastery of Gembloux and celebrating the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul. Having assembled his sons, he addressed them at length and devoutly; with all the eloquence of an accomplished teacher and the tenderness of an affectionate father, he urged them not to turn their eyes away from the plough of the Lord’s work, to beware the leaven of secular people, to provide what is good not only before God but also before men, and to observe other such counsels as flowed from the breast of a pious and wise man.

[Col. 0626B] While speaking, he led them before the altar of Saint Peter. With psalmody and prayer he commended them to the Shepherd of shepherds; he absolved them, by pastoral authority, from all offences committed; and with spiritual sanctification [Col. 0626C] blessed them. Then, bidding them a last farewell not without tears, he went to Liège. For he was pressed by the sorrowful news of the illness of the illustrious Bishop Watho, to whom, beyond the reverence owed through due subjection, he also owed this: Watho had been his fellow pupil and companion from childhood; and from that time the bond of friendship begun between them had grown together with their very age, without complaint, and, so to speak, had grown old with them.

The bishop, rejoicing that he had been comforted by the longed-for visit of his friend, asked him in the name of the Lord to anoint him, according to the command of the Apostle James. When the rite of anointing had been completed and he asked leave of the bishop, still inquiring confidently of him concerning the hope of his life, the bishop, touched by the divine Spirit, said: “Today I shall not die, my friends; but tomorrow, in Christ’s name, come to my aid.”

Despairing of his friend’s life, dissolved in tears and unable to restrain his grief, he said: “May God not permit me to outlive you by seven days.” Returning to the monastery of Saint James, over which he presided, he began to lose his bodily strength and was soon grievously afflicted by fevers. In short: according to the prediction and the wish of these pious men, on the following day, 8 July, the bishop departed to the Lord. The abbot, who had not wished to outlive the bishop, the half of his soul, by seven days, on that very seventh day, 14 July, [Col. 0627A] rendered his blessed spirit to heaven, in the year of the Lord 1048.

**45.** It is superfluous to recount with what honor of veneration and what sorrow of compassion the flock of both monasteries, which had prospered in Christ under his instruction, attended the rites of his burial. For the monks of Gembloux, hearing of the illness of their pious shepherd—to whom, after God and Wicpert, the first founder of our place, they gladly ascribed almost all that they possessed—did not delay to fly there upon the wings of holy love.

They were grievously distressed by the loss of their most loving father; but they were afflicted, beyond what can be said or believed, by the miserable misfortune that they would be deprived of the precious pledge of his body. Had God’s favor opened any way to them, nothing would have settled more desirably in the minds of them all than to accomplish, by some means, the return of the dead man’s body to the monastery of Gembloux. But neither through prayers nor by any possible means could they obtain this, since the citizens rejoiced that the present protection of so holy a man had come to safeguard their city.

[Col. 0627B] He was therefore buried in the church of Saint James, as befitted the first abbot of that place, and this epitaph was inscribed upon the tomb of his burial:

[Note: [Col. 0627] Verses written in red ink.]

> Here lies Abbot Olbert, mirror of abbots, glory of monks,  
> Abbot Olbert, your flower, O Paradise.  
> He presided over two churches by the regular path;  
> Liège possesses his body; Gembloux mourns its loss.

**46.** When this most grievous news was brought to the monks of Gembloux, it became manifest to all, by the testimony of truth itself, [Col. 0627C] with what pastoral concern he had cared for everyone, with what paternal sweetness he had nourished everyone, and with what unanimity of charity he had bound to himself in Christ all alike, from the least to the greatest.

For who could tell—or who, hearing it told, could believe—how great was at once the gathering of everyone, how great the lament of the grieving brethren, how great the cry of the poor, how great the sorrow of orphans and widows? From every mouth sounded thanksgiving for the benefits bestowed upon them; from Christ’s friends there was sent to heaven so devout and hearable a prayer for the absolution of his soul. Who, I ask, having seen such affectionate funeral rites, would doubt that God accepted tears so devout, so deserved, and so abundant—tears not wrung forth by any compulsion of carnal attachment, [Col. 0627D] but drawn forth by the piety of spiritual love pleasing to God?

He therefore who had made for himself so many friends from the mammon of iniquity was received by them into eternal dwellings. And because he ministered well, having acquired for himself a good rank, [Note: [Col. 0627] “for himself.”] and having been enrolled [Note: [Col. 0627] “enrolled”: manuscript d.] [Col. 0628A] in the dignity of the heavenly court, I believe that there he now protects us by his grace, whom here he nourished with such fatherly mercy. Amen. [Note: [Col. 0627] “Amen”: manuscript c.]

## Concerning Abbot Mysach

**47.** When Deodwin had been installed in the episcopal see of the church of Liège, the unanimous election of the whole congregation requested that Mysach, a truly venerable man surnamed Mathelin, be appointed abbot of the monastery of Gembloux. Related to Abbot Olbert by blood, and trained from his earliest years, together with his brother Fulquin—of equally memorable life—in Olbert’s discipline, regular observance, and study, each of the two grew through the exertion of good natural gifts to deserve an office of great usefulness in the Church of God.

Fulquin, the younger in age, distinguished in the exercise of literary learning, was sent to the illustrious Abbot Poppo of Stavelot to govern the boys’ school. Having been sufficiently tested by him for several years in upright conduct, he was advanced, through Poppo’s intervention, to govern the abbey of Saint Vincent the Martyr in the city of Metz; he administered it usefully and praiseworthily until the end of his life.

[Col. 0628B] His brother Mysach, [Note: [Col. 0627] Written in red ink.] meanwhile, was likewise regularly trained at Verdun under Abbot Richard in the school of monastic discipline and was thoroughly tested in every respect in the virtue of obedience. After he was also found patient in labors, energetic and prudent in the management of ecclesiastical affairs, Lord Abbot Olbert attached him to his own side and made him a partner in all his works and counsels. Appointing him his provost, [Col. 0628C] he entrusted to his prudence the second place in all affairs.

In carrying out this obedience he was so strong in submission that he was never stirred by any swelling of pride. For many years he lived so prudently and usefully that, when Abbot Olbert of holy memory yielded to human nature, no one worthier than he could be found to succeed him. Thus, having attained the office of ecclesiastical government on 26 July, [Note: [Col. 0627] After *adeptus*, manuscript c has an erased word.] and having been consecrated on 7 August, he applied diligent attention to himself and to his flock. For, as he had learned, he lived regularly and devoutly; and, as he lived, so he taught others also to live.

The property of the church, whether bestowed in ancient times or acquired later, he never neglected in any respect according to his capacity and means; [Col. 0628D] nor did he diminish it through carelessness or ignorance. Rather, through constant labor and watchfulness, he enlarged it. He always boldly resisted the church’s adversaries, faithfully increased the brethren’s allowances, and, not to go through everything individually, he never held anything dearer, within or without, than the welfare of the church.

## Continuation by Godeschalc

[Col. 0627]

**48.** He too, [Note: [Col. 0627] The first line continues in another hand, written in an erased space.] looking both forward and backward, knowing that the inward person cannot subsist without the outward, [Col. 0628D] divided into two portions whatever he had found in the abbey and whatever he himself had acquired, and distributed it for the food and clothing [Col. 0629A] of the brethren.

He established the wardrobe thus. He assigned five pounds of coin at the estate called Templus; three pounds at Pheroth; three pounds and four shillings at Mannil; eight shillings from Fastrad’s land at Niel; and certain revenues at Esnatica and in the district of Eneis. At the estate also called Castris he established four pounds of pence annually, on the condition that one year furs should be provided to the brethren by the wardrobe-keeper, and the next by the provost of the place; while cowls and tunics should be supplied by the chamberlain.

Moreover, in the estate called Turb, situated in the district of Brabant on the water which the inhabitants call Oilla—“oil”—on account of its sweetness and excellence, [Note: [Col. 0629D] That is, *oleum*, “oil.”] he assigned half the revenues of the whole estate to the wardrobe-keeper. Thereafter Baldwin, a cleric of Soignies, having joined our brotherhood, added the other [Col. 0629B] half, which belonged to him by hereditary right, for the salvation of his soul.

He also decreed that the chamberlain should himself have the steward, investitures, and judicial pleas of the estates subject to him. He allotted one hundred shillings to the cellarer for the purchase of fattening animals. For purchasing utensils for the workshops—that is, the kitchen, bakery, brewhouse, and granary—he ordered thirty shillings from the rent of the enclosures to be given annually. He gave tithes of hay with which the cellarer might feed his oxen; he secured a food allowance and shoes for the oxherd who should bring wood daily from the forest; and he assigned to the oxherd a garden for growing vegetables and an oxherd’s yard with its enclosure.

Establishing all these arrangements under the cellarer’s care, he placed the brethren’s table under that care. Thus: bread of two pounds; a dish of vegetables, peas, or beans; [Col. 0629C] eighteen pence each day for purchasing a second dish—eggs, cheese, or fish. From the Kalends of October until Septuagesima Sunday, he ordered a third dish of garden herbs, two proper measures of cervisia daily, a measure of wine on each of four days of the week, with the charity portion on Saturday; fine wheaten biscuits at the midday meal on the twelve principal feasts of the year; and cakes and wafers with other sweet foods at supper.

Perhaps tomorrow someone, considering the character of the present age, will say: “What is read here is false; monks of that time never lived in such a manner.” God knows, who is highest truth, that I have written what I saw, and [Col. 0629D] suitable witnesses still survive. [Note: [Col. 0629] The same hand continues at another time.]

**49.** He added annually twenty shillings of coin for the church custodian to buy wine, from which [Note: [Col. 0629] *ex quo* corrected.] the daily sacrifice of the Mass must be celebrated. On the anniversary of his death he established that a charity portion of eight shillings should be given annually to the brethren, in grateful remembrance of him. The good steward shall be in everlasting remembrance; he shall not fear evil tidings, because his hope was always in the Lord.

**50.** In his last years he suffered most severely from pain in his feet; yet even in this illness he did not neglect [Col. 0630A] the welfare of the church, nor did he seek physicians’ aid, but trusted confidently in God. And while he thus patiently awaited the good completion of his works, through the virtue of that very patience he prepared a good completion for himself. Thus, long refined in the furnace of tribulation and illness, after completing twenty-three years in office, he paid the debt of human nature on 11 November, in the year of the Lord 1071.

## Concerning Abbot Tietmar

**51.** Upon the death of Abbot Misach, who had been a father so lovable and so useful to the Church of God, much grief and anxiety remained among the monks of Gembloux. They grieved at the loss of so great a shepherd; they were anxious lest one should succeed him who would scatter what had been gathered and fail to gather what had been scattered. But God, the Father of mercies, mercifully comforted [Col. 0630B] them, giving them from the same monastery an abbot named Tietmar.

Following in every respect in his predecessor’s footsteps, he increased rather than diminished the monastery’s resources. While he was church custodian in the time of the aforesaid abbot, he covered the Gospel ambo and the shrine of Saint Exuperius with gold and silver and adorned them with relief work. To this man, who fled worldly glory and followed Christ’s poverty in all things, the assembly of brethren gave as demesne land the estate of the cleric Hucbert, called “the Apostate.” He in return granted the brethren fifty shillings from the revenues of that estate, on condition that he and his successors should annually give two shillings on the principal feasts for the brethren’s use, to purchase fish.

[Col. 0630C] **52.** Through the hands of his provost, Lord Lietard, this father built a crypt in honor of the holy Mother of God; and he rebuilt the screen of Saint Peter’s altar from a low and small structure into the form in which it is now seen. He always cared from his heart for the sick, children, guests, and poor. If he did not increase the brethren’s allowance, he diminished it in no respect, but throughout his life, without any withholding, supplied wine, fish, and fine flour at the appointed times.

**53.** His nephew, the knight Franco Longus, from the estate called Lirul, married the daughter of the steward Albero. The abbot, as his kinsman, granted him by benefice the mill situated in the district of Eneis, on the understanding that he and his heir [Col. 0630D] should enjoy it as long as they lived, and that upon their death it should return to the monastery.

Within five years, therefore, after three children had been born to them, Franco was killed in battle near Distre. Brought back by his friends, he was buried in the cemetery of Gembloux with many tears. His sons too, before their father’s death [Note: [Col. 0629] At first *ejus* followed, then was immediately erased.] and afterward, departed this life. When they had thus died, the abbot reclaimed what he had granted; but the result was otherwise than he had hoped. For the knight Reinfred of Mafa, having married Franco’s widow, seized by marital right all that had belonged to her, with the support and help of her father, the steward Albero.

[Col. 0631A] Indignant over this, the abbot and Franco’s relatives summoned Reinfred before the general court; but his father-in-law Albero defended his son-in-law in every way. The matter, long drawn out, reached the hearing of Bishop Henry. Reinfred’s father happened then to be the bishop’s steward. Thus [Note: [Col. 0631] Manuscript c continues in different ink.] the bishop, softened by flattery and blinded by gifts, consented to sin; and, when injustice had been decreed as law, Reinfred prevailed in every respect. Thus the mill was unjustly taken from the abbot; thus the nearest heirs, disinherited, still make bitter complaint.

For this unfaithfulness Albero was deprived of his stewardship, but he was not punished by God for the injustice; and, ten years after the deed just mentioned, he coveted ecclesiastical property. For, driven by evil greed, he asked that the allod called Ruz—which Peter Calvellus had granted to Saint Peter before suitable witnesses—be redeemed for himself, alleging that, at the time of the grant, Peter had designated him as adopted heir.

[Col. 0631B] The abbot and provost, more astonished than can be said, asked and begged him to desist from the undertaking. But persisting in malice, he was presented to the bishop through his son-in-law Reinfred, who was then the bishop’s steward, and poured his case, and many plausible falsehoods, into the bishop’s ears. The bishop referred the matter to counsel. After deliberation it was decreed that, if Albero established by oath that what he sought was true, he should receive what he requested. The bishop sent the abbot his seal together with a letter to be presented.

When the abbot read the letter, he wrinkled his brow and beat his breast, then handed it to the provost to read. When the provost read it, he fixed a day for the court. On the appointed day the abbot would not attend the court, but entrusted the whole matter to the provost; at his command the assembly was gathered. Albero appeared with his witnesses and, without delay, falsely confirmed by oath what he sought. His witnesses, with genuine perjury, maintained that what he had sworn was true; and so he became the accursed and unjust usurper of church property.

[Col. 0631C] **54.** It must briefly be told what vengeance followed them. By God’s just judgment all were afflicted in different ways because of their perjury, and at last, tortured by prolonged illness, they died. Albero, belatedly repentant of what he had done, decreed that the property he had usurped should be given to his son Reinbald, subject to the assessment of an annual rent.

Once this agreement was confirmed, the dependants of Provost Lietard sought out Stephen the monk and Everard the baker and explained what they had arranged, requesting that, when the abbot and provost had accepted two marks [Note: [Col. 0631] *duabus* corrected to *duobus* in manuscript c.] [Col. 0631D] of silver, they should assent to their settlement, on the condition that Reinbald should pay ten shillings each year from the revenues of that allod on the feast of Saint Servatius.

Persuaded by his men, the provost quickly consented to the arrangement already described. They approached the abbot and asked that he grant his consent. He utterly refused, and angrily turned his eyes away from them. Finally, worn down by their importunity, he ordered that what was requested should be done in the presence of the community.

[Col. 0632A] The case was brought before the community. At the urging of the elders, Albero and all his party were despised, the agreement was rejected, and everyone cried out that he should be regarded as excommunicate. The provost persevered in his decision, accepted what had been offered despite the abbot and brethren, and so the parties separated.

Reinbald therefore succeeded, with his father-in-law Berengarius, to the ill-acquired inheritance; but, as God so willed, fortune turned against them, and both were grievously ruined. One day, while they were taking their customary rest from agricultural labor, they were drowned in a marsh adjoining the estate. Albero, under divine punishment, was afflicted with the loss of his household goods and deprived of the companionship of his wife, a woman quite faithful and chaste. Finally, himself bound by many bodily necessities, he ended in death.

For the present, let the account of perverse people be set aside, and let the praise and devotion of the righteous be described.

**55.** Adelard, a cousin of the aforesaid abbot, having been tonsured from knight to monk, granted to Saint Peter the portion of his allod that belonged to him, with the consent of his mother and stepfather, through the hands of his uncle the abbot and of Advocate Baldwin.

The religious priest named Berold joined our brotherhood at that time. [Note: [Col. 0631] Added above the line in manuscript c.] His works bear witness to how many good things he did for our church. He was a cheerful giver and a ready helper in times of need.

**56.** In the time of this abbot died also the monk Guerin, a man worthy of remembrance for every virtue. For many years, holding the office of prior in the monastery of Gembloux, he benefited all who lived devoutly in [Col. 0632C] Christ, by word and example. He was a relative and disciple of Abbot Olbert, and, imitating his life and conduct, advanced so far that those who knew him called him gold [Note: [Col. 0631] *auro* corrected to *aurum* in manuscript c.] purified by the great fire of merits and a vessel fitted for God’s honor.

For he devoted himself to fasts, vigils, prayers, and daily celebrations of Mass. Yet whenever, as rarely happened, he was free from such work, his spirit had no rest until, as an educated man, he set before the brethren and explained something of worldly or divine philosophy. Divine grace was so present to him in this also that from that time until now our church has had learned men through him and through those whom he instructed.

He died on 17 April; attended by the brethren’s prayers, grief, and tears, [Col. 0632D] he was buried within the church. How highly his contemporaries valued him is shown by his epitaph. We have added this distich, that what we have said about him may be more credible:

> Guerin, rule, glory, mirror, honor of monks,  
> Your teacher, O Gembloux, is covered by this tomb.

**57.** Sigebert, a man of much learning and monk of our church, at the urging of the aforesaid Abbot Tietmar, [Col. 0633A] [Note: [Col. 0631D] From the final chapter of Sigebert’s book *On Illustrious Men*.] revised more carefully by dictation the Life of Saint Maclovius the Confessor; elegantly composed in heroic metre the Passion of the Theban Martyrs; and carried his chronicle from the end of the chronicle arranged by Jerome down to the end of his own time.

To the two books *On Illustrious Men* composed by Jerome and Gennadius he added a third, in which he commemorated many ancient ecclesiastical writers and also many contemporaries worthy of remembrance. At the end of the book he placed himself last in sequence, though not of the least learning. Besides these works which we have mentioned, he composed many things useful to readers.

**58.** Although Abbot Tietmar possessed dove-like simplicity, his speech, wherever it reached—being free from the gall of envy and detraction—[Col. 0633B] was an encouragement to improvement. Therefore, after faithfully governing Christ’s household entrusted to him for twenty-three years, refined by the fire of a long illness, he happily departed this world on 31 May (A.D. 1092), [Note: [Col. 0633] *e* corrected.] and was granted a burial place before the altar of the Holy Cross, always to remain of praiseworthy memory among posterity. Amen.

## Epitaph of the Same

[Note: [Col. 0633] “Epitaph” through “Amen” were written in another ink at the end of folio 43a.]

> Here lies Tietmar, abbot, lamp of the Church,  
> Learned to have followed the eight blessed ways:  
> Poor, peace-making, gentle, pure in heart,  
> Mourning, hungering, compassionate, patient.  
> Your final light shone for him on the penultimate day of May.  
> He who lived for the Lord, may he sleep in the Lord. Amen.

## Concerning Abbot Liethard

[Note: [Col. 0633] Manuscript c continues in another ink.]

[Col. 0633C] **59.** When, after the death of Lord Abbot Tietmar, the monks of Gembloux asked who should succeed him and who was fit to govern them, they held a common deliberation and, by unanimous election, appointed Liethard abbot.

Trained from childhood by Lord Abbot Olbert, he was a lover and constant practitioner of cloistered discipline. He possessed great eloquence of speech, proceeding from the abundance of an enlarged heart. Whenever the sons of this world—who are wiser in their generation than the sons of light—attempted to inflict loss or violence upon church property, he knew how to resist them with prudent and timely reasoning.

Lord Abbot Olbert, already burdened by age and by the administration of two monasteries, observed in this young man [Col. 0633D] such natural ability that he entrusted to him the office of cellarer, so that he might plainly test him. As long as Olbert lived, Liethard obeyed him as a son obeys his father; and whatever had been entrusted to him, he increased, improved, and administered honorably. Though then of youthful age, he was nevertheless a person of dignity, useful in counsel, and welcome in conversation and exhortation to those who knew him.

Finally, many noblemen and men of middling rank, stirred by his counsel and praiseworthy friendship, associated some of their sons with us, together with a small portion of their property, so that among us their memory might be devout and prayer for them [Col. 0634A] frequent before God. Because harmful forgetfulness grows with the passage of time, and dangerous contention follows forgetfulness, I think I shall please our descendants if I endeavor to insert in this little work the acquisitions made by our church during the time of Lord Abbot Olbert through Lord Liethard’s administration. Thus, because he acquired more than other abbots, it may be known what he acquired, how, and from whom. I shall therefore describe, if not everything, at least the more important things.

**60.** Machelm, a nobleman and father of Lord Tietmar, who was the sixth abbot of our monastery, at the request of his son and the exhortation of Lord Liethard, gave to Saint Peter half the church of Saint Mary in the estate called Castra. The other half was afterward given on behalf of our monk Odewalon. He was a man of honorable life and of much learning in divine and human literature.

Likewise Wicher, advocate of Liège, granted Saint Peter half the church of Saint Gaugericus at Genitines, with one mansus. Likewise Robert, son of Boso of Hermereis, a canon of Saint Lambert and a nobleman, granted Saint Peter half of Masniz, and, beyond that half, three mansi. Of the other half our church partly redeemed portions from his relatives or received them as a pledge.

A certain Wibert, a religious man and, as is said, a kinsman of Saint Wibert, granted Saint Peter all that he possessed at Waresch. In the same estate Wolvurad granted half a church—that is, a quarter of the entire church.

[Col. 0634B] Liedwin and his wife Hatheguidis granted Saint Peter one farmstead and six bonuaria for their souls at Harenton. Later they granted half of all the estate they possessed in that same Harenton, and all that they possessed at Valle, which yields fifty shillings annually.

At Belriu Lord Abbot Olbert acquired six mansi and a brewhouse, as well as a sixth part of the mill; this was afterward increased by Abbot Mysach and Abbot Liethard, as shall be said in its place. In the estate of Melenriu, also called Heis after the neighboring wood bearing that name, Abbot Olbert first purchased a portion of the allod; Abbot Liethard and his successor Anselm enlarged it, as shall be said in its place.

Walter of Niel granted Saint Peter all he possessed in that estate. The share of the church which we have there [Col. 0634D] and a share of the estate were afterward given on behalf of our two brethren Albuin and Hellin. Subsequently that holding grew and remained, through much labor and danger undertaken by Lord Liethard. For the disagreement between the co-possessors of the estate and ourselves was so great that it could scarcely have been settled without war, after the shrine of Saint Exuperius had been brought there.

Peter Calvellus granted Saint Peter all he possessed at Ruoz, and at Asnatica one farmstead and three bonuaria. After a long time this estate was seized by Albero through true perjury, as has been said in its place.

With Lord Liethard’s assistance, Lord Abbot Olbert acquired the estate of Suvrei for Saint Peter [Col. 0635A] and imposed upon it an annual rent of three pounds. From this he decreed that twelve shillings should be given for the brethren’s service on the anniversary of his death.

Lambert of Corcellis, a nobleman, and his brothers granted Saint Peter three mansi in that estate; and after Lambert’s death his wife Condrada gave half a mansus. Not content with this gift, she gave to Saint Peter bracelets, rings, necklaces, and all the gold which she possessed as a rich and distinguished woman for her adornment, and asked that a golden cross be made from it. The inscription upon this golden cross survives even today: “Condrada gave me to Saint Peter for herself and her husband Lambert.”

Nor Condrada alone, but all the succession of her descendants—namely Walter of Marebaco, Henry of Lupun, Gerard son of Walter, Henry son of Henry, and all who still survive today from their lineage—have been joined, from then until now, to our brotherhood with such sincere affection that their memory is always devout among us and prayer for them daily before God. For through the benefit of their generosity our possession has often increased.

[Col. 0635B] Count Warner granted one mansus at Dion; his wife, two at Morceshem and one at Malbrovias, which is called in Ruoz. That mansus at Dion pays four shillings and eight chickens. Those two at Morceshem pay ten shillings in the money of Louvain and four chickens. That at Malbrovias pays five shillings in the money of Nivelles; and all were to be free from every service except that owed to the church of Gembloux.

Of the possessions which Lord Abbot Olbert acquired with Lord Liethard, we have described a few, but the more notable ones. In my judgment, we have thereby provided for our posterity, so that if any unjust person, by violence or ignorance—as often happens—attempts to diminish or take away church property, they may know how to resist him justly and reasonably. They acquired many other things also, smaller perhaps, but suited to the church’s advantage; for it is certain that great things are aided by small things, and that a river is filled by many drops of rain.

[Col. 0635C] **61.** The successor of Abbot Olbert, Abbot Mascelin, having experienced in many matters how shrewd-minded Lord Liethard was, entrusted him, at the request of brethren who feared God, with the office of provost. Liethard, considering the position to which he had been raised not an honor but a burden, was to the abbot a staff of strength, because he had no cowardly fear within him, and a relief from anxiety, because he was useful in everything.

Abbot Tietmar, being very simple and unable to guard against the deceitful snares of secular duplicity, entrusted all external matters to Liethard’s care; he himself attended only to internal matters. Thus, because these three abbots were hindered, as has been said, by age, illness, or simplicity, the church’s affairs were, for the most part, sustained in their time by Liethard’s excellence.

Since Lord Liethard had learned, during the time of three abbots, to be subject and to be useful, he was judged worthy, after them, to be asked to preside and to be useful. Once made abbot, as long as he possessed bodily strength and favorable circumstances, he benefited in all respects those over whom [Col. 0636A] he presided. Providing for the welfare of all the brethren, he made no provision for himself, but was always content with scant food and clothing. What he had received from the fathers he faithfully administered to the extent he could.

Although the church was often burdened by many hardships—by barrenness of the land, pestilence among livestock, or the violence of wars—he never made his own advantage out of the brethren’s misfortunes. Rather, at Christmas, Easter, Pentecost, and the feasts of saints, both principal and lesser, he duly dispensed the established allowance in every respect.

In the third year of his rule there was a very great mortality among humankind, and in the following year a great and unavoidable scarcity of provisions, so severe that our cultivated lands and [Col. 0636B] tithes scarcely supplied us with bread for two months’ days. Under the pressure of this shortage of bread, the monastery’s allowance was put up for sale to laymen and clerics alike. The sword of God’s wrath raged everywhere; the roofs of the rich, like the huts of the poor, were battered by the evil of famine as by a great battering ram. The poor and many people of middling rank perished through this plague; cemeteries did not suffice for burial.

In many places broad and deep pits were dug, and the bodies of the dead were lowered into them by ropes. Many were found dead at the exits of roads, many amid the shaded places of forests. Compelled by this plague of famine, many noblemen, unwilling to part from their households, spent much silver to sustain them. Moneylenders oppressed their debtors in every manner; and when they did not receive their money on the appointed day, they doubled it on the day [Col. 0636C] of payment, [Note: [Col. 0635D] Written in an erased space.] under pledge and oath.

62. A certain nobleman, Anolinus, of the village called Halley, oppressed by these misfortunes, sold to Saint Peter for fifteen marks of silver the allod that he held in the village of Jandrinul. Robert likewise, of the same village, sold to Saint Peter for eight marks of silver the small estate which he held in the village called Saint-Gaugeric. Baldwin and John, full brothers from the village called Jalce, conveyed to Saint Peter for seven marks the allod which they held in the village now called Mount Saint Guibert. Lord Abbot Liethard bought from Elbert of Vileyr and his wife Eremburga—with the assent of their sons Godfrey, Arnulf, and Godescalc—for sixty marks whatever hereditary allod they possessed in the village of Gembloux: namely, [Col. 0636D] fields, tilled lands, cultivated and uncultivated ground, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, rights of way, the share of toll accruing to them, a share of the mill, and the other things dependent upon the aforesaid property. Elbert and his wife Eremburga lawfully conveyed all these things to Saint Peter through the hand of Baldwin the advocate, in the presence of Lord Abbot Liethard.

Also, in the presence of the same Lord Abbot Liethard and the brethren, Machelmus, Engo, and Godescalc of Marebaco pledged to Saint Peter, for eight marks, whatever allod they held at Gembloux—in the market, woods, meadows, fields, gardens, and mill, [Col. 0637A] for twelve years.
