If it should not be redeemed after twelve years, the church shall hold it permanently, until the Kalends of October in the following year. Done in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1096, in the fourth indiction, on the Kalends of October.

Gosbert, a layman and citizen of ours, was associated with our brotherhood in those same days. For as long as he lived thereafter, he proved very useful to the church. He paid this silver from his own resources, on condition that, after his death, the entire revenue of that allod should be given in common to the brethren on the anniversary of his death.

63. Lord Berold, a brother of our congregation, concerned for the salvation of his soul, established, with the consent of Lord Abbot Liethard and all the brethren, that every day a Mass should be sung in the church of Gembloux [Col. 0637B] for all the faithful departed; and this ordinance must remain inviolate for ever. To carry this out, he assigned, through the hand of the lord abbot and of all the brethren, one half of the mill at Manilz—which he held in pledge from Elbert and his wife Erenburga for fifteen marks of silver, and had caused lawfully to be conveyed to the church of Gembloux—so that the priest who sings the Mass should receive the income of that mill, apart from the offerings. And if the mill is redeemed, the abbot and brethren shall receive those fifteen marks and shall make provision from them that Mass be sung every day in perpetuity. Whoever destroys this ordinance, let him be anathema.

64. Lord Sigebert, the writer of the Life of Lord [Col. 0637C] Abbot Olbert, spoke truthfully concerning his life and deeds, and could do so without doubt, since he lived with him for a long time. Among other matters, he described and enumerated what that abbot bestowed upon the church of God in gold and silver, in considerable abundance. Since the reader can easily find these things in their proper place, we think it superfluous to repeat them here. Many therefore rightly ask who destroyed them, what was done with them, and what benefit the church of God derived from them.

In answering them, we accuse none of our elders, but excuse ourselves. God knows that we have endured great want of clothing and food, plunderings, burnings, and many tribulations; yet we never put even a single coin from the church’s treasury toward our own expenses. Abbot Liethard, apart from what his predecessors had received, gave from the treasury of the church, when money failed him, more than one hundred and twenty marks’ worth [Col. 0637D] for purchasing estates during a time of distress, when there was an excessive scarcity of grain.

When the brethren, in his time and in that of his predecessors, were greatly saddened that things contributed for the worship of God and the adornment of the church were being destroyed, although a just cause seemed to demand it, the abbots defended themselves by this answer and offered it to the brethren in their own excuse. They said that the purchase of estates brought about an improvement in ecclesiastical possessions, whereas we, alas, see a diminution. They added that one must guard against what they themselves had experienced: namely, lest, upon the discovery of any pretext, episcopal violence should seize the church’s property without profit, though not without our grief. [Col. 0638A] This was their final excuse, and it seemed a very weighty one as well: if any powerful secular person became proud in our neighborhood through the purchase of an estate, our lands would always be devastated by him and our household afflicted.

Saint Jerome says that in every outcome of affairs we ought to weigh more carefully the disposition of the intention than the effect of the act. If, therefore, the abbots’ intention was simple and upright, the effect of their action will not be blameworthy but excusable. Let us return to the matter from which we have digressed.

65. Lord Abbot Liethard, the religious son of a religious father—namely, Lord [Col. 0638B] Abbot Olbert—offered to those over whom he presided an example of religious life. Though he surpassed them in deeds worthy of imitation, he governed what he did with praiseworthy discretion. It had long been his custom to prolong his fast until the evening hour on Wednesdays and Fridays; and he observed this especially in the days of the Lord’s Advent and of Lent. Although he was scarcely or not at all willing to indulge himself, he nevertheless ordered that the brethren be served a refreshment appropriate to the season without delay, preferring that they should voluntarily add something to their undertaking rather than abstain under compulsion from his command.

He rarely or never dined or supped in his own chamber, unless the rank [Col. 0638C] of some distinguished guest compelled him, and charity itself, so to speak, drew him there. If at any time a greater-than-usual concern pressed upon him, he anticipated the dining hour in the refectory, or took food with a few others after the brethren’s meal.

66. [Note: From here onward the script is somewhat smaller, but the hand and author are the same.] The church of the village of Dion, together with its demesne court, having been burned by William of Bellorivo, Lord Abbot Liethard restored to a better condition while he was still provost. He also built from the foundations the church of Saint Nicholas in the village of Sovrei; he renewed, together with all its workshops, the Gembloux court called Capella, which had been burned by the enemy from Namur; and he suitably and well arranged, as far as he could, the cultivation of fields in the villages and estates—that is, Sterias, Jandrigul, Sothejam, Bavenchin, Dion, Genehen, Sovrei, Niel, Picta Villa, Eyneis, and Capella. [Col. 0638D]

He also assigned Salvenerias with its adjoining land, and the mill of the village of Masniz, to our infirm brethren and to the brethren on the anniversary of his death. He added likewise what he acquired in the village called Rosiris, in the village of Saint Paul, and in another called Wastin; and he appointed a brother to care for them.

67. Since we read and know that the village of Salvenerias belonged among the estates of blessed Guibert, it is asked what Abbot Liethard acquired there. We give a true answer to this question. After blessed Guibert’s death, his relatives seized all his [Col. 0639A] estates; and, because they were many, making many shares for themselves, they scarcely left one share out of each to the church, nor did they leave even one village entire to the church. This is still proved today in the principal village of Gembloux and in its other possessions, in which we have many co-possessors. Therefore, whatever pays rent in the village of Salvenerias belonged to the possession of blessed Guibert. But the court and the land belonging to it Abbot Liethard acquired from the possessions of others.

Never idle in vain leisure, but continually aflame with desire for the church’s welfare, he secured the consecration, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, of the crypt which had been built under Abbot Tietmar, through his own special labor, by Otbert, bishop of Liège. On that same day the principal dedication of our church is celebrated. [Col. 0639B]

68. When, on one occasion, he was going to Liège at the invitation of that same bishop, and the heat of the sun, as was to be expected in mid-summer, afflicted everything with excessive burning, compelled by the weariness not of himself but of his companions, he ordered them to be given food, to relieve the extreme heat and enable them afterward to hasten their journey. The horses having been turned out to pasture, he reclined with his companions in an orchard adjoining the road. When many persons nearby saw this, they flocked to him from every direction. He ordered that they should not be turned away, but that they should kindly be given from what he and his companions were using. He also ordered wine to be offered them, although he knew that there was wine there for himself and his companions only in a wineskin of small capacity.

When the meal was finished, [Col. 0639C] he asked the servant whether any wine remained that could be offered to him. The servant said: “Thanks be to God, from the little vessel I have properly served many people wine today, and there still remains enough to serve many more.” Those present marveled that wine from such a tiny vessel had sufficed for so many, and had rather increased than failed. But the abbot humbly ascribed it to God’s grace and mercy that it had sufficed and more than sufficed for himself and his companions. There are still living today people who were present at this event, and they recount to another generation what then happened.

69. How great was his constancy of spirit against those who committed violence against the church’s possessions or tried to seize them may be known, passing over many instances, from this one alone. Onulf of Upper Dion was a nobleman, rich in estates and dependents. At the prompting of his own people and enticed by an unjust covetousness of heart, he provoked Lord Abbot Liethard with disputes before many noblemen, saying that through him and through the prelates of the church of Gembloux he had lost no small part of an estate which he held in Lower Dion, solely because of the adjoining location, and not for any reasonable cause. [Col. 0639D]

Though provoked, the abbot did not provoke in return, but answered moderately that the church held nothing unjustly. He added that it befitted a nobleman to be content with his own possessions, since they could suffice him; that he should not, to the offense of God and the saints, seize ecclesiastical property, because this could not turn out with impunity for him. The man was not recalled from his undertaking by these warnings; laying words aside, he threatened to vindicate his alleged rights by [Col. 0640A] arms.

The abbot, by contrast, armed himself not with the weapons of worldly warfare but with the weapons of Christian religion, enjoining the brethren to continual prayer to God concerning this affair; he himself maintained a three-day fast with much contrition of heart and body. On the appointed day Onulf came to the estate with the supporters of his cause. Duke Godfrey, advocate of our church, was present; the abbot too was there with a few attendants. When Onulf had dismounted from his horse and begun to measure what he called his own, and, after measuring it at his pleasure, wished to set up a boundary-marker, he walked carelessly and drove the spur of his left foot into his right shin, grievously wounding himself. Immediately, as a disease of little worms attacked him, he was almost lifeless; abandoning his undertaking, he returned home. [Col. 0640B] During the three days that he survived, he had no ability to eat or drink, and thus departed this life.

Duke Godfrey confirmed to the church the estate whose dispute had been ended by so manifest a judgment of God; with God’s help, the church possesses and will possess it. May God forgive those whom we have endured and still endure as adversaries and invaders of our possessions. May He acknowledge, and reward as His own, those by whose possessions we have been enriched and by whose means we have been sustained. Foremost among all these was Berold, a devout priest, whom we have mentioned both in this little work and in the Life of Abbot Tietmar. Joined to our brotherhood and most dear to Lord Abbot Liethard, he gave one hundred pounds of money—not at one time, but on various occasions—for the purchase of estates [Col. 0640C] and for his various needs. He died in the time of this abbot and received a burial place before the altar of Saint Gertrude, whose tower he had built at his own expense. He deserved this worthily, because he held nothing dearer than the honor and welfare of our place, to which he was always ready to devote not only his possessions but himself.

70. Oddo, canon and dean of Saint Martin’s at Liège, kinsman of Lord Abbot Liethard, bore toward us a charity not feigned but perfect. For as soon as he began to visit us and our fraternity, he gave a hyacinth-colored cloth to Saint Peter, with which the altar is adorned on his principal feast days. He also gave seven marks of silver upon the pledge of Guarner of Firminis, and established that its income should be given each year to the brethren on the anniversary [Col. 0640D] of his death.

Engrannus of Balastra, having become a brother of our congregation at the urging of Lord Abbot Liethard, gave us at Liège a property from which thirty denarii are paid annually; a vineyard at Juniacum; three solidi at Genitinis; three solidi at Tillir and Huten; and a share of the mill at Gondulpunt. Everelmus of Wisenbech conveyed to Saint Peter the estate which he held at Melenriv, in the presence of Lord Abbot Liethard. Tietbald, our citizen and brother, paid the silver which was due to him, and established its rent for the anniversary of his own death.

71. Vivian, also called Lambert, cousin of Lord Abbot Liethard, was brought up by him from childhood in the clerical habit. He grew into an honorable and religious man and, for as long as he lived, was useful and faithful to the church of Gembloux. From his own hereditary property and from what he acquired by fitting industry, he assigned fifty-seven solidi annually to Saint Peter. He decreed that these should be under the charge of the church custodian, and that from them the custodian should continually supply the light of a suitable lamp before the altar of Mary, the holy Mother of God. [Col. 0641A] On the anniversary of his death, he established that a charitable meal should be sufficiently provided for the brethren, so that his pious remembrance might always endure in our place and devout prayer be made to God for him. May he and all our benefactors possess eternal life and rejoice in the fellowship of all the righteous. Amen.

72. Lord Sigebert, praiseworthy for integrity of character and richness of learning [Col. 0641B], and esteemed by the wise men of his age, has no need of our praises, because his works praise him. While still young, in the time of Abbot Mascelin, he became known to the people of Metz; and, having lived for a long time in the monastery of Saint Vincent the Martyr with Abbot Fulcuin, he was an open fountain of wisdom not only to monks but also to clerics flocking to him from every direction. His memory remains sweet even today to many inhabitants of Metz, among whom traces of his teaching still survive. What and how much he published there at their request while resident among them, he himself shows in the Book of Illustrious Men which he composed.

He was beloved not only by Christians but also by the Jews living in the same city, because he was skilled in distinguishing the Hebrew truth from other versions, [Col. 0641C] and, in matters which they maintained according to the Hebrew truth, agreed with the assertions of the Jews. After a long time, having scarcely obtained permission, he returned to the monastery of Gembloux. He contributed many things to the use and adornment of the church, which he had acquired through the voluntary generosity of those whom he had instructed.

The older men, those higher in rank, and those keener in intellect who lived in the city of Liège frequently resorted to him; if any question arose to them, they were accustomed to bring it to him and discuss it with him. Foremost among these was Lord Henry, archdeacon and dean of the church of Saint Lambert. At his request Sigebert wrote for the people of Trier the book On the Fasts of the Four Seasons, and many other works which he mentions in the Book of Illustrious Men.

At the monastery of Gembloux, he instructed me, who have written these things, and many better men; many of them he sent ahead of himself, and a few, alas, he left behind him. [Col. 0641D] Though a prudent man of great seriousness, he was not stern with indiscriminate severity, but toward all showed a measured moderation suited to circumstances. Reading and meditation upon the Scriptures, especially the divine Scriptures, occupied him; nevertheless, the daily celebration of Masses and devout prayer to God always took precedence for him.

Worn out by old age, when he had taken to bed with his final illness, losing none of his inborn prudence, and although the brethren wished that at his death he should receive a burial place within the monastery, as a man of higher counsel, preferring to be found humble rather than presumptuous in God’s sight, he earnestly requested [Col. 0642A] to be buried in our cemetery with all the fathers. He died on the third day before the Nones of October, in the time of Lord Abbot Liethard.

## Remembrance of Our Departed Brethren

[Note: “Justis … aetas” (vv. 1–5), written by another hand in an erased space.]

Joined to the righteous, may Sigebert live in Christ.

The world changes; it passes away while it seems to stand.

A living human being passes on, but passes utterly away in dying.

Alas! Death spares no human being; it is given to all;

No one’s lifetime passes beyond the boundaries fixed beforehand.

If tears in this world could recall the dead,

How many, and what men, how spiritual for us,

Illustrious in every pursuit—and alas, now rare—

Would be mourned with Sigebert, who had earned his rest.

[Col. 0642B] But since the illustrious and rare cannot be recalled,

Withdrawn from the world, may they be joined to the dwellers in heaven.

God always gives us consolation through himself. Amen.

73. Lord Abbot Liethard lived long with Lord Sigebert, but did not long survive him. After these things which we have written concerning him, and after many things which we have passed over, perceiving that his bodily strength was failing and that he was unequal to administering what he had administered, he divided the burden of his care among brethren whom he knew to be capable, and applied himself more earnestly to prayers, vigils, and fasts, so that he might be more prepared to meet the Lord calling him through the affliction of illness.

Commending to the brethren whom he had treated fatherly and stirred by word and example toward the things of God [Col. 0642C] unanimity in brotherly love and the charity which is the bond of perfection, he bade them farewell amid words of pious exhortation, while they wept. In the twenty-second year of his prelacy, he died on the second day before the Nones of February. The brethren performed his funeral rites with great sorrow, openly showing how affectionate their feeling toward him was. Giving him, therefore, a burial place before the altar of Mary, holy Mother of God, from that time until now they pray to God for his eternal rest.

May God, who is life, grant him blessed life without end. Amen.

## Epitaph

Abbot Liethard, like Judas Maccabaeus,

A good leader like Joshua, presided over the church.

For it he bore wars, threats, and many reproaches;

Yet in the contest he did not abandon the prize.

[Col. 0642D] Through so many labors, a strong man and a diligent Martha,

He ministered to the brethren in every way he could.

At last, weary, despising earthly affairs,

He chose a portion equal to Magdalene’s.

Do not take it away from him, you who freely give all things,

You who alone are good: have mercy on him, O God. Amen. Amen.

## Concerning Abbot Anselm

74. The men of Gembloux, knowing that it belongs to sons to grieve over the loss of a spiritual father, and to wise men to moderate grief arising from whatever source, said among themselves the saying of the blessed Apostle Paul: “We are perplexed, but not in despair” (2 Cor. 4:8). We are perplexed because we grieve at the loss of Lord Abbot [Col. 0643A] Liethard. But we are not in despair, because, by God’s bounty, we have among ourselves one whom we may appoint as a suitable father and provider. Therefore it does not become us, given over to sorrow, to neglect ourselves and our concerns; rather, being diligent and united, we should elect without delay someone who will benefit our place, ourselves, and what is ours. This was the counsel of all, spoken and carried out. They elected Lord Anselm as eighth abbot.

He was a kinsman and disciple of Guerin, worthy before God, whom we mentioned in the Life of Abbot Tietmar. Imitating his prudence, refinement of conduct, and constancy in prayer, he had acquired great reverence among his own people and goodwill among outsiders. [Col. 0643B] Since he was already mature in age and character, his reputation for prudence became known among the Franks, although they were far distant from the monastery of Gembloux. First the men of Hautvillers, and afterward those of Lagny, had him as teacher and almost as a second abbot.

Having remained among them for a long time and become, as it were, a mirror of integrity, he benefited not only those of lesser capacity, but more generously instructed those who were fit to instruct others; through them the root of wisdom which he planted in them continues to bear fruit to this day. At that time many of our brethren, not only in Francia but also in other provinces, were teachers and, as it were, second abbots in many monasteries, because, trained in human and divine writings, they left abundant fruit of wisdom wherever they were employed.

75. When Lord Anselm at last returned to the monastery [Col. 0643C] of Gembloux, he strove day by day to advance in goodness under Lord Abbot Liethard. He was an assiduous investigator of the library, improving it by correcting and enlarging it wherever usefulness demanded. Whenever he was free from reading or prayer, he expounded some portion of human or divine literature to the younger brethren, wishing not merely to flourish in himself but also to live in them after his death.

When made abbot, he showed himself suited to the burden and honor he had assumed; both his person and his prudence were honorable to those who knew him. He associated with himself the brethren whom he knew to be more capable, entrusted ecclesiastical offices to them, and through them did what he did not wish or was unable to do himself. Thus, through them, he adorned with buildings the monastery, cloister, refectory, dormitory, chapter house, every office of the cloistral court, and all the outer courts; and he increased them by purchasing neighboring fields. [Col. 0643D]

76. The prudent reader knows that old charters possess greater authority through their uncultivated antiquity than what modern men now compose with more meticulous elegance. We have therefore inserted in this account certain events occurring in this abbot’s time, as they are contained in the charters: good things to encourage good works, and bad things as a warning to posterity.

77. A certain field adjoined the estate of Eineys. [Col. 0644A] From ancient times it had been granted by the abbot of our house to cultivators on the condition that, after cultivating the land, they should bring the fourth sheaf to the church’s granaries. As time passed, however, it was neglected by the farmers because of its barrenness and lay waste with nettles, brambles, and thorns. Lord Abbot Liethard therefore added this vacant field to the vestry without consulting the heirs. [Note: “Heirs” [German *erben*], as above “cultivators”: possessors of fields.]

The vestry-keeper cultivated the land, enriched with marl and manure, by the plough; he built a house upon it, employed an oxherd, and devoted every kind of labor to Wineritilio—for that was the field’s name. Meanwhile the heirs appeared, complained of injustice, burned the house built upon it, and demanded by every means that the inheritance be restored to them. But while this dispute was prolonged, Lord Abbot Liethard died, and Lord Abbot Anselm succeeded him—a man certainly of good memory and distinguished learning, fit to bear the burden which the united love of the brethren had laid upon him. [Col. 0644B]

But alas! after a short time so great a man was deprived of bodily strength by illness, and while his knowledge, intelligence, and eloquence remained vigorous, he sustained his failing stomach with scanty food and very little wine. The heirs of the field therefore approached him as ruler and altogether demanded that the inheritance lost through neglect be restored to them. After taking counsel with his own men, the abbot heard them in court on the appointed day and, by a ruling issued by the aldermen, found for them on what they claimed. Thus, each having been restored the share which belonged to him, a very large part of the field still remained.

Baldwin the cleric, son of Albero, whom we mentioned in the Life of Abbot Tietmar, was then chief adviser to the abbot. Differing in no respect from his father’s character except that he was greedier in receiving and more cunning in seeking, he coveted the remaining part of the field. Having promised two marks of silver, he asked the abbot to give it to him. The abbot wholly refused. But Baldwin finally deceived the abbot through the provost Adelard, his intimate associate, and through certain brethren who knew nothing at all of the field’s size; without any amount of land being specified, he fixed the rent at five solidi and took twenty-four bonuaria of land at his own pleasure. [Col. 0644C] If this was just, may God, the just judge, see it. When the brethren learned of this, they complained to the abbot of the injustice, but in vain. For laying responsibility for the matter upon those who had been present, the abbot declared himself excused in every respect. [Col. 0644D] Lord our God, judge our cause.

78. Berengar, who with his son-in-law Reinbald unjustly possessed the estate called Ruz, afflicted by many misfortunes, took counsel and sold the harmful possession to a certain layman, Freier. Freier, like a blind man fallen into a pit, learned too late from ill consequences what he had bought. He complained to his own people about his purchase of the estate and silently considered how he might be rid of it. What he desired at once came to pass. He gave his daughter in marriage to Tietger, son of the aforesaid Reinfred, and bestowed upon him, as a dowry together with some money, the estate of destruction. [Col. 0645A] Thus, by God’s ordering, Ruz returned from an outside house to the house of the man who had first seized it.

Not long afterward, as Tietger was going with friends on an appointed day to some court hearing, another knight met him in the middle of the road. Their horses, driven at speed, collided head-on; his horse was thrown to the ground by the other’s horse. He himself was badly struck, shaken in every limb, and carried away by his companions; on the eighth day he died. The prophet David says: “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is upright” (Ps. 118 [119]:137). Since we cannot contradict this declaration, let us commit all things to God’s judgment.

79. Charter concerning the office of reeve. Otbert, by the grace of God bishop of the people of Liège, to the deans, provosts, abbots, and all governors of churches [Col. 0645B] of God dwelling under our authority. We have learned that you know well the dispute which occurred in the parish of Gembloux between the abbot and the reeve; therefore, lest anything of that sort should ever happen in your places, we have taken care to make you cautious and watchful.

The reeveship which Reeve Emmo had attempted to retain by hereditary right, having been rightfully taken from him by our judgment and that of all, the abbot shall give to whatever other servant of the church he chooses. So that this act may remain an example for all churches, we forbid by God’s authority and ours that any abbot should hereafter grant authority to act as reeve to Emmo as though he were an heir, or to his sons as evil heirs of evil men, lest the latter error become worse than the former. [Col. 0645C] If anyone, as though moved by mercy toward him, attempts to restore him, let him be judged not a son of the free woman, who is Mother Church, but an adulterer of an adulteress; let him be anathema maranatha, separated from the fellowship of all Christ’s faithful.

Done at Liège and confirmed by the testimony of worthy men—abbots, archdeacons, and laymen.

Witnesses: Berengar, abbot of Saint Lawrence; Olbert, abbot of Saint James; Rodulf, abbot of Saint Trudo; Stephen, abbot of Brogne; Alexander, archdeacon; Frederick, archdeacon; Henry, archdeacon; Henry, archdeacon; Andrew, archdeacon.

80. Charter of Mount Saint Guibert. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Godfrey, by the grace of God count of Louvain and duke of Lotharingia, to all friends of truth. Let it be known to you that in my days and those of Anselm [Col. 0645D], abbot of Gembloux, near the village called Belrius there was a place now named Mount Saint Guibert after him. The hill was uncultivated, but very suitable for fortification. It belonged to the estate of the church of Gembloux, and the church formerly situated upon it had long since been destroyed; nevertheless, in proportion to its means, it paid in due season what it owed to the church of Liège.

The abbot, monks, and household of the church, fearing what was to be feared—namely, that some unjust invader, upon finding any pretext, might seize the place and, after building a fortress, afflict the neighbors and especially the church’s household—took counsel with me. On the Wednesday of Easter week they carried the shrine of Saint Guibert, with his relics, there; and, with God’s help and with blessed Guibert granting abundant grace of healing to the sick, [Col. 0646A] they built, as is seen today, a church at great expense and labor, so that that place might be not the dwelling of a despoiler but the house of the Savior.

I rejoiced in the work accomplished by my counsel, since it would procure frequent prayer to God for me from the brethren in the monastery of Gembloux, and would bring the neighbors not disturbance but consolation of souls and bodies. When many gathered there because of the unity of peace and concord, and built homes for themselves to live in, I again took counsel with my friends and with the aforesaid abbot and the household of the church. I decreed that the place should have in all respects one legal and customary right with the town of Gembloux. Except for me, no one should possess any jurisdiction there. It should receive no advocate except me. Through the abbot and through me, if necessity required, matters requiring settlement should be settled and matters requiring correction corrected.

Although I, like my predecessors, have been appointed advocate of the monastery of Gembloux through the emperor’s hand, nevertheless, so that my ordinance might be wholly ratified, the bishop of Liège gave this confirmation: if I or any of my successors changes what has been established, let him be anathema. Amen, amen. Done in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1123, first indiction, epact 22, in the episcopate of Albero the First of that name, bishop of the people of Liège. [Col. 0646B]

81. Charter concerning Dudinsart. Let all who love truth, which is God, know that Duke Godfrey the elder and his son of the same name, Godfrey the younger, for the salvation of their souls, gave to God and Saint Peter a certain estate in the parish of Braine called Dudinsart. In the presence of a great [Col. 0646C] multitude of their nobles and faithful men, they decreed that this grant should remain valid and unshaken for ever. Therefore, for the donors and supporters of this gift we pray for the rewards of eternal recompense; upon plunderers and robbers we pronounce the threats and penalties of eternal excommunication.

Witnesses: Godfrey, count of Namur, and his son Henry; Henry the younger, son of the duke himself; William, advocate of Namur, and his brother Anselm; Erfelo of Calvo Monte; Gerard of Wanga and his son Henry; Henry of Birbais; Scherus of Wavre; Gothuinus of Louvain; Franco of Brussels; and many other nobles and servants.

Done at Gembloux in the year of the Lord 1131, while Lothair was reigning, Lord Alexander was bishop of the people of Liège, Anselm was governing our place as abbot, Gregory was governing the Roman see as pope, and Duke Godfrey was our advocate, assisted in the secondary role by his son Sceeri Bernard. [Col. 0646D]

82. Someone may say: “What usefulness is there in copying charters?” We answer: “Much in every way, because they contain the privileges of churches and ecclesiastical possessions.” Therefore our predecessors thought it fitting, and we also thought it fitting, to insert them in appropriate places, lest they be improperly handled by the unwary; so that charters which could be possessed and produced may make known what was unknown and rebuke invaders, while charters neither possessed nor produced may not seem to increase ignorance and add boldness to invaders in seizing what is not theirs.

The church of Saint Peter in the village called Bavenchi was said to have been dedicated [Col. 0647A], and the dead were buried in its cemetery; but because the day of its dedication was unknown, it was judged that it ought to be dedicated again. After the dispute over this matter had continued for a long time, Lord Abbot Anselm, finding an opportunity, caused it to be dedicated by Lord Alexander, bishop of the people of Liège, on the Kalends of September, the feast day of Saint Giles, abbot.

With the consent and at the request of that same bishop, during those same days our church in the village called Castra was consecrated by Lord Godfrey—although bishop of the English, yet our fellow-countryman—on the third day before the Ides of November, the day of the deposition of Saint Martin the Confessor. The consecration of these churches took place in the year of the Lord 1133, [Note: “one thousand one hundred” was added at another time in an empty space left before “XXXIII.”] Lord Abbot Anselm expending much money.

[Col. 0647B] **83.** In the days of this abbot, many people were cured of diverse illnesses through blessed Guibert; many were freed from chains and fetters. Since we aim at brevity, and since we have recorded many notable instances of his miracles in their proper places, lest we be blamed for having passed over everything in silence, we shall write down one instance out of many.

A certain woman of Hagino, through the long duration of illness, already half dead in one side of her body, died daily and yet did not die. She died because, as it seemed to her, she suffered pains more grievous than death. She did not die because the pains themselves were not ended by final death. Through the poverty and disturbance caused by her sickness, she had become a burden and weariness to her neighbours and relatives. Therefore she asked from them this, as though it were a final kindness: [Col. 0647C] that she might be carried in a vehicle to the monastery of Gembloux, so that, while she was there maintained by the alms of the faithful, their concern and weariness might be lightened.

At last she obtained what she requested, and she remained for some time at Gembloux in the hospital for the poor. She was known not only to the townspeople but also to strangers visiting the town, because the greater her illness was, the greater was the assiduity of those attending her. For she could not rise from bed or move from one place to another unless supported by someone else’s help. At length, with the annual cycle, the celebrated anniversary day of blessed Guibert’s death arrived, and a great multitude of citizens and strangers attended his votive solemnity. Since the aforesaid woman could not attend, she lamented and earnestly begged to be carried there.

At last [Col. 0647D] she was carried there. With tearful groans she prayed that God, through the prayer of blessed Guibert, might deliver her from so grave and long-lasting an illness. She was heard, however, not in order that she might depart from life, but in order that she might live as an evident testimony to the miracles of blessed Guibert. For after one hour, [Col. 0648A] strengthened by a divine visitation through blessed Guibert, while the crowd around her marvelled and cried aloud, she stood sound upon her feet and went as far as blessed Guibert’s altar to pray. The abbot, summoned, came with the brethren; and, after suitably addressing the people standing round concerning what had happened, he too glorified God, who thus glorifies His saints.

> O Christ, gracious praise and glory of Your saints,  
> Your power accomplishes the signs by which Guibert shines.  
> Worthily are You praised through him, who work thus;  
> worthily is he praised, who works thus with You.  
> Your praise is his praise; may Your praise and his save us. Amen.

[Col. 0648B] **84.** The sermon of Lord Abbot Anselm, wherever it was delivered, was seasoned with much salt of wisdom: not excessive through verbosity gathered from every quarter, but moderated according to his hearers’ capacity and the occasion. If he spoke to the people, gently, and through matters they could grasp, he offered them, as it were, a cup of milk, teaching them how they ought to live, what they ought to avoid, and what they ought to seek. If he addressed the brethren, or persons who proposed to him knots of questions to be untied, then, like a learned scribe, he brought forth from the treasury of his heart things new and old; and, although they were manifold, he adduced testimonies appropriate to their question and to his answer. They rejoiced, therefore, that things known to them became more certain through him and that unknown things were made known.

At last, worn out by old age [Col. 0648C] and bodily weakness, he devoted night and day to prayer and psalmody. In the twenty-third year of his prelateship, feeling the severity of his final illness advancing in him, he ordered the assembly of the brethren to be summoned. Having fittingly admonished them to hold firm in mind their purpose of God’s service, he comforted their sorrow at his departure, praying God to give them the Holy Spirit as comforter. The loving care of the brethren diligently supplied for him whatever ecclesiastical observance judged proper for such a person at death or after death.

Lord Abbot Anselm himself departed this life on the eighth day before the Kalends of March [22 February], and received a burial place before the altar of the Holy Cross. The monks of Latiniacum and Hautvillers, recalling together both the kindly disposition he had shown toward them while alive [Col. 0648D] and the beneficial study of his wisdom, bore his death with grief and rendered to him the offices of pious remembrance and devout prayer. They also sent us this testimony of his worth, proven in their experience: the epitaph which we have copied below.

[Col. 0647] **EPITAPH OF LORD ABBOT ANSELM, COMPOSED BY THE FRENCH.**

[Col. 0647D]

> Here lies Anselm, remarkable in appearance, rank, and achievement.  
> You enact the reality of *fenicis* [Note: [Col. 0647D] i.e. *phoenicis*, “phoenix”]; for your hope lives.  
> Appearance made you distinguished, rank eminent, achievement gentle—  
> these three things make a man illustrious.  
>
> [Col. 0648D] Widespread fame, an open person, and a house sheltered from murmuring  
> have proclaimed your praises in town and home.  
> Noah, Job, and Daniel adorned you with their virtues—  
> [Col. 0649A] righteousness, calamity [Note: [Col. 0649B] i.e. *plaga*, “calamity”], and virginal purity.  
> Now, because you are dead, we give a tear; but because you live,  
> [Col. 0650A] a psalm: for devotion girds either side.  
> The sun of the north had already yoked his horses to the spring south,  
> when your birthday—your precious death—came.

**85. EPILOGUE, MADE AS A DIALOGUE ADDRESSED TO THE CHURCH.**

[Col. 0649]

[Col. 0649A] **GODESCALCUS.** [Note: [Col. 0649] The manuscript has “G.”; as we shall see below, this is how it must be read.]  
In alternating speech there is consolation for all sorrowful people in every circumstance; you must regard moderation as your mother. Why have you long wept with a mother’s affection?

Sorrow does not take death away, but rather brings it nearer; and this grief of yours directs wounds to my heart.

**THE CHURCH.**  
The feeling of one who weeps gives signs of a grieving heart. I shall tell one who asks what is the cause of my grief.

Alas, death has taken from me abbots who were true fathers; it has also taken wise and spiritual brethren. Through so many citizens I had been a poor woman made rich—not in possessions, but, what was better, in wise men.

[Col. 0649B] Since you, sorrowful, have grieved with me who am sorrowful, your consolation comes gratefully to my weeping mind. Yet she whom either natural affection or the love of fellowship compels to weep does not wish to be consoled.

**GODESCALCUS.**  
The comforter says: “Mother”—[Col. 0649, note: the letter *M* has an *o* written beneath it]—“why do you speak inconsistently?

[Col. 0650A] He who does not wish to be consoled—why does he weep? Why does one shed tears who rejects consoling words and does not judge the comforter’s sympathy fitting?”

**THE CHURCH.**  
My son, I who mourn have said nothing inconsistent to you. Such now is the grief of righteous men. For a time they mourn, while they lament their consolations being taken away from them; yet they do not wish those whom they rejoice to see transferred hence and joined to Christ to be brought back to these things, and to be secure from worldly labours.

Thus in one respect they mourn, and at the same time rejoice; thus they mourn in one respect, and rightly rejoice in the same matter.

**GODESCALCUS.**  
When the comforter sees the knot thus untied, [Col. 0650B] he says: “Spare yourself, I pray; let this sorrow of yours cease. Christ’s grace gave you those whom you have sent before you. What He gave, He has received; He has taken back His own gifts, not yours. Pray gladly for them, and labour for yourself and for the departed, so that they may have rest and a pious reward may increase for you. Amen.”

**86. EPITAPH OF LORD SIGEBERT.**

[Col. 0649]

> Alas, death—the increase of grief, the cause of sorrow—  
> O how many whom the world mourns as snatched from itself through you!  
> [Note: [Col. 0649] “*per te quantos et mundus sibi raptos*” (“through you, how many, and the world [mourns them] snatched from itself”) was inserted in an erased place, in different ink and by another hand, 55.]  
> Your darts strike us; they fix wounds even in the heart.  
> This wound is fixed in the mind, nor can it be resisted.  
> Breaking the hardened heart, anguish strikes it,  
> when death, sundering brothers and changing all things,  
> [Col. 0649, note: “*est caris atque t feruet amor socialis*” was written in an erased place, in the same ink and hand as the correction in verse 2.]  
> among whom there is affection for loved ones and the warmth of fellowship,  
> disturbs by changing, and also breaks with harsh thumb  
> affections both natural and social.
>
> Although man may bloom like a flower in springtime,  
> may heap thing upon thing, and may trouble mind and body,  
> fulfilling anxious cares destined to fall with him,  
> one day makes him wholly wretched and pitiable—  
> whether he be king or prince, or the poor common people rich in possessions.  
> The equal law of death draws them all, though it is most discriminating;  
> for there is a just distinction of lot for the just.
>
> Earthly things please those devoted to earthly things;  
> contempt for vain things and a more sparing use of them,  
> making the righteous leaner, makes them more ready,  
> that they may be in ascent, upright in heart and deed;  
> that, released wholly from the depths, they may be admitted to heaven;  
> that they may strive to gain the devout joys of the highest life.
>
> Let every guarding of the heart be their contest,  
> for the Ravager stretches snares ready for everyone,  
> and his evil mind has so many and such manifold deceits  
> that no bodily sense is safe from them,  
> [Col. 0649, note: *adque* corrected to *atque* in manuscript c.]  
> while the crafty enemy contends by strength and guile  
> to diminish the merit of the righteous or subject them to himself.  
> If he swallows up unstable minds, he counts them as nothing.
>
> Grace be to You, O Christ, because through You the righteous overcome  
> all snares and the destructions which he prepares.  
> Recalling those who follow wandering paths, You join those who stand to Yourself;  
> and Your abundant power, fulfilling hope, aids our hope,  
> making us safe through hope and leading us, made pleasing to You, to the reality.
>
> Like the righteous in his great zeal for integrity,  
> fitted for divine affairs and for conducting worldly affairs,  
> you had been, Sigebert, the law of life and mirror of the rule,  
> [Col. 0651] to whom our discourse pays its due in writing.  
> You lived in harmony; may you live through the ages as a companion.  
> May the same fellowship be granted to our dead as well.  
> They give two verses; our people give verses about themselves, to themselves.

**87. FURTHER, A FEW THINGS ACQUIRED BY LORD ABBOT ANSELM OR UNDER HIM.**

[Col. 0651]

[Col. 0651A] Lord Abbot Anselm bought from Richelde, widow of Herethon of Louvain, from her daughter Amabilis, and from her husband Arnulf of Filforth, for sixteen marks of silver, whatever hereditary allod they possessed at Melenriv, with Duke Godfrey acting as witness. He ordained that the income of this allod should be given to the brethren on the anniversary of his death as an addition to their provisions.

**88.** The pledge which Malchelmus, Engo, and Godescalc gave to Saint Peter for eight marks was confirmed to Saint Peter and Lord Abbot Anselm by William of Marebais and his wife Helvidis, widow of the aforesaid Engo, through the hand of the advocate Seyher, for twenty marks of silver—eight granted first and twelve afterward.

**89. Charter concerning the agreement of the two churches, that of Nivelles [Col. 0651B] and that of Gembloux.** The children of holy Church should cleave to peace and ecclesiastical unity, so that they may be able to become one in Christ, knowing that God is not a God of dissension but of peace and love. We too, the brethren of Gembloux, desire, according to our measure, to be imitators of them, providing for those things that concern peace and benefit for ourselves and our successors.

Therefore let people of good will know what was agreed between us and the nuns of the monastery of Nivelles concerning a small but not insignificant matter. In the village of Asnatica there resides a household belonging to our church, for whom everything from that estate was adequate in their judgment, except that they lacked the means to construct a mill. Nor had the nature of the place entirely denied this; but the course of the water flowed across the Nivelles estate for as much land as a yoke of oxen [Col. 0651C] can plough in one day.

Lest, however, disputes arise between us—disputes which sometimes grow even to homicide—the household of each monastery, with the consent of their prelates, agreed that a watercourse should pass through the Nivelles estate for a mill-work constructed by our resident workers. In return, those who had yielded what was theirs by right received this reciprocal arrangement: they are permitted to use dead wood within our estate, and, as occasion requires, our neighbourhood shall provide them counsel and assistance.

Done in the year 1129 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh indiction, while King Lothair held the sceptres of the Empire; with Godfrey of Louvain as duke of Lotharingia, who also presided as advocate over the household of both monasteries; Henry of Birbais administering matters under him for the people of Nivelles, Bernard of Orbais for those of Gembloux; Lord [Col. 0652A] Anselm as abbot of Gembloux, and Oda as abbess of Nivelles.

**90.** Thanks be to God, because where sin abounded, grace abounded still more. Our fellow citizen Hvilard, having sought and received from Lord Abbot Anselm and the whole convent of brethren our fellowship, was counted worthy to become companion and participant in all our spiritual benefits. Giving thanks for this, he offered the brethren a mark of silver in charity; and for as long as he lived, he was always useful to us and to our house.

For he bought for six marks the part of the allod of Franco of Felliv which belonged to him in the village of Mazniz by hereditary right of his wife Helvidis. Although he wished to retain the income from that land for himself during his lifetime, he did not consume it alone. Rather, on an established day every year, he provided from it the preparation of food and drink [Col. 0652B] for the brethren. Making his will, he ordered that after his death the brethren should receive the same income, namely eleven shillings; and that, mindful of this benefaction, they should cause his name and that of his wife Doda to be inscribed after their death among the names of their own.

**91.** In the time of Lord Abbot Anselm, Henry of Lopun, for the salvation of his soul, gave to God and Saint Peter fifteen *bonuaria* of arable land in the village of Sivirei. Encouraged by this benefaction, his nephew Gerard of Marebaco likewise gave another fifteen *bonuaria* in the same village. The same Gerard, after the death of his son Gerard, granted our church, for his own salvation and his son’s absolution, the tithe which he received from the demesne cultivations in that same village of Sivirei, as well as the tithes of every form of livestock kept there within the demesne court [Col. 0652C].

Through purchase and the grant of their successors, the church of Gembloux now possesses the woodland and whatever rights were theirs in that same village. Thanks be to God.

**WHY IT IS CALLED GEMBLUS.**

**92.** *Gemblus* is interpreted as “gem and staff,” explained thus: *Gem*, “gem”; *Blus*, “staff.”

> Gemblus, fitting gem, staff giving good and striking evil,  
> sustains and guards those whom Christ unites in character;  
> and those whom one heart and true love make one—  
> may these rightly increase in number and also please Christ. Amen.

[Col. 0651] **A SHORT PANEGYRIC**

**ON ABBOT OLBERT.**

[Col. 0651D]

> The voice of one consoling the heart grieving at the death of one dear:  
> Christ, the true peacemaker, the King who rules all things,  
> whose kingdom of peace also has no end,  
> [Col. 0652D] is true God, true man born of a virgin.  
> In mercy He chose for Himself from the world the holy Church as bride,  
> a virgin who might bear for her Bridegroom  
> saints, born into the world and reborn to Christ,  
> [Note: The collected initial letters of the verses read: “Peter, your Godescalc made these verses—kind key-bearer of heaven, I pray, open for him. Amen.”]  
> [Col. 0653A] that they might shine like stars amid the world’s darkness,  
> taught to drive away the black darkness of sin  
> and to spread the light of faith to every believer;  
> not presuming that they were sufficient to themselves  
> nor believing that they had provided for themselves by themselves.  
> They attributed their righteousness to Christ, whose they were and whose work they were,  
> so that, by giving them desire, He might be their gracious patron,  
> and, by giving effect, might increase their merit.
>
> Not content to provide for themselves and their own salvation,  
> they gave to devout persons, present and future, to know through Christ  
> what had been made known to them,  
> so that the seeds of the divine word might grow  
> through such great and such worthy ministers,  
> and the new granaries of Christ might be filled through them—  
> thus anew. For saints multiplied through saints  
> [Col. 0653B] seek with great care new gain for Christ;  
> and while later holy fathers follow the first fathers of the Church,  
> while they imitate the foremost,  
> Christ’s glory grows through the Bride for the Bridegroom.
>
> Abbot Olbert imitated the holy fathers.  
> “Since he is not to be mourned, Mother, why do you weep?”  
> “Weeping with true tears, you are weighed down with grief for him.  
> But take care not to grieve excessively for any cause;  
> and hold in mind how much, why, how, and when  
> you ought to moderate yourself in sorrowful and joyful matters.  
> It will be done wisely, since a moderated thing is fittingly moderated.”
>
> The grieving voice gives this response to the admonitions of the adviser:  
> “I shall tell you what you ask: why I am troubled with lamentations.  
> Tears that are feigned appear to be pretence;  
> tears not feigned confess the secrets of the heart.
>
> [Col. 0653C] I am compelled to true tears when I sadly remember  
> that death took Olbert, my fourth abbot, from me.  
> A fitting member, a suitable head—O head, he has been snatched from me!  
> Hence strength had been special in the other members:  
> gracious affections, suited alike to joy and sorrow;  
> comfort to the sorrowful, restraint to the joyful;  
> approving all things worthy of approval and adorning his name by his character.
>
> He gave out the sweet report of character like the fragrance of incense,  
> nor did he conceal himself by hiding.  
> For thus he was of greater worth, because he pleased the more thereby.  
> To me he was the head and cause of many good things,  
> a man pleasing to God, ready to procure every good thing,  
> and sufficiently cautious, skilled in avoiding every evil.
>
> [Col. 0653D] Distributing each thing and weighing the matter according to the time,  
> he lived for Christ while fulfilling his duties to the world.  
> Never did he wish himself more for himself, but rather held himself within himself,  
> always restrained by moderate care;  
> and, growing within himself, he did not suffer a fall from himself.  
> In order to live justly, Your hand held him, O Christ;  
> supported by it, through You he was pleasing to You.
>
> Flowing from the fountain of his mouth, with the pleasing moderation of his heart,  
> he knew the time for speaking and for teaching:  
> how to speak to the learned, how to teach fitting things to the unlearned;  
> standing between those who learn and those who teach worthy doctrines,  
> sufficiently moderate in either direction,  
> [Col. 0654A] he knew how to give to each person what was suitable.
>
> What was fitting, he taught, when he wisely spoke good things;  
> what he taught was fitting, when after his teaching he lived well.  
> O, if death had not snatched him away, honour and life would have suited him!  
> Alas, death snatched him away—death, which knows how to spare no one.  
> Hence sorrow, hence tears, hence the heat of mind holds me.”
>
> The voice of one consoling the heart grieving at the death of one dear:  
> “What you say I know, because I know what is yours with you;  
> I shall say what you know, because you know what is mine with me.  
> Sinning Adam gave the punishment of sin to all,  
> and all pay by dying for the crime of the first-created man.  
> Each person’s day stands fixed: yours, poor man; yours, rich man.  
> Neither the pleading poor man nor all the furnishings of kings  
> redeems this lot—alas, because it does not take away death.
>
> It is right to weigh the truth by the evidence of deeds.  
> [Col. 0654B] Many monuments of these deeds flourish even today,  
> through which Abbot Olbert proved useful and capable  
> in all the things which public need required.  
> Christ was everything to him; Christ alone sufficed him.  
> He gave Him what ought to be given, because his devout mind asked for what ought to be given.
>
> Wisdom says through Solomon that the man who has become wise makes glad the mother who bore him:  
> for a son’s integrity becomes a support to his mother  
> and an exceptional honour, not support alone.  
> A mother rejoices in the son born from her  
> if, bringing glory to herself, to her own, and to posterity,  
> he shines more brightly in deeds than in words.
>
> Such, in his distinctive excellence, was this son of yours deservedly;  
> and you rejoiced, for you knew that you ought to rejoice.  
> You hoped for joys; you loved him whom you mourn, Mother [Note: [Col. 0653] an *o* is written above, marking the vocative];  
> [Col. 0654C] and, holding the matter certain, you promised yourself enduring hope.  
> But this hope of yours collapsed, because this hope was not hope.
>
> For what in this world remains forever?  
> Nothing is certain in the world; nothing wholly blessed.  
> Hope entrusted to God stands most certain in this certainty.  
> Abbot Olbert, blessed in a happy end,  
> now lives for Him whom he served well while alive,  
> and knows no death because he rests with Christ.  
> Death took him from the world, not at a great age,  
> for posterity will remember what and how great he was.  
> Therefore let sorrow, tears, and the agitation of your mind cease;  
> may God give you consolation and give him rest. Amen.”

**ON ABBOT MATHELIN.**

[Col. 0654D]

> The voice of one consoling the heart grieving at the death of one dear:  
> Who has been able, while living, to escape the common lot of death, or who will be able? Death will retain the rights which it holds in the world through the Fall of the first-created man.  
> Therefore, because through him death passed to all human beings, though there are a thousand kinds of death, death is one cause of fear to every person; each fears death for himself. But who fears well? He who, fearing for himself, lives well.
>
> Death is no pain to him who by death ends the pains of the world, which are so excessive that they cannot be numbered; and, being innumerable, they cannot at all be overcome [Col. 0655A] unless there is devout care to be united to Christ. Eternal honour is that which Christ gives to those dear to Him. It will never fail, because sufficiency will come from Him, through Him, through whom all things exist.
>
> Why do you weep, flock of Christ, for your fifth departed abbot, Mathelin? Rejoice that you had him as a steward, a father not in name alone in the common concern; he did not live as one useful only to himself—he was a rare bird, but dear through a rare gift. He was pleasing in speech and hand, becoming all things to all people.
>
> The gravity of his character adorned him; the honourableness of life beautified him. True love of Christ was his splendour and fervour: it burned within him and, shining, radiated to others, as fire laid beneath logs burns and flashes forth. [Col. 0655B] Brotherly love, like a tree fixed in good roots, yielded fruit both pleasing and fitting.
>
> His care sustains things that would have fallen. In adverse circumstances he was like a strong tower; living with discernment, he tended what needed tending with moderation. He presided in rank, but helped by upright action. He knew how to strive toward the just and resist the wicked. The harsh admired him as gentle, and the impatient as patient, setting him before themselves for imitation.
>
> Speaking what ought to be spoken and first doing what ought to be done, he avoided fault and earned great praise. The bread of grief and drink of sorrow for him was to suffer the body’s prison, and to be delayed from union with Christ, whose love was then an inward fire to him.
>
> [Col. 0655C] Returning earth to earth and his soul to You, O Christ, withdrawn from the world, he rejoices as having become Your portion—if any venial fault binds him in this frail life. For no one is born without vices, and no one exists without them. Flock of Christ, pray; labour by prayers to blot out his faults. Christ wishes to be appeased by vows and wishes to be entreated. Though He is just, He is merciful; He is ready to forgive.”
>
> The flock of Christ says these things to one speaking thus: “I shall do what you urge, for you rightly counsel a just thing. May the prince of darkness, the enemy, not cast the black shadows of sins upon him or upon our dead; but may they have rest, may they have light everlasting through the ages. Amen.”

**ON ABBOT THIETMAR.**

> The voice of one consoling the heart grieving at the death of one dear:  
> [Col. 0655D] The world is uncertain; its course rushes headlong onward. Sorrowful things are mingled with joyful ones in worldly affairs, and they succeed one another, for so the wheel of the world runs. No one, clinging to what is unstable, can be made stable. He passes away with the world who does not live well in it. He who follows Jesus happily reigns for ever; and who follows Him? He who follows in mind by imitation.
>
> In worldly things hope for the future is uncertain; yet it compels many to undergo toil, offering uncertain end but certain labour. Happy is he who departs from this life when Christ is the way of his life, and who has obtained such a way, and life as well.  
> O Christ, as true way and life, You were obtained by [Col. 0656A] the abbot who was our sixth, Thietmar: a simple, upright, patient, humble man, pleasing to You.
>
> Glory and riches, like the movement of an instant’s hour, change masters. Death, not to be placated by gold, carries naked from this world those whom vain outward form had clothed. When a man sees this, why does earth and ash grow proud? What does worldly desire profit any desirer? Why does he strive to acquire, when he sees kings die, and death snatch away rulers and inferiors alike?
>
> When they leave the world, they leave behind what was taken from the world; stripped now of worldly riches, they carry with them only the good or evil they have deserved. But happy is he who, while he lived, lived well. Sharing the lot of the righteous, that he might be free from punishments, [Col. 0656B] this father entered through the gate of life, Christ, and not by another way, and obtained an increase of merits.
>
> Indeed, he served Christ’s flock in the manner of a minister, and corrected it as a pious teacher, giving instruction; he presented himself as a model of zeal and a norm of life. The uncultivated in conduct, cultivated under such a plough, yielded the adornment of good manners and fruits of souls; those who had been righteous advanced with the righteous.
>
> Binding himself to the spirit with a spiritual fetter, he subjected himself to You, Jesus [Note: [Col. 0655D] an *o* is written above], and subdued the flesh, never allowing it to rule the spirit; rather, he compelled it to be subject and weakened it, wishing it to be more feeble than rebellious.
>
> The flock of Christ says these things to one speaking thus: [Col. 0656C] “You speak truth, encompassing very many things in few words. Teaching what is just, avoiding what is unjust, and counselling good things, this father grew through this zeal, pleasing to God, and despised things to be despised.
>
> Raised by his merits of conduct to the burden of honour, attending to the burden he watched over the honour; and he gave himself both substance and distinction by acting wisely, as time, integrity, circumstance, or honour required. He was a cultivator of justice, and thereby an enemy and avenger of sin, finding no hostile snare of sin. If a savage man came near, he departed bewailing his own losses. May he live more fully, he for whom Christ had been life. Amen.”

**ON ABBOT LIETHARD.**

> The voice of one consoling the heart grieving at the death of one dear:  
> No one is granted everlasting use of worldly [Col. 0656D] things; those things which for a time are honours become burdens. The despiser of the world, a happy purchaser, will purchase in exchange for the world’s treasures the treasures and joys of heaven. The purchaser will be happy, and happy the exchange which gives the purchaser that which will be honour to him forever: to be a fellow citizen with the citizens of the heavenly homeland, to enjoy Christ in mind, having overcome the world by merits.
>
> Abbot Liethard, fragrant like true nard, came as the seventh; no storm made him yield, but he was a true shepherd, stern toward the wicked in reason, gentle toward the gentle, pleasing to honourable men. Honour was not an honour to him but a burden; the world likewise was exile.
>
> [Col. 0657A] He did not cling to vanities, but adhered gratefully to Christ, counting it good to cling to Him and his own highest good; he did not deceive himself, but believed that by living thus he would be blessed. Made a mirror, he advanced in sacred actions; eminent in rank, he was more eminent in action; fittingly advancing and fittingly adding to his advances, placing Christ first and handling present things by use. He always rendered pleasing service to Christ.
>
> Retaining the world for a time for the body’s use, he steadfastly walked the narrow path pleasing to the righteous, already worn by the footsteps of many fathers. He directed the gaze of his mind, despising the world with its pomp and thirsting for Christ alone, and desiring that the eager mind be fed with such food; for it is not carnal but spiritual.
>
> [Col. 0657B] As time advanced and every vice receded, he became more pleasing and better with the advance of better morals. Striving finally to attain the desired goal, he hungered, thirsted, wept, sweated, and was cold, offering himself wholly as a pleasing burnt offering to Christ, and not lightly reckoning how brief is the span of life or how short a time worldly offspring endures.
>
> The hope of the end strengthened his mind as it bore hardships, tending toward Christ, the end who remains without end—where, made perfect, blessed without end rejoices whoever worthily loved Him in this life. Persisting in what he had begun, he yielded badly to no unfit person; [Note: The manuscript has a paragraph sign here, which the editors judge should be placed at verse 45.] striving by fitting conduct and deed toward better things, redeeming the time, he yielded pleasing fruits in due season, adding the labour of integrity to his studies.
>
> [Col. 0657C] The flock of Christ says this to one speaking thus: “He speaks truth, I confess; I shall not deny the truth. You commend one worthy, that you may repay worthy things to one worthy. This man was a true shepherd, a diligent imitator of Christ, sparing in words but suited in conduct to honour. He lived as was fitting, because he did not live for himself alone; more useful to others from himself than [Col. 0657, note: perhaps *proficicens*, ‘making progress,’ was originally written.] to himself through himself. He presided over the Church; may he be with Christ without end. Amen.”

**ON ABBOT ANSELM.**

> The voice of one consoling the heart grieving at the death of one dear:  
> By his name a man is marked as to what is the origin of his flesh. A common name, not a proper one, but general. Man reveals you to yourself: frail, likewise akin to mud. Alas, you scarcely subsist, a spiritual substance, [Col. 0657D] unless the body animates you, which God adds to you and takes away; He adds it to one who is to live, and commands it to be taken from one who is to die.
>
> The flower of the world withers; integrity is praised and grows cold. Praise is not feigned when devout deeds confirm it [Note: [Col. 0657] *fa* in an erased place]. [Col. 0658A] Distinguished in divine and worldly philosophy [Note: [Col. 0657] *mundumque* (“and worldly [philosophy]”) was read at first], Abbot Anselm, tested in uprightness of character, was our eighth abbot, worthy of remembrance: a man prudent in speech and of measured gravity, with a worthy bearing, adding to his name such character as was pleasing and acceptable to all.
>
> When questioned about any matter whatsoever, however difficult or knotty the question put to him, he did not refuse anyone asking him; rather, he answered and gave welcome answers, wisely and adequately untying knots. He was pleasing in speaking and pleasing in teaching, for he knew how to say suitable things to each person at the appropriate time.
>
> Since he diligently did what became both himself and his own people, he avoided harmful things and at the same time taught what should be avoided. [Col. 0658B] Knowing how to measure his resources and himself, and fearing what was to come, he acted wisely as circumstances required. His greatest concern altogether was that worldly cares [Note: [Col. 0657] *si* in an erased place], if dearer to him than was right [Note: [Col. 0657] *cure* corrected to *care*], might delay him and prevent him from serving Him who supplies cares and bestows greater gifts than one who hopes asks for, unless he grows lukewarm by not hoping.
>
> Certain in such hope, he strove, sweating in spiritual zeal, to serve Christ diligently. Not unpractised in the works or pursuits of justice, he exercised both together, so that it might be his resolve to set nothing before what was right. Thus governing his mind, though not lacking reason, he left nothing useful unattempted, nothing honourable unattempted.
>
> Not of wavering mind, yet fearing uncertainties with certainties, [Col. 0658C] he strove to deserve by the integrity of a devout heart what Christ, the true guarantor, gives His beloved. Studying to admire the righteous and to imitate the righteous, he strove to be joined to them by similar conduct, accounting all worldly things less than the virtue of the mind, which contains purity of nature.
>
> He pursued this, because through it Christ is approached; mindful of himself and [Note: [Col. 0657] *et* inserted], above all, mindful of Christ, he did not value himself so highly as Christ. Entrusting himself to Him and faithfully cleaving to Him in mind, dead to the world, may he live joined to the righteous. May this be his everlasting reward for good works; may this be the rest and end of worldly labours.
>
> [Col. 0658D] Brethren, let the complaint that now troubles you cease. Let the Almighty be your hope, your anchor, your possession; let Him be all things to you, and, multiplying good things for you, may He add rulers and brethren better than the good. Amen.

[Col. 0657] **ON THE BURNING OF THE MONASTERY OF GEMBLOUX, BY GUIBERT.**

[Col. 0657D, note: He was abbot in 1195–1205; he died in 1208.]

[Col. 0657D] I shall set forth, briefly—if grief permits me—the lamentable cause of the groaning and sorrow that surrounds me: namely, the wretched ruin and destruction of our church, in which I was almost brought into peril of death.

[Note: [Col. 0657] There follows the destruction, or rather the burning, of the monastery of Gembloux, which occurred in [missing [Col. 0659] in MS 2] the year 1137, thirty years after its first burning. Guibert, who later became abbot both of this monastery and of the monastery of Florennes, a man judged by all to be most holy, mourned this pitiable destruction in the following words. MSS 2 and 3 preface this passage thus, mistakenly interpreting Guibert’s letter as concerning the burning of 1136, although it in fact concerns the conflagration of 1185; cf. *Annals of Lobbes*, *SS.* IV, and the chronicle of Gislebert, p. 150. The Aquicinctine continuation of Sigebert gives the year 1186: *SS.* VI, p. 424.]

[Col. 0658D] Our town is known to lie on the border between the duchy of Louvain and the county of Namur; this has often proved a snare, overthrow, and stumbling-block to it, a source of plots against its sanctity, and an evil of the devil. When, therefore, conflict recently arose between the duke [Note: [Col. 0659D] Henry.] and the count [Note: [Col. 0660D] Henry.] [in 1185], that count unexpectedly surrounded it with his army; having set fire to its fortifications—that is, its outer rampart and wall [Note: [Col. 0659] “the same,” MS 2; “same,” Lambecius.]—he devastated it utterly.

Although we feared no such thing, violent gusts of wind arose and carried glowing embers throughout every part of the town. Thus town and monastery alike were consumed together in a most fierce fire, so that in the town no house remained except two very humble ones, newly covered with earth, while in the cloister not even one building escaped burning.

During this burning, while I was singing the morning Mass at the lesser altar, unwilling to leave anything incomplete, I withdrew to safety almost more slowly than I ought. For after the sacred vestments had burned, and since the fires, now ravaging everything far and wide, prevented my breaking out, I entered the nearest open sacristy and found there four of my brethren grieving and anxious. In that place, with flames hemming us in on every side beyond all hope, we were so scorched and suffocated by smoke and heat that two of them were seriously injured but survived; while I and the other two, distressed and breathless, lay upon the ground like dead men until evening. Yet although I survived through the help of [Col. 0659C] God and of our holy patron Guibert, those same two companions in my martyrdom departed this life after a few days.

But, as it is written in the prophets, “report shall follow report, destruction upon destruction, and terror upon terror” (Ezek. 7:26); and “what the locust has left, the cankerworm shall consume” (Joel 1:4). On the ninth day after the burning, the aforesaid count of Namur, having summoned to himself the count of Hainaut, his nephew through his sister, again surrounded the town with a great multitude. After the walls had been torn down in certain places, the armies of both entered; ranging everywhere entirely freely—for they found everyone unprepared and in no way expecting any such event—they plundered everything whatsoever that remained.

In this plundering nothing was left either to us, to the townspeople, [Col. 0659D] or to the people of the countryside who had brought their goods together there. Every animal and domestic fowl was either burned or carried away by the enemy. No reverence was shown to sacred things or altars: indeed, in the middle of the presbytery before the high altar, and throughout the whole extent of both churches, many men were slain while ours and the enemy’s forces fought on foot and horseback [Col. 0660A]; the monks and priests themselves were beaten and stripped.

Not one of the brethren escaped wholly unharmed. I shudder in recounting it: one died immediately after a fatal weapon had been driven through his side; another was left by them as naked as nature had brought him from his mother’s womb into the light. But why do I complain of others? They stripped the abbot himself of the rest of his clothing and even of his stockings; scarcely snatched away by a man known to him, he fled naked and alone through the darkness of a dreadful night.

And, to continue my account, in this aforesaid plundering no reverence at all was shown even to the female sex: women too were left naked, and no mercy whatever was displayed toward nursing mothers. Mothers were stripped of their clothes, children torn from their mothers’ breasts, and, contrary to the laws of nature, carried away into captivity with the greater part of the townspeople.

Thus the enemies, enriched with our spoils, returned triumphantly and jubilantly to their own homes. Even now they rejoice over their victory at our miseries, saying that they scarcely expected to find in any great city such riches as were found among us.

In this destruction something worse befell me than in the conflagration. My chapel—that is, my Mass equipment, which I possessed in the most excellent condition—was taken; likewise the relics, which I loved more than gold and topaz; likewise the delight of my eyes, namely the Life of blessed Martin, upon whose rhythmic rendering I had laboured somewhat [Note: [Col. 0659] “a little,” MS 3.]; and every book that I had composed from early youth onward; all my garments except those [Col. 0660C] which I was wearing; and, to gather much into few words, when I had been carried elsewhere for rest because of illness, all my possessions were taken by the enemy. [Note: [Col. 0659] Missing in MS 2.]

Now, with the other companions in so great a misery, I sit and weep in the open air [Note: [Col. 0659] “in the open air,” MS 3.], roofless among ruins like a night-raven [Note: [Col. 0659] “nyctocorax,” MS 3.], because our choir has been turned into mourning. In the greater church, since it has been defiled by murders, there is neither reading nor singing; instead, in some crypt, as best we can, we perform the divine office.

The harshness of the sky and the inconstancy of the weather burdened me still more—and many others with me—now by heat, now by cold, now by cruel and frequent rains, afflicting us in various ways by day and night [Note: [Col. 0659] “were afflicting,” MS 3.], since no roofs remained upon the houses by which we might be protected [Col. 0660D] [Note: [Col. 0659] “might be protected,” MS 3.], all having been burned by fire.

I was also deeply distressed because the greater altar of the apostles Peter and Paul had remained without the solemn celebration of Mass from the day the church was set on fire until my entry into the abbacy. No one dared celebrate the divine rites upon it, because the vaulting of the arched ceiling, wholly deprived of its cement binding through the penetration of rainwater, [Col. 0661A] seemed to threaten its own collapse and the death of those walking beneath it.

I am no less troubled because almost all the covered walks of the whole cloister, having no roof except the sky itself, are filled with mud and filth throughout the entire winter season and afford their occupants no opportunity to enter, sit, or rest. Finally, certain secular sons of Belial, using the weapons of injustice, persecute us, invade our property, and attempt to seize it for themselves; they were attacking the church. To defend its goods, as has always been our custom, supported by heavenly help, we resist them equally—not arming ourselves with force but with prayers, not with quarrels but with sound counsel.

But why do I complain of the harassment of external or lesser [Col. 0661B] persecutors, when the very highest powers and our princes—those, that is, who were bound by duty to protect us everywhere and without ceasing from their attacks—Albert of Cuch [Note: [Col. 0661] “Aich,” MS 3.], I mean our bishop, and Matilda, duchess of Louvain, while her husband was on pilgrimage at Jerusalem [in 1197] and she ruled alone in the land: the bishop sought by utter force to take away a certain land long possessed by the church; and both sought to take away two beneficed churches belonging to us, which had long before been granted us by another Albert, the duke’s brother, for rebuilding our cloister, burned in the war of his father. They inflicted such losses and disasters upon us that, although they themselves, alike worn out by great calamities, have now died, [Note: [Col. 0661] The bishop was consecrated in 1196 and died in 1200; the duchess died about 1211. The letter was therefore written after that year.] the damages they inflicted still persist from year to year, exhausting us with prolonged hardship. [Col. 0662B]

[Note: [Col. 0661] Here is inserted the miracle which Sigebert reports at the end of his *Chronicle* as having occurred on the occasion of this burning: “The evil of discord,” etc., through “This is Sigebert,” in his chronicle completed by our abbot Anselm, MS 2. These are the words of Abbot Anselm, who augmented Sigebert’s chronicle at its end: “The evil of discord,” etc., through “This is Anselm, abbot of Gembloux,” MS 3.]

[Col. 0661]

# LIFE OF WICBERT

## THE CHAPTER HEADINGS OF THE LIFE OF SAINT GUICBERT BEGIN

1. On the noble birth of the parents of Saint Guicbert.
