2. How he ascended through the stages of life by stages of virtue.
3. How, renouncing the world, he laid aside the belt of military service.
4. How he assigned his hereditary estate of Gembloux to God and Saint Peter for the founding of a monastery.
5. How his grandmother Gisla supported him in this.
6. How Erluin, formerly a canon and then a monk, encouraged him all the more by his friendship toward the good.
7. How, renouncing even himself, he sought the monastic life.
8. On the nobility and religious life of the monastery of Gorze, and how he became a monk there.
9. [Note: [Col. 0661] Opposite this chapter heading a red obelus is visible, indicating that this chapter has fallen out of the text.] How he trained the brethren of Gembloux after the example of those of Gorze.
10. How he placed Erluin over the monastery of Gembloux as abbot.
11. How Emperor Otto, rejecting the malevolence of slanderers, fortified the monastery of Gembloux by imperial authority and granted it immunity in every respect.
12. How he legally confirmed a charter concerning the property of the church, first by imperial authority and then by that of the Apostolic See.
13. How Heribrand, husband of Reinuidis, sister of Saint Guicbert, seized the monastery of Gembloux, and how the holy man temporarily restrained his injustice.
14. [Note: [Col. 0661] This chapter was inserted in darker ink, and the beginning of its text occupies a place from which another text had been erased.] How he converted many of the Hungarian people to Christ.
15. How he encouraged many people from every place toward the fellowship of brotherly charity.
16. [Note: [Col. 0661] Written in darker ink; chapter 19, like chapter 14, also appears to have been inserted.] How he afterwards returned to the monastery of Gorze.
17. [Note: [Col. 0661] Written in darker ink; chapter 19, like chapter 14, also appears to have been inserted.] On his death.
18. How his body was brought back to Gembloux.
19. [Note: [Col. 0661] Written in darker ink; chapter 19, like chapter 14, also appears to have been inserted.] What Abbot Erluin wrote about him in his letter.

## THE LIFE OF SAINT GUICBERT BEGINS

[Note: [Col. 0661] “Guibert” consistently in MSS 2 and 3 through chapter 8.]

[Col. 0661]

## A LAYMAN WHO BECAME A MONK, FOUNDER OF THE MONASTERY OF GEMBLOUX

[Note: [Col. 0661] “From the first manuscript” is absent in MSS 2 and 3.]

[Col. 0661C]

### Chapter 1

The distinguished father Wicbert, happily born in the district of Darnau [Note: [Col. 0661] “Germiensis,” MS 5.], is believed to have been given as an example to the people of his age. All who preserve knowledge of this antiquity affirm that his grandfather Roding [Note: [Col. 0661] “Rodig,” MS 4; “Reding,” MS 5.], his grandmother Gisla, his father Lietold [Col. 0663A], and his mother Osburga all drew out a long line of ancient nobility. [Note: [Col. 0663] Of the nobility of the kings of Austrasia: cf. Richer, Wassebourg, *Antiquities of Belgic Gaul*, book III.]

His mother Osburga, abusing [Note: [Col. 0663] “rejoicing,” MS 2b.] of the apostolic concession which says, “It is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7:9), after the death of her first [Note: [Col. 0663] “former,” MS 3.] husband Lietold—by whom she had borne Lord Wicbert and his full sister Renuidis—rejoicing in polygamy and not refusing union with a second, third, and even fourth husband, bore a numerous offspring by many husbands: namely Hellin, Oilbald [Note: [Col. 0663] “Oibad,” MSS 2, 2b, 3; “Orbald,” MS 4.], Raginard, and Doda, besides those whose names oblivion has erased. Their stock spreading far and wide, Lorraine rejoices that it is almost entirely filled and ennobled by it.

For from the multitude of descendants grew greatness of power; from the multiplicity of possessions flowed abundance of wealth—by which the strength of worldly nobility is customarily amassed [Note: [Col. 0663] “emulated,” MS 4. These examples suffice to show the readings, or rather errors, of the manuscripts used by Henschenius and of Surius’s edition.] and advanced. Yet no one should judge this sufficiently praiseworthy in the servant of God, since, according to the Lord’s saying, “a man’s life does not consist in the abundance of the things which he possesses” (Luke 12:15) [Note: [Col. 0663] Omitted in MSS 2 and 3.], and, according to the Apostle, “there is no respect of persons with God” (Col. 3:25). Rather, what should be highly commended in him is this: although Truth says, “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:24), he, as though casting off the burden of a hump and the swelling excrescence of earthly nobility and wealth, made this human impossibility possible through the ready inclination of his soul.

[Col. 0663C]

### 2

[Note: [Col. 0663] “Chapter II,” and so forth, MS 1.]

This just man, then, planted and rooted in the house of the Lord through steadfast faith, began from his tender years to put forth flowers of virtue in the courts of the house of our God: lofty as the palm in the height of nobility, and destined to multiply, like the cedar of Lebanon, in the fragrant abundance of holiness. But after the beauty and sweet odour of piety had diffused themselves far and wide from the flowers of his good disposition, and in the time of the first [Note: [Col. 0663] The word “first” is written above the line in MS 1.] glorious and victorious King Henry had burst forth into the buds of fruit, at last about the time of Otto I he began to ripen abundantly, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God.

What his life was like in the earliest stages of his growth need not be investigated by us. [Note: [Col. 0663] Between *nobis* and *Nam* a line has been erased in MS 1.] It is superfluous to ask what the root of a tree is like when it lies hidden, buried in the earth, since the nature of the tree is known from the flavour of its fruit alone. Indeed, the voice of Truth says: “Every tree is known by its own fruit. For they do not gather figs from thorns, nor harvest grapes from a bramble” (Luke 6:44).

This tree, then, planted in the Lord’s field, was neither thorn nor bramble: no harshness of pricking, no bitterness of acridity proceeded from it. Rather, such sweetness of fruit flowed from it that its produce even now bears fruit in the Church of God. For while his brothers were thinking of the fruit of bodily descendants, holy Wicbert alone [Note: [Col. 0663] A line and one third have been erased before *spiritualis* in MS 1.] longed for heirs of spiritual generation, being well instructed by the Apostle: “He who is without a wife is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please God” (1 Cor. 7:32).

Therefore, from his patrimony he did not seek to endow a bride for a carnal union, but with undivided affection to enrich his mother, the Church: she would nourish for him not brothers destined shortly to die, but would increase offspring of heavenly adoption who would never die—offspring whom she would neither bear in sorrow nor lose in sorrow, but who would be co-heirs with the Son of God in everlasting joy.

Meanwhile he served in the world outwardly as a soldier; but, so far as the exercise of that occupation permitted, he remained free from the vices of military life. And, not to run through each sort of vice from which, with God’s help, [Col. 0664B] he abstained, or each duty of virtue to which he diligently devoted himself: among his other outstanding merits, this was especially praiseworthy in him. Though men of his class customarily seize the property of others, especially that of the poor and of the churches of God, with insolence, he certainly did not know how to plunder another’s property violently, because he knew how cheerfully to distribute his own among the poor and the churches of Christ.

### 3

After he had long remained hidden beneath the cloak of military dress, because a lamp placed under a bushel ought not to remain hidden any longer, he dissolved as soon as possible the knot and hindrance to divine service, and laid aside the belt of secular military service. Thus, a veteran of the world, discharged from earthly warfare, he began to be a new recruit of Christ; a long-serving slave of the world, made his own through the vindication of divine freedom, he became God’s freedman.

[Col. 0664C] Therefore, after the many windings of the broad road, directed toward the narrow gate of life, so that he might sing as a traveller stripped bare before the robbers of this world, he resolved also to free himself of every burden of harmful possessions. For, lest after complete observance of the legal commandments that one saying of the Lord should be lacking from the sum of his perfection—“Go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, come, follow me, and you shall have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19:21)—he did not indeed sell all his possessions, but strove to lend them at interest to Christ, his faithful debtor. He rejoiced that he should be Christ’s lender, and did not doubt that Christ would faithfully pay him interest. [Note: [Col. 0663] *uersuram*; the letters *er* have been erased in MS 2.]

For, to be one of those of whom the Apostle says, “as having nothing and yet possessing all things” (2 Cor. 6:10), he wished to possess his goods and not to possess them: to possess them by administering them well, not to possess them by keeping them greedily. Appointed by the Lord as the faithful and prudent servant over His household, he took such provident and profitable care to invest the principal of his little capital that, although nothing was diminished from the principal itself, he nevertheless drew from the return of the interest the means by which to distribute the measure of wheat in due season to his fellow-servants.

What, indeed, is more profitable for a faithful steward [Col. 0665A] than to pour out his own resources upon the servants of the Lord, when the Lord Himself graciously deigns to repay them to him as given to Himself? Moreover, he was stirred by another exhortation of the Lord’s word, that by example and assistance he might draw others also to act well. He did not forget that the Lord had said: “He who receives a prophet or a righteous man in the name of a prophet or righteous man receives the reward of a prophet or righteous man” (Matt. 10:41); and Daniel’s saying: “Those who instruct many unto righteousness shall shine as the stars for everlasting ages” (Dan. 12:3).

Therefore, that he might receive the reward for the righteousness of many, it did not seem enough to him if he alone should strive toward righteousness. Rather, he judged that he must exhort others to run with him by his example and encouragement, become the cause of salvation for many, and receive a double crown of recompense.

[Col. 0665B]

### 4

This lover of the brethren, who could cry to God from the deep sighing of his heart with Isaiah, “Before you, Lord, we conceived, as it were laboured, and gave birth: we have brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth” (Isa. 26:18)—what he had conceived in thought and had, as it were, laboured over through the long heat of deliberation, he brought forth as a devout benevolence of soul, by which he might bring children of salvation into being for God upon earth.

From the property of his inheritance he chose an estate called Gembloux and most devoutly assigned it to God, to Peter the prince of the apostles, and to the glorious martyr Saint Exuperius, for the construction of a monastery in their honour. Building dwellings beloved by God and pleasing to men for the Lord of hosts, he, like a sparrow directed in the flight of humility, found a house for himself; and, like a turtle-dove animated by the zeal of chastity and the groaning of contrition, he made himself a nest in which to place his young (Ps. 83:4 [Vulgate]), to be cherished beneath the wings of mother Church.

There a gathered company of monks was to offer sacrifices of praise to God through their service and render their vows to the Most High, sowing spiritual things for Him and reaping temporal things. Wishing to form them according to the right rule of conduct, he caused them to be directed by the model of apostolic life through which he had learned that the primitive Church was founded at the beginning of the faith. Its chief principle was that none of them should possess anything as private property, but all things should be common, so that those whose citizenship was already in heaven might in some manner live an angelic life on earth.

He himself, moreover, laying at their feet as though at the feet of the apostles all that he had, provided with anxious fatherly care that everything necessary for their use should be available in complete sufficiency. Thus, by a legal conveyance, he gave them the aforementioned village, Gembloux, and all its appurtenances, together with many other possessions that devolved upon his share or allotment by hereditary right. [Note: [Col. 0665] At this point one and a quarter lines have been erased in MS 1.]

### 5

This undertaking, begun under a favourable omen, was encouraged not only by divine grace but also by the devout support of his most noble and most Christian grandmother Gisla. Seeing her sweetest grandson [Col. 0666A] pursue the way of truth, she worked earnestly so that, every hindrance removed from the path of piety he had undertaken, he might run with enlarged heart in the way of God’s commandments.

For he did not, like hairy Esau, devote himself to the vain or harmful pursuits of hunting; rather, like mild Jacob dwelling at home, he cultivated simplicity and innocence. Thus she had poured her whole self into love for him. Since she knew that, after the example of faithful Abraham, he had long ago departed in spirit from his land and kindred, [Note: [Col. 0665] *supra* inserted above the line in MS 1.] she believed that the land of promise belonged to him. Nor did she wish to deny her aid to one whom she perceived to be guided in every respect by divine help.

Having therefore found this saving counsel, she legally conveyed to her dearest grandson, for the support of the God-pleasing construction, all the property of her inheritance which her husband Roding had assigned her as a dowry, or which they themselves had added to their patrimony through equal industry. [Note: [Col. 0665] *di* inserted above the line in MS 1.]

### 6

In all these matters divinity had afforded no little comfort to His faithful servant Wicbert, because it had provided him with a certain venerable man, Erluin by name, as teacher and patron: Erluin himself had exchanged the canonical rule by which he had lived for the monastic life. He was a timely and harmonious helper to our devout patron in carrying out every useful plan: in building the church and constructing the cloister buildings, and in gathering brethren to the fold of God and governing them. [Note: [Col. 0665] One and two-thirds lines have been erased in MS 1.]

### 7

To another man striving toward the summit of perfection it might have seemed enough to turn away from evil, renounce the pomp of the world, and distribute all his goods to the poor. But Lord [Col. 0666C] Wicbert, forgetting the things behind, strove to reach forward to those before him, reproaching himself with imperfection unless he were polished to the very point by the pattern of the Lord’s hand.

For, hearing the Lord say, “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23), he applied this whole command of the Lord to himself. Denying [Note: [Col. 0665] Written above the line in MSS 1 and 2; absent in MS 3.] himself [Note: [Col. 0665] A word erased here in MS 1.], he took up in his body the cross of Jesus’ mortification, chastising his body and reducing it to slavery, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, he himself should be found rejected.

He also took up the cross of brotherly compassion when, having been rescued from the sieve of diabolic temptation and himself once converted, he strengthened his brethren, for whom Christ Himself had drunk [Col. 0666D] [Note: [Col. 0665] *bibebat*, “was drinking,” corrected in red in MS 1.] the cup of suffering.

Thus, taking hold of the nail of reason, after casting away his possessions he swam naked out from the shipwreck of this world. [Note: [Col. 0665] In an erased place in MS 1; *ma* seems erased above the line.] At last, having gained the harbour of monastic rest, he cast the anchor of stability from the depth of his breast into the sea of cloistered life. [Note: [Col. 0665] One fifth of a line erased in MS 1; *cau* corrected to *clau*.]

He saw that no refuge was safer for one fleeing the danger of the world: within the cloisters of a monastery the solitude of the desert is not absent; and if anyone is in any way troubled by the unrest of a diabolical assault, the ready strength of brotherly consolation is at hand. [Note: [Col. 0665] An erased place in MS 1; MS 2 inserts text.]

He also saw that he could not rise higher than by attaining that degree of religion to which every ecclesiastical order and every earthly power may indeed be admitted, but from which no one whatsoever may withdraw with impunity for any reason. [Col. 0667A] Moreover, as a prudent man looking both forward and backward, he attended most carefully to the need to do nothing rashly or without foresight.

As an athlete entering the arena carefully surveys the character of the place, lest some obstacle hinder him in fighting or running, so this athlete of ours cautiously considered the suitability and character of the place where he could safely fulfil his purpose: namely, somewhere where a more relaxed discipline would not indulge him, and where more lavish honour would not flatter him improperly because of the regard paid to his known nobility.

For he feared that the Lord might say to him: “Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, I shall begin to vomit you from my mouth” (Rev. 3:15). He also feared that, like one carrying flowers against a blowing wind, he himself, swollen with the emptiness [Note: [Col. 0667] “vanity,” MSS 2 and 3.] of self-exaltation, might lose the flowers of virtue he had gathered, and, like dust, become foul and blinded by the squalor of apostasy.

### 8

Finally, Christ’s dove, unwilling to be tossed any longer amid worldly waves because she could find nowhere for her foot to rest, entered the ark prepared by God for the salvation of many: the cloister of the monastery of Gorze.

Long ago Chrodegang, bishop of Metz—the nephew through a sister of the renowned King Pippin [Note: [Col. 0667] “Pipin,” MSS 2 and 3.]—built that monastery, enriched it with resources as an everlasting memorial of his holiness [Note: [Col. 0667] “monument,” MSS 2 and 3.], and, what was greater still, adorned it with the grace of religious life (cf. the *Life of Chrodegang*).

But as time passed, the wickedness of wars increased; through them the misery of evils grew more cruel; and because laws are silent amid arms, injustice consequently grew strong everywhere. There too, through the corruption of the age and the negligence of prelates, the strictness of regular discipline began to soften. This permission of heavenly wrath endured until at length the eye of divine mercy looked upon the inhabitants of the earth, removed the darkness of unbelief, and restored the light of truth.

For this purpose, among the first sent by God was Adelbero, the first bishop of Metz of that name. Most Christian among nobles and noblest among Christians—for he was brother of Duke Frederick—he first exercised his rule in expelling the vice of irreligion from his diocese by secular power and episcopal discipline alike. Directing the eye of his good purpose first upon monastic discipline, he laboured to restore it to the norm of apostolic life.

Beginning with Gorze, which was pre-eminent among the monasteries of his diocese and where scarcely even traces of established religious observance remained, he did not desist until he had recalled the professed monks from worldly vanity and restored them to the right way. Above all, with the pastoral sword he destroyed the root of evils and wicked stepmother of monks—the desire for private possessions—and shut within the Lord’s sheepfold those who lay exposed to the bites of wolves at the crossroads of the world [Col. 0668A] (cf. the *Life of John of Gorze*).

The devout abbot of Gorze, Agenold, a timely helper in restoring holy religious life, collaborated with him in this. Thus, when harmful roots had been uprooted from the bed of the Lord’s garden, Adelbero planting, Agenold watering, and God giving the increase, the plantations of virtues grew with more than customary abundance.

All who, renouncing the world, wished to take up the sweet yoke of Christ learned here how they ought to be meek and humble in heart after Christ’s example. All who exchanged the military habit for strength in the fear of the Lord received here, as in a field of divine training, proof of themselves. All who, departing from the clerical estate, desired to rise to a higher degree of humility were granted here, with Jacob—not in a dream but in reality—to see the ladder reaching to heaven, by which they might see angels ascending and descending (Gen. 28:12).

Since so great a fervour of holy religious life spread the flames of its warmth so far and wide, every rank of nobility, every dignity, every profession and age without distinction of persons, flowed here to the Lord’s discipline. Nor did anyone believe that he had embraced even the beginning of conversion unless it had happened to him to be initiated into the rule of Gorze.

Here was milk for the infant to suck [Note: [Col. 0667] “suck,” MS 2.]; here solid bread for the perfect person to chew and, like a nurse, at times transform into his own body, so that he might then feed others who were untrained or weak. Among them our patron Wicbert—of no mean nobility, indeed [Col. 0668C] of no mean humility and holiness—was led by the working of God’s Spirit, so that he who had long since renounced all his possessions might here renounce even himself, in order to cling more perfectly to Christ.

Committing himself and all those whom he had won for Christ to the hands of the venerable father Agenold, he devoted himself eagerly to Agenold and hung attentively upon his words. He was not to be fed by this teaching alone, but strove to carry its crumbs to Christ’s poor, whom he himself had gathered. To carry out more earnestly that for which he had come, he carefully considered the particular graces of each person and strove to transfer something of them to himself. One man’s patience instructed him; another’s persistence in prayer kindled him; another’s obedience delighted him. He imitated this man’s humility and that man’s sobriety. In one he admired the labour of the active life, in another the ardour of contemplation.

[Col. 0668D] Thus it happened in a wonderful way that, while he picked something from each person’s virtues as an example for himself, he alone became an example to all. For, as Solomon’s proverb says, “iron sharpens iron,” so each was sharpened by another to act well; and, “as a man makes bright the face of his friend” (Prov. 27:17), so the wholesome shame of brotherly emulation moved them whenever one could not imitate another. [Note: [Col. 0667] “Accordingly,” MS 3, corrected.]

### 9

1. [lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 0667] “He himself … apostolic” occurs in an erased place in MS 1. At this point the text of the entire chapter has fallen out: “How he trained the brethren of Gembloux after the example of those of Gorze.” Hence the chapter numbers have been erased by a seventeenth-century hand, so that X now stands in place of the original XI, and so forth to the end, where a number is again added to meet the numbered arguments. It is unclear who erased the first three lines of chapter nine and wrote in their place the first four lines of chapter ten; the handwriting seems to show that it was neither Sigebert nor Godescalc. In any case, this happened before the other manuscripts were copied from this one. Continuous numbering is found in MSS 2 and 3.]

[Col. 0669A]

### 10

[Note: [Col. 0669] I have restored this number; the manuscripts read VIIII, and so forth, with no lacuna indicated.]

He therefore, having renounced the vanities of the world, feared that he might again be enticed by its pleasures while, under the pretext of administering ecclesiastical affairs, he still outwardly served it. Fearing also [Note: [Col. 0669] A word erased in MS 1.] that apostolic saying [Note: [Col. 0669] A few words erased in MS 1.] that “a teacher ought not to be a novice, lest, being lifted up, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (1 Tim. 3:6), he resolved to forestall the approaching illness as swiftly as possible.

He approached in friendship the venerable Erluin mentioned above: a man pleasing to God, acceptable to men, laudably trained in the school of holy religious life, most intent upon winning souls for God, distinguished by the friendship of the princes of the land and the great men of the Church, and in every respect fitted for carrying out ecclesiastical affairs. He cast himself [Col. 0669B] upon such a man, his father and intimate friend, with familiarity [Note: [Col. 0669] “cast himself,” MS 3.]; he leaned his whole self upon him as upon a couch for his soul, with confidence [Note: [Col. 0669] “leaned,” MS 3.].

Revealing to him in order his intention, trusting him more than himself, and taking counsel with the brethren, he chose him as abbot and, through the efforts of Christ’s faithful, had him placed over the Lord’s sheepfold. Like a good householder instructed to bring forth new things and old from his treasury, Erluin knew that the law of Christ is fulfilled when one bears another’s burdens. Therefore he humbly set his shoulder beneath the burden: certainly heavy, but bearable with God cooperating with him. He was encouraged by the proverb spoken through Wisdom: “A brother helped by a brother is like a city that cannot be captured” (Prov. 18:19).

Thus Saint Wicbert entrusted the ministry of Martha to his energetic fellow-worker Erluin. He himself, sitting with Mary at the Lord’s feet to hear His word, chose the better part which would not be taken from him. For, having returned to the hive of monks—that is, Gorze—he devoted himself more freely to the virtue of contemplation, intent upon fasting, vigils, and prayers.

11. [Note: [Col. 0669] “Already” 1, 2, 3, and so on.] Already the new planting was bearing fruit in the praise of God; already the husbandman, awaiting the precious fruit of the earth, bore patiently, since he did not doubt that he would receive both the early and the latter rain. Already Christ’s glory was growing; already, through those by whom the Lord’s name was blessed, grace was being multiplied, when from Gembloux—the newly founded monastery—there spread far and wide the fragrance of a good savour: for there the flame of holy religion burned fervently, the righteous advanced daily from strength [Col. 0669D] to strength, and the unrighteous, turned from the crookedness of error, were now walking straight.

The whole house of the Church was filled with this sweetness of good savour, and it had already reached the very heights of the imperial court, where the devout conversion to God of the most noble man Wicbert was on the lips of all the courtiers. From his conversion there arose no small edification throughout the whole Church of God, since by his example many renounced the world and submitted themselves to the purpose of holy religion. But where is envy absent—envy which was lacking neither in the paradise of delights nor even in heaven itself? Certain persons, who looked askance at the good deeds of Christ’s faithful servant Wicbert, appealed to the emperor’s ears against him. Enviously disparaging him, they accused him of acting against the commonwealth: Gembloux, they said, had been assigned to his ancestors from the royal fisc by imperial generosity as a benefice, yet he had appropriated it as part of his own property and, having founded a monastery there without the king’s command, had unjustly transferred it into the jurisdiction of the Church—something which public law by no means permits.

The devout founder and holy guardian of our place was summoned by the king’s edict to appear in court [Col. 0670B]. [Note: [Col. 0669] “are summoned,” with *n* added, 1; “is summoned,” 3.] The case was set forth; redress was demanded for the alleged injustice; in deliberating the judgment, different persons expressed differing opinions. Instructed by the Lord, the disciples of the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0669] “taught,” 3.]—“When you stand before kings and governors, do not be anxious how or what you are to speak; for in that hour what you are to speak will be given you” (Matt. 10:19)—did not seek sophistical argumentation, but displayed the humility of Christian simplicity. Knowing that it is dangerous to stretch one’s arms against a torrent, and not ignorant of the Apostle’s sentence, “He who resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. 13:2), they humbly cast themselves at the emperor’s feet and earnestly begged him not to abuse his earthly power against them and Christ’s poor.

They said that imperial majesty ought to rejoice that, in the days of his reign [Col. 0670C], divine mercy had chosen to open the door of its mercy, by deigning to send into the world certain men worthy to be heard when praying for the welfare of the commonwealth. The emperor could earn praise from another’s foundation if he chose, by his royal power, to protect places constructed by others in God’s honour. He could share in another’s labour if he deigned, by the authority of his imperial hand, to confirm possessions lawfully bequeathed to God by others as an inheritance. It was fitting that, in the judgment of an emperor, the equity of truth pleasing to God should carry more weight than the cunning of whisperers and double-tongued persons, or the deceit of flatterers. Of these Wisdom says: “A whisperer and a double-tongued man is accursed; he has disturbed many who lived in peace; and the third tongue” (Ecclus. 28:15)—by which tongue is understood that of flatterers—has stirred up many.

Having spoken these and similar things, they were not disappointed in the good hope which they had in God, proving true the saying of the Wise Man: “Blessed is he who speaks in the ears of the wise.” For the pious King Otto, truly directed by God to restore the commonwealth and repair the Church of God, graciously listened to these counsels of salvation [Col. 0671A] and honourably accepted the petition of Christ’s faithful. He consented to the common counsel of the courtiers and decreed by royal edict that the new foundation of the monastery of Gembloux should remain firm and unshaken. Whatever had been granted to that church by Lord Wicbert himself or by the gifts of other venerable men, no unbeliever or any one of his heirs was altogether permitted to violate.

Moreover, they were granted authority to elect, by command of the king, an advocate and a regular abbot; to build a castle; to establish a market, mint coinage, and take timber. The place itself was made exempt from every service owed to anyone: in city, castle, village, upon waters, at bridges, and in all places of his empire, it was freed from every toll and tribute [Col. 0671B], subject solely to the protection of the royal defence. [Note: [Col. 0671] “and under,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0671] “it is subject to the protection,” 3.]

12. Everything now seemed settled; all things were believed to be secure; nothing was feared from any quarter. A charter concerning the property given to the church and the liberty of the place had been drawn up, confirmed by imperial edict, and authenticated by the impress of the imperial ring. This authentication was solemnly performed at Liège, on 20 September, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 946, in the fourth indiction, in the eleventh year of the reign of Lord Otto I, while Uho governed the see of the Church of Maastricht.

To this confirmation by imperial power there was added the authority of the Apostolic See, when Benedict VII, pope of that name, decreed that the granted immunity of the monastery of Gembloux should remain valid in perpetuity [Col. 0671C]. It was also decreed that no abbot from another monastery should be appointed there, but that the servants of God themselves, living according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, should have the power to elect an abbot from their own congregation; that the abbot himself should be adorned with the privileges and insignia of the Apostolic See; and that this monastery, established under the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Apostolic See, should not be subjected to the jurisdictions of any other church. By the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, under an appeal to divine judgment and under binding prohibitions of anathema, it was declared that no person, small or great, should ever presume to take away or alienate anything from the goods or possessions belonging to that monastery.

This document, written by the hand of Boniface, regional notary and chancery clerk of the holy Roman Church, was issued on 25 March through the hands of Stephen, bishop and librarian of the holy Apostolic See, in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Benedict VII, pope, and in the sixteenth year of Otto, great and peaceable emperor crowned by God, which was the year of the Lord 953. [Col. 0671D]

13. Thus, for a while, the serene sky of prosperity smiled; then suddenly the unexpected onset of a diabolical storm became dreadful. Heribrand of the village of Mainwolt [Note: [Col. 0671] “Maviwolt,” 5.], distinguished among the nobles of Brabant [Note: [Col. 0671] “Brabantines,” 2b.] [Col. 0672A] by birth and wealth, whose nobility was augmented by another nobility—for Reinuidis, the sister of our most noble lord Wicbert, had married him—this man, girded with the sword of injustice and trusting in the weapons of greed, asserted that by hereditary law the fisc of Gembloux belonged to him through his marriage to his wife Renuidis. [Note: [Col. 0671] “Reinuidis,” 2, 3.] He alleged that his kinsman Wicbert had not acted lawfully, since, under the pretext of religion, he had sought unjustly to disinherit his wife, namely Wicbert’s sister.

Therefore, despising the authority of the imperial court and the anathema pronounced by apostolic authority, he joined to himself accomplices in his injustice. He did not fear insolently to invade the abbey and violently plunder the brothers’ substance. Horses were stabled in the workshops of the cloister; secular persons unlawfully wandered through places suited to monastic solitude [Col. 0672B]. The brothers protected themselves as best they could in the hiding-places of the sanctuary, and in this crisis of such tribulation they awaited the aid of divine mercy.

Indeed [Note: [Col. 0671] “for,” 3.], it seemed to the malevolent that this was a fitting time to carry out their injustice, because [Note: [Col. 0671] “for,” 3.] the holy man Wicbert was now dead to the world and far removed from them, having shaken himself free from every reckoning of worldly tumult. Moreover, Abbot Erluin, recently deprived of sight, was thought less capable of restoring what had been lost. When this sinister report struck the ears of the holy man, whose way of life was already in heaven, it is unnecessary to express in words [Note: [Col. 0671] “express,” 3.] what his feelings then were. Although it seemed unfitting to him to turn his eyes back from the plough-handle of the Lord’s field, and though it was grievous to involve himself anew, after earning discharge from service, in the warfare of worldly [Col. 0672C] concern, he nevertheless did not delay to hasten his journey for the consolation of the brothers—he who was prepared even to lay down his life for them.

Arriving, therefore, as one longed for at the beloved place which bore witness to his devotion, he strengthened the sorrowful and desolate brothers with consoling words. With such weapons of humility and moderation as he could, he confronted his opponents, endeavouring by persuasive admonitions to soften their ferocity and greed. They, somewhat reverencing the presence of his holiness, while keeping one thing shut within their breast and another ready upon their tongues, yielded for a time to his will, promising, out of regard for their kinship with him, to desist from this injustice.

14. [Note: [Col. 0671] “The remainder to the end of the page is in an erased place,” 1.] The oft-named and ever-to-be-named Lord Wicbert [Col. 0672D] was so pleasing to God that he was worthy even of the ministry of apostolic preaching. The Hungarian people, shut off behind certain very strong barriers and having had no opportunity to go out either southward or westward, were let loose by Emperor Arnulf after the barriers had been broken. After Arnulf’s death, like a wild storm they ravaged all Italy and all Germany with various kinds of devastation for about fifty years.

In the time of Otto I this people also attacked Lotharingia. Led by Duke Conrad [Col. 0673A] as far as the Carbonarian Forest, they were prevented from advancing farther by the power of God displayed at the monastery of Lobbes, and returned unharmed (cf. Folcuin, *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, *SS.* IV, 66). As the Hungarians passed through the village of Gembloux both on their outward and return journey, the man of God Wicbert met them in the year 954. He was protected not by a material shield [Note: [Col. 0673] “clipeus,” 2; “shield or helmet,” 3.] or helmet, but was girded only with the sword of God’s word, prepared to drink the cup of suffering and to lay down his life for the saving of his brothers’ souls [Note: [Col. 0673] “for,” 3; “souls,” 3.] (John 15:13): according to Truth, there is no greater love than this (1 Cor. 13:13).

First, as a soldier of Christ, he offered them the word of peace in accordance with the Gospel command. He entered upon the way of preaching and, gradually softening their rage, began to work for their salvation. Nor did he cease to reveal to those defiled by the filth of idolatry the doctrines of faith [Col. 0673B] and the mysteries of the eternal King, until he drew some of them away from the kingdom of the devil. Renouncing the vows of the devil’s military service, they were enrolled under the new name of Christian soldiery. Blessed be God in all things, who stood by Wicbert as he served under His standards and granted him the civic crown.

15. The man full of God, foreseeing that it had not been prepared for him by God the Father to drink the first cup of suffering, applied his mind so that he might at least deserve to drink the second cup, that of confession. Thus, wholly intent on providing for himself by providing also for others, he devised a work beneficial not only to himself but also to others. For, embracing above all charity, which is the bond of love [Note: [Col. 0673] “of perfection,” 3.] and in which is the fullness [Col. 0673C] of the law, and especially because this is the Lord’s special command: “A new commandment I give you, that you love one another” (John 13:34), he began to negotiate with many devout and faithful servants of God. They were to be joined together through one love of mutual charity and establish a fraternal fellowship among themselves: since all were one in Christ, they should think one thing, love one thing, will one thing in Christ, and refuse one thing; nothing produced by diabolical rivalry should be found worthy of hatred, nor anything different through opposition. Thus they might truly deserve the blessedness of the peacemakers, the children of God.

This was also done so that, according to James’s command, they might confess their sins to one another (James 5:16) and be saved by praying for one another. And just as Truth says, “He who has bathed needs only to wash his feet, but is wholly clean” (John 13:10), so, washed in the baptismal washing of mutual confession, and with the feet washed that cannot tread the earth without stain [Note: [Col. 0673] “to tread,” 2.]—that is, with the deeds of human life cleansed, a life which can scarcely or not at all be spent without the mark of sin—they might, through the help of fraternal prayer, be made wholly clean: cleansed mutually by alms, fasts, psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs appointed for this purpose.

For they delighted in that saying of blessed Augustine, who, bursting forth in praise of charity, said: “Charity is a sweet sound [Col. 0674A]; charity is a sweet and delightful thing, which gathers brothers, present and absent, into one.”

16. Thus the man of God, touched by a certain foreknowledge of the future—that he would soon have to proceed toward the prize of the heavenly calling—provided for himself in advance, so that, when he laid aside the burden of the flesh and entered upon the way of all flesh, he might place the battle-line of this fraternal fellowship here and there as supports to drive off the assaults of aerial hosts with the weapons of prayer. Leaving the secondary role in completing this undertaking to his faithful vicar, Abbot Erluin, and taking every precaution that, under the pretext of carrying out any business, he should not again become entangled in the world even to the slightest extent, he bade a final farewell to brothers and friends. Leaving them the desired remembrance of peace and love, he hastened [Col. 0674B] on his way to the solitude of Gorze, that rest which was dear to him.

For as a fish taken from the water cannot live, so he feared for the life of his soul whenever he was drawn away from the repose of contemplation. After such numerous and great labours, when he was already expecting moment by moment that God would grant him the longed-for discharge from his military service, the King of kings, rejoicing that His soldier had long stood bravely on behalf of His camps, finally judged it time to render him the rewards of his labour and place upon his head the crown of praise.

17. And now, as the time of his dissolution drew near, he began to grow weak. The supreme craftsman, who always finds in His work something still to be beaten and polished, tested His chosen one as gold in a furnace, in order to purge away completely the dross of his sins. The men of Gembloux [Note: [Col. 0673] “But the men of Gembloux,” 3.], when they heard that their lord and father was mortally ill, could not restrain their grief [Col. 0674C]. Their pain was greatly intensified by the thought that he might die in the land of his pilgrimage while they were absent. Therefore, those among them who seemed to be of greater standing set out immediately for Gorze. They found their lord alive and, having somewhat concealed their sorrow, discussed with him the removal of his body.

He summoned his abbot, named Oilbald, revealed to him his own desire and that of his people, and requested this final favour: that his followers might be permitted, after his death, to carry the clay of his body back to the monastery of Gembloux. After consultation, the abbot answered him as a father to a son: “My sweetest son, I am in difficulties on every side [Col. 0674D]. I reverence your holiness; I fear to trouble your soul as it goes to God. But I fear lest those others [Note: [Col. 0673] “others” corrected to “those,” 1; “others,” 2; “those,” 3.] be troubled over this who venerate you as a father, and who would wish to show in person to you when dying the love which they showed [Note: [Col. 0673] ‘showed,’ 2.] you while living. See: I subordinate my will to yours, if God’s will inspires you and yours. If your people have the means to fulfil their desire, I do not withhold my consent.”

[Note: [Col. 0673] Here chapter XVII begins in manuscripts 2 and 3. Manuscript 1 has only a large T, without a chapter heading or number. A seventeenth-century scribe supplied the number XVII, and shortly below restored XVIII and XIX.]

At last the man of God, perfected in the grace of virtues [Col. 0675A]—which is greater than if he had shone with the glory of miracles, since virtues are sometimes obscured by miracles, whereas miracles are commended only by virtues—on 23 May, in the year 962, gave up his spirit, wearied but not defeated by fruitful labours. Gathered to his fathers, he who had sown in blessings [Note: [Col. 0675] “the wording is in an erased place,” 1.] reaped also in blessings (2 Cor. 9:6), attaining a hundredfold and eternal life according to the Lord’s [Note: [Col. 0675] “God’s,” 2, 3.] promise (Matt. 19:29).

18. The men of Gembloux joyfully received their lord’s body from those reluctant to surrender it and set themselves to their vowed task. Taking precautions lest the excessive heat of summer should harm the holy body, they removed the body’s entrails and buried them in the ground there. They sprinkled the corpse with salt and various [Note: [Col. 0675] “other,” 2.] fragrant spices [Col. 0675B] capable of resisting the putrefaction of bodily decay.

One of them, named Adecho, who had always served the holy man more intimately and therefore now served [Note: [Col. 0675] “attended,” 3.] the holy body itself with greater diligence, procured a cart with oxen and placed the holy body upon it—not with the honour due to his lord, but with the love which he himself owed. They had already gone some distance when, behold, all the people of Gorze blazed with anger and fury, bitterly grieving that the body was being carried away of one whose merits, they believed, obtained God’s [Note: [Col. 0675] “with God,” 2.] help for them. Forming a crowd, they made a popular uproar; many pursued the few, shouting.

At the cry of those running together, the men of Gembloux were stunned and sought God’s help with the silent cry of their hearts. He who fought for the children of Israel against the pursuing Egyptians also fought for them [Col. 0675C]. Suddenly a storm arose [Note: [Col. 0675] “indeed,” 3.], the air became dreadful, and an alien night fell upon the bright day. Thunder crashed, lightning flashed, thunderbolts fell. Palpable darkness turned the pursuers back from their way, while these men [Note: [Col. 0675] “those men,” 3.] travelled on one course and turned neither to the right nor to the left. Thus the former, divinely terrified, withdrew; the latter, divinely aided, advanced freely.

Illustrious through so remarkable a miracle, God’s holy Wicbert was brought back to the monastery of Gembloux with the veneration of all. Buried with due honour in the church of Saint Saviour and Saint Peter the Apostle, he showed those who invoked him that he lived with God. For all who invoke him in person believe that they will be protected perpetually by his guardianship [Col. 0675D]. This holy servant of God died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 962. [Note: [Col. 0675] 3 continues: “Miracles have been suppressed to avoid weariness, since they have been multiplied beyond number. There follows an account of his elevation.”]

19. Lest anyone disbelieve that this man of God was such and so great a person, let there be added the testimony of Lord Abbot Erluin, who lived with him for a very long time and from whom nothing about him was hidden. While Erluin was engaged in arranging the beginnings of the association of the fraternal fellowship established by Lord Wicbert, and inviting to it the venerable man Aletran—whom Bishop Evraclus, after Erluin’s blindness and expulsion, had ordained abbot of Lobbes—he wrote a letter in the following manner [Col. 0676A]. [Note: [Col. 0675] What follows to the end is absent in 2b, 3, 3b, 4, 5, and in the printed editions.]

# HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF ERLUIN

[Note: [Col. 0675] Absent in 2.]  
[Note: [Col. 0675] “Of Abbot Erluin,” 2.]

By a wonderful dispensation divine mercy acts so that the deeds of those who have gone before, rightfully pleasing to God, may be rewarded with a twofold honour in this mortal age and enriched with no lesser reward of grace in heaven. Thus God, the author of all good things, deigned in the present time to distinguish the posterity of a certain beloved servant of His, Wicbert, by these gifts of His generosity. As He Himself testifies, He did not wish the brightness of a shining lamp to remain darkened any longer under the shadow of a bushel, but rather spread far and wide its sweetness of good savour, like the fragrance of spices, for the purpose of edification [Col. 0676B].

Thirsting in heart to attain grace, and not a deaf hearer of the Gospel message, Wicbert despised all worldly things, rejected earthly things, put temporal things aside, and thereafter devoted himself to the observance of monastic religion, so that he might give himself to God’s higher and holier commands. He assigned to God’s servants the inheritance of his own right called the monastery of Gembloux; and, with sincere affection of love, wished to gather a congregation of monastic brothers there. Living himself, as is easily believed, according to the path of the Rule, he performed many works worthy of God. He preferred to strengthen all persons to do good by the example of his own exhortation rather than daily to wander through devious courses by the treachery of evil persuasion.

He provided these examples of his holiness and contests of steadfastness [Col. 0676C] abundantly not only to the brothers remaining in the place already mentioned, but also offered faithful teachings of his exhortation to all laypeople and clerics who did good and sought holiness, to widows and orphans, monks and women dedicated to God. Moreover, as if in open view, he shone forth: he did not delay faithfully to impart the mysteries and doctrines of the eternal King to pagans devoted to the filth of idols, desiring lovingly to associate them with the citizens above.

After his death and the end of his present life, faithful persons of various ages and ranks, stirred by the example of his good activity, took care to promote more widely the godly work begun by him, a work full of the sweetness of love. It pleased many dwelling around the place, whose minds were sounder and whose affection of devotion toward God was strong, to unite themselves in a fraternal fellowship for the redemption of their souls [Col. 0676D], so that, maintaining on earth the union of peace and love, they might deserve to enjoy fellowship in the heavenly homeland.

Accordingly, on the Kalends of May, a considerable company of the faithful assembled at the aforesaid place, surely kindled by the inspiration of the most merciful God. They vowed to God a jointly determined yearly measure of lights, bread, and wine pertaining to the sacramental offerings [Note: [Col. 0675] “for each person,” 2.], so that, on the day of the Kalends appointed for each person, an offering and supplication of the sacred mystery might be made from these things on that person’s behalf [Col. 0677A].

Therefore, on the day specified, both the abbot and the entire congregation of monks of the aforementioned monastery, together with a great multitude of country people, resolved to bind themselves together by the bond of complete love [Col. 0678A], henceforth remaining united in faith and charity. This fraternal fellowship was begun in the first year of the empire of Otto I [Note: [Col. 0677] “first” was later altered by another hand to “second,” 1.], which was the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 963. [Note: [Col. 0677] “It ends,” added by 2, 3.]

# HISTORY OF THE ELEVATION OF SAINT WICBERT

[Col. 0677]

## BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR

**HERE BEGINS [Note: [Col. 0677] “There follows a brief account of the elevation of the body of this holy confessor,” 3. From “Let us rejoice” through “he recognized” are absent there. The *History of the Elevation* is absent in 1, 4, 5.] THE ELEVATION OF THE SAME HOLY CONFESSOR.**

[Col. 0677B]

1. Let us rejoice, beloved; let us rejoice in the glory which God’s grace grants us in observing the festival of this day. For today God has given us the joy concerning His holy confessor Wicbert which He prepared from the foundation of the world, Wicbert whom He endowed, as it is written, with an eternal name in the working of miracles (Ecclus. 15:6). This glory, special to us through his bodily presence, has become general to all Christians: the man whom this place long ago deserved to receive from God as its father, the world today has recognized before God as its patron.

Thus Saint Wicbert, perfected through the exercise of good works over almost forty years, died at Gorze, the monastery of his conversion, and was buried at Gembloux, the place of his first religious life [Col. 0677C]. From the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 962—for in that year he put off his mortal body—he lay for 137 years without public renown; scarcely a few faithful persons, through old charters, remembered the shadow of his holiness. But in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1099 the memory of his name shone forth, through a new grace of signs, God’s magnificence making him wonderful [Note: [Col. 0677] “making him great,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0677] “generosity,” 3.]. This was so marvellous in him during the twelve years before the elevation of his holy body that it won for him the greatest love and honour far and wide from all people.

2. Therefore, many of our own people and many outsiders began to consider it unworthy that a man so highly esteemed among human beings and of such holiness before God should receive from us no reverential cult. Foremost among them was Sigebert, a monk of ancient learning [Col. 0677D] and reverence, the eye of this our Church of Gembloux, who watched over it devoutly by his life, conduct, and fervour of religion. For he was all the more certain of the grace of Wicbert’s holiness because, with much elegance of style, he had pursued in writing his life full of virtues. From the evident display of miracles, having received an opportunity to fulfil his desire, he began to deal with those who possessed the authority concerning the elevation of the saint’s body. Having consulted the will of Lord Abbot Lietard and received his blessing, he undertook a mission from him [Col. 0678B] to obtain the authority of the bishop of Liège on this matter.

3. At that time Lord Otbert drove God’s chariot at Liège, a worthy leader of his church among its predecessors. When he heard the good desire of those desiring good things, he examined and established the truth of the matter, granted his assent to their just request, and rejoiced that in his own time God’s mercy had revealed that through which the whole world might feel itself relieved from the burden of its necessities.

Through Lord Henry, archdeacon of our place, the matter was referred to Frederick, archbishop of Cologne. He brought before a general synod the question of what should be done concerning this affair specially affecting us; and he gladly assented, upon counsel, to that to which the supporter of our faithful cause said he should assent. Thus [Note: [Col. 0677] “Thus … returns” absent in 3.] through the working mercy [Col. 0678C] of divinity, when everything proceeded according to the decision, our lord bishop became more ready in disposition toward us, because he rejoiced that in this matter he possessed even the assent and authority of his metropolitan. Finally, he himself began to press forward with the execution of this affair, though, because of the excessive eagerness of his desire, we had scarcely hoped that he would persist in what he had been consulted about when giving his assent. For the frequent journeys of our embassies to him, and his responses to us when they returned, gave evidence of this purpose.

4. After various answers had been given and received in this matter through the repeated mediators of our embassy, Lord Abbot Lietard determined now to take care personally of what seemed entirely entrusted to others’ care. Therefore, although weakened by old age, he devoted himself to the labour of a long journey and hastened to Liège in the year 1110, borne, so to speak, by a vehicle of good desire [Col. 0678D]. There, addressing bishop and archdeacons, abbots and all the leaders of the ecclesiastical commonwealth, he asked that they unanimously determine when the vow conceived in faithful hearts should be fulfilled. And this was done.

Since the scattered multitude of the faithful could not easily be summoned to such great joys of new salvation, it was decided that the elevation of the holy body should take place on 23 September, the ninth day before the Kalends of October [Col. 0679A], because on the preceding day—the martyrdom of the holy Theban martyrs, especially solemn for us—a very great crowd would gather at this place both because of the announced market and for vowed prayer.

5. Lord Abbot Lietard, delighted by the good things said and done for him, communicated a share in this joy to our expectation. He then admonished us that the duties of our devotion should anticipate the desired solemnities of our good patron. For, to secure from God a prosperous outcome in this matter, he proclaimed a fast by the bishop’s command—a fast which he fulfilled together with us all the more devoutly because he was the more concerned.

And now that day had shone forth, a festival day for heaven and earth: for heaven, because a companion had been appointed; for earth, because a patron had been assigned to it. There was present an innumerable people of both sexes, whom love and honour for the holy confessor had summoned [Col. 0679B] from every place. Many abbots and archdeacons also assembled, and other masters and disciples of ecclesiastical religion, invited by the authority of the lord bishop and by the religious importance of the undertaking to arrange the heavenly treasure. Through their devout services, the pearl of the holy body was raised from the place of burial and carried to a nearby open level place in the field, to be displayed before the awaiting people.

6. Meanwhile, after an address appropriate to the matter and occasion had been delivered to the people, and after all had been satisfied according to their expectation by the sight of the holy body, the holy confessor Wicbert was venerated by everyone and honoured by many with vowed or voluntary offerings. Thereupon, for the protection and preservation of our place, he was placed with his bier [Col. 0679C] in a structure made for that purpose, in the dwelling prepared for him in our Church of Gembloux [Note: [Col. 0679] From “to this purpose” onward absent in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0679] Here 3 ends with: “Thus far the elevation of the holy man.” There follow the privileges of Otto and Benedict VII, and finally an account of the burning of the monastery.]

Indeed, many faithful persons thought that it was not enough that they had been granted a share in the joy of this day unless each one might deserve to receive, as requested, some relics from which they could dedicate crosses, altars, or even complete chapels. Yet how great was the joy of that day, what glory there was among those rejoicing and exulting in the Lord—because no one can adequately express it, it is better to be silent than to say too little. Rather, since the testimonies of events are more ready than those of words, let the innumerable throng of faithful peoples attest it: the grace of the holy confessor invites them to the anniversary day of his very elevation [Col. 0679D], and, as we believe, will always invite them through a new working of miracles. This celebration of the elevation took place in the fourth year of Emperor Henry V of that name, that is, 1110 from the Incarnation of the Lord and Saviour.

7. The day of this elevation was marked by such a privilege of signs that it must be believed to have been arranged not by human rashness but by divine ordination. For while the holy body was displayed for the people to behold in the place described above, those to whom it was granted to see beheld a sign of the cross in the sky above that place [Col. 0680A], seemingly surrounded by a shining circle. The mystery of the event, as is believed, suggested that, since the common enemy was conquered by Christ’s triumph through this sign, the saint’s suppliants might hope through the merits of this patron to be delivered from the power of visible and invisible enemies.

And since enemies have once been mentioned, it must not be passed over that, in honour and love of the holy confessor, as many persons hostile to one another returned to favour as those present had never seen return to favour in their memory. Therefore, without prejudice to the privilege of the Lord’s Nativity, that angelic song is fittingly applied to the grace of our festival: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). For how should glory not be given to God in the highest, who glorified before people by the sign of the displayed cross His saint whom He had glorified with Himself in heaven? Consequently, there ought also to be peace on earth for people of good will [Col. 0680B], to whom divinity provides before Himself such a great intercessor in every offence and necessity.

We may rightly believe that the manifestation of the cross was made to commend the saint’s merit, since we know that, in order to follow God readily, he denied himself and bore his cross after Christ—that is, the mortification of his flesh. Finally, the circle which was seen shining around the appearing cross is not unfittingly considered a sign of the crown which this saint is believed to have deserved from God for his righteous labours [Col. 0680C].

Why some saw this sign while others did not deserve to see it belongs not to our prejudice concerning anyone, but to God’s judgment concerning all. For God, the righteous judge, judges even in this age concerning certain people: He judges some worthy of the consolation of His mercy, while He considers others wholly unworthy. The former, because they do what is right and, if they still err, do nothing out of obstinacy but from ignorance and simplicity; the latter, because though living and seeing, they go into the fire. Thus it must be believed and said that God glorified His saint by this sign for those whom He saw doubting about him not perfidiously but in the human manner. Therefore many who doubted saw it, few who believed in his holiness [Col. 0680D], and none who envied his miracles.

8. But what shall we say of the woman who, though she stood in a suitable place, when the holy pledges were raised up before the people could not see them? Surely this: that in the hidden judgment of the divinity her case was such that she was unworthy to see what had been set before the eyes of all. Yet, appropriately reproving herself, and recognizing that nothing but her own sins obstructed her sight, she humbly made satisfaction to God in prayer within herself for so long, until she deserved to enjoy the sight of the holy relics [Col. 0681A].

9. No less worthy of wonder is what happened in the case of another woman. When she had come with the crowd of people to the new joys of that day, she brought with her in a faithful heart the desire to carry home some small portion of the holy confessor’s body. Therefore, when the holy pledges had been displayed for viewing, as has been said, she stood among those who stood by; and her desire increased all the more because the object that caused its increase was set before her gaze. What then was she to do? Where was she to turn? She was not a person who would presume to petition anyone for so precious a gift, nor one to whom anyone would dare grant it if she petitioned. Since, therefore, complete despair of human aid had seized her [Col. 0681B], she prayed earnestly to God that she might not be cheated of her desire. But while [Col. 0682A] she revealed her case to God alone and prayed unceasingly that she might be heard, wondrous to relate, she suddenly found in her hands—which she had stretched imploringly toward heaven—some of the relics for which she so greatly longed. Those who happened to be witnesses of the matter reported that it was one of the holy confessor’s teeth [Note: [Col. 0681] Here 3b ends.]. Behold how, in one day and in one place, our holy father Wicbert was glorified by God through four miracles: first, by the manifestation of a cross in heaven; second, by the reconciliation of hostile men; third, in the woman whose bodily eyes were both closed and opened; fourth, in the hearing of the other woman’s prayer. Of the glory of these miracles, granted us today by God in such a patron, we can say nothing and render nothing worthy, except that we confess these works of God [Col. 0682B] to be miracles of God, who lives glorious in his saints and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

# Miracles of St Wicbert

[Col. 0681]

By an Anonymous Author [Note: [Col. 0681] These are lacking in 1, 2b, 3b, 4, and 5.]

## Sigebert’s Prologue to the Miracles of St Guibert

[Col. 0681B] Wisdom says: “The memory of the righteous is with praises; the name of the wicked shall rot” (Prov. 10:7). That what Wisdom says is true is attested also by our own times, which recall with God’s praises the memory of the righteous man, namely Saint Wicbert, founder of the monastery of Gembloux. For his name has not decayed through the course of so many years: through him the Lord’s name is blessed and shall be blessed for ever. In the year of the incarnation of Jesus Christ 1099, which was the 137th after the passing of that same Saint Wicbert, the memory of his name flourished anew, made manifest through a new grace of miracles [Col. 0682B]. Although the estimation of a good life does not consist in the display of miracles but in the excellence of deeds, miracles divinely shown through holy men are nevertheless testimonies of good works. Nor without reason does the Apostle Paul say: “Signs are given not to believers but to unbelievers” (1 Cor. 14:22). For how much would the preaching of faith have prevailed if a display of miracles had not accompanied the preaching? Therefore, when God works signs and wonders through holy men, the unbelief of human beings is indeed rebuked, because they do not honour holy men with the fitting devotion of veneration.

## Vision of the Same Sigebert

[Col. 0681]

[Col. 0681C] 1. Some of our own people were greatly offended, and many outsiders were stirred against us even to indignation, because Saint Wicbert—a man of such nobility in the world and such holiness before God—was honoured by us with no devotional observance. Among those moved by this pious indignation was a certain man named Sigebert, foremost among us in age and conduct, learning and religion. He was borne by as great a desire concerning the saint’s veneration or revelation as that ancient Simeon was concerning Christ’s coming or revelation. Accordingly, he had chosen the saint’s tomb as a place of compunction for himself, and frequented it, after the example of the Gospel Mary, with the perfume of prayers. Since he was keeper of the church, he performed this all the more devoutly because he could do it more freely [Col. 0681D]. The sum of his prayer was that, before he died, he might prove by experience what merit, or how great a merit, Saint Wicbert possessed before God.

One night, therefore, he prayed as usual; and there, fed with the bread of tears and made drunk with the cup of compunction, he gave his weary limbs to rest [Col. 0682C]. He had scarcely fallen asleep when, behold, he was delighted by a marvellous vision. He saw entering that very church, as though adorned more festively than usual and illuminated more brightly than usual, an innumerable throng distinguished by episcopal authority, clerical dignity, and the religious profession of abbots and monks. Then, as if to conduct a synod, seats were placed, and the persons took their places to speak. After the ecclesiastical state had been discussed sufficiently fittingly and settled appropriately, a certain elder said:

“Since enough has been done concerning the other matters for which we have assembled, no mention has yet been made of that special matter for which we have come to this place—namely [Col. 0682D], our brother Wicbert.”

“What,” the others asked, “should be deliberated concerning him, except what has been determined before God, who has already made him wonderful with himself and among us, and will again shortly make him wonderful in the world?”

“I shall go,” said that elder, “and shall take care to make this very thing known to that brother who disturbs us day and night over this matter.”

Approaching Sigebert—for he stood at a distance awaiting the outcome—the elder said: “Restrain your sighing; make your face and spirit glad. Your desire shall be fulfilled with good things. God has made his saint wonderful, and will make him wonderful again.”

When these words had been spoken, that holy council was dismissed. But because nothing moves quickly enough for a desiring mind, Lord Sigebert, insufficiently pleased with and insufficiently credulous of this vision, fell asleep again. In the repeated vision he was no longer delighted but rebuked. He saw the holy magnates seated and conversing as before, looking upon him with a sterner, almost angry expression; and he saw his former elder no longer soothing him but rebuking him more harshly [Col. 0683B].

“Why,” he said, “do you believe so reluctantly what you have desired for so long? Why are you ungrateful for the gift of such a vision—something that is not advantageous even for yourself? What I said, I say; and what I say, I say from God: ‘God will make his saint wonderful, and has made him wonderful again.’ Believe, if you believe; you will shortly see that you have not believed in vain.”

Terrified by these words, Lord Sigebert leapt from his bed and ran back to the holy father’s tomb. How great were the thanks he gave to God there, God alone was witness. From that hour, certain of God’s mercy and of Saint Wicbert’s glory, he began to hold him in even greater reverence.

2. The threshing-floor of the holy Church was being cleansed by the winnowing-fan of Lenten observance when our elder received this illuminating revelation [Col. 0683C]. Since the desirable time was soon at hand—that time venerable because of Christ’s death and glorious because of his resurrection—he anchored his intention there: if anything were to be renewed by divine action concerning the memory of the holy confessor, it should happen especially at that time when many bodies of saints are read to have risen and appeared to many, as testimony to the Lord’s resurrection. Therefore, as if nothing at all were what he had previously done, fasted, kept watch, or prayed, he roused himself to greater efforts; and, holding before his eyes the oracles of the divine promise, the more certain he was of the truthfulness of the Promiser, the more he wished to be found ready on the day for which he hoped.

Yet it happened not as he thought—for “the Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain” [Col. 0683D]—but as God had arranged. Not only had that day, famous for Christ’s resurrection, now passed, but also the day of his promise, that is, the awaited coming of the Holy Spirit; and during so great and such a time of mystery nothing new had occurred at the saint’s tomb. One could see our elder, Lord Sigebert, failing in this expectation: wishing to die rather than live; judging himself guilty and foolish, as though he had thought himself worthy for God to deem him worthy of his revelation. But God, who gives grace to the humble, quickly consoled his lack of confidence [Col. 0684A] through the following course of events and miracles.

3. [Note: [Col. 0683] This chapter also occurs in 2b, with its final sentences altered.] A great multitude of people streamed from every side to the town of Dinant [Note: [Col. 0683D] Dinant.], because there much miraculous grace was manifested through the commemoration of Mary, Mother of God. Since desired health was restored there to some, hope of recovered health caused many to lie there. Among others a girl named Hersendis had come there. Deprived of the sight of her eyes through illness, she too begged the Mother of God to grant her health. Yet although she deserved the remedy, she also deserved counsel for recovering the remedy. For she was warned in a dream to come to the monastery of Gembloux, since there the remedy for her health would not fail her.

She came on the Sunday before the martyrdom of the Apostles; and, praying with many tears, she showed the devotion of her heart [Col. 0684B]. But because she did not know where to turn or to whom to disclose her case, grief of heart and bodily pain kept her bedridden for the whole week. On Saturday evening she returned to the church, disclosed her case, and scarcely obtained permission to spend the night in the church. Led to the tomb of Saint Guibert, she spent the night there and, as devoutly as she could, petitioned the saint of God on her own behalf. Nor was this in vain. At dawn, rising from the saint’s tomb, as soon as she went out through the church door, she said: “I give you thanks, O God, because I see the light of heaven, which I have not seen for a long time.” This first grace of miracles, delighting the minds of the faithful, moved all to praise the Lord [Col. 0684C].

4. The fame of Saint Guibert’s name also crossed the sea and gave light to England. The cause was as follows. A man of Gembloux named Hethennus had come to England for trade. His horse fell ill, having been injured when it was taken off the ship. On his companions’ advice it seemed useful to revive the sick horse by bloodletting with a lancet. The lancet was applied and blood flowed; but the flow exceeded all measure and could not be stopped in any way. Many merchants and many Englishmen gathered; they said and did many things customarily useful for stopping a flow of blood. Since all these things were of no use here, the horse’s owner had recourse to aid familiar to him:

“Saint Wicbert,” he said [Col. 0684D], “you who are accustomed to be present for me when I invoke you, behold: in your name I lay a denarius upon the bleeding vein.”

He spoke and laid it there; at the very utterance, the fountain of blood stopped and flowed no more. More than all others the English marvelled at this, inquired about Saint Wicbert’s name and merit, and, learning that invocation of his name was effective, became accustomed to call upon him in their necessities.

5. Who could doubt that it was worthy of a miracle, what God worked through the invocation of Saint Wicbert in delivering Everelm? This Everelm, noble by birth and likewise not undistinguished in the practice of arms, had been captured by his niece, Countess Petronilla, and lay bound in secure custody in the castle called Gocileis [Note: [Col. 0685D] At Gottendeys, a castle in the district of Mechelen.]. Since her nephew was suspect to her and to everyone because of his bodily strength and resourcefulness of mind, Petronilla could not be persuaded by any entreaty or exhortation, nor moved by regard for either the count or the duke, to release Everelm upon receiving hostages until the matter and case had been referred to the hearing of the countrymen.

Despairing, therefore, of human aid, he entrusted his cause to God; and, placing the hope of his liberation in the patronage of God’s saints, he sought the help of Peter, prince of the apostles, whose church Petronilla had burned in order to capture him. While he had long depended wholly on Peter’s mercy, he at last saw in a dream that the apostle himself urged Petronilla [Col. 0685B] to take him as a hostage and release Everelm for a time. When the apostle could not obtain this from her, he departed indignantly, directing Everelm not to worsen his cause by a disgraceful condition.

Meanwhile, since no remission of his punishments was granted him, and he therefore burned with a still greater desire to seek deliverance, he also determined to invoke Saint Wicbert more earnestly, having heard many proclaim the saint’s effective mercy in freeing captives. Fulfilling this desire, he invoked him with a vow. Nor was this enough for him: opening his heart to one of his servants, he instructed him to go to Saint Wicbert’s tomb and offer the saint his vow in person. The servant came and offered his lord’s vow to the saint of God as devoutly as he could; and he made known to those whom he wished why [Col. 0685C] he had come and what he had vowed.

On the third night thereafter, Everelm resolved to begin an undertaking impossible for a human being, through the merits of Saint Wicbert and with the assistance of him to whom nothing is impossible. That this would have been impossible to a human being without God’s aid is easily evident to one who understands. The place in which he lay imprisoned was separated from Petronilla’s bed by only one wall. Since she entrusted his custody to no one at all, she had lodged him so near herself that, if anyone merely muttered while speaking or made any sound at all, she herself, with ears pricked up, would perceive it. A fetter [Note: [Col. 0686D] That is, a chain.] bound both the captive’s feet so tightly on every side that he had no ability whatever to walk [Col. 0685D]. For who can walk with feet tightly bound and immobile? Nor could he move from place to place except by dragging himself on buttocks and hands or crawling on hands and knees.

At the edge of that place lay two pieces of wood, cast there not by chance, as we believe, but presented to him by divine direction. Undertaking by ingenuity to overcome nature, after much labour he hollowed out the earth with his hands, set the pieces of wood in the ground, and began at a suitable point to climb, crawling on hands and knees; having laboriously surmounted the height of the timbers, he strove to reach the house’s ceiling. Tearing out one ceiling-board, he had now reached the upper floor of the house. Although all this could not have been done without some noise [Col. 0686A], none of it could be heard by anyone resting in the house.

Dragging himself by crawling to the window of the house, Everelm threw himself into it with such force as he could. Here indeed he needed to invoke God and God’s saints, and repeatedly call upon the name of Saint Wicbert, to whom he had entrusted the success of his undertaking. For he found the window so narrow that he could neither advance nor retreat in any way. I shall tell a wonderful thing, not in my words but in Everelm’s own. After invoking God and Saint Wicbert, he was astonished that either the window had been enlarged so greatly or his body made so slender that he had full ability both to advance and to retreat. Since retreat was hateful to him, he took courage to proceed [Col. 0686B]; fastening a linen cloth to the window, he lowered himself by it, although dangerously, to the ground.

Having left the house amid such danger, and learned that danger is never overcome without danger, he committed himself to no smaller a danger—namely, getting out over the high wall of the castle. How, with bound feet weighed down by a heavy chain, he climbed the height of the wall, no one can even wonder at adequately, still less explain in words. The steadfastness of so brave a man is indeed exceedingly admirable, and the ingenuity of so prudent a man sufficiently praiseworthy.
