Yet human courage would have achieved little without divine assistance, and human ingenuity would have had little power without divine counsel; therefore all these things are worthy of a miracle.

Having somehow climbed the castle wall, Everelm fastened his stripped-off shirt to the wall [Col. 0686C] and drew himself down it as far as he could; then, falling, he reached the ground, rolled like a smooth log into the depth of the embankment, and miraculously escaped even from there. At last reaching level ground, he had the freedom to depart but not the ability to walk. Yet, now dragging himself on his buttocks, now crawling on his knees as best he could, and satisfying his desire, he discovered that God himself helps the bold. In this way he crossed the nearest wood.

But the shrewd and resourceful man began to fear that he might perhaps be found by those searching if his tracks were detected by tracking dogs. In this fear he gathered strength of mind and body, began to use leaps, and on the third leap threw himself into a passing brook [Col. 0686D]. Hollowing out the muddy bank with his hands, he hid in it all day. He saw those seeking him running about here and there; he saw the dogs, in their scent-tracking manner, following his tracks; he saw and heard women gathering herbs near him. Yet he never in any way abandoned hope of his deliverance.

When day had ended—a day which seemed longer than a whole year to one in peril—and nightfall was approaching, one could see and hear how many men were hunting Everelm in every direction with horns, how many were running everywhere with lanterns and torches, and how many were pursuing him through the wood with tracking dogs. Every road was blocked; every path [Col. 0687A] closed off. But Everelm, trusting in God and Saint Wicbert, lay until cockcrow, encouraged by hope alone. When the cock crowed, he girded himself with courage and rose, intending to go away. But Jesus, who looked upon Peter weeping when the cock crowed, also looked upon Everelm, praying with tears, when the cock crowed. The first sign that he had looked upon him with the eye of mercy was this: at cockcrow, one of Everelm’s feet was released from the fetter’s bond. He fastened the portion of the fetter still attached to his leg and set out under a happy omen, always invoking Saint Wicbert of God.

Thus all those seeking him were frustrated; throughout the whole night he went safely, with Christ as guide and Saint Wicbert as helper. In the morning he came to the church of Fraxinus, which Petronilla had burned in order to capture him [Col. 0687B], and gave thanks to Saint Peter, who had offered himself as Petronilla’s hostage for Everelm’s release. Nor was he ungrateful to Saint Wicbert, to whom after God he had entrusted the outcome of his liberation. He came at a fitting time to the saint’s tomb and, as testimony to divine power, placed the fetter upon it with tears of rejoicing. Whoever sees it ought to give thanks to God, who thus glorifies his saints.

6. A woman from Brania, a village belonging to our community, lay for a long time afflicted by excessive pain in her teeth. Invoking Saint Wicbert’s name, she earnestly implored him to deign to help her. Nor was this in vain. For when the pain had been relieved, she experienced that Saint Wicbert’s name is favourable to those who invoke it. Therefore, as a token of the cure she had received, she made [Col. 0687C] a wax model of gums resembling human gums and brought it to Saint Wicbert’s tomb with thanksgiving. To recount everything individually and repeat each item in sequence is difficult, and not especially useful. Therefore some things out of many are briefly written down, so that from a few instances the existence of many may truly be proved.

7. Hasbania, gladdened by one and then another benefit of Saint Wicbert, was also illumined by a third miracle of his. The people were celebrating the feast-day of Pentecost, and, as the sun declined toward sunset, the church was celebrating the evening synaxis. Behold, a certain man came, supported by his relatives’ hands. With the people following, he was led to Saint Wicbert’s tomb, placed a fetter of great weight upon the saint’s tomb [Col. 0687D], and with tears of rejoicing gave thanks to God and the saint of God.

When asked who he was, where he was from, who had captured him, and how he had escaped, he set everything forth in order:

“I was living in the village of Hasbania called Pellonias, and, though my possessions were modest, I conducted myself vigorously. But however great a person’s prosperity may be, adversity is sometimes not absent. A certain robber named Peter lay in wait for me, captured me, and shut me in the castle called Wanga [Note: [Col. 0687D] Wange, in the district of Landen.]. I assessed the amount of my ransom according to my means, but he assessed it according to his wishes. This disagreement between him and me became the occasion of a worse evil for me [Col. 0688A].

“When he began to grow weary of the long delay in my ransom, how violently he raged against me may be understood from this one thing. Not content with having bound my feet with this heavy fetter which you see, he bound the thumbs and joined fingers of both my hands extremely tightly with a bowstring. What distress could be more grievous than this punishment? Wearied by so many evils, on the Lord’s Day after the Rogation days I spoke with my heart. Saint Wicbert, whom I had been accustomed to invoke more often, I now invoked more devoutly. With tears bursting forth from my heart’s depths, I prayed in these words:

“‘Saint Wicbert, whom all believe by experience to be so merciful and so ready to hear, why have you thus hardened yourself against me, a sinner who calls upon you confidently above all saints? Such distresses constrain me that I now fear, in my despair, danger to my soul unless you deign to help me at once.’

“As I prayed thus, I felt such heat in the place where I lay that I thought a furnace had been kindled beside me. Shaken with great terror, I was drenched in such sweat over all my limbs that I had never so burned with heat for any reason. While I was distressed in both heart and body, the bound fingers of my hands began to come apart; shortly thereafter the bolts of the fetter also began to loosen. Thanks to God and God’s saint, the use of my hands and feet was restored to me. Forgetting every pain and not fearing the five guards lying around me, whom I even thought awake, I began to leave in hope of safety.

“The moving door-hinge made such a creak that it filled me myself with great fear [Col. 0688C] and struck heavy terror into all resting in the house. I came to the castle enclosure. Here indeed all hope failed me. What could I do? I did not dare go back; I did not know how to get out of the castle enclosure, for I had neither counsel nor strength by which I could somehow seek a way out. As I stood there stunned with fear, I began to invoke Saint Wicbert; blaming him for the cause of my flight, I said weeping:

“‘You have deceived me, Saint Wicbert, and I have been deceived: while fleeing the loss of my possessions, I have run into danger of death. If I am found here, there will be no ransom for me thereafter. But you, saint, complete what you have begun, for to you alone after God I entrusted my cause.’

“While I was saying these things to myself, I felt what seemed like the sound of a bird’s wings flying around me. Shaken with dread in addition to the fear that made me tremble, I stood beside myself and estranged from my senses. I call God and Saint Wicbert to witness that I do not know at all what happened to me meanwhile—namely, how I was placed beyond the castle enclosure or how I escaped the steep embankment. When I came to myself and understood this, it cannot be said or believed how greatly I was astonished, and still am astonished. Yet I set out on the road, now carrying good hope with me.

“I heard the household of the castle making an uproar and seeking me with horns, torches, and dogs. I saw the dogs tracking me; when they saw me, they fell silent and drew back as though struck by a stick. Giving thanks [Col. 0689A] for this to God and God’s saint, I passed the night as best I could by travelling, and in the unexpected morning reached my home. Because bodily pain prevented me from coming here at once, behold, on the eighth day after my release I come to offer thanks to God and Saint Wicbert.”

When this had been heard, all praised God in his saint; they praised God in his mighty acts; they praised God with cymbals of rejoicing; and the church resounded with praises of the holy Trinity.

8. After the death of Lord Abbot Lietard, of good memory (4 February 1113), many great adversities befell us. Certain members of our household, disregarding the church’s rights, claimed them for themselves and harshly asserted claims against us concerning our own property as if it were theirs. Since this tragedy has been sufficiently sung upon the theatre of the world [Col. 0689B], I refrain from recounting it here, because its full relation demands its own place.

Therefore Duke Godfrey of Louvain had come to Gembloux to decide our case against unjust men, and a great multitude both of his magnates and retainers [Note: [Col. 0689A] *satellum*, corrected to *satellitum*—“retainers.”] had assembled. The bodies of the saints—Exuperius the martyr, and Maclovius and Wicbert the confessors—lay upon the ground in the middle of the church, so that, because our sins prevented us from deserving to be heard in our tribulation, God’s mercy might be reconciled to us through this propitiatory appeal to the saints. Many of those assembled for that day therefore turned to venerate these saints, especially Saint Wicbert, whose name was at that time celebrated by the glorious novelty of miracles [Col. 0689C].

Among the others was a certain nobleman, Henry of Bierbais. Though a son of the world, he was a close kinsman by birth of Saint Wicbert himself. As he passed by with many companions, he said: “Come, let us stand, and, worshipping God in his saints, let us greet my kinsman Saint Wicbert.”

At these words he had begun to approach [Col. 0690A], when a young knight, as frivolous in mind as in age, said: “Tell him to help me, for I have no leisure to stop here.”

Horrified by the frivolity of the remark, Henry fell down to pray. But the foolish youth wished to pass on and could not, being chastised by a divine stroke. His face was suddenly distorted; a trembling of some limbs and forgetfulness of mind seized him; and as his steps failed he could scarcely stand, much less walk. His eyes stared wildly, his ears became deaf, and his tongue stammered, so that he no longer seemed to retain anything human. Yet, by whatever effort he could, he crawled as far as the place of the choir. Seeing there a brother sitting [Note: [Col. 0689A] *frm.*, “brother.”], he tried to attach himself to him. The brother recoiled from the man’s dreadful appearance, but pitied his feeble gait. Thus horror urged flight, compassion compelled him to remain [Col. 0690B]. Compassion prevailed; and he approached the wretch whom he had at first sight recoiled from. He led the man aside and asked in order who he was, where he came from, and how he had been changed into this condition.

Explaining his identity, place, time, and cause, the man said:

“I am Gerard of Morealmes. Today I entered this chapel with certain leading men and companions of mine. While they were conducting themselves devoutly in reverence for the saints, especially Saint Wicbert, I began to mock their devotion with unbecoming remarks. For that reason I know and confess that I have been changed into the pitiable condition which you see. I pray you, give me counsel, that I may deserve pardon from the saints—especially Saint Wicbert, whom I particularly offended.”

The brother then corrected him, as he humbly confessed his sin, with corporal chastisement, and imposed penance upon him [Col. 0690C]. His repentance was so heartfelt that he immediately obtained pardon, being at once restored to the beauty of youthful age so completely that he marvelled that he had been returned to himself so suddenly.

[Col. 0689]

# Life of Theoderic, Bishop of Metz, by Sigebert of Gembloux

(Edited by Dom Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores*, vol. IV, p. 461.)

## Notice

Sigebert, born about the years 1027–1030 [Note: [Col. 0689C] He appears to have lived about eighty-five years.], entered the monastery of Gembloux under Abbot Olbert, distinguished for learning and merits [Note: [Col. 0689C] Compare Sigebert, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 142.]. After spending a few years under Olbert’s successor Macelin, he was summoned to Metz by Folcuin, brother of the abbot and then provost of the monastery of Saint Vincent at Metz, to instruct boys. In that most pleasant city he spent his early years. There he wrote many small works [Note: [Col. 0690C] Sigebert, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 171.] and became famous for humane cultivation, wisdom, and learning. As Anselm relates [Note: [Col. 0690C] *Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux*, continuation, p. 768.], he was “an open fountain of wisdom, most beloved not only by monks and clerics flocking to him from every quarter, but also by Jews dwelling in the same city, because he was skilled at distinguishing Hebrew truth from the other versions, and in matters stated according to Hebrew truth he agreed with the assertions of the Jews” [Col. 0691].

Indeed, the very first book which he declares himself to have composed, the *Life of Bishop Theoderic* [Note: [Col. 0691B] *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 171: “I wrote the Life of Bishop Theoderic, founder of that church and abbey; in it I also, by way of digression, declaimed in heroic metre the praise of the city itself.”], shows him as a young man well disposed, devout, a lover of truth and beauty, distinguished by varied learning: a diligent reader of Holy Scripture, classical authors [Note: [Col. 0691B] Especially Horace, from whom he inserted many passages into his writings.], the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0691B] For example, Augustine; see ch. 5, end.], and writers even of his own time [Note: [Col. 0691B] For example, Ruotger and Widukind, ch. 1.]; an assiduous investigator of his country’s antiquities; and a lively, elegant, somewhat florid writer. He delights in verses and expressions gleaned from poets, and in sentences answering one another in rhythm and sound, so that he often turns the limbs of hexameters and pentameters into the same syllable-counts. He undertook to write the *Life of Theoderic* at the request of the brothers Ulric and Rudolf, and from devotion to the founder of the monastery in which he himself lived [Note: [Col. 0691B] Ch. 14.], Saint Vincent’s. He combined, into a composition in praise of the bishop and city of Metz, whatever ancient records they could provide for this undertaking [Note: [Col. 0692B] Chs. 13, 16, 17, 18, 21]: charters and privileges of emperors and popes [Note: [Col. 0692B] Chs. 14, 20], and an account of the translation of relics gathered by Theoderic in Italy, written by a cleric who had been present at the events [Note: [Col. 0692B] Ch. 16.].

Yet, although Theoderic had some faults deserving no slight censure, Sigebert did not touch them even with a needle-point, content to say that the bishop had inveighed rather too severely against those who violated Saint Vincent’s possessions. Whether this should be attributed to ignorance or to a purpose of concealment is unclear, since Sigebert apparently neither read what Thietmar [Note: [Col. 0692B] III.9.] had alleged to Theoderic’s discredit, nor is it certain that, when he published the *Life of Theoderic*, he already knew what Alpert [Note: [Col. 0692B] Whose book he used in the *Chronicle*.] had related concerning Theoderic’s death.

He wrote in the time of Abbot Folcuin, while the consecration of Saint Vincent’s church, celebrated in 1030, still clung as though recent to the memory of those who had been present [Note: [Col. 0692B] Ch. 22.]; therefore, between the years 1050 and 1060.

A book apparently corrected in his own hand survives in a codex of the late eleventh century, written in two columns in a very small script, fols. 1–5. From it Leibniz first published the text in vol. I of the *Scriptores Brunsvicenses*, pp. 293–313. We offer a more correct text, indicating by the letter c) the reading of the codex, by the number 1) the hand of the author himself, by 2) that of the corrector, and adding 3) the variant readings of Paris, Bibliothèque royale MS 5294, a parchment manuscript of the eleventh century. This manuscript contains the history of the translation of relics collected by Theoderic, published by D’Achery in *Spicilegium*, V, p. 139; corrected by Baluze in the second edition of that work, vol. II, p. 133; and now again collated by Waitz with the editions.

Sigebert himself inserted certain extracts from the *Life of Theoderic* into his *Chronicle* under the years 964 and 969; and the author of the *Chronicle of the Bishops of Metz* praises it in D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, II, 228. The epitaph inserted in chapter 21 is also found in an eleventh-century manuscript, formerly of the Collège de Clermont, later Meerman’s, now belonging to the most distinguished Sir Thomas Phillipps at Middlehill in England, no. 1711. From this manuscript it was formerly copied by André Duchesne; Baluze published it in *Miscellanea*, IV, 554, and our Lappenberg copied it again in 1836.

We append the rhythms composed by Sigebert in honour of Theoderic, which Meurisse published in his *History of the Bishops of Metz*, pp. 329–330, from Sigebert’s autograph preserved in the monastery of Saint Vincent at Metz.

# Rhythms in Honour of Theoderic

[Col. 0691]

[Col. 0691A] The life of Theoderic, first in merits and in time [Note: [Col. 0692B] The second Theoderic held office from 1005 to 1047.],

Set forth in this book, shall be recited by an age that remembers.

I scarcely composed this and wrote it in humble characters,

I, Sigebert, Christ’s orphan, humble in mind.

Here, Vincent the Levite, I have reread your trophies;

Here too, Lucy, are your triumphs, and those of the remaining three,

Whose titles have been set forth in order above [Note: [Col. 0692B] See chapter 16.].

Whatever error I have committed must be charged to you,

O Ulric, and likewise to your brother Rudolf,

Whom divine love, and zeal for your [Note: [Col. 0691] Thus c.] bishop,

[Col. 0692A] Impelled to compel me, unwilling and strongly resisting,

To consent to lift this burden with my feeble limbs,
So that, while you receive praise, my fault may bring blushes upon me.

Who could deny that praise should be added to your reward,

you who have bestowed such a book, suited to divine use,

upon the saints from your own possessions, and dedicated it as their own?

The gift is smaller than the affection, but the devotion greater than the means. [Note: [Col. 0691] “in understanding” in witness 1.]

He who sows seed in hope shall reap more abundantly.

God, who gives all things freely, receives nothing freely from one who gives.

Praise to the giver, peace to the keeper, the cross to the plunderer.

## LETTER CONCERNING THE LIFE OF LORD DEODERIC, THE FORMER BISHOP OF METZ

[Note: [Col. 0691] *devita* added.]

[Col. 0691]

[Col. 0691B] To the reverend lord, venerable father, lord abbot and mirror of abbots, F. . . . the least, would that he were the least, little servant of the servants of God, S. . . . what God has promised to those who love him. Concerning the deeds of our lord and patron Deoderic which I have been able to learn through truthful report, I have endeavoured faithfully to record them according to my capacity—an undertaking indeed rash, but an affection voluntary. For I do not think that anything added to the praises of his lord displeases the mind of a faithful steward.

My heart urged me to inscribe this work to your name; [Col. 0692B] yet it was not my intention, through the grave fault of my slowness, to diminish your praise—you whom all acknowledge to excel in the dignity of literary learning. You therefore, who are accustomed to delight in the continual sweetness of divine reading, permit, I pray, your mouth to be made bitter by the taste of uncultivated speech, so that the sweetness, repeatedly tasted, may please you all the more after an unaccustomed lover has for a time caused you pain; just as a fastidious stomach often prefers very humble turnips and scallions [Note: [Col. 0691] I correct thus; the manuscript has *ascidas*. Everyone knows that the lowest scallions are the tenderest. Leibniz corrected it to *acidas jurulas*, “sour little broths.”] before all poverty has yet been banished [Col. 0693A] by the feasts of kings. For today there is room for cheap eggs and black vegetables. [Note: [Col. 0693] That is, greens or vegetables.]

Do not attend to who I am, or with what style I have written, but to what I have written and concerning whom. Apply, if you please, the rod of paternal criticism; pierce the superfluities with a sharp spit. If it displeases you, prefix the deadly theta. Let the silent page speak the sequence of events, and let it not cover the writer’s face with shame. Fare well.

[Col. 0693] HERE ENDS THE LETTER.

## PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING WORK

[Col. 0693A] “Let us praise,” says Jesus son of Sirach, “glorious men, and our fathers in their generation, who [Note: [Col. 0693] “and in” in witness 1.] attained glory in their generations and were held in praise in their days. Those born from them left behind a name for the telling of their praises. And there are some of whom there is no remembrance: they have perished as though they had not existed; they were born as though not born, and their children with them. But these were men of mercy, whose righteous deeds have not fallen into oblivion” (Ecclus. 44:1, 8–10).

See how the lover of wisdom, embracing the pious glory of his fathers, rightly deplores the indolence of those who suffer the memory of their ancestors to be effaced through forgetfulness or neglect. For since “the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance,” and “the memory of the righteous” [Col. 0693B] “is always with praise,” surely, just as blessed immortality is prepared for the soul of the righteous by good works, so lasting renown must also be prepared for his name by remembrance of good works.

If, therefore, he who gives only a cup of cold water in the name of a righteous man shall not lose his reward, then, I believe, he too shall receive a righteous man’s reward who prevents the praises of a righteous man from growing old with age or being buried in oblivion. For without doubt it pertains to the praise of God, and increases the reward of the righteous, when the integrity of their lives invites others by its example to good conduct. [Col. 0694A]

Accordingly, very many people are accustomed to complain: some, because oblivion has so utterly erased the life of their predecessors; others, the lives of their particular patrons; that, apart from [Note: [Col. 0693] “apart from” in witness 1; “except for” in witness 2.] the name, and apart from the fact that they are known to have pleased God in their own days, no mention of their deeds is made, so that through them the name of God may be blessed—the God who works all things in all. This same complaint troubled us more and more each day concerning our lord and patron Deoderic, because the decay of forgetfulness had almost consumed his many great works as worms consume wood, or moths garments.

We ought not transmit to our descendants this concern, left to us by our elders. Rather, searching these matters out with careful eyes, and aided by him who makes the tongues of infants eloquent, [Col. 0694B] we shall attempt to set them forth plainly with the pen of certainty. Let us therefore prove our devotion toward our patron; let us offer our offering to him who was truly God’s temple. And if we do not possess the gold of purity, the silver of eloquence, the fine linen of cleanness, scarlet dyed with the double [Note: [Col. 0693] Perhaps “genuine”; yet *gemina*, “double,” occurs frequently in Thietmar; cf. *SS.* III, 859.—L.] love (Exod. 35:6), let us at least weave from goats’ hair a haircloth covering—whether to cover the tabernacle of his body [Note: [Col. 0693] “or at least to cover his tabernacle,” in witness 2.] or at least to wipe the dust from his tomb.

## INVOCATION

[Col. 0693]

[Col. 0693C] Therefore, as we are about to enter upon the road whereby we may come to recount truthfully the life of the righteous man, let us invoke the grace of him who is the Way, the Truth, and the Life: that he who feeds toothless infants with milk may feed us with the nourishment of his teaching and instruct us through the discourse of his wisdom.

Lord Christ, almighty God, ruler without beginning,

*Kyrie, Christe, theos, pantocraton, archos, anarchos*—  
“Lord, Christ, God, almighty, ruler, without beginning,”

be for me beginning, guide, way, and protection,

that through you I may be able worthily to write concerning you.

[Col. 0694C] My mind depends upon you: what can anything be without you?

In saints who are praised, you are praised and hallowed.

And what is the honour of the righteous? The love of the one who makes righteous.

When I proclaim a saint, I proclaim the Holy One of saints;

the praise of a beautiful work is praise of its craftsman.

Behold, I restore to you your righteous man Deoderic;

be present, one Trinity, threefold unity of soul.

I can scarcely utter a sound; I pray, open my mute mouth.

You yourself teach the she-ass, that she may teach Balaam.

The law of nature does not hinder you, lawgiver beyond law;

for nature, following your nod, cannot retain its fixed order.

You give speech to the mute and take speech even from the eloquent;

touch the rock of my heart, and the rock will pour forth water.

## HERE BEGINS THE LIFE OF LORD DEODERIC, THE ELDER BISHOP

[Col. 0693]

[Col. 0693D] **Chapter 1. On the nobility of his lineage.** Thus we have learned that Deoderic, a man memorable in life and venerable in memory, [Note: [Col. 0693] “true man” in witness 1.] was descended from the district of Hamaland in Saxony, [Note: [Col. 0693D] On both banks of the IJssel.] born of Count Everard as father and Amalrada [Note: [Col. 0693] Thus Leibniz rightly corrected it; cf. chapter 21. The manuscript has AMALRABA.] as mother—born, as we truly believe, for the adornment of the world. [Note: [Col. 0694D] A hexameter verse.]

Another writer, relying on his talent, would begin the web of his narrative from the cradle; he would praise his teachable childhood and magnify the noble character of his youth. When he had reached the fork of Pythagoras’ letter, he would send the world with its allurements to the left-hand path, but lead the mind of the righteous man, striving toward the prize of immortality, along the narrow path to the right. Why say more? At every stage of life he would arrange in that man’s heart the ascents of virtues.

We, because we distrust our strength and can scarcely suffice for matters properly our own, pass over what is common; and because we seek brevity, we are content to praise in him only uprightness of character and nobility of birth. His noble manner of life was daily increased [Note: [Col. 0695] “increased” in witness 1.] by the presence of divine cooperation; while his religious nobility was raised by the eminence of his kinsmen [Col. 0695B] and connections, namely the foremost men of Gaul and Germany, and was further enhanced by the splendour of imperial blood.

For we know that his mother was sister to Queen Matilda, who by King Henry bore Otto the Great and Duke Henry, and their brother Bruno, worthy of much praise, who shone among all mortals of that age as the moon among the lesser fires (Horace, *Odes* 1.12). These women were daughters of Duke Theoderic, and their brothers were Widukind, Immed, and Reinbern. Reinbern himself fought against the Danes, who had long been ravaging Saxony; he defeated them and freed his country from their incursions. They were of the stock of the great Duke Widukind, who waged mighty war against Charlemagne for almost [Col. 0695C] thirty years. Moreover, Bruno, whom we mentioned above, was commended by such divine favour through his merits that he whom the dignity of the archbishopric of Cologne made illustrious was also marked out by the high authority of rule over all Lotharingia. [Note: [Col. 0965D] Compare the *Life of Bruno*, chapter 22.]

**2. [Note: [Col. 0695] In the manuscript the word “Chapter” is repeated consistently.] How he advanced under the instruction of Lord Bruno.** Deoderic, the cousin for whom this work is composed, [Note: [Col. 0695] DEODERIHCUS in the manuscript.] was weaned in his earliest years from the breast of maternal piety in the bosom of the holy church of Halberstadt. Raised, as was fitting, in a lofty manner, he promised sweet and abundant fruits of nature and character. But when Bruno, the jewel among bishops, ascended the pontifical throne in 953, Deoderic assumed the role of disciple and acted as his inseparable companion.

[Col. 0695D] Since he was one day to serve in the ranks of the heavenly army through civic service, he was trained under Bruno in the school of the holy church of Cologne by a long preparatory course in liberal education, and was commendably tested through prolonged preliminaries. There he learned humbly to be subject, though he was someday usefully to preside over many and to benefit those subject to him by humble and judicious governance. Each possessed something which the other could cherish in him; [Col. 0696A] and, as iron sharpens iron, each was built up by emulation of the other’s virtues.

At first the natural bond of kinship had produced friendship between them; then habitual intimacy nourished goodwill. Though goodwill may be removed from kinship, it cannot be removed from friendship, because kinship without goodwill retains an empty name, whereas friendship cleaves indivisibly to goodwill. Thus friendship corresponded to kinship in these cousins, and mutual goodwill made their friendship firm. Nor could it prove futile that a man destined to become so great in Christ and in the Church—whom Mother Church had nurtured for her own adornment and support, whom nature, or rather the Author of nature himself, had enriched with native excellence of mind—should have deserved to be instructed and polished by the devotion and teaching of so great [Col. 0696B] a master.

For, as he says indeed (Horace, *Odes* 4.4):

> Instruction develops inborn strength,  
> and right cultivation strengthens hearts;  
> yet, wherever character has failed,  
> faults disgrace well-born natures.

**3. On his promotion to the episcopate.** Therefore, lest a man born for the benefit of many should lack material for virtue, lest so great a craftsman lack a workshop in which to exercise good works, heavenly providence provided this also, not only for him but for the advancement of very many: that, as a cultivator of righteousness planted in the house of the Lord, he might flourish in the courts of our God like a palm tree in the height of his merits; that, multiplied like a cedar of Lebanon, he might give forth the incorruptible fragrance of examples; and that, like an olive tree, [Col. 0696C] he might bear the rich fruit of joy and blessing.

In the year 962 from the incarnation of the Lord, when the first Adelbero, restorer of holy religion, had entered the way of all flesh, the see of the holy church of Metz, bereft of its own shepherd, was vacant. Bruno, sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, did not fail it; I say, he did not fail either it or the welfare of the whole kingdom. But, as he was accustomed to do in other matters, so in this matter too he sought not what was his own, but what belonged to Jesus Christ.

For among the other arts in which he excelled he had added this one: when he saw the innocence of the dove, the prudence of the serpent, and the simplicity of especially secure faith flourishing in leading men of every rank, he attached his friendship especially to them [Col. 0696D] and obtained for them the king’s favour more abundantly. If private life still obscured any such persons, he suitably advanced them through his own efforts into the places of eminent men who had died, thereby stirring them to good action. [Note: [Col. 0695] Thus Leibniz; the manuscript has “approached.”] For he had become all things to all people because he wished to gain all.

Seeing, then, that a suitable place and time had come to him for establishing in the Church of God, as support of the spiritual structure, a solid pillar shaped by his own hand, [Col. 0697A] he judged it useful that his cousin Deoderic, distinguished by birth and religion, should be installed there. For the balanced scale of his judgment weighed place, time, and person: he judged Deoderic worthy to rule so noble a city, and a city of such power not unworthy to be entrusted to a man of such high birth—especially since that time required its defence through the aid of a prudent and courageous ruler.

For in the preceding years public calamities had pressed heavily upon it, when it was attacked by Cono, author of every evil, [Note: [Col. 0697D] Compare Ruotger, *Life of Bruno*, chapter 24.] it was almost plundered and destroyed in 954. Thus, with the unanimous agreement of all the clergy and people, and with the support of the entire senate of the palace, [Col. 0697B] Bruno caused him to be enthroned in the august see of Metz, amid the joyful harmony of all, not without great applause from the heavenly powers.

Adorned, therefore, with the pontifical mitre, and with Henry, metropolitan of Trier and a man of great merit, officiating, [Note: [Col. 0697D] Read “Theoderic”; Henry had died in Italy in 964; cf. *Continuation of Regino*, under 965.] he was consecrated with the oil of blessing on 5 March, the third day before the Nones, in 965. He strove to fulfil the title of the office he had assumed through good works, preferring to be rather than merely to seem a bishop. At first he did not deviate from the footsteps of his predecessor; and the man whose high birth made him his equal he intended also to imitate in excellence of character and fervour of religion. His own good purpose stirred him toward good; as we have said, the recent example of his predecessor formed him; the sound instruction of his good teacher had not fallen from his mind; and, surpassing every human teaching, [Col. 0697C] he was further inspired by a heavenly oracle.

**4. On the initial letters of names given by an angel.** Let us therefore recount a matter known through the report and writing of our elders and, because of its novelty, rightly to be laid up in the treasury of memory. Saint Clement, disciple of Peter, prince of the apostles, and first apostle and preacher of the people of Metz, among the other things which the devout lover of our salvation bestowed upon him for strengthening the first foundations of the growing Church, merited this special gift from heaven: he received, sent to him by an angel, the names of future bishops in the church of Metz, with only the first letters of each name recorded.

When the blessed man of whom we speak had attained the episcopal seat, he was one day enjoying the agreeable and serious conversation [Col. 0697D] of familiar friends and wise men—for God’s providence had also provided faithfully for him in this respect, so that he should not lack the company of wise and good counsellors—and he ordered those memorials of the angelic writing brought before him. Examining them carefully, he marvelled that some were formed in the variety of gold, others of silver, and still others of some different colour; and he understood by a deeper interpretation that the variety of colours signified the varied quality of each person’s merits.

[Col. 0698A] Among the rest he saw the letter of his own name shining white in a silver colour. Turning to himself, he marvelled on the one hand at the deep and unchangeable counsel of divine foreknowledge, [Note: [Col. 0697] “presence” in witness 1.] and on the other considered the purpose of his own good will. “If,” he said, “God, the co-worker in every good thing, grants my good intention its desired fulfilment, I trust that I shall accomplish such great good in my episcopate that this silver letter will someday be changed into gold.”

Thus the good man, bringing forth good from a good treasure, spoke from the abundance of his heart; nor was he slower in carrying out good works than he had promised. Although the neglect of our forebears has deprived us of some part of these deeds, and though, lulled by the sleep of their indolence, they thought him to be buried with them, still many of his wonderful works remain, [Col. 0698B] in a manner presenting him to us as alive. [Note: [Col. 0697] The manuscript has “with.”] [Note: [Col. 0697] “is lacking” in witness 1.] Thus we may plainly testify to the Lord’s saying in the Gospel: “If these should be silent, the stones will cry out” (Luke 19:40).

For who does not know that, by the vitality of his intellect, the shrewdness of his counsel, and his singular prudence—qualities for which he was greatly esteemed among the chief men of the realm—the condition of the state was improved and the episcopate of the holy church of Metz, over which he presided by God’s appointment, was augmented for the better?

**5. On the demolition of the old church and construction of the new.** To say nothing for the moment of the monastery of the glorious martyr of Christ, Vincent, in building which he spent the whole devotion of his heart, let us first demonstrate his energy from the works he undertook in his spare time. [Note: [Col. 0697] Thus L.; the manuscript has *subciuis*.]

[Col. 0698C] First among the witnesses to his magnificence stands the greater church of the precious protomartyr Stephen, which, threatening dangerous collapse through age, he fittingly rebuilt from its foundations. At that time there still stood the oratory of ancient reverence, preserving a treasure surpassing gems and gold: the precious pledge of the protomartyr’s blood. Because not everything is known to everyone, we shall give a brief account of this oratory.

Long ago, when the cry of Gaul had multiplied before God and the sin of its wickedness had become excessively grievous, the stirring of the righteous Judge gave the cities of the scarlet harlot the cup of wrath and indignation to drink. Finally, the Huns were unleashed for their utter destruction, incited like rabid dogs to devour the beasts and animals of the field. [Col. 0698D] Every shepherd sought by every means, with rightful concern, to rescue his sheep; but the people’s sins had grown so strong that, although the priests were judged worthy of the Lord’s hearing, those for whom they prayed were unworthy to be heard.

A divine revelation concerning this oratory was made to certain persons, especially to Saint Servatius, bishop of Tongeren, the close friend of Auctor, then bishop of Metz. [Note: [Col. 0698D] Compare the *Life of Saint Servatius of Tongeren*.] By apostolic assurance he was promised that this oratory alone in Belgic Gaul would, through the intercession of the protomartyr, be immune from barbarian devastation.

[Col. 0699A] You would lament to see a populous and wealthy city reduced to ashes, while rejoicing nonetheless that flames licking all around were kept far away from the oratory; and you would marvel that the barbarians, struck with the blindness called in Greek *aorasia*, were kept away from its entrance, so that the efficacy of the martyr’s fruitful faith might be revealed. [Note: [Col. 0699] A second hand adds: “If anyone asks what *aorasia* is, he may learn from the words of Saint Augustine, who says thus in his book *Questions on Genesis*: ‘They struck the men who were at the door of the house with blindness.’ The Greeks have *aorasia*, which more accurately signifies, if it can be said, ‘non-seeing,’ causing a person not to see—not everything, but what is necessary. Those who sought Elisha were struck with this *aorasia*. Those who, after the Resurrection, walked with the Lord on the road and did not recognize him also had it.”]

As I said, it still stood—though shaken by long age, like something already falling, indeed almost fallen. Yet although collapse seemed to threaten danger, its presence was thought to represent an ancient protection. But the bishop, whose mind was bent upon restoring the church and providing all that its use [Col. 0699B] or dignity required, believed that the worship of divine reverence does not consist only in handmade dwellings, and that a place does not commend us; rather, we commend it if we endeavour to live well. Therefore he did not fear to demolish it utterly, though he offended the hearts and eyes of many, as though he had removed from their midst a manifest sign of divine favour and a present testimony to the merits of the protomartyr.

Having built the church anew, he generously honoured it with ecclesiastical ornaments and enriched it with precious gifts, partly given by himself and partly offered to God’s Church by the magnates of the realm out of love for him. These came especially from the generosity of the glorious Emperor Otto and his wife Adelaide, whose life was nothing other than an example of piety and [Col. 0699C] chastity. The glory of their offspring, Otto the Younger, was no less generous in this respect. Since this faithful householder stored up treasure not for himself but for the benefit of the Lord’s household, to give them their measure of wheat at the fitting time, the devotion of many faithful Christians cooperated with his good intention.

**6. On the construction of the monastery of Waulsort.** [Note: [Col. 0699D] Waulsort, in the diocese of Namur.] To introduce one instance among many: at that time there was a count illustrious for noble rank and highly renowned for reverence of holiness, related by blood to this our father; his name was Elbert. Touched by the prompting of heavenly desire, he began to set aside all the deceptive joys of the world that smiled abundantly upon him, judging it unworthy to suffer loss to his soul for their gain.

Sending the embassy of his salvation [Col. 0699D] to the king who came against our single force with a double army, he chose as a fitting mediatrix between himself and God the most devout Mary, his virgin mother. Desiring to bargain away not merely his possessions but even his life itself for the love of eternal life, he gave all that was his to God and to God’s mother in this blessed exchange. In her honour he built a monastery in the village of Waulsort, which the Meuse washes, in the diocese of Liège; and there, under the habit of monastic religion, [Col. 0700A] he gathered persons fit for divine service, that they might sow spiritual things for him and he might reap their material things.

Since he took pride in kinship with our aforesaid bishop, [Note: [Col. 0699] “our” in the manuscript.] especially because he saw that the bishop had considerable influence with the king through intimate friendship, and understood that he had earned the grace of the King of kings by the purity of his heart, he preferred no one after God and God’s mother to appoint as his heir except him. For love of him, he bequeathed the same monastery by testament to the jurisdiction of the holy church of Metz, and confirmed this forever by imperial decree. [Note: [Col. 0699D] On 19 September 946, at Rheims, Elbert’s gift was confirmed by Otto; Miraeus, *Opera* I, 239. Compare [Col. 0700D] the *Chronicle of Waulsort*, ed. Dachery, 2nd ed., II, p. 709, and the *Life of Forannan*, Mabillon, *Acta* V, p. 587.]

The bishop, being a man of no ordinary prudence and not ungrateful for so great a benefit freely bestowed upon his church, ensured that Elbert should not lack a worthy earthly recompense besides eternal reward. He joined to the same monastery a nearby estate under his own authority, called Hasteria, with its appurtenances.

**7. Which men flourished in that age.** I would rightly call Otto’s times happy, when the commonwealth was restored by distinguished bishops and wise men, the peace of the churches renewed, and the integrity of religious life restored. One might see and prove in fact that the philosopher’s saying was true: a state is fortunate if either kings are wise or wise men reign.

[Col. 0700C] For those set over the people of the kingdom were not hirelings but most distinguished shepherds. Among them, deservedly comparable to shining stars, that greatest of magnates, the renowned and ever-to-be-renowned Bruno, archduke [Note: [Col. 0699] *archidus* in the manuscript.] and archbishop, gleamed red as the morning star. After him our Deoderic, ruler of the Church, pillar of the realm, and model of virtue, spread everywhere the light of his name.

At Trier Henry [Note: [Col. 0699] *henricus* in the manuscript.] guided the chariot of God, and after him Egbert; whoever does not know their holiness can readily find those from whom to learn it. Gerard governed at Toul; Wicfrid held the episcopate at Verdun. Their quality may be known even from this: they were colleagues of our Deoderic, trained under the celebrated Bruno, by whose judgment they too deserved [Col. 0700D] to be advanced to the episcopal rank.

Moreover, Wicfrid made ready use of Bishop Deoderic’s assistance in every matter, particularly in building the monastery of Saint Paul the Confessor in the suburb of Verdun. From Deoderic he also obtained the bones of Saint Gregory, martyr of Spoleto, more precious than [Col. 0701A] gold and topaz, and fittingly deposited them in that same church, as may still be seen today.

I could list more persons eminent in every rank at that time, but I do not wish to weary other minds or ears. These men, besides those whom obscure fame has hidden away, were contemporaries of this our father; some were even his comrades-in-arms, some members of the same tribe. These, I say, were his fellow workers for good; these were comrades of this outstanding standard-bearer in the camp of the Lord Sabaoth; all these, serving as auxiliaries in peace and in business, supported the king’s causes, and wonderfully honoured his nephew Deoderic—some with a father’s honour, others with a brother’s love.

**8. On the death of Lord Bruno.** [Note: [Col. 0701D] From Ruotger’s *Life of Bruno*, chapters 43–46.] After the venerable Archbishop Bruno had set all [Col. 0701B] Lotharingia in order, he travelled to Compiègne to bring France also into order, taking with him his cousin Deoderic, his most faithful helper in every good work. From the beginning of Deoderic’s installation Bruno had employed him as his collaborator in all affairs, foreseeing that he would be the imitator of his works and, not long afterward, heir to the grace and virtue granted him from heaven.

The man of peace, wishing to be called a son of God, was intent upon bringing his works to a good completion when he fell into bed, held fast by bodily illness. He returned as far as Rheims, but there his illness grew stronger and detained him. Feeling that his end had been made known to him by God, that the number of his days was completed, and knowing what was yet lacking to him, he resolved to redeem his sins by alms [Col. 0701C] and to lay up his treasures in the treasury of heaven—that is, to spend them for the use of the poor and the churches of Christ.

Calling to himself Deoderic, the relief of his pain and consolation in life and death, and Wicfrid of Verdun—for he too was present—he dictated and sealed his testament before them, appointing them witnesses of his ordinance and executors of his testament. Then, as the dreadful hour of his dissolution approached, he turned himself as best he could toward his nephew Deoderic, and from heartfelt affection bade him a final farewell: “Lord,” he said, “pray.”

Immediately, amid the devout and confused sound of everyone’s singing and weeping, in the year of the Lord 965, on 11 October, the fifth day before the Ides, [Col. 0701D] he paid nature’s debt, sending joy to heaven and leaving mourning to the world. Deoderic, with his fellow bishop, conveyed the body of his friend to Cologne; he opened the testament before the clergy and citizens, and did not deny the dead man the faithfulness and devotion he had shown him alive.

The emperor, grieving that he had been bereft of his only comfort, transferred to his cousin the affection he had borne for his brother. The bishop, grieving that he had survived the half of his own soul, represented Bruno to the emperor in faithfulness and service, lest he should appear unequal or unworthy in the king’s estimation. And as it is written, “The spirit of Elijah rested [Col. 0702A] upon Elisha, to perform signs and wonders” (4 Kings 2:15), so one might marvel that every gift of spiritual grace by which God’s grace had distinguished Bruno was transferred to Deoderic for ordering the affairs of the realm.

**9. On the unanimous fraternity of the clergy of Metz and Halberstadt.** This man of imperial nobility and episcopal dignity kept continual watch over the guard entrusted to his flock and had a particularly earnest concern for the honour and advancement of the clerical order. Therefore he carefully promoted whatever seemed conducive to their welfare.

Among other things, he united the clergy of Metz and Halberstadt—both relying upon the same patron, the victorious protomartyr Stephen—with such a bond of mutual charity that he infused into them one heart and [Col. 0702B] one soul in the Lord. That is, there was to be a perpetual communion of love between them in temporal matters and an undivided union of charity in spiritual matters. What Deoderic’s care began was completed by the industry of his successor and nephew, Adelbero of good memory.

Because the bishop of Halberstadt used, on solemn feast days in the celebration of Mass, a *logium*, that is, a rational [Note: [Col. 0701D] A vestment or ornament resembling the *rationale*, or breastpiece/stole, of the Jewish high priest.]—a mark of doctrine and truth—which had been granted to his church by decree of Pope Agapetus, the aforesaid Adelbero requested by letter that Bishop Hildward of Halberstadt, since they were one in all things, should communicate to him also that one thing which belonged to Hildward alone.

The latter replied [Note: [Col. 0702D] See Hildward’s letter in Labbe, I, p. 682.] that it was one and indivisible; but because love of unity could refuse nothing, he sent him a similar one and so communicated it to him, [Col. 0702C] on the stated condition that thereafter neither might transfer it to any other church, but that these two alone—sisters enjoying one father, one mother, one kinship, and one protector—should adorn themselves modestly and honourably in the eyes of the Bridegroom; and that, if a blemish or wrinkle existed in one, it should be wiped away or corrected by the hand of the other.

For this, however, he requested the reciprocal return of a praiseworthy recompense: namely, that his church be given even a very small portion of the protomartyr’s blood, which blood is believed in true faith to spring forth in the church of the city of Metz, and relics of the glorious virgin of Christ, Glodesindis. Thus, as Solomon says, “A threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Eccles. 4:12), this unanimity of fraternity has been preserved, unshaken and with the greatest firmness, by both sides down to the present [Col. 0702D] day.

**10. On the special honour of the bishops of Metz.** Happy Mother Church, in so sweet an affection of sons! Happy, I say, city of Metz, in so constant an advancement of bishops! Few cities of Gaul would dare prefer themselves to it, claiming to have received from God priests greater in authority, more illustrious in birth, or more distinguished in holiness. Hence certain bishops of Metz, honoured beyond the ordinary rank of bishops, often received from the Apostolic See such a privilege, whether for the grace of holiness or [Col. 0703A] the glory of noble birth, that, while retaining subjection to their metropolitan, they exercised the office and honour of archbishop.

The first among these was the ancient Urbicius; much later, Chrodegang, nephew of King Pippin through his sister; after him Angilram; and another Drogo, son of Emperor Charlemagne. Walo also, a man of great reverence in Christ, deserved the use of the pallium by decree of Pope John; Robert after him likewise received the insignia of an archbishop.

Yet all these, providing for their individual dignity rather than for the common honour of their mother Church, could each be adorned with this privilege only during his lifetime. But our men, Deoderic and Adelbero, laid up this prerogative of honour not merely for themselves in the present, but forever for the descendants and sons of their mother Church. They received it not temporarily or from a desire for ostentatious eminence, but wishing through it to admonish themselves and their successors that, the more eminent they appeared above others, the more ardently they should devote themselves to doctrine and truth, taking heed to themselves and to the flock.

Let no one interpret malignantly our ascribing to our Deoderic what was confirmed by Adelbero; rather, let him observe in the former the beginning of the cause and in the latter its effect. Having said these things in part by anticipation, [Note: [Col. 0703] That is, “by prolepsis.”] let us gird ourselves for the work we have begun.

### 11. On the immunity of the ecclesiastical households

Our shepherd, called good, imitating the footsteps of that Shepherd who is good in essence, did not sit over the sheepfold like a hireling, who flees and leaves the sheep open to attack by their enemies; but, standing by his own on every side, an untiring defender, he protected them from the assaults of visible and invisible foes, so that, when the Prince of Shepherds should appear, he might receive the unfading crown of glory. For he feared—as no deaf hearer—the voice of the supreme Shepherd, who through Ezekiel (ch. 34, vv. 4–6) threatens wrath and judgment against shepherds who feed themselves rather than the Lord’s flock; who rule them with harshness and power; who abuse the prosperity of the rich; who despise the weakness of the exiled; and who through their negligence allow the flock to go into dispersion or become food for the beasts of the field.

Therefore unceasing concern troubled him even for the lay households of his mother, the holy Church; and against the insolence of the proud or the injustice of the wicked he laboured justly and powerfully to defend them continually, lest the prophetic saying be applied to him: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56:10). Nor did it suffice for his good will merely to assist them for the present, unless he also provided for them and for their descendants in the future. Accordingly, lest they lack against the iniquity of judges the authoritative support of ecclesiastical liberty, he carefully sought out the laws established for them by earlier kings or pontiffs; he recited those which he had found in the emperor’s presence; and he caused those which had been recited to be confirmed by an imperial edict and, moreover, strengthened by a written instrument and the impression of the royal seal.

### 12. On the construction of the castle or monastery of Spinal

[Note: Epinal.]

This husbandman of the Lord, not idly concerned for the vineyard which the master of the house had entrusted to him, diligently pruned it, cultivated it with the hoe, enriched it with the manure of the word, and finally supplied in due season whatever the needs of cultivation required, awaiting the denarius agreed upon with the Lord. And because, according to the Apostle (2 Tim. 2:6), “the labouring husbandman must be the first to receive of the fruits,” and because many evidences of his diligence are available, it does not seem to us that the following should be counted among the least of his deeds.

In the district of Calvomont, in the diocese of Toul, in a village called Spinal by an accidental usage of the rustic tongue, he built a castle [Note: manuscript *c*: *estruxit*.], which he richly furnished with buildings and necessities, adequately fortified with defenses, and sufficiently supplied with arms and armed men. For that region was harassed by sudden and continual raids of plunderers and by the unbearable ambushes of brigands; and especially calamitous was the proximity of the Burgundians. Against these dangers he set it up as a most secure barrier and an impregnable bulwark of the country.

Yet he did not assign the care of souls a secondary place. Seeing that the site was suited to the services of the divine household, he also built there, in honour of the most high God, a monastery, assigning adequate estates and whatever necessities were required by those serving God there. Moreover, under the inspiration of the Angel of Great Counsel, he removed to that place the body of the most holy Goeric, confessor of Christ and bishop of Metz, from the church of Saint Symphorianus, which lies in the suburb of Metz, with the greatest chanting of psalms and worthy rejoicing of clergy and people, so that strangers and natives alike might have a faithful protector, through whose intervention they might commend their vows and prayers to the ears of the Almighty.

And, so that the place might be held in greater distinction and that provisions might be supplied from every direction to townspeople and inhabitants, he established the striking of coin there and the holding of a public market. He did not omit to sanction this also by imperial decree and seal. Thus he solemnly distinguished that place, as may still be seen today. Hence even now its countrymen, having experienced the aid of the holy confessor’s presence in times of need, bless God through him with greater reverence and praise more earnestly the pious industry of their provider, Theoderic.

### 13. On the laying of the foundations of the basilica of Saint Vincent

As good fortunes succeeded one another and God’s grace heaped joy upon joy, Emperor Otto, returning for the second time to Italy, caused his son, bearing his own name—a youth of good disposition, answering his father’s virtues—to be made co-emperor with him. The son had long since been anointed king at Aachen. Otto assigned him a share in the imperial authority, while he himself, yielding to old age, might pass the remainder of his life more peacefully.

We suppose that this occurred in the year of the Lord 968 [967, 25 December], in which year, as we have learned from the writing of our elders, the foundations of the church of Saint Vincent were also laid. And lest anyone disparage my words, I gladly insert here the very words of the elders, few though they are:

> In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 968, while Lord Theoderic, bishop, was adorning this holy see with the imperial greatness of his blood, with strength of mind and a singular industry in every kind of learning and noble action, divine and human, public and private, most successfully and with the utmost resources and magnificence; while the most holy, inseparable company of the emperors—the Italian expedition of Otto and his most glorious namesake, worthily answering his father’s virtues—and the august Empress Adelaide, the ornament of the Empire in most splendid dignity, were engaged there for almost three years: the foundations of this entire holy structure were newly laid with expenditures worthy of it and with ample resources.

### 14. On immunity for the place obtained from the Apostolic See

The emperor, moreover, providing for the continued propagation of his bloodline, betrothed to his son Theophanu, daughter of the emperor of Constantinople, and celebrated her marriage at Rome with imperial magnificence (A.D. 972, 14 April). In this expedition and in the arrangement of these affairs, the venerable bishop Theoderic, as we have stated, held a foremost and especially prominent place. Since he yielded to no one in birth, dignity, or favour, and since he was a weighty adviser in counsel, he held a rank inferior to none before the emperors and the lord apostolic.

Although occupied on all sides with imperial and ecclesiastical business, he nevertheless returned day and night in mind to his special desire, namely the construction of the church of Saint Vincent. He had entrusted its construction to Odilbert, abbot of Gorze [Note: Odilbert did not succeed Abbot John until A.D. 974], a man most dear to him and renowned in every respect for divine and human learning. Meanwhile, like a most prudent bee [Note: *apes*, corrected to *apis* in manuscript *c*], he gathered industriously from every quarter what might fill his hives, store up flowing honey, and expand the cells with liquid nectar, in which he might rear the grown offspring, the hope of the holy race.

And, in order to keep idle cattle from the feeding-troughs, he first obtained from John, bishop of the Apostolic See, immunity for that place (A.D. 970). He committed that place and everything he had bestowed upon it to the lock of apostolic protection, and marked it with the key of an indissoluble anathema, so that, if the monstrous obstinacy of anyone’s callous breast should block it [Note: manuscript *c*: *obtutaret*; L: *obturaret*, “should shut/block”], so that even this apostolic immunity would not restrain him from violence or injustice against the holy Church, all impunity thereafter might be denied him. Thus this man beloved of God, while wishing to be more secure concerning his own people and to appear victorious in his purpose, seemed perhaps, if I may say so without offense to him, somewhat severe.

Let us therefore place before our eyes the privilege of apostolic authority, which, as it is the safeguard of our possessions, may likewise be the proof of our words.

> John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most beloved son Theoderic, bishop of the holy church of Metz.
>
> Since the due concern of pastoral solicitude compels us, in setting forth the praises of God, to promulgate abundantly those things which are known to pertain to the stability of pious places, and to confirm them by the authority of apostolic institution in privileges and decrees: it is fitting that we, by apostolic governance, suitably order holy and venerable places which formerly lay in ruins and lived in great want and poverty, or undoubtedly bring them into a better condition—especially where things are requested which concern not temporal advantage, but the perpetual provision for the souls of those who serve God.
>
> Thus the venerable place, gathered together and joined into one by our most beloved son Theoderic, with its proper communities, which according to rule keep watchful vigils for God our Saviour Jesus Christ in psalms, hymns, and prayers, may continually be protected from outward assaults and be able to perform the offices of pious service in the monastery of Saint Vincent. And since your religious devotion is known to seek from us the apostolic confirmation of this privilege, because of the changes of temporal affairs and the various chances of humankind, we have judged that the fortification of Saint Vincent, martyr of Christ, with all things belonging to that monastery, should be confirmed, and that you, your community, and your successors should be strengthened in perpetuity [Note: “in perpetuity,” added by a second hand].
>
> Thus, as these matters are now arranged by you, so they may be preserved henceforth unto the end; so that the community, remaining firmly joined in one, may be able to render diligent praises to God, may be permitted to persevere continually as its observances have been inspired by God, and, established under one abbot, the aforesaid place may remain undivided in honour of Saint Vincent, as may the community itself.
>
> Nor shall anyone be allowed, fleeing the discipline of the rule diligently imposed upon him, to wander here and there or seek transfer to other monasteries [Note: corrected reading: *aliis se conferre*, “to transfer himself to others”; manuscript *c*: *aliis reconferre*]. We prohibit this, contrary to the rule, under the bond of anathema.
>
> Therefore, establishing and promulgating before God and His terrible future judgment, through the document of this our apostolic privilege and decree, we ordain, decree by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and solemnly charge both future pontiffs of the Apostolic See and those who administer episcopal office, as well as persons great or small, or anyone endowed with power of whatever rank: let no one in any manner have license to disjoin or alienate anything from the often-named place of Saint Vincent, united into one and spiritually joined by the writing of apostolic authority, from those things piously handed over and granted to the venerable place by our aforesaid beloved son Theoderic.
>
> We command that the monastery of Saint Vincent shall look to the episcopal see of Stephen, the first martyr of Christ; and that the abbot of that place shall be elected under the authority of its bishop [Note: added by a second hand]. If, however, the bishop is absent, the abbot may on feast days come to the episcopal see and there celebrate Mass wearing the dalmatic and sandals which we send him.
>
> But if anyone—which we do not believe—should rashly attempt to oppose what has been piously and firmly established by this our authority through this privilege; or should presume to resist, take away, or alienate those things established by our aforesaid beloved son Theoderic, bishop of Metz, for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Vincent: let him know that by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he is bound by the bond of anathema and is to be burned in the punishment of eternal fire with Judas, betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ. So condemned, may he never be absolved from the bonds of the aforesaid anathema.
>
> But whoever, with pious intention, proves an observer of these things in all respects, may he receive in manifold measure the grace of blessing from our most merciful Lord God, become a sharer in eternal life, and may this chain of blessed Peter open to him the gate of paradise. But if any bishop should wish to diminish anything therefrom, may this chain, as we have said, close against him the kingdoms of heaven.
>
> Written by the hand of Stephen, notary and *regionarius* of the holy Roman Church, in the month of September, in the fourteenth indiction. Fare well.

[Note: All chronological indications agree.]

Given on the third day before the Kalends of October [29 September], by the hand of Guy, bishop and librarian [Note: manuscript *c*: *bibliotecharius*] of the holy Apostolic See, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord John, supreme and universal pontiff, the thirteenth of that name, presiding [Note: manuscript *c*: *PR.*] in the most sacred see of blessed Peter the Apostle; in the ninth year of the empire of Lord Otto the Elder, and the third of Otto the Younger; and finally in the year 970 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

### Letter of the same bishop Theoderic concerning the giving of tithes to the church of the same holy martyr

Theoderic, bishop in office and name, though unworthy, servant of the servants of Christ, together with the entire household of Saint Vincent, to the Christians of our churches: the joys of this present life and the abiding rewards of eternity.

To poor, richer, and moderately prosperous persons who strive, each according to his ability, to render to God without any withholding the tithes appointed from their possessions—namely, from the first fruits of sheep, from flax and wool, wine and grain, or from whatever other things not set forth here—we make known that they should rejoice, and that they shall obtain the gift of divine grace which the Apostle Paul declares is granted to the willing dispensers of their goods, saying: “For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7).

Let them know also that in this present life they will obtain blessing and an abundance of temporal goods for this very reason, provided that they persevere in this kindly disposition; and they will be filled with that good of peace which the angels, announcing the Lord’s birth to the shepherds of the flocks, assigned only to people of good will. But those who delay in paying the tithes owed to God and strive through the malicious faithlessness of obstinacy to defraud Him must fear the judgment of dreadful condemnation which the same Apostle terribly threatens against them and their followers, declaring that neither thieves nor the rapacious shall possess the kingdom of God.

### 15. On the ninths and tithes of the church of Saint Vincent, levite and martyr

Having considered this sequence of events and agreement of writings, let anyone look more carefully and observe how this man, wholly “smooth and rounded” in himself (Horace, *Satires* II.7.86), left praiseworthy memorials of his diligence in every direction and in every matter. It is known even to the simple and unlearned, from both the Old and New Law, that tithes of possessions are owed to God and to God’s ministers, and that by synodal enactment they are called God’s due.

Therefore he, whose desire it was that “the lines of an unfailing inheritance should fall to him in pleasant places,” wished that the Lord’s portion of the inheritance should be defrauded in nothing. Accordingly, by synodal authority and episcopal censure, he withdrew from lay persons—to whom his predecessors had assigned them in place of stipend or benefice—the tithes of the churches of his diocese, although they resisted and protested. And, according to the written saying, “Those who serve at the altar should live by the altar,” he assigned the property of the churches to church officials, being careful to render to God what was God’s and to Caesar what was Caesar’s.

Hence today the holy churches of God rejoice, especially those whose restoration he had undertaken, namely those of Saint Vincent the martyr and Saint Goeric the confessor. Because this seemed to him a common obligation shared with others, he also desired to do something beyond what was required, so that, when that true Samaritan came, he might receive, in addition to the two denarii of the twofold love, the unfading crown of glory.

He withdrew from their own uses the ninths of all revenues of the bishopric belonging to the lordly estate, together with one *mansus* in every court, and added them to the church of his pious patron Vincent. And, knowing that another’s foundation was often either undermined or neglected by successors, he forbade any of his successors to render void this decree of his generosity, under an indissoluble anathema, adding an imperial sanction and, moreover, the curse of apostolic excommunication.

### 16. On his eagerness in seeking relics of the saints

This scribe learned in the kingdom of heaven—that is, in the holy Church—was like the householder bringing forth from his treasure things new and old. He considered that God is not greatly pleased by dwellings made by hands, but rather by what is spiritually done within them. As the outstanding preacher of truth says: “You know, brethren, that you are the temple of God and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you. But if anyone violates this temple, the Lord will destroy him; for the temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3:16–18).

For what are the beauty of walls, the gleam of metals, the brilliance of gems, and the splendour of precious vestments, except allegorical ornaments of diverse virtues? Understanding, I say, that the purity of the inward person is more to be desired than the superficial attractiveness of outward beauty, the man of God strove in this matter also to bring his work to perfection. Anyone may readily perceive this from this fact alone, if he considers how earnestly he sought to gather together in that place the pledges—that is, relics—of the saints, so that those dwelling there might be stirred to good conduct by their examples and [Note: the editor supplied *vocem*, “voice”] if they were worn down by any evils or dangers, might be defended by the saints’ present patronage.

Even in this matter scarcely anyone could adequately admire his praiseworthy life. For although he had merited from heaven so great a privilege of grace that those who had in any way offended the imperial majesty sought him alone as intercessor and mediator to appease the indignation of royal authority [Note: “to appease the indignation of royal authority,” added by a second hand], he expected no reciprocal temporal advantage from them for this service [Note: “Compare Thietmar III.9”]. The only riches he most eagerly sought from every quarter were those by which he might obtain bodies or relics of saints. This alone was the blameless desire that consumed his mind.

Therefore let the document be brought forward, fully composed by those who were present, concerning the translation of the saints:

[Note: In manuscript 3, where this history occurs on fols. 36–41, it bears the heading: “Discovery of saints found by Lord Bishop Theoderic.” It begins: “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation …”]

> In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 970, while the great and most glorious Caesar Augustus Otto, together with his namesake, his august son, a youth of admirable character, and likewise with his wife Adelaide [Note: manuscript 3: *Adelheide*], endowed with great virtues—than whom nothing could ever have been more just, gentle, prudent, or more pious—were peacefully and securely governing the sceptres of Italy with pious and just moderation as far as the borders of Calabria: Lord and venerable Theoderic, bishop of holy Metz [Note: manuscript 3: *Mettis*], bound to that magnificent emperor by blood, marvelous affection, and kinship [Note: manuscript 3: *familiaritate*, “familiar association”], and one by whose counsel, because of his extraordinary wisdom, all affairs of the palace were conducted, was present on that Italian expedition, in which he served for almost three years.
>
> While chiefly devoted to divine worship [Note: manuscript 3: *cultu*], he eagerly sought everything that might contribute to the honour, adornment [Note: manuscript 3: *decoremque*, “and adornment”], or defense of his holy see; and [Note: manuscript 3: *et*], since all things effectively answered his desires, with God’s grace assisting him he gathered an immense quantity of saints’ bodies from diverse places in Italy. He sought to bring them to his holy see of Metz [Note: manuscript 3: *sancte sedi metensi*], there to be venerated with fitting worship and with honour more splendid than elsewhere.

#### On Saint Elpidius

[Note: These headings are always absent in manuscript 3.]

The first of these was Saint Elpidius, the venerable confessor of Christ, whom he took from the province of the Marsi, with the consent of Alberic, bishop of that Marsian territory, from a church near the episcopal see. That see lies above Lake Fucinus [Note: manuscript 3: correct; manuscript *c*: *Sticinum*], and what it once was is attested by the ruins of the city and by the abundance of churches and monasteries around it.

The bishop himself and the other inhabitants told us that Elpidius belonged to a company [Note: manuscript 3: *collegio*, “college”] of servants of God who, at an earlier time, had come from Greece to the province of the Marsi, seventy in number. Shining in various places and cities all around with the radiance of venerable signs [Note: manuscript *c*: *universis mirabilium* (“of all miracles”); manuscript 3: *s.*; manuscript 3 also reads *fulgentes* for *refulgentes*], wherever the end of life had come to them in holy conduct, they were laid in venerable burial and are honoured far and wide by the reverence of their neighbours because of the continual delight of miracles.

Three of them, of whom Elpidius was the third, lay in the same cemetery: Calistratus, Eutychius, and Elpidius. Emperor Otto [Note: omitted in manuscript 3] had previously removed Eutychius. To prevent any deception in receiving Elpidius, the tomb was found intact and securely fortified, showing no signs of violation since the day of burial. Before any inhabitant could know beforehand what was occurring, and with only Bishop Alberic and a few of his clergy present, our priest Theudo [Note: manuscript *c*: *Leudo*; see below] and Heriward, the emperor’s priest, opened the saint’s coffin—which they could not do unless they first broke apart the altar above it. They themselves [Note: omitted in manuscript 3] received the sacred bones, of wonderful whiteness and no less fragrant odour [Note: manuscripts *c* and 3: *flagrantis*], all complete in number and quantity, and placed them in a shrine. We celebrate his feast on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October [16 September].

#### On Saints Eutyches, Victorinus, and Maro

Coming soon afterward into the territory of the city of Amiternum [Note: Amiterno], which itself now displays only ruins, he received from the same Bishop Alberic, from the monastery of Rieti subject to his jurisdiction, the precious martyr Eutyches [Note: manuscript 3: “most precious”]. In the preceding year he had obtained the relics of Eutyches’ blessed companion Victorinus, together with a portion of Saint Maro, who suffered with them [Note: manuscript 3: *simulque et*, “and likewise together with”]. We saw both the places of their martyrdom and the waters of Cotiliae [Note: manuscript 3: “the waters themselves”], breathing a foul smell, in which the martyr had been suspended upside down. Written accounts of their passion are preserved in the acts of Saints Nereus and Achilleus.

The venerable Lord Theoderic himself, present there, received Eutyches from his marble coffin, strongly secured, with wondrous exultation and veneration, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [24 September]. Adelard [Note: manuscript 3: *Adhelardus*], son of Gerard, carried these two saints to their homeland.

#### On Saint Felician, bishop and martyr

Felician protected the stronghold of Foligno [Note: Foligno], not far from Spoleto, with his sacred body, while a great multitude of people flocked there from every direction. Benedict, bishop of Foligno [Note: manuscript 3: *fuliniensis*], granted him [Note: manuscript *c*: *cum*] with much weeping; and on the fourth day before the Nones of October [4 October], Bertraus the deacon and Heriward the priest [Note: manuscript 1: *scilicet. est et per.*] raised him from his innermost tomb. His Passion has been written.

#### On Saint Asclepiotatus, martyr

In the wood called Collis [Note: manuscript 1: *sancto*, “holy”], adjoining the city of Perugia, where the emperor was then engaged in the autumn hunt, there stood a very ancient monastery above the River Tiber. Flowing there through a moderate ford, the river thereafter increases in the depth of its waters until it reaches the city of Rome. This monastery, once constructed, as was apparent, in handsome workmanship and marble ornament, but then ruined by age, held the venerably buried remains of the eminent martyr Asclepiotatus.
