When Theudo [Note: manuscript 3: *theudo*], Bertraus [Note: manuscript 3 omits *et*], Rotard, and Heriward [Note: manuscript 3 omits both occurrences of *et*] had at last, with great difficulty, penetrated his tomb, which was blocked by an exceedingly strong mass of stones and earth, and had uncovered the marble nearest the saint’s body [Note: manuscript *c*: *corpore* for *corpori*], they found a monument extending deep downwards [Note: manuscript 3: *profundo*, corrected from *profundum*] and naturally divided through the middle, from head to feet, by a sort of line in the very stone. On more careful inspection, however, it was shown to be one continuous whole.

One half of the blessed body lay on one side and one half on the other, with the limbs arranged opposite one another from side to side, except for the head alone, which lay carefully placed whole on one side [Note: manuscript 3: *integram*]. The sacristan and the others said that antiquity [Note: manuscript *c*: *antiquitate*] had intended by this sign to indicate what they themselves firmly asserted: that the martyr had been cut alive through the middle of his body by a cruel form of martyrdom, and had therefore been placed divided within a divided tomb [Note: manuscript *c*: *attestante* for *attestandae*].

The venerable bishop received him, when he had been removed with the honour fitting to him, on the seventh day before the Ides of October [9 October; Note: manuscript 3 reads “Kalends”]. We learned from the inhabitants that his feast day [Note: added by a second hand] was the ninth day before the Kalends of November [24 October]. For we were entirely unable to obtain his acts from the bishop of Sisa [Note: perhaps Assisi?], to whose jurisdiction the place belonged.

#### On Saint Serena and Gregory of Spoleto

The most holy virgin Serena lay at Spoleto, in the monastery of Saint Savinus the martyr outside the city walls, where she also shone through many miracles. An immense crowd of people came to her almost daily, so that watchful throngs also spent the nights there with lamps and other offerings. The venerable bishop obtained her too, with all her bones intact throughout her body, having sent there the deacon Rothard with other men faithful to him. He also obtained there the relics of the blessed martyr Gregory of Spoleto. His Passion has been written.

Besides what we found in the Passion of Saint Savinus—that Serena herself buried the blessed martyr—we could discover nothing further concerning her deeds. Yet she commends herself by such continual signs of power that, with the living reading of these signs placed before one’s eyes, she needs no attestation of her deeds in order to show what she was in life. Her feast is celebrated on the tenth day before the Kalends of December [22 November], the same day as that of Saint Savinus the martyr.

#### On the chain of Saint Peter the Apostle

Meanwhile, after sending the aforesaid deacon Rothard to Rome, Theoderic obtained, as a gift from Pope John, thirteenth of that name, no small portion of the chain of blessed Peter. The pope cut off that portion from the chain in the basilica called *ad Vincula* [Note: Saint Peter in Chains]. With it the same lord pope sent the privilege of the monastery of Saint Vincent, together with the dalmatic and sandals [Note: manuscript 3: *scandaliis*] granted by apostolic prerogative to the abbot of that place. Adelbert the cleric and Count Cono brought all these things.

It has not seemed tiresome to insert in this account how the occasion of so memorable a gift came about. One day, while Emperor Otto was in Rome, the devil attacked one of his counts, a man very close to him; and, before everyone’s eyes, the possessed man pitifully tore himself apart. When the king heard this, he was deeply grieved and devoted himself to this one remedy: that the man should be brought to Lord Pope John, who was then distinguished by the apostolic office. For at that time the emperor was, by chance, kept a little apart by civic concerns.

When the demoniac was brought into the pope’s presence, the Roman clerics—since it was always their custom to mock simple people concerning the request for the chain—offered a certain piece of iron chain to be bound about the raving man. Though the pope objected that the lord emperor should not be mocked, they offered another; until, stirred by the third deception, the lord pope commanded that the true chain of Saint Peter be brought.

The bishop of Metz, Theoderic, and the aforesaid Rothard were present among the venerable men sent by the king to witness this spectacle, awaiting its outcome. As soon as the chain touched the demoniac’s neck, the invading spirit departed at once, foaming and crying out loudly. When Lord Theoderic of Metz saw this, he seized the chain and wrapped it round his hand, saying that he would by no means release it unless his hand were cut off.

The lord emperor hurried to the dispute and began eagerly to investigate what this great commotion meant. When it had been explained to him and the bishop answered with the words already stated, the king himself turned petitioner and urgently asked that it be done. The pope most willingly consented, although a great part of the order of the Roman Church strongly opposed it; and, when a saw had been brought, the guardian cut it off. Because of the intervention required by another affair, the pope commended that portion to the man most dearly loved by both parties [Note: L: *alius*, “another”; manuscript *c*: *aliis*].

Later, after Deacon Rothard had been sent, he carried it away from the church called *ad Vincula*, where this had occurred, with the lord pope’s consent. Moreover, healing comes to the sick if anyone who deserves it touches it in faith at Saint Vincent’s, where it is deposited and venerated by the people.

#### On Saint Vincent, levite

Bertraus the deacon removed the blessed martyr and levite Vincent [Note: manuscript 3: *m. magnum et l.*], though with great difficulty and no small danger to his life, from a nearby monastery of considerable beauty in a most ancient city called Corduno [Note: Cortona], which had long been destroyed to its very foundations and lies twelve miles from Arezzo [Note: manuscript 3: *aretio*]. A cleric of the bishop of Arezzo, named Crisulfus [Note: manuscript 3: *ei* for *cui*], who knew the place, accompanied him. They firmly maintained that Vincent had been brought from Spain into Italy [Note: manuscript *c*: *italia*].

We learned the fuller manner of his translation later, when the lord bishop came to Benevento, having been sent to meet the imperial daughter-in-law arriving from Greece. Near Capua we found an almost ruined monastery named Saint Vincent’s [Note: Saint Vincent at Volturno]. The few old monks then seen there [Note: manuscript 3: *veteratini* for *veterani*] said that it had formerly been built in grand and remarkable workmanship by three noble brothers; that the body of Saint Vincent had later been secretly brought there from Spain by two monks; and that it had thereafter been held in the highest veneration for many years, until pagans devastated that monastery and the holy body was removed from there and transferred to the aforesaid city of Corduno.

At that time the bishop of Arezzo [Note: manuscript 3: *aretinus*] also gave—not without reluctance, and while he and all his property were placed in the utmost danger before the emperor—a considerable portion of the blood of the most blessed proto-martyr Stephen, in a crystal vessel excellently adorned with gold and gems; some of the blood of the Innocents in another casket; and hair of Saint Peter, with little written labels attached to each. Because his resources for securing his own ransom pressed hard upon him, he thereby made our venerable bishop his advocate [Note: manuscript 3: *sui* for *suum*], both through these gifts and through the body of Saint Vincent; and thus, through the bishop’s intervention, he scarcely returned to the emperor’s favour.

Several Italian bishops had often previously attempted to obtain this same blessed martyr, among them Ambrose of Bergamo, because the see of his bishopric was dedicated in honour of Saint Vincent. A short time earlier he had fixed, with such people as he could gather, the day on which he was to receive him. But by the Lord’s ordering, on the preceding night—the day before the one he had appointed—the saint was forestalled by our people. Clerics of the Mount of Remiremont [Note: Remiremont] carried this relic.

#### On Saints Protus and Hyacinthus

In the Sabine region, not far from the city of Rome, about forty miles away [Note: manuscript *c* and manuscript 3: “fortieth”], the holy martyrs Protus and Hyacinthus were kept under somewhat negligent guard. A certain abbot from the monastery of Saint Mary called Farfa [Note: Farfa], while asking our venerable bishop to intercede for his cause before the emperor, first offered him a portion of them. For he had learned that no gift delighted the bishop so greatly. But later, at the lord bishop’s remarkable insistence, he added whatever he could find of them, himself taking an oath with his monks upon the holy Gospels that these were truly the bones of Saints Protus and Hyacinthus. This was done after Christmas, as we were returning from Rome, in the vicinity of the city of Orta [Note: Orta].

[Col. 0714B] On Saints Digna and Emerita [Note: [Col. 0713] Emerentia?]. While we were then staying at Rome, by the gift of Lord Pope John he received the relics of the holy women Digna and Emerita, whose bodies are laid in the portico of the church of the blessed martyr Marcellus, which stands before [the church of] the holy Apostles; together with other relics of various saints, separately deposited and accompanied by their own labels, among them a sandal of Saint Stephen. All these were sent through Willard, monk of the monastery of Maur [Note: [Col. 0714D] Marmoutier in Alsace.].

On Saint Vincent the bishop. He obtained another Saint Vincent, a bishop, from a certain monastery in the district of Urbino, about fifty miles from Ravenna, near Pietra Pertusa [Note: [Col. 0714D] On the Metaurus River, south of Urbino.]. Its abbot was greatly reduced in the necessities of life and, having nothing else to give for the relief [Note: [Col. 0713] Thus I print it; the manuscript has “revelation.”] of the place, first offered a portion. But when Bertrao had been sent there and had acted vigorously with much skill [Note: [Col. 0713] Thus manuscript 3; manuscript *e* has “with much fortress.”], he obtained it. We have described this saint’s Passion. He was sent through Count Immo.

On Saints Leontius and Carpophorus. The city of Vicenza lies not far from Venice; the Lombards are said first to have come there among the cities when they invaded Italy. In it the martyr Leontius was venerated in a famous monastery. The bishop of that place promised our most reverend prelate his relics, if he would intercede with the imperial majesty concerning his case. Rothard the deacon was promptly sent there; and when the bishop made himself exceedingly difficult about giving more than he had promised, he was at last overcome by the unremitting insistence of the petitioner [Note: [Col. 0713] Manuscript *c* has “continuous.”]. Retaining only a few relics for himself, he bestowed the entire remainder of the body.

The inhabitants affirmed that he and blessed Carpophorus suffered at Rome, and had been translated from that city not long before. There, too, had once stood the distinguished monastery of Saint Felix, where they were said first to have been deposited. But after it had been burned by the Hungarians, who are almost neighbors of those very regions, and because their continual raids prevented its restoration, they were placed beneath an altar at the episcopal see within the city [Note: [Col. 0715] Omitted in manuscript 3.]. Accordingly the aforementioned Deacon Rothard took the whole of Saint Leontius and no small relics of Saint Carpophorus from the very altar-enclosed tomb, after breaking open the altar. They said that the account of their Passion had perished in a fire. Their feast is celebrated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August [20 July]. Teudo conveyed them.

On Saint Lucy, virgin and martyr. How Lucy of Syracuse, the virgin and martyr renowned in the great and universal celebration of the Church, came in due order to the most eager devotion of our most religious [Note: [Col. 0715] Manuscript *c*: *reliogiossimi*.] prelate, Wigeric our priest can adequately explain. At that time he performed the office of cantor, now that of keeper of Saint Stephen; he himself lifted those sacred bones with his hands from the urn in which they were enclosed by no slight protection, and he is known to be wholly trustworthy. She rested at Corfinium [Note: [Col. 0715] Manuscript 3: *confinio*.], once an ancient city, now entirely ruined. It was reliably affirmed to us that she had been translated there from Sicily by a certain Faroald, duke of Spoleto. The bishop of the place himself, placing his hand upon the holy Gospel, confirmed that this was that same Syracusan Lucy concerning whom responsories and antiphons are sung everywhere together with the Mass. [Note: [Col. 0715] Manuscript 3: “the bishop himself also.”]

On the gridiron of Saint Lawrence. When, after the royal wedding had there been celebrated with great magnificence, we were arranging our return home from Rome, the lord pope enriched the venerable prelate with a final benefit, more abundant than many others: four portions of the gridiron of Saint Lawrence. Wigeric and the monk John struck these off from the sacred gridiron itself. They were the ends of the bars which lay crosswise, fixed into the outer ribs. For all six bars which it had possessed had long before been bestowed by various popes as gifts upon various kings; of these, one, which remained until a few years ago, was granted by Octavian to the great Emperor Otto. When these pieces were struck off [Note: [Col. 0715] Manuscript 3: “were struck off.”], the ribs remained closer together, while the ends on the inside, which were firmly held below, remained in place. Yet they were detached, though with laborious effort, by applying iron and striking with the hand.

We have received this account of the translation of the saints from our elders. But why they made no mention of Saint Fortunatus, bishop of the city of Todi—of whom Gregory included a memorable account in his *Dialogues*—nor of the martyr Minias, causes no slight disturbance to our minds. For we truly believe that their bodies also were translated from Italy to us by him. We read that Minias was brought to us with Protus, Hyacinthus, and Bishop Vincent on the sixth day before the Nones of July [2 July]. The truth of the matter itself also shows that the relics of Fidentius and Terentius, together with Vincent the martyr and levite, Felician, Eutices, Elpidius, Asclepiota, and the chain of Saint Peter, were sent to us by him on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May [14 April]. He also described their Passions and noted the day of their martyrdom or burial: Fortunatus’s, the third day before the Kalends of July [29 June]; Minias’s, the eighth day before the Kalends of November [25 October]; and those others’, the fifth day before the Kalends of October [27 September].

This diligent lover of saints also translated relics of Quintianus, priest and martyr, from the Campanian city of Alatri [Note: [Col. 0715D] Alatri.], and of Florentius, martyr, from the fortress of Thiel [Note: [Col. 0716D] Thiel on the Meuse.]. He did not bring accounts of their Passions, but reported only the day of martyrdom: Quintianus’s, the third day before the Nones of July [5 July]; the other’s, the sixth day before the Kalends of November [27 October].

17. Praise of the city of Metz [Note: [Col. 0715] Manuscript *c*: “of the city.”]. Thanks be to you, holy and indivisible Trinity, who, pouring out everywhere upon earth the immeasurable riches of your mercy, have most abundantly prepared incomparable delights for this city. Individual cities rejoice in the particular guardians of their salvation divinely bestowed upon them; and those whose glorious confessions they remember as having made them illustrious, they believe assist them by their pious intercessions. Some cities are also adorned by the glorious victory of martyrs; yet there the voice of their blood, shed upon the earth as testimony to the truth, still cries to God from the ground, demands vengeance, and, held in suspense by the promise of the divine response, awaits the completion of the number of their brethren.

This city too received prophets, wise men, and scribes sent to it; quickly recognizing the time of its visitation and eagerly embracing the light of a new radiance, it drove from itself the darkness of inveterate error. And since no righteous blood is to come upon it—since it has never devoted itself or its children to anyone’s blood—it nevertheless possesses glorious martyrs present with it, to whom it may commend itself and its children. Since, I say, no blood is required from this generation, it glories in reverently preserving the bodies or relics of holy martyrs.

Therefore I would call the holy church of Metz truly blessed: having received from God the earnest of faith, it rejoices that through faithful stewards the measure of its spiritual dowry is increased a hundredfold. Rejoice therefore, fortunate city of the Mediomatrici! Again and again reflect what you owe to so great a man—I mean Theoderic—through whose pious zeal you have received the relics of so many saints, besides the patronage of your native saints. Enriched by him beyond the abundance in which you uniquely flourish by nature, you have raised your head among other cities.

Even the etymology of your name, Mediomatricis, accords with the grace of your good fortune. As a womb embraces and cherishes a child in a mother’s belly, so you, situated in the midst and sustaining the surrounding regions, cherish them in a manner with a motherly bosom through merchandise native or imported [Note: [Col. 0715] Manuscript *c*: “importation.”]. Moreover, that you are called Metz is popularly said to derive from your having been ruled by Mettius Suffectus, a Roman commander. Hence someone says:

> Another Sigibert ruled the south with the sceptre;  
> Mettius Suffectus gave his name to the city.

Others relate that this distich was found inscribed thus on stones dug from the earth:

> At the time when Caesar brought his arms against the Gauls,  
> then Mettius overcame the city of the Mediomatrici.

Nor should you think it happened without some presage that antiquity records you as having been called Divodunum in addition to these customary names. For that *dunum* means “mountain” in the Gallic language is well known to scholars. One who interpreted from the *Neoterics* why the city of the Aedui is called Augustodunum says among other things:

> Thereafter it wished and began to be called Celtic Rome,  
> and finally, having been conceived, to be called Augustodunum,  
> because the Celtic language renders this “Augustus’s mountain.”

Therefore, just as Augustodunum is named “Augustus’s mountain,” and Viridunum “the mountain of men,” so you acquired the name Divodunum, as it were “mountain of the gods.” This was not only because of the merited grace of your inhabitants, whom pagan superstition considered worthy of that name, but also because, as we have said, you were prophetically foreshadowed as destined to become the host of so many saints. Nor is it foreign to the rectitude of faith for saints to be designated by the name “gods,” since much Scripture—and above all God of gods in the Gospel—declares that those to whom the word of God came are called gods.

Let us leave controversy over the name to others. But since we often tread the middle way through the city, we would be ungrateful if we left it without greeting; and therefore we delight to linger briefly in its praise.

> Hail, renowned city; hail, most noble land,  
> City most populous, land most fertile in fields.  
> Flowing with honey and milk, abounding in bread with wine,  
> Overflowing in wares, rich in gold and gems.  
> Golden Pactolus yields to you, sweet Hymettus too,  
> And the Italian land, three-cornered Sicily, and Africa. [Note: [Col. 0717D] Italy, Sicily, Africa.]  
> If I look around, I see nothing not worthy of praise.  
> I praise the massive wall built of squared stone,  
> Not easily broken down, not to be stormed by an enemy.  
> For a slope protects the wall, rivers protect the slope;  
> Thus secure without, within it is strengthened by the power of its rampart.  
> Where nature fails, strength, human hand, and skill provide support.  
> Measuring its breadth, you marvel at its increasing length.  
> Looking up at its towers, I imagine Babylon’s citadels.  
> Ram, tortoise, great bow [Note: [Col. 0718D] A great bow.], siege-shed, and sickles  
> Shall never batter them even vainly, nor shall hostile flame consume them.  
> When I see its houses, I think them Roman palaces.  
> When I seek its theatre, I think it Daedalus’s labyrinth.  
> And if you consider the beauty of its site, what anywhere is fairer?  
> Its position measured according to its natural character,  
> It pleases in beauty of appearance, yet is fairer in usefulness by nature.  
> Set upon a modest hill, fortified by a double stream,  
> Its rivers give a murmur; they give strength to its defenses.  
> Behold its four quarters through its four gates:  
> East, west, south, and north.  
> Whoever sees its churches judges them heavenly halls.  
> When I seek the chief sanctuary of Stephen, the first martyr,  
> and see the clergy, I seem to myself to ascend to heaven  
> and to hear heavenly choirs sweetly singing hymns.  
> And to you, Savior, I give thanks that new walls have arisen—  
> the pillar of the fatherland, the visible summit of life—  
> which pious Adalbero built, its entire glory in his age.  
> The Lamb of the Virgin, the Sheep, and Spouse of virginity  
> establishes virgin bridal chambers, threefold in the threefold Name,  
> in the midst of the walls of this city for himself.  
> The virgin Mother of God becomes the diligent bridal attendant of her Son;  
> the heavenly key-bearer likewise becomes God’s best man.  
> Worthy of the virgin bridal chamber of her heavenly Spouse,  
> the virgin Glodesindis sings wedding songs for the royal bridegroom,  
> a ewe leading [Note: [Col. 0718D] *Minare* means “to lead,” French *mener*.] ewes to be driven into the sheepfold of salvation.  
> Moreover Felix, blessed in deeds and in name,  
> protects the long boundaries of the great city  
> together with pious Clement, the first bishop of Metz.  
> With them, gracious Symphorianus, you share the watches.  
> John, borne aloft on the wings of virginity,  
> lovingly embraces holy Arnulf in his bosom;  
> between them he stands, conspicuous to be seen from the city,  
> and flying on high draws behind him a train from below.  
> O Vincent, the island has been granted to you by Christ’s gift;  
> here your lofty dwelling rises through Theoderic’s zeal.  
> Nor has Martin’s guardianship been lacking to the city:  
> he stands farther away, yet watches all things close at hand.  
> It would be shameful here to mention you only briefly, mother Gorze.  
> I marvel that aqueducts have gone six miles by arches;  
> Gorze, the daughter, visits her mother Metz.  
> Neither high mountains nor deep valleys,  
> nor even the force of the intervening Moselle  
> impeded its course: what have I ever seen more laboriously wrought?  
> Art sent waters which nature had denied you,  
> until age alone at last broke the long course.  
> Even its ruins preserve the praise of the construction.  
> I pass over very much; I leave aside what is far away.  
> Who could describe the waters? Who the springs, or the saltworks?  
> Shall I be silent about the Seille? I am reminded to mention the Moselle:  
> from springs in diverse and distant regions  
> it runs through long stretches to yield you its fruits;  
> embracing your walls on alternate banks,  
> and at last mingling kisses with joined lips,  
> it gives beauty and fruit, affords defense and usefulness.  
> Usefulness feeds the belly, beauty the mind, sound the ear.  
> What water-organs modulate so sweet a voice?  
> Wherever the horizon permits the eye to range,  
> you see nothing but what is delightful, nothing but what is pleasing.  
> Who could fail to marvel at the mountain that overhangs the city  
> on several sides? It is most pleasing to the eye, rich in fertility;  
> nature has nursed it from her full breast.  
> Few mountains receive such favor from nature.  
> All the hills rise with sloping summit.  
> You see hills crowned with vines and valleys drowned in them.  
> Meadows grow green, woods leaf out, the field ripples [Note: [Col. 0719D] With ears of grain stirred by the wind. Leibnitz.].  
> If you seek pastures, roam through every plain.  
> How variously the birds sing again; how the swarms play!  
> Few experience a better temperateness of sky.  
> Whom would the charm of so many things not delight?  
> That pleasing delight even nourishes the country folk themselves,  
> and while the bounty of the land answers their greedy wishes,  
> they console their hated labor with love of repose.  
> One prunes vines, another digs, another marries them [to supporting trees];  
> one shades springs, another plants mountains with trees.  
> One diverts streams, another enriches fields with seed;  
> I fish with hooks, you with wicker traps, another with nets.  
> Who could recount the spectacles of so many things?  
> Homer himself, and another Homer [Note: [Col. 0719D] Virgil.], would be mute before them.  
> Many cities are rich through fortune’s gift;  
> nature’s abundance enriches you with a full horn.  
> Besides the goods of fortune, which it supplies abundantly,  
> neighboring cities yield to you in the honor due a mother:  
> the Vangiones, Leuci, Verdun, Liège [Note: [Col. 0720D] Liège.], Rheims,  
> and Trier, the mother, gladly rises in loving homage.  
> May he who reigns above all things forever preserve you.

[Col. 0719C] 18. On the dedication of two altars. While zeal for the begun construction was thus ardent, and the bishop of holy memory had returned through Christ’s favor from his long exile, two adjacent altars were dedicated in the same church in the year 972, with the reverend bishops Wigfrid of Verdun and Gerard of Toul present and assisting. One was dedicated in the presence and honor of Saint Lucy of Syracuse, the great martyr celebrated throughout the whole world; the other in the presence and honor of the martyrs Protus and Hyacinthus, equally renowned throughout the world. Their most sacred bodies were genuine—as surely as the faith of Christ is true—and no others. With the aid of the emperors themselves and by the authority of Lord Pope John, then reigning, he obtained them in those regions of Italy and, under the Lord’s favorable guidance, brought them here with many other bodies of holy martyrs, under a fortunate omen. The solemn days [Note: [Col. 0720D] That is, the feast days. Leibnitz.] of this dedication were the eighth day before the Ides of August [6 August], in the ninth year of his pontificate.

19. On the death of his kinsman Everard. But because the changing course of events does not permit the joy of shadowy prosperity to endure long, not long afterward a wound of bitter grief was renewed for him in his deep sorrow. He had a kinsman, the sweetness of his soul and image of piety, named Everard. With paternal affection he had undertaken to raise him from the cradle, to extend the hope of his posterity and enlarge the glory of his nobility. Alas, uncertain hope of the future! Alas, the ill-trustworthy fate of human affairs! He had scarcely crept from infancy into childhood; he had scarcely begun to display his ancestral grace of good character; it had scarcely become apparent what a great man he would be. And behold: as in early spring a tender little flower is suddenly scattered by the whirlwind, so this boy—O grief!—was snatched from the world by untimely death and filled all with no small mourning.

To comfort his miserable grief, his uncle held funeral rites that were not so much mournful as magnificent; he had the body borne with fitting honor to the monastery of Saint Vincent and buried it before the altar of Christ’s virgin Lucy. So that, for the purity of his innocent life, he might receive the golden rewards of everlasting life, he gave that place for the salvation of Everard’s soul a gold chalice of great weight and marvelous workmanship, interweaving the memory of himself and Everard in the same work in these letters: “Theoderic, builder and guardian of this holy shrine, for the soul of Everard, dear to him in life.” [Note: [Col. 0719] The codex divides the phrase not here but after *constructor*, “builder.”] And believing that the name of the one was inscribed in golden letters in the book of life [Note: [Col. 0719] The abbreviation “i. l. h. t. e. s. a.” was added by a second hand.], he added to his tomb an epitaph engraved in gold letters as follows:

> In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 978, Theoderic, humble bishop [Note: [Col. 0719] Manuscript *c*: “pious bishop.”], builder of this place from its very foundations, through pious zeal committed to stone, under the human lot, on the fourth day before the Nones of September [2 September], his kinsman Everard—his sole love for as long as he was permitted to live; illustrious through orthodox parents and royal blood; himself promising by the exceptional character of his childhood a gracious future; raised from the cradle with tender affection by Theoderic as the greatest hope of himself, his family, and his native land—cut down by the untimely scythe of death before he had completed ten years, a dear pledge mourned beyond measure by people and fathers.

ANOTHER EPITAPH.

> The death of the righteous is not harmful, but precious,  
> always possessing its day before God’s face.  
> That day is full, serene with shining sun:  
> it is a day without night and rest without end.  
> May Everard remain glad in this rest, sustained by the comfort of light,  
> so that he may be able to behold  
> the King who reigns, ruling the realms of those who reign—  
> Christ, whom he worshipped while he was able to live.  
> This distinguished boy, flourishing in life at ten years,  
> adorning all his pursuits with purity,  
> passed from the world on the second day of September’s sun.  
> Reader, say at last: “May he rest in peace.” Amen.

ANOTHER EPITAPH OF THE SAME COUNT EVERARD.

> In this tomb is enclosed a dove long without gall,  
> the child Everard, noble and pious,  
> nobly born of the blood of the illustrious  
> Bishop Theoderic, from whose brother he was born.  
> Tomorrow’s light of September was the last for these limbs.  
> O Christ [Note: [Col. 0721] Manuscript *c*: *Criste*.], grant him your rest and your day!

20. Renewed immunity of the church of Saint Vincent. After calming all disturbances throughout Gaul, Emperor Otto set out toward Italy in the year 980. At his side was not absent Bishop Theoderic, the honor of bishops: privy to all his counsels and partner in all his affairs, whom the reverence due to his twofold dignity made greater than, or equal to, all others. Yet no remoteness of lands separated him so far, no length of roads burdened him so heavily, no multitude of occupations troubled him so greatly, that he did not continually direct his mind to the honorable completion of the monastery of Saint Vincent, and that no other care pressed him more urgently.

Therefore it was not enough for him, ever intent upon good, that he had formerly secured that place and all entrusted to it firmly and lawfully by the authority and blessing of Pope John. He still strove by every means to forestall the injustice of wicked men who wrongfully appropriated the goods of others. Thus, prompted by the opportunity of place and time, in 981 he judged it worthwhile to renew the very privilege formerly written and sealed by Pope John. It was written by the authority of Benedict, then exercising the apostolic office, by the hand of Bonigo, notary and regional official of the holy Roman Church, in April of the eighth indiction. [Note: [Col. 0721] In 981 the ninth indiction was current; but the emperor’s residence at Rome then shows that it was 981.]

21. On the strengthened immunity of his deeds. Thus the faithful and prudent servant of the Lord, looking both backward and forward, was guided by a foreknowledge of the future, lest at some time the enchantment of vanity darken his good works. As long as life and opportunity allowed, he protected those of the household of faith—to whom he did good especially for the remedy of his soul—by apostolic and imperial support. Nor did he seek immunity for this place alone; desiring that his other acts too should remain valid forever, he did not delay to confirm them by a legal document, strengthen them by imperial edict, and authenticate them with the impression of its seal. Let it not, therefore, be burdensome to insert here the charter itself, a fitting witness both to the works of our bishop and to our words.

Decree of Otto II [Note: [Col. 0721] Manuscript 1: “secret.”].

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. Otto, by divine favor and clemency emperor augustus. Let it be known to the diligence of all our faithful, both present and future, how our faithful servant Theoderic, venerable bishop of the church of Metz, humbly petitioned our highness that we should confirm by the gift and authority of our imperial command the monastery of Saint Vincent, built outside the walls of his city called Metz, which he first began to build with the permission and consent of our father Otto, emperor augustus of blessed memory; and the market which he first established with our permission in the place called Épinal. He also petitioned that we should newly grant and strengthen, by the authority of our gift, the law which had been granted to the households of the church of Saint Stephen, the first martyr of Christ, over which he presides, by our predecessors, namely kings and emperors.

Receiving his petition graciously for divine love, we have taken under the immunity of our protection the aforesaid monastery consecrated in honor of Saint Vincent the martyr. We confirm by royal and imperial munificence and magnificence everything granted there by him or by others, and everything still to be granted there by anyone. We command by imperial authority that the market established in the aforesaid place shall henceforth stand and remain firm without dispute from any persons. And we grant and strengthen, to be held henceforth by the households of the aforesaid church, the law which the aforesaid Bishop Theoderic requested us to grant them, by imperial gift and protection. [Note: [Col. 0721] Here and above, “we confirm” and “we would confirm” are to be understood.]

And so that this grant of our donation may be held more firmly by all faithful persons through the course of future ages, we have ordered this command of our highness to be drawn up and sealed with the impression of our seal, and have confirmed it with our own hand.

Sign of Lord Otto, most invincible emperor augustus. (L. M.) I, Hildibold, bishop and chancellor, have recognized it on behalf of Willigis, archchaplain. Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July [20 June], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 983, the eleventh indiction, the twenty-fifth year of the reign of the most invincible Otto [Note: [Col. 0721] XXIII should be understood; of his empire, XVI. But the remaining diplomas of this period suffer from the same error.], and the fifteenth of his empire. Done at Mantua; happily, amen.

22. On the worthy completion of Lord Theoderic’s works, and his death. The man of God Theoderic, intensely devoted to the pursuit of good works and anxiously watchful over the talent entrusted to him, strove to bring before his Lord deeds of mercy multiplied. As a faithful servant, he endeavored to supply the household committed to him with the saving food.

> Made bishop, he fulfilled a bishop’s acts;  
> he benefited and governed the sheep entrusted to him.

For he loved those whom he saw zealous in ecclesiastical duties, and encouraged them with fruitful teaching not to abandon their perseverance. But those more negligent persons, who adhered less than they ought to the Gospel’s work, he rebuked, exhorted, and reproved according to the command of the Doctor of the Gentiles; nor did he cease to fortify them with the wall of spiritual defense, lest they be harmed by the bites of invisible wolves.

The perfection of his conduct was particularly praiseworthy because what he taught by discernment and abundance of doctrine, he demonstrated by examples and uprightness of character. He opened the bowels of mercy to the needy and orphaned; he offered the sweetness of consolation to the afflicted; he did not deny the benefits of kindly hospitality to guests. No one ever drew him away from justice to injustice. Rather, when the possessions of provincials were crushed, now by private plundering, now by public exactions, he grieved no less than those who suffered. He did not remain silent about words of truth before princes; he did not conceal the demand of justice for orphan and widow.

In his heart was humility; on his lips, consummate discernment; in his countenance, disciplined cheerfulness; in his work, outstanding charity. A haven and altar to his people, he devoted himself wholly to the growth of the Church. Finally, so that his memory might be eternal and the course of his life might multiply in the house of the Lord like a flourishing palm tree, like a cedar of Lebanon, he was a diligent builder of churches. As the preceding narrative relates, he shone as their indefatigable adornment with temporal goods and relics of saints, as may still be seen today.

O man worthy of remembrance, who regarded human favor as a passing shadow, set aside friendship with the children of men, and won for himself the favor of the citizens above! Indeed, although he was held first among courtiers and counselors of the empire, and the affairs of the kingdom were entrusted to his wisdom and direction, he no longer wished, as he had hitherto done, to entangle himself in secular affairs, so that he might serve God more freely. Dwelling alone with himself, he exercised and cleansed [Note: [Col. 0723D] That is, he cleansed with a broom.] his spirit.

Casting, therefore, from his soul all the nausea of courtly anxiety—where manifold trouble sometimes excludes all moderation, and where anyone may behold the changing wheel of Fortune—he wholly passed from the active to the contemplative life. Warned by divine inspiration that the day of his death was at hand, he performed fruits of repentance worthy of all the excesses of his life, hastening to be enrolled among the dignitaries of the heavenly court. He set before his mind’s eyes what we described at the beginning of his enthronement: namely, the letter of his name inscribed from heaven in silver among the names of the bishops of Metz. For this he had promised that he would perform such great good works in his bishopric that, by God’s favor, the silver letter would be transformed into gold. Nor did his expectation deceive him. For, adding the increase of good works to his good will, he confirmed the beginning of a good life by a memorable and righteous end.

> Thus the good athlete of the Lord, flourishing perfectly  
> above the joyful courts while striving to live rightly,  
> completed his course and afterward rested in peace.

When he was removed from this unstable life, on 7 September 984, and, as we believe, received into the heavenly court, how dear he had been to the city could be measured by the immeasurable mourning at his funeral. He was therefore borne to the monastery of Saint Vincent, the splendid testimony of his devotion, and there buried with the honor befitting a bishop of so great a name. He left the work itself unfinished, yet did not fail to assign sufficient funds and expenses for its completion.

He died in the year of the Lord 983 [Note: [Col. 0724D] It is established that Theoderic died in 984.], in the eleventh indiction, with epact 15 and concurrent 7, on the seventh day before the Ides of September [7 September], the sixth weekday, in the first year of the reign of Otto III. On that same day of the month the anniversary of the death of his mother Amalrada was commemorated. [Note: [Col. 0723] Thus the codex.] His father Everard had departed from the world on the Kalends of May [1 May].

EPITAPH. [Note: [Col. 0723] Manuscript *c*: “epitaph.”]

> Here lies Theoderic, born of noble blood,  
> of royal descent and bearing a famous name;  
> he was touched by the bloodline of Emperor Otto,  
> by whose counsels he gave laws to peoples.  
> He shone upon the world like a star filled with light,  
> in distinguished deeds and excellent character.  
> Therefore he deserved to ascend the see of Metz,  
> which he governed in the worthy office of a bishop.  
> He built this hall for the heavenly King as an offering  
> and adorned it with marvelous and countless things.  
> When the Ides of September had now returned,  
> by the lot of death he was enclosed beneath this stone.

23. On the dedication of the church of Saint Vincent. Since we have now completed our account of the life of this most excellent bishop, we take care to leave before posterity’s eyes the day of the dedication of the church of Saint Vincent. After that bishop’s death, through the succession of many abbots presiding over the place, the work that had remained unfinished was finally completed in the time of Lord Heribert, abbot of venerable life, in 1030. Among the other things which he accomplished zealously and devoutly, he arranged for the church itself to be dedicated by Lord Theoderic the Younger.

How lavishly furnished with every resource, with what pious fervor of devotion, with what great concourse of all people, and with how much zeal the joy of this dedication was celebrated, still clings almost fresh in the memory of those who were present. The first and principal altar was consecrated in honor of Saint Vincent, martyr and levite; the second in honor of Saint Benedict the abbot, the bishops and confessors Fortunatus and Elpidius, and Pope Gregory the confessor; the third in honor of the most glorious and victorious cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, John the Baptist, Quintianus priest and martyr, and Remigius bishop and confessor.

This dedication was celebrated on the second day before the Ides of May [14 May], in the year 1030 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the thirteenth indiction, epact 14, the seventh year of Conrad’s empire, and the twenty-fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Theoderic the Younger. Moreover, as has been handed down to us from our elders, the altar of Saint Peter was dedicated by Egbert, archbishop of Trier, in honor of the same Saint Peter the Apostle and Felician, bishop and martyr, on the third day before the Nones of February [3 February].

Let this suffice to have said about this dedication. But let the faithful reader conclude the reading with this prayer: that the Lord God may visit and bless this place, defend the brethren dwelling in it from every evil, and always hear the prayers of all faithful people—he who lives and reigns through all ages. Amen.

RHYTHMS IN HONOR OF BISHOP THEODERIC

[Col. 0725A]

> Theoderic, illustrious in blood and character,  
> indeed more illustrious than all,  
> was second in brilliance to the king,  
> scarcely second to anyone beneath him.  
>   
> This cousin of the renowned emperor  
> stood by him in war and peace,  
> holding second place in the kingdom  
> and lightening the emperor’s cares.  
>   
> Through him all affairs of the realm  
> and the laws of the Church stood firm.  
> Soldier, senate, and royal court  
> looked expectantly to his words.  
>   
> While King Otto, by the helm of government,  
> sought everywhere to calm the excessively turbulent  
> waters of Italy through the laws of peace,  
> driving evils away,  
>   
> this man too was there, influential and intimate,  
> at the emperor’s mouth, ears, and heart;  
> whom he favored, was favored through him;  
> scarcely could anyone prevail without this.  
>   
> Because of this pre-eminent magnificence,  
> all honor him with generosity,  
> being made welcome through him  
> so that they might obtain their desires.  
>   
> Yet he did not demand this greedily, but with pious desire:  
> he sought what would be useful,  
> what was known to be free from fault,  
> what might prepare hope of pardon for him.  
>   
> For your bodies, holy martyrs,  
> this holy man’s faith sought,  
> translated by whatever effort,  
> so that he might possess them reverently.  
>   
> The city of Metz rejoiced in such a bishop,  
> trusting in his double protection,  
> powerful through his holiness  
> and secure through his noble birth.

VITA OF SAINT SIGEBERT THE KING, BY SIGEBERT OF GEMBLOUX.

(See *Patrologiae*, vol. LXXXVII, col. 303, under King Sigebert.)

SHORTER VITA OF SAINT SIGEBERT, WRITTEN BY THE SAME SIGEBERT

(Duchesne, *Historiae Francorum Scriptores*, II.)

[Col. 0725C] Since you ask about the Life of Sigebert, king of the Franks, I shall set forth briefly what we read concerning him, whether in histories about the ordering of the kingdom or in saints’ deeds about the propagation of holy religion, gathered from those sources. And since we know that there were three Frankish kings of this name, I shall trace the antiquity of his nobility farther back, so that it may be made clearer to you who the first King Sigebert was, who the second, and who this third one of whom we are now speaking. At the same time, let it become plain to all whence the Frankish people derive their name or origin, and whence and when they invaded Gaul, which they have now held for almost six hundred years and, still holding it, govern powerfully and prosperously.

After the Greeks had destroyed the noble city of Phrygia, Aeneas and Antenor, nobles of the Trojans, withdrew with the remnants of the Trojans to foreign nations. That Aeneas came to Italy and laid the foundations of the Roman Empire is sung even by schoolboys. But twelve thousand Trojans who followed Antenor wandered through the regions of Scythia, settled around the Maeotian marshes, and were called Antenoridae after Antenor. Hence Virgil also writes:

> Antenor, escaping through the midst of the Achaeans,  
> was able to penetrate the Illyrian bays, and safely reach  
> the innermost realms of the Liburnians, and pass beyond the spring of Timavus.

Their descendants founded the metropolitan city of their kingdom, which they called Sicambria; and from it they themselves were also named Sicambri. They grew into a great people, always having a king of their own nation; nor did they ever permit themselves to be subjected to the yoke of any people, but were always a terror to neighboring nations. But when, by God’s dispensation, the whole world had been subdued to the Roman Empire and, after a census had been taken, reduced under taxation, they too became tributaries of the Romans. Yet they continually harassed the Roman provinces with incursions and spread their name far and wide. From the destruction of Troy down to these times of the Emperor Valentinian, such was the course of Frankish affairs.

During the reign of Valentinian—at the time, namely, when Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, was renowned throughout Gaul for holiness and miracles—a certain people of Scythia called the Alans rebelled against the Romans. Since the Romans could not conquer them because of the inaccessible marshes of the Maeotian river, they proposed an agreement: whoever defeated them should be free from tribute for ten years. The Sicambri, whose king at that time was Priam, defeated the Alans. For this they were judged worthy of honor and reward by the Emperor Valentinian, who in the Greek tongue called them *Franci*, that is, “fierce ones.” After ten years, when they refused to pay tribute demanded by the Romans and moreover rebelled boldly, Valentinian defeated and crushed them in war, and killed their king Priam. After Priam, his son Marcomir reigned; the Franks left Sicambria and settled in Thuringia, a province of Germany. After Marcomir came his son Faramund, the long-haired king, from whom the Franks began to have long-haired kings. After him his son Clodius reigned. Bringing the Franks from Thuringia, he invaded Gaul; having captured the city of Tournai, he advanced as far as Cambrai and killed many Romans in Gaul.

For Gaul had been under Roman rule from the time of Julius Caesar, who subdued it in a ten-year war, and received its rulers from the Romans. But, deprived of all assistance and exposed to plunder by Vandals, Goths, and other barbarian peoples, it lay open to devastation. After Clodius, his son Merovech reigned; because he was very serviceable, he gave the Franks from himself the name Merovingians. In his time Attila, king of the Huns, rushing from the North like a wild storm, flooded all Gaul and destroyed with dreadful devastation Metz, Trier, Tongeren, Rheims, and nearly all cities, forts, and towns as far as Orléans. But at last, defeated in battle by Aetius, commander of the Romans, with the Franks assisting him, he returned to his homeland. This destruction of Gallic cities occurred fifty-four years after the death of Saint Martin, in the fifth year of Merovech.

*A leaf is missing here in the manuscript codex.*

For although King Dagobert was an outstanding warrior, a devout lover of God’s priests and churches, a generous supporter of Christ’s poor, and a practitioner of many good works, he nevertheless suffered excessively from the disease of carnal incontinence. From it he had incurred a shameful stain of infamy upon the brightness of his name; and, what was more serious, he had kindled against himself the wrath of the King of kings. For, on pretexts invented for the purpose, he repudiated one queen for another; and even over those to whom he was betrothed he brought the loves of concubines. Although he was so given to sexual intercourse, he had no hope of propagating offspring, having received no son from any of so many wives.

He grieved greatly, therefore, because he felt that he had incurred God’s displeasure, especially since he knew that none of the royal stock of his fathers survived except himself and his brother Charibert. Charibert, because of excessive simplicity, was less fit to hold the helm of the kingdom. Yet although Dagobert despaired of descendants, he did not despair of God’s mercy; he prayed from his heart that, by God’s will, a son might be given to him to succeed him in governing the kingdom. The just and merciful Lord, who is provoked to wrath by human errors, is also moved back to mercy by the prayers of the humble.

In the ninth year of his reign, while King Dagobert was travelling through Austrasia, he took as his wife, with the honor of royal state, a certain maiden named Ragnetrude, praiseworthy in beauty of face and of a family not ignoble among the Austrasians. By God’s will she bore him a son in that same year; regenerated in the sacred font, he was named Sigebert.

After some time had passed, King Dagobert, rejoicing with great joy and accompanied by his entire army, came to Metz in the eleventh year of his reign. There he ordered an assembly of nobles and bishops to attend; by their counsel and consent he elevated his son Sigebert to the kingdom of the Austrasians, allowed him to have Metz as the royal seat, and gave him a sufficient portion of the treasures. A year later a son was born to King Dagobert, named Clovis. Again, when all the chief men of Austrasia and Neustria had been gathered in a general assembly, Dagobert arranged a division of the kingdom between his two sons and confirmed it by their counsel and assent, with mutual agreements and oaths given and received: namely, that the definite boundary of each kingdom having been determined, Sigebert should reign over Austrasia and Clovis should rule Neustria. They called Austrasia that part of Francia which looks toward the south and east; they called Neustria that which inclines toward the north and west.

King Dagobert, having arranged both kingdoms so justly and prudently, lest at any time the brothers should quarrel with one another in fraternal hatred, or a kingdom divided against itself be devastated by the scandal of civil war, died in the seventeenth year of his reign. He was buried at Paris in the basilica of Saint Denis, and left the kingdom at peace with foreign peoples and in no respect diminished from its borders. After his death the two kings and brothers, Sigebert and Clovis, each governed wisely in his own kingdom and exercised power strongly among his own people.

Meanwhile Pippin, mayor of the palace, was removed from this life. He had nurtured Sigebert himself from childhood with paternal care and supported him with the strong arm of his aid. In every respect useful to the kingdom, eminent above all for birth, power, prudence, and courage, he made his son Grimoald heir of his possessions. He also left behind two daughters, Gertrude and Begga, for the praise and glory of his line. One of them, Gertrude, preferring Christ as spouse to a carnal husband, devoted herself to the profession of holy religion; in the monastery of Nivelles, founded by her mother, she still does not cease to bear spiritual offspring for God. Her sister Begga, married to Ansegisel, son of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, restored through her descendants the splendor of royal dignity which had wholly dissipated through the unprecedented indolence of the Frankish kings. She bore Pippin; Pippin bore Charles, surnamed Tudetes, that is, “the Hammer”; Charles bore Pippin, the first king; Pippin bore Charles, surnamed the Great, king of the Franks and emperor of the Romans. He attained such a height of honor and power that no king of the Franks, either before or after him, could be compared with him.

Grimoald, appointed mayor of the palace in his father Pippin’s place, ruled powerfully in the court of King Sigebert and courageously defended the kingdom at home and in war. Since King Sigebert had found Grimoald, his mayor of the palace, faithful, obedient, and cooperative in all things, he had designated Grimoald’s son Childebert heir to the kingdom of Austrasia, but on the condition that he himself should die without children. The king, being ignorant of future events, did what then appeared suitable to the circumstances; but afterward he fathered a son, whom he called Dagobert after his own father. Setting aside the former testament as void, he entrusted this son’s upbringing to Grimoald, mayor of the palace, so that Grimoald’s power might safely raise and preserve him against all opposition in the kingdom of the Austrasians.

Sigebert himself built twelve monasteries in various parts of his kingdom and, with royal generosity, supplied them from his revenues with necessities, so that those living there under the rule of apostolic life, while they reaped carnal things, might sow spiritual things for him. Among these, prominent in our neighborhood, are the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy, situated within the forest of the Ardennes. The same king built them, with Grimoald, his mayor of the palace, assisting him, and handed them over to Saint Remaclus, bishop of Tongeren, to organize.

When he had completed thirty-one years of life and twenty-eight of reign, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 642, two hundred and forty-three years after Saint Martin’s death, the terrible King, feared by all kings of the earth, who takes away the spirit of princes, snatched him by a bitter death from this present wicked age in the flower of youth and bestowed upon him in the heavenly court the glory of true dignity. He died on the Kalends of February [1 February] and was buried in the city of Metz, which had been the seat of his kingdom, in the basilica that he had built by royal generosity for the praise and glory of God in honor of Saint Martin, the glorious confessor. It is situated at the foot of a mountain which rises high over the city and looks down upon the opposite citadels.

Oh, how often ambition has deceived many! Oh, how often divine vengeance has cast down many traitors! When King Sigebert had died, Grimoald, mayor of the palace, had his son Dagobert—entrusted to his fidelity, in order that he might obtain the kingdom of the Austrasians—tonsured as a cleric, on the advice of Dido, bishop of Poitiers, uncle of Saint Leodegar the martyr; and through Dido’s own hand he sent the innocent little boy into irrevocable exile in Scotland. He then established his own son Childebert as king of the Austrasian kingdom. The Franks, bearing Grimoald’s treachery with indignation, captured him and sent him to Paris for the judgment of King Clovis, Sigebert’s brother. Clovis committed him in chains to prison and cruelly tortured him, as he deserved, until death. The Austrasians chose Hildric, son of Clovis, and established him as king in the kingdom of Austrasia, which his uncle Sigebert had held. This is King Hildric, in whose time Saint Lambert was martyr and bishop. . . .

[Col. 0729]

# Life of Saint Maclovius, or Machutes, Bishop and Confessor, by Sigebert of Gembloux

*(In Surius, Acts of the Saints, 15 November.)*

## The Author’s Letter

[Col. 0729D]

### To Thietmar, Abbot of Gembloux

The Life of the most devout confessor of Christ, Maclovius, who is also called Machutes, had been diligently set down in the style of the ancients, insofar as historical truth was concerned. But because it was arranged rather disorderly, written rather incoherently, and moreover excessively confused with barbarisms and solecisms, it lay concealed beneath the long accumulation of oblivion and neglect so completely that, as though worthy of no one’s ears, it had already passed from human memory.

But, venerable Father Thietmar, considering that precious metal does not wholly lose the estimation of its value even if it lies buried beneath the rubbish of the earth or discolored by the roughness of rust, it pleased your fatherhood to command my smallness to examine the text of the history, erase as far as possible the accumulated defects, and improve it with whatever modest ornament of expression I could supply. I, who ought not to have opposed the command, carried out the imposed task—not as I wished, indeed, but as I could, given the weakness of my ability.

For I undertook the assigned work in the manner of a rustic smith, who, by blowing bellows and striking with hammers, removes dross from the crude mass of precious metal so that it may be made readier for the hand of a skilled craftsman, displaying to others the splendor of the material, so that anyone wishing to exercise the power of his craft may find material prepared for his use. Therefore I shall do what seems easy to do: namely, remove superfluities, correct faults, and restore confused matters to order. Yet I shall in no way depart from the truth of the history, so that I may seem to have introduced nothing new, but only to have renewed what was old by filing and polishing it.

## Prologue

The praises of the saints, which are very precious in the eyes of the Lord, must by no means be passed over in silence, but must be committed to all remembrance. Likewise, it must be believed that the saints’ miracles were accomplished through the power of almighty God, their hearts first having been endowed by heavenly generosity for their blessed life. Therefore the life of Christ’s friends must first be investigated, so that, while we strive to imitate it, it may profit us to admire their virtues. For it does us no good to marvel at miracles without the beneficial imitation of a blessed life.

Now let the life of the blessed man be brought forward, so that, while we are encouraged to imitate him by recalling his merits, we may deserve to obtain the grace of his intercession in times of need.

## Chapter I

Saint Maclovius, then, distinguished among his contemporaries in the world by no small nobility of parents, was born near the shore of the British sea. His father, named Guent, was a count and founder of the city called Gimicastrum. We have received that his mother was called Darual. Since God’s providence is never absent from any event, it was also evident at the beginning of this holy man’s birth. For he was born on the holy day on which the whole world celebrated the joys of the Paschal solemnity, so that divine mercy might add this joy also for mortals on the day which the Lord made, “that we may rejoice and be glad in it.”

At that same point of the day thirty-three other boys were born in the same neighborhood. Since this was believed to have occurred through God’s providential ordering, it pleased the parents of them all that those who had received at birth the beginning of one contemporaneous life should maintain one fellowship of living in Christ. For all were instructed together with Saint Maclovius in scholarly studies, and all together were dedicated to divine service.

## Chapter II

Thus, for the boy of good disposition, chosen by God for the accomplishment of blessed works, there was already then divinely inspired what Holy Scripture says: “A child is known by his pursuits, whether his works are pure” (Prov. 20); and, “Blessed is he who has borne the yoke from his youth” (Lam. 3). From his earliest years he renounced the occupation of worldly vanity and joined himself to the freedom of divine service. In order more fully to possess learning in doctrine and knowledge of God, he devoted himself more strictly to instruction in the holy Scriptures. In the pursuit of this, idleness—which is the enemy of the soul—is restrained; in its meditation God is known; in its practice eternal life is attained.

He sought the knowledge which builds up through the humility of charity; he fled that which puffs up through vain self-exaltation. Beginning also to chastise his body and bring it into the service of the spirit (1 Cor. 8), he accustomed himself to be content with simple food and clothing. He made light of bodily cold, and judged it unworthy to be distended by an abundance of foods, lest through indulgence of bodily necessity the wantonness of flesh should in any way rule his soul. Therefore, except for what the simple necessity of nature required, he spent all else upon works of almsgiving.

## Chapter III

God, therefore, who can sometimes sanctify his servants and prophets even in their mother’s womb (Jer. 1), did not delay to make his servant wondrous in virtues and signs in his very earliest childhood (Luke 1). Even in the simplicity of childish age he did not cease, through good intention, to prepare himself to serve God.

One day, having gone with boys of his own age to the shore of the sea for play, while the others were occupied in the idle business of play, he laid his head upon the ground and began to yield to sleep. Suddenly the returning tide of the sea came flooding in—as regularly occurs in the British sea according to the course of the moon. The other boys fled to preserve their lives, not thinking to awaken him as he slept in so great a danger. But God’s protection [did not stand apart], wrought through a great miracle, was not far off from the boy born for the salvation of many. For though waters flowed around on every side, and waves, swelling and rising over waves, roared around with violence, they did not dare to touch the place where the boy lay, a circle having been drawn around it on every side. God’s omnipotence made an island rise there, extending by its height to the summit of the water, and rescued the future bishop of Christ from the danger of death.

When so unexpected a miracle appeared before everyone’s eyes, the boy pleasing to God was promptly brought out of danger from the sea by the efforts of his parents, who procured a boat. And lest the novelty of this event should ever fall from memory, and so that the holy man’s sanctity might shine forth the more through it, the Divinity caused that same island to remain until the present day; and, as we believe, posterity will have it as a testimony until the end.

## Chapter IV

Afterward, as Saint Maclovius passed from mature infancy into boyhood, the more abundant a grace of divine inspiration he drank in with the increase of his years, the more eagerly and urgently he prepared his heart to seek the holiness of angelic life. Knowing from the Lord’s mouth that the blessedness of seeing God is promised to the pure in heart (Matt. 5), he dedicated himself from the very beginnings of boyhood to works of purity. Wishing to please God in body and spirit, he chose to spend all his life in the celibacy of virginity.

For as a fresh vessel retains for a long time the odor with which it is once imbued, so it seemed good to him to fit the unformed vessel of his body as soon as possible for sanctification and honor, lest it be corrupted by the passion of carnal desire. So that he might carry this out more freely and perfectly, through his parents’ devotion and his own will he assumed the habit of the monastic order. Placed there under the guardianship of regular discipline, how vigorous and prompt he showed himself beyond the others in obedience may at least be proved from this: he could not escape the envy of his equals, which always arises from another’s advancement and glory and wastes away within itself.

For among his fellows he suffered what Joseph formerly suffered among his brothers. Joseph, clothed by his father in a many-colored tunic (Gen. 37) and loved by him more than all his brothers because he rebuked their faults, had drawn envy upon himself. So this boy also, because he deserved to receive from God the ankle-length tunic of perfection, variegated with the color of virtues, could not escape the envy of his equals.

It was the custom of that order that boys should carry a lamp with its light before their teacher, each in his week, when they entered or left the oratory at night. When the happy boy’s week arrived, his companions extinguished the fire from which the lamp ought to have been lit, hoping that at least for this offense he would suffer the teacher’s blows. What was the simplicity of the boy to do? He ran to the workshop where beer was made from grain steeped and boiled in water, and asked the attendant to give him fire. But even in the uncultivated breast of the rustic there was no lack of the malice of diabolical envy. Despising the humble request of the suppliant boy, he refused to offer him a firebrand.

Distressed by fear of the teacher, the boy placed glowing coals from the hearth upon his garment and hurried back to light the lamp. But finding that it had already been lit by divine power, he shook the coals from his clothing, which nevertheless appeared unharmed to everyone. The teacher, astonished by the double miracle, threw himself at the knees of his pupil. Thereafter Maclovius was held in due veneration; though he surpassed all in glory, he was beloved by all.

## Chapter V

Because the holy man was to become a priest of Christ, and knew that both the head and the tail of the sacrificial victim ought to be offered as a sacrifice to God, he advanced day by day from virtue to virtue and labored to climb step by step, by the ladder of good works, to the summit of perfection. Whatever he had faithfully vowed to God in tender age, he sincerely fulfilled at the proper time. Above all he devoted himself to the purity of chastity, knowing that unless a vessel is pure, whatever is poured into it is corrupted.

Having therefore his loins girded with this virtue of chastity, he also held a burning lamp in his hands when, through good works, he showed his neighbors examples of light. Thus he faithfully and wisely doubled the talents of understanding and action entrusted to him by God (Luke 12), drawing by word and example all whom he could to the purpose of holy conduct, and joining them to himself as companions and partners in climbing the way of perfection.

How friendly frugality was to him, how pleasing restraint, and how, drawing back the rope of temperance from either side, he always held the middle path of virtues in all things, is sufficiently evident from the fact that he happily reached the highest summit of holiness. By the uprightness of his life the whole people were directed in no small degree toward improvement of morals; delighted beyond measure by the glory of his miracles, they caused him to be promoted to the episcopal order, that they might more abundantly deserve to be sanctified by his blessings.

## Chapter VI

Rumor, which is accustomed to speak alike of truth and falsehood, reported that there was a certain island in the sea which, besides the other blessings of happiness in which it was said to abound beyond other lands and islands, was held worthy to possess this marvelous distinction: that citizens of heaven were said to dwell there. If the truth of the matter is considered, that happiness of life was attributed to those islanders because among them the integrity of moral uprightness in no respect departed from its course; indeed, in all things the holiness of the natural law reigned powerfully.

Delighted by so favorable a report, the blessed man’s whole mind was carried toward seeking such a praiseworthy island. Since his manner of life was already in heaven and the manifold injustice of humankind offended him as he lived amid the scandals of the world, he desired at least to live where he had heard that traces of justice remained. He was further encouraged by the example of his teacher and abbot, Brendan, whose whole purpose burned no less ardently to seek the happy island. Brendan was, indeed, the originator and author of this new pilgrimage, as the written account of his life shows. Whoever wishes to read it should learn from the judgment of the wise what ought to be thought of it.

Therefore, setting aside the sweet love of their homeland, they undertook the uncertain labor of their desired pilgrimage. Whether the desire alone to seek a happy dwelling persuaded them to follow this course, or whether the pleasure of human curiosity in some degree crept into their minds, our rashness has no right to investigate. Yet we understand sufficiently that this journey did not displease God, since even during this pilgrimage he did not cease to adorn his servant with wonderful miracles.

## Chapter VII

The world was celebrating the joy of the Paschal solemnity, when the holy Church more solemnly commemorates the remembrance of our redemption, fulfilled in those days by the Lord’s passion and resurrection. While others celebrated this more festively, Saint Maclovius observed it more devoutly, giving himself to psalms, hymns, and prayers, as one who ought to intercede with God not only for his own sins but also for the offenses of the people.

Wishing, therefore, to celebrate the solemnities of the Masses, but having no suitable place for this purpose—for, turning his sight about as far as the horizon permitted, he saw nothing but heaven above and the expanse of waters below—he turned with all his heart to God and prayed earnestly that a suitable place might be provided. The attentive ear of almighty God was at hand for the prayer of one asking profitable things; and he who once prepared a whale for Jonah when he was in danger, for his sure salvation (Jonah 2), now also caused a whale to be present.

Its body was so vast that people thought it a rock; moreover, it had been made so motionless that it was believed to be a stable island. The priest therefore solemnly celebrated the order of the sacraments, and devoutly distributed to all the provision of the Lord’s Eucharist, by which alone they might be fortified against all adversities of both the inner and outer human being. Then, cheerfully casting off the ship’s mooring, they committed themselves to their intended voyage. There were about one hundred and eighty persons in that company.

When they were already out at sea, secure under the sail of faith, only then, looking back, did they understand from what great danger the merciful power of the Lord had rescued them: he had prepared a whale for them as an island in the middle of the sea and had made it so firmly motionless that it caused them no fear of danger. Who could then doubt that all would have encountered an unavoidable danger of death if that most enormous beast had moved its body? Therefore all, singing a joyful sailors’ chant, raised with one accord voices of thanksgiving to the stars.

## Chapter VIII

Miracles greater than great ones follow, and by their novelty stir the devotion of the faithful more strongly to praise the mighty works of God. While they labored so greatly to seek that island of praiseworthy report, it happened, by God’s disposal, that they landed at another island. Having gained the desired shore, and exploring its features to relieve the weariness of navigation, they came upon the mound of a buried man. The appearance of the body’s dimensions showed that he had been of giant size and stature.

The holy man, moved by the compassion of human pity and moreover strengthened by the force of heavenly inspiration, invoked with greatness of faith and tearful contrition of heart the name and power of the holy Trinity. Opening the tomb’s enclosure, he raised the man from the dead. When he had been restored to the full functions of life, the priest addressed him kindly, asking who he was, whence he had come there, where he had been, and whether he had ever believed in Christ.

He answered that he had been killed by his parents and had received a place of burial there. He had been assigned to the prisons of hell and had endured a dreadful and unending torment. Then the man of God added: “Do you, whom unbelief has consigned to the penal prison-house of hell, possess any confession of faith, any knowledge of the holy and undivided Trinity?”

The man replied: “Certainly we possess knowledge of the holy Trinity, but now it profits us nothing either to know or confess it. Indeed, because in life we were unwilling to know it, it harms us mortally. Therefore I beg that I may at least now deserve to be reborn through saving baptism, so that I who until now have been condemned to eternal death may henceforth be rescued from destruction in hell.”

Hearing this, the saint of God entered upon the way of apostolic preaching. After instructing and catechizing him in the rudiments of the Catholic faith, he consecrated and regenerated him through the sacraments of baptism, and strengthened him with the provision of the Lord’s body and blood. He survived for fifteen days; rescued from the death of the soul, he was restored to bodily death, laid again in the same tomb, and at the general regeneration of all will rise more happily with Christ.

These, good Jesus, are the wonderful works of your divinity; these are the splendid gifts of your promise, by which your mercy comforts those who faithfully believe in you. “He who believes in me,” he says, “will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John 14). That these things could be accomplished through a human being would scarcely win belief among people, unless it had been promised that they would be done through the Lord’s human being—that is, Christ—and through a faithful human being.

> **Note [Col. 0735].** By “the Lord’s human being” (*Dominicum hominem*) he means Christ; Augustine regretted having used this expression. See *Retractations*, book I, chapter 19.

## Chapter IX

After the prolonged labor of navigation had been spent in vain, and no hope of finding the desired island breathed upon their pious longing, they reconsidered the matter together and decided to put an end to so long an exile from home. They had already completed seven years in this pilgrimage and had celebrated seven returns of the Paschal feast, yet through certain toil still possessed nothing certain in their minds.

The holy man therefore returned to his ancestral homeland and restored to his parents the presence of himself for which they had long desired. Since he had been unable to find on earth the island of happiness he sought, he gave unceasing attention by night and day to deserving a homeland of perpetual blessedness in heaven. God, who precedes a person by his grace so that he may will the good, and follows him so that he may be able to accomplish it, made him attain his desire.

For while he was wholly intent on setting out at once upon the way of perfection, as he was present, according to custom, at the mystery of the ecclesiastical office, he heard the deacon proclaim the Gospel: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate father and mother, and wife and children, and brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14); and, “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (ibid.).

Seizing upon the words from the deacon’s mouth, and believing this counsel to have been delivered to him at that moment from the Lord’s own mouth, he immediately approached his father on the occasion of the reading, set before him the message of the Lord’s command sent to him through the deacon, and humbly asked leave to renounce himself and all that belonged to him. He declared that he wished to undertake a pilgrimage across the sea for Christ.

His father, loving his son with excessive carnal affection and rejoicing that he had returned from so distant a pilgrimage, wished to oppose his good intention. Running ahead to the shore of the sea, he removed all boats from the area and sternly forbade all sailors to provide his son with any means of crossing the sea. But the man of apostolic life, knowing that the Lord commanded: “If your right hand, or foot, or eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it away from you” (Matt. 18), preferred to enter life alone rather than be cast into Gehenna with his parents, loved to his destruction.

> **Note.** “Augustine regrets having said this. See *Retractations*, book I …”

Setting aside, therefore, every affection of carnal kinship for the love of Christ, he renounced his father, renounced his paternal property, and indeed renounced himself, that naked and unencumbered he might follow as a disciple in the footsteps of the Master.

## Chapter X

Having therefore summoned all who shared with him the purpose of the monastic order, and having also called his teacher, Abbot Brendan, companion of the earlier pilgrimage, he came to the shore of the sea. There, with the boats and sailors all removed in accordance with his father’s prohibition, and no means of crossing available, he recalled the Psalmist’s words: “It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man” (Ps. 117 [118]).

As he fixed his heart upon God alone, behold, he saw a ship, empty of people, standing ready; Christ himself was guiding it, though the holy man believed him to be a boy. The boy immediately invited him to sail and asked where he wished to direct his journey. He replied that wherever the Lord’s will wished to direct his journey, he wished gladly to follow.
