The boy added: “In this gulf of the sea is a certain island inhabited by a man greatly tested in monastic life. He is called Aaron; therefore the place is also named Aaron’s Island. I will direct you to him and ensure that you are received by him with the utmost courtesy and treated kindly.”

From this exchange the man of God at last understood that the boy with whom he spoke was the God whom he had invoked. When he hastened to throw himself at the speaker’s knees, the boy vanished from his sight more quickly than words can tell.

## Chapter XI

Thus he undertook the way of a happier voyage and, with favorable winds and a straight course, was directed to Aaron’s Island. According to the Lord’s promise, he was received by God’s servant with attentive hospitality. There he lived holily with the holy man, acted innocently with the innocent, and, each becoming the other’s mirror, whenever they saw in themselves something to be corrected or added, one improved the other by charitable emulation.

There the pilgrim of this world remained for some time, until it pleased divine omnipotence to render him even in this age a reward for his labor, while reserving for him in the future the fullness of recompense.

## Chapter XII
Already the report of him had made his name famous everywhere; already all the people spoke of how that pilgrim was powerful in miracles and surpassed men in the abundance of his teaching. All the people had now turned to love of him, because they saw in him both the affection of a compassionate father and the authority of an eloquent teacher. Therefore, with divine grace cooperating, they caused him to be enthroned in the episcopal chair in the city called Aletha, not far from Aaron’s island. The river named Rinctus washed this city on one side, and the sea on the other. In those regions the filth of demons still prevailed; and although the grace of the Gospel reigned widely, traces of idolatry still remained there. Thus the man of God, girded with the sword of God’s word, showed how faithful he was to his king, undertaking for love of him to overthrow the kingdom of the devil. Nor did he desist until, by the wonder-working power of miracles and the abundance of his teaching, he had bent the hearts of unbelievers to faith, driven them from the devil’s kingdom, and subjected them to Christ’s yoke.

In this neighbourhood Saint Samson lived, a kinsman of blessed Maclovius. In the territory of the city in which he exercised the episcopate, he laboured no little to drive paganism out of the kingdom of his Lord and to enlarge Christianity for the praise of God. Thus in that region, through the mighty soldiers of Christ, the power of the opposing party was diminished, and the splendour of Christianity was spread far and wide.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0738B] The Christian people were observing the vigil of Easter, and the priest was intent upon celebrating the mysteries of the Mass. And behold, the sorrowful funeral rites of one who had died were brought forward, and the tears of the mourners moved the hearts of the hearers to compassion. More deeply moved than all was the priest himself, wholly given to mercy; he ordered them to wait until the Mass was finished. As a crowd of people stood around, he urged all to call upon the Lord’s mercy, that he who has dominion over death and life might deign to restore the life-giving warmth of the soul to the stiffened limbs.

It was not long; he who said, “All things are possible to one who believes” (Mark 9), came to the aid of the faithful people’s devotion. The dead man rose, striking all with awe, and made it openly manifest that God favours those who ask faithfully. When he stood alive, he asked that a cup of wine be offered him. What was the holy man to do? He had no wine to give the thirsty man; and the thirsty man refused to touch the cup of water that was offered. Strengthened once more in faith, he returned to the fountain of mercy, asking that he who had granted the greater thing in response to the faithful people’s prayer might deign also to grant what was less.

At once, having a marble vessel at hand, he raised his hand in blessing over it and changed it into a glass vessel. Pouring water into the vessel, through the power of the holy blessing he changed it also into the nature of wine. Thus, presenting in a glass vessel a cup of new wine to the man restored to life, he showed all no small miracle of divine compassion.

O truly devout and magnificent worshipper of the holy Trinity, whom divine power, according to the faith of his heart, glorified in one day by three miracles: in the name and power of the holy Trinity he raised a dead man, made glass from marble, and wine from water. Thus the man whom others had brought there in a cart for burial himself gladly drove it home; and for as long as he lived he remained a competent witness of his own resurrection.

## CHAPTER XIV

The often-mentioned man, in whom faith lived through good works, performed no small miracles even in small matters, so that Christ’s glory might increase through him in all things. Once, while he was travelling about the region of Brittany in order to sow the seed of the divine word in the field of the Lord’s cultivation, he came upon a swineherd in a field, afflicted by great bitterness of grief. While guarding [Col. 0739A] a herd of pigs, he had been trying to keep a sow, greedily and persistently ravaging the crops, from damaging his neighbours’ property; but through an unwary blow with a stone he had killed her.

For this offence he feared his master, whose anger he believed would be especially inflamed because seven wandering piglets, accustomed to draw milk from the teats of their dead mother, sought it but could find no nourishment of life in her lifeless body. Maclovius, wholly claimed by compassion, could not see the swineherd’s tears without tears of his own. After offering prayer to God, he placed his staff upon the dead sow’s ear; and when she was restored to life at the mere touch, he returned joy to the grieving man. The swineherd reported the event to his master and spread abroad, through every mouth, the praises of God’s servant. The master mounted his horse, thanked the holy man face to face, and granted one estate to the church for the use of the servants of God under him.

## CHAPTER XV

He also did something else similar, highly praiseworthy even solely in view of his compassion. Imitating the Apostle Paul (Acts 20), whose own hands, by labouring, supplied whatever he lacked, he too devoted himself to manual work whenever he was free from the office of evangelizing. One day, while he was pruning a vineyard with the brothers, he put aside his cloak in a secluded place so that he might work more freely. When the work was finished and he wished to recover the cloak, he found that a little bird, commonly called a *bitrio*, had laid an egg upon it.

Knowing that God’s providence does not fail even the birds—for not one of them falls to the earth without God the Father (Matthew 10)—he left the cloak there until the bird, having brooded on the eggs, should in due time hatch her young. In this matter there was also this wonder: throughout the time that the cloak lay there, no rain damaged it. All who heard of it magnified God’s power with thanksgiving and praised the compassion of the man of God.

## CHAPTER XVI

In the district of the city of Aletha, in which the venerable Maclovius presided as bishop, a certain very noble man had a daughter grievously afflicted by an intolerable suffering caused by demonic assault. She bit everyone who came near her, sparing not even her parents. The violence of this evil condition could neither be restrained nor quieted unless that dreadful madness were bound fast in iron chains. Her father, to whom nothing could be pleasant while his daughter was ill, invited the blessed Maclovius to heal her, having formerly heard that he was renowned for effective cures.

Maclovius did not delay his mercy. Believing that God can easily grant healing to one who asks faithfully, he went to the girl. Wishing to restrain the deceit of demonic malice, he cast his handkerchief around the frenzied girl’s neck. Then indeed one might have heard the horrible voices of the demons reproaching God’s servant in these words:

> “O inhabitant from beyond the sea, could not your own country endure you, that you have come here to seek what belongs to others and to drive us out of our region?”

Christ’s disciple despised these insults of the enemy, rejoicing that he shared this with his Master and Lord, to whom the demons cried in a deceitful confession: “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of the living God? Have you come before the time to destroy us?” (Matthew 8). Following the example of the Lord’s rebuke, he restrained their empty falsehoods.

Knowing this demon to be of the kind of which the Lord says, “This kind cannot be cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matthew 17), he poured forth an exorcistic prayer over water and, adding an episcopal blessing, gave the girl a drink. Through the cup of blessed water, the power of the blessing flowing through the girl’s limbs—long battered by demonic intrusion—she fell to the ground as though dead. Shortly afterwards, having regained consciousness, she rose whole and joyful. The assault of the most wicked invader had fled, and her fully restored health brought joy to others.

Seeing his wishes fulfilled, the father, in thanksgiving, enriched God’s holy Church with landed estates and precious gifts. Since glory is rarely, if ever, without envy, the cunning of the ancient enemy did not long endure so great a glory of Maclovius. Lest the grace of the good soldier should grow still stronger in Christ’s kingdom, he stirred up against him enemies armed with the deceit of injustice and supported, moreover, by considerable secular power.

## CHAPTER XVII

A certain Hailoch, who held powerful rule over all Brittany, prompted by the instigation of demonic malice, began to destroy a basilica which blessed Maclovius had founded on an estate within his diocese. The man of God pleaded at the prince’s ears with tears and prayers, asking that he might deign to desist from destroying the church building. But Hailoch, made savage by the arrogance of iniquity conceived within him, could not be softened or restrained by any grace of pious admonition.

Against the power of such secular domination, Maclovius took patience alone as his defence and support. But he who says to his faithful people through the prophets, “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zechariah 2), and, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deuteronomy 32), did not leave unavenged the injury done to his poor. As he struck Saul, resisting him, with blindness for three days (Acts 9), so that afterward Saul might illuminate the whole world with eternal brightness, he also struck this man with temporary blindness, so that through passing darkness he might be freed from the darkness of sins.

Immediately returning to his senses and pierced with heartfelt repentance, Hailoch hurried as quickly as possible to make satisfaction to the bishop, declaring himself guilty with bitter sobs and confessing through tearful lament that he had deserved to be blinded. Maclovius, who had learned from the Master of highest goodness that good must be done even to enemies, and prayer offered for persecutors and slanderers (Matthew 5), quickly and mercifully pardoned the penitent man’s offence. Providing for the salvation of both the inward and outward person, he sprinkled him with blessed water, anointed his eyes with holy oil, and thus restored his former sight. Yet for his rash deed he imposed upon him a fitting manner of repentance.

The duke, seeing that his satisfaction benefited both soul and body, assigned no small inheritance of lands to God’s Church and bestowed an abundant endowment in slaves and property. Thereafter, for as long as he lived, he loved the servant of God with a son’s unique love as his father, and in every matter was a timely protector and helper to him and his people.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Thus the ancient enemy departed defeated in this first encounter, yet yielded without being exhausted. For just as formerly, when he contended with the Lord himself (Matthew 4), he did not withdraw after being overcome in the first temptation but dared to renew his weapons a second and third time, so after Maclovius’s first victory Duke Hailoch did not cease from his efforts. Hailoch had humbly submitted himself wholly to Maclovius’s service and, for his sake, had vigorously devoted himself to the defence of God’s Church; but after he entered the way of all flesh, his death gave the wicked an opportunity to oppress the Church.

For after him rose an impious generation which, turning its face away from God, wholly abandoned the counsel of righteousness. The devil seized this opportunity and, using such agents, rose against the man of God with a thousand devices. The sons of Belial, attacking Maclovius with detestable hatred, assailed him with this reproach:

> “Who is this wicked foreigner who has entered our realm and everywhere stirs up troubles for us? Who is this seductive impostor who alienates men’s hearts from us with his flatteries? Who is this greedy hunter after inheritances, who here procures advantages for himself from our misfortunes? Though apostles and successors of apostles ought to possess nothing on earth, this man conceals the vice of greed under a show of poverty; under the pretext of almsgiving he pursues the profit of avarice; under the cover of long prayer he plunders widows’ houses. He lies that he has left everything for Christ, and boasts that he possesses everything in Christ; yet he disinherits us and our sons and greedily seeks our inheritances for himself. He pretends not to care for what is his: why, then, does he administer what belongs to others?

> “Therefore nothing is more useful to us than now at last to provide for our exhausted affairs, drive him far from our realm, and reoccupy the inheritances unjustly made over to churches. For he has left nothing to us or our sons, having appropriated all our property for himself. At the price of all our possessions, he sells us only hope of future things, while he himself presently enjoys their usufruct.”

Frequently provoking the holy man with such injurious attacks, they harassed him with every kind of persecution, tortured his people with savage beatings, and utterly devastated God’s Church through every form of plunder.

## CHAPTER XIX

How severe and intolerable this persecution was may be understood from one example. They unjustly seized his baker, named Riman, shamefully beat him, bound him hand and foot with willow bonds so that he could use none of his limbs for assistance, and left him alone on the seashore so that, when the tide came in, he might be swallowed by the deep. They also took the holy man’s horses so that he could not bring aid to him. They left the bishop only a mare, supposing that they would thereby insult him if he had to mount a worthless mare.

The priest gave such aid as he could to his servant in danger by prayer. The Almighty did not fail the praying bishop: through his faith and prayer, the man who lay at the point of death escaped marvellously. By the will of him whom all nature serves, the tide of the sea was held back on every side for the distance of one mile from the baker where he lay, and it feared to touch the innocent youth exposed to death. The bishop therefore at once went to the baker, afflicted because of hatred directed against himself; he found him unharmed and brought him back with him in good spirits.

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 0742B] Bishop Maclovius, who wished to maintain justice blamelessly before God and men, bore more heavily than can be said the scandalizing of Christ’s little ones by the impious. He also grieved deeply for those sacrilegious people, goaded by so sharp a spur of greed: no excuse of ignorance could acquit them before God, for greed was dragging them headlong while they saw and knowingly willed it. Their eye was evil and darkened by envy precisely where their fathers’ had been good. Their fathers had redeemed their sins by giving alms; these men had accumulated their sins by speaking against almsgiving.

Trained to possess his soul in patience, he said: “If my Lord Jesus avoided the faithlessness of the Jews by flight, why should I, a mere man, not avoid these people’s malice by yielding? Behold, these men have, like foxes, dens of deceit, and, like birds, nests of vanity; while we, with the Son of Man, have nowhere among them to lay our head” (John 8 and 12). “Let us withdraw and, at least by fleeing, remove from them the opportunity to sin against us. The dust must be shaken from our feet as a testimony against them. And because they are not children of peace, among whom Christ’s peace may rest, may our peace return to us” (Matthew 10). “When our Lord Jesus said, ‘When they persecute you in this city, flee into another’ (ibid.), he surely foresaw that at some time this occasion for flight would be forced upon us. Therefore, brothers, let us act without delay; let us withdraw, I beg you, patiently.”

Thus the devout man, having execrated that most wicked generation, pronounced upon them a deserved curse, because they had driven blessing far from themselves. Thus Moses, the meekest of all men dwelling on earth (Numbers 121 [an erroneous citation]); thus Isaiah and Jeremiah, offended by the stiff-necked hardness of an ungrateful people, bound them under a most grievous imprecation—namely, praying because of their impenitence that God should not heed their vows or sacrifices. Elisha cursed the boys who mocked him and consigned them to the punishment of the curse (4 Kings 2). What shall I say of the Lord of lords, who, after cursing the fig tree because of its barrenness and causing it to wither (Matthew 21), subjected the faithlessness of the Jews to an imprecation deservedly accursed?

Following this example, blessed Maclovius cursed his own persecutors, so that, delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh while the hope of salvation was nevertheless reserved for their souls, they might desist from the work of iniquity; and so that those who, through hardness of heart, had stored up God’s wrath for themselves might at last, softened through repentance, reconcile God’s mercy to themselves.

## CHAPTER XXI

Driven from his episcopal see by the offences of the impious, he prepared every provision for departure and gathered together his faithful company of monk-disciples. After completing a long voyage, he finally reached the harbour of Aquitaine. Arriving in the region of the city of Saintes, he considered it first necessary to inquire whether the observance of Christianity flourished in those places. He received an answer than which he could hear nothing more gladly: the religion of Christian worship was fervent everywhere there.

He went on to ask who presided there in the episcopal chair, and gladly heard that Leontius [Note: [Col. 0743] Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux. On him see Venantius Fortunatus, poems, books I and IV of the new edition.] supervised the Church’s governance, a man endowed with the dignity of divine wisdom and human learning. Rejoicing that the first auspices of the prosperity he desired smiled upon him, Maclovius conceived hope from the agreement of circumstances that henceforth all things should turn out according to his wish.

He therefore confidently sent chosen envoys from his own company to the bishop, set out in order the reason for his journey, and humbly requested that a place to live might be granted him. Filled with a prophetic spirit, Leontius rejoiced that God had visited him by providing the consolation of a brotherly fellowship. Freely and gladly extending his hand of generosity, he gave him a suitable dwelling-place, prepared, in accordance with the Apostle’s command (2 Corinthians 8), to supply the other’s need from his own abundance. The local people too, delighted by the fragrance of his good conduct, supported him and his companions with many gifts, themselves wishing to share in the fruits of another’s labour.

## CHAPTER XXII

This was not occurring by chance, but by the providential plan of the Divinity: the more widely the pilgrimage of so great a man was reported in different places, the more widely knowledge of his name was magnified. The daughter of a count who ruled the district of Saintes was walking for exercise with her attendants through her father’s garden. There, as she walked carelessly, she was wounded by the venomous bite of a hidden serpent; she groaned and gave all a great occasion for lamentation. Her father mourned inconsolably; her mother knew not how to restrain her maternal sorrow as she saw her daughter’s life wavering between hope and fear. The entire household lamented; the whole city was afflicted by funeral mourning.

At last grief admitted this single counsel: since no human aid could avail, divine help should be sought from blessed Maclovius. As it was advised, so it was done. They came to Maclovius’s feet, and the petition of those asking faithfully was not disappointed. The bishop resorted to the aid of prayer and blessed exorcized water. He sprinkled a leaf of ivy with it and laid the leaf upon the place of the wound. The force of the venomous pest could not withstand the power of the sacred blessing.

One could see the deadly poison drawn out from the deepest entrails and contracted at the place covered by the ivy leaf. Dripping thence drop by drop to the ground, it left the girl’s body unharmed. Thus through Maclovius’s merits the girl’s health was restored, her parents’ joy increased, and the novelty of the miracle strengthened in faith in Christ all who saw and heard it. The father, not ungrateful for the benefit, granted an estate from his own property to God’s servant, so that he might have resources to give to those suffering need for Christ’s sake.

## CHAPTER XXIII

The venerable Leontius, seeing blessed Maclovius glorified by merits and miracles, began to rejoice greatly within himself that divine compassion had chosen to console him with so great and such a guest. Therefore, when he was about to visit his diocese, he urgently compelled Maclovius with entreaties to go with him.

They came to an estate which antiquity called Bream, nobly distinguished by two churches in honour of God. In order to bind Maclovius more closely to himself, Leontius assigned one of them to his dwelling, retaining the other for his own jurisdiction. How much this pleased God was clearly shown by the miracle with which the Lord there gladdened them in their presence.

At daybreak, when the bishop wished to wash, a household boy hurried off to draw water. While drawing it carelessly, his foot slipped, he fell into the well, and, overwhelmed by the mass of water, died. Suddenly cries and groans arose, and people crowded together from every side. The grieving father rushed up; the wretched mother did not delay to come, dishevelled in appearance, her body uncovered and her hair loose, moving all to compassion. The delightful flower of youth moved everyone, especially the parents: for the boy was already twelve years old. The countless multitude of those gathering increased the commotion, for the boy was of noble family.

Leontius, keeping sorrow in his heart but retaining hope and good faith in the Lord, ordered the dead body to be carried into the church which he had assigned to Saint Maclovius’s portion. Until dawn of the following day, the parents kept watch beside the body according to solemn custom. But the servants of God, spending the night in prayer, did not despair of God’s goodness.

When morning came, Saint Maclovius sent everyone out of the church, keeping only two monks with himself, that with them he might more intimately entreat the Lord. With them, then, after bending the knee seven times, he prayed to God with all the devotion he could until he perceived the soul of the innocent boy restored to his stiffened limbs. When the boy rose and stood present as testimony to the miracle, it is superfluous to repeat at length the joy of the bishops, the astonishment of the people standing by, and the thanks all rendered with one voice to the Almighty.

For the Divinity’s miracle, shown to commend the sanctity of his servant, was spread more widely by the nobility of the boy restored to life and received more gladly through the devoted love of his parents. O man praiseworthy in every respect! O saint comparable with saints in the magnificence of miracles! He too, following the example of his Lord Jesus, raised three dead persons by the most efficacious invocation of the Trinity.

## CHAPTER XXIV

Nor shall I omit from the catalogue of such great miracles what was also done in the district of Saintes. A certain woman named Bona, who lived her life laudably in the continence of widowhood, had been overwhelmed by blindness for fourteen years. When she was faithfully brought before the gaze of the holy man, she was restored to her former sight.

## CHAPTER XXV

Moreover, the people in Brittany who had harassed the man of God and, through the wickedness of their obstinacy, had brought upon themselves and their land his curse, could not escape the vengeance of that curse. The land, cursed because of the deeds of the impious, was rendered barren and unfruitful, both in crops and in fruits of every kind. Its inhabitants, consumed by a thousand forms of disease, began variously to waste away: some were crippled by weakness of their limbs; others were disfigured by leprosy; others lamented the loss of sight; some found themselves deprived of speech; others bewailed the impairment of hearing. There was none among them who escaped the judgment of heavenly vengeance.

At last, learning their fault too late through punishment for it, and neither wishing nor being able any longer to endure the affliction of curse and retribution, they took counsel together and resolved humbly to implore pardon from the holy man. Having therefore sent an embassy to him, they asked with contrition of heart to be released from that curse, promising that, if he would deign to return to them, thereafter they would obey him without any opposition.

Maclovius, a lover of compassion and mercy, when he received the repentance of his countrymen, referred the chief decision to the venerable Leontius. Leontius judged that the matter should be referred to God himself. Both, imposing upon themselves a three-day fast, prayed that the Lord would reveal to them what ought to be done concerning it.

While he was praying, an angel of the Lord stood beside Maclovius and conveyed to him these words from God:

> “You must, O friend of God, revisit Brittany, remove every curse, heal the people with a saving blessing, and restore the land’s fertility. Thereafter you must return to Saintes, for there you are shortly to die.”

The holy man therefore returned to his homeland in accordance with the angelic revelation. He sanctified the land and its people with his blessing, and commended them in prayer to God, the giver of all good things. Thus the entire land was filled with abundant fertility through his blessing, though it had formerly been condemned through his curse. It was thereby evident to all that the compassionate bishop had not imposed the curse through any intemperance of ill will, but rather through the benevolence of salutary severity, so that through this necessity they might at least be drawn unwillingly to repentance.

The Bretons, having obtained the fulfilment of their desire, joined together—prince and nobles of the kingdom, clergy and bishops alike—and earnestly asked the blessed man to remain with them for the rest of his life, so that through living with him they might deserve to acquire God’s grace. He refused that this could be done, humbly explaining to them the reason for its impossibility. He foretold that the time of his calling was imminent and said that, from the angel’s words, he had learned that this had been appointed for him by God at Saintes. The Bretons, weeping and fearing that traces of heavenly wrath might still remain, judged themselves unworthy to have such a patron either in his life or in his death. They accompanied him with the joy of peace and love, and only with difficulty at last allowed themselves to be separated from him.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Having returned to Saintes, he worked more vigilantly at guarding himself night and day because he had learned more certainly that the Lord was near, so that at whatever hour he came, he might open to the one knocking while watchful and prepared. For he who had fought the good fight through so long a lifetime and had at last finished the course claimed, by reason of his religious life, the crown of righteousness which the just judge had laid up for him.

He gave back to the earth what was earth’s; heaven received his spirit with the rejoicing of its saints. Led in a wondrous way by the hands of angels, he went to receive the reward of his labours. For having lived an angelic life on earth, he now rejoices eternally in heaven in the company of angels. He lived one hundred and thirty years and died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September [16 August].

## CHAPTER XXVII

Bishop Leontius, rejoicing in the treasure sent to him from heaven and destined to benefit his successors eternally, resolved to honour him with the distinguished office of burial. He built a new church and buried his body there with fitting reverence as an instrument of the Holy Spirit. Nor could he whose merit was now in heaven remain hidden on earth. For on the very day when he was placed in the mausoleum, sight was restored to two blind persons, and one possessed was freed from demonic assault. On the third day after burial, healing was restored to a crippled man and speech to a mute person.

Afterwards the Lord worked there through the merits of Saint Maclovius miracles so great that no tongue can recount them and no parchment contain them. May almighty God help us through the many and frequent intercessions of this saint, and all who celebrate his praises: he who lives and reigns through the eternal ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0747]

# THE LIFE OF SAINT THEODARD, BISHOP OF MAASTRICHT AND MARTYR, BY SIGEBERT OF GEMBLOUX

*(Bollandists, Acts of the Saints, September, vol. III, 10 September, p. 580.)*

## CHAPTER ONE. His life before the bishopric of Maastricht; the virtues by which he adorned his church

[Col. 0747A]

Blessed Theodard, born in Gaul, was distinguished by the noble lineage of his parents, being destined to become an ornament of the kingdom and a glory of the Church. At that time the kingdom of the Franks was ruled by Lothar, son of Chilperic [Note: [Col. 0747C] The Acts of the Saint, written by Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, who flourished at the end of the eleventh century and the beginning of the following century, are here reprinted from Surius’s edition, which I shall correct here and there from two manuscripts. Thus, from those manuscripts, I have here printed “Lothar, son of Chilperic” instead of “Clothar, son of Childeric,” as it is found in Surius. First, it is certain that the father of Lothar II, king of the Franks, of whom this passage treats, was a king of Soissons named Chilperic, not Childeric. I preferred, however, to write “Lothar” rather than “Clothar” from the said manuscripts, because the former reading appears to me more genuine: in Sigebert of Gembloux’s *Chronicle* and in his other works, I have everywhere found “Lothar.” He reigned from 584, when his father Chilperic was murdered, until 628—not from 587 until 631, as Sigebert maintains in the *Chronicle*. He is also mistaken when he says that this same Lothar II obtained the monarchy of all France in 610; that occurred in 613.], resembling his grandfather Lothar in name and bravery, the son of Louis [Note: [Col. 0748C] Or Clovis I.], who enrolled the Frankish people—baptized with himself by blessed Remigius [Note: [Col. 0748C] His feast will be given on 1 October.]—in the military service of the eternal King.

Thus under Lothar II, Theodard, advancing from childhood to the crossroads of adolescence, despised the broad way upon which he saw many of the called wandering to the left; and he chose the narrow way by which the few chosen proceed to the right. [Col. 0747B] Through the devotion of his parents he was committed to monastic discipline, and willingly bore Christ’s light yoke. Since, according to the Lord’s saying, a good tree cannot bear bad fruit (Matthew 7:18), he showed in the flower of his growing years how sweet and how abundant a fruit he would bear in its season. Indeed, the grace of God, which had preceded him so that he might will what was good, also followed him so that he might be able to accomplish it.

For just as the earth bears fruit more abundantly when favourable weather smiles upon the season, so in the reign of King Lothar [Note: [Col. 0748C] The following matters are to be referred to Lothar’s monarchy, that is, to the period from 613 to 628.], under the favour of tranquillity in public affairs, the holy Church bore more abundant fruit in God’s saints, whom no storm of worldly affairs, or only a rare one, troubled outwardly. For while wars raged through almost the whole world—while the Lombards afflicted Italy, which they had invaded only recently [Col. 0748A] [Note: [Col. 0748C] The Lombards entered Italy in 568.], and while Asia and Africa were attacked now by Persians, now by Saracens—Gaul alone, inhabited by the Franks, enjoyed secure peace; and while other peoples fought for survival, the Franks fought for glory.

2. Yet this must be ascribed not so much to human valour as to divine mercy, which at that time had armed the leading men of kingdom and Church with prudence and courage, holiness and wisdom, so that through them kingdom and Church prospered far and wide. Almost the whole world felt how highly God valued them, especially in this: at that time the Roman Emperor Heraclius, having defeated the Persians, brought back to Jerusalem the cross of Christ, which the Persians had carried away when they burned Jerusalem and had held for fifteen years; and he ordered its feast of Exaltation to be celebrated [Note: [Col. 0748C] Consult the standard writers on ecclesiastical history.].

That we may know who those were by whose example or institution Theodard emulated the better gifts, let us gather the unknown from the known: the many from the few, the distant from the near. Among them Arnulf, bishop of Metz and formerly mayor of the palace, was preeminent [Note: [Col. 0748C] The Acts of this saint were discussed on 18 July, where in the preliminary commentary, §2, it is demonstrated that before his episcopate he had not been mayor of the royal palace. Saint Arnulf is here followed by Saint Eligius, whose entry is to be given on 1 December, and Saint John Agnus, given on 25 July.]; Eligius, formerly a goldsmith and later bishop of Noyon; and John of Tongeren, likewise chosen by God from lay status to be bishop by the same sign as the first Aaron: his staff also, which he carried in his hand, was fixed in the ground at an angel’s command, and grew green, put forth leaves, flowered, and bore fruit. By imitating such men Theodard advanced in the twofold knowledge; attached to their side, he was known and dear to the princes of the palace [Note: [Col. 0748C] What is asserted here about Saint Theodard appears highly suspect to me.].

[Col. 0748C] 3. The fame of his name had already risen to the throne of [Col. 0749A] Dagobert, who reigned after his father Lothair [Note: [Col. 0749D] After Lothair II, who died in 628, his son Dagobert I reigned until the beginning of 638, when he died. Sigebert wrongly places Dagobert’s death in the year 645 in his Chronicle.]; and after the report, the truth of the matter also brought him into the king’s notice. And now God, who was able to make all grace abound in his servant Theodard, was preparing an occasion to make this man, too, worthy of great renown among men of many names. For under Dagobert, amid the happier fortunes of that age, the grace of the Holy Spirit kindled far more persons to labor for the winning of souls for God by founding monasteries.

First among these comes before us Landelinus, transformed from a robber into a herald of the faith, who made the monastery of Lobbes the foundation of his devotion. Aldegundis established the bridal chamber of her virginity for Christ her bridegroom in the monastery of Maubeuge. Her sister Waldetrudis [Col. 0749B] sowed the sixtyfold fruit of continence in the monastery of Châteaulieu. Her husband Vincent, having conquered the world, raised God’s banner at Hautmont. And what need is there to proclaim the nobility of Gertrude of Nivelles, whose name’s glory is more widely spread than all Gaul? As these cultivators of the faith begged the Lord of the harvest to send many laborers into the plentiful harvest, he directed foreign laborers from regions beyond the sea: Bertuinus, Etto, and others; Foillan with his brothers Ultan and Fursey. Of these, Foillan founded the monastery of Fosses and consecrated it by his martyrdom. [Note: [Col. 0749D] Our predecessors have treated most of the saints named in this section: Fursey on 16 January; Aldegundis on the 30th of the same month; Gertrude on 17 March; Waldetrudis on 9 April; Ultan on 1 May; Landelinus on 15 June; Etto on 10 July; and finally Vincent on the 14th of that month. Foillan will be treated on 31 October, and Bertuinus on 11 November. Of the monasteries which Sigebert in this same section writes were founded under Dagobert I, there is none whose beginnings may safely be believed to precede that king’s death, or the beginning of 638. Indeed, I would almost venture to say that Sigebert committed as many errors as he here asserts monasteries to have been founded under the said king.]

4. But the eye of divine providence foresaw that, among so many and such men, his beloved Theodard should not lack a place in which he too, having raised a triumphal arch, might [Col. 0749C] portray his victories and hang up the spoils captured from enemies. Sigebert, reigning in Austrasia after his father Dagobert, honored royal power with devotion to divine religion, so as to prove that the miracle God had shown concerning him was not idle. For when Saint Amand was catechizing him, when he was scarcely forty days old, at the end of the prayer, since none of those standing around responded “Amen,” God opened his mouth, and he answered in a clear voice, in the hearing of all: “Amen.” [Note: [Col. 0750D] Saint Amand was treated on 6 February, where the same miracle is reported in chapter 4, no. 17, of his Life written by his disciple Baudemund. Sigebert of Gembloux also relates it in the Life of King Saint Sigebert, published for 1 February, chapter 2, no. 5, and likewise in his Chronicle under the year 633; but it must be held to have occurred three years earlier.]

This king, making God the heir of his possessions, established twelve monasteries; but he applied himself more earnestly to founding the monastery of Stavelot, while Grimoald, mayor of the palace, cooperated with him in building a monastery at the place called [Col. 0750A] Malmedy. Having taken counsel together with Remaclus, bishop of Tongeren, and Cunibert, [Note: [Col. 0750D] He is entered in the Roman Martyrology on 12 November.] bishop of Cologne, to whose dioceses those places belonged, they found no one more suitable than Theodard to place over those sites, so that he might lay a spiritual foundation upon the supreme cornerstone, Christ Jesus (Eph. 2:10).

5. But Theodard, knowing that presiding over others is a burden, not an honor, for one who does not know how to govern, preferred to be an abbot rather than be called one, so that, becoming all things to all people, he might gain all. At last he showed himself such that both kingdom and Church might deservedly say to him: “Your wisdom is greater, and your works greater, than the report which we heard concerning you.”

Remaclus labored with fatherly concern for the government of the bishopric of Tongeren, but [Col. 0750B] he was distressed that the yield of its fruits answered his efforts poorly. Wearied therefore by his labors, he turned in mind toward the harbor of the solitary life; from there King Dagobert [Note: [Col. 0750D] Yet in his Chronicle Sigebert writes that Saint Remaclus was ordained bishop of Maastricht in 646, after the death of Dagobert I. He is mistaken in both places; for that holy prelate did not begin to occupy the see, transferred from Tongeren to Maastricht, before 650 or the following year.] had drawn him out to undertake the steering of the ship of the Church. He approached King Sigebert and, pleading the reasons for his incapacity, requested dismissal and the canonical appointment of a pastor for the Church in his place. The matter was referred from the palace to the judgment of the Church. The Church agreed with the palace. Relieved of the burden of the episcopal load, and rejoicing that he had swum clear of the shipwreck of the world, Remaclus sought the harbor of the monastery of Stavelot; there, devoting himself to contemplation, he dwelt with himself.

When a common deliberation had been held concerning the appointment of a replacement bishop, recourse was had to Theodard. Of all men he alone pleased them as the one who ought worthily to preside over all. [Col. 0750C] For, according to the Apostle, because he had ministered well, he had acquired for himself a good standing [Note: [Col. 0750D] In the manuscript of Rouge-Cloître these words are added: “and, faithful in a few things, he was worthy to be set over many.”] (1 Tim. 3:13). Therefore, by the equal consent of Church and palace, and by the unanimous applause of clergy and people, Theodard was chosen, consecrated bishop by Bishop Cunibert, and presided over the Church of Maastricht as the twenty-eighth from Maternus, [Note: [Col. 0750D] He will be treated on 14 September.] the first bishop of the Tungri.

6. Since, as he went from strength to strength, so he was advanced from honor to honor, he held before his mind as a mirror the Apostle Paul, who, while his living voice still speaks, declares what a bishop ought to be. By this teaching, because he conformed himself to all, he drew the affection of all to himself; and although he surpassed all in glory, he was nevertheless beloved by all. [Col. 0751A] He was able to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradicted it (Tit. 1:9), because what he taught by word he demonstrated by example. For by the command and example of the Lord Jesus, because he was greater than all, he was the servant and minister of all. Above all, having put on the armor of God, girding his loins with truth, clothed in the breastplate of righteousness, and with his feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace; fortified with the helmet of salvation, the shield of faith, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, he was strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might, so that he might stand against the snares of the devil and wage war against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavens (Eph. 6:10).

His daily insistence pressed upon him—the care, that is, of all the churches. He permitted nothing slack; he gave no place to idleness, but night and day [Col. 0751B] worked out his salvation. Moreover, mindful that through the prophet Ezekiel God threatens those shepherds who feed themselves and not God’s flock (Ezek. 34:2), he fed God’s flock according to God: not for shameful gain, but willingly; not lording it over the clergy, but becoming from the heart an example to the flock (1 Pet. 5), so that when the chief Shepherd came he might receive the unfading crown of glory.

## CHAPTER II. He instructs Saint Lambert; approaches the king to recover ecclesiastical property; is martyred by its unjust possessors

7. At this time Lambert, of good natural disposition, was growing up in good promise. His father, the most illustrious man Aper, had entrusted him to the man of God Landoald, [Note: [Col. 0751D] We have treated this saint on 19 March.] archpriest of Bishop Amand, [Col. 0751C] so that he might imbue the boy’s years with regular discipline and liberal learning. Delighted that Landoald had initiated his son, as he wished, into the rudiments of both kinds of knowledge, the father also entrusted him to Theodard’s instruction, so that the more fully he drank from the learning of many men, the more abundantly he might advance in grace.

Just as silver is improved when it is gilded by a goldsmith, so Lambert, shining with the silver of natural talent, was improved by the added instruction of Theodard and was adorned all the more, as though by gold laid over it. Theodard, having experienced in himself that all things work together for good for those who love God (Rom. 8:28), rejoiced that everything turned out favorably for him, and a good yield of fruits lightened his labor. Therefore, although by God’s grace and his own diligence he restored many things, this concern afflicted him more sharply: he knew that the possessions of his Church had been plundered by domestic enemies and unjust robbers, and that, alienated from the Church for a long time, they had passed from right into the possession of the unjust.

8. He grieved that this had happened through the recognized character of the times and the negligence of his predecessors: through the character of the times, because security bred by the long repose of peace had turned many away from the regard of divine fear; neglect of good morals had crept in through abundance of possessions; and, external wars having ceased, they were endangered by internal wars of the soul. Hence, since injustice prevailed everywhere against the Church of God—an injustice that always directs its first assaults against the innocence of the good—[Col. 0752B] no one’s justice came to the aid of God’s Church, and no power of princes protected it.

No slight grief lay upon Bishop Theodard: the Church of Maastricht had been mutilated of a great quantity of its possessions, and for about thirty years no one had contended, or even lodged a protest, for the right of God’s Church. Amand, whose holiness ought not to be praised in few words, had been compelled by the entreaties of King Dagobert to accept the bishopric of Maastricht, after Bishop John died, because he had baptized King Sigebert and received him from the font. But, with stormy tempests rushing from every side against the ship of the Church, reflecting on the Apostle’s saying that no one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs (2 Tim. 2:4), after three years he left the bishopric and withdrew into the harbor [Col. 0752C] of his desired repose. His archpriest Landoald suitably performed his duties for nine years, but could not stand up for the Church because he possessed no pontifical authority. All these circumstances were more favorable to the robbers. Concerning Remaclus, because he had been unable to stretch out his arms against the torrent of flooding evils, Theodard trusted his own eyes and ears. [Note: [Col. 0751D] In this section Sigebert of Gembloux advances not only falsehoods but also accusations injurious to the saints. He says that Saint Theodard grieved because, partly “through the negligence of his predecessors,” the Church of Maastricht had suffered a great loss of its possessions and had endured it for many years. So that you may understand with greater difficulty that those men were entirely free from blame, he assumes that the alienation of sacred goods was known to them and yet declares that “for about thirty years no one had contended, or even lodged a protest, for the right of God’s Church.”

The reasons he adds for such dissimulation do not wholly erase, as is evident to anyone considering the matter, the stain of negligence and excessive dejection of spirit which he had earlier cast upon Saint Theodard’s predecessors. To these he adds Saint Landoald, the archpriest, who, he says, administered the Church of Maastricht in a vicariate capacity for nine years after Saint Amand had resigned a bishopric accepted at the entreaties of King Dagobert, who died in 6[.....]8. These assertions are certainly false. Saint Remaclus succeeded Saint Amand immediately in 650 or the following year; it is established that Amand occupied the see at the end of 649, and that he had presided no longer than about three years under King Saint Sigebert.

In no. 27 and following I have proved that Saint Theodard suffered in 668 or 669; Sigebert wrongly asserts in his Chronicle that this happened in 658. Whether we adopt our own view or that of the erring Sigebert, thirty years did not elapse between our saint’s martyrdom and the death of Saint John Agnus. Therefore he too must be added to Saints Amand and Remaclus, upon whose negligence and excessive dissimulation the same Sigebert expressly lays the blame that Saint Theodard found the Church despoiled of a great part of its possessions. But from where did this author learn that this should be reckoned a fault in the said holy bishops? Certainly the anonymous writer of the Life of Saint Theodard contains nothing from which this can be forced.

“For after all these things,” he says above, [Col. 0753C] chapter 1, no. 8, “had been investigated in order, and the accounts alike faithfully examined, it was discovered that certain estates [Col. 0753D] had been held by their fathers less than justly. And, turning over within the secret recesses of his heart this concern for the Church’s possessions that had been badly damaged, he began to doubt which he preferred: whether to allow matters to remain as he had found them, or to proceed in this business and appeal to royal ears. At last, trusting in the Lord as protector and not fearing what man might do to him, he stood firm in his resolve,” set out for Childeric II, king of Austrasia, and was slain on the journey.

From the anonymous account and from the fact that Childeric was at Maastricht in his palace on 6 September 667, it is sufficiently inferred that our holy bishop learned no earlier than the said day and year that the goods of his Church were held by unjust possessors. Undoubtedly he would have claimed them earlier in accordance with his office, had this become known to him earlier. The same [Col. 0754C] must be presumed of Saint Remaclus. Since he had found King Saint Sigebert exceptionally devoted to him—as the benefactions with which the king enriched him attest—he would easily have recovered the alienated goods. Nor should one think otherwise of Saint Amand, who, requesting from Pope Martin I release from the burden of the episcopate, did not mention even once the property of his Church unjustly occupied, but addressed only the corrupted morals of the clergy. Even if some persons had received estates less justly from Saint John Agnus and afterward possessed them in bad faith, that saint is not therefore to be blamed: he could have been deceived by fraud, which Theodard eventually uncovered.]

Having himself undertaken the governance of the Lord’s ship, he feared the reproach of inconstancy should he yield his place under the pressure of dangers.

9. Therefore, lest the long impunity of injustice become still more deeply rooted, he girded himself manfully and, standing in defense of the camp of the Church, did not cease to cry out. Raising his voice like a trumpet, he declared their crimes to the people and [Col. 0753A] their sins to the robbers. Like an eagle standing over God’s house, he foresaw the devices of the wicked with the keenness of his eyes, and defended himself with his claws. Since his life was upright and his word sound and irreproachable, the one who opposed him respected him, having nothing evil to say of him. The favor of King Sigebert [Note: [Col. 0754D] Our saint did not occupy the see under King Sigebert, unless perhaps for a very brief period.] protected him against all men, for the king, a lover of divine religion, had eyes of dovelike simplicity.

When Sigebert died, his brother Clovis gave the kingdom of Austrasia, which Sigebert had held, to his own son Childeric. [Note: [Col. 0754D] After Clovis II, his son Chlothar III became monarch of the Franks; in 660 he yielded the kingdom of Austrasia to his brother Childeric II.] Then all malice and injustice prevailed in the kingdom, and a violent whirlwind of domestic storm thundered against the Church. But Theodard, because he was not a hireling, did not flee from the face of the wolves, but stood more steadfastly [Col. 0753B] against them on behalf of his sheep. And because the Shepherd who is good in his very being had said, “No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13), he was not a deaf hearer in this matter, but was ready to lay down his life for the sheep.

10. Yet, lest he leave anything untried, he resolved to approach King Childeric and lawfully complain before him of the injustices inflicted upon the Church, in the hope that through royal judgment the Church might recover her possessions. Divinely instructed by the oracle of his own mind that the time of his passion was impending, he set his house in order; bidding a final farewell to all, entrusting his sheep to him who had entrusted them to himself, and guided by steadfastness of mind, he set out with a few companions.

But the sons of Belial, who because of the hardness of their unrepentant hearts were storing up wrath [Col. 0753C] for themselves, could by no means be brought into any way of repentance. Knowing that justice would not answer for them in any respect if a dispute concerning the Church’s seized possessions were litigated before the men of the palace, they heaped evil upon evil. In the peril born of desperation they plotted the death of the innocent bishop and carefully spied out his route.

The holy man, steadfast in his righteous purpose, armed by the living and effective word of God saying, “Do not fear those who kill only the body” (Matt. 10:28), had already passed far beyond the boundaries of his diocese and had halted in the district popularly called Alisatia, while his journey was still prospering. And behold, a band of God’s enemies emerged from ambush and rushed upon the innocent man’s death [Col. 0754A] with leveled spears. Protected by the sure shield of patience, he wished to invite them to the good of peace; but, because they were not children of peace, peace, finding no place in them to rest, returned to its friend.

As wolves surround a lamb, the impious surrounded the pious man. Though he raised his eyes to heaven and prayed for them after the example of Jesus hanging on the cross, they assailed him with insults and threw him to the ground. And because power cannot satisfy anger, they cut into pieces the head anointed with holy oil and tore the holy body limb from limb.

11. Thus the earth was indeed given into the hands of the impious; but his spirit, purged of every earthly dross by the fire of suffering and tested like gold in a furnace, returned to the Lord who made him. Surely the faith [Col. 0754B] which opened the heavens to the protomartyr Stephen, so that he saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:35) to assist him, opened the heavens also to the martyr Theodard and caused him, bearing the marks of Jesus, to be enrolled with the martyrs in the book of life.

God, who noted the unbelief of the Jews when he said, “Unless you see signs and wonders, you will not believe” (John 4:48), notes our unbelief also: we do not judge the merits of those pleasing to God from the power of their deeds, but from the display of signs. For signs do not make a person blessed, but show that he has lived a blessed life; and by the novelty of events they lead us to venerate the saints. Behold Theodard, who had been an instrument of the Holy Spirit, lay slain by the impious, as though cheap and despised, and as though [Col. 0754C] struck down and humbled by God. But divine mercy removed from humankind every stumbling-block concerning him when it showed manifest signs in testimony to his holiness.

## CHAPTER III. A woman punished with blindness and restored to sight; funeral rites celebrated by a great multitude; miracles at the place of first burial; the body removed thence and deposited at Liège

12. A boy from the household of the holy bishop, who alone, while the others had fled, kept watch beside the lifeless body, grieved that the limbs of the blessed body had been scattered from one another and endeavored by every means to join them. Fitting limb to limb or part to part, [Col. 0755A] he had nothing with which to bind them. Indeed, after committing their crime, the enemies of justice had also carried off all the baggage. The boy did what alone he could: he bound together with the bands of his clothing all the limbs he could join. When his own bands were still insufficient, he began to lose heart. Turning over many thoughts within himself, he went, on the counsel of his own mind, to the nearest village, hoping that God’s aid would not fail him; nor was his hope disappointed. For on his way he met a poor woman, occupied with feeding sheep and drawing thread from a distaff as she spun.

He addressed the woman, humbly begged her to give him thread, explained why he asked, and unfolded the whole matter in order. Hearing the severity of the execrable crime, she was at first horrified and astonished. Then, moved almost to tears by human sympathy, she said: “What you ask, O boy, I would willingly give, but there is a definite reason why I must refuse. I owe my daily stint to the mistress whose maidservant I am; if it should prove short, I shall not suffer without punishment and shall not escape the loss.” She spoke; then, preferring compassion of heart to fear, she willingly gave the thread to the petitioner.

13. Having obtained what he desired, the boy returned as quickly as possible; and, lest he be weary of his labor, he received from God a consolation greater than his request. For he found two lights shining on either side, at the martyr’s head and feet. Who would not marvel at your mighty works, O Christ? Because Theodard had been light in the Lord and had walked as a child of light, you, the true light enlightening every person, through angelic ministry provided the service of light for the funeral rites of him whom you had called from the darkness of the world to [Col. 0755C] the true and eternal light.

Divine power confirmed this miracle by a greater miracle, so that the martyr’s name and merit might become known more swiftly and widely. The woman who had shortened her allotted task in service to him, after bringing the sheep back to their folds in the evening, rendered her daily stint to her mistress. When the mistress perceived that it was short, accusing the maid of fraud, she struck her head with a heavy blow. But God’s mercy acquitted the maid of fraud: the mistress was suddenly struck with blindness of the eyes and cried out in lamentation to the servant, while the servant too cried out, pitying her mistress. The household made the matter public; the report astonished the whole village. Before all, the maid explained the cause of the blindness inflicted, and urged that, in order that the fault might be forgiven, [Col. 0755D] her mistress should be reconciled to the bishop, so that the light which the offense had taken from her might, when obtained from God, come back and restore her.

14. Distress compelled the mistress, trusting the servant’s words, to seek a remedy for her misery. Led by the servant, she came to the place where the venerable body lay, a body whose scattered condition was pitiable to all who saw it. The mistress confessed her guilt in unjustly striking the maid; and, that she might deserve to obtain pardon, she sought to appease the grace of the holy martyr by vows and gifts. When has it been difficult for God to hear the prayers of the wretched who faithfully cry to him? Having obtained forgiveness, the woman rejoiced in restored sight. Seeing the limbs of the holy body [Col. 0756A] bound with her threads, she at last recognized how greatly she had sinned in striking a guiltless maid devoted to the holy martyr.

All wept for joy; all cried, “Praise to God! Thanks to God!” The reverence due to the martyr increased; the report flew through all the surrounding country and spread farther through the entire province. Wherever one turned one’s eyes, one could see throngs gathering. The mistress of the household, who was the cause and witness of so great a miracle, gave herself wholly to the grace of the holy martyr, inviting everyone by word and example to the service of celebrating the funeral. The turn of events taught them to grieve for a stranger, while the compassion inherent in human nature drew forth tears. For who could see without tears that a man once of such great nobility in the world, [Col. 0756B] of such dignity in the Church, and of such holiness before God, required even burial?

15. Accordingly, all pressed for the proper completion of the funeral rites. Some dried the wounds with soft cloths; others reserved the garments stained with holy blood as a means of obtaining his protection. They placed the sufficiently lamented limbs upon a bier and spread precious coverings over them. The mistress of the household secured a burial place and, according to her agreement, caused a tomb to be prepared at the place called Nec. [Note: [Col. 0755] Near Landau, an imperial town in the diocese of Speyer.] When the coffin containing the body was raised, now these, now those gladly took turns in bearing its weight. Others went ahead to show level roads to the bearers. With so great a multitude of every rank and age and of both sexes, with such reverence of humanity and devotion, the funeral rites of the holy martyr [Col. 0756C] were celebrated, and the body was honorably buried.

The cause that checked the tears of all was their belief that they ought to rejoice: they considered themselves so valued by God that, unexpectedly, he had sent them a patron of such merit, one who would be their protection or remedy against every adversity. Bands of sick persons gathered from every side, hoping through the merits of the new martyr to obtain from God remedies for their illnesses. How many works of mercy, how many benefits of healing, how frequent illuminations of the blind, how many cures of feverish persons occurred there through Theodard’s intercession is attested by many seats of paralytics and by numerous memorial objects hanging there, affixed by the inhabitants, so that through them the memory of posterity might recount [Col. 0756D] how great the grace of God shone there through Theodard’s name.

16. Spreading far and wide, the report entered the city of the Wangiones, now called Worms; and after filling the ears and tongues of the people with much whispering, it made its way even to the bishop of the city. When the bishop heard of the blessed Father’s departure, after long sighs drawn from the depths of his breast he was torn by conflicting emotions, for he was both saddened and glad. He was saddened because a monstrous crime had been committed within his diocese; but he was glad because heaven had granted his diocese the patronage of a new martyr.

The report advanced further and reached the city of Speyer, [Col. 0757A] which antiquity called that of the Nemetes; nor did it withhold its course from the city of Strasbourg, called Strazborch in the German tongue. The report traveled through the whole region watered by the Rhine more swiftly than the wind. Nor does the Rhine’s water flow more swiftly or farther than the report of this event ran; not content to roam within the bounds of the nearer bank, it reached the boundaries of Germany on both sides.

The bishop of the Wangiones, more deeply concerned than all others by this event, invited to himself the bishops of neighboring cities and summoned the chief men and nobles of the entire province. He entrusted to their counsel what he ought to do regarding this deed which the Lord had done and shown to them: whether it was permissible to remove the holy bishop’s body from a less worthy place and transfer it to a greater church. It is easy for a decision to be carried where [Col. 0757B] the will of all breathes as one. From their common counsel the devotion of all conceived one agreement: for the martyr’s greater glory, his body ought to be transferred from there.

17. On the day appointed for this, all assembled, and the number of the gathering people was no more countable than the stars of heaven. They were already preparing for the work; the tomb of the holy martyr was about to be opened. But “there is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel against the Lord” (Prov. 21:30), because the order of nature, serving the Lord of nature, resisted those who themselves were resisting. Heaven suddenly grew terrible, and by its terror shook the earth. The rushing murmur of winds foretold a storm; the immediate flashing of lightning dazzled the eyes; thunder louder than usual terrified the ears and minds of all. [Col. 0757C] Such a tempestuous flood of rain burst forth that, if it had continued, it could have sufficed to create a deluge.

As all these things threatened immediate death, everyone fled. They abandoned what they had undertaken from their own hearts, and because they had not asked the Lord’s mouth concerning it, they understood that they had thought against God. “Who has ever been God’s counselor?” (Isa. 40:13). So that by this miracle also Theodard’s glory might shine far and wide, God had drawn together from afar and broadly so many thousands of people, so that while all proclaimed one man’s merits, God might be blessed by all through his name.

18. When the people of Maastricht were informed of their bishop’s death, the magnitude of their grief showed the love with which they burned toward him. His loving fatherhood had sunk deeply into all their hearts; they recalled the great diligence of their father for the Church’s welfare, for which he had resisted enemies unto blood. Each had a personal reason [Col. 0757D] to mourn the bishop’s death in a particular way.

But Lambert, who during Theodard’s life had been the other hope of the Church of Maastricht, had through the development of his good disposition reached the point that, upon the death of his bishop, the whole Church leaned upon him and rested in him. He mourned his teacher’s death more than all others, because the teacher had loved him more than all others. Yet, after the wound of grief had been inflicted upon his heart, taking up the shield of steadfastness, he devoted himself wholly to recovering at least his teacher’s body. Traversing the long road with the swift flight of desire, he came to the place [Col. 0758A] where the body of his departed father lay in a foreign land. When he had shed the tears owed by a son to his father, he disclosed to the inhabitants of that region the reason for his arrival and asked that none of them oppose his wish to carry back his father’s body.

With one voice all opposed Lambert. They all declared that Theodard was rightfully theirs, since God had freely sent him to them as their patron, had shown them so many miracles through him, and by a great miracle had forbidden the bishops of the province to carry the holy body elsewhere.

19. Thus Lambert returned to Maastricht disappointed of his desire, in order to negotiate the matter with clergy and people. The clergy and people, however, placed the entire weight of the affair upon Lambert. Lambert, undertaking to prevail by another means, prepared abundant expenses and provisions for the journey, gathered much gold and silver and other valuables, and, placing his hope in the Lord, returned to the desired place.

The inhabitants, therefore, perplexed by his return so soon after leaving them, received him with favorable feeling. Attending to his face and bearing, and recognizing the reverence due to him, they attached themselves to him with service. But Lambert won them over by an affection of piety. Repeating the reason for his journey, he added entreaties that they should no longer deny him his Father’s body, saying that it was absurd for a father to be denied to his children and a bishop to his citizens; that it was enough for them that he had consecrated their land with his blood; and that the protection of the holy Father would not fail them, since they had esteemed him highly enough to bury him honorably.

Their firmness was now yielding, because [Col. 0758C] the angelic man had softened them with his honeyed speech. To draw them yet more fully to his purpose, he opened the lap of his generosity and honored each of them with suitable gifts. Nor did he withhold his hand from the poor common people: to each old person and each child he gave a coin, but to pregnant women two coins. Having overcome them by such affection and resourcefulness, and made them his own, he used their hearts according to his will.

20. Therefore, since they no longer resisted but assisted in every way, he took the beloved body of his Father, brought it back with hymns and praises, and buried it honorably in the public village of Liège, as befitted a martyr. Who does not see God’s providence here? God’s providence worked in Lambert when it ordained that Liège should be adorned with Theodard’s tomb. For since Lambert’s place of suffering was designated there, and Liège itself was destined through Lambert to be enlarged into a city and raised by the honor of an episcopal see, God did not wish those whom he foresaw as alone equal among the bishops of the Tungri, by the glory of martyrdom, [Col. 0758D] and also equal by the grace of their merits, to be separated far from one another in burial.

Theodard only forestalled Lambert, so that he should not be the first martyr in this Church; Lambert forestalled Theodard, so that he should not be the only martyr in this Church. O happy Liège! You are adorned by the equal martyrdom of those whose equal patronage before God assists you. Let us magnify God through the glory of his saints, so that through the saints’ merits we may obtain the grace of him who lives and reigns unto ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0759]

# THE DOUBLE LIFE OF SAINT LAMBERT, BISHOP OF MAASTRICHT AND MARTYR, AT LIÈGE IN BELGIUM, BY SIGEBERT OF GEMBLOUX

*(Bollandists, Acts of the Saints, September, vol. V, p. 518.)*

## NOTICE

[Col. 0759]

Sigebert, a monk of Gembloux in Brabant, who flourished at the end of the eleventh and beginning of the twelfth century, says the following in the final chapter of his book *On the Illustrious Writers of the Church*, where he also lists his own works:

> “I also improved the Life of St Lambert, first of all in an elegant style; afterwards, at the request of Henry, archdeacon and dean of the church of St Lambert, I adorned it with comparisons drawn from the ancients, in accordance with the sequence of events. Although they embrace the earlier work, as being simpler, more readily and copy it more carefully; for it is more straightforward in meaning and clearer in language.”

I possess a copy of the Life written by him second, hitherto unpublished, from our college at Louvain. Its first part is marked as transcribed from the second part of the *Hagiology of the Brabanters*, collated with the manuscript of Rouge-Cloître; from that manuscript the second part too has been added in a different hand. The title prefixed to it is: “Life and Passion of Saint Lambert the Bishop, according to Sigebert of Gembloux.”

From Sigebert’s cited words, moreover, I can no longer doubt that the Life published by Chapeaville under the name of Reiner or Rener, monk of St Lawrence near Liège, is not Reiner’s, but Sigebert’s own: namely, the one first composed and mentioned by him. The reason is evident: apart from comparisons inserted in various places, chiefly drawn from the Old Testament, and one miracle of St Lambert in childhood, all the rest in the two Lives is so similar that they differ here and there only in a few words. This difference may indeed be attributed to Sigebert himself, who, while weaving the said comparisons into the earlier Life, could readily have added to the rest this single miracle, learned later, and altered a few phrases, as commonly happens. I could demonstrate this here by citing texts from each Life; but, lest I become too lengthy, I prefer to refer the reader to compare the Life to be published with that published by Chapeaville. [Note: [Col. 0759] We give both, editors of the *Patrologia*.]

I add, however, another argument: namely, Reiner’s own silence. In Book II of *On the Writers of His Monastery*, when he lists his own small works, including several Lives of saints and the *Boulogne Triumph* of St Lambert, he does not so much as mention a Life of the same saint.

# THE EARLIER LIFE OF ST LAMBERT

Published under the name of Rener, monk of Liège, in Chapeaville’s *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*, vol. I, p. 411.

[Col. 0759]

## CHAPTER I. On the noble birth of St Lambert, and during the reign of which princes he was born.

[Col. 0759A]

The glorious Lambert, an accepted martyr of the eternal King and a beloved priest of the true Priest, was born of a distinguished lineage in a village of the town of Maastricht. In him and in his forebears great grace in the Church of God, and great glory and loyalty in the Frankish commonwealth, stood forth conspicuously. Among the orthodox, their unwavering guardianship of Christianity increased reverence for them; their nobility of flesh, through the abundance of their possessions, produced worldly rank and great influence among the magnates of the realm. His father and mother gave immediate distinction to this splendour of ancestry, transmitted to him from afar.

His father, named Aper, excelled among the distinguished men of the royal palace by the rank of his nobility. Tradition received from the fathers says that his mother, pre-eminent among Frankish noblewomen, was called Herisplind.

Now Dagobert, son of the middle Lothair, ruled the kingdom of the Franks. He entrusted the kingdom of Austrasia to his son Sigebert and gave him as guardians Cunibert, bishop of Cologne, and Pippin the First, mayor of the palace, father of the holy women Gertrude and Begga.

[Note: [Col. 0761D] This Pippin was the son of Carloman, who, having taken as wife Sueva from the Aquitanian people, defeated in war the Suebi and other peoples of Germany. He had three children: the daughters Begga and Gertrude—the latter was afterwards enrolled among the saints—and the son Grimoald, who, after his father’s death, became duke and presided over the commonwealth. Barlandus, *Chronicle*, chapter 1.]

## CHAPTER II. That he was first brought up by St Landoald.

What manner of man this boy would be in the world was foreshown from his cradle by God’s providence. Whatever beginnings of good character, whatever features of beauty, nature—or, more truly, the Author of nature himself—usually forms beforehand in a child of good promise, all these were already evident in his infancy. For he was handsome in limb; and beyond what his age suggested, he seemed kindly in expression and affection toward kinsfolk and servants, and thereby worthy of the love of all.

Therefore his father, grateful to God, from whom he expected so much in his son, conformed his own will to the divine will and devoted his son to divine service, toward which he already perceived him in some measure aspiring. And because instruction develops an innate capacity, while disciplined training strengthens the bodily faculties, he chose a holy teacher for his holy son, lest some fault in the master should darken the single eye of the pupil.

Thus he entrusted him, to be initiated into literary study, to Landoald, a man highly esteemed for wisdom and learning, holiness and diligence. This Landoald was a priest of the holy Roman Church. Because, as has been said, he was eminent in holiness and learning, Pope Martin deputed him to St Amand, bishop of Maastricht, to assist in preaching; he came to Gaul and, ordained archpriest of the church of Maastricht, there served God under Bishop Amand. Since that bishop, in his zeal for preaching, had freed himself from the episcopal burden, Landoald carefully and suitably discharged the bishop’s functions; and for nine years he governed the church while the see was vacant, until Remaclus received the cathedra of the church of Maastricht.

## CHAPTER III. On the spring brought forth through the saints’ prayer.

[Col. 0762A]

Landoald, receiving the tender years of the holy boy into his fatherly care, shaped the conduct of his earliest age according to the rule of holy life.

But the illustrious Aper, in order to make his son Lambert more steadfast in his purpose, assigned in perpetual right to him and to his guardian Landoald an estate belonging to him, called Wentershovum. There, once a church had been built, the one might devote himself more earnestly to teaching and the other to learning, inasmuch as they would live farther from worldly vanity.

While work on the church was under way, the craftsmen complained about the lack of drinkable water. The water there, gathered from stagnant marshy runoff, tormented those who drank it more with bitterness than it refreshed them with any sweetness. The holy master and the disciple holier than his master, placing faith in him who gave sweetness to bitter waters from the sea (Exod. 15:25), and who also brought water from the rock (Exod. 17:6), united in a vow and together implored the mercy of the Almighty. The name of the Holy Trinity having been invoked, a place was marked with a staff in the shape of the holy cross; and—an extraordinary thing, though not unfamiliar to faith—a most clear spring issued forth there. It both revealed how much the saints could accomplish with God and, from then until now, has served the inhabitants for every use.

As the fathers hand down the memory of this benefit by recounting it generally to their children, they add to the merits of the saints, since through them they cause the Lord’s name to be blessed. Thus all things worked together for good for Lambert and Landoald, who loved God and were called according to God’s purpose, that they might be saints (Rom. 8:28).

[Col. 0762C]

The vigorous boy, already striving with all his strength to become a perfect man, made such progress under the rod of his holy teacher and received the words of piety and learning with such a pure heart that it is needless to press the matter with words here, when even today we see everywhere the fruit of so profitable a labour overflowing.

The blessed youth, not lightly trained under Landoald, returned to his father. It is not easy to say with what joy each was filled, as the son rejoiced in fatherly affection toward him and the father rejoiced in his son’s progress.

## CHAPTER IV. That Lambert was instructed by St Theodard.

When St Theodard succeeded as bishop of Maastricht, Lambert too was commended to him by his father, to be educated after his example—Theodard being greatly esteemed both in the Church and at court.

At this man’s side Lambert advanced so far that in every matter he was an example to all, not only by conduct but also by miracle.
