For he was truly worthy: lovable in appearance, gracious in conversation, upright in conduct, and accommodating to all, scarcely imitable by anyone. He made little of present things, as he had vowed in childhood, reckoning everything as nothing except the grace of eternal salvation. Cleaving in mind to heavenly things, he offered himself as a holocaust to the Lord.

But what need is there to colour him with artificial pigments of praise sought here and there, when wisdom itself has coloured him with virtues? It is superfluous to seek matter for praise elsewhere, when the Creator fashioned him with such grace that scarcely any defect of nature crept over his whole body, and scarcely any harmful stain appeared in his soul.

## CHAPTER V. On St Lambert’s bodily appearance and gifts of mind.

Yet, since he must be praised, it is fitting that we praise him truthfully. One who either knew his bodily appearance or learned it from those who knew him wrote that he was strong, swift, very agile, steadfast in battle, distinguished in beauty, tall of stature, comely of face, beautiful in hair, bright-eyed, with well-shaped hands, long fingers, and white flesh: from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head he was without reproach.

[Note: [Col. 0763D] He means Godeschalc, who says in chapter 3 of the *Life of St Lambert* that he learned both Lambert’s bodily appearance and his virtues of mind from Theodoenus, St Lambert’s servant.]

And, to come to the goods of the mind: he was full of charity, girded with chastity, grounded in humility, attending at the proper times to prayer, reading, secular business, or household affairs. Behold: you see a man so enriched with gifts of grace and gifts of nature that you would say he had been fashioned by God into a perfect man. Behold, I say, you have a man fitted to adapt himself to every station: if you consider the qualities of a layman, what would you say was lacking in him as a layman? If you seek the qualities of a cleric, you find in him the whole cleric.

These things readily brought it about that he was judged worthy of every honour and of everyone’s love. Accordingly, he was so dear to Bishop Theodard that Theodard would have preferred to choose him as his successor, had he not known it decreed by apostolic authority that priests should not dare, by naming designated persons, to appoint others in their own place, lest the episcopate be thought not a divine gift but a hereditary possession, and lest anyone think that what belongs to God is owed to a human being.

[Note: [Col. 0764D] You have this decree: “On whether the sons of priests are to be ordained,” chapter 7. “No less must the decree of the apostolic rescript be observed,” it says, “which detests hereditary succession in the Church of God.”]

Furthermore, at the royal court Lambert’s name was held in no small esteem: both the king’s care and the multitude of magnates revered him.

## CHAPTER VI. On the recovery of St Theodard’s body.

[Col. 0763D]

When Bishop Theodard had been led by the path of innocence to the glory of martyrdom, the Vangiones, in whose territory he had met his death, did not believe this had occurred by chance, but by the will of God, who orders all things. They hoped that the present protection of a new martyr had been provided for them. Therefore they would not allow his body to be carried away from their district, whose presence they wished to be their eternal glory.

This bitter situation deeply struck the people of Maastricht and, I believe, distressed Lambert’s mind more than all others. But, mastering his grief—for the entire city depended upon him after God—he prepared himself to recover the bishop’s body. At first he was unsuccessful; yet he did not give up. Applying his entire mind and understanding to carrying out his task, he achieved the result he desired.

The holy body having thus been recovered, he buried it at Liège, a public estate, foreseeing that divine providence had appointed that place to be specially consecrated by Lambert’s own blood and name, and was preparing to enlarge it into a city in order to increase the glory of the martyrs.

## CHAPTER VII. That he was elected to the episcopate.

There was much deliberation in the Church of God about who ought to be appointed bishop of the church of Maastricht; much was also discussed on this matter at the court of King Hilderic, who, after the death of his uncle Sigebert, had received the kingdom of Austrasia from his father Clovis. Little by little the report spread from palace to church and from church to the multitude of the people: no one was better than Lambert, and consequently no one was worthier of the episcopate of Maastricht. It belonged to him, by canonical authority, to receive in his own church the fruit of his service.

The Church agreed with the palace; the clergy consented with the people. The hearts of all desired one thing; thousands of people acclaimed with one voice. He declared himself unequal to that burden and thereby deserved all the more to be compelled. At last the man, enriched with honours of holiness and made illustrious by the practices of frugality, agreed to comply with all, so that all might glory in the one man in Christ.

Having attained the summit of lasting religious office, he strove to increase works of mercy, now adorned with the pontifical mitre. Each day he offered a holocaust to the Lord, not from another’s flock. He always directed his counsel and action toward God, and set his heart and feet toward preaching peace. For the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are inherent in Christ substantially, were also present in him accidentally, according to the capacity of human nature. The spirit of counsel flourished outstandingly in him, and whatever he did he governed by the spirit of wisdom.

King Hilderic, seeing that he surpassed all others, valued him above all the leading men of the realm and even above the bishops. He gave him the first place in his heart, at his ears, and upon his lips; believing Lambert’s heart to be an oracle of the Holy Spirit and holding his tongue to be an instrument of truth, he willingly granted him the fullness of his friendship and made him his confidential adviser. As is reported, Lambert was also his *a commentariis*, keeper of records. Thus all Austrasia depended upon Lambert’s heart and mouth, and the entire royal court revered him.

Theodoric, brother of King Hilderic, who ruled in that part of Francia called Neustria, likewise sought Lambert’s presence. Among his magnates and friends he reserved an abundance of favour for him; and if anything in his realm required authorization, it was not thought sufficiently ratified unless it had also been approved by Lambert’s counsel.

## CHAPTER VIII. Which bishops and abbots were contemporaries of St Lambert.

The Frankish kings themselves, Theodoric and Hilderic, although through simplicity they had little wisdom of their own, were nevertheless wise in this: they listened to wise men. For the first degree of wisdom is to be wise; the second, to listen to a wise person. Therefore, because they managed the affairs of their kingdoms by the counsel of Lambert, so holy and prudent a man, and of other holy bishops, the condition of affairs was fair in both kingdoms and the faith of the Church prospered.

At that time there were holy bishops, endowed with learning and wisdom, who administered the second rank of the kingdom in holiness and justice. Foremost among them were Ouen of Rouen, Austregisilus of Bourges, Eligius of Noyon, Vindicianus of Cambrai, Audomar of Thérouanne, Leodegar of Autun, and Faro of Meaux. Lambert shone among them, a golden star of the Church, as the moon shines among lesser fires. Lambert revered them as fathers and elders; by imitating them, he drew some grace from each of them. They, moreover, loved Lambert from their hearts as a son already bringing forth fruits from the flower of youth. They rejoiced that, as by hereditary succession, the governance of the Church would belong to him after them, seeing that he walked blamelessly in all things as righteous before God and humanity (Luke 1:6), and went day by day from strength to strength.

There were also abbots, renowned for holiness both then and now: Bertin, Philibert, and Wandregisel; Ursmar of Lobbes was growing into a novice of Christ. These were Lambert’s contemporaries; such were his companions. Like cherubim, they beat the wings of their virtues, each toward the other, and in God’s praise set the world in motion (Ezek. 10:11). By their merits the Church of God was kept tranquil for a long time, and the condition of the kingdom prospered for a long time.

Afterward, because of the people’s sluggishness, while Jesus slept in the ship of the holy Church, behold, a great disturbance arose upon the sea of this world (Matt. 8:24). The cause of so great a disturbance is easy to learn.

## CHAPTER IX. On the killing of King Hilderic.

The brothers Theodoric and Hilderic ruled the kingdom of Francia in two parts. But because Theodoric was of duller intelligence, Ebroin, mayor of the palace, abused his simplicity and stirred the hatred of all the people against the king. The Franks, turning another man’s envy against Theodoric, deposed him from the throne and, summoning his brother Hilderic from Austrasia, set him over themselves as king.

So long as Hilderic held them, he governed both kingdoms moderately and powerfully. But when he too exceeded due measure and acted too insolently, he could not long stretch out his arms against the torrent. Being harsher than justice allowed, he caused a certain Frankish nobleman, Bodilo, to be beaten against the law while bound to a post; later, caught by that same Bodilo while hunting, he perished. Theodoric recovered the whole kingdom. Ebroin’s malice revived: all whom they found to have supported Hilderic’s party too steadfastly they crushed, slaughtered, deprived of honours, punished by proscription, and banished into exile.

## CHAPTER X. That St Lambert was deprived of his episcopate.

Because no one had been more loyal or more friendly to Hilderic than Lambert, the whole weight of persecution fell upon him. It seemed that nothing had been accomplished by Hilderic’s death if Lambert, Hilderic’s intimate, went away unpunished; for they firmly knew that he would never assent to their faction of iniquity.

Therefore, on Ebroin’s counsel, King Theodoric convened a crowd of bishops in synod. Like dumb dogs unable to bark (Isa. 56:10), they unlawfully deprived other bishops of office on false testimony. And so that no one might remain in the kingdom or Church who would dare to raise the shield of faith in defence of truth, either by Lambert’s example or at his urging—for he dared, more freely than the rest and on behalf of the rest, to oppose injustice—all the devil’s accomplices rose against Lambert, the friend of truth. Having contrived charges of injustice, they deposed him from the episcopate.

The bishop of Cologne is said to have conspired in this wicked faction, led by envious zeal, and by money given to the leading men of the people to have stirred them to hatred of Lambert. He even allowed Pharamund, a cleric of his own church, to be advanced to the episcopate of Maastricht, contrary to right and justice. Because that wretch walked in the counsel of the wicked and sat in the seat of pestilence (Ps. 1:1), what else can be said of him than what Truth says: “He who does not enter by the door into the sheepfold, but climbs in another way, is a thief and a robber; but he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep” (John 10:1–2). “The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy” (ibid., 10).

## CHAPTER XI. That he sought the monastery of Stavelot.

Lambert, the good shepherd, following the example of the Shepherd who is good in essence and ready to lay down his life for his sheep, did not flee like a hireling (John 10:11–12). Rather, he turned aside from the shipwrecking storm of persecution at home. Bearing everything gently, he relinquished the sceptre of his episcopal office, entrusting the care of the sheep to him who washed them in baptism and redeemed them by blood.

He therefore sought the monastery of Stavelot, founded some years earlier by King Sigebert and renowned everywhere for the fervour of its holy religious life. He chose the harbour of monastic quiet and there, living an angelic life for seven years, dwelt with himself. Of the entire household of the church, only two boys remained attached to his service. One of them, named Theodoenus, was the truthful informant and fitting witness to Lambert’s deeds for the man who first wrote the holy man’s Life.

Behold, we have a man set before all as an example of virtues. Knowing that the supreme Master alone had commanded him to learn from him, he sought rest for his soul in humility, gentleness of heart, and patience (Matt. 11:29). In obedience he conformed himself as co-heir to his Christ, who obeyed the Father unto death (Phil. 2:8).

What, I ask, was it like to see a man noble in age, renowned for holiness, a bishop in office, formerly powerful in possessions, become in so short a time a proven monk—something that scarcely any other person could attain in many years? Truly, prosperity did not delight him beyond measure, since its reversal did not shake him. For what is possessed with love is never lost without pain. Whoever desires also fears; whoever fears never lives free or secure. Our Lambert grieved to lose nothing of the world, because he desired nothing; and thus he was always secure in himself and free in Christ.

When he was unjustly removed from the episcopate, to whom did he complain of the injury done him? Whose person did he invoke? To whose hearing did he commit himself? To what jurist did he entrust his cause? He stirred up no scandal in kingdom or Church. He did not wish to mingle anyone else’s ruin with his own fall, but revealed his cause to God alone, saying what the Son of God said to the Father through the Prophet: “Arise, O Lord, and attend to my judgment, my God and my Lord, to my cause” (Ps. 34:23).

## CHAPTER XII. On the obedience and humility of St Lambert.

[Col. 0767C]

Let us now see, in one testimony of obedience, how highly Lambert’s monastic way of life was valued. Ever tending toward perfection, he added something to the measure of his servitude, knowing that whatever he gave beyond requirement would be repaid to him by the true Samaritan. Therefore, anticipating the canonical night offices, he offered God private vigils by night.

On one of these nights, wishing to leave the dormitory, he disturbed the sleeping brothers when one of his sandals slipped from his hand. Knowing that by the discipline of the Rule one who had disturbed the brothers’ rest ought to go to the cross, he immediately rose secretly from bed, wearing only one rough hair-shirt. More swiftly than speech, at the command of the angry abbot, leaving behind his sandals and what he had in his hands, he went barefoot, with unshod feet, almost naked, to the cross. There he remained motionless all night, intent on psalms and hymns.

This was a stone cross, set between the oratory and the dormitory for this purpose: that, looking upon that cross, those who belonged to Christ might more devoutly crucify their flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5:24); and, should they commit somewhat grave faults, they might be assigned to it for regular penance.

The frost intensified the cold of that night, and snow fell abundantly, yet did not rise above the bishop’s ankles. The whole face of winter was utterly dreadful. But that most gentle man, burning inwardly with the flame of the Paraclete Spirit, did not therefore feel outwardly the torments of the cold. Heaven was opened to his prayers, and his prayer reached the hearing of those above. As he sang the verse of the psalm, “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41:3), the cocks gave their song earlier than usual.

The brothers rose for the prescribed duties of the vigils and afterwards, having entered the house, lit a large fire. While warming themselves, the abbot asked where Lambert was, since he was absent from the assembly of the brothers. One brother said that Lambert was the man who, by regular judgment, had been assigned to the cross through the unseasonable night. The abbot was alarmed and urgently ordered the brothers to go and call him back. They went and found him singing: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. 50:19).

When he had been summoned back, the abbot and the whole community threw themselves at his knees. The abbot accused himself and, excusing his fault, asked forgiveness for ignorance or excess of severity. Lambert, his own accuser, laid the fault upon himself, saying that there was nothing for him to forgive them. The brothers repaid the grace of his goodwill, prepared a bath for him, and changed his clothes. Then, kissing his hands and feet, they all rejoiced together, saying that this had occurred to increase his glory.

The outstanding bishop then raised his hands to heaven and blessed the brothers thus:

> O almighty God, filling the heavens with light,  
> You who govern heaven, earth, and sea by your dominion,  
> So that all things in their time are subject to your will:  
> I pray you, bless these your servants for ever;  
> Protect them from snares; preserve them in gracious virtues,  
> Until they behold you and attain the kingdoms of heaven,  
> Through your gift, O God, who now and ever throughout eternity  
> Are blessed in the threefold power of your being.

## CHAPTER XIII. That St Lambert was recalled to the episcopate.

When the seven-year period had elapsed, at last it pleased the Most High, after a dreadful and long-lasting storm, to make the face of heaven serene. Pippin the Second, son of Ansegisel and Begga, after he had bravely conquered all those who were tearing Francia apart by fighting one another, alone obtained, under King Theodoric, the chief rule of all Francia, and set in order the disturbed condition of kingdom and Church.

Among other matter for praise, this came to him: Pharamund, the hireling at Maastricht, was at last rejected by the just judgment of clergy and people and expelled not only from the church of Maastricht but from the whole province. Immediately the prayer of all was lifted to heaven, and the prayer of all was directed to Prince Pippin, that the people of Maastricht might no longer lack the comfort of their pious father Lambert. The prince approved the just petition and commanded that the shepherd be restored to his sheep.

Thus the veteran soldier, purified by most grievous tribulation, was lifted up by the voices of all his people and fittingly restored to the cathedra of Maastricht. Rightly so: for sincerity and the fullness of the law were in his heart; truth and beauty were in his mouth.

No eloquent tongue would suffice, should it wish to run through each detail, to describe how great was the rejoicing at his return among every rank, age, and sex; how greatly clerics and monks, strangers and pilgrims, old men and boys, young men and virgins, each in their own circumstances, rejoiced.

The apostolic man therefore returned to his own city and restored the rule of ecclesiastical discipline, corrupted by pseudo-Christians.

## CHAPTER XIV. That St Lambert freed Taxandria from idolatry.

Preferring to be rather than to be called a bishop, he watched over himself and the entire flock all the more earnestly. He did not shrink from declaring the whole counsel of God to all (Acts 20:27–28). Fearing the reproach of the wicked and slothful servant who put his lord’s money away in a napkin (Luke 19:20), he made no concession to ease in heart or body. He visited cities and towns and, in hearts cultivated by the mattocks of the word, sowed the seed of life in due season.

At times he even crossed the boundaries of his diocese, lest the Lord call him an unprofitable servant because he had done only what he ought to have done. Nearby was the province of the Tessandri, where idolatry still flourished. The mighty athlete of Christ grieved that enemies of the Christian name, so near at hand, should oppose the kingdom of his King. He armed himself with the weapons of faith, and, inflamed with the zeal of virtue, harassed them with repeated assaults.

Offering them the peace of the Lord, he tried by every means whether somehow his peace might rest upon sons of peace (Matt. 10:13). At one time he soothed them with the sweetness of speech, to bring those wandering to the way of truth; at another, entering willingly into conflict, he destroyed the temples and images of the pagans, in order to restrain their rage by whatever means. They raged like barbarians and wished to tear him apart like the fiercest beasts. Yet sometimes, moved by regard for humanity, they considered the virtue and piety of the holy man, who fulfilled in deed what he preached with his mouth. Wishing to imitate him, they allowed themselves to be strengthened by him in Christ’s faith.

Thus Christ’s warrior gradually abolished from their hearts the barbarism of paganism, enticed them toward the gentleness of Christianity, removed the stench of idolatry, and spread everywhere the good fragrance of Christ (2 Cor. 2:15). Nor did Christ’s standard-bearer desist until he had led that entire people, removed from the kingdom of the devil, into the kingdom of the King of kings.

This, O Christ, is your grace; this is the steadfastness of your good soldier, who, undertaking the apostolic work, brought such a distinguished triumph into your camp. Behold the apostle of Tessandria, deservedly to be compared with the apostles and apostolic men. For when the Prince of shepherds comes to judge, and each shepherd presents to him what portion of the world he has brought to faith by his preaching, this our shepherd will not appear empty among shepherds. Rather, he too will draw after himself many whom he has reclaimed from idolatry or wickedness by his labour, and will receive a manifold crown of glory.

## CHAPTER XV. A vision shown to St Lambert concerning the burial of St Landrada.

[Col. 0770A]

How glorious God is in himself could in no way be apprehended by human beings unless he worked certain marvellous things in his saints, through which we might understand that he is truly wonderful.

While Pippin was governing the Franks, the holy virgin Landrada built a monastery in the estate of Belisia, encouraged in every way by St Lambert’s counsel and aided by him. When the day of her departure drew near, so that, prepared for the Bridegroom’s wedding feast, she might enter with the lamp of good works alight, she affectionately summoned the same St Lambert to receive from him the provision for the journey of life.

While the holy man hastened on his way, she was meanwhile released from the prison of flesh. But God, to whom nothing is more pleasing than brotherly charity, would not allow either him or her to be deprived of the fruit of their mutual friendship.

For, as he travelled, a delightful vision appeared to the bishop. Before the eyes of the one lying down and, as though in ecstasy, half-awake, Christ’s virgin Landrada herself stood visibly in radiant brightness. Addressing him with the friendly grace of face and speech, she said: “How is it, my friend, that this unfamiliar neglect of me has caused you such delay in coming to visit me?”

Lambert, pleading the affection of friendship, offered this reply in excuse: “You have no ground to accuse me either of neglect or of delay. As I was hastening to come to you, the swifter necessity of your death forestalled me. Behold, I am here, and you have already entered into the joy of your Lord (Matt. 25:21). I shall now render you what is justly due; but tell me, I ask you, in what place I am to bury your body according to your wish.”

She said: “Look up to heaven, and carefully mark on earth the place where you now see the sign of the holy cross appearing from heaven through flashing light.”

Following her pointing with eyes and mind, Lambert saw a place on earth marked by heavenly light in the shape of the holy cross. From the mouth of the virgin speaking with him he received these last words: “Lambert, know that this place, indicated to you from heaven, was long ago assigned by God for my burial.”

When the holy virgin had been received into heaven at the close of this conversation, the holy man awoke from sleep and rejoiced in himself at the miracle of the heavenly vision.

The place irradiated by the sign of heavenly light was Wentershovum, where St Lambert himself, having been brought up by St Landoald, had marked the first character of his novicehood.

Lambert hastened on his way all the more quickly because he knew that this would be more pleasing to God and to his bride. Coming to Belisia later than he wished but not later than his feet could carry him—for to a desiring mind nothing is ever hurried enough—he disclosed the vision to all and sought, as gently and eloquently as he could, to persuade them to carry it out.

All protested against one man; all raised a clamour with one voice: “Far be it, Lambert! Far be it, blessed bishop! Here this holy virgin was consecrated to God by you. This church, built by her labour and at her expense, was dedicated through her by you. Here all her possessions were relinquished by her to God through you. Here the community of those serving God was raised up through her and through you. And where could her bones rest more worthily than here, where the present testimonies of so many of her good works are visible?

“And all these things, Lambert, add to the merits of your holiness as well, since through the zeal of your pastoral care the gifts of faith and virtue here overflow among the faithful people, increased both in worth and in number.”

Lambert, offended by the obstinacy of all, said: “It is pleasant to preside over fellow-citizens, but burdensome to please everyone. Behold, because the word of God and my word find no place in you (John 8:37), I shall follow you all against my will. Yet I am certain that the heavenly oracle will not lack its fulfilment.”

Lambert, therefore, after the holy virgin had been buried, was more unsettled in mind by the people’s decision than by his own [Col. 0771B]: on the one hand certain of the heavenly oracle, on the other uncertain concerning the virgin’s buried body. For this reason, devoting himself to every manner of prayer, he sought the answer from Him to whom, as he knew, nothing is impossible (Luke 1:37). Thus, after three days had passed, he summoned the people and said:

“The virgin of Christ, long since deceased, was, in your own judgment as well, a woman of great merit; and therefore I judge that what I hold to have been made known to me from her lips—she who now reigns with Christ—is not a trivial matter. Therefore, lest you resent what I ask: let the virgin’s tomb be opened, so that you may test the matter itself with your eyes.”

All obeyed him. The tomb was opened; but nothing was found there of the holy body that had been buried, since the sarcophagus itself had been transferred elsewhere. Everyone’s face grew pale; Lambert alone [Col. 0771C] rejoiced, and, soothing their astonishment with fatherly gentleness, said:

“Since you have experienced your lack of faith, let us now experience God’s wondrous power; and let us seek the soil containing the holy body in the place indicated to me.”

With him as their guide, they hastened to Wentershoven. Recalling in mind and before his eyes the traces of the heavenly sign shown to him, he pointed out the place pleasing to the holy virgin. O new wonder! There they found the soil containing the holy body, together with the sarcophagus, transported thither and set down so orderly and fittingly that no one could doubt that the holy virgin had been transferred there by angelic ministry.

All extolled the mighty works of God; above all, they proclaimed the faith and merit of the glorious Lambert, whose manner of life was already in heaven (Phil. 3:20), although [Col. 0771D] he was still held in the body upon earth. In him they saw fulfilled that saying of the Lord: “All things are possible to one who believes” (Mark 9:22). O man worthy of God, lacking nothing for the fullness of perfection, ready even to ascend to that love than which no one has greater: to lay down his life for his friends! (John 15:13). For what greater glory could the King grant to His veteran soldier than to bestow upon him, crowned with martyrdom, the light of eternal rest?

Let us now, in order to put the finishing hand to our work, raise the banner of his passion.

## CHAPTER XVI. How Lambert rebuked Pippin for an unlawful marriage

Pippin, as we have said, ruled preeminently [Col. 0772A] over all the princes of the Franks, and the frequent trophies of his victories increased his glory. At least the nobility descended to him from both parents and the memorials of sanctity could have spurred him to virtue.

For, to pass over the holiness of his maternal aunt Gertrude, or of Clodulf, son of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, who was Pippin’s godfather: who does not marvel at the life of Saint Begga, his mother? Who does not know the sanctity of his paternal grandfather Arnulf, who was first mayor of the royal household and afterwards bishop of Metz, marvelous to the world both in life and in death? Moreover, the power of Arnulf’s sons still flourished in the kingdom. Of these, Drogo was duke of Champagne, while Grimoald awaited the hereditary principate of his father. [Col. 0772B] His lawful wife Plectrude had borne these sons to Pippin.

Although Pippin lacked nothing in glory, power, or prosperity, Fortune was never more favorable to anyone’s exertions than she was to his. O, nothing is ever secure in the devil’s presence! A man so victorious could not triumph over himself; he allowed his iron breast to be pierced by the soft dart of lust. He took as an additional wife over his lawful wife Plectrude a noble and beautiful girl named Alpaïs. By her he also had a son, Charles, later surnamed Tudens, or Martel (“the Hammer”), because of his untamed valor in war. She was the sister of Dodo, who was an officer in the household of Prince Pippin, a man rich in possessions, distinguished by birth, and possessed of great power in the kingdom through friends, relatives, and many retainers [Col. 0772C] obedient to him.

Since there was no bishop to stand in opposition and “set himself as a wall for the house of Israel, to stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezek. 13:5), Lambert alone, “zealous with zeal for the house of the Lord” (3 Kings 19:14), rebuked the prince “in season and out of season” (2 Tim. 4:2), presenting himself as another Elijah or John. Herodias felt toward John, when Herod gladly listened to John reproving him for adultery, what Alpaïs likewise felt toward Lambert when Pippin obeyed Lambert rebuking him for his concubinage. Indeed, Pippin—otherwise a praiseworthy and devout man, save for this one matter—took great pleasure in Lambert’s counsels and was moved by his admonitions. [Col. 0772D] Had he been able to deceive his loving concubine, he would undoubtedly have gladly listened to the bishop who rightly reproved him.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the war waged by Dodo’s nephews against Saint Lambert’s household

The concubine reported the matter to her brother Dodo. Entrusting her entire plan to him, she begged him by his help to erase the disgrace to her family, which would grow too great if Lambert’s censure should result in her separation from the prince. Dodo shared his and his sister’s cause with the stronger members of his kindred, and strove, both personally and through them, to restrain the bishop from reproving the prince. Finding him inflexible, and perceiving that he showed no regard for anyone’s person against [Col. 0773A] justice, he promised his kinsmen and friends vengeance for his sister’s cause.

Accordingly, two brothers, Gallus and Rioldus, Dodo’s relatives, pitying the plight of their kinswoman Alpaïs, sought an opportunity to provoke the bishop. Rising with all their followers against the entire household of the Church of Maastricht, by whatever artifice they could they fabricated accusations against them. They omitted no injury they could inflict, if by this means they might bend the bishop’s judgment so that he would at least desist from reproving the prince on account of his own people. But the event turned out otherwise than they had expected. For the righteous man, “bold as a lion” (Prov. 28:1), protected himself against every attack with the shield of patience; girded himself, against the threats of earthly power, with “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God”; and, wearing “the helmet of salvation” (Eph. 6:17), pursued the cause of truth without hesitation. At first he addressed them gently; and by all the means available to a father’s compassion and a bishop’s discipline, he tried to deter them from unjust violence. But because he poured his words into the wind, he cast himself with familiar confidence upon God, saying: “Arise, O Lord, and judge my cause; remember the reproach of thy servants” (Ps. 73:22). Yet the sons of Belial attacked God’s faithful more fiercely and harassed the innocent by every kind of injury.

Those whose cause concerned their lives, and whose entire hope rested solely upon innocence, without consulting the bishop prepared to meet them with arms, either to avenge their wrongs or not to die unavenged. They came together [Col. 0773C] and fought. The one side fought in recklessness; the other resisted for safety. Pride placed Gallus and Rioldus, Dodo’s kinsmen, in the first line of battle; justice set Peter and Andoletus, the bishop’s kinsmen, against them in the foremost rank. Fear exposed the degenerate spirits of Gallus and Rioldus (Vergil, *Aeneid* IV, 13); innocence raised the hands of Peter and Andoletus to valor. The strength of innocence prevailed, and victory fell to the ecclesiastical party. Gallus and Rioldus, leaders of the wicked faction, fell slain; Peter and Andoletus, defenders of the Church, bore off the standard of victory. The wicked were confounded, yet did not blush; they were defeated, but did not withdraw exhausted.

For Dodo, who had been the instigator of every evil, [Col. 0773D] now himself became the author of war. Despising what God says concerning priests—“He who touches you touches the apple of my eye” (Zech. 2:8)—he raged against the very head of the holy bishop, vowed him to death, and directed against him alone the vengeance for his nephews.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How Saint Lambert was invited by Pippin to Jupille

In those days Prince Pippin had come to Jupille, a place adjoining the estate of Liège. There Saint Lambert was invited to his court, ostensibly on business of the realm, and did not refuse his presence. The prince and the prince’s concubine made their faces serene toward him; some concealed anger, others feigned joy, and many, each according to his own inclination, changed the expression of their hearts.

[Col. 0774A] The concubine was considering how she might suitably procure someone to plead for her, through whose persuasion she could reconcile the bishop’s mind to herself, or at least for the present soften his importunate rebukes of the prince.

A banquet was prepared, the bishop was invited, and the whole courtly company rejoiced exceedingly. The prince signaled that the cup offered to him by the cupbearer should be presented to the bishop. He regarded it as a blessing if he received from the consecrated hand of the holy bishop a cup which, as he knew, the Emperor Maximus Caesar had once requested from Martin, bishop of Tours. But Pippin would have received a greater blessing from Lambert than the great emperor received from Martin, had Pippin’s wife deserved from Lambert the favor which Maximus’s wife obtained from Martin. Martin considered his priest better than the great emperor and handed the cup to him before the king. Lambert preferred no one to Pippin.

Following the prince’s example, the lesser nobles all demanded that a cup be handed to them by the holy hand of the holy bishop. As all rushed indiscriminately toward this and crowded in confusion, each trying to get ahead of another, behold, the concubine secretly mingled her own hand among the hands of the others, striving even thus to snatch a cup from the bishop’s hand. He, seeing before and behind, prudently perceived the woman’s snares and, turning to the prince, complained of the excessive presumption of a woman who had craftily sought to stamp upon him [Col. 0774C] the mark of a communion displeasing to God. Thereupon he rushed from the hall and diminished all the gaiety of that princely banquet. Yet even thus the woman’s cunning did not rest, unwilling to leave any expedient untried.

When evening came and the bishop prepared to depart, the prince, at the concubine’s prompting, commanded him not to leave without greeting his wife. The bishop, with the Spirit of truth speaking steadfastly within him, said:

“I call you to witness, most mighty prince; I call Jesus truly to witness, the hope of our life: I shall never communicate with a fornicator, because Paul wrote and commanded us, saying, ‘Do not associate with fornicators’ (1 Cor. 5:9). I call God to witness, I say, that I shall never greet her, because I know that John, the friend of God, said: ‘If anyone does not remain in the doctrine of Christ, do not receive him, nor say to him, “Greetings”; for he who says to him, “Greetings,” shares [Col. 0774D] in his evil works’ (2 John 2). I grieve deeply that you share fellowship with her; I bear with pain that you will not repent. Therefore I fear God’s wrath for you.”

The concubine, seeing that nothing remained for her cause and fearing that, should Lambert live long, her separation was imminent, furiously laid out the whole matter in order to her brother. Adding oil to the furnace, she implored him to act as quickly as possible to kill the bishop. The grief Dodo felt over the death of his nephews was intensified by the doubled grief at the rejection of his sister; and now his entire purpose was to satisfy himself and his sister.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Dodo’s fury as he hastened to kill Saint Lambert

[Col. 0775A]

Lambert, herald of truth, now pressing toward the prize of the heavenly calling, had come to Liège. Dodo, however, had withdrawn to the village of Auridum, quite near Liège. He prepared arms, assembled companions, and summoned auxiliary forces obtained from the royal household in his own name or in that of his sister. He hated the delays of postponement; by delaying, he accumulated anger, and through anger sharpened the goads of fury upon the whetstone of his very hard heart.

Meanwhile, Lambert, foreknowing that his contest was at hand, passed that night without sleep—not because any dreams of death frightened him, but because the hope of the joys of future rest had taken possession of him. For, rising in the very dead of night to confess the Lord, [Col. 0775B] he performed on earth an angelic service. At the hour for celebrating the nocturnal office, he awakened his disciples and said: “Rise quickly; God has promised a crown to those who watch.” When the office was completed, the others returned to their beds; he himself persisted in completing the course of good work.

Toward dawn, as the corruptible body weighed down the soul, he began, after the example of the Lord going to His passion, to be distressed. His eyes heavy with sleep, he sought in slumber a little rest, when, behold, around daybreak, as the darkness grew thinner, Baldoveus, watchman of the bishop’s house, saw a hostile army advancing in close ranks and reported it. Although the mist rising in the morning dulled clear sight, the matter was easy to discern, whether from the multitude of men seen or the clash of weapons heard. Breastplates flashed, helmets rose above their heads, left hands were covered by shields, right hands armed with swords and lances; slingers advanced before them with archers.

## CHAPTER XX. On the vision of the sign of the cross

Hear a marvelous matter, a token of divine mercy.

For, in order that it might be manifest that Lambert gloried in nothing except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world was crucified to him and he to the world (Gal. 6:14), and that his ascent from earth to heaven was now prepared through the power of the cross, certain persons following the army saw an extraordinary sign. Astonished, they saw above the house in which the bishop was a figure like the Lord’s cross, glowing more brightly than every metal, from earth up to heaven.

Those who deserved to see this, I believe, followed Dodo [Col. 0775D] more because of the wage due them and hope of the promised reward, and to increase the number of soldiers, than from any zeal to persecute the innocent or lust to shed blood.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the killing of Saint Lambert and his companions

The hostile battle-line, now as though prepared for action, was drawing near. The watchman of the house cried out to the sleepers, for the army already surrounding him could itself have been the messenger of terror.

Lambert, Christ’s witness, startled by the heaviness of sleep and the bitterness of the event, rose barefoot and seized a sword, as though about to defend himself and his people. But coming to himself, he condemned himself for rashness; and because he had at least unlawfully attempted to take up arms, [Col. 0776A] he imposed upon himself fitting penitence before God’s eyes. “Good Jesus,” he said, “thou who hast said, ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay’ (Heb. 10:30), I beseech thee: do not let me lose my victory, for it is better for me to die in thee than to lay hands upon the wicked in battle. Thou, mighty warrior, take up weapons and shield, and arise to help me” (Ps. 34:2).

The gates had already been burst in; the doors already broken open. They struck the very walls of the house with their lances; some had even entered and were threatening fire. Peter and Andoletus drove out those who entered, and with so few men they strove in vain to resist so many.

The saint comforted them for the moment, saying: “Brothers, if you have loved me in return, love Christ as I [Col. 0776B] love him. Confess your sins to Jesus, and pray for one another that you may be saved” (James 5:16). “I must now be dissolved and live with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). “You know, O my nephews, that you were guilty and culpable in the offense for which vengeance is now being sought. What you did unjustly then, I pray you now expiate justly and patiently. God will not judge twice for the same thing, nor will a double tribulation arise. I beg you, do not let your sin overflow before God: let not blood touch blood through your hands” (Hos. 4:2). “Let us not fear the cruelty of persecutors, because the sword and fire that will consume their flesh to the marrow shall be their punishment. You, only keep your hands innocent, so that your spirit may be saved forever; give even your bodies to them to be torn apart.”

[Col. 0776C] Encouraged by these final admonitions of their father, all who were now in their agony were strengthened to die for innocence.

Taking up the psalter, he received as an omen the first verse of the psalm that occurred: “For the Lord will seek the blood of his servants” (Ps. 9:13); and he added this final saying: “May God see and require it” (2 Chron. 24:22). When all had gone out of the chamber and had been exposed like lambs amid raging wolves, he himself, stretching out his hands, prostrated himself upon the ground in the form of a cross. Praying with tears, he commended his soul into the Lord’s hands (Luke 23:46), as no one ever commended himself to God more fervently.

Meanwhile the executioners killed Peter and Andoletus, and all of the Church’s household whom they found there.

[Col. 0776D] One man, more savage than the rest, climbed to the summit of the roof and, seeing him clinging to the floor, pierced his heart with a hurled weapon. Angels bore his soul to heaven, while he uttered a low murmur of prayer.

Therefore Lambert, precious priest of the Lord, who here had been the companion of all who keep God’s commandments (Ps. 118:63), rejoices there and exults in the fellowship of all the saints. With the continent and virgins he is crowned with the garland of chastity; a confessor among confessors, he drinks before God the holy cup of confession; a monk among monks, he receives the hundredfold of eternal recompense; an apostle among apostles, he sits upon the seat of judicial authority; [Col. 0777A] a prophet among prophets, he rejoices in hope; a patriarch among patriarchs, he shines in faith; finally, a martyr among martyrs, taking the cup of salvation, he calls upon the name of the Lord (Ps. 115:13), because he had nothing greater to render to the Lord for all that the Lord had rendered to him. Among the nine orders of angels also he has a place in which, according to the merit of each, he shares in the office proper to them. Thus made a participant in all, he has been admitted as a citizen into the eternal court, where he possesses the palm of everlasting glory and the robe of eternal joy.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the funeral rites of Saint Lambert

A few of Saint Lambert’s retinue who escaped the danger of death covered his body, drenched in rosy blood, with a cheap covering and carried it as quickly as possible by boat to Maastricht [Col. 0777B]. The report flew through the people, shaking all with fear and horror. All feared because of the prince’s offense; all shuddered because of the bishop’s undeserved murder. The people of Maastricht lamented that they had lost the loving-kindness of their pious father, but they still did not sufficiently dare to offer the reverence due to so great a father. They scarcely had leisure to mourn their beloved; scarcely had leisure to hate the guilty.

When the holy body was set down at the harbor, people without name or number assembled. From the confused lamentations of all, one could judge how highly he had been esteemed by everyone.

Placed upon a bier, the saint was borne with due honor to the basilica of Saint Peter. The clergy accompanied him with psalms and hymns; the people clapped their hands amid lamentations. The people spent the night in solemn vigil; the clergy [Col. 0777C] duly kept watch. All delighted in kissing the footprints of their pious father; anyone who was permitted to press kisses upon the holy limbs counted himself to have obtained great assistance. It was pleasant and devout to see the sheep render their shepherd this pledge of love.

But it was both pitiful and strange to observe the anger of the pious shepherd toward wandering sheep. For it is handed down from the elders that, though all were freely allowed to approach and kiss the saint, if any concubine thrust herself forward to kiss the martyr’s body, she was driven backward as if by a whirling storm. Thus, by the repulse of concubines, it was made very plain that the concubine was hateful to God and the holy martyr—a woman who had disgraced Francia by a double crime and troubled the holy Church.

[Col. 0777D] Yet such fear seized the people of Maastricht because of the harshness of this affair that they did not dare to prepare a mausoleum worthy of a man of so great a name. Therefore, when the tomb of Aper, Saint Lambert’s father, had been opened, they buried the body of the most holy son in the morning together with his father’s bones.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the angelic service at Saint Lambert’s tomb

Heavenly power did not abandon his lifeless limbs;

It showed the peoples how great had been his goodness.

For, lest the people should be frightened by human fear from venerating Saint Lambert of the Lord with due honor, an angelic choir singing psalms began to be heard at his tomb, night and day, whenever it appeared that human silence prevailed there. Nor were there lacking persons who [Col. 0778A] investigated the truth of the matter itself. When they applied every attention of mind and ear, it seemed to them—judging by the quality of Saint Lambert’s voice, well known to them—that the saint himself, with the others who had fallen with him, sang a sweet melody to the divine majesty. If anyone at that hour wished to approach the basilica, he could not enter because of fear; and the nearer anyone ventured, the less he received the angelic voices, his ears being checked. But when he withdrew farther away, the angelic melody was repeated more fully.

O Christ, thine ineffable power! Who can repay thy mighty works? Behold, thou openly showest what thou didst say with thy mouth: “God is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Mark 12:27), for all live to thee, who livest and reignest for ages of ages.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On God’s vengeance upon Dodo and his accomplices

[Col. 0778B]

The glorious soldier of Christ, Lambert, immediately began to reveal on earth how great he was with the King of kings in heaven—being thereby much more blessed, because through him, even after death, the Lord’s name was blessed among the peoples.

For, appearing by night to a treasurer named Amalgisilus, formerly his judge, he addressed him in gentle speech. When that man carefully asked him the reason for his coming, he said: “We have gone to Rome; behold, we return from Rome, intending to visit Dodo and his accomplices. For the blood of the innocent, shed with Christ upon earth together with me, now [Col. 0778C] demands vengeance from God; nor has God withheld his favor from them.” Having said this, I disappeared; but the outcome of events proved that the vision was not illusory.

Dodo, the murderer of the holy bishop, at once incurred the wrath of divine vengeance. All his entrails, putrid and foul, he expelled through his private parts, and by his miserable end of life showed everyone his wretchedness. He who here had abused the pomp of the world was assigned in hell to unquenchable fire and to the undying worm (Isa. 66:24). It is also reported that, because the stench was intolerable, his body was thrown into the river Meuse, where it was consumed by worms and decay. He deserved no other burial, having acquired the miserable memory of so great a crime.

[Col. 0778D] One equal to Dodo in guilt—the man who killed the saint of God with his own hands—engaged his brother in a wretched battle and, killing his brother, was in turn killed by his brother.

To conclude everything briefly: within the space of that same year, scarcely anyone escaped who had been guilty in the killing of the holy martyr; and if anyone survived, he felt himself so ruined even in mind that he considered fortunate those who had been consumed by swift, though miserable, death.

But Christ’s crowned martyr triumphs; holding the palm of victory, he exults in Abraham’s bosom. Thus, O Christ, in thy saints thou triumphest over enemies: loving those who love thee (Prov. 8:17), thou honorest those who honor thee (1 Sam. 2:29).

## CHAPTER XXV. On the miracles shown at Liège, at the place of Saint Lambert’s passion

[Col. 0779A]

Liège, which deserved to be made illustrious by the martyrdom of its patron, although it grieved to have been temporarily bereft of his body, was nevertheless not without his miracles.

In the chamber conscious of his martyrdom, lamps kindled by divine power often shone, so that the entire house gleamed as though with the rays of the sun, and the human eye could scarcely endure that light.

The subsequent grace of miracles confirmed these beginnings of renown; their chief points must here be set down.

The holy man warned a certain Theoduin once and twice in a vision to return his finest comb, which Theoduin’s wife had snatched away from him. When Theoduin did not obey a third time, he afflicted his breast with an incurable stroke, and thus recovered what was his from the unwilling man.

Baldigisil, commanded in a vision to keep watch at the place of Lambert’s martyrdom, and another man, Raginfrid, instructed to clean that same place, both received the light of their eyes, which they had lacked, each in his own time.

The virgin Oda also came in faith to this place. She too was blind and lived nearby; as soon as she invoked the name of the holy martyr, she received what she desired. By these things the fresh veneration of the new patron grew, and the people’s devotion, inflamed, built a basilica for the saint all the more quickly because it was more devout. A bed of the saint, made by the faithful, was also placed in the spot where the saint had been pierced by the weapon of the wicked man.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the translation of Saint Lambert and the miracles manifested therein

[Col. 0779C]

This devotion of the people of Liège so pleased the Lord that heavenly visions now frequently appeared to many of God’s faithful, directing that the holy martyr, transferred to Maastricht, should be restored to the place of his martyrdom. Saint Hubert, Saint Lambert’s disciple and successor, did not resist the will of God and the martyr.

Therefore, in the thirteenth year of his episcopate, opening the saint’s tomb, he found his body whole and unharmed, suffused with a marvelous fragrance. He changed its garments and sealed the former ones for preservation, so that relics might be given from them.

It was made manifest during the translation that this was pleasing [Col. 0779D] to the Lord. For when the people were resting in the village of Nivelles, a poor blind man was enriched by the restoration of the use of his eyes.

Not long afterwards, in the village of Harmala, while all were resting to relieve their weariness, a paralytic brought there was restored, before the holy bier, through the strengthening of the structure of his limbs.

In each of these places basilicas were immediately founded in honor of the holy martyr.

With such rejoicing they approached thee, O city of Liège. How great and what sort of procession of clergy and people there was; how great and what kind of rejoicing among those streaming in from every side; how great the generosity of all in giving gifts to the saint; how great the purity with which the faithful prayed and made vows—these and like matters can more easily be estimated by a wise person [Col. 0780A] than narrated by anyone’s speech or pen.

Thou hast, O Liège, thy joy; behold, thou holdest thy special patronage. Here began the beginning of thy advancement. Through him, raised into a city, thou art advanced from daughter to mother; through him, promoted to an episcopal see, thou hast advanced in every dignity. While other cities in some measure decline into old age, thou, through him, hast flourished into the state of beautiful youth. May the holy martyr protect thee forever by his intercessions, he who advanced thee to this condition: that among cities thou mayest be made great in name and in merit.

From that time onward there has been neither limit nor number to the miracles. For to all who invoke God there in truth through Lambert’s name, the door of divine mercy has always [Col. 0780B] stood open. There one could see the fetters of prisoners and the supports of the infirm hung up as testimonies to God’s power. Whoever came steadfast in faith never returned without effect.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Grimoald’s killing before Saint Lambert’s altar

This holy martyr, as he was a gracious and ready helper to the pious and faithful, so he was either a severe rebuker or a just avenger against the impious.

A few years after his translation, when the often-mentioned Pippin, mayor of the household, had fallen ill, his son Grimoald went to visit him. Devoted to Saint Lambert—perhaps the more so because he had died [Col. 0780C] defending the marriage of Grimoald’s mother Plectrude—Grimoald turned aside to Liège and approached the saint’s tomb to pray. While praying, he was attacked there before Saint Lambert’s altar and killed by a retainer of Radbod, duke of the Frisians. Grimoald had been awaiting marriage to Radbod’s daughter, to whom Pippin, Grimoald’s father, had betrothed him. But Radbod did not go unpunished for this, at whose instigation the innocent Grimoald had died. For not long afterward, Radbod himself, marvelously deluded by a demon, perished by sudden and eternal death.

Because it would be long and tedious to recount each of Saint Lambert’s miracles individually, let us universally praise the power of God working through him.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Epilogue

[Col. 0780D]

Godescalc, a deacon and cleric of Lambert’s own community, first wrote the Life of Saint Lambert by command of Bishop Agilfrid. He lived in the time of Pippin and Charlemagne and truthfully recounted Lambert’s deeds, but spoke with insufficient freedom concerning the cause of his martyrdom. He is believed to have done this lest he seem to reproach the kings of his own time with the guilt of their ancestors. For Charles Martel was born from the unlawful union of Pippin and Alpaïs; from Charles came Pippin III, who was raised from princely rank to become king of the Franks; from Pippin came Charlemagne, than whom none before or after him was greater among the kings of the Franks. Of him one may doubt whether he was stronger or [Col. 0781A] more fortunate, more powerful in government or more devout in ecclesiastical discipline.

Saint Lambert suffered martyrdom on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October [17 September], in the fortieth year of his episcopate, under Hildebert, king of the Franks [Col. 0782A], son of King Theuderic. From that Theuderic onward, the kings of the Franks reigned in name alone, while the power of the kingdom remained with the mayors of the household until Pippin III.

# THE SECOND LIFE OF SAINT LAMBERT, BY SIGEBERT

*(Bollandists, September, vol. V, p. 589, from the manuscript of Rouge-Cloître and the Brabant Hagiology.)*

## CHAPTER I. The saint’s distinguished parents; his education under Saints Landoald and Theodard; gifts of body and mind; the translation of Saint Theodard’s body to Liège

[Col. 0781B]

1. The glorious man Lantbert, a martyr acceptable to the eternal King and a priest beloved by the true Priest, was born from a distinguished lineage in a village of the town of Maastricht. Born of good and religious parents, he was also reborn in Christ through good and religious men. For he was the spiritual son in baptism of Remaclus, later bishop of Maastricht. [Note: On Saint Remaclus, bishop of Maastricht and afterwards abbot of Stavelot, we have treated under the third day of this month of September. Yet it seems scarcely probable that Saint Lambert was baptized by him or received by him from the font.]

Great grace in the Church of God shone forth in this boy and his ancestors, and great glory prevailed for them in the kingdom of the Franks. For their steadfast Christian faith increased their esteem among the orthodox, while nobility of flesh brought them worldly rank through abundance of possessions and great power among the nobles of the realm. His father and mother enhanced at close hand this distinction of lineage which had come down to him from afar. His mother, most noble among the nobles of the Franks, posterity received from its forebears as having been called Herisplind. His father, named Aper, belonged to the first order of senators, called *viri illustres* (“illustrious men”), who are placed in the royal court before the second and third orders of senators, called *viri respectabiles* (“respectable men”) and *viri clarissimi* (“most renowned men”); among the foremost of these, he excelled.

[Col. 0782B]

2. At that time the kingdom of the Franks was ruled, after Lothair the Younger, by his son Dagobert. [Note: This was Dagobert I, son of Chlothar II.] While he reigned in Neustria, he entrusted the kingdom of the Austrasians to his son Sigebert, [Note: He considers this Saint Sigebert king of Austrasia, whose deeds are elucidated in our work under 1 February.] and, while Sigebert was still a child, gave him as guardians Cunibert, bishop of Cologne, [Note: Saint Cunibert, bishop of Cologne, will be treated under 12 November, on which day he is venerated.] and Pippin the First, mayor of the household, father of the holy women Gertrude and Begga. [Note: The Acts of Blessed Pippin of Landen have been illustrated under 21 February; those of Saint Gertrude, abbess of Nivelles in Brabant, under 17 March; and those of Saint Begga will be given under 17 December.]

What this boy would be in the world, God’s providence foreshowed from his cradle. For whatever first indications of good disposition and whatever features of beauty Nature—or rather, the Author of Nature himself—usually fashions beforehand in a boy of good promise, all these appeared already in his infancy. For he seemed handsome in form, and, beyond his years, gracious in expression and affection toward relatives and servants, [Col. 0782C] and thus worthy of everyone’s love. Therefore his father, not ungrateful to God, who promised him so much in his son, conformed his own will to the divine will and devoted his son to God’s service, toward which he already saw him in some manner aspiring. And because instruction develops innate capacity and the cultivation of righteousness strengthens hearts, he chose a holy teacher for his holy son, lest some fault in the teacher darken the disciple’s single eye.

3. Accordingly, for initiation in literary studies he entrusted him to Landoald, [Note: The Life of Saint Landoald, archpriest, from which Sigebert drew these matters, has been published by us under 19 March.] a man greatly esteemed for wisdom, learning, holiness, and diligence. This Landoald [Col. 0783A] was a priest of the holy Roman Church and was assigned by Pope Martin [Note: This was Saint Martin I, pope of that name.] to Amandus, bishop of the people of Maastricht, as assistance in the work of preaching. He came to Gaul and, ordained archpriest of the Church of Maastricht, served God there. Since the same bishop had freed himself from the episcopal burden for the sake of preaching, Landoald diligently and suitably fulfilled the bishop’s duties. For nine years he governed the Church while it was without a bishop, until Remaclus received the chair of the Church of Maastricht. [Note: It has already been proved that the claims concerning the see of Maastricht’s vacancy for nine years and its administration by Saint Landoald are false; see Saint Amandus, vol. I of February, p. 833, and Saint Remaclus, vol. I of September, p. 674.]

Therefore Landoald, receiving the tender years of the holy boy into his fatherly care, shaped the conduct of his earliest age according to the rule of holy life. Formerly the spirit of Elijah rested upon Elisha; yet this did not suffice Elisha, who asked for a difficult thing, though one possible to God: that Elijah’s spirit might become double in him. So now the spirit of Landoald rested upon Lantbert; and I believe that the teacher’s spirit became double in Lantbert, whose grace in the world increased beyond the grace of his teacher.

4. The illustrious Aper, in order to make his son Lantbert more steadfast in his purpose, granted in perpetual right to him and to his guardian Landoald an estate of his own property called Wentreshovum, so that, once a church had been built there, they might devote themselves all the more earnestly—the one to the desire to teach, the other to the desire to learn—the farther they lived from the vanity of the world.

> [Note: [Col. 0783D] Winterhoven is a district of Belgium between the towns of Hasselt and Tongeren. Gottefrid Wendelin also mentions it in *The Native Soil of the Salic Laws*, p. 104, where he identifies this place as none other than the residence of Windogast, one of the four framers of the laws, called Windoheim or Windehove.]

While work on the church was under way, the builders complained of a lack of drinkable water; for water collected there from marshy runoff tormented those who drank it more by its bitterness than it refreshed them by any sweetness. The holy master and the disciple holier than his master, placing their faith in him who gave sweetness to the bitter waters of Marah, joined their prayers and together implored the mercy of the Almighty.

5. Therefore, when the name of the Holy Trinity had been invoked, a place was marked with a staff in the form of the holy cross. A wondrous thing, yet not unfamiliar to faith: immediately there sprang forth a most clear spring, which both revealed how much the saints could do with God and, from that time until now, has proved fit for every use to the inhabitants. As the Fathers, recounting this benefit from generation to generation, hand down its memory to their children, they increase the merits of the saints, because through them they cause the Lord’s name to be blessed. Thus, for Lantbert and Landoald, who loved God, all things worked together for good, since they were called according to God’s purpose to be saints.

Here the history of antiquity is renewed. Moses and Aaron, commanded by God to relieve the thirsting Hebrews’ scarcity, struck the rock twice with the rod and drew forth abundant waters. Yet they, reproved for unbelief by the Searcher of hearts, did not deserve to enter the Promised Land; whereas these men, strengthened in faith, sanctified God before all.

6. Once the righteous holy boy was sent by his master to bring fire for his use. Since there was nothing in which to carry it, yet he judged it sinful not to obey his master, he brought the fire placed in his garment, to his master’s astonishment. He who preserved the three boys cast into the Chaldeans’ furnace with their garments so that not even their clothing was altered likewise kept this man’s garment unharmed, so that it might be clear that, through the fire of the Holy Spirit burning within him, he had overcome material fire.

The vigorous boy, already then striving with all his powers to become a perfect man—how greatly he advanced beneath the rod of his holy master, how pure-heartedly he received the words of devotion and learning—it is unnecessary to repeat in words here, since even today we see everywhere the fruit of such profitable labor overflowing. The fortunate youth, rigorously trained under Landoald, returned to his father; nor is it easy to say with what joy each was moved, while the son rejoiced in filial affection and the father in his son’s progress.

7. When the holy Theodard was appointed bishop of Trajectum, Lantbert was also commended to him by his father, to be educated according to the example of one highly esteemed both in the Church and at court.

> [Note: [Col. 0784D] What he here relates about St. Lambert’s education by St. Theodard, he drew from Godescalc and Stephen.]

At this man’s side he advanced so far that in every undertaking he was an example to all, and even a miracle. For he was truly worthy: pleasing in appearance, gracious in conversation, upright in conduct, conformed to everyone, scarcely imitable by anyone. He made little of present things, as he had vowed in childhood, reckoning all things as nothing apart from what belonged to the grace of eternal salvation. Clinging in mind to heavenly things, he offered himself to the Lord as a holocaust.

Here I seem to see Joshua, Moses’ minister, who, while Moses remained with God on Mount Sinai, kept watch at the foot of the mountain and took no part in sinners’ feasts and games; and when Moses returned to the camp, did not leave the tabernacle of the covenant. Therefore, when Moses laid his hands upon him, he deserved to become Moses’ successor.

8. But what need is there to color him with cosmetic praises sought here and there, when Wisdom herself has adorned him with virtues? It is superfluous to seek material for praise elsewhere when the Creator formed him in such grace that scarcely any defect of nature could steal into his whole body, and scarcely any harmful stain appear in his mind. Yet, since he ought to be praised, it is fitting that we praise him truthfully.

One who either knew his bodily appearance or learned it from those who knew him

> [Note: [Col. 0785D] He indicates Godescalc, whose words he soon uses.]

wrote that he was strong, swift, very agile, steadfast in battle, distinguished in beauty, tall in stature, handsome in face, beautiful in hair, with splendid eyes, well-shaped hands, long fingers, and fair flesh; so that from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head he was beyond reproach.

And, to come to the qualities of his soul: he was full of charity, girded with chastity, grounded in humility, applying himself at the right time to prayer, at the right time to reading, and at the right time to secular business or household affairs. Behold: you see a man so richly endowed with the gifts of grace and the goods of nature that you would say he had been formed by God into a perfect man. Behold, I say, you have a man suited to conform himself to every station. If you consider what belongs to a layman, what could you say was lacking to him as a layman? If you seek what belongs to a cleric, you find the whole cleric.

9. Who now could wonder at the beauty and good disposition of Moses the lawgiver? Because of his elegance Thermuth, Pharaoh’s daughter, reared and adopted him as her son; and such surpassing grace of beauty is recorded to have been in him that whenever he was carried or walked through the streets, all who looked at his beauty stood entranced, abandoned the occupations in which they were engaged, and delighted rather in Moses’ appearance. Moses, placed in Pharaoh’s hands by the daughter, refused the king when he sought to flatter him by placing the royal diadem on his head: he threw the diadem to the ground and trampled it underfoot.

> [Note: [Col. 0785D] Sigebert drew all these matters from Flavius Josephus.]

Lantbert likewise despised the ruler of this world when he wickedly sought to flatter him, and by his humility cast down and trampled upon the diadem of that ruler’s pride. Tarbis, daughter of the king of the Ethiopians, admired and loved Moses as he fought bravely and wisely against the Ethiopians; preferring his love to the safety of her father and native land, she clung to his embraces.

> [Note: [Col. 0785D] These too are drawn from the tales of the same Josephus, no. 53 and following.]

The holy Church chose Lantbert as her bridegroom, because he manfully fought against the Ethiopians of the world.

10. For these reasons it was easy to agree that Lantbert should be judged worthy of every honor and every affection. Therefore Bishop Theodard desired to choose him as his own successor, had he not known that apostolic authority decreed that priests must not dare appoint named persons as their own replacements, lest the episcopate be thought not a divine gift but a hereditary possession, and lest anyone suppose that what belongs to God is owed to a human being.

Moreover, at the royal court Lantbert’s name was held in no slight esteem: both royal majesty and the multitude of nobles revered him. When Bishop Theodard had been led by the path of innocence to the glory of martyrdom,

> [Note: [Col. 0785D] St. Theodard was more probably killed in the year 669, on 10 September, among the Nemetes in Germany, as we have said elsewhere.]

the Vangiones,

> [Note: [Col. 0785D] A people of Germany whose chief city is now called Worms.]

in whose territory he had met his death, believed that this had not happened by chance. They hoped that, by the will of God who gently disposes all things, the present protection of a new martyr had been provided for them; therefore they would not allow his body to be carried from their diocese, in whose presence they desired eternally to glory.

11. This bitter event had greatly struck the people of Trajectum and, I believe, had distressed Lantbert’s mind more than that of all others. But he moderated his grief—for upon him, after God, the entire city rested—and girded himself to recover the bishop’s body. Though frustrated at first, he did not desist; but employing all his mind and effort to accomplish the task, he brought the matter to the desired conclusion.

Thus, when the holy body had been brought back, he buried it in the public estate of Liège,

> [Note: [Col. 0785D] Nothing whatever is read in Godescalc or Stephen concerning the recovery and translation of St. Theodard’s body by St. Lambert. But Sigebert may have learned these things from the very ancient anonymous author of the *Life of St. Theodard*, printed by us for 10 September, pp. 588 ff.; in chapter 2 of that work are related more fully the same matters which we summarized from it in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 40 ff. The same translation is related by Sigebert in his *Life of St. Theodard*, printed third under the aforementioned date in September.]

foreknowing that the Godhead foresaw that it would also be especially consecrated by his own blood and name, and was preparing to enlarge it into a city for the increase of the martyrs’ glory.

> [Note: [Col. 0786D] I take these statements as Sigebert’s conjecture; for neither Godescalc nor Stephen handed down that St. Lambert had already then been informed of his own martyrdom.]

Such was Joseph’s devotion toward his father Jacob, who died in Egypt; such also was Moses’ diligence in seeking the bones of the patriarch Joseph, buried in Egypt, so that each of them might be returned for burial with his fathers.

## CHAPTER II. The saint’s episcopate at Trajectum, beneficial to Church and kingdom; bishops and abbots contemporary with him; his expulsion from his see; monastic life at Stavelot.

12. Much deliberation took place in the Church over who ought to be appointed bishop of the Church of Trajectum; much discussion also took place at the court of King Hildric,

> [Note: [Col. 0786D] That is, Childeric II, then king of Austrasia, as we said above.]

who, after the death of his uncle Sigebert,

> [Note: [Col. 0786D] St. Sigebert, king of the Austrasians, brother of Clovis II through Dagobert I, though by a different mother. His deeds were illustrated under 1 February.]

had received the kingdom of Austrasia from his father Clovis.

> [Note: [Col. 0786D] Sigebert is mistaken when he writes that Childeric had been appointed king over the Austrasians by his father Clovis, who is known to have died some years earlier.]

And gradually talk passed from the palace to the Church, from the Church to the assembled people: there was none better than Lantbert, and consequently none more worthy of the episcopate of Trajectum. By canonical authority it was fitting that he should receive in his own Church the fruit of his service. The Church agreed with the palace; clergy consented with people; the hearts of all desired one thing; thousands of people shouted with one voice.

He declared himself unequal to the burden and was thereby all the more deserving of compulsion. As once the unanimous zeal of Israel and Judah moved them to choose David as king—the man whom the Lord had found according to his own heart—so favorable was the clergy’s and people’s agreement in choosing Lantbert, whom the Lord had likewise found according to his own heart, to do all God’s wills. Though all had one heart, nevertheless you might think that, above the rest, the people of Tongeren said to Lantbert what the men of Judah said to their kinsman David:

> “We are your bone and your flesh. Yesterday and the day before, you were the one who led Israel out and brought it back; for the Lord your God said to you: ‘You shall feed my people Israel’; and: ‘You shall be prince over us.’”

13. At last the man enriched by the honors of holiness and made illustrious by the commerce of self-restraint consented to comply with all, so that all might glory in the one man in Christ. Having attained the summit of religious office, he strove continually to increase works of devotion, now adorned with the pontifical mitre. Every day he offered a holocaust to the Lord, not from another’s flock but from his own body. He always turned his counsel and work toward God, directing heart and feet to proclaim the gospel of peace.

For the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which belong to Christ substantially, were also present in him accidentally, according to the capacity of human nature. The spirit of counsel flourished remarkably in him, and whatever he did, he governed by the spirit of wisdom. King Hildric, seeing him surpass all others, esteemed him above all the leading men of his realm and its bishops. In his own heart, at his own ears and lips, he gave him first place; believing his heart to be an oracle of the Holy Spirit and holding his tongue to be an instrument of truth, he freely granted him the fullest measure of his friendship and made him his secretary for confidential matters—who, it is said, was also his keeper of official records. Thus all Austrasia depended upon his heart and mouth, and the whole royal court revered him.

14. Theoderic, brother of King Hildric, who reigned over the part of Francia called Neustria, likewise sought Lantbert’s presence and reserved abundant favor for him among his nobles and friends. If anything in his kingdom had to be authorized, he did not think it sufficiently ratified unless it had also been approved by Lantbert’s counsel.

> [Note: [Col. 0787D] All these statements that Sigebert here writes concerning Theoderic III, then king of Neustria and later monarch, are not very plausible.]

The Frankish kings Theoderic and Hildric, though because of their simplicity they possessed little wisdom in themselves, were wise in this: they listened to wise men. For the first degree of wisdom is to be wise; the second, to listen to a wise person. Hence, because affairs of the realm were conducted by the counsel of Lantbert, so holy and prudent a man, and of other holy bishops, the condition of affairs in both kingdoms was good and the Church’s faith prospered.

For at that time there were holy bishops, endowed with knowledge and wisdom, who holily and justly assisted the secondary administration of the kingdom. Foremost among them were Audoenus of Rouen,

> [Note: [Col. 0787D] His Acts were illustrated under 24 August.]

Austregisilus of Bourges,

> [Note: [Col. 0787D] The Life of Austregisilus of Bourges was given under 20 May; yet he had died many years before St. Lambert was made bishop, indeed before he was born.]

Eligius of Noyon,

> [Note: [Col. 0787D] St. Eligius will be treated under 1 December; but neither did he survive as far as St. Lambert’s episcopate.]

Vindicianus of Cambrai,

> [Note: [Col. 0787D] His Life is found in our work under 11 March.]

Audomarus of Thérouanne,

> [Note: [Col. 0788D] St. Audomarus was treated under 9 September.]

Leodegarius of Autun,

> [Note: [Col. 0788D] This saint’s deeds will be elucidated under 2 October.]

and Faro of Meaux.

> [Note: [Col. 0788D] St. Faro is commemorated on 28 October.]

15. Among these Lantbert shone forth, the Church’s golden star, as the moon gleams among lesser fires. Lantbert revered them as fathers and elders, and, imitating them, drew from each something of grace. They, in turn, loved Lantbert deeply as a son now producing the fruits of maturity from the flower of youth; and they rejoiced that, as though by hereditary succession after them, the governance of the Church should belong to him, whom they saw walking blamelessly in all things, righteous before God and men, and advancing day by day from virtue to virtue.
