There were also abbots, renowned for holiness both then and now: Bertin,

> [Note: [Col. 0788D] St. Bertin, abbot of Sithiu, was treated under 5 September.]

Philibert,

> [Note: [Col. 0788D] He means St. Filibert or Philibert, abbot on the Gallic island of Herio, concerning whom see our work under 20 August.]

and Wandregisel;

> [Note: [Col. 0788D] He was abbot of Fontenelle, whose deeds are set forth in our work under 22 July; but he died before St. Lambert’s episcopate.]

while Ursmar of Lobbes was growing into a novice of Christ.

> [Note: [Col. 0788D] See concerning him under 18 April.]

These were Lantbert’s contemporaries; such were his companions. Like Cherubim, they beat the wings of their virtues one against another and stirred the world to praise God.

16. These and others who shone in that age like stars in the firmament of heaven, like David’s thirty-six mighty men prefiguring the steadfastness of faith through the equality of a square number, with our David—that is, Lantbert—by the mighty hand of Christ illumined the world with wisdom and strength; and in their hands warfare against God’s enemies prospered.

Among them Lantbert, like another David given by God to govern the Church; like a growing forest-tree rising to the summit of perfection; like the tiniest wood-worm, by the power of humility destroying things hard and strong; like a worker in embroidered many-colored cloth,

> [Note: [Col. 0789D] He seems to indicate the patriarch Joseph, of whom Genesis 37:3 reads: “And his father made him a coat of many colors.”]

himself adorned with various virtues and adorning others, attained with an ascent easy to very few the three foremost degrees of virtue: governing the throne of the Church by wisdom, marking out by humility the footsteps for following Christ, and conquering adversities for God by fortitude. Through their merits the Church of God long remained tranquil and the realm’s condition long prospered. Afterwards, because of the people’s torpor, while Jesus slept in the ship of the holy Church, behold, there arose a great commotion upon the sea of this world. The cause of so great a disturbance is easy to learn.

17. The brothers Theoderic and Hildric ruled the kingdom of Francia in two parts. But because Theoderic was of duller intellect, Ebroin, mayor of the palace, abusing his simplicity, stirred up the hatred of all the people against the king. The Franks, turning another’s envy against Theoderic, deposed him from the kingdom and invited his brother Hildric from Austrasia, appointing him king over themselves. So long as Hildric governed them moderately,

> [Note: [Col. 0789D] I have restored this word, since our manuscript read only *modera*, followed by a blank space for two or three omitted letters.]

he ruled both kingdoms powerfully. But when he too exceeded the measure and acted too arrogantly, he could not long hold his arms against the torrent. For, having caused a certain Frankish noble named Bodilo to be beaten more severely than was just, bound to a stake and against the law, he was killed by that same Bodilo while hunting.

Theoderic recovered the whole kingdom. Ebroin’s malice flared up again: he ruined, slaughtered, stripped of honors, punished by confiscation, and exiled all whom he found to have supported Hildric’s party too steadfastly.

18. Since no one had been more faithful or friendly to Hildric than Lantbert, the whole weight of tribulation fell upon him. It seemed that Hildric’s death had accomplished nothing if Lantbert, Hildric’s intimate, went unpunished; for they held it certain that he would never assent to their faction of iniquity. Therefore, by Ebroin’s counsel, King Theoderic summoned a crowd of bishops to a synod. Like mute dogs, they could not bark against false testimony;

> [Note: [Col. 0789D] In place of *valebant* (“were able”) in the erased text, another hand has written in the margin *volentes* (“willing”).]

they deposed some bishops and, by doubled injustice, ordained others.

And lest anyone remain in kingdom or Church who would dare, by Lantbert’s example or prompting, to raise the shield of faith in defense of truth—he who, beyond and on behalf of the rest, dared more freely to oppose injustice—all the devil’s accomplices rose against Lantbert, the friend of truth; fabricating grounds of injustice, they deposed him from the episcopate.

> [Note: [Col. 0789D] We have said that this pseudo-synod, at which St. Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, was most unjustly condemned, was held some years later, while our saint was already an exile at Stavelot.]

The bishop of Cologne is said to have conspired with this faction of wicked men; he even allowed Faramund, a cleric of his church, to be advanced to the episcopate of Trajectum against right and justice.

> [Note: [Col. 0790D] Godescalc and Stephen also teach that Faramund was unjustly intruded into the holy bishop’s see; but neither of them makes any archbishop of Cologne guilty of that crime.]

19. Wretched Faramund, because he followed their counsel, sat in the seat of pestilence. What else could be said of him than what Truth itself says:

> “He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs in another way, is a thief and a robber. But he who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep. The thief comes only to steal and slaughter and destroy.”

Lantbert, the good shepherd, following the example of the essentially good Shepherd, was ready to lay down his life for his sheep. He did not flee like a hired servant, but withdrew from the stormy shipwreck of domestic persecution; meekly bearing all things, he relinquished the scepter of his episcopate, commending the care of the sheep to him who washed them in baptism and redeemed them by blood.

The patient man indeed had as leader in his exile King David, who, when his own people conspired against him at the instigation of his son Absalom, took up the course of patience; and, lest he be the cause of ruin in Israel, fled weeping, with covered head and bare feet, committing the cause of his justice to God.

20. He therefore sought the monastery of Stavelot, founded some years earlier by King Sigebert and renowned everywhere for the fervor of holy religion. He chose the haven of monastic quiet and there lived for seven years, leading an angelic life in his own company. Of the entire household of the Church, only two boys remained attached to his service. One of them, named Theodoenus, was the truthful narrator and competent witness of his deeds for the man who first wrote the holy man’s Life.

> [Note: [Col. 0790D] Thus he himself states in the first Life, no. 6.]

Behold, we have a man set before all as an example of virtues. Knowing what alone the supreme Master had commanded him to learn, he sought the rest of his soul in humility of heart and in patience. In obedience he conformed himself to Christ, his co-heir, who obeyed the Father unto death. What, I ask, must it have been like to see a man noble in birth, renowned in holiness, a bishop by office, formerly powerful in possessions, in so short a time become an accomplished monk—a thing that scarcely any other could attain over many years?

21. Truly, prosperity did not delight beyond measure the man whom altered circumstances did not shake; for what is possessed with love is never lost without grief. Whoever desires also fears; whoever fears never lives free or secure.

> [Note: [Col. 0790D] In the margin of our manuscript, another hand notes *erit* (“will live”) instead of *vivit* (“lives”).]

Our Lantbert grieved to lose none of the world, because he desired nothing; therefore he was always secure in himself and free in Christ. When unjustly removed from the episcopate, when did he complain of the injury done him? Whom did he appeal to? To whose hearing did he commit himself? To what jurist did he entrust his cause? He stirred up no scandal in kingdom or Church; he wished to mingle no one else’s ruin with his own. Revealing his cause to God alone, he said what the Son of God said to the Father through the prophet:

> “Arise, Lord, and attend to my judgment, my God and my Lord, to my cause.”

Now let us see, in one testimony of obedience, how highly Lantbert’s monastic conduct was esteemed. Always tending toward perfection, he added something to the discipline of his service, knowing that whatever he performed beyond obligation would be repaid to him by the true Samaritan. Hence, anticipating the canonical night-watch offices, he discharged private vigils to God at night.

22. One night, wishing to leave the dormitory, he disturbed the sleeping brothers because one sandal slipped from his hand. Knowing that, by the discipline of the Rule, one who had troubled the brothers’ rest ought to go to the cross, he immediately leapt from bed at the signal of the angered abbot. Leaving behind the sandals and what he held in his hands, clothed only in a rough hair-shirt, barefoot and nearly naked, he went to the cross.

> [Note: [Col. 0791D] Godescalc, who could have heard this from Theodoenus, expressly states that the abbot—who did not know by whom that noise had been made—had given this order.]

This stone cross stood between the oratory and the dormitory. The Israelites in the wilderness, murmuring because of the weariness of their long journey and labor, were struck down for this offense by the bites of fiery serpents; they were healed by looking upon the bronze serpent, raised by Moses as a sign prefiguring the crucified Son of Man. In this manner it is credible that this cross too was set up as a sign, so that those who belonged to Christ, looking upon it, might crucify their flesh with its vices and desires; and if any, wearied by the long labor on God’s way, became discouraged, then at the sight of the cross they might recover from Christ’s death the long-suffering of hope and thus escape the burning poisons of the ancient serpent.

23. Lantbert therefore went to the cross with the same patience and obedience with which Christ obeyed the Father unto death on the cross.

> [Note: [Col. 0791D] That is, he imitated Christ’s example as far as he could.]

There those sentenced under the Rule performed penance if they had committed rather serious faults; and Lantbert remained there unmoving through the night, intent upon psalms and hymns. The cold of that night was sharpened by frost, and though snow fell abundantly, it did not rise above the bishop’s ankles.

> [Note: [Col. 0791D] I do not know what miracle of snow Sigebert intended to indicate here; neither Godescalc nor Stephen mentions it.]

The whole face of winter was altogether terribly harsh; but this gentlest man, because the flame of the Spirit the Paraclete plainly burned within him, did not feel the outward torments of cold. Heaven opened to his prayers, and his prayer reached those above and was heard. While he sang the psalm verse,

> “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?”

the cocks crowed earlier than usual. The brothers rose for the prescribed duties of the vigils and, after this, entered the house and kindled a plentiful fire. While they warmed themselves, the abbot asked where Lantbert was, since he was absent from the brothers’ assembly. One of the brothers said that Lantbert was at the cross, sentenced by the Rule through the unseasonable night.

24. The abbot was terrified and urgently ordered the brothers to go and call him back. They went and found him singing:

> [Note: [Col. 0791D] In the manuscript margin, another hand again notes *attendunt* (“they attend”) in place of *offendunt* (“they find”).]

> “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.”

When he had been recalled, the abbot and the entire community fell at his knees. The abbot accused himself and, while excusing the fault, asked pardon for ignorance or lack of restraint. Lantbert, his own accuser, imputed the fault to himself, saying that there was nothing for him to forgive them. The brothers repaid the grace of his goodwill; preparing a bath for him, they changed his clothes. Then, kissing his hands and feet, they congratulated him unanimously, saying that this had happened for the increase of his glory.

The distinguished bishop, stretching his hands to heaven, blessed the brothers thus:

> O almighty God, who fillest the heavens with light,  
> Who rulest heaven, lands, and sea by thy dominion,  
> So that all things in their season are subject to thy will,  
> I ask thee: bless these thy servants through all ages;  
> Protect them from snares; preserve them by kindly virtues,  
> Until they see thee and attain the kingdoms of heaven,  
> By thy gift, O God, who now and forever through eternity  
> Art held blessed in the threefold power of thy being.

> [Note: [Col. 0792D] He borrowed these verses from the second Life, no. 22.]

## CHAPTER III. The saint’s restoration to his see and pastoral care; the Taxandrians brought from idols to Christ; the burial of St. Landrada made illustrious by a miracle through him.

25. When seven years had passed, at last it pleased the Most High, after a dreadful and long-lasting storm, to restore serenity to the face of heaven. Pippin II, son of Ansegisel and Begga,

> [Note: [Col. 0792D] St. Begga, daughter of Pippin of Landen, wife of Ansegisus, Ansegis or Ansigilius, and mother of Pippin of Herstal, is commemorated on 17 December.]

after bravely defeating all those who, contending among themselves, had torn Francia apart, alone obtained under King Theoderic the leadership of all Francia and undertook to improve the disordered state of kingdom and Church. Among other grounds for praise, this occasion presented itself: at last Faramund, the hireling of Trajectum, having been removed by the just judgment of clergy and people, was expelled not only from the Church of Trajectum but also from the whole province.

> [Note: [Col. 0792D] We have shown in Commentary §6 that Faramund’s expulsion and St. Lambert’s restoration to his see should be assigned to 681 or 682, when Pippin held the mayoralty of the palace of Austrasia alone.]

Immediately all raised their prayer to heaven, and all directed an embassy to Prince Pippin, that the people of Trajectum might no longer lack the consolation of their pious father Lantbert. When Absalom, invader of his father’s kingdom, had been divinely punished, such was Israel, God’s people, in its exultation; so great then was the joy of God’s people at the repulse of the invader Faramund. They longed for Lantbert’s recall to the episcopate as greatly as those others had labored for David’s return to the kingdom. The prince approved their just petition and ordered the shepherd restored to his sheep.

26. Thus the veteran soldier, purified by most grievous tribulation, was raised up by his sheep’s voices and fittingly restored to the chair of Trajectum. And rightly so: for in his heart were sincerity and the fullness of the law; in his mouth, truth and beauty. How great was the rejoicing at his return among every rank, age, and sex! How each rejoiced in his own particular cause, he knows who alone discerns all affections.

The apostolic man, therefore, having returned to his own city, restored the rule of ecclesiastical discipline that had been corrupted by pseudo-Christians. And as David said, “I know that today I have been made king over Israel,” so he believed himself now for the first time made bishop; forgetting what lay behind, he stretched himself toward what lay before. Preferring to be rather than to be called a bishop, he attended most earnestly to himself and to the entire flock. He did not evade declaring the whole counsel of God to all; fearing the reproach of the wicked and slothful servant who stored his master’s money in a cloth, he did nothing negligently with heart or body. Instead, he visited cities and towns, and sowed the seed of life in season in hearts cultivated with the hoes of the word.

27. At times he even crossed the boundaries of his diocese, lest the Lord call him an unprofitable servant because he had done only what he ought to have done. Nearby was the province of the Tessandrians,

> [Note: [Col. 0793D] Taxandria is a region two miles distant from the town of Trajectum.]

where idolatry still flourished. The valiant athlete of Christ grieved that enemies of the Christian name should oppose his king’s realm from so nearby a territory. He girded himself with the arms of faith; inflamed by the zeal of virtue, he harassed them by frequent assaults and, offering them the Lord’s peace, tried every means to see whether his peace might in any way rest upon children of peace.

Although they raged like barbarians and wished to tear him apart, he freely entered the conflict, destroyed their temples and images, and at other times softened them with the sweetness of speech, addressing them thus:

> “Brothers, concern for myself, for what is mine, and for your welfare urges me to admonish you concerning true salvation, so that both you may be saved and I may receive from you the fruit of my labor. Nothing is more useful to a human being than to seek salvation. But who can seek salvation unless he knows what salvation is? How can he seek it if he does not know from whom it must be sought? Whoever seeks it from any source other than God, who is salvation itself, accomplishes nothing.
>
> “If a person, neglecting the soul, cares only for the body, he differs in no way from a beast, which, in accordance with the posture of its body, looks down at the earth and attends only to the body. For that person is a human being who knows himself. Know, O human being, who you are, how you were created, and what you will become.”

28. “You are human because you were formed from clay;

> [Note: [Col. 0793D] The margin reads *humo*, ‘soil,’ instead of *limo*, ‘clay.’]

you are a rational and mortal creature, midway between beasts and angels. By reason you are better than a beast; by mortality you are lower than an angel. What manner of being you were created is shown by the posture of your body. Why was the human being alone created with face uplifted, breast erect, and hands straight? Surely so that in body, heart, and action he might always attend to heaven.

“Do you wish to know what you will become? You are earth, and to earth you shall return. Yet if

> [Note: [Col. 0793D] The margin notes *sed cum*, ‘but when,’]

you seek the salvation of your soul, you will attain immortality. To attain this, a person must know who or what God is. If he does not know who or what God is, let him at least know who or what God is not.

“Do you wish to know what God is? God is he who created all things from nothing, governs all things, and always lives without beginning, without end, without spatial or temporal limitation, and without change of substance. Hear also what God is: God is eternal and eternity itself, wise and wisdom; and whatever virtue belongs to anyone else accidentally belongs to God alone substantially.

“But who does not know what God is not? A human being, a stone, wood, or anything of that kind is not God; in short, no creature is God. God is not any of those things that are spoken of through the privation or opposition of good—such as being unjust, evil, or anything of that sort. Whoever is human will learn these things from the teaching of nature alone and, by contemplating creation, will understand the Creator.”

29. God created heaven and earth, and last of all creatures fashioned man, granting him freedom of choice, so that through a voluntary desire for good he might deserve also the reward of good. [Col. 0794C] [Note: [Col. 0794D] In our manuscript this word is corrupted; it reads *oppe-*.] He created him such that, if he did not sin, he would be immortal; if he sinned, he would become mortal. Trusting the devil more than God, he fell into death together with all his race; and humankind broke out into such great wickedness that God repented of having made man, and by the Flood destroyed from beneath heaven all flesh, preserving only eight persons in the ark for a whole year. Their descendants, wishing to have a refuge against God, raised a tower up to heaven; but God, taking the pride of Adam’s children to heart, divided the human language, which had been one for all, into seventy-two languages, and so divided them from himself. Idolatry grew worse than every evil; because Abraham almost alone recoiled from it, he deserved from God a blessing and the promise that in his seed—that is, Christ—all nations would be blessed. Born of the Virgin, true God and true man, performing in his one person the works of divine and human nature, he did and suffered in human nature everything belonging to humanity except sin; and, shining forth in words and signs, he did not conceal what belongs to God.

30. But as wax softens and clay hardens under the one heat of the sun, so under the heat of the divine word the good were softened unto faith, while the evil were hardened against faith. [Col. 0795A] Therefore, in order that God might accomplish his work—namely, save humankind—he performed a work so strange and alien that he who is the life of all things tasted death, even death on a cross, in human nature and for humankind. Having despoiled hell, rising from the dead on the third day, ascending into heaven, and sending the Holy Spirit upon the disciples together with knowledge of every language, he sent them into the world to preach and baptize in the name of the Holy Trinity. Hence the sound of the apostles and apostolic men went out into all the earth. At last this sound has reached even you. Therefore, brothers, I grieve for you unto my very soul, because, rejecting God’s word, you judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life. Flee idolatry, most beloved ones. I speak to the wise: judge for yourselves what I say. [Col. 0795B] What advantage is there in worshipping images that have neither soul nor life? Flee, I say, from idolatry, because there is no greater injury against God, who says through the prophet: “My glory I will not give to another.” Flee darkness, you who possess the light of natural reason.

31. By now almost the whole world has believed. As the sun touches with its presence the three quarters of the world—East, South, and West—but illuminates the northern quarter from afar by casting its rays, so Christ, the Sun of the world, sanctified the East by being born there, visited the South in fleeing into Egypt, and did not leave the West, where he sent the apostles, through whom Rome, now the head of the world, has bowed its neck. This fourth quarter, which you inhabit, though because of the sun’s absence it receives the light more slowly, nevertheless sees that it is illuminated from afar; and if it lacks the sun’s presence, it has no less need of the use of sunlight. In this way, most beloved ones, though you have not seen Christ himself or Christ’s apostles, blessed are you if you believe in him whom you have not seen. If you cannot fix your gaze upon the sun itself, direct your eyes to the mountains illumined by the sun. Through these mountains—that is, apostolic men—by the light of faith transmitted far and wide, Spain, the threefold Gaul, Germany, and the remote Britain and Scotland under another sphere have now believed. Francia close at hand reproaches you for stubborn unbelief. Since the earth is full of the Lord’s mercy, why does God’s wrath remain upon you as upon children of unbelief? Run to the light; believe in God [Col. 0795D] the Father, and in Jesus Christ his Son, and in the Holy Spirit. Believe in the future resurrection of the flesh; fear the final day of judgment, on which we shall all be judged: the wicked, that they may go into eternal punishment; the good, that they may have eternal life with the angels—not changed into angelic nature, but advanced to angelic glory in the various orders of angels according to the diversity of their merits.

32. With these and such words the Preacher of Christ gradually removed the barbarism of paganism from their hearts and enticed them toward the gentleness of Christianity; [Col. 0796A] removing the stench of idolatry—[Note: [Col. 0795D] In the margin stands *fervorem*, “ardour.”]—he spread everywhere Christ’s sweet fragrance. Yet, moved by regard for his humanity, they observed the power and piety of the holy man, who fulfilled in deed what he preached by word; wishing to imitate him, they allowed themselves to be confirmed by him in faith in Christ. Nor did Christ’s standard-bearer cease until he had led that whole people, driven out of the devil’s kingdom, into the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0795D] In the margin, in place of *regnum* (“kingdom”), stands *aeterni* (“eternal”); consequently, shortly afterward *regum* (“of kings”) ought to be read as *regnum* (“kingdom”). Moreover, that entire speech is Sigebert’s, not [Col. 0796D] the saint’s.] of the King of kings. This, O Christ, is your grace; this is the steadfastness of your good soldier, who, undertaking the apostolic work, brought an illustrious triumph to your camp. Behold the apostle of Toxandria, rightly comparable with the apostles and apostolic men. For when the Prince of Shepherds comes to judge, and each shepherd presents to him what portion of the world he has brought by his preaching [Col. 0796B] to faith, this our Shepherd will not appear empty among the shepherds; rather, he himself will draw after him many whom by his labor he has recalled from idolatry or wickedness, and he will receive a manifold crown of glory.

33. How glorious God is in himself could in no way be grasped by human beings, unless he worked certain wonders in his saints, through which we might understand that he is truly wonderful. While Pippin ruled the Franks, the virgin Saint Landrada built a monastery in the estate of Belisia, [Note: [Col. 0796D] The Life of Saint Landrada, virgin and first abbess of Belisia, was published under 8 July, by Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Trond.] guided in everything by Saint Lambert’s counsel and using his assistance. When the day of her departure was imminent, in order to enter prepared for the wedding of her Bridegroom with the lamp of good works alight, she summoned Saint Lambert himself familiarly, so that she might receive from him the viaticum of life. [Col. 0796C] As the holy man hastened on his way, she was meanwhile released from the prison-house of the flesh; but God, to whom nothing is dearer than brotherly love, did not allow either him or her to be deprived of the fruit of their mutual friendship. For as he travelled, a pleasing vision appeared to the bishop. Before his eyes, as he lay there and was, as it were, half-awake in ecstasy, the virgin of Christ, Landrada herself, stood visibly radiant; addressing him with the grace of a friendly face and voice, she said: “Why, my friend, this unusual neglect of me on your part? Why has such delay kept you from coming to visit me?”

34. Lambert, alleging the affection of friendship, made this excuse: “You have no cause to accuse me either of neglect or delay, for, as I hastened to come to you, the swifter necessity of your death forestalled me. [Col. 0796D] Behold, since I am here and you have already entered into the joy of your Lord, I shall pay you what is due in justice; but you, I ask, tell me in what place, according to your wish, I should bury your little body.” And she said: “Look up at heaven, and carefully mark on earth the place where you now see the sign of the holy cross appearing from heaven through flashing light.” Lambert followed with eyes and mind as she pointed; behold, he saw a place on earth marked by heavenly light in the form of the holy cross, and from the mouth of the virgin conversing with him he received these final words: “Lambert, know that this place, divinely shown to you, [Col. 0797A] was long ago appointed by God for my burial.” When the holy virgin had been received into heaven after this exchange of words, the holy man awoke from sleep and rejoiced in the oracle of the heavenly vision. The place irradiated by the sign of heavenly light was Wentreshovum, [Note: [Col. 0797D] See the notes on chapter I, letter i.] where Saint Lambert himself, having been brought up there by Saint Landoald, had distinguished the beginning of his religious training.

35. Lambert accordingly hastened his way all the more eagerly because he knew that this would be more pleasing to God and to his bride. Arriving at Belisia later than he wished, though not later than his feet could carry him—for to a desiring mind nothing hastens sufficiently—he disclosed the vision to everyone, seeking, as gently and eloquently as possible, to persuade them to carry it out. All protested against one; all cried out tumultuously with one voice: “Far be it, Lambert—far be it, blessed bishop! Here this holy virgin was consecrated to God by you; this church was built by her work and expense and dedicated by you at her request; here all her possessions were assigned to God by her through you; here the community serving God grew up through her and through you. And where could her bones rest more worthily than here, where the visible testimonies of so many of her good works are present? Indeed, all these things also increase the merits of your holiness, Lambert, since here, through the care of your pastoral office, gifts of faith and virtue abound in a body of believers increased both in worth and in number.” Lambert was offended by the obstinacy of all. “It is pleasant,” he said, “to preside over fellow citizens, but hard to please everyone. Behold, since the word of God and my word find no place [Col. 0797C] in you, I shall reluctantly follow you all; nevertheless, I am certain that the heavenly oracle will not lack its fulfillment.”

36. Therefore, after the holy virgin had been buried more by the people’s wish than by his own, Lambert’s mind wavered: on the one hand he was certain of the heavenly oracle; on the other, uncertain about the buried body of the virgin. For this reason, devoting himself to every manner of prayer, he sought the matter from him to whom he knew nothing was impossible. After three days had thus passed, he summoned the people and said: “I declare that the virgin of Christ, long deceased, was of great merit even in your judgment; and therefore I do not consider lightly what I know has been told me from her mouth now that she reigns with Christ. Therefore do not be troubled by what I request: let the virgin’s tomb be opened, that we may test the matter itself with our eyes.” Everyone obeyed; the tomb was opened, but nothing was found there of the holy body [Col. 0797D] buried there, since it had been moved elsewhere together with the very sarcophagus. All faces grew pale; Lambert alone rejoiced, and gently comforted the astonished people like a father. “Since,” he said, “you have experienced your disbelief, let us now experience God’s wondrous power and seek the mound of the holy body in the place shown to me.” With him as guide they hurried [Col. 0798A] to Wentreshovum; reviewing in mind and sight the traces of the heavenly sign shown to him, he pointed out the place pleasing to the holy virgin. O new event! There they found the mound of the holy body, transported together with the very sarcophagus and reset so suitably and decently that no one could doubt that the holy virgin had been transferred there through angelic ministry.

37. And what wonder is it if he who prepared for his martyr Clement, by angelic hands, a dwelling in the sea in the form of a marble temple [Note: [Col. 0797D] Saint Clement, pope and martyr, whom this passage indicates, is venerated on 23 November; on that day these matters may be examined.] also transferred this virgin’s body so fittingly through angels, the ministers of God’s mysteries? [Note: [Col. 0797D] The same things are read in the Life of Saint Landrada, from which Sigebert could have learned them.] If anyone disbelieves this miracle as unprecedented, let him at least be moved by an argument from the contrary. For since [Col. 0798B] he knows that the bodies of many people, unworthily buried in holy places, have been cast far away by evil angels, let him not doubt that holy angels, at God’s command, performed this service for the holy virgin and confirmed the wish and words of Saint Lambert. Therefore all exalt God’s power; above all they proclaim the faith and merit of glorious Lambert, whose citizenship was already in heaven although he was still held bodily upon earth. In him they saw fulfilled that word of the Lord: “All things are possible to one who believes.” O man worthy of God, lacking nothing for the fullness of perfection, prepared even to ascend to that love than which no one has greater: to lay down his life for his friends! For what greater discharge would a king give his veteran soldier [Col. 0798C] than to bestow on him, crowned with martyrdom, the token of eternal rest? Let us now, to lay the final hand upon the work, raise the banner of his passion.

## Chapter IV. Pippin rebuked for taking Alpaïs as a concubine: the concubine’s hatred and intrigues; the saint’s martyrdom at her instigation

38. Pippin, as we have said, ruled preeminently over all the princes of the Franks. His glory was enhanced by frequent trophies of victory; and the memorials of nobility and holiness descending from both parents could at least have prompted him to virtue. To pass over the holiness of his maternal aunt Gertrude, [Note: [Col. 0797D] He refers to Saint Gertrude the virgin, abbess of Nivelles in Brabant, whose deeds were elucidated under 17 March. She was the daughter of Pippin I, surnamed of Landen, and sister of Saint Begga, by whom and Ansegisel [Col. 0798D] Pippin II was born.] or of Chlodulf, bishop of Metz, [Note: [Col. 0798D] He intended to refer to Saint Chlodulf, or Clodulf, bishop of Metz, whose deeds are set forth under 8 June, the day on which he is venerated.] who was Pippin’s godfather: who would not admire the life of his mother Saint Begga? Who does not know the sanctity of his paternal grandfather Arnulf, [Note: [Col. 0798D] Before entering the episcopate Saint Arnulf was married in secular life and fathered Saint Chlodulf, mentioned just above, and Ansegisel. From Ansegisel and Saint Begga Pippin was born, as we have said. For Saint Arnulf’s deeds, see 18 July.] who was first mayor of the royal household and afterward bishop of Metz, wonderful to the world both in life and death? Moreover, the power of his sons already flourished in the kingdom. Of them [Col. 0799A] Drogo [Note: [Col. 0799D] Drogo, duke of Champagne, Pippin’s son by his lawful wife Plectrude, is recorded in various annals cited by Cointius as having died in 708.] was duke of the Champenois, while Grimoald [Note: [Col. 0799D] This was Pippin’s other legitimate son. While in 714 he was praying in the church of Saint Lambert at Liège for the recovery of his sick father, he was murdered.] awaited his father’s hereditary principate. His lawful wife Plectrude had borne these sons to him. Since Pippin lacked neither glory, nor power, nor good fortune, fortune was never superior to his diligence.

39. O, nothing is ever safe in the presence of the devil! A man so victorious could not triumph over himself; allowing his iron breast to be pierced by the soft weapon of lust, he took a noble and graceful maiden named Alpaïs in addition to his lawful wife Plectrude. By her he also had a son, Charles, who was later surnamed Tudetes, or Martellus, because of his untamed bravery in war. She was the sister of Dodo, [Note: [Col. 0799D] Godeschalc and Stephen also testify that Dodo was a member of Pippin’s household and a powerful man; but the first writer known to me to state that he was Alpaïs’s brother was the anonymous author whose words we cited in the Commentary, no. 128.] who belonged to the household of Prince Pippin, [Col. 0799B] a man rich in resources, illustrious by birth, and possessed of great power in the kingdom through friends, relatives, and many retainers obedient to him. Since there was no bishop to stand opposed and set himself as a wall for the house of Israel, to stand in battle on the day of the Lord, Lambert rebuked the prince in season and out of season. He presented himself as another Elijah or John, and, imitating their zeal, he also aspired to their merit, so that, being equal to them in constancy in struggle, he might be equal in the glory of victory. Elijah endured and overcame Ahab [Note: [Col. 0800D] Read *Achab*. Here, in our manuscript, one word and then another have dropped out, as the blank space indicates.] … king of Israel as an enemy, and by rebuking him brought him so far that he postponed from himself God’s threatened wrath—a wrath he might perhaps have escaped altogether had not his wife Jezebel, inciting him against God, sold him into sin.

[Col. 0799C] 40. Herod feared John when he rebuked him and did many things because of him; but his wife Herodias likewise drove him, through the sensual dancing of her daughter, to an oath and thereby to the Saint’s death. Our third Elijah, or second John—Lambert, that is—sent in the spirit and power of Elijah and John to prepare the Lord’s way, likewise rebuked Prince Pippin freely and did not fear the rage of a second Herodias. For Alpaïs had the same disposition as Herodias had when Herod willingly gave ear to John rebuking him for adultery, [Note: [Col. 0800D] In our manuscript Alpaidis is wrongly read here. Moreover, at this point Sigebert begins, contrary to the testimony of Godeschalc and Stephen, to invent a new cause for Saint Lambert’s martyrdom.] while Pippin obeyed Lambert rebuking him for his concubinage. Though otherwise a praiseworthy and devout man, Pippin took much pleasure in Lambert’s [Col. 0799D] counsels and was moved by his admonitions. If he could have deceived his loving concubine, he would doubtless have listened profitably to the bishop who rightly rebuked him. Elijah, taken up into heaven, still awaits the palm of victory through Antichrist’s sword; John devoted [Col. 0800A] his head to martyrdom for truth; Lambert, third of these two, likewise showed himself worthy to drink the Lord’s cup.

41. The concubine reported the matter to her brother Dodo and, entrusting her entire plan to him, begged that by his help the disgrace to her family might be removed—a disgrace that would grow too great if Lambert’s rebuke should bring about her separation from the prince. Dodo, sharing his own cause and his sister’s with the more powerful members of his kin, strove personally and through them to restrain the bishop from rebuking the prince. When he found Lambert inflexible and realized that he did not respect anyone’s person against justice, he promised his relatives and friends vengeance for his sister’s cause. Thereupon two brothers, Gallus and Rioldus, kinsmen of Dodo, [Note: [Col. 0800D] That Gallus and Rioldus were Dodo’s kinsmen and grievously oppressed the church of Maastricht by their depredations, he learned from Godeschalc and Stephen; but they assign no cause for the oppression and never mention Alpaïs.] pitying the plight of his niece [Col. 0800B] Alpaïs, sought an opportunity to provoke the bishop. Rising with all their followers against the entire household of the church of Maastricht, they fabricated accusations against them by whatever art they could and omitted no harassment they were able to inflict, hoping somehow thereby to bend the bishop’s judgment, so that at least for the sake of his own supporters he might cease rebuking the prince. But the outcome differed from what they had expected. The righteous man, confident as a lion, protected himself against every assault with the shield of patience; girding himself with the sword of the Spirit, which is God’s word, against the threats of earthly power, and putting on the helmet of salvation, he pursued the cause of truth without wavering. At first, indeed, he addressed them gently and, by every means [Col. 0800C] available to a father’s compassion and a bishop’s discipline, deterred them from unjust violence.

42. But because he was pouring words into the wind, turning with intimate confidence to God, he said: “Rise up, Lord, and judge my cause; remember the reproach of your servants.” But the sons of Belial attacked God’s faithful more fiercely and afflicted the innocent by every kind of injury. Those for whom the matter concerned their lives, and whose whole hope depended upon innocence alone, prepared, without consulting the bishop, to meet force with arms, either to avenge their wrongs or not to die unavenged. They came together; they fought. The former fought out of recklessness, the latter resisted for safety. Pride placed Gallus and Rioldus, Dodo’s kinsmen, in the foremost line of battle; justice set Peter and Audolecus, kinsmen of the bishop, [Col. 0800D] opposite them in the first rank. Fear exposed the cowardly spirits of Gallus and Rioldus; innocence raised Peter’s and Audolecus’s right hands to valor. The power of innocence prevailed, and victory went to the ecclesiastical side: Gallus and Rioldus, leaders of the wicked faction, [Col. 0801A] fell slain; Peter and Audolecus, defenders of the Church, carried off the banner of victory. [Note: [Col. 0801D] Sigebert embellished this entire battle according to his own fancy, whereas Godeschalc and Stephen say only that Gallus and Rioldus were killed by Peter and Audolecus, who could no longer endure the plundering of ecclesiastical property.] The impious were confounded, yet did not blush; they were defeated, but did not withdraw exhausted. For Dodo, who had been the instigator of every evil, now himself became the author of war; despising the words God speaks concerning priests, “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye,” he attacked the very head of the holy bishop, devoted him to death, and directed upon him alone vengeance for his nephews.

43. In those days Prince Pippin had come to Jopilia, [Note: [Col. 0801D] Jopilia, Jopila, Jopilum, Jupila, Jobii-villa—commonly Jupille—is a village on the Meuse near Liège, where Pippin had an estate and is believed also to have died.] an estate adjoining Liège. There the holy man, invited to Pippin’s court ostensibly on public business, did not withhold his presence. The prince and the prince’s concubine made their faces serene toward him; some [Col. 0801B] concealed anger, others feigned joy, and many altered the expression of their heart according to their individual inclination. The concubine, however, was considering an opportune way to procure an intercessor for herself, by whose intervention she might reconcile the bishop’s mind to her, or at least for the present mitigate his persistent rebuke of the prince. A banquet was prepared; the bishop was invited; the entire courtly company was altogether merry. The prince indicated that the cup offered him by the cupbearer should be brought to the bishop, considering it a blessing if he received a cup from the consecrated hand of the holy bishop—something he knew Emperor Maximus had once sought from Martin, bishop of Tours. [Note: [Col. 0802D] This story is related by Sulpicius Severus in chapter 23 of the Life of Saint Martin, who is commemorated on 11 November.] But Pippin would have received a greater blessing from Lambert [Col. 0801C] than Emperor Maximus received from Martin, if Pippin’s wife had deserved such favor from Lambert as Maximus’s wife obtained from Martin. [Note: [Col. 0802D] See the Dialogues of the same Sulpicius Severus, book II, chapter 7.]

44. Martin judged his own presbyter worthier than Emperor Maximus, to whom he handed the cup before the king; Lambert preferred no one to Pippin. The lesser nobles followed the prince’s example: all demanded that the cup be handed to them from the holy hand of the holy bishop. While everyone rushed in together and crowded forward in confusion, each trying to precede the other, behold, the concubine, secretly mingling her own hand among the hands of the others, strove even in this way to snatch the cup from the bishop’s hand. He, seeing before and behind, prudently guarded against feminine snares, and turning to the prince, [Col. 0801D] complained of the woman’s excessive presumption. He protested that she had craftily sought to brand him with the mark of a communion displeasing to God. Then he hurried from the hall and diminished all the pleasure of the princely banquet. [Note: [Col. 0802D] Sigebert was likewise the first to invent this entire banquet, unknown to all earlier writers, and narrated it as though he himself had attended it.] Nor did feminine cunning rest even then, wishing to leave nothing untried. [Col. 0802A] As evening compelled the bishop to return, the prince, at the concubine’s prompting, commanded him not to depart without greeting his wife.

45. The bishop, with the Spirit of truth speaking in him, said: “I call truly to witness Jesus, the hope of our life, O most great prince: I shall never hold communion with a fornicatress; for Paul commanded us: ‘Do not associate with fornicators.’ I call God to witness, I say, that I shall never greet her, because I know that John, God’s friend, said: ‘If anyone does not remain in the teaching of Christ, do not receive him, nor say “Hail” to him; for whoever says “Hail” to him shares in his evil works.’ I grieve exceedingly that you associate with her; I bear with pain your unwillingness to repent; and because of this I fear God’s wrath for you.” Thus the concubine, seeing that nothing remained for her cause and fearing that, if Lambert lived long, separation was now imminent, recounted the whole matter in order to her enraged brother. Adding oil to the furnace, she implored him to arrange the bishop’s murder as quickly as possible. Dodo’s grief over the death of his nephews was intensified by his doubled grief over his sister’s rejection; and he was now wholly intent upon satisfying himself and his sister.

46. Lambert, herald of truth and now hastening toward the prize of the heavenly calling, had come to Liège. Dodo, meanwhile, withdrew to the village of Auridum, sufficiently near Liège. He prepared weapons, gathered companions, and summoned auxiliaries acquired from the royal household in his own name or that of his sister. He hated delay; by delaying he gathered his anger, and by anger he sharpened the goads of rage upon the whetstone of his exceedingly hard [Col. 0802C] heart. Lambert, foreknowing that his contest was near, spent that night without sleep, not because any dreams of death frightened him, but because hope anticipated the coming joys of rest. For at the very middle of the night, rising to confess the Lord, he exercised upon earth an angelic service. At the hour for celebrating the nocturnal synaxis, [Note: [Col. 0802D] That is, the night Office.] he awakened his disciples and said: “Rise quickly: God has promised a crown to those who keep watch.” When the office was finished, the others returned to bed; he continued—perhaps, “remained steadfast”—to complete the course of good work. Near dawn, as the corruptible body weighed down the soul, he began, after the example of the Lord going to his passion, to feel weariness; and, his eyes heavy with sleep, he took in sleep a little [Col. 0802D] rest.

47. Then behold, near dawn, as the darkness grew thinner, Baldoveus, watchman of the episcopal house, saw and announced an enemy army advancing in wedge formation. Although the morning mist rising up obstructed clear vision, the matter was easily perceived [Col. 0803A] both from the multitude of men seen and from the clash of arms heard. Cuirasses flashed, helmets projected above their heads, shields covered their left hands, and swords and lances armed their right; slingers and archers marched ahead. Hear a wonderful thing, an indication of divine mercy! To make clear that Lambert gloried in nothing except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world had been crucified to him and he to the world, and that through the power of the cross an ascent from earth to heaven was now being prepared for him in heaven, certain men following the army saw in astonishment an admirable sign above the house where the bishop was: a likeness of the Lord’s cross, brighter than every metal, gleaming from earth up to heaven. It is established that to some who followed Dodo in hope of promised payment, not from eagerness to shed blood, and merely to increase the soldiers’ numbers rather than commit the crime, the holy cross was visible; whereas it was hidden by the covering mist from those who, through desire of plunder and expectation of reward, were bent upon the destruction of the holy bishop. [Col. 0803B] [Note: [Col. 0803D] Sigebert appears to have stated merely from conjecture to whom this cross was visible and from whom it was hidden; for the earlier biographers say only that it appeared in this way to certain persons from the army itself or following the army.]

48. To Emperor Constantine, the first Constantine, as he went to war against his rival, the sign of the cross appeared in heaven, shining with fiery brilliance; upon it appeared to be inscribed: **Τούτῳ νίκα**, “In this sign you will conquer.” [Note: [Col. 0803D] The deeds of Emperor Saint Constantine were elucidated under 21 May; there, in chapter 3, the miraculous cross which he saw when about to move against Maxentius is discussed. I have restored the Greek words, since in our manuscript they were corruptly read as *Duthoyca*.] A sign of the cross likewise appeared above Lambert’s house as he stood on the eve of battle, clearly foretelling that for him—who had borne the marks of Christ’s cross in his heart and body—victory and a crown were now being prepared by God. To certain persons it also appeared that for the Lord’s beloved Benedict a road was prepared, strewn with garments and lit by lamps from earth to heaven, by which he might ascend to heaven. [Col. 0803C] [Note: [Col. 0803D] The Life of Saint Benedict, founder of his order, by Saint Gregory the Great, was published under 21 March; there this vision is narrated in chapter 6.] But a way more glorious than Benedict’s was prepared for Lambert, who ascended to heaven by the very cross gleaming from earth to heaven. Lambert was also happier than Elijah himself. Elijah, carried into heaven in a fiery chariot, has had death deferred and still holds a long expectation of eternal life; Lambert, having undergone death, was led to heaven by the cross of fiery light and rejoices with Christ in eternal life.

49. The enemy battle line was now approaching as though to attack. The house watchman cried out to those sleeping; the army surrounding them could now itself have been [Col. 0803D] the messenger of terror. Christ’s witness Lambert, stunned by the heaviness of sleep and the bitterness of the event, rose barefoot and seized a sword as if intending to defend himself and his own. But recovering himself, he condemned himself for rashness [Col. 0804A] and, because he had even unlawfully attempted to use arms, bound himself before God to fitting penance. [Note: [Col. 0804D] Godeschalc and Stephen also say that the saint, immediately casting aside the sword which, heavy with sleep, he had first seized in an impulse of mind for self-defense, changed his purpose; neither mentions penance imposed upon himself for this. The anonymous poet cited in no. 174 fabricated from rumor that he resolved, if he survived, to do penance for seven years.] “Good Jesus,” he said, “you who said, ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,’ I pray you: do not let me lose my victory, because it is better for me to die in you than to lay hands upon my enemies in battle. You, mighty warrior, take up weapons and shield, and rise to help me.” Now the gates had been broken in, the doors smashed, and they were striking the very walls of the house with lances; some had even entered and were threatening fire. Peter and Audolecus drove out those who entered, and with the strength of so few men they vainly strove to resist so many. The saint comforted them for the time: “Brothers, if you have loved me in return, love Christ as I love him. Confess your sins to Jesus [Col. 0804B] and pray for one another, that you may be saved. It is now necessary for me to depart and live with Christ.”

50. “You know, my nephews, that you were guilty and liable in that crime [Note: [Col. 0804D] Namely, in the killing of Gallus and Rioldus.] for which vengeance is now sought. What you then did unjustly, I pray you now expiate justly and patiently. God will not judge the same matter twice, nor will double affliction arise. I beg you, do not let your sin overflow before God, nor let blood touch blood through your hands. Let us not fear the savagery of persecutors, for sword and fire will be their vengeance, consuming their flesh down to the marrow. Only keep your hands innocent, so that your spirit also may be saved eternally; give even your bodies to them to tear apart.” Encouraged by these final admonitions of their Father, all those now placed in the agony were strengthened to die for justice and innocence. Taking up the Psalter, he accepted as an omen the first verse of a psalm that came to hand: “For the Lord will require the blood of his servants.” To this he added as his final saying: “May the Lord see and require it.” When everyone had gone out of the chamber and been exposed like lambs amid raging men, he himself, with arms extended, prostrated himself upon the ground in the form of a cross, and praying with tears commended his soul into the Lord’s hands, as no devout person had ever commended himself to God.

[Col. 0804D] 51. Meanwhile the executioners killed Peter and Audolecus and all the members of the ecclesiastical household whom they found there. One man, more brutal than the rest, climbed to the roof’s summit and, seeing Lambert clinging to the floor of the room, [Col. 0805A] pierced his heart with a hurled spear. [Note: [Col. 0805D] Sigebert was the first to write that Saint Lambert’s heart was pierced. Godeschalc says:

> “At the stroke of the weapon he struck him down.”

Stephen says:

> “He struck with a weapon one who would live with Christ through the ages.”

The anonymous poet says:

> “Piercing him with a weapon, he increased the wounds of his own guilt.”]

But angels bore Lambert’s soul to heaven together with the very murmur of his prayer. The precious priest of the Lord, Lambert, who here had shared the lot of all who keep God’s commandments, rejoices and exults there in the fellowship of all the saints. Crowned with the garland of chastity among the continent and the virgins, as a confessor among confessors he drinks before God the second cup of confession; as a monk among monks he receives a hundredfold of eternal recompense; as an apostle among the Apostles he sits on the seat of judicial authority; as a prophet among prophets he rejoices in hope; as a patriarch among patriarchs he shines in faith. Finally, as a martyr among martyrs, taking the cup of salvation, he calls upon the Lord’s name, because he had nothing greater that he could render to the Lord [Col. 0805B] for all that the Lord had rendered to him. He also has a place among the nine orders of angels, in which he participates according to the merit of each order’s office. Thus made a participant in all, he was chosen as a citizen of the eternal court, where he possesses the palm of everlasting glory and the robe of eternal joy.

## Chapter V. Burial of the body at Maastricht; punishment of Dodo and his companions; miracles performed at Liège and a church built there; transfer of the body there; Grimoald’s murder divinely punished; the Northmen repelled from the sacred body; the author’s observation; date of the martyrdom.

52. A few of the attendants of the holy martyr who had escaped the danger of death covered the body, drenched in rosy blood, with a humble shroud and conveyed it as swiftly as possible by boat to Maastricht. Rumour flew through the peoples, shaking all with fear and horror: all trembled at the offence against the prince [Note: That is, against Dodo, as has often been said elsewhere.]; all recoiled at the undeserved murder of the bishop; the people of Maastricht wept that they had lost the goodwill of their loving father, yet did not dare sufficiently to render the reverence due to so great a father. They scarcely had leisure to mourn their dear one, scarcely to hate the guilty.

When the holy body had been brought ashore at the harbour, an innumerable, nameless crowd ran together; and from the confused lamentation of all one could judge how highly St Lambert had been valued by everyone. Laid upon a bier, the holy martyr was borne with due honour to the basilica of St Peter; the clergy followed with psalms and hymns, the people clapped their hands amid lamentations. The people kept solemn vigil through the night; the clergy duly observed the watch-services.

53. All delighted in kissing the footprints of their loving father; whoever was permitted to press kisses upon the holy limbs considered that he had obtained great aid. It was pleasant and devout to see everyone offer his shepherd a token of love; but it was pitiable and strange to observe the anger of the loving shepherd against wandering sheep.

For it is handed down by the elders that, although everyone was freely allowed to kiss the saint, if any concubine thrust herself forward to kiss the martyr’s body, she was whirled about as if by a whirlwind and driven back. [Note: Sigebert, the first of the biographers, recorded this remarkable repulse of the concubines.] Thus, by the repulse of the concubines, it was made very plain that this concubine was hateful both to God and to the holy martyr—the woman who had disgraced Francia by a double crime and disturbed the holy Church. [Note: He means Alpaida, whom we do not believe to have been responsible for St Lambert’s death.]

Such fear had seized the people of Maastricht because of the bitterness of this event that they did not dare prepare a tomb worthy of a man of so great a name. Therefore, opening the tomb of Father Aper, St Lambert’s own father, at daybreak they resolved to bury the body of his most holy son for the time being with his father’s bones.

54.

The heavenly power did not abandon his lifeless limbs, and  
showed the peoples how great had been his goodness.

For fear that the peoples might be frightened by human terror and thus fail to venerate Saint Lambert of the Lord with fitting honour, angelic chanting of psalms began to be heard at his tomb by night, and sometimes by day, whenever human silence seemed to prevail there. Nor were there lacking persons who investigated the truth of the matter itself; and when they applied every attentiveness of mind and ear, it seemed to them—judging from the quality of the voice, well known to them as St Lambert’s—that the saint himself, together with the others who had died with him, was singing a sweet melody to the divine Majesty. [Note: The words enclosed in brackets have been restored from the shorter Life, written by the same Sigebert and wrongly attributed to Reiner. In our manuscript, where the text is defective, it reads, in its dislocated form: “It seemed to them, from a voice familiar to them, whence [that] of St Lambert, that the saint himself,” etc.]

If anyone at that hour wished to enter the basilica, he could not go in because of terror; and the nearer he pressed forward, the less his blunted ears admitted the angelic voices. But when he withdrew, the angelic melody was repeated more fully. O Christ, your power is ineffable! Who can requite your mighty works? Behold, you openly show what you said with your own mouth: “God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” For all live to you, who live and reign for ages of ages.

55. The glorious soldier of Christ, Lambert, immediately began on earth to reveal how great he was in heaven before the King of kings. In this he was far happier, because through him even after death the name of the Lord was blessed among the peoples.

For, appearing by night to the treasurer named Amalgisus, formerly his judge, he addressed him in gentle speech. When that man diligently asked the reason for his coming, he said: “We have gone to Rome; behold, we are returning from Rome, to visit Dodo and his accomplices. For the blood of the innocent, shed upon the earth with me for Christ, is now demanding vengeance from him; nor will God withhold his favour from them.” Having said this, he disappeared.

But the outcome proved that the vision was not imaginary. Dodo, the murderer of the holy bishop, immediately incurred the wrath of divine vengeance. For, vomiting through his mouth all his vital parts, putrid and foul, he displayed his wretchedness to all by his miserable end of life. He who here had abused the pomp of the world was assigned in hell to unquenchable fire and the worm that does not die.

[Note: Godescalcus calls him *Amalgisilus*, and this reading likewise occurs in the shorter Life just cited.]

56. It is also reported that, because the stench was intolerable, his body, corrupted by worms and decay, was thrown into the River Meuse; nor did he deserve any other burial, he who had acquired for himself the miserable memorial of so great a crime. [Note: Godescalcus says nothing of the body having been thrown into the Meuse.]

One equal to Dodo in guilt—the man who had slain the saint of the Lord with his own hands—entered miserably into battle with his brother; after killing his brother, he was in turn killed by that brother. To put everything briefly, as they say: within the course of that same year scarcely anyone escaped who had been guilty in the murder of the holy martyr. If anyone survived, he grieved so deeply that his understanding had been destroyed that he considered fortunate those who had been carried off by swift, though miserable, death. [Note: Our manuscript reads *censu*; perhaps *sensum*, “understanding,” should nevertheless be read.]

But Christ’s crowned martyr triumphs; holding the palm of victory, he rejoices in Abraham’s bosom. [Note: Our manuscript has *Victoriam palmae*; I have corrected it from the same shorter Life.] Thus, Christ, you triumph over enemies in your saints; loving those who love you, you honour those who honour you.

57. Liège, which was privileged to be made illustrious by the martyrdom of its patron, although it grieved that it had for a time been widowed of his body, was nevertheless not deprived of his miracles. In the chamber that knew his martyrdom, lamps kindled by divine power often shone, so that the whole house gleamed as though it were one single ray, and scarcely could a human eye endure that light. [Note: The words enclosed in brackets have again been restored from the cited shorter Life. In our manuscript, after the word “gleamed,” with the rest omitted, there followed only “eye.”]

The grace of the miracles which followed confirmed these first reports, the chief points of which should here be summarized. The holy man once warned a certain Theodimus in a vision to return his excellent comb, which Theodimus’s wife had snatched from the saint. When he did not obey on the third occasion, the saint struck Theodimus’s breast with an incurable blow, and thus recovered what was his from an unwilling man. [Note: The shorter Life has *Theoduinus*; Godescalcus, *Theodoenus*.] [Note: Godescalcus testifies only that the saint appeared to him twice; Sigebert added the third occasion.]

Baldigisilus was commanded in a vision to keep vigil at the place of his martyrdom; another man, Raginfrid, was instructed to clean that same place. Both received, each in his own time, the sight of which they had been deprived.

58. The virgin Oda also came in faith to this place, herself blind; and, as soon as she invoked the name of the holy martyr near the place, she received what she desired. [Note: Godescalcus treats of these three persons who received sight in chapter 3; it was from him that Sigebert learned this, as also what follows concerning the church built at Liège.]

By these things the new veneration of the new patron increased, and the devotion of the people, once kindled, built a basilica for the saint—the more swiftly, the more devoutly. A bed made by the faithful for the saint was also set in the place where the saint had been pierced by the weapon of the wicked man.

This devotion of the people of Liège so pleased the Lord that heavenly visions now frequently appeared to many faithful persons, directing that the holy martyr be brought back from Maastricht to the place of his martyrdom. Saint Hubert, the most holy Lambert’s disciple and successor, did not resist the will of God and the martyr. Therefore, in the thirteenth year of his episcopate, he opened the saint’s tomb and found the body whole and untouched, suffused with a wonderful fragrance. He changed the clothing and sealed up the former garments, to preserve them for distribution as sacred relics. [Note: This year, which we have shown fell in A.D. 721 or 722, was taken from the biographer of St Hubert in Surius.] [Note: That is, to be distributed as sacred relics.]

59. It was made manifest also during the translation that this was pleasing to the Lord. For, when the people rested in the village of Nuella, a poor blind man was enriched by the restoration of his faculty of sight. [Note: The shorter Life reads *Nivella*.] Not long afterwards, in the village of Hermala, while all rested to recover from their labour, a paralytic brought there was restored to himself, his limbs made sound, in the sight of the holy bier. [Note: The shorter Life has *Harmala*.] [Note: Godescalcus calls him *contractus*, “crippled.”]

In each of these places basilicas were immediately founded in honour of the holy martyr. With such rejoicing they approached you, O Liège, their civic community! [Note: Liège, or Leodium, had been only a village during St Lambert’s lifetime; yet it is likely that, because it was the place of his martyrdom and became illustrious through miracles and a church, it had already then begun to grow.] How great and what kind was the procession of clergy and people; how great and what kind the rejoicing of those running together from every side; how great was everyone’s generosity in giving gifts to the saint; how great the purity with which the faithful prayed and discharged their vows—these and similar things may more easily be estimated by a wise person than described by anyone’s speech or pen.

60. You have your joy, Liège; behold, you possess your special protection. Here the beginning of your advancement began; through him, raised from a daughter into a mother, you have been promoted into a city. [Note: An alternative reading is *provectus*, “advancement.”] [Note: I have restored “mother” from the shorter Life; our manuscript wrongly reads “martyr.”] Through him you were advanced to an episcopal see and grew into every form of dignity. While other cities declined, as it were, into old age, you through him blossomed into the condition of beautiful youth.

May the holy martyr, who brought you to this height—that you should be magnified on earth in merit and in name—protect you forever by his holy intercessions. From that time onward there was neither measure nor number of miracles; for to all who invoked God there through Lambert’s name in truth, the door of divine mercy always stood open. There one could see the chains of prisoners and the supports of the weak hung up as evidence of God’s power. Whoever came steadfast in faith never returned without effect.

61. This holy martyr, moreover, just as he was a merciful and ready helper to the devout and faithful, was toward the impious either a stern reprover or a just avenger.

For a few years after his translation, while the often-mentioned Pippin, mayor of the palace, was sick, his son Grimoald was going to visit him. Devoted to St Lambert—perhaps all the more because Lambert had died in defence of his mother Plectrude’s marriage—he turned aside to Liège and came to pray at the saint’s tomb. While praying, he was killed there before St Lambert’s altar by a retainer of Radbod, duke of the Frisians, whose daughter, betrothed to Grimoald by his father Pippin, he expected to marry. [Note: What is narrated here has been shown in the preliminary Commentary, no. 118 and following, to have happened in A.D. 714. Sigebert therefore erred in asserting that it happened some years after the saint’s body had been brought there.] [Note: Sigebert is mistaken. Cointius, at A.D. 711, no. 7, proves from the Annals of Metz and the Deeds of the Kings of the Franks that Teutsinda, or Theodosinda, daughter of Radbod, duke of the Frisians, had in fact married Grimoald, namely in A.D. 711 according to the cited Annals.]

But Radbod did not go unpunished for the death of innocent Grimoald, who had died at his instigation. For not long afterwards Radbod himself, wonderfully deceived by a demon, perished by sudden and everlasting death. [Note: Here again Sigebert tells a fable when he says that Radbod, shortly after Grimoald’s murder—of which he truly fell under suspicion—died after being deceived by a demon. For the Annals cited by Cointius at A.D. 719, no. 14, establish that he did not die until that year, 719, having already earlier been defeated with his army by Charles Martel, as may be seen in Cointius at A.D. 716, no. 1. For the alleged deception by a demon, consult the Appendix to the Life of St Wulfran, bishop of Sens, vol. III of March, from p. 146.]

62. After St Lambert’s death, the Northman people, breathing bestial savagery, violently burst into Leodium, that is, Liège. Having broken into and burned the towns, slaughtered the citizens indiscriminately, and plundered their property, they finally consumed St Lambert’s church by fire. Levelling it to the ground, they left only traces of ruin and burning.

Then, wishing in barbarous presumption to approach the place where the holy body was venerated and to plunder whatever best things they found there, they recoiled in divinely inflicted terror and fled. As they fled, they consoled themselves for their flight by saying that they had suffered a loss because they had not carried away the structure alone, now so precious, gleaming thus around the martyr’s body. [Note: On this Northman incursion, see the preliminary Commentary, §14. There I showed from the older anonymous author that what Giles of Orval relates about terror being inflicted upon the Northmen at St Lambert’s body is wholly improbable; but I had not then observed that Sigebert had preceded Giles in this matter. We nevertheless think the anonymous author should be followed.]

Since it is lengthy and wearisome to narrate each of St Lambert’s miracles individually, let us praise universally the power of God working through him.

63. Godescalcus, deacon of his community, who lived in the time of Pippin III and Charlemagne, first wrote the Life of St Lambert at the command of Bishop Agilfrid. Though, owing to the simplicity of his understanding, he expressed it with many faults of barbarism and solecism, he himself, a writer in gold, wrote the whole of it in golden letters in honour of the holy martyr. He truthfully recounted Lambert’s deeds, but spoke with insufficient freedom about the cause of his martyrdom. [Note: Our manuscript wrongly reads *represserit*.] [Note: The same erroneous reading, *represserit*, occurs in our manuscript.] [Note: I have corrected this from the Life published under Reiner’s name; our manuscript corruptly reads: “and when of martyrdom.”]

He is believed to have acted thus in order not to seem to reproach the kings of his own time with the fault of their ancestors. For Charles Martel was born from the illicit union of Pippin and Alpaida; from Charles came Pippin III, who was elevated from prince to king of the Franks; from Pippin came Charlemagne, than whom none before or after was greater. Of him one may doubt whether he was stronger or more fortunate, more powerful in public affairs or more devout in ecclesiastical discipline. [Note: The word *Pippini*, “of Pippin,” had dropped out of our manuscript; it has been restored from the Life just cited.]

St Lambert suffered on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October [17 September], in the fortieth year of his episcopate, under Childebert, king of the Franks and son of King Theuderic. From that Theuderic onward, the kings of the Franks reigned in name alone, while the power of the kingdom rested with the mayors of the palace, until Pippin III was elevated to the kingship.

[Col. 0811]

# SIGEBERT’S SERMON ON SAINT LUCY

(MEURISSE, *History of Metz*, p. 320.)

At the time when Justinian II, and after him Philippicus, ruled at Constantinople, while among the Franks Pippin the Elder, son of Ansegisel, and after him Charles Martel administered the chief power of the realm, Aripert ruled the kingdom of the Lombards vigorously, and after him his son Liutprand reigned.

Under these men—Aripert and Liutprand, that is—Faroald, duke of Spoleto, son of Trasamund, a most valiant duke, was distinguished among the Lombard dukes by power and courage at home and in war. Not only did he manfully defend his own frontiers from others; he also frequently harassed his neighbours by hostile raids, and, abusing his power, was exceedingly hostile to the holy Roman Church itself.

Extending the reins of his dominion even across the sea, he came to Syracuse in Sicily. From there he took the sacred body of the venerable Lucy and transferred it to Italy, to Corfinum, a city of his dominion. In this, indeed, God’s wondrous providence was at work: the lamp of such great light, kindled in the world, was not to lie hidden in the narrow corner of a small island extending only a little more than sixty miles; rather, set openly upon a lampstand, it was to illuminate the world far and wide by the grace of its manifold radiance.

Thereafter his son Trasamund rose against Faroald, deprived him of his principality, and had him tonsured as a cleric. Let us observe here also God’s ordering and the holy virgin’s mercy toward the duke devoted to her. Since worldly occupation stained the good deeds of such a duke with the blemishes of negligence, yet his devotion toward God’s handmaid was affectionate, it is credible that through the merits of the holy virgin God repaid his sins in the present world; and, since God granted him a place and time for repentance, provision was made for his soul in the world to come.

But Trasamund, who despised God’s commandment saying, “Honour your father, that you may be long-lived upon the earth,” did not escape God’s vengeance. For rebelling against King Liutprand, he at last lost the duchy that he had snatched from his father; tonsured as a cleric, he himself received the sentence that he had imposed upon his father.

How strong in ancient times were Corfinum’s walls, how rich the city was, the reader can learn both from poets’ verse and from the trustworthiness of histories. Duke Faroald greatly increased its nobility when he transferred there the body of the holy virgin Lucy. The city rejoiced in that blessed pledge for about two hundred years, until it too, its sins demanding it, was reduced by barbarian incursions, along with other cities of Italy, to such a condition that its former character and greatness can now be shown only by the remains of its walls.

After the passage of many years, when many great storms from the four winds of heaven had long and violently shaken the whole world far and wide, at last the eye of divine mercy looked upon the children of men, when it found a man after its own heart to govern the state of the commonwealth: Otto I, a king strong, wise, and devout.

By God’s inspiration working upon his good will, after he had utterly extinguished internal and domestic wars by his courage and industry and expelled barbarian peoples from the territories they had invaded, he devoted himself wholly to restoring the order of the empire. Nor was he less concerned for the peace of the Church and the reform of religion. Going to Rome, the head of the empire, he received the imperial crown; and, traversing Italy for three years, he freed it from every oppression of tyrants.

On this three-year expedition Deoderic, of glorious memory, forty-sixth bishop of Metz, remained inseparably attached to him. A cousin of the emperor himself, he surpassed all the courtiers in the glory of his lineage and the grace of his wisdom. Through him all the business of the empire was conducted; through him ecclesiastical affairs were improved; through him whomever the emperor favoured was favoured; through him each person obtained what he sought to obtain.

Already united to the emperor by extraordinary affection and intimacy, and devoted to the worship of divine religion, he eagerly sought everything that might contribute to the honour, adornment, or protection of his holy see, the Church of Metz. So that all things might effectively answer his desires, aided by divine grace he collected a very great number of saints’ bodies from various places in Italy, sought to bring them to his holy see at Metz for veneration there with more excellent worship and honour, and honourably placed them in the church which he had founded on the island of Metz in honour of St Vincent, levite and martyr.

Among the other sacred pledges which he had gathered to himself from every quarter with praiseworthy eagerness, the memorable virgin and martyr Lucy of Syracuse at last came, amid a great and universal celebration of the Church, to the object of his most ardent devotion. Uvigeric, priest of the aforesaid bishop—a man of very trustworthy faith, then serving as cantor and later as keeper of the church of Blessed Stephen—brought her from the city of Corfinum. With his own hands he removed those sacred bones from the urn itself, though it was enclosed by no slight protection.

Because this seemed incredible on account of the greatness of the matter, the bishop of that place, laying his hand upon the holy Gospel, confirmed by oath that this was indeed that Lucy of Syracuse about whom responsories, antiphons, and the Mass are sung throughout the Church.

The body of this holy virgin was translated in the year 970 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and, with the marvellous acclamation of both orders, was placed in the church of St Vincent, martyr and levite. Here too the incomprehensible wisdom of God worked providentially, so that the name and merit of the holy virgin might cross the Alps on its journey; and she whom all Italy had long proclaimed should now be known also throughout the threefold Gaul. For the more recent the memory of the holy virgin was made by a more frequent translation, the more celebrated everywhere became reverence for so great a name.

Since nothing is done quickly enough for an eager mind, Bishop Deoderic, wholly inclined to the service of the virgin Lucy, immediately hastened to construct an oratory in which he might fittingly place the treasure divinely given him, more precious than gold and topaz. When this work had been laudably completed, he solemnly dedicated that basilica in honour of the glorious virgin Lucy on the eighth day before the Ides of August [6 August], in the ninth year of his episcopate, namely in the year 972 of the Lord’s Incarnation. His fellow suffragan bishops Gerard of Toul and Winfrid of Verdun were present and assisted him. They had formerly remained attached to him in close fellowship at the emperor’s court, and now, in performing the offices of ecclesiastical religion, they mutually complied with one another in unanimous devotion.
