In the fifty-second year after these events Conrad II was chosen emperor, a dignity which belonged to him by hereditary succession from the royal stock and which even more fittingly suited him because of his outstanding wisdom and courage. Although Conrad watched diligently over the external affairs of the empire, he did not rank the concerns of the King of kings as secondary. Thus, among other works, in the diocese of the Church of Speyer, at the place called Lindiburg, he founded by royal munificence a monastery in honour of St Mary, Mother of God, his wife Gisela of good memory cooperating with him.

But death, striking with equal step at the towers of kings and the cottages of the poor, prevented him from bringing his begun work to completion. His good son, succeeding his good father—Henry, the third emperor of that name—took upon himself, as though by hereditary right, the work of the monastery founded by his parents. He built it royally and completed it nobly. Since he lacked no abundance of earthly wealth, he directed his mind toward gathering sacred pledges from every quarter, so that the ready intercessions of those saints whose memory was celebrated there day and night in their bodily presence might aid him in his necessities.

Yet he did not believe his wishes fulfilled unless he should also deserve to possess relics of the holy virgin Lucy, whose name was celebrated in the Church and whose aid was sought with faithful devotion throughout Gaul.

The Church of Metz, which specially rejoiced in the body of the holy virgin, was then governed by Deoderic the Younger, its forty-eighth bishop, a man greatly powerful in the world because of the nobility of his family and held in great reverence in the Church because of the dignity of his wisdom. Emperor Henry requested from him that an arm of St Lucy be given to him; and though with difficulty, he obtained it.

That same bishop therefore conveyed the holy arm, in fulfilment of the emperor’s desire, to the monastery of Lindiburg; nothing could have been more welcome to the emperor. It was translated in the third year of Henry’s reign, in the year 1042 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

[Col. 0813]

# SIGEBERT OF GEMBLOUX’S DOUBLE LETTER ON THE DIFFERENCE CONCERNING THE FOUR SEASONS, WRITTEN TO THE CLERGY OF TRIER IN THE NAME OF THE CLERGY OF LIÈGE

(MARTENE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 294.)

## LETTER

[Note: A manuscript of Gembloux, where we saw this letter, teaches us that its author was Sigebert, monk of Gembloux; this is also established by the other letter that he wrote in the name of the clergy of Liège to the clergy of Trier, “On the Rule of Berno.”]

When we asked whether one ought to fast immediately on the first Saturday of March, even if that month begins on a Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, or whether it should be postponed to another Saturday because of the Wednesday, you replied in a definite judgment based upon the writings of the holy and ancient Fathers, and especially upon the authoritative custom of your Church: the first weekday of the month must always, without any objection, be awaited. For the fast which begins on Wednesday and ends on Saturday is in no way reckoned to February but wholly to March, so that our first fast may be consecrated to the Lord in that month in which the beginning of the year and the creation of the world itself began.

We who sought certainty from you on one question are entangled in manifold doubt. Saving your goodwill, therefore, permit us still to discuss with you those matters about which we doubt. We do not take lightly what is decided by men so weighty and learned as yourselves.

What is said erroneously and improperly is idly drawn into an example of truth. March, which Romulus erroneously placed as the first month of the year, we too improperly call the first month of the year; but we do not believe it to be so, because we have learned from God’s own mouth which month is the first. “This month,” he says, “shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year” (Exod. 13:2).

Who does not know that in the Law and the Prophets March is reckoned as the twelfth month? All divine Scripture depends upon Moses; all who discuss divine Scripture rest upon him. Unless we walk by the straight way, we shall always be learning and never come to knowledge of the truth.

Therefore, because according to the pagan arrangement the first day of the world is assigned to the middle of March, namely to the eighteenth day of that month, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April [18 March], are we for that reason to take the first part of March as the first month of the year? The first part of March agrees better with the year’s end than with its beginning. If the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April was truly the first day of the world, there will be the beginning of the first year and therefore of all the years of the world. In the month in which the first day of the world falls, that month ought to be held first; consequently, Romulus’s arrangement concerning his first March, and Numa’s concerning his January, would disappear.

But if someone says that the whole may be taken from a part, so that from its last part the whole of March is taken as the first month of the year, then March itself, so to speak, will not concede to you that it can be at once the first and the last month of the year—especially since you yourselves do not concede to it that it may borrow three or two days, or even one weekday, from February, so that from a part its entire fast, which you assign wholly to March alone, might be its own.

Moreover, retaining the pagan arrangement of the months, if by a certain figurative understanding we refer the last part of March to the beginning of the world—which is assigned not to March but to April—then, if by this same figurative understanding we place the beginning of March not on its Kalends but, counting backwards, for example on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, understand that to be the beginning of March, so that the fourteen days which the creation of the world takes from March at its end may be restored to it before its Kalends. In this way perhaps we shall obtain that you do not begrudge our fast its Wednesday or Friday, which, though pronounced to be in February, may nevertheless be understood to belong to March.

Caught at such a crossroads of divine and human writing, we remain uncertain in our understanding; and while neither party believes the other concerning which way is more direct, we strive laboriously toward what we desire—and may we arrive without error.

You say: “The prophetic reading agrees with this judgment, showing that there is a fast of the first, a fast of the fourth, and a fast of the tenth, and not a fast of the twelfth; and this could in no way remain undisputed if the aforesaid fast of the first month happened to be celebrated on a Wednesday or Friday of February.”

If our understanding does not deceive us in this matter, you seem to have understood these four months as follows: you assign the fast of the first month to March; the fast of the fourth to June, which is the fourth from March; the fast of the seventh to September, which is the seventh from March; and the fast of the tenth to December, which is the tenth from March. You added “and not of the twelfth”—February being the twelfth from March—so that we might understand that this was your meaning.

Why do you so greatly disparage February that you do not admit even one of its days to the first fast, as though you fear that the fast of the tenth month might perhaps in some way be transferred to it? If this passage of the prophet stands thus in your copies, as you have presented it, that is your concern. We say that it is not so written either in the edition of the Seventy Interpreters, which the ancient Greeks and Latins used, or in the edition now used by the Church, which Jerome translated from Hebrew into Latin and expounded.

In the Septuagint it reads: “The fourth fast, and the fifth fast, and the seventh fast, and the tenth fast shall be to the Lord,” and the rest (Zech. 8:19). In Jerome’s edition it reads: “The fast of the fourth, and the fast of the fifth, and the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall be to the Lord,” and the rest. Where here is any mention of a fast of the first month, on which you rely in support of your case against us? If the prophet had here named the first month, he would have meant no first month other than April, and would have derived the order of the other months from April.

Jerome explains the order of the months and the causes of the fasts thus:

> “The fast of the fourth”—that is, of the month—which is July, the fourth from April, falls on the seventeenth day of the same month, when Moses descended from the mountain and broke the tablets of the Law. It was also in that month that Nebuchadnezzar first captured Jerusalem.  
>
> “The fast of the fifth,” the fifth month from April, which for us is August, was on the tenth day of that month, because an uprising arose after the scouts returned from inspecting the promised land; because of this all but two perished in the wilderness over eleven years. It was also in that month that Nebuzaradan, commander of the cooks of King Nebuchadnezzar, demolished the walls of Jerusalem, which had previously been captured, and burned the Temple; and much later, in the same month, Titus Caesar destroyed and razed the Temple of the Lord.  
>
> “The fast of the seventh month” from April, which for us is October, was because in that month Gedaliah, whom Nebuchadnezzar had set over the conquered Jews, was killed, and the remnant of the Jews was destroyed to utter annihilation.  
>
> “The fast of the tenth month” from April, which for us is January, was because Ezekiel the prophet and the other captives in Babylon, learning in this month that the Temple of the Lord had been destroyed, lamented and proclaimed a fast.

These are Jerome’s words. Therefore, do not be troubled to see how little the prophetic reading agrees with your position: since it supports you neither regarding the order of the months nor regarding the cause of the fasts, it has force here only insofar as it urges us, by the example of the Jews, to celebrate four fasts in the year.

You say: “The fast which begins on Wednesday and ends on Saturday is in no way assigned to February but wholly to March, so that our first fast may be consecrated to the Lord in that month in which the beginning of the year and the creation of the world itself began.”

We do not refute this opinion of yours presumptuously, since we are readier to learn than to teach; but there is a reason that dissuades us from agreeing with you on this point, concerning which the unprejudiced judgment of your charity will decide. Pope Calixtus, seventeenth from the Apostle Peter, decreed that a fast be kept three times a year, on Saturday, for grain, wine, and oil. This decree was amended for the better: he decreed that a three-day fast be held at the four seasons of the year, writing thus to Bishop Benedict:

> “The fast which you have learned is celebrated among us three times a year—that, as we are filled with grain, wine, and oil for the nourishment of our bodies, so we may be filled with fasting for the nourishment of our souls—we now decree should more suitably be held at the four seasons of the year. Thus, as the year revolves through four seasons, so we too may observe a fourfold solemn fast through the four seasons of the year; as, among other things, the prophet Zechariah says in the words of the Lord: ‘The fast of the fourth [month], and the fast of the fifth, and the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall be to the house of Judah joy and gladness and splendid solemnities. Only love truth and peace,’ says the Lord. Therefore we must be of one mind in this: that, according to apostolic teaching, we may all say the same thing, that there may be no schisms among us, but that we may be perfected in the same understanding and the same knowledge.”

Thus Pope Calixtus, I believe, foresaw in a prophetic spirit the future dissensions of the Church concerning the fast instituted by him. From these words of Calixtus our fathers were instructed, and instructed us, that the year should have as many fasts as it has seasons; and that each season should have as many days of fasting as it has months; and that, while three days are assigned to each of the four seasonal fasts—the fourth and sixth weekdays and Saturday—each day should be assigned to one of the several months: so that whatever we have sinned during a whole month may be forgiven us through fasting on one day of that month, and so that God may grant us, in every season, month, and day, a good and healthful tempering of the air for our needs.

Since, therefore, this fast of the Four Seasons is distinguished by the settled order of the seasons, understood and arranged by holy, learned, and ancient Fathers, let us select a few things from many, and the more certain from two. Bede says in his book *On Times*:

> “Different people assign different beginnings to the Four Seasons. Isidore, bishop of Seville, says that winter begins on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, spring on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, summer on the ninth day before the Kalends of June, and autumn on the tenth day before the Kalends of September. But the Greeks and Romans—whose authority ought rather to be followed in this matter—determine that winter begins on the seventh day before the Ides of November, spring on the seventh day before the Ides of February, summer on the seventh day before the Ides of May, and autumn on the seventh day before the Ides of August. They mark the beginnings of winter and summer by the morning or evening rising or setting of the Vergiliae, also called the Pleiades; likewise, they place the entrance of spring and autumn when the Vergiliae rise or set at approximately midday or midnight.”

And, in order to show on what basis the Greeks or Romans fix the beginnings of the seasons in this way, Bede adds the words of the holy, learned, and ancient man Anatolius, bishop of Laodicea, disputing thus concerning the equinoxes and solstices:

> “Do not fail to observe this: although the actual boundaries of the seasons—the two equinoxes and the two solstices—fall near the Kalends of the succeeding months, each occupies the middle of its season; and the beginnings of the seasons do not commence where the Kalends of the months begin. Accordingly, each season must be begun in such a way that the equinox on the eighth day before the Kalends of April divides the season from the first day of spring; that the solstice on the eighth day before the Kalends of July occupies the middle of summer; that the equinox on the eighth day before the Kalends of October occupies the middle of autumn; and that the solstice on the eighth day before the Kalends of January occupies the middle of winter.”

[Note: Anatolius of Alexandria, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, flourished under the emperors Probus and Carus. He was a man of remarkable learning in arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic; Jerome says in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* that we may understand the greatness of his talent from the volume which he composed on Easter and from his ten books on the principles of arithmetic.]

According to the words of blessed Anatolius, if you count upward from the seventh day before the Kalends of April as far as the seventh day before the Ides of February, you will have forty-six days, which is the middle of spring. By this authority of Anatolius the Greeks and Romans place the beginning of spring on the seventh day before the Ides of February; from there to the Kalends of February, the remaining six days belong to winter. This is according to the ancients, who placed the equinoxes and solstices on the eighth day before the Kalends.

But we moderns, who according to the decree of the Nicene Synod place the equinoxes and solstices on the twelfth day before the Kalends, if, placing the equinox and the middle of spring on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, we count upward forty-six days, which divide spring in half, shall find the beginning of spring on the third day before the Nones of February. In this way, only four—or indeed only two—days of February belong to winter, and spring possesses the whole of February.

Accordingly, February would seem to be the first month of spring, and the fast of the first season ought to be celebrated in it—and rightly so. But lest contentious persons be given an occasion for calumniating the fast of the first season, since it would include a few days of the final season, namely winter, the spring fast is more suitably postponed into the following month of March. Yet it is not thereby entirely assigned to March. For although the three days of fasting are contained in one week of one month, because of the continuity of the mysteries, nevertheless the individual days of fasting are assigned to individual months: the fourth weekday to February, the sixth to March, and the seventh to April.

Therefore, when March begins on the fifth, sixth, or seventh weekday, what impropriety is there in anticipating the beginning of March by fasting on the third-last and final days of February? Although those days are not days of March, they are days of spring, to which this entire fast belongs, distributed in parts among the months of that same season. What, I ask, is unsuitable in fasting on the fourth weekday in February—especially since that fast is itself observed to obtain a good and healthful tempering of the air in February? What is unsuitable for March in fasting on the sixth weekday in February on behalf of March itself? Will April not deserve a good and healthful tempering of the air because its Saturday fast is anticipated in March?

For this reason I maintain what I said: that the fourth and sixth weekdays are attendants and, as it were, preparations for that Saturday of March, and are of the same character as the Saturday to which they render the service or ministry of preparation—those who either receive or celebrate the mysteries pertaining to Saturday preparing themselves by the fast of the third and sixth weekdays. Nor is it necessary, for this purpose, either to extend February by a number of days or to shorten March, since the weekdays of February and March are of one character precisely because they belong to one season.

If anyone does not accept this division of the fasts according to the division of the months, at least he will take the whole fast collectively as belonging to the season. But because what is divided among many is not the whole possession of any one, and what is common to many is not proper to any one, the spring fast will not belong wholly to March, since it is equally assigned to three months. It will not, I say, be proper to March when it is common to three months.

Moreover, we read neither idly nor falsely that the holy Roman popes Simplicius, Gelasius, Symmachus, and Felix performed ordinations during February. Whether spring arises on the eighth day before the Kalends of March according to the Spaniards, or on the seventh day before the Ides of February according to the ancient Greeks and Romans, or on the third day before the Nones of February according to the Nicene Synod, we must believe that men of apostolic rank did not exclude from the fast of the Kalends of March the fourth and sixth weekdays of February, which belonged to the spring season. Perhaps they even admitted a whole week of February in order to complete the spring fast and celebrate the mysteries appropriate to that fast. For in ordinary years February often contains several weeks of Lent.

Your charity, then, may consider why the spring fast is not assigned wholly to March: namely, because the days of the spring season count on behalf of February, lest it be excluded from the spring fast. But if the order and rationale of the season should prove that spring begins on the very Kalends of March, I shall add no further word against excluding the fourth and sixth weekdays in February from the fast, if, together with their month, they are wholly alien to the spring season.

But apart from the crude institution of Romulus, nowhere do we find the authority of Scripture stating that the beginning of spring and of March coincide on the very day of the Kalends. The authority of Anatolius and of other Fathers opposes those who place the beginning of spring on the Kalends of March; heaven and earth also oppose them. Heaven, because philosophers have discovered the beginnings of the seasons through the risings and settings of stars, which God made for signs and seasons, months and years. Earth, unless some irregularity of weather intervenes, shows the rising of spring in the dew upon trees and grasses long before the beginning of March.

The rule of Anatolius, which denies that the beginnings of the seasons occur on the Kalends of the months, and explains where they ought to begin in words such that it can also be shown to the eyes, still further demonstrates, through the beginning of summer, where the summer fast should be celebrated. If, according to the ancients, the summer solstice and the middle of summer are placed on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, and you count upward forty-six days, you will find the beginning of summer on the sixth day before the Ides of May. From there to the Kalends of May only eight days belong to spring; thus almost the whole of May is assigned to summer.

Nor are there lacking certain moderns who, the more recent they are, the more clear-sighted they claim to be, and who, marking with their eyes and fingers the ascent or descent of the sun at the solstices, contend that the equinoxes and solstices ought more correctly to be placed on the fifteenth day before the Kalends. If this should be proved, who would contradict the truth that spring ought wholly to claim February for itself?

Therefore, since on this account the days of February ought freely to be admitted to the spring fast, and the days of May to the summer fast, when June begins on the fifth or sixth weekday, what impropriety prevents the second fast—which belongs wholly to summer—from being celebrated on its second Saturday, or in the second week, though you assign it only to June? In the spring fast, it seems an impediment that the fourth and sixth fast-days fall in one week; what reason is there why you postpone the fast into a later week? Why do we cling so tightly to the killing letter that we depart from the life-giving spirit? Why do we cling so tightly to seeking the first Saturday of the month? We are always striving to find it, and find it only once.

For if Saturday is compensated by the number of days, we keep such a Saturday only in those years in which June, March, September, and December begin on the first weekday. In all other years, we always observe the Saturday of an incomplete week. You, indeed, who assign the seasonal fast, common to three months, solely to the middle month of the three, whenever the fasting months begin on the fifth, sixth, or seventh weekday, always have the second Saturday in place of the first, the third in place of the second, and the fourth in place of the third; because, once the first month’s week is completed, you place Saturday on the third or second day of the second week.

But we, who take the seasonal fast according to its name and admit without distinction the days of the season to the seasonal fast, regard the first Saturday occurring in the fasting month as the first Saturday, referring it not to the month but to the week on whichever weekday that month begins—the month which seems more suitable for celebrating the seasonal fast and the mystery of the fast.

Perhaps someone among those opposed to us will think these disputes, questions, and conflicts to be the quarrels of the law which Paul writes to Titus, and through him to us, must be avoided as vain and useless. Whoever accepts what we have said concerning the succession of the seasons in spring and summer will readily perceive, through Anatolius’s rule, the corresponding order of autumn and winter, and will see that the spring fast must not be assigned wholly to March, but also to February.

You say:

> “When the first Saturday fast before Lent falls, it seems strange to us that, according to your Church’s custom, it should be observed on the second or third Saturday of March.”

We are surprised that you are surprised at us on this point. Do we do this without the authority of ancient or modern Fathers? For not long ago, by order of Emperor Conrad, a general assembly and council of bishops was held at Tribur. Among other matters the bishops wished to decree this chapter:

> “That, if at any time the fast of the first month should fall within the week in which the beginning of the fast is observed on the fourth weekday, the celebration of both fasts should be completed by the performance of one office.”

But a few of our people, opposing the decree of many, prevailed by the sounder counsel that the fast of the first month should be celebrated in the other week in which the office is held, according to the custom of the ancients. Authority confirms this ordering of the fasts.

For Pope Gelasius, following the judgment of Pope Zosimus, says:

> “Ordinations of priests or deacons ought not to be performed except at fixed seasons: that is, at the fast of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months, and also at the beginning of Lent and in the middle of Lent; and they should know that these are to be celebrated on Saturday, in fasting, about evening.”

Thus Gelasius. Who does not see that he foresaw by the Holy Spirit the contentious discord of posterity concerning this fast, when, deliberately using the designation “first month” and disregarding the first Saturday, he identified the time appropriate to the matter for fasting—namely, at the beginning or in the middle of Lent? For he took precautions because the calculation arising from the variation of Easter would entangle us in the uncertainty with which we are now burdened.

Lest anyone’s contentiousness dare to weaken this chapter of Gelasius, it was also confirmed at the fifth council of bishops, held by order of Emperor Charlemagne:

> “We decree that priests and deacons are not to be ordained except at fixed seasons, as is contained in the decrees of Zosimus and Gelasius.”

Holy and apostolic men, whom the Church regards as competent authorities, testify that they follow in the footsteps of this judgment. Let us cite the words of Isidore of Seville alone:

> “There are four Saturdays on which the greater fasts and offices of readings and prayers are established: that is, the first Saturday in the month of March, in accordance with the observance of Lent and the spring season, and the rest.”

Since the custom of our Church is confirmed by such competent witnesses and testimonies, the spring fast ought not to be celebrated before Lent; nor should it seem a marvel to you, unless you have persons whose authority outweighs these.

You say:

> “Of this pre-Lenten fast, if we may so call it—saving your favor—it appears that the position of the first Saturday is driven from its place, since Nebuzaradan is still battering the walls of Jerusalem.”

Saving our favor, we accept whatever you say, provided that, saving your favor, you accept what we say. For we seek nothing from contentiousness, but everything from charity. You have raised a difficulty for us when you say that the position of the first Saturday is driven from its place. We do not believe that you are mistaken in this; rather, we charge ourselves with slowness, since perhaps we do not properly understand your well-spoken words.

Although Saturday is named from its cause, not from a number, and therefore is sometimes referred not to number but to cause, nevertheless the Saturday with which we are concerned always retains its place in the number: namely, on the weekday designated seventh from the number. No one knows better than you that the position of Saturday is as immovable as the number which established that position for Saturday. For we call no day of the week except the seventh “Saturday”; rather, all the days are named from the Sabbath: that is, the first, second, or third day of the Sabbath.

But if something which cause or usage assigns to Saturday is occasionally driven from its place, Saturday does not thereby rise from its own seat. Therefore, if the fast assigned to the first of March is driven from its prescribed place by some cause or necessity, we should like to hear from you how the position of Saturday itself is thereby driven from its own place. For if Saturday’s seat could be moved from its place, and if Saturday, so to speak, could follow the day of fasting driven from its place, that Saturday would always be first, nor would it permit the second Saturday to take its place.

Why, then, are you so troubled by such a removal of the first fast—not always necessary, indeed, but sometimes appropriate? Why is denied to the first fast what is granted to the other seasonal fasts, which may fittingly be moved from their place? See: there is no complaint about the winter fast, though Christmas Day has transferred it from week to week and from Saturday to Saturday. And we thank you for allowing the transfer of the autumn fast for our festival.

And because perhaps you do not fear that Nebuzaradan must storm the walls of our Jerusalem, you say to us, in a certain manner, with Ezra: “Eat rich foods and drink sweet wine, and send portions to those who have prepared nothing for themselves; for this day is holy to the Lord. Do not be sorrowful, for the joy of the Lord is your strength” (2 Esdras 8:10).

What is granted to us can also be granted to any Church: if a special feast occurs during any seasonal fast, the position of the fast may be changed. Thus, if the Saturday of the summer fast coincides with the Saturday of Pentecost—both Saturdays being designated by the title of the twelve readings—the fast is deferred to the week of Pentecost, because two authoritative offices and two mysteries cannot be performed in one celebration: one, that of baptizing; the other, that of ordaining.

Although in almost our own memory three archiepiscopal sees—yours, namely, Trier, Cologne, and Mainz—wished these two mysteries of the double fast to be completed in a single office on one day, this proposal could not attain either the agreement of all or the practice of the Church. Why, I ask, are you so troubled by the alteration of the first fast alone that you say Nebuzaradan, chief of the cooks of Nebuchadnezzar—or of the devil—is still storming the walls of Jerusalem if this fast is transferred into Lent?

At the latest Easter, which is on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, March begins on the second weekday of Sexagesima; at the next-to-last Easter, which is on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, it begins on the third weekday; at the third-from-last Easter, which is on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, March begins on the fourth weekday of Sexagesima. Since, therefore, in these years the fourth, sixth, and seventh weekdays fall in the week of Lent for celebrating the mysteries of the spring fast and ordinations, we leave it to your judgment whether fasting and ordination are suitably performed on the Saturday of Sexagesima.

Popes Zosimus and Gelasius were more moderate in this, assigning this fast and the mysteries appropriate to it to Lent. And, to add something from ourselves, this fast is sometimes postponed by holy and prudent men to the last Saturday of March or to the next-to-last week of Lent, so that both those ordaining and those ordained may be more prepared, should Nebuzaradan still storm the walls of Jerusalem—as God forbid. Those returning from Babylonian captivity will labor in penitence to rebuild the walls of their Jerusalem, doing the work of prayer with one hand and holding the sword of fasting with the other.

We too take pleasure in allegorizing over the number of weeks that distinguish the seasonal fasts. But, as Origen says, there is free license to wander in the fields of allegory; this freedom ought to have a limit in its progress. The three ranks of Christ’s generations correspond allegorically to the three orders of fasts: what then will be assigned to the fourth fast, which is also deficient in number of weeks? This allegory is pleasing, but not to such a degree that it should be fixed as a certain rule for the fasts.

Berno’s rule is also pleasing, which leads you by a certain intellectual thread of linear number from the first fast to the second, from the second to the third, and from the third to the fourth—would that it did so without error. It would please far more if it returned also by fourteen [weeks] from the fourth fast to the first. But, to speak with your peace and favor, this line of his seems to some not sufficiently straight, because it does not divide equally the weeks of the year through the Four Seasons’ fasts. For if it is tripled by fourteen from the fourth fast to the recurrence of the first, only ten weeks remain. If it is quadrupled by fourteen, it runs four weeks beyond the fifty-two weeks of the year.

We do not dare set our foot upon this intellectual thread, lest, if we leap into a narrow place, we may be unable freely to draw back or extend our foot. Someone disputing about this linear number of weeks says:

> “If some number ought to delimit these four intervals of the fasts, no number would be more suitable than fourteen, which, multiplied fourfold, yields the fifty-two weeks of the year. Thus, if present practice allowed it, the fast of each season would always occur, by the line of this number, on the first Saturday of the month assigned to fasting.”

Although this man spoke truly, he spoke in vain, because he thought outside established practice—Berno, upon whose words you depend, whose words serve you as a rule, and who entitles your sacramentary book with his exemplar. He also pleases us; we hold him in great esteem, because he offered to God’s tabernacle what he was able according to his capacity.

But the Apostle commands us to test all things, hold fast what is good, and abstain from every appearance of evil. Discord in the Church is an appearance of evil; concerning it we all pray daily, that God may first deign to pacify and unite it throughout the whole world. Yet we do not allow it to be united as one while we divide ourselves from one another through disagreement in ecclesiastical rite. We do not condemn you or your rites; but whether we rightly retain what we hold from the ancient tradition of the Fathers, we submit to the judgment of good men.

Above all, in determining the beginnings of seasons we follow Anatolius. Eusebius in his *Ecclesiastical History* and Jerome in his book *On Illustrious Men* testify how great he ought to be considered:

> “Anatolius of Alexandria, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, flourished under Probus and Gaius, restorers [of the state], a man of remarkable learning in arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic.”

And if we must come to more recent authorities, we follow Waterho, bishop of our city, and Olbert, abbot of the monastery of Gembloux, men who were just and learned in their generation, worthy of comparison with—or even preference over—the just and learned men of their time and ours.

[Note: He is commonly called Watho, or also Wazo, bishop of Liège; he died in 1048, as we read in the *Book of the Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux*, where much is also said about Abbot Olbert.]

These men were contemporaries of Aribo and Berno. They read Berno’s writings with his own guidance; but though they read much and tested everything, as the Lord commands preachers, they did not pass from house to house—that is, from this man’s opinion to that man’s—but, walking the royal road of the Fathers, turned neither to the right nor to the left. Taking the fasts of the Four Seasons according to the rationale of the seasons, they did not exclude from the spring fast the days of the season before the Kalends of March. Rather, they performed the fast and the liturgy of the fast immediately on the first Saturday—indeed, sometimes on the first day of the month.

We follow these and other holy and learned men in this matter, not because they were holy and learned, but because they are proved to be defenders of truth. For Augustine teaches us thus in writing to Jerome:

> “I accord this honor and authority only to those writings which are called canonical Scriptures: I most firmly believe that none of their authors erred in anything. But I read other authors in such a way that, however much they excel in holiness and learning, I do not think something true merely because they themselves thought it so, but because, through those canonical authors or by probable reasoning, they have been able to persuade me of what does not depart from truth.”

Following Augustine’s example, we read the writings of many; but we need not believe all of them. Seeking whom we ought rather to follow, we write these things to you not from obstinacy—for we do not believe that you wrote your letter from obstinacy either, since you concluded it with so delightful an epilogue, which we return to you in kind. If it is certain to you, by Catholic reasoning, to show us something better, we are ready to yield to your understanding rather than to serve our own obstinacy any longer to no purpose.

This also must be added: in the year 1095 of the Lord’s Incarnation, almost the whole Church received from the See of the Roman Church a decree of apostolic authority that the spring fast should always be celebrated in the first week of Lent, and the summer fast always in the very week of Pentecost. Since February often contains one, often two, and sometimes—at the earliest Easter—three weeks of Lent; and similarly May often extends one, often two, and sometimes—at the earliest Easter—three weeks beyond Pentecost Sunday, it is clear that they celebrate the whole spring fast in February, while they remove the summer fast not only from the second week of June but even far from the beginning of June.

Certainly there is no controversy among these people about observing the fourth or sixth weekday before the Kalends of March, June, or September, since they refer the seasonal fast not to fixed months but to the rationale of the season. Farewell.

Likewise, a letter of the men of Trier to the men of Liège, questioning why Berno’s rule is sometimes said to increase and sometimes to decrease.

[Note: Concerning this rule Sigebert says the following in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: “I wrote on the fasts of the Four Seasons, concerning whose celebration there is disagreement among many. Some, according to the consideration of the seasons, admit to the fast of the fourth and sixth weekdays the days of February, May, or September, and, when Saturday falls on the Kalends, conclude the fast; but others, without consideration of the seasons, do not fast unless the fourth and sixth weekdays of the fast, together with Saturday itself, fall in March, June, or October. Many authorize such a manner of fasting, especially the Germans.”]

Although you seem to have replied well and properly in other matters, on this one point we doubt whether Berno’s rule is rightly criticized for sometimes increasing and sometimes decreasing, as though he had not considered that from the last fast until the recurrence of the first there are only ten weeks, after three groups of fourteen weeks have been assigned to the intervals between the fasts. For he seems to extend his line from the first fast to the fourth, and not to deal with the period from the last until the recurrence of the first; so that the descent of forty-two weeks may correspond to the forty-two generations of Christ. We think this was Amalar’s intention, since he took the first week of March as the figure of the first generation, Abraham, and the final week of December as the figure of the last generation, Christ; and he called the three consecrations of fasts three groups of fourteen weeks, which are their intervals. Why, then, do you say, “What will happen with the fourth?” We have stated our doubt to you. Farewell.

## Reply of Lord Sigebert on Behalf of the Clerics of Liège

Because, as someone says, a letter alone is the thing that makes those who are absent present, it delights us to speak with and hear you whom we love by letters sent and received—especially since, as Jerome says, a friend finds great consolation for longing when he receives a friend’s letter. You have stated your doubt to us: namely, whether Berno’s rule is rightly or wrongly criticized as sometimes increasing and sometimes decreasing, and why we said, “What will happen with the fourth?”

Concerning the latter question, I first say that I did not say, “What will happen with the fourth?” but, “What will be assigned to the fourth fast?” You rightly asked about this, because, in leaving it to be understood, I left ambiguous what I intended to be understood. For when I said that the three ranks of Christ’s generations correspond allegorically to the three orders of fasts, I added implicitly: “What,” that is, “what allegory,” will be assigned to the fourth fast?

[Note: From these words it is clear that Sigebert was the author of the preceding letter to the men of Trier.]

What I asked, I still ask of your prudence: what can be assigned to those ten weeks which remain from the fourth fast until the first, so that every week of the year may have its corresponding allegory? For if you had understood this at first, it would have seemed to you that those generations which, according to the Hebrew truth, are counted as ten from Noah to Abraham could be assigned to these ten weeks, if no more fitting explanation connected with the number ten can be assigned. The following generation of Abraham will suitably occupy the first week of March.

As for whether Berno’s rule sometimes increases or decreases, or whether it can rightly or wrongly be criticized, your prudence, which practises it, knows. What does it matter to you, we have said and say, to criticize it? Let Berno have his rule to himself, because we do not wish to be constrained by it: in accordance with the suitability of the matter and the time, we freely place the intervals of the four fasts either at fourteen or at fifteen [weeks].

But since you offer it to us for inspection, while you hold it on one side, let us look at it together and see what it is like. And this, indeed, is its rule:

> “From the Saturday of the spring fast, as by a certain intellectual thread, let the line of the rule be drawn most exactly through fourteen weeks as far as the second Saturday in the month of June; then through another fourteen weeks to the third Saturday of September; likewise, either through fourteen or through thirteen [weeks], to the Saturday nearest before the Lord’s Nativity, so that the limits of those Saturdays may be determined without error.”

Why does this perfectly straight line return from fourteen to thirteen? Plainly because it must follow the appropriateness of the time. In counting these weeks Berno satisfied himself; I do not know whether he satisfied you as well.

You seem, indeed, to intend that the forty-two weeks should correspond to the forty-two generations of Christ in such a manner that the first generation, Abraham, occupies the first week of March, while the last generation, Christ, corresponds to the final week of December. You think rightly in this, if Berno’s line could direct you to it. But if Christ is born in the final week of December, how will you give Abraham the first week of March? Berno’s line excludes Abraham from it; for if Abraham possessed it, the final week of December would not correspond to the final generation.

Therefore, because, as Cicero says, the first cause of victory is carefully to learn the case for which we are going to plead, let us seek together the cause of this difficulty, so that by common labor we may perhaps be able even to perceive the difficulty itself.

From the Kalends of March to the eighth day before the Kalends of January there are forty-two weeks and six days. Subtracting these six days from the number of weeks, Berno begins to count them not from the Kalends of March but from the Saturday of the spring fast. Thus he has indeed guarded himself so that his line neither increases nor decreases in the number of weeks; yet he has not thereby freed himself from every stumbling-block.

Because of these six subtracted days, disagreement sometimes arises between us and you; but between Abraham and the Christ being born there is agreement in no year. Abraham, as it were unwilling to depart from the first week of March assigned to him, always reclaims the six days taken from him; receiving one day each year, he seems to accuse Berno’s rule of sometimes increasing and sometimes decreasing. For however many days of his week he receives, Christ loses that many days of his own week.

The farther Abraham is removed from his week, the more days he appropriates to himself, so that in some cases he possesses more than one week, and in others more than two—namely, in the three years in which you place the Saturday of the fast around the sixth day before the Ides of March. But the child whose name is “the Lord our righteousness,” as the line increases again toward his portion, receives only his own days each year and demands nothing beyond his rightful share.

Thus you never give the Christ being born a complete week except in one year—unless perhaps you sew the days subtracted in March onto Christ’s shortened week, so that in this way you may give poor Christ, as it were, a little shirt resewn from torn scraps, though even his enemies did not tear his seamless tunic. It does not become you to offer such half-garments to him to whom, with the Magi, you have offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh.

Let us prove what we say by the sequence of the years. In the year in which March begins on the first feria, Berno begins to count the weeks from the Saturday of the spring fast, set on the Nones of March, leaving Abraham only one day; and only in that year does Christ have a complete week. In the following year, with the Saturday of the fast set on the first day before the Nones, in the third year on the third day before the Nones, in the fourth year on the fourth day before the Nones, and in the fifth year on the fifth day before the Nones, Berno restores the six days deducted during these six or five years, with a leap-year intervening; and according to the variation of the Nones of March, his line appears to grow or shrink in either direction. According to you, however, the farther the Saturday of the fast is placed, the more extensively the line varies. What of the fact that sometimes, through Berno’s line growing beyond its proper measure, the birth is driven outside the forty-second week and generation? For, since Berno begins the weeks and generations on Saturday, he always completes them on Friday.

Therefore, in the year in which March begins on the second feria, the forty-two weeks and generations are completed on the ninth day before the Kalends of January—that is, on the eve of the Lord’s Nativity, which in that year falls on Friday—beyond which Berno’s rule ought not to be extended. Thus, as the forty-third week begins, Christ is born on the following Saturday, as though in a foreign place, because in that year there is no room for him in Berno’s inn. Yet we trust concerning you in the Lord that he who is born, the Angel of great counsel, will inspire and breathe upon you, so that even in this year he may have a place in the inn of your wisdom. Someone might perhaps wish to excuse Berno on the ground that on the eighth day before the Kalends of January the final week of December begins, which ought to correspond to Christ’s generation. He could indeed be excused on this ground if, in that year too, the fast were deferred to the second Saturday of March. But the way of escaping by this argument is barred to him, because, when the Saturday of the fast is set on the second day before the Nones, and Abraham occupies more than the second week of March, Christ does not even have the penultimate week of December.

Whether I have said these things justly or not concerning Berno’s rule, the eye of your diligence will see; and if anything has been said by us incautiously, the simplicity of our eye will excuse us and obtain pardon. For we do not disparage B[.....]rno in any respect. We judge him to be holy and wise, to be counted among the number of distinguished men, because he offered for the advancement of posterity what he had received from God, and because that very thing which he offered was thereby to be approved by God. He offered the gold of holiness and wisdom. “As gold in the furnace, the Lord proves his chosen”; he offered the silver of eloquence. What does Wisdom suggest to you through Solomon concerning such a man? “Remove,” she says, “the dross from the silver, and a vessel most pure shall come forth.” I should wish to walk in the house of God in agreement with such a man; but the prophet Amos says: “Shall two walk together unless they have agreed?” [Col. 0829A] (Amos 3:3.) We thought that Berno and ourselves agreed in accepting the allegorical correspondence of the generations; but the discordance between the first week of March and the last week of December calls us away from that agreement. Yet concerning the number of fourteen weeks, Berno and we agree; and in accepting them, we do indeed walk together upon the same road, but not everywhere in the same footsteps. For, while Berno goes six days before us, we enter upon the road of counting the forty-two weeks not with him from the Saturday of the fast, but always from the Kalends of March; and, like you, we divide them into three fourteen-week periods. Yet in the first of these fourteen-week periods we set the weeks of the appointed fasts: namely, the first of March, the second of June, the third of September, and the fourth of December. The six days that remain do nothing to hinder the distinction of the intervals between the fasts. I added this outside the scope of your question [Col. 0830A] in order to remove from you the charge of inconsistency which your earlier letter laid upon us: namely, that when March begins on the sixth or seventh feria, in one year we celebrate the June fast, and in the other the September fast, in the fifteenth week. With your favour, let us say that we are pressed by your judgment according to the tenor of your rule, not ours. Behold, you see the cause of our mutual disagreement: namely, the six days taken from March by Berno; and because you do not admit the trope of synecdoche—the days of the seasons in the fasts of the seasons. Who does not know in how many places Scripture would falter unless it were supported by the trope of synecdoche? Christ did not rise from the dead unless we admit the trope of synecdoche. May God, who has made you rich in him, in all utterance and in all knowledge, confirm you [Col. 0830B] blameless unto the end. Farewell.

[Col. 0829]

## SIGEBERT’S LETTER TO THE PEOPLE OF LIÈGE

(Marten, *Anecdota Collectio*, I, 587.)

When Robert, Count of Flanders, returned from the holy war in the year 1101, Pope Paschal wrote letters exhorting him to expel from the Church the schismatics of Liège who adhered to Emperor Henry. Sigebert attacks the pope’s judgment in a letter sent to the people of Liège. Because of the excessively hostile spirit with which he inveighs against the Holy See, we have refrained from publishing it. It appears in Labbe’s volumes of Councils (X, 630), without the author’s name, under this title: “A most vehement responsive declamation of the schismatics of Liège, who, like their fellows in the schism of the Donatists, rebelling against princes while claiming the Catholic name, thus entitled their declamation: Letter of the People of Liège against Pope Paschal.” EDITOR OF THE *PATROLOGIA*.

[Col. 0829]

## SIGEBERT’S LETTER AGAINST THE CALUMNY OF LAYMEN AGAINST MARRIED PRIESTS

(Marten, *Thesaurus*, I, 230.)

This letter appears to have been written on the occasion of the decree of Pope Gregory VII, who, in order to bring incontinent priests back to soundness of mind, forbade any one of the faithful to hear their masses, much less to receive ecclesiastical sacraments from them. In attempting to attack this judgment, our author thinks less correctly in more than one place. We have judged this little work also to be omitted. EDITOR.

[Col. 0829]

## SIGEBERT’S RESPONSE TO HILDEBRAND’S LETTER, WRITTEN TO HERMANN OF METZ IN CALUMNIATION OF ROYAL POWER

See above, in the Prolegomena, col. 16, note 40.

[Col. 0829]

## FRAGMENT OF A RHYTHMIC POEM ON ST LUCY, BY SIGEBERT

(In Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. IV, p. 372.)

[NOTE.]

In the year 1042, the relics of St Lucy, virgin and martyr, were translated to the monastery of Limburg, in the diocese of Speyer. They were given as a gift to Emperor Henry, son of Conrad the Salian, by Theodoric, bishop of Metz, [Col. 0831] who had received them from the monastery of St Vincent. This is taught us by the letter of the monks of Limburg on this matter, which it will not be burdensome to reproduce here:

“To the monastic community of blessed Vincent and St Lucy—that is, the chosen vine of God—the little flock of the monastery of Limburg wishes that they may bear fruit worthy of God.

“Let your brotherhood know that we possess the pledge of the relics of the holy martyr Lucy as something more dear than every precious pearl; but by what manner and through what persons it was translated to us, a certain account, based upon our own experience, will be made known to you. The lord Emperor Conrad of divine memory, with his wife Gisela, was a most devout founder and builder of our place. While he was still alive, the crypt and certain altars of the monastery were dedicated. After he departed from this light, his son Henry repaired the same place with no less zeal; and, having gathered relics of very many saints far and wide, he requested and obtained from Theodoric, the second bishop of the Church of Metz, an arm of St Lucy. When it had been brought to us by that bishop himself, they relate that, in confirmation of whether she was Lucy of Sicily, when this was sought from the Lord by prayers, it was declared by signs. And even to this day, through her aid, cures of many infirmities occur. With her veneration added, our church is dedicated in honour of the Holy Cross, St Mary ever Virgin, and St John the Evangelist. We have no other accounts of her deeds except her Passion under the proconsul Paschasius. As you promised, deign to send us this Passion composed in verse, that we may share in that distinguished little work, whose precious little body we possess with you as joint owners. Farewell in the Lord, most beloved brethren, aided by the prayers of St Lucy and of all the saints.”

Thus far the letter of the people of Limburg, which we extracted from the codex of St Vincent. It was written after the beginning of the twelfth century, when Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, who taught letters at St Vincent, composed the rhythmic poem on St Lucy, a copy of which the people of Limburg request in this letter. To this belong the following rhythmic verses of Sigebert:

For the pledge of so blessed a virgin,  
the parish priests of the church of Speyer  
glory that they are fellow participants  
in praises sung to Christ.

I speak of you, Limburg, noble in name,  
founded for the service of the highest Father  
by the hand of the reigning Conrad  
and of Gisela, his consort.

Although many churches flourish in splendour,  
to which the generous hand of kings has contributed,  
among your rich possessions you hold  
nothing so pious, nothing so beautiful,

as the sacred pledges of the holy virgin,  
whom you honour with renowned praise together with us:  
you possess Lucy in her arm alone,  
while we possess her wholly in her sacred body.

Young Henry brought this to you;  
young Theodoric took it to us:  
glorious Emperor Henry,  
and Theodoric adorned with the stole.

And at the end the author says:

Lucy, strong and renowned martyr,  
Lucy, noble and pious virgin,  
draw me—me, poor Sigebert—  
away from the fires of hell.

[Col. 0831]

## FRAGMENT CONCERNING ST LULL

(In Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, vol. IV, p. 392, in the Eulogy of St Lull.)

[NOTE.]

It is easy to believe that a dispute arose between Lull and Abbot Sturmi over the jurisdiction of the monastery of Fulda and that, as happens in similar cases, bitterness was not absent from the contention. While Sturmi vigorously defended the rights of his monastery, granted by the Roman pontiffs and secured by royal authority, dissension arose among his own followers; one party sought to ingratiate itself with Archbishop Lull and imputed crimes to Sturmi. When Lull, being too credulous—as this fault easily befalls persons stirred by emotion—reported these charges to the king, he incurred the mark of envy among Sturmi’s friends and admirers, and perhaps for this reason he was spoken of ill before Pope Adrian. Yet the anonymous writer of Gembloux, author of the Life of Lull, whom I suspect to have been Sigebert, monk of that place, judged this action quite differently. After describing the translation of the body of St Boniface to the monastery of Fulda, he adds the following:

“After these matters had been successfully accomplished as desired, the archbishop devoted all his effort to the place itself. But events turned out very differently from what he had hoped. For at that time a man named Sturmi presided over the monastery, a man of outstanding ability and praiseworthy holiness, but of a nature excessively vehement and fierce. He disturbed the minds of the brethren, warning them that this favour shown by Bishop Lull towards them had some purpose other than that which they imagined. By these and similar words he alienated the minds of the brethren from blessed Lull and, though Lull suspected nothing, stirred up no small envy against him.

“Moreover, the spirit of the man of God was already afflicted by no slight weariness, when he saw that so many and such great labours of his were flowing away in vain, that envy was not extinguished by benefits, and that it was the height of folly to expend such great resources upon this place without fruit, when elsewhere he could construct an enduring monument of his devotion. There was a place in the forest of Buchonia, which posterity named Herolfeld, exceptionally suitable for the dwelling of monks. There Abbot Sturmi had settled at the time when, with fervour of spirit, he had first eagerly devoted himself to the solitary life in the forest. Having uprooted the shrubs, he had constructed, in rough workmanship, small cells for himself and his brethren, and had already spent nine years there. But although the pleasant situation of the place and the convenience of water attracted blessed Boniface, he was offended by its side adjoining the Saxons, who still remained bound by pagan rites and frequently inflicted on Christian places slaughter of men and no small devastation of fields. Therefore, to escape this disadvantage, they occupied a place farther within Buchonia, where the monastery of Fulda is now seen.

“The place of Herfeld, by the gift of blessed Boniface, passed into the possession of St Lull, who perhaps even then had conceived in his mind a desire to build a monastery there. Accordingly, he devoted all his resources to this place and, having abundantly cut down the shrubs, set about making room for the brethren of a larger monastery and building it up with cultivators and buildings. In a short time the name of Herfeld rose to an immense summit of glory and greatness. Since blessed Lull, from the laying of the foundation onward, had dedicated the church of the monastery to the blessed apostles Simon and Thaddaeus, he was warned in a dream by an angelic voice to translate there the body of blessed Wigbert.”

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1112. THE CHRONICLE OF THE POLES, EDITED BY J. SZLACHTOWSKI AND R. KÖPKE, DOCTORS OF PHILOSOPHY

(In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. IX, p. 418.)

[Col. 0833]

## PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 0833A] A hundred years ago Godfrey Lengnich was the first to publish the *Chronicle of the Poles*, which he had persuaded himself should be ascribed to a certain Martin Gallus. The later editor, J. V. Bandtkie, seemed to think no differently; he published the same *Chronicle* from our more copious codex, and after them this same name has been repeated by all learned men who have undertaken to elucidate the most ancient affairs of the Poles. But not with good reason. For neither the name Martin nor the name Gallus can stand, since the reports handed down by later writers lack every authority to which credit ought to be given. Upon somewhat more careful examination of the matter, one finds only a single support—and that one ought rightly to be called very much into doubt here—by which certain persons thought they could defend this opinion: namely, the testimony of Długosz, a fifteenth-century writer of Polish affairs.

It is true that the name Martin Gallus is read in this author [Note: [Col. 0833B] Długosz, *Historia Polonica*, Leipzig edition, I, 36: “Martin Gallus is the authority for the statement that Lech defeated their duke.” I, 65: “Some maintain that this Lesko was defeated and slain in a battle begun with Emperor Charlemagne; for I found that Martin Gallus wrote this concerning him.” Semler, in his *Specimen of Observations on the More Ancient History of Affairs*, in the *Transactions of the Jablonowski Society*, “On the Slavs Lech and Czech,” Leipzig, 1772, p. 30 ff., observed that the words cited by Długosz had been copied from Ekkehard under the year 805, and that Długosz followed an interpolated codex of some Martin. [Col. 0834B] Others thought that this Martin Gallus was not the author of our *Chronicle*, but another person.], but, regrettably, the words which he cites from him are not found in our codices. Who, then, would rely upon such authority? Since, therefore, our codices display neither of those two names, both must be rejected. Nor did it seem proper to retain the name Gallus because of those few words, written in a later hand, which were read in the now-lost Heilsberg codex [Note: [Col. 0834B] According to Lengnich, the following was read at the beginning of the Heilsberg codex: “Gallus wrote this history, as I suppose some monk, as may be inferred from the prologues, who lived in the time of Bolesław III.” And at the end: “Thus far Gallus.”], or because of a mention made by other Polish writers before Lengnich [Note: [Col. 0834B] B. Paprocki, in his *Herby rycerztwa Polskiego*, Cracow, 1584, under the heading “Orzeł,” published the poem on the death of Bolesław I, I, 16, and the song concerning Bolesław III, III, 11, 13, 14; their author is anonymous to him. [Col. 0835C] Cromer, *Polonia*, Cologne, 1589, p. 46, writes: “A certain Gallus, who not long after these times set forth in three books the deeds of Bolesław III and of the earlier kings of Poland.” Sarnicki, *Annales Poloniae*, Leipzig edition of Długosz, II, 894: “Gallus and Kadłubek were almost contemporaries of King Wrymouth.” Compare p. 1056. Herburt, who was to publish our *Chronicle*, calls him “the anonymous Gallus” in his preface to Kadłubek. But in the *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, fourteenth century, Stenzel, *Scriptores rerum Silesiacarum*, I, our author’s book is cited by the simple name *Chronica*. Compare pp. 60, 66.].

For by that latter name they doubtless wished to indicate the author’s native country. But this question concerning his country is no less obscure than that concerning his name. In the book itself, indeed, the author appears to have concealed himself in almost impenetrable darkness: nowhere has he stated in explicit words who he was or in what land he was born. Yet one thing cannot be overthrown by any doubts: he was not a Pole. He proved this in words clearer than light in [Col. 0835A] the letter to the ducal chaplains before the third book: “I did not begin so great a work in order that I, an exile among you and strangers, might exalt my native land or parents, but in order that I might carry back some fruit of my labour to the place of my profession. … I undertook this labour … in order to avoid idleness, preserve the practice of composition, and not eat the bread of Poland in vain” [Note: [Col. 0835C] Bandtkie, p. XXV, strangely twists himself at this point: in order to make the author a Pole, he wishes the word *tamquam* (“as if”) to be understood.].

Can anything clearer be read? The author, an exile among the Poles, undertook his work not in order to extol his own country or parents with praise, but in order, by writing Polish affairs, to repay the favour of their hospitality and to carry back some recompense [Note: [Col. 0835C] That he expected some reward for his labour is indicated by III, epistle.] to the monastery in which he had professed himself a monk, when he should at some time return there. For this, we believe, is how “the place of my profession” must be understood [Note: [Col. 0835C] This also appears to be Bandtkie’s view, p. XXII. The opinion of Kownacki and Lelewel—that he was a Benedictine monk on the Roman Caelian Hill—has been rejected; see Ossoliński, *Vincent Kadłubek*, translated from Polish by Linde, Warsaw, 1822, pp. 375, 600, together with the false reading of the Gdańsk edition, “above the hill of St Gregory,” in the first epistle.].

Nor do the passages in which he calls Poland his native country oppose the view we have proposed. [Note: [Col. 0835D] Bandtkie, p. XXIII, collected these passages carefully. For the author, *patria* often means simply “land” or “region”; for example, I, prologue, 12, 20. He uses the word in its proper sense in I, 7; 15; II, 33, 35, 45; III, epistle 1, 5, 7; none of these passages concerns the author’s native country. But in the epistle before Book III he considers that his work will not be useless for the honour of his country, and in the epistle to Book II he testifies that it was written for the praise of the princes and “our country.” If one retains the words cited above, he indicated nothing else here than that Poland was a second native country. In nearly the same sense [Col. 0836C] he calls the Poles “ours” in II, 33. Elsewhere he fears the envy of the inhabitants as a foreigner: II, 12, “I, an exile, shall not please everyone”; add what he said concerning detractors and hatred in I, epistle; II, epistle.]. Nor does his knowledge of the Polish language, which he undoubtedly possessed, prove that he was a Pole [Note: [Col. 0836C] Polish expressions include: *Gnezen Sclavonice nidus*, “Gniezno, in Slavonic, ‘nest’,” I, 1; *cebri*, that is, “buckets,” I, 2; *Lapis (castrum) Kamin, Kamien*, that is, “stone,” II, 37; *in vacuum*, Polish *na próżno*, “in vain,” I, 16; *se quinto solummodo*, II, 33, that is, “he himself with four companions,” Polish *samopiąt*.].

An immigrant from the western parts of [Col. 0835B] Europe settled in Poland [Note: [Col. 0836C] That immigrants often moved to Poland from western Europe appears to be proved by the “castle of Gallus,” mentioned in II, 38, 39.], and by habit made it a second homeland for himself. But where, finally, did he first see the light? Some wished him to be a Frenchman, others a German [Note: [Col. 0836C] Besides Lengnich, the author was thought Franco-Gallic by Bentkowski and Lelewel; see Ossoliński, pp. 373, 606; German by Semler, cited work, p. 47, who in the cited dissertation rightly corrected the corrupt edition of Lengnich; a German from beyond the Rhine, in almost the same sense as “Galli” occurs in Lambert, by Samuel Bandtkie, *Dzieje Królestwa Polskiego*, Wrocław, 1820, I, 345; a Pole by Kownacki, Ossoliński, ed. Linde, p. 377, and J. V. Bandtkie, p. XIX. Bandtkie observed that the words, II, epilogue, “we have passed through so many lands,” must not be referred to this question but understood metaphorically.]; but he derived his origin from neither people and appears to have been an Italian.

This is chiefly confirmed by the one word which he uses, *vastaldiones* [Note: [Col. 0836D] I, 12 reads *vastandiones*; II, 1, *vastaldiones et comites*. The word *potissando*, I, 12, also appears to reveal an Italian.], which, unless we are mistaken, is the same as the Lombard *gastaldiones*. This word occurs only among Italian writers; nor can one clearly see how a Polish or German monk could have encountered such a word, which scarcely reached the ears of foreigners. It also appears Italian that he calls the Germans generally *Alemanni* [Note: [Col. 0836D] II, 37; III, 1, *impetuosi Alemanni*, “impetuous Alemanni”; III, 3, *impetus Alemannorum*, “the assault of the Alemanni.”], something which, as everyone knows, German authors at least never did. Finally, one may add that in a northern man of those times one would seek in vain the evidence, apparent in one passage, that he was by no means unacquainted with the art of painting or had often inspected painted panels [Note: [Col. 0836D] II, epistle.].

We do not know whether we indulge conjecture more than is right if [Col. 0835C] we say that this Italian monk not only came to the court of Duke Bolesław III but was also received among the ducal chaplains. [Col. 0836A] For in the dedication of Book III, written to the ducal chaplains and other worthy clerics throughout Poland, he calls them “dearest brethren.” He also saw Duke Bolesław, on account of his brother Zbigniew having been blinded, fasting, rolling upon the ground in ashes and haircloth, bathed in tears, and separated from human society [Note: [Col. 0836D] III, 25.]. Thus one might readily believe that the author was among the very few to whom the duke’s secret journey to the monastery of St Giles in Hungary was known and that he was one of the duke’s companions; so precisely did he describe the duke’s penance and his journey into Hungary and to the tomb of St Adalbert.

One may connect with this also the fact that, although the crime committed against Zbigniew was not slight, he nevertheless attempts to excuse Bolesław; he did not openly state the act itself for which the duke repented, but only cautiously and obscurely hinted at it [Note: [Col. 0836D] In the passage cited.]. This is not at all surprising if one considers the purpose which the author set before himself in composing the book: to celebrate Bolesław III with his praises [Col. 0836B] rather than to transmit the deeds of the Poles to posterity. He expressly sets forth this plan in these words in the prologue to Book I: “Our principal intention is to describe Poland and Duke Bolesław, and, for his sake, to recount certain memorable deeds of his predecessors.” He professes the same thing no less openly elsewhere in the work [Note: [Col. 0836D] I, epilogue 30; II, 45.].

He kept this end quite consistently in view throughout the whole work, for one may often regret that, because of this purpose, he dispatched in very few words matters which he could undoubtedly have related in fuller discourse. Thus he included in one first book the deeds of all the earlier dukes of Poland, but set forth in a very full narrative, in the other two books, the life of Bolesław down to his twenty-eighth year—that is, down to the year 1113; the duke died in 1139. Yet he did not write the book in one continuous stretch, but, as he himself proves at the end of Book II, rested for a time [Note: [Col. 0836D] II, 50.]. For he composed the first two books in 1109 or 1110 and dedicated them, together with certain others, to Bishop Paul of Kruszwica and Bishop Maurus of Cracow. The former died in 1110 [Col. 0836C] [Note: [Col. 0836D] Thus Długosz in the *Lives of the Bishops of Kruszwica*, in a manuscript in the Ossoliński Library, 4, no. XVIII, paper, fol. 101v. In the Leipzig edition of Długosz, I, 391, Paul is called, through a printer’s error, Paulinus, bishop of Cracow; the codices examined by Szlachtowski rightly read “of Kruszwica.”], while the latter was consecrated in 1109 [Col. 0837A] [Note: [Col. 0837C] Compare the notes at the beginning of the dedicatory epistle to Book I. On Syroslaus I, who is said in the *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, Stenzel I, 158, to have held office in 1112–1120, while in the catalogue of the bishops of Wrocław, ibid. II, 132, in 1111–1120, compare ibid.].

He appears to have written the third book shortly after Bolesław’s journey to St Giles, perhaps in the very year 1113. The patrons and assistants of this work were those five bishops to whom he dedicated the first book. Relying upon their authority and help, he undertook the task of writing; their kindness opened certain inner goals to him [Note: [Col. 0837D] I, epistle.]. One can scarcely doubt that they supplied the author with resources for writing, and above all Chancellor Michael, whom he calls the maker of his begun labour and his fellow-worker [Note: [Col. 0837D] In the cited passage, II, epistle.].

The materials which he used were almost entirely prepared in such a way that he merely transmitted to posterity what he had either drawn from others’ narratives or witnessed himself. Of books, he cited only one Passion of St Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0837D] I, 6. He did not have before him the Life of St Adalbert by either John Canaparius or Bishop Bruno; rather, there seem to have been older miracles of that kind, as printed in *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores*, IV, 613 (*Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVII, col. 889), in which little work our *Chronicle* has been copied.]. The letters which he inserted appear rather to have been written by the author himself than by those to whom they are attributed [Note: [Col. 0837D] I, 30; III, 2, 13, 14.]. He inquired into events from persons who knew them [Note: [Col. 0837D] II, epilogue.], and in recounting the most ancient tales of the Poles [Col. 0837B] he followed the old men of former times. Yet because these tales derived their origin from pagan times, he preferred to consign them to oblivion rather than memory [Note: [Col. 0837D] I, 3.]. Elsewhere he cites the report of the ancestors [Note: [Col. 0837D] II, 42.]. Nor did he reject popular Polish songs, as the song composed in honour of Bolesław proves [Note: [Col. 0837D] II, 28.]. But someone might not without reason doubt whether that other poem, made by Germans in praise of Bolesław, really arose from the mouth of the people or from the author’s own invention [Note: [Col. 0837D] III, 11.].

More cautiously and modestly, he marked by the word *fertur* (“it is reported”) or in some other manner everything which appeared doubtful because of its antiquity, or was not sufficiently investigated and known [Note: [Col. 0837D] I, 2, 7, 18, 21, 27, 28, 29; II, 8, 16, 17, 22, 23, 24, 49.]; finally, he openly professed ignorance of other matters [Note: [Col. 0837D] I, 18; II, 7, 16, 33.]. He likewise praised witnesses who had been present at events [Note: [Col. 0838C] III, 1.]. He set historical truth before himself, as it were, as a norm and law [Note: [Col. 0838C] II, 31.], which one cannot deny that he generally observed rather carefully, although he wrote more cautiously concerning Bolesław III and the death of St Stanislaus [Note: [Col. 0838C] III, 25; I, 27.].

The author was undoubtedly an educated man, sufficiently steeped in ancient literature, as he proved in those [Col. 0837C] passages in which he brought forward recollections of the deeds of ancient peoples [Note: [Col. 0838C] III, epistle.]. Among historians he read Sallust above all [Note: [Col. 0838C] I, prologue 3, 6, 7; II, 6, 13, 16; III, 8.], and among poets Lucan [Note: [Col. 0838C] II, 5.]. His style of writing is far removed from that natural charm which attracts the mind in other writers of those times. It is swollen and daring in images and metaphors, so that in more than one place one hesitates whether what one reads should be understood literally or metaphorically. Moreover, he composed almost the whole book [Col. 0838A] in those verses which occur very frequently among writers of the twelfth century. Of these we have preserved only those which, being somewhat more carefully composed, possess a rhythm readily perceived by the ear.

Among writers of later times, our author was adapted to their own use by Kadłubek [Note: [Col. 0838D] Długosz, Leipzig edition, II, 651, and elsewhere; he appears to have had the *Chronicle* before him.], the compiler printed by Lengnich [Note: [Col. 0838D] Bielowski maintained in his book *Wstęp Krytyczny do dziejów Polski* [Critical Introduction to the History of Poland] that the *Chronicle* published by Lengnich under Kadłubek’s name was that of Miorszi.], the author of the *Chronicle of the Dukes of Poland* [Note: [Col. 0838D] Stenzel, *Scriptores rerum Silesiacarum*, I, 45 ff. Semler had already shown this in the cited work, p. 36.], the Polish annals [Note: [Col. 0838D] Lengnich edition, p. 33. The Cracow annals flowed, if not from our *Chronicle*, at least in part from another source whose author had read ours; and that author copied Cosmas no less.], Długosz [Note: [Col. 0838D] Compare above, note 1.], and Sarnicki [Note: [Col. 0838D] Długosz, Leipzig edition, II, 1063.].

In order to establish the text of our edition, we called to aid the two codices of which information survives today. Yet in many places, since these are neither ancient nor of the best quality, a remedy could be applied only by conjectures. We have marked Pertz’s conjectures with P, Szlachtowski’s notes with S, and Köppe’s—who also attempted to establish the chronology—with K.

1) The Warsaw codex of the library of the Counts Zamoyski, on parchment, made about the middle of the fourteenth century, has ninety-seven numbered leaves. Besides [Col. 0838B] our *Chronicle*, written in two columns from fol. 20v to fol. 54v in a neat hand, with chapter headings and initial letters painted in cinnabar, it contains:

a) fols. 1–20, the *Life of Alexander M.*;

b) fol. 55r–74, the *Life of St Stanislaus*, which J. V. Bandtkie published together with the *Chronicle of Gallus* [Note: [Col. 0838D] Except for the miracles of St Stanislaus, which do not occur in the Warsaw codex.];

at the end of this folio begins

c) the Polish annals of Traska, continued from Duke Mieszko to the year 1341, fol. 89v;

d) fols. 90–96v, a mixed Chronicle of Hungarians and Poles [Note: [Col. 0838D] H. Kownacki published this chronicle at Warsaw in 1823 from our codex 2. From that less accurate edition S. Endlicher published it in the *Monumenta Arpadiana regum Hungariae S. Galli*, 1848, I, 60.];

e) on fol. 96 and the final fol. 97r are recorded various events of the sixteenth century; on the verso is found a poem written in the Polish language on the killing of the Count of Tęczyn, perpetrated at the same time.

Augustyn Bielowski, a distinguished man, most kindly communicated to us the readings of this most excellent codex, which he had copied from the codex itself at Warsaw with the utmost care.
