2) The Kłodawa codex, later the Puławy codex, of Santko of Czechel, on paper, made at the end of the fifteenth century, consists of 945 pages numbered by a later hand—page 25 being numbered twice—and two final parchment leaves. It was given to the monastery of St Giles at Kłodawa by its provost, Santko of Czechel, as is proved by the following inscription [Note: [Col. 0838D] Read less correctly by Bandtkie.] on p. 1: “Chronicles of the Poles and another work called *Flowers of Time*, concerning the supreme pontiffs and emperors; at the end, an inventory of all the ornaments of the church of Gniezno; given by Brother Santko for the monastery of St Giles at Kłodawa.”

The codex then came to the church of Gniezno, whence it passed into the library of Jan Zamoyski, who, as the inscription on [Col. 0839A] p. 1 testifies, bequeathed it to the library of the Zamoyski Academy in the seventeenth century. By what fortunes it subsequently came into the library of Tadeusz Czacki cannot be discovered. After Czacki’s death, the codex was bought with the whole library by Prince Adam Czartoryski and was kept in the library at Puławy. J. V. Bandtkie prepared his edition of 1824 from this codex, which he calls the Gniezno codex.

Besides our *Chronicle*, written on pp. 242–307 in two columns, with the chapter initials painted in cinnabar and their headings underlined in cinnabar, the codex contains not a few documents useful for elucidating ancient Polish history:

a) the Polish annals—the Benedictine annals of Gniezno; Traska, pp. 14–21, 117, 118, 326–349; the longer and shorter Cracow annals, pp. 942, 943, 944, 945;

b) the *Chronicle* of Bogufał, bishop of Poznań, and of the man who continued it, Basco, custos of Poznań, pp. 23–117;

c) the *Chronicle* of the anonymous archdeacon of Gniezno, pp. 118–224, with Polish annals inserted which also occur jointly with this chronicle [Col. 0839B];

d) the *Life of St Stanislaus with Miracles*, pp. 307–326;

e) a mixed *Chronicle of Hungarians and Poles*, pp. 349–359;

f) Passion-legends of St Wenceslaus the martyr, St Podven, St Procopius, and St Ludmila, pp. 500–533;

g) documents concerning the disputes of the kings of Poland with the Teutonic Knights, pp. 2–14 and 534–855;

h) Martin of Poland’s *Chronicle of Emperors and Pontiffs*, pp. 904–912;

i) the Wiślica Statute of Casimir the Great, pp. 858–901;

k) three letters of Santko of Czechel, pp. 234–237;

l) finally, on the two final leaves, pp. 946–949, an inventory of the church of Gniezno, added to and bound with the codex at a later time.

Szlachtowski collated this codex. It derives either from one and the same source as codex 1, or at least codices 1 and 2 derive from codices which flowed from a single source; for the corrupt passages and erroneous readings are nearly the same in both codices.

3.) The Szamotuły Codex, later the Heilsberg Codex, on paper, of the late fifteenth century, displays on its first page, in smaller gilt letters, the inscription: “The book of the magnificent lord Peter of Szamotuły, castellan and captain of Poznań, 1471.” [Note: [Col. 0839D] These are Bandtkie’s words.] Written quite neatly, with many blank spaces left between nearly all chapters, doubtless for painting their initial letters, it comprises 279 pages, numbered on both sides in Arabic numerals by a later hand; the text is arranged in two columns on each page. This codex too was in the hands of J. V. Bandtkie when he prepared his edition of Gallus; he had received it together with codex 2 from the Puławy library. From that edition we have drawn our description of this codex, which today would be sought in vain in libraries, having been lost through the injuries of time. We have adopted variant readings from Bandtkie’s edition. The codex was undoubtedly of the lowest quality, for it is mutilated and interpolated. Chapters I.21; II.9, 16, 20, 27–33, 44–47; and III.16–26 are wanting. [Note: [Col. 0839D] Chapters I.27 and 28, which one might readily miss, are found on p. 44 of Lengnich’s continuation of Kadłubek.] Almost all the remaining chapters are abridged; direct speeches are frequently cut short; here and there one finds letters and the like in the text. [Col. 0840B] Chapters 11, 14–16, and 32 from the *Life of Saint Stanislaus*, together with certain other passages copied from the *Life of Saint Stephen*, have been incorporated into the text. [Note: [Col. 0839D] Pp. 73, 76, as Prazmowski had already noted in Ossoliński, p. 304.]

The first edition from the Heilsberg codex was prepared by G. Lengnich at Gdańsk in 1749, under the title *Vincentius Kadlubko et Martinus Gallus scriptores historiae Poloniae antiquissimi*, p. 56; it was reprinted by Mizler de Kolof in the *Great Collection of Writers on the Histories of Poland and Lithuania*, Warsaw, 1769, vol. III. The third was that of J. V. Bandtkie, who, following the same codex and the Kłodawa codex, was the first to publish Martin Gallus’s *Chronicle*, Warsaw, 1824, octavo, in its entirety and with reasonable accuracy.

Aided by these resources, we have endeavoured to restore the text, as far as possible, to its genuine form. In spelling words, however, in accordance with the usage of the early twelfth century, we have restored the diphthong *ae* and the syllable *ti* in place of the simple *e* and *ci* found in fourteenth- and fifteenth-century manuscripts.

Lviv and Berlin, December 1849.

J. SZLACHTOWSKI and R. KOEPKE.

[Col. 0839]

# HERE BEGIN THE CHRONICLES AND DEEDS OF THE DUKES, OR PRINCES, OF THE POLES

# HERE BEGINS THE EPISTLE AND CERTAIN PRELIMINARY MATTERS CONCERNING THE CHRONICLES OF THE POLES, IN THIS MANNER

[Note: [Col. 0839] “Here begins—manner” is absent in 2 and 3.]

[Col. 0839C] To lord M., [Note: [Col. 0839D] Lengnich had already observed, in his Gdańsk edition, fol. 2, that this letter indicates Martin, Archbishop of Gniezno. According to Długosz’s *Polish History*, Martin attained this dignity in 1092 and died in 1118. S.] by God’s grace supreme pontiff; and likewise to [Note: [Col. 0839] “likewise” 3.] Simon, [Note: [Col. 0839D] Simeon, appointed bishop of Płock, according to Długosz, in 1107; he died in 1129. S.] Paul, [Note: [Col. 0840D] Paul, bishop of Kruszwica, or Włocławek, appointed in 1098, died in 1110. S.] Maurus, [Note: [Col. 0840D] Maurus, bishop of Cracow, appointed in 1109, died in 1118. S.] Syroslaus, [Note: [Col. 0840D] Zyroslaus, bishop of Wrocław, appointed in 1091, died in 1120: Długosz, *Polish History*, I, 321, 416. In his *History of the Bishops of Smogorzów and Ryczyn*, Długosz adds that Zyroslaus was finally consecrated in 1100, and certainly not in 1112, as the fifteenth-century writer Rozicius erroneously has it; Sommersberg, *Scriptors rerum Silesiacarum*, I, 64. Bandtkie followed him in his edition of Gallus, p. 3, n. 3. S.] pontiffs of the Polish land, worthy of God and venerable; and also to their fellow-worker, the venerable chancellor Michael, craftsman of the work undertaken: may the author of the following little work, entrusted to the flock of the Lord’s saints upon Mount Sion, [Note: [Col. 0839] “of saints” 1; “of the saints” 2.] watch over it with vigilant study, and, advancing from strength to strength, contemplate face to face the God of gods. [Note: [Col. 0839] 3 corruptly reads: “sent above Mount Spondia of Saint Gregory,” for “upon Mount—entrusted.”]

Unless I were supported by your authority, fathers named above, and sustained by your assistance, I should vainly undertake, with my own strength, the burden of a task so weighty; and with a frail little skiff [Note: [Col. 0839] 1 had *iembo*, and 2 had it also, but deleted it and wrote *limbo* in the margin.] I should dangerously [Note: [Col. 0839] 3 reads “with a frail dangerous *iembo*.”] enter so vast an expanse of sea. But the sailor seated safely in his little vessel can navigate through the waves of the raging strait if he has a skilled helmsman, who knows how to steer it [Note: [Col. 0839] “them” 3.] surely by the governance of winds and stars. Nor should I know how to avoid shipwreck in so great a Charybdis, unless your charity had been pleased to sustain my little vessel by the rudders of your rowing; nor could I, ignorant of the way, emerge from so great a density of forests, unless your kindness had been pleased to reveal to me inwardly reliable landmarks. [Note: [Col. 0839] 1 reads *cecitas*; 2 originally had the same, but deleted it and supplied *certas*, “reliable,” in the margin.]

[Col. 0841A] Therefore, furnished with the assistance of such great rulers, [Note: [Col. 0841] “therefore” 3.] I shall safely enter harbour, free from the storms of winds; nor shall I hesitate to grope with weak-sighted eyes along an unknown path, [Note: [Col. 0841] 3 reads “broad …” for “with weak-sighted eyes—unknown path.”] since I have learned that the eyes of the rulers who go before shine more brightly than light itself. [Note: [Col. 0841] “I have learned” 1.] And since I have sent ahead such advocates [Note: [Col. 0841] singular “advocate” 3.] as defenders, I shall make light of whatever jealous detractors may mutter in whispering complaint. [Note: [Col. 0841] 1 and 2 read “in customary practice”; 2 later corrected it.] And because favourable fortune has provided you as supporters of a just cause, I have thought it fitting to insert such great men, as it were, in the sequence of a chronicle. [Note: [Col. 0841] 3 reads “a chronicle to be written” for “in the sequence of a chronicle.”] For in your time and through your precious prayers God has made Poland illustrious through the memorable and famous deeds of Boleslaus the Third. [Note: [Col. 0841] “famous” 1; 2 first had the same and then corrected it.] Although I pass over many great and magnificent deeds performed while you are living, I shall nevertheless not fail subsequently to suggest certain matters [Note: [Col. 0841] 3 reads *ty*; perhaps 1 and 2 read “only.”] to the memory of posterity. [Note: [Col. 0841] 3 reads “of those that follow”; Warsaw second edition reads “subsequently.”] [Note: [Col. 0841] “I shall omit” 3.] But now [Col. 0841B] let us, unanimously with one voice and one praise, [Note: [Col. 0841] “one praise” absent in 3.] praise in unison those who are united in mind, and whom the indissoluble bond of charity binds together; let us add them also to our praises. [Note: [Col. 0841] “your” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0841] singular “let me add” 3.]

For it is fitting that those who have devoted themselves even to the deeds of affairs should be distinguished in advance—[Col. 0842A] those whom divine grace causes, by gifts of charisms, to rule the princes themselves; and that the patronage of those by whose stewardship the faithful are supplied, according to the capacities of their subjects, with the heavenly nourishment, should protect by its aid the little work of our insignificance. [Note: [Col. 0841] This seems to be the proper reading; *donis* is Pertz’s conjecture. 1 reads: “For it is fitting that those who have applied themselves even to the deeds of affairs should be distinguished in advance, whom divine grace causes from these charisms to rule the princes themselves, to you by whose stewardship what is supplied to the faithful from the capacities of subjects of the heavenly food, may the patronage of the same protect the little work of our insignificance.” 2 reads: “For it is fitting that those who have applied themselves even to the deeds of affairs should be distinguished in advance” (adding in the margin, “may we distinguish your dignities in advance”), “whom divine grace causes from these charisms to rule the princes themselves, food by whose stewardship …”; 3 has comparable corrupt readings. Bandtkie reads: “in the balance before … likewise by whose stewardship … by the summits of heavenly nourishment the faithful.”]

For those whom God has ordained to excel all other persons by so great a privilege of rank ought to provide more zealously for the advantages and necessities of each individual. [Note: [Col. 0841] “of others” 3.] Therefore, lest we appear to be lowly persons extending the fringes of vanity, [Note: [Col. 0841] “to extend vainly” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0841] “fringes” 2.] we have resolved to entitle this little book not with our names but with yours. Accordingly, let us ascribe the praise of this work and the honour of this homeland to its princes; but let us confidently entrust our own labour and the recompense of that labour to the judgment of your discretion. [Note: [Col. 0841] “honour” 3.] May the grace of the Holy Spirit, which ordained you shepherds of the Lord’s flock, [Col. 0842B] suggest such counsel to your minds that the prince may give worthy gifts to one who merits them, whence honour may come to you and glory to him who bestows them. [Note: [Col. 0841] “in” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0841] “bestowing,” manuscripts.] Rejoice always; favour us and our work.

# HERE ENDS THE EPISTLE

# HERE BEGINS THE EPILOGUE

[Note: [Col. 0841] “epilogue” 1 and 2.]

Boleslaus, illustrious duke,  
Born by God’s gift,  
Through the prayers of Giles  
Here received the source of his beginning.  
How this came about,  
If God here [Note: [Col. 0841] absent in 3.] grants it, [Note: [Col. 0841] At this point 1 and 2 add in the margin: “Prologue of the third book.”]

# FIRST PROEM

[Note: [Col. 0843] “Here begin—first” absent in 3.]

[Col. 0843B] Since, throughout the wide expanse of the world, very many things worthy of remembrance are done by very many kings and dukes, [Note: [Col. 0843] absent in 1 and 2.] [Note: [Col. 0843] “do” 3.] which are covered in silence by the wearisome negligence of philosophers—[Note: [Col. 0843D] Sallust, *Catiline*, IV; *Jugurtha*, XVII. S.] perhaps through want—[Note: [Col. 0843] “of very many [philosophers]” 3.] we have thought it worthwhile to set down in a simple style certain deeds of the princes of the Poles, for the sake of a certain most glorious and victorious duke named Boleslaus, [Note: [Col. 0843] 3 omits this and leaves a blank space.] rather than leave nothing at all noteworthy to the memory of posterity. [Note: [Col. 0843] “changeable” 1, 2, 3.] This is especially so because he was born by God’s gift and through the prayers of Saint Giles, through whom, as we believe, he was fortunate and always victorious. [Note: [Col. 0843] absent in 1 and 2.] But because the land of the Poles is remote from the routes of travellers, and is known to few except those who pass into Rus’ [Note: [Col. 0843] “Russia” throughout in 3.] for trade, if we say a little about it, [Note: [Col. 0843] “be abandoned” 1 and 2; corruptly in 3.] [Col. 0843C] let no one regard this as absurd; and if, in describing a part, [Note: [Col. 0843] “describing a part” 3.] the whole is introduced, let no one deem it burdensome.

Thus Poland lies in the northern part of Slavonia, [Note: [Col. 0843] “Slavonia” 2, but the corrector deleted the first *c*.] having Rus’ on the east, Hungary on the south, Moravia and Bohemia toward the sunrise, and adjacent to it on the west Denmark and Saxony. On the northern, or Amphitritean, sea [Note: [Col. 0843] “or Amphitritean” absent in 3.] it has three neighbouring and most fierce nations of pagan barbarians: Selencia, [Note: [Col. 0843D] By Selencia the author means neither Silesia nor the land of Schleswig, but Luticia—or, as the author of the *Life of St Otto* calls it, Leuticia—as S. Girtler already demonstrated in the *Index lectionum* of the University of Cracow, 1823. S.] Pomerania, [Note: [Col. 0843] “Pomorania” 3.] and Prussia. [Note: [Col. 0843] “Prussia” 2; “Russia” 3.] Against these regions the duke of the Poles constantly fights, in order to convert them to the faith. Yet neither the sword of preaching could recall their hearts from faithlessness, [Col. 0843D] [Col. 0844B] nor could the brood of vipers be wholly destroyed by the sword of slaughter. [Note: [Col. 0843] “unless” 2.] Nevertheless, their rulers, often defeated in battle by the Polish duke, sought baptism; and then, gathering their forces and renouncing the Christian faith, they again prepared war against Christians.

Beyond them also, and below the arms of Amphitrite, are other barbarous nations of pagans and uninhabitable islands, where snow and ice are perpetual. [Note: [Col. 0843] “perpetual” 3.] Thus the land of Slavonia, situated in the north and in part divided or bounded by these its regions, [Note: [Col. 0843] “divisions” 2 and 3.] [Note: [Col. 0843] “constituted” 2 and 3.] is bounded, from the Sarmatians, who are also called Getae, by Denmark [Note: [Col. 0843] “Ducy” 2.] and Saxony; [Note: [Col. 0843] plural “are bounded” 1 and 2.] and, from Thrace, descending through Hungary, once occupied by the Huns, who are also called Hungarians, [Note: [Col. 0843] “of this” 1 and 2.] [Note: [Col. 0843] “formerly” 2.] [Note: [Col. 0843] “Huns—occupied” absent in 3.] and through Carinthia into Bavaria, it is delimited. [Note: [Col. 0843] “Carinthia and Bavaria” 3.] To the south, [Col. 0844C] along the Mediterranean Sea, extending from Epirus through Dalmatia, Croatia, [Note: [Col. 0843] “Scrovacia” 1; “Stromacia” 3.] and Istria, [Note: [Col. 0843] “Istria” 3.] it is bounded by the shores of the Adriatic Sea, [Note: [Col. 0843] “Atriatic” 1; 2 originally had the same but subsequently corrected it.] where Venice and Aquileia [Note: [Col. 0843] “Venacia and Aquilegia” 3.] stand, and is separated from Italy.

Although this region is very wooded, it is nevertheless abundantly supplied with gold and [Note: [Col. 0843] absent in 1 and 2.] silver, bread and [Note: [Col. 0843] absent in 3.] meat, fish and [Note: [Col. 0843] absent in 3.] honey. Above all, it deserves preference over other lands because, though surrounded by so many peoples mentioned above, both Christian and pagan, and often attacked by all together and by each individually, it has nevertheless never been completely subdued by anyone: a homeland [Note: [Col. 0843] absent in 3.] where the air is healthy, [Col. 0844D] the soil [Note: [Col. 0843] “land” 3.] fertile, the forest honey-bearing, the water rich in fish, [Col. 0845A] the soldiers warlike, the peasants industrious, the horses enduring, the oxen fit for ploughing, the cows full of milk, and the sheep wool-bearing.

But lest we seem to have made too long a digression, let us return to the purpose of our undertaking. Our intention is chiefly to describe Poland and Duke Boleslaus, [Note: [Col. 0845] “Boleslaus chiefly” 3.] and, for his sake, to recount certain memorable deeds of his predecessors. [Note: [Col. 0845] “predecessor” 2.] [Note: [Col. 0845] “memory” 3.] Let us now begin our subject in such a way that we may ascend through the root to the branch of the tree. How the honour of the dukedom came to this line will be made known by the following sequence of the narrative. [Note: [Col. 0845] “will have made known” 3.]

# BOOK ONE

[Note: [Col. 0845] Absent in 1, 2, and 3.]

[Col. 0845]

## 1. Concerning Duke Popiel, called [Note: [Col. 0845] “spoken” 1; “dctus” 2; “said” 3; Bandtkie conjectured “led.”] Chosisco.

[Note: [Col. 0845D] That is, “praised,” “blessed.” P.] [Note: [Col. 0845] “Choszysto” 3.]

[Col. 0845B]

There was in the city of Gniezno, whose name means “nest” in Slavonic, [Note: [Col. 0845] “Slavonic” 2, but the corrector deleted the first *c*.] a duke named Popiel, who had two sons. In accordance with pagan custom, he prepared a great feast for their tonsure, [Note: [Col. 0845] “was preparing” 1 and 2.] to which he invited very many of his nobles and friends. By God’s hidden counsel it happened that two guests came there, who not only were not [Note: [Col. 0845] Absent in the codices; added by the editors.] invited to the feast, but were even driven away with insult from the entrance to the city. Horrified at once by the inhumanity of those citizens, [Note: [Col. 0845] “inhumanity” 3.] they went down to the suburb and happened to arrive before the little house of a ploughman belonging to the aforesaid duke, while that duke was holding a feast for his sons. This poor man, full of kindly compassion, invited those guests [Note: [Col. 0845] “the aforesaid [guests]” 3.] into his own [Note: [Col. 0845] “proper” 3.] little house, and most generously placed his poverty at their disposal. [Col. 0845C] They, gladly accepting [Note: [Col. 0845] “he” 3.] the poor man’s invitation [Note: [Col. 0845] “invitation” 3.] and entering the hut of hospitality, said: “May you rejoice that we have come, and may our coming bring you an abundance of goods and, from offspring, honour and glory.” [Note: [Col. 0845] 2 had *hor.*, which the corrector deleted and supplied *honorum*, “of honours,” in the margin; “of honour” 3.]

## 2. Concerning Piast, son of Choscisco.

[Note: [Col. 0845] “II” absent in 1, 2, and 3.] [Note: [Col. 0845] “Past” 2.] [Note: [Col. 0845] “Choszyszko” 3. The whole heading, “Chapter—Choscisco,” is set by 1 in the margin, without interrupting the thread of the narrative from the preceding chapter.]

For Piast, son of Chostko, [Note: [Col. 0845] “Chossistko” 2; “Chosiszko” 3.] and his wife, called Rzepka, [Note: [Col. 0845] “Repta” 2.] were householders of that lodging. [Note: [Col. 0845] “lodging” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0845] “household” 2.] [Note: [Col. 0845] 2 originally read “Piasto,” but the *o* was erased, though it remains plainly visible.] [Note: [Col. 0845] “were called” 2, but the final *a* was altered to *i*.] With great affection of heart, they strove according to their means to serve the needs of their guests. Observing their wisdom, they resolved to carry out, with their counsel, whatever secret matter there might be. [Note: [Col. 0845] “who of them” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0845] “which” 3.] And while, according to custom, they conversed at leisure [Note: [Col. 0845] “knowing” 3.] about many things, and the travellers asked whether there was anything to drink there, [Note: [Col. 0845] absent in 3.] the hospitable ploughman replied:

“I have,” he said, “a little vessel of fermented ale, which I prepared for the cutting of the hair [Note: [Col. 0845] “to cut” 1 and 3; “to store” 2.] of my only son; but what use is this small amount? If you wish, drink it.”

For that poor peasant had determined, when his lord the duke was preparing a feast for his sons—since at another time, because of extreme poverty, he could not—to prepare some food [Note: [Col. 0845] corrupt readings in 1 and 2.] for the tonsure of his own little boy, and to invite some friends and poor people, not to a midday meal but to an evening supper. He was also rearing a piglet, which he was reserving for that occasion. I shall tell something marvellous; but who [Note: [Col. 0845] “what” 1; 2 suggests that “who” should be read.] can comprehend God’s mighty works? Or who dares dispute about divine benefits—he who sometimes raises up the humility of the poor in temporal things [Note: [Col. 0845] “of the poor” 1 and 2.] [Note: [Col. 0845] 3 reads: “moderates the humility of the poor sometimes.”] and does not refuse to reward even the hospitality of pagans?

The guests therefore command him [Note: [Col. 0845] “therefore” 2 and 3.] [Note: [Col. 0845] *em* added by 2 and later deleted.] confidently to serve the ale, knowing well that in drinking [Col. 0846C] [Note: [Col. 0845] corruptly “prtisando” 2; “potisando” 3.] it would not fail but increase. Indeed, the ale is said to have increased so much that all the borrowed vessels were filled, as well as those empty vessels of the feasting duke which they found. They also order the aforesaid piglet to be killed, from which, marvellous to tell, ten buckets—called *cebri* in Slavonic—are said to have been filled.

When Piast and Rzepka [Note: [Col. 0845] “Repta” 2 and 3.] saw the miracles taking place, they sensed some great portent [Note: [Col. 0845] “prestige” may also be read in 3.] concerning the boy, and already thought of inviting the duke and his guests. Yet they did not dare, unless they first asked the travellers about this. Why delay? Thus, by the counsel and exhortation of the guests, their lord the duke and all his guests [Note: [Col. 0845] absent in 3.] are invited by the farmer Piast; and the duke, though invited by his peasant, does not think it beneath him to go down to him. [Note: [Col. 0845] In 3 this word is placed after *dedignatur*, “thinks it beneath him.”] For the Polish dukedom was not yet so great, nor did the ruler of the world swell with so much arrogant pride, nor, surrounded by so many ranks of retainers, did he proceed with such magnificence. [Col. 0846D] [Note: [Col. 0845] plural “proceeded” 1 and 2.]

When the feast had been begun in customary fashion, [Note: [Col. 0845] 3, perhaps through a scribe’s error, reads *puto*, “I think.”] [Col. 0847A] and everything had been abundantly prepared, those guests tonsured the boy and, as a prophecy of future events, gave him the name Siemowit.

[Note: [Col. 0847C] Compare the *Life of Saint Ladislaus, King of Hungary*, in Endlicher, *Rerum Hungaricarum monumenta Arpadiana*, *S. Galli*, 1848, I, 236. S.]

## 3. Concerning Duke Siemowit, who is called Siemowit, son of Piast.

[Note: [Col. 0847] “III” is absent at this point in the codices, as are the chapter numbers in all subsequent chapters of all three books; the word “chapter” is also absent, except in chapters where we have noted only the absence of the number.] [Note: [Col. 0847] “Concerning Duke—Piast” absent in 3.]

When these things had been done, the boy Siemowit, son of Piast Choscisco, [Note: [Col. 0847] “Chossisco” 2; “Choszysco” 3.] grew in strength and age, and [Note: [Col. 0847] absent in 3.] from day to day began to advance in increasing virtue, [Note: [Col. 0847] “began” 3.] to such an extent that the King of kings and Duke of dukes [Note: [Col. 0847] absent in 3.] appointed him, by common consent, duke of Poland, and utterly rooted out Popiel and his offspring from his kingdom. [Note: [Col. 0847] 2 had *Pumpil*, later corrected to *Popiel*; “Popel” 3; *Popiel* is the customary Polish form.] The old men also relate that this Popiel [Note: [Col. 0847] accusative “this [man]” 1 and 2; absent in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0847] 2 originally had *Pumpil*, again changed by the corrector to *Popiel*; “Popel” 3.] was expelled from the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0847] “by” 3.] and suffered such great persecution from mice [Note: [Col. 0847] “so great” 3.] that, on this account, he was carried to an island by his followers. [Note: [Col. 0847] “followers” 2; “persecutors” 3.] There, after those most wicked beasts had swum across, he was protected in a wooden tower only until, overcome by the pestilential stench of the multitude, abandoned by all, and gnawed by monsters, he expired in a most shameful death.

But let us neglect to recount the deeds of those whose memory the oblivion of antiquity has effaced and whom error and idolatry have defiled. Let us pass them by with this brief naming and proceed to recount those matters which faithful remembrance retains. Siemowit, having attained power, did not spend his youth in pleasure or folly, [Note: [Col. 0847] absent in 2 and 3.] but through experience of labour and warfare he acquired a reputation for virtue and the glory of honour, and extended the borders of his dominion farther than anyone before him. [Note: [Col. 0847] “before that” 3.] Upon his death his son Lestek succeeded him, [Note: [Col. 0847] 3 reads: “Upon his death, his son Lestko succeeded him,” for “In whose place—succeeded.” In the margin, 1 and 2 write: “Concerning Duke Lestek.”] and equalled his father’s virtue and boldness by his military deeds. [Col. 0847C] [Note: [Col. 0847] “equalled” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0848C] Sallust, *Jugurtha*, IV. S.] Lestek, [Note: [Col. 0847] “Lestko” 3.] when he died, was succeeded by his son Siemomysł, [Note: [Col. 0847] “Szemimisl” 3. In the margin 1 and 2 write: “Concerning Duke Zemimysł.”] who increased the memory of his parents threefold in both lineage and [Note: [Col. 0847] absent in 3.] dignity. [Note: [Col. 0847] “multiplied eightfold” 3.]

## 4. Concerning the blindness of Mieszko, son of Duke Siemomysł.

[Note: [Col. 0847] “Mechko” 2; “Mieszko” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0847] “son” in the dative, 1 and 2.] [Note: [Col. 0847] “Siemomysł, etc.” for “Duke Siemomysł,” 3.]

This Siemomysł begot the great and memorable Mieszko, [Note: [Col. 0847] “Meschko” 2; “Mieszko” 3.] who was the first called by that name. [Note: [Col. 0847] “that” 3.] He was blind for seven years from birth. But when the seventh anniversary of his birth came round, the boy’s father, having according to custom summoned an assembly of counts and other princes of his own, [Note: [Col. 0847] absent in 3.] celebrated a lavish and solemn feast. Yet amid the feast, mindful of the boy’s blindness as though of grief and shame, [Col. 0848A] [Note: [Col. 0847] “however” 1 and 3.] [Note: [Col. 0847] “truly every day” 3.] he secretly sighed from the depths of his heart. [Note: [Col. 0847] “one” 2; after this word was cancelled, the corrector supplied *intimo*, “innermost,” in the margin.]

While the others rejoiced and clapped their hands according to custom, one joy heaped upon another, indicating that the blind boy had recovered his sight. [Note: [Col. 0847] We have corrected thus; the manuscripts and editions read “invited.” P.] But the father did not believe anyone who told him this, [Note: [Col. 0847] “that person” 3.] until the mother rose from the feast and entered where the boy was. She cut away the knot [Note: [Col. 0847] “not yet a wound” 3.] of doubt for the father, and, while all remained seated, [Note: [Col. 0847] “standing against” 2.] announced that the boy could see. [Note: [Col. 0847] “presented” 2.] Then indeed all were full of joy, when the boy recognized those whom he had never seen and turned the disgrace of his blindness into inexpressible gladness.

Then Duke Siemomysł carefully asks the older and wiser men present [Note: [Col. 0847] “adhering” 2.] whether some portent was signified by the boy’s blindness and restoration of sight. [Col. 0848B] They replied that through the blindness Poland had formerly been, as it were, blind, but that hereafter it would be enlightened through Mieszko and raised above the neighbouring nations. [Note: [Col. 0847] “prophesied” 2.] This indeed came to pass, although it might also be interpreted otherwise. Truly Poland had formerly been blind, knowing neither the worship of the true God nor the teaching of faith; but through the enlightened Mieszko it too was enlightened, [Note: [Col. 0847] The corrector of 2 erroneously repeats “was.”] because, when he believed, the Polish people were delivered from the death of unbelief. [Note: [Col. 0847] “because” 2.]

For Almighty God, in fitting order, first restored bodily sight to Mieszko and afterwards bestowed spiritual sight as well, [Note: [Col. 0847] 2 adds “and moreover.”] so that through visible things he might penetrate to knowledge of invisible things, and through knowledge of created things might contemplate the omnipotence of their Maker. But [Note: [Col. 0847] 2 has the abbreviation *d’r*, perhaps to be read *dicitur*, “it is said.”] [Col. 0848C] why does the wheel run ahead of the cart? [Note: [Col. 0848C] That is, why does the narrative run ahead of the deeds? P.] [Note: [Col. 0847] Thus emended by P.; 1, 2, and the editions read “runs ahead” without a question mark. “Then indeed—runs ahead” is absent in 3.] Siemomysł, worn out by old age, then bade his final farewell to the world. [Note: [Col. 0847] 3 adds “afterwards.”]

## 5. How Mieszko received Dobrawa as his wife.

[Note: [Col. 0847] “Mescho” 2.] [Note: [Col. 0847] absent in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0847] “How—wife” absent in 3.]

Mieszko, [Note: [Col. 0847] 3 reads: “In the year of the Lord 965, Mieszko,” for “But Mieszko.”] having obtained the dukedom, began to exercise his native ability and bodily strength, [Note: [Col. 0847] absent in 3.] and frequently to attack in war the surrounding peoples. At that time he was still so entangled in the error of paganism [Note: [Col. 0847] “was entangled” 3.] that, in accordance with his custom, he made use of seven wives. [Note: [Col. 0847] Here 1 adds at the foot of the column: “In the year of the Lord 965 he took a wife.”] Finally he sought in marriage a most Christian woman from Bohemia, named Dobrawa. [Note: [Col. 0847] “He sought Dąbrówka by name, daughter of the duke of Bohemia,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0848C] Compare Cosmas, I.26. K.] [Col. 0849A] (A.D. 965). But she refused to marry him unless he abandoned that wicked custom and promised to become a Christian. [Note: [Col. 0849] 3 adds “also.”] Accordingly, when he had pledged [Note: [Col. 0849] “therefore” 3.] that he would renounce the practice [Note: [Col. 0849] “himself” 3.] of that paganism and receive the sacraments of the Christian faith, [Note: [Col. 0849] “but” 3.] the lady entered Poland with a great retinue of secular and ecclesiastical rank. She did not, however, join herself to him in the marriage bed until he had gradually and diligently considered Christian custom and the religion of the ecclesiastical order, renounced the error of the pagans, and united himself to the bosom of Mother Church [Note: [Col. 0849] “joined himself” 1; “himself—united himself” absent in 3.] (A.D. 966).

## 6. Concerning the first Boleslaus, who was called the Glorious, or Chrobry.

[Note: [Col. 0849] “Concerning—Chrobry” absent in 2 and 3.]

Thus Mieszko, the first duke of the Poles, attained the grace of baptism through his faithful wife. For his praise and glory it sufficiently and abundantly avails that, in his time and through him, the Dayspring from on high visited the kingdom of Poland. [Col. 0849B] [Note: [Col. 0849] “He was born in 967” is added in the margin in 1.]

By this blessed woman he begot the glorious Bolesław, [Note: [Col. 0849] “In the year of the Lord 967, from this blessed woman Dąbrówka the glorious duke Bolesław was begotten” replaces “Thus Mieszko … begot” in 3.] who, after his father’s death (25 May 992), [Note: [Col. 0849] “father” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0849C] Cf. Thietmar IV.37 and the Annals of Hildesheim for 992; the Merseburg Calendar gives the date as the fifth day before the Ides of May. See Roepell I.103. K.] governed the kingdom manfully. With God’s favor he grew to such excellence and power that, if I may so speak, by his merit he gilded all Poland. For who could worthily recount his brave deeds or the battles he fought against the surrounding peoples, much less commit them to enduring written record? [Note: [Col. 0849] “could” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0849] *memoralibus* in 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0849] An uncertain siglum for “N. q. n. i.” in 3.] Did he not subdue Moravia and Bohemia, [Note: [Col. 0849] “and Bohemia” added in the margin by corrector 2.] establish himself in the ducal seat at Prague, and assign it to his suffragans? [Note: [Col. 0849C] Cf. Cosmas I.35. K.] (A.D. 1003.) Did he not repeatedly defeat the Hungarians in battle and subject their entire land as far as the Danube to his rule? [Note: [Col. 0849C] On these matters see Roepell I.651. K.] (A.D. 999.) He also subdued the untamed Saxons by such prowess [Note: [Col. 0849] 3 transposes “by such prowess [he subdued] the Saxons” to “the Saxons by such prowess.”] [Note: [Col. 0849C] Unpublished Cracow Annals of Poland. S.] that, in the river Saale, in the midst of their land, he marked the bounds of Poland with an iron boundary-post. [Note: [Col. 0849] “which” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0849C] Cf. Annals of Quedlinburg for 1007, 1012, and 1017. K.]

Why, then, is it necessary to enumerate by name the victories and triumphs over unbelieving peoples, [Note: [Col. 0849] “therefore” in 2 and 3.] [Note: [Col. 0849] *nominali* in 3.] whom he is known to have trampled, as it were, beneath his feet? [Note: [Col. 0849] “it is established” in 3.] Indeed, he so crushed Selencia, Pomerania, and Prussia when they resisted in unbelief, or so firmly established them after their conversion to the faith (A.D. 995), that through the apostolic [pope] he appointed many churches and bishops there—or rather, that the apostolic [pope] appointed them through him. [Note: [Col. 0849] *nucas*, i.e. *magnificas* (“splendid”), in 3.]

He likewise received with great reverence Saint Adalbert, who, during a long pilgrimage and at the hands of his rebellious Bohemian people, had suffered many injuries, when he came to him; and he faithfully obeyed his preaching [Note: [Col. 0849] 3 places *fideliter* before *obedivit*, “obeyed.”] and instructions. But the holy martyr, kindled by the fire of love and zeal for preaching, when he saw that the faith had now begun to sprout somewhat in Poland and that the holy Church had grown, fearlessly entered Prussia and there completed his contest by martyrdom (A.D. 997). [Note: [Col. 0849] *consionavit*, apparently for *consignavit*, “completed/sealed,” in 3.]

Afterward Bolesław purchased his body from the Prussians for its weight in gold [Note: [Col. 0850C] Bruno, *Life of St Adalbert*, ch. 34, and *Miracles of St Adalbert*, ch. 9. S.] and placed it with fitting honor in the metropolitan church of Gniezno. [Note: [Col. 0849] “Gniezno” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0849] “buried” in 3.]

We also judge this worthy of commemoration: [Note: [Col. 0849] “worthy” added in 3.] in his time [Note: [Col. 0849] “namely, in the year of the Lord 1000” added in 3.] the emperor Otto Rufus [Note: [Col. 0850C] Rather, Otto III. K.] came to Saint Adalbert for prayer and reconciliation, and also, attracted by the fame of glorious Bolesław, to make his acquaintance, as may be found more fully in the book concerning the martyr’s passion. [Note: [Col. 0850B] Cf. the preface. K.] Bolesław received him with such honor and magnificence [Note: [Col. 0850C] Cf. Annals of Quedlinburg, 1000. K.] as befitted the reception of a Roman emperor and so great a guest.

For, at the emperor’s arrival, Bolesław displayed marvellous wonders: first, battle-lines of soldiers of many kinds; then, on a broad plain, companies of magnates arranged as if in choirs. [Note: [Col. 0849] 3 reads: “At the emperor’s arrival Bolesław displayed battle-lines. First …” for “For … first …”] Each separate battle-line was distinguished by the varied colors of its clothing. [Note: [Col. 0849] “each also” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0849] “separately” in 3.] Nor was this any cheap variety of adornment. Rather, whatever could be found anywhere among the nations that was most precious was there: in Bolesław’s time all soldiers and all women of the court used mantles in place of linen or woollen garments; nor were hides, however precious and even if new, worn at his court without a mantle [Note: [Col. 0849] *pellio* in 3.] and gold embroidery. In his time gold was held by all as something common, like silver; silver, however, was considered cheap, as though it were straw. [Note: [Col. 0849] “as” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0849] 2 adds “was held,” but subsequently marks it as superfluous with dots.]

When the Roman emperor beheld his glory, power, and wealth, he said in admiration: “By the crown of my empire, what I see is greater than what I received through report.” [Note: [Col. 0849] Omitted in 2.] And, on the counsel of his chief men, he added before all: “It is not fitting that so great a man and such a one [Note: [Col. 0849] “a man and citizen” for “a man and such a one” in 3.] should be called duke or count, like one of the princes; rather, crowned gloriously with the royal diadem, he should be exalted to a royal throne.” [Note: [Col. 0850C] This in fact occurred only in 1025, as the Annals of Quedlinburg prove. Cf. Roepell I.162. K.] (A.D. 1025.)

Taking the imperial diadem from his own head, [Col. 0851A] he placed it upon Bolesław’s head as a pledge of friendship; and, in place of a triumphal banner, [Note: [Col. 0851] *trmphas* in 3.] he gave him as a gift a nail from the Lord’s cross together with the lance of Saint Maurice. In return for these Bolesław gave him the arm of Saint Adalbert. That day they were united in such affection [Note: [Col. 0851] *cog’ti* in 1 and 2; *99’ti* in 3; the author frequently uses *couniti*.] that the emperor made him brother and co-worker of the empire [Note: [Col. 0851] “appointed” in 3.] and called him friend and associate of the Roman people.

Moreover, in ecclesiastical honors [Note: [Col. 0851] “men” in 3.] he granted to his authority and that of his successors whatever belonged to the empire in the kingdom of the Poles, or in other regions of barbarians conquered or yet to be conquered by him; Pope Sylvester confirmed the decree of this compact by a privilege of the holy Roman Church. [Note: [Col. 0851] “King Bolesław lived in the time of Pope Sylvester” added in the margin in 2.]

Thus Bolesław, so gloriously raised to royal rank by the emperor, exercised [Note: [Col. 0851] *exeruit* in 2.] the generosity bestowed upon him. [Col. 0851B] During the three days of his consecration [Note: [Col. 0851] “coronation” in 3.] he held a feast in royal and imperial fashion; each day he changed all the vessels and furnishings, presenting others, different and much more precious. When the banquet had ended, he ordered the cupbearers and stewards to gather all the gold and silver vessels—there were no wooden ones there—namely cups and goblets, dishes and small plates, [Note: [Col. 0851] “dishes” in 2.] and horns, from all the tables of the three days, [Note: [Col. 0851] “to be gathered” in 3.] and presented them to the emperor as a mark of honor, not as the principal gift.

Likewise he ordered the chamberlains to collect the spread cloths and curtains, [Note: [Col. 0851] Omitted in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0851] *cortinias* in 3.] tapestries, coverings, tablecloths, towels, and whatever had been supplied for service, and carry them into the emperor’s chamber. [Note: [Col. 0851] “to be gathered” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0851] “to be carried” in 3.] [Col. 0851C] Moreover, he gave many other vessels—of gold and silver, of varied workmanship—cloths of different colors, [Note: [Col. 0851] Omitted in 3.] ornaments of an unknown kind, precious stones, and so forth; [Note: [Col. 0851] “and so forth” omitted in 3.] and he offered so many and such great gifts that the emperor regarded so great a present as miraculous. He bestowed gifts upon each of the emperor’s princes so magnificently that from friends [Note: [Col. 0851] “of the boundary,” or *limicis*, erroneously in 3.] he gained most devoted friends. [Note: [Col. 0851C] Sallust, *Jugurthine War*, 10. S.]

But who could enumerate what gifts, and how great, he gave to the greater men [Note: [Col. 0851] “nobler men” seems to be written in abbreviation, but without a siglum, in 2.], when not even one inhabitant among so great a multitude departed without a gift? The emperor returned joyfully to his own lands with great gifts; Bolesław, however, reigning, renewed his old wrath against his enemies.

## 7. How Bolesław powerfully entered the land of Rus’

[Note: [Col. 0851] *Rusie* in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0851] The heading “How … entered” is omitted in 3.]

[Col. 0852A]

It must therefore first be inserted into the sequence how gloriously and magnificently he avenged the injury done him by the king of the Ruthenians, [Note: [Col. 0851] “For in the year of the Lord 1018 he fought manfully against the king of the Ruthenians” replaces “It must therefore first … avenged” in 3.] who had refused to give him his sister in marriage. [Note: [Col. 0851C] Bolesław’s daughter had married Sviatopolk, son of Vladimir, prince of Rus’. K.]

King Bolesław took this indignantly and invaded the kingdom of the Ruthenians with great force. Those who first tried to resist with arms, but did not dare to engage, [Note: [Col. 0851] “but [they] did not dare” in 3.] he scattered before his face like dust before the wind. Nor did he delay his march by immediately taking cities in the manner of an enemy or gathering money; rather, he hastened to Chyov [Note: [Col. 0851] *th’yon* in 2; Kyow in 3.] the capital of the kingdom, so that he might seize both the stronghold of the realm and the king (A.D. 1018). [Note: [Col. 0851] Omitted in 3.]

The king of the Ruthenians, [Note: [Col. 0852C] Yaroslav, son of Vladimir. K.] in the simplicity of that people, happened at that time to be fishing with a hook from a small boat, [Note: [Col. 0851] *naviculati* corruptly for *navicula tunc* in 3.] when they unexpectedly announced to him that King Bolesław was at hand. [Note: [Col. 0851] “to whom” in 3.] He could scarcely believe it; but at last, as one messenger after another told him, he was convinced and was terrified.

Then at length, putting his thumb and forefinger together to his mouth, [Note: [Col. 0851] “his own” in 2 and in the fragment of 3, p. 93.] and moistening the hook with spittle in the fishermen’s manner, he is said to have uttered, to the disgrace of his people, this proverb: “Because Bolesław has not applied himself to this skill, but has been accustomed to carry military weapons, [Note: [Col. 0851] *bajolare* in the fragment of 3, p. 93.] God has therefore ordained to deliver into his hand this city, the kingdom of the Ruthenians, and its riches.” So he spoke; and without pursuing the matter further, he took to flight.

But Bolesław, entering the great and wealthy city with no one resisting him, drew his sword and struck the Golden Gate. When his men, in rather jesting astonishment, [Note: [Col. 0851] *ammirantibus* in 3, fragment p. 93.] asked why he had done this, he explained: “As at this hour [Col. 0852C] [Note: [Col. 0851] Omitted in 2.] the Golden Gate of this city is struck by this sword, so on the following night the sister of the most cowardly king—who was forbidden to be given to me—will be violated. [Note: [Col. 0852C] Commonly called Predslava. K.] Yet she will not be joined to Bolesław in a marital bed, but only once in a singular act of concubinage, so that by this deed the injury to our lineage may be avenged and it may be counted to the Ruthenians as disgrace and dishonor.” Thus he spoke, and fulfilled his words by deeds.

King Bolesław therefore held the very rich city [Note: [Col. 0851] “etc.” added in 3, fragment p. 93.] and the most powerful kingdom of the Ruthenians for ten months, never being idle in sending money thence into Poland. In the eleventh month, however, because he held very many kingdoms and did not yet consider the boy Mieszko fit to reign, [Col. 0853A] he appointed in his own place to rule there a certain Ruthenian of his own family [Note: [Col. 0853C] His son-in-law Sviatopolk. K.] and returned to Poland with the remaining treasure.

[Note: [Col. 0853] “the most powerful kingdom of the Ruthenians … returned” is absent from 3 in the fragment, p. 93. In the continuous text, p. 135, from “Then at length he put his thumb …” through “returned,” 3 abbreviates the account as follows: “Then Bolesław entered the great and wealthy city with no one resisting him and struck the Golden Gate with his sword. And when they had gained the most powerful city and kingdom of the Ruthenians, he returned to Poland with great treasure.”]

As he returned with great joy [Note: [Col. 0853] “sword” in 3.] and wealth [Note: [Col. 0853] “to his own lands” for “and wealth” in 3.], already approaching the borders of Poland, [Note: [Col. 0853] “already … approaching” omitted in 3.] the fugitive king followed him from behind, having assembled the forces of the Ruthenian dukes together with the Plauci and Pinciniatiri; [Note: [Col. 0853] “with the Plauci and Pinciniatiri” omitted in 3.] and at the river Bug he tried, confident of victory, to join battle.

For he thought that the Poles, rejoicing after so great a victory in their booty, would each be drawing near to his own home—as victors nearing the borders of their own land, having remained so long abroad without children and wives. Nor did he think this without reason, since a great part of the Polish army had already slipped away without the king’s knowledge. [Note: [Col. 0853] “For he thought … had slipped away” omitted in 3.]

But King Bolesław, seeing that his own soldiers were few and the enemy perhaps a hundred times as numerous, [Note: [Col. 0853] *cencias erat* in 2; a corrector altered *a* to *e*.] [Note: [Col. 0853] “then” in 1 and 2.] addressed his men, not as a coward or timid man, but as one bold and provident: [Note: [Col. 0853C] Sallust, *Catiline*, 18. S.]

“There is no need to exhort for long good and experienced soldiers, nor to delay the triumph that offers itself to us; but it is time to exercise bodily strength and courage of spirit. For what does it profit to have had so many and such great victories before, or what does it profit to have subjected so many kingdoms to our rule and amassed so great riches from others, if it should now happen that we, conquered, lose these things and what is ours? But I trust in God’s mercy and in your proven valor that, if you withstand manfully in battle, if you attack courageously in your accustomed manner, and if you recall the boasts and promises made at my feasts when booty was divided, [Col. 0853C] today you will end your continual labor as victors and, moreover, win enduring renown and a triumphant victory. But if you are defeated—which I do not believe—then, though you are lords, you and your sons will be servants of the Ruthenians, and you will moreover pay most shamefully the penalties for the injuries inflicted.”

While King Bolesław spoke these and similar words, all his soldiers together extended their spears and answered that they preferred to enter their homes with triumph [Col. 0854A] rather than shamefully with booty. [Note: [Col. 0853] 2 transposes “shamefully [enter] their homes.”]

Then King Bolesław, exhorting each of his men by name, [Note: [Col. 0853] 3 abbreviates from “But King Bolesław, seeing his soldiers few …” to: “But King Bolesław, seeing that his soldiers were few and the enemy perhaps a hundred times as numerous, encouraged his men and trusted in God’s mercy.”] charged into the densely massed enemy like a thirsty lion. [Note: [Col. 0853] The Warsaw edition corrects *confortissimos* in the manuscripts to *confertissimos*, “densely massed.”] It is not within our power to recount how great a slaughter he made there of those who resisted him, [Note: [Col. 0853] “there he laid low the enemy” for “how great a slaughter … he made” in 3.] nor can anyone calculate with an exact number the thousands of enemies slain, since they were known to have assembled for battle beyond numbering, and only a few survivors escaped in flight. [Note: [Col. 0853] 3 reads: “to recount how many thousands of slain enemies fell there,” for “the thousands of enemies slain … escaped”; in it the word *enarrare*, “recount,” also appears added by another hand.]

Indeed, many who came after many days from distant regions to the place of battle to find friends or relatives affirmed with certainty that the shedding of blood there had been so great that no one could walk across the whole plain except through blood [Note: [Col. 0853] “blood” in 3.] or over corpses, and that the whole river Bug [Col. 0854B] bore more the appearance of blood than of a river. [Note: [Col. 0853] “the whole” in 3.] From that time Rus’ was tributary to Poland for a long while.

## 8. On the magnificence and power of Bolesław the Glorious

[Note: [Col. 0853] “king” in 3.]

The deeds of Bolesław are more numerous and greater than can be described by us or even recounted in bare words. [Note: [Col. 0853] “already” in 2; omitted in 3.] For what arithmetician [Note: [Col. 0853] *arthimeticus* in 1; *arthimaticus* in 2, where a corrector changed the latter *a* to *t*; *arismeticus* in 3. The Warsaw edition recommends *arithmeticus*.] could calculate with sufficient exactness the number of his armored formations, much less describe and recount the victories and triumphs of so great a multitude?

[Note: [Col. 0853] “On the great population of the cities of Gniezno and Poznań” added in the margin by an old hand in 2.] From Poznań there came 1,300 armored soldiers with 4,000 shield-bearing soldiers; from Gniezno, [Note: [Col. 0853] “Gniezno” in 3.] 1,500 armored men and 5,000 shield-bearers; from the fortress of Władysław, [Note: [Col. 0853] “Władysław” in 3.] 800 armored men and 2,000 shield-bearers; from Gdech, [Note: [Col. 0853] Gdeth may also be read in 2 and 3, because *c* and *t* are not easily distinguished. A later but old hand erased *Gdehc* and wrote Gdańsk in the margin in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0853C] Gdecz, now Giecz, in the greater duchy of Poznań, between Września, Środa, and Kostrzyn. The Bohemians destroyed this fortified town in 1039. Not far from the aforesaid town, Gdecz, one came to the metropolitan city of Gniezno. Cf. Cosmas II.2. S.] 300 armored men and 2,000 shield-bearers. All these, most valiant and highly trained for war, [Note: [Col. 0853] *de … ssimi* in 3.] came forth in the time of the great Bolesław. [Note: [Col. 0853] Omitted in 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0853] “From other” omitted in 1; it was also absent in 2, but supplied in the margin in the same hand.] To recount the forces from other cities and castles [Note: [Col. 0853] “and” omitted in 3.] would be a long and endless labor for us, and perhaps tedious for you to hear. But, to spare you the weariness of counting, I shall set before you a numberless number of the multitude. King Bolesław had more armored soldiers [Col. 0855A] than all Poland in our time has shield-bearing soldiers. [Note: [Col. 0855] “had” was written in 2, but a corrector marked the final *b* as erroneous.] [Note: [Col. 0855] “in comparison with” in 3.] In Bolesław’s time there were almost as many soldiers in Poland as there are in our time people of every sort. [Note: [Col. 0855] 2 and 3 transpose “in Poland almost” to “almost in Poland.”]

## 9. On the virtue and nobility of Bolesław the Glorious

Such was the military magnificence of King Bolesław; [Note: [Col. 0855] Omitted in 3.] nor was the excellence of his spiritual obedience inferior to it. [Note: [Col. 0855] *spal.* in 3.] He held his bishops and chaplains in such reverence that, when they stood present, he did not presume to sit, and he addressed them only as “lords.” He worshipped God with the highest devotion, exalted the holy Church, and adorned it with royal gifts. [Note: [Col. 0855] “worshipped” in 1.]

He also possessed a great quality of justice and a notable humility. If at any time a poor peasant or any little woman complained against any duke [Col. 0855B] or count, [Note: [Col. 0855] Omitted in 3.] then, although he was occupied with great affairs and surrounded by many companies of magnates and soldiers, [Note: [Col. 0855] Omitted in 2.] he did not leave his place until he had heard in order the case of the complainant. He then sent word to the chamberlain concerning the person against whom the complaint was made. Meanwhile he entrusted the complainant himself to one of his faithful men, who would provide for him and state his case when his opponent arrived. Thus he admonished the peasant as a father admonishes a son: he must not accuse an absent person without cause, nor, by making an unjust complaint, heap upon himself the anger that he was stirring up against another.

The accused did not delay in coming when promptly summoned, nor did he evade by any excuse the day fixed by the king. When the prince against whom the summons had been issued arrived, Bolesław did not show himself maliciously [Col. 0855C] [Note: [Col. 0855] “malicious” in 1 and 2.] angered against him. Rather, receiving him with a cheerful and gracious expression, he invited him to table, and investigated the case not that day but on the second or third. Thus he dealt as carefully with a poor man’s affair as with that of some great prince. [Note: [Col. 0855] 3 adds here, “This is the justice and equity of Bolesław,” omitting the remainder of this chapter.]

O Bolesław’s great discernment and great perfection! He showed no respect of persons in judgment; he governed the people with such justice; he maintained the honor of the Church and the condition of the land at the highest level. Bolesław rose to this glory and dignity through justice [Note: [Col. 0855] This appears to be the correct reading in place of *in mirum*.] and equity, [Note: [Col. 0855] From the words “Justice *in mirum* and equity,” a corrector in 2, by adding two words and lines above, made two clauses: “He loved justice in a wonderful manner and equity.”] the virtues through which in the beginning the power and empire of the Romans grew. Almighty God adorned King Bolesław with as much valor, power, and victory as he recognized in him goodness and justice [Col. 0855D] toward God himself and toward human beings; and as much glory, abundance of possessions, and joy attended Bolesław [Col. 0856A] as his worth and generosity deserved.

## 10. [Note: [Col. 0855] 3 prefaces: “Likewise.”] On Bolesław’s battle with the Ruthenians

But let us defer the recollection of these matters to the following page, and recount one of his battles, memorable enough for the novelty of the event, so that by considering this occurrence we may prefer humility to pride. [Note: [Col. 0855] 3 reads, “But let us recount an event worthy of remembrance,” for “But let us defer … memorable.”]

It happened [Note: [Col. 0855] “happens” in 2.] that at one and the same time King Bolesław entered Rus’, and the king of the Ruthenians entered Poland, each hostile toward the other and neither knowing of the other. They established military camps facing one another on a river lying between them, in the territory of the other’s land. When it was reported to the king of the Ruthenians that Bolesław had already crossed beyond the river and settled with his army on the border of his kingdom, [Note: [Col. 0855] *confinie* in 3.] the foolish king, thinking that he had enclosed him like a wild beast in nets with his multitude, is said to have sent him a saying of great pride, which would be turned back upon his own head: “Let Bolesław know that, like a boar in a wallow, he is hemmed in by my dogs and hunters.”

The Polish king replied: “Good: you have called me a boar in a wallow, because I shall stain the feet of my horses in the blood [Note: [Col. 0855] “blood” in 2.] of your hunters and dogs—that is, of your dukes and soldiers [Note: [Col. 0855] “your” in 3.]—and, like a solitary wild beast, [Note: [Col. 0855] “wild beasts in the plural” in 3.] I shall devour your land and cities.” [Note: [Col. 0855] The editor emends *cum*, “with,” in 1, 2, and 3, to *ceu*, “like.”]

After these words had been exchanged, [Note: [Col. 0855] “true words,” incorrectly, in 1.] a feast-day was imminent on the following day. [Note: [Col. 0855] 3: “A feast was imminent, which …”] Bolesław, intending to celebrate it, [Note: [Col. 0855] “those who were intending to celebrate” in 2.] put off engaging in battle until a fixed day. [Note: [Col. 0855] “the third day” in 3; 2 repeats “until a fixed day.”] For on that day countless animals were slaughtered, to be prepared in the customary manner for the king’s table on the ensuing feast, when he and all his princes would dine. [Col. 0856C] [Note: [Col. 0855] “for eating” in 3.]

Accordingly, all the cooks, household servants, attendants, [Note: [Col. 0855] singular *apparitor* in 2.] and camp parasites were gathered on the riverbank to clean the flesh and entrails of the animals. From the opposite bank the Ruthenian retainers and armed servants taunted them with loud cries, provoking them to anger with disgraceful insults. The Poles answered no insult in return, but threw the filth and useless parts of entrails before their eyes as an insult. [Note: [Col. 0855] “threw forth” in 3.]

When the Ruthenians incited them with ever more insults and attacked them more fiercely with arrows, Bolesław’s camp servants, abandoning the dogs [Note: [Col. 0855] “all,” in 2; a corrector wrote “dogs” in the margin, deleting “all.”] which [Note: [Col. 0855] The editor corrects *que* (“which”) in the manuscripts and editions to *quos* (“whom”).] they held and the birds, [Note: [Col. 0855] The editors emend *comissis* in the manuscripts and editions to *omissis*, “having abandoned.”] crossed the river swimming, with the weapons of the soldiers who were sleeping at midday [Note: [Col. 0855] “at midday” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0855D] That is, at the hour. P.] and triumphed over so great a multitude of Ruthenians. [Col. 0856D] [Note: [Col. 0856D] That is, boys or servants. P.]

King Bolesław [Col. 0857A] and the whole army, roused together by the shouting and clatter of weapons, [Note: [Col. 0857] “army” in 2.] asked what this might be. Learning the reason, and suspecting that the action had been done by design, [Note: [Col. 0857] 2 suggests *factam*, “done,” instead of *facta*; omitted in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0857] “thinking” in 3.] they fell upon the enemy as they fled on every side with their battle-lines marshalled. Thus the camp servants alone did not have either the glory of victory or the guilt for the bloodshed. [Note: [Col. 0857] “blood,” incorrectly, in 1 and 2.]

The multitude of soldiers crossing the river was so great [Note: [Col. 0857] Omitted in 1, 2, and 3; added by the Gdańsk edition.] that those below could not see water, but rather a kind of dry roadway. Let this small account of his wars suffice, so that the recollection of his life, imitated by hearers, may be fruitful. [Note: [Col. 0857] *prof.* in 3.]

## 11. On the organization of churches in Poland and Bolesław’s virtue

[Note: [Col. 0857] “equity” in 3.]

King Bolesław was so devoted to divine worship [Note: [Col. 0857] “toward divine worship” omitted in 3.] in constructing churches, appointing bishoprics, and conferring benefices [Col. 0857B] that in his time Poland contained two metropolitans with their suffragans. He was in every way and in all things so benevolent and obedient toward them that, if any of the princes began a lawsuit against any cleric or bishop [Note: [Col. 0857] “against any of the princes” for “if any of the princes against” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0857] *quelibet* in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0857] “friends and priests” for “clerics and bishops” in 3.], or if anyone appropriated anything from ecclesiastical property, he commanded silence from everyone by a gesture of his hand and, as patron and advocate of the bishops, defended the case of the Church.

The barbarian peoples around him whom he conquered he compelled not to pay a money tribute, but to promote true religion. Moreover, he built churches there from his own resources [Note: [Col. 0857] “built” in the plural in 3.] and honorably established bishops and canonically established clergy among the unbelievers with the necessary resources. [Col. 0857C] [Note: [Col. 0857] “he was appointing the same persons” for “he established them” in 3.]

By such virtues—justice and equity, namely fear [Note: [Col. 0857] “namely” in 3.] and love—King Bolesław excelled, and with such discernment administered the kingdom and commonwealth. Bolesław shone far and wide in many virtues and worthy qualities; yet it was especially through three virtues—justice, equity, and piety—that he rose to so high a summit of greatness. Through justice, because he decided cases in judgment without respect of persons; through equity, because he loved princes and people with discernment; through piety, because he honored Christ and his bride in every way.

And because he practiced justice, loved all persons [Note: [Col. 0857] “all things” in 3.] impartially, and exalted mother Church and ecclesiastical men, [Col. 0857D] the Lord exalted his horn in glory through the prayers of holy mother Church and the intercessions of her prelates [Col. 0858A] (Psalm 88:25), and he always advanced well and prosperously in all things. And although Bolesław was thus devout in divine matters, he nevertheless appeared very glorious in worldly affairs.

## 12. How Bolesław travelled through his lands without injury to the poor

For in his time not only counts but also all nobles wore gold torcs of immense weight, [Note: [Col. 0857] *bajulabant* in 3.] so abundant were they in superfluous wealth. Women of the court proceeded so laden with golden crowns, necklaces, little collars, [Note: [Col. 0857] The word has been corrected, and its reading is uncertain, in 2.] armlets, gold embroidery, and gems that, unless supported by others, they could not bear the weight of the metal.

God had also bestowed such favor upon him, [Col. 0858B] and he was so desirable in the sight of all, that if he removed anyone from his presence for a moment because of a venial offence, [Note: [Col. 0857] “and momentary” in 3.] even though that person possessed his property and personal freedom, he considered himself not alive but dead, and not free but thrust into prison, until he was restored to Bolesław’s favor and presence. [Note: [Col. 0857] “and” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0857] “himself” in 3.]

Nor did he constrain his peasants as a lord to forced labor; rather, as a kindly father, he allowed them to live in peace. [Note: [Col. 0857] “and his” for “moreover his” in 3.] Where he had his fixed stations and service, [Note: [Col. 0857] *determinari*, “to be fixed,” in 1; 2 originally had the same, but a corrector changed the final *i* to *um*.] he did not willingly dwell in tents like a Numidian [Note: [Col. 0857] “at home” in 3.] or in the fields, but frequently in cities and fortified places. [Note: [Col. 0857] “or in” in 3.]

Whenever he moved his station from one city to another, leaving some persons on the border, he changed others, the *vastandiones* and estate-stewards. [Note: [Col. 0857] “changed” in 3.] And as he passed, no traveller [Col. 0858C] or laborer hid oxen or sheep; [Note: [Col. 0857] “and” in 3.] rather, poor and rich alike smiled upon him as he passed, [Note: [Col. 0857] “or” in 2.] and the whole country hastened to see him. [Note: [Col. 0857] *proberabat* in 2.]

## 13. On the virtue and piety of Bolesław the Glorious’s wife

[Note: [Col. 0857] The heading “On the virtue … the Glorious” is omitted in 3.]

He loved his commanders, companions, and princes as though they were brothers or sons, and, without detriment to due reverence, honoured them as a wise lord should. He did not rashly believe those who complained against them; he tempered with mercy the judgment against those condemned by law. [Note: [Col. 0857] MS 2 reads *illos*, “them.” [Col. 0857D] P.: *contra*, “against,” i.e. *erga*, “toward.” [Col. 0857] MSS 1–3 read *legem*, “law” (accusative); the Warsaw edition recommends reading *lege*, “by law”; MS 3 adds *cum*, “with.” [Col. 0857D] “Those condemned contrary to law, when he understood this, he released.” *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, Stenzel, I, 52. Cf. *Life of St Ladislaus* in Endlicher, *Rerum Hungaricarum monumenta Arpadiana*, I, 238. S.]

For his queen, a prudent and discerning woman, often snatched many persons condemned to death for offences from the executioners’ hands and freed them from imminent peril of death. She mercifully kept them alive in prison, sometimes without the king’s knowledge and sometimes while he deliberately overlooked it. [Note: [Col. 0858D] Bolesław took four wives; the last was Oda, daughter of Ekkehard, margrave of Meissen. K.]

The king had twelve friends as counsellors, with whom, together with their wives, he often enjoyed dining and feasting, free from cares and deliberations; and with them he discussed, more intimately, the mysteries of the kingdom and of counsel. [Col. 0859A] [Note: [Col. 0859] MS 2 reads *consiliatores*, “advisers,” but the corrector changed it to *consiliarios*, “counsellors.” MS 3 reads *et eorum*, “and their,” instead of *eorumque*, “and their.” It also reads “with all cares and counsels settled” instead of “free from cares and deliberations.”]

While they were feasting and rejoicing together, the memory of those condemned men happened to arise among other conversations, perhaps through some mention of their family. King Bolesław grieved, in his goodness of heart, at their deaths for the sake of their parents, and regretted having ordered them killed. Then the venerable queen, gently stroking the king’s pious breast with her hand, asked him whether it would please him if some saint perhaps raised them from death. The king replied that he possessed nothing so precious that he would not give it if anyone could recall them from death to life and free their descendants from the stain of disgrace. [Note: [Col. 0859] MS 2 reads *permittebat*, “allowed,” for *poenitebat*, “regretted.” MS 3 omits *blanda*, “gently,” *forsitan*, “perhaps,” and *tam*, “so.”]

Hearing this, the wise and faithful queen accused herself as guilty of, and privy to, a pious theft; and, with the twelve friends and their wives, she threw herself at the king’s feet to seek pardon for herself and for the condemned men. The king kindly embraced her, raised her from the ground with a kiss and with his hands, and praised her faithful theft—indeed, her work of mercy. [Col. 0859B] [Note: [Col. 0859] MS 2 reads *eciam erat*, “and indeed was,” but the corrector deleted *eciam*, “indeed,” and wrote *cum*, “with,” above it. MS 3 reads *commendabat*, “commended,” for *collaudabat*, “praised.”]

Accordingly, that very hour he sent numerous horses for those captives whom, through the woman’s prudence, he had preserved alive, setting a deadline for the messengers’ return. Their joy increased manifold as they sat there, since the queen so wisely maintained the king’s honour and the kingdom’s advantage, and the king heard her petitions with the counsel of his friends.

Those for whom the messengers had been sent, when they arrived, were presented not immediately to the king but to the queen. Having been reproved by her with harsh and gentle words, they were brought to the king’s bath. King Bolesław corrected them as a father corrects sons while they bathed with him, and praised their lineage by recalling it:

> “You, sprung from so great and such a family, ought not to have committed such deeds.”

He rebuked those more advanced in age only with words, both personally and through others; but upon the younger he inflicted blows together with words. Thus, after fatherly admonition, he adorned them with royal garments and, granting gifts and conferring honours, dismissed them to go home rejoicing. Such was King Bolesław’s conduct toward the people and the princes; in this way he wisely caused all his subjects both to fear and to love him. [Col. 0859C–D] [Note: [Col. 0859] MS 3 reads *levibus*, “light,” for *lenibus*, “gentle.” MS 2 reads *moribus*, “customs,” for *minoribus*, “younger.” MS 3 omits *in*, “upon,” and reads *subjectis*, “subjects.”]

## 14. On the splendour of Bolesław’s table and his generosity

[Col. 0860A]

He maintained his table so methodically and so honourably that every day, apart from lesser tables, he had forty principal tables set up; yet he spent nothing in all this from others’ resources, but from his own. He also had fowlers and hunters from almost every nation, who by their arts caught every kind of bird and wild beast; and daily, from every individual species, both four-footed and winged, a separate dish was placed upon his tables. [Note: [Col. 0859] MS 3 omits *privato*, “on an ordinary day,” and *cottidie*, “daily.” MS 2 has an unclear marginal reading, *tn*.]

## 15. On Bolesław’s ordering of the castles and cities of his realm

The great Bolesław was also often occupied in preserving the frontiers of his lands from enemies. When his stewards and viceregents asked what was to be done concerning garments prepared for the annual festivals, and concerning food and drink in each city, he would cite a proverb as an example for posterity, saying:

> “It is more fitting and more honourable for me to preserve a chicken here from enemies than, while I feast idly in this or that city, to give my hostile enemies an opportunity to attack me. For to lose a chicken, through valour, I do not count as losing a chicken, but as losing a castle or a city.”

[Col. 0860B] [Note: [Col. 0859D] That is, occupied in preserving the frontiers from enemies. K. [Col. 0859] MS 3 reads *obser­vandis*, “to be preserved,” for *conservandis*, “to be conserved.” It also reads *animalibus*, “animals,” for *annualibus*, “annual.”]

He then summoned such members of his household as he wished and assigned them one by one to individual cities or castles, so that in his place they might celebrate feasts for the castle-dwellers and townspeople and present his faithful men with garments and other royal gifts which the king customarily gave. [Col. 0860C] [Note: [Col. 0859] MS 3 reads *praeferebat*, “appointed before,” for *deputabat*, “assigned.” It reads *prepararent*, “prepared,” for *celebrarent*, “celebrated.” MS 2 has *indomita*, “untamed things,” for *indumenta*, “garments.”]

At such words and deeds all marvelled at the prudence and intelligence of so great a man, saying among themselves:

> “This man is truly the father of his country, its defender, its lord—not a squanderer of another’s money but an honourable administrator of the commonwealth. He regards the loss violently inflicted by enemies upon a peasant as comparable to the loss of a castle or city.” [Note: [Col. 0859] MS 2 reverses the order, reading “intelligence and prudence” for “prudence and intelligence.” MS 3 omits “this man is its lord.”]

Why prolong the matter? If we wished to write down piecemeal every memorable deed or saying of the great Bolesław, it would be as though we laboured with a pen to dry up the sea drop by drop. Yet what harm is there in idle readers hearing what scarcely can be discovered by a historian except with labour? [Note: [Col. 0859] MS 2 reads *vir*, “man,” incorrectly for *vix*, “scarcely.”]

## 16. On the lamentable death of Bolesław the Glorious

[Col. 0860D] [Note: [Col. 0859] MS 2 reads *lauli*, apparently an error, for *lamentabili*, “lamentable.” MS 3 omits the entire title.]

Although, as has been said, King Bolesław surpassed every other king in such and so great riches and worthy soldiers, he nevertheless always complained that he lacked only soldiers. Whatever worthy guest proved himself in military service at his court was called not a soldier but the king’s son. If at any time he heard, as often happens, that one of them had suffered misfortune with horses or in other matters, he would lavish endless gifts upon him, jesting with those standing by:

> “If I could rescue this worthy soldier from death with riches as I can overcome his misfortune and poverty with my abundance, I would load greedy death itself with riches, in order to preserve this flower so bold in war.”

[Col. 0861A] [Note: [Col. 0861] MS 2 reads *honorarem*, “I would honour,” for *onerarem*, “I would burden.” MS 3 reads *onerarem*, “I would burden,” and MS 1–2 read *talem*, “such a one,” for *hunc florem*, “this flower.”]

Therefore his successors ought to imitate such a great man in his virtues, that they may be raised to such glory and power. Whoever desires after death to acquire such fame, let him acquire while living so great a palm of victory in virtues. If anyone seeks to be compared with Bolesław in the title of remembrance, let him strive to make his own life conform to that venerable life. Then virtue in military exploits will deserve praise, when a soldier’s life has been adorned with honourable morals. This was the memorable glory of great Bolesław; such virtue should be recounted for later generations to imitate. [Col. 0861B] [Note: [Col. 0861] MS 3 adds *ut*, “so that,” before *recitetur*, “may be recounted,” and reads *recitatur*, “is recounted.” MS 2 reads *vita*, “life,” for *militis*, “of a soldier.” MS 3 corruptly reads *gestis est collauda*, apparently “deeds are praised,” for *in gestis militaribus collaudanda*, “to be praised in military exploits.”]

For God did not heap grace upon grace on him in vain, nor did He without cause set him above so many kings and dukes; but because he loved God in all things and above all things, and because he overflowed with the affections of charity toward his own people as a father toward his children. Therefore all, but especially the bishops, archbishops, abbots, monks, and clerics whom he reverenced, diligently commended him to the Lord in their prayers; while dukes, counts, and other nobles prayed that this ever-victorious man might remain alive among them. [Col. 0861C] [Note: [Col. 0861] MS 2 adds *et*, “and,” before *archiepiscopi*, “archbishops.” MS 3 reverses the order, reading “archbishops and bishops,” and has *presbyteri*, “priests,” for *clerici*, “clerics.”]

Thus the glorious Bolesław, bringing a happy life to a praiseworthy end, knew that he must fulfil the debt owed by all flesh. He therefore gathered around him from every side all his princes and friends, made private arrangements concerning the governance and condition of the kingdom, and prophetically announced to them that many evils would come after him:

> “Would that, my brothers, whom I have tenderly nourished as a mother nourishes her sons, the things that I see about to be born while I am set in the contest might turn out prosperously for you; and would that those who kindle the fire of sedition might fear God and man! Alas, alas! Already, as through a mirror in an enigma, I see the royal lineage exiled and wandering, and mercifully supplicating those enemies whom I trampled underfoot.
>
> “I also see from afar, proceeding from my loins, something shining like a carbuncle; joined to the hilt of my sword, it makes all Poland radiant with its brightness.”

[Col. 0862A] [Note: [Col. 0861] MS 2 reads *noscitura*, “about to know,” for *nascitura*, “about to be born.” It also reads *tuti namque*, apparently “securely, indeed,” for *utinamque*, “would that.” MS 3 has *sediciones accedentes*, “approaching seditions,” for *seditionis accendentes*, “kindling sedition”; and *homines*, “men,” for *hominem*, “man.” MS 3 reads *regem talem*, “such a king,” for *regalem prosapiam*, “the royal lineage.” It reads *exultantem*, “exulting,” for *exulantem*, “exiled.” [Col. 0861C] Paprocki, *Herby rycerstwa polskiego*, perhaps from another manuscript, gives this speech somewhat differently: “I see the kingdom being vainly divided into many and various parts,” etc. If this could be understood of the division of the kingdom among Bolesław’s sons reported by Thietmar, it would be evidence of great importance. S.]

Then grief and sorrow pierced the inmost hearts of those standing by and hearing this, and overwhelming pain seized the minds of all with violent stupefaction. After they had for a while restrained their grief, they asked Bolesław how long they should observe his funeral in mourning dress and habit. He answered truthfully:

> “I set you no limit of grief in months or years. Rather, whoever knew me and obtained my favour will mourn me daily in remembrance of me. And not only those who knew me and enjoyed my goodwill will mourn me, but their sons and their sons’ sons also will grieve when others tell of the death of King Bolesław.”

[Col. 0862B] [Note: [Col. 0861] The wording of MS 1–3 is uncertain at the beginning of the sentence: *Cumque paulisper dolore compresso* may be read “when, after grief had been restrained for a little while.” MS 3 adds *nocteque*, “and at night,” after *die cottidie*, “daily,” and omits the clause *me plorabunt*, “will mourn me.”]

When King Bolesław departed from earthly life, the golden age was changed into an age of lead. Poland, once a queen crowned with gleaming gold and gems, sits in the dust, clothed in the garments of widowhood; the lyre is turned to lamentation, applause to mourning, the organ to sighs.
