In that whole ensuing year no one in Poland publicly held a feast; no noble man or woman adorned himself or herself in ceremonial garments; no applause and no sound of lyre was heard in taverns, no maiden’s song and no voice of joy echoed in the streets. [Col. 0862C] [Note: [Col. 0861] MS 1 has *aureas*, “golden,” for *aurea*, “golden”; MS 2 reads *plumbeas*, “leaden,” agreeing with a plural form. MS 2–3 read *sedens*, “sitting,” for *sedet*, “sits.” MS 1–3 read *pallium*, “cloak,” for *plausus*, “applause”; the edition of Gediminas prints *plausus*. MS 3 reads *gaudium*, “joy,” for *organum*, “organ.” MS 3 reads *audiebatur*, “was heard,” for *resonabat*, “resounded.” Cf. *Life of St Ladislaus*, ed. Endlicher, I, 241. S.]

This was observed universally by all for a year; but for noble men and women, mourning for Bolesław ended only with the end of their lives. When King Bolesław passed away from among men, peace, joy, and abundance of things seemed to have departed Poland with him. Let us here set a boundary to the praises of the great Bolesław, and lament his death for a little while in a mournful song.

## Verses on the death of Bolesław

Every age, every sex, every rank—run!

Behold with grief the funeral of King Bolesław,

And mourn with me the death of so great a man!

Alas, alas, Bolesław, where is your glory?

Where is your valour, where your splendour, where your abundance of riches?

[Col. 0863A]

Enough remains to be wept for—woe to me, Poland!

Support me as I fall from grief, companions;

Bereaved soldiers, I pray you, grieve with me;

Desolate guests, answer: “Alas for us!”

How great was the pain, how great the mourning among the bishops!

No strength, no feeling, no mind remained in the dukes.

Alas, alas for the chaplains; alas for all themselves!

You who wore torques as a sign of military service,

And you who changed royal garments daily,

All together cry out: “Woe, woe to us today!”

You matrons, who wore golden crowns,

And whose garments were wholly woven with gold,

Strip yourselves of these and put on mournful woollen clothing.

Alas, alas, Bolesław, why do you forsake us, father?

Why, O God, have you ever permitted such a man to die?

[Col. 0863B]

Why did you not first grant us all one death together?

The whole land is desolated, widowed of such a king,

Like a house left empty after its possessor is gone;

At your death it mourns, grieves, reels, and is uncertain. [Note: [Col. 0863] MS 1–2 read *mutans*, “changing,” for *nutans*, “reeling.”]

Every human being, remember with me the funeral of so great a man:

Rich and poor, soldier and clergy, and likewise farmers,

All you inhabitants, Latins and Slavs alike! [Note: [Col. 0863] MS 3 reads *Sclavorum*, “of the Slavs,” for *Slavorum*. [Col. 0863C] This distinguishes the Poles of the Western and Eastern Churches. S.]

And you, reader of good disposition, whoever you are who read this,

I pray that, moved by compassion, you will shed tears;

You will be most inhuman unless you weep with me. [Note: [Col. 0863] MS 3 omits *haec*, “this,” and reads *quidque*, “whatever,” for *quicumque*, “whoever.” It reads *si non*, “if not,” for *nisi*, “unless.”]

## 17. On the succession of Mieszko II, son of Bolesław the Glorious

[Col. 0863C] [Note: [Col. 0863] MS 2 reads “son of Bolesław” instead of *Bolezlaydes Gloriosi*, “of the Bolesławid the Glorious.” MS 3 omits the entire title.]

After the great Bolesław departed from the world, his son Mieszko II succeeded to the kingdom. During his father’s lifetime he had married the sister of Emperor Otto III, and by her had begotten Casimir—that is, Charles—the restorer of Poland. [Note: [Col. 0863C] Richeza, daughter of Ezzo, count palatine of the Rhine, by Mechthild, sister of Otto III. S. Cf. the *Foundation of Brauweiler*. K. See also *Miracles of St Adalbert*, chapter 9. S. [Col. 0863] MS 2 reads *procrearet*, “might beget,” for *procrearat*, “had begotten.”]

This Mieszko was a worthy soldier and performed many military deeds too numerous to relate. Yet because of his father’s unpopularity, he was hated by all his neighbours, and, unlike his father, was not abundant in life, morals, or wealth. [Note: [Col. 0863] MS 2 has a marginal addition, *MXXV*, “1025,” perhaps by the original or an early hand.]

It is also said that he was taken by treachery at a conference by the Bohemians and, lest he should be able to beget children, was bound tightly at the genitals with thongs, because his father King Bolesław had inflicted a similar injury upon them in 1003, when he blinded their duke, his own uncle. [Col. 0864A] [Note: [Col. 0863] MS 2 reads *faceret*, “might do,” for *fecerat*, “had done”; MS 3 reads *fecit*, “did.” MS 3 reads *Bohemis*, “Bohemians,” for *Bohemicis*, “Bohemian.” [Col. 0863C] The duke was Bolesław III the Red, in 1003; Cosmas, I, 34. Nothing about Mieszko’s captivity is found in other writers. K.]

He did indeed emerge from captivity, but did not thereafter know his wife. But let us be silent concerning Mieszko and turn to Casimir, the restorer of Poland. [Note: [Col. 0863] MS 3 omits *sed*, “but.” It adds: “For Mieszko, as is read elsewhere, fell into madness and died in the same year as his father.”]

## 18. On Casimir’s succession and expulsion after his father’s death

**(A.D. 1034.)** When Mieszko died—having lived only a short time after the death of King Bolesław—Casimir remained a very young boy with his imperial mother. [Col. 0864C] [Note: Cf. the *Annals of Hildesheim*, 1034. K. [Col. 0863] MS 3 reads *patris*, “of his father,” for *regis*, “of the king.” It reverses the order of *remansit parvulus*, “remained a little boy.”]

While she freely reared her son and governed the kingdom honourably as a woman might, traitors expelled her from the kingdom out of envy, while retaining her boy with them in the kingdom as a kind of screen for their deception. [Col. 0864B] [Note: [Col. 0863] MS 3 reads *licet puerum*, “although a boy,” for *libere filium*, “her son freely.” [Col. 0864C] The monk of Brauweiler narrates this affair very differently. See Roepell, I, 662, on Richeza. K.]

When he had reached adulthood and begun to reign, the malicious faction, fearing that he would avenge his mother’s injury, rose against him and forced him to withdraw to Hungary. At that time St Stephen ruled Hungary and was then for the first time converting it to the faith by threats and persuasions. He maintained peace and friendship with the Bohemians, the bitterest enemies of the Poles, and, while he lived, did not graciously allow Casimir to go free. [Note: [Col. 0863] MS 3 reads *Bohemis*, “Bohemians,” for *Bohemicis*, “Bohemian.” It reads *blanditus*, “having used persuasion,” for *blanditiis*, “persuasions.” It also reads *pro*, “for,” instead of *tunc primum*, “then for the first time.”]

After Stephen’s departure from this life in 1038, Peter the Venetian received the kingdom of Hungary. He began the church of St Peter at Bazoar [Borsod, in Borsod County], which no king has completed, down to the present day, on the scale on which it was begun. [Note: [Col. 0863] MS 3 reads *Bazcario*, “Bazcario,” for *Bazoario*. [Col. 0864C] Borsod in Borsod County. S. MS 3 omits *nullus rex*, “no king.”]

When the Bohemians asked Peter not to let Casimir go if he wished to maintain the friendship received from his predecessors, he is said to have answered in kingly fashion:

> “If ancient law has determined that the king of the Hungarians is to be the jailer of the duke of the Bohemians, I shall do what you request.”

So he replied indignantly to the Bohemian embassy, taking little account of their friendship or hostility; and he honourably dismissed Casimir, furnishing him with one hundred horses, an equal number of soldiers who had followed him, arms, and clothing. Nor did he forbid him to go wherever he wished. [Note: [Col. 0863] MS 3 reads *Bohemorum*, “of the Bohemians,” for *Bohemicorum*.]

Casimir gratefully set out on his journey and hastened into the land of the Germans. He stayed, I do not know how long, with his mother and the emperor Henry III; but in military action he proved himself an exceptionally bold soldier. [Col. 0865A] [Note: [Col. 0863] MS 3 reads *igitur*, “therefore,” for *vero*, “however.” MS 2–3 read *terram*, “land,” for *regionem*, “region.” MS 2–3 spell *Theutunicorum*, “of the Germans,” for *Theutonicorum*. [Col. 0865C] The emperor was Henry III. K. MS 3 reads *fuerat*, “had been,” for *extitit*, “proved himself.”]

Let us allow him to rest a little with his mother, and return to the desolation and devastation of Poland. [Col. 0865A] [Note: [Col. 0865] MS 3 inserts here chapter 10, taken from the *Life of St Stanislaus*.]

## 19. On the restoration of the kingdom of Poland by Casimir, who was a monk

[Note: [Col. 0865C] Although “who was a monk” is expressly found in the manuscripts, we judge with Bandtke that these words are a later addition, both because the narrative of this chapter proves it and because the author, who calls Casimir a learned man, would not have passed over his monastic life in the text. S. Cf. Roepell, I, 180. K.]

Meanwhile, the kings and dukes all around were trampling Poland from their respective sides, each either annexing to his own dominion the neighbouring cities and castles or levelling them to the ground by conquest. And while Poland suffered such injury and calamity from foreigners, it was still more absurdly and abominably harassed by its own inhabitants. For servants rose up as lords against their masters, and freedmen against nobles; they raised themselves to dominion, held some in servitude in a reversal of roles, killed others, and wickedly seized their wives in incest and their dignities with utter criminality. [Col. 0865B]

Moreover, departing from the Catholic faith—something we cannot say without tearful speech—they began a sedition against God’s bishops and priests. Some they killed with the sword as though they were more worthy of such a death; others, as though deserving a baser death, they crushed beneath stones. At last Poland was reduced to such desolation by foreigners and natives alike that it was almost wholly stripped of wealth and people in A.D. 1039. At that time the Bohemians destroyed Gniezno and Poznań and carried off the body of St Adalbert. [Col. 0865C] [Note: [Col. 0865] MS 3 reads *dignos*, “worthy,” for *dignius*, “more worthily.” It omits *non*, “not,” and *viliori*, “baser.” It also reads *indignis*, “unworthy,” for *indigenis*, “native.” MS 3 places *vero*, “indeed,” before *tam*, “so,” where the text has *autem*. [Col. 0866C] Cf. Cosmas, II, 2. K.]

Those who escaped from the hands of enemies, or avoided the sedition of their own people, fled beyond the River Vistula into Mazovia. The aforesaid cities remained desolate for so long that wild beasts made their dens in the church of St Adalbert the martyr and St Peter the apostle. It is believed that this calamity befell the whole land in common because Gaudentius, St Adalbert’s brother and successor, for some reason unknown to me, is said to have struck it with an anathema.

Let this much be sufficient concerning Poland’s destruction; may it serve as a correction to those who did not keep faith with their natural lords. [Col. 0866A]

Casimir, then, having spent some time among the Germans and won there great renown for military glory, decided to return to Poland and secretly informed his mother of it. His mother tried to dissuade him from returning to a faithless people not yet thoroughly Christian, urging him instead to possess peacefully his maternal inheritance. The emperor likewise asked him to remain with him and wished to give him a very splendid duchy. But Casimir, as a free man, answered proverbially:

> “No inheritance of uncles or maternal inheritance will be possessed more justly or honourably than a paternal inheritance.”

[Col. 0866A] [Note: [Col. 0866C] The uncles were Archbishop Hermann of Cologne and Otto, duke of Swabia, brothers of Richeza. K. [Col. 0865] MS 3 omits the passage from *Kazimirus ergo* through *paterna*, “Casimir, then … paternal inheritance.”]

He took with him five hundred soldiers and entered the borders of Poland. [Col. 0866C] [Note: [Col. 0865] MS 3 reads *sexcentis*, “six hundred,” for *500*, “five hundred.” Cf. the *Saxon Annalist*, 1039. K.]

Advancing farther, he gained a certain castle which his own people surrendered to him. From it he gradually freed, by valour and intelligence, all Poland, occupied by the Pomeranians, Bohemians, and other neighbouring peoples, and brought it under his dominion. [Col. 0866B] [Note: [Col. 0865] MSS 1–2 omit the words corresponding to “by conquering, he levelled them to the ground.” MS 3 reads *tam virtute quam ingenio*, “by valour as well as intelligence,” for *virtute cum ingenio*, “by valour with intelligence.” It reads *Pomonis*, apparently an error, for *Pomoranis*, “Pomeranians”; and *Bohemis*, “Bohemians,” for *Bohemicis*. It also reads *finitimis nationibus*, “neighbouring nations,” for *finitivis gentibus*, “neighbouring peoples.” [Col. 0866C] Cf. the *Saxon Annalist*, 1039. K.]

Later he took as wife a noblewoman from Rus’, with great wealth—Dobroniega, sister of Prince Yaroslav—and by her begot four sons and one daughter, betrothed to the king of Bohemia. [Col. 0866C] [Note: [Col. 0865] The word *uxorem*, “wife,” was supplied in the margin by the corrector of MS 2. MS 3 reads *uxorem* in the text. Dobroniega, sister of Prince Yaroslav. K.]

The names of his sons were Bolesław, Władysław, Mieszko, and Otto. [Note: [Col. 0865] MS 3 reads *Meszco*, “Mieszko,” for *Mescho*.]

But let us conclude by treating first of what Casimir did, and afterwards set forth in better order which of his sons ruled first and which later. [Col. 0866C] [Note: [Col. 0865] MS 3 reads *primitus*, “first,” for *prius*, “earlier”; *quis vero*, “which indeed,” for *quisve*, “which”; and *regnavit*, “ruled,” for *regnaverit*, “will have ruled.” MS 2 reads *educamus*, “let us educate,” for *edicamus*, “let us set forth.”]

## 20. On the battle of Count Miecław with the Mazovians

After the fatherland had thus been liberated and won back, and the foreign peoples driven out, no less a task remained for Casimir: the expulsion of the hostile members of his own people, his subjects by hereditary right. There was a man named Miecław, cupbearer and servant of Casimir’s father Mieszko; after Mieszko’s death, by his own persuasion, he became leader and standard-bearer of the Mazovian people. [Col. 0866C] [Note: [Col. 0865] The title is corrupt in MS 2, which reads *Mesth Metzzslaus*; the first form is marked as erroneous.]

At that time Mazovia, owing to the Poles who had earlier fled there, as has been said, had become so populous that its fields were spacious for cultivators, its pastures for animals, and its places for inhabitants. [Col. 0866C] [Note: [Col. 0865] MS 2 reads *ante ea*, “before that,” for *antea*, “earlier.” MS 3 omits *ut dictum*, “as has been said.”]

Miecław, confident in the boldness of his soldiery—or rather blinded by the ambition of ruinous greed—strove by presumptuous audacity to obtain what did not belong to him by any right or natural claim. He had also risen to such arrogance that he refused obedience to Casimir and moreover resisted him with arms and ambushes. [Col. 0867A] [Note: [Col. 0865] MS 3 reads *ambitiose cupiditate*, “by ambitious desire,” for *ambitione perniciosae cupiditatis*, “by the ambition of ruinous greed.” It omits *nisus est*, “he strove.” MS 3 reads *competebat*, “belonged,” for *cedebat*, “yielded.” It adds *et*, “and,” after *ren­nuebat*, “refused.”]

Casimir, indignant that his father’s and his own servant should violently hold Mazovia, and considering that great harm and danger would threaten him unless he avenged himself by force, gathered a band small in number but accustomed to war. Entering battle, he killed Miecław and triumphantly won victory, peace, and the entire fatherland in A.D. 1047. [Col. 0867A] [Note: [Col. 0867] MS 2 reads *vi se*, “by force himself,” for *nisi se*, “unless he should avenge himself”; an older hand subsequently supplied *nisi* in the margin, so that the sense is “unless he should avenge himself by force.” MS 3 reads *armatorum*, “armed men,” for *bellatorum*, “warriors,” and *asseveta*, “accustomed,” for *assueta*, “accustomed.” MS 2 reads *Meczlawo*, “Miecław,” for *Meczslawo*, “Miecław.” It also reads *tantamque*, “so great,” for *totamque*, “the entire”; and *provinciam*, “province,” for *patriam*, “fatherland.” [Col. 0867C] Nestor says that this was done with Yaroslav’s aid. Yet a different victory over the Pomeranians occurred a little earlier, since, according to the Annals of Altaich, peace between Casimir and the duke of the Pomeranians was concluded in 1046. K.]

So great a slaughter of Mazovians is remembered to have occurred there as the battlefield and the precipice on the bank of the river still testify. Casimir himself became exceedingly exhausted by cutting down men with his sword there; his arms, whole breast, and face were bloodied with flowing blood. He pursued the fleeing enemy alone so far that he would have died, unsupported by all his own men, had not a certain man—not of noble birth but one of the common soldiers—nobly aided him as he was near death. Casimir later repaid him well: he granted him a city and raised him by rank among the nobler men. [Col. 0867B] [Note: [Col. 0867] MS 3 reads *Mazovitarum*, “of the Mazovians,” for *Mazovitorum*. It reads *minis*, “threats,” for *nimis*, “exceedingly.” It reads *quidem*, “indeed,” for *quidam*, “a certain man.” It also reads *cum*, “with,” for *eum*, “him.”]

In that battle the Mazovians had thirty ordered battle-lines, whereas Casimir scarcely had three full battle-lines of warriors, since, as has been said, almost all Poland lay deserted. [Col. 0867B] [Note: [Col. 0867] MSS 1–2 read *habebant*, “they had,” for *habebat*, “he had.” MS 3 omits *tota Polonia*, “all Poland.”]

## 21. On Casimir’s battle with the Pomeranians

[Note: [Col. 0867] MS 3 omits this whole chapter and the beginning of the next. Immediately after the final word of the preceding chapter, *jacebat*, “lay,” it adds: “He killed St Stanislaus, bishop of Cracow, a most venerable man.”]

After this battle had been memorably won in A.D. 1046, Casimir hastened without hesitation with a few men to meet the Pomeranian army that was coming to Miecław’s aid. [Col. 0867C] [Note: MS 2 reads *Meczlao*, “Miecław,” for *Meczzlao*. MS 2 originally had *propetravit*, an error; the corrector cancelled it and supplied *properat*, “hastens,” in the margin.]

It had been reported to him beforehand, and he knew that they were arriving to aid his enemies. Therefore he prudently arranged first to settle the issue with the Mazovians alone, and afterwards to enter the field of battle more easily against the Pomeranians.

On that occasion the Pomeranians brought four legions of soldiers under arms, while Casimir’s soldiers did not amount even to half of one legion. But what then? When they came to the battlefield, Casimir, an eloquent and experienced man, encouraged his soldiers in this fashion:

> Behold the day long expected from the first!  
> Behold the complete end of labour!  
> Having overcome so many false Christians,  
> Now fight securely against the unruly.  
>
> Multitude does not make victory,  
> But he to whom God has given His grace.  
> Remember your former valour  
> And put an end to your labour.

[Col. 0868A] [Note: [Col. 0867] MSS 1–3 read *pugnare*, “to fight,” for *pugnate*, “fight.”]

Having said this, he entered battle with God’s help and won a great victory. He is also said to have honoured Holy Church with great devotion, and especially to have increased the communities of monks and holy nuns, because as a small child he had been offered to a monastery by his parents and liberally instructed there in sacred letters. [Col. 0868B] [Note: [Col. 0867] MS 2 reads *quoniam*, “because,” for *qui*, “who.” [Col. 0868C] The words “because he had been offered to a monastery … instructed there” were misunderstood and perhaps gave rise to the tale that he was a monk; Bandtke, p. 98. S.]

## 22. On the succession of the second Bolesław, called the Generous, son of Casimir

[Note: [Col. 0867] The chapter heading was added by the corrector in the margin of MS 2. MS 3 omits the entire title.]

### English translation of the substantive editorial notes

**[Col. 0857D–0858D].** The *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland* says that Bolesław freed those condemned contrary to law when he understood the matter; compare the *Life of St Ladislaus* in Endlicher’s *Monuments of Hungarian Affairs*, I, 238. Bolesław married four times; his last wife was Oda, daughter of Ekkehard, margrave of Meissen.

**[Col. 0859D].** That is, he was often occupied in guarding the frontiers against enemies.

**[Col. 0861C–0862C].** Paprocki’s *Heraldry of the Polish Knighthood*, perhaps from another manuscript, gives this speech in a slightly different form: “I see the kingdom being vainly torn into many and varied pieces,” etc. If this can be understood of the division of the kingdom among Bolesław’s sons reported by Thietmar, it would be important evidence. For the day of death see Cosmas, I, 41; compare the *Life of St Ladislaus*, ed. Endlicher, I, 241.

**[Col. 0863C–0864C].** “Latins and Slavs” distinguishes Poles of the Western and Eastern Churches. Richeza was the daughter of Ezzo, count palatine of the Rhine, by Mechthild, sister of Otto III; compare the *Foundation of Brauweiler* and the *Miracles of St Adalbert*, ch. 9. The duke blinded in 1003 was Bolesław III the Red (Cosmas, I, 34); other writers say nothing of Mieszko’s captivity. Compare the *Annals of Hildesheim* for 1034. The monk of Brauweiler tells Richeza’s affair very differently; see Roepell, I, 662.

**[Col. 0865C–0866C].** Henry III was the emperor. The manuscript heading “who was a monk” is judged, with Bandtke, to be a later addition: this chapter’s narrative disproves it, and an author calling Casimir learned would not have suppressed his monastic life. Borsod is in Borsod County. Casimir’s maternal uncles were Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, and Otto, duke of Swabia, Richeza’s brothers. Compare the Saxon Annalist for 1039; Dobroniega was sister of Prince Yaroslav.

**[Col. 0866C–0867C].** Compare Cosmas, II, 2. Nestor attributes the 1047 victory to Yaroslav’s aid; but an earlier victory over the Pomeranians is implied by the Annals of Altaich, which record peace between Casimir and their duke in 1046. MS 3 omits this entire chapter and the beginning of the next; after *jacebat* (“lay”) it adds: “He killed St Stanislaus, bishop of Cracow, a most venerable man.”

**[Col. 0868C].** The words “who had been offered to a monastery … instructed there” were misunderstood and may have occasioned the tale that Casimir was a monk (Bandtke, p. 98).

The supplied source ends here, with the heading of chapter 22 only; no body for that chapter has been supplied or inferred.

Source preparation: embedded foreign-language text was recovered from the supplied local archive and translated as part of this section.

With these memorable deeds of Casimir thus set forth in advance, and several others passed over in silence because of haste, let us bring to an end both him whose life was ending and the writer. [Note: [Col. 0867] “Casimir died in 1038,” is written in the margin by 1.] After Casimir had therefore taken his final leave of the world (A.D. 1058), his firstborn son Bolesław—[Note: [Col. 0867] “This man killed Stanislaus” is added here above the column, over the word *Bolesław*, by 1.] a generous and warlike man—ruled the kingdom of the Poles. He equalled the deeds of his predecessors by his own considerable achievements, [Note: [Col. 0867] In place of “With these memorable deeds of Casimir … equalled,” 3 reads: “Casimir died in the year of the Lord 1058, and Bolesław his son succeeded him in the kingdom—his firstborn son, I say, a generous and warlike man, who equalled the deeds of his predecessors by his own considerable achievements.”] except that a certain excess of ambition or vanity impelled him. For, when at the beginning of his rule he held sway over both Poles and Pomeranians, and gathered an innumerable multitude of them to besiege the fortress of Gradec [Col. 0868C] [Note: [Col. 0867] Omitted by 2.] [Note: [Col. 0867] *Gradek*, 3.] [Note: [Col. 0868C] Königgrätz in the kingdom of Bohemia. S.] (A.D. 1061), through the negligence arising from his obstinacy he not only failed to take the fortress, but also barely escaped Bohemian ambushes and thus lost dominion over the Pomeranians. Yet it is not altogether surprising if someone goes somewhat astray through ignorance, provided that later he corrects through wisdom what he has neglected. [Note: [Col. 0867] 3 reads “had gone astray.”] [Note: [Col. 0867] 3 reads “had corrected,” etc.]

### 23. On Bolesław’s agreement with the duke of the Ruthenians

It is not fitting, therefore, [Note: [Col. 0867] Omitted by 3.] to pass over in silence the manifold excellence [Col. 0869A] and liberality [Note: [Col. 0869] “freedom,” 2 and 3.] of King Bolesław the Second [Note: [Col. 0869] Omitted by 3.], but rather to disclose a few instances out of many as an example to governors of kingdoms. King Bolesław the Second, then, was a bold and vigorous soldier, a kindly receiver of guests, and most lavish in generous gifts. [Note: [Col. 0869] 3 omits “generous gifts.”] He too, like the first great Bolesław, entered by force the chief city of the Ruthenian realm, Kyiv, [Note: [Col. 0869] *Kyow*, 2; *Kyyevo*, 3.] and left on its Golden Gate the mark of a stroke from his sword, as a memorial [Note: [Col. 0869] 2 reads *reliquit* (“left”) for *dereliquit*.] (A.D. 1069). There he also established on the royal throne a Ruthenian of his own kin, to whom he entrusted the government, [Note: [Col. 0869] 3 reads: “to whom the kingdom belonged.”] and deprived all rebels of power. [Note: [Col. 0869D] Iziaslav, prince of Kyiv, who had been expelled by his own people.]

O pomp of temporal glory! O boldness of martial confidence! O majesty of royal power! Thus Bolesław the Generous, asked by the king whom he had made to come to meet him [Col. 0869B] and, in honour of his nation, give him the kiss of peace, consented to this as a Pole; but the Ruthenian gave what he wished. For, having counted the Generous Bolesław’s horse-steps [Note: [Col. 0869] “horses,” 2 and 3.] from his quarters to the place of meeting, the Ruthenian placed down the same number of marks of gold. Yet he did not dismount from his horse; instead, plucking Bolesław’s beard with a smile, he gave him a kiss sufficiently precious. [Note: [Col. 0869] 1 reads *exibuit* for *exhibuit* (“gave, offered”).]

### 24. On the Bohemians’ deception of Bolesław the Generous

(A.D. 1068.) At the same time it happened that the duke of the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0870D] Vratislav. II. K.] entered Poland with all the strength of his troops; after passing through the thickets of the forests, he pitched camp on a plain quite suitable for battle. When Bolesław heard this, he hastened energetically to meet the enemy; hurrying on, he occupied and blocked the route by which they had come. Since much of the day had passed and he had wearied his own men by the rapid march, he informed the Bohemians through envoys that he would come to battle on the following day, begging them earnestly to remain there and not tire themselves further.

“You used formerly,” he said, “when coming out of the forest, like hungry wolves after seizing prey, to penetrate with impunity the forest hiding-places while the shepherd was absent. But now, with the hunter present, armed with hunting-spears and with his dogs loosed upon the tracks, you will be able to avoid the stretched nets neither by flight nor by ambush, but by courage.” [Note: [Col. 0869] “Formerly … courage” is omitted by 3.]

In reply, the Bohemian duke sent Bolesław a message with crafty cunning: [Note: [Col. 0869] 3 reads: “With the crafty cunning of the Bohemians he sent Bolesław this reply,” in place of “In reply … sent a message.”] it was unworthy for so great a king to stoop to an inferior [Col. 0869D]; but on the next day, if he were Casimir’s son, let him be ready there to await the service of the Bohemians. Bolesław, wishing to show himself Casimir’s son, satisfied the Bohemians’ trickery by remaining there. [Col. 0870A] But, when the following day was already half spent, scouts reported to the Polish camp [Note: [Col. 0869] “is reported,” 3.] that the Bohemians had entered upon flight during the preceding night, not battle. At once Bolesław, grieved that he had been deceived [Note: [Col. 0869] 3 adds *sic* (“thus”).], pursued them fiercely as they fled through Moravia; he captured and killed many, and because they had thus escaped, returned in indignation against himself.

The following must also be attached to the account: the cause that almost entirely abolished in Poland the use of coats of mail, which the army of King Bolesław the Great had formerly employed with great zeal. [Note: [Col. 0869] Two small stars are placed in the margin here, near the end of the following chapter, in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0869] We have emended *racionem* (“account/reason”) to *narrationi* (“narrative”); 3 has *romani*.]

### 25. On Bolesław the Generous’s victory [Note: [Col. 0869] Omitted by 3.] over the Pomeranians

The Pomeranians suddenly invaded Poland [Col. 0870B], and King Bolesław heard of it while he was far away in those regions. [Note: [Col. 0869] Repeated twice by 2.] Burning with desire to free his homeland from the hand of the heathen, and before the army had yet assembled, he rashly hurried forward too hastily. When they reached the river beyond which the bands of heathen were stationed, the armed mail-clad soldiers entrusted themselves to the deep current without looking for either bridge or ford. Many men in mail were consequently presumptuously drowned there; the surviving remainder threw away their coats of mail, crossed the river, and, though at great loss, won the victory. From that time Poland abandoned the use of mail; thus each man attacked the enemy more swiftly and crossed an intervening river more safely, unburdened by the weight of iron.

### 26. On Bolesław’s liberality [Note: [Col. 0869] 3 reads *libertate* (“freedom”) for *liberalitate*.] and generosity, and [Note: [Col. 0869] 1 and 2 omit “and.”] a poor cleric

[Col. 0870C]

I shall likewise not conceal one memorable deed of exceptional liberality by the second Bolesław, but shall relate it to his successors as an example for imitation. [Note: [Col. 0869] 3 reads: “a memorial deed of Bolesław and of generosity” for “one memorable deed of the second Bolesław.”] One day in the city of Cracow, Bolesław the Generous was seated before his palace in the court, inspecting tribute from the Ruthenians and other revenues spread out upon carpets. It happened that a poor foreign cleric was present [Note: [Col. 0869] “had been afflicted,” 2.] and saw the magnitude of so great a treasure. Gazing greedily with his eyes upon that abundance of money in wonder, [Note: [Col. 0869] 2 reads “and with the reasoning of his mind”; 3, “in wonder.”] while thinking of his own misery, he sighed with a deep groan.

But King Bolesław, being fierce by nature, heard the man groaning pitifully and, thinking that someone had struck one of the chamberlains, angrily asked [Col. 0870D] who had dared groan in this fashion, or who had presumed to beat anyone there. The wretched cleric, trembling, would rather never have seen the money [Col. 0871A] than have entered the king’s court for this reason.

But why do you hide, poor little cleric?

Why do you hesitate to confess that you groaned?

That groan will trample down all your sorrow;

That sigh will bring you great joy.

Do not, generous king, do not allow the poor little cleric to gasp longer from fear; rather, hasten to load his shoulders with your treasure.

Thus, when the king asked the cleric what he had been thinking as he sighed so tearfully, he answered with trembling: “My lord king, considering my misery and poverty, and your glory and majesty, and comparing happiness with misfortune as things so unequal, I sighed because of the greatness of my grief.” [Col. 0871B]

Then the generous king said: “If you sighed because of need, you have found in King Bolesław consolation for poverty. Go, then, to the money you admire, and let whatever you can manage to carry in one load be yours.” The poor man approached and filled his cloak with so much gold and silver that it burst from the excessive weight, and the money itself came into view. [Note: [Col. 0871] “and the money itself came into view” is omitted by 3.] Then the generous king took the mantle from his own neck and handed it to the poor cleric as a sack for the money; helping him, he honoured him with still better things. The generous king loaded the cleric with so much gold and silver that the cleric cried out that his neck would come apart if he put on any more.

The king lives in fame; the poor man, enriched, departed. [Note: [Col. 0871] 3 transposes *pauper ditatus* (“poor [man] enriched”).] [Note: [Col. 0871C] “He went away made rich.” *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, Stenzel, I, 61.8.]

### 27. On Bolesław the Generous’s exile in Hungary

[Note: [Col. 0871] In place of this and the following chapter, which are missing from the continuous text, 3 contains a fragment inserted elsewhere and printed on p. 44 of the Ged. edition; it also contains other fragments from the book on the Passion of St Stanislaus and from the Life of Blessed Stephen, King of Hungary, which are printed in the Life of St Stanislaus, chapters 10, 11, 14, 15, 16, and 22.]

[Col. 0871C] (A.D. 1064.) He also drove King Solomon out of Hungary by his own forces and placed Władysław upon the throne, a man as outstanding in body as he was abundant in piety. [Note: [Col. 0871] 1, 2, and 3 read *sic* (“thus/as”) for *sicut* (“just as”).] [Note: [Col. 0871C] Ladislaus I was not made king until A.D. 1077. K.] This Władysław had been brought up in Poland from infancy and had become, as it were, Polish [Note: [Col. 0871] 2 reads *eciam* (“also”).] in habits and manner of life. They say that Hungary never had such a king, nor that the land was ever afterward so fertile. It would take long to tell how King Bolesław was expelled from Poland; but this at least may be said: a Christian ought not to inflict bodily punishment for any sin upon Christians. [Col. 0872A] For it greatly harmed him when he added sin to sin, when, on account of treason, he subjected the bishop [Note: [Col. 0871C] Stanislaus, bishop of Cracow. K.] to mutilation of his limbs (A.D. 1079). We neither excuse a traitorous bishop nor commend a king who takes vengeance so disgracefully; but let us leave this matter undecided and explain how he was received in Hungary.

[Note: [Col. 0871] The text read *Epm.* (“bishop”); in 2 a pious hand of a later age, evidently moved by zeal, erased the final two strokes of the letter *m*, leaving the first intact, and thereby made *Epi—*, “of a bishop.” A corrector contemporary with the scribe never used a knife but always a pen.]

### 28. On Bolesław’s reception by Władysław, king of Hungary

When Władysław heard that Bolesław was coming,

Władysław rejoices in part at his friend; in part there remains room for anger against Bolesław.

Władysław rejoices in part at receiving his brother and friend,

[Col. 0872B] But Bolesław grieves to render deference to Władysław, made his enemy. [Note: [Col. 0872C] The marginal attributions are: Władysław, P.; Bolesław, P.]

He did not receive him as each man is accustomed to receive a stranger, guest, or equal; rather, as a soldier ought by right to receive a prince, a duke a king, or a king an emperor. [Note: [Col. 0871] In the fragment, 3 instead reads: “For this Władysław Bolesław, after driving King Solomon from Hungary by his own forces, placed upon the royal throne.”]

Bolesław called Władysław his king;

Władysław acknowledged that through Bolesław he was king.

Yet one thing must be attributed to vanity in Bolesław, and it greatly harmed his former excellence. For, although he entered a foreign kingdom as a fugitive, and though no peasant was bound to obey a fugitive, [Col. 0872C] the humble Władysław hastened to meet Bolesław and, dismounting from his horse at a distance, waited respectfully for his approach. But Bolesław did not regard the humility of the gentle king; rather, he raised his heart to the pride of pestilential arrogance. “I brought up this fosterling in Poland,” he said; “I placed this man as king in Hungary. It is not fitting that he should honour me as an equal; he ought, while seated on horseback, to kiss me as he would any of the princes.”

Władysław was somewhat distressed by this intention and turned aside from the road; nevertheless, he ordered that Bolesław be served throughout the whole land [Col. 0873A] quite magnificently. Later they came together in harmony and friendship, like brothers. The Hungarians, however, noted the affair more deeply in their hearts; hence Bolesław accumulated great Hungarian enmity for himself, and consequently, as they say, his last day overtook him sooner (A.D. 1081). [Note: [Col. 0873] In the margin of 1 and 2, between red lines: “Bolesław the Generous died 1081.”] [Note: [Col. 0873] 3 adds: “But he died miserably in the year of the Lord 1081.”]

### 29. On the son of the same Bolesław, Mieszko the Third

King Bolesław had one son named Mieszko, who would not have been inferior in excellence to his forefathers, had the envy of the Fates not broken the thread of life of the boy, now reaching adolescence. This boy [Note: [Col. 0873] 3 omits *Illum enim* (“for this [boy]”).], after his father’s death, was reared by Władysław, king of the Hungarians, who loved him in the place of a son, out of regard for his father. The boy indeed surpassed all his contemporaries, Hungarians and Poles alike, [Col. 0873B] in honourable conduct and beauty; by evident signs he drew all minds to himself with hope of his future rule. Therefore his uncle, Duke Władysław, thought fit to summon the boy back to Poland under an ill omen and marry him to a Ruthenian girl [Note: [Col. 0873D] Eudoxia, if Długosz is to be trusted. K.] despite the envy of the Fates (A.D. 1087).

Having married, this beardless and handsome young man conducted himself so gravely and wisely, and observed the ancient custom of his forefathers so well, that he pleased the whole country with extraordinary affection. But Fortune, the enemy of mortals’ prosperity, turned joy into sorrow and cut short both the hope of his excellence and the flower of his age. For some say that certain rivals, fearing that he might avenge his father’s wrong, killed the boy of good disposition with poison [Col. 0873C] (A.D. 1089), and that some who drank with him scarcely escaped the danger of death.

When the boy Mieszko died, all Poland mourned as a mother mourns the death of an only son. Not only those who knew him lamented, but even those who had never seen him followed the dead man’s bier with lamentation. Farmers abandoned their ploughs, shepherds their flocks, craftsmen their occupations, and labourers their work [Note: [Col. 0873] 3 omits *operatores opera* (“labourers [their] work”).] [Col. 0874A] because of grief for Mieszko; little boys and girls, moreover male and female servants, celebrated Mieszko’s funeral rites with tears and sighs. At last the wretched mother, when the lamented boy was laid in the coffin, lay for one hour as though dead, without the breath of life, and was scarcely revived after the funeral by bishops with fans and cold water. No king’s or prince’s death, even among barbarian peoples, is recorded as having been bewailed with such protracted grief; no funerals of magnificent tetrarchs are so mournfully celebrated, nor has the anniversary of an emperor ever been observed with such a mournful chant. But let us be silent about the grief for the buried boy and come to the joy concerning the boy who was to reign.

### 30. On the marriage of Władysław, father of Bolesław the Third

[Col. 0874B]

When King Bolesław had died and his other brothers were dead, Duke Władysław ruled alone. He took as wife Judith, daughter of Vratislav, king of Bohemia, and she bore him Bolesław the Third, concerning whom our purpose has set its title, as the following account will make clear. But now, since we have passed briefly along the tree from its root through its branches, let us direct pen and mind to grafting a fruit-bearing branch into the catalogue.

The parents of the future boy, still without offspring, persisted in fasting and prayer, and gave abundant alms to the poor, so that almighty God—who makes barren mothers rejoice in their children, who granted the Baptist to Zechariah, and opened Sarah’s womb so that he might bless all nations in the seed of Abraham—might give them such a son as heir: one who would fear God, exalt the holy Church, exercise justice, and hold the governance of Poland for the honour of God and the salvation of the people. While they did this unceasingly, Franco, bishop of Poland, [Note: [Col. 0873D] The author calls this Franco a Polish bishop; Vincent Kadłubek calls him simply a prelate, Leipzig edition, p. 668, but his commentator, p. 672, calls him bishop of Cracow. Długosz followed him, book IV, A.D. 1085, p. 305, naming him Lambert. After St Stanislaus, bishop of Cracow, was killed by Bolesław the Generous in A.D. 1079, Gregory VII placed Poland under ecclesiastical interdict, and the see of Cracow was without a bishop for four years. The same judgment should be made concerning the bishopric of Kruszwica, which the author calls Polish in the letter in Book III; for according to Długosz’s unpublished *Lives of the Bishops of Kruszwica*, Andrew, bishop of Kruszwica, died in 1081, and only in 1087 was the Roman Baptist appointed in his place. *Lives of the Bishops of Kruszwica*, manuscript, Ossoliński Library, Lwów, quarto no. XVIII, fols. 100–101. Thus Franco was probably a bishop of Kruszwica elected by the king or chapter during the interdict, who either could not obtain papal confirmation or died before obtaining it. This is why he is vainly sought in Długosz’s succession-list of bishops of Kruszwica. S.] came to them with salutary counsel [Col. 0875A] and said:

“If you most devoutly carry out what I shall tell you, your desire will without doubt be granted.” Gladly hearing the bishop concerning such a matter, and promising, in hope of offspring, that they would do great things, they urgently begged him to state the matter as quickly as possible. To this the prelate replied: “There is a certain saint in the regions of Gaul, to the south, near Marseilles, where the Rhône enters the sea—the land of Provence—and his name is Saint Giles. [Note: [Col. 0875D] The monastery of Saint Giles in the Flavian valley, near Nîmes in the diocese of Arles; in French, Saint-Gilles. The *Chronicle of the Poles* in Stenzel, *Scriptures of Silesian Affairs*, I, 12, calls this monastery Saint Gall’s. S.] His merit before God is so great that everyone who places devotion in him and keeps his memory, whatever he asks of him, will obtain without doubt. Therefore have a golden image made in the likeness of a boy, prepare royal gifts, and hasten to send them to Saint Giles.”

Without delay, a child’s image and a chalice of the purest gold were made; gold, silver, mantles, and sacred vestments were prepared, to be conveyed to Provence by faithful envoys [Note: [Col. 0875D] One of them was Peter, chaplain to Queen Judith, as Cosmas, II.36 reports. Długosz affirms that he was a canon of Cracow, I, 305. S.] with this letter:

### Letter of Władysław to Saint Giles and to the monks

[Note: [Col. 0875] In 2, a pious reader erased the final two strokes of the *m* in *sanctum Egidium*, and rather ineptly made a genitive out of the accusative; he also deleted the repeated preposition *ad* but forgot to delete the now-superfluous *et*.] [Note: [Col. 0875] 3 adds *capitulum* (“chapter”) after “monks.”]

Władysław, by the grace of God duke of Poland, and Judith, his lawful wife, to O., [Note: [Col. 0875] Omitted by 3.] [Note: [Col. 0876D] Odilo, who was then abbot of this monastery. Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictines*, V, 128. S.] venerable abbot of Saint Giles, and to all the brethren: the service of most humble devotion.

Having heard the report that Saint Giles is pre-eminent in the dignity of his special mercy, and that he is a ready helper by the power divinely granted to him [Col. 0876A], we offer him these gifts of our devotion in hope of offspring, and humbly implore your holy prayers in aid of our petition.

### 31. On fasts and prayers for the birth of Bolesław the Third

When the letter had been read and the gifts received, the abbot and brothers made return to those who had sent the gifts [Note: [Col. 0875] Semler, loc. cit., p. 35, advises adding *sua* (“their own”) or *gratias* (“thanks”), taking *gifts* to refer not to the monks but to the parents.] and kept a three-day fast with litanies and prayers. They besought the omnipotence of the divine Majesty to fulfil the devotion of the faithful, who were sending such great gifts to Him in person [Note: [Col. 0875] *miptencium*, 3.] and vowing much more, in order that He might exalt the glory of His name among nations unknown to Him and spread far and wide the fame of His servant Giles.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] Władysław, to whom Bolesław his son was born through the prayers of the monks of Saint Giles in the Flavian Valley, built and endowed many churches and monasteries under Saint Giles’s title. This appears from the Codex of Kłodawa, which at the head of p. 36, where the Chronicle of Bogufał speaks of Władysław, has the following, written in a fifteenth-century hand: “This Władysław, in honour of Blessed Giles, endowed and founded the parish church at Kłodawa; the collegiate church in honour of Blessed Giles at Cracow; another collegiate church at Łęczyca; a parish church at Krobia; and many others in honour of Blessed Giles the Confessor, through whose prayers he had a son.” At the same time King Ladislaus of Hungary founded an abbey of Saint Giles, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in Hungary, in Somogy County. [Col. 0878D] Cf. Bel, *Compendium of Hungarian Geography*, Pressburg, 1777, p. 178. S.]

[Col. 0876B]

Well done, servant of God: bring this undertaking to completion;

Fulfil the vows which your servants ask.

For a boy, make a boy; for the false, make the true;

Fashion the fleshly one, keeping the material one for yourself.

What more need be said? The fast had not yet been completed by the monks in Provence, and already the mother in Poland rejoiced over a son conceived. The envoys had not yet departed thence, and already the monks foretold that their lady had conceived. Thus the envoys, returning home more swiftly and joyfully, and proving the monks’ prophecy true, rejoiced over the son conceived, but would rejoice still more over the fulfilment of their vow.

[Col. 0875]

**Here ends the First Book.**

## Book Two

[Note: [Col. 0875] “Book Two” is added by Bandtkie; it is absent from the manuscripts.]

[Col. 0875C]

### The Epistle Begins

To Lord Paul, by the grace of God bishop of Poland, of venerable discernment, and to Michael the chancellor, his fellow-worker in a religious undertaking, the humble steward of a small provision offers the service of paternal reverence and due obedience.

As I reflected upon many things, remembrance came upon me of your most abundant charity, and of your fame, spread far and wide, of the wisdom divinely bestowed upon you and of your human excellence. But because the intention of an able mind often conceives what a slow faculty of speech cannot express, let the intention of good will suffice in place of speech. For when a man does what he can, complaint is then made unjustly.

Nevertheless, lest we seem to pass over in silence the glory of such great men and the memory of such religious prelates, let us endeavour, in dwelling upon their praises, to carry, as it were, a drop from a little spring to the floods of the Tiber. Although that which is perfect cannot naturally be increased, reason does not forbid its being honoured in writings and proclamations of praise. Nor is anyone thought unsuitable in paintings if, for variety in the work, black is blended with beautiful colours. [Col. 0877A] At kings’ tables likewise some humble dish is often served, by which distaste for daily delicacies may be driven away. Moreover, although the ant is an animal unequal to the camel in bodily size, it nevertheless diligently performs a task proportionate to its strength.

Encouraged by these examples, I endeavour, in the manner of one who stammers, to form childish words in praise of men praiseworthy in themselves, without praise, or in a truthful and unfeigned encomium upon Israelites. Their life is laudable, their teaching clear, their morals worthy of imitation, and their preaching salutary. Their wisdom, flowing from the two-peaked mountain of philosophy, so shrewdly illuminates the dense forests of Poland that they do not first scatter the wheat-seed of faith upon the untilled ground [Col. 0877B] of the human heart until they have uprooted from it thorns and thistles with the spades of the divine word. They resemble the householder who knows how to bring forth things new and old from his treasure; or the Samaritan, binding the wounded man’s wounds and pouring wine and oil upon them. They also faithfully distribute wheat to their fellow servants by measure, and do not hide the talent but put it out at interest.

But why does one mute strive to speak about eloquent men? Why does a child of scant ability entangle himself in matters so deep? Yet let the discernment of your holiness, great fathers, spare both ignorance and goodwill; let it consider not what, or how much, is offered of its own labour, but what the desire of our capacity seeks to offer. For when a poor friend renders to a powerful man even the least amount of work within his ability, the powerful man, considering not the gift but the giver’s affection, does not refuse to accept it as a great gift.

Therefore, venerable fathers, may your eminent authority and the benevolence of your mind receive and commend this little work, childishly written with the pen of our small ability in praise of our princes and country, so that almighty God may increase you with the growth of temporal and eternal goods.

The epistle ends.

### The epilogue begins

Stand by us; read this work for us!

Through you, if you wish, this work becomes praiseworthy to many.

[Col. 0878B]

It is no wonder if we have rested a little from our labour:

It was time to rest; we have crossed so many lands.

Nor have we known well the road we began,

But we gradually inquire through those who know.

Let us now rise from sleep, for we have slept enough;

We have already sought the journey of but one day.

When this has been accomplished, we shall think sufficiently of what is to come.

With God as guide, let us continue what we have set aside;

Let us fulfil what we have often announced above,

And add anything that we have said too ignorantly.

## Supplementary textual apparatus

Each entry is keyed to its source locus. Every reading retains its manuscript number or editorial siglum, its actual form, and an English meaning; “omits” gives the exact omitted scope.

### Chapters 23–26

- **23:** 2–3 *libertatem* (“freedom”) for *liberalitatem* (“generosity”); 3 omits *Bolezlavi secundi* (“of Bolesław II”) and *datorque largorum* (“giver of generous gifts”). 2 *Kyow*, 3 *Kyyevo* are spellings of Kyiv. 2–3 *equis* (“horses”) for *passibus equinis* (“horse-steps”); 3 additionally inserts *de* (“from/of”) before horse.
- **24:** 2 *non* (“not”) for *nec* (“and not”); 1–2 repeat *exeuntes* (“coming out”); 3 omits the whole speech from *Antea quidem* (“Formerly indeed”) through *devitare* (“avoid”). 3 substitutes its whole sentence “With Bohemian crafty cunning he sent Bolesław this reply” for *At contra … remandavit* (“In reply … he sent back”). It reads *nunciatur* (“is reported”) for *nunciavit* (“reported”), *sequitur* (“follows”) for *secutus est* (“followed”), and construes *ineatur* (“is undertaken”) with flight rather than battle.
- **25:** 2 repeats *partibus* (“regions”), *namque* (“for/indeed”) for *itaque* (“therefore”), and *eodem* (“the same”) for *eo* (“that/from that”); 3 preserves the chapter heading only in its displaced fragment.
- **26:** 2 *affluisse* (“to have afflicted”) for *affuisse* (“to have been present”); 2–3 *prospexisse* (“to have looked out”) for *perspexisse* (“to have looked/gazed closely”). 2 inserts *et animi racione* (“and with the reasoning of [his] mind”); 3 *admiratione* (“in amazement”) and *ibidem* (“there”). For *oculis inhiaret* (“was gaping/eagerly fixed his eyes”), 1 has corrupt *iniaret*, 2 corrupt *oclis miaret*, 3 *inhire't*. 3 uses *ingemuisse* (“to have groaned”) for *gemivisse* (“to have sighed”), *fuit* (“was”) for *fuerit* (“was/has been”), *presumpsit* (“presumed”) for *praesumpserit* (“has presumed”), omits *te gemuisse confiteri* (“to confess that you groaned”), *noli* (“do not”), and *et pecunia ipsa apparuit* (“and the money itself came into view”). It has *gemuisse* (“to have groaned”) for *gemivisse*, *illud* (“that”) for *istud* (“this”), *onerare* (“to burden”) for *honerare* (“to honour”), *disparaliter* (“unequally”), and *onere* (“with a burden”) for *honere* (“with honour”). All three have corrupt *tollere* at “to carry”; Ged. corrects it. 2 *clerico* (“to/for the cleric”) for *clericum* (“the cleric”).

### Chapters 27–29

- **27:** 3 lacks chapters 27–28 from the continuous text and instead inserts the specified Ged. p. 44 fragment and Passion/Life fragments. 1–3 *Ungaria* (“Hungary,” nominative) for *Ungariam* (“into Hungary”); 2 *christianum* (“a Christian,” singular) for *christianos* (“Christians”); 2 transposes *peccatum peccato* (“sin to sin”); its supplied *n* makes *tradicioe* read *tradicione* (“by treason”). In *Epm.* (“bishop”), a later hand in 2 erased strokes to make *Epi—* (“of a bishop”); the contemporary corrector used a pen, never a knife.
- **28:** 3’s fragment adds *enim* (“for/indeed”) and “king of Hungary,” omits *partim* (“in part”) and both verses from “Władysław rejoices” through “made his enemy.” Margins attribute the paired lines respectively to Władysław and Bolesław. 1–2 *fugitivus* (“a fugitive,” nominative) for *fugitivo* (“a fugitive,” dative); 2 wrongly *Wladislavo* for *Bolezlavo*, *Qui* (“who”) for *Quod* (“that/which”), *osclari* for *osculari* (“to kiss”). 3 *igitur* (“therefore”), *appellat* (“calls”) for *appellabat* (“called”), *fastum inanis* (“empty pride”) for *pestiferae fastum* (“pestilential pride”), *jamque* (“and now”) for *indeque* (“and thence”), and transposes *extrema dies cicius* (“his last day sooner”).
- **29:** 3 omits the heading. 1–2 *Mesconis*, 3 *Mieszkone*, for *Mescone*: forms of Mieszko’s name; 1–2 “III” for *tertio* (“third”). 3 substitutes “Bolesław the most wicked king had one son,” uses *Mesconem/Mieszkonem* for *Meschonem*, omits the sentence from *qui non fuisset inferior* (“who would not have been inferior”) through *adolescentiam* (“adolescence”), adds erroneous *virtutes* (“virtues”) after *omnium* (“of all”), omits *puer* (“the boy”), and has *cumque* (“and when”), *satis* (“enough”), *igitur* (“therefore”) for *eumque* (“and him”), *fatis* (“fates”), *ergo* (“therefore”).
- **29, funeral:** 1–2 omit *se* (“himself”) after *sapienter* (“wisely”); 2–3 *Mescone* for the name; 2 adds erroneous *vivit* (“lives”) after “mother”; 3 *noverant* (“had known”) for *viderant* (“had seen”); 3 *poneretur* (“was laid”) for *conderetur* (“was buried”), 1–2 *suscitatur* (“is raised”) for *suscitabatur* (“was being revived”), 3 *et* (“and”) for *vel* (“or”), 2 repeats then cancels *nec exequiae* (“nor funeral rites”), 2 corrupt *retharcharum* (initial corrected to *t*) and 3 *thetharchar* for *tethrarcharum* (“of tetrarchs”). 1–2 *magnificum* (“magnificent,” singular) for *magnificorum* (“of magnificent [ones]”); 3 *celebrabantur* (“were celebrated”), *mesticiam* (“mourning,” corrupt spelling), and omits *veniamus ad gaudium de puero regnaturo* (“let us come to the joy concerning the boy who was to reign”).

### Chapter 30, Letter 31, and closing verses

- **30:** 3 omits *Mortuo itaque* (“Therefore, when [he] had died”); *Bohemie* (“of Bohemia”) for *Bohemici* (“the Bohemian”). 2 omits *filium* (“a son”), has *cathelogo* for *cathalogo* (“catalogue”), and 1–2 *oracionis* for *orationi* (“prayer,” spelling/case variant). 2 omits *ut* (“that/in order that”); 3 omits *justitiam exerceat* (“he may exercise justice”) and has *regnum* (“kingdom”) for *regimen* (“government”). In Franco’s speech, 3 has *compleveritis* (“you will have fulfilled”) for *compleatis* (“you may fulfil”), *quantocius* (“as quickly as possible,” spelling) for *quantocitius* (same sense), *certa* (“certain”) for *terra* (“land”), *habet devocionem* (“has devotion”) for *devotionem suam ponit* (“places his devotion”), and *quicquid* (“whatever”) for *si quid* (“if anything”). The Saint-Gilles note identifies the monastery and its sources and cautiously records Franco as a possible unconfirmed/short-lived Kruszwica bishop during the interdict.
- **Letter heading/address:** 3 *Polonie* (“of Poland”) for *Poloniensis* (“Polish”), *S. Egidio* (“to Saint Giles”) for *Sancti Egidii* (“of Saint Giles”), and adds *capitulum* (“chapter”) after the brethren. O. is Odilo, then abbot (Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini* V.128).
- **31:** 1–3 omit the numeral “31”; 1–2 retain *capitulum* (“chapter”), 3 omits it. 2 *uti* (“to use”; the note tentatively construes *navitate*) after an unexplained siglum; a later hand adds *donacioni* (“to the donation”) after *Bolezlavi*. Semler proposes *sua* (“their own”) or *gratias* (“thanks”) after *mittenti munera* (“to the one sending gifts”). 3 corrupt *miptencium* for *mittentium* (“of those sending”), *adimplent* (“they fulfil”) for *adimpleret* (“might fulfil”), and *et* (“and”) for *atque* (“and also”); 1 had *exdilataret* (“might spread out”) before *ex* was deleted, while 2 retains it. The long note gives the named Saint-Giles foundations and its cited Kłodawa/Bel evidence.
- **Closing verses:** 3 *materie* (“material,” ablative/spelling form) for *materiei* (“of material”), and *pro* (“for”) for *de* (“from/about”). The source verse is retained as printed: “For a boy, make a boy; for the false, make the true; fashion the fleshly one, keeping the material one for yourself.”

### Book Two: epistle and epilogue

- **Address:** 3 *suo quoque* (“his also”) for *suoque* (“and his”); 2 *imitende*, 3 *imitande*, for *immittendae* (“to be sent/undertaken”). *paternae venerationis* means “of paternal reverence,” not filial reverence.
- **Opening:** 3 omits *Meditanti mihi de plurimis* (“As I reflected on many things”) and leaves a blank. 2–3 *caritatis* for *karitatis* (“charity,” spelling). 2 *humatus* (“buried”) for *humanitus* (“humanly”); 3 *pietatis* (“piety”) for *probitatis* (“uprightness”); 2 *tarde* (“slowly”) for *tarda* (“slow”); 1–2 *facultate* (“by/with ability”) for *facultas* (“ability”). 3 *petunt* (“they ask”) for *potest* (“can”), omits *tunc* (“then”), and all three give corrupt *juste* (“justly”) for *injuste* (“unjustly”); the corruption must not reverse the sense.
- **Praise:** 2 repeats *Licet enim* (“Although indeed”); 3 *preciosis* (“precious”) for *speciosis* (“beautiful”), 2 *verietate* for *varietate* (“variety”), corrupt *magni aaau* for *operis* (“work”), 1–2 *insereatur* (“is inserted”) for *misceatur* (“is blended”). 3 omits *suis* (“its own”) after the ant’s strength; 2 repeats erroneous *vita laudabilis* (“a praiseworthy life”); 3 *existunt* (“they exist/are”) for *existentes* (“being”), 1 and 3 *hominum* (“of men”) for *homini* (“to a man”). 3 *vulnerato* (“to the wounded man”) for *vulnerati* (“of the wounded man”); 2 *oleum desuper* (“oil from above”) and 3 *dei super* (“God above”) for *deinde oleum* (“then oil”). 3 omits *fideliter* (“faithfully”), 2 *abscondit* (“hides”) for *abscondunt* (“they hide”), 3 omits the whole question “Why does a child of scant ability …,” and 2 erroneous repeated *libet* in *quantumlibet* (“however much”). 3 *commendat extollens* (“commends, exalting”) for *commendat excellens* (“eminent [authority] commends”).
- **Epilogue:** 3 *epilogus* (“epilogue,” nominative) for *epilogum* (accusative). Its fragment replaces the lines from “It is no wonder …” through “It was time to rest.” It has *a* (“from”) for *de* (“from/about”) in *a sompno* (“from sleep”), all three *qui* (“who”) for *quod* (“which/that”), and 2 *minus* (“less”) for *nimis* (“too much”). The final heading is *Tertii Bolezlavi primo de nativitate* (“First, concerning the birth of Bolesław III”); 3 omits *primo de nativitate* (“first, concerning the birth”).

Thus the boy Bolesław was born on the feast-day of Saint Stephen the King [Note: [Col. 0878D] This appears to be an error: the day of Stephen the King was 20 August, that of Stephen the Protomartyr 26 December. Cosmas, II.36, relates that Judith gave birth on 23 December and died on 25 December. K.] (A.D. 1085, 23 December). His mother, however, subsequently fell ill and died on the night of the Lord’s Nativity (25 December). Before the day of her death especially, this woman performed works of piety toward the poor and captives, and with her own resources redeemed many Christians from enslavement by the Jews. After her death, Duke Władysław—because he was a serious man and infirm [Note: [Col. 0877] “and weak,” 3.] in his feet, and had a very small child [Note: [Col. 0877] “a small child,” 1, 2, 3, erroneously; read *parvulum*, namely “a small son.”]—betrothed in marriage the sister [Note: [Col. 0878D] Likewise Judith. K.] of Emperor Henry III, formerly the wife of Solomon, king of Hungary [Note: [Col. 0877] “in marriage” omitted by 3.]. By her he begot no son but three daughters [Col. 0878C] [Note: [Col. 0877] “generated,” 3.]: one of them married a husband in Rusʹ; another [Note: [Col. 0877] “the other,” 3.] covered her head with the sacred veil; while a certain man of her own people married one [Note: [Col. 0877] “but the third,” in place of “while one,” 3.].

But lest we pass over the father of so great a boy in bare words, let us clothe him in some adornment of military achievement. Thus Duke Władysław of the Poles, related by marriage to the emperor of the Romans, triumphed over the Pomeranians—with his own men coming to his aid—by besieging their stronghold [Note: [Col. 0878D] The unpublished Cracow Polish Annals place this battle under the year 1090 and call the place Psechen; it seems to be modern Pszczew, Betsche, near Międzyrzecz, Meseritz. S. Later writers believe that this occurred in 1091. K.]. Trampling their obstinacy beneath his feet [Note: [Col. 0877] Omitted by 1, 2.], he destroyed it; and the Assumption of the Mother of God [Note: [Col. 0877] “of God” omitted by 3.] brought forth the joy of this victory (A.D. 1090, 15 August). Having defeated them, he violently occupied their cities and boroughs inland and along [Note: [Col. 0877] Added by a corrector in 2; omitted by 3.] the coast [Col. 0879A], and stationed his own *vastaldiones* and counts in the chief [Note: [Col. 0879] “more principal,” 3.] and best-fortified places. And because he wished entirely to cut off the pagans’ confidence in rising again through treachery, he ordered his own commanders, on a specified day and at an appointed hour, to burn all the fortifications in the heart of the realm [Note: [Col. 0879] “of the land,” 3.]. This was accordingly [Note: [Col. 0879] “thus,” 3.] done [Note: [Col. 0879] “was,” 2.]. Yet not even so could the rebellious people be subdued. For those whom Setheus [Note: [Col. 0879] “Szeczecheus,” 3.] had set over them [Note: [Col. 0879] “was setting over them,” 3.], and who was then commander of the army [Note: [Col. 0879] “was” omitted by 3.], they partly killed in requital for their wrongs; but the more noble men, who had conducted themselves more wisely and honourably, scarcely escaped with the approval [Note: [Col. 0879] “consent,” 3.] of their friends [Note: [Col. 0879] “put to flight,” 3.].

## 2. On the war with the Pomeranians

[Note: [Col. 0879] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 134; the manuscripts have none, but continue after a space from the preceding chapter.]

But Duke Władysław, recalling the injury inflicted upon his people [Note: [Col. 0879] “such an injury,” 2.], entered their land with a strong force before Lent, and there observed much of the fast. [Col. 0879B] When he had completed a very great part of the fast there, he unexpectedly entered Stettin [Note: [Col. 0879] Thus I emended it. P.; absent in 3; “highest,” 1, 2. *Stetin* and *summi* are written with the same strokes.], a city [Note: [Col. 0879] Absent in 1, 2.] more populous [Note: [Col. 0879] Absent in 2; “foremost in population,” 3.] and wealthier than any in that land (A.D. 1091, 2 March), and from there [Note: [Col. 0879] “there,” 3.] gathered immense plunder and countless captives.

And when he was now returning with his plunder, fearing nothing, and was safely approaching the boundaries of his realm, the Pomeranians suddenly pursued and attacked him upon the river Nakła [Note: [Col. 0879] “a certain [river],” 3; “wave,” 1, 2; clarified by the reading of the *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, which has Nacka or Nakla. Długosz likewise adopted Nakla.] [Note: [Col. 0879C] Władysław’s battle appears indeed to have been fought in the plain near Drezdenko, Driesen; hence Lelewel recommends reading Drzn, not Drzu. But the river at that city is the Noteć, Netze, already called so by Długosz; more similar to the reading of MSS 1 and 2 would be the name of the river Drwa, Drage, which near Drzen—Drezdenko [Col. 0880C]—flows into the river Noteć. S. Compare Barthold, *Geschichte von Rügen und Pommern*, I, 428. K. It is the river Netze. P.], and engaged with him in a bloody and grievous battle on the day before Palm Sunday [Note: [Col. 0879] “Palms,” 1, 2.] (5 April), disastrous to both sides [Note: [Col. 0879] “not grievous,” in place of “and grievous,” 2.]. For that battle began at about the third hour of the day [Note: [Col. 0879] “day,” 1, 2.] and ended at evening twilight [Note: [Col. 0879] “was broken off,” 3.]. At last the Pomeranians [Note: [Col. 0879] “however,” 3.] put on the darkness of night as their defence, while the Poles held the field of victory called Drzu [Note: [Col. 0879] “Drzy,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0880C] Probably modern Drezdenko, Driesen; Długosz has Drizen, I, 321. S.]. For it remained uncertain [Col. 0879C] whether there had been there a slaughter of Christians [Note: [Col. 0879] “forces,” 3.] or of pagans [Note: [Col. 0879] “where,” 2.] [Note: [Col. 0879] “had been,” plural, 3.]. This scourge [Note: [Col. 0879] “Who,” 2.], as we believe, God Almighty inflicted upon those transgressing the observance of Lent [Note: [Col. 0879] “of Lent,” 3.] as a correction [Note: [Col. 0879] “inflicted,” 2.], as he later revealed to certain persons delivered from that very danger. And because, as has been said, the victory was grievous and costly to many, and the day of the Lord’s Resurrection [Note: [Col. 0879] “Reservation,” 3.] was drawing near (13 April), the counsel of those urging pursuit was overcome by the wiser course of returning.

## 3. Siege of the fortress of Nakło

[Note: [Col. 0879] “Siege of the fortress of Nakło” is not in the manuscripts; it is the heading of the Warsaw edition, p. 136.]

Likewise, having summoned three battle-lines from Bohemia to his aid [Col. 0880A], Władysław invaded Pomerania about the feast of Saint Michael [Note: [Col. 0879] In place of “having summoned … Władysław invaded about the feast of Saint Michael,” 3 has: “having summoned *inacubilium* [uncertain reading] … Władysław [invaded] about the feast of Saint Michael.”] (29 September). While they were besieging there the fortress [Note: [Col. 0879] Absent in 3.] of Nakyel [Note: [Col. 0879] “Nakel,” 2.] [Note: [Col. 0880C] Nakło, Nackel, on the river Noteć, Netze. S.], unheard-of marvels occurred which every night disturbed them with terrors, armed as though [Note: [Col. 0879] Absent in 2.] they were about to fight enemies. And when they had endured this deception for a long time and wondered more intensely what it might be, one night, roused by their customary fear, they went farther from the camp [Note: [Col. 0879] “fortress,” 3.] and, deceived by a succession of enemies, pursued the night-shadows, seeming to palpitate [Note: [Col. 0879] In place of “night-shadows, seeming to palpitate,” it has “nightly shadows, as though panting.”]. Meanwhile [Note: [Col. 0879] “again,” 2.] the townsmen hastily [Note: [Col. 0879] “hastening,” 1.] descended from [Note: [Col. 0879] Absent in 3.] the ramparts [Note: [Col. 0879] singular “rampart,” 3.] and burned their engines and part of their encampment (A.D. 1091). Thus, when the Poles saw that they had achieved nothing [Note: [Col. 0879] “done,” 3.] and had found no battle, and when a great [Col. 0880B] part of the army, especially the Bohemians, had no provisions [Note: [Col. 0879] “had,” 2.], they returned after expending their labour in vain [Note: [Col. 0879] “returned,” corrupted, 3.].

Thus the Pomeranians gradually raised themselves in pride [Note: [Col. 0879] “into pride,” 3.] against Poland, to be extirpated by the child of Mars [Note: [Col. 0879] “mother,” 2.] whom we portray with the pen. But lest we appear to eviscerate a joyful subject, let us endure the odium arising from misfortunes rather than the disgrace of detraction. Nor should it seem in any way absurd to any discerning person that, in this history, the son of a concubine is introduced alongside the legitimate son. For in the principal history two sons of Abraham are remembered, but they are separated from one another by their father because of discord; both indeed begotten from the seed of the patriarch, yet not both made equal in the right of inheritance.

## 4. On the rebel Zbigniew

[Note: [Col. 0879] “On the rebel Zbigniew” is absent from the manuscripts; it is the heading of the Warsaw edition, p. 138.]

Therefore [Note: [Col. 0879] Absent in 3.] Zbigniew [Note: [Col. 0879] “Zbigeuus,” 2.], born to Duke Władysław by a concubine, was, when he had now reached an age for it, assigned to letters in the city of Cracow [Col. 0880C] [Note: [Col. 0879] “readings,” 2.]; and his stepmother sent him to Saxony to be taught in a convent of nuns [Note: [Col. 0879] “and,” 3.]. At that time the palatine count Setheus [Note: [Col. 0879] “Stephen,” 2; “Szeczeus,” 3.] was a man [Note: [Col. 0879] “a certain” added by 1; “indeed” added by 3.] wise, noble, and handsome, but blinded by avarice, and he practised many cruel and unbearable acts. Some he sold away on a trifling pretext; others he drove from their homeland; and he preferred men of low birth [Note: [Col. 0879] Absent in 3.] to noblemen [Note: [Col. 0879] “set before,” 3.].

Accordingly many [Note: [Col. 0879] “much,” 3.] fled of their own accord, not under compulsion, because they feared that they themselves [Note: [Col. 0879] “the other self,” inserted above the line in the hand of the corrector, 2.] would suffer the same thing without fault. [Col. 0881A] But those who had first been fugitives, wandering in various places, were gathered together in Bohemia by the counsel of Duke Bretislaus [Note: [Col. 0881] “Brzeczlaus,” 3.]. And so [Note: [Col. 0881] “therefore,” 3.] by Bohemian cunning they hired certain men for money, who secretly drew Zbigniew [Note: [Col. 0881] “Sbigneum,” 2.] out of the nuns’ cloister [Note: [Col. 0881] “monastery,” 3.]. Once Zbigniew had been received [Note: [Col. 0881] Absent in 3.], the fugitives in Bohemia sent an embassy in these words [Note: [Col. 0881] “letagacionem,” 2.] to the count of Wrocław named Magnus [Note: [Col. 0881] “Whose,” 3.]:

“We indeed, Count Magnus [Note: [Col. 0881] Absent in 3.], though exiles, endure in whatever way we can the insults of Zetheus; but for you, Magnus—whose title of duke brings you more disgrace [Note: [Col. 0881] “honour,” 1, 2, 3; *dedecori*, ‘disgrace,’ is more correctly found in the *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, ed. Stenzel, p. 65.] than honour—we grieve tearfully [Note: [Col. 0881] “tearfully,” corrupted, 2.], since you possess the burden of rank but not [Note: [Col. 0881] “not,” 3.] its honour, and do not dare to rule over the *pristaldi* [Note: [Col. 0881D] That is, officers of execution. K.] of Zetheus [Note: [Col. 0881] “Zetheus,” 1, 2, 3.]. But if you wish to shake the yoke of slavery from your neck, hasten to receive the boy whom we have as the shield of your defence.”

And the Bohemian duke himself urged all this, since he gladly sowed discord [Col. 0881B] among the Poles. Having heard this, Magnus at first hesitated for a long time; but after consulting and winning the approval of the greater men, he agreed, accepting their words.

> At this deed Władysław,  
> His father, is grieved;  
> But Zetheus with the queen  
> Is disturbed far more.

[Note: [Col. 0881] “And,” 2.]

Therefore they sent an envoy [Note: [Col. 0881] “envoy,” ablative, 3.] to Magnus and the magnates of the region of Wrocław [Note: [Col. 0881] “to Wrocław,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0881] “and the magnates,” 3.], asking what this meant: that they had received Zbigniew [Note: [Col. 0881] “Sbigneum,” 2, 3.] with fugitives without his father’s command, and whether [Note: [Col. 0881] “but,” 1, 2, 3.] they wished to be rebels or to obey him [Note: [Col. 0881] “wished,” 1.]. To this the people of Wrocław unanimously [Note: [Col. 0881] Absent in 3.] replied that they had not handed over their country to Bohemians or [Note: [Col. 0881] “and,” 3.] foreign peoples [Note: [Col. 0881] Absent in 3.] [Col. 0881C], but had received the son of their lord duke and their own fugitives; that they would faithfully obey in all things and in every respect both their lord duke and his legitimate son [Note: [Col. 0881] “his,” 3.] Bolesław [Note: [Col. 0881] “and him,” 3.]; but that they would oppose Setheus and his evil deeds by every means. The people wanted to stone the envoy [Note: [Col. 0881] “to obey” added erroneously by 2, but subsequently deleted.], because he defended Setheus’s party with deceitful evasions [Note: [Col. 0881] Absent in 3.].

Therefore Władysław was greatly [Note: [Col. 0881] “excessively Władysław,” in place of “greatly Władysław,” 3.] angered, and Setheus was exceedingly inflamed with wrath. They summoned King Władysław of Hungary and Duke Bretislaus [Note: [Col. 0881] “Brzeczlaus,” 3.] of Bohemia to aid them against [Note: [Col. 0881] “in,” 3.] the people of Wrocław (A.D. 1093), from which they gained more [Note: [Col. 0881] Absent in 3.] disgrace and loss than honour and advantage [Note: [Col. 0881D] Cosmas, III.1, gives another account. K.]. For King Władysław would have carried Setheus [Note: [Col. 0881] “Zecheum,” 3.] away in chains with him to Hungary [Note: [Col. 0881] “King Władysław” absent in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0881] Absent in 3.], had he not fled for safety with little Bolesław [Col. 0881D] [Note: [Col. 0881] “for” absent in 2.]. And since they could accomplish nothing by force against the people of Wrocław [Col. 0882A] [Note: [Col. 0881] “not,” 3.], because they were unwilling to wage war against their own people, the father reluctantly made peace with his son, and then for the first time called him his son.

Meanwhile Setheus, having returned from Poland [Note: [Col. 0881] “from the place”; the *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, ed. Stenzel, p. 66.], to which he had fled, cunningly tested the leading men among them with promises and gifts, and gradually bent them [Note: [Col. 0881] “them,” 1, 2.] to his side. Finally, when he had won over many, Duke Władysław approached the city of Wrocław with an army [Note: [Col. 0881] “approaches,” 3.], and was already taking possession of the surrounding forts that had been surrendered to him. Zbigniew, seeing that the nobles had failed him both within and without, realizing grimly [Note: [Col. 0881] “dreadfully,” 2.] that he had kicked against the goad, and mistrusting the loyalty of the common people and his own life, fled by night; and in his flight he entered the fortress of Kruszwica [Note: [Col. 0881] “Cruszwicz,” 3, and it always observes this spelling.], rich in soldiers, having been received by the townsmen.

## 5. The capture and destruction of the fortress of Kruszwica

[Note: [Col. 0881] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 144; absent from the manuscripts. MSS 1 and 2 insert a space, but continue without beginning a new chapter.]

But his father, grieved that he had thus escaped unpunished and that the people of Kruszwica had received him against himself, pursued the fleeing Zbigniew [Note: [Col. 0881] “fleeing,” 3.] with the same army and attacked the fortress of Kruszwica with all his strength. Zbigniew, however, having summoned [Note: [Col. 0881] “mingled,” 3.] a multitude of pagans and having seven battle-lines of men of Kruszwica, came out from the fortress and fought against his father [Note: [Col. 0881] “peace,” 2, 3.]. But the just Judge judged between father and son. There indeed a war more than civil [Note: [Col. 0882D] Lucan, *Pharsalia*, I.1. K.] was waged, in which son bore impious arms against father, and brother against brother. There, I hope, wretched Zbigniew earned by his father’s curse what was to come; but there God Almighty showed Duke Władysław such mercy that he slew an innumerable multitude of enemies [Col. 0882C], while death took from his own men very few.

So much human blood was shed, and so many corpses fell into the lake [Note: [Col. 0881] “into the lake” absent in 3.] adjoining the fortress, that from that time onward every good Christian recoiled from eating fish from those waters. Thus Kruszwica, formerly rich [Note: [Col. 0881] “at first,” 3.] in wealth and soldiers, was reduced almost to desolation. Zbigniew therefore fled into the fortress and was saved with very few [Note: [Col. 0881] “is” added by 3.], uncertain whether he would lose his life [Note: [Col. 0881] Absent in 1, 2.] or some limb. But his father, not avenging the folly of youth—fearing lest he should attach himself to pagans or foreign peoples, whence [Note: [Col. 0881] “one,” 1, 2, 3; we have adopted Bandtkie’s reading.] greater danger might threaten—granted him, upon faith being sought and pledged, safety of life and limbs [Note: [Col. 0881] “granted,” 3.]. He took him with him into Mazovia and for some time wore him down by imprisonment in Setheus’s fortress [Col. 0882D]. Later, at the consecration [Col. 0883A] of the church of Gniezno, he summoned him at the intervention of bishops and princes [Note: [Col. 0883] “to,” 2.], and through their prayers Zbigniew regained the favour which he had lost [Note: [Col. 0883] “and in their sight,” in place of “through their prayers,” 3.].

## 6. Miracle of Saint Adalbert

[Note: [Col. 0883] Heading in MS 3; absent in 1 and 2.]
