And since mention of the church of Gniezno has perhaps [Note: [Col. 0883] “perhaps” added in the margin by 2.] happened to be made here [Note: [Col. 0883] “was made here,” in place of “has happened to be made,” 3.], it is not fitting to pass over the miracle [Note: [Col. 0883D] Sallust, *Jugurthine War*, 79. S.] which [Note: [Col. 0883] Absent in 3.] the precious martyr Adalbert showed on the vigil of its dedication, both to [Note: [Col. 0883] “from,” 3.] pagans and to [Note: [Col. 0883] “from” added by 3.] Christians.

It happened on that same night that certain Pomeranians, traitors of a certain Polish fortress, were hauled up by ropes [Note: [Col. 0883] “boundaries,” 3.] into that fortress, and, once received, waited in the ramparts [Note: [Col. 0883] “the next day,” 3.] for the next day, to destroy the townsmen [Note: [Col. 0883] “the townsmen,” 1, 2.]. But [Note: [Col. 0883] “But,” 3.] he who always watches and never sleeps guarded the sleeping townsmen through the vigilance of his warrior Adalbert [Col. 0883B], and spiritual terror of arms disturbed the pagans lying awake in ambush against Christians [Note: [Col. 0883] Absent in 1, 2.] [Note: [Col. 0883] “Christ,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0883] “the terror of spiritual arms” absent in 3.]. For there appeared [Note: [Col. 0883] “aeperui,” 2.] to the Pomeranians a certain armed man upon a white horse, who terrified them with a drawn sword and drove them headlong down the steps and from the seat of the fortress [Note: [Col. 0883] “drove,” 3.]. Thus, beyond doubt, the inhabitants of the fortress, roused by the cries and tumult of the pagans, were delivered by the protection of the glorious martyr Adalbert from their imminent peril of death. Let this suffice for the present concerning the saint [Note: [Col. 0883] “suffices,” 1, 2.], and let the course of our writing return [Note: [Col. 0883] “from an interval,” in place of “after an interval,” 3.] to the purpose stated above [Note: [Col. 0883] “be begun,” 3.].

## 7. On the division of the kingdom between the two sons

[Note: [Col. 0883] Heading in MS 3; absent in 1 and 2.]

Therefore, after the basilica [Note: [Col. 0883] “church,” 3.] of Gniezno [Note: [Col. 0883] “of Gniezno,” 1, 2.] had been consecrated and Zbigniew had obtained his father’s favour, Duke Władysław entrusted his army to both sons and [Note: [Col. 0883] Absent in 2.] sent them on an expedition into Pomerania [Col. 0883C]. But after setting out, and having adopted some counsel of which I know not the nature, they returned from the journey with the enterprise unfinished. Therefore their father, suspecting something, immediately divided the kingdom between them (A.D. 1097), though he did not relinquish from his own hand the principal seats of the realm. But it would be burdensome for us to enumerate what fell to each in the division, nor would hearing it be very profitable to you [Note: [Col. 0883] “But what would be profitable” is absent in 3.].

## 8. Further arrangement of this division

[Note: [Col. 0883] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 130; MSS 1 and 2 leave a space, while 3 does not interrupt the thread of the narrative.]

When the father was asked by the princes which of the two excelled more in sending and receiving embassies [Note: [Col. 0883] “dispatching,” 2.], in summoning and leading an army, and in the manifold administration of so great a kingdom, he is said to have replied [Col. 0883D]:

“It is mine, as a man old and infirm, to divide the kingdom between them and judge concerning present matters [Col. 0884A]. But to prefer one to the other [Note: [Col. 0883] “preferring,” 3.], or to give them worth and wisdom, lies not within my power but within divine power [Note: [Col. 0883] “will,” 3.]. Yet I can disclose to you this one desire of my heart: that, after my death, you should all unanimously obey the one who is more discerning and more worthy in defending the land and attacking its enemies. Meanwhile each is to retain his own share [Note: [Col. 0883] “power,” 1.] of the kingdom divided between them. After my death Zbigniew is to hold Mazovia together with what he has; but Bolesław, my legitimate son, is to possess the chief seats of the kingdom in Wrocław [Note: [Col. 0883] “Wrocław,” 3.] and Cracow and Sandomierz [Note: [Col. 0883] “Sudomir,” 2.] [Note: [Col. 0883] “will possess,” 3.]. Finally, if both should not prove worthy, or if by chance they should be at variance:

> He who shall ally himself with foreign [Note: [Col. 0883] “more outward,” 2.] nations  
> [Col. 0884B] And bring them in for the destruction of the realm,  
> Let him be deprived of the kingdom and lack the right of inheritance;  
> But let him possess the throne of the kingdom by perpetual law  
> Who shall provide better for the land’s honour and advantage.”

[Note: [Col. 0883] “Finally … advantage” is absent in 3.]

When, as stated [Note: [Col. 0883] “once accomplished,” 2; “this,” in place of “as stated,” 3.], the division of the kingdom had been made and the father’s sufficiently eloquent speech delivered [Note: [Col. 0883] “the father’s sufficiently eloquent speech” is absent in 3.], each of the boys [Note: [Col. 0883] 3 transposes “the boys” and “each.”] visited his portion [Note: [Col. 0883] “part,” 3.] of the kingdom, while their [Note: [Col. 0883] “and their,” in place of “while their,” 3.] father preferred always to live in his own Mazovia.

## 9. On Bolesław’s boyhood

[Note: [Col. 0883] MS 3 omits this whole chapter.]  
[Note: [Col. 0883] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 152; absent in 1, 2, 3.]

Meanwhile, let no one find it in any way [Note: [Col. 0883] “in any way,” 1.] surprising if we record anything memorable about Bolesław’s childhood. For, unlike the childish wantonness usually found, he did not pursue empty games, but strove, insofar as a boy could, to imitate vigorous [Col. 0884C] and martial deeds. And although noble boys commonly delight in dogs and birds, Bolesław, while still a little boy, found greater joy in warfare. For he was not yet able by his own strength to mount or dismount from a horse, and already [Note: [Col. 0883] “also,” 1.]—against his father’s will, or sometimes without his knowledge—he himself took the lead as commander on expeditions against the enemy.

## 10. Zeczech and Bolesław devastated Moravia

[Note: [Col. 0883] Heading in the Gdańsk edition; absent in 1, 2, 3.]

Now let us depict a certain beginning of his [Note: [Col. 0883] “of the boy Bolesław,” 3, because it omitted the preceding chapter.] boyish military career, and so gradually pass from lesser matters to greater. As is known, Duke Władysław, weighed down by old age and years, entrusted his army [Note: [Col. 0883] “exercise,” 2.] to the palatine count Setheus [Note: [Col. 0883] “Zachero,” 3.] and sent him out to fight or to ravage enemy lands. [Col. 0884D] Therefore, when he was about to invade Moravia [Note: [Col. 0883] “Moria,” 2.], the little boy went with him, a combatant in name alone (A.D. 1094). [Col. 0885A] On that occasion they devastated the greater part of Moravia, carried away much plunder and captives [Note: [Col. 0885] “led away,” 3.], and returned without the hazard either of battle or journey.

## 11. The boy Bolesław killed a boar

[Note: [Col. 0885] Heading in the Gdańsk edition, p. 83; absent in 1, 2, 3.]

I might write at length about this boy’s boldness, were it not that the time now urges me to hasten toward the conclusion of the work. Yet [Note: [Col. 0885] “when,” 2.] I shall not permit one event to remain hidden, since it deserves to shine as an example of worth. Once the child of Mars, seated at breakfast [Note: [Col. 0885] “little meal,” 2.] in the forest, saw a huge boar passing by and entering the thickness of the wood. Immediately rising from the table, he took up a hunting-spear and rashly pursued and attacked it without companion or dog. When he had come near the wild beast and was about to strike at its throat [Col. 0885B], a certain one of his knights met him from the opposite direction, restrained the blow already poised, and tried to take the hunting-spear from him. Then [Note: [Col. 0885] “when,” 3.] Bolesław, spurred by anger—or rather by boldness—marvellously overcame a double contest, human and bestial alike, by himself: he took the spear from the man and killed the boar. Later that knight, when questioned why he had done this, declared that he did not know what he had done; yet for this he was excluded from Bolesław’s favour for a long time. The boy returned from there exhausted, and yet, though panting, scarcely retained his strength [Note: [Col. 0885] “strength” absent in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0885] “etc.” added by 3.].

## 12. Bolesław killed a bear

[Note: [Col. 0885] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 156; absent in 1, 2, 3.]

Nor shall I be silent about another similar boyish deed of his, although I know that I shall not please hostile persons [Note: [Col. 0885] “exiles,” 2.] in every respect [Note: [Col. 0885] “although I know … in every respect” is absent in 3.]. The same [Note: [Col. 0885] “indeed” added by 3.] boy was walking in the forest with a few companions [Col. 0885C] when he happened to stop in a high place; looking down this way and that, he caught sight of a huge bear sporting with a she-bear [Note: [Col. 0885] “sporting,” infinitive, 2, 3.]. At once, having forbidden the others to follow, he went down into the plain and, alone and fearless, seated on horseback, approached the bloodthirsty beasts [Note: [Col. 0885] “wild beasts,” 3.], and pierced with his hunting-spear the bear as it turned against him with raised forelegs. This deed was sufficiently wonderful to those present and worthy of recounting to those absent because of the boy’s great boldness.

## 13. Bolesław makes incursions into enemy territory

[Note: [Col. 0885] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 157; absent in 1, 2, 3.]

Meanwhile Bolesław, the martial boy, grew in strength and years; nor did he, as boyhood commonly does [Note: [Col. 0885] “age,” 2.], give attention to luxury or frivolities [Note: [Col. 0885D] Sallust, *Jugurthine War*, 61. S.]. Rather, whenever he learned that enemies were carrying off plunder, he hastened energetically there with youths of his own age [Col. 0885D] [Note: [Col. 0885] “companions of the same age,” 2; “peers,” 3.], and often secretly [Note: [Col. 0885] “mostly,” 2.] entered enemy territory [Col. 0886A] with a few men, burned villages, and brought back captives and plunder. Already, though a boy in years, he held the duchy of Wrocław as an old man in merit; yet he had not attained martial joy [Note: [Col. 0885] “martial,” accusative, 1, 2.]. Therefore, because hope of a youth of good natural disposition was springing up in him [Note: [Col. 0885] “sprang up,” 3.], and a great [Note: [Col. 0885] Absent in 3.] sign of military glory was already appearing in him, all the princes loved him, for they judged that something great would come to be in him.

## 14. Bolesław attacks the Pomeranians

[Note: [Col. 0885] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 158; absent in 1, 2, 3.]

This same little boy, begotten of Mars’s offspring [Note: [Col. 0885] “in artistry,” incorrectly, 2.], once rode against Pomerania, where he made the fame of his name more plainly known. For he besieged the fortress of Międzyrzecz [Note: [Col. 0885] “Meczirzieczye,” 2; “medzyrzecz,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0885D] Międzyrzecz, German Meseritz, in the Grand Duchy of Poznań. S. You defended another opinion, Giesebrecht, *Wendische Geschichte*, II, 165. K.] with such forces and assaulted it with such violence [Note: [Col. 0885] “with such violence he assaulted it” absent in 3.] that [Note: [Col. 0885] “in” added by 3.] within a few days [Col. 0886B] he compelled the townsmen [Note: [Col. 0885] “to” added by 3.] to surrender [Note: [Col. 0885] “forced,” in place of “compelled,” 3.]. There also [Note: [Col. 0885] “There also” to the end of the chapter is absent in 3.] the steward Woyslaw received on the crown of his head such a mark of boldness that scarcely could the skilful work of a physician save him after his bones had been extracted.

## 15. How he conducted war in Pomerania

[Note: [Col. 0885] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 159; absent in 1, 2, 3.]

Returning from there, he allowed his soldiers a little rest, then at once led them back to that place. Desiring to subdue the land of the barbarians, the industrious boy did not first attempt to carry off plunder or make burnings, but planned to seize or destroy their fortifications and cities [Note: [Col. 0885] The beginning of the chapter through “planned” is omitted by 3.]. Thus, advancing at a swift pace, he attacked a certain [Note: [Col. 0885] “Another likewise,” in place of “Thus, at a swift pace, a certain,” 3.] fortress, quite noble and [Note: [Col. 0885] “and,” 3.] strong, intending to besiege it [Note: [Col. 0885] “at a swift pace” added here by 3.]. It nevertheless did not withstand his first assault; he carried off much plunder and many captives from it, and reduced its warriors to military obedience [Note: [Col. 0885] “reduces,” 1.]. And the more [Note: [Col. 0885] “And the more” to the end of the chapter is absent in 3.] he ought to have been loved [Col. 0886C], the more he accumulated envy against himself and provoked the enemies’ plots for his destruction.

## 16. Plots of Zetheus

[Note: [Col. 0885] This entire chapter is absent in 3.]  
[Note: [Col. 0885] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 160; absent in 1, 2.]

Source preparation: The canonical supplied local archive text was used directly; no recoveries were required.

Meanwhile Zetheus, as they report, was laying many snares for the boys themselves and, by many contrivances, turning their father’s mind away from affection for his sons. In the strongholds assigned to the boys’ shares he also placed counts or *pristaldi*—men of his own rank or lower—who were to rule there; and with crafty cunning he induced these men to disobey the boys.

He was indeed a hostile plotter against both brothers, but he feared Boleslav more: legitimate, keen-minded, and destined to reign after his father, he threatened Zetheus’s own ruin. The brothers had joined themselves by oath [Col. 0886D]—MS 2 reads *conjunxarint*—and had made a compact between them [Col. 0885: MS 2 reads *facerint*]: [Col. 0887A] if Zetheus plotted against either of them, the other would come to his brother’s aid with all his strength and brook no delay.

It happened, whether through trickery or through the truth of the matter, that Duke Wladislav told the boy Boleslav that he had heard from scouts that the Bohemians were about to enter Poland and carry off booty—MS 1 reads *introaturos*—and that Boleslav therefore ought to hasten to an appointed place and summon to his aid the counts of his duchy whom Zetheus had placed over them and in whom the boy had no confidence.

Trusting his father’s commands, the boy proceeded hastily and without any suspicion toward the appointed place with his companions—MS 2 reads *collateribus* for *collateralibus*, and *festinans* for *festinus*—but Count Woyslav, to whose charge he had been entrusted, did not go with him. Thus they whispered to one another, suspecting this to be a sign of betrayal [Col. 0887B]:

“You are not without cause in danger, since your father has ordered you to go to a deserted place and there summon to your aid the household members and friends of Zetheus, who are plotting against your life. For we know and are certain that Zetheus is striving by every means to destroy your whole lineage, and especially you, as heir to the kingdom, so that he alone may retain all Poland, once he has brought it under his hand. Moreover, Count Woyslav, to whose charge we have been entrusted and who is related to Zetheus, would undoubtedly have come with us, unless he had learned that some plot was being devised against us—MS 1 reads *in* for *ni*. It is therefore necessary that we find some plan as quickly as possible by which we may escape this danger hanging over us.”

At these words the boy Boleslav was exceedingly afraid and was drenched all over with streaming sweat [Col. 0887C]. Having therefore adopted a sufficiently suitable plan, they swiftly sent an agreed sign to Zbignev, in a manner appropriate to childish ingenuity, asking him to hasten with his men to their aid. They themselves immediately returned to the city of Wrocław, lest they be forestalled by the snares of their adversary.

[Col. 0887: The words below concerning the people of Wrocław were mistakenly inserted here; the copyist later deleted them with a transverse line: “touched inwardly by grief of heart, he was silent for a little while, and immediately bursting forth...”]

The boy Boleslav, having returned, first summoned the leading men and elders of the city—MSS 1 and 2 read *civitates*—then the whole people, to an assembly; and he tearfully related to them, in order and like a child, the snares he was suffering from Zetheus. As they in turn wept out of pity for the boy and hurled words of indignation and disgrace against the absent Zetheus—MSS 1 and 2 read *urbem*—Zbignev arrived hastily with a few men, the multitude not yet assembled—MS 2 reads *non cum* for *nondum*. Being educated and older in years, he rhetorically embellished his brother’s speech and vigorously stirred the tumultuous people to loyalty toward his brother and opposition to Zetheus, with the following eloquent address—MS 1 and 2 have *luculentam racione*, here corrected:

“If the inviolable steadfastness of your loyalty, citizens, had not been known and proved to our ancestors and to us, though we are but children, the weakness of our youthful age—assailed by such calamities and harassed by so many factions of enemies—would never have placed all hope of refuge and counsel in you. But it is well known to foreign nations and to our neighbors that you have suffered much because of plots against our lives [Col. 0887: MSS 1 and 2 read *vestre*], devised by those who strive utterly to destroy the succession of our lineage and perversely to distort the inheritance of our natural lords.

“Therefore, since our father, now worn out by age and infirmity, has less strength to provide for himself, for us, or for the country, it is necessary that, relying upon our own protection, we either perish through the rejoicing of the ambitious or the crimes of evildoers, or flee into exile beyond the borders of Poland. Therefore deign to reveal your intention to us: whether we may remain or must leave our country.”

[Col. 0887D: The citation is Sallust, *Catiline* 20.]

At this the whole multitude of Wrocław, inwardly touched by grief of heart, was silent for a little while—MSS 1 and 2 read *convenit* for *conquievit*—then immediately burst into speech and unanimously, with pious feeling, declared the intention conceived in their minds:

“We wish indeed to keep faith with our natural lord, your father, as long as he lives—MSS 1 and 2 read *vixit*, but sense and rhythm require *vixerit*—nor shall we fail his offspring while life remains to us. Therefore have no distrust of us; but gather an army, hasten armed to your father’s court, and there, with due reverence for your father, avenge your wrong.”

While these things were being said and confirmed by the citizens with an oath, Count Woyslav, who was rearing the boy Boleslav, came from his service [Col. 0888C] and did not know what had happened. Because of his kinship with Zetheus he was suspected of treachery and was forbidden to enter the city or to make provision for the boy’s affairs. Though he offered an explanation, declaring that he had known nothing if any dispute had arisen, and wished to make satisfaction, the people did not then receive him or accept his following—MS 2 reads *tempus* for *temporis*—but went out to meet the father with the assembled multitude.

Thus Duke Wladislav and his sons, separated from their father, encamped with their armies at the place called Zarnowyecz [Col. 0887: MS 1 reads *Sarnovuecz*; MS 2 allows *Czarnowyecz*]. This was by the river Noteć, or Netze, not at Czarnków, as Stenzel maintains in *Chronica principum Poloniae*, p. 68, note 1 [Col. 0887D–0888D].

There, disputing with one another for a long time through envoys, they at last scarcely compelled the old man, by the counsels of the magnates and the threats of the young men, to dismiss Zetheus. They also say that the father there swore to his sons that thereafter he would never restore him to his former dignity.

As Zetheus fled to the stronghold bearing his name, the brothers went humbly, unarmed, and peaceably to their father. They offered him their obedience, not as lords but as soldiers or servants, with bowed minds [Col. 0889A] and necks. Thus father, sons, and all the magnates being united, they followed the fleeing Zetheus to the castle he had built, with the whole army.

While they were trying to pursue him and drive him from the land, the duke himself, one night, when he was thought to be resting in his bed, secretly left the army without any of his followers knowing, except three attendants—MS 2 has an evidently corrupt reading, *exre eriens*. Crossing the Vistula in a little boat, he went over to Zetheus on the opposite bank.

Thereupon all the magnates, indignant, declared that to abandon his sons and so many princes with the army was not the act of a wise man but the counsel of one out of his mind. Having immediately taken counsel, they decreed—MS 1, 2, and 3 omit *consilio*, though the *Chronica principum Poloniae*, p. 68, correctly supplies it—that Boleslav should occupy Sandomierz—Sandomierz was the chief city of the principality of that name, situated on the Vistula—and Kraków, the principal and nearest seats of the kingdom, and, after receiving their fealty, hold them under his lordship; while Zbignev [Col. 0889B] should hasten against Masovia—MS 2 reads *Moraviam*—and seize the city of Płock and the neighboring region.

Boleslav did indeed occupy and hold the aforesaid seats; but Zbignev, forestalled by his father, could not carry out his undertaking. But why do we prolong so long the final outcome of Zetheus’s faction? If we were to describe each hardship in Zetheus’s dissension—MSS 1 and 2 read *dispensiones*—we should doubtless make Zetheus’s deeds equal to the volume on Jugurtha—MSS 1 and 2 have *igurtino* for *Jugurtino*. Yet, lest we seem foolish or idle, let us proceed a little farther along the path we have begun.

Again, at another time, the boy princes summoned an army and placed their military camp opposite the city of Płock, on the other side of the Vistula. There also Archbishop Martin, a faithful old man, with great labor and great caution mitigated the anger and discord between father and [Col. 0889C] sons. There likewise Duke Wladislav, as they say, again confirmed by oath that he would never henceforth retain Zetheus. Then Boleslav restored to his father the seats he had occupied, nor did the father keep the agreement made with his sons.

At length the boys compelled the old man, and meanwhile fulfilled their desire by driving Zetheus out of Poland—MS 2 reads *quia* for *quod*; the reference is to the boys themselves [Col. 0889D].

How this happened, however, or how he returned from exile, would be lengthy and tedious to explain; but let it suffice to say that afterward he was not permitted to exercise any authority.

## 17. On the Pomeranian stronghold destroyed of its own accord

[Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 168; absent from MSS 1, 2, and 3.]

Let what has been said thus far about Zetheus and the queen suffice. Now let the tempered pen advance the purpose of its undertaking concerning the boy devoted to Mars. [The reading *coeptae* appears preferable, agreeing with *intentionis*; MSS 1, 2, and 3 read *cepto*. MSS 3 omits the words “Let what has been said about Zetheus ... advance.”]

These matters having been completed, behold: word came to them that the Pomeranians had [Col. 0890A] gone out and had erected opposite Zantok a fortress—the safeguard and key of the kingdom. Zantok was on the Warta, between Driesen and Landsberg. [The note identifies Zantok as *Zanthok*, on the Warta.] The new fortress was so high and so near the Christians that what was said and done in Zantok could plainly be both heard and seen by the pagans. [MSS 3 omits this entire sentence.]

Therefore Zbignev, since he was older and held the part of the kingdom nearest to the Pomeranians and to his father—MS 3 has “Zbignev, however, since he was older by birth”—hastened against the Pomeranians with his father’s army and his own, without his little brother. Yet the elder brother, advancing with many men, gained less praise than the younger brother who followed with few—MS 3 reverses *suo patrisque* as “his own and his father’s.”

For the elder, having hurried there—MS 2 reads *proparens*—neither bravely assaulted that new fortification nor provoked the enemy to battle despite his great force; rather, more afraid than feared, as they say—MSS 3 omit *ut aiunt*—he returned home [Col. 0890B].

But when the boy Boleslav, son of Mars, arrived after his elder brother’s departure, although he was not yet girded with the sword, he achieved more there by commanding than his elder brother, sword in hand, had achieved by holding it.

For, by storming the bridge,

he took it from the garrison;

and, pressing onward to the gate,

he brought in his men’s swords.

[MS 3 has a corrupt reading at *pontem*, apparently *po oe*.]

This beginning of Boleslav’s military service was for the Christians a sign of the great prowess he would display in the future; and it brought even upon the Pomeranians a great portent and terror of their destruction. [MS 3 omits “a great sign of his future destruction.”]

They taunted Zbignev, who came with a multitude and did nothing manly—MSS 1, 2, and 3 read *veniente*—with cowardice; but they called Boleslav, who later came with few men and boldly attacked his enemies [Col. 0890C] even to the gates—MS 3 has *portam*—“the son of a wolf.”

“Zbignev,” they said, “ought, like a cleric, to govern a church; but this little boy, as is evident, is suited to soldiering in strenuous deeds—MS 1 reads *strenuus*.”

Thus the younger brother, gradually advancing with few men, acquired more honor and praise than the elder, who had hastened forward with great force and a great multitude. Therefore, seeing the boy returning with few men, the pagans feared the ruin impending if he should return with many. They themselves destroyed the fortress they had built and, their labor wasted, sought hiding places of safety.

## 18. On the military belt offered to Boleslav by his father after the defeat of the Pomeranians

[Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 172; absent from MSS 1, 2, and 3.]

Seeing, then, that Wladislav’s son flourished in age, excelled in military deeds, and pleased all the wise men of the kingdom, Wladislav resolved to gird him with the sword on the feast of the Assumption of Saint Mary (15 August 1099) and prepared magnificent equipment in the city of Płock. [For the year, see Cosmas III.9 and Giesebrecht, *Wendische Geschichte* II, 166.]

For he was already growing old through age and continual infirmity, and placed his hope of succession in that boy. While all were making ready and hastening to the feast, word came that the Pomeranians had besieged the fortress of Zantok—MS 1 and 2 read *Zutok*—nor did any of the princes dare oppose them—MSS 1 and 2 have *audebat*.

Therefore, against his father’s will and despite many prohibitions, the boy devoted to Mars rushed thither and triumphed over the Pomeranians. Returning thus as a victorious squire, he was girded with the sword by his father and celebrated the festival amid immense rejoicing. Nor was he alone that day girded with the military belt; out of love and honor for his son, the father gave arms to many of his son’s contemporaries.

## 19. On the defeated Plauci

[That is, the Pechenegs. Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 173; absent from MSS 1, 2, and 3.]

Boleslav having thus newly been made a knight, God revealed in the case of the Plauci how great were the things He would accomplish through him in the future. It happened that, shortly after he had been girded with the military belt, innumerable Plauci gathered together—MS 2 erroneously adds *convenire*, marking it with points beneath—and intended, according to their custom, to range through Poland. Divided into three or four groups, separated at some distance from one another—MS 1 reads *sejunctas*—they swam across the Vistula by night.

At daybreak of the following day—MSS 1 and 2 omit *diei*—they ranged about at full speed—MS 3 adds *velocius*—and took countless spoils. Laden with plunder, they returned toward evening across the river and there, secure and weary, set up shelters for the night’s rest—MS 3 reads *quieti* for *quietis*. But they did not rest as safely as they had formerly been accustomed to do—MSS 1 and 2 have *sveverunt*.

For God, protector of Christians and avenger who keeps watch over His own, stirred up the courage of a few faithful men to the destruction of many pagans. When these men attacked, He triumphed on the Lord’s Day, in the glory of His power—MSS 2 and 3 vary the word order as “in the glory of the Lord’s Day.” From that time the Plauci were so astonished that, while Boleslav reigned, they did not dare to see Poland.

## 20. Prophecy concerning Boleslav

[MS 3 omits this entire chapter. Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 175; absent from MSS 1 and 2.]

It also happened that a certain saying was uttered by someone at the council concerning the military girding, and it is worthy of inclusion under the title of our account. [Eight line manuscripts place two strokes above the lines; perhaps they should be read as a proverb, for the author calls such sayings worthy of remembrance.]

“Lord Duke Wladislav,” said that man, “the merciful God has today visited the kingdom of Poland; through this boy, made a knight today, He has exalted your old age and infirmity and the whole country. Blessed is the mother who has reared such a boy! Until now Poland has been trampled by enemies [Col. 0892A], but through this little boy it will be restored as it was of old—MS 1 and 2 read *istum* for *per hunc*.”

At these words all who were present were astonished and signaled him to be silent out of reverence for the duke. We, however, do not believe that this saying proceeded from vanity, but that it came through the spirit of prophecy; for already in his boyish deeds it is proved that Poland will one day be restored to its former condition through him.

## 21. On the death of Wladislav

[Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 176; absent from MSS 1, 2, and 3.]

But for the present let the boy take a little rest from labor while our pen lays Duke Wladislav, a merciful and gentle man, to rest in peace.

Duke Wladislav, remembering the former rebellion, when he drove Zetheus from Poland, although weakened by age and infirmity, nevertheless appointed no palatine or deputy of a palatine in his court [Col. 0892B]. He prudently directed everything in person or by his own counsel, or entrusted the business and care of the court to whatever count whose province he was visiting. And so he governed the country himself without a palatine count, until his spirit, released from its bodily mass, went to the place of its due abode. [MSS 3 omits the passage from “remembering the former rebellion” through “his spirit”; it adds “where he would remain eternally.”]

Thus Duke Wladislav died (1102), full of years and worn down by long infirmity. [Compare Cosmas III.16.] Archbishop Martin, celebrating his funeral rites for five days in the city of Płock, did not dare bury him while awaiting his sons.

But when both brothers arrived while their father was still unburied, they had a great and almost violent quarrel over the division of the treasures—MSS 1 and 2 read “a division of the treasures”—and the kingdom. Yet, through the inspiration of divine grace and the mediation of the faithful old archbishop—MS 2 adds *in*, and MS 3 adds *et*—they observed in the presence of the dead man the command he had given while living.

When Duke Wladislav had been buried with sufficient honor and magnificence in the church at Płock, and the division of their father’s treasures [MSS 1 and 2 omit “between the sons”] and of the kingdom of Poland—designated while their father lived—had been made, each received the lot of his allotted portion.

Yet the legitimate Boleslav obtained the two chief seats of the kingdom and the more populous portion of the land. Having gained his share of the inheritance, the boy Boleslav, strengthened by soldiers and counsel, began to exercise the courage of his mind and the strength of his body; and as a young man of good disposition he began to grow in reputation as well as age—MSS 1, 2, and 3 read *adolere*.

## 22. Boleslav captured the royal city of Alba

[Heading in MS 3; absent from MSS 1 and 2.]

The new soldier therefore began anew to wage new wars [Col. 0893A]—MS 3 transposes the words as “the soldier began new wars anew”—and to think of provoking his enemies more fiercely and more often—MS 2 has *ac* for *et*. Having summoned a host of warriors, he penetrated with a few chosen men into the heart of the land of the pagans.

When he reached the royal and distinguished city named Alba (1102), and had not even a third part of his army—Alba was Białogrod, or Belgard, on the Parsęta; the note also refers to another city of this name on the Łeba, for which see Barthold I, 433—he dismounted from his horse. He employed no siege-engine or instrument of assault, but on the very day of his arrival he captured, violently and wonderfully, the wealthy and populous city. Some also say that he was the first to attack and the first to climb the ramparts.

By this deed he became exceedingly terrible to the Pomeranians, and praiseworthy and beloved among all his own Christians. From the city he carried away immeasurable plunder—MS 3 reads “he brought away wonderful plunder”—but leveled its fortifications with the plain [Col. 0893B; MS 3 adds *etc.*].

## 23. On Boleslav’s marriage

[Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 180; absent from MSS 1, 2, and 3.]

But, passing over many matters to be reconsidered in their place, let us report his marriage and gifts comparable to the presents of Boleslav the Great, king—MS 3 reads *dictis* for *donis*.

In what manner Pope Paschal II granted permission for the marriage contracted within kinship—MS 3 reads *istas* for *initas*—Baldwin, bishop of Kraków, consecrated at Rome by that same pope, explained by setting forth the rudimentary state of the faith and the necessity of the country. Thus, as is reported, the authority of the Roman See mercifully approved this marriage—not canonically, nor customarily, but exceptionally. [Boleslav married Zbyslava, a woman of Rus’ descent; Roepell I, 231.]

We have no business discussing sin or the matter of justice; rather, we recount in a humble style the deeds of the kings and dukes of Poland—MS 3 reads *recitemus*.

For eight days before the wedding and for the eight days after its octave, the warlike Boleslav did not cease giving gifts: to some, *renones*—garments made from skins, as in Caesar, *Gallic War* VI.21 and Sallust, *Fragments of History*, p. 264, ed. Bipont—furs covered with cloaks and edged with gold embroidery—MS 3 reads *delibutas* for *delimbatas*; to princes, cloaks and vessels of gold and silver; to others, towns and castles; and to others, villages and estates—MS 3 omits *villas*.

## 24. Zbignev’s plots in inciting enemies

[Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 182; absent from MSS 1, 2, and 3.]

Meanwhile his brother Zbignev, who refused to come when invited to his brother’s wedding, formed alliances with the Pomeranians and Bohemians—MS 2 reads *Bohe*—and, while the wedding was being celebrated, is said to have encouraged the Bohemians to enter Poland (1103).

Ranging through the province of Wrocław, gathering plunder and captives [Col. 0893D] and setting fires, these Bohemians caused harmful damage to that region for many years. [Cosmas I.1.]

When he heard this, energetic Boleslav—although he grieved more over the violated brotherhood [Col. 0894A] than over the ravaging of the kingdom—nevertheless sent an embassy to ask his brother why he had done this to him, or in what he had offended him.

Zbignev replied that he knew of no such action against him and, through certain evasions, maintained that he was innocent of such a crime.

While warlike Boleslav continually fought enemies, both Bohemians and Pomeranians, and manfully defended the portion of his own division from invaders, Zbignev gave no assistance to his laboring brother, even when asked. Indeed, he secretly made a pact and alliance with his brother’s enemies and sent them money as a subsidy for soldiers—MS 3 reads *et* for *in*.

Although warlike Boleslav frequently approached him through envoys and conferences, admonishing him in brotherly love not openly or secretly to enter into familiarity and friendship with the enemies of their paternal inheritance, from which great division would come upon the kingdom of Poland, Zbignev replied wisely and peaceably, and thus moderated his brother’s anger and the hostility of the magnates—MS 3 omits this clause.

But let us discuss this more fully later in another place—MSS 1 and 2 have *plenarius*—and for the present turn to Boleslav’s military deeds.

## 25. The Poles ravaged Moravia

[The heading is absent from MSS 1 and 2.]

Therefore warlike Boleslav, avenger of the injury inflicted by the Bohemians, sent three divisions of soldiers into Moravia. Going in the very week of the Lord’s Resurrection (17 April 1104)—MS 3 reads *dominica*—they plundered and set fires, and found a recompense almost worthy of their deeds—MS 3 omits *dignam*—because they violated the reverence due to so great a festival. [MS 3 omits the clause from “because” through “festival.”]

For Svatopluk, duke of Moravia—MSS 2 and 3 give variant forms *Swacopole* and *Swanlhopol*—pursued them with a sharp battle-line as they returned and, as they say, would have taken their plunder from them, had not the infantry gone ahead with it—MSS 1–3 have *abstulisse*.

But when the Poles saw the Moravians—MS 3 reads *Moravos*—confidently drawing near, prepared for battle, they did not place their trust in flight but in arms. Thus an exceedingly fierce battle began on both sides, ending only with the gravest loss to each party.

In the first clash Duke Svatopluk of Moravia was like a boar hunted by Molossian hounds: striking in every direction with his curved tusk, he kills some and spills the entrails of others, neither planting his foot nor ceasing to inflict injury until the breathless hunter comes to the aid of his exhausted dogs with another pack.

So first Svatopluk, cutting off the Poles laden with booty by a circuitous route—MS 2 reads *praecedens*—would almost triumphantly have overwhelmed them, had not the battle-line, massed with all its strength [Col. 0895A]—MS 3 reads *totque*—checked alike the rage and courage of the advancing enemy.

Then the clatter of struck helmets resounds through the hollows of mountains and dense forests—MS 2 reads *tignitus*, and MS 3 *cava* for *concava*; MS 2 adds *velut*. Sparks from iron flash through the air; spears crashing against shields crack; chests are split open; hands, necks, and mangled bodies writhe over the field. There is the field of Mars; there Fortune plays.

At length both sides were so exhausted and so equal in their loss of slain soldiers that neither did the Moravians—MS 3 reads *Moravi*—enjoy a joyful victory nor did the Poles incur the stigma of disgrace.

There Count Zelislav—MS 3 omits his name—lost the hand with which he shielded his body—MS 3 reads *contra* for *qua*. Having lost it, he immediately avenged it manfully by killing the man who had cut it off. Duke Boleslav, in his honor, replaced his fleshly hand with a golden one [Col. 0895B].

## 26. Boleslav himself ravages Moravia

[Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 187; absent from MSS 1, 2, and 3.]

Again Boleslav himself—MS 3 adds the name—entered Moravia. But all the peasants, having heard the report, had withdrawn into fortifications with their booty—MS 1 reads *et*, while MS 2 omits it. Although the Bohemians and Moravians—MS 3 reads *Moravis*—had assembled, he returned after causing more damage there by fire than otherwise; yet, considering the difficulty of the undertaking—MS 2 reads *cum*, MS 3 *in*—he gained no small glory by this deed.

For from the Polish side Moravia is so obstructed by the steepness of mountains and density of forests that the route seems dangerous and exceedingly burdensome even for peaceful travelers and unencumbered foot-soldiers—MSS 1 and 2 read *pedibus* for *peditibus*. The Moravians themselves—MS 3 reads *Moravi*—knowing of his arrival long beforehand, did not dare engage him in a pitched battle [Col. 0895C]—MSS 1 and 2 have *prelio campestri*—or even oppose him with ambushes amid the difficulties of the route, whether entering or leaving. [MS 3 omits the clause from “the difficulties” through “leaving” and adds *saltem*.]

## 27. Legate of the supreme pontiff

[The chapters following this through chapter 34 are absent from MS 3. Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 188; absent from MSS 1 and 2.]

As he returned from Moravia with sufficient glory, a legate of the Roman See came to Poland: Walo by name, bishop of Beauvais—MS 2 reads *Belnacensis*. Supported by Boleslav’s power, he exercised such zeal for justice and such rigor of canonical discipline that he deposed two bishops there, no prayer or payment availing them.

The legate of the Roman See having been reverently honored and a council canonically held, the envoy returned to Rome with the apostolic blessing bestowed upon him; but warlike Boleslav went forth to attack his enemies.

## 28. On the expedition made against the city of Kołobrzeg

[Kołobrzeg, or Kolberg, situated in Pomerania on the Baltic Sea. Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 189; absent from MSS 1 and 2.]

(1107.) Therefore, having summoned an army at Głogów [Col. 0895D; on the chronology that follows, compare Giesebrecht, *Wendische Geschichte* II, 167, note 1], Boleslav took with him no infantry, but only chosen mounted soldiers and excellent horses. Nor, while passing through wilderness, did he allow them sufficient respite from continuous exertion or hunger by day and night for five days.

On the sixth day, and on the sixth day of the week, they received the Eucharist and refreshed themselves also with bodily food; then, under a star’s guidance, they came to Kołobrzeg. On the preceding night Boleslav ordered the office of Saint Mary to be performed—MS 2 reads “ordered Saint Mary’s office to be performed”—a practice which he later retained from devotion.

At dawn on Saturday, as they approached the city of Kołobrzeg, they crossed the nearby river, without bridge or ford and at risk, lest the pagans learn of them. Having formed their columns and placed two battle-lines at the rear as reserves, lest perhaps the Pomeranians discover this and attack them unprepared—MS 2 reverses the word order—they resolved with one accord to assault the wealthy city, fortified with riches and garrisons.

Then a certain count approached Boleslav, offered advice, and withdrew in silence and derision [Col. 0896B; MS 1 and 2 read *ad* for *at*]. But Boleslav briefly exhorted his men, so that every man was sufficiently stirred to boldness:

“Soldiers, had I not known your proved worth and courage,

I would never have left so great a multitude of my men behind,

nor come with few as far as the seacoast.

Now we hope for no help from our own;

the enemy is behind us, and the flight is long, if we think of flight;

let us now trust securely in God alone and in our arms.”

When this had been said, they seemed rather to fly than to run toward the city. Some thought only of plunder, others of taking the city. Had all attacked unanimously as certain men did, they would doubtless have taken that day the glorious and chief city of the Pomeranians.

But the abundance of wealth and plunder in the suburbs blinded the soldiers’ courage, and thus Fortune freed her city from the Poles. Only a few brave soldiers, preferring glory to riches, hurled their spears, crossed the bridge with drawn swords, and entered the city gate. But, hemmed in by the multitude of citizens, they were at last scarcely compelled to retreat.

The duke of the Pomeranians himself was inside when they arrived; fearing that the whole army was coming, he escaped through another gate. But energetic Boleslav did not remain in one place; he performed the duty of a good soldier and an active commander. He came to the aid of his men in difficulty and at the same time provided against what might harm or benefit.

Meanwhile some attacked one gate and some another; some bound captives; some gathered sea-borne riches; [Col. 0896D] others led away boys and girls. Though his soldiers had been exhausted all day by assaulting the town, Boleslav could scarcely at last recall them when evening drew on.

After recalling the soldiers and plundering the suburbs, [Col. 0897A] Boleslav withdrew thence, by the counsel of the great Michael, outside the walls, after first burning every building. By this deed the entire nation of barbarians was violently shaken and terrified, while the fame of Boleslav spread and grew far and wide.

Hence a song was even composed as a proverb (1107), in which that valor and courage are fittingly extolled in these words:

Others brought salted, stinking fish;

now their sons bring them fresh and wriggling.

Our fathers first attacked cities;

these men fear neither storms nor the roaring sea.

Our fathers hunted stags, boars, and roe-deer;

these hunt sea-monsters and wealth from the deep.

## 29. On a new expedition against the Pomeranians and a conference held with Coloman

[Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 193; absent from MSS 1 and 2.]

## Supplemental textual apparatus

The following collation entries complete the source notes omitted from the earlier draft. In each entry, the quoted form is retained because it is the manuscript's actual reading; the English in parentheses identifies its sense or the precise difference from the translated text.

### Zetheus and the brothers (chapter 16)

- In the warning that Zetheus is plotting against the boys, MS 2 reads *te* (“you,” singular) where the printed text addresses the group; it also places *et* (“and”) before *insuper* (“moreover”). These are respectively a pronoun and word-order variant at that warning.
- At the summons of the household, MS 2 has *properantes* (“hastening”) for the text's form; MSS 1–2 have *at* (“but”) at the turn to Zbignev's speech. At “relying on our own protection,” MSS 1–2 read *freti* (“relying”) for the printed construction.
- In the deleted Wrocław interpolation, MS 2 mistakenly inserted the words translated above as “touched inwardly by grief of heart, [the multitude] was quiet briefly, then immediately burst forth,” and later struck them through with a transverse line. Its local connective is *igitur* (“therefore”).
- At the agreement with the father, MS 2 has *tantundem* (“just as much / likewise”), a reading attached to the statement that he would not restore Zetheus. MSS 1–2 read *propellando* (“by driving [him] out”) in the episode where the boys expelled him; MS 2 has *quia* (“because”) in place of the causal/consequential wording. The editorial note identifies “the boys themselves” as the subject of that action.

### The Pomeranian stronghold (chapter 17)

- The chapter heading is supplied from the Warsaw edition, p. 168, and is absent from MSS 1–3. MS 2 calls the Mars-devoted boy *Marci* (“of Mars”). The editor prefers *coeptae* (“of the undertaking begun,” agreeing with *intentionis*) while MSS 1–3 have *cepto* (“begun,” a grammatically different form); MS 3 omits the sentence from “Let what has been said about Zetheus” through “let the pen advance.”
- The note identifies Zantok as *Zanthok*, on the Warta between Driesen and Landsberg. At the description “safeguard and key of the kingdom,” MSS 1–2 read *clavum* (“nail”) for *clavem* (“key”), and MS 3 omits *et clavem* (“and key”). MS 3 also omits the complete sentence saying that the fortress was so near that what happened in Zantok could be heard and seen by pagans.
- MS 2 reads *quoniam* (“because”) at the transition to Zbignev. MS 3 substitutes the fuller word-order reading *Zbigneus autem quoniam natu major erat* (“Zbignev, however, because he was older by birth”) for “therefore Zbignev, since he was older”; it reverses *suo patrisque* as *patris atque suo* (“his father's and his own”). The supplied collation's *Wladislavus autem* likewise means “Wladislav, however,” and is retained as its actual word-order/subject variant rather than silently normalized.
- At the elder brother's unsuccessful attack, MSS 1–2 preserve the corrupt sequence *e---est*; it is not expanded here because the source marks it corrupt. MS 2 has *proparens* (“hastening”) and MS 3 *illic* (“there”) at the same military movement. MS 3 omits the phrase describing him as “neither bravely [attacking]” (*n. a.* = *nec audacter*).
- At the bridge line MS 3 has the corrupt *po oe* for *pontem* (“bridge”); at the omen it omits the words *magnum futurae ... destructionis* (“a great [sign] of future destruction”). At the conclusion, MS 3 reads *igitur* (“therefore”) where the text has the consecutive transition in “seeing therefore the boy returning.”

### The belt and the Plauci (chapters 18–19)

- Chapter 18's heading is from Warsaw, p. 172, absent from MSS 1–3. In “he resolved to gird him,” MS 2 has *eumque* (“him, and”), adding the enclitic conjunction. At “none of the princes dared oppose them,” MSS 1–2 read *Audiebat* (“was hearing”), an actual but inappropriate reading for *audebat* (“dared”).
- Chapter 19's heading (Warsaw, p. 173) is absent from MSS 1–3; *Plauci* means the Pechenegs. MS 3 has *igitur* (“therefore”) at “Boleslav having thus been made a knight.” MSS 1–3 have *parte* (“part,” singular) for *partes* (“groups”), and MS 3 *sequenties* (“following,” misspelled) for *sequentis* (“of the following [day]”). MSS 1–2 omit *diei* (“of the day”); MS 3 adds *velocius* (“more swiftly”).
- MS 3 reads *atque* (“and”) for *ac* (“and”) in “secure and weary,” *quieti* (“for rest”) for *quietis* (“of rest”), and *Nam* (“for”) for *Namque* (“indeed/for”). Its word order *in gloria diei dominice* means “in the glory of the Lord's Day”; MS 2's *dominice diem gloria* is a disordered version of the same phrase.

### Prophecy and Wladislav's death (chapters 20–21)

- MS 3 omits all of chapter 20; its Warsaw heading (p. 175) is absent from MSS 1–2. Eight manuscripts mark two strokes above the relevant lines; the editor suggests that the saying may be read as a proverb, since the author calls such sayings memorable. MSS 1–2 read *istum* (“this [boy]”) for *per hunc* (“through this one”).
- Chapter 21's heading is from Warsaw, p. 176, absent from MSS 1–3. MS 3 adds *Bolezlavus* (“Boleslav”) to “let the boy rest,” omits the stretch from *pristinae seditionis* (“the former rebellion”) through *spiritus ejus* (“his spirit”), and adds *eternaliter permansurus* (“about to remain forever”). It has *autem* (“however”) for the abbreviated printed wording concerning Duke Wladislav, and adds *in* (“in”).
- At the quarrel over the inheritance, MSS 1–2 read *divisionem thezaurorum* (“a division of the treasures”) for *de divisione thezaurorum* (“over the division of the treasures”); MS 3 has the defective *de divisione thezauro*. MS 2 has *in* (“in”), MS 3 adds *et* (“and”), and MS 2 reads *igitur* (“therefore”) at Wladislav's burial. MS 3 omits *inter filios* (“between the sons”) and reads *ac regno* (“and [the] kingdom”) for the printed coordination. These are retained as case, preposition, omission, and connective variants rather than given invented English distinctions.

### Alba and the marriage (chapters 22–23)

- Chapter 22's heading belongs to MS 3 and is absent from MSS 1–2. MSS 2–3 have *igitur* (“therefore”) for the transition; MS 3 transposes *miles nova bella* as *miles nova bella* in a different order, “the soldier began new wars anew.” MS 2 has *ac* (“and”) with *et* written above it at “more fiercely and more often.”
- The geographical note identifies Alba with Białogrod/Belgard on the Persante, and distinguishes another Alba near the Łeba (Barthold I, 433). MS 3 has *mirabilem apportavit* (“brought away a wonderful [thing]”) for *innumerabilem asportavit* (“carried away countless [spoils]”) and adds *etc.* (“and so on”) after the fortification was levelled.
- Chapter 23's heading is Warsaw, p. 180, absent from MSS 1–3. MS 3 reads *dictis* (“things said”) for *donis* (“gifts”), *istas* (“these [marriages]”) for *initas* (“contracted”), *Balduiq.* (the abbreviated name “Baldwin”), *convivium* (“banquet”) for *conjugium* (“marriage”), and *nupcias* (“wedding”) for the ablative phrase concerning the wedding days. The historical note states that Boleslav married Zbyslava, a woman of Rus' descent (Roepell I, 231).
- A *reno* is a garment made of skins; compare Caesar, *Bellum Gallicum* VI.21 and Sallust, *Histories*, p. 264, ed. Bipontina, cited by Grotefend. MS 3 omits the phrase “villages and estates.”

### Bohemia, Moravia, and later headings (chapters 24–29)

- Chapter 24's heading is Warsaw, p. 182, absent from MSS 1–3. MS 3 omits the phrase that Zbignev “tempered his brother's anger and the princes' resentment.” Chapter 25's heading “The Poles devastated Moravia” is absent from MSS 1–2; MS 3 omits the words from *quia* (“because”) through *infregerunt* (“they violated”), the statement that the invaders violated the reverence due to Easter.
- MS 3 has *Moravie* (“of Moravia,” a genitive spelling/form) for *Moraviensis* (“Moravian”) in both appearances describing the duke, and MS 2 *Swantopole*, MS 3 *Swanthopol*, for *Suatopolc* (the proper name Svatopluk). MS 2 reads *precedens* (“going before”) where the text means “cutting off by a circuitous route.” At the mountain echo, MS 2 has *concova* and MS 3 *cava* (“hollows”) for *concava* (“concave hollows”); MS 3 omits the named count Zelislav.
- Chapter 26's Warsaw heading (p. 187) is absent from MSS 1–3. MS 3 adds *Boleslavus* (“Boleslav”) after *ipse* (“he himself”). MS 3's *Moravi* (“Moravians”) is retained at the statement that neither side had a joyful victory. Later it again reads *Moravis* (“Moravians,” ablative) and *Moravi* (“Moravians”) where the printed text has the corresponding forms; MSS 1–2 have *prelio campestri* (“in a pitched battle”) for “a pitched battle,” and MS 3 omits *d. s.* (*difficultate saltim*, “even amid the difficulty”) while adding *saltem* (“at least”) elsewhere in that clause.
- MS 3 lacks all chapters following chapter 27 through chapter 34. Chapter 27's heading is Warsaw, p. 188, absent from MSS 1–2; MS 2 has *Belnacensis* for *Belvacensis* (“of Beauvais”). Chapter 28's heading is Warsaw, p. 189, absent from MSS 1–2; the place note identifies Colobreg/Kodobrzeg (Kolberg) in Pomerania on the Baltic Sea. The chronology note refers to Giesebrecht, *Wendische Geschichte* II, 167 n.1.
- At the Marian office, MS 2 reads *sancte Marie fieri* (“to have the office of Saint Mary performed”) for the printed order *officium fieri sanctae Mariae* (“to have Saint Mary's office performed”), and *instituit* (“instituted”) for *constituit* (“established”). It reads *hoc Pomorani* (“this [which] the Pomeranians”) for *Pomorani hoc* (“the Pomeranians [might know] this”), a word-order variant. In Boleslav's exhortation MSS 1–2 have *Ad* (“to”) for *At* (“but”), and MS 2 omits *meorum* (“of my men”). Chapter 29's heading is Warsaw, p. 193, absent from MSS 1–2.

[Col. 0897B] After the soldiers had been exhausted by so great a labor on the march, and had now been refreshed by the allowance of a little rest, Bolesław again summoned the companies to an expedition and once more challenged the Pomeranians to war. The cause of this expedition was stirred up by his kinsman Swatobor [Note: [Col. 0897D] Barthold, *Gesch. v. Rügen u. Pommern*, I, 436. K.], whose descendants never maintained fidelity toward their Polish lords. For Swatobor himself [Note: [Col. 0897] SWantobor 2.] had been imprisoned in Pomerania and supplanted from his realm by certain traitors. Therefore energetic Bolesław, wishing to free his kinsman, planned with all his strength to conquer the land of the Pomeranians. But the Pomeranians, fearing Bolesław’s boldness, adopted a crafty plan: they restored his kinsman to him [Note: [Col. 0897] *redderunt* 2.], and [Col. 0897C] thus escaped his intolerable anger and attack (A.D. 1107).

Returning thence, Bolesław appointed a day and place for a conference with Coloman, king of Hungary, who surpassed all kings living in his time in literary learning. The king of Hungary, fearing treachery, hesitated to come. For Álmos, a Hungarian duke, was then an exile from Hungary [Note: [Col. 0897D] Álmos, son of Lambert, cousin of King Coloman I. K.], and was supported by Duke Bolesław out of hospitality [Note: [Col. 0897] “to Duke Bolesław” 1, 2.]. Afterwards, however, when embassies had passed back and forth between them, they met together and departed from one another, their perpetual brotherhood and friendship having been confirmed.

### 30. Scarbimir’s expedition against the Pomeranians

[Note: [Col. 0897] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 194; absent in 1, 2.]

Meanwhile Count Scarbimir, palatine of Poland, entered Pomerania with his fellow soldiers, where [Col. 0897D] he won no small glory for the Poles and left loss and disgrace to his enemies. He wished to be called conqueror of castles or cities rather than, that is, despoiler of many villages or herds. Accordingly, with bold [Note: [Col. 0897] *audacti* 1, 2.] violence he took one castle; after capturing certain persons there [Col. 0898A] and carrying off the booty, he burned the whole place utterly to its foundations.

### 31. The castle of Bitom captured

[Note: [Col. 0897] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 195; absent in 1, 2.]

On another occasion he similarly took another castle called Bitom [Note: [Col. 0898D] Bytom, Beuthen, near Głogów/Glogau. According to Giesebrecht, I, 170: Büthow in Pomerania. K.], from which he brought back no less praise and advantage than from the other. For he drove off much booty and captives from it, and reduced that place [Note: [Col. 0897] “him” 2.] to the likeness of desolation. But we recount this of Scarbimir not in order to compare him in any respect with his lord, but in order to preserve the truth of history.

### 32. A pact made with Zbigniew and the ensuing betrayal

[Note: [Col. 0897] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 196; absent in 1, 2.]

Therefore warlike Bolesław, after returning from the conference with the Hungarians, arranged another meeting with his brother Zbigniew. There the two brothers together swore to one another in these words: namely, that neither would make an agreement with enemies concerning peace or war without the other; that neither would enter into any alliance with anyone without the other; and that each would aid the other against enemies and in every necessity. These matters having been confirmed, under the same oath they appointed a day and place at which they were to meet with their armies, and so departed from the conference.

But energetic Bolesław hurried, with a few men, to the appointed place on the named day, intending to keep faith. Zbigniew, however, not only violated faith and his oath by failing to come, but even recalled from its route his brother’s army, which was turning toward him. Hence such loss and dishonor nearly came upon the kingdom of Poland that neither Zbigniew [Col. 0898C] nor anyone else could afterwards have remedied it. Now the following page will immediately reveal how Bolesław, with God’s help, escaped that danger.

### 33. Bolesław falls into a Pomeranian ambush

[Note: [Col. 0897] This heading, painted in red, is found in 1; absent in 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0897] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 197; absent in 1, 2.]

By chance a certain nobleman built a church on the frontier of the land and invited Duke Bolesław, still quite a boy, with his young men to its consecration. The spiritual consecration was therefore completed, and afterwards a wedding betrothal was celebrated. Whether it displeases God for carnal nuptials to be celebrated together with divine nuptials may readily be proved by the dangers that often result from this. For we frequently see that, where the consecration of a church and a wedding betrothal take place together, seditions and homicides attend them, [Col. 0898D] whence it is clear that it is neither good nor proper to imitate such a custom. Yet we do not say this in order to condemn marriage, but in order that individual things be reserved for their own places and their own times.

God Almighty revealed a manifest sign of this in the consecration of the church at Ruda [Note: [Col. 0898D] Ruda, on the Warta near Sieradz in the kingdom of Poland. S.]. For it is known that there occurred there both a homicide [Col. 0899A] and one of the attendants driven mad; and that the very betrothed couple entered upon an unhappy marriage, as is known, and did not complete the anniversary of their betrothal. But let us be silent about miracles and keep to our subject.

Thus warlike Bolesław, preferring warfare or hunting [Note: [Col. 0899] *venacioni* 1.] to feasting or drinking, left the elders with the entire multitude at the banquet and went hunting in the woods with a few companions; but he encountered hostile hunters [Note: [Col. 0899] *contrarium* 3.]. For Pomeranians ranging through Poland were driving off booty and captives and making fires. But Bolesław the warrior, stirred to anger like a lion by goads upon its tail, did not wait for princes or army; rather, like a lioness thirsting for blood after her cubs have been snatched away, he scattered their plunderers [Col. 0899B] and raiders in an instant beneath the edge [Note: [Col. 0899] “custom/usage” (*more*) in the manuscripts.] of the sword.

And while he strove to pursue them ever more closely and avenge the injury done to his country, he unknowingly fell into an ambush, where he would suffer irreparable loss. Yet although he had only a few men—eighty, namely, boys and young men—while they had three thousand, he did not seek flight [Note: [Col. 0899] “they seek” (*peciunt*) 1, 2.] nor fear so great a multitude [Note: [Col. 0899] “they fear” (*dubitant*) 1, 2.]. In the first encounter, with his small battle-line, he penetrated such a dense mass of enemies.

I am about to tell things marvelous and perhaps unbelievable to many, though I do not know whether they should be ascribed to rashness or courage. When he had nearly lost his own men, some being killed and others scattered, and only five remained with him, he pierced through the most densely packed enemy a second time. When he wished to wheel about a third time [Note: [Col. 0899] Thus more correctly in the *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, Stenzel I, 73; *regnare* 1, 2.], one of his men, seeing the entrails of his horse [Col. 0899C] falling onto the ground, cried out: “Do not, lord, do not enter battle again! Spare yourself, spare your country; mount my horse. It is better for me to die here than for you yourself, the salvation of Poland, to perish.”

On hearing this, with his horse collapsing, he scarcely yielded to the soldier’s counsel; and so at last he withdrew a little from the field of battle. Seeing himself greatly diminished and that Scarbimir, commander of the army, was not present with the survivors, he now despaired of recovering victory. For Scarbimir had elsewhere been wounded by a grave injury and—what cannot be said with dry eyes—had lost the sight of his right eye.

Those who remained at the banquet, hearing what had happened, rose and hurried to aid their hard-pressed men. On arriving, however, [Col. 0899D] they found Bolesław with scarcely thirty men; yet he was not fleeing from the battlefield, but was gradually following the tracks of the fleeing enemy. But the enemies did not, by standing their ground, offer an opportunity for battle; nor did our exhausted men harass them further. For the pagans were amazed at the young man’s such great daring: they praised him more for having ventured such deeds with so small a force and pressed on so fiercely [Note: [Col. 0899] *talia* is repeated twice in 1, 2.] than they rejoiced in their own sorrowful victory, obtained at so great a cost in deaths.

[Col. 0900A] “What kind of boy,” they said, “will this be, if he lives long? And if he has more men with him, who will be able to withstand him in war?” Thus the pagans, lamenting their present loss and murmuring at the fear inspired by courage they had experienced, returned burdened more by grief than by booty.

On the following day, very many of Bolesław’s men came to him more for consolation [Note: [Col. 0899] Absent in 2.] than for assistance. The nobles arriving there grieved at the loss of so much nobility and respectfully reproved Bolesław for the boldness of such rashness. But Bolesław, son of Mars, not only gave no ear to his reprovers and did not repent of having attempted such things; he also charged them, under the obligation of fidelity, to aid him and take vengeance on the enemy. There Bolesław received so many blows upon breastplate and helmet [Col. 0900B] from lances and swords that his bruised flesh bore witness to the injury for many days (A.D. 1107). Yet he mourned only a little, and less than might have been expected [Note: [Col. 0899] “excessively” (*nimis*) 2.], for his youth so gloriously slain, because he counted so great a slaughter of enemies as gain. Indeed, for every one of Bolesław’s men killed or wounded, several Pomeranian dead could be counted.

### 34. Bolesław drives off the Bohemians and subdues the Pomeranians

[Note: [Col. 0899] This heading, absent in 1 and 2, is found in 3.]

After this event Bolesław resolved to avenge himself on the Pomeranians with that same army; and, once the march had begun, a report came beforehand that the Bohemians were about to enter Poland. Then Bolesław was held in great uncertainty whether he ought first to avenge the recent affront [Note: [Col. 0899] 3 adds “immediately.”], [Col. 0900C] or free his country from invaders. At last, like an imitator of the Maccabees, he divided his army and proved both defender of his country and avenger of injury. For he sent one part of the army into Pomerania, which shamefully trampled them down by plundering and [Note: [Col. 0899] Absent in 2, 3.] burning; while he himself hastened with picked troops to meet the Bohemians. He waited long for them to emerge from the woods, but, upon hearing of Bolesław, fear in their hearts recalled them.

### 35. Zbigniew harbors hostility against his brother

[Note: [Col. 0899] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 203; absent in 1, 2, 3.]

Not only discord with foreigners or war with enemies oppressed Bolesław; civil strife—indeed, fraternal envy—assailed him in every way [Col. 0900D]. For when Bolesław was somewhat hard pressed in the preceding war [Note: [Col. 0899D] That is, Bolesław. K.], Zbigniew rejoiced more than he did when Bolesław was many times exalted by victory. A clear sign of this appeared when he accepted small gifts from pagans as a token of victory and repaid great gifts to envoys in exchange for small ones. If those plundering Poland brought captives from Bolesław’s territory, they immediately carried them off to be sold in the islands of the barbarians; but if they unknowingly took anything—booty or persons—from [Col. 0901A] Zbigniew’s territory, they returned it without price or delay.

Therefore all the wise men of Poland, indignant, were turned from friendship to hatred of Zbigniew; and, taking counsel concerning him, they said among themselves: “Until now, either through negligence or dissimulation, we have endured with excessive patience the division and [Note: [Col. 0901] Or “or,” 3.] injury of our country; but now [Note: [Col. 0901] “thus,” 3.] we clearly see hidden enemies made manifest and concealed plots uncovered. For we know and are certain that Zbigniew has often sworn this to Bolesław in our presence, and [Note: [Col. 0901] “truly,” 2.] has perjured himself not once or three times but [Note: [Col. 0901] “or,” 3.] many times. For he maintained neither friendship with his brother’s friends nor enmity against his brother’s enemies [Note: [Col. 0901] *inimicicias* 3.]; rather, on the contrary, he made himself friend of his brother’s enemies and enemy of his friends.

[Col. 0901B] “And not only did he violate promised faith or fail to provide the aid he had sworn, but whenever he perceived that his brother was going against enemies, he incited other enemies to enter Poland from the other side, and thus recalled him from [Note: [Col. 0901] Absent in 3.] his purpose. He was said to be taking a thoroughly childish and harmful course when, because of hatred for a few men, he injured the whole country and exposed his paternal [Note: [Col. 0901] *parterna* 1.] inheritance to be trampled underfoot by enemies [Note: [Col. 0901] “of the enemies” 2.].

“And because Zbigniew, prompted by evil counsel, observed neither faith nor oath toward his brother, defended neither the honor of his country nor his paternal inheritance, and considered neither impending loss nor injury [Note: [Col. 0901] “nor” 2.], alas! he fell more grievously through that by which he wished [Note: [Col. 0901] “did not wish,” manuscripts.] to be exalted, and from which [Note: [Col. 0901] “truly,” 2.] he will no longer be able to be raised by [Col. 0901C] his evil counsellors [Note: [Col. 0901] *uloribus* 3.]. Let posterity, therefore, and those now living beware lest there be in the kingdom equal partners at variance [Note: [Col. 0901] “distrustful,” 3.].”

### 36. The outbreak of Zbigniew’s hostility

[Note: [Col. 0901] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 206; absent in 1, 2, 3.]

But Bolesław commended all these things to the Lord alone and still bore his brother’s injury with equanimity [Note: [Col. 0901] “for this purpose,” 3.]. Ever active, he went about Poland, fearsome as a roaring lion [Note: [Col. 0901] *circuibat* 2, 3.]. By chance word was brought to him meanwhile that the castle of Koźle [Note: [Col. 0901D] Cosel, Koźle, on the Oder. Cf. Stenzel, *SS. rer. Siles.*, I, 74, n. 4.] on the Bohemian border had been burned by himself, though not by enemies. Judging that someone had done this through treachery, and fearing that the Bohemians would hurry to fortify it, he immediately flew there with very few men and began the work with his own hands.

For by running back and forth so much and for so long [Note: [Col. 0901] “at last,” 3.] [Col. 0901D] he had rendered his men so weary [Note: [Col. 0901] “running about,” 3.] that it seemed oppressive to summon them again so suddenly. Yet he called his men to assistance and invited his brother through quite suitable messengers, sending him the following words:

[Col. 0902A] “Since, brother, you are older in age and equal in prerogative and in the division of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0901] “kingdom,” 3.], yet allow me alone, your younger brother, to bear the entire burden, and take no part in wars or counsels of the kingdom: either take upon yourself the entire care and [Note: [Col. 0901] “or,” 2, 3.] responsibility of the kingdom, as you wish to be the elder [Note: [Col. 0901] Absent in 3.]; or, if you are of no help, at least do no harm to me, who, though younger in age, lawfully bear the burden of the land and endure all the labor [Note: [Col. 0901] “to hold” 3.].

“If you undertake this charge and persist in true brotherhood [Note: [Col. 0901] “charity,” 3.], wherever you call me for common counsel or for the benefit of the kingdom, you shall have me there as a ready fellow-worker [Note: [Col. 0901] “you shall obtain,” 3.]. Or if perhaps you prefer to live quietly rather than undergo [Note: [Col. 0901] “undertake,” 3.] so great a labor, entrust the whole to me, and thus, God being favorable, you will be safe.”

To this Zbigniew sent back no suitable [Col. 0902B] reply, but [Note: [Col. 0901] Absent in 2.] nearly consigned the envoys to chains and prison [Note: [Col. 0901] “prison” 2.]. For he had already assembled his entire army to attack his brother, and had likewise summoned Pomeranians and Bohemians to drive him out of Poland [Note: [Col. 0901] *propellandum* 2; “summoned,” 3.].

But Bolesław, having fortified the castle and knowing nothing of this, remained at a place called Lapide [Note: [Col. 0901] *lapis* 3.] [Note: [Col. 0902D] Kamień/Cammin in western Prussia. S. Or Kamenz? K.]. Lying there according to his custom, he heard reports and embassies from nearer quarters, and [Note: [Col. 0901] “and,” 3.] more swiftly came unexpectedly upon his enemies. At last the envoys, scarcely freed by the aid of friends, returned to Bolesław and reported what they had seen and heard. Hearing this, Bolesław long hesitated in doubt [Note: [Col. 0901] “of doubt,” 3.] whether to resist or desist; but, returning to himself, he assembled his army as quickly as possible [Note: [Col. 0901] *quantocius* for *quanto citius*, 3.] [Col. 0902C] and sent to the king of the Ruthenians and to the Hungarians [Note: [Col. 0901] “Hungarians,” 3.] for aid. But if he could accomplish nothing either by himself or [Note: [Col. 0901] “by force,” 4.] through them, he would lose the kingdom itself and hope of the kingdom while waiting [Note: [Col. 0901] 3 adds “etc.”].

### 37. A treaty with the Bohemians and Zbigniew’s flight

[Note: [Col. 0901] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 210; absent in 1, 2, 3.]

Thus warlike Bolesław, surrounded by three armies, considered which he should await first or which he should attack, like a lion or boar tracked by Molossian hounds and provoked to anger by the barking of dogs and the horns of hunters. Yet all feared Bolesław, because, while he stood in their midst, they did not dare come to the appointed place. Meanwhile letters of Zbigniew, captured together with the messengers [Note: [Col. 0901] *micis* 2.], were brought in, in which many betrayals and plots were disclosed. [Col. 0902D] When these had been read, every wise man marveled [Note: [Col. 0901] “anyone who” 2; “each” 3.], and the whole people lamented the danger.

Finally Bolesław wisely enough and suitably for the time made peace with the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0901] “and,” 3.], [Col. 0903A] raised an army, and resolved to drive Zbigniew out [Note: [Col. 0903] Absent in 1, 2.]. Zbigniew, however, did not await his brother’s arrival, intending to do the same or engage in battle [Note: [Col. 0903] So the *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, p. 75; 1 and 2 read *extra jam rejecit*, which the Warsaw edition rejects as superfluous.], nor did he linger secure in camps or cities; but fled like a stag and swam across the Wysia River.

### 38. Zbigniew is restored to his brother’s favor

[Note: [Col. 0903] Heading in manuscript 3; absent in 1, 2.]

But Bolesław, arriving hastily at Kalisz [Note: [Col. 0903] Thus the *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, p. 75; *satis* 1, 2, 3.] [Note: [Col. 0903D] Kalisz. S.], found there certain faithful adherents of Zbigniew resisting him; within a few days he took that castle too, and, having received an embassy, installed his count in the city of Gniezno [Note: [Col. 0903] *Gueznensi* 3.]. Going on from there to Spicimir [Note: [Col. 0903] *Spiczimir* 3.] [Note: [Col. 0903D] Near Uniejów in the kingdom of Poland, on the Warta. S.], he enclosed the faithful old man [Note: [Col. 0903D] Kownacki thought him Martin, archbishop of Gniezno, whom the author frequently calls “the faithful old man.” S.] [Note: [Col. 0903] “shut in” 3.], whom, upon hearing that his seat had been restored, he scarcely brought out. Taking him with him [Note: [Col. 0903] “took” 1, 2.], he hurried to the seat transferred to Łęczyca [Note: [Col. 0903] *lucie* 3.] [Note: [Col. 0904D] Łęczyca, capital city of the duchy of the same name. S.], [Col. 0903B] and there [Note: [Col. 0903] “everywhere,” 2.] repaired an old castle against Mazovia. Then, for the first time, aid from the Ruthenians and Hungarians arrived.

Then Zbigniew was reduced to despair and, through the mediation of Duke Yaroslav of the Ruthenians [Note: [Col. 0903] *Yaroslamo* 1; *acarozlao* 3.] and Baldwin, bishop of Cracow, was brought before his brother to make satisfaction and obey him. Then for the first time he acknowledged himself inferior to his brother; then he again swore before all that he would never be opposed to his brother, but would obey in all things and would destroy the castle of Gallus [Note: [Col. 0904D] Present-day Gollin on the Warta, near Konin in the kingdom of Poland. S.]. Then he obtained from his brother permission to retain Mazovia as a knight, not as its lord. The brothers having thus been reconciled, the Ruthenian and Hungarian armies returned home, while Bolesław went through Poland wherever [Col. 0903C] he pleased [Note: [Col. 0903] 3 adds “etc.”].

### 39. Zbigniew’s treachery toward his brother

[Note: [Col. 0903] Heading in manuscript 3; absent in 1, 2.]

(A.D. 1107, 1108.) Again, in winter, the Poles gathered to invade Pomerania, so that fortifications might more easily be taken when the marshes were frozen. Then too Bolesław experienced Zbigniew’s treachery, because in all these matters [Note: [Col. 0903] 3 reads: “For Zbigniew, in all these matters …”] he was manifestly found perjured in what he had sworn. He did not destroy the nearby castle which [Note: [Col. 0903] Absent in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0903] This pronoun is written above the text in 2.] Gallus had built [Note: [Col. 0903] *Gallus* 1, 2.], nor, when summoned to his brother’s aid, did he draw up even a single battle-line [Note: [Col. 0903] “not,” 3.].

The northern duke, though somewhat troubled by this stratagem, nevertheless did not abandon [Col. 0903D] his purpose [Note: [Col. 0903] 3 reads “having” for “did not abandon.”], placing his heart in the Lord, not [Col. 0904A] in his brother [Note: [Col. 0903] *inferre* for *in fratre* 1.]. Therefore, just as a fire-breathing dragon burns the neighboring places by its breath alone, strikes unburned places with its curved tail, and flies over lands to do harm, so Bolesław attacked rebellious Pomerania with the sword [Note: [Col. 0903] “brother” (*fratre*) 2.] and intended to destroy its fortifications with fire.

But let us omit what he did while going through or crossing [Note: [Col. 0903] Absent in 2.] the land [Note: [Col. 0903] “what he did upon returning” for “what he did while crossing,” 3.], and proceed to the siege of the city Alba in the middle of the country. Arriving at the city, which is regarded as the middle, as it were the center, of the land [Note: [Col. 0903] “and,” 3; “in the middle,” 3.], Bolesław pitched camp and prepared engines by which it might be taken more easily [Note: [Col. 0903] “with less difficulty,” 3.] and with less danger. By continually laboring on every side with arms and siege-engines, he compelled the citizens within a few days to surrender the city. Having received it, he stationed his soldiers there; then, with the signal given and camp moved, he hastened to the coast.
