When [Col. 0904B] he was already turning toward the city of Kołobrzeg [Note: [Col. 0903] *Gologum* 3.] and was considering taking a castle near the sea before approaching the city [Note: [Col. 0903] “was taking” 3; “to approach,” manuscripts.], behold: citizens and townsmen came out to meet Bolesław with bowed necks, offering themselves, their faith, and their service. The duke of the Pomeranians himself also came, bowed to Bolesław, and, while remaining on horseback, committed himself to his service and military following [Note: [Col. 0903] Absent in 1, 2; *debutavit* 1.].

For five weeks Bolesław rode through Pomerania, waiting for battle or seeking it, and subdued almost the whole kingdom without a battle. Therefore Bolesław deserves to be praised with such titles of renown and crowned with such triumphs of wars and [Note: [Col. 0903] “and,” 3.] victories.

### 40. A son is born

[Note: [Col. 0903] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 217; absent in 1, 2, 3.]

But with this joy of triumphant victory there arose [Col. 0904C] a greater joy: a son of royal lineage was born to him [Note: [Col. 0904D] Władysław II. K.]. May the boy grow in years, advance in virtue, and increase in good character. As for the father, it is enough for us [Note: [Col. 0903] Absent in 3.] if we keep to the subject begun.

### 41. Zbigniew is defeated again

[Note: [Col. 0903] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 218; absent in 1, 2, 3.]

Therefore Bolesław, seeing [Note: [Col. 0903] “however,” 3.] that his brother was in every matter and [Note: [Col. 0903] “character” for “in every matter and,” 3.] in promises and oaths [Note: [Col. 0903] “things sworn,” 3.] utterly faithless [Note: [Col. 0903] “faithless,” 3.], and that [Note: [Col. 0903] “that,” 3.] he was harmful and burdensome to the whole land, drove him from the entire kingdom of Poland. With Ruthenian and Hungarian aid he took those resisting him and defending a castle on the frontier of the land [Note: [Col. 0903] “castle,” 3; *intrare* for “of the land” 1; absent in 3.]. Thus Zbigniew’s dominion, through evil counsellors, came to an end, and [Col. 0905A] the whole kingdom of Poland was united under Bolesław’s rule. Although performing these deeds in winter would have been enough labor for many, Bolesław nevertheless counted nothing burdensome where he knew the kingdom’s advantage or honor could be increased.

### 42. Saxons came by ship into Prussia

[Note: [Col. 0905] Heading in manuscript 3; absent in 1, 2.]

Accordingly he entered Prussia, a thoroughly barbarous land, and returned with much booty, after making fires and taking many captives [Note: [Col. 0905] “many,” 3.], having sought battle but found none. But since this region has happened to come to mind [Note: [Col. 0905] “the mention of this region came to memory” for “this region came to mention,” 3.], it is not unfitting to add something from the report of our elders [Note: [Col. 0905] “to add,” 3.].

For in the time of Charlemagne, king of the Franks, when Saxony was in rebellion against him and accepted neither the yoke of his dominion nor the Christian faith, [Col. 0905B] this people crossed over from Saxony in ships and occupied both this region and its name [Note: [Col. 0905] “region” 2.]. To this day they persist without king and without law, and do not abandon their original perfidy or [Note: [Col. 0905] “nor,” 2.] ferocity. For the land is so protected by lakes [Note: [Col. 0905] *lacis* 1; “enough,” 2.] and marshes [Note: [Col. 0905] *counita* 2.] that it would not be so fortified even by castles or cities [Note: [Col. 0905] Absent in 3.]. Consequently it has still not [Note: [Col. 0905] Absent in 3.] been subdued by anyone, because no one has been able [Note: [Col. 0905] “could,” 3.] to transport an army across so many lakes [Note: [Col. 0905] *lacis* 1, 2.] and marshes.

### 43. A miracle concerning the Pomeranians

[Note: [Col. 0905] Heading in manuscript 3; absent in 1, 2.]

But now let us leave the Prussians with their brute animals and [Note: [Col. 0905] Absent in 3.] recount an account intelligible to those capable of understanding an account [Note: [Col. 0905] “capable,” 3.]—indeed, a miracle of God. [Col. 0905C] It happened, perhaps [Note: [Col. 0905] “for,” 3.], that Pomeranians burst forth from Pomerania and, according to their usual practice [Note: [Col. 0905] Absent in 3.], ranged through Poland to seize booty [Note: [Col. 0905] “captives,” 2.]. Scattered and roaming in different directions, and all doing evil and perverse things, some of them nevertheless broke out into greater crimes and attacked the metropolitan himself and the holy church.

Accordingly Martin, archbishop of Gniezno, the faithful old man, was at Spicimir [Note: [Col. 0905] *Spiczimir* 2, 3.] in his church, making confession with the priest and intending to hear Mass; he was also preparing to depart elsewhere, his horses already saddled [Note: [Col. 0905] *insallatis* 2.]. Thus, without doubt, all there would either have been slaughtered together [Note: [Col. 0905] “together,” 3.] or, master and servant alike, consigned together to the bonds of captivity [Note: [Col. 0905] 3 adds “would have been”], had not one of the attendants standing outside recognized their arms, hurried to [Col. 0905D] the church door, and cried out that the Pomeranians were already present [Note: [Col. 0905] Absent in 3.].

Then the bishop, priest, and archdeacon, terrified, were forced already to despair of temporal [Col. 0906A] life: what counsel they should take [Note: [Col. 0905] *caperentur* 1, 2.], what they should do [Note: [Col. 0905] *agerentur* 1, 2.], or where they should flee [Note: [Col. 0905] “or,” 3; *fugerentur* 1, 2.]. They had no arms, few retainers, enemies at the doors, and—what seemed more dangerous—the wooden church was thought readier to be burned with them inside.

At last the archdeacon went out through the enemy and wished to reach the horses by way of the covered upper chamber, thinking thus to escape. But abandoning salvation and seeking safety, he strayed from safety, because [Note: [Col. 0905] “but,” 3.] he encountered the Pomeranians rushing in there. When he was seized, the pagans thought that he was the archbishop and rejoiced greatly. Having placed him in a cart, they did not bind him or beat him [Note: [Col. 0905] “imprison” 3.], but guarded and honored him [Note: [Col. 0905] “they guard, they honor” absent in 3.].

Meanwhile the archbishop commended himself to God with vows and prayers and marked himself with the holy sign of the cross [Col. 0906B] [Note: [Col. 0905] *asignavit* 3.]. And where a young man might have hesitated, the trembling old man did not hesitate to climb [Note: [Col. 0905] “for” 1, 2; “there” 3; *dubitaverit* 1, 2.]. Wonderful to tell: the strength denied by old age [Note: [Col. 0905] “once,” 3.] was supplied by peril of death and sudden fear. The priest, moreover [Note: [Col. 0905] “after this” for “the priest,” 3.], being as he was prepared, concealed himself behind the altar; and so both bishop and priest, with God’s help, escaped the hands of the enemy.

For the divine majesty so blinded the pagans breaking into the church that none of them thought to climb upward or look behind the altar. Yet they carried off the archbishop’s portable altars [Note: [Col. 0905] *vitica* 3.] and the church’s relics, and immediately departed with them and with the archdeacon whom they had taken [Note: [Col. 0905] “approached,” 3.]. But Almighty God, just as [Note: [Col. 0905] “thus”: P’s correction; “as” 1, 2, 3.] he delivered the bishop, priest, and church, so afterwards he restored to the archbishop the relics and the whole sanctuary [Col. 0906C] unpolluted and unharmed.

For whoever among the pagans possessed relics, sacred vestments, or vessels of the sanctuary [Note: [Col. 0905] “sacred” absent in 3.] was afflicted either by a wasting sickness or terrible madness. Therefore, terrified by God’s mighty power, they were compelled to restore everything to the captive archdeacon [Note: [Col. 0905] “archbishop,” 3.]. The archdeacon himself also returned safe and sound from Pomerania; and when all his possessions had been restored [Note: [Col. 0905] “returned,” 3.], the archbishop praised God as wondrous in these [Note: [Col. 0905] “his,” 3.] works. From that day the Pomeranians gradually began to be brought to nothing [Note: [Col. 0905] “to be admired,” 3.] and thereafter did not dare range so freely through Poland [Note: [Col. 0905] 3 adds “etc.”].

### 44. The baptism of the Pomeranians

[Note: [Col. 0905] Chapters XLIV–XLVIII are absent in 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0905] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 226; absent in 1, 2.]

(A.D. 1108.) Accordingly energetic Bolesław again entered Pomerania [Col. 0906D] and attacked the castle of Czarnków [Note: [Col. 0905D] Czarnków on the Noteć/Netze. S.] with great forces, intending to besiege it. Having prepared machines of various kinds and raised towers [Note: [Col. 0905] “towers,” 2.] [Col. 0907A] higher than the castle’s fortification, he assailed the stronghold with arms and [Note: [Col. 0907] “from,” 1, 2.] engines until, after its surrender, he brought it under his authority. Moreover, he recalled many from unbelief to the faith, and raised the lord of the castle himself from the baptismal font.

When the pagans and the lord of the pagans himself heard that the obstinacy [Note: [Col. 0907] “of the obstinate persons,” 1, 2.] of the men of Czarnków had thus easily fallen, that duke was the first of all to bow before Bolesław; but neither he nor they maintained loyalty for long. For later that baptized man, Bolesław’s spiritual son, committed many betrayals worthy of capital punishment. But let us presently pass over these matters in silence, to be related in their proper place, until we bring back the emperor from Hungary and Bolesław from Bohemia, and introduce whatever may have happened earlier [Col. 0907B].

### 45. War waged with the Moravians

[Note: [Col. 0907] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 227; absent in 1, 2.]

But now let us turn from the Pomeranians to the Bohemians, lest, by lingering too long on the same subject, we seem sluggish. (A.D. 1108, September.) While Bolesław persisted in guarding the land and strove with all his strength for his country’s honor, it happened that Moravians arrived, wishing to anticipate the Poles in seizing the castle of Koźle without their knowing it. Then Bolesław also sent certain valiant soldiers to take Racibórz [Note: [Col. 0907] *Rathibor* 2.], if possible; he himself, however, did not on that account cease either hunting or resting.

Those valiant soldiers departed and engaged the Moravians in battle. There certain brave Poles fell in combat, but their companions [Col. 0907C] gained both the field of victory and the castle. Thus the Moravians were slain in battle, and thus those in the castle, unaware, were caught off guard [Note: [Col. 0907] “slain,” 1.]. Meanwhile Emperor Henry IV entered Hungary, where he gained little advantage or honor [Note: [Col. 0907D] Cosmas, III, 22. K.]. We are not at present treating of the deeds of emperors or Hungarians; but in recalling these things we proclaim Bolesław’s fidelity and courage.

### 46. War brought upon the Bohemians

[Note: [Col. 0907] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 228; absent in 1, 2.]

For it had been agreed under oath between Coloman, king of the Hungarians, and Boleslav, duke of the Poles, that if the emperor entered the kingdom of either, the other should meanwhile harass Bohemia. Therefore, when the emperor entered Hungary, Boleslav too, keeping faith, [Col. 0907D] joined battle amid the forests and, victorious, harassed Bohemia. There, during three days and nights, by burning he destroyed three castellanies [Note: [Col. 0907] *castellanuas* in the manuscripts] and one suburb [Col. 0908A]; and thus he swiftly returned, because the Pomeranians were taking his fortresses through treachery.

### 47. The rebellious Pomeranians

[Note: [Col. 0907] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 229; absent in 1 and 2.]

Already during his absence the Pomeranians besieged Uście [Note: [Col. 0907D] Uście, on the River Noteć/Netze. S.], a fortress of Boleslav; and the Poles there surrendered it to the Pomeranians, Gnevomir now urging this through treachery [Note: [Col. 0907] *tradiderunt*, “surrendered,” 2.]. For this Gnevomir was from the fortress of Czarnków, which Boleslav captured; Boleslav himself had lifted him from the baptismal font and, after the others were killed, spared his life and installed him as lord in that very fortress. But this traitor, perjurer, and forgetful recipient of kindness advised the garrison to surrender the fortress, falsely asserting that Boleslav had been defeated by the Bohemians and had now submitted to the Germans.

Accordingly, although the army was returning from Bohemia after so arduous and dangerous a journey [Col. 0908B], he spared neither himself nor his weary men nor his emaciated horses; he rested neither by day nor by night until, hastening thither with the few whom he could choose from many—and, even if he did nothing else, he at least made known his intention to avenge the wrong—he showed himself alive and undefeated. For no one prepared himself to fight against him; no one even came out to meet him in battle as he returned; and so he returned, neither inflicting nor receiving injury.

### 48. Boleslav punishes the rebellious Pomeranians after taking the fortress of Wieleń

[Note: [Col. 0908D] Wieleń, [uncertain: “…enne”], on the River Netze. S.]  
[Note: [Col. 0907] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 231; absent in 1 and 2, and in 3, which begins again at this point.]

Meanwhile [Note: [Col. 0907] “Again,” 2 and 3.], after the horses and soldiers had recovered somewhat [Note: [Col. 0907] 3 has: “Therefore Boleslav,” in place of “after the horses and soldiers had recovered”], Boleslav prepared to return into Pomerania [Note: [Col. 0907] *Pomeraniam*, 3.], his companies again restored for war [Note: [Col. 0907] “Boleslav again” absent in 3.]. [Col. 0908C]

Entering the enemy’s land [Note: [Col. 0907] Absent in 3.], he did not pursue plunder or herds, but besieged the fortress of Wieleń [Note: [Col. 0908D] Sallust, *Jugurtha* 94. S.] and prepared siege-engines and implements of various kinds [Note: [Col. 0907] 3: “and of various kinds,” for “of various kinds”]. The garrison, on the other hand, despairing of life and trusting only in arms [Note: [Col. 0907] “only,” 3.], raised the defensive works, repaired what had been destroyed, lifted palisades and stones already prepared, and hurried to block the gates.

When the engines had been prepared and all armed [Note: [Col. 0907] *universibus*, 1 and 2], the Poles vigorously attacked the fortress on every side [Note: [Col. 0907] “besieged,” 3], while the Pomeranians defended it no less vigorously. The Poles pressed the attack so fiercely for justice and victory; the Pomeranians resisted for their innate treachery and for the preservation of their lives [Note: [Col. 0907] “The Poles … resisted” absent in 3.]. The Poles sought glory; the Pomeranians defended liberty [Note: [Col. 0907] “The Poles sought glory … defended liberty” absent in 2.].

At last, however [Note: [Col. 0907] “Therefore,” 3.], the Pomeranians, exhausted by continual [Note: [Col. 0907] Absent in 3.] labours and vigils [Col. 0908D], reflecting that they could not withstand such great forces [Note: [Col. 0907] *meditari*, “to reflect,” 1, 2, and 3], descended from the first arrogance of their pride and surrendered themselves and the fortress, after receiving Boleslav’s glove [Col. 0909A] [Note: [Col. 0909] *cyrotheca*, 3.] as a pledge [Note: [Col. 0909] “handed over,” 3] (A.D. 1108).

But the Poles, recalling so many labours [Note: [Col. 0909] “so many labours” absent in 3], so many deaths, so many harsh winters, so many betrayals and ambushes, killed them all, sparing none; nor did they heed even Boleslav himself when he forbade it. Thus little by little the rebellious and obstinate Pomeranians were destroyed by Boleslav, as faithless men ought rightly to be destroyed [Note: [Col. 0909] “are accustomed to be destroyed,” 2.]. Boleslav strengthened the fortress for more secure retention [Note: [Col. 0909] “fortified,” 3], furnished it [Note: [Col. 0909] “it also,” 3] with necessities, and stationed his own soldiers there.

### 49. Six hundred Pomeranians are slain in Masovia

[Note: [Col. 0909] Heading in manuscript 3; absent in 1 and 2.]

(A.D. 1109.) Yet in the following summer the Pomeranians assembled and crossed into Masovia [Note: [Col. 0909] *Maiozoviam*, 2.] to seize plunder. But just as they attempted to make the Masovians their plunder, so they were compelled to become plunder for those same Masovians [Col. 0909B] [Note: [Col. 0909] 3 has *de*, “from,” for *sic ab*, “so by”]. For they themselves were roaming through Masovia, gathering booty and captives and burning buildings [Note: [Col. 0909] *concrementes*, 3.], and now stood secure with their spoil, entertaining no fear of battle.

And behold, a count named Magnus, who then ruled Masovia [Note: [Col. 0909] “who … ruled” absent in 3], entered into a terrible battle against the more numerous and innumerable pagans with the Masovians—few indeed in number, but numerous in valour [Note: [Col. 0909] 3: “and in strength”] [Note: [Col. 0909] *numerosos*, wrongly, 1 and 2]. There God revealed his omnipotence. For they say that more than six hundred pagans perished there [Col. 0910A], that the Masovians took from them all the plunder and captives, and that the remainder undoubtedly either were captured or fled.

Indeed Simon, bishop of that region [Note: [Col. 0909] “religion,” 1 and 2], followed with his clergy his sheep, torn by wolfish bites, with mournful cries, clothed in priestly vestments [Note: [Col. 0909] “pontifical,” 3.]. What he could not accomplish with material arms, he strove to accomplish with spiritual weapons and prayers [Note: [Col. 0909] “laboured earnestly,” 3.]. And just as in ancient times the sons of Israel overcame the Amalekites by the prayers of Moses [Note: [Col. 0909] *Moysi*, “of Moses,” 1, 2, and 3], so the Masovians won victory over the Pomeranians, aided by the prayers of their bishop [Note: [Col. 0909] “prelate,” 3.].

On the next day as well, two women gathering strawberries along byways brought news of a new victory: they found a Pomeranian soldier, stripped of his weapons, bound his hands behind his back [Col. 0910B], and brought him before the count and bishop.

### 50. The defeat of the Bohemians and Zbigniew

[Note: [Col. 0909] Heading in the Gdańsk and Warsaw editions; absent in 1, 2, and 3.]

Zbigniew’s soldiers, together with the Bohemians, were plundering and burning through the Silesian region [Note: [Col. 0909] “religion,” incorrectly, 3.] [Note: [Col. 0909] *Zlesiensem*, 3.]. They too were defeated in like misfortune by the neighbouring inhabitants [Note: [Col. 0909] 3 has only *af*], some being captured and others slaughtered with the sword [Note: [Col. 0909] “slaughtering with the sword,” in place of “slaughtered with the sword,” 1 and 2.].

Let us rest a little from these lesser matters already set forth, so that, following the thread of the narrative, we may proceed to the third book, concerning greater matters.

[Col. 0909] **HERE ENDS THE SECOND BOOK; THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS.**

## THIRD BOOK

[Note: [Col. 0909] Title in the Warsaw edition, p. 237; absent in 1, 2, and 3.]

[Col. 0909]

### The epistle of the third book begins

[Note: [Col. 0909] Manuscript 3 has “and first the prologue,” in place of “The epistle of the third book begins,” joining it to the preceding book.]

To the venerable ducal chaplains and to the other worthy clerics to be remembered throughout Poland, the author of the present little work: may you so pass beyond temporal goods that you may readily leap from things perishable to those enduring.

First of all, dearest brothers, I wish you to know that I did not undertake so great a work in order thereby to enlarge the fringes of my own insignificance, nor in order to exalt before you, as an exile and stranger, my country or my relatives [Note: [Col. 0909] Absent in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0909] “strangers,” 2.], but in order to bring back some fruit of my labour to the place of my profession. Again, I make this clear to your discernment: I undertook this labour not as though preferring myself above others [Note: [Col. 0909] “others,” 3.] or presenting myself as more eloquent in speech, but in order to avoid idleness, preserve the habit of composition, and not eat Polish bread in vain.

Moreover, the abundant matter of wars stirred my ignorance to presume upon a burden unequal to my strength [Col. 0909D], and the valour and magnanimity of Boleslav himself, the warlike duke [Note: [Col. 0909] Absent in 3.], furnished me confidence to dare [Note: [Col. 0909] “to please,” 2; “to hear,” 3.]. Therefore receive not what is mine but what is yours [Note: [Col. 0909] “your,” 1.]; weigh not the craftsman but the gold; drink not the vessels but the wine. And if perhaps you criticize the poverty of language in this work, at least from these things [Note: [Col. 0909] “at least,” 2.] you may have material for treatment more profound [Note: [Col. 0909] Absent in 3.] and more richly argued.

But if you judge Polish kings or dukes unworthy of annual chronicles [Note: [Col. 0909] *aialibus*, 2 and 3.], you must without doubt assign the kingdom of Poland to whatever uncultivated barbarian nations you please. And if perhaps you object that I, a man unworthy both in character and in life, have presumed to undertake such matters, I shall answer: I have written the wars of kings and dukes, not the Gospel. For never would the fame or military power of the Romans or Gauls have become so renowned throughout the world unless, through writers’ testimony, it had been preserved for the memory and imitation of posterity [Note: [Col. 0909] “and” absent in 3.].

Great Troy too, though it lay destroyed and deserted, was nevertheless inscribed in the titles of poets for everlasting remembrance [Col. 0910D]. Its walls lie levelled [Note: [Col. 0909] *quoequati*, 1.], its towers destroyed; spacious and pleasant places lack inhabitants; in the palaces of kings and princes there lurk dens of wild beasts and hidden lairs. Yet the Pergamum of Troy [Note: [Col. 0909] *Pargama*, 2.] is proclaimed throughout all lands by the voice of writing [Col. 0911A] [Note: [Col. 0911] singular “is proclaimed,” 2 and 3.]; Hector and Priam are recounted more often in the dust than upon the throne of kingship [Note: [Col. 0911] “is recounted upon the throne of kingship,” in place of “are recounted …,” 3.].

What should I recount of Alexander the Great, of Antiochus, of the kings of the Medes and [Note: [Col. 0911] “and,” 3.] Persians, or of barbarian tyrants? If I were merely to recite their names, I would prolong today’s work until tomorrow [Note: [Col. 0911] “tomorrow,” feminine form, 3.]. Yet their fame is immortal in the praises of later-born men [Note: [Col. 0911] “by birth,” 2; “one born,” for “of later-born men,” 1 and 3.], though their life is not everlasting but winged [Note: [Col. 0911] *penalis*, “penal,” 1, 2, and 3.].

For just as holy men [Note: [Col. 0911] The reading of the Gdańsk edition is absent in 1, 2, and 3.] [Note: [Col. 0911] *su*, 2 and 3.] are celebrated for good works and miracles, so worldly kings and princes are exalted by triumphant wars and victories. And just as it is a religious act to proclaim in churches the lives and sufferings of the saints, so it is glorious to recite in schools or in the palaces of kings and dukes their triumphs or [Note: [Col. 0911] “and,” 3.] victories. And just as the lives or sufferings of saints, preached in churches, instruct the minds of the faithful in religion [Col. 0911B] [Note: [Col. 0911] “are instructed,” incorrectly, 1 and 2.], so the military exploits or victories [Note: [Col. 0911] “military exploits or victories” absent in 3.] of kings and dukes, recited in schools or capitols [Note: [Col. 0911] *capitolis*, 2; “palaces,” 3.], inflame the spirits of soldiers toward valour.

For just as pastors of the Church [Note: [Col. 0911] “of churches,” 3.] ought to seek the spiritual fruit of souls, so defenders strive to extend the honour and fame of their country and temporal glory. For God’s ministers ought spiritually to obey God in matters which are God’s, and in matters which are Caesar’s to render honour and service to worldly princes. What wonder, then, if triumphant and illustrious men seek fame and glory through valour, when even Cleopatra, queen of Carthage [Note: [Col. 0911] *Karthaginis*, 3.], eager for praise [Note: [Col. 0911] *avidia*, 3.], wished to transfer the Roman empire by manly boldness [Note: [Col. 0911] *viri*, 2.] [Note: [Col. 0911] *auda*, 3.], not by natural or [Col. 0911C] feminine excellence?

And if a woman seeking empire, defeated in a naval battle, preferred to kill herself by a terrible death rather than serve, what wonder is it if those defending their fatherland or paternal inheritance, or pursuing an injury inflicted upon them, prefer to perish in war by a famous, not poisonous [Note: [Col. 0911] “veined,” 2.] death [Note: [Col. 0911] Absent in 2 and 3.] rather than obey their own dependants in disgrace?

It is therefore clear, from the foregoing established examples, that the deeds of Polish rulers have not been recounted in vain [Note: [Col. 0911] The Warsaw edition judged *non*, “not,” to be added, although it is absent in 1, 2, and 3.]; and it is also clear that, by your judgment, the present work should be approved and recited with a truthful [Note: [Col. 0911] Absent in 3.] interpreter [Note: [Col. 0911] 3 adds *vero*, “truthful”]. Moreover, may the cause of God and the cause of Poland provide [Note: [Col. 0911] “will provide,” 3.] that your discerning goodness does not hinder the reward for so great a labour through hatred or through an occasion arising from any vanity of mine. For if my work is judged by wise men to be good and useful for the honour of the country, it is unworthy and unfitting that, by the counsel of certain persons, the craftsman should be deprived of the reward for his work [Col. 0911D].

[Col. 0912A] **The epistle ends.**  
[Note: [Col. 0911] “Prologue,” 3.]

### The epilogue begins

[Note: [Col. 0911] “Epilogue,” 3.]

To God be praise and honour, kingdom, power, and glory,

Under whose might Pomerania is subdued;

To Boleslav [Note: [Col. 0911] “For Boleslav,” 2.], triumphant, safety [Note: [Col. 0911] abbreviated *sal’*, 2.] and victory [Note: [Col. 0911] abbreviated *victo*, 2.].

Let us refer all things to the honour of Jesus Christ,

Who governs the whole world by his wisdom;

This was not done by human strength, nor by military force.

Boleslav was besieging a most ancient fortress,

Most strongly defended by men, arms, and [Note: [Col. 0911] “and” absent in the manuscripts.] its natural position,

And most dangerous to the detriment of his kingdom.

The Pomeranians came to aid the besieged

And hurried to attack the unsuspecting besiegers [Note: [Col. 0911] “In” absent in the manuscripts.].

But, deceived in vain hope [Note: [Col. 0911] “received,” 2.], they were brought to ruin.

Almost all, proceeding on foot through shadowy places [Note: [Col. 0911] *opaga*, 1 and 2.] by devious ways [Note: [Col. 0911] “would be,” 1, 2, and 3.],

[Col. 0912B] The soldiers, lest they place hope of flight in horses [Note: [Col. 0911] *cabellis*, 2.],

Emerged unexpectedly by unknown paths.

Duke Boleslav, armed, with a few soldiers,

Palatine Skarbimir with his companions,

Seven hundred clashed with thirty [Note: [Col. 0911] “twenty-nine,” 3.] thousand.

For on the preceding night they had kept watch,

And, hearing that the enemy were coming, had laid ambushes;

Thus the duke had sent forces hither and thither [Note: [Col. 0911] Absent in 2.].

But the others, bending down, drew up their battle-line [Note: [Col. 0911] “drew up,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0911] 3 adds “forces” only at this point.],

Bringing their spears together on every side into a hedgehog [*ericium*] [Note: [Col. 0911] “they are,” 1, 2, and 3.] [Note: [Col. 0911] *prolectentes*, 2.] [Note: [Col. 0911] *ericium*, 3.] [Note: [Col. 0911D] That is: the Pomeranian battle-line bristled, formed into a circle like a hedgehog, with spears. K.],

And they did not advance in companies, but stood in a circle [Note: [Col. 0911] *cyntinnium*, 1; *cyncinnium*, 2 and 3.].

Duke Boleslav, sufficiently shrewd in such a [Note: [Col. 0911] “their,” 3.] situation [Note: [Col. 0911] “shrewd men,” 3.],

Prudently rode around them on every side,

[Col. 0912C] As a bold and warlike man eager for praise.

Skarbimir, from the opposite side, threw himself into their midst

And exhorted and encouraged his comrades to fight:

“Pomeranians, you have not felt swords such as these!”

But why say more? The Pomeranians turned their backs in battle,

And no slaughter as great as this had ever been inflicted upon them [Note: [Col. 0911] 3: “Nor was such a slaughter inflicted upon them at any other time.”],

The duke gained seven fortresses as the prize of war.

In these things [Note: [Col. 0911] 3 adds “therefore.”] let us praise God and Saint [Note: [Col. 0911] Absent in 3.] Lawrence,

On whose most sacred day this battle was fought [Note: [Col. 0911] 3: “the battle was joined,” for “this battle was fought.”],

And there let a worthy building be made for him.

To Boleslav’s victory, so illustriously described,

Let peace and friendship with Augustus be assigned;

Let brotherly concord, as is fitting, be confirmed.

For this reason, it is clear [Note: [Col. 0911] “thus,” 1, 2, and 3; the Gdańsk edition reads *per quas partes*, “through which regions,” a reading adopted by the Warsaw edition.], the emperor had come into these parts.

[Col. 0912D] With what arrogance and what power he had entered this kingdom!

Whom he had already decided to depose, whom to appoint [Note: [Col. 0911] “now,” 3.]!

[Col. 0913A] But what strength or counsel prevails against God?

Without whose will nothing happens, nor does a leaf move,

Who, if he wills, turns mountain ridges into valleys.

Boleslav stands in the kingdom as a great duke and lord,

And is ready for war like a lion at close quarters:

Whoever resists is overcome, or else flees at once.

Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0913] *Bohemenses*, 2 and 3.], why do you delay to bow your necks?

Since you see the king himself yield to Boleslav,

So that [Note: [Col. 0913] “here,” 3.] you may know that you cannot resist by force.

There is no enemy capable of engaging so great a duke,

[Col. 0914A] Or who dares openly to declare himself his equal,

Nor any neighbour who does not rejoice in peace with him.

For against enemies he proves a marvellous conqueror [Note: [Col. 0913] “marvellous,” 3.],

Toward all he is a generous giver, with honour,

And through him the king of the Hungarians remains at peace.

There is no time to recount each of the things he has done,

Which those know who have endured prisons and chains [Note: [Col. 0913] “who,” 1 and 2.].

We offer these small gifts for praise, not for deceit [Note: [Col. 0913] “here,” 1 and 2.].

## THE THIRD BOOK OF THE DEEDS OF BOLESLAV THE THIRD BEGINS

[Note: [Col. 0913] The entire title is absent in 3.]

[Col. 0913]

### 1. Victory over the Pomeranians

[Note: [Col. 0913] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 247; absent in 1, 2, and 3.]

[Col. 0913B]

Among the many and innumerable military deeds of Boleslav the Third, this above all deserves to be recorded: how it happened to the Pomeranians on Saint Lawrence’s day; how the emperor’s wrath was restrained; and how the impetuous Germans were resisted [Note: [Col. 0913] *ostentum*, 3.].

There is a certain fortress called Nakło, on the border between Poland and Pomerania, known to be strong both by marshes and by workmanship. The warlike duke, encamped with his army to take it, was labouring with arms and siege-engines. When the townsmen saw that they could not withstand so great a multitude, though they expected aid from their own rulers, they sought a truce and fixed a definite day, before which, if their people did not help them, they would give both themselves and the town into the enemy’s power [Note: [Col. 0913] “power,” 3.] [Col. 0913C].

A truce from attacking them was indeed granted [Note: [Col. 0913] 3: “a truce from attacking was granted to them”], but the preparations for assault were by no means delayed. Meanwhile the envoys of the townsmen found the Pomeranian army and reported to them the agreement which their people had made with the enemy. Then the Pomeranians, astonished at the news, swore together [Note: [Col. 0913] 3 adds “either themselves” here.] either to die for their country or [Note: [Col. 0913] “or themselves” absent in 3.] to gain victory over the Poles [Note: [Col. 0913] “against the Poles,” 3.].

They dismissed their horses so that, with danger equally shared, all might have greater confidence [Note: [Col. 0913] “and,” 3.] and courage. They followed neither road nor path, but broke through the lairs of beasts and the dense places [Note: [Col. 0913] “and dense places,” 3.] of the forests. Not on the appointed day, but on the most sacred day of Saint Lawrence (A.D. 1109, 10 August), they emerged like mice from hiding-places [Note: [Col. 0913] 3 repeats “day”] and perished by their own evidence, not by human but by divine hand [Note: [Col. 0913] “and were indicated,” wrongly, 1 and 2; “and utterly,” for “by their own evidence,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0913] The Warsaw edition rightly observes that the Romans liked to say: “I myself have perished today by my own evidence, like a mouse.” Terence, *Eunuchus* V.7.23. S.].

God is glorious in his saints. For the day of Saint Lawrence the martyr was venerable [Note: [Col. 0913] Absent in 3.]; and at that hour the Christian congregation [Note: [Col. 0913] *consio*, erroneously, 1 and 2.] was leaving the solemn celebration of Mass, and behold, suddenly the army of barbarians was threatening close at hand.

[Col. 0914B] **Verse** [Note: [Col. 0913] The sign *v* placed here in 1 and 2 indicates verse.]

> Martyr Lawrence, aid the people who deserve aid.

What now will the Christians do [Note: [Col. 0913] “What more? What are they to do?” 3.]? Where will they turn [Note: [Col. 0913] “may they turn,” 3.]? The enemy army was unforeseen; there was no time [Note: [Col. 0913] Absent in 3.] to form a battle-line. They themselves were few, the enemies many; flight, slow and never pleasing to Boleslav, was out of the question.

**Verse** [Note: [Col. 0913] 1 and 2 again place the sign *v*; absent in 3.]

> Martyr Lawrence, take away the violence endured by the people!

Therefore, all the soldiers who were present were arranged in only two divisions. The warlike Boleslav himself led one division, and his standard-bearer Skarbimir the other. For some of the remaining multitude [Note: [Col. 0913] “to the remaining multitude,” 1 and 2; 3: “but the remaining multitude”] were seeking fodder [Note: [Col. 0913] *babulum*, 1.] for the horses, others provisions, while still others watched the roads and paths [Note: [Col. 0913] *intramites*, in place of *et tramites*, 2.] and the enemy’s approach [Note: [Col. 0913] Absent in 1 and 2.].

Without delay, energetic Boleslav led out the divisions, encouraging them with these very few words: “Your valour, the necessity of the approaching danger, and love of country, rather than my speech [Note: [Col. 0913] *uia*, 2.], should exhort you, unconquered young men. Today, with God’s favour and Saint Lawrence’s intercession, Pomeranian idolatry and military pride will be crushed by our swords.”

Having said no more, he began to ride round the enemy, because they had planted their spears in the ground with their points turned outward against the enemy and had packed themselves together [Note: [Col. 0913] *sese*, 2.] so closely that no one could penetrate to them by strength unless also by ingenuity. For, as said above, nearly all were infantry, and they were not arrayed for battle in the Christian manner, but, like wolves lying in wait for sheep, were bent at the knees toward the ground [Note: [Col. 0913] “ground,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0913] *poblitibus*, 1; *poblicibus*, 2.].

And while tireless Boleslav seemed more to dart about everywhere than [Col. 0914D] to run, with the enemy facing him crosswise, Skarbimir found a place to enter and, from the opposite side, did not delay [Note: [Col. 0913] “will not delay,” 2.] to penetrate the densely packed wedges. When the barbarians had been penetrated and enclosed, they at first resisted fiercely [Note: [Col. 0913] *acritus*, 2.], but at last, compelled, sought flight.

Of the Christians a number of worthy soldiers fell there [Col. 0915A] [Note: [Col. 0915] “some” absent in 3.]; but of forty thousand pagans scarcely ten thousand escaped. I call God to witness, by whose aid, and Saint Lawrence, by whose intercession, this slaughter was wrought [Note: [Col. 0915] “was,” 3.]: those present marvelled how so great a carnage could have been accomplished so suddenly [Note: [Col. 0915] “also,” 3.] by fewer than a thousand soldiers [Note: [Col. 0915] “were accomplished,” in place of “could have been accomplished,” 3.] (A.D. 1109).

The Pomeranians themselves are said to have counted with certainty twenty-seven thousand of their own who fell there; had the marshes not intervened, not even those could have escaped. The townsmen, seeing that they had lost all [Note: [Col. 0915] 3 adds “thus.”] hope and could expect aid from nowhere or from anyone, surrendered the town after their lives had been spared. When the inhabitants of six other fortresses heard this [Note: [Col. 0915] “certain persons there,” 3.], they likewise [Note: [Col. 0915] Absent in 3.] adopted the plan of surrendering themselves and their fortifications.

### 2. The emperor’s letter to Duke Boleslav

[Col. 0915B]

While these things were taking place [Note: [Col. 0915] 3: “While these things were thus being done”], the Emperor Henry the Fourth, not yet crowned at Rome but to be crowned in the second year thereafter [Note: [Col. 0915D] In the year 1111. K.], sent an embassy beforehand to Boleslav in words such as these, intending to invade Poland with a powerful army:

“It is unworthy of an emperor, and forbidden by Roman laws [Note: [Col. 0915] “prohibited,” 3.], to enter hostile territory—especially that of his own vassal—before [Note: [Col. 0915] Absent in 3.] asking him concerning peace, whether he wishes to obey, or concerning war, if he resists [Note: [Col. 0915] “resists,” 2.], so that he may make provision for himself [Note: [Col. 0915] “to make provision,” 2; “may be able to make provision,” 3.].

“Therefore you must either receive your brother into half of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0915] “half of the kingdom,” 2 and 3.] and give me three hundred marks yearly in tribute, or an equal number of soldiers for an expedition; or, if you can, divide the kingdom of the Poles with me by the sword.”

To this Boleslav, duke of the North, answered: “If you demand our money or Polish soldiers as tribute, and if we do not defend our liberty, let us be considered women, not men [Note: [Col. 0915] “let us be considered,” 3.]. No violence of power will compel me to receive a seditious man, or to divide even a single kingdom with him [Note: [Col. 0915] “one,” 3.], unless the common counsel of my men and the decision of my own will require it.

“But if you had requested money or soldiers as aid for the Roman Church in kindness rather than ferocity, perhaps you would have obtained from us no less aid or counsel than your predecessors obtained from ours [Note: [Col. 0915] “would obtain,” 2 and 3.]. Therefore consider carefully whom you threaten: you will find war, if you make war [Note: [Col. 0915] “if you make war,” incorrectly, 2.].”

### 3. The beginning of the war with Henry

[Note: [Col. 0915] Heading in the Warsaw edition; absent in 1, 2, and 3, which do not even leave a blank space.]

Provoked to extreme anger by this reply [Col. 0915D], the emperor conceived such designs and began upon such a course that he would not leave or return from it without being chastened with the greatest possible injury to himself and his own [Note: [Col. 0915] “one,” 1, 2, and 3.] [Note: [Col. 0915] “most greatly,” 3.]. Zbigniew too stirred the emperor’s anger still further, since he promised that few in Poland would resist him. Moreover, the Bohemians, accustomed to live by plunder and robbery, encouraged the emperor to enter Poland, boasting that they knew the roads and paths through Poland’s forests [Note: [Col. 0915] Thus corrected by P.; 1, 2, and 3 read “they incited.”].

The emperor, therefore, led by such warnings and counsels into the hope of conquering Poland [Note: [Col. 0915] “conquered,” 3.], entered it and reached Bytom; but in all these matters he was deceived [Note: [Col. 0915] “led back,” 2.]. For he saw the fortress of Bytom so armed and fortified [Note: [Col. 0915] Manuscript 3 omits “For he saw the fortress of Bytom …” here and places it below.] that the emperor looked angrily upon Zbigniew with words of indignation [Note: [Col. 0915] 3: “and the emperor [looked] upon Zbigniew”] [Note: [Col. 0915] 3 places “because he saw the fortress of Bytom so armed and fortified” here.].

“Zbigniew,” said the emperor [Note: [Col. 0915] 3 repeats “Zbigniew.”], “is this how the Poles acknowledge you as lord? Is this how they demand that your brother [Note: [Col. 0915] 3 adds “your.”] leave, and that your lordship be established?”

When he wished to pass by the fortress of Bytom, impregnable because of its fortification, natural position [Note: [Col. 0915] “bosom,” 1 and 2.], and encircling waters [Col. 0916B], with his battle-lines arrayed, certain renowned knights among his men turned toward the fortress, wishing to prove their own military prowess in Poland [Note: [Col. 0915] “into Poland,” 2 and 3.] [Note: [Col. 0915] “to be proved,” 1.] and to test the strength and boldness of the Poles.

But the garrison, opening the gates and drawing their swords, came out. They feared neither the multitude of so many different peoples, nor the German attack, nor the presence of the emperor, but resisted them [Note: [Col. 0915] “him,” 1 and 3.] boldly and manfully face to face. Seeing this, the emperor was greatly astonished: men without armour fighting with bare swords against shielded men, or shielded men [Note: [Col. 0915] “or shielded men” absent in 3.] against armoured men, and hurrying to battle as joyfully as to a feast.

Then, as though angered by the presumption of his soldiers [Col. 0916C], he sent his crossbowmen and archers there, so that at least through fear the garrison might yield and withdraw into the fortress [Note: [Col. 0915] “and withdraw” absent in 3.]. But the Poles counted the javelins and arrows that flew everywhere [Note: [Col. 0915] Absent in 2.] as though they were snow or drops of rain. There the emperor first tested Polish courage, because he did not recall all his men from that place unharmed [Note: [Col. 0915] 3: “he did not recall all his men thence unharmed.”].

But now let us allow the emperor to wander for a little while through the forests of Poland, until we bring back the flame-devouring dragon from Pomerania.

### 4. Boleslav prepares for war

[Note: [Col. 0915] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 260; absent in 1, 2, and 3.]

(A.D. 1109.) Thus tireless Boleslav, after winning the above-mentioned battle in Pomerania and acquiring seven fortresses, learned for certain that the emperor had entered Poland. His men and horses had been exhausted by the long siege [Col. 0916D], some soldiers had been killed, some wounded, and others sent home with them; yet he rode with those whom he could assemble. He gave orders by every means that the crossings [Col. 0917A] and fords of the River Oder should be blocked [Note: [Col. 0917] “entrusted,” 3.].

Accordingly, all places were blocked which could be forded even in low water, as well as any places that perhaps might be secretly attempted by the inhabitants themselves. He also sent certain worthy soldiers beforehand to Głogów [Note: [Col. 0917] Absent in 2.] and to [Note: [Col. 0917] Absent in 2.] guard the river-crossings. They were to resist the emperor until, when he came to their aid upon the riverbank, they either won complete victory or at least held the enemy there while awaiting the army or reinforcements.

Boleslav himself stood there with a small army not far from Głogów; nor is this surprising, because he had wearied his men for a very long time [Note: [Col. 0917] “would weary,” 1 and 2; “had wearied,” 3.]. There he heard reports and embassies; there he awaited his army; from there he sent scouts in every direction; from there he assigned chamberlains for his own men, the Ruthenians [Col. 0917B], and the Pannonians.

### 5. The siege of Głogów

[Note: [Col. 0917] Heading in the Warsaw edition; absent in 1, 2, and 3.]

But as the emperor proceeded on his march, he did not turn aside to test fords upstream or downstream. Rather, beside the city of Głogów he crossed with an attack through a place beyond estimation [Note: [Col. 0917] *inestiabile*, 2.], where no one knew of a crossing [Note: [Col. 0917] 3 adds “or made one.”], and where no one resisted. With dense ranks of armed men, while the citizens were unprepared, he forded the river [Note: [Col. 0917D] Cosmas, III.27. K.] at that place, which the garrison had never suspected or hoped needed to be suspected.

For it was the feast day of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle (24 August) when the emperor crossed the river, and the whole population of the city was then hearing the divine office. It is therefore evident that he crossed safely and without danger, acquiring much plunder, people, and even tents around the town [Col. 0917C]. Many also of those who had come to defend the fortress and were staying in tents outside it were prevented by the emperor from entering the fortress [Note: [Col. 0917] 3 adds “into”]; some were suddenly held there [Note: [Col. 0917] “detained,” 3.], while others were saved when flight came to their aid [Note: [Col. 0917] “flight,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0917] “coming to aid,” 2.].

One of these, fleeing, met Boleslav and told him everything that had happened. Then Boleslav did not vanish like a timid hare, but encouraged his men like a courageous soldier:

“O most valiant soldiers, wearied with me in many wars and expeditions, now too be with me, ready either to die or to live for the liberty of Poland [Note: [Col. 0917] “ready,” 2.]. I myself would gladly enter battle against the emperor even with so small a force, if I knew for certain that, even should I die there [Col. 0917D], I would bring the peril to my country to an end. But since the enemy outnumber us by more than a hundred to one, it is more honourable to resist here than presumptuously to go there with a few men and die. For if we resist here and bar their passage, that will be counted enough as a victory for us.”

Having said this, [Col. 0918A] he began to block with felled trees the little stream beside which he stood.

### 6. The truce of the people of Głogów

[Note: [Col. 0917] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 264; absent in 1, 2, and 3.]

Meanwhile, the emperor received hostages from the people of Głogów under oath, on this condition [Note: [Col. 0917] “with,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0917] “accepted,” 3.]: if, within five days, the citizens should arrange peace or some agreement by sending an embassy, then, once an answer had been returned—whether peace was concluded or refused—the citizens should nevertheless receive back their hostages. This was certainly done by stratagem. The emperor received the hostages with an oath because he believed that through them he could gain the city, even by perjury. The people of Głogów, moreover [Note: [Col. 0917] Absent in 3.], gave those hostages because in the meantime they fortified the places in the city which had been weakened by age.

### 7. The truce is broken

[Note: [Col. 0917] Heading in the Warsaw edition, p. 265; absent in 1, 2, and 3.]

[Col. 0918B]

Boleslav, however, angered when he heard the embassy’s report concerning the hostages that had been given, threatened the citizens with the cross if they surrendered the fortress on their account [Note: [Col. 0917] “through,” 3.], adding that it would be better and more honourable for both citizens and hostages to die by the sword for their country than, by surrendering, to purchase a dishonourable life and serve foreign nations. Having received their answer [Note: [Col. 0917] “return” 3.], the citizens reported that Boleslav was unwilling for peace to be made on these terms, and demanded back their hostages, as they had sworn (A.D. 1109). To this the emperor replied: “Indeed, if you surrender the fortress to me, I shall not retain the hostages; but if you rebel, I shall slaughter both you and the hostages.” The defenders replied [Note: [Col. 0917] “the fortress,” incorrectly, 1, 2.]: “You may indeed commit both perjury and murder against the hostages; but know that through them you will by no means obtain what you demand.” [Col. 0918C]

### 8. The siege of the fortress of Głogów [Note: [Col. 0917] heading, Warsaw edition, p. 266, absent in 1, 2, 3.]

Having said this, the emperor ordered engines to be made, arms taken up, the legions divided, the town surrounded with a rampart, and standard-bearers to sound their trumpets; and he began to assail the city on every side with iron, fire, and engines. In response [Note: [Col. 0917] “against,” 1.], the citizens divided themselves [Note: [Col. 0917] “if,” 2.] among the gates and towers, fortified the defences, prepared engines, and brought stones and water up upon the gates and towers. Then the emperor, thinking that the citizens’ spirits might [Note: [Col. 0917] absent in 3.] be bent by compassion for their sons and friends, ordered the nobler hostages [Note: [Col. 0917] “towns,” 2.] of that city, and [Note: [Col. 0917] absent in 1, 2, 3.] the count’s daughter, to be bound upon the engines, believing thus that the city would be opened to him without bloodshed. But the defenders spared their sons [Col. 0918D] and kinsmen no more than they spared Bohemians or Germans; rather, with stones and [Note: [Col. 0917] “or,” 3.] arms they compelled them to withdraw from the wall. Seeing, however, that by such a device he would never overcome the city, nor ever turn the citizens’ minds from their purpose, the emperor strove to obtain by strength and arms what was denied him by stratagem.

[Col. 0919A] Therefore the fortress was assailed from every side, and a mighty clamour rose on both sides [Note: [Col. 0919] “between the two parties,” 3.]. The Germans [Note: [Col. 0919] *Thetonici*, 1, 2.] attacked the fortress; the Poles defended themselves. Engines hurled masses everywhere; crossbows rang; javelins [Note: [Col. 0919] “missiles and,” 3.] and arrows flew through the air; shields were pierced, cuirasses penetrated [Note: [Col. 0919] “pierced through,” 3.], helmets shattered [Note: [Col. 0919] “struck,” 2.]; the dead fell, the wounded withdrew, and the healthy men took their places.

The Germans discharged crossbows; the Poles engines together with crossbows [Note: [Col. 0917D] Compare Sallust, *Jugurtha* 57; *Catiline* 56. S.]. The Germans shot arrows; the Poles javelins together with arrows. The Germans whirled slings with stones; the Poles millstones with sharpened stakes. Protected by beams [Note: [Col. 0919] “drawings/tractions,” 1, 2.], the Germans tried to approach the wall [Note: [Col. 0919] “they crept up,” for “they tried to approach,” 2.]; but the Poles made them a bath of burning fire and boiling water [Note: [Col. 0919] “themselves,” 3.]. The Germans brought iron rams up beneath towers; [Col. 0919B] but the Poles rolled down from above [Note: [Col. 0919] absent in 3.] wheels studded with steel [Note: [Col. 0919] *calliberatas*, incorrectly, 3.]. The Germans climbed upward on raised ladders; the Poles, with iron hooks fastened upon them, suspended them in the air.

### 9. The Germans carry off the wounded and corpses as tribute [Note: [Col. 0919] heading, Warsaw edition, p. 269, absent in 1, 2, 3.]

Meanwhile Boleslav did not cease by day and night [Note: [Col. 0919] “and by night,” 3.], but harassed all who went out from the camp for provisions; he also frequently terrified the emperor’s camp itself, running now here, now there, while lying in wait for plunderers or burners. By such means, therefore, for many days the emperor strove to take the city, and gained nothing but the freshly killed human flesh of his own men every day [Note: [Col. 0919] absent in 3.]. For noble men were killed there daily; after their entrails had been removed, their bodies were preserved with salt or spices, to be carried in loaded wagons into Bavaria to the emperor [Note: [Col. 0919] “into Bavaria, to the emperor,” for “into Bavaria, by the emperor,” 3.] or into [Note: [Col. 0919] absent in 2, 3.] Saxony, as tribute from Poland [Note: [Col. 0919] “from the Poles,” 2, 3.]. [Col. 0919C]

### 10. Panic among the Germans at the head and tail attacks of their harasser [Note: [Col. 0919] heading, Warsaw edition, p. 271, absent in 1, 2, 3.]

When the emperor saw that he could bend the citizens neither by arms [Note: [Col. 0919] “not,” 3.] nor threats, gifts, or promises, and that by remaining there any longer he could achieve nothing [Note: [Col. 0919] “accomplish there,” repeated, 3.], he took counsel and moved his camp against the city of Wrocław, where [Note: [Col. 0919] “there,” 3.] he also recognized Boleslav’s strength and ingenuity. For wherever the emperor turned, or wherever he made camp or halts, Boleslav too followed, though later, [Col. 0919D] and always remained near the emperor’s position [Note: [Col. 0919] *presistebat*, 3.].

Whenever the emperor was on the march and moved his camp, Boleslav likewise became his travelling companion; [Col. 0920A] and whoever [Note: [Col. 0919] “whosoever,” 2.] left the ranks [Note: [Col. 0919] “went out,” 2, 3.] immediately forgot all thought of returning. And if several men, seeking provisions or fodder for the horses [Note: [Col. 0919] “*habulum*,” 2.], ventured farther from the camp in reliance on their numbers, Boleslav immediately placed himself between them and the army; thus, while desiring plunder [Note: [Col. 0919] “desiring” entered in the margin by the same or a contemporary hand; “taking” had been written, 2.], they themselves became Boleslav’s booty [Note: [Col. 0919] “made,” erroneously, 1, 2.].

Thus he brought so great and such an army to such terror that he compelled even the Bohemians, naturally rapacious, either to eat their own goods [Note: [Col. 0919] “*bo*” added by 2, but marked with dots above; Bandtkie reads *bona*, “goods.”] or to go hungry (A.D. 1109). No one dared leave the camp [Note: [Col. 0919] “heard,” 1, 2.]; no man-at-arms dared gather grass; no one even presumed to go beyond the appointed lines of guards to relieve his bowels [Note: [Col. 0919] absent in 3.]. By day and night [Note: [Col. 0919] “and by night,” 3.] Boleslav was feared and remembered by all; [Col. 0920B] he was called “Boleslav who does not sleep” [Note: [Col. 0919] “indeed,” 2.]. If there was a little wood or a thicket [Note: [Col. 0919] absent in 3.], they cried: “Watch yourself—he is lurking there!” There was no place where Boleslav was not thought to be.

In this way he continually exhausted them: at one time he seized some from the head, at another from the tail, like a wolf; at another time [Note: [Col. 0919] “sometimes,” 3.] he pressed them from the flanks. Thus the soldiers went forth armed every day and continually expected Boleslav as though he were present. At night too all slept in armour, or stood at their posts; some kept watch, some continually circled the camp [Note: [Col. 0919] “camps,” 3.] through the night, some cried, “Keep watch! Beware! Guard!” [Note: [Col. 0919] absent in 3.], while others sang songs celebrating Boleslav’s valour [Note: [Col. 0919] “sang,” 3.] in this manner [Note: [Col. 0919] “etc.” added, 3.]:

### 11. A German song in praise of Boleslav [Note: [Col. 0919] heading, Warsaw edition, p. 274, absent in 1, 2, 3.]

[Col. 0920C]

> Boleslav, Boleslav, most glorious duke,  
> You defend your land with utmost zeal.  
> You do not sleep, nor do you let us sleep even a little,  
> Neither by day, nor by night, nor at dawn [Note: [Col. 0919] “nor,” 3.].  
> And while we thought to drive you from the land [Note: [Col. 0919] “think,” 3.],  
> You hold us as though shut up in prison.  
>
> Such a prince ought to rule a kingdom and land,  
> Who knows, with few men, how to chastise so many and so great.  
> What [Note: [Col. 0919] “Who,” 3.] if perhaps he should gather all his own men together?  
> The emperor could never withstand him in war.  
>
> Such a man would be worthy of a kingdom and empire,  
> Who with few men thus subdues so many bands of enemies.  
> And although he has not yet recovered from Pomerania,  
> Yet through him our arrogance is so exhausted;  
> And though he should be met with triumph,  
>
> [Col. 0920D] We [Note: [Col. 0919] “Nor,” 3.] instead intend to attack his fatherland.  
> He indeed wages lawful wars against pagans,  
> But we wage unlawful wars against Christians;  
>
> [Col. 0921A] Therefore God is with him, granting victory,  
> While to us He justly repays the injury we inflicted [Note: [Col. 0921] “inflicted,” 3.].

### 12. The emperor is compelled to implore peace [Note: [Col. 0921] heading, Warsaw edition, p. 276, absent in 1, 2, 3.]

Certain noble and discerning men, hearing this, marvelled and said among themselves [Note: [Col. 0921] “saying,” 3.]: “Unless God were helping this man, He would never grant him so great a victory over pagans, nor would he stand against us so manfully. And unless God exalted him so powerfully, our people would never praise him in this way.” But perhaps God did these things by a hidden counsel [Note: [Col. 0921] “this,” 3.], transferring the emperor’s praise [Note: [Col. 0921] “praise,” singular, 2.] to Boleslav; for the voice of the people is always accustomed to accord with the voice of the Lord. One thing is certain: the singing people obey God’s will.

The people’s song displeased the emperor, and he very often forbade it to be sung [Note: [Col. 0921] “to the singer,” 1, 2.]; but this moved the people all the more [Col. 0921B] to such boldness [Note: [Col. 0921] “of the people” seems to have been written in 2; 3 has a corrupt reading for “moved the people.”]. The emperor, however, recognizing from examples and events that he was exhausting the people in vain and could not resist the divine will, devised something more secret and pretended that he would do something else [Note: [Col. 0921] corrupt reading in 3 for “and pretended that he would do something else.”]. For he reflected indeed [Note: [Col. 0921] “therefore,” 3.] that so great a host could not live longer without booty [Note: [Col. 0921] absent in 3.], and that Boleslav was continually circling them [Note: [Col. 0921] absent in 3.] like a roaring lion. Horses were dying; men were tormented by watchfulness, labour, and hunger; dense forests, clinging marshes, biting flies, sharp arrows, and biting peasants did not permit their purpose to be fulfilled [Note: [Col. 0921] “permit,” 2.].

Accordingly, pretending that he wished to go to Kraków, he sent envoys concerning peace to Boleslav and asked for money—not so much, nor so arrogantly, as he had previously demanded—in these words [Note: [Col. 0921] “etc.” added, 3.]:

### 13. The emperor’s letter to the king of Poland [Note: [Col. 0921] “Bo.” added, 3.]

[Col. 0921C]

(A.D. 1109.) “The emperor, to Boleslav, duke of Poland: favour and greeting. Having learned of your valour, I assent to the counsels of my princes; and, on receiving three hundred marks, I shall return hence in peace. This is enough for my honour, if we have peace and friendship together [Note: [Col. 0921] absent in 3.]. But if it does not please you to approve this, you may soon expect me at the see of Kraków” [Note: [Col. 0921] 3 gives a corrupt text for “if it does not please you … you may soon expect me.”].

### 14. Reply to the emperor [Note: [Col. 0921] heading absent in 3.]

To this the northern duke replied to the emperor [Note: [Col. 0921] “Boleslav,” 3.]: “Boleslav, duke of the Poles, certainly desires peace [Note: [Col. 0921] absent in 1, 2, 3; *recepit*, ‘received,’ in the Warsaw edition from the Gdańsk edition], but not in hope of pennies. It rests with your imperial power to go or to return; but from [Col. 0921D] me, neither through fear nor on terms, shall you be able to find even a single [Note: [Col. 0921] “indeed one,” 3.] worthless [Col. 0922A] obol [Note: [Col. 0921] absent in 3.]. For I would rather lose the kingdom of Poland with its liberty intact, for honour’s sake [Note: [Col. 0921] “of the kingdom of Poland,” for “the kingdom of Poland,” 2, 3; “liberty,” for “with liberty intact,” 3.], than retain it forever peacefully with disgrace.”

### 15. The emperor returns, carrying corpses as tribute [Note: [Col. 0921] heading, Warsaw edition, p. 280, absent in 1, 2, 3.]

Having heard this, the emperor approached the city of Wrocław, where he acquired nothing but dead men from the living. And while for a long time, pretending to go to Kraków, he wandered to and fro around the river [Note: [Col. 0921] “circled,” 3.], planning thus to strike terror [Note: [Col. 0921] “fear,” 3.] into Boleslav and turn back his spirit, Boleslav for that reason [Note: [Col. 0921] “rather,” 3.] had no distrust whatsoever, nor did he give the envoys any answer other than that given above.

Therefore the emperor, seeing that by remaining longer he faced rather loss and disgrace than honour or [Note: [Col. 0921] “and,” 3.] profit, resolved to return carrying as tribute nothing but corpses. [Col. 0922B] Thus, because he had first arrogantly demanded a great sum of money, in the end, though asking for little, he acquired not even a penny [Note: [Col. 0921] “nor,” 2.]. And because [Note: [Col. 0921] “because,” 3.] he had arrogantly planned to subject Poland’s ancient liberty, the righteous Judge made that counsel foolish and avenged both that wrong and another upon his adviser Swatopole [Note: [Col. 0921] 3 reads instead: “because the emperor returned to his own land with sufficiently abundant confusion.”].

### 16. [Note: [Col. 0921] Everything which follows from this point to the end of our edition is absent in 3, which breaks off the narrative with this addition: “This Boleslav was surnamed Krzywousty [‘Wrymouth’]; after the war which he had with Emperor Henry, he later waged many wars successfully against the Bohemians, Pomeranians, and Ruthenians, and triumphed gloriously.”] On the death of Swantopole [Note: [Col. 0921] Swathopole, 2, throughout.]

And since we have perhaps recalled Swatopole to memory, it is worthwhile to relate something concerning his life and death for the correction of others. Swatopole was first hereditary duke of Moravia [Note: [Col. 0921] *hereditaree*, 1, 2.]; later, full of ambition, he supplanted his lord Borivoy [Note: [Col. 0921] Borivou, 1.], duke of Bohemia [Note: [Col. 0921] “lordship,” 1, 2.]. He was noble by birth, fierce by nature, vigorous in war, [Col. 0922C] but of scant faith and crafty in disposition.

It was by his counsel that the emperor entered Poland. He had sworn not once but often to Boleslav; he had joined himself to Boleslav as one shield; by Boleslav’s valour and aid he had acquired the kingdom of Bohemia. Did not [Note: [Col. 0921] thus corrected by P.; “Nuq'o non,” 1, 2.] Boleslav, in order to install Swatopole at Prague [Note: [Col. 0921] “to set forth,” 2; “to promote,” 3.], enter Moravia with Coloman, king of Hungary, and penetrate the forests of Bohemia as its king was returning? Certainly he did. Nor would he have returned from there unless Borivoy gave him, by agreement, the fortress of Kamenz [Note: [Col. 0921D] Steinau on the Oder, between Lüben and Winzig in Silesia. Compare Cosmas III.4. S. Kamenz not far [Col. 0922D] from Frankenstein, in Stenzel’s opinion, *Scriptores Rerum Silesiacarum* I, 80. K.].

Moreover, Boleslav both retained and fed many men from Bohemia who had already fled to him, anticipating his favour and hoping that he himself would become duke, because Swatopole then possessed little land and little wealth. [Col. 0923A] Conversely, Swatopole swore to Boleslav that, if he ever became duke of Bohemia by whatever means or stratagem, he would always remain Boleslav’s faithful friend and their two persons would be one shield; and that he would either restore to Boleslav the border fortresses of the kingdom or utterly destroy them.

But once he had obtained the duchy, he neither kept faith, violating his oath, nor feared God, committing murders. Therefore, as an example to others, God gave him a recompense worthy of his deeds: secure, unarmed, seated upon a mule amid his own men, he fell when pierced by the spear of a single worthless soldier (September 20); and none of his own men lifted a hand to avenge him [Note: [Col. 0923D] Cosmas III.27–28. K.]. Thus the emperor returned triumphantly from Poland—namely, he carried home in memorial fashion mourning instead of joy, and the corpses of the dead instead of tribute. But Boleslav, duke of the Poles, undoubtedly feared him little when present, and less when absent [Note: [Col. 0923] thus corrected by P.; “doubted,” 1, 2.]. [Col. 0923B]

### 17. [Note: [Col. 0923] 1 and 2 retain the heading but omit only the number.] On the Bohemians

(A.D. 1109.) Therefore, after so great exertion, the northern duke, somewhat refreshed, was not delayed long before riding against the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0923] thus corrected by P.; “refreshed,” 1, 2.]. For he intended both to avenge upon the Bohemians his own injury and to restore his friend Borivoy to the seat from which he had been supplanted.

While travelling through the midst of the forests, he engaged the Bohemians who met him in battle and won the victory. Part of his army was already stationed in the plains of Bohemia, and Borivoy, now received by the Bohemians, rendered Boleslav thanks for such loyalty and labour. Thus indefatigable Boleslav [Col. 0923C] returned from Bohemia with a twofold honour (December 24). But let us hear what he did upon returning, so that we may derive some benefit from the example of such great valour.

### 18. [Note: [Col. 0923] “XVIII” absent in 1; “Chapter XVIII” absent in 2.] On the Pomeranians [Note: [Col. 0923] “On the Pomeranians” absent in 2.]

For he did not immediately allow the army, wearied by so great a journey, to go home; nor did he himself rest amid luxuries or banquets when the harshness of winter came on [Note: [Col. 0923] “came on,” 2.]. Instead, with selected soldiers from the army, he visited the land of the Pomeranians. How long he stayed there, or how much burning or plundering he carried out across the land, need not be set down point by point; rather, since we hasten to greater matters, it will suffice to explain the sum of the affair. On that expedition Boleslav captured three Pomeranian strongholds; having burned and levelled them, he took only booty and captives. Afterwards [Col. 0923D] Boleslav rested a little without warfare, while in the meantime making his cities, where the emperor had been, impregnable.

### 19. [Note: [Col. 0923] “XIX” absent in 1, 2.] On the Bohemians and Poles

While Boleslav was fortifying the city of Głogów and staying there with his army, Zbignev’s soldiers went out with Bohemians to plunder across Poland. Immediately, without Boleslav’s knowledge, the margraves of that region gathered together, and these men, coming out like mice from their hiding-places, were captured or left dead there, except for a few who sought the aid of the forest, friend of robbers. [Col. 0924A]

### 20. [Note: [Col. 0923] this heading is absent in 1, 2.] On the treachery of the Bohemians

A little above, I recall having said that the Bohemians had received Duke Borivoy to the seat from which he had been expelled, and that Boleslav had therefore returned so suddenly from Bohemia [Note: [Col. 0923] “therefore,” 2; in the margin of 1, in red, “No.”]. But because Bohemian faith is as changeable as a wheel, just as they had treacherously deceived Borivoy by expelling him, so they received him again treacherously, intending to deceive him again [Note: [Col. 0923] “so they received … again” absent in 2.]. (A.D. 1110.) For within a short time he was not only deprived of his dignity, supplanted by his middle brother [Note: [Col. 0923D] Vladislav. Cosmas III.30 ff. K.], but also lost the means of recovering it, having been captured by the emperor.

He also had a third brother [Note: [Col. 0924D] Soběslav. K.], [Col. 0924B] younger in age indeed [Note: [Col. 0923] “named Soběslav,” added in the margin by a fifteenth-century hand in 1.], but not inferior in valour. Duke Boleslav kept him in Poland because he remained loyal to his brother, and gave him support and assistance in contesting his elder brother’s dignity.

### 21. [Note: [Col. 0923] “Chapter XXI” absent in 1, 2.] On war and victory against the Bohemians

From there warlike Boleslav, having assembled a multitude of soldiers, opened a new route into Bohemia—an exploit that may be compared with Hannibal’s remarkable deed. For, as Hannibal, intending to attack Rome, was the first to make a road through Mount Jupiter, so Boleslav, intending to invade Bohemia, penetrated through a terrible place previously untried [Note: [Col. 0923] “first,” 2.]. Hannibal gained such fame and remembrance by laboriously crossing one mountain; but Boleslav ascended, as though climbing backward, not one but several cloud-bearing mountains. [Col. 0924C] Hannibal laboured only by cutting through the mountain and levelling rocks [Note: [Col. 0923] *scapulos*, not well, 2.]; Boleslav did not cease rolling logs and stones, climbing steep mountains [Note: [Col. 0923] “steep,” feminine, 2.], opening a way through dark forests, and making bridges in deep marshes.

Having travelled for three days and nights through such labour for Borivoy’s justice and friendship, weary Boleslav did such a thing in Bohemia that he will always be remembered in triumphant memory. After he had at last entered Bohemia amid such danger, he did not immediately make booty and return like a wolf snatching prey, as the Bohemians did from Poland. Rather, with standards raised, trumpets sounding, columns arrayed, and drums resounding, he advanced slowly through the open [Col. 0924D] plains of Bohemia, seeking battle and finding none; nor did he wish for booty or burning before an end had been made to the war.

(September.) Meanwhile the Bohemians appeared several times in companies, but immediately fled in constant flight when the Poles attacked (A.D. 1110). Many soldiers also went out from nearby fortresses; when the Poles attacked, their return afforded an opportunity to burn the suburbs. [Col. 0925A] Borivoy’s youngest brother, mentioned above, begged Boleslav not to seize booty, burn, or devastate the land, for in childish simplicity he believed that he could acquire the kingdom without war, through the words of traitors and without victories.

When Boleslav, now on the fourth day [Note: [Col. 0925] “fourth,” 2.], was expecting battle and hastening directly toward combat, and approached a certain river, not large indeed but difficult to cross, the duke of Bohemia was stationed on the opposite bank with an assembled army. Not daring to do so elsewhere, he awaited Boleslav there, trusting in the difficulty of the site, intending to bar the crossing.

But Boleslav, having found the enemies he sought, fumed like a lion that sees prey enclosed by barriers, because he had no opportunity to fight. For as the Poles considered crossing, now upstream, now downstream, [Col. 0925B] to the other side of the river, so the Bohemians stood opposite them. The river, according to the Bohemians who were with it lying [Note: [Col. 0925] *mcientes*, 1, 2.], was marshy and dangerous for so great a multitude to cross if none resisted.

Boleslav, seeing that in acting thus he was wasting time in vain and that the day was declining as the sun moved toward sunset, offered the Bohemian duke the choice demanded by military courage: either Boleslav should give him room to cross, or he himself would cross there if the Bohemian duke yielded the place. He further declared that he had not come to seize the Bohemian throne, but had undertaken, as was his custom, to defend the justice of exiles and the cause of the wretched, as Borivoy had formerly done for him. Therefore the Bohemian duke should either restore his brother peacefully to his share [Col. 0925C] of the paternal inheritance, or the just Judge of all should reveal true justice between them [Note: [Col. 0925] thus corrected by P.; *interesse*, “to be present,” in the manuscripts.] in a pitched battle.

The Bohemian duke replied: “I am ready willingly to receive my brother if you receive yours; but I have not dared to divide the kingdom with him except by the emperor’s counsel. But if I had either the will or the power to fight you hand to hand, I would not wait for your permission, since I formerly had ample [Note: [Col. 0925] “ample,” 1, 2.] freedom to cross.”

### 22. [Note: [Col. 0925] “XXII” absent in 1, 2.] On the devastation of the Bohemian land by the Poles

Boleslav, seeing that in the answers sent by the Bohemian duke there was no certain reason, but only bare words, broke camp at twilight, the time for rest, and, proceeding down that bank of the river to the River Elbe, did not move away from it. There, beside the Elbe, he crossed that little stream without obstruction [Note: [Col. 0925D] the Cidlina. K.] and hastened to seek battle where he had left it.

When he reached the Bohemians’ positions and found nothing of them but tracks [Note: [Col. 0925] “found,” 1, 2.], he called together the elders and took counsel, where he determined with sound reasoning what seemed sufficiently more beneficial and honourable. Some of the elders said: “For three days it is enough that we have stood by our valour in an enemy land and have not found battle, though all of them were assembled and present.” Others said: “God’s judgments are true and hidden from men. We have prospered well to this point, but if we delay longer [Note: [Col. 0925] “we diminish,” 1.], it hangs in doubt which way these fates may turn.”

On the other hand, Boleslav and the young men set aside the elders’ counsel and approved continuing onward to Prague. And the young men’s counsel would indeed have prevailed over that of the elders, had bread not failed—which has more power than civil law can exercise. Therefore, when Boleslav’s plan of return had scarcely been approved, he granted permission to burn and plunder as they returned. He himself always advanced with his cohorts in order, often remaining with the rearmost columns to provide support. He also had ordered lines of soldiers to go ahead of the burners and plunderers [Col. 0926B] and watch for Bohemians approaching.

Having led out and brought back his army so prudently and sagaciously, and having already pitched camp at the entrance to the forests on Friday, he ordered more frequent watches, greater readiness, and that each legion, should any disturbance arise, remain at its own post. That night, while Boleslav remained at prayer after matins, a certain terror by chance seized the entire camp [Note: [Col. 0925] “in,” added in 1, 2.], and raised a sudden cry throughout the army. Then every province and every armed cohort, as had been commanded, remained at its own [Note: [Col. 0925] “seen,” 1, 2.] station to defend its position. But the courtly battle-line, armed in courtly fashion [Note: [Col. 0925] “courtly men,” 1, 2.], stood around Boleslav, [Col. 0926C] ready to conquer or die there.

Boleslav, hearing the people’s cry, immediately surrounded by a crown of young men standing about him, climbed to a somewhat higher place in order to speak. There, by his speech, he increased the courage of the brave and removed from the fearful both horror and fear, beginning thus:

### 23. [Note: [Col. 0925] “XXIII” absent in 1, 2.] On Boleslav’s courage and foresight [Note: [Col. 0925] “prudence,” 2.]

(A.D. 1110.) “O youth illustrious in character and nature [Note: [Col. 0925] *juventus* added by the Warsaw edition; absent in 1, 2.], always trained with me in war, accustomed with me to hardship, hold yourselves securely; together await joyfully this present day, which will crown us with triumphant honour. Until now the Bohemians, like sea-monsters or woodland beasts, mocked the Poles and counted it soldiering to snatch something from our herds and flee with it through the woods. But you have now for seven days traversed their land, burned villages and suburbs, seen their duke and his assembled army, and sought battle without being able to find it.

“Indeed, today, whether the Bohemians do not engage in battle, or whether they do engage, today [Note: [Col. 0925] “today” repeated in 2.], with God’s help, the Poles will avenge their wrongs. And when you enter battle, remember the plunder, captives, and burnings; remember the girls carried off, wives and matrons; remember how often they provoked you [Note: [Col. 0925] absent in 2.]; [Col. 0927A] remember how often, while they fled, they exhausted you who pursued them. Therefore hold out a little, brothers and glorious soldiers; be strong in battle, my joyful young men. This day will give you what you have always desired; this day will erase the pain which you have borne for so long.

“Dawn is already at hand. Soon that glorious day will blaze forth [Note: [Col. 0927] *exarebit*, 1, 2.], which will expose the treachery and faithlessness of the Bohemians, trample down their presumption and pride, and avenge the wrongs done to us and our fathers: that day, I say—that day ever to be remembered in Poland; that day ever great, bitter, and dreadful to the Bohemians; that day glorious to the Poles, hateful to the Bohemians; that day, I say, joyous amid the rejoicing of all, [Col. 0927B] on which it will bow the foreheads of the Bohemians to the ground [Note: [Col. 0927] “to the ground with oars,” erroneously for *humotenus*, 1, 2.], on [Note: [Col. 0927] absent in 2.] which almighty God will exalt with the right hand of His greatness the horn of our humility [Note: [Col. 0927] “His,” 2.].”

When this speech had been completed, Mass was celebrated throughout the whole camp; the divine word was preached by the bishops to their parishioners; and all the people were strengthened by the most holy communion (October 8). After these rites had duly been performed, they left their positions with the battle-columns arranged as usual and gradually reached the entrance to the forests.

When so great a multitude had entered the woods, having neither knowledge of the place nor a trace of the route, every man made his own path through trackless ground, and so they could no longer keep either the standards or their order [Note: [Col. 0927] “now,” 2.]. For they heard that the road by which they had come, and all other roads, had been blocked; therefore they were returning [Col. 0927C] by another road, incapable of accommodating so great a multitude.

Duke Boleslav, however, remained behind on the right flank with the courtly battle-line, sending his whole army ahead like an excellent shepherd.
