Count Skarbimir too lay concealed for Boleslav on the other side, in a narrow wood; there he waited in ambush for the Bohemians, should they perhaps follow. The Gniezno battle-line, consecrated to the patron of Poland, together with certain palatines and other spirited soldiers, awaited its lord who had halted [Note: [Col. 0927] “who were halting,” 2.] in a small plain. This plain divided the greater woods from the smaller intervening wood.

As Boleslav followed his army obliquely through the narrow wood, seeing his own men and seen by them, he took them for enemies; and they likewise thought him an enemy. But when they came closer to one another and looked more carefully at their arms, they recognized the Polish standards and so refrained from a crime almost begun. [Col. 0927D]

Meanwhile the Bohemians, as though already certain of victory, hurried on—not, as before, in ordered companies [Note: [Col. 0927] absent in the manuscripts.], but one before another—because they believed they would capture the Poles, now withdrawn into the forest, as hares: men who could not be recalled to battle, disordered, hiding [Note: [Col. 0927] absent in 2.], and scattered. But warlike Boleslav, seeing the enemy already near, cried: “Young men, let the beginning of striking be ours, and ours the end also!” Having said this, he immediately laid low the first man in the line with his hunting-spear from his charger; and at the same time Dirsek, the cupbearer, offered another a deadly draught. Then [Note: [Col. 0927] “when,” 2.] the Polish youth rushed forward in rivalry, first making war with lances, and, when these were spent, drawing their swords. Shields [reading uncertain: *clepunt*] protected only a few of the approaching Bohemians there; cuirasses gave them weight, not assistance; helmets brought honour to their heads, not safety. There iron sharpened iron; there the bold soldier was recognized; there valour was overcome by valour. Bodies
Bodies lie strewn; faces and breasts are drenched with sweat; streams of blood flow; the young Poles cry out: “Thus must valour be proved by men; thus is fame won—not by secretly snatching booty and seeking the forest, in the manner of swift wolves.” [Col. 0928B] There the glittering first line of armoured Bohemians and Germans, which had been first, was first to fall, weighed down rather than helped by its armour. Yet the duke of the Bohemians, a second and a third time, though now the flower of his soldiery lay prostrate, strove to avenge his loss by wheeling his companies back; and ever the heap of his fallen men increased. Scarbimir also, with the palatine division, the forest lying between them, fought against other Bohemian columns, so that Boleslav knew nothing at all of where Scarbimir stood or whether he was fighting, nor Scarbimir of Boleslav. (A.D. 1110.)

On whichever side Mars exerts his strength, Fortune plays: the Bohemians’ wheel is overturned; the Fates cut the Bohemians’ threads [Note: [Col. 0927] “occantur,” MSS. 1 and 2]; Cerberus opens his devouring mouths; Charon, the ferryman, toils in sailing upon Acheron; [Col. 0928C] Proserpina laughs; the Furies spread out for them viperine garments [Note: [Col. 0927] “cuperinas,” MS. 2]; the Eumenides prepare sulphurous baths; Pluto commands the Cyclopes to fashion fitting crowns for soldiers deservedly to be honoured—with serpentine teeth and dragon tongues. Why prolong the matter? Seeing that their cause did not please the divine judgement, and that the Poles’ courage prevailed together with justice, their better troops there having been struck down in masses, the Bohemians scattered and took flight. The Poles did not at once perceive that they were fleeing [Note: [Col. 0927] “precipiunt,” MS. 2], but thought that they were feigning flight. For a certain valley in the middle and a forest assisted the Bohemians, concealing either their flight or an ambush. Therefore Boleslav, duke of the Poles, forbade his impetuous soldiers rashly to pursue them, [Col. 0928D] because he suspected Bohemian guile and ambushes. But when the Poles at length learned that the Bohemians’ flight was genuine, they immediately gave rein to their horses in pursuit.

Thus, having obtained a triumphant victory, the Poles delayed the journey they had begun back to Poland. As they returned, they carried their wounded with them out of Bohemia; with seven added to the three [Note: [Col. 0927] “superioribus,” MSS. 1 and 2], they completed the number ten of the expedition [Note: [Col. 0927] “perfectionis,” MSS. 1 and 2]. Through the treacherous plots of that warlike people, the Bohemians, they were reduced to this loss and disgrace: almost their worthy and more noble soldiers [Col. 0929A] [Note: [Col. 0929] “nobilibus,” MS. 2] were crushed beneath the Poles’ feet. Zbignev also was present there with the Bohemians; and, like them, he benefited more by fleeing than by remaining. But the Poles, returning from Bohemia with immense rejoicing, rendered everlasting thanks to almighty God and offered triumphant praises to triumphant Boleslav.

24. [Note: [Col. 0929] “XXIV” absent in MSS. 1 and 2.] Concerning the devastation of the land of Prussia by the Poles

Likewise, energetic Boleslav did not rest idly in leisure during the winter season, but entered Prussia, a land adjoining the north and bound by frost—although even Roman commanders, when fighting barbarian nations, wintered in prepared fortifications and did not campaign throughout the whole winter. Entering there, he used the ice of lakes and marshes as a bridge, because [Col. 0929B] no other entrance [Note: [Col. 0929] “nullus,” MSS. 1 and 2] into that country [Note: [Col. 0929] MS. 2 reads “illius”; MSS. 1 and 2 give “nullam pat’am” for “in illam patriam”] is found except through lakes [Note: [Col. 0929] “lacis,” MSS. 1 and 2] and marshes. Having crossed the lakes and marshes and reached habitable land, he did not settle in one place, nor lay siege to castles or cities—for there were none there. Indeed, the site and natural situation of the region are fortified by islands amid lakes [Note: [Col. 0929] “lacis,” MSS. 1 and 2] and marshes, and divided among peasants and inhabitants by hereditary allotments.

Therefore warrior Boleslav, ranging everywhere through that barbarous people, seized immense booty [Note: [Col. 0929] “in mensam,” through a scribe’s carelessness, MS. 2]; he took countless men and women, boys and girls, male and female servants captive; he burned many buildings and villages; and with all these he returned to Poland without a battle—though at that time he desired to find a battle more than all these things.

25. [Note: [Col. 0929] “XXV.,” absent in MSS. 1 and 2.] Concerning Zbignev’s false reconciliation with Boleslav

[Col. 0929C]

After Boleslav had thus checked his enemies, as was said, he compelled the Bohemian duke to receive his younger brother, whom we mentioned above, into a share of the inheritance, certain towns being assigned to him (A.D. 1111). [Note: [Col. 0929D] The province of Žatec; Cosmas, III.37. K.] When this had been done, Zbignev sent an embassy to his brother Boleslav, humbly begging that he too might grant him some small portion of their paternal inheritance, as the duke of Bohemia had granted to his brother, upon this condition: that he would in no respect [Note: [Col. 0929] “null’a,” MSS. 1 and 2] make himself Boleslav’s equal, but would always and in all things obey him as a soldier obeys his lord. For he trusted that he could not overcome him either through the emperor, the Bohemians, or the Pomeranians [Note: [Col. 0929] “enim,” MSS. 1 and 2]; but what he could not gain by power and arms, he hoped at least to gain by humility and brotherly affection. [Col. 0929D]

The words indeed seemed sufficiently good and peaceful; but perhaps one thing was ready upon the tongue and another concealed in the breast. Let us defer these matters to their proper place, and hear Boleslav’s reply. When he heard the report of his brother’s most humble supplication, Boleslav softened his mind in forgiveness—despite so many former perjuries, so many injuries inflicted, and foreign peoples brought into Poland [Col. 0930A]—and summoned Zbignev back to Poland, on terms expressed as follows: if a humble intention accorded with the words of his embassy; if he regarded himself as a soldier and not a lord; if henceforth he displayed neither pride nor any claim to dominion, then in brotherly affection Boleslav would give him certain castles [Note: [Col. 0929] “praedam” was wrongly added by MS. 3 and later deleted by that scribe; perhaps he forgot to delete “nec superfluum,” which the manuscripts add], and, if he found in him true humility and true affection, would promote him daily to better things (A.D. 1111) [Note: [Col. 0929] “die cottidie,” manuscript reading]. But if he concealed in his heart that old obstinacy and discord, it would be better for him to declare open discord [Note: [Col. 0929] “aperte discordia” for “apertam discordiam,” MSS. 1 and 3] than again bring a new sedition into Poland.

But Zbignev, yielding to foolish counsel and entirely forgetful of the subjection and humility he had promised, entered Boleslav’s presence [Col. 0930B] not humbly but arrogantly. He did not behave as a man chastened by so long an exile and wearied by so many labours and miseries; rather, like a lord, with a sword borne before him and with the accompaniment of musicians playing drums and lyres, he indicated that he had come not to serve but to reign, and pretended not to perform military service under his brother but to exercise rule over him.

Certain wise men understood this in a sense other than Zbignev perhaps intended, and suggested to Boleslav counsel which he immediately regretted having trusted and would always regret having followed [Note: [Col. 0930D] Ib., III.54. K.]. They inflamed his mind with words such as these: “This man, crushed by such calamities and driven into such long exile, enters at his very first approach with such haughty pride, although he is still uncertain of every particular. What will he do in future if some power in the kingdom of Poland is granted him?” They further alleged something graver and more dangerous: namely, that Zbignev had already found and enlisted a man of any rank, rich or poor, who, after observing Boleslav in a favourable place, would stab him with a knife or some other iron weapon; and that, if Zbignev then escaped the danger of death, he would exalt that murderer to the summit of high honour as one of the princes.

But we are more inclined to believe that this plot was contrived by those evil counsellors than that such a crime was ever conceived by Zbignev himself, a man sufficiently humble and simple. Therefore it is less surprising that a young man flourishing in age and established in power, spurred by anger [Col. 0930D] and prompted by the counsel of wise men, should commit any crime whatever in order to avoid the danger of death and rule secure from every ambush. Yet let no one believe that that sin was committed “in spirit” [Note: [Col. 0929] Thus restored; perhaps “in anger”: “anima impetu,” P.; “in hope,” the manuscripts], but rather out of presumption; that it proceeded not from deliberation but from occasion [Note: [Col. 0929] “peragatum,” MS. 2].

For if Zbignev had come humbly and wisely, as one seeking mercy [Col. 0931A] [Note: [Col. 0931] “misericordia,” MSS. 1 and 2], and not as a lord intending to reign, as it were, beneath the burdens of vanity, neither would he himself have fallen into irreparable ruin nor brought others into lamentable guilt. What then? Do we accuse Zbignev and excuse Boleslav? By no means. But it is a lesser sin to commit, through the anger of haste occasioned by another, than to ponder in deliberate counsel the very deed that is to be done [Note: [Col. 0931] “ipe deliberacionis” for “ipsa deliberatione,” MSS. 1 and 2].

We do not deny repentance even to a sin of deliberation; yet in repentance we must weigh the person, age, and circumstances. For after irretrievable evil has been committed, it is not fitting that worse evil should follow; rather, one who can be healed ought to receive aid from the physician’s medicine of discernment. Therefore, since what has been done cannot on one side be restored to its former condition [Col. 0931B], the weaker party, capable of medicine [Note: [Col. 0931] “artem,” MS. 2], must be preserved in a condition of dignity by the vigilant [Note: [Col. 0931] Thus corrected by P.; “vigilandi,” MS. 1; “jugulandi,” MS. 2] care of discernment. Thus it is clear that aid is administered one way to a sick body and that a sick person is sustained by spiritual medicine in another way.

We accuse Boleslav in this, that he committed such a deed; but we praise him in this, that he made worthy and very humble repentance. For we saw such a man, so great a prince, so pleasure-loving a youth, keeping his first Lent fast [Note: [Col. 0931D] The Lenten fast. K.], continually prostrate on the ground in ashes and haircloth [Note: [Col. 0931] “pervolutum,” MS. 2], drenched with tearful sighs, separated from human company and conversation, regarding the ground as his table, grass as his covering [Note: [Col. 0931D] “Stragulo,” a coverlet. K.], harsh bread [Note: [Col. 0931] “acrum,” MS. 2] as delicacies, and water as nectar. Moreover, bishops, abbots, and priests assisted him, each according to his ability, with Masses [Col. 0931C] and fasts; and at every principal feast or consecration of churches they relaxed some part of his penance by canonical authority. He also caused Masses to be celebrated daily for sins and for the dead, and psalters [Note: [Col. 0931] “psalteriaque,” MS. 2] to be sung; and he bestowed great consolation of charity in feeding and clothing [Note: [Col. 0931] “vescendis,” the manuscripts] the poor.

And what is considered greater than all these things and especially important in penitence [Note: [Col. 0931] “deputatur erat,” MS. 2; “de” marked for deletion and “e” written above], making satisfaction to his brother by the Lord’s authority, he was reconciled when forgiveness had been granted. Boleslav also showed one very worthy fruit of penitence . . . [Note: [Col. 0931] A word has fallen out, e.g. “ostendit,” “showed”], which may be regarded as a sign to all penitents in the case of so great a prince. For although he governed not a duchy but a magnificent kingdom [Col. 0931D], and feared enemies from various Christian and pagan nations, he commended himself and his kingdom for preservation to divine power, and, with very few knowing it, undertook and completed with utmost devotion a pilgrimage to Saint Giles [Col. 0932A] and Saint King Stephen, on the occasion of a meeting.

[Note: [Col. 0931D] The abbey of Blessed Aegidius in the county of Semich, Hungary, founded by King Ladislaus at the end of the eleventh century, was formerly fortified. Bel, *Compendium of Hungarian Geography*, Pozsony, 1777, p. 178. Cf. Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, V, 128, where a papal diploma confirming the foundation of this monastery is cited; it was subject to the abbot of Saint Aegidius, Saint-Gilles, in the Flavian valley of France.]

Throughout all the days of that Lent [Note: [Col. 0931] Reading of the *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*; “illis quadragesima” is incorrect for “illius quadragesimae,” MSS. 1 and 2], he fasted, content with refreshment of bread and water alone—except when, because of the demands of so great a labour, the discernment of bishops and abbots, through Masses and prayers, relaxed that fast in the service of charity. Each day he went on foot from his lodging, sometimes barefoot, with bishops and chaplains, until he had completed the Hours of the perpetual Virgin, the canonical offices of the day, and the seven penitential psalms with the penitential litany; and he often added the whole course of the psalter after the vigils for the dead. He was so devout and diligent throughout the whole journey of that pilgrimage [Col. 0932B] in washing the feet of the poor and giving alms that no needy person who sought mercy from him departed without mercy.

Whenever the northern duke came to an episcopal see, abbey, or provostship, the bishop, abbot, or provost of that place, and sometimes King Coloman of the Hungarians himself, came out to meet Boleslav in an ordered procession. Boleslav himself everywhere made some offering in the churches; but in those principal places he presented only gold and rich cloths. Thus he was received religiously throughout Hungary by bishops, abbots, and provosts [Note: [Col. 0931] “prepositibus,” through scribal error, MS. 2]; they prepared for him bodily service most generously and with the greatest care, and he gave gifts to them while they gave gifts to him. Everywhere the king’s servants and retinue followed him, [Col. 0932C] and Boleslav’s reception, whether more careful or more negligent, was recorded by his attendants for report to the king. Whoever seemed to receive him more carefully and honourably was said without doubt to be the king’s friend or to obtain favour from this.

With such spiritual devotion and such temporal honour [Note: [Col. 0931] MS. 2 wrongly added “de,” but marked it with dots], Boleslav returned from his pilgrimage. Yet, returning to his kingdom, he did not renounce the life of a penitent or the practice of pilgrimage; rather, he continued with the same pilgrimage intention [Note: [Col. 0931] “preposito,” MS. 2] until the tomb of blessed martyr Adalbert, where he was to celebrate the Lord’s Passover [Note: [Col. 0931] “pacha,” wrongly, MS. 2] (A.D. 1113, 13 April). And as he came day by day nearer to the holy martyr’s place, he walked all the more devoutly barefoot, with tears and prayers. When he reached the city and the martyr’s tomb, how many alms he distributed among the poor! What ornaments he presented in the church and upon the altars [Note: [Col. 0931] “alteribus,” MS. 2]! The gold work is proof of the workmanship [Note: [Col. 0931] “extitit comperacionis,” corruptly for “existit operationis,” MS. 2] [Col. 0933A] which Boleslav made for the martyr’s relics as a memorial of his devotion and penitence. That shrine contains eighty marks of the purest gold, apart from pearls and precious gems, which appear no less valuable than the gold.

At that most glorious holy Easter, he celebrated so magnificently and generously in gifts to his bishops, princes, chaplains, and soldiers that he adorned every one of the greater men and almost all the lesser with precious garments. And he made such liberal provision for the canons [Note: [Col. 0933] “canoniciis,” MS. 1] of the blessed martyr, the guardians and ministers of the church, and the citizens of that city, that he honoured all without omitting one, each according to the rank and order of his dignity, with garments, horses, or other gifts.

When this pilgrimage, so religiously devout, had been completed, the siege previously undertaken was not thereby [Col. 0933B] erased from the memory of our heart. Nor should anyone consider the order misplaced, since, if it were inserted here, it could disturb the entire sequence of the narrative begun.

[Note: [Col. 0933D] The events which the author narrates in the following chapter precede Boleslav’s journey to Saint Giles. Thus, with Giesebrecht, *Wendische Geschichte*, II, 168, on account of the mention of King Coloman, who died 4 February 1114, that journey seems to be assignable to the year 1113, and the war against the Pomeranians—placed by Roepell, I, 263, in connection with 1118—to 1111 and 1112. K.]

26. [Note: [Col. 0933] “XXVI,” absent in MSS. 1 and 2.] The Pomeranians surrendered the castle of Nakło to the Poles

Accordingly, Boleslav had granted Nakło Castle—the place where that great battle mentioned above is said to have occurred (A.D. 1111), and from which continual loss and unceasing hardship had always arisen for the Poles—to a Pomeranian related to him by birth, named Suatopole, to hold along with several other castles on this condition of fealty: that he should never withhold from Boleslav either his service [Col. 0933C] or the castles for any reason. But afterwards he never maintained the fealty he had sworn; nor did he ever render the promised service when he came [Note: [Col. 0933] Thus emended; the manuscripts and editions read “neque venientibus neque promissam”]; he did not open the gates of the castles to those who came; rather, as a faithless enemy and traitor, he defended himself and his own possessions by force and arms.

Boleslav, northern duke, being stirred to anger, gathered companies of warriors and besieged the very strong castle of Nakło [Note: [Col. 0933] “Nakyel,” MS. 2] (A.D. 1111, 29 September), intending to avenge his insult. There he remained from the feast of Saint Michael until the Lord’s Nativity. Though he laboured daily and diligently in warfare against the castle, he spent his effort entirely in vain, because the wet, watery, marshy ground did not permit siege-engines [Col. 0933D] and equipment to be brought forward. Moreover, the castle was so well supplied with men and necessary resources that it could not have been taken by arms or want of any sort [Col. 0934A] in a whole year. Boleslav himself was wounded there by an arrow, and was thereby spurred to greater anger in seeking revenge.

Suatopole therefore continually sought peace or some agreement through Boleslav’s friends and retainers, offering him a large sum of money and hostages. After considering these matters, Boleslav abandoned the siege and returned, awaiting a suitable time to go back and avenge his insult; he carried away part of the money with him, together with Suatopole’s eldest son as a hostage [Note: [Col. 0933] MS. 2 added “idem” wrongly, then deleted it].

Likewise, in the following year (A.D. 1112), because Suatopole kept neither his pledged faith nor the agreement made, gave no thought to the danger faced by his son, and took no care either to come to the appointed conference with Boleslav or to send grounds of excuse, [Col. 0934B] Boleslav gathered his army and visited the faithless enemy somewhat with an iron rod, though not fully. When he came to the Pomeranian frontier, where any other prince would have been afraid with his entire host, he left the army behind and hurried forward with chosen soldiers, intending to take by sudden assault the castle of Wyszogród, whose garrison had neither anticipated nor prepared for it.

But when they reached the river which, where it joined the Vistula [Note: [Col. 0933] “Wysle,” MS. 2], separated from them on the other side that castle situated at the angle of the rivers, some swam that river hastily [Note: [Col. 0933] “cursum,” MSS. 1 and 2], one before another, while others of the Mazovians came by boat along the river Vistula [Note: [Col. 0933] In MS. 2 this whole column, down to the words “burn that mound,” is written in smaller letters, in the same but hurried hand]. Thus it happened, unknowingly in war, that [Col. 0934C] civilian loss—that is, loss among citizens, namely Poles [Note: [Col. 0934D] P.]—was greater than the loss inflicted by the enemy in eight days of assaulting that castle.

Nonetheless, once the entire army had gathered around the castle and equipment of various sorts had been prepared for storming the town, its inhabitants, fearing Boleslav’s stubborn resolve against his enemies, gave themselves up under a guarantee of safety [Note: [Col. 0933] “fidem,” MS. 2], and so escaped Boleslav’s hand and death. Boleslav gained that castle in eight days, and, remaining there eight more days, strengthened it for retention; having left garrisons there, he advanced and surrounded another castle with a siege [Note: [Col. 0933] “illud” added by MS. 2, then marked as superfluous; “cremavit” was added and marked superfluous by MS. 1, and also inserted without deletion by MS. 2]. Boleslav took this castle with greater effort and after a longer delay, because he found there more and stronger defenders and a place more securely fortified against a military assault.

Accordingly, the Poles prepared implements and engines for the assault, and the Pomeranians likewise made every kind of equipment for resistance [Note: [Col. 0933] Correctly added by the *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, p. 91]. The Poles levelled ditches [Col. 0935A] and brought together earth and wood so that they might approach the castle more easily and on a flatter way with wooden towers. The Pomeranians, by contrast, prepared lard and resinous wood, with which gradually to burn that mound. Three times the garrison secretly came down from the wall and burned all the engines; three times the Poles built them again. Thus [Note: [Col. 0935] “namque,” MS. 2] Boleslav’s wooden towers stood close to the castle, and the garrison resisted them from the battlements with weapons and fire. Whenever the Poles attacked the castle with weapons, fire, and heaps of stones [Note: [Col. 0935] “statis,” MSS. 1 and 2], the garrison in every fashion returned a contrary resistance. The garrison wounded many Poles with arrows [Note: [Col. 0935] This appears to be the correct reading; cf. *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, p. 91] and stones; the Poles, however, killed more of the garrison every day.

For they were pagans [Col. 0935B], secure concerning death [Note: [Col. 0935] “secum,” wrongly, MSS. 1 and 2], if they were captured through martial valour; and therefore they preferred to die defending themselves with honour rather than stretching out their necks in cowardice. At times they considered making an agreement with Boleslav and surrendering the castle; at other times [Note: [Col. 0935] “interim,” manuscripts], requesting a truce or awaiting aid, they postponed that plan. Meanwhile the Poles, never idle and never slothful, did not cease despite exhaustion from such labours and vigils, but persisted in taking the castle, whether by force or stratagem. The Pomeranians recognized Boleslav’s purpose and intention: they could in no way escape his hands unless they surrendered the castle. Their greatest despair arose because they expected no aid from Suatopole, their lord. Therefore they entered upon an arrangement quite suitable for both parties at the time: they surrendered the castle after receiving a guarantee of safety, and they themselves departed unharmed with all their people [Col. 0936B] wherever they wished.

**IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1112. BERENGOSUS, ABBOT OF SAINT MAXIMINUS OF TRIER**

[Col. 0935]

**HISTORICAL NOTICE**

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. I, p. 214.)

Berengosus, of the Order of Saint Benedict, abbot of Saint Maximinus at Trier, flourished not, as Bellarmine stated in the first edition of his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, in the seventh century, but at the beginning of the twelfth. In 1112 he obtained from Emperor Henry V a privilege concerning the advocacy of his abbey. He wrote the following works: the *Three Books on the Praise and Discovery of the Lord’s Cross*, published at Cologne in 1555, reprinted in the *Libraries of the Fathers*, and most recently at Lyons, vol. XII, p. 349; *On the Mystery of the Lord’s Wood*, and *On Visible and Invisible Light, by Which the Ancient Fathers Deserved to Be Enlightened*, p. 367; and five sermons *On Martyrs, Confessors, the Dedication of a Church, and the Veneration of Relics*, p. 376. Oudin is mistaken (*vol. II*, p. 1004) in attributing to this Berengosus a commentary on the Apocalypse, which has already been shown to belong to Berengar of Tours. Likewise, the work *On the Fasts of the Four Seasons*, attributed to Berengosus by some, belongs to Berno, not Berengosus.

[Col. 0935]

**OF ABBOT BERENGOSUS: ON THE PRAISE AND DISCOVERY OF THE HOLY CROSS**

(*Bibliotheca Patrum*, XII, 349.)

**HERE BEGINS THE FIRST BOOK ON THE PRAISE OF THE HOLY CROSS**

**CHAPTER I. How the Lord first sent prophecy and the Law before himself, and then, having been born and having suffered, ascended the tree of the cross.**

[Col. 0935C]

When the ancient Godhead foresaw the fitting time [Col. 0936C] to gather into one the children who had been scattered, he sent first and second servants, and thirdly the Son, into the vineyard of the Church in order to redeem the human being whom free choice of his own will had divided from God. Desiring to show himself the true king, he sent prophecy and the Law before himself as servants, when, in preparing the way of humanity’s heavenly homeland, he came first to Abraham, second to Moses, and third to Mary. From her, lest he be hidden either as man by sufferings or as God by miracles, he presented himself to human sight as true God and true man, so that, with no hindrance from obstacles of things, he might be proved man by afflictions and God by miracles.

For in ascending the tree of the cross in order to suffer for our salvation, he undoubtedly showed himself to be truly man; but in trampling down his death by the glory of resurrection, he showed himself to be truly God. Nor should it be attributed any less to his divinity that the very day of his Passion appeared to be darkened at the hour [Col. 0937B] in which he suffered for the redemption of the human race by cross, nails, and spear. These indeed are the most holy marks of human salvation, by which the true Isaac brought us the oil and marks of heavenly medicine; when, like a ram caught among thorns by the horns of the cross of sins, he deigned to heal every sick head and every grieving heart (Isaiah 1). These are those marks by which the highest priest of priests willed wholly to free the human race in one man upon the altar of the cross, when by a singular sacrifice and common grace he provided in one for all and in all for one. These also are the marks by which the Son of God showed us the inestimable sign of paternal love, when he bore [Col. 0937C] our sins in his body upon the tree (1 Peter 2), so that the ancient enemy might be tortured in himself by the all the sharper dark torment of his envy, insofar as he was conquered by that same wood by which he had conquered.

**CHAPTER II. How the wood of the cross was discovered by Queen Helena, or had first been hidden by the Jews; and concerning the presentation of three errors, according to the threefold mystery of that same wood**

Therefore, just as that day of the Lord’s Passion was once desirable to the whole world, so this most holy day ought no less to be revered by us: for just as on that day our Saviour completed the work of our redemption, so on this day he decreed to make known to us the wood of the Lord. This day ought therefore to be celebrated by us with greater festivity, because on it that same wood of the Lord, Christ revealing it, was uncovered—especially since divine Scripture says nothing else about this day except that today the Lord’s cross was discovered by Queen Helena. For, as the Calendar testifies in the catalogue of saints for the present day, this day is called the Discovery of the Holy Cross, because on this day the very cross was discovered upon which the human race was redeemed by Christ’s Passion.

But because many still seem not to know why that wood of the Lord had long been hidden by the Jews, we shall now, according to our capacity, set causes against causes and matters against matters, and say a few things out of many on this subject. You know that, just as faithlessness is opposed to faith and vice to virtue, so Jewish impiety is always hostile to Christian salvation. For, as it assailed on the wood of the cross the author of human salvation, so it still execrates the honour of Christian religion. It is therefore not surprising that those same Jews, clothed in the mantle of envy, should begrudge divine mercy and human salvation; since, through that same envy by which they killed in the Passion the very author of light, they hid the wood of the cross after his Passion, so that the salvation offered us in the cross by the author of life and salvation might be lacking to us more plainly than the sun and more manifestly than light.

For these were those of whom it is written: “They shall be portions for foxes” (Psalm 62), since, choosing the fox Caesar in place of the supreme King, they would change neither face nor mind toward God. Therefore, in order to show their faithlessness more fully—for through their lack of faith in Christ the nations have not yet been disturbed and kingdoms have not been shaken (Psalm 45)—our discourse will now range more broadly through the fields of the Scriptures, as an example, since the matters to be set forth are better shown by example than by speech. Thus, that the Jews’ envy may justly be put to rest, three men from the ancient Fathers must be proposed, lest the words of Truth addressed to us seem neglected: “In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (2 Corinthians 13). It should be understood that, just as these men are three—Joseph, Isaac, and Moses—so, through the chief ministry of the ancient Godhead, they must bring us a threefold mystery.

**CHAPTER III. On the comparison which Joseph bears to the wood, and his brothers to the synagogue of the Jews**

[Col. 0938C]

Although Joseph was the youngest of the three, he will nevertheless be first for us in this presentation, so that, in the ladder of the Church, ascending gradually as it were from step to step, we may briefly pass from one to another. Nor should it weary any of us if, together with Joseph, we bring forward his brothers and the Jews; for the Jews were filled with the same envy toward the Lord that Joseph’s ten brothers had felt toward Joseph. The Jews always had toward the Lord the same cause of envy that Joseph’s brothers were accustomed to have toward Joseph; for, on account of his singular grace, they seemed so to boil in the furnace of envy that they could not [Col. 0938D] speak peaceably at all (Genesis 37).

The Jews, holding the same envy toward the Lord, sharpened their tongues like serpents against his death, lest that prophecy should seem false: “They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue” (Psalm 108). Although no fellowship exists between light and darkness, or between darkness and light, those brothers and the Jews are nevertheless to be compared with the Lord’s cross, especially because by antiphrasis they have the same relation to the cross that darkness seems to have to light. For just as brotherly love began to fail among Joseph’s brothers when, in betraying him, they went away to Dothan, which means “defection,” so the Jews were divided from God by the lot of great defection when they devised his death, even death on a cross, for him (Philippians 2).

[Col. 0939A] But it must be understood that, among the other twelve brothers, only two imitated the ancient Fathers: Joseph and his brother Benjamin did not wish to go with their other brothers to Dothan, because, being sons not of Leah but of Rachel, they ought not to have shared their brothers’ counsel. The other brothers, born of the handmaids or Leah, were, as it were, scattered abroad outside the way through their brother’s betrayal, just as in the net of the Church the order is distinguished between good and bad fish: the bad are cast out and the good remain within. Therefore, since those brothers and the Jews bore the figure of those fish of whom it is written, “but they cast the bad out” (Matthew 13), it is no wonder that the brothers’ envy toward Joseph appeared to be like the Jews’ faithlessness toward Christ.

It should be understood, however, that just as Joseph deserved to bear the type of the Saviour by the merit of his good action, so it was not by works of the flesh but by works of light that the mystery of the cross was prefigured in him. For just as Joseph was enclosed for a time in a pit, so the Lord’s cross was long enclosed in the earth, until, by the cooperation of heavenly grace, both the cross was raised from the earth and Joseph from the pit. And just as Joseph was sold by his brothers to the Ishmaelites, so Christ was sold by Israelites to the chief priests; for just as Joseph was handed over into exile by the counsel of Judah the patriarch, so Christ was handed over to the death of the cross by the counsel of Judas Iscariot, the arch-heretic.

Accordingly, the manifold malice of those brothers is not inappropriately compared with the malice of the Jews, [Col. 0939C] since both they and these blasphemed one and the same mystery of Christ. For as those men, according to the written judgement of the ancient Godhead, sold their brother Joseph into Egypt, the land of dark falsehood, so these, in imitation of the sign of that same malice, had hidden the Lord’s wood in a certain most dark place. And as Joseph was once thrust into prison through the wickedness of his brothers, so through the malice of the Jews both the cross lay hidden and Christ enclosed in the tomb, in order that the human race might be deprived, in this twofold mystery, of the sign of divine love: so that neither life might come to it from Christ nor salvation from the wood.

#### Chapter IV. How, as Joseph was freed from prison and Christ from death, so the sign of the cross was freed from confinement

[Col. 0939D]

Therefore, just as it has been related with sufficiently clear reasoning how the wood of the cross seemed long to have been hidden as a type of the Lord’s burial, so now it must be set before you, as a sign of the Lord’s resurrection, how the wood of the holy cross was raised up in the same manner. For since the burial of the Lord’s body could be a figure of the cross that was to be found, it is fitting that, as we compared the hiding of that same cross with Joseph’s prison and the Lord’s burial, so we should now assign its discovery to the opening of the prison and to the Saviour’s resurrection. For as Joseph’s drawing forth from the pit signifies the Lord’s resurrection, [Col. 0940A] so the drawing of the cross from the earth can bear the same meaning: because, as Joseph was drawn from the pit for the salvation of his brothers, so the Lord’s cross was today drawn from the earth for the salvation of the peoples.

And, as it concerns one and the same lot that Joseph escaped prison and Christ escaped death, so we may fittingly ascribe to the Lord’s cross the corresponding sense of both acts, since it too was today released from the prison-house of the earth in the same figure. Moreover, this too must not be passed over by us but rather spiritually examined by you: the Lord’s cross was today freed from its ancient confinement in the same manner in which Joseph and the cupbearer were once freed from Pharaoh’s prison. Therefore thanks be to God that, as Joseph and Christ spiritually shared one [Col. 0940B] lot—Joseph being sent to prison and Christ to death—so the Christian people would by no means spare the Jews until the Lord’s wood was led forth from the prison of its ancient confinement, under the same lot of spiritual understanding by which Joseph was brought out of prison and Christ from death.

#### Chapter V. How, as Joseph was clothed by Pharaoh with a golden collar, ring, and robe, so the wood of the cross was adorned with gems and gold by Queen Helena

Therefore, just as it has sufficiently been said how Joseph in prison, and Christ in death, became a curse for us, so what was done to Joseph by Pharaoh after his release from prison must not remain untouched by us. [Col. 0940C]

But because the following statement seems so joined to the preceding one that no reason for silence ought to impose silence upon the mouth, it is fitting that we say something about what follows, for the strengthening of the souls of the faithful.

For as Joseph, released from the prison-house of the aforesaid prison, was figuratively clothed with a golden collar, and also with a ring and a robe, so Christ, rising from death for human salvation, “was clothed with strength and girded himself with power” (Ps. 92 [93]). Yet, lest this statement alone seem insufficient, we must say what is signified by the golden collar, the ring, and the robe. For as a twofold meaning lies hidden in the linen robe and the golden collar—since the virginal flesh is signified by linen, and heavenly wisdom by the collar—[Col. 0940D] so in the ring is prefigured the office of faith of the supreme Priest, who says through Peter: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2).

Thus it should be known that, as Joseph was figuratively adorned by Pharaoh with ring, robe, and golden collar, so most blessed Helena adorned the wood of the cross historically, when from the treasury of royal munificence she decorated that same cross with gems and gold. Again, as Joseph sets forth a type for us when, adorned with diverse gifts, he mounted the chariot of joy, so most sacred Helena today raised up for us the horn of salvation, when for our salvation she brought the Lord’s cross up from the depths to the heights. Moreover, as Joseph, raised up in the royal chariot, deserved to be proclaimed everywhere by a herald’s voice, so [Col. 0941A] in this same event he left us a great mystery of twofold grace: in the same figure, the wood of the cross is proclaimed by the people and Christ by John.

#### Chapter VI. How, as Joseph, intending to sell grain to the Egyptians, opened the king’s storehouses, so Queen Helena merited to open for us the wood of the cross in the storehouse of the Church

Therefore, having related what Joseph, king of Egypt, did, we must also recount what Joseph himself did for the Egyptians out of humanity, lest any of you should think it unworthy that his deed concerning the Lord be referred to the wood. For as the prison in which he was confined and the chariot in which he was exalted have fittingly been compared with the Lord’s cross, so the distribution of Egyptian grain must be compared with that same venerable cross on a similar principle.

[Col. 0941B] For it should be known that, as Joseph, intending to sell grain to the Egyptians, opened the storehouses of charity, so most sacred Helena merited today to open for us the wood on which the grain of wheat died, lest it should be given over any longer to oblivion with Manasseh, whose name is interpreted “forgetfulness,” but should rather be increased into the Christian religion with Joseph, who is called “increase.” Therefore, because through the faithlessness of the ancient enemy the bread of faith and charity has now almost failed in our granaries, we must return to the true Joseph for our Father’s bread with that prodigal son, guilty in faith, who, returning to his father, said: “How many hired servants in my father’s house abound in bread, while I here perish from hunger” (Luke 15).

For unless, in order to obtain the kingdom of eternity, we make for ourselves bundles from the tares of vices to be burned, [Col. 0941C] we shall by no means reach God with that sheaf of good work of which it is written: “Gather the wheat into my barn” (Matt. 13). Accordingly, as by Joseph’s command a fifth part of the Egyptian crops was given to the king, so our five senses must be offered in God’s service, in order that, in place of the fifth part owed to kings, we may always subject the keeping of our five senses to the divine laws. For unless, according to the example of the legal sacrament, we redeem the firstborn of a human being with five shekels of silver, the scars of Christ’s five wounds will profit us nothing—wounds by which, upon the altar of the cross, he willed to heal the scars of our five senses.

Therefore, lest these same senses of ours appear, with the Egyptians, to be fasting from faith and charity, [Col. 0941D] we must implore the true Joseph in common prayer, that he who once willed, for human salvation, to hunger in the Egypt of this tribulation may deign to open for each of us the storehouses of charity, offering the grain of the heavenly word to the inner mind—he who, through the death of the cross, willed to compare himself to a grain of wheat.

#### Chapter VII. How Joseph hid the cup in the sack of his younger brother, and the Jews likewise hid the Lord’s wood

Therefore, as the marrow of wheat, which lay hidden for a very long time beneath the chaff of Egyptian servitude, has now been made most plainly manifest to us by the winnowing of the heavenly grain, so that cup of Joseph’s must by no means be concealed from your charity, [Col. 0942A] which he once commanded to be hidden in the sack of his younger brother. For it is fitting that, as the marrow of the heavenly grain was first extracted from Joseph’s storehouses, so now the flask of the spiritual sacrament may be offered to you from his cup, that in observing so great a mystery you may be partakers of the grace of God which the Jews once lost in their concealment of the Lord’s wood.

For by hiding the wood of the cross so deeply, as though in the mouth of the earth, the Jews refused to imitate Joseph’s deed. After he had suitably answered every inquiry concerning his brothers, Joseph finally hid the silver cup in the mouth of his younger brother’s sack. As the brilliance of the heavenly word is expressed through the cup, and the letter of the Law through the sack, so the mouth of the younger brother’s sack signifies the human soul—provided that it clings more amply and perfectly [Col. 0942B] to that knowledge of which it is written: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.”

Therefore, because Joseph always enclosed in the summit of his heart, as though in the mouth of the sack, that knowledge of which it is written, “The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom” (Ps. 16 [17]), his heart never departed from its law. But because that same cup of truth was far removed from the faithlessness of Jewish impiety, they could not preserve in the inward part of the mind that desirable treasure of which it is written: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise.” It is therefore no wonder that, although Joseph and the Hebrews were of one stock, Joseph had one intention in this deed and the Jews another, since, according to the differing quality of their merits, the will of each was also different.

For as Joseph, in order to chastise the audacity of fraternal impiety, changed insult into favour by the concealment of that cup, [Col. 0942C] so the Jews, on the contrary, in order to obscure the remembrance of the Christian religion, preferred to procure for us insult rather than glory by concealing the cross. In this they acted most wickedly, hiding for so long the treasure of the Divinity to our disgrace, when it would have been better for them to find Joseph’s cup of truth than, out of envy for Christians, to conceal the wood of the cross for so long.

And although, according to the command of the Law, they ought, together with Joseph, to carry beneath the belt of their heart the peg of compunction for covering the dung of Jewish filth, they instead lost the peg of faith, hope, and charity, while through the goad of envy they wove the banner of the Lord’s [Col. 0942D] cross. Yet it is no wonder that they did not have the peg of compunction beneath the belt of the heart, since in the inward part of the mind they possessed the cup of love only to destroy it. Cast headlong by the chariot of their pride into the prison of diabolic captivity, they were separated from the storehouse of the Church and the cup of wisdom.

Therefore, lest we likewise seem to be imprisoned by the ancient Pharaoh, we must be raised with Joseph in the chariot of humility and patience, so that in the storehouse of the Church we may merit not only to be nourished with the measure of spiritual wheat but also to drink, with Christ making us drunk, from the cup of heavenly speech. And thus, distinguishing by the spiritual sacrament, as though by embossed workmanship, what is signified by the same prison and chariot, and by grain [Col. 0943A] or cup, it is fitting that we should not today pass over in silence the discovery of the holy cross, to which the opening of the prison and ascent into the chariot, the distribution of grain, and the finding of the cup bear witness.

#### Chapter VIII. As the eyes of the Jews grew dim after the example of Isaac when they hid the wood of the cross out of envy for Christians, so that same people unwillingly disclosed the wood of the cross, as Isaac unknowingly blessed his son

See: because our discourse has been somewhat prolonged with Japheth, while we lingered for a time with Joseph in order to proclaim the mystery of the cross, it remains for us now, exchanging wine and milk freely from each Law, to pass from Joseph’s storehouses to Isaac’s wells. But before saying anything about these wells, it does no harm to preface a few words concerning the dimness of his eyes, especially since, by comparison of good and evil, his blindness can fittingly be compared with the blindness of the Jews.

[Col. 0943B] It is not without significance that the son of Abraham incurred this blindness, although that blindness which befell Israel was not from Abraham and Sarah, but from Hagar and Ishmael. For if Sarah is compared with Hagar, the one differs from the other in freedom yet is alike in condition; for you know well what each was, one being free and the other a slave-woman. Therefore, because God has endowed us with the freedom of the one, we ought not to be oppressed by the servitude of the other, so that with Isaac we may attain so perfect a freedom that, after his example, we may by no means imitate the blindness of the Jews.

For if Isaac’s outward eyes grew somewhat dim because he spiritually prefigured in himself the blindness of the Jews, much more did that same Jewish people lose inwardly the light of truth when, by concealing the Lord’s wood, it separated itself from the unity of the Church. But thanks be to God that, as the eyes of the Jews once grew dim, as it were with Isaac, when they concealed that same treasure of the Divinity in order to injure Christians, so that same people, in the discovery of the holy cross, unwillingly bestowed upon us [Col. 0943C] the same blessing by which the aforementioned Isaac once unknowingly blessed his son. For as Isaac unknowingly extended the blessing to his son, and yet foresaw long beforehand what would happen to him, so that Jewish people, following the example of that Israelite, [Col. 0943D] unwillingly disclosed the wood of the cross which it had refused voluntarily to reveal.

#### Chapter IX. As the Philistines filled up Isaac’s wells, so the Jews concealed the wood of the cross; and as Queen Helena found that wood, so Isaac found pure water in those same wells

Since [perhaps: “It is now time”] for us, as we have said, to pass to those wells, from which we may offer you cups of clearer water. For it does no harm if today, in honour of the holy cross, we call to mind the wells which Isaac once dug among a foreign people, lest we choke that mystery beneath the dark smoke of human silence: namely, how the hostile Philistines filled those wells with earth.

What, then, is signified by the [Col. 0944A] Philistines except the Jews? And what by the wells except the depth of God’s Scriptures? For the Jews are not unfittingly compared with the Philistines, since in concealing the Lord’s wood they long lay in ambush against human salvation, failing to heed the maxim of the ancient proverb: “The wicked shall be caught in their own snares” (Prov. 11). It is therefore no wonder that, as the Philistines buried the living water when they filled with earth the wells which Isaac had dug, so the Jews, by concealing the Lord’s wood, buried that heavenly water of which it is written: “Whoever drinks the water which I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4).

But thanks be to God that, as Isaac merited to find wells of living waters in order to quench the thirst of believers, so Judas the Hebrew, although he declared himself unworthy of this work, found the Lord’s wood on this day. Moreover, as the Philistines strove to fill up the wells of the Scriptures with the earth of their wickedness so that the true water of spiritual understanding might not flow from them, [Col. 0944B] so the Jews wished for a long time to smother the wood of the holy cross with earth, so that the stream of the saving mystery might not flow to us from it.

Therefore, as Isaac used to remove earth from the wells of his fathers in order to find the heavenly water of saving grace, so we also, in seeking the stream of spiritual understanding, must penetrate the depths of our thoughts until, the earth of all wickedness having been removed from the well of our heart, the pure water of true innocence shines forth for us through the mystery of the cross.

#### Chapter X. How the well called “of the Living and the Seeing One” can correspond to the well of the divine blood and to the mystery of the cross

[Col. 0944C]

Therefore, as in Isaac’s wells we have found spiritual water for cleansing the sewer of carnal impurity, so it now benefits the watering of our mind if with Isaac we hasten on to the well called “of the Living and the Seeing One.” Although there are many wells there and only one here, nevertheless through them all the gift of one sacrament is offered to us, because one figure is at work in all of them, while in each one sacred Scripture is signified.

But who is the Living One except God, of whom it is written: “The Lord lives, [Col. 0944D] and blessed be my God” (Ps. 17 [18])? And who the Seeing One is, he himself showed us when he said to Nathanael: “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 1). This is that living well of which the Apostle said: “Christ indeed lives in me” (Gal. 2), so that after his example each one of us may draw from that same well and live, of which it is written: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink” (John 7).

For every believer has eternal life from his well, who lives for all and sees all, dying and living with the aforesaid Isaac in him, because he is called both Living and Seeing. As Isaac, according to the higher understanding of the mind, walked by the way that leads to the well called “of the Living and the Seeing One,” so the true Isaac, through the mystery of the cross, deigned to open for the world [Col. 0945A] the well of life, from whose depth it might draw the water of divine knowledge. But as the well, as has been said, signifies the depth of sacred reading, so the road which leads to the well signifies the humility of the Lord’s Passion, through which the spiritual streams of sacred Scripture were opened to us, though before the Lord’s Passion they lay hidden under the chaff of the Law.

Therefore, that we too may, after Isaac’s example, be made drunk from that well of the Most High, of which it is written, “Drink and be drunk, beloved” (Song 1 [5:1]), it is fitting that we follow, as our forerunner and guide on the way which leads to it, him who bore in his body nails, lance, and cross in running the course of the Passion.

#### Chapter XI. How, as Moses was found by Pharaoh’s daughter beside the river-bank, so the wood of the cross was found by Queen Helena in the place of Calvary

[Col. 0945B]

Therefore, because, according to the Apostle, we have given you not solid food but milk, while we have related to you certain matters concerning Joseph and Isaac under the figure of the Lord’s cross, it is fitting that we now pass from Isaac to Moses in the same way, in order to explain another matter to you. For as Moses was found by divine providence beside the river-bank on the day when Pharaoh’s daughter went down to wash in the river, so today the wood of the cross was found at Calvary by the Church of the people of twofold origin.

Since, by the hidden judgment of the Divinity, it seemed to have been buried for a long time in that very place, we must not let slip from memory [Col. 0945C] what history records as arising therefrom through the envy of the Jews. At the instigation of the Jewish chief priests, the Emperor Hadrian committed a dreadful crime: to display an example of Jewish perversity, he built a temple to Venus in the place where the Lord’s wood lay, so that Christian devotion might neither bend the knee there nor offer to God the oblations of its vows.

But thanks be to God that, as Pharaoh’s daughter emptied that little vessel in which Moses lay hidden and enclosed for a time, so Queen Helena today destroyed, to the confession of the devil, that temple which Hadrian had built to God’s insult. Moreover, as Moses merited to draw from the river of spiritual understanding the water of divine knowledge, so in the mystery of the cross we ought to draw the waters of our redemption, [Col. 0945D] of which it is written: “You shall draw waters with joy from the springs of the Saviour” (Isa. 12).

Again, as Moses used to sweeten for the children of Israel the most bitter waters in the desert of Mount Sinai, where the Son of Man had never rested, so the true Moses sweetened bitter and incurable waters through the mystery of the cross; by imparting sweetness, he made them drinkable for us. And as the true Moses deigned to free the children of Israel from Egyptian slavery when he cast Pharaoh’s chariot and army into the sea, so most blessed Helena today freed the Lord’s cross from Jewish captivity and placed it in the bosom of the Church, as on a long-desired shore.

Therefore we must pray that, as Moses instructed the Hebrew people by a miracle of the Divinity, when he brought forth water from the rock to heal [Col. 0946A] their bodies and minds, so that true Moses may cleanse us by the waters of repentance from the sewers of vices—he “brought water out of the rock and made waters flow down like rivers” (Ps. 77 [78]).

#### Chapter XII. As Moses was hidden by his mother in a basket, so the Lord’s cross was long hidden in the Synagogue; and the cross was found in the earth as Moses was found on the bank and Christ in the Church

Moreover, this too must by no means be concealed by silence: after the example of Moses, the Lord’s cross once seemed to be hidden. For as Moses was hidden by his mother in a basket beside the river-bank, so the wood of the cross was long hidden in the earth by the Synagogue. But as Moses was found on the river-bank, and Christ at the water of baptism, so Thermuth, Pharaoh’s daughter—that is, the Church of the Gentiles—merited to find the Lord’s wood for the salvation of believers.

But it should be known that, as the Jews seemed to stand at a distance there, as though with Mary the sister of Moses, to observe the outcome of the matter, so all who are still clothed in the robe of the ancient Law appear to stand far off with the Synagogue from the mystery of Christ’s cross. [Col. 0946B] But as Pharaoh’s daughter preserved Christ for us in the male child, since she used to lift Moses enclosed from the little vessel, so the Church of the Gentiles today disclosed for human use the wood of the cross which, through Jewish envy, had long lain enclosed.

And as she found the basket in the shelter, so the Church today found the Lord’s cross in its confinement; for by one and the same grace the cross is found today in the earth, just as Moses is found daily on the bank and Christ in the Church! O wondrous mercy of God! O light brighter than other light—the light of that day on which, after the example of that Israelite leader, the wood of the cross was raised from the place of confinement!

For thanks be to God that, as Pharaoh’s daughter showed great kindness to the Hebrew children, preserving her father’s male child together with the females, so by great grace the Church of God has been preserved in the true Moses, since today Queen Helena has displayed the Lord’s cross both to males and to females. Therefore, if we rightly consider Pharaoh’s wickedness, it is no wonder that he commanded the male children of the Hebrews [Col. 0946C] to be killed and the females preserved. For as males and females are distinguished in two kinds of persons, so virtues are signified in males and vices in females.

Therefore, lest the ancient enemy be received into the vessels of our hearts by preserving females and killing males, we must pray that the true Moses may deign to grant us these twofold virtues: that, in gathering virtues and cutting off vices, we may preserve the males and kill the females, lest we appear to fall under the dominion of the true Pharaoh, who commanded the male sex to be killed and the female preserved.

#### Chapter XIII. Moses, as a figure of the eternal King, crushed beneath his feet the royal diadem which Pharaoh placed upon his head at his daughter’s request

[Col. 0947A]

Therefore, although we have spoken once and twice concerning Moses and Pharaoh’s daughter, nevertheless, about to speak a little with them for a third time, we shall touch briefly upon both her and him. For it should be known that this same boy, clothed in royal attire, handsome in bearing but more handsome in face, prefigured by his appearance and beauty that Lord of whom it is written: “You are beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44 [45]).

It is therefore no wonder that, by the counsel of the ancient Divinity, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him as her son, since this adopted son prefigured in hope that Son [Col. 0947B] of whom it is written: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2). Accordingly, under the type of him “who makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a joyful mother of children” (Ps. 112 [113]), she offered the child to her father Pharaoh, asking that through the inmost love of paternal affection he should make him successor to his empire.

Thus transferred into Pharaoh’s house, he was not deprived of royal goods there, the prophetic saying being fulfilled in him: “He will not deprive of good things those who walk in innocence” (Ps. 83 [84]). For, as Josephus relates in the books of the *Antiquities*, he held great authority in Pharaoh’s house, typifying him of whom the eminent prophet says: “The government has been placed upon his shoulder” (Isa. 9). [Col. 0947C] Therefore, although Pharaoh did not know the noble stock of that race, nevertheless, for his daughter’s favour, he placed upon him the diadem of his kingdom, fulfilling in himself what the Gospel saying testifies: “The kingdom shall be taken from him and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21).

Moses himself also promptly showed this well in his action, when, casting that royal diadem to the ground, he trampled it under foot. He thereby signified that he would not succeed an earthly man upon the throne of an earthly kingdom, since he was to receive “a kingdom of glory and a diadem of beauty from the hand of the Lord.” In this deed he foresaw that the kingdom of the devil would one day be destroyed, when he crushed beneath his feet the crown which Pharaoh had set upon him; thus he typified for us that by the power of the cross we shall always utterly crush him of whom the Apostle says: “God will crush Satan under your feet swiftly” (Rom. 16). [Col. 0947D]

#### Chapter XIV. These three men—Joseph, Isaac, and Moses—according to their prophecy and Law, spoke differently, indeed, concerning the mystery of the cross, yet held one mind

See: as through the riddles of spiritual words, in explaining the three men, we moved from one to another, so now it seems suitable and timely to gather these same men here together into one. But because these men—Joseph, Isaac, and Moses—had three figures in three persons, we must consider with both eyes in what respect the third seems to differ from the two.

Thus, in proclaiming the King of all ages, two of them offered prophecy and the third the Law; for as the Law was given through Moses, so prophecy was offered to us through Joseph and Isaac. Therefore, although two of them are patriarchs and the third a prophet, the Law and prophecy of each seem almost to be fulfilled in the mystery of the holy cross, except for those matters which, promising us either reward or punishment, still await the future judgment.

[Col. 0948A] It should be observed that wherever they proclaimed God as living, they had different speech but one mind; for if we examine the words of each more carefully, whatever one testifies, the other and the third testify also. For it was fitting that all whom the ray of heavenly light had penetrated should speak together from the mystery of the cross, in which blood and water came forth from the Saviour’s side to cleanse the sewer of original impurity (John 19).

Thus it should be known that, as Abraham showed himself to possess a type of the Saviour when he saw three beneath the tree of the cross and worshipped one, so these three also honoured the divine and human nature in God when they used to worship the form of the holy Trinity in that same figure. But although all had the worship of one God, they nevertheless possessed in themselves a single figure: one held the worship of piety and the type of the living God by the testimony of the prison, [another] of the ram, and the third of the serpent. Therefore, lest we appear to be imprisoned, as Joseph was, in the prison-house of Egyptian captivity, [Col. 0948B] we must imitate the other two men, Isaac and Moses, so that we may be armed in mind with them against the wiles of the ancient serpent by the weapons of righteousness, imitating the Saviour’s strength in the ram and prudence in the serpent.

[Col. 0948C]

#### Chapter XV. That, in the figure of the Lord’s cross and evangelical grace, double or triple nourishments suitably belong to those three men—Joseph, Isaac, and Moses

These matters having been considered, we must also consider in them other works of piety, so that we may know what ought rightly to be sought from each of them, whose figures differed according to the diversity of grace. For as Joseph merited both to feed others and himself to be fed with the bread of life and understanding, [Col. 0948D] so Isaac and Moses merited to drink the water of wisdom, that, through differing grace but equal goodwill, one might be joined to another in mutual charity.

For spiritual gifts are so disposed that one virtue is always sustained by another, since among the virtues of spiritual men there is such reciprocity that the virtue not possessed by one is possessed by another. It is therefore no wonder that, as Joseph, according to the sacrament of higher understanding, is accustomed to distribute to us spiritual grain from the storehouse of charity, so Isaac and Moses, according to the grace given to each, are to give us the water of heavenly wisdom.

For as Joseph in the mystery of the cross figuratively showed us that bread of which it was said, “This is the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6), so Isaac and Moses must give us to drink the secret streams of that rock [Col. 0949A] of which it is written: “They all drank from the spiritual rock that followed them” (1 Cor. 10). Therefore, lest we perish from thirst or hunger, it is fitting that through the mystery of the cross we be refreshed with the water and bread of the heavenly Word, especially since these same three men can wholly remedy the thirst of souls from there: if one gives us bread and two give drink.

But meanwhile it seems no obstacle if Joseph is separated for a little while from the other two, so that where one argument seems to agree with another he may again be restored to his proper place in the former station. For we must briefly note in two ways how, in Isaac and Moses, causes correspond to causes and things to things, especially since through the abundant clause of the following sentence they can completely ward off for us the peril of inward thirst.

[Col. 0949B] For as Isaac, from that well called “of the Living and the Seeing One,” must irrigate the dryness of the mind in the figure of the Saviour, so that the thirst of our hearts may be quenched by Moses, we must, with Noah, be made drunk in the ark of the Church with the cup of charity. There, through the mystery of the cross, when the sevenfold flood of God’s grace inundates us, Isaac ministers to us the water of wisdom from the well, and Moses from the river.

#### Chapter XVI. Which of the three men named immediately above, according to the threefold grace of the Divinity, is to give bread, while the others give water
Behold, if anyone now wishes to consider the time and hour more carefully, the third must again, as we said before, be recalled to his place [Col. 0949C], so that in the heavenly chief-ministry of the Holy Trinity he may be joined to the other two both in number and in mystery. For just as Joseph, on the altar of the cross, prefigured for us among the Hebrews that bread of which it is written, “He gave them bread from heaven” (Ps. 77), so Isaac and Moses ought to minister to us certain secrets of heavenly wisdom in the two measures of twofold love.

For *metron* in Greek is called *mensura*, “measure,” in Latin; and the two measures suitably belong to the teaching of these men, because they filled those upper water-jars with two or three measures, concerning which it is written: “Each holding two or three measures” (John 2). It must indeed be understood that, just as two measures signify twofold love, so three measures typically indicate faith in the Holy Trinity [Col. 0949D]. Moreover, just as, by the insight of an inward kernel, the two measures figure Law and grace, so the three measures signify the threefold order of believers: namely, married persons, virgins, and the continent. Therefore, since upon the two commandments and faith in the Trinity hang the whole Law and the Prophets (Matt. 22), two or three measures fittingly belong to these three men, because heavenly nourishment is daily ministered by them to these three orders: married persons, continent persons, and virgins.

For just as Joseph, through the mystery of the cross, restores the strength of souls with that bread of which it is said, “You have fed us with the bread of tears” (Ps. 79), so Isaac and Moses customarily intoxicate our hearts with the figure of that drink of which Scripture says: “You will give us drink in tears by measure” [Col. 0950A] (ibid.). And therefore it is necessary for us, through the grace of almighty God, to strive to fill the jars of the mind with the Lord’s commandments: that is, by the double coinage of Law and grace, to fill them with good works even to the brim.

Otherwise, when the ceremonies of the Hebrew Law fail, the wedding in Cana of Galilee was made for us in vain (John 2), unless in the Church of God the wedding-feast of those reclining at table is daily fulfilled by the good conduct of believers. But because, in the mystery of the Lord’s Passion and cross, a twofold grace has been given us—so that in the Lord’s sacraments we ought to lack neither wine nor water—both must therefore be brought for God’s service, lest either the Law be lacking to grace or grace to the Law.

For it must be understood that if [Col. 0950B] wine alone is brought by either one or the other in the Redeemer’s sacrifice, his blood begins to be without us. But if water alone is ministered, whether by this one or that, the people alone begin to be without Christ. Therefore, as we have learned in the school of holy mother Church herself, neither wine alone nor water alone is to be brought for the Lord’s sacrifice; rather, both are to be mingled together, so that one sacrament may be completed from both by spiritual sanctification.

For this reason, as we have from the tradition of the faithful, at the wedding banquet water was changed into wine, and the Law into the Gospel, so that we too may be transformed by the Almighty into another image: that, as we were once changed in body, so we may now be changed in mind. But it must be understood that the Law changed into the Gospel, and the water changed into wine, ought first [Col. 0950C] to be brought to the steward of the feast, because in the Church of God, which has a threefold dining-hall in its three orders, the chief authority appears to be held in the figure of the teachers.

For *archos* in Greek is called *princeps*, “chief,” in Latin; and this name seems fitting for the pastors of Churches, because over the three principal orders of ranks in the Church’s dining-hall they customarily hold primacy. Therefore, because wine was then spiritually made from water when the mystery of the Lord’s Passion and cross appeared to have been accomplished, it was fitting that the grace which previously lay hidden in water and wine should first be brought by the children of the Church to the steward of the feast. Otherwise the twofold grace would have been kept for us in that wine and water in vain, unless that wine from water were brought by us [Col. 0950D] here and to him there, concerning which it is written: “But you have kept the good wine until now” (John 2).

Such wine ought not to be put into rotten skins, but rather into new wineskins, because every company of the faithful ought carefully to guard against making old wine in new skins. And what are signified by new skins except new people—provided that, renewed through the grace of almighty God, they possess not newness of body but newness of mind? He who long ago, through the death of the cross, raised decayed dead persons, likewise always requires new wineskins to receive his blood: persons renewed from the old into the new human being according to that same pattern by which Peter, Paul, and the rest were renewed.

Therefore, lest the wineskins of our hearts be found unlike those wineskins concerning which [Col. 0951A] Truth says, “They put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved” (Matt. 9), it is necessary that, through the frost of heavenly grace, our inward parts should grow cold along with that wineskin of our vices, concerning which it is written: “I have become like a wineskin in the frost” (Ps. 118). For since no one can possess inward beauty unless he has coldness in vices and warmth in virtue, it is fitting that each of us should possess within himself the same warmth of divine love concerning which it is said: “He trampled my heart within me” (Ps. 38).

Otherwise we cannot confidently cry out that which is in the Song of Songs: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind” (Song 4), unless the coldness of all wickedness is so shut out from the enclosure of inward thought that the door of the heart is closed to the north wind and opened to the south wind. Therefore, because we can by no means please the divine gaze unless we possess coldness in vices and warmth in virtues [Col. 0951B], we must fill the jars of the mind with good morals and upright deeds in order to celebrate the wedding-feast of almighty God, so that in the mystery of the cross we may worthily draw from that wine of spiritual joy concerning which it is written: “Draw now, and carry it to the steward of the feast” (John 2).

Since, then, the wedding-feast of those reclining at table has now been more than sufficiently supplied, while in the banquet of spiritual words we have filled the jars of our minds, it is time, in order to take up again the measures of the preceding argument, to return from the wedding and the jars to the patriarchs and prophets. For just as, through the power of divine mercy, we lately turned from Law to grace [Col. 0951C], so now, to proclaim the King of all things, we must return from wine to water and from grace to Law.

But although we must draw out with great force whatever is to be drawn from Isaac’s wells and from the Law of Moses, nevertheless, because we have once experienced the severity of both, we ought again to return to them by our former reading. For these prophets exert upon us the same force that we see the magnet-stone exert upon rings and straw: we are compelled to obey these same prophets in the same manner as a straw or a ring is compelled to yield to the magnet’s power. For just as that stone, by an art of wondrous force, draws to itself whatever meets it from the opposite direction, so we too appear to be drawn indirectly back to these same prophets for the completion of our former undertaking.

Accordingly, lest Joseph stray too far from the path of the other two in pursuing the theory of the proposed argument [Col. 0951D], it is necessary that he should now all the sooner be joined to the other two, because by number and mystery he must aid them both. These men are indeed the more worthy of the ministry of human service because they were few in number and many in mystery; for the two-edged sword of the two Testaments fittingly indicates to us that their meaning is manifold.

Therefore, because beneath the single profession of faith there was in them a manifold grace of Christ—since one office belonged to this man and another to that—we must diligently consider what we ought worthily to hope from each of them. For we need their patronage and God’s grace in one way, and the Jews in another; because in the mystery of the cross such a great chasm seems to have been fixed between us and them [Col. 0952A] (Luke 16) that neither we wish to pass to them nor they to us.

Therefore, lest we suffer hunger with those Jews like dogs (Ps. 58), through the mystery of the cross we must daily seek spiritual loaves from the true Joseph, so that, just as he meets the fugitive with the marrow of wheat or with loaves, Isaac and Moses may bring water of heavenly speech to the thirsty mind. For it must be understood that, just as the true Joseph formerly fed us spiritually and the Hebrews bodily with that bread of which the prophet David says, “He satisfied them with bread from heaven” (Ps. 104), so the true Isaac and the true Moses gave us spiritual drink, and the Jews figurative drink, with that heavenly water concerning which it is written: “He gave them to drink of the water of wisdom” (Ecclus. 15).

And therefore it is necessary that, just as the true Joseph [Col. 0952B], through the mystery of the cross, daily gives us that heavenly manna to be chewed with the teeth of faith, concerning which the Psalmist says, “He rained manna for them to eat” (Ps. 77), so the true Isaac and the true Moses should individually remedy for us that thirst of souls of which it is written: “He turned rivers into a desert, and springs of water into thirst” (Ps. 106). It is also necessary that, just as the true Joseph customarily feeds us daily, by the mystery of the heavenly sacrament, from the fatness of wheat in the granary of the Church, so Isaac may wish to give us drink from the wells, and Moses from the rock, by two or three measures of spiritual understanding.

Thus, as may be recognized by the clarity of the inward eye, a threefold grace meets us in these three men: through the grace of him who satisfies the empty soul, two offer us [Col. 0952C] water and the third bread. But although one kind of food often does not suit three persons according to their condition, we must nevertheless show here, with singular devotion and common reasoning, how in the mystery of the cross one is suited to all and all to one.
