Therefore, since our faith and our hope are in him alone whose figure Joseph, Isaac, and Moses bore, we must pray that, just as the true Joseph daily feeds us, through the mystery of the cross, with that bread in the house of the present Church, concerning which it is written, “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77), so the true Isaac may show himself so devoted to our devotion that from the well of his blood he may grant us the drink of heavenly grace; in order that, upheld by the threefold rowing of faith, hope, and love through the true [Col. 0952D] Moses, we may cross the sea of this present age with dry feet. Thus through his Passion and cross may we always be mortified in body and made alive in mind—his death being prefigured by Joseph in prison, Isaac in the ram, and Moses in the serpent.

May he deign to grant this to us, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

For since we must now swiftly conclude all that we have proposed concerning Joseph, Isaac, and Moses, we must consider what the word of God, which is living and effective, finally accomplishes here as one in three. And so our discourse, as though after conquering the shadow or crowd of worldly care, will attain its summit in Christ Jesus.

## HERE BEGINS THE SECOND BOOK ON THE DISCOVERY OF THE HOLY CROSS

[Col. 0953]

## CHAPTER I. Blessed Helena and her son Constantine the Great obtained grace from God.

[Col. 0953A]

Although it cannot be unknown that after the Lord’s Passion the Lord’s wood had long been hidden by the Jews, it is nevertheless fitting, in proclaiming the victory of that most sacred cross, to recall when and by whom it was discovered. Blessed Helena, once a native of the city of Trier, after the grace of baptism began to labor earnestly in works of piety. Perfect in faith and more perfect in love, she was noble by birth but nobler in holiness. By the nobility of her character she surpassed the nobility of others, knowing that this is unquestionable nobility: that which is proved to be adorned with good morals.

Accordingly, from the seed of noble senators she bore a noble son, who, according to the greater luminary which appears to rule the day, was a splendor of empire in worldly matters and in the things of God [Col. 0953B]. Therefore, as the divine ordinance had predetermined for him, Constantine was not inappropriately named from Constans and Constantius, demonstrating that he himself possessed greater constancy toward God than either of his parents, Constantius or Constans, possessed. Yet although in the dignity of the world he was noble from his father’s lineage, he was nobler in the things of God through his mother’s descent, since after receiving the grace of the living God he preferred nobility of mind to nobility of body.

For after the grace of baptism, by which both were reconciled to the heavenly Father, the same power that was granted to the son was granted also to the mother. For if we consider the history of each more subtly, the God whom the mother worshipped was worshipped by the son.

## CHAPTER II. Through the mother Helena Syria, and through the son Constantine Rome and Greece, were converted; and to these two alone was entrusted the grace of discovering the cross.

After the son received from the Almighty, through Bishop Silvester, this grace—to be cleansed in the pool of salvation from bodily leprosy and from vices in mind—he immediately began, in order to lead others also out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth (Ps. 39), to proclaim the faith of the Holy Trinity both to Romans and to Greeks. Although he was greater in strength and might [Col. 0953D], he nevertheless labored with equal balance for the salvation of Jews and Gentiles. Running, as it were, between Jews and Gentiles, he began to call back unbelievers and strengthen believers.

Meanwhile, as with such devotion he subjected the world to himself and himself to God, his mother likewise acted here and there, drawing frequent sighs from the depths of her heart because Syria also had for so long previously resisted the Christian faith. Therefore mother and son followed the commandments of life all the more diligently because the grace granted to one was granted to both [Col. 0954A]. For, as the heavenly Father had inspired both, the faith that the son preached was preached also by the mother.

When they cast their nets in both places to catch people, Rome and Greece were immediately drawn to Christ’s faith. Moreover, lest the hearts of other nations, as though fasting from faith, should fail on the way, Syria was converted through the mother and Romania through the son. Therefore, since from such good works both mother and son were worthy, it is no wonder that the grace preserved for one was preserved for both: for a singular grace above all others was reserved to both in their search for the mystery of the saving wood.

For, by the counsel of the ancient Divinity, the office of discovering the cross was reserved for this mother and son, so that each might know that he or she had received from divine grace what no one before them could possess [Col. 0954B]. Therefore, since the banner of the Lord’s cross was discovered through the effort of both, it is uncertain whether in this discovery we should prefer her or him, especially as one counsellor out of a thousand guided them so long in this investigation, until she and he attained the accomplishment of the same work.

For through the inward persuasion of divine inspiration, the son furnished the beginning and the mother the ending of this discovery. Since each devoted himself or herself to this inquiry, the son imposed its origin and the mother its completion.

## CHAPTER III. Constantine armed himself against the barbarians with the sign of the cross, and, following the sign he saw in heaven, overthrew and conquered his enemies.

[Col. 0954C]

But since it is known only to the heavenly Father why the discovery of the most sacred cross was reserved for this son and mother, we must say how the hidden counsel of the ancient Divinity prompted mother and son to seek the Lord’s wood. At a certain time, no small multitude of barbarians began everywhere to ravage the territories of the Greeks and, breaking forth as it were into open apostasy, customarily occupied almost the whole of Romania.

Constantine, still not fearing God but respecting men, armed himself against his enemies as a veteran soldier; day and night he began with his followers to consider and reconsider how or by what means [Col. 0954D] he could drive them away. But as he was distressed by this every night and every day—since, as always happens, an anxious mind changes its purpose amid troubled circumstances—at last he was divinely raised up by such a sign, for the manifestation of the most sacred wood of the cross against his enemies.

One night, as he rested in his bed, he saw the sign of the cross in heaven; and after this vision he immediately heard a voice from heaven to this effect: that on the day of battle and at the time of fighting he ought to obtain a triumphant victory through this sign [Col. 0955A]. Therefore, although he was still a pagan and had as yet received no instruction concerning the mystery of the cross, he nevertheless at once had another sign made in the form which he saw in heaven.

When the fitting day arrived, on which the Crucified One would show the power of the cross to confirm the sign of heavenly grace, that wooden sign was carried before Constantine’s battle line. In that conflict, although each side faced the other with resolute countenance, battle line attacked battle line most fiercely until the immense line of his forces, through the power of the cross, defeated the line of the adversaries.

For when recruits and veterans were bent upon arms on both sides, and beside the bank of the Danube party met party and nation met nation [Col. 0955B], immediately, as divine grace had previously shown him in the vision, he partly destroyed and partly put his enemies to flight by the power of the cross. Thus, after he deserved to obtain victory through the power of the cross, to the praise and glory of the Divinity, he experienced in himself that grace of the divine promise concerning which it is written: “I shall put to flight those who hate him” (Ps. 88).

For because the Lord does not leave the rod of sinners upon the lot of the righteous (Ps. 124), on that day he clearly showed this in the strength of his own, when through the power of the cross he chose to free them from barbarian nations, concerning whom it is written: “But the Lord strengthens the righteous” (Ps. 36). Though they were not yet righteous in the eyes of human beings, they were nevertheless righteous before the Lord [Col. 0955C], because even then that remedy of heavenly grace was beginning to draw near to them, by which they would walk blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord (Luke 1).

## CHAPTER IV. After Constantine obtained victory through the sign of the cross, he first began to inquire about the mystery of the cross from worshippers of idols; then, baptized by Silvester, he caused Christ’s faith to be preached throughout the world.

After the rout of his enemies and victory for his own forces, Constantine began to inquire about the mystery of the cross from priests of idols, as though those who had not yet experienced the power of the holy cross could tell him anything certain about it. But certain Christians who were then present, hearing this, first preached to him something concerning the coming [Col. 0955D] of the Son of God; then, unfolding in full sequence the mystery of his Passion and cross, they told him all that had happened concerning Jesus of Nazareth.

Constantine, to appease the Maker of the whole work, by whom he was strengthened and baptized in the Lord’s name, began to learn what he owed to God and what to humankind. Putting on a new garment and assuming a new mind, he received two kinds of remedies in the font of the Savior: because he had refused to shed innocent blood, leprosy left his body and vices his mind.

Therefore, trusting in divine power, he waged inward wars against the vices of the flesh. Since he had impressed the form of the Divinity more deeply upon himself, the war which he had formerly fought with enemies he afterwards waged with vices. For after many sins had been forgiven him, because he loved much (Luke 7), he immediately turned to the worship of the one God. So that he might no longer sacrifice in a common temple of idols to diverse idols [Col. 0956A], he afterwards chose to sacrifice not to many gods but to one.

From that day, unwilling to make himself guilty before God, he worshipped the God who is three in persons and one in majesty. His heart leaned all the more firmly upon love of the Creator because he chose to know nothing except Christ Jesus, and him crucified (1 Cor. 2). Thus, as through daily advances he grew from virtue to virtue and from salvation to salvation, he became more powerful everywhere throughout the world in proportion as he began to be more fervent in the Creator’s service.

And because he served on earth, humble in thought and faithful in action, him whom angels serve in heaven, his throne was established in faithfulness as the days of heaven (Ps. 88) [Col. 0956B]. But because by the observance of faith and the fruit of good works he brought joy to Christians and grief to idolaters, we also ought to give greater thanks on his account to the Creator of grace, because his faithfulness advanced both himself and us.

For he had led almost the whole world to the same faith in which he himself had been instructed through the blessed bishop Silvester, knowing long ago that, just as the strength of an entire garment depends on its warp, so the whole salvation of the soul depends upon faith in Christ.

## CHAPTER V. Constantine sent his mother, blessed Helena, to Jerusalem to seek the Lord’s wood; when she arrived, she diligently questioned the Jews concerning the holy cross.

[Col. 0956C]

Therefore, when by the hidden chief-ministry of the ancient Divinity the Emperor Constantine had formerly ruled the Roman Empire, he passed from nation to nation and from kingdom to kingdom (Ps. 104), scattering everywhere, here and there, the seed of faith: joyful for the faithful and sorrowful for the unbelieving, he commended the faith of the Holy Trinity to the former and the latter.

Meanwhile, as he labored in this way for Jews and Gentiles, he began to seek the Lord’s wood from wise men, desiring all the more earnestly to venerate the memorial of that cross because through it he had earlier deserved victory over his enemies. But because he divided his attention among many matters for the faith of Christ and the affairs of the empire [Col. 0956D], he sent his mother, blessed Helena, to Jerusalem in his place, that she might there seek the Lord’s cross all the more diligently because, in this inquiry, she had the Crucified One himself as her guide and leader.

Blessed Helena, using wise counsel, immediately obeyed God inwardly and her son outwardly. She not only went with strong resolve to Jerusalem for that inquiry, but also diligently investigated among the Jews where the Lord’s wood was. Having already passed from vices to virtues by acting well, she deservedly sought that treasure of the Divinity, found it when sought, and preserved it when found.

Therefore, that we too may hasten with her as from darkness to light, we must tell how she found that cross [Col. 0957A], lest any hearer ever be so foolish as later to claim ignorance of these things despite knowing them. Choosing from among the Jews one thousand men, she asked them what this one or that one thought concerning it. Seeing that they all agreed in one and the same conclusion, she again began to separate five hundred from them.

Although they had been instructed in the divine Law, they did not know what the queen intended to do with them, except insofar as Judas, one of them, could explain the matter to the other Jews. Accordingly, he gave them a proper explanation: “She wishes to make inquiry concerning the Lord’s wood.” Yet he said that absolutely nothing had been written concerning it, except what he confessed had been foretold to him by his father or grandfather.

Therefore, recalling the sayings of his father and grandfather of old, he began to explain them to the others, recounting to the two peoples—the Jews and the Gentiles—whatever he had received concerning both sets of ancestors. For they had told him that he and all his descendants could know this: whenever an inquiry concerning the wood should occur, their race would no longer be able to reign, but their kingdom would be transferred to the salvation of believers, concerning which it is written: “The kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule over the nations” (Ps. 21) [Col. 0957B].

## CHAPTER VI. Blessed Helena judges that those Jews who refuse to reveal the holy cross should be punished with death and burned with fire; she orders Judas to be confined in a pit for seven days.

The queen, summoning the whole company of Jews back to herself, set before them life and death: life, if they disclosed the wood of the cross; death, if they scorned to reveal it [Col. 0957C]. But since their hearts were hardened toward these matters and they said that they did not know what they knew, she compelled them all the more speedily to say what had to be said because she wished the sooner to learn from them what she did not know.

When the truth of the matter could by no means be discovered from them, she immediately ordered them all to be burned with fire, so that at least in this way she might compel them to obey divine admonitions—those whom she could bring to this neither by coaxing nor by threats. But the Jews, fearing for themselves and desiring rather to live than die, at last handed Judas over before them all in order to reveal to her the bare truth.

Since she could neither frighten him by threats nor entice him by persuasion to say anything true about the matter, she immediately selected one man from among them all [Col. 0957D] and ordered him to be kept fasting in a pit for seven days, until, when the seven days had passed, he should ask to be brought out on the condition that he render the Lord’s cross the service due to it.

When he was brought out of the pit at these words, joy immediately arose among the Christians and grief among the Jews; for all the Jews assembled there envied us and feared for themselves. But he who is our salvation in the time of tribulation (Ps. 36), taking pity on them and on us, turned to us and returned to them; on that day he chose to make Christians glad and Jews enlightened.

## CHAPTER VII. Judas, then drawn from the pit, offered prayer to the Lord and found three crosses; a dead man restored to life there bore witness to the Lord’s cross.

[Col. 0958A]

For this reason, when a crowd of the twofold people gathered from every direction at the place of Calvary, side began to draw toward side, lest art should be mocked by art through Jewish impiety. Judas, standing among the others before the eyes of the children of men, poured out this prayer to the Lord from the depths of his heart: that he might deign to show him where the pit of the Lord’s cross was, he who had formerly deigned to show Moses the bones of our father Joseph.

But because he could not find a sure trace of that place unless divine mercy chose to show some heavenly wonder, the place itself was suddenly shaken, to strengthen the hope of unbelievers and the faith of believers [Col. 0958B]. Moreover, another sign immediately followed to make known the wood of the Lord’s cross: smoke of aromatic spices at once rose from that place, to tame the untamed heart of the Jews.

Judas, who had previously hung between hope and fear, began to experience joy instead of sorrow and weeping instead of joy, giving thanks to God for everything gloriously done by him. Then, humbly bending to the ground and taking up a digging-tool, he began to dig vigorously. Others after others likewise began to dig with him until, in place of the one cross they sought, they found three together.

O how wonderful and unheard-of a thing: one cross was sought and three were found [Col. 0958C], although one was much more precious than the other two for enlightening the souls of the faithful. It is therefore no wonder that Judas himself, among the others, was the first troubled as to what ought to be done with the three crosses. For, as many Jews from the synagogue of the Jews affirmed, two crosses were those of thieves and the third was God’s.

Thus, though Judas himself did not know among so many crosses whose this or that one was, a certain dead man who was restored to life there immediately gave greater credence to the Lord’s cross than to the other crosses. Nor would human discernment fail to recognize what honor and reverence ought to be given to the two or to the third. Therefore, after the people had fruitlessly brought that dead man to one cross and then another, when he was brought to the third he recognized the power of the holy cross. After the crowd on foot had in vain extended him to two crosses [Col. 0958D], he was immediately placed upon the third and rose.

Accordingly, all deservedly blessed God, since the resurrection of the dead man bore witness to them of the power of the Lord’s wood. The same dead man also deservedly blessed it above the others, for he had been dead and was restored to life that very day.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the testimony borne to the holy cross both by the living and by the dead, and concerning the spiritual joy of blessed Helena.

O precious and wondrous wood! O wood worthy of angelic and human proclamation, through which the ancient Divinity restored both life to the dead and liberty to the captive, and thus plainly declared that that wood seemed not dead but living! O sacred and venerable cross [Col. 0959A]! O glorious and wonderful cross, which, that fitting honor might be shown by all, had proclamation from the living and testimony from the dead!

O immeasurable love of charity! O ineffable dispensation of divine mercy, which by the hidden counsel of the ancient Divinity gave God over to death on the cross for humanity, and the Son for the servant, so that after the bitterness of that death had been overcome, the servant might receive liberty and the Son inheritance! Although that most sacred cross has no need of human proclamation, since it is commended of itself by prophetic and evangelical testimony, it is nevertheless fitting that we should pursue it with boundless praise all the more zealously because our salvation seemed in some fashion to be suspended upon it.

This is the cross which, long held captive under Jewish custody, is proved today to have been discovered by Queen Helena, so that we too, admonished by this example, may strive to be found in its pattern [Col. 0959B]. This is the cross upon which the Son of God, lifted up, drew all things to himself (John 12), he of whom the angel said to Mary: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you” (Luke 1).

This is likewise that sacred and most renowned cross on which that light hung which said, “Let there be light,” and there was light (Gen. 1), so that he who deigned to undergo nails, spear, and cross for us might lead us with himself to eternal light. This is the cross which, as the mysteries of Holy Scripture testify, is proclaimed as found by the blessed Queen Helena, the evangelical words being fulfilled in it today: “Ask and you shall receive; seek and you shall find” (John 16).

But no one at all can know how joyful or glad that queen was made today [Col. 0959C], when the Lord’s cross appeared raised up from the earth, except him who alone knows how to open the seven seals in the book of life. Therefore, so that what had been begun under a good omen might be concluded with a good omen and end, it was fitting that that most beautiful gift should first be brought to that most beautiful queen, so that she who was greater in imperial authority might be first in the gift through the chief-ministry of heavenly grace.

## CHAPTER IX. With what zeal and joy of clergy and people the life-giving wood of the cross was received.

Meanwhile, while through the saving mystery the Lord looked down upon the children of men (Ps. 32), crowds of people flocked together, blessing the Lord in hymns and confessions [Col. 0959D]; and, moreover, after a speech had been made in greeting of that same saving grace, great rejoicing immediately arose among the people. For the ancient unbelief of the Jews having been excluded, there resounded there the harp and lyre of a spiritual song, the tambourine and flute; since, lest any suitable person of any rank or age should be absent, neighbour and resident, pilgrim and stranger, hastened thither: so that, just as none of them seemed exempt from guilt, so that singular grace might be common to all alike. How great was the gathering of nations and the joy of the peoples there neither the hearing of the ears nor the sight of the eyes can comprehend; for all who were present had such joy and such dancing there that, through their desire to see [Col. 0960A], they even abandoned at that hour their concern for eating.

There, while one begrudged another’s swiftness, charity became the rival of charity, when charity began to delay charity in order to behold the dignity of that same heavenly mystery. O praiseworthy separation and marvellous exchange, in which the running of the swift delayed the running of the sluggish; where, although the swifter persons seemed to delay the sluggish, nevertheless neither party appeared deprived of God’s grace. But because they had not yet experienced the power of the holy cross, the sluggish clung to the swift and the swift to the sluggish, so that one seemed less sluggish than another insofar as each wished to be more diligent than the other in running the course. For just as the Jews began to be saddened when they saw God’s glory upon the Lord’s wood, so [Col. 0960B] the Christian people rejoiced when the shrine of that same heavenly mystery was seen.

There, undoubtedly, the eager and the tearful gathered together; there the strong and the weak alike assembled, while, through the different lots of the two groups, the eager were joined with the tearful and the strong with the weak. There also the blind and the lame were united in divine praise, as though someone had invited them there in those Gospel words in which it is said: “Bring the blind and the lame in here” (Luke 14). Moreover, there every deaf and mute person lay in wait for his own salvation, since those devout persons came thither for the sake of the grace of him who made the deaf hear and the mute speak (Mark 7). Therefore, since clergy after clergy and people after people ran from every direction to see the shrine of the most holy cross, it is no wonder if so great a multitude of peoples [Col. 0960C] seemed to be wheeled round from circle to circle, where, in the collision of crowds, a man struck a woman and a woman a man.

For where clergy and people were massed in a wondrous column, what good did it do if there a neighbour and a husband clung to a wife, and a wife to a husband, especially when both were there subjected to divine honour, and wife envied husband and husband wife? For the greeting of the shrine of that most precious treasure produced clamour among the clergy and tumult among the people, while, through their hasty visitation of that heavenly shoot and divine seed, sweat broke out on the men and modest shame upon the women. Although here and there the people seemed to stand like a wall, nevertheless father hastened with son, mother with child; and although the wailing infant was left at home in the cradle, none of them wished to be deprived of that same joy [Col. 0960D].

For, that one might behold the life-giving mystery before another, each began to obstruct another’s desire; because, just as at the funerals of loved ones one person joins another at the bier in pious devotion, so at that divine service each strove to outstrip another through another. Indeed, each caused the other a long delay, while one restrained another from seeing this grace from hour to hour; for although every sex and age ran together to this spectacle, each of them exceeded the bounds of customary pace. Thus only those who were present could know how much grief all those who were absent felt—especially since those absent were swallowed up by so much greater sadness as they saw those present rejoicing with more abundant gladness [Col. 0961A].

But perhaps none of those over whom the discipline of heavenly teaching presided was absent there, “in the council of the righteous and the congregation” (Ps. 110), since a greater punishment would have bound him if he had happened to be missing from that assembly. For there each began all the more eagerly to forestall the other at that spectacle, as each wished before another to behold the divine miracle: the most holy cross, stained with the liquid blood of the Lord, is read to have been uncovered by divine agency through Queen Helena.

## Chapter X. How we too ought to rejoice at the honour of the holy cross, and what difference there is between Christians and Jews

[Col. 0961B] Yet although we were not bodily present with them on that day, we ought now to rejoice with the same joy as they; because, though absent there in bodily presence, we nevertheless seemed in some manner to be present with them in Christ’s body. Through participation in spiritual joy and exultation, on that day we were present to them and they to us; for, in the unity of the Church, he held us together with them in himself—the one who said to the Father concerning his elect: “I will that they may be one in me, just as I am in thee” (John 21).

See how blessed—indeed, what is more blessed than every good fortune—is that unity of God and man, and that common communion, such that man has in God and God in man the same union that the body has in the head or the head in the body [Col. 0961C]. That God is the head of Christ and Christ the head of the Church may especially be proved from the saying: “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6). Hence it is written that the Jews, divided from Christians in this union, seem entirely cut off from the body of the Church, because they think one thing about the mystery of the cross and Christ’s incarnation, and Christians another.

For just as we, for the instruction of believers’ souls, believe in three persons and worship one God, so, conversely, the Jews wrongly transform themselves into another form of belief, worshipping one person in God and rejecting the other two. Yet it must be noted that, although Christians believe one way and Jews another, both render worship to one God [Col. 0961D]; for although the Christian thinks one thing and the Jew another concerning the mystery of the cross, one God is nevertheless worshipped by both. But because in the Saviour’s death one is innocent and the other guilty, the Christian ought rightly to rejoice and the Jew to mourn; so that from the fruit of a good or evil tree, in respect of the mystery of the cross, one may be in joy and the other in mourning.

And it fittingly befalls both believers and unbelievers that the former ought to rejoice with those who rejoice, and the latter to weep with those who weep (Rom. 12); for, as the Apostle says: “The word of the cross is foolishness to those who perish; but to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God” (1 Cor. 1). Hence it is no wonder that, just as among believers that future laughter will be seen of which Truth says, “Blessed are you who now weep, for you shall laugh” [Col. 0962A] (Luke 6), so among unbelievers that laughter will at some time be seen of which it is written: “Laughter shall be mingled with sorrow” (Prov. 14).

And therefore, that we may always embrace by good merits that spiritual joy of which James says, “Count it all joy, brothers, when you fall into diverse temptations” (James 1), we must pray that through the grace of the Godhead that full joy may always remain in us, of which Truth says to the disciples: “No one shall take your joy from you” (John 22).

## Chapter XI. A comparison of Constantine and his mother Helena

Therefore, since we have now somewhat forgotten the preceding argument while we sought, with good reason, to oppose the unbelief of the Jews [Col. 0962B], it is fitting that, just as in the concealment of the Lord’s wood we sufficiently experienced their hardness, so now we should return by our former discourse to Constantine and Helena. For he, instructed in the school of the heavenly sign, burned first of all with desire to seek the cross; yet his mother has now brought the affection of his good will to its accomplishment.

For it must be known that, after their prayer had been made pure through good works, in the search for the saving wood he became first and she second. For although the two had one purpose in finding the cross, the search ennobled the son and the discovery the mother. Since both devoted effort to the same search, the son sought the wood of the cross, but the mother found it; she who, while beginning to explore the depths of the earth for this cause [Col. 0962C], became first in discovery and second in the search.

Thus, although it is not unknown to the eternal Father whether we ought to render greater reverence to son or mother, we nevertheless believe, in him who always regards the vows of the humble, that the mother is of greater merit than the son. Yet we ought to show some reverence to both on this account: each has now received the rewards of life. Although, as “star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15), so the mother differs from the son in the magnitude of merits. For if we wish to weigh their deeds more carefully, the mother is believed to be of greater worth before God than the son; because, after both were reconciled to the heavenly Father, the son had great care, but the mother greater care, in building God’s churches [Col. 0962D].

For although the son built many churches in Greece and Rome, to which he bestowed many royal gifts in treasures and estates, the mother, as the diverse martyrdoms of saints still attest, built many more churches in Gaul and Syria. Therefore churches consecrated everywhere to God in her honour rightly testify how greatly she prevails in holiness before the Lord—especially since only the ancient knowledge of the Godhead fully knows what and how great her holiness and magnificence are. Accordingly, since the power of her holiness is so great that she herself is deservedly numbered holy among the other saints, it is no wonder that, as catalogues of saints are accustomed everywhere to testify, her feast ought always to be celebrated by us in its annual recurrence.

But [Col. 0963A] since her son has no mention in the same catalogue, but rather his memory is there obliterated in every way by silence, it is necessary that the Church offer prayer to God for him, so that he too may please God in the land of the living.

> [Note: [Col. 0963] Constantine the Great, though a most pious prince, has not yet been entered by the Roman Church among the number of the saints.]

Since, in the dwelling-place of the present Church, the office of festal solemnity is owed rather to the mother than to the son, everyone ought therefore to take care, in the offices for the dead, to keep the son’s memory among the departed. Consequently, to reconcile God the Father to us, we ought no longer to pray to that same son, but to the mother, so that she may, by the aid of her most holy intercession, plead for us and for her son before God.

Because the evils we have committed are many, we ought most diligently to commend both ourselves and him to the prayers of that woman [Col. 0963B], although there is no doubt that the mother who bore him prays all the more earnestly for her son, insofar as that son grew old not in vices but in virtue. Nor without reason ought we commend both ourselves and him to that widow, that she may be willing continually to entreat God for us and for him—especially since she may thereby have us more willing in her service if, together with her son, she protects by her prayers both those of her household and strangers.

For, because that saying is great in substance and brief in words, in which it is said, “The continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful” (James 5), it is necessary that she now deign to intercede more humbly for us and for her son, insofar as the mother is declared more righteous than the son. Therefore, that it may go well with us and with him in this present age and in the age to come, we ought always to pray to God for ourselves and him in secret [Col. 0963C], so that the grace which he prepared here and there for his elect may never be lacking either to us or to him.

Moreover, lest rest ever be lacking to our souls or peace to our bodies, we ought every day to entreat God for ourselves and him, that he who is rich in promises and richer in gifts may, according to the riches of his glory, have mercy on him and on us. But because he has perhaps now long paid after his death for whatever sin there was in him before death, it is fitting that we ourselves always entreat God for him with all the more earnest prayer, insofar as he perhaps is now at rest and we are in toil. And because he does not yet possess the complete perfection of future rest, but still hopes with us to find a better resurrection [Col. 0963D], we must pray that he who by his blood chose to sanctify the banner of the life-giving cross may someday bring both us and him into perfect rest.

For it must be known that, although he was not such and so great in the perfection of merits that he can worthily be counted among the number of saints, nevertheless he will truly and beyond all doubt have a share “in the council of the righteous and the congregation” (Ps. 110). And not without reason: although Philip and Gaius—only these two kings before him—were Christians, he was the first of all emperors and kings who most zealously subjected the monarchy of the Roman world to divine laws [Col. 0964A]. Therefore, because by works of this kind he drove from himself every power of the enemy, he could rightly be called, if not a saint, yet a righteous man; for after the example of that righteous man he always desired to live for God, of whom it is written: “The righteous shall live by faith” (Gal. 3).

For if anyone searches his deeds more diligently in histories, he will clearly see that this man, though not a saint, was nevertheless righteous; for, after the example of that righteous man, he was weak against vices and strong in virtue, of whom it is said: “The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” (Ps. 111). And because both he and his mother possessed a thousand virtues, she was rightly righteous and he righteous, but she more righteous.

Hence it is no wonder that, just as the son will forever bear the figure of that righteous man of whom it is written, “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree” (Ps. 91) [Col. 0964B], so the mother, fair through the grace of diverse virtues, appears no longer misshapen like a thorn but beautiful like a rose. But although, according to the differing quality of merits, roses belong to martyrs, and so forth, lilies to confessors, nevertheless, because through the mortification of vices their hearts were barren of vices and fruitful in virtue, the son shall rightly flourish like a palm tree and the mother like a rose.

Furthermore, by the counsel of the eternal Godhead, the son shall flourish like an olive tree and the mother like a lily; because, now that the exile of this present life has run its course, the crown of righteousness cannot be lacking either to mother or son. Nor without reason are those worthy of so great a reward for whom the discovery of the Lord’s wood was reserved, although the mother entered with her son into so great a covenant of love that the son sought [Col. 0964C] that wood and the mother found it. For although, in seeking the banner of the Lord’s cross, he urged her and she urged him, each fulfilled what was pious: the son sought the same cross and the mother found it.

Therefore it must be known that, if that son ought fittingly to receive a reward for having first sought the wood of the Lord’s cross, the mother herself deserved far greater glory, since on this day she elegantly disclosed the Lord’s wood to us. And if she who found the cross is worthy of glory and honour, much more is he to be honoured who redeemed us on the cross, because upon that same wood which she is accustomed to reveal to us today he graciously accomplished the work of our redemption.

Therefore [Col. 0964D], because every day we worship the life-giving cross in honour of him who once upon the cross turned night into day and darkness into light, we must pray that, through the glorious power of that most holy cross, he may someday deign to grant our souls rest and now health to our bodies; so that through his grace we may then deserve to be delivered from punishments and now from sins, because on the altar of the cross Jesus Christ our Lord offered himself as a sacrifice to God the Father, “for an odour of sweetness,” he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever.

# Here begins the third book, concerning Constantius and Helena

[Col. 0965]

## The author’s brief preface

[Col. 0965A]

Since, dearest brothers, we have already said something concerning the discovery of the holy cross, we shall say something concerning Constantius and Helena, through whom the cross was discovered, so that in the sequence of this work the authors of the subject may be brought forward after the subject. For it is fitting that [we who] treat [have treated] the discovery itself should set forth something about its discoverers, so that, once their glory and magnificence are known, the preceding argument may proceed more effectively to what follows.

## Chapter I. How Constantius joined Saint Helena to himself

Constantius Caesar, who was Emperor Claudius’s grandson through a daughter, always preferred foreign wars to civil ones, so that by foreign wars he might shorten the course of those civil wars of which it is written [Col. 0965B]:

> “Now a second age is being worn away by civil wars.”

Accordingly, taking military fellowship upon himself in the order of his turn, he waged distinguished war here and there, defending the commonwealth by public command and subjecting many cities and provinces to Roman rule. For this reason he set out from Rome for Gaul with a large army; here and there he brought arms against rebels and gifts to suppliants, so that, according to the differing conduct of individuals, their reward of gifts might also differ.

Accordingly he was held in all the greater affection by the Gauls because he was a mountain to the proud and a valley to the humble: by repressing the hated and advancing the beloved, he began to tame the arrogant and raise the subject. Thus, after travelling throughout Gaul on every side, he at last turned aside to the most famous city of Trier [Col. 0965C], which at that time was the more abundant in riches and resources insofar as it appeared more powerful in arms and soldiers. For although it was strong through its surrounding provinces and cities, it was made stronger by divine grace through its believers; especially since, through blessed Eucharius and his companions, idolatry was so barren and faith so fruitful that it was deservedly called a second Rome.

Meanwhile, while Constantius everywhere extended the Roman Empire through Gaul, he loved the blessed virgin Helena because of the extraordinary beauty she possessed. For she was not merely beautiful to see and pleasing in appearance, but seemed even more admirable in glory and honour. Thus, while he devoted his whole mind and all his effort to this matter [Col. 0965D], he at last pursued his beloved desire and joined her to himself in marriage. By her, as divine providence had ordained, he begot a son called Constantine the Great.

Therefore, since she was superior to Galerius and nobler than Chlorus and Cyrus, it is no wonder that so noble a woman was joined to so noble a man. For, as she was noble to the world and therefore more noble, so he was useful to himself and more useful to the empire [Col. 0966A]. In worldly matters he was, as it were, a ray of empire after the likeness of a human mirror. But she, imprinting herself by the ray of divine faith upon the law, was a mirror of empire in the things of the world and the things of God. Thus, by the nobility of mind which divine ordinance bestowed upon her, she seemed far nobler than Constantius, because through the inestimable efficacy of heavenly mercy she deserved to possess by grace that nobility of mind which he did not possess by nature.

Therefore, since Constantius could nowhere find a refuge more pleasing to his love, it is no wonder that so noble a man joined so noble a woman to himself in wedlock. By her, as history more subtly declares to us, through God’s grace there was given to us so great and illustrious a son: one who would not be inferior in virtue to preceding kings, and would be prior in salvation to those following. Therefore blessed was the man who had such a son; blessed also the woman who, after this man, did not go to another! Yet he could have become much more blessed if he had wished to be more fruitful through the fruit of righteousness.

Still, in some manner, happy was the father of so great a son; happy also was the mother. Yet both would appear happier if they now together possessed the reward of life. Nevertheless, through the grace of whatever virtue, each seemed happy in some respect: he happy in temporal power or victory, she happy in everlasting grace and glory. Hence, by the grace of some virtue, she was happy in part, he happy, and each was happy; but one was happier than the other insofar as that one seemed more learned in God’s law [Col. 0966C].

Although that man, the mirror of the Roman world, was happy as regards the world, nevertheless, because the darkness of paganism had blackened [him] in God’s eyes, he was by no means happy as regards God. But if it may in some way be granted that he was called happy in any respect through God’s grace, he would nevertheless have been far happier had he attained faith with his wife, because he could then have enjoyed more prosperous success by guarding more carefully through faith in Christ against monstrous transgressions.

## Chapter II. What attests Saint Helena’s nobility of birth

On the other hand, that precious woman appeared noble not only in birth but also in virtue, since by the grace of almighty God she always raised the nobility of her body through nobility of mind. Thus, although the noble descent of her parents is passed over in histories, the antiquity of her buildings at Trier still testifies to her nobility: there the pavement of her house, once laid with diverse marbles and Parian stone, clearly declares how great was the precedence she seemed to possess above others [Col. 0967A].

Moreover, the very surfaces of the walls, painted in tawny gold as though with hyacinthine weaving, well attested the marks of her unconquered nobility; and, further, the abundance of her estates, long since bestowed everywhere upon God’s churches, clearly shows how eminently she possessed the most noble antiquity of lineage. Her bed too, furnished and adorned with golden bristles, in some sense bore witness in her to the nobility, as it were, of the Roman Quirites; especially since no bed like this could be found from the rising of the sun to the furthest Thule, because that chamberlain never defiled the chamber of her heart with any pollution, of whom it is written: “He stood in his bed in every way that was not good” (Ps. 35).

But perhaps all these things occurred figuratively. She who was one day to become queen began to possess by grace what she had previously possessed by nature; for after she deserved to be called back to Christ’s faith by heavenly help, she drew the ornaments of bodily rank into the salvation of her soul. Thus, by labouring for human salvation in discovering the holy cross, she became glorious through this work, but more glorious in virtue: namely, as a type of the Church, adorned within by the dignity of diverse virtues [Col. 0967B], of which it is written: “The queen stood at thy right hand in clothing of gold, surrounded by variety” (Ps. 44).

Therefore, since she was inwardly adorned with such and so many virtues, she was in every respect pleasing to every divine gaze. Yet because she was outwardly adorned with beauty and loveliness, she seemed dear and pleasing to her husband Constantius; for she was furnished with such a rule of inward devotion and everlasting beauty that she pleased God in soul and Constantius in form. According to popular opinion and the truth of the matter, she was dutiful in service to her husband, but more dutiful in service to God; for love of Constantius and of God was distinguished in her heart by a twofold principle, so that she was subject outwardly to Constantius and inwardly to God.

After Constantius had in Gaul partly settled the business of war himself and partly entrusted it to others to settle, he finally revisited his native land and people with his fellow soldiers, so that he might receive a greater crown of triumphal laurel insofar as he had returned from Gaul to Rome with a greater palm of victory. But although it is unknown to us whether the blessed Helena went with Constantius [Col. 0967D], or remained in Gaul because of the child’s tenderness, it may nevertheless be believed that she was either all the more safely taken with him, or all the more quickly conveyed after him without great delay, since she was loved by him above all other women. It must also be believed that whenever she was brought there, she was immediately reared with royal adornments and expenditure, and carefully equipped, so that, just as she was elegant in dress and more elegant in countenance, so nothing should be lacking to her in royal expense or ornament.

## Chapter III. How Constantius joined Helena to himself in lawful marriage, and concerning their son Constantine’s proclamation as Caesar

After Theodora, Constantius’s wife, died [Col. 0968A], the blessed Helena was joined to him in marriage, so that she who had previously exercised authority in the palace in a somewhat more obscure condition might afterwards share with him both marriage and empire. For it was fitting that he should deem her worthy of greater honour insofar as he had now learned with her in peace what she had earlier suffered for him in toil; especially since every labour seems altogether burdensome unless it is lightened in tribulation by the grace of consolation.

Then, when the empire of the Roman world was divided between the two Augusti, Constantius and Galerius, Illyricum and Asia fell to Galerius, while Africa and Europe came to Constantius. And since, by the permission or assistance of divine favour, one ruled Asia and the other Europe, Constantius had so much less concern for the Italians and Africans as he had greater care for the Spaniards and Gauls [Col. 0968B].

Meanwhile Constantine, his son, suited to offices and acceptable to men, was elected Caesar by the Romans on the senate’s counsel; for, in view of the virtue of both, it seemed fitting and just to them that son should be advanced to be Caesar and father to be Augustus. In this matter divine power clearly showed in him that “there is no authority except from God,” since by the hidden aid of the Godhead, at the same time that it advanced the father, it advanced the son also.

But after Constantine had defended the Roman Empire for several years with power both vigorous and fortunate, he further showed what spirit he bore toward the commonwealth when, to acquire the crown of greater glory, he again migrated from Rome to Gaul with a strong hand.

## Chapter IV. How Constantius departed after defeating the Germans and Britons, and Constantine was attacked by leprosy

[Col. 0968C]

Although the peoples of Britain and Germany, by old tyranny and new rebellion, again stirred him up to new wars, he was nevertheless filled with so much less sorrow on that account as a new army and old wisdom were at hand for his triumph. Meanwhile his son Constantine, leaving his mother in Roman territory, followed his father into Gaul with remarkable skill, so that father and son might more easily resist the tyrannical party, insofar as the son aided his father and skill aided skill. For because both were shrewd in natural ability and provident in counsel, through the mutual office of affection son met father [Col. 0968D], and father son, so that one side might overcome the other more strongly insofar as skill more cunningly outwitted skill.

Yet although Constantine was of remarkable shrewdness and admirable strength in military affairs, the peoples of Britain and Germany became for him “a grape of gall and a cluster of bitterness”; for by continuing the delays of war against them for seven years, he scarcely subjected them to Roman rule in the seventh year. Thus, after Germany and Alemannia had been conquered, at last the victor over all died and was buried in Britain, and, sending his son Constantine to the seat of Romulus, left him heir both of the Roman Empire and of Gaul.

But Constantine, after arranging the affairs of the kingdom in Gaul as he could, was revealed, immediately upon returning to Rome, as to what sort of man and how great he would be, when [Col. 0969A], through the inestimable grace of heavenly teaching, after a short time he assumed the monarchy of the Roman Empire. How wisely and vigorously he governed that Roman Empire everywhere is attested to this day by his ancient achievements—except that, through manifold worship of idols, he soon became a persecutor of Christians.

Therefore, to avenge upon him the guilt of excessive persecution, God gave him over to dishonourable sufferings: although he was of great power and greater constancy, he was struck with elephantine leprosy. In this event, because “many are the scourges of the sinner,” the power of the Creator was clearly displayed in him, so that he might fittingly recall that prophetic saying: “Scourges have been multiplied upon me, and I did not know it” (Ps. 34). Although, because of the various medical arts, different physicians were gathered from different regions [Col. 0969B], nevertheless no physician and no medicine availed to heal that plague sent by God.

Accordingly, to seek a more powerful kind of remedy, more than three thousand infants and nursing children were gathered from throughout the kingdom, as though a more effective medicine for healing him might be found if he were washed in a pool of their milky blood. But on the appointed day, when for this purpose he had proceeded from the palace to the Capitol and saw mothers on every side, their hair loosened, mourning and wailing for their children, he immediately rejected the priests’ counsels and began to recoil from the dreadful crime.

He who had formerly been stronger than the bravest men in many battles yielded on that day, indeed, to women, being moved by an inward inspiration to such mercy that he ordered each mother’s child restored to her, together with very ample gifts [Col. 0969C]. Consequently, just as none of them had previously been exempt from sorrow, so the cause of the ensuing joy appeared common to all; especially since they had not experienced so much sorrow in coming as they seemed to have joy in returning.

Thus Constantine, who had formerly conquered others, rejoiced on that day that he had conquered himself. Conquered by women’s tears to the praise and glory of the Godhead, he deserved to obtain victory. For he preferred still to bear leprosy alone in its shifting course than to stain a drawn sword with the blood of innocents; and therefore, by divine action, he became pious from impious, since he postponed the health of one person for the salvation of very many [Col. 0969D].

## Chapter V. He compares Constantine with Herod, setting one’s piety alongside the other’s cruelty
Since Constantine’s piety and Herod’s impiety are known to you, dearly beloved, in many ways, it does no harm if, by a special rule of comparison between good and evil, we set one against the other. For if one is compared with the other, it may be proved whom death and whom life follows, since the two are now separated from one another by death and life: one has the reward of death, the other of life. Therefore, Christian, that you may know what the divine and human laws judge concerning each, imitate this man and cease to imitate that one; for that man sinned in one manner, [Col. 0970A] and this man in another. King Herod sinned knowingly, when he shamelessly loved himself in bringing about the Saviour’s death. Constantine, on the contrary, erred in ignorance, when, for the life of one man, he pronounced a sentence of death upon so many men. Herod, striving to extinguish the birth of the everlasting King, was wont to draw his sword more tightly, staining it with blood upon the necks of nursing children; Constantine, wishing to show himself gentler than he, began, in pious devotion, to withhold his blade from the necks of infants. Herod took evil counsel and made evil provision for his own welfare when, on account of one child, he killed many children; Constantine, however, was wont to provide far better for his own welfare, since he would not prefer the life of one man to the safety of many. Herod also, seeing that he had been mocked by the Magi, [Col. 0970B] increased punishments upon punishments and wounds upon wounds in the slaughter of the little children; Constantine, seeing that he had been badly advised by diviners and Magi, wished, by releasing the children, to calm the sobbing of their weeping mothers. Herod, touched by ambition for an earthly kingdom, was deprived by divine vengeance of the joy of the heavenly kingdom; Constantine, by suspending the force destined to kill, rather than being killed, worthily earned entrance into the kingdom of paradise. Herod, fearing to lose his share of earthly rule, inflicted death upon many for the death of one; Constantine, however, preferred alone to bear the scab of wandering leprosy rather than, by killing many, incur leonine frenzy. Herod, the chariot of evils and driver of the wicked, became the very murderer of his three sons; Constantine, [Col. 0970C] the chariot of the Greeks and driver of the Romans, refused to become the murderer of other men’s sons. Herod has already been consigned to punishments in many ways, since he did not spare his pleasing weapons in shedding the blood of his sons [the wording is corrupt: *armis non parcebat amoenis*]; Constantine, on the contrary, was freed from eternal punishments because, in redeeming others’ children, he spared others’ sufferings. Herod cast himself far from the face of the Lord when, in slaughtering the little children, he rather killed himself; Constantine spared himself better, since, sparing the blood of the innocent, he did not wish to kill himself.

But since mention of that same accursed Herod has now fallen into our hands, we ought not to pass over in silence the torment of his illness and his death—especially since, after his death, his poisonous aconites bore good witness [Col. 0970D] to what sort of man he had been in life. Before his death, therefore, not only the end of his present life but also punishment in the life to come seemed to hang over him. Divine vengeance pursued him through diverse illnesses so that no medicine at all could help him. For his limbs were rotting and his eyes failing of themselves; he was hateful to those standing by and more hateful still to those sitting beside him, because, through extreme decay of body and strength, he was foul in breath and hideous in appearance. And although in his lower parts he was almost wholly fluid and pallid, there was nevertheless discharge in his feet and swelling in his legs; moreover his private parts, rotten and swarming with worms, scarcely awaited the arrival of the end of that miserable life. [Col. 0971A] The more fiercely the divine scourge raged in his putrid genitals, the more ruin was multiplied in them; and because his mind was fierce and his belly swollen, his pain was always before his eyes. For although fever tormented him in one part and itching in another, an insatiable desire for food seemed to possess him, so that frequent urging, excessive bloating, and coughing often testified to the voracious appetite of one eating. Moreover, although inwardly and outwardly he burned with excessive heat, he would still gladly have prolonged his present life, had not an even greater bodily illness overtaken him: his intestines seemed within to be blocked by various ulcers. Therefore, although warm water was poured over him and he was often anointed with warm oil as a healing remedy, in the end [Col. 0971B] he died an evil death and came to an evil end. For after many kinds of punishment, by which he had formerly bloodied others, he finally killed himself of his own accord with his own knife.

Thus, since he had formerly afflicted innocent others with various wounds, it is no wonder that he died an evil death, he who had always lived evilly; nor is it surprising that he is to be tortured eternally and beyond by his own punishments, he who could never be satisfied with the sufferings of others. For although before his death he had often profaned God’s temple by killing the righteous, yet in death itself he left a wicked example to his descendants. He ordered that the noblest men, whom he had caused to be assembled from all Judaea into one place, should all be slain by the sword at the very departure of his soul, so that their survivors might rejoice the less at his death because they had something in their hands [Col. 0971C] by which they might mourn more over the killing of their own. O wickedness of a king! O injustice of Herod, known through such and so great evils to us and to you! Under the pretext of piety, he summoned a company of Jews and, by the savagery of torments, inflicted death upon those who hoped for life—thus dedicating the entrance of death and the exit of life under such auspices, so that those who had not wished to grieve at his death might grieve against their will.

## CHAPTER VI. How the apostles Peter and Paul appeared to Constantine, and how he was made a catechumen.

But because to reject evil and choose good is the gift not of human but of divine bestowal, [Col. 0971D] it is time, just as a little earlier we turned from Constantine to Herod, now to return in the same order from Herod to Constantine. For just as Herod was struck in both the inner and the outer man by that twofold crushing of which it is written, “Crush them with a double crushing, O Lord” (Jer. XVII), so Constantine, by contrast, was struck by God with a simpler wound for a simpler fault: for the persecution of Christians he was punished with wandering and shifting leprosy. But because he did not make himself guilty before God of the same fault as Herod, when Herod sought the child in order to destroy him, neither was he rewarded with the same recompense with which that same Herod is known already to have been repaid.

Since, therefore, the mention of that accursed king has been sufficiently amplified, we now wish to efface his memory by silence, [Col. 0972A] because in the furnace of eternal fire he has to be cooked eternally in such torments that there is no need for us to say anything further about him. Armed by the monstrousness of his cruelty for the death of the innocent, he undoubtedly fell into the lot of eternal death. Constantine, however, by the humanity of his piety deferring the death of the innocent, undoubtedly escaped the lot of eternal death. How he escaped that death, and who showed him beforehand the way of escape, we wish to explain to you more fully, because in matters so necessary we do not wish to omit anything.

Accordingly, when the day had passed on which he had refrained from the accursed crime of shedding innocent blood, on the following night he was instructed by a divine oracle through the blessed apostles Peter and Paul to this effect: that he would receive health [Col. 0972B] of flesh and spirit from the supreme Creator if first he sought the salvation of his soul from Bishop Sylvester. O how great the kindness and humanity of the Saviour! Though he is the Creator of all creatures, he chose to reveal in a dream to so great a man such a great mystery: that by heavenly judgment he would obtain health of body and soul.

Constantine therefore, in confirmation of the grace of divine mercy and glory, committed that vision most diligently to memory, so that, his cruelty having been softened, he might more quickly report it to Sylvester, who had long hidden in mountains, caves, and caverns of the earth through fear of him. Who among you can imagine how quickly he immediately caused Sylvester to be summoned to him? Who can imagine how long the delay seemed to him when he could scarcely await even one hour for his presence? In order that the blessed man might be brought quickly, messenger after messenger and envoy after envoy were sent after him all the more urgently, because, through the cooperating grace of divine power, he was to receive from that man the medicine of salvation.

Sylvester, however, was the less afflicted by faintness of spirit and agitation because he feared being summoned to martyrdom all the more, although for the Lord he was ready to go to prison and death, even if compelled by that same man to undergo every kind of torment. And although in this anxiety he had, as it were, a thousand thoughts before a thousand others, nevertheless he thought in one way and Constantine in another; for by the inestimable gift of divine mercy, what Sylvester considered [Col. 0972D] evil, Constantine was turning to good. Though he had not yet obtained from the bishop the counsel for recovering health, the blessed man was nevertheless received by the emperor with great joy; for Constantine had not previously shown as much eagerness in seeking him as he afterward displayed rejoicing in receiving him.

What more need be said? As the two sat together here and there and conversed with one another about faith in the holy Trinity, that same Wisdom was undoubtedly believed to be present in their conversation which, after the Resurrection, spoke with the two disciples on the road. Yet although amid these mutual conversations the faith of one was still tender at the root, so that neither might grow too weary of the other amid their differing propositions and judgments, each laid before the other what had been revealed to him. Constantine related to Sylvester the vision (*horama*, ὅραμα) in the very words in which it had earlier been revealed to him by Christ’s apostles. [Col. 0973A]

And although that man, soon to become a soldier of Christ, was somewhat assured concerning this vision, he still wished to be more certain and began to ask whether images of them were available. Therefore blessed Sylvester, to block the abyss of his distrust, had a true image of those apostles brought to him, so that the image on the painted panel might more fully testify whether that vision should be judged an actual event or a tale. Since he sought no images other than these two, he immediately recognized them in the hands of those presenting them as his own. In proportion to this, he gave all the greater thanks to divine power, because, assured about the vision, he seemed nearer to salvation.

Thereupon, after his mind rose to praise those whose faces he had seen in the vision, he began to delight all the more in the inquiry into the Catholic faith, the more certain he was made of his coming recovery by the two images. Thus, when a small shoot of divine knowledge had sprung up in his heart, he passed from the old image to a new image. He renounced evil knowledge and shameful deeds so that he who bore the image of the earthly man might bear also the image of the heavenly. [Col. 0973B] In order, as it were, to pass from image to image, and thus from vice to virtue, he sought rest in place of toil and health in place of illness. Through the ineffable efficacy of divine mercy, he passed from death to life and from fault to grace.

Wishing in this manner to restrain himself from every crime, he rested from carnal action as though from the journey prescribed by the legal Sabbath. In order that he might depart from fault and rest in grace, he began, as it were, to decrease with lamp and light in one respect and increase in the other. Enlightened through Sylvester by knowledge of the divine light, as he failed in fault so he advanced in grace and wisdom—except for this one thing still charged against him: that he had not yet fully known God through the wisdom of God. Therefore, in order to be wisely foolish among those foolish ones of whom it is written, “God chose the foolish things of the world in order to confound the wise” (I Cor. II), he began to inquire more zealously of the wise concerning faith in the Trinity [Col. 0973C] and the mystery of the cross, because, after the Apostle’s example, he wished to be debtor both to the wise and to the foolish (Rom. I). And in order someday to reach the harbour of everlasting salvation, he brought about within himself the setting of idolatry and the rising of faith. For after he had been instructed by blessed Sylvester in faith in the holy Trinity, faith there took its beginning in his heart and idolatry its end.

In accordance with Sylvester’s admonition and the Lord’s revelation, he obeyed God and man inwardly and outwardly. Like a catechumen taking the right-hand path at the Pythagorean fork, he deserved to be instructed by Sylvester in the creed of faith.

## CHAPTER VII. By whom Constantine was baptized.

But since Sylvester and Constantine are now before us, we shall say something about the name of the one and the baptism of the other, because a great schism has often arisen in the hearts of some from the fact that here Constantine is said to have received baptism from Eusebius and there from Sylvester. [Col. 0974A] For if one searches diligently in Greek records, he is asserted to have been baptized by Eusebius, bishop of the city of Rome. But if one investigates earnestly in Roman histories, he is undoubtedly read to have been baptized by Sylvester. Therefore it must briefly be explained here, in the name of the Lord, how these two names belong to one man, so that the question which commonly arises among some persons may be quieted by sound reasoning.

According to the definition of the wise, and not according to popular opinion, some called him Sylvester and others Eusebius, because, as Christians report in many places, he was called Eusebius by the Greeks and Sylvester by the Romans. Therefore, since Eusebius was a Greek name, it was not inappropriate that he bore that Greek name among Greeks, for just as one is called *lector* from reading and *pictor* from painting, so Eusebius is said to mean “good writer” from writing.

[Note: [Col. 0973D] These explanations do not seem adequately to reflect the Greek meaning.]

For, like a scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven, he wrote with the stylus of preaching upon the hearts of his neighbours what and how great the Lord had narrated in the Scriptures of the peoples, when, among the other miracles of divine power, he brought forth from his treasury things new and old. And because he had diligently inscribed upon the tablet of his heart the decree of both the Old and New Law, he therefore learned day [Col. 0974C] and night from the Scripture of truth how he should hate every way of iniquity. Hence, after he dipped the pen of his heart deeply in the springs of the Saviour, he painted the inner parts of his mind into the image and likeness of God, so as to be transformed into another form by the pen of the scribe who says: “My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe” (Ps. XLIV).

Therefore, since we have now satisfied the foot-soldier multitude concerning the name Eusebius, it is fitting that we should satisfy, as it were, the cavalry concerning the name Sylvester. For just as *eques* (“horseman”) is derived from *equus* (“horse”), and *pedester* (“foot-soldier”) from *pes* (“foot”), so the same man was not inappropriately called Sylvester from *sylva*, “wood.” Who can doubt that this man, instructed in prophetic and evangelical laws, continually grew into a wood of virtues through the foliage of good works? [Col. 0974D] In order that he might not be cut down by the evangelical sickle together with that tree of which it is said, “Every tree which does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. III), he therefore always wished, through the eminence of his merits, to bear the likeness of that tree of which it is written: “There is no bad tree bearing good fruit” (Luke VI). And because, with mind free and flesh captive, he always flourished in the house of God like a fruitful olive, he will therefore possess eternally, for the blossoms of virtues, the type of that palm of which it is written: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree” (Ps. XCII). Since, then, he continually grew through the shoots of good works into, as it were, a wood of virtues—fulfilling in works what he taught in words—he was not undeservedly called Sylvester, as though from *sylva*, while he appeared to be minister of the heavenly word and guardian of divine love. [Col. 0975A]

But just as some things have now been said separately about each name, so both names must now be joined together in summary. Although one seems to differ from the other in word, not in deed, he nevertheless took the greatest care to observe the etymology of both through spiritual practice. He therefore undoubtedly did not deceive himself in any respect, who received both names in this one man. Whoever entertains any doubt on this point is truly seeking a knot in a reed. Since every Roman pontiff even to this day has two names, one from another person and the other his own, it is no wonder if the same man, raised by the efficacious mercy of God to the rank of apostleship, had one name by nature and another by grace. Since he was always exhorting by writings and words for the gathering of sheep and the conversion of God’s people, and was stern in rebuking, therefore, as in his labour of preaching he treated some more gently and others more severely, he was not undeservedly called both Sylvester and Eusebius. [Col. 0975B]

## CHAPTER VIII. How Constantine devoted himself wholly to works of piety in preparation for receiving holy baptism.

Behold: since our discourse has for some time lingered in a level place in explaining the two names, Eusebius and Sylvester, it is fitting that, for a loftier mystery, we now ascend the mountain, as it were, with Jesus, and follow King Constantine in the procession [Col. 0975C] of our reading to the font. For just as no one can worthily seek heavenly things in exchange for earthly unless he first wishes to abandon earthly things for heavenly, so Constantine could in no way reach the font of everlasting life unless he first ascended the mountain with Jesus, as it were, by steps of virtue. Therefore, by Sylvester’s counsel and instruction, he no longer wished to remain in the level place with the secular multitude. For love of God, after the grace of baptism, he ascended Jacob’s ladder more highly with angels ascending, in proportion as before baptism he had more zealously descended that same ladder with angels descending out of compassion for his neighbours.

In order that he might heal the various wounds of his soul by the remedy of repentance, he devoted seven continuous days to works of mercy, so that the less labour weighed upon him day by day in secular matters, the greater rest seemed to stand before him in spiritual concerns. Thus, preparing himself throughout seven days for divine praise, he ordered the churches of Christians to be opened and the temples of idols closed. Wishing also to do good to all and spare all, he freed captives from captivity and released prisoners from prison, so that, rejoicing with him in God for his deliverance, they might rejoice all the more because he dismissed them free from every yoke of servitude, as though in an annual jubilee. Thus, when those tormented by cold, nakedness, hunger, or thirst were freed from every distress and tribulation, it came about that through these varied consolations of heavenly mercy the injury of preceding evil [Col. 0976A] was lightened by the grace of subsequent joy.

Constantine, desiring to erase the ignorance of his former error, began, after the example of Mary the sinner, to wash the Saviour’s feet with tears of repentance. For the washing away of the leprosy of his vices, he strove all the more to draw near to his feet because he no longer wished to stand far off with the ten lepers of the Gospel. Therefore, at the admonition of blessed Sylvester, renouncing all idolatry, he showed the leprosy of sin to that priest according to the Lord’s command, lest he be driven by the various impulses of vices with those ten lepers to whom Truth said, “Go, show yourselves to the priests” (Luke XVII). What more need be said? So long did each use the other’s counsel, so long did each speak with the other as a father with his son, until the son, obedient to the father, deserved to be reconciled to Mother Church. [Col. 0976B]

For just as our Saviour once sought in the Idumaea of this present world the hundredth sheep, having left the ninety-nine sheep of heaven in the wilderness (Luke XV), so blessed Sylvester, grieving that the hundredth sheep had strayed from the Lord’s fold, strove to carry it upon the shoulder of paternal love back to the Church. Lest the grace of heavenly power for that sheep be delayed longer, the acceptable time and day of salvation arrived, in which that hour drew nearer and nearer which was to reward Constantine with worthy recompense for the release of the little children. Therefore, after blessed Sylvester had more fully shown him the discipline of Christian faith, he began to show him medicine for medicine and pool for pool: reformed by prophetic and evangelical institutions, he baptized him in the pool of salvation in place of the pool of blood. [Col. 0976C]

O venerable day and splendid hour, in which an intolerable light penetrated the eyes of all, when divine power, making a covenant with him in ancient love, deigned to restore what had fallen and strengthen what had been broken! O holy and most celebrated day, in which rest was given to his soul and to his body, when in that same font there fell from his body the shameful kind of wandering leprosy, like the scales of great fishes! O bright day, brighter than other days, in which an end and a beginning were bestowed upon two things: when a sound arose in the water like that of a hissing frying-pan, there was given in his heart an end to idolatry and a beginning to faith! For in place of the outward leprosy of his body and the inward offence of his soul, a twofold power of divinity was shown in him: [Col. 0976D] just as the tracks of a serpent are not found upon a rock, so no stain was found in his soul nor leprosy in his body.

## CHAPTER IX. The leprosy of Constantine compared with that of Naaman the Syrian.

But because no one except God can make possible things out of impossible things, or similar things out of dissimilar things, it does no harm if we, conversely, set similar things beside similar things and compare Constantine’s leprosy with that of Naaman the Syrian. Although each was renowned for the worship of idols, each was nevertheless strong and rich, but leprous; for, if we examine their lives attentively, each had leprosy in body and leprosy in mind. Therefore, when one sought the help of Elisha (IV Kings V) and the other the help of God for the salvation of both aspects, it came about that, although one was believed to be healed by God and the other by Elisha, yet both were truly healed by God. [Col. 0977A] For the right hand of the Lord wrought power when it wished to grant both the salvation they desired; yet that same hand bestowed the greater grace on him who was healed inwardly and outwardly in the Saviour’s font.

Therefore, lest we leave untouched how God acted with each of them, it must briefly be stated here in Christ’s name by what power of divinity he aided this one or that. To Naaman the Syrian, the word of the king of Israel was bitter as gall when he saw the king of Israel tear his garments for the sake of his healing. To Constantine, on the contrary, the word of truth seemed sweet as honey when he perceived a prophet in Israel in his salvation. Naaman, setting out toward the shadow of the Old Testament, took with him ten talents of silver; Constantine, penetrating the shadow of the Decalogue by the splendour of the sacrament, preserved in the ark of his heart the remembrance of the weight of silver.
