Naaman took with him ten changes of clothing as a figure of the ten legal commandments; Constantine, carrying with him ten changes of the legal Scriptures, changed them by mystical understanding into the salvation of souls. [Col. 0977B]

Naaman, not yet seeing the glory of God, stood at the door of Elisha’s house to seek healing. Constantine likewise began to stand at the door to seek salvation—at the door of whom the Lord says in the Gospel, “I am the door” (John X). Naaman, never marking himself with the sign of the cross upon his forehead, turned away from Elisha and departed in anger. Constantine, however, marking himself continually with Christ’s sign, did not wish to turn away from God and depart in anger. Naaman, still oppressed with Hagar under the yoke of servitude, was the less willing to rest with Issachar within the boundaries of eternal blessedness because he judged the river Jordan inferior to the rivers of Damascus, Abana and Pharpar. Constantine, however, desired all the more to be healed in body and reborn in mind in the Saviour’s font because he judged it better than Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus. [Col. 0977C]

Naaman, obeying the words of Elisha, servant of God, obeyed his own servants in the Jordanian washing. Constantine, often disobedient to the Son of God, began to obey the counsel of Sylvester, servant of God. Naaman, washed seven times in the river Jordan, was made wholly clean from bodily leprosy. Constantine, immersed three times in the Saviour’s font by the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, was healed outside and within. Naaman was not reborn by water and Spirit because Christ had not yet been glorified; Constantine, reborn by water and Spirit in the washing of regeneration, appeared healed in both body and soul. Naaman returned to the house of the man of God and gave him thanks for the health received. Constantine, long exiled from the house of his heavenly homeland, returned to the house of his father with the prodigal son. Naaman, resisting the divine will with frivolous willfulness, rejected idols for bodily health; Constantine, for the health of his soul [Col. 0978A] and love of the heavenly homeland, brought about in his heart an end of unbelief and the setting of idolatry. Naaman, kindled by a small torch of Jewish faith, seemed to depart in peace from Elisha, the man of God; Constantine, strengthened in the Catholic faith by the aid of the true Elisha, proclaimed peace to those far off and peace to those near.

## CHAPTER X. What the names Naaman and Constantine signify.

Since we have considered morally the comparison of Naaman and Constantine, it remains that the name Naaman be examined separately in the same manner, so that the salvation by which each man was saved may appear to agree with the name. Because Naaman always possessed a manly spirit in the strength of war, he not inappropriately seemed to signify the Gentile people. This is also aptly indicated by the interpretation of his name, for Naaman is interpreted as “their adornment” or “their stirring.” [Col. 0978B] Since he did not wish to serve God without the adornment of virtues, face to face, he stirred the Gentile people toward the worship of the one God (IV Kings V), lest he become like them in the eyes of his inner self, of whom it is written: “You have made us a likeness among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples” (Ps. XLIII). Coming, as it were, with the Gentile people into Judaea, to the house of Elisha, he observed the worship of God according to the Law of Moses, lest in transgressing one commandment he become guilty of all before the eyes of him of whom it is written: “God is known in Judaea” (Ps. LXXV).

But since we have set forth the name Naaman morally, we must proceed by other steps in setting forth Constantine’s name, so that, if it cannot be explained by us allegorically, it may at least be explained historically by a certain likeness. For just as *longinquus* (“distant”) is derived from *longinquitas* (“distance”), and *vicinus* (“neighbouring”) from *vicinitas* (“neighbourhood”), so Constantius comes from Constans, and Constantine is named from Constantius, thus displaying in himself the steadfastness of his father and grandfather, one of whom was called Constantius and the other Constans. [Col. 0978C] He possessed from both Constantius and Constans such great constancy that his shield in war never turned back but remained before him; the assault of hostile fear was so completely wiped from his mind that his spear in battle never seemed turned aside. Therefore, although Constantius is derived from Constans and Constantine from Constantius by the same formation through which *humanus* is derived from *humanitas* and *divinus* from *divinitas*, Constantine was nevertheless wont to labour more abundantly for the Church of God than either Constans or Constantius before him had ever laboured.

After receiving health, he began with Naaman to worship the same God whom Abraham appeared formerly to have worshipped (Gen. XVIII). Abraham foreshadowed for us faith in the holy Trinity when, as though beneath the tree of the cross, he saw three and worshipped one. Yet one received a purity of greater grace than the other: Naaman followed the shadow, Constantine the truth; for, as is evident and plain to all, Naaman followed straw, Constantine grain. [Col. 0978D] It is therefore no wonder that greater grace than had once befallen Naaman the Syrian under the shadow of the Law was bestowed upon this most blessed man through the grace of truth. For as Naaman, washed seven times, returned from paganism to Judaism, so Constantine, reborn by the sevenfold Spirit, came to baptism. Although one was washed unwillingly and the other willingly, one was healed in the Jordan and the other in the font. Although, through the Spirit of God dwelling in their hearts, the former followed the killing letter and the latter the life-giving Spirit (II Cor. III), nevertheless each deserved, after experiencing the benefits of healing, to attain the grace of the Creator. But just as in these two matters—the shadow of the Law and the grace of truth—they were unequal, so in these two ways they appeared equal: just as through the one the Lord gave salvation to Syria, so through the other he gave salvation [Col. 0979A] to the Church.

## CHAPTER XI. The difference between Constantine and the leprous Gehazi.

Therefore, since we have spoken sufficiently thus far to your charity, most beloved, about the typological healing of this man, it is time now to pass from these matters to the rest, and once again to bring forth things new and old for the expression of other subjects. Accordingly, that another leper near at hand may be found by us to take Naaman’s place, and may be suitably compared with the same Constantine on account of bodily infirmity, nothing prevents us, as we descend in the scale of the Church from a higher rank to a humbler one, from still comparing that most illustrious man with a lesser man. But who can that leper be except Gehazi, who by deceit and force extorted his money from the aforesaid Naaman (IV Kings 5), when, not in his own name but in Elisha’s, he carried away double gifts from that man? It is therefore fitting that, just as mercy was once joined to severity in Moses’ breast, so now we compare Constantine’s mercy with Gehazi’s malice; for, just as Gehazi fell into infirmity through cupidity and avarice, so Constantine deserved to receive healing through mercy and justice.

For Gehazi received from Naaman two talents of silver without the gain of the divine sacrament. Constantine, however, likewise receiving two talents from God, bore them truly to Elisha together with the gain of a good work. Gehazi, unwilling eternally to enjoy the heavenly reward, hid his master’s money without reckoning; Constantine, however, in order to increase his Lord’s money, desired that he himself and all that was his should be held in common for God and humankind. Gehazi, on account of the two changes of garments which he had received, was struck by Elisha, the man of God, with the plague of Naaman’s leprosy; Constantine, however, freed from the plague of elephantine leprosy, was clothed by God with the twofold garment of immortality and innocence. Gehazi deceived himself through cupidity and avarice when he enclosed the double gifts in two bags; Constantine, however, refused to enclose his money in the malice of that old bag, concerning which it is written: “You have torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness” (Ps. 49 [Vulgate numbering]).

Gehazi, swollen against his fellow-servants and proud toward the humble, refused to obey his lord as a servant; Constantine, however, humble toward the humble and proud toward the proud, ruled servants as a lord and obeyed the Lord as a servant. Gehazi also, forgetful of the Lord his Creator, contrary to the precept of the Law coveted his neighbour’s possession; Constantine, however, contrary to neither the Lord’s precept nor Moses’ Law, refused with Gehazi to covet his neighbour’s possession. Gehazi likewise, because of the iniquity of his cupidity, did not bear the type of those of whom it is written: “From usury and iniquity he shall redeem their souls” (Ps. 71); Constantine, however, deserved to bear the figure of that righteous man who “did not give his money at usury” for earthly gain (Ps. 14). Gehazi refused to avoid those gatherings of deceivers of which it is written: “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4). Constantine, however, observed toward his neighbour that saying of the Wise Man in which it is said: “Do not love falsehood against your brother” (Ecclus. 7).

Gehazi, not possessing the Creator’s faith perfectly like Abraham, was not undeservedly struck with Naaman’s leprosy. Constantine, however, possessing faith in Christ, refused to let that leprosy cling to him concerning which Elisha said to Gehazi: “Naaman’s leprosy shall cling to you” (IV Kings 5). Gehazi, blackened like pitch by the darkness of vices, went out from Elisha leprous as snow; Constantine, whitened as snow from the blackness of his sins, refused any longer to be blackened like pitch by the darkness of idolatry.

But since Gehazi went farther from himself down the precipices of vices into the valley of cupidity, when he seized from Naaman’s goods whatever he saw that pleased him, it is not surprising that the reward he received is signified by the interpretation of his very name. For *Gehazi* is interpreted “seeing a precipice,” or “vision of a valley.” Since he refused spiritually to dwell with the ibexes upon inaccessible cliffs and precipitous rocks, as though upon mountains of virtues, he was therefore, raging against virtues and smiling upon vices, not inappropriately called “seeing a precipice.” And because he refused to ascend from the valley of vices to the mountain of virtues, he was not undeservedly called “vision of a valley,” since he did not set in his heart those ascents by the steps of good works, “in the valley of tears, in the place which he appointed” (Ps. 83). Therefore, since the path of justice was so rarely seen by him upon the mountain of virtues that his name was deservedly called “vision of a valley,” it is not surprising that, because of the leprosy of his vices and far removed from the salvation of believers, he cannot “see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26).

But since we have lingered long in comparing Gehazi and Constantine, comparing the impiety of the one with the piety of the other, it remains that, just as for their consideration we have drawn out a long thread in this discourse, so now we should turn again the stylus of our speech from Gehazi to Constantine. For, lest this same Constantine should be struck further with bodily leprosy together with Gehazi, he began spiritually to observe Moses’ Law—although after the grace of baptism the Jews began greatly to reproach him for this, because he sought so often the mercy of the true Elisha. For when, through the admonitions of blessed Sylvester, he had not only been freed from the bonds of idolatry but had also been washed in the laver of divine regeneration, he enclosed in his heart the love of heavenly charity all the more perfectly, inasmuch as perfect charity casts out fear (I John 4). And rightly indeed did he love God with the love of inward affection, for God was “his helper in due seasons, in tribulation” (Ps. 9), while he deserved to be raised by the remedy of a twofold grace from the twofold infirmity of body and soul: when in the laver of regeneration he received these two medicines of healing, so that he might be cleansed in body from leprosy and in soul from vices.

[Col. 0981]

# The Distinguished Little Book of Abbot Berengos on the Mystery of the Lord’s Wood and on the Visible and Invisible Light by Which the Ancient Fathers Once Deserved to Be Enlightened

*(Bibliotheca Patrum XII, 366.)*

[Col. 0981B] Since the first man, beloved brethren, because of the food of cupidity which he unlawfully ate (Gen. 3), once sat for a very long time in darkness and in the shadow of death, it was necessary that the only-begotten Son of God should intervene so worthily on his behalf as to open for him a path to the way of eternal light. For long it was that, having lost the light of truth, he was not unjustly hemmed in by the abyss of ancient blindness, because by his voluntary will he separated himself from the divine light when, against the Lord’s command, he loved the darkness of wrongful action. But because he could return from darkness to light in no way unless our Saviour himself should be willing to open the way for him, therefore, in order to show him the brightness of most loving light, he became obedient for us to the Father unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2).

Therefore thanks be to God: while the Son obeys the Father, the blind man of the Gospel returns to light, so that the human race is now assailed less by the inclination of its former blindness, since through Christ’s blood it is daily illumined by the sight of heavenly light. Otherwise it shall not behold that lovable light of which it is written: “The people who walked in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. 9), unless through the fruit of good work it deserves to be joined to the choirs of those concerning whom it follows: “For those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light has arisen” (ibid.).

This, then, is that light of which the first man deserved to be deprived when guilt assailed him and grace deserted him. For, while upon the tree of death he impressed upon himself more deeply the delight of sin, divine power took one light away from him and granted another. He himself who is “the faithful witness in heaven” (Rev. 1) assigned him one light on earth and another in heaven; for, when at the very creation of the world he distributed his gifts to every creature as was fitting, he gave one light to humankind and promised another. But since, from the one light which is promised, we are able to be the more secure because we daily see with bodily eyes the other which was given, it is fitting that for the sake of the light promised we imitate in all things the actions of those of whom it is written: “They worked righteousness; they obtained promises” (Heb. 11).

For since one light is earthly and the other heavenly, it is fitting that we always pursue the heavenly light with honourable conduct; so that, just as through the tree of death we are earthly from the earth, so through the tree of life we are heavenly and from heaven. Otherwise we can by no means behold that visible light which we must someday see, not with bodily but with spiritual eyes, unless we are first instructed on earth by this visible light, so that we may know what and of what sort is that light reserved for us in heaven.

[Col. 0982B] Therefore, since mention has here been made by us of temporal and eternal light, we ought not to pass their differences over in silence; for the pearl of perpetual light is to be acquired by us at the greater price in proportion as the distinction between this light and that appears great. For just as prosperity differs from adversity and joy from sorrow, so one light is shown to be distinct from another—especially since the one appears so unequal to the other that one is eternal and the other temporal. Yet, although unquenchable waters cannot extinguish either light, there is great diversity in them both; because, as the page of sacred Scripture testifies, one illumines and is illumined, while the other illumines and is not illumined.

For if we consider carefully the brightness of both, we are undoubtedly illumined by the one in body and by the other in mind. Such is the power of the light which comes from divine splendour that it cannot be comprehended by bodily eyes but only by the gaze of the mind. Therefore, if we are accustomed to marvel as we gaze upon this temporal light, by which not hearts but bodies appear illumined, believers ought much more to marvel at that eternal light through which both their bodies and their minds are illumined. Moreover, if peoples marvel at the visible light of sun and moon, because of whose intolerable brightness human eyes are very often dazzled, much more should that hidden light of the angels be marvelled at, which cannot be grasped by hearing of the ears or sight of the eyes.

[Col. 0983A] And behold: since here a fitting occasion presents itself for us to say something, among other stars, about the sun and moon, it is fitting that, with the course of the reading, we hasten eagerly forth to consider these very luminaries, concerning which the Lord said: “Let lights be made in the firmament of heaven.” He spoke, and they were made (Gen. 1). For after the first command of the Lord’s voice, each appeared to have been placed in its own order, so that, as ancient divinity had once ordained, each always rises and sets in its own place and time.

For it must be known that, just as on the first day the skin of heaven was stretched out, so on the fourth day it was clothed with stars. Thus I could, if I wished, compare this skin with that heaven concerning which it is written: “Stretching out heaven like a skin” (Ps. 103). Yet although different stars are still fixed in that same heaven or skin, the sun and moon appear to rule the other stars all the more because they can not inappropriately be compared with Christ and the Church. For just as in the firmament of heaven no created star seems more outstanding in brightness than those two luminaries, so in the firmament of the Church no two persons can be more exalted than these—although, just as “star differs from star in brightness” (I Cor. 15), Christ excels the Church in heavenly dignity.

Therefore it should be noted that, just as in the creation of the world a new world shone forth with new light, so in his Passion Christ joined the Church to himself by the ray of a new brightness, so that, in the outward affection of twofold charity, through the mystery of the cross each now delights in the sight of the other. For he who once rejoiced “as a giant to run the way” of his Passion (Ps. 18), upon the altar of the cross deigned typologically to join the chariots of sun and moon—that is, bridegroom and bride—signifying to us that those are truly believed to possess faith in Christ and the Church who are guided in Christ Jesus by the chariot of twofold love.

For this purpose the Sun of righteousness “placed his tabernacle in the sun” (ibid.), when for human salvation he was conceived from female offspring; so that you too, O human being, may rejoice all the more in God your Saviour, because God went forth for you “as a bridegroom from his chamber” (ibid.). We must therefore know that, if we compare this visible sun with the invisible Sun, we by no means rule in this prophetic utterance which, revealing the invisible Sun to human knowledge, says: “For those who fear God the Sun of righteousness shall arise” (Mal. 4).

But in the course of the moon, which is accustomed to illumine us thirteen times in the year, this especially ought to be considered: that none of us, by the various changes of his mind, should imitate the foolishness of him of whom it is written, “A fool changes like the moon” (Ecclus. 27). For after the Sun of righteousness, through the fire of divine charity, willed to illumine the moon-like loss arising from the dissension of angels and humankind, he immediately shone everywhere upon human minds, through apostolic preaching, with the full moon of new faith and ancient love, so that they might follow to faith in Christ the teaching of those of whom it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. 18).

[Col. 0984A] For you know that, as divine Scripture testifies (Acts 4), apostolic teaching was prefigured for us by sun and moon, provided only that we have one heart and one soul after their example, whose teaching shines in the Church like sun and moon. Therefore it is necessary, O Christian, that you consider more carefully within yourself how these two luminaries are distinguished by days and nights, years and months; for Christ and the Church will likewise be for us signs, seasons, days, and years, in order to irradiate and enlighten the souls of believers. Since sun and moon bear the type of Christ and the Church, they will deservedly continue to be for us signs, seasons, days, and years; for as sun and moon daily shine upon us outwardly with their brightness, so Christ and the Church always shine in our hearts with inward light.

For it must be known that, just as on the first day of the world God created heaven and earth (Gen. 1), so on the fourth day he willed to give us heavenly light, when, to illumine the shadows of three-day darkness and the newly formed clouds, he deigned on the fourth day to bring forth sun, moon, and stars (Gen. 3).. Therefore, although the brightness of the sun is one thing, that of the moon another, and that of the stars another, it is fitting nonetheless that we draw the brightness of all to the salvation of souls, so that, while the breath of eternal light blows upon us, our bodies and souls may be illumined by both lights.

[Col. 0984C] It is fitting indeed that, for our bodies and souls now illumined by eternal light, we should always give unceasing thanks to God. For just as by the word of divinity he once brought forth sun and moon on the fourth day in the firmament of heaven, so in the firmament of the Church the bridegroom shone upon the bride with a ray of new brightness, when the same one, God and man, offered his human limbs to be crucified for us—he through whom, of old, “there was evening and there was morning, the fourth day.”

Therefore, just as yesterday we treated of sun, moon, and stars, so today we ought to contemplate temporal and eternal light with the greatest care, especially since in so great a miracle we ought to acknowledge the Creator in respect of both lights: wonderful in one, if more wonderful in the other. For one illumines earthly things only, not heavenly, while the other is confined neither by heaven nor earth. Therefore, if anyone wishes to weigh more closely the quality of both, one is wonderful and the other more wonderful. Hence, if this visible heaven, which seems stretched out like a skin and through which we are daily illumined by sun, moon, and stars, is to be marvelled at, much more is that heavenly Light to be marvelled at through which heaven and earth are illumined in angels and human beings.

[Col. 0984D] For this is that light through which we, who are children of light and children of God, must someday behold the brightness of God—provided that he now illumines in us “the hidden things of darkness,” he who will hereafter illumine us by the vision of holy souls. And because, to make known to us the truth of perpetual light, he willed to grant us the shadow-like brightness of this temporal light, it is fitting that, while we live in this light, we should always strive through good works for that other light, so that, when we depart from this life, we may be able to attain eternal light.

For it must be known that, just as one light is small and the other great, so one is needy and the other generous. For the generous one abounds and overabounds in every good thing, since from what it possesses it gives to all. Therefore, since the relation between these two lights is such that what is not possessed in one is found in the other, it is necessary that by this light which we already possess in reality we hasten toward the other, which we still await in hope. It must indeed be known that although in one way we are illumined by the other, and in another by this one, we ought nonetheless to hope for both from Christ; for he from whom we have one light temporally possesses the other eternally with the Father and the Spirit.

[Col. 0985B] For just as in the three persons there is, according to the nature of divinity, one Godhead, so in them there are not three lights but one light. Yet this light is accustomed to shine more than other lights inasmuch as it illumines human beings and is not illumined by human beings. Therefore, although there is nothing which we can worthily compare to that light, we ought nonetheless to compare certain figures to it in some manner, so that through these enigmas of things it may more easily be understood that the Light of lights and Day of days is unlike this visible light.

For the same disparity, if it may be said, exists in this twofold light which is manifested in male and female, especially since the lesser is subjected to the greater in the same way, I think, as a wife seems not greater than her husband but lesser. Moreover, just as the greatest differs from the least, as the large differs from the small, so this light seems to differ from that; for although both seem to shine upon us from Christ, a greater grace is accustomed to come to us from that than from this. For it must be known that, as spiritual things differ from carnal and heavenly things from lower, so this temporal light differs from eternal light—especially since heavenly things do not agree with earthly, nor highest things with lowest, in the same way that first things do not agree with last, nor last with first.

[Col. 0985D] Again, one light differs from another in the same way as spirit from letter or grain from chaff, lest we too, after the manner of the Jews, receive the grace of God in vain, in following spirit in place of letter and grain in place of chaff. For it is certain that, just as Christians follow the grain and Jews the chaff in knowing the one Law and the other, so each Law speaks to one people and is silent to the other: for one is blind and the other sees in beholding the Creator’s light.

It must surely be believed that, just as the light of the elect is not extinguished by temptation but is made brighter, so the blindness of the Jews is shown to endure until the evening of the ageing world, so that Christians and Jews may know themselves to be the two peoples of whom it is written: “That those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9). For just as Christians to this day bear the type of those of whom it is said, “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20), so the Jews go with those blind men of the Gospel into the precipice, of whom it is written: “If a blind man offers guidance to a blind man, both fall into a pit” (Matt. 15).

[Col. 0986A] Christians always smile upon those blind men of whom it is written, “The blind see” (Matt. 11); thus Jews shall remain like those blind men until the wrath of consummation, of whom it is said: “They have eyes and shall not see” (Ps. 113). Since Jews are not joined to Christians, nor Christians to Jews, the light of truth has therefore been given to us and taken away from them—although they too must someday worship Father and Son with us, fulfilling what is said: “That they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent” (John 2).. But it must be known that, although Christians understand one thing and Jews another in the mystery of the cross, nevertheless all have sinned and need the glory of God; so that all must be justified freely by his grace, by whom the impious is to be justified and the pious glorified.

Therefore we must pray that the true light, “which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 17)., may deign so to enlighten the depths of the Jewish heart that they too may deserve to be suffused with us by that same light of which it is written: “I am the light of the world” (John 9)..

[Col. 0986B] This, then, is that light through which the Son of God, drawing all things with himself upon the altar of the cross, enlightened that blind man of the Gospel, who, sitting beside the way of faith and earnestly imploring the glory of God, said: “Son of David, have mercy on me” (Matt. 10; Luke 18). For this purpose the grain of wheat willed to be put to death by the death of the cross: so that heavenly light might shine upon every believer, by which, as is known to all and plain to all, he enlightened the human race in that same blind man.

For God divided his light in a twofold way when he restored two lights to that blind man who had lost two. For, if we consider carefully the twofold grace of his healing, through the mystery of the cross he received light in body and light in mind. Therefore, if we wish with that same blind man to obtain the grace of eternal light, concerning which the Lord said to him, “What do you wish me to do for you?” (Luke 18), it is fitting that each of us frequently say with him this brief prayer which he answered, saying: “Lord, that I may see” (ibid.).

Otherwise the crowds of thoughts, which take from us the seedbeds of good will, stifle together with that blind man the voice of our entreaty, unless by continual prayers we drive away from the eyes of our hearts the phantasms of the vices which we have committed. Moreover, in that this blind man sat beside the way and not upon the way, he furnished us an example of faith still imperfect, so that each of us, by mortification of the flesh, may always afflict his heart in such a way as to plant his step in the truth of good work.

[Col. 0986D] But this cannot happen unless the dawn of new light dispels from our eyes that night which the lingering hour of original sin had brought upon us, so that, when the whole darkness of blindness in us has been dissolved, the beauty of the ancient origin may be refashioned into new light. Otherwise it profits us nothing that Jesus repaired lost light in that blind man, when, passing by, he heard the cry of his blindness and, standing still, enlightened him—unless he who alone beholds hearts and reins deigns in the same way, by passing by, to hear our blindness and, by standing still, to enlighten it.

For he who in his humanity has to pass by and in his divinity to stand still deigned in a wonderful manner to enlighten that blind man, when he added the very voice of the man’s faith in these words: “Go; your faith has made you well” (ibid.). Therefore, since we, beloved brethren, are now oppressed by so great a blindness that we are not only blind for a time but blind from birth, we must pray that he may offer himself to us as guide toward the brightness of perpetual light—the one from whom that blind man wished to request not gold but light.

[Col. 0987B] For if the same light of divinity illumines our hearts—a light which neither beginning extends nor end confines—it is necessary that we never be restrained, by any threats of passing demons, from seeking that light, whose faith is the beginning and whose operation is the end. And because it accords neither with human salvation nor divine praise that we should seek a light which can either end in time or be confined in place, it is fitting that we seek without ceasing that light which we may have in common, not with beasts, but with angels.

This is the eternal light which willed to join heavenly things to lowly, when, rich in the grace of divine compassion, through the mystery of the cross it made angels and human beings fellow citizens. This is that light on account of which, that causes may correspond with causes and things with things, we must introduce here certain ancient Fathers, so that our discourse may more fittingly fly to its end through what remains, since invisible light brings forth from its treasury things new and old for us.

[Col. 0987C] For since the light of divinity is proved so marvellous and holy that none at all seems like it or so great, it is fitting that human praise should not be lacking to it, for it is accustomed to have prophetic and evangelical testimony. But since the love of twofold charity is assigned to two persons, it is fitting in this reading that women be joined to men and men to women. For it is just that the eternal Law should have testimony from the male and female sex, since in the mystery of the cross it willed to free both from diabolical dominion. And rightly indeed should eternal light receive glory from men and women, since it willed to perpetuate its memory in both sexes: those whom the Creator’s power once formed for life, the light of divinity illumined for grace.

Therefore, since here we wish to treat of the affairs of the ancient Fathers, it is fitting that we strive to invite eternal light into the little ship of our mind, because we must now apply ourselves more zealously to the oars of the holy Scriptures, inasmuch as we must toss for several days upon the sea of the book of Genesis. Since we have now entered in mind this great and spacious sea, it is necessary that we be endangered neither by empty thoughts nor vain words, nor that the shoulder of our heart be weighed down by those creeping things of vices of which it is said: “There are creeping things without number” (Ps. 102).

[Col. 0988A] Thus, with all heresies and heresiarchs driven from that same ship, we must first treat of the righteous, then of kings and patriarchs. Yet before we pass from patriarchs to prophets, we appear to have not one or two but many stages; and therefore it is necessary that he who once deigned to show the royal way to patriarchs and prophets may also deign to extend his right hand to us on this journey. For the little ship of our mind is then truly steered by the divine right hand if it is strengthened within and without by the bitumen of charity.

But since we seem now to linger in vain in the ship of the Church unless, together with the ancient Fathers, we deserve to be illumined by divine light, we must pray in this treatise that he may will to reveal himself to us as guide—he who said of himself to his disciples: “While you have the light, believe in the light” (John 12).

This, then, is that light which made Adam, our first parent and prototype, pious from impious and chaste from incestuous upon the altar of the cross, when through the saving effect of its mystery it restored in him the vision of ancient brightness. This is that light through which, on the very day of the Lord’s Passion, Eve’s curse was changed into Mary’s blessing, when, in order to purchase for us the pearl of perpetual light, through the mystery of the cross punishment passed into glory and death into life.

[Col. 0988B] This is that light through which the Lord God of Israel once willed to illumine Abel, when, as the outstanding lawgiver testifies, “the Lord looked upon Abel and upon his gifts” (Gen. 4). This is that light which shone upon Noah—whose name is interpreted “rest”—when he constructed an ark from incorruptible woods as a type of the Church, setting before us the sign of saving baptism and of the Lord’s cross, since by the wood he saved himself and his own.

This is that light by which Noah was figuratively illumined when the dove brought him an olive branch, typologically signifying that no one is able to fly upward from the depths to the heights upon the wings of virtues unless he strives, with the dove, to bring back to the ark of the Church the branch of good work. This is that light by which Noah was illumined when he became drunk on the wine which he himself had planted, signifying that the cup of the Lord’s Passion is sweet to believers and bitter to Jews; concerning it the prophetic utterance says: “My cup, which intoxicates me—how splendid it is!” (Ps. 22).

[Col. 0988D] This is that light through which Shem and Japheth deserved to be illumined when, approaching from the opposite direction, they covered their father’s genitals, signifying that we in like manner should present our face to virtues and our back to vices, just as they walked backward to cover their father’s shame. This is that light which once shone upon the mind of Melchizedek the priest when he offered bread and wine to Abraham returning from slaughter (Gen. 14), foreshadowing for us that sacrifice of the priest of the Most High, concerning which the Bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “Eat; become drunk, my dearest ones” (Song 5).

This is that light through which the Lord God Sabaoth once deigned to illumine Lot when, fleeing burning Sodom as carnal concupiscence (Gen. 19), he saved body and mind in the little city of Zoar. This is that light which divinely illumined Abraham when, according to the Lord’s command, he went out from Aram, where this abundant blessing was given to him by the Lord: “I shall bless those who bless you, and curse those who curse you” (Gen.).

[Col. 0989A] This is that light which also shone upon the eye of the inward man when he aided Lot, his brother, and Lot’s women and people, when, by the help of the holy Trinity, he had been refined by the strength of his adversaries as in the fire of tribulation.

> [Note: Col. 0989D: Something seems to be missing.]

This is that light which gave the same Abraham a share of its own light when, at sunset, he drove birds away from the Lord’s sacrifice, signifying that no one can drive away the birds of demons from the sacrifice of prayer unless he has first driven from the eyes of his heart the phantasms of vices.

[Col. 0989B] This is that light which divinely illumined him in the valley of Mamre when, beneath the tree of the cross, he saw three and adored one—illumined, that is, with such brightness of divine light that he adored as one in majesty him whom he knew to be three in persons. This is that light which also shone upon him elsewhere, when the Lord said to him: “Offer me your son upon one of the mountains which I shall show you”; thereby setting before us diverse signs of the Lord’s Passion and cross, when in the same mysteries he bound the son and the wood together.

This is that light through which Isaac, Abraham’s son, was illumined when Sarah and Hagar quarrelled with one another; for, in the figure of the Saviour, he was accustomed to live so honourably in his father’s house that the son of the slave woman could not become heir together with the son of the free woman. This is that light which showed us a pattern of humility when Rebecca, seeing Isaac, descended from the camel (Gen. 24), typologically signifying that ancient Gentile society abandoned the structure of all idolatry when, as though through a vision in the Lord’s Passion, it deserved to recognize the feather [perhaps *palmam*, “palm/victory,” rather than printed *plumam*, “feather”] of faith.

[Col. 0989C] This is that light which divinely shone upon Isaac at the time when, loving Rebecca his wife, he brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother (ibid.); through this, that entrance is set before us in figure concerning which the Church says in the Song of Songs: “The king brought me into his storerooms” (Song 1). This is that light which guided Isaac by the governance of heavenly discipline when he loved Rebecca his wife with exceeding love (Gen. 24), signifying that the only-begotten Son of God loved the Church exceedingly, when he assuaged the grief which had come upon him from the death of his mother, the Synagogue.

[Col. 0989D] This is that light which heavenlyly illumined Isaac and Rebecca when, in the figure of Christ and the Church, it joined each to the other in mutual charity, so that the Church may know herself to be joined to Christ with such love (ibid.) that, because of love for him, she may never become another’s wife.

This is that light by which Isaac himself deserved to be illumined from heaven, when our Savior chose to be sacrificed for him, as though a ram. And when he was caught by the horns of the cross amid the thorns of our sins, he restored to us the eternity of everlasting light. [Col. 0990A]

This is that light which, in that same Isaac, made manifest to us the Son of Mary, when he went out to meditate in the field as the day was already declining (Gen. XXIV): signifying, namely, that the only-begotten Son of God walked, as if to meditate, in the field of this world, when through nails, spear, and cross he hastened even unto death.

This is that light which chose also to illumine Isaac in another way, when he himself deserved to carry the wood for the burnt offering: mystically intimating to us that, just as he bore the wood for the sacrifice, so Christ carried his own cross in that very Passion (Matt. XXIV; Mark XV; Luke XXIII; John XIX).

This is that light which, in that ass, set before us the chaos of Jewish blindness, concerning which it is written: “Wait here [Col. 0990B] with the ass, until we return to you” (Gen. XXII); mystically indicating that the Jews, who have not yet experienced faith in the Holy Trinity, must return near the end of the age with the pledge of faith.

This is that light which, by the fact that the ram was sacrificed and Isaac escaped, took care to irradiate us with a twofold mystery: typically suggesting to us that, although Jesus endured diverse mockeries in his Passion, he nevertheless suffered in his humanity and remained unharmed in his divinity.

This is that light which shone from heaven upon Jacob under the type of the gentile people (Gen. XXVII), when his mother’s grace first introduced him to his father’s blessing, so that this younger brother might render greater thanks to the Creator, since even today the elder ought to serve the younger.

This is that light through which Jacob himself [Col. 0990C] saw the Lord in a dream, when, journeying from Beer-sheba to Aram, he slept on the road (Gen. XXVIII): mystically indicating that the light of divinity shines upon no one at all unless, in passing through this world, he rests from every carnal desire.

This is that light which there still illumined Jacob by divine power, when in the ladder of the Church it showed him in a vision angels ascending and descending (Gen. XXIX), intimating to us by the descent that one must love one’s neighbor, and by the ascent that one must love God.

This is that light through which Jacob seemed also to be illumined in another manner, when, in order to water the sheep, he removed the stone by which the well was closed; signifying, namely, that the true Jacob deigned to open for us at the altar of the cross the well of truth, so that we might be refreshed from the well of the Lord’s [Col. 0990D] blood by the water of charity.

This is that light through which Jacob knew that Rachel would become his wife, when, after watering her flock, he began to kiss her as his own; typically suggesting that, after the outpouring of his blood, the Church ought to enjoy eternally with Christ that kiss of charity. Concerning the bride in the Song of Songs: “Let my beloved,” she says, “kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Cant. I).

This is that light by which Jacob, being illumined, placed rods in the water-channels (Gen. L), so that, according to their varied appearance, the offspring of his sheep might become varied: typically intimating to us that in the channels of our hearts we cannot prepare a temple worthy of God [Col. 0991A] unless, for conceiving a diversity of virtues, we always take examples from good things.

This is that light through which we too have the lives of the Fathers as examples for the illumination of our minds; through these, once the bark of the Law has been removed and the whiteness of grace received, we ought to bring forth the offspring of good work—if you, almighty God, deign to make us fruitful in your virtues among those fertile sheep, of whom it is said: “Their sheep, fruitful and abundant in their goings forth” (Ps. CXLIII).

This is that light which shone upon Jacob in two ways, when he first took Leah and then Rachel as wife: thereby intimating to us that saving mystery of which the Apostle says, “Not first that which is spiritual, but that which is natural” (I Cor. XV).

This is that light by which Jacob, [Col. 0991B] being illumined, made a separation between flock and flock corresponding to that same distinction, which is seen even today between Law and Law, so that the whole assembly of the faithful may not fail to know what the new Law says through the saving mystery, or what the old.

This is that light which still illumined the vision of his inward eye, when, carried beyond himself, he saw the Lord face to face; although he never saw him in his divinity, as John testifies when he says: “No one has ever seen God” (I John IV).

This is that light which illumined Jacob at Bethel, where, after changing the name Jacob, he called him Israel: mystically indicating that only with spiritual eyes ought we to see that true Nazarite, through whom Jacob himself was called Israel—that is, “one seeing [Col. 0991C] God.”

This is that light through which Rachel, whose name means “sheep,” deserved to be illumined, when, sitting down, she concealed Laban’s idols which she had secretly taken; mystically teaching that we ought to cover the idols of vices with the garment of good works and confession of sins.

This is that light which, through understanding the saving mystery, illumined the appearance of Leah and Rachel: especially since Leah’s weak eyes and Rachel’s beauty intimate this to us, that with one we labor on earth and with the other rest in heaven.

This is that light which illumined Martha and Leah in one way, Rachel and Mary in another: so that we too may labor in this life, together with Martha and Leah, with such diligence in the Creator’s abundant service, that in the other life we may enjoy divine contemplation [Col. 0991D] together with Rachel and Mary.

This is that light through which, in Judah, whose name is interpreted “confession,” the profession of the Christian religion has been illumined: because we, the Church of Christ, shall always confess God by good works, concerning whom it is written: “Whoever shall confess me before men, him will I also confess before my Father” (Matt. X).

This is that light which wished to illumine Judah, who came to shear the sheep, as a type of the Savior, who chose to be bloodied by five wounds at the altar of the cross so that he might strip the sheep of his pasture of the fleeces of their sins.

This is that light which afforded Judah access to the spiritual marriage with Tamar, who, having laid aside the clothing of widowhood, changed both her name and her attire—signifying, namely, that Judah who, at the altar of the cross, sought [Col. 0992A] the hundredth sheep, and from a harlot made a bride and from the Synagogue made the Church.

This is that light through which Judah gave the same Tamar a ring, staff, and bracelet, which were tokens of a pledge, as a pledge of calling, justification, and glorification, when Christ united the Church to his body at the altar of the cross by this threefold pledge, of which it is written: “Those whom he called, them he also justified; and those whom he justified, them he also glorified” (Rom. VIII).

This is that light through which heavenly grace smiled upon Perez, whose name means “division,” when it separated him, as a type of the gentile people, from Jewish unbelief, so that he too might receive among others those divisions of ministries of which it is written: “To some, kinds of tongues; to others, interpretation of utterances” (I Cor. XII).

This is that light which shone upon Zerah, who is called “rising,” more than was necessary, when he who ought first to have arisen first put forth his hand; thereby setting before us, in a figure, the Jewish people, who as it were offered a hand when it showed itself ready to fulfill the Creator’s commandments.

This is that light which briefly illumined that same Zerah, when his midwife vainly bound upon him the scarlet of the Lord’s Passion and cross; for, when he refused to receive the mystery of faith which was offered to him in the scarlet, he immediately withdrew the hand which he had put forth toward faith. [Col. 0992B]

This is that light which partly darkened his eyes, when he raised his hand as though toward faith and withdrew it to unbelief; signifying, namely, those who stretched bloodstained hands against him through the death of the cross, concerning whom it is written: “He came unto his own, and his own did not receive him” (John I).

This is that light which also shows the light of its charity to everyone who does not stretch out his hand to iniquity: namely, to one who always follows him in good works, who will stretch out his hand in recompense at the reward of the saints.

This is that light which shines upon each of us every day, if we do not stretch our hands out to iniquity but withdraw them from iniquity, because the Savior showed this example in himself: at the recompense of the righteous he draws back his hand for the reprobate and stretches it forth for the righteous.

This is that light which once wished to illumine Joseph through a dream, when he saw his sheaf adored by the sheaves of his brothers, signifying, namely, [Col. 0992D] that he ought always to be adored by us with sheaves of good works, who after his resurrection openly chose to appear to his disciples.

This is that light through which Joseph himself deserved to be illumined in another way, when he saw himself adored by the sun, moon, and stars: designating, namely, him whom the whole Church of saints ought to adore in the sun, moon, and stars, by which the brightness of the righteous is figured.

This is that light which illumined Joseph with this singular grace, that alone among his brothers he wore a long robe: mystically instructing us that he shall possess eternally the reward of good work, concerning whom it is written: “He who endures to the end, he shall be saved” (Matt. X).

This is that light through which Joseph, illumined, began to provide for his own salvation when he gave his cloak to the adulteress who wished to use it wickedly: typically suggesting that the covering of the letter of the Law, from which the Jews derive no profit, ought through the light of divinity to be transparent to us. [Col. 0993A]

This is that light through which a twofold fruit of shining grace shone forth in Joseph, when alone he was sent into prison and alone brought out from it; thereby figuring for us the resurrection of him who, rising from the dead, most powerfully freed his own from the prison of hell.

This is that light which breathed into Joseph so great a knowledge of inward brightness that his tongue spoke wisdom among princes, when in Pharaoh’s house his servants served him in the basket.

This is that light which turned his back away from burdens, when the splendor of that same divine light splendidly irradiated his heart, lest in Egypt he should be burdened by the tribulation of carnal riches, concerning which it is written: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. LXI). [Col. 0993B]

This is that light which illumined Joseph by divine laws when throughout all Egypt he assigned a fifth part of the crops to the kings: signifying, namely, that he who commanded the firstborn of a man to be redeemed with five silver shekels redeemed through the mystery of the cross the guarding of our five senses by his five wounds.

This is that light through which Joseph himself deserved to be illumined when, for the distribution of grain, he opened the king’s granaries: typically indicating that every prelate over the Lord’s household must have such care as to give them, in due season, a measure of spiritual wheat.

This is that light which sat spiritually within his inward eyes when he gave three hundred silver pieces to Benjamin his brother, so that you, most beloved brethren, ought to understand in those silver pieces nothing else than the mystery of the cross and faith in the Holy Trinity. [Col. 0993C]

This is that light which, through the number three hundred contained in the letter Tau, daily shows us the figure of the cross in the image of Jesus, signifying, namely, that our heart ought to be fixed upon the Lord all the more deeply because we ought to know nothing except Christ Jesus, and him crucified.

This is that light which shone unequally upon those two men whom Pharaoh brought unequally out of the prison of captivity, typically intimating to us that the gentile and Jewish peoples received unequal benefits of divine recompense: through the mystery of the cross, one received reward and the other punishment. [Col. 0993D]

This is that light through which, although one of them was brought out for punishment and the other for glory, both nevertheless signified the victory of the Lord’s resurrection, because by one and the same allotment of the heavenly mystery they came out of prison after three days, and Christ rose from death.

This is that light through which, in Manasseh, whose name means “forgetfulness,” the Jewish people are subjected to the vengeance of divine forgetfulness, lest you, O Christian, following his example, forget your Creator, concerning whom it is written: “He forgot the Lord his Creator” (Deut. XXXII).

This is that light through which, in Ephraim, whose name is interpreted “fruitful,” the fruitfulness of the gentile people is illumined even today—provided, however, that in us the field of souls be made fruitful with those fruits [Col. 0994A] of virtues, concerning which it is said: “Honor the Lord from your substance and from the first fruits of your produce” (Prov. III).

This is that light which wished to illumine Manasseh and Ephraim by a twofold mystery, when their father Joseph placed one at Jacob’s right hand and the other at his left for the blessing: typically signifying that both possessed in Christ Jesus the same figure which the gentile and Jewish peoples previously possessed in Jacob and Esau.

This is that light which wished to prefigure the mystery of the cross in Jacob’s hands, when he used to place his right hand upon the younger and his left upon the elder; mystically instructing us that in this crossing of hands nothing else is to be understood by left or right except that, through the mystery [Col. 0994B] of the cross, one people is now within the Church and the other outside it.

This is that light which chose to illumine the elder in one way and the younger in another, so that in Ephraim and Manasseh the elder might serve the younger in the same way in which, in Esau and Jacob, the greater seemed to serve the lesser.

This is that light which by the same mystery in some degree illumined Reuben, whom previously it had not wished to illumine in Esau and Manasseh, since by the ineffable judgment of heavenly instruction each of them seemed to bear the figure of the former people.

This is that light through which Reuben, the firstborn and his father’s strength, paid the penalty of iniquity as his sins demanded, when he deserved to enjoy less than the others the order of primacy before his father, in proportion as the fault of the firstborn increased the beginning of his sorrow.

This is that light which was wholly darkened in [Col. 0994C] Reuben’s inward eyes when he went up into his father’s bed and defiled his couch: signifying, namely, that the Jewish people, defiled, went up into the bed of God their Father when they suspended his body upon the tree of the cross with iron nails.

This is that light which was greatly obscured in Reuben’s eyes when he was poured out like water through the wantonness of excessive pleasure: destined to pay the penalties of sin all the more among his brothers as he grieved that he had lost the primacy of the firstborn.

This is that light which seemed to illumine Reuben less by the ray of spiritual grace, though priestly and royal dignity were due to him, when he burned with excessive desire for unrestrained lust—he who formerly had been first in gifts and greater in rule.

This is that light through which [Col. 0994D] Simeon and Levi, warlike instruments of iniquity, are darkened like wandering stars because of works of darkness; for it would be altogether unworthy that their inward eyes should be illumined by heavenly light, through whom the scribes and priests of the Jewish people were prefigured.

This is that light which made the light of truth dark in their hearts, they who “in their fury killed a man, and in their wrath undermined a wall”: signifying, namely, that those are far removed from everlasting light who crucified the Lord’s body with nails, spear, and cross.

This is that light which illumined Jacob in one way at Bethel, but divided Simeon and Levi in Jacob and scattered them in Israel in another; because there “his foot at his foot” did not have the meaning which division here has in relation to scattering.

This is that light [Col. 0995A] through which the reciprocal conversion of these names is so variously changed that in believing Jews “division” is understood, and in unbelievers “scattering”; for as through this division the faith of those is intimated to us of whom it was said, “He received them from the way of their iniquity” (Ps. CVI), so through this disposition we must note the unbelieving Jews, concerning whom it is written: “He gave them into the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them” (Ps. CV).

This is that light through which Judah deserved to enjoy eternally his father’s blessing, for which his father said to him: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you” (Gen. XCIV); intending, namely, to set before us figurally that Judah who was to be born from the tribe of Judah for the punishment of the wicked and the praise of the good.

This is that light through [Col. 0995B] which Judah’s brothers praised him in the same figure in which the apostles afterward praised God, when through the ineffable efficacy of divine mercy his brothers were not so by nature but by grace.

This is that light which long lay hidden from their eyes, concerning whom it is added: “Your hands are upon the necks of your enemies” (Gen. XLIX), signifying, namely, that the true Judah ought to humble the necks of the proud with the heavenly sword of power, concerning whom it is written: “The righteous Lord shall cut off the necks of sinners” (Isa. XII).

This is that light by which Jacob, illumined in blessing his son, immediately added: “The sons of his father shall adore you” (Gen. XLIX); through whom, namely, were prefigured for us those true worshippers of God of whom it is written, [Col. 0995C] “All kings shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. LXXI).

This is that light which set before this Judah, in a figure, that lion concerning whom it is added: “Judah is a lion’s whelp” (Gen. XLIX), signifying, namely, that in the Lord’s resurrection the strength of that lion was made manifest to us, concerning whom it is written: “Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. V).

This is that light through which Judah was illumined by the mystery of Christ when his father said to him: “You have gone up to the prey, my son” (Gen. XLIX): thereby intimating to us the majesty of that conqueror who, ascending into heaven, led captivity captive with him (Eph. IV).

This is that light through which Judah, resting, lay down like a lion, while Christ rested in the tomb for three days in God; for God deigned to rest in the tomb for three days in the same way in which a lion’s whelp, when born, is said to sleep for three days. [Col. 0995D]

This is that light which, in the figure of this Judah, wished to raise God, concerning whom it is added: “Who shall raise him?” (Gen. XLIX), signifying, namely, that through the light of divinity, with which his humanity was filled, he was to be raised by God the Father as a lion and as a lioness.

This is that light through which it ought to be set before this Judah in a figure how great were Christ’s humility in sleeping and power in rising; while through the light of divinity he spiritually beheld him who died and rose for us (Rom. VIII).

This is that light in which Christ rested as a lion, who fulfilled the sleep of death for three days and three nights, when through the saving mystery of that death [Col. 0996A] he destroyed the dominion of ancient death.

This is that light through which that distinguished patriarch was illumined, of whom it is said: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor a leader from his loins” (Gen. XLIX); typically indicating that from the tribe of Judah that leader was to be born for the salvation of believers, concerning whom it is added: “He shall be the expectation of the nations” (ibid.).

This is that light which illumined Judah as a type of apostolic preaching when, in the figure of the gentile people, he tied his colt to the vine; intending that in this vine should be understood the Church of Christ, concerning which it was said: “You transplanted a vine from Egypt” (Ps. LXXIX).

This is that light through which Judah, to distinguish the dispute between Jews and gentiles, tied his ass to the vine under the type of the gentile people, [Col. 0996B] signifying, namely, that he who, appearing to his disciples after his resurrection, pretended that he was going farther on (Luke XXIV), bound the Church of the gentiles to himself with the bonds of charity through the mystery of the cross.

This is that light through which Judah knew Christ’s Passion to be forthcoming when, in the figure of the Savior, he washed his garment in wine (Gen. XLVI): mystically intimating that Christ’s flesh, which hung upon the cross, fell a little short of the angels (Ps. VIII), when in the winepress of the Passion he pressed out for the Church of the gentiles the cluster of his blood.

This is that light through which that true Judah washed his cloak in the blood of the grape: he who through the mystery of the cross cleansed the Church of the gentiles from all iniquity, when he aided its twofold sin with a twofold remedy, washing it with water from his side and redeeming it with blood. [Col. 0996C]

This is that light through which he who is “the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Cant. II) deigned, for the salvation of believers, to wash his cloak in the blood of the grape, when through the mystery of his saving blood he gave them a garment of praise in place of a spirit of mourning.

This is that light which still illumined Judah’s eyes with a divine mystery, where it is added: “His eyes are more beautiful than wine” (Gen. XLIX): intending that nothing else should be understood by the purity of this wine except the severity of legal observance.

This is that light through which Judah’s eyes were more beautiful than wine, when the apostles and evangelists were brighter than the legal tradition, having poured into us divine knowledge through evangelical and apostolic teaching.

This is that light through which his teeth also were whiter than milk [Col. 0996D] (ibid.), when the teachers of the Church were brighter than legal obscurity, for, testifying by the whiteness of milk to the brightness of virtues, they instilled in us the sweetness of evangelical truth.

This is that light through which Christ’s preachers are understood in his teeth; through them unbelievers, indeed, are conveyed into the body of the Church like food, and at first are nourished, after the manner of little children, with milk because they are not yet able to become accustomed to solid food.

This is that light in which Christ, encountering the audacity of the ancient enemy, illumined the wine and milk of the old Law by the ray of new grace; when at the altar of the cross he chose to confer this twofold grace upon believers, so that thereafter neither dimness might appear in their eyes nor pain in their teeth.

This is that [Col. 0997A] light which illumined Zebulun by the ray of divine brightness, when he dwelt at the shore of the sea and at the station of ships (ibid.): signifying, namely, that he chose to place the Church in the harbor of eternal rest—he who in apostolic preaching extended his branches as far as the sea (Ps. LXXIX).

This is that light through which Zebulun, whose name is interpreted “dwelling of strength,” seemed to be more greatly illumined as if at the shore, when the Church of the gentiles deserved to receive from him strength of virtue, who through the mystery of the cross chose to show it the harbor of salvation.

This is that light through which Issachar, who was called a strong ass, cast off the burden of death for the reward of heavenly life, because the more the Lord’s yoke was sweet and his burden light (Matt. XXX), the more the present age seemed to him transient [Col. 0997B] and light.

This is that light through which Issachar, whose name appears to mean “reward,” together with the gentile people is accustomed to serve God without ceasing with the rewards of faith; typically instructing us that a great distinction obtains between gentiles and Jews, although many from both peoples have been purchased at the price of the Lord’s blood.

This is that light which still illumined Issachar—that is, the gentile people—in another manner, when, lying down between the boundaries of eternal blessedness, he bore the excellent land upon his shoulder; signifying, namely, that almighty God crowns no one at the end of the age with the reward of heavenly life unless he first here submits his shoulder to bear the burden of righteousness in good action.

This is that light through which Jacob, illumined with knowledge of future things, said: “Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent [Col. 0997C] in the path” (Gen. XLIX), signifying, namely, the Antichrist, who at times must rage against God’s elect with a twofold madness, since he is called both serpent because of cunning and horned serpent (*cerastes*) because of power.

This is that light which also illumines us with Jacob through spiritual allegory when, in that same Dan, it shows us that the path is narrower than the way, lest, instead of the narrow and confined way which leads to life (Matt. VII), we seek that broader way of which it is written: “Broad and spacious is the way which leads to destruction” (ibid.).

This is that light which seemed to be greatly darkened for Dan when he used to pitch camp apart from his brothers in the northern region: thereby imitating the deed of him who rose up against God and said: “I shall place my throne in the north” (Isa. XIV).

This is that light through which God’s elect at times disdain to follow the tracks of his hoofs, concerning whom Jacob adds: “Biting the hoofs of the horse” (Gen. XLIX); for it is altogether unworthy that a Christian should take from Antichrist an example of wicked living, who, through pride and ambition, foams like a horse in the course of this passing age. [Col. 0997D]

This is that light which is also accustomed to illumine us daily by repentance for sins together with Peter, lest, after the example of Dan, we fall backward with the rider of this horse—that is, with any proud person—knowing, namely, that only those go with the blind men of the Gospel into the precipice who, with Saul, fall backward and not upon their face.

This is that light through which the person of Christ is set before us under a suppressed name, where Jacob adds: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord” (ibid.), mystically signifying that by this “salvation” his resurrection is most clearly indicated—he who is interpreted Jesus, that is, “saving” or “salvation.”

This is that light which also spiritually set God before us in Gad, where it is added: “Gad, girded, shall fight before him” (ibid.), signifying by this battle that battle which Christ was to wage against the devil for the salvation of the faithful. [Col. 0998A]

This is that light which in that same Gad sent us the sword of the heavenly Word, by which the only-begotten Son of God separated daughter-in-law from mother-in-law and son from father, when, coming into the arena of this present life, he said: “I came not to send peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matt. X).

This is that light through which, in the figure of Gad, were illumined those most unconquered warriors of whom the Church says in the Song of Songs: “All,” she says, “holding swords and most trained for wars” (Cant. XXX); signifying, namely, that those are believed in the Church of God to be as the strong among the strongest of Israel who strive always to resist with the spiritual sword the excesses of carnal desire.

This is that light through which that true Gad, most strongly girded with the sword of the heavenly Word, is meant, concerning whom it is written: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, most mighty one” (Ps. XLIV); mystically suggesting that we must always gird the loins of our minds with the armor of God, so that we may be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked one (Eph. VI).

This is that light which also illumined Gad in the words that follow, though still obscurely, where it is added: [Col. 0998C] “He himself shall be girded behind” (II Thess. II), that is, in the future: signifying, namely, that Christ will at some time kill Antichrist with the spirit of his mouth, so that God’s elect may enjoy eternal blessedness with him more securely.

This is that light through which Jacob, the distinguished patriarch, was illumined where, adding concerning another son, he says: “Asher, his bread is rich” (Gen. XLIX); thereby setting before us in a figure the richness of that bread concerning which it is written: “This is the living bread which came down from heaven” (John VI).

This is that light through which Jacob himself was still illumined by divine laws when, adding concerning the same Asher, he says: “He shall provide delicacies for kings” (ibid.), thereby signifying those kings who have governed themselves well according to divine laws. [Col. 0998D]

This is that light through which Asher, whose name means “blessed” or “rich bread,” deserved to be illumined as a type of the Savior, when he was enriched with the abundance of those riches for providing delicacies to kings, concerning which it is written: “Riches of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge” (Isa. XXXIII).

This is that light through which in Naphtali the abyss of the heavenly sacrament is opened to us, where it is added concerning him: “Naphtali, a released hind” (Gen. XLIX), signifying, namely, that the swiftness of apostolic preaching desired the salvation of souls as the hind desires the springs of waters (Ps. XLI).

This is that light through which that same Naphtali, who bore the figure of the strength of a hind, gave his brothers words of beauty, when in the beauty [Col. 0999A] of the heavenly word he prefigured for us the preaching of those concerning whom it is written: “Their sound went forth into all the earth” (Ps. XVIII).

This is that light through which, in Naphtali, whose name means “expansion,” apostolic preaching began to be expanded through the breadth of the world; through it the hearts of the faithful are daily enlarged toward God, even to the last elect, to whom the Psalmist says: “I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. CXVIII).

This is that light through which Jacob, burning for himself and shining for us, repeated concerning Joseph: “Joseph, an increasing son, an increasing son” (Gen. XLIX); typically indicating that through this boy was prefigured the power of that child concerning whom it is written: “The child Jesus increased in age and wisdom” (Luke II).

This is that light through which Joseph, illumined with the affection of pious devotion, was splendid in clothing and handsome in appearance: mystically prefiguring that Lord concerning whom it is written: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV). [Col. 0999B]

This is that light which did not wish the mystery of his beauty to be obscure to the children of the gentiles, concerning whom it is added: “The sons ran upon the wall” (Gen. XLIX); signifying, namely, that the children of the Church, through firmness of faith, ought to love Christ above gold and topaz if they desire in his beauty to see the God of gods in Zion.

This is that light from which Joseph’s brothers were long alienated, concerning whom it is written: “They embittered him and quarreled,” when, mocking his dreams and his power, they said: “Will you indeed be our king, or shall we be subject to your dominion?” (Gen. XLIX, 37).

This is that light through which the torch of divine charity began to grow dark in those same brothers, concerning whom it is said: “They envied him”—that is, Christ—“having arrows” (Gen. XLIX), prefiguring by the darts of their envy the wickedness of those concerning whom it is written: “The arrows of little ones became their wounds” (Ps. LXIII). [Col. 0999C]

This is that light through which that same distinguished father was illumined, concerning whom it is added: “His bow sat in the strong one” (Ps. LXV), signifying, namely, that the power of the Son of God remained most firmly in the Father when he suffered in the ark of the cross for the Church his mother.

This is that light through which, in the same way, the bonds of his arms were loosened by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob, as Job was afterward freed from the bond of a woman’s reproach: typically intimating that through the power of God the Father the bonds by which Christ’s body had been bound were loosened, when his brothers—that is, the Jews—led him bound to Pilate (Matt. XXVII).

This is that light through which that blessing was first promised to Jacob the patriarch at Bethel, concerning which it is added: “Judah went forth, the shepherd, the stone of Israel” (Gen. XLIX), signifying, namely, that the fullness of the gentiles ought to enter into faith in Christ through him from whom the stone—that is, the firmness—of believers came forth. [Col. 0999D]

This is that light through which his son Joseph was illumined, where his father said to him: “The God of your father shall be your helper” (ibid.); mystically suggesting that that heavenly Father strongly helped his Son in the Passion, [Col. 1000A] concerning whom it is written: “A help in due times, in tribulation” (Ps. IX).

This is that light through which that fatherly blessing was also given to him, concerning which it is added: “God Almighty shall bless you” (Gen. XLIX); typically instructing us that the Father is to be believed to have confirmed in the Son that blessing concerning which it is written: “May he who blesses you be filled with blessings” (Gen. XXVII).

This is that light through which Joseph deserved to be illumined separately before his brothers by those blessings, concerning which it is added: “With blessings of heaven above, and blessings of the deep lying beneath” (Gen. XLIX); mystically suggesting to us that we ought especially to refer these blessings to him through whose grace we live from the dew of heaven and from the richness of the earth.

This is that light through which Joseph, among the other blessings of his brothers, was still illumined with “blessings of breasts”—that is, of the two Testaments, or blessings of the breasts by which Christ’s infancy was nursed—concerning which it is written: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts which you sucked” (Luke XI). [Col. 1000B]

This is that light which wished to shine upon Joseph also through another blessing, concerning which it is added: “With blessings of breasts and womb” (Gen. XLIX); thereby prefiguring in hope that virginal womb concerning which Jeremiah says: “Before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jer. I).

This is that light through which...

…by which Joseph, strengthened by those blessings, was confirmed among the blessings of the righteous, concerning which Jacob says: “The blessings of your father have been strengthened by the blessings of your fathers” (Gen. XLIX); thereby typologically intimating [Col. 1000C] that, just as Joseph’s blessing prevailed over the blessings of his brothers, so the blessing of God the Father surpasses in faith the blessings of all fathers.

This is that light by which Joseph, illumined with these and other blessings as a figure of the saints, endured until the desire of the everlasting hills should come: signifying, namely, that God’s elect, by reason of their eminent holiness, are rightly seen as made equal to those hills of theirs, concerning which it is written: “The lovely places of the wilderness grow rich, and the hills shall gird themselves with rejoicing” (Ps. LXIV).

This is that light by which all these blessings, repeatedly confirmed in words, came upon him, of whom it is added: “Let them be upon the head of Joseph and upon the crown of the Nazirite” (Gen. XLIX). Through them, indeed, he allegorically sets before us the alabaster vessel of that most precious ointment [Col. 1000D] which descends without interruption from the head of Christ through all the members of the Church, down to the last elect person.

This is that light by which Jacob, still foretelling the obscure mysteries of future things, says: “Benjamin is a ravening wolf; in the morning he shall eat the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoils” (Gen. XLIX). By this he prefigures, indeed, the final salvation of the Jews, because Benjamin, the last, received his father’s blessing.

This is that light which, through the efficacy of the saving mystery, sets before us in the same Benjamin both Law and grace: for by “morning” and “evening” it signifies that letter and spirit concerning which it is written: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (II Cor. III).

This is that light by which, in Benjamin, [Col. 1001A] who was called by his mother “son of sorrow,” the conversion of blessed Paul is allegorically signified: inwardly struck by sorrow of heart, he was made godly from ungodly, and a teacher from a persecutor.

This is that light by which your charity has well understood that Benjamin was called by his father “son of the right hand,” signifying Paul, who, after the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, daily increased through its grace unto salvation; concerning whom it is written: “The right hand of the Lord has wrought mightily” (Ps. CXVII).

This is that light by which Paul, who before his conversion was a ravening wolf, after conversion was made capable of the divine Law: for Paul was called “great” because, from a reprobate, he became upright, and from a wolf he became a lamb.

This is that light through which, from the same Apostle, He bestowed the great gift [Col. 1001B] of divine illumination, while in his heart, as it were, “evening and morning” became one day; because, when Christ offered Himself to him as guide upon the way of truth, He changed his night into day and his darkness into light.
