This is that light by which Benjamin, who ate prey in the morning and divided spoils in the evening, lost the cause of his ravening through the shedding of prophetic blood; signifying, indeed, that just as Saul’s rapacity was prefigured for us in the prey which he ate in the morning, so Paul’s preaching was figured in the spoils which he divided in the evening.

This is that light by which everything formerly foretold historically concerning Benjamin was afterwards fulfilled allegorically in Paul, when, in the ecstasy of his mind, he pursued that same Benjamin with unrestrained step toward the Church of God, concerning whom it is said: “There is little Benjamin, in ecstasy of mind” [Col. 1001C] (Ps. LXVII).

Accordingly, blessed also is he who, after that man’s example, has few vices and a thousand virtues; blessed, indeed, is he who, through the dryness of the outward person and the verdure of the inward person, is accustomed also to instil in others the sweetness of a good fragrance. But far more blessed is he if, through the ineffable aid of the holy Trinity, he strives to put forth shoots of good works unto his end, like a lily in the falling drops—namely, beginning the shoot of that good work and bringing it to completion in that same work—concerning which it is written: “In its falling drops it shall rejoice as it sprouts” (Ps. LXIV).

Behold, dearest brethren, since we have long been tossed upon the sea of the Scriptures, while, with Christ as helmsman, we have sought to bring the blessings of the ancient Fathers into harbour, [Col. 1001D] it is time that our discourse, roused from the deep of mysteries as though by lifting waves, should with the little ship of the mind be brought as swiftly as possible to shore. Yet because we cannot as yet perfectly see the end of our discourse, as it were the level ground of land, it is fitting that we most firmly cast the anchor of our hope in Christ Jesus, so that, while heavenly grace overshadows us in this night, tomorrow’s day may find us where today’s has left us. For as today we treated fully of Jacob and his sons, so tomorrow we shall treat briefly of his wives and children, and of the matters which still remain, lest we seem to pass hastily from their deeds to other matters, when in their history some grain still appears to lie hidden beneath the chaff. Therefore, since we have passed this day joyfully [Col. 1002A] from morning until evening, it is time now to entrust our hearts to the Creator and our limbs to rest, so that tomorrow’s day may find us the more cheerful, in proportion as the night’s rest has more relieved today’s labour.

And behold, since this night, beloved, like yesterday’s day which has passed away, has now almost vanished with the dawn glowing red, it is now time for us to rise from darkness to light in the name of Him of whom it is written: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us” (Ps. 4). But since it is written, “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added unto you” (Matt. 6), we must first offer prayers to God, so that, for pursuing the journey of the present day, the little ship of the mind may more easily be loosed from the side of the body. Yet since [Col. 1002B] clean things should be compared with clean, and spiritual things with spiritual, it is time now that a tablet be taken in one hand and a stylus in the other; for today we shall treat very briefly of Jacob’s wives and children—the matters which from yesterday and the day before yesterday we had reserved for treatment on this day.

You know indeed, beloved, that the light of the ancient Godhead illuminated Jacob in many ways, when he begot twelve sons by two free women and two handmaids, lest we should be ignorant what is signified in these or in those, since the New Law is figured in the free women and the Old in the handmaids. But, in order that the words of history may support the mystery of allegory, it must be known that six of the twelve sons were Leah’s, so that the other three wives might the better recognize their sons, since Bilhah and Zilpah had four, [Col. 1002C] and Rachel had two. But we must note that, among those brothers born of the free women, the sons of the handmaids also were consecrated by their father’s blessing, so that we, following their example, may have the greater confidence through Christ toward God, because in their blessings there was with Him no respect of persons (Col. 3). For grace of paternal blessing was given to them all alike by Him who “divided the land to them by the measuring-line of distribution” (Ps. 77), plainly signifying that almighty God wills no one to perish by the death of sin, but wills all to come to the knowledge of truth (1 Tim. 2).

For there is no distinction whether you are Jew or Greek, barbarian or Scythian, since through the grace of the Saviour eternal [Col. 1002D] life receives all, provided that here they are reconciled by faith to His body—He who with the Father and the Spirit is ever one and the same. Therefore, if we attentively consider the mercy of the Creator, it matters nothing whether anyone is noble in the flesh, unless he is proved nobler in mind; for in the eternal homeland the ranks of birth do not distinguish those whom here the unity of charity makes equal. Thus the kingdom of God is common to all, so that king sits beside soldier and soldier beside king, where in God the Father and His coeternal Son servant shall reign with lord, and shepherd with king. There disciple and teacher, servant and free person, Jacob and Rachel, Hagar and Ishmael, all dwell together alike; for it is fitting that there the son of the handmaid should be with the son of the free woman, since all are one in Christ and to live is one thing.

With these words, [Col. 1003A] therefore, since we have passed this day joyfully until evening, while in the hull of our mind we dictated what was to be read and reread what had been dictated, now that the sun is setting we ought all the sooner to yield to the day’s labour, because in Christ Jesus we ought to fear less the terror of the night. Therefore, since after the example of prophetic reading we sometimes ought even to be silent from good things, silence must now be imposed upon the mouth all the more diligently, because tomorrow we wish again to devote ourselves to reading.

Behold, since the last hour of this night now indicates that the dawn of today’s day ought already to glow, we must rise all the more quickly from the sleep of dullness and sloth, because today we desire to reach more swiftly the shore of our discourse. For as yesterday, [Col. 1003B] illuminated by the star of heavenly light, we briefly unfolded concerning Jacob’s wives what either the handmaids or the free women prefigured, so today, while sailing, we wish to touch upon nothing else except how this discourse, with favourable breezes blowing, may reach harbour. Therefore, for completing the journey of one day, the anchor of hope must now be drawn back by the chain of faith, because in the little ship of our heart we ought to have the greater hope in God, since He will not abandon any who hope in Him. And because we now need the heavenly rowing-power of divine mercy, if we wish to arrive at our appointed place in a prosperous vessel, we must the more diligently apply ourselves in the little ship of the mind to the oars of faith, hope, and charity, because, in these last stages, we must row ever more eagerly in hope of seeing the shore.

[Col. 1003C] Yet while we hasten toward the end of our discourse, as from shore to shore, we must by no means lose the way of truth; rather, we must now look farther before us with the inward eyes, lest the little ship of the mind be dashed against the windings or rocks of some error. For it must be known that, just as in the book of Genesis we have plainly sailed for some days already, so in the other books of Moses we must henceforth fish for some time, especially since those great fish have already been shown to us in the patriarchs and prophets, of whom Truth said to His disciples: “Cast the net on the right side of the vessel, and you shall find” (John 21:6; cited here as John 12). For as many prophets bore the figure of those fish of whom it is said, “Although they were so many, the net was not [Col. 1003D] torn” (ibid.), so all heretics even to this day bear the type of those of whom it is written: “But their net was breaking” (Luke 5:6). And as those good fish are daily found in the enclosure of the present Church, of whom Truth says, “They gathered the good into vessels” (Matt. 13:48), so heretics will always bear the figure of those fish of whom it is written: “But they cast the bad outside” (ibid.).

For since some in the Church of God are so perverse, while others are so holy, that they are not undeservedly like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind (ibid.), it is fitting that by the just judgment of the Creator some should remain within and others without. But those who are outside, dearest brethren, you ought all the more quickly to drive out because within the Lord’s sheepfold they use a wolf’s tooth [Col. 1004A] and a sheep’s fleece: being wolves, they pretend to be sheep, and divide the Church of God by diverse heresies. For since it is written, “Beware of false prophets” (Matt. 7:15), these are those of whom you must beware. Although perhaps some among you may honour them as gods, nevertheless “by their fruits you shall know them” (ibid.). Therefore, since our discourse is so fortified by divine protection against their snares that, freed from heretical power, it may safely hasten to shore, it is time that the sea should cast us out, as it were with Jonah, all the more swiftly onto the land of this argument, because we desire sooner, as it were with Jesus, to stand upon the shore.

But lest we appear to have given what is holy to dogs or pearls to swine, if we return empty-handed to [Col. 1004B] land without the multitude of fish which we have caught, it is fitting that the net of our heart should now gather those great fish by whom the patriarchs and prophets were formerly signified. For what else were they but fish, who by the little fins of virtues were accustomed to fly from the depths to the heights, while they were ever fortified against the devil’s snares by the scales of righteousness, lest they be caught by the barbs or hooks of carnal vices? Fish which possess the little fins of scales can leap above the waters, plainly signifying that only those are made most worthy of the body of the Church who know how to raise themselves from earthly to heavenly things by the little fins of virtues. But no breeze of divinity touches those whom the inward frost binds beneath the covering of vices, unless, with the warmer winds of God’s sevenfold grace breathing upon them, they [Col. 1004C] ascend by leaps of the mind from vices to virtues.

Such leaps, therefore, the patriarchs and prophets made, while supported by the little fins of virtues they were accustomed to fly from the lowest things to the highest, imitating Him who, ascending on high after the glory of His resurrection, made a great leap from earth to heaven. Therefore, since they were like those great fish—namely, the one hundred and fifty-three—of whom food pleasing to God must ever be prepared in the Church of the saints, it is necessary that we, after their example, should have with them the same faith which that same number has shown us through mystery. And since it may be more sincerely unfolded by us if the mystery of one number is separated from the mystery of another, therefore, lest one food be [Col. 1004D] wearisome to us and another desirable, it is fitting that the hundred, which is first among these in number, should also be first in mystery.

You know, certainly, that according to the ancient reckoning of the wise, ten times ten make one hundred, mystically signifying both that the fulfilment of the Decalogue is understood in ten, and that the fullness of perfection is understood in one hundred. For it must be known that unless with whole faith and perfect charity we endeavour to fulfil the ten commandments of the Law, we can by no means be united to that perfect rest where not night declares knowledge to night, but day to day. Yet another mystery is still shown to men in the same number, whereby it is customarily assigned to virgins for the crown of virginity, since, in the bending of the fingers, under the Law as teacher, it has in the right hand the same position [Col. 1005A] which ten has in the left.

Behold, since by the shoulder of pious devotion and fraternal charity we have brought you two mysteries in this same number, it remains, according to the teaching of diligent men, that we add a third to these two. Attentive readers should certainly observe that the letter T, *tau* (*thau*), is assigned the number three hundred; plainly signifying that, as the sacrament of the New Law testifies, the Trinity is represented in three and charity in one hundred. For unless we wish to possess the quality of that charity of which it is written, “Perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4:18), the perfection of that love cannot [Col. 1005B] flow into us, of which it is said, “Love is the fulfilment of the law” (Rom. 13:10).

And since the allegorical senses hidden in that same number have now been disclosed to your charity, beloved, for the third time, it is fitting that, because a new mind requires new limbs, a fourth be added to the three. For you know in Christ Jesus that not the cross itself, but the form of the cross, is contained in the letter T, *tau*, because if one further part remained at its upper end, it would no longer be the shape of a cross but a complete cross. Hence in the same letter, by which the number three hundred and the form of the cross are displayed, Gideon’s battle is not inappropriately set before us figuratively, in which he deserved through the grace of the Almighty to triumph over his enemies with three hundred men. For through the mystery of the cross and the form of the Trinity he fought armed men without arms, when he subdued them not by pleasant weapons [Col. 1005C] but by trumpets, lamps, and jars.

We must also note that the prophet Ezekiel, wishing to express the faith of believers by the same letter, says: “Mark T, *tau*, upon the foreheads of men who groan and mourn” (Ezek. 9:4), thereby figuratively intimating through this sign of new sanctification that the wood of the Lord’s cross is stronger than the enemies’ sword. Through this cross, therefore, our Saviour, wishing to draw all things to Himself, says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross and follow me” (Matt. 16:24; Mark 8:34), plainly signifying that we seem to take up the Saviour’s cross more truly in proportion as we have greater charity of compassion toward our neighbours.

Behold, since the form of the number one hundred [Col. 1005D] has been examined for you morally, it is time that the number fifty likewise be examined. For although the former is first and this second, each is nevertheless deep in mystical interpretation. Therefore, although this number is now to be examined allegorically, it must first be multiplied historically by natural calculation, so that it may be discerned by the clarity of the inward eye what is owed to it by nature or by grace. You know, certainly, that if anyone wishes to assess its parts separately, it plainly consists of ten and five; for, as the more skilful calculators know well, ten times five, or five times ten, makes fifty. Therefore, although by the hidden judgments of divinity there are many mysteries in this number, we do not wish to say more about them than a few things, since for the present a few things appear [Col. 1006A] sufficient in place of many. For its parts possess spiritual meanings so many and so manifold that human arts would scarcely suffice to explain them all; therefore it must now be examined by us not wholly but in part through allegorical art.

But before one comes to its total, its parts must first be considered, lest, when one proceeds from the part to the whole, a mystery known to some should remain unknown to others. You know, therefore, that divine power consecrated the number five when, from five loaves and two fish, it fed five thousand; by the five loaves signifying the sacraments of the Law, and by the two fish the two persons of priest and king. Since, then, in sacred discourse we learn daily with you that in that [Col. 1006B] refreshment of the Lord’s Passion neither fish were lacking to loaves nor loaves to fish, it is fitting that, for the continual observance of that example in the Church of God, neither kingship be separated from priesthood nor priesthood from kingship.

An example of this may easily be seen in the Creator Himself, who wished to be shown as both king and priest, to sanctify the people and govern it, when, to prepare for us the unfading crown of eternal life, He wished in Himself to bear the sacerdotal and royal person. Therefore you err greatly, O Christian heretic, who, after the manner of madmen, are accustomed madly to agitate kingship and priesthood, since you do not fear to separate from one another through diverse heresies the two persons who have always been exalted in the Church of God. But perhaps you do not know that it was long ago established by the law of ancient [Col. 1006C] divinity that in the kingdom of the Romans king should not be separated from pontiff, nor pontiff from king, so that the sons of the Church may be able to see clearly in their concord that, by divine ordination, one possesses the office of priesthood and the other that of kingship.

Therefore there is no obstacle if the aforesaid refreshment of the Lord’s Passion is compared by a certain likeness with these two persons, since in the mystery of the nourishment which these same men ought to provide for Christians, one has the form of a fish and the other of bread. For it is not unknown to you that the art of baking is indoors and fishing outdoors, so that each may strive all the more to benefit the other in Christ’s charity because one art can always be useful to another. Thus, for the love of divine and fraternal [Col. 1006D] charity, these same two men ought always to be at work, because in the Church of God their order is so distinguished that in matters of the world and matters of God one works outside and the other within. For each bears a certain badge of divine charity, while, as it were, one works in water and the other in fire: just as one, for love of God, is baked like bread in the fire of the Holy Spirit, so the other, for defence of neighbours, is fortified like a fish by the scales of righteousness.

Therefore, since it may be learned most plainly from sacred discourse that in the Lord’s refreshment neither fish was absent from bread nor bread from fish, it must be known that it is contrary neither to Catholic faith nor to Christian law if, for the honour of kingship and priesthood, king obeys pontiff and pontiff obeys king. [Col. 1007A] These are they who, by the twofold dispensation of the ancient Godhead, have come together in the firmament of the Church as two great lights, so that in matters of the world and matters of God the lesser light may be said to preside over the night and the greater light over the day. Nor without reason can they be compared with those two lights which appear to rule more than the other stars, because just as in the firmament of heaven no created star seems more excellent in brightness than those lights, so in the firmament of the Church none can be higher than these two persons in rank and dignity.

The action of Moses also seems not inappropriately to suit them: he used often to enter and leave the tabernacle of the Lord, so that, in demonstrating the admirable union of priesthood and kingship, kingship may in this place be understood in the going out and priesthood [Col. 1007B] in the entering in. For while one offers others an example of good living within, and the other sits outside to arrange the causes of the infirm, undoubtedly one seems, as it were, to return with Moses to the tabernacle, while the other appears to go out with him. As one is raised upward on the wings of virtues like a dove, while for heavenly secrets he hastens from low things to high, so the other, to repair the breach of worldly dissension and discord, must continually descend from high things to low.

Therefore, in order that, following Moses’ example, one may return within to the tabernacle for ordering inward things, while the other may worthily sit outside with him for arranging outward things, it is necessary that through the office of mutual charity each should so help and strengthen the other in Christ’s power that one orders spiritual things within, while the other [Col. 1007C] bears outside the burden of carnal matters. Thus kingship and priesthood can have peace between themselves if these two men wish worthily to exercise their office, especially since in the Church of God they can daily find a cause for which one may enter the tabernacle of the Church and the other worthily go out.

Moreover, we should observe that the banquet long ago, at which Mary sat and Martha ministered, accords well with this mystery; for, as is plainly evident from the words of the Gospel, Mary would eat poorly if Martha did not minister. For it must be known that, according to a fitting order and suitable rationale, these two persons may be compared with those two persons, because in the Church of God they have the task in nourishing bodies and enlightening [Col. 1007D] souls which was formerly prefigured for us in these two sisters. For you know that through these two sisters two lives are morally expressed, one of which now appears to be present in hope and the other in reality; and, as the grace of evangelical truth testifies, one is called active and the other contemplative.

But in order that the twofold life may rest upon a twofold path, it must be known that the active is assigned to Martha and the contemplative to Mary. Although one is preferred to the other, nevertheless each appears necessary to the other. Thus there is no objection if I suitably compare these two sisters with those two persons who seem to bear in the Church of God the sacerdotal and royal office, because it is fitting that in arranging [Col. 1008A] ecclesiastical and worldly matters they should exercise the same dispositions which those two sisters once displayed in the house of the Pharisee. For as Martha was busy with much serving, while Mary was accustomed to sit at the Lord’s feet and hear His word, so in ordering the honour of ecclesiastical and worldly dignity, one of them will be at rest and the other at labour.

Yet lest one leave the other to minister alone, it is fitting that each should always aid the other in Christ’s charity, lest one cry out vainly to God concerning the other in those Gospel words: “Tell her therefore to help me” (Luke 10:40). Although heavenly gifts are not equal in them, it is nevertheless fitting that each sow to the other his carnal things, that he may reap the other’s spiritual things. Therefore, so that person may be relieved by [Col. 1008B] person and part by part in the same manner in which Mary’s rest was once relieved by Martha’s service, it is fitting that in running the way of royal and sacerdotal justice, one should be Martha and the other Mary to the other.

Behold, that prayer also seems to accord with this reasoning, in which the twofold offering of legal sacrifice is shown to us, where Moses, establishing sacred observance for the people of Israel, says: “Let him offer a lamb from the flock, or a goat. But if he cannot offer livestock” (Lev. 5:6–7), by which he may offer to God the whole glory of true innocence, then at least, for amendment of bodies and expiation of souls, “let him offer two turtledoves, or two young pigeons” (ibid.). Since, therefore, these different [Col. 1008C] sacrifices of the Law are set before us in the person of the Roman pontiff and king, it is fitting that, for enlightening the souls of the faithful, we should first explain those which we first proposed.

Thus, so that abundant piety and great virtue may be in these two men, the goat and lamb of this legal sacrifice are figured; for, as the grace of the New Law testifies, the active life is signified by the lamb and the contemplative life by the goat. Hence it is not inappropriate that this quality of each life should be compared with each of these men, because under the legal signification of this same lamb or goat, for the Church of God one will always be in action and the other in contemplation. Yet because by the lamb the innocence of the active life is signified, it is not inappropriately compared with the royal person—provided that in his heart he possesses, through God’s grace, that innocence of which it is written: “I walked in the innocence of my heart [Col. 1008D]” (Ps. 100:2). For unless he so continually afflicts his heart for diverse faults that he lives laudably before God in the innocence of his heart, that prophetic saying will by no means be fulfilled in him: “He will not withhold good things from those who walk in innocence” (Ps. 83:12).

But if he has subjected the hearts of evildoers to divine laws by the material sword, he seems no longer to offer a goat but a lamb from the flock, plainly signifying that among the two lots and two lives of the elect, the active life belongs to many and the contemplative to few.

Therefore, since the legal person has now been morally compared with the legal lamb, [Col. 1009A] it remains that the legal goat be compared likewise with the Roman pontiff. For as, according to the higher understanding of the Law, the legal lamb expresses the person of the king, so the goat, by which the summit of Catholic faith is figured, is not undeservedly likened to the apostolic office. For when the apostolic man abandons low things and seeks high things, he not inappropriately bears the appearance of this legal goat—provided that by God’s grace he is so raised above the miseries of the present age that, hanging as it were upon the highest cliffs, he seeks his food upon the heights. And when he nourishes the souls of the faithful with the udders of both laws, he undoubtedly slaughters the goat as a sacrifice of his condition, provided that he is not lifted up thereby with the swollen pride of arrogance, but first satisfies himself with the food of inward compunction. But if, for a more exalted food, he softens the hardness of his heart with the milk of charity, then, like a goat, he worthily raises his feet and lifts up his head, because by the food of innocence [Col. 1009B] he desires spiritually to enjoy with those of whom it is written: “He fed them in the innocence of his heart” (Ps. 77:72).

Behold, as certain things have been said by us separately concerning the person of pontiff and king, so other things must yet be said generally concerning both men, so that each may strive all the more carefully to cleave to the other because the Church of God ought in no way to lack either one. For it is fitting that, as goat and lamb are offered together in the Creator’s sacrifice, so between the two there should be whole faith and great charity. Although in the Church of God they are separated from one another in rank and dignity, they must nevertheless always be joined in love of the Godhead. For as one, through the active life, usually shows himself so devoted to all that for love of the Creator he gives food to the hungry [Col. 1009C] and drink to the thirsty, so the other, through the contemplative life, ought to practise nothing else than, for the unity of the Church, to cleave to God alone through prayers and fasts.

For if the confidence of both is great in God, they are not undeservedly compared with goat and lamb; and if in them the mind is free and the flesh captive, the active and contemplative lives are not inappropriately likened to them. Therefore, so that one may be able most courageously to draw the material sword on the occasion of the lamb, while the other may be able most powerfully to gird himself with the spiritual sword for the immolation of the goat, it is fitting that, by the sacred observance of sacerdotal and royal dignity, one should offer a lamb and the other a goat in sacrifice to the Creator.

[Col. 1009D] Therefore, as it has already been explained to us by evident reasoning how lamb and goat are to be slain in these two men as a sacrifice to the Creator, so now it must be related to you, in few verses but many words, how these same two men may be compared with two turtledoves. [Col. 1010A] Moreover, it must also be unfolded for us from the inner marrow of the Scriptures how these same men are to be equated with two young pigeons, so that each may rejoice in God his Saviour if these two turtledoves or these two young birds suitably correspond to him.

For it must be known that by dove and turtledove the twofold office of sacerdotal and royal dignity is signified: kingship is understood in the dove and priesthood in the turtledove. By the dove, indeed, which usually flies in a flock, the royal person may not inappropriately be represented generally, provided that in this active life that fellowship of good people does not seem burdensome to him, of which it is written: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). But in the turtledove, which loves solitude, we ought to admire [Col. 1010B] the dignity of the sacerdotal person, provided that with that solitary sparrow he pursues with a perfect heart the sweetness of the contemplative life, of which it is written: “I have become like a solitary sparrow upon the roof” (Ps. 101:7).

But because turtledoves and doves possess the groaning of a twofold repentance, they may not inappropriately be likened to these two persons, provided that, like Achsah, daughter of Caleb, they possess this twofold groaning for the two water-springs: that they may both lament sins past and guard against sins to come. For as a twofold gift must be brought to God in the two turtledoves or young birds, when two young birds or two turtledoves, and not one, are offered, so likewise these same two rulers of the earth ought together to offer themselves in pious devotion as sacrifice and holocaust to the Lord.

[Col. 1010C] But another point must still be noted concerning these two turtledoves, which may not inappropriately apply to both these men. Since the turtledove, when deprived of the companionship of its marital union, has groaning instead of song, it may not undeservedly be equated with these two men, because it is fitting that if through some misfortune one loses the other, they ought not to have song on that account but groaning. For they must know that then that charity truly exists in them of which it is said, “Love of neighbour works no evil” (Rom. 13:10), if that fraternal companionship does not seem burdensome to them, of which it is written: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in one” (Ps. 132:1). Thus, for expiation of bodies and regard for souls, let these two men offer two [Col. 1010D] turtledoves or two young pigeons, if, after the poison of all malice has been wholly drained from their hearts, when one is deprived of the other’s consolation they make bitter mourning for themselves.

[Col. 1011]

# SERMONS OF BERENGOSUS, ABBOT

(*Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XII, p. 376.)

## SERMON ONE: ON THE FEAST OF THE MARTYRS

[Col. 1011A]

On the passage of Psalm 58: “O God, thou hast cast us off and destroyed us,” etc.

Because our Lord Jesus Christ, beloved brethren, took upon himself the weakness of our flesh in order to drive from us the power of the enemy, this is undoubtedly attested by the prophetic prayer which has often been read among you, when David of old uttered it under the figure of the faithful: “O God, you have rejected us and destroyed us.” For by this David, who, as is narrated in the books of Kings, subdued very many regions by slaughter and fire, is spiritually signified that true mighty-handed one, Jesus Christ our Lord [Col. 1011B], who, coming into this world in order to divide son from father and daughter-in-law from mother-in-law, brought fire with which to burn and a sword with which to kill: so that, making havoc of vices in the hearts of the faithful—not with iron but with the word, not with the sword but with the Spirit—by the fire of love he might restore them to the harmony of twofold love.

This destruction of vices, therefore, and this succession of virtues shone forth most perfectly in these most holy martyrs of Christ, whose feast we celebrate today. When divine grace inspired them, the world and its concupiscence wholly withered away within them; and thus, with every sin destroyed in them, they may rightly say among the rest: “O God, you have rejected us and destroyed us.” For those who in our first parents were rejected by God on account of the grafted fruit [Gen. 3], that same God and man afterward drew to himself upon the wood of the cross. Thus the rejection is devout, and the destruction fatherly: it rejects a person in order to call him back; mortifies in order to give life; humbles in order to exalt; destroys in order to rebuild.

For such destruction both adorns the hearts of the faithful with virtues and cleanses them of vices, concerning which it is said: “Will not one who sleeps rise again?” [Ps. 40.] This is that destruction by which God destroyed these most holy men, in order that he might change Saul into something better—into Paul. Though in the first flower of life, as though in the morning of some wickedness, they devoured prey with Saul, yet afterward, in the evening of this present life, they divided among their neighbors the spoils of truth with Paul [Col. 1011D].

Yet God destroyed differently those of whom it is said, “You will destroy them and not build them up” [Ps. 27:5], and differently those who are changed for the better, of whom it is said here: “O God, you have rejected us and destroyed us” [Col. 1012A]. The former he destroyed unto ruin, not unto resurrection; the latter unto correction, not unto perdition. The former, that they might not be changed for the better; the latter, that they might be built up and healed. The former he destroyed, that they might be cast down with Saul [Acts 9]; the latter, that they might be raised with David [2 Sam. 3]. The former, that they might look back with Lot’s wife; the latter, that they might return to repentance with Peter.

In this manner, then, he rejected and destroyed these most holy men when, through the light of faith and the fire of charity, he graciously shone upon them, so that, kindled by the fire of divine love, they might cleave perpetually to that fire which no temptations can ever extinguish [Matt. 27—citation uncertain]. He also rejected and destroyed them [Ps. 16] when in his mercy he brought them back from darkness to light and from death to life, so that through him they might be delivered from the hell of eternal death—he who says through the prophet: “O death, I shall be your death; O hell, I shall be your bite” [ibid.].

He rejected them, I say, and destroyed them when, displaying his mercies in them, he says according to Isaiah, “He blots out your iniquities” [Isa. 34—citation uncertain], so that every hardship for Christ in the oppression of the present Church might seem the easier to them, because he immediately adds: “I shall not remember your sins” [Ezek. 18—citation uncertain]. He rejected and destroyed them when he took every iniquity from them as a cloud, fitting them for every good work so that they might do his will. The unconquered charity of Christ rejected and destroyed them [Col. 1012C] when it made them alive with him [Col. 2], forgiving them all their offenses.

He rejected and destroyed them when, in order to receive the unfading crown of eternal life [1 Pet. 1], they maintained good conduct among the Gentiles, so that, confirmed by the living and enduring word of God, they might be delivered from the voice of the reproacher and slanderer. He rejected and destroyed them when each, touched inwardly by sorrow of heart, became not only a hearer of the word but also a doer. Whenever he looked in the mirror upon the countenance of his birth in the divine law, he kept himself undefiled from this world.

He rejected and destroyed them when the spirit of discipline, which flees deceit, uprooted every offense from their hearts, so that they might guard themselves all the more diligently from the inclination toward evil thoughts because that same Spirit of truth withdraws himself from thoughts without understanding [Col. 1012D–1013A]. He rejected and destroyed them when each remembered within himself that “the tongue of the imprudent is his own overthrow,” and refused to attach himself to that imprudence, so that through him to whom all the buffoonery of babblers is ever hateful he might be delivered from wicked lips and a deceitful tongue.

He rejected and destroyed them when, filled with the fruit of righteousness, they refused to feast upon the leaven of malice and wickedness; rather, despising the food of falsehood, they feasted upon the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth [1 Cor. 5]. He rejected and destroyed them when, so that in them the threshing of the divine harvests might overtake the vintage, they refused to commit blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, knowing indeed that the Spirit of God’s glory truly rests upon the person who is not ashamed of the name of Christian.

He rejected and destroyed them when, hating every way of iniquity [Ps. 118], they chose instead the way of truth: that is, continually praying in word and deed to him to whom the Psalmist says, “Remove from me the way of iniquity” [ibid., adapted]. He rejected and destroyed them when, in order that the treasure of heavenly wisdom might rest in them, in accordance with Solomon’s command they did not exalt themselves in the thoughts of their soul like a treasure, lest perhaps their strength be dashed to pieces by folly [Ecclus. 6—wording/citation uncertain], should they appear to love iniquity and hate righteousness [Col. 1013B].

He rejected and destroyed them when each, drawn by the love of divine charity, in giving to the poor did not receive a sinner, knowing that one who does good to the righteous will find recompense from the Lord. He rejected and destroyed them when, hating every robber and double-tongued person, they extinguished within themselves the entire fire of detraction and wrath, knowing that, just as confusion and repentance are upon a thief, so the worst devouring is upon a double-tongued person.

He rejected and destroyed them when, freed from sin by the possession of virtue and the laying aside of malice, they became servants of righteousness [Rom. 6], refusing, with that people, to glory in wickedness, concerning whom David says: “Labor and injustice are in its midst” [Ps. 54]. He rejected and destroyed them when that noble saying of the Apostle bore fruit in their hearts: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires” [Rom. 6; Col. 1013C–D].

He rejected and destroyed them when, wholly abandoning earthly care, they did not lend their money at interest, lest any one of them alone incur the punishment of that people concerning whom David says: “Usury and deceit have not departed from its streets” [Ps. 54]. He rejected and destroyed them when, recalling within themselves that every sinner is envious and double-tongued, they refused to share in their unworthy works, lest they imitate with their poisonous tongue the faithlessness of those of whom the Prophet says: “They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue” [Ps. 108].

He rejected and destroyed them when they dwelt with those in divine contemplation to whom it is said, “Blessed are the undefiled in the way” [Ps. 118], so that one day they might receive among them the reward of their labors, of whom it is written: “The Lord knows the days of the undefiled” [Ps. 36; Col. 1014A]. He rejected and destroyed them when, observing the commands of a certain wise man, they fled sins as from the face of a serpent, lest they follow in every respect the errors of those of whom it is written: “Sinners have drawn the sword” [ibid.].

This, beloved brethren, is that destruction by which these most holy martyrs were destroyed among the elect and circumcised fathers, when, clothed with the armor of God, with the weapons of righteousness, they were circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, in the stripping away of the body of flesh. And because no one can drive away the chaos of our vices except one of whom it is said in thanksgiving, “O God, you have rejected us and destroyed us,” therefore the prophet, about to enumerate still other benefits of the Redeemer, immediately adds: “You were angry and had mercy on us” [Col. 1014B].

O merciful anger and health-giving indignation, through which every fruitless manner of life is made fruitful! O merciful anger, which is angry so as to help; threatens so as to spare; takes away so as to restore; hands over so as to rescue; destroys so as to fortify; casts aside so as to receive! O how health-giving is that indignation which turns away so as to look again; closes so as to open; exacts so as to remit; casts down so as to raise; loses so as to seek; lets go so as to preserve!

But what this anger or indignation is, the excellent Prophet testifies, clearly expressing both: “Anger is in his indignation, and life in his will” [Ps. 29]. Anger is, as it were, present in his indignation when he is so angry with the impious and criminal that he does not have mercy. Not that he is to be believed to grow angry or to possess anger, but because his reproof or indignation is called anger in the manner of human speech. And therefore, just as anger in his indignation is the death of sinners, so life in his will is believed to belong to the converted, because he humbles and raises up those who are converted in heart, since he does not will the death of a sinner but that he should be converted and live.

Yet this anger of God is also called, in another sense, his just vengeance, which is not at all completed in the present age but will rather be fully executed without mercy in the future against those who showed no mercy, when he avenges upon the impious and sinful the blood of his servants. For just as then the supreme judgment of heavenly anger will be fulfilled upon the children of the devil, when the impious shall hear: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” [Matt. 25; Col. 1014D], so God’s mercy must be fulfilled in the elect and righteous, when the righteous shall hear: “Come, you blessed of my Father” [ibid.].

These most blessed martyrs N. ought therefore rightly one day to hear this voice of the Son of God with the elect, since formerly in themselves they were accustomed, by living well, to experience what and how great were the Lord’s anger and mercy—of which David, setting before us an example of divine compassion, says: “You were angry and had mercy on us” [Ps. 39—citation uncertain]. For he was, as it were, angry with this most sacred choir of martyrs whenever it sinned through weakness of the flesh; merciful when it cleansed itself after its crimes with tears of repentance. Angry when he destroyed within it the superstitions of every error; merciful when he shone upon it with the light of true faith and truth [Col. 1015A].

God was also angry with it whenever, offending in one commandment of charity, it became guilty of all [Jas. 2]; merciful when it strove to cleave to that charity which “does not rejoice in iniquity but rejoices together with truth” [1 Cor. 13]. Angry whenever it was not merciful to orphans as a father; merciful when, by works of mercy, it took pity on them more than a mother. Angry whenever—far be it—it set falsehood forth with its mouth and did not possess truth in its heart; merciful when, avoiding assemblies of deceivers, it refused to love a lie against its brother.

Angry whenever, burning with a contentious spirit, it walked with a furious man against Solomon’s command [Prov. 25—citation uncertain]; merciful when, obedient to the same eloquent man, it refused to befriend an angry person. Angry whenever by works of mercy it made itself neither pleasing to God nor kindly toward the congregation of the poor; merciful when, through love of the living and enduring word, it delivered one suffering injury from the hand of the proud [Col. 1015B].

Angry whenever, despising the lot of the innocent, it did not rescue those being led to death; merciful when, by the merit of good action, it rescued those dragged to destruction. Angry whenever, setting aside Solomon’s sentence, it returned evil for good to its neighbors [Prov. 17]; merciful when, pursuing the apostolic command with an unconquered heart, it did not return evil for evil or curse for curse [1 Pet. 2].

Angry whenever it imitated the wickedness of those of whom it is written: “The mouth of fools bubbles forth folly” [Prov. 15]; merciful when it followed the wisdom of those of whom it is written: “The tongue of the wise adorns knowledge” [ibid.; Col. 1015C]. Angry whenever, forgetting human weakness, it refused compassion to one needing bread; merciful when it gave its bread to that neighbor of whom Truth says: “Break your bread for the hungry” [Isa. 58].

Angry whenever—far be it—it became an exactor of temporal gain, a hearer of the heavenly word but not a doer; merciful when, neither giving God’s pearls to swine nor the holy thing to dogs, it was a doer of the word and not a hearer only. Angry whenever it delighted in the burden of those riches concerning which it is written: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” [Ps. 61; Col. 1015D]; merciful when, rich in faith and poor in understanding, it was a child in malice and perfect in understanding.

Angry whenever, unarmed against the words of the wicked and contrary to the Apostle’s command, it was deceived by empty words [Eph. 3—citation uncertain]; merciful when, through the incomparable gift of the divine word, it could not be deceived by loftiness of speech. Angry whenever it refused to show cheerful mercy to the poor and did not share their sorrow by distributing its goods to them; merciful when, distributing its possessions for Christ, it desired that its name be inscribed with theirs in the book of life—those who sent portions from what they possessed to those who had prepared nothing for themselves.

Angry whenever it went in the way of those of whom it is written: “The way of the impious shall perish” [Ps. 1]; merciful when it had avoided the lot of that way of which Solomon says: “A wandering path leads to death” [Prov. 13; Col. 1016A].

Therefore, since such anger and so great a mercy of the Creator are benefits solely of divine condescension, the unwavering voice of the martyrs rightly says to him with the Church: “You were angry and had mercy on us.” O merciful anger and incomparable mercy, which always cleanses human hearts of every vice! By it the sinner is invited to pardon, the righteous to life, the martyr to the palm, the confessor to glory. For he does not have mercy unless he is angry, since he is first angry for this purpose: that afterward he may have mercy.

Anger goes before so that mercy may follow; tears go before so that pardon may follow; repentance goes before so that forgiveness may follow; humiliation goes before so that exaltation may follow; confession goes before so that remission may follow; calling goes before so that justification may follow; justification goes before so that glorification may follow. “Those whom he called, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, them he also glorified” [Rom. 8; Col. 1016B].

Therefore let one who is a sinner repent, that he may be justified; but let one who is righteous practice righteousness still further, that he may be glorified. For the efficacy of pure confession, when it has gone before, kills sin and grace arises. Then any sinner seems to sail through this great and wide sea while already in harbor, when before God’s eyes both his sin is setting and the grace by which he is delivered is rising. Thus, while sin appears to fall and grace to rise within us, God is, as it were, angry with us and merciful to us, because, as rain follows wind, so mercy follows anger [Col. 1016C].

Through the works of this mercy these most holy martyrs sought to be delivered from every evil of wickedness; concerning it the Psalmist says: “I shall sing forever of the mercies of the Lord” [Ps. 88]. The same excellent Psalmist expresses this more plainly elsewhere: “His compassions are over all his works” [Ps. 144]. And rightly indeed is the mercy of the Lord exalted above every work: through it a slave is made free, the weak are raised, the humble exalted, the proud humbled, the deaf hear, the mute speak, the lame are cured, the sick are healed, the blind enlightened, lepers cleansed, the dead raised, the sea calmed, and one possessed by a demon delivered.

This is that mercy through which the same flock of martyrs was cleansed by God from all vices. Speaking of himself through the Prophet, he says: “I shall not scatter my mercy from him” [Ps. 88; Col. 1016D]. Through him, now also transferred by God from the night of this present age into his glory, it can rightly say: “In the morning I shall exalt your mercy” [Ps. 59]. For it could not have arrived at this mercy unless it had first experienced the disturbance of heavenly anger. Once this had calmed in its heart all the pools of vices, immediately, through God’s mercy, there came to be a great calm.

But the prophetic utterance witnesses what heavenly anger or mercy is. If you diligently call it to mind, it says: “When you are angry, you shall remember mercy” [Hab. 3; Col. 1017A]. In these words, therefore, beloved brethren, we must take care not to think that God forgets, or is forgetful of us, in such a way that, like a human being, he remembers mercy after anger. Rather, just as that remarkable prophet was disturbed by God’s anger when he said to him, “When you are angry, you shall remember mercy,” so we too, in the manner of human speech, should cry out to God with the Psalmist, as though he had forgotten mercy for us, in words and deeds: “Do not forget the voices of those who seek you” [Ps. 73].

For he seems to remember mercy after anger when, being angry, he does not immediately strike but threatens, so that, when human hearts have been disturbed by his anger, mercy may exclude anger rather than anger exclude mercy. Therefore, lest God be angry with a person in the house of the present Church, it is fitting that the person first be angry with himself through the mercy of God: that is, he should strive to cease from past sins in accordance with that prophetic admonition, “Be angry, and do not sin” [Ps. 4].

For this purpose he must restrain himself from the concerns of fleshly concupiscence: just as he is angry at past sins, so he must beware of future ones, lest he seem to incur the blame of that defense of which the Apostle says: “Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath” [Rom. 12; Col. 1017B]. Thus above all others that person’s anger is praised by the prophetic voice who, after he is angry, remembers mercy.

Accordingly, because such anger and such mercy are signs of divine condescension and compassion, this most holy man, as though giving thanks with the other faithful for the Redeemer’s mercy, rightly says: “You were angry and had mercy on us.” But because, beloved brethren, it would be far too long if on this day we were to compress the exposition of this entire psalm into one sermon, it is good that we reserve what remains to be said for another day, so that then we may have something in our hands from which always to give thanks to God our Creator.

For the present psalm, so that each person who diligently applies himself to divine reading may have something from it, I think it fitting to divide the same psalm into four parts, so that the silent sermon may make those speak who wish to be silent about the martyrs at so many of their feasts [Col. 1017C]. Therefore, since the time is now at hand to bring this sermon to its close, it is fitting that we seek without ceasing the protection of these same martyrs of Christ, so that, through the intercession of their merits, that charity which covers all offenses may reign unconquered in us unto the end, of which the Apostle says: “The end of the commandment is charity, from a good conscience and unfeigned faith” [1 Tim. 1].

But since no one can be active in the workshop of that same perfect charity unless he has first been rejected from the evil person—that is, from himself—by divine destruction, we must pray, beloved brethren, that he who daily in his mercy is angry with and has mercy upon his elect may deign to be angry with and have mercy upon us so gently and so graciously that we too, with these martyrs of Christ, may worthily cry out to him that refrain of prophetic rejoicing: “You were angry and had mercy on us.” May he deign to grant this—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit unto ages of ages. Amen [Col. 1018A].

## Sermon II on the Martyrs

Likewise, on the verse of Psalm 54: “O God, you have rejected us and destroyed us.”

Since, dearest brothers, in the other sermon we have sufficiently explained, as far as we could by the Lord’s grant, what and of what kind the wrath or mercy of God is, it remains for us, under the figure of the holy martyrs N., whose solemnity we celebrate today, to recall some of what follows, so that we may be able to commend the earlier things by the later.

For after the Prophet describes how the only-begotten Son of God, in order to destroy the weakness of human conduct, was angry [Col. 1018B] and had mercy upon us, he immediately wishes to declare that, for the salvation of earthly persons, he stretched the footwear of his Incarnation into Idumaea: “You have moved the earth,” he says, “and troubled it” (Ps. 59). For he moved and troubled the earth—that is, the hearts of earthly people—understood, by the consciousness of sins, when he said to them through the Gospel: “Unless you are converted and become like little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18).

But here, before all else, we must consider that moving is one thing and troubling another, since these two words have a double meaning: namely, because agitation gives birth to groaning, while disturbance gives birth to pain. What this agitation is like Scripture shows, if you ask, where it says: “When you have groaned, you shall be saved.” [Col. 1018C] And what this disturbance is like is declared by the sentence in which the Psalmist says: “Heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled” (Ps. 6).

Through this agitation and disturbance the Lord moved and troubled the hearts of holy righteous persons when he said to them through the prophet: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. 3), lest they should see themselves as unworthy of divine salvation if, having heard this, they were not moved and afraid. In this way their minds were also disturbed and moved when Isaiah said to them and to us: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. 1), so that from their hearts and ours the cry of that heavenly spiritual washing might rise to God, of which the Psalmist says: [Col. 1018D] “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50).

He also moved and troubled them when he said among other things: “Unless you are converted, he has brandished his sword” (Ps. 7); and, lest they should wish to defer even for a little while the remedy of their conversion, he immediately adds: “He has bent his bow and made it ready” (ibid.). In these words, dearest brothers, there is a great abyss of divinity, because, just as open wrath is signified by the sword, so hidden warfare is signified by the bow.

Thus the soul of these martyrs was girded with the sword of this heavenly word “upon your thigh, O most mighty one” (Ps. 44), when through it it had conquered both persecutors without and the devil within, so that it escaped the opposing errors of that sword concerning which it is written: “Sinners have drawn the sword” [Col. 1019A] (Ps. 36). He also bent this bow, by which the New Testament and the Old are denoted, when he meditated restlessly upon the law of the Lord day and night, lest he should be struck by the bow of that evil one, of which it is written: “He shall break the bow, shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire” (Ps. 45).

For these most holy martyrs were thus moved and troubled by the sword of the heavenly word when they were transferred from ancestral oldness into newness of life: instead of worshipping many stone images, they worshipped the one God and Lord, who says through the Prophet: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands” (Ps. 113). They were moved also away from wickedness, so that all unrighteousness might not rule them, when, in order worthily to receive from God the nourishment of heavenly life, [Col. 1019B] they pursued peace with all people and holiness.

They were moved and troubled whenever they despised that path of perversity of which Solomon says: “There is a way which seems right to people” (Prov. 14), lest they should fall into the most evil lot of that same path, concerning which it is added: “Its end leads to death” (ibid.). He also daily moves and troubles the earth of the human conscience when he says: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3), lest we transgress those prophetic commands in which it is said: “Repent and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 3).

One is indeed moved, not unto resurrection but unto ruin, of which Solomon says: “Poverty and disgrace come to one who abandons discipline” (Prov. 13). Others are moved, indeed, not unto ruin but nonetheless unto resurrection, of whom the Prophet says: [Col. 1019C] “Lay hold of discipline, lest at any time the Lord be angry” (Ps. 2). Therefore, since the faithful soul is not worthy to be healed unless through this movement it is unknown to the devil and known to God, the Prophet adds: “Heal its breaches, for it has been shaken” (Ps. 59).

For this most tried man knew that he could by no means be worthily healed unless he first deserved that within himself the water of repentance be troubled; and therefore perhaps he held before the eyes of his mind that sick man of the Gospel who became well after the moving of the water. This breaking, then, made the mind of the holy martyrs stronger in Christ, and rendered their weakness strong for God against the world, [Col. 1019D] concerning which David—whose word does not fail—says: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50).

“Heal,” he says. This is that healing, dearest brothers, which the Psalmist formerly prayed for himself when, turning to the Lord, he said: “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40). This is that healing through which our same Lord healed the brokenness of the saints, who says through the prophet Hosea: “I will heal their brokenness” (Hos. 14), lest they should be continually broken by God through that breaking of which Jeremiah says: “The virgin daughter of my people has been broken by a very grievous wound” (Jer. 14).

Further, their brokenness was healed through him and by him through whom that nation was once struck with the deformity of blindness, for which Elisha said to the Lord: [Col. 1020A] “Strike, I beseech you, O Lord, this nation with blindness” (4 Kings 6). He healed their brokenness, he who “called them and justified them” (Rom. 8); for through him and in him they were cleansed from every stain of vices—he “heals those broken in heart and binds up their wounds” (Ps. 146).

Therefore, because after the wounds of the saints have been healed they must enter the kingdom of heaven through many tribulations (Acts 14), the prophet, declaring how much they suffered under the pressure of the present Church, immediately adds: “You have shown your people hard things” (Ps. 59). For hard things were shown by God to the holy martyrs when, in the persecutions endured by the Church, they suffered harsh and most inhuman [Col. 1020B] torments for him. Therefore we may not undeservedly compare them with the apostolic men, of whom the Apostle says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (Rom. 8).

These holy sons of the Church also suffered hard things for Christ when, following in the footsteps of the apostles, they went away rejoicing from the presence of the council (Acts 5), knowing that they would please divine mercy all the more because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus (ibid.). Thus he showed hard things to his people when he set before them the examples of the fathers who went before, so that they might be instructed by the words of the apostolic reading: “The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8).

But he also showed hard things to his people in another way when, speaking to each person through the Gospel, [Col. 1020C] he says: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart” (Matt. 22). And because no person is established as perfect in this love alone unless he has also the other love which he shows in what follows, declaring how greatly one ought to strive in love toward another, he immediately adds: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (ibid.).

Therefore, dearest brothers, strive as quickly as possible to fulfil these two commandments of love in yourselves, “on which hang all the law and the prophets” (ibid.); and thus each of you may easily weigh within himself how hard the things are which he commands, and how hard the things are which he shows. For, as I judge, he must be sought among the number of angels, [Col. 1020D] not of human beings, who can love the Lord as the Lord commands; or who can so extend himself toward another in accordance with such teaching as to love his neighbour as himself. And therefore each person is his own witness that no one, or scarcely anyone, can be found who wishes another as much good as he wishes himself.

But lest the claims of the preceding sentence lead us too far away, the Lord also once deigned to show hard things to King Hezekiah, when, as a rich man, he gloried in the multitude of his riches: “Set your house in order,” he said, “for you shall die and not live” (Isa. 38). And see how harsh this command seemed to him: he himself showed it when, turning to the wall, he wept most bitterly (ibid.). And so, while through desire for a longer life he wished to escape the lot of sudden death, [Col. 1021A] he gave to everyone who lives and shall see death an example of how willingly he would live.

Our Lord also showed hard things in this manner long ago to his patriarch when, testing his servant Abraham and proving him by testing, he commanded him, in the figure of his Only-Begotten, to kill his son Isaac: “Offer him to me upon one of the mountains which I shall show you” (Gen. 22). And see how harsh and hard that command was: only the person who has an only son, and one beloved, knows.

Likewise, the Lord deigned to show hard things in this way to the sons of Zebedee when he foreshadowed for them, in the figure of his Passion, what they would suffer for him. As you have often heard and will hear in the Gospel reading, he said to them: “You shall drink my cup” (Matt. 20). Thus, then, God and our Lord, who for us “bowed the heavens and came down,” showed hard things to his holy martyrs when, foretelling to them what they would suffer for him, he said: [Col. 1021B] “You shall be hated by all for my name’s sake” (Matt. 10).

Therefore, because after many tribulations by which a person is struck with the hammer of human persecution, he often returns to himself and is bathed in the grace of inward compunction, the Psalmist, after already setting forth the showing of tribulation, immediately adds: “You have given us to drink the wine of compunction” (Ps. 59). This is that cup of love which brought these most blessed martyrs to fellowship in divinity, after the abundance—not of wine but of compunction—had extinguished all the flames of vices found in their hearts.

And the Psalmist, foreseeing that this drink is a drink not of the mouth but of the mind, sweet to the faithful and bitter to the reprobate, says: “My inebriating cup, how excellent it is!” (Ps. 22). [Col. 1021C] From this cup, then, is poured that draught of divine love with which Christ purchased for himself in his blood a Christian people; and the Church, giving it to her beloved in the Song of Songs in the figure of the saints, says: “I will give you a cup from spiced wine and must of my pomegranates” (Cant. 8).

Wine without mixture of another thing is love without pretence; but spiced wine is love with action. Therefore wine that is not plain, but is seasoned with good works and holy virtues, seems especially pleasing to the divine gaze. Truth shows this in the Gospel when he says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14).

And rightly, on account of the affection of excessive love, the Church offers to her beloved not just any drink but must; because must, when it is most fermenting, is never found to fail in its heat until, by its excessive ferment, it seems to cast all impurity out of itself. Therefore by this must of pomegranates is not unfittingly signified the strong love of the saints, who, cleansed in their passion from every stain of vices, seemed to love God with such burning love that neither death nor any tribulation could separate them from the love of Christ.

Now the Punic apple, which is especially abundant in Africa, is called the pomegranate because it overflows with the multitude of its seeds. [Col. 1022A] By this is signified that, just as there are many dwelling places in the kingdom of heaven, so in the present Church there are many tribulations of the righteous. And because the Punic apple has a blood-red colour, it seems to typify not only the blood of Christ’s martyrs but also the Lord’s own blood; and this is why in the Song of Songs he is called by the Church “white and ruddy,” so that he may be understood as white from the innocence he possesses and ruddy from the Passion he suffered.

In that Passion the saving cup was poured out for us, through which these most unconquered martyrs were given the wine of compunction to drink. The power of the Most High, applying the Song of Songs to itself, says: “Drink, friends, and be inebriated, dearly beloved” (Cant. 5). Therefore, whoever lives not for himself but for God drinks worthily from this cup of love, becoming a participant in that saving drink concerning which it is said: [Col. 1022B] “You have given us the wine of compunction to drink” (Ps. 59).

And rightly is he given wine of inward compunction to drink who is stung inwardly in his mind over his sins; for the impurity of defilement is perfectly washed away in proportion as it is often washed by the tear of the heart. For raging destruction does not follow where this burning medicine has gone before. This is indeed that reconciling compunction by which Mary the sinner was reconciled to God when, by the hidden judgment of divinity, her many sins were forgiven her because she loved much (Luke 7).

David the patriarch also, perceiving that he had formerly offended divine mercy, was turned by this wine of compunction to repentance when, through inward inspiration, he acknowledged his iniquity: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy” (Ps. 50). Blessed Peter likewise deserved to trouble himself in repentance by such compunction when, after his threefold denial of the Lord, returning to himself he wept bitterly. Previously, when accused by a maidservant of being one of God’s friends, he answered her: “I do not know what you are saying” (Matt. 26).

Thus these martyrs of Christ also, desiring in every respect to please divine mercy, were very often given this wine of compunction to drink through the Lord’s inward inspiration, when the oppression of the present life not only fed them with bread of tears but also gave them drink in tears by measure. Therefore, so that we too, dearest brothers, may give glory to God [Col. 1022D] with these martyrs of Christ, let us humbly implore his mercy: since he who remained and remains always one and the same with the Father and the Holy Spirit, may now heal our brokenness with most merciful compassion; so that he who showed hard things to his saints in the present world through many tribulations may, through the intercession of their merits, grant us also with them drink in tears by measure. Thus, pierced by divine inspiration, we may worthily sing with them that saying of prophetic rejoicing: “You have given us the wine of compunction to drink.” May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. ON ONE CONFESSOR

[Col. 1023A]

On the passage in which fine flour is commanded by the Law to be offered in sacrifice, where it is said of it: “In a frying-pan, sprinkled with oil, it shall be fried; the priest who has succeeded his father by right shall offer it hot as a most sweet savour to the Lord, and it shall all be burned upon the altar” (Lev. 6:21–22).

Always, dearest brothers, every faithful person is built up by the history of sacred reading if he often calls the precepts of the ancient Law to mind, because he receives from it the fruit of righteousness more fervently if he savours spiritually what he reads carnally in those precepts. Accordingly, we do not think it will greatly harm your charity if, from the different kinds of royal sacrifices, we say here a few things out of many, by which this most sacred bishop [Col. 1023B] N., whose feast we celebrate today, following the example of Moses, often appeased the wrath of the Lord for his own soul and for those of his subjects.

For while the vices of himself and of his subjects were still tender at the root, he applied different kinds of legal sacrifices. Among these, this first comes to mind: fine flour is commanded by the Law to be offered in sacrifice. Because this alone cannot make a person perfect, oil must, according to the precept of the ancient Law, be mixed with it, so that one may be joined to the other in the unity of faith: “Sprinkled with oil, it shall be fried in a frying-pan,” it says.

For just as fine flour signifies purity of life, and oil works of mercy, so the frying-pan, made of strong iron, signifies the strong frying of spiritual zeal. Knowing this, this most holy man made his heart a frying-pan, [Col. 1023C] in which he burned strongly through zeal for righteousness against the vices of his neighbours, when for the sins of those who erred the anger of that sternness was kindled within him of which the Apostle says: “Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11).

Although he seemed greatly tormented in the frying-pan of his heart whenever he saw any weak persons abandoning eternal things and delighting in temporal affairs, nonetheless he always moderated the burning of spiritual zeal against his neighbours’ vices in such a way that he was never, or only rarely, carried headlong in fury beyond the bounds of patience. For he knew that no sacrifice is so pleasing and dear to almighty God as zeal for souls. Hence the Psalmist, bearing witness to truth in this matter, says of himself: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. 68).

But how gladly almighty God receives this frying of spiritual zeal is made most plainly clear to us by the same Law, where fine flour itself is commanded to be offered in sacrifice, concerning which it is written: [Col. 1023D] “Sprinkled with oil, it shall be fried in a frying-pan.” This fine flour in the frying-pan is nothing other than the pure mind of the righteous person, whitened with the fine flour of virtues from the blackness of vices; and it is shown to be worthily sprinkled with the oil of mercy through the care of spiritual zeal when one person is joined to another in love.

Therefore, because the clean mind of this most sacred priest had no stain in itself of the principal vices, he seems not undeservedly to have expressed in himself the pure and sincere substance of this legal fine flour. And because through the oil of mercy he always burned and shone before the Lord like a lamp, he mixed with the fine flour—that is, with the love of mercy—without interruption.

For he recalled within himself what was commanded in the Law: he sprinkled with oil the flour which was cooked in the frying-pan of the heart, when through the affliction of spiritual zeal he was accustomed to burn in the frying-pan of his mind against his neighbours’ vices in such a way that, through works of mercy, he seemed no less to burn and shine in the sight of the Lord. [Col. 1024A] Therefore, because it helps nothing if anyone has zeal for uprightness in his mind unless through the fire of love he shines forth by the merit of good action, the ancient Law adds: “He shall offer it hot as a most sweet savour to the Lord.”

For fine flour, sprinkled with oil and fried in a frying-pan, is commanded to be offered hot as a most sweet savour to the Lord, because unless zeal possesses love in the teacher’s mind, the fine flour does not seem to have heat. Hence this most pious priest N., who bore in the breast of his mind the ornaments of the four virtues, often offered this hot fine flour as a most sweet savour to the Lord through the ardour of holy zeal, when, through the fire of divine love by which he took away the coldness of wickedness from his neighbours’ hearts, he himself always burned and shone in the sight of almighty God.

He is further shown to have offered this fine flour—by which, as we have said, purity of mind is signified—hot as a most sweet savour to the Lord when, lest that same flour of faith lose heat in his heart, he stirred up within himself through the uprightness of spiritual zeal the love of twofold charity. [Col. 1024B] He also offered this fine flour hot to God as a most sweet savour in another way: when, out of compassion for his neighbours, he mixed the oil of the fine flour, that is, the love of mercy, lest he should be thought less worthy to preside over the Lord’s sheep if one seemed to lack something from another through the pastor’s negligence.

For, lest one person seem in any respect to lack something from another, it is fitting that in the hearts of teachers one thing be mixed with another without interruption, because any work whatsoever without mercy is like a lamp without oil. Therefore this most tried man was accustomed always to temper with the oil of gladness the frying of the heart produced by spiritual zeal toward his neighbours, when, kindled by the heat of that zeal, he both slew the vices of his subjects with the sword of severity and loved through the love of charity those whom he seemed to pursue.

Hence, that we may know what the Law still suggests that we should do concerning the same fine flour, it immediately adds: “The priest shall offer it, who has succeeded his father by right.”

[Col. 1024C]

For that priest succeeds his father by right who attests by his work what he believes; because the one who stands immovable in faith and work in the service of the Creator shows himself to be the son of the supreme priest. [Col. 1024D] That priest also succeeds his father by right who in himself somehow imitates the form of the divine nature, so that he who is earthly from the earth may strive also to become heavenly from heaven.

Thus this most worthy priest of Christ, Bishop N., [Col. 1025A] by worthily carrying out for God the business of the pontifical office, succeeded his Father, namely Christ, by right in the priesthood. His mind was intent upon love of that supreme High Priest who “entered once into the holy places through his own blood, having found eternal redemption” (Heb. 9). He is shown to have succeeded his Father by right because he attested in work what he believed in heart, when, for love of him, he went from virtue to virtue—him through whom “one believes with the heart unto righteousness, and confession is made with the mouth unto salvation” (Rom. 10).

He succeeded his Father by right because in his inward person he expressed in some degree the form of divinity, when he renounced evil thoughts and unchaste deeds in order that he who had borne the image of the earthly might bear also the image of the heavenly. He succeeded his Father by right because in a good and excellent heart he never resisted virtues or yielded to vices, when he was unwilling in any way, through the baseness of his works, to oppose the nobility of mind with which he appeared to be ennobled in Christ.

Thus we too, dearest brothers, following the example of this most sacred man, must always labour sleeplessly that we may be called and may be sons of him who says: “I have said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81), lest we at some time be found guilty before the supreme Judge and disinherited from the kingdom of heaven—the Judge who transferred this most holy man into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

For if, following his examples, we wish by doing good works to pursue one another what is good, that fine flour of the Law will seem to be wholly burned upon the altar, concerning which the same Law, giving command, adds: “And it shall all be burned upon the altar” (Lev. 6). By this altar nothing other than purity of mind seems to be understood, which is said to be not only a sacrifice but even a holocaust to God, provided that within it the frying of strong zeal burns so ardently for the salvation of souls that the virtue of mercy burns and shines no less within it.

Otherwise a holocaust, which in Latin is called *totum incensum*, “wholly burned,” is truly accomplished by no believer unless, through the fire of love—which that legal fire spiritually signifies—he burns up every vice that makes evil noise in his heart. Therefore, since in God’s sight, as the judgment of sacred Scripture testifies, a holocaust is greater than sacrifice, it is necessary for every believer, by the sacrifice of praise, to consider diligently both what he owes to God and what he owes to his neighbour, [Col. 1025D] so that through the fire of charity he may set his whole mind aflame in the love of the Creator.

He offers sacrifice who, with Leah and Martha, pleases God by rightly serving with temporal goods; but he offers holocaust who, with Rachel and Mary, gives himself more attentively to divine contemplation. He offers sacrifice who reads historically that a dry rod once brought forth a flower; but he offers holocaust who believes spiritually that an unwedded virgin bore the Saviour. He offers sacrifice who abandoned the gains of worldly desire with Matthew; but he offers holocaust who climbed the tree of the cross with Zacchaeus by the merits of virtues.

Therefore this most holy man too was a sacrifice when, lifted up in divine contemplation, he set his whole mind aflame with the fire of divine love.
