He was a sacrifice whenever, through love of neighbour, he descended the ladder of virtues with descending angels; but a holocaust when, through love of God, he ascended that same ladder with ascending angels. [Col. 1026A] He was a sacrifice whenever, with Mary the sinner, he washed the feet of the Lord’s Incarnation with tears of repentance; but a holocaust whenever, with the ointment of good work, he raised the head of his own mind to the heights of divinity.

He was a sacrifice when, in the course of the present life, he slept as it were with Jacob on the way, away from the love of temporal things; but a holocaust when, resting with him upon the ladder of virtues from above, he passed to the heights through the vision of contemplation. He was a sacrifice when, announcing the commandments of the Law historically to the people of God, he descended as it were from the mountain with Moses; but a holocaust when, examining them spiritually, he ascended as it were the mountain with Moses.

He was a sacrifice when, descending as it were from the mountain with Jesus in order to give the lower commandments of God to the crowd on foot, he stood in a level place; but a holocaust when, because he was a bishop, making a bridge from the hearts of his subjects to the supreme High Priest, he ascended the mountain as it were with Jesus when he saw the crowds. He was a sacrifice when he showed to Christ’s priests, according to the command of truth, whatever he found vicious in his mind; [Col. 1026B] but a holocaust when, by reason of the outstanding nobility of mind which he drew from the knowledge of divinity, he always flew with the wings of virtues from low things to high.

He was a sacrifice when, having renounced the world but not yet perfectly clinging to the Lord, he still limped as it were on one foot with Jacob; but a holocaust when his other foot remained sound because in his mind everything that passes away seemed to pass away. He was a sacrifice when, serving as a soldier for God, he did not involve himself in worldly business, in order to please him to whom he had proved himself; but a holocaust when, applying himself to divine contemplation, he likewise desired to please him concerning whom the Psalmist says: “Be still, and see that I am the Lord” (Ps. 45).

He was a sacrifice when, weeping through fear of punishment, he received the lower watered land, as it were with Achsah, daughter of Caleb; but a holocaust when, weeping for love of the kingdom of heaven, he possessed the upper watered land with the same Achsah.

But because the judgment of sacred reading has sufficiently stated how this most pious man was both holocaust and sacrifice, it remains, since place and time aptly present the occasion, briefly to say how he offered himself to God as both together. For he offered sacrifice and holocaust to God when, recalling what he owed to God and what he owed to his neighbour, he rendered “to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22). [Col. 1026D] He desired to be sacrifice and holocaust to God when, like Moses, he often entered and went out from the tabernacle of the Lord: sacrifice indeed when, for the weakness of his neighbours, he praiseworthily went out into the things of the world; but holocaust when, lifted up in divine contemplation, he humbly entered into the things of God.

He was sacrifice and holocaust when he had the loins of his mind girded with the virtue of chastity, and yet himself shone no less within before God with the lamp of good works, following in this the grace of the life-giving Spirit and not of the killing letter, while wishing both to do this and not to omit that.

These things, then, dearest brothers, which we have now said particularly about this most holy man, we may apply generally to ourselves. For if we desire to share with him the reward of eternal recompense, we must walk as he walked. Therefore, to repeat what we have already said, we offer fine flour if we preserve purity of mind in the heart, cleansed by the example of those from every defilement of vices of whom it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart” (Matt. 5). [Col. 1027B]

We appropriately mix oil with this fine flour when we show our neighbours works of charity and mercy, because our sacrifice is especially pleasing to almighty God if, together with the severity supplied by spiritual zeal, the hand is not idle from mercy. Then we rightly put the same fine flour, sprinkled with the oil of gladness as the Lord commanded in the Law, into the frying-pan if our heart, through the consuming power of spiritual zeal—shown more perfectly in care for souls—is proved to be not only a sacrifice but also a holocaust to God. We offer it hot to God as a sweet savour when zeal for uprightness possesses the love of charity.

For we ourselves are the frying-pan in which that fine flour is offered if, through the heat of virtues, every smoke of vices has vanished from us. We offer sacrifice if we make no provision for the flesh in its desires; but we offer holocaust if we set our whole purpose ablaze in love for Divinity. We also offer sacrifice if, after the leaven of malice and wickedness has been removed from us, we sacrifice to God upon the altar of our heart a sacrifice of righteousness; but we offer holocaust when, by the completion of good work, we desire to be enrolled in perpetual eternity with him to whom the Psalmist says: “I will offer you fat holocausts” (Ps. 65). [Col. 1027C]

But we offer sacrifice and holocaust without blemish if our heart, stripped of all vices, has been wholly burned by the fire of divine love, so that through the incense of good action it may worthily be compared with this legal fine flour, concerning which it is said: “And it shall all be burned upon the altar.” For then the fine flour is wholly burned upon the altar if God is loved by us with the whole mind and the whole strength—provided, however, that through the inward ardour of spiritual zeal we also kindle in the frying-pan of our heart love for brotherly correction.

For those who correct their erring neighbours and yet know how to moderate spiritual zeal in that correction become indeed both sacrifice and holocaust to almighty God. Therefore, dearest brothers, it is necessary that in this evil time we seek the aid of this most sacred priest, so that through his merits and prayers God may fill us with that spiritual zeal concerning which it is written: “My zeal has made me waste away” (Ps. 118); so that we too, [Col. 1028A] with him, may through love of neighbour mix the oil of mercy with this legal fine flour in such a way that, through love of God, we may be able continually to offer that same fine flour hot as a most sweet savour to the Lord, lest, oppressed by the coldness of all iniquity and wickedness, we pass into the number of those concerning whom it is said: “The charity of many shall grow cold” (Matt. 24). May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages.

## SERMON IV. ON ONE CONFESSOR AND BISHOP

On the passage in which the Law commands: “Fire shall always burn upon the altar; the priest shall feed it, laying wood upon it every morning; and, after the holocaust has been placed upon it, he shall burn upon it the fat of the peace offerings. This is a perpetual fire, which shall never fail from the altar” (Lev. 6:12–13).

[Col. 1028B]

Because our Lord Jesus Christ, dearest brethren, willed that through the preachers of the Church his name should at that time be spread everywhere among the nations—when, to enlighten the hearts of the faithful, he sent his fire upon the earth and willed it to burn vehemently—we have judged it fitting, on the feast of this most holy priest N., whose solemn observance we celebrate today, to recall that fire of the Law which this same outstanding preacher of Christ once continually kindled in the souls of those subject to him. For the ancient Law, formerly foretelling to us in a figure how each of the faithful ought diligently to burn continually with the fire of divine love, instructs us in a certain place concerning this: “Fire,” it says, “shall always burn upon the altar.” [Col. 1028C] And immediately it foreshadows how, for the nourishment of this same fire, no rest from daily exercise is to be granted to any priest: “Which,” it says, “the priest shall nourish, placing wood upon it every morning, day by day.” Then it indicates what kind of holocaust ought to give forth fragrance to God in the hearts of the elect: “When,” it says, “the holocaust has been laid on it, he shall burn above it the fat of the peace-offerings.” And because this same fire ought always and without cessation to burn upon the altar of our heart, it immediately adds: “This fire,” it says, “is perpetual; it shall never fail from the altar.”

Therefore, if we are to examine what has now been related historically, it is time to return by expounding these four points which we have set forth. “Fire,” it says, “shall always burn upon the altar.” For our heart is the altar of God, provided that we ourselves are children of light and [Col. 1028D] children of the day; so that, as if cut from living stones and squared by virtue, gifts and sacrifices for sins may worthily be offered to God within us. Hence that legal fire shall not without reason always burn upon the altar—that is, the ardor of divine love ought to burn without interruption upon the altar of our heart, continually receiving strength to burn from that fire of which we have spoken, which the Lord sent upon the earth and willed vehemently to be kindled (Luke 12).

Lest this fire should at any time seem to fail in the hearts of those subject to him, this most holy priest was accustomed every morning, day by day, to place wood upon it—that is, examples of the ancient Fathers—so that, when every twisting of vice had been burned away in their hearts by that same fire, the fire and lamp of faith and charity might kindle them to [Col. 1029A] divine love. Therefore, lest the righteous Judge should justly condemn us at some time in the future judgment because of the blindness of our heart, it is fitting that each of us, most beloved brethren, should inflame himself with the pursuit of charity by whatever efforts he can; thus laying up in his heart the testimony of evangelical truth, so that the flame of charity may never fail upon the altar of his heart.

For it often happens to some who are still less perfect in charity that a certain night of wickedness extinguishes in their hearts whatever fire of divine love was once kindled; and so, gradually failing, it will very swiftly be extinguished in their minds unless it is inwardly renewed among them each day by the use of examples from the Scriptures. Knowing this, this most holy man not only continually renewed [Col. 1029B] this fire upon the altar of his own heart, but also, in nourishing it in the hearts of the faithful, daily supplied them most abundantly with wood—that is, testimonies of Scripture—so that that legal holocaust might give fragrance to God in their hearts, concerning which the ancient Law adds: “When,” it says, “the holocaust has been laid on it, he shall burn above it the fat of the peace-offerings.”

For whoever wishes to make peace between himself and God must first kindle within himself the torch of twofold love; for then he worthily renders to God from himself a most sweet fragrance, if, for love of God and neighbor, he bends himself toward every lowly thing through the practice of charity. Accordingly, after this most holy man had been kindled by the same fire, he governed his soul not by strength and power but by counsel and mercy; considering the inward things of his thoughts, [Col. 1029C] he laid himself upon the holocaust of his heart, when, spiritually kindling within himself what the Law commanded carnally, he spiritually cast out every vice that had lived carnally in him.

For, in order that by this offering, making peace between himself and God, he might attain the sweetness of everlasting peace, he was accustomed to burn the fat of the peace-offerings—that is, the inward richness of his new manner of life—to God. When all sins had been burned in his heart by the fire of divine love, he offered himself to God as a sacrifice of a sweet fragrance. And because the love of this same divine charity remains always unquenchable in the hearts of the elect, this most blessed man also strove [Col. 1029D] to follow the remaining commands of the same Law, in which it is said: “This fire is perpetual; it shall never fail upon the altar.”

For no one is proved truly to love God unless neither tribulation nor distress can separate him from God’s charity (Romans 8); because the love of inward affection never wastes away in idleness in the minds of those in whom the fervor of divine charity continually increases from day to day. Knowing this, this blessed priest was increasingly accustomed to despise worldly prosperity for Christ, precisely because he never permitted the fire of divine charity to fail upon the altar of his heart; so that he might cling through everlasting ages to that fire which no temptations can ever extinguish.

Moreover, through that same fire of charity he recalled the sheep entrusted to him from death to life, from darkness [Col. 1030A] to light, so that, by the lamp of good works, they might follow him as their forerunner and guide to the very Author of light. For he had so accustomed himself continually to burn inwardly through the fire of faith and the flame of charity that he appeared no less to shine outwardly to his neighbors through examples of good work. Therefore, because by such teaching he was always accustomed to present himself to Christ’s ministers as a model of good living, we believe that in the future he will have nothing in common with those at the left; rather, he must at some time have his portion with those men of apostolic preaching at the right, to whom evangelical truth once said: “Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12).

And therefore it is necessary that you also, O Christian, carefully consider within yourself day and night how, after the example of this man, you may continually kindle in yourself the fire of divine charity through the testimonies of Scripture, knowing that you will become a member of the supreme Priest in no other way unless you place before yourself every morning, day by day, the examples of the ancient Fathers. And so, in order that you may be able to serve God worthily every day, you must nourish without cessation the flame of divine charity upon the altar of your heart, lest something worse happen to you if the night of some blindness extinguishes in your heart the fire of heavenly love.

For this is that fire which the ancient Godhead formerly scattered more widely through his preachers, when, for the enlightenment of the nations, fire blazed in his sight, by which the hearts of the faithful might be kindled to faith by God with those coals of which the Prophet adds: “Coals,” he says, [Col. 1030B] “were kindled by him” (Psalm 17). For what else were the Apostles and their successors but coals, since through the example of good work and the light of preaching they burned both inwardly for themselves and outwardly for others? For this purpose they were accustomed, by mighty force, to strike the hearts of the faithful with those arrows of the heavenly word, of which it is written: “Sharp arrows of a mighty one” (Psalm 119), so that they too, laid waste of vices and cleansed of sins, might be made like those coals of which the same Prophet adds: “With desolating coals” (ibid.).

By “desolating coals” are signified all converts who, as though first extinguished by sin and afterwards rekindled by righteousness, turn from dead works to Christ, so that in the desolation of vices and the practice of virtues they may continually learn from heavenly words how to revive without cessation from darkness to light and from death to life. This teaching was by no means hidden from the man of whom we speak, since by the mystery of the heavenly word he always directed his life through good morals and upright deeds, so that in his heart, from incestuous he might become chaste, and from impure, pure; that it might become a desolate place, ever ready to be made a dwelling-place of God in the Holy Spirit. Therefore he was not without reason one of those same coals, since by the light of good work he was accustomed always to burn and shine inwardly and outwardly for himself and the Church; so that, although the ardor of divine charity in him seemed rarely or never to be extinguished, all his glory was nevertheless always, like the glory of a king’s daughter, [Col. 1031A] from within (Psalm 44).

And those two disciples likewise burned like coals with the fire of that same divine charity. After the Lord’s resurrection, they did not know that he was speaking and walking with them; later, in repentant recollection, they recalled that they had spoken with the Messiah: “Was not,” they say, “our heart burning within us while he spoke on the way?” (Luke 24). Thus long ago the lawgiver Moses burned; thus Aaron and Phinehas burned; in this manner David too burned with Elijah, just as did those two disciples to whom the Lord spoke on the way.

Did not Moses burn with the fire of charity, when, resisting God’s wrath, he wished to exchange the death of the falling people for his own death? For he said to the Lord, as you have often been able to read in the book of Exodus: “Forgive them this sin; otherwise blot [Col. 1031B] me out of the book which you have written” (Exodus 32). Did not Aaron too burn, kindled by the same fire of charity, when, likewise resisting God’s wrath, he stood between the living and the dead, taking a censer so that he might appease the wrath of God’s immense fury with the smoke of incense? Did not Phinehas burn strongly with the zeal of charity, when he was accustomed to slay those engaging in wantonness with foreign women in the very act of intercourse, and thus, by pouring out abundantly the blood of the Israelite people, appeased the divine fury? Did not Elijah too, a man like us and subject to suffering, possess in his heart an unquenchable fervor of the same charity, when grieving that rain from heaven had long been withheld from the parched earth, he obtained by his prayers both rain from heaven and fruitfulness for the earth? Did we not recognize David as kindled by the same fire of charity, who, as [Col. 1031C] we read in the books of Kings, once placed himself as a barrier before his sheep, when he prayed for those who had perished through the smiting angel: “It is I,” he said, “who have sinned” (2 Kings 24); “these, who are sheep—what have they done?”

We see also another great mystery similar to these in John, who once recalled God’s people in the wilderness to his ways. According to the testimony of the Godhead, he was “a burning and shining lamp” (John 5): when, showing himself worthy to receive the word of Truth, he burned inwardly in desire and shone outwardly to others by his word. Since, therefore, we have sufficiently set forth the greatness of the charity in the hearts of the preceding Fathers, it remains to relate something similar about Paul, the teacher of the nations. For he too burned strongly with the same fire of charity as they did, when he wished himself to become accursed [Col. 1031D] for his brethren. And elsewhere he likewise showed how great was the fervor of divine charity within him: “Who is weak,” he says, “and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Corinthians 11).

We can also know the example of his charity more clearly from this: that he said he was in travail for the salvation of the Galatians, when, for the restoration in them of the power of divine love, he said: “My little children, for whom I am again in travail until Christ be formed in you” (Galatians 4). Therefore, because these most blessed Fathers did such things not with the zeal of bitterness but with the zeal of loving-kindness, when they kindled the fire of divine charity in the hearts of their neighbors, it must be known that, just as [Col. 1032A] there are two kinds of zeal in sacred discourse—the zeal of bitterness and the zeal of love—so also there are two fires: the fire of wrath and the fire of love.

That woman once seemed to possess the zeal of bitterness who, envying the son of another woman, said: “Let it be neither mine nor yours, but let it be divided” (3 Kings 3). But the Psalmist possessed the zeal of love when, sighing over the iniquity of the Jews, he said: “Zeal for my house has consumed me” (Psalm 68). Therefore, since we have briefly treated historically of the two kinds of zeal, let us likewise distinguish the two fires. You may learn more fully what the fire of divine wrath is from him who spoke through the prophet Moses: “A fire,” he says, “has been kindled in my wrath” (Jeremiah 15). But you may learn from the Law what the fire of love is, [Col. 1032B] where, instructing us concerning the eating of the paschal lamb, it says: “If anything,” it says, “remains, you shall burn it with fire” (Exodus 12).

Therefore, dearest brethren, so that we may be able both to extinguish the one fire in our hearts and kindle the other, it is fitting that with all our mind and all devotion we seek the aid of this most holy priest, so that through his merits and prayers the fire of divine wrath may be quenched within us, and the fire of love may deign always to enlighten our hearts. And since all flesh will one day waste away before the fire of the Lord’s wrath, when, to distinguish the good and the evil, fire shall blaze in his sight (Psalm 49), we must pray that we may not then be devoured with the reprobate and wicked by the eternal fire, when “in his wrath he shall trouble them, and fire shall devour them” [Col. 1032C] (Psalm 20); but that we may instead deserve to be delivered from it through that fire of divine charity which long ago came in a dove upon the only-begotten Son of God and in fire upon the disciples. May he himself deign to grant this to us, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the same Holy Spirit, unto ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON V. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH AND THE VENERATION OF RELICS

I rejoice, and our heart is made glad with manifold exultation whenever it festively celebrates the memory of the saints, by whose annual observances our Church flourishes in splendor. For our Church, made joyful by very many solemnities of saints and rendered beautiful with varied adornment, [Col. 1032D] shines as though blossoming in the flowering beauty of spring and smiles joyfully upon all who behold it. And not without reason: for as often as, having celebrated the saints’ festal birthdays with due honor, we glory in the Lord, so often are we, aided by their prayers and merits, flooded with the abundant grace of the blessing of our Creator.

For whatever praise and honor is bestowed upon the soldiers of a king is all credited to the glory of the king whose sceptre marks those soldiers. Nor is there any doubt that we always have as our advocates in heaven those whose festivals we observe on earth with the zeal of devout devotion. For if our spirit, though not yet stripped of the material of flesh and yet sometimes raised to the stars by the fervor of twofold love, strives to pour out prayers to the Lord for those whom it loves, then much more [Col. 1033A] must we believe that the souls of the saints, ardent with the fullness of the highest love, descend at their solemnities, cherishing the pledges of their bodies, intercede for the salvation of their faithful, and bestow the gift of due recompense upon their venerators.

Having, therefore, the eminent pledges of this hope—the remains of those blessed spirits themselves—let us celebrate the praises of the saints with fitting honors; and let us all the more extol with due praises their festal joys, whose ashes and bones this our particular church shelters more abundantly in her bosom. You know, dearest brethren, these unique endowments of our particular church: in whose weighty bosom we rest joyfully; behold how joyfully she cherishes, whence she flourishes richly; how exceedingly wealthy she is through the ashes of saints and virgin flowers, [Col. 1033B] in that she preserves intact the coverings of those truly blessed, and possesses bones gathered far and wide from both sexes. “Therefore rejoice and exult in her, all you who love her” (Psalm 31). Rejoice with great gladness, and joyfully receive the celebrated joys of today’s festival.

And so that we may glory more splendidly in the Lord during this solemnity, the authority of Scripture commends the same thing to us when it records these words: “Rejoice,” it says, “in the Lord, and exult, you righteous; and glory, all you upright in heart” (Psalm 96 [printed *XCXVI*]). But if we are not yet numbered among the righteous and upright, still through desire and choice, under the patronage of the righteous saints, we must strive at least not to be found altogether devoid of righteousness.

Therefore celebrate with joyful gratitude the saving [Col. 1033C] solemnities of this day: namely, for the chosen and illustrious pearls of this Church and for the blooming and glittering flowers of our chosen nurse. We declare that we ought to exult today for this reason. First, because our Church shines, wreathed in the blooming freshness of apostolic verdure and in emerald gems. Second, because she gleams brightly with the blood-red roses of martyrs. Next, because she shines adorned with the most brilliant pearls of confessors. Then, because she grows white with flowering virgin lilies. Finally, because enriched by the abundance of very many saints of both sexes, like the fragrance of many spices, she gives forth the sweetest scent, blossoms, flourishes, thrives, and is mighty. The constancy of faith of all these strengthens us; the height of their hope lifts us up [Col. 1033D] and the fullness of their charity gives us joy.

Let this be a joyful day among us, commended to us, dearest brethren, by the commemoration of so many and such great saints. Let it proceed in melodious jubilation, since the welcome fellowship of angels and saints alike celebrates it with harmonious song. For of this festal joy of great salvation we sing from Scripture in the psalm: “The voice of exultation and salvation has been heard in the tents of the righteous” (Psalm 32). Most fittingly indeed may the voice of exultation and salvation be heard today in this dwelling, because, in the celebration of this day, while a general commemoration is made of all the saints whose relics are contained in this Church, we believe their praises resound alike in heaven and on earth: while we on earth [Col. 1034A] embrace ashes and bones with devout love, and the rejoicing angels sing in heaven over the fellowship of souls: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2).

Indeed, we believe that an angelic presence comes together with the saints for this solemnity also—provided that we duly celebrate it with fitting honor, through holiness of life, so that our voice may deserve to be joined to the voice of both kinds of dwellers in heaven. Otherwise, we do not fittingly commemorate the great celebration of this day with worthy praises unless through holiness of life we ourselves have become the praise of God. For it is written: “Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclesiasticus 15). Therefore, renouncing the vices of sins, let us circumcise the foreskin of our heart, so that, touched by the fire of divine love and with cleansed lips, we may gratefully sing hymnic praises [Col. 1034B] to the Lord of Hosts with saints and angels, and may at last deserve to be associated with their fellowship in heaven.

Let us therefore wipe the sinful, corrupting dust from the eye of the mind, look upon those in whose praise this day is called celebrated, and follow their footsteps. For we believe that we shall attain the glory of those whose life we imitate. And if we struggle to be impressed with the model of their form, we shall doubtless also be set apart from their fellowship. What share has the faithful with the unfaithful? Or what has sobriety to do with light and darkness? What has God’s temple to do with idols?

For every soul loves what is like itself. Hence a certain wise man says: “Every animal loves what is like itself, and so does every human being his neighbor” [Col. 1034C] (Ecclesiasticus 13). “All flesh shall join itself to what is like itself, and every human being shall associate with his like. How shall the wolf have fellowship with the lamb, and likewise at some time sin with the righteous? What fellowship has a holy man with a dog?” What share or fellowship, then, I ask you, do you think the incestuous will have with the chaste; the drunkard with the sober; the robber or unjust person with the righteous or holy; the blasphemer or slanderer with the good speaker; the liar with the truthful; the obstinate or avaricious with the generous; the shameful person with the devout?

You therefore, dearest brethren, who are called faithful by the name of Christianity, refuse to be reckoned unbelievers by pagan manners. You who are styled “light in the Lord” by the apostolic character, do not allow yourselves to be assigned through the gloomy darkness of vices to the prince of darkness. [Col. 1034D] You who are portrayed in the page of sacred discourse as the temple of God, struggle with all your strength not to set up images of gods in your hearts. For whoever loves anything more than God has plainly already set up an idol in the sanctuary of his heart; he falls down in service to it as often as he cultivates it persistently and subjects himself to its dominion.

For it is written: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with all your strength” (Matthew 22). Thus he alone must be loved supremely, who alone must be worshipped and cultivated with the greatest earnestness. Whatever, therefore, is contrary to the worship or exercise of this love must assuredly be eliminated from the very marrow. Yet we are taught by apostolic doctrine that the structure of our body has been chosen as the dwelling-place of God. “Do you not know,” he says, [Col. 1035A] “that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 6). And again: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are. But if anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Corinthians 3).

For this reason, dearest brethren, judge it necessary to cleanse God’s temple from every filth of sin; to eradicate utterly all idols of transitory things; to drive out the impediments of vicious action; to spread more broadly the fabric of prayers; to illuminate it with the splendors of charitable ardor; and to sprinkle it with the fragrance of every virtue, so that you may gain for yourselves the inhabitant of this temple as gracious and as the giver of grace. And in order that we may become effective workers in this task, suitable patrons must be sought by earnest prayers—the predecessors in this work whom we venerate today. [Col. 1035B] Thus first they are to be rendered favorable by devoted veneration; afterwards they are to be invoked with greater confidence. But we make their ears more certainly attentive to us if, by the witness of our conduct, we have been emulators of their goodness.

Behold, they themselves, clothed in the material of flesh, as evident signs make clear, lived honorable lives before God and human beings, free from and untouched by every criminal deed; and they kept their hands undefiled by the pollution of this world. They despised the flower of the world with all its pleasures and sought heavenly things more urgently with every intention of their hearts. Persevering in fasts and prayers, they subdued the claims of the flesh and strengthened the spirit. They did not hesitate to engage the enemy of salvation with a warlike hand, [Col. 1035C] and, girded with divine arms, they overthrew him; [Col. 1036A] yielding in no respect to his savagery, but resisting by fighting bravely to the end.

When they had overcome his tyranny by victorious hand, they inscribed for themselves the triumphal titles of the supreme King in the court of their own blood, by which their memorial shall flourish through the ages. With the turning cycle of the year it always blooms again with the renewed fruit of praise, and, while we gain merit for it, it puts forth new shoots. Therefore it is written: “The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” (Psalm 3). Again, elsewhere it is said: “The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree; he shall be multiplied like the cedar of Lebanon. Planted in the house of the Lord, they shall flourish in the courts of the house of our God” (Psalm 91). “They shall still increase in a more advanced old age, and shall be steadfast,” until they announce to posterity what they have come to know: namely, that the Lord [Col. 1036B] our God is righteous and upright, and that there is no iniquity in him.

It is true, brethren, that though they died many years ago, they still speak vividly, since every day the faithful are converted to the Lord through their teaching and strengthened for good work through their example. Therefore, as long as the course of this world continues to turn, their venerable merit continually receives increase. Let us then, dearest friends, offer boundless praises and thanksgivings to our Creator on their feast, since he has already granted them in heaven the kingdom prepared before the ages, and has promised us that, through salvation restored by his blood, we too shall be participants in that same kingdom. To him, therefore, King of all ages, be praise and glory for endless [Col. 1036C] ages; to us, everlasting mercy. Amen.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1112: JOHN OF THE MARSICANS, BISHOP OF TUSCULUM

[Col. 1035]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE CONCERNING JOHN

*(UGHELLI, Italia Sacra, I, 230.)*

John, called “the Marsican,” was appointed cardinal-bishop of Tusculum by Urban II. At the Council of Vasto in 1106 he delivered an exceedingly weighty judgment, and he was of such great and ready courage that, when the impious Emperor Henry IV had cast Pope Paschal II into prison, he himself, together with Cardinal Leo, fled to Rome in a feigned manner of dress. Having summoned the Roman people to an assembly, he persuaded them to take up arms against the emperor and avenge the injuries done to the pontiff. He died under that same Paschal.

[He was also present at the Roman council of 1112. That he acted as the pope’s vicar in the City may be inferred from the title attached to the letter quoted by Baronius, *Annals*, vol. XI, which he wrote to Richard, bishop of Albano, warning him of Henry’s wicked deeds and of the most miserable condition of the City and the universal Church. With many cardinals he reproached Paschal for the concession of investitures made to Henry. Yet Paschal sharply rebuked him in turn because he censured him with excessive zeal; for John had not noticed that the pope had done this in order that the City might not be consumed by schism and a worse disaster. LUCENT.]

[Col. 1037]

## ADDRESS OF JOHN OF THE MARSICANS, BISHOP OF TUSCULUM, TO THE ROMAN PEOPLE

*That they may avenge the injury done to the supreme pontiff, who, with his followers, was detained and insulted by Emperor Henry.*

*(BARONIUS, Annals, under the year 1111, nos. 11, 13.)*

[Col. 1037A] Although, dearest sons, there is no need to apply the spurs of exhortation to your eagerness and courage—for by words neither does the vigorous man become so from weak, nor anyone robust from timid—yet your entire battle and every contest concerns life and liberty, glory and the defense of the Apostolic See; all these things have been entrusted to your hands. For whoever desires peace should prepare war.

Your sons are held in chains contrary to every right and law. The basilica of the Apostle Peter, venerable throughout the whole world, is filled with arms, corpses, gore, and blood. What conclusion of all evils can we draw from this? What more monstrous calamity has ever been heard of? The pontiff of the Apostolic See is held in chains by [Col. 1038A] barbarous men; the entire priestly order, all ecclesiastical dignity, has been consigned to prison and darkness. The ministers of the Lord mourn; the holy altars are wet with tears; mother Church herself, utterly crushed, groans and implores your aid. In grief she prays and beseeches her sons to rescue her from such disasters.

Therefore, with all the feeling we can, we beg you to come to the aid of her in danger and to devote yourselves with all your mind and all your strength to avenging your mother’s injury. For if there are any who oppose you, the enemies will be readier to flee than to stand. Therefore rise more eagerly to avenge so great a crime. Trusting in the mercy of our Lord and of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, we absolve you from all sins.

[Col. 1037]

## JOHN’S LETTER TO RICHARD, BISHOP OF ALBANO

*Concerning the wicked deeds of Emperor Henry.*

*(BARONIUS, as above.)*

[Col. 1037B] **JOHN**, by the grace of God bishop of Tusculum, acting in the place of Lord Paschal, pope and prisoner of Jesus Christ, to his venerable brother **RICHARD**, bishop of Albano: greeting in the Lord.

Because, as the Apostle says (Romans 12), we are one body in Christ, and if one member suffers, the other members suffer with it, we make known to your brotherhood what has been done to our head and to almost the whole Church.

When Henry, king of the Germans, had reached Sutri, he sent certain envoys to Rome. They confirmed by oath that they would conduct safely the envoys of Lord Pope Paschal; that they would bind the king himself by oath utterly to renounce every investiture of churches; that he would also give hostages, lest he return again to this outrage; and that he would leave wholly free and [Col. 1038B] undisturbed ecclesiastical property, royal rights, and the patrimonies of blessed Peter. They were also to provide hostages as security when the pope should go out to crown him at the basilica of blessed Peter.

Afterwards, on the Church’s part, it was confirmed by laymen that, if the said king observed those things which had been promised, our lord would receive him kindly, place the royal diadem upon him, and allow him, once crowned, to enter the City if he wished. He also received hostages for his crossing of the bridge, and for them he gave an oath that if on that Sunday he crossed the bridge, he would restore them into the free control of our people.

Thus, when all these oaths had been concluded by each side and hostages had been given, as the pope went out to the Church of blessed Peter to crown him, Henry disregarded the oaths and dismissed the hostages; in the very church he violently seized the pope, together with bishops, cardinals, and many Romans, and keeps them under the strictest imprisonment. On the next day the Romans gathered together, attacked the enemies of the Church, and forced them to flee from the portico [Col. 1039A], killing many of their men and capturing or destroying horses, tents, money, and an immeasurable quantity of equipment. After this, all unanimously swore against him to fight with one mind and one will.

You therefore, prudently, keep watch; and the more you see the need, the more earnestly labor, and do not cease to assist the mother of all Churches [Col. 1040A]. Cause prayers to be offered wherever you can for the deliverance of our lord—indeed, for the Church herself. Farewell.

This took place in the year of the Lord 1111, in the fourth indiction, on the day before the Ides of February, in the basilica of Saint Peter, prince of the Apostles, on the Sunday before the beginning of the fast.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1113: BLESSED ODO, BISHOP OF CAMBRAI

[Col. 1039]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(Cameracum Christianum, by D. LEGLAY, p. 30.)*

[Col. 1039B] Odo, honored with the title “Blessed,” who is sometimes called Odoardus and was a citizen of Orléans, was the first abbot of Saint Martin of Tournai after the restoration of that monastery; the history of the abbots of that place should be consulted concerning him. He was elected and consecrated at a synod of the province of Reims in 1105, on 2 July, a Sunday, as is inferred from his own charter made that year for Roger, abbot of Anchin, which is called the first year of his episcopate and is subscribed by Baldwin, dean; and from the instrument by which the foundation of the college of canons at Dendermonde is confirmed.

After his ordination, Odo did not for some time obtain possession of the episcopal see. But after Emperor Henry died, Henry his son, who had embraced the papal party against his father, ordered the people of Cambrai, having expelled Walcher, to receive Odo, in 1106. From the narrative of the restoration of the Abbey of Saint Martin of Tournai, *Spicilegium*, vol. XII, chapter 82.

In 1110 he granted Count Robert and his wife Clementia [Col. 1039C] permission to build a chapel at New Borough near Oudenaarde. In 1113, from the cartulary of the place, he confirmed for the monastery of Saint-Denis near Paris the church of Solesmes. In 1112, the seventh year of his episcopate, he confirmed the foundation of the Abbey of Bournehem. But because he refused to receive from Emperor Henry [Col. 1040B] IV the staff and ring which he had already received in his ordination by ecclesiastical authority, he was driven from his see and lived in exile at Anchin, as he himself writes in the book *On Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit*.

Burdened by bodily weakness, says Herimannus (*Spicilegium*, vol. XII, p. 469), he resigned the episcopate and had himself carried in a litter to Anchin, where he died within eight days. More on Odo may be found in Molanus, *Natalia Sanctorum Belgii*; Miraeus, *Codex Donationum Piarum*; Lindanus and other hagiographers; and Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he says that Odo was learned in Scripture, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, and more than moderately distinguished in delivering homilies to the people. Besides the homilies which he composed, he expounded the Canon of the Mass and produced other learned writings.

He passed to the better life on 19 June, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the year 1113, at the monastery of Anchin. There he was buried beneath a tomb of white marble, bearing his carved image [Col. 1040C] and this epitaph:

> Here lies Bishop Odo, manifest to all the world;  
> he was an exile, faithful to God;  
> he shines in heaven like a star.

[Col. 1039]

## ANOTHER NOTICE

*(MABILLON, Benedictine Annals, vol. V, p. 299.)*
[Col. 1039D] At this time (A.D. 1090) many learned men flourished among the French. Balderic, abbot of Bourgueil, celebrated most of them in his verses: among them his teacher Hubert, who [Col. 1040D] taught letters at Meung; Frodon of Angers; Audebert of Le Mans; and Godfrey of Rheims. Yet it is surprising that he passed over his fellow-countryman Odo, a native of Orléans, who [Col. 1041A] taught publicly first at Toul and then at Tournai for five years, with great renown and a large attendance of pupils.

This man deserves more than a brief notice, since he restored the monastery of Saint Martin at Tournai, where he became both monk and abbot. He was a cleric, born, as I have just said, in the city of Orléans, the son of Gerard and Cecilia. Commonly called Odoard, he had from childhood been so well trained in letters that he was regarded as second to none among the French masters of his age. He first held the schools at Toul; then, summoned by the canons of the church of Tournai, he taught letters there for five years with such distinction that pupils flocked competitively to him—not only from Flanders and neighbouring regions, but even from the most distant provinces, Burgundy, [Col. 1041B] Italy, and Saxony—to the number of two hundred clerics.

Although he was especially proficient in every liberal art, he excelled particularly in dialectic. He adhered to the old school of those called Realists, rather than to the new school of the Nominalists, which a certain Raimbert, a celebrated master, was then lecturing upon to his pupils at Lille. When disputes arose on this subject, one of the canons of the church of Tournai, named Gualbert—who later became a monk at Tournai and finally abbot of Saint Peter’s monastery at Châlons—consulted by gestures a certain deaf and mute diviner concerning the matter, and learned from him that Odo was to be preferred.

[Col. 1041C] When Odo had presided over the school of Tournai for nearly five years, a certain cleric offered him Augustine’s book *On Free Choice of the Will*. The master bought it to supplement his library, but threw it into a chest along with his other books; for, wholly devoted to secular learning, he took greater delight in reading Plato than Augustine. It happened, about two months later, that he was lecturing to his pupils on Boethius’s books *On the Consolation of Philosophy*. When he reached the fourth book, which deals with free choice, he remembered the book he had bought and ordered it brought to him, in case he might find in it something noteworthy on this question.

Then, after reading two or three pages, he was so affected by the reading that he immediately summoned his pupils, [Col. 1041D] wishing them to share in the treasure he had discovered. “Truly,” he said, “until now I did not know how great Augustine’s eloquence and learning were.” At once he began the book itself from the beginning, read it to his pupils, and explained it on that day and the following day. But when he reached the third book, in which the holy doctor sets forth the wretched condition of sinners who prefer the world—like a foul sewer—to heavenly glory, he drew deep sighs from the depths of his breast in profound grief and said: “Alas!” How sternly this judgment touches and oppresses us, who devote all our studies to acquiring vain knowledge, wholly forgetful of divine worship and heavenly glory, and therefore destined after death to be unworthy of it!” With these words he rose and, entirely bathed in tears, entered the church.

At this, [Col. 1042A] the whole school was disturbed, and the body of canons was struck with astonishment. Thereafter Odo gradually withdrew from the school, attended church more than usual, distributed the money he had amassed among the poor, especially clerics, and finally so wore down his body with fasts that he was soon scarcely recognizable to many because of his emaciation.

Not long afterward four clerics joined him: namely Odo the abbot, Gerbert, Rodulf, and William, besides Lanfrid, who slipped away in flight and perished miserably. Yet they hesitated over which state to embrace, that of canons or that of monks. Having investigated both in various places, they meanwhile began to live together in the suburban little church of Saint Martin, where there had once been an abbey of monks, but which had been destroyed by pagans and reduced almost to solitude.

[Col. 1042B] Encouraged by this example, the citizens of Tournai asked Bishop Radbod not to permit Odo and his companions to move elsewhere. This pleased the bishop, and he therefore spoke with Odo about the matter. But when Odo left the episcopal residence without giving any definite reply, the most devout prelate enlisted a religious priest named Gislebert—then regarded in those regions as a prophet and later buried in the church of Saint Peter at Elnone—to persuade Odo to agree with him and the citizens.

Overcome by Gislebert’s words, Odo promised to remain there, provided that the bishop would grant him a free place. Greatly delighted, the bishop sought the consent of the canons; they, as though foreknowing the future, repeatedly refused. Then the bishop, by the authority he possessed, [Col. 1042C] unconditionally gave the aforesaid little church of Saint Martin, which was under his jurisdiction, to Odo and his companions. He led them there in solemn procession on the sixth day before the Nones of May—that is, 2 May—which was a Sunday, in the year 1092 of the Incarnation of the Lord; and he left them there to serve God under the Rule of Saint Augustine, in clerical dress.

Herimannus the abbot recounts all this at length in his book *On the Restoration of the Abbey of Saint Martin of Tournai* (*Spicilegium*, vol. XII, p. 398 ff.). At that time almost the whole province, and especially the city of Tournai, was afflicted by the sacred fire. Very many people burned by that fire, not only from the city but also from distant regions, were brought in crowds to the church of Blessed Mary. Then, on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, the bishop appointed a solemn procession from that principal [Col. 1042D] church to the little church of Saint Martin. It was made barefoot and, Herimannus says, has continued on that same day down to our own time.

Moreover, besides what that author records about Odo, we also learn some things from the verses of his friend Godfrey, master of Rheims. In them Odo’s noble birth and the excellence of his talent and learning are highly praised. Among his other small works Godfrey commends a little book *On the Trojan War*, which, he writes, Odo had published. We found Godfrey’s work, entitled *The Dream of Odo of Orléans*, hitherto unpublished, as I think, in a manuscript of the Jesuit college at Paris, written five hundred years ago. Since it perhaps seemed superfluous to reproduce the whole little work, [Col. 1043A] we have excerpted several verses from it below.

In the same manuscript we saw another poem of no small size on the opening verses of Genesis, or the work of the six days. Although it bears the name of “Odo, bishop of Orléans,” we suspect it to be by our Odo, since no bishop of that name occurs in the entire catalogue of bishops of Orléans, while Odo was both an Orléanais and a bishop. It begins:

> Almighty One, in the beginning, both heaven and earth.

In 1113, Odo, burdened with bodily illness, resigned his bishopric and had himself carried in a litter to Anchin. On hearing this, Segard, abbot of Saint Martin of Tournai, hurried there with several of his monks and asked him to permit himself to be brought to his own monastery, [Col. 1044A] which he had restored and where he had first been a monk and first abbot. But Alvisus, abbot of Anchin, opposed this and declared that he would by no means allow it. Odo therefore remained there, and within eight days was carried off by death, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, that is, 20 June. With great honour he was buried in the church before the image of the Crucified, beneath white marble on which his likeness was engraved.

He wrote several little books: namely, on the Canon of the Mass; a disputation against a Jew; and *On the Origin of the Soul*, as Hermannus, his contemporary, asserts in his history of the monastery of Saint Martin of Tournai. Blessed Odo, or Odoard, is venerated in the church of Cambrai; Burchard succeeded him in the bishopric. Amandus, prior of Anchin, wrote a circular letter concerning his life and death.

[Col. 1043]

## LITERARY NOTICE

(*Literary History of France*, vol. IX, p. 594.)

[Col. 1043B] Until now, none of the bibliographers who have undertaken to discuss our holy and learned prelate has made known all the writings that issued from his pen. We shall try to remedy this deficiency; and this will be the first complete catalogue, both of those that still exist and of those that have been lost but of which some knowledge remains. They belonged to two different classes. Some, composed before the author’s conversion, concerned purely secular sciences or profane subjects; the others dealt with various points of the Christian religion. We shall begin by examining those of the first class and then proceed to the others.

1. Before Odo left the city of Orléans, the place [Col. 1043C] of his birth—and consequently while still young—he had already composed a poem on the famous Trojan War (*Mabillon, Annals*, vol. V, p. 651, no. 1). Godfrey, scholastic of Rheims, another poet of the period and the author’s close friend, having heard of this production of his muse, gave him no rest until he communicated it to him. It prompted Godfrey to compose in praise of the poet a long and fairly ingenious piece of verse, which he entitled *The Dream of Odo of Orléans*.

Odo’s poem is not otherwise found anywhere. It appears to have been the first of his writings, and our only knowledge of it comes from the following verses of Godfrey. He depicts the poet as [Col. 1043D] borne on the winds from Orléans to Rheims, in order to offer him the poem himself, speaking as follows:

> Therefore, entrusting myself to the winds for your sake, my friend,  
> I did not fear to travel, suspended, along uncertain paths.  
> And because my little works are always dear to your heart  
> and are not to be cast away at your discretion,  
>   
> [Col. 1044B] I have brought the little book that sings of the Trojan wars,  
> which you often make me recite to you.

Besides, in the verses preceding those just read, Godfrey greatly extols the sweetness, harmony, and rhythm of his friend’s poetry. Thus, if the poem on the Trojan War possessed all the beauties this scholastic discerned in it, its loss would be regrettable. But it is an eleventh-century poet praising another poet, and one knows what weight to give such praise.

2. When Odo directed the school of Tournai, he composed, as has already been mentioned, several writings to strengthen and render more useful the lessons in dialectic which he gave his pupils. One of these writings was entitled *The Sophist*, and aimed to teach [Col. 1044C] how to discern sophisms and avoid them (*Spicilegium*, vol. XII, p. 361).

3. Another work on the same discipline (*ibid.*) bore the title *Complexionum*, “On Conclusions or Consequences,” in which Odo apparently laid down the rules of the syllogism, so as to put what the schools call an argument into proper form and thereby teach correct reasoning.

4. A third work, again on dialectic (*ibid.*), was entitled *On Being and the Thing*, because he discussed there whether being is the same as the thing, and the thing the same as being. These three writings are known only from the little that Herimannus considered fit to transmit to us [Col. 1044D] concerning the early events in their author’s history. Sanderus, who found among the manuscripts of Belgian libraries most of Odo’s other writings, discovered none of the three in question here. It was principally in these works [Col. 1045A] that the author, when occasion arose to name himself, used the name Odard, under which he was then more commonly known.

By his manner of teaching dialectic, Odo, like Saint Anselm, greatly helped to uphold sound philosophy, since both were strongly attached to the method of the Realists and opposed that of the Nominalists with equal force. But it is unknown, if Odo wrote on this subject, whether he did so in one of the three treatises just noticed. However that may be, the service he rendered philosophy in this regard contributed greatly to the support of sound theology; so too did the works [Col. 1045B] he composed on theological subjects. We shall now examine these.

5. Amandus of Chastel, Odo’s panegyrist (*Bollandists*, 19 June, p. 913, no. 8), and Herimannus, his principal historian (*Spicilegium*, *ibid.*, p. 469), attest that he wrote an explanation of the Canon of the Mass. Henry of Ghent (*Henry of Ghent*, ch. 4), Trithemius (*Writers*, ch. 371), and all later bibliographers likewise agree in assigning him this work, which has had a happier fate than the preceding ones. It is in fact found at the head of the other productions of its author’s pen which escaped the shipwreck suffered by so many others (*Library of the Fathers*, vol. XXI).

Odo was already bishop when he undertook it, [Col. 1045C] as appears from the title he assumes, with a touch of humility, at the head of the short preface or letter addressed to Odo, monk of Afflighem, at whose urgent prayers he undertook the work. He began to work on it under that friend’s eyes and completed it after leaving him. This means either that the author had gone to Afflighem and that the monk Odo would not let him leave until he had begun to grant what he so ardently requested, or that the monk had himself gone to the author to induce him seriously to put pen to paper.

[Note: [Col. 1045D] Sanderus (*Bibliotheca Belgica, Manuscripts*, part I, p. 167) read “Wolbodon” in place of “Odo,” unless the manuscript he encountered was more correct than the one from which the opusculum was printed.]

In this preface Bishop Odo begs those who undertake to make a copy of his explanation to take care to transcribe correctly at the head of each paragraph or chapter the text of the Canon [Col. 1045D] which he explains. He gives this notable reason: to prevent any alteration from creeping in through additions or deletions that might be made; and nothing may be changed in it without the authority of the Supreme Pontiff. From this one sees the respect this pious bishop had for this principal part of the liturgy. He shows it again by his humble confession of incapacity to treat mysteries so profound. Yet he succeeded in a manner at once clear, exact, full of piety, and full of unction.

For greater order and clarity, he divided his [Col. 1046A] text into four parts, forming as many sections or chapters in the exposition he gives. At the end is a short epilogue or conclusion, asking copyists to preserve this same division carefully and to write the titles in capital letters, so that it may be noticed at first glance.

The author passes over scarcely a word of his text without, so to speak, turning it on every side and giving it all the senses it can bear. Throughout his exposition he carefully indicates the points of doctrine, morals, and discipline to which the passages he explains relate. On this basis he unequivocally establishes transubstantiation in the Eucharist, and consequently [Col. 1046B] the real presence. He observes that, in order to pray as one ought, prayer must be made with confidence and humility; that in the first centuries of the Church no Mass was celebrated without an assembly of the faithful; and that the practice of private Masses was introduced only later, especially in monasteries.

On the first invocation of the saints in the Canon, the author observes, against the enemies of this ancient practice, that whoever does not honour the members does not honour the head either; whoever does not honour the saints does not honour Jesus Christ either; and whoever does not honour Jesus Christ, who is the Son, does not honour [Col. 1046C] the Father either. Many other edifying observations might be drawn from Odo’s work, but these suffice to show its merit. The author did not pause to explain the Lord’s Prayer, because several others had done so before him.

Nothing could better indicate the value of Odo’s treatise than the large number of editions it received. As early as the fifteenth century there were three different editions. Guyot le Marchand, printer in Paris, produced two octavo editions: one dated from the royal house of the College of Navarre at Champgaillard, 16 August 1490; the other 4 January 1496, according to the French reckoning. This latter had been preceded by another edition, [Col. 1046D] printed at Paris by George Mitthelhuf in 1492, in a small quarto of that period.

The same work appeared again in octavo, together with the treatise *On the Ceremonies of the Mass* by Francis Titelman, Franciscan of Antwerp: at Antwerp, with William Vosterman, in 1528 and 1530; at Caen, with Michel Angier, in 1529, in the same format; and at Mainz, with Francis Behem, in 1554, again in the same format, through the care of Philip Agricola, citizen of Mainz. Father Labbe records two further editions, which we have neither seen ourselves nor found elsewhere: one printed at Antwerp in 1532, and the other at [Col. 1047A] Lyons in 1556. The same is true of two others indicated by Lipenius as printed at Cologne in 1563, octavo, and in 1575, folio, apparently in some collection. Finally, Odo’s work, having been published in the same year in Margarin de la Bigne’s *Library of the Fathers*, was reprinted in all the other collections bearing that title. It appears in volume XXI of the final edition; and before appearing there it had also been separately printed in quarto at Paris in 1604.

6. After the preceding work in the *Library of the Fathers* comes another by Bishop Odo concerning original sin. It is divided into three books, and his two historians already cited explicitly acknowledge it as his work. [Col. 1047B] It is true that Herimannus announces it only under the title *Treatise on the Origin of the Soul*, because that subject forms the principal matter of the third book, which is the most extensive, and also part of the second. It is not addressed to Amandus of Chastel, prior of Anchin, as Possevin says; in this matter he confused it with another work to be mentioned later.

Odo declares that only with extreme difficulty did he resolve to treat this question, which had so often been discussed before him without being fully clarified and which seemed to him to contain much obscurity. But overcome by the requests of some of his brethren and by the [Col. 1047C] charity he bore them, he could not refuse to undertake it. It appears that he was not yet bishop when he put pen to paper for this purpose. Struck by the difficulty of succeeding, he begins by imploring the enlightenment of the Holy Spirit, so that he may write nothing displeasing to Him. Then he reduces the entire question to this: how we sinned in Adam and derived original sin from him. Taking as granted the doctrine established by Saint Paul—that all sinned in Adam—Odo enters upon the matter and treats his subject purely as a philosopher. Before concluding, he explains why he has proceeded in this manner: not in order to establish truth by philosophical arguments, since it supports itself, but to clarify it and make it better known.

[Col. 1047D] This treatise, though wholly philosophical, is written with great clarity and precision. It contains excellent material concerning the notion of evil in general, including a sound refutation of the Manichaean opinion that moral evil is a substance, or something real—which amounts to the same thing. Since the question of the soul’s origin greatly aids in explaining the question of original sin, the author enters into an extensive discussion of this issue, which had already greatly occupied many philosophers. Refuting opposing opinions, he maintains that each soul is immediately created by God and that it nonetheless [Col. 1048A] contracts original sin; he explains this through a sequence of questions, which he always treats philosophically.

7. Another work of Odo’s, printed under his name after the preceding two and reckoned among his opuscula by his two historians, is a disputation in dialogue form which he held with a Jew named Leo. It concerns chiefly the Incarnation of the Word and the redemption of humankind, which is its principal effect. Around Christmas 1105, Odo went to Femy, an abbey in his diocese, and spoke to the brethren gathered in chapter about the motive and cause of the Incarnation. One of them, named Acard, moved by this discourse but unable to retain its contents, later asked the bishop to set it down in writing.

[Col. 1048B] The good prelate was seriously considering satisfying him when he was obliged to set out for the council which the legate Bruno, bishop of Segni, had summoned at Poitiers for May 1106. Passing through Senlis, he happened to have occasion to use what he had said in this discourse against the Jew Leo, who had come to dispute with him. After some time Odo arranged this disputation, which contains the substance of his discourse. At the head of the Jew’s questions or objections he placed an “L.” for Leo’s name; and at the head of his own replies an “O.” for Odo. He sent the work, thus arranged, to Acard along with a [Col. 1048C] short preface or letter in which he himself relates the history of the work just recounted.

Henry of Ghent and Trithemius, perhaps following him, say that this *Dialogue* is addressed to Wolbodon, monk of Afflighem. Were there two different dedications? Not only the title but also the text of the preface in the printed editions expressly names Acard, monk of Femy.

The author’s manner of reasoning in this *Dialogue* is again almost wholly philosophical, and he makes very little use of Holy Scripture, which his opponent acknowledges as such. Nevertheless, although everything is treated through reasoning with some assistance from revelation, Odo succeeds in convincing his Jew [Col. 1048D] that God alone could make satisfaction for the sins of humankind, from which he infers the necessity of the Incarnation of the Word. Then, having brought him to this point, he asks why he refuses to believe. The Jew replies that he does not wish to expose the truth of his religion to Christian arguments.

8. In the same collection the final three works of Odo are followed by another concerning blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which Amandus of Chastel—who ought to have known well—attributes to him along with the preceding works. It was indeed at Amandus’s solicitation, while he was still merely a monk of Anchin, before soon becoming its prior and later abbot of Marchiennes, that Odo undertook this opusculum. Amandus [Col. 1049A] even says that Odo did him the honour of dedicating it to him; but this dedication does not appear in the printed text.

The author composed it at Anchin, where he was then staying after being expelled from his church on the occasion recounted above. In occasional conversations on spiritual matters with this friend, Amandus expressed a strong desire to be instructed about what is meant by blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Odo referred him to what the Holy Fathers had said in expounding the Gospel. But Amandus, finding nothing there to satisfy him, pressed the good bishop for an explanation of his own. Odo, overcome by his entreaties and knowing besides that the attention he had given to his treatise *On Original Sin* had enabled him to discover [Col. 1049B] many things he had previously not known, resolved to grant his request.

He remembered having once read that Saint Augustine had treated the same subject. But he despaired of recovering what Augustine had written, because neither he nor anyone he knew had yet managed to read it. He therefore decided to produce an entirely new treatise.

First, the author begins by copying the passages of the Evangelists Saint Matthew, Saint Mark, and Saint Luke in which blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is spoken of as irredeemable in this life and the next. He then states the difficulty that results: the Church has always taught and [Col. 1049C] still constantly teaches that there is no sin which cannot be forgiven. Odo resolves the difficulty by saying that the Gospel presents blasphemy against the Holy Spirit as irredeemable, while implicitly adding “without repentance,” because this blasphemy is impenitence itself. The Church, in teaching that there is no sin which cannot be forgiven, implicitly adds “by means of repentance.”

Here the author introduces what Saint John the Evangelist says in his First Epistle concerning the sin persisting unto death, for which he does not wish prayer to be made. He observes that in this the beloved disciple agrees with the three Evangelists, because this sin is none other than blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, or final impenitence. Finally, Odo explains why this blasphemy is called against the Holy Spirit rather than against the Father or the Son. He gives this reason: since the Holy Spirit is properly and especially charity, it is He who forgives sins; and, since nothing is more opposed to that forgiveness than final impenitence or blasphemy, it is rightly described as against the Holy Spirit.

Bishop Odo, moreover, follows throughout this work his habit of philosophical reasoning, which seems to have been very familiar to him. He has left a very clear mark of it in the square figure crossed by a line in the form of a cross, used to indicate the angles enclosed within it. This diagram serves to show at a glance the contraries [Col. 1050A] and opposites, with the effects of each, concerning the subject under discussion. For example, forgiveness of sins and repentance are contrary to unforgiveness and impenitence. Forgiveness is opposed in justice to impenitence, and unforgiveness in mercy to repentance. Repentance produces forgiveness, and impenitence unforgiveness. This is what the diagram displays.

9. In the same collection follows another work by Bishop Odo, on the Gospel Canons, listed among his other opuscula by Amandus of Chastel. This work, which required the diagram represented in it in order for its meaning to be understood, teaches how to make tables showing [Col. 1050B] the respects in which the Evangelists agree throughout all that they wrote. Odo distinguishes ten such tables, as the ancients did, and as they may be seen engraved, for example, at the beginning of Robert Estienne’s fine folio edition of the Greek New Testament.

The first table includes the four Evangelists; the second is assigned to Saint Matthew, Saint Mark, and Saint Luke; the third to Saint Matthew, Saint Luke, and Saint John; the fourth to Saint Matthew, Saint Mark, and Saint John. The fifth contains Saint Matthew and Saint Luke; the sixth, Saint Matthew and Saint Mark; the seventh, Saint Matthew and Saint John; the eighth, Saint Mark and Saint John; the ninth, Saint Luke and Saint John. Finally, the tenth is [Col. 1050C] reserved for what is distinctive to each Evangelist and common to none of the others. This arrangement shows that there is no table for Saint Mark, Saint Luke, and Saint John together, because nothing is found in their Gospels in which all three agree. At the head of each table are respectively placed the names of the Evangelists for whom it is intended; then the passages in which they agree are entered there.

10. Odo’s panegyrist, Amandus of Chastel, counts among his writings a homily on the Gospel of the bad farmer, read at Mass on the eighth Sunday after Pentecost, but merely mentions it without further description. Henry of Ghent (ch. 4), however, who places it first among the other works of our prelate which he discusses, calls it a fine homily: *homiliam pulchram*. One homily printed under Odo’s name follows the works just reviewed and concerns the same parable. At least one other on the same text from Saint Luke is found among sermons formerly attributed to Saint Bernard, though it bears no author’s name.

Finally, Dom Martène and Dom Durand published a third (*Anecdota*, vol. V, pp. 854, 859–878), bearing the name “Odo, bishop of Cambrai,” in a manuscript supplied to them by the abbey of Préaux. They maintain that this is the one attributed to him by Henry of Ghent and Trithemius. Their reason [Col. 1051A] is that it retains more closely the characteristics by which those bibliographers describe it than does the homily printed in the *Library of the Fathers*. They do not, however, absolutely deny that the other may also be Odo’s work, since it would not be extraordinary for him to have composed two on the same subject—of which there are many examples among other authors of homilies.

But there is such a great and perceptible difference, especially in style, between the homily printed in the *Library of the Fathers* and that published by Dom Martène, that whoever has read both attentively will never judge [Col. 1051B] them to be the work of one and the same author. The first is brief, written in a clear, segmented, highly concise style, and develops the meaning of the sacred text naturally and without extensive argument. The other, by contrast, is very lengthy, almost four times longer than the first. Its style is diffuse, though clear, and its arguments are lengthy and numerous.

Moreover, it appears later than the first, which its author seems not to have been unaware of. At least he begins by saying that many others before him had explained the same parable in their own manner, according to the needs and dispositions of their contemporaries. Given this, compare each homily with the other writings of Bishop Odo, and one will certainly recognize [Col. 1051C] his entire manner of writing and character in the first. Above all, attention should be paid to his *Explanation of the Canon of the Mass*. If, however, one considers only the substance of these two pieces—that is, the teachings they contain—each has its merit and contains excellent moral instruction.

As for the one found without an author’s name in the old editions of Saint Bernard’s works, it cannot belong to our prelate, since it is addressed to Cardinal Matthew, bishop of Albano, who had not yet been raised to those dignities during the lifetime of Odo of Cambrai. Moreover, it was subsequently recognized that this homily is the work of a Bernard, monk of Cluny, distinct from the holy abbot of the same name; and it has been reprinted under his name [Col. 1051D] in the newer editions.

11. Besides the homily on the wicked farmer, or the unfaithful steward, Trithemius further attributes other homilies indiscriminately to Bishop Odo; this seems grounded on the fact that he sometimes, at least, as has been said, made advantageous use of the gift of speech he had received. There are indeed several other homilies bearing his name. Vatican Library manuscript no. 1506 (MONTF., *Bib. bib.*, p. 48), among the manuscripts of the Queen of Sweden, contains two: one on the Canaanite woman, bearing the name of our prelate with the title Bishop of Cambrai; the other, without an author’s name, [Col. 1052A] on the Passion of the Saviour, but judged likewise to be his work.

12. Another manuscript from the College of Louis-le-Grand in Paris, containing the poems of Godfrey, scholastic of Reims, also includes a long poem on the opening verses of Genesis, or the work of the six days. Its inscription assigns it to an Odo, Bishop of Orléans. But since that city never had a bishop of that name, and since our prelate was a native of it, there is no doubt that he himself is intended by the inscription. Moreover, Dom Mabillon, who had seen this manuscript, tells us nothing either of the manner in which the poem treats its subject or of the characteristics of its author’s versification. We have seen above [Col. 1052B] that Godfrey of Reims praised it highly in general terms.

13. Valerius Andreas (*Bib. Belg.*, p. 707), Aubertus Miraeus, and others attribute to Odo a collection of parables, giving us no further information except that a manuscript copy formerly existed at St Michael’s, Antwerp. Even in our own day two further copies may be seen in the Vatican Library (MONTF., ibid., p. 37): one under the name of the great Odo, bishop and doctor of theology, among Queen Christina’s manuscripts; the other under the name simply of Odo, bishop and doctor, among the manuscripts of Alexander Petau.

14. Trithemius (ibid.) and Simler (*Bibl.*, p. 530) further enlarge the catalogue of Bishop Odo’s [Col. 1052C] writings with a collection of letters. Yet none appear to have been printed except those placed at the head of some of his minor works and serving as their prefaces. But these are not in question here; moreover, they have already been made known. As for the others, we have discovered only one, among the manuscripts of the abbey of Vauclere (MONTF., ibid., p. 1301). It is addressed to a certain William, monk of Afflighem, where, as we have seen above, our prelate had connections.

15. In the same manuscript, Odo’s *Explanation of the Canon of the Mass* is joined to the preceding letter, along with two further treatises also under his name, bearing the following titles: *Treatise on the [Col. 1052D] Canon*; *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. Since we are unable to examine this manuscript ourselves, we can speak of it only conjecturally. It seems highly probable that this *Treatise on the Canon*, here distinguished from the *Explanation of the Canon of the Mass*, is none other than the minor work on the canons of the Gospels. Apparently the same is true of the other treatise, which may be only an extract from what Odo says on transubstantiation and the other matters concerning the Eucharist in his *Exposition of the Canon of the Mass*.

16. It seems that one may rightly count among the works of our learned bishop the Tetrapla of the Psalter (SAND., *Bib. Belg.*, manuscript part I, [Col. 1053A] p. 107), which he had made when he was abbot of Saint-Martin, as was stated in his history, and which were still preserved there in the time of Sanderus. Even if he had had no greater role in this rare collection than conceiving the plan and directing its execution, he would thereby have rendered a great service to learning.

17. Since it thus appears that he had a taste for the Hebrew language, might one not be justified in identifying him with that Odo, author of an introduction to theology in which several passages of Holy Scripture are quoted in Hebrew? (*Bib. Angl.*, manuscript part III, p. 545). It is true that this author, whose work exists in manuscript in English libraries, is called simply [Col. 1053B] Odo, with nothing indicating either his country, rank, or dignity.

18. A manuscript in the Pauline Library at Leipzig contains a *Treatise or Exposition of the Number Three* under the name of Odo, who is not otherwise identified there (MONTF., ibid., p. 545). The work is adorned with twenty-eight figures to make its contents more perceptible. Simler (*Bib.*, ibid.), who mentions it, says that its author was highly skilled in mathematics. These traits almost all suit Bishop Odo and seem to identify him. He was a Platonist, belonging to a school of philosophers [Col. 1054A] who reason extensively about combinations of numbers. He also customarily adorned his writings with figures, as is evident from his minor works on the irremissible sin and on the canons of the Gospels. Finally, he was an astronomer, a science which presupposes knowledge of some part of mathematics. Despite all these conjectures, we do not venture to pronounce that the treatise in question is his work.

19. Valerius Andreas and Cave (*Script.*, p. 560) also credit him with a collection of conferences. But here those two bibliographers have confused Odo, Bishop of Cambrai, with St Odo, Abbot of Cluny, to whom this work belongs; nor is any other work of this kind known that bears the name [Col. 1054B] Odo.

29. Finally, there is a very short letter from our prelate to Lambert, Bishop of Arras (BAL., *Misc.*, vol. V, p. 345). It is merely a letter of dismissal on behalf of a cleric moving from the diocese of Cambrai to that of Arras. There is another letter from Lambert to Odo. It was being circulated as proceeding from the latter that the emperor wished to alter the boundaries of the two dioceses. Lambert sets before him the injustice that would result from this rearrangement and asks Odo whether he has any part in the scheme; we do not possess the reply of the Bishop of Cambrai.
