# SACRED MINOR WORKS OF ODO, FIRST ABBOT OF TOURNAY, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF CAMBRAI, NOW FOR THE FIRST TIME PUBLISHED IN LARGE PART THROUGH THE LABOUR OF ANDREAS SCOTUS, S.J.

(*Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XXI, p. 221.)

[Col. 1053]

# EXPOSITION OF THE CANON OF THE MASS

## PREFACE OF ODO

[Col. 1053C] ODO, unworthy minister of the Church of Cambrai, to ODO, his beloved son, serving in the Lord’s camp under the venerable Fulgentius, abbot of Afflighem: greeting.

I fear to be accused of presumption because I have dared to touch a difficult subject and have attempted to stretch out into profound heights: namely, to expound the canon of the altar and prove such great mysteries, as it is written: “Do not seek things higher than yourself, and do not investigate things stronger than yourself” (Ecclus. 3). But however others may judge me, you know, brother, with what earnestness of entreaty you overcame me so that I undertook so great a burden, trusting rather to be helped by your devotion and prayers than by my own strength. For it was impious not to yield to so great a desire, even if it exceeds my powers; and I judged it preferable to collapse beneath the load rather than wholly to refuse you. Therefore, [Col. 1055A] trusting in God’s help, I began for you in your presence, through your prayers, and completed in your absence without you.

But I ask that the text of each chapter be set before the entire exposition, lest additions, omissions, or alterations in the sacred Canon be rashly presumed; for we hold it unlawful that this should be done without the Roman pontiff.

## TEXT OF THE CANON. FIRST DIVISION

“You therefore, most merciful Father, through Jesus Christ your Son,” etc.

## EXPOSITION OF LORD ODO

Because it is fitting and right that we should give you thanks: “You therefore, most merciful Father,” we ask that you receive the sacrifice from us. And because you admit our voices in humble confession: “You therefore, [Col. 1055B] most merciful Father, through Jesus Christ your Son, we humbly beseech and ask” that you accept the real sacrifice, so that a substantial sacrifice may follow the praises of our voices.

“We beseech and ask.” Beseeching displays humility; asking, confidence. One who implores anything ought to display humility and be confident of obtaining it. Therefore we humbly beseech and confidently ask. Hence it is written: “Let him ask of the Lord, doubting nothing. For he who doubts is like a wave of the sea” (James 1). And again: “Whatever you ask in faith, you will receive” (Mark 11).

“That you may receive and bless [these gifts].” “Receive” means pleasing and acceptable. May you receive them, granting pardon for our faults, not offended but rather appeased by our devotion. [Col. 1055C] “And bless”: by multiplying grace, increasing dignity, indeed by converting them into the most excellent creature of immortality and incorruption.

“These gifts.” These gifts, which we give to you, that they may remain yours, made firm by your blessing; these gifts, which we give to you, that they may stand before you uncorrupt through your blessing; these gifts, which we give to you, that they may be taken up by you, O God, since “the Word was made flesh” (John 1).

“These offerings.” We customarily give gifts to those from whom we seek to obtain something. These offerings by which we present you with a gift in earthly bread, that we may obtain him who is heavenly; these offerings by which we present you with a gift in bodily food, that from it we may receive spiritual nourishment; [Col. 1055D] these offerings by which we present you with a gift in the substance of bread and wine, that from it we may receive Christ’s body and blood.

“These holy, unspotted sacrifices.” Holy, because offered to God; unspotted, because still whole and untouched. For they ought not to be touched until they have received spiritual power and have been converted into Christ’s body and blood. For if consumed beforehand, they would nourish only the body. Hence some join what follows to the preceding words, dividing it thus: “Unspotted first of all,” that is, untouched at first, until, fortified by the divine blessing, they are received for the salvation of soul and body. By this word we are admonished that the bread set forth should be whole and violated by no breaking or injury.

[Col. 1056A] “First of all, which we offer to you for your holy Catholic Church.” “First of all,” which is joined to the preceding words in the sense already stated, is also joined to those that follow, signifying that we offer the victim first for the whole Church and then for the others who follow.

“Be pleased to grant her peace” from visible and invisible enemies, so that she may be trampled down neither by the persecutions of human beings nor defiled by the instigation of demons into sins.

“To guard her.” In that very peace.

“To unite her.” So that she may not be divided by any schisms or heresies, but that the whole Church may be united in every respect in the unity of the sacraments of Catholic faith.

“And to govern her throughout the whole world.” So that in her counsels, dispositions, judgments, decrees, institutions, [Col. 1056B] and actions she may be deceived by no error and in all things may be guided by your governance.

“Together with your servant our pope, our bishop, and our king, and all orthodox believers and worshippers of the Catholic and apostolic faith.” From the whole we descend to the parts, so that, having first prayed for the entire Church, we may afterwards be concerned for individuals. For the entire Church needs one kind of governance, individual churches another, and individual persons another. One kind of care must be given to public affairs, another to private matters. Yet concerning the three persons for whom he proposed prayer, this seems to be observed: the other priests should pray for the true pope, bishop, and king.

“Orthodox.” That is, glorious in life and doctrine, whose renown is spread among the people by the merit of their life [Col. 1056C] and doctrine.

“Worshippers of the faith.” Not merely persons possessing faith. For possessing faith is one thing and cultivating faith another. The one who cultivates faith is he who strives and is intent on living according to faith, whereas many possess faith but do not do this.

## TEXT OF THE CANON. SECOND DIVISION

“Remember, Lord, your servants, men and women, N. N., and all who stand around, whose faith is known to you and whose devotion is manifest, for whom we offer to you—or who offer to you—this sacrifice of praise,” etc.

## EXPOSITION OF LORD ODO

[Col. 1056D] The first period, extending thus far, prays for the whole Church and for all worshippers of the faith. The second, which begins here, turns its attention to those present, who are assistants and fellow-workers in the holy sacrifice. “Remember, Lord, your servants, men and women, and all who stand around”: that is, remember indeed those whom I proposed above, namely all worshippers of the Catholic faith, both male and female, and all standing around, that is, those bodily present, fellow-workers in the holy mysteries. For I am not sufficient to celebrate such great sacraments unless aided by the prayer of the gathered multitude, whom I have previously urged to prayer as well, saying: “Pray, brethren.” And as the first period descends from the whole to the parts, so this second proceeds from the universal [Col. 1057A] to the particular. Then all those standing around follow as particular cases. And lest some betrayers of the faith and persons of corrupt life be among those present, it adds:

“Whose faith is known to you.” That is, who are of proved faith and of [devotion] before you. [The supplied text prints *depositionis*, literally “deposition”; “devotion” conjecturally repairs it to *devotionis*.] For God’s knowing is approving. Alternatively: “Remember, Lord, your servants, men and women.” And because in some codices the following letter N is found, it signifies that remembrance is made by name of certain persons. Hence some maintain the practice in this place of remembering those whom they hold dearer, then adding: “And all who stand around,” so that, after remembrance has been made of beloved persons absent, it is also made of those present.

[Col. 1057B] “And all who stand around.” Although at first Masses were not celebrated without a congregation, the Church subsequently adopted the practice of celebrating solitary Masses, especially in monasteries.

And since they have no congregation whom they may greet in the plural, nor can they alter the plural greetings, they turn themselves toward the Church, saying that they greet the Church within the Church, address the whole body in the body, and that by the power of the communion of the whole Church the holy mysteries are celebrated in the Church through God’s grace. Nor is there any believer anywhere who does not become a participant and fellow-worker in the life-giving most holy rites, provided that, within the body of the Church, he adheres to the head as a useful member. In this sense, those standing around are understood here to be all believers everywhere, who, in the unity of the whole body, adhere [Col. 1057C] both to one another and to the supreme head, so that whatever good is done in the whole body, no one who is not separated from that body can in any way be alien from it; rather, every good may be supplied to every member as health-giving nourishment, so that the whole body may be made vigorous by God’s Spirit. In this manner the prayer previously offered for all worshippers of the Catholic faith is repeated by solitaries, who say that prayers ought frequently to be repeated, so that God may at least be overcome by importunity.

“Whose faith is known to you”: that is, therefore, Lord, remember all who stand around, namely all believers, because their faith is known to you and their devotion is manifest. Thus solitaries understand this passage.

[Col. 1057D] “For whom we offer to you, or who offer to you.” Not only priests and clergy, who, according to their different ranks, are occupied with divine riches, offer; those also who hear and stand by as fellow-workers with vows and prayers offer, and, as it were, communicate by the kiss of peace, confirming what has been done.

“This sacrifice of praise” is truly a sacrifice of divine praise, as we have testified in this office: “It is fitting and right, just and salutary, to give thanks to God the Father”; and with angelic praises we have prayed that our voices might be admitted.

“For themselves and all who are theirs.” We offer for ourselves when, by the sacrifice, we ask God to be both a protector against dangers to body and soul and favourable toward the attainment of good outcomes in either respect. [Col. 1058A] We offer for all who are ours when we pray for our friends and possessions. For we supplicate for peace for friends when they are at war; for a safe return when they are travelling; for health when they lie ill; for conversion when they live perversely; and against the misfortunes of friends, that, with God’s help, they may escape them. In missal books we frequently find petitions for our possessions. At the time of sacrifice, we pray against fires for our places; against excessive dryness of the air or storm for our crops; against plague for our animals; and against other harms for other possessions. For according to the Apostle, in Christ we have consolation for the present life and the future life (1 Tim. 4).

[Col. 1058B] “For the redemption of their souls.” For this alone is the sacrifice by which we could be redeemed; its good is sufficient against our evil, because it is more good than our sin is evil, and therefore it redeems us from our evil at a greater price.

“For the hope of their salvation and safety.” This most holy sacrifice not only frees us from evils but also fills us with goods; it not only rescues us from punishments but also increases the joys of salvation and safety. Salvation, I say, means the eternal salvation of souls; safety means the perpetual incorruption of bodies. This is what we offer so precious a gift for.

“And render their vows to you.” By offering the sacrifice of praise, they render their vows to you. Otherwise perhaps [Col. 1058C] they would not render their vows unless they offered such a sacrifice. They are aided by the power of the sacrifice so that they may be able to render their vows. It is difficult to restrain vices and bring virtues into a settled habit. But for the saints to be able to render these vows, they must necessarily be strengthened by God.

“To the eternal God, living and true.” This distinguishes him from false and insensible gods, to whom the nations vainly paid their dues. “Communicating,” they offer to you the sacrifice of praise and render their vows to you.

“Communicating.” For outside communion there is no place for offering God a true sacrifice or rendering vows.

“And venerating the memory.” We do not otherwise offer God a pleasing sacrifice, nor otherwise render vows usefully to God, [Col. 1058D] unless we venerate the memory of the saints. For one who does not honour Christ’s members cannot honour Christ, who is the head. And one who does not honour the Son does not honour him who sent him. Let us therefore honour the head in the members, God in his saints, so that by their merits and prayers we may in all things be fortified with the aid of divine protection.

“First of all, the glorious,” etc., as far as “may we be fortified by aid through the same Christ our Lord.” In the veneration of the saints this order must be observed: first and above all the blessed Mother of God is to be honoured; second, the apostles; third, the holy martyrs; then all the other saints.

“This oblation therefore.” Because we offer you this sacrifice, communicating in the body of the Church and [Col. 1059A] venerating the memory of the saints. Therefore we ask that you receive this oblation favourably: namely, that if we are hindered by our sins, you may nevertheless be pleased, through communion with the holy Church and veneration of your saints, to receive the sacrifice we offer to you.

“Of our service,” that is, of the clergy, who, according to the ranks received, serve you in this offering of sacrifice.

“But also of your whole family,” that is, of the whole congregation standing by. Solitaries understand “of our service” thus: of me with my minister. “But also of your whole family,” that is, of the whole Church.

“We beseech you, Lord,” etc., as far as “be granted a place in the flock through Christ our Lord.”

“And order our days in your peace.” He significantly says “your.” For there is peace of the world and peace of God. [Col. 1059B] The peace of the world is useless; the peace of God is health-giving. The world establishes peace so that it may freely indulge its pleasures. God gives peace to the saints so that, intent upon the divine commandments, they may secretly devote themselves to virtues.

## TEXT OF THE CANON. THIRD DIVISION

“Which oblation, we beseech you, O God, deign in all respects to make blessed, enrolled, ratified, reasonable, and acceptable, so that it may become for us the body and blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.”

## EXPOSITION OF LORD ODO

In the preceding periods, namely the first and second, we prayed for the Church, for worshippers of the faith, and for the congregation standing by. This third period, which we now enter, is chiefly occupied with the sacrifice, that it may become [Col. 1059C] perfect and be changed into another substance, immortal and incorruptible. “Which oblation,” and the rest, as far as “deign to make acceptable.” Blessed in every respect with glory, that it may become glorious; blessed with immortality, that it may become immortal; blessed with incorruption, that it may become incorrupt; blessed with divinity, that it may become God. He descends from the whole to the parts, praying for the parts of universal blessing for the victim for which he had prayed for universal blessing; thus, having first said “blessed in all respects,” he adds in particular “enrolled,” “ratified,” “reasonable,” and “acceptable,” which are the parts of complete blessing.

“Enrolled” (*ascriptam*). We know that in the Trinity, which is God, [Col. 1059D] the Son is the brightness of the Father’s glory and the image of his substance. Therefore he who is the Father’s figure and image represents and portrays the Father, as it were a certain sculpture of him, or a writing in which the Father shines forth; that is, he appears clearly, so that the Son is rightly called his brightness. Therefore the Father is engraved and inscribed in the Son, whose figure and image the Son is, so that the Son is his writing, having him inscribed in himself. Alternatively, the Son is called “writing” because he has within himself the form of all things. For all things were created in such a way that the forms of the divine Word arranged them; nor did they come forth into being otherwise than the forms in the supreme Word prescribed. There the forms are not one thing and the Word itself another, where nothing is one thing and another, but all things are the very same thing. Thus, although the diversity of forms shines forth there intelligibly, [Col. 1060A] nevertheless they are all only the one and same Word; and although there is there true and perfect unity, yet, in relation to created things, a certain diversity appears there. Thus, when God spoke once in the Psalm (Ps. 61), the Prophet understands two things in one word. Hence it is written: “What was made, in him was life” (John 1). It was made from nothing, yet it was in the Word; it was made as a creature, yet it was eternally [in the Word]. It was in the supreme art; it was made in actuality. It lived formally in the reason of the artificer; it was made substantially in the reality of subsisting. It came forth from nothing, so that what was made might exist substantially. It lived in the Word, so that it might exist formally before it existed substantially. What was made was manifold; the Word is simple. What was made manifoldly was simple in the Word. Wondrously, [Col. 1060B] plurality is seen in one thing and multiplicity in what is simple; it is seen, yet not comprehended. It can be seen but cannot be explained how the one Word is inscribed with all the forms of all things, as is written elsewhere: “The pen of a swiftly writing scribe” (Ps. 44). The Father is the scribe who swiftly inscribes all things with his Word. He writes swiftly because he does not delay one thing for another. He writes swiftly because he writes all things without delay. Therefore the Son of God is the written Word.

But the assumed body too is rightly called writing. For just as a passing voice is written down so that what flees of itself may remain in writing, so something corruptible is written when it passes into incorruption, so that what was transient through corruption may remain through the writing of incorruption. Thus Christ’s body is a kind of writing: from passible flesh it was made impassible in the resurrection, and from earthly bread it daily becomes heavenly upon the altar. Thus in Christ both the Word is called writing and the body likewise is called writing. What, then, is “enrolled” except writing placed beside writing? Christ’s body is therefore not only writing but also enrolled writing: that is, writing set beside writing, namely the body joined to the Word. When, therefore, we pray that the victim may become enrolled, what else do we desire than that what is still corruptible bread may become an incorruptible substance? That is, that from a voice it may become writing joined to writing, namely to the Word. Therefore make, Lord, our oblation enrolled: that is, writing joined to writing, [Col. 1060D] so that it may become Christ’s precious body, united to God’s Word and joined in unity of person.

“Ratified.” We call that ratified which we hold to be certain and fixed. Let it therefore become ratified: that is, let it not remain unstable and subject to change through corruption, but become lasting and fixed through incorruption, and thus certain.

“Reasonable.” The blood of bulls or calves is not sufficient to cleanse us from sins (Heb. 10). For it is inferior to a human being. Therefore for a rational human being only a rational victim suffices. Let our victim therefore become rational, since the man assumed by the Word subsists from a rational soul and human flesh. Let our victim become rational, that we may offer a true human being for human beings, and that in the rational victim God may be propitious to human beings. Let it become reasonable, [Col. 1061A] so that we may offer reasonably. For one who offers without striving to amend himself offers unreasonably. One who offers with an unrepentant heart offers unreasonably, like Cain, who offered rightly indeed but did not divide rightly. He indeed offered to God rightly, but did not divide rightly, because he did not strive to amend himself. Hence it is written: “He did not look upon Cain and his offerings” (Gen. 4). For God neither knows nor receives the offering of one whom he does not know. The victim of the wicked is unreasoning, as it is written: “The prayer of him who did not hear the law shall be an abomination” (Prov. 28). Let the victim therefore become reasonable, so that we may offer it reasonably with fear and repentance.

Or let the victim become reasonable, that is, for a rational, right, or honourable cause. For if anyone offers in order that he may find again what was stolen, [Col. 1061B] kill an enemy, commit robbery, or acquire money or favour, the cause for offering is not called reasonable; therefore such a victim is not acceptable. Thus let our victim become reasonable both by the merit of those offering it and by the cause of offering it, so that it may consequently become acceptable as well.

“Acceptable.” What has the preceding three kinds of complete blessing cannot fail to be acceptable. God cannot hate God. But because God is love (1 John 4), God loves God, and a victim which is God is acceptable to God. Why then do we pray that it may become acceptable, when it cannot displease? For what is acceptable in itself displeases on account of the offerer. It is rejected on account of the offerer, though accepted so far as its own nature is concerned. It is accepted for the holy, [Col. 1061C] but the very same thing is not accepted for the wicked. It helps the godly and condemns the wicked. It benefits the godly unto salvation and harms the wicked unto condemnation.

“So that it may become for us the body and blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.” He had said “blessed in all respects” and added four kinds: enrolled, ratified, reasonable, acceptable. But all these were closed, less intelligible, less apparent. He opened the door and disclosed everything: namely, that for us it may become Christ’s body and blood. Here everything is completed; here everything is perfected: that it may become only Christ’s body and blood. Christ’s body and blood alone are the victim blessed in all respects, enrolled, ratified, reasonable, and acceptable. “That it may become for us body and blood.” He significantly says “for us,” that is, for worshippers of the Catholic faith. [Col. 1061D] By “for us” he excludes pagans, Jews, and heretics: for us who communicate and venerate the memory of the saints. For there is no place for a true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church.

“Who, the day before he suffered,” as far as “his hands.”

“He took bread”: still bread, not yet flesh.

“And lifting his eyes to heaven, to you, God the almighty Father, giving you thanks, he blessed [it].” He blessed it: he made it his body. What had previously been bread became flesh through the blessing. Now it is flesh, no longer bread.

[Col. 1062A] “And broke [it].” O miracle! It was broken between his fingers while he sat unharmed among the disciples. He was whole, and yet divided into parts; he held himself in his hands and from his hands offered himself to the disciples to eat. David signified this, who, according to another translation, was carried in his hands before King Achish (1 Sam. 21). Thus we daily consume Christ on the altar, and he remains; we eat, and he lives; we crush him with our teeth, and he is whole. We consume, eat, and crush him not only in appearance but also in reality; not only in form but also in substance. And in a wondrous way he is consumed while remaining, crushed while incorrupt, distributed while undivided, just as after the resurrection he offered his spiritual body to be touched. Yet by a like contradiction what is spiritual is not tangible, nor is what is tangible spiritual. [Col. 1062B] For under the appearance and taste of bread and wine we eat and drink the very substance of body and blood, the substance having been changed under those same qualities, so that beneath the appearance and taste of the former substance the true substance of Christ’s body and blood may have come to be.

“He gave [it] to his disciples,” etc., as far as “my body.” It is clear that the bread, on receiving the blessing, became Christ’s body. For after the blessing he would not have said, “This is my body,” unless in the blessing it became his body.

[Note: [Col. 1061D] For bread is not transubstantiated into Christ’s body except by the power of those words, “This is my body”; nor does it become the body through any blessing before those words, which are indeed effectively operative of transubstantiation, are pronounced. See St Thomas, Part III, question 78, article 4. [Col. 1062D]]

“Likewise, after supper, taking also this excellent chalice.” If Christ had taken the chalice of the supper, he is said to have taken “this” chalice. Therefore this chalice and that one are the same. For unless they are one, it cannot be said [Col. 1062C] that in that [supper] he took this [chalice]. Therefore it is one also when it is taken in the hands at the altar to be blessed, and is not yet blood but still wine, because of the unity of faith and of him to whom, and in whose honour, it is faithfully offered. For it is daily taken to be blessed in the faith that what was then to come about may now come about. And because this faith is one throughout the whole Church, and he to whom it was then and now is offered is one, therefore the chalice, when taken even for the divine words, is one; just as the altar of all churches is called one, because upon it, according to one faith, one sacrifice of the Lord’s body is daily offered.

“Excellent.” He calls the chalice, still containing wine, excellent until it immediately becomes excellent when it is blood, as it is written: “My inebriating cup, how [Col. 1062D] excellent it is!” (Ps. 22). Or this is in comparison with that which Melchizedek offered and with the other offerings of the Old Testament; or on account of the excellent majesty of him to whom it is offered. Hence in what follows it is said: “We offer to your excellent majesty.” “Chalice”: by a metaphor, that which contains is put for that which is contained—that is, the vessel for the liquid of wine and water.

“Into his holy,” etc., as far as “he blessed [it],” that is, he made it his blood. “He gave [it] to his disciples,” etc., as far as “my blood,” is said intransitively and employs one grammatical case for another. “The chalice of my blood” means, as if he had said, [Col. 1063A] “the chalice, namely my blood.” Likewise, here it is clear that it became blood by the blessing. For after the blessing previously mentioned he added: “This is the chalice of my blood.”

“Of the new and eternal testament.” For he confirmed the new testament of the Gospel for eternity by the blood of his death. Thus Abraham, after offering sheep and oxen, made a covenant with Abimelech and Phicol, commander of the army: that is, he struck sheep and oxen for a covenant, so that the covenant might be confirmed by the blood and death of animals (Gen. 21). And Jacob, fleeing in Gilead, after making an oath with Laban his uncle, sacrificed victims so that the covenant of the oath might be confirmed by the blood of victims (Gen. 31). And Moses, in order to confirm the testament he received on Sinai, sprinkled the blood of a victim with hyssop [Col. 1063B] upon the whole people and the tabernacle (Heb. 9; Exod. 24).

“The mystery of faith” pertains to Catholic faith: one must believe that after the blessing there is true blood, so that one who does not believe this is an unbeliever. Again, something hidden beneath sensible things is called a mystery, just as the reality of blood lies hidden in the taste and appearance of wine. Therefore the altar’s chalice is a mystery of faith because under the appearance and taste of wine true blood is believed to be hidden. It is a mystery of faith because what is believed is covered by certain sensible things. For true blood is believed where wine is perceived by sight and taste. It is a mystery of faith because what faith believes is hidden within. Within is true blood in true faith; outwardly is false [Col. 1063C] wine in true appearance. Wine is perceived, yet is not [there]. Blood does not appear, yet is [there]. Sense is deceived by the quality; faith securely holds to the truth of the thing. Therefore the blood is called the mystery of faith, because faith believes the blood to be hidden within. What is perceived is manifest; what is believed is hidden. And whatever is hidden belongs to faith, just as what is manifest belongs to sense. Therefore the blood is a mystery of faith, since, being hidden, it pertains to faith.

“Which shall be shed for you and for many unto the remission of sins.” “For you,” namely those present; “for many” distinguishes them from pagans, Jews, and false Christians.

Whenever you do these things, you shall do them in memory of me. [Col. 1063D] For without this remembrance we do not effect the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood. Take away Christ’s words, and Christ’s sacraments do not come to be. Do you wish Christ’s body and blood to come to be? Add Christ’s utterance. The utterance of Truth accomplishes what it says: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 48). Undoubtedly, in the creature, Christ’s utterance says what it does concerning the creature. “For your almighty utterance, O Begetter.” Therefore Christ’s body and blood come to be by Christ’s utterance. Whenever we receive them through the mighty word, we commemorate the Lord’s death until he comes (1 Cor. 2). [Col. 1064A] And lest this remembrance should withdraw from us under these mysteries, he adds:

“Wherefore, O Lord, we your servants remember”—that is, we who, according to the ranks of clergy received, serve in the office of this sacrifice; or, according to the solitaries, who minister here in the present.

“But also your holy people,” who are devoutly assembled here in the present out of reverence for this sacrifice; or, according to the solitaries, who live faithfully everywhere in the unity of the Church.

“Of the same Christ your Son,” and so forth, down to “gifts and things given.” A gift (*donum*) is something prepared for giving, even if it is not given. A gift is that which can be given. But a thing given (*datum*) is what has already been transferred into another’s possession; what has gone from possibility into act; what is already possessed. Therefore Christ’s body and blood are gifts prepared for us by God. They are gifts which can usefully be given. They are true gifts, but placed in heaven in Christ. But they are things given when, for us, they come to be from the creaturely bread and wine; given when we receive them at the altar, when we are thereby refreshed sensibly. Gifts in heaven; things given on earth. Gifts with God in Christ; things given upon the altar in the sacrament. Gifts naked and open in heaven; things given at the altar, covered by sensible forms and hidden—yet in both places the same true realities.

“A pure victim.” Formerly the victims of the old law, taken from irrational animals, were fleshly, full of the foulnesses of carnal impurity and of odors, and reduced by the crushing of teeth to dregs and excrement. But this victim is pure because, although it is true flesh [Col. 1064C] and blood, it is nevertheless spiritual and incorrupt.

> [Note: [Col. 1063D] When Odo says that the eucharistic victim is not carnal or corporeal but spiritual, he does not deny that Christ’s true flesh is truly and really present in it. Rather, he means that it is not corporeal—that is, it is not immolated merely by a bodily and outward rite, as the other fleshly victims were; rather, a spiritual and divine power is present in it, and Christ’s body is not sacrificed in the outward appearance of flesh, etc. [Col. 1064D]]

It is divided, yet cannot be consumed. It is consumed, yet remains incorrupt. It is ground, yet is unharmed. It is broken, yet remains whole. This victim is flesh—not fleshly flesh, but uncontaminated light, and therefore pure. It is a body, yet not corporeal, but spiritual light, and therefore pure. Pure in cleansing, pure in purifying; pure because divine, purer than bodily light.

“A holy victim.” The former victims were indeed holy, but not holy in themselves; they were holy because they bore the type of this consecrated victim. They were imperfect, and therefore less holy; this one is perfect, and therefore wholly holy. They remitted the sin of one person; this one takes away the sins of the whole world. In them there was only remission; [Col. 1064D] in this one there is full payment and perfect redemption. They obtained pardon for a debt without payment; this one pays the debt, with full recompense. Therefore this one is fully and perfectly holy; those were holy, but less so and imperfectly.

“An immaculate victim.” That is, without every stain of fault: conceived and born without sin, and thereafter living in the world without fault; therefore immaculate. It was indeed born from human flesh, but without the condition of human propagation; therefore immaculate. It was conceived without a man, from the holy Virgin; therefore immaculate. [Col. 1065A] It was conceived without human action, by divine power alone; therefore immaculate. For a work accomplished by God alone and by no other cannot have a culpable beginning; therefore immaculate. For we cannot blame the beginning of a human being who, without human agency and with God alone as author, was created—even though from a sinful mass—unless we wish to ascribe sin to God; therefore immaculate. Yet it is believed to have been conceived and born from a virgin pure from every sin; therefore immaculate. For from the time when she heard in the angelic salutation, “Full of grace” (Luke 1), she is believed, having been purified by faith, to have lived the rest of her life without every fault, with the Holy Spirit as guardian.

> [Note: [Col. 1065D] Read cautiously: for the Mother of God, while still existing in the womb, attained before her birth that sanctification by which she would never actually sin, although at the incarnation of the Word she received a more abundant overflowing of grace. See St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, III, question 27, articles 4 and 5, reply to objection 2. [Col. 1066D]]

Thus this victim was taken from the immaculate one, and therefore is itself immaculate. In this place we are also warned that the bread placed upon the altar ought to be very white, [Col. 1065B] and such that no stain can be perceived in it, so that the figure may visibly display what is preached concerning the substance: the outward figure is seen to be pure and immaculate, whose inward substance is said to be pure and immaculate.

“The bread of eternal life.” When you hear “bread,” do not suppose it to be what it was before the blessing, lest you be deceived by the changed substance. Previously it was bread; now it is not bread, but flesh alone. Yet he called it bread, as though he said “food,” as it is written: “I am the living bread” (Matt. 6). And: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77). How is it bread of eternal life when it is received by many unto condemnation? The power of this bread is faith, which works through love (Gal. 5). For the bread also is a mystery of faith, as was said concerning the chalice [Col. 1065C]. Therefore, received without faith, it does not profit. For if this bread is a mystery of faith—that is, something hidden, seen by faith alone—what benefit is there in receiving without faith what is not seen without faith? You have lost your eye: what benefit are riches in a chest to a blind person? What benefit is it to store within yourself the riches of human redemption when you do not see them, the eye of faith having been lost? Hence it is written: “Whoever eats and drinks the body and blood of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 15). For one eats unworthily who eats without the faith that works through love. Therefore this is the bread of eternal life, not for those who receive only with the mouth, but for those who receive also with the mind; not for those who press it with the tooth, but for those who touch it by faith. Hence it is written: [Col. 1065D] “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20). As though he were saying: You wish to touch me with hands; you wish to touch me bodily. Not in that way: I desire your faith. Touch me by faith; believe that I have ascended to the Father—that is, that I am equal to the Father.

“And the chalice of perpetual salvation.” What we have said concerning the bread can likewise be said concerning the chalice; and what was said of eternal life, of perpetual salvation.

“Upon which,” etc., down to “an immaculate victim.” The end looks back to the beginning. “Upon which”—namely, the holy sacrifice and immaculate victim—“may you deign to look and to hold acceptable”; as if it said: May you look upon them [Col. 1066A] and accept them, because they are a holy sacrifice and an immaculate victim, so that we who distrust our own merit may be aided by the majesty of so great a sacrifice. But why do we pray that the Father be propitious and serene toward the victim, and accept it, when nothing is more acceptable to him and he always looks upon it propitiously and serenely? For it is written: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3). Yet this must be referred to those who offer: those who are frightened because of sins and distrust themselves set before themselves an acceptable victim, so that, shielding themselves with its shield, they may ask that the Father be propitious and serene toward them beneath it, and may desire that they themselves be accepted under that which they never doubt is acceptable. [Col. 1066B] Thus those who do not dare to offer themselves to the Father in their own persons, lest they provoke him by their evils, set forth the beloved Son, that they may enter beneath him and, under his protection, come before the Father’s sight. Therefore we pray that this victim may be acceptable and may please for us, so that, when we offer what pleases, God may be pleased with us. Hence the examples of the saints are also introduced: righteous Abel, the patriarch Abraham, and Melchizedek the high priest, so that, as God accepted their sacrifices by being propitious to them, so he may receive this victim by having mercy on us. Melchizedek is called high priest because he was regarded as such among the priests of that time.

“We humbly beseech you,” down to “before your divine majesty.” Here too it is remarkable how we pray for the Lord’s body and blood to be carried into God’s presence, when [Col. 1066C] it is written that Christ always stands before the Father’s countenance, interceding with God for us (Heb. 7); and when we read that Christ, ascending into heaven, was exalted above all things and sits at the Father’s right hand (Mark 16). How, then, do we pray for Christ to be carried where he always is? But above we prayed that the Father’s countenance might become propitious and serene over the victim of the Son, not because the Father could be severe toward his Son, but so that, under the occasion of the Son, we might bring ourselves into the Father’s propitiation: that for love of the Son he may have mercy upon us, and may, as it were, count the Son of little worth if he does not receive us for his sake. So also here we pray that the Son, who is always with the Father for us, may be carried to the Father, so that our vow and devotion may come through the Son to the Father, and that, by the power of so great a sacrifice, our prayers may be presented before the sight of God—as though [Col. 1066D] the Son does not ascend to the Father if our devotion does not reach there.

For this reason we pray that, just as Christ was lifted from the earth into heaven before the disciples and became invisible to their sight, afterward to send the gift of the Holy Spirit, so this victim may be transferred from the earthly altar upon which it is immolated to the sublime altar before God’s sight; so that from there we may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace, and that what is visibly handled on earth may work invisibly in heaven. Offered here, accepted there—not by a change of place or by the passage of time, as though a motion of transfer begun from this place must afterward be completed at another place. [Col. 1067A] Rather, in the same place, that which was bread becomes the flesh of the Word. It is not transferred in place in order that flesh may come from bread; yet it is transferred from the altar to heaven because it is transferred from bread to God. But because God is everywhere, no change of place occurs in order that the flesh made from bread may be joined to God. It is invisibly transferred inwardly to God, and is not visibly moved outwardly from the altar: offered at the altar through human devotion, accepted in heaven through God’s propitiation. For then it is, as it were, accepted by God, when God is propitiated toward us and sends us heavenly blessing.

But Christ did not need the aid of angels when by his own power he ascended into heaven. Why then do we ask that this victim be carried by the hands of an angel before God’s sight, when angelic offices are not necessary for this carrying? But this is [Col. 1067B] what was said: that by the carrying of Christ’s body and blood we ask for our prayers to be carried. Yet angels have been assigned to us, who daily offer our prayers to God. Hence it is written: “Their angels always see the face of the Father” (Matt. 18). We therefore pray, under the occasion of Christ, that our prayers may be carried by the hands of an angel, so that good angels may present good prayers under the pretext of so great a sacrifice.

“We humbly beseech you, almighty God.” We supplicate you, we bend before you, we pray more earnestly: show your omnipotence; stretch out your mighty hand, so that those things upon which you look with a propitious and serene countenance may also be carried to your invisible and sublime realities and admitted before the sight of your majesty. Here is the necessity of bending, [Col. 1067C] here the work of supplication, here rests the completion of all our labor: that this victim may be carried to your sublime altar, before the sight of your divine majesty. What is this? What is it for the victim to be carried to the sublime altar, except for the sheep to be placed upon the Shepherd’s shoulders? And what is the sheep placed upon his shoulders, except the human being assumed by the Word? And what is more sublime than the Word of God? Daily the Word of God assumes believers to himself through participation in this sacrifice. Therefore the Word of God is the sublime altar to which we pray that the victim may be carried before God’s sight, and through which we may be brought in. The sight of God is the Father’s Word, in which he beholds everything that he has made. For everything the Father does is in his Word. For “what was made in him was life” (John 1); and “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1), [Col. 1067D] that is, in the Word; and “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. 32); and “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103). What could more properly be called God’s sight than his Wisdom, in which he beholds all that he does? Therefore, for the victim to be carried to the sublime altar before God’s sight is nothing other than for our offering to be joined to the Word, united to the Word, made God; and for us, through it, to be assumed into God and for our prayers to be accepted.

“That as many as shall receive from this,” etc., down to “may be filled with every blessing and grace.” Through the same our Lord. Amen. The Church has a visible altar on earth; there is also an invisible altar in heaven with God. The victim that we offer to God upon this altar is joined to God and becomes God. In this sacrifice earthly things are joined to heavenly things, the creature to God. When from this altar we receive this creature, we receive [Col. 1068A] God from the sublime altar. When here we receive Christ’s body and blood, we receive God from heaven, in whom we are filled with every heavenly blessing and grace. Here we visibly receive Christ’s body and blood; invisibly we receive from heaven, to which they have been carried, God’s blessing and grace. We receive, I say, grace and blessing if we worthily receive Christ’s body and blood. For one who receives unworthily indeed receives with the mouth and physically grinds with the tooth, but gains nothing spiritually. Indeed, one who receives Christ’s body and blood unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself (1 Cor. 2). Therefore we pray that all of us who have received the most holy body and blood of your Son from this participation at the altar may, from there to which they have been carried, be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace. [Col. 1068B]

## TEXT OF THE CANON. FOURTH DISTINCTION

“Remember also, O Lord, your servants, male and female, who have gone before us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace. To them, O Lord, and to all resting in Christ, we beseech you to grant a place of refreshment, light, and peace; through the same Christ our Lord. Amen.”

## EXPOSITION OF LORD ODO

This fourth period begins at the point at which the third, which labored in effecting Christ’s body and blood, has thus far ended. Once Christ’s body and blood have been effected, it returns to praying for the dead, [Col. 1068C] more confident of being heard through the advocacy of the sacrifice. “Remember also, O Lord.” Here commemoration is customarily made of deceased friends and family.

“To them, O Lord, and to all resting in Christ.” To them—that is, those whose remembrance we have made—and afterward grant pardon also to all the rest.

“To us also, your sinful servants.” Namely, we who are present and celebrate the office of this sacrifice; or, according to the solitaries, we who faithfully serve you in the body of the Church throughout the whole world. I do not know how to make the whole text that follows clearer by other words, down to “through whom, O Lord, you always create all these good things.” “Through whom” is said in relation to what had been said, “through Christ our Lord.” But it is remarkable [Col. 1068D] that he said in the plural, “all these good things,” although Christ’s body and blood are only one. Yet in Christ’s one body there are many forms; and although the substance is one, the figures are many. For however many loaves are placed upon the altar, so many figures remain, the plurality of substances having been converted into one body, so that plurality may visibly appear where there is invisibly a unity of substance, and one individual reality may be present in substance where the figure is manifold. Several loaves are placed as figures, and in substance become Christ’s one body; the plurality of figures remains, the plurality of substances ceases. It is one individual reality; many things appear. Accordingly, we speak of the Lord’s body sometimes as it is and sometimes as it appears. We often say, in the distribution of the Lord’s body: “We have expended many victims,” or, “With several victims [Col. 1069A] we have refreshed many people with the one body of Christ,” showing in one verse both the plurality of what appears and the unity of the invisible substance itself, when we call the victims many and the body one. So in this passage we say, “all these good things”: namely, all the victims which the Church immolates throughout the whole world. If indeed you consider their sensible qualities, they are infinite in number; if their substance, there is one blood and one flesh. These are always created by God, because he who once created the body of his Word from the Virgin daily creates his flesh from bread and his blood from wine.

“You sanctify.” Daily he sanctifies, through the prayer of the priest and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit.

“You give life.” Daily he gives life, giving life to the body previously inanimate. Hence this victim was earlier called rational.

“You bless.” Daily he blesses, as above we prayed that it might be made blessed in every respect, and added four kinds of blessing.

“And grant them to us.” Daily he grants us the body of his Son, because what is with the Father on high, he daily grants us upon the altar. And what is a gift with him in heaven is a thing given among human beings on earth.

“Through him and with him.” Through him, the Son, by whom the Father creates flesh from bread, sanctifies, gives life, blesses, and grants; through that same Son, to God the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, is all honor and glory. There is honor and glory to the Father through the Son, as it is written: “Father, I have made your name known to the people whom you gave me” (John 17). And: “Father, glorify your Son, that [Col. 1069C] your Son also may glorify you” (ibid.). For the Father has honor and glory with the Son, with whom he has power and divinity in common. For with him with whom he has all things, the Father also has honor and glory; and he has them in the one in whom he is. For it is written: “The Father is in me, and I am in the Father” (John 10). Because the Father is in me, whatever the Father has, he has in the Son; for he cannot have it except in the one in whom he is.

“Let us pray: Instructed by saving commands.” He exhorts us to pray, adding the reason: because we are instructed in this by a saving command. Read the Gospel and you will find the command. Why is this prayer alone preceded by an exhortation, when we make many prayers in this canon and have been exhorted to none of the others? Because those are lesser and composed by human reasoning; this one is perfect and formed by God alone. Hence follows:

“And formed by divine instruction.” As the Gospel relates, the apostles asked the Lord, “Teach us to pray” (Luke 11); and the Lord instructed them by establishing this prayer.

[Col. 1070A] “We dare to say.” For weak human beings, divine instruction appears to be daring and presumption. We dare through obedience, not through audacity. Those who dare through audacity are guilty; those who dare through obedience are praiseworthy. The daring of obedience is good; the audacity of pride is evil. And, just as the reason for praying was added—because it was commanded—so the reason for daring came before, because we have thereby been formed by divine instruction. Therefore we pray because we have thereby been instructed by saving commands; and we dare to say because we have thereby been formed by divine instruction. For we pray because from it we received the command; and we dare because God has encouraged us in our fearfulness to do so. He gave the command to pray for salvation; he gave confidence to dare because of fear.

“Our Father, who are in heaven.” [Col. 1070B] I do not expound the Lord’s Prayer, because I find that many Fathers have expounded it. Nor is there need to set down here what can readily be found in many places.

“Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord.” After the Lord’s Prayer has been confirmed by saying “Amen,” all the text that follows prays for pardon of sins and for peace, taking its own beginning from the end of the Lord’s Prayer, which prays against sins by saying, “But deliver us from evil.” Then the following text begins concerning sins, saying: “Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord, from all evils.” Then it proceeds concerning peace: “Graciously grant peace in our days.” Again concerning sins: “That we may always be free from sin.” Then concerning peace: “And secure from every disturbance.” Again it proceeds concerning peace: “May the peace of the Lord be always with you.” [Col. 1070C] Then concerning sins it is repeated:

“Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.” Again concerning peace: “Grant us peace.” And thus the end and completion of the sacrifice is made in peace, and we remain in peace. Hence, at the completion of the sacrifice, we receive the kiss: by this we show both assent to and participation in the sacrifice, and signify that we ought to remain in peace.

## CONCLUSION

Having most diligently investigated the text of the most holy canon, I beseech you, whoever you are who transcribe it, that, carefully observing the distinctions, you mark the beginnings of the individual chapters in somewhat larger letters, and illuminate with capital letters the periods in which this work of four books is wholly enclosed; adding titles by which both the diversity of the periods may shine clearly at first sight and the beginnings of the individual chapters may present themselves at the first glance; and so that altered colons and commas, through confused distinctions, may not throw the sentences into confusion. [Col. 1070D]

[Col. 1071]

# THREE BOOKS ON ORIGINAL SIN

## BOOK ONE

### Prologue

[Col. 1071A]

As I am about to speak on the famous question of original sin, which is frequently debated among the orthodox, I call upon you, Holy Spirit, that you may be with me, guarding my mind and tongue in all things, lest anything be done in this matter without your good pleasure. But I ask the brethren not to accuse me of presumption because I undertake to examine a matter very frequently stirred up and yet always undiscussed, and to pour new light upon an ancient chaos. For certain brethren compelled me to do this. When I pleaded the burden of outward occupations, they urged upon me the need to avoid the curse of the hidden talent. When I set forth my dullness of intellect, they answered with that saying from the psalm: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80). When I feared the difficulty of the question, they set against it the promise [Col. 1071B] of God who says: “I have laid help upon one who is mighty” (Ps. 88). And I too recalled to myself that, while writing, more than once things had occurred to me which I did not know. Therefore, overcome by my brethren’s unwearied prayers and by charity which, when it burns, often exceeds measure, trusting in God’s mercy and in the help of fraternal prayers, I descended into a dark pit and entered the hiding places of a difficult question, hoping that light would shine from darkness. It should therefore be known that this question of original sin arises from what the Apostle says: “In whom all sinned” (Rom. 5), that is, in Adam. And it is asked how we sinned in Adam, deriving the origin of sin from Adam. Before setting forth the knots of this question, [Col. 1071C] it seems necessary to say what is meant by what is called sin.

### In What Ways Evil Is Said

Sin, then, is an evil which God does not make. For evil is spoken of in two ways: namely, that which God makes and that which God does not make. Hence it is written: “Making peace and creating evil” (Isa. 45); and: “Is there evil in a city which God has not done?” (Amos 3). For punishment for sins is an evil for those who suffer it, and God makes it. For God repays evils for sins. But the evil called injustice God does not make at all, but punishes, so that he is by no means the author of that of which he is the punisher.

### That Sin Is Not in the Body

This evil is not found in bodily things, nor do we properly say that we sin by means of the body. For in homicide, what is called evil? If you accuse the sword, God made iron. If you blame the hand, God also [Col. 1072A] made it. If you blame the movement of the hand or of the sword, who does not know that movement has essence? If it has essence, it was made by God. For every essence other than God was made by God. Therefore the movement made by God is not evil. Thus neither is the human mind itself an evil which God did not make. But if neither mind, nor iron, nor hand, nor any movement is evil, what then is called evil in homicide? It is not found at all in bodily things. Likewise in adultery, neither person, neither sex, nor movement, discharge, or even lust itself, is an evil which God does not make. Finally, those bodily things themselves which God made are not the evil which God did not make. Nor is evil in them, such that they may rightly be called evil on that account. Finally, if bodily things were to charge themselves with evil because they commit adultery, they could rightly make this defense: By the Creator’s ordinance we are subject to the mind so long as we are animated by it; the Lord established for us that mind which we must serve and obey in all things. Therefore, by divine ordering, we are moved to all things at its command. What sin, then, do we commit by obeying reason, as God commanded? Do we commit adultery? Our mistress, reason, commands it, whose authority we were unable to resist. We are not evil workers, because we do not do our own evil but another’s. Praise the obedient servant; blame the master who commands the fault. What sin does a horse commit by carrying an enemy? What sin does a spear commit by wounding a human being? [Col. 1072B]

### That Sin Is in the Rational Spirit Alone

He truly errs who seeks sin in the body. It is found nowhere but in the rational spirit and its will; [Col. 1072C] yet reason, will, and the spirit itself are not the evil which God did not make. Rather, the injustice of the will is itself the evil we seek. God did not make it at all, and it is what must not be imputed to God. Nor need an author of all evils be sought, just as God is known to be the author of all goods.

### That Evil Is Something According to the Manichaeans

The heresy of the Manichaeans asserted this, considering evil to be an essence because they see it divided in many ways, like a genus, into species. They speak of the evil of injustice, pride, fornication, and many other species; so that, plainly subordinate to a genus, we see their subdivisions descend in an ordered way even to individuals, and conversely [Col. 1072D] many individuals are truly united into one species and many species into one genus; likewise, higher things are most aptly predicated of lower ones. Who would deny substance to that which answers the question “what?” Who would refute the claim of essence in what no one denies to be universal?

### Otherwise

Moreover, every name is significant by convention. Therefore who would deny that this utterance—namely, *evil*—which the grammarian calls simple in form and declines through all cases, and which also receives singular and plural numbers, is a noun? Therefore it signifies something by convention. A Greek hears this utterance, and a Latin hears it. To the Greek who hears it, it is only a sound; he understands nothing by it. So too the Latin, if he says that he does not understand, plainly lies: let him question his conscience, and he will find a movement of mind caused by that utterance. For this utterance, when heard by a Latin, truly conveys something to the mind. For when he hears, “He does evil,” he either denies it or grants it—something [Col. 1073B] the person who does not understand does not do. Since, then, that utterance is a noun, it signifies something; if something, then an essence, for what has no essence is not something. Therefore what is called evil is an essence, and evil is not nothing.

### That Evil Is Nothing

We, on the contrary, say that evil is nothing and has no essence. For that which God did not make is nothing; but God did not make evil. Therefore evil is nothing and has no essence, because, if it is, God made it—he who made everything that is. But to say that God made evil is impious. Therefore evil is nothing, because evil is a privation of good; and everyone who knows rightly knows that a privation is not something. Finally, there are four kinds of opposition: those of contraries, relatives, affirmation and negation, privation and possession. The first two of these—contraries and relatives—set one thing against another: for example, white and black, which, as contraries, both exist and each has its own essence. Likewise master and servant, which are relatives: both exist and each has a true essence. But the other two kinds of opposition set against something that which does not exist; as when *not-man* is set against a human being as a negation. A human being indeed exists, but *not-man* has no essence. Likewise, when *impious* is set against pious as a privation, piety exists, [Col. 1073C] but impiety has no essence; it is only the privation of piety. For just as *not-man* merely denies that a human being exists, so impiety denies piety. But what merely denies that something exists could not itself exist; therefore privation or negation has no essence. Thus evil also does not exist, if it is only the privation of good. But it is only the privation of good. And, to show this more clearly, because good and evil are spoken of in many ways, lest their multiplicity produce error, let us take justice for good and injustice for evil. For our purpose is to speak of sin, which we have called injustice and evil.

### That Privation Is Nothing

Therefore injustice is the privation of justice, since the privative particle merely removes justice and does not posit another essence. For just as *not*, a negative adverb, denies the existence of what is joined to it and does not posit another existence, so the privative particle removes the joined [Col. 1074A] essence and does not posit another essence. For just as *not just* denies the attached “just” and does not posit another existence, so *unjust* removes justice and posits nothing else. Privation differs from negation only in this: negation exists wherever it exists, whereas privation does not exist wherever the deprived thing is absent, but only where it ought to be present; and privation is never without an obligation that the deprived thing should be present. Nor can we properly speak of privation where the deprived thing ought not to be present. Hence *irrational* is not properly said of that to which the use of reason is not due. Yet privations are sometimes used for negations, and, when names for things are lacking, they are often used even for the things themselves. But here we are treating privation in its proper sense. Therefore, since injustice is the privation of justice, it has no essence, [Col. 1074B] and is therefore nothing. Thus sin and evil are nothing, since sin and evil are nothing but injustice.

### That Evils Have No General Species

Therefore evil is neither a genus nor are those things into which it is divided—namely adultery, homicide, and the rest—species, since they have no essence. For what has no essence is neither genus, species, universal, nor particular.

### That Reasoning Concerning Evils Proceeds from Goods

That there is an orderly division, ascent, or descent in evils belongs to goods. For whatever we say concerning privations, we derive wholly from the things deprived; nor does a privation do anything except where the account of the deprived thing precedes. For we cannot even form a privation unless we have the thing that is deprived. [Col. 1074C] Therefore the species and genera of things come first, so that by them we judge the differences of privations. Unless we know the essences of justice, piety, and patience, we cannot understand their privations—namely injustice, impatience, and impiety. Thus truth belongs to genera and species in essences, whereas in privations there is imitation, as also in negations. It is clear in them that they are not essences, genera, or species; nevertheless, conversely, from the things negated they take the likeness of genera and the alteration or semblance of species. For just as man is a species under animal, so *not-animal* is, as it were, a species under *not-man*. This is what Boethius calls contraposition in the *Antepredicaments*. But this is not the truth of genera and species, but an alteration; and it is so in privations as in negations. Yet in negations the imitation alone is evident; in privations, however, it is not merely evident, because they are more similar to things, so much so that many think them to be things and to have their own essence. For they are said only of those in whom the deprived thing ought to be present but is not; and they have proper names, sometimes without a privative particle, as essences do. Negations, however, nowhere have proper names without a negative particle, nor do they admit an obligation of the thing negated; rather, they are said of all things in which the negated thing is not found. Thus *not-man* is everything that is not a human being; but *unjust* is only one who ought to be just and is not. [Col. 1074D]

### That the Names of Privation and Possession Signify the Same Thing

Privations often have names without [Col. 1075A] a privative particle, just as possessions do: evil as good, darkness as light, blindness as sight, fornication as chastity. And although privation does not set essence against essence, because privation has no essence, the name of privation nevertheless signifies an essence—but the essence of possession, not its own. Therefore the name of privation and the name of possession signify the same thing. But the name of possession signifies its own reality, while the name of privation signifies an alien reality: the name of possession signifies its own essence by positing it; the name of privation signifies that same essence by removing it. The name of possession offers what you understand; the name of privation removes what you understand. Therefore the name of privation is significant of something, not of its own thing, but of another thing which it signifies to be deprived.

### Epilogue of the Preceding Matters
[Col. 1075B] From the foregoing, then, it may be concluded that evil exists only in the rational spirit; it is not a thing in a subject, but the privation of a thing from a subject. And when you say that evil is in the will, you do not say that something is there; you say only that good is not there where it ought to be. And this is plainly evil: that good is not present where it ought to be. For injustice is the absence of justice where it ought to be, and a person is unjust when he is not just although he ought to be. What, indeed, could be said more rightly than that he is unjust who, though able, refused to retain the justice entrusted to him, and voluntarily abandoned the gift of so great a good?

### That rational nature cannot lack the debt of justice

You received justice: a good entrusted to you, to be guarded most carefully and nevertheless returned, because he who entrusted it [Col. 1075C] demands his deposit. Do you wish to return it well? Guard it well. The more you guard it, the more you return it. And the more you return it, the more you guard it: justice is a marvelous good, which you return by guarding it and do not lose by returning it. Indeed, the more you return it, the more you preserve it.

It is a good, I say, to be guarded with all one’s strength so that you may return it; for if you lose it, you have nothing to return. Yet you owe the deposit to him who entrusted it. He entrusted it; therefore you owe it. But perhaps you lost it voluntarily, because you voluntarily abandoned it. Nevertheless, the one who bestowed it demands the deposit. But you do not possess it, because you voluntarily abandoned what you ought to return. Thus the one who bestowed it is found to be a just claimant; but you, who do not return it, are an unjust debtor. Unjust, I say, not because you possess any essence in this privation, but because you do not possess the due essence [Col. 1075D] of justice—due because you received it, not preserved but voluntarily abandoned.

The error of the Manichees is therefore clear. Thinking evil to be a real essence, and being unable to ascribe it to the good God, they were compelled to invent some author of all evils, so that two contrary authors might be the authors of contrary things—the good author of good things, and the evil author of evil things—and thus they might establish two first principles of all things.

### That one who is punished for evil is not punished for nothing

Someone may perhaps say: “What then? If evil is nothing, are we punished for nothing when we are punished for evil?” And it seems foolish to be accused for injustice, since injustice is no essence. But if the matters said concerning privations are carefully considered, no one will be troubled [Col. 1076A] by this objection. For without a possession, privation can neither be spoken of nor understood; nor is privation anything other than the removal of what is possessed—for example, injustice is the removal of justice.

Therefore, when we are punished for injustice, we are punished for justice abandoned. But justice is something; therefore we are punished for something. Thus, although injustice is said to be nothing, something is nevertheless understood in it, on account of which we are punished because it has been abandoned; we are punished, therefore, for the justice which we abandon. Accordingly, privation too is nothing; yet, when we are punished for it, we are punished for that which is something. And most justly does he punish one who has voluntarily abandoned that which he gave to be preserved always. He punishes, indeed, on account of justice—not because it is possessed, but because it is not possessed; not because it is present, but because it is absent. But the absence of justice is injustice. Therefore, justice not being present where it ought to be is injustice.

[Col. 1076B] But “justice not to exist,” neither where it ought to be nor where it ought not to be, signifies being. Therefore injustice too does not signify being, because it merely denies that justice exists, although only where justice ought to exist. But tell us what injustice posits as existing,

> and keep Phyllis for yourself alone.  
> (Virgil, *Eclogues*, III.108.)

### That essences are predicated of non-existent things

But perhaps someone says: “We certainly say that injustice is a privation, a relative, and an opposite. No sound-minded person will deny that privation, relation, and opposition exist, since ‘relative’ is called a most general genus, while privation and opposition are called its species. How, then, is injustice said not to exist, [Col. 1076C] when so many essences are predicated of it? For everything exists of which something is predicated. Otherwise, can anything be said of that which does not exist?”

Certainly it cannot be done by ordinary usage, but it can by necessity. For we necessarily speak of things that do not exist; and because they have no words of their own, we speak of them by means of the words of things that do exist. Since we cannot speak of them in their own terms, we are compelled to speak of them in borrowed terms.

Consider: when we devise many things in thought, forms are indeed shaped in the mind, but the things for which they are shaped are not found. Thought takes its figures from existing things, but the things for which it takes them do not exist. Nor can the mind think that which does not exist unless it takes forms from that which exists, so that by the forms of things which are, it thinks of things which are not. Therefore, [Col. 1076D] when we say what we think, just as the mind cannot think what does not exist unless it is formed after the likeness of what exists, so the tongue cannot speak of things which do not exist except through the words of things which do exist.

For speech follows thought, so that the tongue arranges words only as thought dictates images. A painter likewise cannot paint things which do not exist except through the figures of things which do exist. He paints outwardly, for things which do not exist, those forms which thought dictates inwardly from things which do exist. And this practice of speaking and painting what does not exist is common, as a certain wise man says:

> Painters and poets  
> Have always had equal power to dare whatever they please.  
> (Horace, *Ars Poetica*, 9–10.)

At times we wish to recount the phantasms of dreams [Col. 1077A] and describe the deceits of dreams. And how can their emptiness be recounted except through words denoting things? It is therefore no wonder that, when we speak of privations, we employ words taken from things and explain privations through the names of things.

### That each person is the author of his own evil

Before returning to our subject, another point occurs which may trouble the reader unless it is resolved. For, since it has been said against the Manichees that there is no one author of all evils, someone may perhaps doubt and ask: “Whence come evils, if there is no author of all evils?” But truth shows that each person is the author of his own evil. For although you may have sinned through example, exhortation, or coercion, [Col. 1078A] the sin you committed belongs to no one but you who committed it. No necessity could compel you unless you willed it. Remove the will, and you will see that no necessity has force. Are you oppressed? Are you slaughtered? It is nothing, unless you will it.

Therefore you sin from no necessity, but from will alone. And for this reason the will alone is either punished or rewarded. It is punished if you suffer what you do not will; it is rewarded if you attain what you rightly willed. You, therefore, are yourself the author of your own evil: you sinned by the choice of your will. Do not ascribe to another what you yourself did, nor seek another author, when you yourself made yourself its executor. But, having reached the end of these matters, let us rest a little, so that refreshed by repose we may rise more vigorously, from another beginning, to what follows.

[Col. 1077] Here ends the first book.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1077]

### The twofold account of original sin

[Col. 1077B]

Our purpose was to speak of original sin, because the question is asked how we have sin from our origin, which is Adam and Eve. This question arises from what is read in the Apostle: “In whom all sinned” (Romans 5).

The question, then, is how we sinned in Adam. It is certainly true that we were all in Adam and are from him, but according to the flesh. Concerning the soul, however, the authority of the orthodox Fathers says otherwise. For it does not hold that soul is sown from soul as flesh is sown from flesh, nor that a part is separated from a soul in order that another human being’s spirit may arise from it, just as a part is separated from flesh in order that another human being’s body may arise.

There are, nevertheless, many who maintain that the soul comes by propagation (*ex traduce*) as the body does, and that the power of the soul proceeds together with bodily seed. Since their arguments are not wholly to be despised, it seems proper that, as we have set forth both views, we should pursue both as well, beginning with the path of the orthodox.

### Why God is said to have rested from working, if He now creates souls from nothing

Their teaching concerning the human soul is this: nothing from a parent’s soul is separated with the offspring’s seed; nothing is ever transmitted from a parent’s soul to an offspring’s soul; nor does the later soul derive anything from the earlier. Rather, just as God breathed a new soul into the first human being, so He always breathes fresh souls into fresh bodies. Fresh, I say, and new: either newly made from certain existing secret and hidden sources, or newly created, as was the whole creation in the beginning, from nothing.

Against this is urged the reading of Genesis, in which God is said to have rested from all the work that He had accomplished (Genesis 2), as though the daily labor of producing creatures could not agree with rest after creatures have been created, and as though He could not truly be said to rest from the things He had accomplished if He still labors daily to make other things from nothing.

[Col. 1078B] But the answer is that this passage describes only the creation of bodily things. God is not said to have made any bodily thing from nothing after that first creation; for whatever bodily things are created daily arise from the seed-principles of the first creation, and no bodily thing anywhere comes to be which does not descend from that first origin.

God therefore rested from the first creation of bodily things, since He is not found afterward to have made any bodily thing from nothing. But concerning incorporeal things it is written: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5). Thus the orthodox say that the human soul in no way descends from a soul, but that new souls are made daily by God in fresh bodies. Hence it is written: “Let the dust return to its earth, whence it was, [Col. 1078C] and let the spirit return to God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12). Observe how distinctly it is said that dust belongs to earth, whereas God gave the spirit. And again: “We have had the fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we revered them; shall we not much more submit to the Father of spirits and live?” (Hebrews 12).

Here again it is distinctly shown that human beings are fathers of our flesh, but God is the Father of our spirits: flesh alone comes from a human being, while a new spirit is given by God in new flesh. According to this view, the question is very difficult. If I have only my body from Adam, but my soul not from Adam but from God alone, and if sin is only in the soul and not in the body, how am I said to have sinned in Adam? Adam sinned, and the sin was in his soul alone, not in his body. But I do not have from him the soul in which sin exists. How, then, am I said to have sinned in him? When he sinned, my body was then in him; I would rightly be said to have sinned in him if sin were in the body. But now, since sin is in the soul alone, how am I said to have sinned when he sinned, if my soul was not at all in him?

### On genera, species, and individuals

Against this question the orthodox answer as follows. They say that individuals stand differently in relation to species than species stand in relation to genera. Species possess more substantial being than genera, and a genus does not suffice for the substance of a species, because a species possesses a difference substantially in addition to its genus; thus a species is substantially more than a genus. For a human being is more than an animal, because a human being is rational, whereas an animal is not rational.

Individuals, however, have nothing substantially more than species, nor is Peter substantially anything other than a human being.
