That there are several individuals under one species does not result from anything substantial, but from accidents. Therefore only an individual can be under a species, whereas a species cannot be under a genus by itself. Thus, if all individual human beings except Peter were destroyed, the species “human being” would have Peter alone as its individual. Peter is an individual because of the collection of accidents; “human being” is a species because it can be common to many individuals.

For the phoenix bird, though it has only one individual, is a species, because it can be common to many. For “phoenix” is one thing and “this phoenix” another. “Phoenix” is a specific nature capable of being common; “this phoenix,” however, is a nature which is only individual and can be nothing but singular. The phoenix is delimited by genus and differences; this phoenix is distinguished by the property of accidents. An individual can be predicated of only one thing. A species, even if it is predicated of only one thing, is universal; an individual, however, is only singular.

Reason apprehends a species from genus and differences; sense recognizes an individual from the properties of accidents. The inward faculty of reason pertains to universals; external sensory knowledge pertains to singulars. We perceive individuals bodily, but apprehend universals rationally. And when a species is predicated of one individual alone, an accident can equally be said of the individual and of the species, although accidents are principally and primarily in individuals.

### That, in each thing, the individual must be distinguished from the species

Therefore, when the first human being was made, the human soul was first made in one individual and afterward divided in another; the nature of the human soul itself was wholly and entirely in two persons—wholly, I say, because it existed nowhere outside them; entirely, because no person lacked anything of the human soul.

Hear three things and distinguish them. There was the human soul; there was Adam’s soul; and there was Eve’s soul. These three are different. Adam’s soul is an individual—or, if you prefer, a singular or a person—which is predicated of nothing. Similarly, Eve’s soul is an individual, or a person, or a singular, which is predicated of nothing. The human soul is a specific nature, not individual but common, which is predicated of the two persons and divided among them. Distinguish these three, and in distinguishing them use not sense alone but reason as well. For an individual is distinguished from a species not by sense but by reason alone. But, so that these points may be grasped more easily, a few things must be said concerning the individual, the singular, and the person.

### On the individual

[Col. 1080A]

An individual is something contracted by the property of accidents, so that it is predicated of nothing. For higher terms are predicated of individuals, while individuals are predicated of nothing. Even if a species does not inhere in several things but has only one individual, the species itself is predicated of the individual, while the individual is predicated of nothing—for example, “phoenix” of this phoenix, “world” of this world, and “sun” of this star.

This is the meaning of “individual” with respect to a universal, not with respect to a whole. For there is also an individual in a whole: being a part of the whole and the whole being divided in it, it itself, because of its smallness, cannot be divided—for example, a unit in number, a point in a line or time, a letter in speech, or an atom in a body. Thus what is lowest among universals, and smallest among wholes, [Col. 1080B] is called an individual. The latter is so called because it is not divided into smaller things; the former because it is not predicated of lower things.

The individual of a whole constitutes and is not constituted; the individual of a universal divides and is not divided. The individual of a whole comes first in the constitution of the whole; the individual of a universal comes last in the division of the universal. The individual of a universal has the universal itself wholly and completely in itself; the individual of a whole has nothing of the whole in itself beyond itself.

### On the singular

A singular is that which is distinguished from all other things by some property. This distinctness of each thing from all others exists not only in individuals but also in universals. Universals too have their own properties, by which, though not by sense, they are nevertheless distinguished from others by reason. For reason, through the power of its discernment, both apprehends the nature of universals and distinguishes them from one another and from individuals. Thus, although universals are common, they nevertheless possess a certain singularity of their own essence, just as individuals do.

Therefore every essence, whether individual or universal, is singular insofar as it has the singularity of its own essence, by which it is considered separately from others. Thus every individual is singular; but not every singular is an individual, because only that which is predicated of nothing is an individual, whereas everything is singular.

### On the person

A person is an individual of rational nature. Hence, among all individuals, only those which do not lack reason are called persons. There is, therefore, no person among universals, nor among those individuals which are not rational. Every person, then, is an individual, but not every individual is a person. And the relation of person to individual is the relation of individual to singular.

The grammarian divides person into three: first, second, and third. The first, which speaks, and the second, to which speech is addressed, can only be rational individuals. Therefore they are rightly persons. The third, concerning which speech is made, is likewise rightly a person when it is rational. But in this third person there is a problem according to the grammarian, who calls every thing concerning which speech is made a third person. How can that be a person which is not a rational individual?

Yet just as a painting, because of its likeness, is called a human being although it is not a human being, and things used on the stage are called persons because of a resemblance although they are not proper persons, so an individual lacking reason is indeed called a third person, but is not one. For reason has the proper characteristic of speech, so that only what has reason has speech. Accordingly, the personhood of reason is divided according to the diversity of speech: the first person is that which makes the utterance; the second is that to which the utterance is made; and the third is that concerning which the utterance itself is made.

When persons are divided in this way according to the three modes of speech, the term “third person” applies to all things by a certain resemblance. For just as speech is made concerning a rational individual, so discourse can be made concerning all other things. It is proper and familiar to rational beings to speak to and about one another, and to retain within their own genus what is proper to it; to transfer this to another seems, as it were, foreign. But because rational beings must sometimes go beyond their own genus and speak about foreign things, we call those foreign things third persons, though they are not persons, because the likeness of third personhood prevails in them insofar as speech is made about them. Thus other things are third persons by resemblance, but rational things by propriety, because the office of speech belongs properly to the rational individual. Let us now return to the subject.

### That there are many goods of the soul

In the beginning, when God created the human soul, He endowed it with many goods. He gave it reason, [Col. 1081C] by which it might distinguish the Creator from the creature. He gave it will and freedom of will, so that it might will what it willed by choice and not by necessity; for it was not to be compelled to blessedness, which is attained only through voluntary justice. He adorned it with justice, by which it might deserve to become blessed. And He subjected justice to the choice of its will, so that it might be just by will and not by necessity.

He also gave it the debt of justice, so that one who has received justice ought to retain justice and is bound, as guilty by the debt of justice, if by will he abandons what he ought always to possess. And because a heavenly city was to be brought to perfection from humankind, the human soul was given the power of bodily propagation, so that by the cooperation of male and female it might be able to generate from its own body the body of another soul. Behold the human soul, thus honored with so many goods at the beginning of its creation, enclosed in two persons and not extended anywhere outside them.

### That the fault of a person is the fault of nature

Behold, both persons sinned through the serpent’s suggestion. Both sinned, I say, while their substance existed nowhere other than in themselves, for it was not yet elsewhere. If, then, the person sinned, it did not sin apart from its substance. Therefore the substance of the person was corrupted by sin, and sin infects the substance which exists nowhere outside the sinful person. But the substance, common and specific to both persons, is one and the same.

Therefore in the sinful persons the specific nature was infected by sin; it existed nowhere except in them. Thus, in Adam’s soul and Eve’s soul, which sinned personally, [Col. 1082A] the whole nature of the human soul was infected by sin. It is a common substance and is specific to both. For it did not yet exist outside them. Had it been divided among others, it would not all have been infected on account of these alone. For if these had sinned, perhaps the others would not have sinned, and in them the nature of the human soul would have remained sound. But now where could the human soul be clean, when it was sinful everywhere?

### How human nature does not sin through itself, but through a person

But perhaps someone will say: “If the common nature—the human soul—sinned in the persons, who can deny that the species sinned?” But it is absurd to say this of the species itself and to ascribe to universals what belongs to persons alone. Moreover, universals are always what they are; however individuals may vary, universals remain immutable. And although the mutability of individuals may truly be predicated of universals, it is not in the universals themselves.

Nor do we say that the species itself sinned through itself, but only in persons. And although accidents of individuals are predicated of universals, they are not in the universals themselves as such, but in them secondarily from individuals. For species differ from individuals, and likewise their properties differ. Thus the property of a human being whereby it is a species, a universal, common, an essence immutable in itself, and predicated of many things, together with the other marks by which universals are distinguished from individuals, does not belong to individuals themselves. Likewise, the facts that Peter is an individual, a person, predicated of nothing, mutable, and the other marks by which individuals are separated from universals, nevertheless belong to universals themselves [Col. 1082C] secondarily.

### On the properties of species and individuals

Since the occasion has arisen and this is useful to our purpose, it should be noted that the properties of universals which are common to universals themselves do not at all belong to individuals. Likewise, those properties of individuals which individuals have in common cannot be fitted to universals, such as those set out above.

But those properties of universals by which each is separated from all others exist principally and primarily in the universals themselves, and are applied secondarily to lower things down to individuals. Likewise, those properties of individuals by which each is separated from all others exist principally in the individuals themselves, but belong secondarily to higher things. Thus the property of body, namely that it is corporeal substance, belongs to all lower things, but primarily to body.

Likewise, the properties by which Peter is separated from other individuals—that he is Andrew’s brother and the chief of the apostles—are principally in Peter himself; universals receive them secondarily from him. Therefore there is a twofold property of universals, and likewise a twofold property of individuals: one property of universals by which they differ from universals, another by which they differ from individuals; likewise, one property of individuals by which they are separated from individuals, another by which they are separated from universals.

For since one and the same substance is in individuals and species, they must have properties by which their difference from one another is apparent. Thus human being and Peter, though one and the same substance, have differences by which they differ from one another: this one is an individual and a person, whereas that one is a common and specific nature. They are one in substance and different in properties. By what they have, they are different; by what they are, they are one. The unity of substance makes one what is different; the diversity of properties makes different what is one.

Thus a species does not have in an individual that whereby it differs from the individual; rather, it has that whereby it differs from the individual in itself and separately from the individual, as though it were not at all in the individual. But that whereby the species differs from universals it has only in the individual, and it has it in the individual as though it were nothing other than the individual itself, although it is a species and not an individual.

Similarly, an individual does not attribute to its species that whereby it differs from the species. Rather, it holds in itself and separately from the species that whereby it differs from the species, as though it had nothing from the species, although it has wholly one and the same substance with the species. But that whereby an individual differs from individuals it has only together with the species, and it has it with the species as though it itself were nothing other than the species.

### That in the soul, because of the fault of the person, there is a fault of nature

Therefore, to speak in accordance with the authority of Scripture—which takes the two persons of the first creation as one and calls them by one name, namely Adam—if Adam’s soul sinned, the human soul sinned. The nature of the person, which is specific and capable of being common, therefore sinned. Yet it did not sin through itself and apart from the individual, for sin is not among those properties by which it differs from the individual. Rather, it sinned in the individual itself and through it, because it has no substantial being other than the human soul, and because sin belongs to those properties by which the individual itself differs from individuals.

Therefore the person does not possess sin apart from its species, with which it has one and the same substantial being. In the first human being, then, the sin of nature is personal, not natural. For sin is principally in the person which itself sinned; it is in the species secondarily, which indeed sinned but not itself. A person could not sin without substance, nor could a person possess sin except in substance. But the person possesses sin; therefore the whole substance possesses it as well. Whole, because it existed nowhere except there; whole, because it had not yet been divided into other persons; whole, since we properly say “whole” (*tota*), not rather “all” (*omnis*).

### The difference between “whole” and “all”

For “whole” is said with reference to parts, whereas “all” is said with reference to individuals. “All” belongs to universals, while “whole” belongs to composites; for “all” gathers individuals, whereas “whole” gathers parts. But a species gathers not parts but individuals. Composition, moreover, is found only in individuals, so that they are called wholes; universals, however, are all of a simple and uncompounded nature, although several things are sometimes said by a certain resemblance to be composite—for example, a species from differences and genus, after the likeness of matter and form.

### That human nature cannot pass to other persons without fault

[Col. 1084A]

Since the human soul is wholly in Adam liable to sin, it cannot be transferred to other persons without sin. The human soul can no longer come to be without the defect of sin, and everywhere it draws with itself the defect which it has had conjoined to itself from the beginning. Therefore every soul created after Adam draws from its natural origin that for which it is blameworthy. Otherwise it will not be a human soul if it is without fault, nor will it belong to sinful nature if it is not itself sinful. Or, if it declares itself not sinful, it must profess that it is not a human soul. No soul shown to be a human soul is created in this life without sin.

### How Christ came without fault

[Col. 1084B]

What, then, do we say of Christ’s soul, which is human and without fault? It was said earlier that propagation was given to the human soul so that, through the cooperation of male and female, it might propagate a human body from a human body. By the authority of divine justice and by the necessity of nature, it was necessary that such a soul and such a body as it was to produce should be followed by a soul of the same kind in such a body. Thus, as the origin and root-principle was, so by a just necessity the process of the human race should follow; and what was produced through the propagation of male and female should not be unlike its beginning.

Christ, however, because He came neither by marital union nor by the embrace of marriage, but was made holy in the Virgin and from the Virgin by divine power alone, was rightly free from sin. Nor ought sin [Col. 1084C] to be sought where there is divine work alone. He who was made without human action could rightly be without sin, so that he who was not made through human beings might not possess sin together with human beings.

Adam’s soul joined fault to the propagation given to it, and added the sin which it itself committed to the good of propagation which God had given. What has been joined together in the origin cannot be separated in posterity. Therefore those who are born through human propagation draw natural sin. You are born through human propagation; fault follows by necessity. Thus one whom human propagation does not produce can be without sin. Remove human propagation: where will you find fault? Christ therefore had no fault because He did not have human generation. Nor is human nature liable to sin except where human generation occurs; for where there is divine operation alone in propagation, there is no fault unless you blame God. Thus Christ would have been born without sin even if He were not God.

### Why Christ had punishment without fault

Perhaps it is asked: Why did Christ, who did not sin, endure such great things? He voluntarily retained, not by necessity but out of compassion for human beings, our weakness—which is useful and in which virtue can be exercised. Since He exercised virtues in weakness even unto death, He gave an example of patience, lest we fail in weakness but endure adversities patiently, because “virtue is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12).

For what harm did the hardship of afflictions do Him, when the marks of hidden virtues were being expressed? Who says that grapes are uselessly pressed in winepresses when he sees pure wines sweat forth? Who would not resolutely grind a compound (*synaxis*) if he wished to experience its hidden power? So in Christ our weakness was outwardly present, so that by its crushing the strength that was within might be made manifest. And thus, though without sin of His own, He deigned to suffer punishment for our sin—not only that which we commit, but also that with which we are born.

### The difference between natural and personal sin

Sin is spoken of in two ways: personal and natural. Natural sin is that with which we are born and which we draw from Adam, in whom all sinned. For my soul was in him by species, not by person; not individually, but by common nature. For the whole common nature of the human soul in Adam was liable to sin. Therefore every human soul is blameworthy according to its nature, even if not according to its person.

Thus the sin through which we sinned in Adam is natural in me but personal in Adam. It is graver in Adam and lighter in me. For I sinned in him not as the one I am, but as what I am. It was not I who sinned in him, but that which I am. I sinned as a human being, but not as Odo. I sinned in substance, not in person. And because substance exists only in a person, the sin of substance is also the sin of person, but it is not personal sin.

Personal sin, however, is that which I do as the one I am, not as what I am: in it Odo sins, not humanity; the person sins, not nature. But because person does not exist without nature, the sin of the person is also the sin of nature, though it is not natural sin.

### What it means to come by propagation (*ex traduce*)

But an objection may be made: it has been shown that every soul comes by propagation, although the orthodox deny this. For every soul is created in a body and has no substantial being other than specific being. But the first soul also had specific being; therefore every soul has its substantial essence from the first soul. Every soul, then, comes by propagation, since it derives its substantial essence from the first.

But this objection is answered by saying that those who speak of propagation from the species do not understand propagation rightly, and they wrongly ascribe to the species what belongs to the individual. For although an individual cannot exist without a species, the individual does not nevertheless have the species from the species. An individual has propagation from an individual, but not according to the same species. For it comes from an individual of one species, through an individual of another species, into an individual of the same species as the first. Thus the extreme terms are individuals of the same species, but the middle is of another.

The source and the result are of the same species; that through which the process occurs is of another. The middle is that through which it occurs; the extremes are that from which and that into which it occurs; the first is that from which, the last that into which. Thus in an animal we say that propagation comes from the first parent, through the middle—seed—and into the final offspring. It comes, therefore, from the first through the middle into the last. The first and last belong to the same species under animal, namely human being: for the parent is an animal and a human being, and the offspring is an animal and a human being. But the middle, the seed through which it occurs, is neither animal [Col. 1086A] nor human being, but of another species.

Likewise in plants, the first is that from which the seed comes; the middle, that through which propagation occurs, is the seed itself; the last, into which the propagation of the plant occurs, is the plant. Thus the last plant comes from the first plant through the middle seed of the plant, which is not itself a plant. We must not therefore suppose that a later individual has propagation from the first individual, beyond their common species, unless it comes about through the middle seed. A species may pass many times from other individuals to a new one, yet we call there no propagation unless it occurs through a middle seed.

And because rational souls do not flow through any seed, the species always passes from the first soul to a new soul without any propagation. Even if the new soul receives the substance of the preceding soul, it nevertheless has no propagation where no seed intervenes.

### How God does not cause fault when He creates a sinful soul

[Col. 1086B]

The arguments set out above prove that the human soul is created sinful in each individual, and that it cannot be created except by God, who creates all things. We must therefore fear lest God be the author of sin, since he is the creator of the sinful soul. But, conversely, we say that God creates the soul sinful and is not the author of evil. For consider, in the human race, who first made the soul and who first made guilt, and you will find that the soul is God’s work and guilt man’s work. God’s work is good; man’s work is evil. Therefore, when you say, “God creates a sinful soul,” you say two things—soul and sin—and refer each to its own author: namely, the soul [Col. 1086C] to God and sin to man. Therefore, in the sinful soul which God creates, assign to God his work and praise it; assign to man his own work and condemn it. He creates a sinful soul. What you hear as “soul” belongs to God; what you hear as “sinful” belongs to man. In this manner God both creates the sinful soul and is not the author of sin.

Further, to speak more plainly, let us substitute “injustice” for “sin.” God creates an unjust soul. Blessed be God, because even in this he is just. For what is more just than to create a human soul unjust? Certainly he ought to create it in me such as it was in the first man, because in being born each person ought to possess such a nature as the propagation of male and female ought to produce. Therefore he creates it unjust, and most justly, because he creates it such as it ought to be. If he created it just, he would be unjust [Col. 1086D] and contrary to himself. For he who had established that human posterity propagated by human generation should follow its own beginning, if this posterity is born [otherwise], denies his own institution, severing the body from its head, so that the end is not contiguous with its own beginning and the human race becomes a two-formed monster, having a head discordant with its body and a beginning discordant with its end. Take care, then, lest, while you recoil from God’s creating unjust souls and foolishly flatter him, you make him unjust; and while you think you honour him, you dishonour the supremely just one.

Further: God gave justice to the soul, and therefore it ought to possess it; but the soul voluntarily abandoned the justice which it ought to possess. Whose fault, then, is its lack of that which it ought to have? Its own—the justice which it voluntarily abandoned—not God’s, who did not compel it. Yet it ought to have that which it does not have. Therefore, that God makes the soul without the justice which it ought [Col. 1087A] to have is not God’s fault but the soul’s. But if he now makes it without the justice which it voluntarily abandoned, is he not greatly to be praised, since he has left it so many goods? It still retains its obligation to justice and its propagation, freedom of rational choice, and reason itself, by which it surpasses the other animals. Foolish soul, who are you to accuse the Creator and to call him unjust because he did not make you just? Let what you have suffice you, for you did not deserve even that. Praise the kindness that gives undeserved goods; do not accuse the rectitude that does not give unjustly. If it does not please him to give to the soul being created everything you desire, give thanks for what has been granted and pray for the rest. Do you wish to make him unjust [Col. 1088A] so that you may be just? But the Immutable cannot be changed, nor can the Omnipotent be compelled. He creates unjust, but this is nothing other than creating without justice and not giving justice to the soul being created. If he does not wish to give more, receive what you have with thanksgiving, and do not trouble him about the rest except by prayer.

But perhaps you say: “I ought to have it.” If you owe it, pay it back. “I do not have it.” You had it. “I lost it.” Who took it away? No one. How, then, did you lose it? “I let it go voluntarily.” Therefore you cannot recover it except by a great recompense. Some matters still remain to be said for the orthodox, but because we are weary, they must be reserved for another beginning.

[Col. 1087] Here ends the second book.

# BOOK THREE

## That the whole human being is said to sin through the soul, not through the body

[Col. 1087B]

The foregoing establishes that injustice has no essence, and that it exists not in the body but only in the soul, where justice ought to be; that souls are not produced by transmission, but by God alone, either from certain existing things or from nothing; that in Adam’s sin the human soul sinned—every soul and wholly; and that after him no soul except Christ’s is made without sin, this being required by divine and natural justice. Since, therefore, human sin is found not in the body but in the soul, we have so far spoken of the soul. Yet the human being, for whose sake we have undertaken this whole discussion, consists of soul and body and is not whole from either one separately, nor even from both taken merely as such; although a human being is sometimes named according to one or the other. Thus a certain sage, descending from the most general genus to the lowest species, places the human being under body, saying that a human being is an animate, sentient, rational body—here taking reason for speech, because, just as the mind uses reason inwardly, so the body uses speech outwardly.

And because, when speaking of a whole, what belongs to a part and is said of a part cannot often be denied of the whole—as the same person may be called black in body and just in soul—so every human being, although consisting of soul and body, is nevertheless called a sinner through the soul. Is the whole composed of many parts? What belongs to one part is said of the whole, though not of all its parts: one who consists of body is called a sinner, yet sinning does not belong to the body [Col. 1087D].

## That in several substances there is one person

Thus Peter is called a person. Although personhood does not belong to the body, the body is nevertheless joined to the soul, so as to possess with the soul what it does not possess by itself. Therefore the individual human being is called a person, not by reason of the body but of the soul; for the soul assumes the body into its own person, so that in one person there are two substances. This is the chief difference between Creator and creature: the Creator has several persons in one substance, a condition which [Col. 1088B] cannot at all be found in a creature. A creature, however, is found to have one person in several substances, which cannot be in the majesty of the Creator. Therefore an individual human being is of multiple substance and one person: one person, multiple substance. A human person consists of several things and is not said of several things; it is divisible, as a whole is through its members; it is indivisible, as a singular is with respect to subjects. Because it has parts, it is a whole; because it has no subject, it is an individual.

## That in the human being, through the fault of the person, there is a fault of nature

And just as something universal is said with reference to an individual, so something is said of a part with reference to the whole. Thus an individual human being who has both soul and body is called a sinner on account of the soul alone [Col. 1088C]. He who has body and soul together is called a sinner through the soul alone. Sin does not belong to the body; yet the one who has a body is a sinner. Therefore it is not said that the soul alone sinned in Adam, but Adam himself also sinned through the soul: that is, the whole, composed of many parts, sinned through one part. Adam, then, is said to have sinned because the soul that he possessed sinned. And if Adam sinned, the human being sinned; for if that human being sinned, human nature sinned, since the human being is human nature. But the whole of human nature was then in him, nor was the specific human being anywhere else. Therefore, when the person sinned—that is, that human being himself—the whole nature sinned, that is, the common human being. And through the sin of the person, the human being of common nature became culpable [Col. 1088D]. And such as Adam made human nature in himself, such he handed it down to his descendants after himself. And such as human nature was made through the folly of the sinner, such it must necessarily be transmitted to descendants through the justice of the Creator, so that what was said above concerning the part may hold of the whole, and what was said of the soul may be found in the whole human being.

## That no one can escape justice

This must be understood not only of guilt but also of punishment: because God rendered punishment to the first human being [Col. 1089A] for guilt, punishment is transmitted to descendants together with guilt, and those who are created with guilt are born with punishment. For, by justice, one rightly suffers what one does not wish, who did what one wished against justice. And one rightly suffers punishment unwillingly who voluntarily abandoned justice. He who voluntarily did evil is justly punished unwillingly, so that he who deserts justice may not escape justice. For when he abandons it by doing evil, he falls into it by being justly punished. If he leaves it through disobedience, he falls back into it through harsh suffering. If he does not wish to be subject to justice by obeying, he is subject to it, willing or unwilling, by suffering. The justice he avoids by will, he incurs by necessity. And a just necessity presses upon him whom an unjust will holds fast.

## That the merit of rational nature lies in the will alone

[Col. 1089B]

We sin or do good in the will, because our whole merit lies in the will. Whatever we merit, we merit by will; and where will is absent, there is no merit at all. But where there is merit, there is just punishment or reward. Blessed be God, who has placed in our will which of the two outcomes shall be ours. What then? As we will, so shall we have. If we will justice, the merit of the victor’s palm follows in accordance with the will. If we will injustice, the merit of punishment follows contrary to the will. Therefore it lies in our power which of the two we attain, because it lies in our will. For nothing is so much in our power as our will. Indeed, those things which are in our power are so much the more in our power as they are more in the will; and because our will is more immediately present to itself and is more within itself than other things, it is especially in our power. For my power does not include what does not depend on my will; what is not in the will presses more by necessity than it delights by power. Therefore in all things the Lord is upright, and there is no injustice in him (Psalm XCI [92]). Whichever we will, he is good: if justice is in our love, the merciful one rewards the merit of the will with a prize; if something else contrary to justice is in our love, the just one repays the merit of the will with punishments [Col. 1089C].

## That rational nature is punished in what it loves

[Col. 1089D]

And because a human being is punished against the will, he is punished in what he loves, so that he may grieve at the loss of what he loves. He is punished, therefore, in himself and in what is his, because he loves himself and what is his. He is punished in himself, namely in soul and body. In soul and body the human being immediately received conditions of infirmity by which he might be punished for sin, which he had not previously possessed because he had not yet deserved them. In the soul, indeed, he is confounded by ignorance, wastes away through fear, is saddened by sickness, is tormented by his own and his body’s difficulty, and is stretched out by countless anxieties. In the body, however, the wretched human being is continually tormented by the heaviness of sluggishness, the pains of diseases, the fatigue of work, exhaustion from labours, the inequality of fasting and gluttony, cold that contracts with its severity, summer that dissolves in sweat, and [Col. 1090A] countless other inequalities, and finally by death. He is punished in what is his through the deaths of relatives, the various misfortunes of friends, and the many losses of his possessions.

## That guilt cannot exist without punishment

These are the evils which God made, so that the human being might suffer for the evil which God did not make but the human being made. And by these evils which God made, the human race is justly punished for the evils which God did not make but the human race made. The human race contracts the evil made by God, so that the wretched human being may always have punishment joined to sin and may live temporal life with punishment, since he lives temporal life with [Col. 1090B] guilt; thus the one whom guilt holds is always wearied by punishment. This is the miserable condition of the human race; this is the inescapable necessity: that we always have guilt and always have punishment as well. In this life we can neither free our neck from the yoke of guilt nor wholly escape the necessity of punishment. This guilt and this punishment for guilt existed in the first human being: the punishment from God, but the guilt from the human being. Human guilt is a work against God; punishment is God’s work against the human being. And just as guilt passed from Adam into all human beings, so too did the punishment of guilt; for guilt could not exist in human beings without punishment. Therefore God’s retribution for our guilt must exist in us, just as God’s retribution came upon the first human being for his guilt, so that those who contract guilt may contract punishment also.

We must receive human nature as it was later in the first human being, not as it was earlier in him [Col. 1090C]. For human nature demands of you what was later in the first parent, not what had been earlier in him; because what had been earlier in him he lost, while what was later remained. What had been good earlier, he lost; what was bad later remained. Humanity cannot be propagated except as it was. Therefore we are only what it was. And for that reason we are miserable, because it was miserable.

## That each person’s soul cannot be made except as belonging to human nature

It may be asked how human souls are created daily by God. For if the substance of a new person is the same as its species, how is it called new when its substance is old? In what way is that created now whose substance existed from the beginning? For the specific nature remains, the nature of which the new soul is created. How, then, is it made new today when its nature remained in the species—made now, yet already existent? What is this? The answer to this question is as follows. It is clear, according to the Catholic faith, that a new soul is created in a human body. But the soul which is created is either of human nature, or of a nature other than human, or of no nature. But it is impossible for a person to be made of no nature, and to be created among natures while having no nature. If, however, a soul of a nature other than human is created in a human body, it is equally absurd to say this. It remains, therefore, that when a new soul is created it is made of human nature [Col. 1091A]. Thus it follows that something new is made of a nature which is not new. Therefore God makes a new soul which does not have a new nature. The same nature is therefore new and not new: new in person, not new in species; new in personal property, not new in common property. A soul new personally, of that nature which has existed universally from Adam, is created by God either from existing things or from nothing.

When you say, “The person of a human soul is created,” you do not say that a human soul is created, but a person. A person of a human soul is an individual soul. Therefore it is not a human soul that is created, but an individual soul. The individual soul is created because it did not exist before; the human soul is not created because it existed before and existed in other persons. Yet the individual soul is a human [Col. 1091B] soul; and, in substance, the individual soul is the same thing as the human soul. This and the human soul are one and the same substance: that is, what is now created and what has remained from the beginning; the individual and the specific, the singular and the common. They are one and the same substance because, when an individual soul is created, it is made of human nature and, though now made from nothing, assumes within itself that which was made from the beginning. I say that the individual assumes the common, so as to have the same substance as it. And although they differ in their properties, in substance they are altogether the same.

Thus new individuals of the human soul are created, which become in substance the same thing as the human soul is. A new individual of the human soul is created; and it must be of the same nature as the human soul, because it is impossible for an individual of a human soul to be created in a human body with a nature other than human [Col. 1091C]. Further, it may also be said that new souls are created not in what they are but in what they have: that is, in property, not substance. Thus not a new substance but a new property comes to be, so that, by the production of a new property, there is said to be a creation of an old substance, and the old substance is called new because it is formed by a new property. And although a person is not without substance, it is not substance but a property of substance that makes a person; and therefore the soul is called new on account of the new property. God gives a new property to the existing soul and makes a new person. The species subsists; a property is given by God; and a new person comes to be. A property comes to the common [Col. 1091D] nature, and by the property an individual comes to be which had been common. Thus the property alone comes to be, not the nature; the property alone, not the substance. Yet substance is said to be created through the property, so that the soul whose property is new may be new.

We do not prefer this account to the former, because we scarcely dare say, in the creation of souls, that God creates not substance but property alone, lest we seem to detract from supreme omnipotence if he is said to create accidents alone in persons and not substances. Nevertheless, we give the reader liberty to hold whichever view he prefers. By these arguments it is shown, according to all orthodox believers, that all human beings contract guilt originally and that all sinned in Adam, although souls are not produced by transmission.

## On the material whole

[Col. 1092A]

We must now turn to those who say that souls too came from Adam, and that thus all sinned in Adam. But here we must first speak of part and whole, as above of universal and individual; for, just as the earlier discussion of universal and individual was effective for demonstration, so here speaking of parts and whole will be useful for understanding.

“Whole” is used in several ways. In one sense it means an integral whole, which naturally consists in the composition of parts, using composition as form and parts as matter. For the composition that comes upon the parts completes the whole. Without composition, indeed, the parts accomplish nothing. Thus in a human being the parts are soul and body; in the human [Col. 1092B] body the parts are all its members. The former complete the human being; the latter, the human body—provided that they have an appropriate composition. And as the whole is constructed by composition, so it is destroyed by the dissolution of its parts.

It frequently happens that whole and part belong to different genera, as the human body belongs to the human being and the body, and the human soul belongs to the soul; but the human being as whole is subordinated to neither, but to that which consists of both. In this whole, neither is the whole itself predicated of the parts nor are the parts predicated of it. Such a whole is always an individual of a species. No such whole is found among universals. For universals, in what they are through themselves, are uncompounded and of a simple nature. If they are called wholes, they are so called in their individuals, not in themselves. Likewise quantities, and genera and species—which seem to signify nothing other than such wholes made up of parts—have parts and are wholes in their individuals, but in themselves they neither have parts nor are wholes; rather, they are of a simple and absolute nature. This is so with genera and species of numbers, whose entire reasoning is contained in the consideration of parts, while they themselves, in their own right, are neither wholes nor have parts; but in individuals they are wholes everywhere through the composition of parts [Col. 1092C].

Nevertheless, philosophical inquiry attributes a constitution to universals, not properly but by analogy with matter and form; for they say that a species consists of genus and difference, as of matter and form. Yet in this constitution of universals the simplicity of nature is not lost, just as parts do not produce the quantity of a whole; rather, the quality that comes upon it simply informs matter. A figure is not the composition of many things into one, but the simple informing of underlying matter; nor does quality create any quantity in the underlying matter by informing it, as does the number of material parts by composition. For the number of material parts establishes quantity. But figure establishes a quality in underlying matter, since figure is a quality. Quality, however, does not belong to the whole made of material parts; quantity belongs to it because of their number. Therefore, because universals do not admit a number of material parts, the quantitative whole does not apply to them, so that they are said to be composite in their constitution; rather, they are of a simple and uncompounded nature, always remaining in themselves what they are and immutable in themselves [Col. 1092D].

## On the formal whole

[Col. 1093A]

There is another sense of “whole,” the formal whole, which consists of form and matter. Peter’s body consists in one way of human figure and the matter of bodily mass, and in another way of its several members and their composition. Figure is present in the mass, and the formal whole consists. This whole does not consist in quantity, because the multitude of material parts is not under consideration here, but only the mass and the forming form; nor should it be called a “how much,” but rather a “what kind,” because it is formal, for form is also quality. It should be known that this whole is found only in individuals of species. Species do not have this constitution, but one similar to it.

## On the virtual whole

[Col. 1093B]

There is also a whole which may be called virtual, consisting of powers, and it is found especially in individual souls. Every soul has powers and certain capacities by which it is constituted and accomplishes many things according to its capacity, so that its bodies flourish in many respects according to the soul’s powers. Thus the human soul has a rational power, which it uses inwardly for invisible knowledge and the discernment of all things; and outwardly it performs in its body many actions, especially speech. It also has a power called sensitive, by which it endows the body with the five senses so that it can perceive each sensible thing, and it apportions among the body’s parts the kinds of sensation according to the distinct qualities of sensible objects: sight in the eyes perceives shapes and colours; hearing in the ears receives sounds [Col. 1093C] and voices; the nostrils receive odour through smell; the palate judges flavours by taste; touch throughout the body, without differentiation, discerns rough and smooth, hard and soft, sparse and dense, cold and heat, and shapes. Although these senses are in the body from the soul, they are neither the soul nor powers of the soul, but affections imparted by the soul to bodies.

It also has a vegetative power, by which it nourishes its body and administers, without conscious knowledge, even the successive stages of the body’s condition. What shall we say of the souls of plants? Medicine certainly does not wholly ignore their powers, since it investigates their capacities in their plants according to their various species. Souls possess powers inwardly, while plants are affected outwardly. The efficacy of the soul flourishes, and this is found in the plant; in the plant we experience the powers [Col. 1093D] that lie hidden in the soul. It is remarkable that, after the soul has died, the powers of the soul remain in the body, and traces remain in the plant of the powers which were in the soul, until they too gradually perish in the body through age.

This whole has a feature peculiar to it beyond other wholes: although it has several powers, it is whole in each one; and in each individual power the soul is present, although the whole consists of one power alone. The whole is in one power alone, yet one power alone does not constitute the whole. The whole is indeed in each single power, but does not consist of each single power. The whole is said of a part alone, but the whole does not consist of the part alone. Although the soul of this plant is said of each of its powers, nevertheless those powers must not be regarded as its species, because it is an individual and is not said of any subject. For the powers of this soul are its parts [Col. 1094A], not individuals subject to it; nor is the soul of this plant whole in each of its individual powers as a species is whole in each of its individuals. Now let us return to the matter proposed.

## How souls come by transmission

The advocates of the seminal origin of souls, whose account we have undertaken after that of the orthodox, say that every soul comes by transmission: that is, a soul comes from a soul through seed, just as its body is propagated from a body through seed, or as a tree comes from a tree; and thus there is a seminal power in the soul just as there is in the body. For unless an animal’s seed draws from its parent a vegetative power, it does not advance to the creation of the ensuing offspring. For how, when seed is emitted into a female, does it sprout [Col. 1094B] unless it draws the vegetative power of the soul? How does that which has been sown cohere within the womb of the pregnant woman unless it has in some way been animated?

Let urine from a parent, spittle, or anything else be introduced: it does not advance to birth or any offspring, nor has an animal ever been born from such an infusion, because such an infusion lacks animation. It draws no power of soul and therefore does not advance to birth, nor does anything sprout from it. Let seed be introduced into a woman, and let something else also be introduced. Why is the latter always unproductive, while the former often advances to offspring? Why is the one never of any effect while the other promises offspring to come, except that the one has no animation at all and the other retains vegetative power? Therefore the seed of the body draws along with itself the seed of the soul: namely, the power of vegetation, which causes the bodily seed to grow into human form, itself growing with it into a rational soul. Thus, as a particle which is not a human body flows from a human body into seed, so a particle which is not a human soul flows down from a human soul as seed.

And just as bodily sexual excitation does not customarily occur without delight of the soul, so bodily excitation does not discharge seminal fluid unless delight of the soul at the same time brings forth from the soul its seminal power—that is, vegetative capacity—so that the vegetative power is the seed of the human soul, just as seminal fluid is the seed of the body. And as the causes, delight and excitation, proceed together, so their effects likewise follow together: vegetative power and seminal fluid. Together also, as they grow, the latter advances to human form [Col. 1094C] and the former to rational soul; thereafter together they remain in one person until death. Causes joined together join their effects together into one individual, namely that which consists of soul and body. But that individual, composed under its species by its causes, advances to an individual of another species. To make this clearer, let us begin elsewhere, so that knowledge of the conclusion may become clearer from a higher principle.

## The descent of substance to individuals through that which consists of body and soul

There is a subalternate genus of substance, which is subordinated neither to body nor to soul, but to that which consists of both.

[Col. 1095A]

[Col. 1095B] This in turn has another subalternate [genus] beneath it, namely, that which consists of vegetative soul and body, having animal opposite it. But that which consists of vegetative soul and body itself has beneath it another subalternate [genus], namely animal seed, which is not an animal but only seed of an animal, having a plant opposite it. Thus, under that which consists of body and vegetative soul, animal seed is one thing and plant another. Under animal seed, the most specific species is human seed, and beneath that is the individual seed of each human being [Col. 1095C]. Human seed, however, under animal seed, is not a human being or an animal, but gradually advances into an individual human being.

Therefore animal seed, which is not an animal, descends and gradually advances into another individual of animal. Thus an animal is propagated from an animal through animal seed, which is not an animal, so that animal seed, losing the specific nature of seed which it had, receives through a certain advancement the substance of another species, which it subsequently possesses [Col. 1095D].

## That species and individuals change in relation to the same matter

In this connection it must be noted that species and individuals undergo change in relation to the same matter; in the same mass now one species comes to be and now another. Thus in the mass of seed there is first seminal nature and afterward human nature. Although the mass is materially the same, it changes its predicable substance with time, so that, while the mass of matter remains the same, just as the figure in relation to it is at one time changed [Col. 1096A], so the specific nature is changed, and likewise the individual, because the individual follows the species and not the matter. For it looks not downward to the underlying matter, but upward to the formed species.

This is frequently evident in bodies: just as figure changes in relation to bodily matter, so species changes according to predication. Figure shapes the mass, and a formal bodily whole comes to be; difference shapes substance, and a substantial species comes to be when incorporeal form changes. Matter is visibly altered in individual things when figure changes; the difference of common substance in visible matter is invisibly changed; and the specific nature is changed in the same visible matter. Thus the bodily change of figure in the mass may be called the cause of the incorporeal change of difference in substance. For just as bodies change figures so that other formal wholes arise from matters, so genera of bodies change differences in the matters of bodies so that other species arise. There, figure shapes matter by means of the differences themselves, so that matter itself consists of material parts; genus is shaped by difference, so that species is predicated of individuals in those matters.

Here you have the parts of matter; there, substance; and matter itself placed in the middle, because matter has parts and also has substance [Col. 1096B].

Substance is predicated of matter; matter is composed of parts. Matter receives the predication of substance from one side and has the composition of parts from the other. On this side it is an individual of the species of substance; on that side it is a whole in respect of its parts. It is referred to the species as an individual and looks to the parts as a whole; and, under both relations, it is later than each, for it is later than the species as individual and later than its parts as whole [Col. 1096C].

## That the integral whole is the intermediate end of the extreme principles

Every integral whole therefore presents itself as a middle between parts and predicaments. It contains parts from below and receives predicaments from above. From higher things it receives its substance; from lower things it has its integrality. From predicaments it has the highest principle of its being; from parts it has the lowest principle from which it comes to be. After the highest principle of itself, it receives from predicaments the differences of species, descending gradually into itself; before its lowest principle, it receives from parts the compositions of parts, ascending gradually into itself. It receives predication from predicaments and composition from parts. The same thing is both whole and individual: individual because it is something; whole because it is from something.

It is an individual because higher things are said of it; it is a whole because lower things compose it. It is an individual because it is not said of a subject; it is a whole because it is composed of several things. Composition does not belong to the individual, nor predication to the whole, because the whole is not said [of something] so as to receive predication, nor is the individual [so called] so as to receive composition [Col. 1097A]. Therefore every integral whole capable of some figure has two principles: for the one the lowest, for the other the highest. It is lowest in relation to the highest because it is its individual; it is highest in relation to the lowest because it is its whole. It is lowest in relation to the highest because it is not said of a subject; it is highest in relation to the lowest because it is constituted from it as its ultimate. It is lowest because it descends from the predicaments so as to be said of nothing; it is highest because it ascends from the parts so as to proceed no further. It presents itself as the middle end of both principles, so that it terminates in itself the office of both. For the end of predication comes from the highest principle, and the end of composition from the lowest. The ends of the extremes meet together in it, so that each course finds its end there. Thus a certain hundred has extremes: unity on one side and quantity on the other; it is an individual, lowest with respect to quantity according to predication, and a whole, highest with respect to unity according to composition [Col. 1097B].

## On the highest and lowest principles

The extremes are, from above, principles to be predicated of individuals; from below, they are principles from which wholes are composed. The end of the principle of predicaments is the individual; the end of the principle of parts is the whole.

First principles enclose the totality of their things at each extreme; and because they leave no thing outside, they turn the propagations of things inward against one another into the same thing, so that the same thing, according to diverse relations, is the middle of both processes. Nor are the lowest subordinated to the highest by predication; rather, they face one another as opposites. The highest are neither predicated of the lowest nor composed from them. For a point of a line, though not yet a line, is nevertheless not wholly non-line, but is almost a line.

Therefore it is in some way a line, although it is not a line in every respect. Similarly, a letter is not fully a sound, but almost; it is not a sound in every respect, but in some respect; it is not a perfect sound, but an imperfect one.

Therefore quantity also exists in some way; likewise an atom of body is almost a body, a point of time almost time, and unity almost number. Thus an atom is in some way substance, while the others are in some way quantity. The grammarian observes these things, who calls the singular number “plural-like.” Common usage also calls the present tense a particle of time, to which, as though to a common boundary, past and future are joined. Thus the ultimate principles can be referred to the first principles, as though subordinated to the genera themselves and receiving their predication within themselves [Col. 1097D].

## On figure

From the preceding it may therefore be inferred that figure is the cause of all bodily things. For without figure neither matter itself can exist, nor can any species in bodies be predicated of individuals, nor can a material whole exist or be composed. Bodily matter may indeed be conceived by the mind, but it cannot exist without figure [Col. 1098A]. Remove the figure which was forming it, and the species which was predicated perishes. For if the figure of a human body perishes, the species itself fails in that body, and according to another figure which it receives, it assumes another species in respect of the body itself. For because it receives the figure of ash or worm, it changes its species in relation to the same mass. Thus that mass of which “human being” was formerly said according to the former figure is called worm and ash according to another. Likewise, a material whole cannot exist without the figure of its mass. For how are its parts distinguished? Therefore figure is the cause of all bodies. Indeed, they can neither be wholes nor individuals, nor have species, nor subsist at all without figure.

## On forms

[Col. 1098B]

Likewise, all incorporeal things cannot exist without their forms: thus all species and individuals receive forms, as do differences and properties, by which they exist. But the first genera of things receive essence as their form; for just as forms give being to their things, so the highest genera cannot exist except through essence. And all other forms belong to their own things, whereas essence is common and universal to all things. Other forms make their own things be something; essence makes all things simply be. And whereas all things have their proper forms by which they are formed so as to be something, the first genera of things have essence, by which they are formed unto being. [Col. 1098C] Other forms make their things be what they are. And since being something is one thing, and simply being another, other forms pertain to being something, not to being. Although being something entails being, it is nevertheless not the function of the other forms to cause being; they do cause it, however, by consequence, not by nature. But essence is primary in the first genera, so that the first genera may principally exist, being first formed through essence unto being; thence lower things have, through forms, being something, as a body has substantial being through bodily form. Therefore forms are causes of all things; for all other forms are causes for their own things, that they may be something, whereas essence is the cause for all things that they may be.

And matter is prior to forms in substantial nature; but if you consider being, forms are prior to matter, because they cause it to exist. [Col. 1098D] We make many and lengthy digressions in this work. The difficulty of the matters proposed compels us to do so, since it produces questions of many kinds. These must be resolved with clarity, lest the matters proposed remain in obscurity. The subtlety of the questions drives us to length, for they scarcely arrive at understanding even through a multiplicity of words. And when, as it were, we cut off one head of the living Hydra, many are sometimes reborn, which we cannot remove except with great effort.

### That the vegetative power is the seed of the soul, although it is not the soul

It was shown above that the seed of an animal belongs to things composed of soul and body, and that in the seed, just as the body, so also the vegetative power advances into the animal that is to come. Accordingly, it cannot be denied that, just as body comes from body, so an animal soul comes from an animal soul through the vegetative power. But perhaps someone will say that the vegetative power in the seed is no soul at all, coming from the parent’s soul and advancing into the offspring’s soul. Yet what was said above stands watch against this: namely, that the soul is affirmed to be spoken of both as a whole and in respect of its individual parts.

But if an obstinate person perhaps does not yield to this argument, then let it be so: certainly no one possessing intelligence can say that the vegetative power is not of the soul. And if, as he says, it is not a soul, it is nevertheless a power of the soul. For unless there is a soul in the body, it cannot produce seed. Remove the soul: it produces no seed; it does produce seed, therefore it has a soul. [Col. 1099B] Therefore the seed has from the soul its vegetative power. It has it either from the soul or from the body. If from the body, remove the soul and discharge the seed, and we shall yield you the palm of victory if we see offspring follow. But if this cannot happen, confess the truth and grant the vegetative power to the soul. And although that power itself is not a soul, yet through it soul is propagated from soul, and the seed becomes seed of a soul propagating a soul. Therefore, whether that power is called soul or not, it is clear that it proceeds from the parent’s soul and advances into the offspring’s soul.

Moreover, we often see the parent’s likeness in the offspring both in the condition of the body and in the dispositions of the soul. What is this except that seed draws from the body a small quantity of fluid and from the soul a vegetative power? For unless seed transmitted to offspring each thing which it draws from each parent, it would not reproduce in each respect so great a likeness of the parent in the offspring. [Col. 1099C]

### That we were all in Adam, soul and body

Therefore, if there is found in seed both that which comes from the soul and that which comes from the body, it is clear that the offspring’s soul comes by propagation, and that all our souls were in Adam’s soul. And when Adam sinned, nothing of human nature had yet gone forth from him; rather, whatever constituted humanity was still wholly in him. Therefore, when he sinned, we all sinned, because we all were in him. We were there in body, and we were there also in soul. Therefore, in him we are all infected with sin; and because punishment justly followed in him on account of guilt, punishment too is born in us together with guilt.

And we are justly born wretched, since we issue from one who is wretched, so that such as the origin is, such also may the offspring which follows be. [Col. 1099D] And thus we are born with sin, which is original to us. Since it was personal to the first man, we are born with the sin which we ourselves did not commit but which he committed; and he poured into us the misery which he himself deserved. This is original sin, by which the human race wastes away and from which Christ delivered us.

### Why God is called Father of souls

By the authority of Scripture the orthodox affirm that soul is not propagated from soul. For the Savior says: “Let the dust return to its earth, whence it was, and let the spirit return to God who gave it” (Eccles. XII). And the Apostle says: “We indeed had fathers of the flesh as instructors, and we revered them; shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live?” (Heb. XII).

Against this, the advocates of propagation of souls say that God made the human body from earth but gave the soul from nothing. Therefore, although parents generate both soul and body in their offspring, God is properly called Father of the soul because a human being received it, not from elsewhere, but from God alone; thus, since the body was received from elsewhere, God is deservedly called Father of that which did not come from elsewhere. Therefore, since according to Scripture God is rightly called Father of the soul, it remains that a human being be called father of the flesh, although he generates both.

### That souls do not come by propagation

The advocate of propagation of souls proves that soul comes from soul because the vegetative power is drawn into the seed, saying that this power is part of the soul and is separated from the whole in order to produce offspring. [Col. 1100B] But the orthodox man says that this person thinks carnally and does not properly understand the nature of the soul. For the human soul is simple and uncompounded in nature. It is not composed of many things, although it consists in many things. It is one and has many powers, just as the sun is one and has many rays. It is simple and nourishes many things from itself for the body—many things externally; but that from which they come is simple within. These are parts of the soul, but it does not have composition, because the whole itself does not admit quantity.

Here the advocate of propagation of souls errs, because when he hears “parts,” he thinks of quantity. He seeks what belongs to body in that which is not body; and he thinks that, just as in a body, a part can be hidden in a soul, that its indivisible unity, which is not local, can be broken apart into diverse places and held by distinct parts in distinct locations, and that it has parts occupying different places, as does a body. He thinks carnally because he judges spiritual things bodily, seeking the quantity of body in a spiritual substance. He hears “parts,” and there comes to mind quantity and composition, such as commonly belong to body. Going out from itself toward body and thinking of itself according to body, the mind thus forgets itself within itself, seeking itself outside itself; it imagines itself extended by quantity and spread out through spatial intervals, although it has no number and is uncompounded—like unity in number, far simpler than the point of a line or the atom of a body, which, although it is from body, is no longer body but, because of its simplicity, incorporeal.

Therefore, when you hear of parts of the soul, [Col. 1100D] remove from your mind every notion of quantity or composition. Cleanse it of phantasms of bodies; set aside sense and imagination, raising yourself to reason, so that by reason you may think of reason. For the parts of the rational soul are not bodies but powers; they belong not to matter but to efficacy. They do not compose it as limbs do; rather, they proceed from it as rays. It is wholly itself, and is not extended in length; it is wholly itself, and does not swell in depth. It consists in many things without losing simplicity, because it admits no composition. It consists in many things and preserves the indivisibility of its unity, because plurality itself does not create quantity.

It is indeed true that a power comes into seed through animal propagation, but that power is an affection of body, not an efficacy of soul. Efficacy is in the soul, [Col. 1101A] and the body is affected by its presence. I name three things: distinguish and consider them—the soul, the soul’s power, and the body’s power. The soul is substance; but the soul’s power is called both soul and substance. The body’s power, however, is neither substance nor a power of the soul nor soul; it is an affection of body, that is, a quality introduced into the body by the soul’s presence. Yet this quality can in some manner be called a power of the soul, not because it is a part of the soul, but because it is introduced into its subject through the soul’s power.

Nor does the soul affect the body only through its efficacies, but also through its qualities. Thus we often see the face grow pale from fear or reverence in the soul, or be suffused with blushes; and many bodily affections arise from the efficacies or qualities of souls. Thus the soul governs and changes the body by its powers and qualities. Remaining wholly in itself, the soul nevertheless causes the body to be affected by many qualities which are not the soul. Thus the soul exercises its powers throughout the whole body, though it is not itself a whole [body]. Indeed, it pours its whole self through all the spaces of the body, while possessing no space. The body has parts; the soul fills the body, and fills its individual parts not with its own parts but wholly, fully, and perfectly. It fills, I say, many things without plurality, things numerically many without number, many things without multitude.

Thus supreme Wisdom has all the forms of all things. Many forms shine in the supreme Art, because many things are in the work; for diverse things in the work were made according to the diverse forms of the supreme Art. For the supreme Art saw inwardly within itself how all things were to be created outwardly, and so all things came forth into essence as the eternal forms showed. Behold, we speak of many forms of the supreme Art, though they are not all in one. Whatever is there is nothing but one thing, the selfsame thing: O one Light, many rays. The rays are one in the one light; they appear many in the manifold creation. [Col. 1101C] Many forms belong to the one Art, and the Art itself is uniform. Simple in itself, it appears multiple in creation. Created things also receive their forms from the supreme Art, because their own forms are imparted to things from the eternal forms. From eternal forms temporal forms proceed; from the highest, lower forms. Yet the forms of things do not proceed from them in such a way as to be those forms themselves, but as things of another nature, because He is Creator and these are creatures.

They do not proceed from the Highest as though the supreme essence flowed piecemeal into creation and bestowed parts of its substance upon creation, so that our forms should be what that supreme essence itself is. Rather, the supreme essence creates, so that these things come to be through its efficacies. [Col. 1101D] It fills the whole creation yet is not a whole; it fills all spaces while possessing no space; it fills all times at once, without time; wholly, fully, and perfectly, it fills the individual parts of the whole creation without its own parts. In like manner the soul fills its body, because God made the soul after His likeness. [Col. 1102A]

Therefore the soul governs its body, and through the soul’s presence the body has many things which are neither the soul’s substance nor parts of its substance, but bodily affections and qualities. And the body has many things from the soul which it retains for a time after the soul. For a limb freshly cut from its body continues for a while to twitch after the soul [has departed], retaining the motion which it had from the soul. Likewise, after a plant has long been dried and reduced to the finest powder, although it has now entirely lost its soul, it nevertheless retains from the soul it has lost a fragrance pleasant to the nostrils and powers against ailments.

Similarly, seed discharged through sexual pleasure from a living body draws with it from the soul the power of propagation; it had that power in the body from the soul. Certainly it was not of the soul, [Col. 1102B] but of the body: that is, a bodily quality and affection from the soul, but an effect of the soul. It is discharged and separated from its body; it carries away with it the vegetative power which it had. The seed carries the power with it outside the body, but the body keeps the soul with itself. Nothing is separated from the soul with the seed; the soul remains wholly in the body. The seed carries with it its affection, but the body retains its whole soul; from a simple nature nothing can flow forth. Therefore the soul cannot generate a soul from itself, nor can we find the propagation by which, you said, a soul comes to be.

### Why philosophical considerations are included in this work

I beg that the brethren not accuse me, because I have introduced philosophical considerations, as though I had wished to fortify the Catholic faith by philosophical reasoning. I did not do so in order to fortify it, but in order to teach. Who can fortify truth? Truth cannot become stronger, because it cannot be fortified. But truth is weighty and grave; it is not easy for superficial minds, nor does the unlearned person quickly grasp what even the learned scarcely discover. Therefore arguments must be sought from every side, so that what is hidden may be opened—not so that what is strongest may be fortified; so that what is closed by mysteries may be uncovered—not so that what is immutable may be strengthened.

For this reason we have employed certain philosophical matters, because we know that Catholics among the clergy, educated in the liberal arts, see more quickly through what is closed by means of what they know. [Col. 1102C]

### Why advocates of propagation of souls are introduced here

I have willingly set forth the advocates of propagation of souls so that, when everything has been viewed from every side, what ought to be chosen may more readily become evident; and so that, amid the many things presented, the authority of truth may freely stand out and the consideration of the positions themselves may appear fair. [Col. 1102D]

Here ends the Treatise on Original Sin of the most reverend lord Odo, formerly abbot, from its first restoration, of the monastery of Saint Martin among the people of Tournai, and afterwards bishop of the Church of Cambrai.

[Col. 1103]

# DISPUTATION AGAINST A JEW NAMED LEO CONCERNING THE COMING OF CHRIST, THE SON OF GOD

### Prologue

[Col. 1103A]

ODO, bishop of Cambrai, to ACARDUS, monk of Phideme.

While, at the chapter-house of Phideme, with the Nativity of the Lord approaching, I had given an explanation of the divine incarnation, what you heard pleased you, as you said, but your understanding could not retain it in memory. For things which endure through careful discussion fall away through a more abundant outpouring. Therefore you asked that a very slender sequence, arranged in lasting writing, might shape the memory which the flood of thoughts was overwhelming.

At length, overcome by your prayers, I undertook to do what you requested. But as I was going to Poitiers for a council, because on the day when at Senlis, with God’s help, I had fittingly carried out this very matter against a certain Jew, it seemed appropriate to me to pursue this question in dialogue form: the Jew asked and I answered. And because the Jew is called Leo and I am called Odo, let the distinction of the persons be made by the first letters of the names. Now I invoke the Holy Spirit, that what He gave me for convincing a Jew He may restore for instructing a faithful monk.

And so, after the afternoon sleep, when the Jew had come to our lodging at about the ninth hour, we sat down, and he began to speak as follows.

### That remission of sins is not sufficient for glory

LEO. Tell me, bishop: what benefit did the coming of your Christ bring to the world?

ODO. Tell me, Jew: what benefit do you believe your Messiah, whom you still believe is to come, will bring?

LEO.
