What we read in the prophets: namely, that all kingdoms are to be subjected to us in him; that under him we shall have perpetual peace; that from all kingdoms we shall be gathered with glory into Jerusalem; that Jerusalem shall have dominion over all kingdoms; and the other blessings which the prophets happily enumerate. Since we do not see all these fulfilled in your Christ, we wonder what you expect from him.

[Col. 1103C]

ODO. Through Christ we expect the kingdom of heaven; we hope through Christ for a heavenly happiness, whereas you hope for an earthly one.

LEO. You seem to be mistaken. For we too hope, through the Messiah, for temporal happiness from that time onward and, through observance of the Law, for a heavenly kingdom after this life. The prophets promise us temporal goods; from the Law we expect the heavenly kingdom. For the Law teaches what sacrifice should be made for each sin, and thus that sin is forgiven. Moreover, when King David confessed the sins of adultery and homicide, the prophet Nathan said to him: “Your sin has been forgiven” (II Kings XII). [Col. 1104A] Therefore, if under the Law there is remission of sins without your Christ, eternal blessedness follows as well. For “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. XXXI). What, then, does your Christ accomplish?

ODO. You do not sufficiently consider the rectitude of justice. The person whose sin is forgiven is not immediately advanced to glory. Remission of sin removes punishments; it does not confer glory. The person from whom punishment is taken is not immediately given glory. The person toward whom wrath is remitted is not immediately adorned with favor. For David too, when he forgave his son the guilt of fratricide, did not yet allow him to be brought into his presence, nor did he give favor to him whose punishment he had remitted (II Kings XIV).

A human being indeed sinned in a singular way; but for one who repents, obeys again, and serves well, punishment is remitted even under the Law. Yet he does not thereby merit the glory to which he cannot justly attain except through recompense for sin. For it is unjust to rank a sinner among those who have not sinned without satisfaction for sin. Thus under the Law remission of sins was given to a human being. But because under the Law a human being cannot make satisfaction for sin, he cannot arrive at glory through the Law. Therefore Christ is necessary for the world, because in him we make satisfaction for sin, so that we may arrive at glory. [Col. 1104B]

### That the practice of good works is not sufficient to erase sin

LEO. I do not know how a human being makes satisfaction for sin in your Christ; but under the Law I see how sin is amended. For through prayers and sacrifices, offerings and alms, and other exercises of good works, we make satisfaction to God for sin under the Law.

ODO. If a servant, bound to his lord by an old debt, afterwards sins against that lord, will the later sin be purged by payment of the old debt? Or will payment of the earlier debt rightly be reckoned satisfaction for the subsequent offense? Will not a just lord separately exact both the former debt and the subsequent wrong?

LEO. Yes.

ODO. Therefore a human being could not amend sin through the practice of good works. For every good which he was able to do before sin he owed to God, from whom he had received it. Let the human being therefore render every good which he has received; nevertheless, the evil which he has committed is justly required of him. Therefore a human being under the Law cannot redeem what he has sinned by any holiness. [Col. 1104D]

### That endurance of hardships is not sufficient to erase sin

LEO. Let it be granted that a human being could not redeem sin through that which he owed beforehand. Yet he was not obliged previously to suffer labors and death; for who would say that he was obliged to suffer when he had not deserved it? But we read that God imposed punishments on human beings because of sin: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death” (Gen. II)—there is death. “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread; thorns and thistles the earth shall bring forth for you” (Gen. III)—there are labors and tribulations. [Col. 1105A]

If God gave these punishments to a human being for sin, they either suffice for the expiation of sin or they do not. If they suffice, it follows that, sin having been expiated, we arrive at heavenly glory without your Christ. If they do not suffice, God must be said improperly to have imposed punishments which do not suffice for expiation of sin. Since it is impious to say this of God, it is proved that the wise God established a measure of punishments according to the measure of sin. For the just God ought to exact a just punishment, neither less than the sin nor exceeding its measure. The just God ought not to punish the sinner less, nor should the merciful God punish him more, than he deserved.

Therefore, if a human being patiently endures the labors, tribulations, and finally death of this life, he amends sin by the good of patience—a suffering which one who had not sinned was not formerly obliged to undergo. Thus sin is erased by recompense of good, because patience recompenses as much good as guilt had been evil. Once sin has been discharged, then, what hinders entry into the kingdom?

ODO. You would not say these things if you knew how great a weight sin possesses. Therefore let us seek the smallest sin we can, so that from it we may see how great the weight of other sins is. Now, propose whatever seems fitting to you.

LEO. Nothing occurs to me smaller than a brief vain thought.

ODO. Therefore, if God prohibited you from turning the intention of your thought away from Him in any direction, and someone else truthfully told you that, unless you turned yourself quickly elsewhere, you would immediately perish and return to nothingness, would you think that you ought briefly to turn your thought elsewhere against God, for your own sake, lest you perish, and commit this tiny sin for your own redemption? Or do you judge it better to live through sin than to perish for righteousness?

[Col. 1105C]

LEO. Why should it not be better?

ODO. Because omnipotent God can restore you, after righteousness has been preserved, to a better state than you can live through sin. And He who would justly make you miserable if you lived through sin would justly restore you blessed if you were destroyed for righteousness. Therefore the sin which you proposed outweighs you: it ought not to have been done even for your own redemption.

LEO. What you say pleases me, for I had not perceived that such a small fault bore so great a weight.

ODO. But tell me: would you owe this for an angel, though you do not owe it for yourself?

LEO. According to the reasoning which you gave concerning me, neither for one person, nor for all persons, nor for the whole creation, ought even the least thing against God be done. For omnipotent God is able to restore to a better state whatever could perish for righteousness; and to those to whom He mercifully gave being without merit, He would justly give, with merit, a better being.

ODO. You have understood well. For all creation cannot abolish that which is against God in any creature, lest God appear to need creation to abolish that which is against Himself in creation. A servant cannot free a fellow servant. Since all creation is God’s handmaid, can creation free from sin a creature which has subjected itself to sin? The creature that has subjected itself to sin has departed from God. Therefore, a creature which frees a creature from sin restores it to God and makes it blessed. But to be blessed is better than to be. Thus what is greater is attributed to creation and what is less to the Creator: the Creator makes that which is being, while creation makes that which is blessed being. Since this is impossible, creation cannot free a creature from sin.

For every creature is outweighed by the least sin, because the least sin is against God, and God is greater than every creature. Therefore all creation does not suffice to recompense the least sin. [Col. 1106B]

LEO. We are in great danger, since we sin daily, if sin, as you say, bears so great a weight.

### Why God imposed on humanity a punishment that does not suffice to erase sin

But why did God impose punishment on the sinner if that punishment does not suffice for sin?

ODO. For remission of sins—which the good possessed before sin could not effect. For all such things, namely endurance of every affliction, the manifold disciplines of mind and body, and all things by which one is exercised toward good, can avail, without full recompense for sin, only for pardon, not for glory.

### That humanity was made for the completion of the heavenly city

[Col. 1106C]

LEO. How then can a human being make satisfaction, or what can he recompense for sin, if the whole creation is less and cannot suffice to erase sin?

ODO. In no way by himself.

LEO. Therefore our rational dispute has come to this: if a human being escapes punishments through forgiveness of sins but nevertheless does not attain glory, he may have an intermediate state in which he rests forever; so that angels who did not sin remain in glory, while a human being who has received remission of sin obtains a repose suited to his condition, and one without remission incurs eternal punishments. We have therefore arrived at the conclusion that your Christ is in no way necessary to the world. For that state of repose is obtained without Christ through the Law, in which remission of sins is read. And you, who proposed to show the power of your Christ, have proved that a human being can in no way attain glory.

[Col. 1106D]

ODO. I shall endeavor to prove to you not only that a human being can attain the glory of angels, but also that it is necessary. When, with Christ’s help, I have done so, I ask that you abandon error and become a Christian.

LEO. Leave that aside and proceed with what you promise.

ODO. It will be established that human glory is possible if it can be proved necessary; for what must exist can exist.

LEO. It is so.

ODO. I believe you will not deny the truth of what is read concerning God in many places of your Scripture: “Whatever He willed, He did” (Ps. CXIII, CXXXIV).

LEO. It is most true.

ODO. God willed to make the heavenly city, whose citizens He created as angels. [Col. 1107A] The good God created all angels only good; those who became wicked were justly cast out from that city. Therefore, when the city was vacated in part, the work God had begun remained imperfect. But God’s purpose cannot be frustrated, and the city which God had begun must be completed, lest God be said to have foolishly begun what He afterward did not wish, or was unable, to complete. But it is impious to ascribe either mutability of will or impotence to God. Therefore God will complete what He began. He therefore made humanity and gave it propagation, so that He might complete what He had begun. It is therefore necessary that God’s purpose concerning humanity be fulfilled. For whatever He willed, He did.

### That the number needed to complete the heavenly city is greater than the number of angels in the first creation

[Col. 1107B]

LEO. Since you have introduced the subject of the first creation, I ask whether the number in which angels were made sufficed for the city’s completion before angels became evil.

ODO. It does not seem so. For if the number of angels made had sufficed merely for those who fell, a human being could rejoice at their fall, whose glory he would hold. But since no one except the just enters heavenly glory, how could one be just who rejoiced in another’s sin? Therefore we say that with God the number for completing the city is greater than the number of angels in the first creation. Humanity, however, was so made that, if all angels had remained in righteousness, the remainder of the city would have come from humanity; but if they fell away, the whole would be completed from humanity.

### That God alone can make satisfaction for sin

[Col. 1107C]

LEO. If God’s purpose cannot be frustrated, a human being must be transferred into the glory of angels; and God is omnipotent, therefore He can do everything that He has purposed. Thus a human being must be transferred into glory. Yet the arguments above prove this impossible. How then is that necessary which is impossible? What great diversity of arguments is this! When I consider God’s purpose, it is necessary that a human being pass into glory; when I consider human impotence and God’s justice, it is altogether impossible for a human being to come to glory. What is more contrary than necessary and impossible?

ODO. Let our Christ come—let Him come and dissolve this contradiction.

LEO. How?

ODO. Listen. If you have properly understood what was grasped above, satisfaction for sin alone prevents human glory. For if a human being could make satisfaction for sin, he could certainly attain glory; but a human being cannot. What then? Is what a human being cannot do altogether impossible? Can God not do what a human being cannot? Otherwise God is not omnipotent. Therefore God can make satisfaction for sin.

[Col. 1107D]

LEO. How will God make satisfaction, when it does not pertain to Him? How will one who has not sinned make satisfaction for sin? The sinner ought to make satisfaction; God ought not.

ODO. Since it is necessary for a human being to come to glory, which he cannot do without satisfaction, and since God can make satisfaction but ought not to do so, while a human being ought to make satisfaction but cannot, it is therefore necessary that the two natures meet and that God become human: that Jesus Christ be one, God and human—not one person God and another human, but wholly whatever He is. He is human not by a confusion of natures, as if one were emptied into the other, but with the property of each nature remaining intact in one true person. Therefore Jesus Christ is not two but altogether one and undivided in person. Because He is omnipotent God, He can make satisfaction for sin; because He is human, He ought to do so. He can as God; He ought as human. [Col. 1108A]

### That it pertains to Christ, who did not sin, to make satisfaction for sin

LEO. How does He owe it, even though He is human, when, as you say, He is not a sinful human being?

ODO. Through compassion and mercy. Because we could not amend sin, He amended it for us, as a brother for brothers and as one sharing our nature. For it is alien to no one to condescend to his own nature and to make satisfaction for those who belong to his own nature. Thus, because of the identity of nature, He bore our sins; for our sins He willingly endured stripes and death, punishments which He did not owe, for He had not merited such things.

He feeds us with His flesh and blood, so as to incorporate us into Himself, so that we too may be Himself and He may be one with us. Therefore He makes our miseries His own; He attributes our sins to Himself; in the Psalms and prophets He transfers our words into His own person, as in: “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me? Far from my salvation are the words of my offenses” (Ps. XXI). In His own person He was neither forsaken by God nor possessed those offenses; but because He counts us as being in Himself, He says of Himself what we possess. [Col. 1108C]

### That Christ willed to give for sin something greater than every sin

LEO. How does He make satisfaction for a human being? How did He recompense human sin, for which the whole world does not suffice?

ODO. He gave a price—His life—and endured death, an undeserved punishment.

LEO. How can the life and death of one human being recompense sin, for which the whole world does not suffice?

ODO. You cannot deny that nothing can be compared with God, but God incomparably surpasses all things. Therefore human sin cannot be compared with God, because God is far more good than sin is evil. Since God gave His life, He gave a price surpassing every sin. If this price merely equaled sin, it would suffice to erase it. But now, since it greatly outweighs sin, it makes satisfaction all the more.

Further, if God’s life is better than all things, His death is worse than all things, because necessarily the corruption of that whose generation is better is worse. But Christ’s life is good beyond all things; therefore His death is evil beyond every sin. Thus, when Christ suffered death, He bore a punishment beyond every sin and greater than all sin deserves. [Col. 1108D] Therefore He discharged the whole sin of the world, who both suffered a greater punishment—that is, death—and gave a greater price, namely His life, than the sin of the whole world. [Col. 1109A] “This is the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world” (John I).

This is the victim which, once offered, erases the sins of all the righteous: sins past from the beginning, present sins, and sins yet to come until the end. This victim mercifully gives Himself to us, so that, while He always offers Himself in heaven to the Father for us, we may continually sacrifice Him to the Father on earth—not by inflicting death again, but by most devoutly commemorating His death for the remission of sins, both of the living and the dead.

It remains, therefore, that, having received remission of sins, we proceed by the straight way to heaven through manifold acts of righteousness, now that satisfaction for sin has been accomplished through Christ. But this satisfaction benefits only those to whom remission is granted, through the cooperation of their own merits or those of their neighbors. For Christ’s satisfaction benefits nothing to one who cannot receive remission. Therefore, “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven” (Ps. XXXI). For when sin is forgiven to someone, there is no reason why that person should be delayed from the kingdom, since satisfaction has been fulfilled through Christ.

Therefore our Christ is exceedingly necessary to the world; without Him a human being cannot come to the glory for which he was made. Remission of sin in the Law does not suffice unless Christ’s satisfaction follows in the Gospel. Therefore, although sins had been forgiven to the ancient fathers and prophets, they were not yet in glory until satisfaction for sin was fulfilled through Christ’s Passion.

LEO. Where were they?

ODO. In a place suitable at that time for the righteous, yet not glorious.

LEO. I have no rational objection to raise against one who speaks rationally. Yet I do not believe, lest, deceived by subtlety and verbal cunning, I should vanish from the most firm stability of the holy Law. [Col. 1109C]

### Whether there is grace where there is necessity

LEO. But what gratitude is owed to God for your salvation, if He was led to it by necessity? Surely He needs human salvation, upon which the power of His purpose depends. For if He does not save humanity, He displays the impotence and falsity of His purpose. Therefore, lest so great an impropriety occur in Him, He must procure human salvation.

ODO. It is indeed necessary to render what it was not necessary to promise. For one who promises voluntarily binds himself by the necessity of rendering; thus, although the subsequent rendering is of necessity, the preceding promise is of will and grace. But this necessity which proceeds from grace must not be separated from grace itself, so that what was first promised by great grace may rightly be called something done by grace. [Col. 1109D]

### Why God, who gave every good, does not owe satisfaction for sin
LEO. What troubles me is what you said above: that God ought not to make satisfaction for sin unless he became man. For satisfaction for sin is a great good. But every good is from him who is supremely good. How then was it said that God ought not to do what is his own? Who owes good more than he from whom every good comes? Therefore God owes the good of satisfaction, since he owes every good.

ODO. God both owes and does not owe, because “owed” is spoken of in two ways: as a debt of grace and as a debt of merit. For perhaps I ought to help this man because of his merits, but that man by my grace. Likewise, perhaps I ought to suffer—or, if I have sinned, to suffer either by merit or by grace alone—for another. Therefore God ought not to make satisfaction for sin by a debt of merit, because neither had he himself earned it by his own fault, nor had man earned it by his righteousness; yet he ought to make satisfaction by grace alone. Thus God ought not to make satisfaction by a debt of merit, and ought to make satisfaction by a debt of grace. Therefore, when it was said above that God alone could make satisfaction but ought not to, whereas man could not but ought to, in both cases a debt of merit must be understood: God did not owe it by merit, while man did owe it by merit. And in this sense it is true that God ought not to make satisfaction for human sin unless he is man. But because God became man, although this must be ascribed to ineffable grace, nevertheless in the satisfaction there is a strong fragrance of merited obligation: because he had become man and the brother of men, by merit he would not despise his own nature in men, but as brother would aid his brothers by merit and make satisfaction for his brothers by merit. [Col. 1110A–B]

### How God became man from a virgin without injury from female impurity

LEO. In one matter we mock you greatly and judge you mad. For you say that God, shut up in the maternal womb—in the foul prison of a fetid belly—endured there for nine months, and at last in the tenth month came forth by a shameful exit, which cannot be looked upon without embarrassment; thus you inflict upon God such disgrace as we do not speak even of ourselves, though truly, without great shame.

ODO. God fills all things and is wholly everywhere. Therefore, although he fills us and is wholly in us who are sinners, he is not touched by the impurity of our sins, but remains uncontaminated and pure. He sees all things, and nothing harms him. He sees darkness while himself pure from darkness, because “the light shines in the darkness” (John 1), and “night shall be illuminated as day” (Ps. 138). He sees sins while most pure, and our injustices while most just, because he justly orders every evil which he sees. For the light of righteousness is not choked by the illumination of sins, just as the corporeal light of this world illuminates a filthy body without itself becoming filthy.

Why then are you offended if God is conceived in a virgin, he who preserves his purity everywhere? Further, there are two things by which we judge all things: sense and reason; but reason judges in one way, sense in another. Sense judges by habit and desire, by appetite and its opposites. We prefer familiar things to unfamiliar, useful things to harmful ones, and what gives pleasure to what displeases by its unpleasantness. Reason, however, investigates the nature of a thing more subtly. Reason prefers animate things to inanimate, sentient things to insentient, heavenly things to earthly.

For a peasant would sooner choose that a serpent perish from a rocky hollow than that a stone perish from his wall, consulting his desire and the pleasure of sight, because it is dreadful to see a serpent and not dreadful to see a stone. Reason, however, prefers a serpent to any precious stone whatsoever. Sense prefers an excellent house to a fruit-bearing tree, so that it would rather have the tree cut down than the house burned. Reason, however, prefers a living tree to an inanimate house. A peasant would rather have many wild beasts perish in the forest than one denarius from his purse, though reason judges that no denarius should be compared with an animal. And the peasant would rather have several stars perish from heaven than one small tree from his field, though reason rightly puts heavenly things before earthly ones. [Col. 1110C–1111A]

Thus sense despises our genitals, entrails, and excrement, and judges them unclean. Reason, however, judges nothing unclean except sin, because God created all things good (Gen. 1). The Gospel of the Lord Jesus itself testifies to this: “To eat with unwashed hands does not defile a person. Everything entering the mouth goes into the belly and is expelled into the privy, and does not defile a person. But the things which come forth from the heart— thefts, murders, adulteries—these are what defile a person” (Matt. 15).

Our Apostle agrees with this—formerly your Jew and instructed in the Law, but now raising himself against you, who judge certain foods unclean according to the Law: “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Tim. 4). Although the Law judges many things unclean according to sense, behold: the Gospel of the Lord Jesus and the teaching of his apostles declare every creature good and clean by the judgment of reason. Reason is preferred to sense and judges concerning the senses; but sense cannot rise to reason, and often considers the subtle judgment of reason foolish and mad.

We, setting aside the sense of the flesh, consider the human body under the guidance of reason: joined by unity of person to the mind, destined to possess with it an eternal union, ever a participant either in honour or dishonour. We judge it superior to every body—purer than a file, more precious than the sun—because it will come to judgment and, with its own mind, undergo glory or punishments, either displaying in itself God’s eternal mercy or suffering his justice; now animal, but destined to be spiritual at the judgment. What body is exalted anywhere by so great a prerogative? If I compare heaven, the comparison is not fitting. If I consider the brilliance of sun and stars, precious to the eyes, something lesser presents itself.

But what does sense do? In the face of so great a thing, the fool does not fear to revile what displeases him. Sight recoils from the form of the genitals, the nostrils mock the smell, touch shrinks from filth. Behold what sense judges concerning a thing with which not even heaven can be compared. If our body is so great, though we are sinners, what shall we say of the body of the virgin from whom the Lord was born? Certainly the holy angel Gabriel said of her: “Full of grace” (Luke 1). If full, nothing in her was at all empty of grace. Therefore nothing in her was vacant to sin, since grace filled her whole being. Therefore glorious was her sex, glorious her womb, glorious her entrails, glorious her whole being, because her whole being was full of grace.

Truly that woman surpassed sense and had understanding, who said: “Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts which you sucked” (Luke 2). Where now is what you called female impurity, a foul prison, a fetid belly? Confess, miserable man, your folly. Was she then sensual among animals, without reason among human beings? This virgin became, in her conception, the bridal chamber of almighty God, the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit. In her God dwelt uniquely and in another manner than even in the spirits of the highest heavenly powers. The hidden places of her blessed entrails were so much holier—indeed, more divine—as divine mysteries more intimately sprang up there. Blessed virgin, from whose entrails was taken the seminal material that would become God. What in the whole creation was holier, cleaner, or purer than the Virgin from whom was taken that which would become God? O womb, O entrails, in which and from which the Creator was created, God was made flesh.

Certainly we have set other human bodies above all bodies. But I set the body of this most blessed Virgin even above angelic spirits: from which God chose to take that from which he would be made, from which he began [to take] what he would inseparably unite to himself, from which he would redeem the earth, restore heaven, despoil the realms of hell, heal the earth, and perfect heavenly things—something for which he chose none of the heavenly spirits.

LEO. I hear what I have never heard before; until now I did not know that you were supported by such great arguments.

ODO. Why then do you not believe?

LEO. Because I do not dare to commit the truth of our matter to your words.

ODO. Brother Acard, I gave these arguments concerning Christ’s coming to the Jew, because certain Catholics who were present on the Jew’s side compelled me to argue certain matters more subtly. [Col. 1111B–1112C]

[Col. 1111]

## On Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit

### Prologue

[Col. 1111D]

Blessed Augustine says in the *Enchiridion* that he wrote a little book on blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. But this book has not come into my hands, nor do I know that I have seen anyone who had read it. Therefore the venerable man Amandus, a monk of Anchin, complained to me anxiously that a solution to so great a question could not be found.

For Anchin was then a sweet refuge of my exile, because royal power drove me from the see of Cambrai, since I refused to receive anew, as a gift of the emperor, the staff and ring which I had received from the Church when consecrated. When the aforesaid brother, often speaking with me about spiritual things, devoutly demanded from me the solution of the aforesaid question, I referred him to the expositions of the orthodox Fathers. But he said that they did not treat the matter in the manner of his doubt, nor could his uncertainty be removed through their expositions.

Thus it seemed better to me to take up the burden—though I might fall—than, by wholly refusing, to make him think it pride or contempt; and I would rather have him see me exhausted and failing through effort than have him be ashamed at being repulsed because I had set aside the labour. I was also greatly encouraged by the little book *On Original Sin*, which I had recently written, in which, while I was struggling, many things occurred to me which I had not known. [Col. 1112D–1113A]

### In which canon and chapters the blasphemy against the Spirit is found in the Gospel

First the words of the Gospel itself which create the question must be set forth; then the difficulty of the question must be shown before we undertake its solution. They are contained in the second canon: in Matthew, chapter 12; in Mark, chapter 34; and in Luke, chapter 47.

Matthew says thus: “Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven to human beings; but blasphemy against the Spirit shall not be forgiven. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.”

Mark says thus: “Amen I say to you: all sins shall be forgiven to the children of men, and the blasphemies by which they have blasphemed. But whoever shall have blasphemed against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness for ever, but shall be guilty of an eternal sin.” Because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.”

Luke says thus: “Everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man shall be forgiven; but to him who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit it shall not be forgiven.” [Col. 1113A–B]

### That some sins can be forgiven and some cannot

Behold: these three chapters of the second canon say that every sin can be forgiven except one; that one alone can in no way attain pardon, while every other can in some manner obtain the mercy of forgiveness; one alone is altogether incapable of release, while every other can be absolved. Over that one alone the pit presses its mouth, so that it may be shut in eternal oblivion; over every other the mouth of the pit stands open, so that it may somehow be able to come out.

But first let us see how God forgives remissible sins.

### That sin cannot be forgiven to one who is unrepentant

God forgives either the repentant or the unrepentant. Now God cannot forgive sin to the unrepentant, for God cannot be unjust. A person sins against another person, and sins also against God. He is unrepentant toward another person, and unrepentant also toward God. A human being ought to forgive the unrepentant, but God ought not, because a sinner ought to forgive a sinner, whereas God ought not forgive the unrepentant. A sinner forgives even the unrepentant, because he fears from above that he himself may not be forgiven even when repentant. God does not forgive the unrepentant, because he does not fear that he himself will not be forgiven. A human being ought to forgive an unrepentant sinner because he too is a sinner; God ought not, because he is not a sinner.

Further, all impenitence is pride, and all pride is principally contrary to God. Therefore, if God forgives pride to the unrepentant, he forgives it against himself, joins to himself that which separates every good from him, and associates with himself that to which every good is opposed. But it is impossible for the supreme good in any manner to enter into alliance with the supreme evil, or for the supreme good to lend support to any evil—much less to that which is chiefly its contrary. For “what fellowship has light with darkness?” (2 Cor. 14). “What has the temple of God to do with idols?” [Col. 1113C–1114A]

### That God has certain goods which he himself cannot do

Therefore, if a human being can forgive the unrepentant and God cannot forgive them, a human being can do a good which God cannot do. But from whom does a human being have good except from him who is the supreme good? A human being possesses a great good: forgiving the unrepentant—a great good, and one fitting only for the perfect. But from where has he this, if God himself cannot do it? Certainly a human being does not have so great a good from himself, but from God, from whom comes every good. For God has this good also, although he does not do it. He has it in himself and gives to a human being from himself what he has. God has it so as to command; a human being receives it so as to do it. God does not have it in himself for himself, but has it in himself for humanity; he does not have it in himself for himself, but has it in himself for us. He has it in himself, and we do it; he has it in himself, and it belongs to us.

There are therefore goods which, although God cannot do them, God nevertheless has; he has them because otherwise we would not do them unless we had them from him. There are thus goods appropriate to the majesty of the Creator and goods appropriate to the service of the creature. Yet both these and those are from him from whom and in whom are all good things. [Col. 1114A–B]

### That even sin is able to be forgiven to the unrepentant, if they repent

Although, as has been shown, no sin is forgiven to the unrepentant, every sin is forgiven to the repentant. Perhaps impenitence itself, because it is unforgivable, is blasphemy against the Spirit. But what if the sinner repents of his very impenitence and finally abandons what he held obstinately for so long? Does he obtain pardon, and is this impenitence of one now repentant forgiven? He was unrepentant for a long time, but now repents; he has now softened the long hardness of his heart. We see tears, hear groans, and God sees inner compunction of heart. If the door of mercy is shut to such a person, for whom is it opened? Far be it that God should reject him, that he who is most merciful should cast him away, when it is written: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, I will receive him” (Ezek. 33). Far be it that any fault of the repentant should be incurable before the supreme physician.

Therefore, if impenitence, which appears unforgivable, is itself forgiven through repentance, what fault is wholly unforgiven? What is the blasphemy called that of the Spirit? [Col. 1114B–D]

### Inquiry into what sin is blasphemy

Here the Gospel proclaims blasphemy against the Spirit wholly unforgivable; there the Church, the firmest pillar of truth, preaches repentance against every sin. Here the Gospel, in three chapters, confirms that some sin cannot in any way be dissolved; there the Church promises certain pardon through repentance from every sin. It is wickedness to contradict the Gospel; and who would dare to declare the Church false? The Gospel denies something; the Church affirms everything. They are contradictory and cannot both be true if the same understanding is preserved everywhere. Therefore they must be understood differently, so that both may be true.

Let a mode therefore be found through whose sameness they divide truth from falsehood between themselves, and through whose difference they may both be true. The universal affirmation of the Church, which says that every sin can be forgiven, is true if the mode of repentance is understood. What then, if it is understood likewise in the Gospel’s particular negation, which says that blasphemy against the Spirit cannot be forgiven through repentance? It is false. Therefore, for it to be true, the mode of repentance must not be understood: for blasphemy against the Spirit cannot be forgiven without repentance.

But so that the Gospel may at the same time be true with the Church, let us understand, on the other hand, a different mode of repentance: when the Church in its affirmation introduces the understanding of repentance, let the Gospel remove it from its negation. Thus both statements will be true: that blasphemy against the Spirit is not forgiven without repentance, and that every sin is erased through repentance. The same mode will divide truth and falsehood between them, and the different mode will make them both true.

In this way the Gospel does not differ from the Church when it says that blasphemy against the Spirit cannot be forgiven, implying “without repentance,” since the Church says the same concerning every sin. But it is strange why the Gospel excepts blasphemy from every sin, since, like every sin, it can be forgiven through repentance. Yet I think this is strange because the door has not yet been opened to me. Open, Christ, to one who knocks; reveal the mysteries of your most holy word. You say that every sin can be forgiven except blasphemy against the Spirit; and no sin can be forgiven except through repentance. Does repentance not follow blasphemy too?

Perhaps someone will say that blasphemy against the Spirit is so great a sin that no repentance can follow it. And though some blasphemer seems to beat his breast and may be heard sighing, perhaps it will be said that he does this not from the heart. But in this way we are sent on to infinity: we judge uncertain things and presumptuously claim knowledge of the inscrutable abyss of the human heart; we proclaim that we penetrate a hidden depth which God alone can know. When we see blasphemers beating their breasts and shedding tears, and hear deep groans and long sighs, who would dare call it deceit and say that they do not repent from the heart? I do not believe that supreme Wisdom wished to write in the Gospel something that a human being cannot grasp, or to teach a human being what a human being cannot know. Therefore I judge that I have not yet understood the blasphemy against the Spirit which is not forgiven, lest I be forced to invent an impenitence of heart which cannot be known. [Col. 1114D–1115D]

### That the sin unto death is blasphemy against the Spirit

But let us consult the First Epistle of John the Evangelist, one of the Catholic Epistles, in which something similar to the Gospel is said. For in this saying he appears to agree through the Epistle with the three evangelists, concerning which he had set down nothing in his Gospel—almost as if he supplied in the Epistle what he had said less fully in the Gospel—so that the saying we seek may be known as firmer because it is confirmed by all four evangelists.

We have heard what the three evangelists said, from which the question arises. Let us hear what John, the fourth, said, from which the solution may arise. Three entangle us by the obscurity of their words; the fourth disentangles us by the evident clarity of his statement. For he says: “There is a sin unto death; concerning it I do not say that anyone should pray” (1 John 5). Why is prayer for it forbidden unless it is in no way to be forgiven? Certainly one should not pray for that which cannot at all be forgiven.

The evangelist calls this “sin unto death,” so that one who closes his last day in sin has an unforgivable fault, for which God admits no one praying. This is blasphemy against the Spirit, which is not forgiven: when someone is held by sin until the end, so that eternal punishment receives him whom this life leaves with the will to sin. Such a sinner is not absolved in this age, because he remained in the will to sin; nor in the age to come, because he passed over with the will to sin. And he is justly punished forever who would have sinned forever, had he lived forever in this age, so that an everlasting punishment may accompany an everlasting will to sin, and the necessary justice of punishment may not fail in one in whom the will to sin does not fail. [Col. 1115D–1116B]

### How the sin unto death is one sin alone, like blasphemy against the Spirit

Here a very difficult question arises: the three evangelists say in the Gospel that one sin alone is unforgivable—namely, blasphemy against the Spirit—separating it from all others; but John the Evangelist, in the Epistle, says that no sin is separately unforgivable, but rather any sin unto death. How do John’s Epistle and the Gospel agree, if what the Gospel denies of every sin except one named sin, John affirms of any sin, not of one separately?

The Gospel says: “Blasphemy against the Spirit alone is unforgivable.” John says: “Whatever sin is unto death deserves no prayer.”

The Gospel names blasphemy against the Spirit singularly and definitively; the Epistle names nothing singularly, but speaks indeterminately of sin unto death. By “sin unto death,” said indeterminately, we understand any one sin indefinitely; by “blasphemy against the Spirit” we understand a sin not any whatsoever, but one definite sin.

Thus John’s Epistle seems in this respect to disagree with the Gospel, since the Epistle says that no prayer should be made for any sin unto death, while the Gospel says that blasphemy against the Spirit alone is an unforgivable sin. But as an unconsidered confusion of things entangles this question, so a carefully considered distinction of things resolves it.

For repentance or obstinacy accompanies every sin. Repentance is a good; sin itself is evil; persistence in sin for a time is worse; persistence unto death is the worst and final evil. Thus among evils, one is earlier, another later, another last. Earlier, such as fornication, theft, robbery, hatred, envy, and countless other things; later, such as impenitence for a time; last, impenitence unto the end.

The earlier evils precede as if they were principal, regarding which one either repents or remains unrepentant. Unless sin is first committed, there is nothing for someone to repent of or in which to remain unrepentant. From every evil people are first directed to the first good, namely repentance, which forgiveness follows. From the first evil one falls into the later evil, and from there into the last: impenitence unto the end, which unforgiveness follows. When the sinner has reached these two, the later and the last, he “despises” (Prov. 18). [Col. 1116B–1117A]

Here four opposites are considered: two goods opposed to two evils. To make their arrangement more evident, let a square diagram set them out, so that the upper line contains two opposite one another and the lower line likewise contains two opposite one another. Thus their primary opposition appears in both lines. And they are found on both sides so as to follow one another: on one side two goods through mercy, the lower of virtue and the upper of the palm; on the other side two evils through justice, the lower of fault and the upper of punishment. Diagonally, however, they are opposed on both sides in such a way that they cannot coexist: two by the immutability of justice, two by the certainty of mercy, as the diagram set below shows. [Col. 1117A–B]

[Col. 1117C]

Therefore, with this distinction of things understood, when the Gospel says that every sin is forgiven, it means the sins which are earlier and impenitence for a time, which is later. But blasphemy against the Spirit, which cannot be forgiven, is impenitence unto the end, for which one must not pray. And while in the Gospel there are many and countless sins which can be forgiven, blasphemy against the Spirit alone cannot be forgiven; it is identical with the sin unto death in John’s Epistle, that is, impenitence unto the end, for which alone one should not pray.

Thus there is one unforgivable sin alone both in the three evangelists and in John: in the Gospel it is called blasphemy against the Spirit; in the Epistle, sin unto death—that is, impenitence unto the end. [Col. 1117C–1118A]

### Why unforgivable blasphemy pertains more to the Spirit than to the Father or the Son

But although in John it is emphatically and properly called sin unto death, the question arises why in the Gospel it is called blasphemy not against the Father or the Son but against the Spirit alone. The response is that, although the majesty of the supreme Trinity is wholly love and each individual person in the supreme Trinity is most certainly love, nevertheless the Holy Spirit is specially and properly love, because he is the true communion of Father and Word, and the sweet mutual love of both toward each other and toward all things.

Since love itself cannot admit its contrary, it cannot hate anything created, but loves all things; for all that anything is, it is through true love. Unless it loved every essence, each thing could not exist as it is. Certain essences, however, have admitted fault; yet true love also loves those which have sinned, ready to pardon them if they repent. For one who truly loves gladly forgives an offence.

The desired forgiveness of sins is indeed the office of true love. And just as love in the supreme Trinity is properly referred to the Spirit, so forgiveness of sins is properly ascribed to the Spirit as an office of love, although forgiveness of sins is common to the whole Trinity. [Col. 1118A–B]

Therefore, if the Holy Spirit properly forgives sins, that which most excludes forgiveness of sins rises more against the Holy Spirit; and by greater wrong the sinner afflicts the Holy Spirit more, insofar as by greater wickedness he rejects forgiveness of sins. Thus that sin is rightly called blasphemy against the Spirit which rejects the sweet office of love and takes no care to receive the gift of pardon, which love desires to bestow upon all. This is the sin unto death, that is, impenitence unto the end: the final evil, alone unforgivable, although every other sin can be forgiven.

And this is to speak against the Holy Spirit: namely, by condemning divine works and interpreting them perversely, to persist enviously and proudly, unrepentant until the end—just as the malicious Jews were then doing, who attributed his divine powers to an unclean spirit. Therefore, seeing by divine knowledge their impenitence unto the end, he said that they would be condemned forever and instructed later generations to avoid so great an evil. From these Gospel chapters we find that the orthodox Fathers speak otherwise; whoever wishes to know this should consult them. [Col. 1118C–D]

[Col. 1117]

Here ends the treatise of the most reverend Lord Odo, *On Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit*.

[Col. 1117]

## On the Canons of the Gospels

The reading of the holy Gospels is a certain canon—that is, an institution or rule—of perfect religion. Hence those who live according to the institution of the holy Gospels are called canons regular. We therefore call the individual statements of the holy Gospels “canons.” But because the rules or canons of the Gospels are completed in the four books of the four Evangelists, it happens that in some statements all four agree together: what is said in one evangelist is found in the same or a similar manner in the other three. In some statements, however, only three agree, so that what three evangelists say similarly is not found in the fourth. In others, only two agree, the other two being silent concerning the same thing. In still others, individual evangelists state their own particular sayings, while the others are silent about what one has said.

Thus a clear division of the genus may be made, as into certain species of canons: some in which four evangelists agree; others in which three agree; others in which two agree; and others in which individual evangelists pronounce their own canons, that is, rules. [Col. 1118–1119A]

Among the canons in which four agree, there is no subdivision. Among those in which three agree, because there are four evangelists, there are four varieties, since their threefold combination can be varied in four ways. One is when Matthew, Mark, and Luke agree; another when Matthew, Mark, and John agree; the third when Matthew, Luke, and John agree; the fourth when Mark, Luke, and John agree. The threefold combination of four things cannot be varied in more ways.

But the fourth of these four combinations—Mark, Luke, and John—is absent here, because, in the entire Gospel text, I think it cannot be found that these three evangelists have said something together within the class of those sayings in which three agree.

Among the canons in which two agree, because there are four evangelists, there are six combinations, and no more can occur. For in four, pairs may be joined as follows: Matthew and Mark; Mark and Luke; Luke and John; Matthew and John; Matthew and Luke; or Mark and John. The last of these, Mark and John, is again absent here, because I think they nowhere agree within the class of those sayings in which two agree.

The canons in which one evangelist alone appears are fourfold according to the four evangelists. For in each of the Gospels many things are said so peculiarly that no likeness of their canons occurs in the others. Yet although these canons are fourfold according to the four evangelists, they are rightly reduced to one form, so that, because they belong to the class in which one alone appears, they may also be called of one species.

There are therefore ten canons according to the division stated above. The canon in which four agree is the first. The one in which three agree—where Matthew, Mark, and Luke agree—is the second; where Matthew, Luke, and John agree, the third; where Matthew, Mark, and John agree, the fourth. Of those in which two agree, Matthew and Luke are the fifth; Matthew and Mark, the sixth; Matthew and John, the seventh; Mark and Luke, the eighth; Luke and John, the ninth. The tenth is the canon in which one alone appears. Although it runs through the four Gospels, it is understood uniformly, and becomes the tenth, retaining in some way a likeness to the first canon—though far less perfectly—because it relies on the authority of one evangelist alone. [Col. 1119A–1120B]

I wonder that the evangelists do not admit agreement in two combinations, so that the number becomes ten. I do not believe this happens without profound teaching, except that it occurs to me that this itself reveals the solidity of the Holy Gospel: beneath the letter of the Old Testament, as beneath a veil, it lay hidden; and from there, through the grace of the Lord Jesus, it came forth into the light of understanding. Just as the Old Testament consists in the Decalogue of ten commandments, so the Gospel, as though proceeding from it, is completed in the number of ten canons. And so that what has been said may appear more clearly even to the eyes, the diagram below demonstrates it. [Col. 1120B–C]

### What the numbers of the canons and the numbers of the chapters signify

[Col. 1121A]

Since the ten canons mentioned above contain all the chapters of the Gospels—whether of four evangelists, three, two, or one—the numbers of the canons must be joined to the chapters of concordant sayings. Thus, through the chapter numbers, the sayings may be found; and through the canon numbers, which are customarily added in red, one may know whether a saying is shared with others or not, and, if it is shared, among how many and which evangelists the sharing occurs.

To make the principle clear, let us demonstrate by examples what we mean. Let us take one saying, namely that marked in Matthew by the eighth chapter. If you compare it with that of Mark marked by the second chapter, that of Luke marked by the seventh, and that of John marked by the tenth, it is similar in all four. Therefore the first number must be added to the aforesaid four chapters of the four evangelists, so that, when the saying is marked by the aforesaid chapters, it may be known to belong to the first canon, as shared by four evangelists.

Again, if we take the saying marked by the seventh chapter of Matthew and compare with it those in the sixth chapter of Luke and the second chapter of John, we find similar sayings. To know which evangelists, and how many, agree in the saying of the aforesaid chapters, we mark the number three in red. From the number we know both that three evangelists agree and which they are by name. For in the preceding diagram, the species of the canon in which Matthew, Luke, and John agree was called the third canon. Thus, through the chapters, the sayings of the Gospel text are sought, found, and marked; through the canon number, we know how many evangelists there are and who they are by name. [Col. 1121A–C]

Again, concerning the canon in which two agree: compare Matthew’s third chapter with Luke’s second chapter, and a similar saying is found in the chapters. But with the chapter numbers set down by themselves, we do not know which evangelists agree or whether more than two agree. But if the number five of the canon is placed in red, it is known that this is the fifth canon, the canon in which two agree, according to which Matthew and Luke plainly agree.

Thus through the canon numbers we know not only how many evangelists agree, but also their names, although I have seen the names of the evangelists everywhere written alongside the canon numbers. But I think this is done more because of the slowness of our memory than for any other reason. Since combinations of names arise in many ways, each of which is signified by its own number, when you see a number or hear what combination it signifies, you do not quickly recall it; therefore, together with the canon number, I set before you also the names signified.

But in the canon in which one evangelist alone appears, we do not understand the evangelists’ names from the canon number. For because the lack of form of this species is unified from the plurality of four evangelists, none is understood to be specified in it. Therefore both the canon number and the evangelist’s name are written beside the chapter of the saying. By the chapter number the saying is identified; by the canon number it is understood that the saying is not shared among several, but is peculiar to one evangelist; and the name is also necessary in order that it may be made clear whose saying it is in particular. Therefore the name is also written in the preceding cases, not only because of the slowness of memory already mentioned, but also because of their resemblance to these. [Col. 1121C–1122B]

### Why one is repeated beside several chapter numbers
It also happens that a saying common to more than one Evangelist is found in only one place in one Evangelist and in several places in another, so that in one it has only one section, but in another several; as the little saying which in Matthew ends with the eleventh section, in Mark with the fourth, and in Luke with the tenth, is found in John in four places and ends with four sections. Hence, in that collection of sections in which all the sections of the entire Gospel text are arranged under their respective canons, it happens in the aforesaid saying that the tenth section of Luke, the fourth of Mark, and the eleventh of Matthew are repeated four times in relation to the four sections of John. And as many sections as a saying has in one Evangelist, so many times is it repeated in another.

[Col. 1121]

# HOMILY ON THE UNJUST STEWARD

ON LUKE, CHAPTER XVI: “There was a certain rich man who had a steward,” etc.

[Col. 1121D] “There was a certain rich man,” etc. Who is the rich man but Christ—rich in heaven, rich on earth, rich everywhere; rich, “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14)? And “of his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16). Rich is he “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2:3), rich “unto all and upon all who call upon him” (Rom. 10:13).

The steward, moreover, is every Christian, who in baptism received the stewardship of himself and of his neighbour. [Col. 1122D] For every Christian lives not only for his own sake, but also for his neighbour’s. Nor will he render an account only for his own soul, but also for that of the person with whom he lives in this life: exercising himself in body and mind, helping his neighbour by instruction and example, seeking not only what is his own but also what belongs to others. This is the noble concern and holy stewardship of Christians; hence comes the fearful judgment of God and the future reckoning.

“And he was accused before him, as though he had wasted” [Col. 1123A] “his goods.” We are accused daily before the Lord, because our angels always see the face of the Father (Matt. 18:10) and report to him all that concerns us. What, then, do we do? Where do we hide? They accuse us; they behold us and God; they behold all that concerns us and God, because in beholding us they report to God. There is no obstacle, no darkness, by which they are prevented from seeing all that concerns us, because the divine light by which they are illuminated penetrates everything: “the light shines in the darkness” (John 1:5), and “night shall be illumined as day” (Ps. 138 [139]).

“And he was accused as though he had wasted his goods.” Who administers well in every respect all the goods entrusted to him? Who does not sometimes slumber? “Sometimes even good Homer nods” (Horace, *Art of Poetry*, 359); and, “In many things we all offend” [Col. 1123B] (James 3:2); and, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:3).

“And he called him and said to him: What is this that I hear of thee?” The Lord calls us daily: “Come, children, hear me” (Ps. 33 [34]:12); “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are burdened” (Matt. 11:28); and, “O men, unto you I cry, and my voice is to the sons of men.” Daily he speaks to us through the prophets; he speaks through the apostles; he speaks through himself in the Gospel; he speaks through teachers; he speaks in the conscience: “What is this that I hear of thee?” He reproves those who think evil, those who speak evil, those who act evil, those who live evil lives.

“What is this that I hear of thee? Render an account of thy stewardship.” For “of every idle word which men shall have spoken, they shall render account on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12:36). Render an account of thy stewardship. What do you do concerning yourself? What concerning your neighbour? What do you think in your heart? What sort of word do you utter? What delights your hearing, and upon what do you fix your eye? Render an account of thy stewardship. You waste my goods; you use my goods badly; you give my goods to strangers. I call, and you do not answer; I stretch forth my hand, and you do not look. Render an account of thy stewardship. For now you can no longer be steward. You have reached the end; it is the time of judgment: render an account; now you can no longer be steward. You are soon to depart hence, soon to die. Now you can no longer be steward. After this life there is no stewardship. Here we serve by stewarding; there, by resting, we receive our reward. Here [Col. 1123D] we acquire what we shall possess there; here is labour, there reward.

“But the steward said within himself: What shall I do, because my lord is taking away from me the stewardship?” Happy is he who thinks of the end; happy he who knows himself to be daily about to die, because “the end of a discourse is better than its beginning” (Eccl. 7:9 [Vulgate]). What shall I do? How shall I escape the consequences of a badly administered stewardship? “I cannot dig,” once the stewardship of this life has failed. After this life no action remains by which we may merit eternal life. There I shall no longer be able to dig, because there one cannot refresh the poor, visit the sick, persevere in holy vigils and prayers. For what else is digging but cultivating the soil of mind and body through the exercises of holy works? We dig the soil when [Col. 1124A] we root out vices from ourselves in order to plant virtues; and this cannot be done after this life.

“I am ashamed to beg.” Lest that be said to me which was said to the foolish virgins: “Lest perhaps there be not enough for us and for you, go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves” (Matt. 25:9). There is good begging and bad begging. Good begging is here. Here we rightly beg wisdom and instruction from teachers; in the litanies we beg the saints to pray for us. In the other life, begging is shameful. For who would not be ashamed to say: “Give us of your oil, because our lamps are going out” (ibid., 8)? Therefore I am ashamed to beg. Truly, begging is shameful where nothing is recovered and perpetual want of every good accompanies one. Therefore I am ashamed to beg. There the begging of another’s good is of no use, where [Col. 1124B] one’s own every good has failed; nor can anyone expect from another what he himself has not merited, when each scarcely has enough for himself and “the righteous man is scarcely saved.” Therefore I am ashamed to beg.

“I know what I shall do, that, when I have been removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.” He who had administered his stewardship badly found, at the end, a healthful counsel: namely, to give a little in order to receive more, and to be received into the houses of others when his own failed him.

“Having therefore called together each of his lord’s debtors, he said to the first: How much dost thou owe my lord? And he said: A hundred measures of oil.” We have one common Lord, whom we worship as one Lord, to whom we all owe whatever good we can do. But because we are all stewards, a share of the debts owed to the Lord comes to us by right of our stewardship, so that we are found to be debtors not only to God but also to one another. [Col. 1124C] For we are commanded not only to love God but also our neighbour. Therefore we are debtors to God and debtors also to our neighbour. Yet to God we owe the whole, even that which we refer to our neighbour, so that whatever we owe, we owe to God.

We have spiritual goods and bodily goods. Spiritual goods are faith, justice, charity, and the like, which we owe to God and our neighbour. Bodily goods are gold, silver, wheat, wine, and the like, by means of which we serve God and assist our neighbour. What can be understood better by oil than spiritual goods? Oil is rarer and gentler than the solidity of wheat; it nourishes light—that is, its power illuminates [Col. 1124D] the mind for beholding truth—and it excels all liquids, as spiritual goods excel bodily ones. What is understood by wheat but bodily goods? For the genus is often understood through a species.

Therefore the steward first addresses the debtor in oil, because spiritual things come before bodily things. He owes a hundred measures of oil because he owes God whatever spiritual good he possesses. The measures of oil are many just as the kinds of spiritual good are many. For the vessel containing a hundred measures of oil signifies all the kinds of spiritual goods. The number one hundred often signifies fullness, and a finite number is often used for an infinite one. Therefore he owes his lord a hundred measures of oil who owes God the perfection of spiritual good. But much of what is owed to God concerns one’s neighbour. For we offend greatly unless we render faith, [Col. 1125A] justice, and charity to our neighbour.

When, therefore, the steward orders fifty to be written out of a hundred measures, what is owed to God is confirmed in writing, because it is not remitted. What is owed to himself he does not order to be written, because it is remitted. He remits what is his own; he leaves what is God’s. Concerning that which is owed to himself, he makes the debtor secure by pardon; concerning that which is owed to God, he makes him anxious by a written record. Hence it follows:

“And he said to him: Take thy bond, and sit down quickly, and write fifty”; as though he said: What you owe to me, I remit to you; as for what you owe to God, take up the obligation; and you who stood proudly, sit down quickly and humble yourself. What you despised, or through forgetfulness regarded as nothing, write on the tablets of your heart and hold in memory, so that you may frequently repent and make expiation until that too is remitted [Col. 1125B] to you. “Sit down quickly,” that is, do not put it off from day to day. “Write fifty.” This number belongs to repentance and remission: so too the fiftieth year is a year of release, and the fiftieth psalm is penitential. Fifty are written and fifty remitted. A like number signifies a like offence against God and man. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, and with thy whole soul, and with thy whole mind. This is the first and great commandment. The second is like unto it: Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself” (Matt. 22:37–39). For where love is alike, offence is alike.

It follows:

“Then he said to another: And thou, how much dost thou owe? And he said: [Col. 1125C] A hundred cors of wheat.” A *cadus* is a measure for liquids, and a *corus* for seed. Greatly must we fear, who owe the fullness of bodily goods—we owe them to our neighbours—and yet do not pay; we owe the whole and scarcely pay a little. What then shall we do? If we cannot pay all that we owe, at least let us remit to others what is owed to us. Hence it follows: “He said to him: Take thy note, and write eighty.” For he who writes eighty out of a hundred remits a fifth part, because from bodily things that is owed to one’s neighbour which the five senses of the body require. What is thus commended in writing is left to divine grace through the number eight. You have seized what is mine, taken away what was lent, denied what was entrusted. If I remit to you what concerns me, write eighty—that is, commit to memory [Col. 1125D] that you still need the pardon of divine grace. For the grace of the Gospel is signified by the number eight, just as the severity of the Law is signified by seven. But he merits the grace of eight who keeps the commandments signified by ten; thus, by joining eight to ten, we bind grace acquired to the commandment, so that he who writes eighty, through keeping the Decalogue, may attain the grace of the number eight.

“And the lord praised the unjust steward because he had acted prudently.” A remarkable thing: the steward is wicked and is praised; he administered badly and is spared; he did not make good what he did, and yet is pardoned. But he acted prudently, because he remitted a little so as to receive more; he remitted temporal things so as to receive eternal things. For he had heard: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6:37), and, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” [Col. 1126A] (Matt. 6:12). He truly acted prudently who strives to make God his debtor, so that he may demand from him the remission owed because he himself remitted. He acted prudently because he makes the very one to whom he was indebted indebted to himself. And he who had a harsh exactor now has a gracious debtor, so that he may confidently say: Forgive, because I forgave; render the pardon which you owe, because I granted pardon.

“For the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light.” The children of light labour and scarcely merit their wage; they run and scarcely reach the prize; they travail and scarcely escape. The children of the world, after praises, enticements, and illicit loves, merely forgive, and hold God as their debtor; they spare, and are spared; they pardon, and are pardoned. Therefore [Col. 1126B] the children of this world are wiser than the children of light in their generation—that is, when they are reborn to God and renewed by spiritual life.

“And I say to you: Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of iniquity.” *Mammon*, that is, riches, are called riches “of iniquity” because they are not acquired without iniquity, and because it is unjust to reclaim for private use what the Lord created for common use. Hence it is written: “For iniquity I saw the tents of Ethiopia” (Hab. 3:7); that is, for the sake of acquiring riches I saw men made into tents of blackness—that is, of vices and demons—so that those who could have been tabernacles by pursuing poverty were made tents of vices for the gathering of iniquity. Who does not see many incur perjury, commit murders, devise frauds against their neighbours, and become betrayers of states and rulers for the sake of riches? These become, for iniquity’s sake, tents of Ethiopia.

But since above the steward made friends both from spiritual and from bodily goods, why does the Lord conclude his parable by speaking of bodily goods alone? We more quickly forgive an injury done to us than money lent; we give faith more readily than possessions; we are more inclined to forgive hatreds than to spend what is ours. Therefore the Lord, having instructed us parabolically in mercy, concludes his discourse with that kind of mercy which he knows to be more difficult among human beings; and at the end he urges us more earnestly toward that to which he sees us more reluctantly inclined, because “the end of a discourse is better than its beginning” (Eccl. 7:9 [Vulgate]). [Col. 1126D]

Let us therefore make friends from the riches of iniquity, by distributing them to the poor and forgiving debtors and those who have taken them away. But because some riches of iniquity are possessed by paternal succession, others acquired by just labour, and others usurped by crime or impiety, those which come from crime or impiety certainly do not make friends of God. Nor should anyone suppose that he ought to seek aids to salvation from wealth which he has amassed by the commerce of iniquity. For it is written: “The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable” (Prov. 2:2), because they are offered from crime; and, “He who sacrifices from what is unjustly acquired, his offering is defiled” (Ecclus. 34:21); and, “He who offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son in his father’s sight” (ibid., 24).

When, therefore, we are commanded to make friends from the mammon of iniquity, [Col. 1127A] we must distinguish such riches as arise from inheritance or just labour. Yet these too are called riches of iniquity, as though of inequality, because when we hold them as private property, we do not preserve equality with other human beings. Thus the riches from which we are commanded to make friends are riches both of iniquity and of justice: of iniquity in relation to God, who creates all things for common use; of justice in relation to the world, because human beings possess them by worldly justice. Thus riches justly possessed on earth are unjust in relation to divine justice and just in relation to earthly justice. Divine justice condemns the possession of any private property; earthly justice defends the possession of some private property. Through earthly justice, men gather possessions as their own; [Col. 1127B] through divine justice, they make their possessions common.

But riches obtained by crime are altogether unjust. No justice approves them; even earthly justice condemns them. And these must in no way be offered to God, [Col. 1128A] because they were acquired by crime. Nevertheless they must be restored quickly—indeed, cast away—lest the evildoer be found persisting in what he began wickedly.

“That when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings.” Here he explains what he had said: “that they may receive me into their houses.” For eternal abodes are the houses of those upon whom mercy is bestowed: their houses, I say, not by possession but by cause; not by possession, as though they possess them—perhaps they will not possess them—but by cause, because they are the cause that their benefactors possess them. Therefore they receive you into their houses when they cause us to be in eternal dwellings. We count as theirs those dwellings which we receive only through them, which they render to us, as it were, for the benefits and mercies they have received [Col. 1128B] in temporal things; they become requiters with eternal things through him who repays for them what they themselves owed, our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1127]

# BOOK, OR HOMILY, OF BLESSED ODO, BISHOP OF CAMBRAI, ON THE UNJUST STEWARD

(Martène, *Anecdota*, V, 853, from a manuscript of Pratelles Monastery.)

## PREFATORY NOTICE

[Col. 1127C] Concerning Odo, bishop of Cambrai, and his writings, besides Herimannus, who treats of him at greater length in the *History of the Restoration of the Monastery of St Martin of Tournai*, vol. XII of the *Spicilegium*, Henry of Ghent has the following in Book 4 of *On Illustrious Writers of the Church*:

> Odo, bishop of Cambrai, wrote a beautiful homily on the Gospel according to Luke: “There was a certain rich man who had a steward.” He also expounded the canon of the Mass, *Te igitur*. He also wrote to Wilbodon, monk of Affligem, a disputation which he had held with a certain Jew concerning the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, in dialogue form, marking the first letter of his own name and the first letter of the Jew disputing with him.

And John Trithemius, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, says:

> Odo, bishop of Cambrai, a man learned in the Holy Scriptures and nobly educated in humane letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in speech, remarkably eminent, after the manner of the ancients, in composing and delivering homilies to the people, wrote a disputation [Col. 1127D] which he had held with a certain Jew concerning the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, in dialogue form, marking the first letter of his own name and that of the Jew disputing with him.
>
> To Wilbodon the monk: one book. On the canon of the Mass: one book. On the unjust steward: one book, “There was a certain rich man.” Several homilies and letters. And he composed not a few other works which have not come to my knowledge.

From these two testimonies it follows that the homily [Col. 1128C] on the unjust steward, published under Odo’s name together with his other short works in volume XXI of the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, is not the work of our Odo, since by reason of its brevity it can be called neither a beautiful homily nor, much less, a book—unless perhaps one says that he wrote two homilies on the unjust steward (for he composed several homilies), one shorter and the other longer and beautiful, which can also be honoured with the name of a book. These two characteristics agree excellently with the following homily, here published from an old manuscript of Pratelles, whose style also agrees very closely with his other works.

Odo, formerly abbot of St Martin of Tournai, was elected bishop of Cambrai in 1105. He died in the monastery of Anchin in 1113, to which he had withdrawn after resigning the episcopate. We have concerning him a notable encyclical letter of the monks of Anchin, which it is fitting to place here first from the manuscripts of Alnes and Tournai.

The humble community of the monastery of Anchin, to all [Col. 1128D] who are concerned for their salvation, greeting in the Lord.

Beloved, we send you greeting, that through your prayers we may deserve to be relieved from the sorrow that weighs upon us. Alas, bitter death, who dividest brothers and severest friends! Whence comes this power to thee? After the cross of Christ, who restored these powers to thee? Surely he cast thee down, he conquered thee, who long ago threatened thee through the prophet: “I will be thy death, O death; I will be thy bite, O hell” (Hos. 13:14). If therefore Christ’s death took from thee the power to harm, how dost thou compel to die those whom he himself redeemed from death to live with him forever?

For these are his words in the Gospel: “Everyone who believes in me shall not die; and though he be dead, he shall live” (John [Col. 1129A] 11:25–26). But perhaps someone will say: “What an opening has he given on his arrival! What is the point of this?” Believe, brothers and lords to whom these words come, that it was not unbelief but sorrow of heart that forced from us this beginning of speech and made us launch, as it were, an attack upon death, though we know that in the Scriptures the departure of the righteous from this world is called sleep or falling asleep. Hence the Psalmist says: “When he shall give sleep to his beloved” (Ps. 126 [127]:2); and the Lord says in the Gospel: “The girl is not dead, but sleeps” (Luke 8:52).

Yet we cannot command ourselves not to grieve when we recall Lord Odo, bishop of Cambrai, who recently departed this world among us. Held by a grievous illness, he resigned the episcopate and had himself brought to Anchin; and in the end he showed how greatly he had loved our church during his life. While he lived here, he was a father to us in counsel, a mother in tenderness, a friend in beneficence. [Col. 1129B] Nor is it surprising that we cannot endure the longing for his presence, since it has happened to us to lose the consolation of his present life. We grieve for our condition, not his, because we believe that, while we still walk among the snares of this world, he has escaped to better things.

We believe, I say, that he now joyfully sings with the righteous: “As we have heard, so have we seen, in the city of the Lord” (Ps. 47 [48]:9); and marvels with Moses, saying: “Passing by, I shall see this great vision” (Exod. 3:3). Surely he now has the great vision of God to behold, he who, while in the body, loved not his own will but God’s. But who could worthily recount the virtues which he possessed? What should one praise in him above all? If you proclaim his patience, kindness, and humility, whatever you say will be less than the truth. He so excelled in each one as though he possessed no others. And how can I briefly describe his daily life in worn and commonplace words?

He was gentle in address, sweet in speech. Nothing was more cheerful than his severity, nothing more serious than his cheerfulness; the gaiety of his countenance tempered the gravity of his character, and the gravity of his character tempered the gaiety of his countenance. He either did not know how, or did not wish, to lie or swear. He prudently avoided the tongues both of flatterers and detractors, and fled from both kinds of people in spirit as plagues of the soul.
