Against the latter he fenced his ears with thorns, “that he might not hear an evil tongue” (Ecclus. 28:28). Against the former he knew it was written: “The words of flatterers are soft, but they strike the inward parts of the belly” (Prov. 18:8). [Col. 1129C]

He rendered evil to no one for evil, nor curse for curse (1 Pet. 3:9); and, like a lamb sent among wolves, he had no bite of malice. He provided things good not only before God but also before men (Rom. 12:17), that he might preside without offence over the church entrusted to him. He also shone with the grace of apostolic teaching; and, so far as lay in him, he recalled men from the world both by the word of preaching and by the excellent discipline of his life.

Among the distinguished marks of these virtues, I think it superfluous to praise his chastity, since even before his conversion his life, because of the continence he maintained, was an example to all; and this should have been said first. But I have not undertaken to say everything. At that time too—that is, before his conversion, to return to what went before—he was so wholly absorbed in books that he seemed to think he could have no rest except the labour he had undertaken in the study of Scripture. He was grounded in grammar, adorned with rhetoric, armed with dialectic; and a great multitude of pupils followed him as he was incessantly occupied in these studies, having assembled from every direction because of the fame of so great a man and thirsting to be shaped by his discipline and instructed by his teaching.

Here perhaps someone might pause and speak of how ardent his intellect was, how tenacious his memory, how restrained he already was in manners, sober in speech, diligent in teaching, cautious in disputations, prompt in resolving questions; and of the great quiet in his schools, the great peace among his students, and the ordering of life [Col. 1130A] achieved through his discipline, so that he seemed deservedly to be called not so much a master of letters as a bishop of souls.

But after the books of blessed Augustine, *On Free Choice of the Will* and *On True Religion*, came into his hands, he was immediately changed into another true self: he began to hate what he had loved and love what he had formerly hated. Good Jesus! What a transformation in the man! His goods were distributed to Christ’s poor; he practised abstinence from food and drink, mortification of the flesh; and turning into true philosophy all the study he had spent on secular disciplines, he made companions out of his pupils, converted many by his example and teaching, and afterwards, leaving behind the secular clerical state, became a monk and built the monastery called St Martin’s at Tournai. He was chosen and consecrated abbot by all who had left the world through him or with him. I pass over many things, because I hasten to others.

Then indeed it was as though a light had arisen in that region. For the people were converted by his preaching. In marriages, holy separations took place with the consent of both parties; fathers were divided from sons, and sons from parents, by the sword of God’s word. All, as in the time of the apostles, brought into common the price of what they possessed. Young men and virgins, old men together with younger, vied with one another in casting off the burden of this world; and, as though they no longer belonged to this world, they desired to fly naked and unencumbered to heaven. Their city seemed a prison to them; the monastery, paradise.

He himself, becoming all things to all, weak with the weak (1 Cor. 9:22), appeared strong to the strong; and, as though he were father of all, he bore heartfelt care for all. Alas for the uncertain ordering of human affairs! Temptation attended those happy beginnings, and Satan, who was present even among the sons of God, demanded them “that he might sift them as wheat” (Luke 22:31). Let the scorpion here cease to pour the venom of detraction from its curved wound, and let no one cite against so great a man the fact that certain persons, abandoning their holy purpose, returned to the world—unless he dares to reproach Christ because many of his disciples [Col. 1130B] “went back and walked with him no more” (John 6:67). Let each spare his tongue, spare his soul, and strive to escape this most wicked vice as though it were the devil’s final snare. For few there are—even to say nothing of religious persons—who make their own lives so blameless that they do not gladly find fault with another’s.

Why say more? Christ did not permit so great a lamp to lie hidden under a bushel, but, by God’s grace, that it might shine “for all that are in his house” (Matt. 5:15), he was raised to the episcopate of the church of Cambrai. How great and what manner of life he then lived, and how mindful he remained of his former humility and poverty, we can produce as many witnesses as there are people in that city.

But because we have strayed too far from what we began, let us now, leaving everything else aside, return to our sick man; and, lest he suffer delay on our account, let us briefly recount his passage to glory. As we have said, he had himself brought to Anchin. There, after all that is fitting for a dying Christian had duly been performed, he appeared to await his final hour with such cheerfulness and security as though another, not he himself who was ill, were to die for him. Therefore a certain brother, overcome with astonishment, dismissed every witness and approached him alone; placing his ear close to his mouth, he carefully inquired whether he was afraid.

Then he, to use his own words, when he said, “Why should I be afraid?” and the brother set before him the peril of death, the fact that “the judgments of the Lord are a great deep” (Ps. 35 [36]:7), that “no living person shall be justified in thy sight” (Ps. 142 [143]:2), and other such things, he was silent a little while and, as though first considering something within himself, answered: “I am not afraid.” The brother, astonished, was silent and perceived that he had great confidence.

This blessed man died on the third day before the Kalends of July [29 June]; he rendered his soul to Christ, and left us his body for burial. Therefore we ask all brothers and lords to whom this writing may come: pray for him, as he prayed for himself through us. For, having summoned privately to himself the abbot of our house, [Col. 1131A] he said, to give his own words: “Ask, dearest one, the community of brothers to deign to intercede for me before God, whose judgment I shall not be able to endure without his mercy.”

But I preferred to undergo the judgment of many through this writing and endure reproach from evil men rather than disobey my abbot’s command or fail to follow his will. For the man of whom we speak raised for himself a monument more enduring than bronze (Horace, *Odes* 3.30.1), which no antiquity can erase. There remain among us certain of his short works, judged worthy of remembrance: namely, two treatises, one on the canon of the Gospels and one on the canon of the Mass; a disputation against a Jew; and a homily on the steward; one book on original sin and another on blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which he deigned to compose in response to my question and dedicate to my name. Farewell.

# HOMILY ON THE UNJUST STEWARD

[Col. 1131B] “There was a certain rich man who had a steward; and he was accused before him as though he had wasted his goods,” and the rest. (Luke 16.)

1. Beloved brothers, after the reading from the holy Gospel has been set forth, many people, according to the customs of their times and the purposes of their undertakings, have expounded many matters elegantly, bringing to the ignorance of their contemporaries no contemptible instruction suited to the character of those to be taught. Yet they did not discuss all that can usefully be understood concerning this passage, any more than they did concerning many other Scriptures; rather, they left much to be discussed by teachers who would publish teaching suited and necessary to later times. And, to confess the truth, they could not do so, because just as no persons of the present age possess its complete understanding, so neither did those before us possess it.

For the utterances of the Holy Spirit possess by nature such fertility of meanings that they can neither be contained, nor ought to be contained, within the narrow limits of any human minds. But the Holy Spirit himself, who implanted their multiplicity in his utterances, mercifully distributes them to persons according as he sees them to be expedient in the times to which he spoke. Thus he has deigned to impart also to our humility an understanding of the aforesaid reading that differs in many respects from the interpretations of earlier expositors. Though scholarly, it is nevertheless not to be disregarded. If he himself should choose to grant strength of eloquence for this purpose, admonished by certain brothers, I wish according to the powers of my small ability to share it with many by setting it forth. [Col. 1131D]

But because, for fullness of understanding in any reading, it is not enough to know what is intimated by the words unless one also knows the beginning of the whole narrative and its final cause, we must look back at the preceding words of the holy Gospel, so that we may discover on what occasion and for the purpose of indicating what the Lord set forth the parable of the unjust steward.

2. In what precedes, St Luke the Evangelist relates that tax collectors and sinners came to the Lord, and that the same Lord did not disdain to take bodily food with them. He also relates that the Pharisees and scribes, who falsely gloried in their own righteousness, seeing this, murmured; and on that occasion they defamed him and his teaching as far as they could.

But the merciful Lord, who took bodily food with them not by sharing in their sins but, through the familiarity of a bodily meal, by inviting them to the refreshment of spiritual food, set forth the likeness of a man who had a hundred sheep and lost one of them. He did this in order to make known to them and to all others the folly of their iniquity, and to show himself to be the true shepherd of mankind and men to be his precious possession. [Col. 1132B] To this he added another likeness, of a woman who had ten drachmas and had lost one of them.

Having completed these similitudes, he then, as it were adapting them to their intended meaning and demonstrating by its effect how great a good repentance is, in order to summon them to it—and also indicating why he received sinners—added, saying: “Thus there shall be joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance” (Luke 15:7). In order that this saying might become for sinners a secure incentive to repentance, he added the following narratives of three parables. For because the Saviour, as he himself says, had come [Col. 1132C] to call sinners to repentance, he wished no one to be able to despair of repentance for any reason, or to think himself excusable. Therefore, after mentioning repentance, he added the parables of the prodigal son, of the unjust steward, and of Lazarus, covered with sores and lying at the rich man’s gate; in these he displayed, according to the differing kinds of sinners, differing modes of conversion and varied works of repentance.

3. [Cols. 1132D–1133A] For it is certain that some sinners, recognizing the wretched foulness of their sins without any admonition from anyone—though prompted by divine grace—shudder at it; and, shuddering, seek pardon from the Lord with the keenest affliction of mind. Others, however, remain so irrational in them that they pay no attention whatever to them until at last they are roused to awareness of them by terrible rebuke and threat, or by their being plainly set before them. This commonly happens to those who serve God in many respects, yet do not wholly withdraw from carnal pleasure. When these persons learn their evils through the rebuke of others and fear future condemnation, because, through their habitual carnal pleasure, they are unable to practise in themselves the severity of penance, they make amends for their sins through works of mercy. There are also others whose sins are exceedingly grave and numerous, and, like ulcers which, their skin having burst, have grown out upon the surface from an inward discharge, are not concealed. These too, often ashamed at the public and grievous foulness of their evils, yet not despairing of pardon from the merciful Lord, utterly humbled, seek from all whom they judge learned in the law and followers of righteousness the teaching of eternal life—although they are despised by many of them—as beggars seek bread from the rich; and they disclose their evils to all whom they know to have care for the humbled, as though to dogs licking Lazarus’ sores, and ask their aid by prayers and instruction in satisfaction.

4. [Cols. 1133A–1133D] Therefore, because the Lord, the true and supreme priest, had come to save sinners not only by his own sacrifice but also by exhortation to conversion and instruction in satisfaction, having mentioned repentance he wished in the parables already set forth to display the varieties of it which we have indicated, and perhaps many others besides. In this he also refuted the Pharisees and scribes who rejected fellowship with sinners. Since he had added these parables to what he had said about joy arising in heaven over sinners who repent, it seems without error that he invited sinners of every kind to repentance, as though addressing them thus:

Whoever you are who, living lavishly and according to your own desire, have withdrawn from the Creator into the far country of unlikeness, do not grow sluggish in returning, by returning into yourself for the correction of repentance, as though despairing of pardon. Rather, consider that the son who had squandered with harlots the portion of property which his father had entrusted to him, at last returned to himself, sought his father with tears, and asked to be received no longer as a son but as a servant; yet he was received as a most beloved son, and received with festivity (Luke 15:12).

You also, whom the shameful and manifest ulcers of sins disfigure, do not delay to humble yourself by fleeing to repentance. Rather, as a suppliant made humble, ask the guardians of souls to assist you by prayers and instruction in amendment; and urgently desire to be strengthened by the consolation of the Scriptures from those who seem wise in the Scriptures, even though most of them shut the door of speech. For if you do this, while those who disdain to strengthen you by the Scriptures perish in the torments of hell, you will attain rest in Abraham’s bosom. For Lazarus, lying full of sores at the door of the rich man clothed in purple and fine linen, desired to be fed with the crumbs falling from the table when no one gave him anything; he attained the refreshment of Abraham’s bosom, while that rich man, who had not given him crumbs from his table, was consigned to infernal torments (Luke 16:20).

But you also, whoever are subject to me and obey in many things, and therefore, secure in many respects, sin through negligence by following your desires: because you do not notice that you sin, nor show yourself resistant to correction, when through some rebuke you have come to know the evils of your negligence, do not despair of pardon. Do not plead as an excuse that you cannot exercise in yourself the severity of penance; but carefully consider from the parable which I recount to you how you may be able to appease your Lord.

5. [Cols. 1133D–1134A] “There was a certain rich man who had a steward,” and so forth. This rich man, concerning whom the Lord proposes a parable to his disciples, is understood most reasonably as none other than the Lord himself. Although he lived among human beings as a poor man, nevertheless, in that he is God, he rules by the right of creation over all things whatsoever. He alone truly is and is understood to be rich; for whoever else is believed to be rich, unless he receives from him who is rich that which he may possess eternally, is found poor in the midst of his riches. It does not seem necessary to say much in order to show this, since no believer disputes this interpretation. But because we have not yet found anyone who has sufficiently investigated whom the steward ought to signify, it must be diligently and reasonably explored through the likeness of the thing itself.

6. [Cols. 1134A–B] The name *villicus* (“steward”) is either formed from or derived from *villa* (“estate”), and properly signifies anyone appointed to guard the tenants of an estate, exact their rents, and restrain them so that they do not withhold from the master the service due to him. Hence we could already recognize the steward of this rich man, that is, of our Lord, if we knew the estate and the tenants whom he appointed the steward to guard. This too can easily be known if we take care to examine closely the character of an estate.

7. [Cols. 1134B–D] An estate is called the dwelling of a countryman, established not for ornament and pleasure but for cultivating land, fitted so as to yield the benefit of fruits. If it receives industrious tenants, so that what ought to be in it is found there, it is regarded as a possession greatly dear to its owner, because it is very useful. Indeed, from the goods which he gathers from it he takes pride in his pleasant urban dwelling. But if it has useless tenants, then in a short time, laid waste and lacking the necessities of life, it will appear a worthless possession and a habitation of wild beasts. If we fittingly apply these things to their counterparts, what can we discover more rightly signified by the estate than our temporal life? For what is this life in which we live temporarily, except a kind of rural and laborious dwelling, with no beauty and no pleasure, far removed from the city of true happiness?

In it, while we strive through the limbs of the body to perform actions pleasing to the Lord; while we foster good thoughts in the mind; while we judge everything earthly to be transient, useless while possessed but not used, and unstable—and therefore contemptible—once it begins to be used; while we think upon the heavenly things, enduring and delightful, which, though always enjoyed with the greatest delight by their possessors, never pass away and therefore ought to be desired; and while we reason that we must apply ourselves especially to knowing the praise of our Creator, so that we may know how to serve him without error: what else are we doing but laboring to cultivate the ground, that it may bear fruits pleasing to our possessor?

8. [Col. 1135A] If, therefore, the estate is understood as our temporal life, what are signified by the tenants except the two powers of the mind? One of these moves the limbs of the body to perform whatever it wills; the other turns itself about in many ways for meditation and contemplation. When these two exercise the mind in meditating and the body in doing what pleases the Lord, what can our temporal life offer the Lord more pleasing than the powers of the mind? And indeed, when it is so cultivated, it is thought to become pleasing to the Lord; for then, as the Apostle himself exhorts, he is glorified in all things through it (1 Corinthians 10:31). But if they give themselves over to carnal desires and temporal glories, what will our life be except a thing empty and deserted of every good, a habitation of demons?

9. [Cols. 1135A–C] Therefore, lest those powers of the mind—that is, the powers of acting and meditating—should be able to bend themselves wherever they wished at their own will, the Lord set reason over them. It ought to examine each of their movements and, whether they wished it or not, recall them from what displeased the Lord to what pleased him. Whoever discerns that this is true already recognizes without doubt the steward whom we sought. For reason itself performs the role of steward within us when it recalls from vices and exhorts to virtues those powers which move the body to act and the soul to meditate. It performs the role of steward when it guards them carefully lest they ever be broken by the temptations of evil spirits. It also holds the place and carries out the office of steward when it impels them, as though by force, toward what is just, although it may appear lowly and contemptible. Thus it compels them to render to the Lord the service which they ought to render, but which their desire for their own pleasure would not fear to withhold.

When it gives them harmful assent by flattery, and assists them in what they demand, it as it were casts away, dissipates, and tramples underfoot the good of discernment and authority which the Lord entrusted to it. This cannot be concealed from the Lord by any cunning devices, since, as the Apostle says, he is the discerner of thoughts and intentions of the heart, and no creature is invisible in his sight (Hebrews 4:12). To indicate this, the Lord added: “And he was accused before him as though he had squandered his goods.” For I do not think he says anything else by this than that he cannot be ignorant of what that steward has done wickedly. For when someone is accused, the crime which he perhaps wished to be hidden is made public. Thus the accusation of the steward seems to mean nothing other than the Lord’s manifest knowledge of reason’s negligences and harmful assents.

10. But what does he intend to indicate when, in the significant language of the parable, he says “as though he had squandered,” rather than saying simply that he had squandered? If we consider the nature of the matter, namely, that reason never ceases to possess discernment and the power to direct those powers of the mind to the Lord’s glory, what the Lord wished to show by “as though” is sufficiently clear. For it is certain, and no rational person can doubt, that discernment of good and evil, the authority by which reason rules the aforesaid powers of the mind, those very powers, and the grace of faith, are goods of the Lord God neither small nor contemptible. If reason could destroy all these things, and did destroy them, how great a crime deserving condemnation would it commit against their maker and giver?

Therefore the Lord shows, by “as though,” that reason is known to be deserving of as great a condemnation because it does not use the goods granted to it by the Lord, nor rule the aforesaid powers of the mind as it ought, as it would be judged to deserve if it utterly cast down from their very being the goods entrusted to it and the powers of acting and meditating subjected to it. Whoever is not devoid of understanding can see that this is just, if he wishes to weigh the merits of things in the just balance. For when reason does not use the aforesaid goods according to the purpose for which it received them from the Lord, what does it appear to do except utterly extinguish them? And when it does not compel the powers of the mind of which we have spoken to serve the Lord by doing what is just, it does not make them more dishonourable to their Creator than if they did not exist at all.

11. [Cols. 1136A–B] But because the most merciful Saviour wishes to indicate that he is appeased by the satisfaction of many such people, he added, in order to show how: “And he called him and said to him.” When someone is said to be called, this shows that he does not come of himself but is invited to come; it also shows that he is far from the caller, and that the calling itself works to make him near. What, then, is understood by the calling in which the steward is said to be called by his master, except that those who do not exercise the power of reason do not turn of themselves to awareness of their error; and that the negligence of reason separates many from the Lord, whom the Lord mercifully exhorts to return to him? The gracious Saviour himself also wished to make this exhortation clear by saying that the master said to the steward: “What is this that I hear of thee? Render an account of thy stewardship.”

12. [Cols. 1136C–1137A] Whoever love the Lord and desire to find him gracious toward us, let us carefully attend to these words of his, love them when understood, and hold fast to them when loved. For they are the words of one who is powerful, whose ordinances it is unsafe to transgress: words expressing disturbance with gravity, yet calling the transgressor to amendment with mercy, and reasonably declaring that correction must not be delayed.

For by saying, “What is this that I hear of thee?” he shows himself as it were astonished that faithful reason sins against him by not using, or misusing, the abundance of his goods. What is said to the steward in these few words is as though reason were addressed in the following, expanded utterance:

“I, the Lord of all, creator of the universe, most mighty of the mighty, most sufficient of the sufficient, who need no one outside myself, who by my will alone do whatever I will: although I had no need of you, by my goodness alone I made you; by the imprint of my image I implanted in you discernment of good and evil; I granted you power to restrain every movement of the will; I bestowed the grace of true faith and the consolation of hope for attaining heavenly things; and I helped you by my commandments and examples. Yet you, treating all these things as though they were contemptible, follow the movements of temporal desire.

“What is this that I hear of thee? Neither the immensity of my power nor the severity of my justice brought you fear of me. The granting of so many and such great benefits, my patience and gentleness, did not bring you worthy love for me. What is this that I hear of thee? You have made yourself so worthless, so useless—though I had made you so great, though I had raised you so high. You have committed a great evil; you have prepared a great punishment for yourself. Yet because I cannot fail to be merciful, render an account of thy stewardship, and I am ready to be appeased toward thee.”

13. [Cols. 1137A–B] Whoever, when called to account by another, answers as he ought until the other is justly satisfied, renders an account. In accordance with this form the most gracious Saviour exhorts us to render an account to him: that is, to make satisfaction to him, in response to the sins for which he rebukes us, through repentance, humility of mind, works of mercy, and prayers. Nor should we delay, because the time is near when we shall be unable to render it. For death threatens at every hour; and after it, nothing can be changed according to our will. The gracious teacher indicated this to us when he added: “For now thou canst no longer be steward.” For after death the right of reason is of no benefit to the lost, because it cannot escape the punishments of deserved condemnation. He who is rich above all wished plainly to indicate this to us by saying to the steward, “For now”—that is, shortly—“thou canst no longer be steward.”

14. [Cols. 1137B–D] But we must consider how the Lord speaks thus to negligent reason, lest what we have said seem far from the truth to those of lesser understanding. The Lord speaks in many ways through which he wishes to make his will known, to each person in a mode suited to him, as he sees each person’s nature and capacity require. For he speaks to some by a hidden inspiration occurring without any outward sign, as the Prophet says: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me.” To others he speaks by a voice, though they do not know whence it comes, as to Samuel. To others by dreams, as to Joseph, Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, and Daniel. To others by angelic ministry, as to Moses, Abraham, Jacob, and many others. To others by certain signs, as to Belshazzar, when fingers wrote upon the wall. To many he speaks through faithful human beings: to the ancients through prophets; to us through ecclesiastical teachers; to some through the reading of the divine Scriptures; to very many through bodily affliction; and to some also through temporal adversity. There are many other modes of divine speech, all of which our weak understanding cannot enumerate.

But this should be known: the Lord speaks to reason when, by one of the aforesaid modes or by any other, he recalls it from its error and negligence to the knowledge of his will. He speaks most especially to the reason of believers who have followed the concupiscence of the flesh through teachers, readings of the divine Scriptures, bodily distress, or adversities. This speech takes place within reason when, aroused by the Lord through any of the aforesaid means and recalling its errors to mind, it says to itself: “What have you done, wretch? How improperly and unjustly you have handled the goods which the Lord bestowed upon you! Have you not held in memory his immensity and unchangeable justice? By following, against his good pleasure and command, a most worthless thing—namely, the flesh—you have defiled yourself. What have you deserved by treating yourself so badly, especially when you knew that he could not be ignorant of these things?” When reason, admonished by any of the aforesaid causes, reflects thus with itself, it is then rebuked by the Lord as though he were saying to it, “What is this that I hear of thee?” and the rest.

15. [Cols. 1138A–B] We must observe that such reflection often occurs in a person’s reason without the ensuing search for repentance and fitting satisfaction that ought to follow. But when this happens, the Lord is not then speaking to it; rather, it surveys itself and wanders abroad without the confusion of fear. The speech of the Lord, however, always accomplishes that for which it is made. Therefore, whenever he himself rebukes reason for its evil deeds, anguish of heart and the search for satisfaction accompany it. This is plainly indicated to us by the Lord’s words. For he adds: “But the steward said within himself.”

Reason speaks, as it were, outside itself when it plans to do evil things or considers without fear the evil things it has done. But it speaks within itself when it carefully investigates what it ought rightly to do. For the former is naturally separate from it; the latter is always proper and innate to it.

16. [Cols. 1138B–D] Therefore, when the Lord has in some aforesaid way rebuked reason for transgressing his ordinances, it immediately remains neither idle nor stupefied, but says within itself: “What shall I do, because my master is taking the stewardship away from me?” That is, according to the force of its nature, it considers how it may avoid incurring the Lord’s wrath, which it recognizes that it deserves. For the steward’s words, “What shall I do, because my master is taking the stewardship away from me?” express reason’s concern lest it be subjected to the Lord’s judgment for condemnation, reasoning and judging in the manner of the Apostle Paul’s counsel:

“I know that I have not served my Creator as I ought, and that he has justly appointed infinite punishment for transgressors of his commandments. I also know that he will soon take life away from me and turn to its opposite the power which I now have to do whatever I will. Yet I know nonetheless that he is merciful, desiring the sinner’s life rather than death, and therefore calling me to the amendment of repentance. With this anxious confidence I seek what I ought to do while I remain in my own power, lest, when I lose it, I be crushed by a most shameful and unbearable poverty.

“But I do not fail to know that it is easy for anyone to begin some kind of severe penance. Anyone, even a coward, may declare war; but I have learned, from the Lord’s teaching, that salvation is earned not by beginning but by persevering. Therefore I think it necessary to consider such a manner of amending my life as I can endure without failure as long as I live. Hence I deliberate how I ought to punish my evils, not daring to commit myself, since I fear a fall into a punishment which I cannot bear. For I do not wish to run uncertainly or fight as one beating the air, but, if it please him who sets the prize, to attain the prize and the crown. For this reason I show myself weighing my strength, when I say: ‘What shall I do, because my master is taking the stewardship away from me? I cannot dig like the strong; yet I do not wish, like the slothful, to remain idle. But I shall do what I can, because I am ashamed to beg.’”

17. [Cols. 1139A–D] Since, when earth is dug, it is pierced and broken by the hard blow of the spade, and turned over so that it may produce the sustenance of life, “to dig” fittingly signifies the mortification of the flesh practised by one whom sharp sorrow for sins and a desire to live with the Lord exercise. Since one who begs, lacking life’s necessities, desires the goods of another, “to beg” signifies want of and desire for the good works in which the saints abound.

Thus reason’s saying, “I cannot dig,” means weighing the weakness of its infirmity in bearing the mortification of the flesh. It declares itself ashamed to beg when it diligently considers the good things which it can do, lest it appear in the life to come poor and empty of good works, desiring those of others, and be put to shame. Because of this pure examination of itself and humble desire to know what would profit it, no one who considers sincerely and humbly how he may please the Lord will be left in doubt. The Lord clearly promises this to those who seek how to escape eternal poverty, when he shows the steward submitting to his own concern: “I know what I shall do.”

For after first showing him doubtful and concerned when he says, “What shall I do?” and so forth, why does he immediately show him made certain by adding, “I know what I shall do, that, when I have been removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses,” except to teach mercifully that however weak a sinner’s reason may be, it should not despair through ignorance of its salvation? For if it grieves bitterly over past evils and, while anxiously examining its powers, seeks how to escape eternal poverty, it will be made certain when the remedy is revealed to it.

Accordingly, when the steward says, “I know what I shall do, that, when I have been removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses,” this indicates the consolation of reason perceiving the ways of its salvation: “A little while ago, terrified by the threat of my Lord, I was held doubtful and anxious, considering my weakness and wondering whether I might recover his grace. Now I know—that is, I understand as the matter truly is—what I ought to do, in order to merit entrance, when I have completed the course of life, into the houses which just bodily action and good meditation build, and which are therefore called their houses. I say that I shall be received into them by those actions because they are the cause why those who are received are received, just as I trust that I shall be received. For, as the Apostle says, before the fearful tribunal of the Lord we shall receive nothing other than what we have done in the flesh, whether good or evil. And the manifold diversity of dwellings which the Lord says are in the Father’s house surely corresponds to the diversity of merits by which each person, aided by grace, has deserved them while living.”

What else are those houses into which after this life we reasonably wish [Note: “[Col. 1139D] Some word is missing, perhaps *introire* (‘to enter’).”] to enter, except dwellings of rest? They come to each person according to the character of the actions of body or mind which are his own; hence they are rightly said to belong to actions, since they are possessed only by those who have merited them.

18. [Col. 1140A] But lest you craftily object to me, saying that, on this interpretation, the houses can also signify the punishments of the wicked, since, just as good actions establish and merit rest, so evil actions establish and merit those punishments, know that a house is called only a dwelling able to protect from rains and every inclement condition of the air. In hell, however, there are only sulphur, fire, stormy blasts, and unspeakable tribulation.

What the steward does whereby he trusts that he will be received into the houses of his subjects, the Lord himself then added when he said: “Having therefore summoned each of his master’s debtors, he said to the first: ‘How much dost thou owe my master?’ And he said: ‘A hundred casks of oil.’ And he said to him: ‘Take thy bond, sit down quickly, and write fifty.’ Then he said to another: ‘And thou, how much dost thou owe?’ He said: ‘A hundred cors of wheat.’ And he said to him: ‘Take thy papers and write eighty.’”

19. [Cols. 1140A–C] We are confident that no one will deny that the powers of the soul by which it moves itself and the body are debtors to the Lord. For they ought, without contradiction, to refer all their acts by right to his glory. Reason summons them, therefore, when it recalls them to its jurisdiction after they have withdrawn from it by following their own desires, and restrains them from the desires which they followed. It asks how much they owe when, setting them before its consideration, it investigates by reasoning why they were made by the Lord, and how diligently, sincerely, in what manner, for what purpose, and for how long they ought to serve him.

That the first answers that he owes the master a hundred casks of oil shows that reason knows, concerning that power of the mind which moves the body to act, that it was made by the Lord, who himself created all things, in order that it might honour him with the utmost zeal in works of charity and mercy, for which he made it: in confession of faith in the eternal Trinity; virginally—that is, incorruptly, without admixture of evil works; steadfastly; through the whole course of temporal life; and for the recompense of eternal blessedness alone.

For oil penetrates more deeply than other ointments, so much so that it draws pain from the very marrow, and naturally floats above every liquid with which it is mixed. In this it fittingly bears the likeness of mercy and charity, because this excuses condemnation for sin, however grave; and the Apostle proves charity to be higher than the other gifts of the Holy Spirit.

20. [Cols. 1140D–1141B] A *cadus* (“cask”) is said to be a measure filled by three amphorae; therefore it fittingly signifies faith in the holy Trinity, by which every spiritual good is measured out to believers. Moreover, a hundred is the number produced by multiplying ten by itself, and thus indicates zeal for perfection and steadfastness. For it is known that ten is a perfect number, because after it there is no other elementary counting; and therefore perfection is fittingly understood through it. But when it is multiplied by itself to produce a hundred, the hundred indicates how perfectly one must strive toward the perfection of charity and mercy, and how rightly and steadfastly one must persevere in it.

For since ten is multiplied by ten to make a hundred, there is no doubt that a hundred is the plain, equilateral square of ten. The equal-sided plane square is a sign of the justice and uprightness which it possesses through equality of sides; and because it lies firmly upon a plane, it is also a sign of steadfastness. This number is divided into two fifties. Fifty represents the joy of the jubilee, in which, according to the law, both a slave attained freedom and one deprived of an inheritance recovered his own inheritance. Therefore a hundred, in which that number is doubled, expresses the joy of eternal blessedness, in which those received will attain freedom of body and soul and will receive, never again to lose it, the inheritance which they lost in the first parent.

The same number, a hundred, also contains four times twenty-five. This is called a circular number; and therefore a hundred signifies the whole span of temporal life, distinguished into four seasons and perpetually recurring in itself like a circle. Those who expound the nature of the number hundred also say that its power is signified by transferring the sign to the right hand, using the same fingers with which thirty and sixty are signified on the left. Since thirty signifies the sanctity of marriage and sixty the chastity of widowhood, they say that a hundred, because it is transferred to the right hand, signifies eternal blessedness; and because it is marked by the same fingers with which those two numbers are marked on the left, it is understood to represent virginity.

21. [Cols. 1141C–D] If, therefore, we rightly weigh both the nature of oil and the quantity contained by the cask, as well as the force and manifold significance of the hundred which we have shown, we shall understand—as we have shown above—how each person ought to serve the Lord as indicated by that answer. Because reason alone, judging and examining itself as to wherein it has sinned, recognizes this concerning the bodily movement subject to it, that first debtor answered the steward that he owed his master a hundred casks of oil.

For we see no other meaning in the debtor’s answering that he owes so much by bodily movement, except that reason, examining the faculty of bodily action, perceives concerning it what we have expounded. For who dares deny that throughout the whole course of our life we ought, with the utmost zeal, without the admixture of any evil, and for the reward of eternal life alone, to exercise the body in order to fulfil true faith through works of mercy and charity? For if we leave faith devoid of works, we prove that we possess the corpse of faith, not living faith or faith that gives us life.

But since a debtor of this sort who can pay this debt as fully as we have shown that it is owed is scarcely found—and that is true—it is necessary for the steward carefully to strive to moderate the debt for debtors. Unless it is moderated as it ought to be, when it can no longer be repaid as owed because it was badly secured, both steward and debtor will undoubtedly perish together. Therefore the steward says to him: “Take thy bond, sit down quickly, and write fifty.”

22. [Cols. 1142A–C] In many places expositors of the sacred Scriptures testify that the number fifty signifies correction and repentance for those who sin according to the flesh. Anyone who wishes and is able to consider will readily learn this from the nature of the things themselves. Fifty is produced if five is multiplied by ten, or ten by five. When the flesh, which had multiplied sins through the five senses, returns to obedience to God’s commandments, commonly understood by the number ten, when it is recalled by rebuke in whatever manner, then five is spiritually multiplied by ten.

But it is impossible for flesh which has followed the pleasure of the senses to be subjected in obedience to the divine commandments unless it first grieves in repentance over the defilement which it had at some time contracted through pleasure. Hence repentance can very fittingly be understood as signified by the number fifty.

There is, however, something else that we wish to observe in fifty: namely, that we are taught to cleanse bodily life from the filth of vices through the grace of the Holy Spirit, for the hope of eternal blessedness. For this reason the number fifty itself is produced from seven multiplied by seven, with one added: seven times seven is forty-nine; with unity added, fifty is completed. In the Scriptures, unity, which has not undergone the diminution of division, is known to signify eternal blessedness, which never experiences any loss of itself. This is made clear by the Lord’s own words in the Gospel, when he says to Martha, anxious in her many tasks, signifying eternal blessedness: “But one thing is necessary.”

Moreover, seven signifies the operation of the Holy Spirit because of his sevenfold grace. It also signifies human life, since it is conducted in seven days, and from generation itself advances by sevens to perfection and then, by the same course, declines into failing and weakness. Therefore, when carnal life, which of itself succumbs to many vices, is cleansed of them by the grace of the Holy Spirit—without whose help iniquity is not cast off—what else happens except that the sevenfold number of humanity is multiplied by the spiritual sevenfold number? If this is done in hope of eternal blessedness, unity is added, and fifty is completed.

23. This, then, is what the steward advises the Lord’s debtor to do: he who has confessed that he has not at any time rendered the hundred, but owes it, should take his bond and, sitting down quickly, write that, since he is unable to render a hundred, he will render fifty. [Col. 1142D] The steward, as we have already said, is reason; the debtor is the capacity for bodily action. Its bond is rightly said to be that which most forcibly recalls to it its debt to the Lord—namely, the thought of approaching death and the fear of infernal punishment. For nothing else makes the capacity for bodily motion so cautious and provident in paying its debt to the Lord as continually holding before the eyes of the mind imminent death and the condemnation of Gehenna. Then it does not readily commit deeds deserving punishment, and those it remembers having committed it strives, by whatever means it can, to erase.

It should be noted, moreover, that what is written is thereby provided against ever perishing through forgetfulness. Therefore, when reason, which fears the Lord’s threats and recognizes that it has not served him with bodily motions as the law of creation required, sets before the mind—which wishes not to carry out through the body what it ought not—death as ever imminent and the horror of infernal punishments, does it not then compel it, as it were, to take up its bond? It likewise bids it, as it were, to sit down quickly, when it urges it, through restraint, to rest without delay from the evils in which it formerly stood. But it then exhorts it to write fifty when it considers that the Holy Spirit’s help must be sought, that by his aid bodily motions which would offend the Lord must all be corrected, and that this must be done not for an hour but unchangeably, throughout the remaining span of life and without cessation, in hope of attaining eternal blessedness—so that faith in the undefiled Trinity may thus be preserved and usefully fulfilled through works of charity and mercy.

For it does not profit one to possess faith in the Trinity, or to practise works of mercy and charity, if one refuses to put away and remove from oneself the unclean works of the flesh. To summarize briefly what has been said at length by reasoning: when reason, recognizing that it has not lived well, either cannot bear or dreads the bitterness of repentance and seeks how it may placate the Lord, it firmly resolves continually to look upon imminent death and the ineffable horror of torments awaiting the ungodly, against the will’s carnal delights that constantly recur; consequently, it resolves to desist without delay from the evils by which it had offended the Lord, continually to invoke the Holy Spirit as helper so that it may lead the remaining life unstained, and to perform works of mercy and charity appropriate to faith in the undivided Trinity. [Col. 1143C] Then the steward bids the Lord’s debtor take up his bond, sit down quickly, and write that he owes the Lord fifty measures of oil.

24. That another answers that he owes a hundred measures of wheat signifies that reason recognizes concerning the power of meditation that at all times, without any admixture of an unclean or in any way harmful meditation, with utmost zeal and steadfastly—without vacillation—in the hope of obtaining blessedness, it ought, according to the rule of Catholic faith, to rehearse God’s commandments through meditation and to consider in wonder the Creator’s boundless goodness and grace. For we believe that the hundred here signifies nothing other than it did in the first debtor’s answer; but wheat signifies something different from [Col. 1143D] oil—namely, God’s commandments and his grace, Christ, by whom we are fed. This is plainly found in many passages of Scripture.

A *corus*, moreover, is said to be a measure containing thirty modii; and since thirty contains ten three times, the *corus* fittingly figures faith in the Trinity, as divine Scriptures—signified by the number ten—establish it. But because one who pays this debt can rarely be found—for it is evident that nearly all human minds are occupied for the greater part of their time with countless vanities—the steward must also moderate this debt for salvation. He therefore says to him: “Take your documents and write eighty.” Since it is manifest that memory is guarded by letters, reason bids the power of meditation, as it were, to take up its documents when it resolves unwaveringly to stir up memory to preserve divine teachings. For memory accomplishes for the certainty of meditation what letters accomplish for awakening dormant memory.

25. It then, as it were, orders eighty to be written when it determines to meditate without forgetfulness upon the commandments of God, signified by ten, together with those things signified by eight which kindle the mind to fulfil their command. For the number eight signifies the simplicity of the divine substance, which is changed by no increases, no diminutions, and no alterations whatsoever; and the abundance of his goodness, which created so many and such great things while needing none of them, by which created things subsist, are held together in wonderful order, and are differentiated and changed by manifold forms and every kind of motion, and are mercifully bestowed upon us by him as he sees fit for each.

The same number eight also signifies the twofold love of God and neighbour, and the perfection of the six virtues—faith, chastity, humility, sobriety, generosity, mercy, and concord. It likewise signifies possession of faith, hope, and charity, and the eternity which they confer upon those who faithfully possess them. By this same number may also be understood the frailty of bodily corruption, which comes from the separation of the four mutually discordant elements, and preparation for the body’s incorruption, which comes through observance of the four virtues—prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. In the same number may likewise be recognized how widely [Col. 1144C] charity ought to be spread by its possessor. The eight states by which true blessedness, though apprehended in whatever manner, remains one, are also signified by this number; the Lord himself fully indicates them to us in the Gospel by declaring blessed the poor in spirit and the rest that follows. The same number also signifies equity and stability that cannot waver in any respect. When all these things are rehearsed in meditation upon God’s commandments, what else happens than that ten is multiplied by eight, producing eighty? In these, moreover, nearly the whole subject-matter of holy meditation is contained.

26. But perhaps someone will ask by what analogies these things are shown in the number eight. Such a person must first recognize that, apart from meditation on the matters stated above, no minds are justified except perhaps those of the simple. For how can any mind preserve the form of justice if it either will not or cannot contemplate the simplicity of the divine substance, which most perfectly contains every good and is in no way changeable; if it does not observe that the many and manifoldly changing things it sees exist by the goodness alone of him who does not need them, and pass into so many changes by his command; if it does not recognize that whatever goods it knows itself to possess, whether bodily or spiritual, are given by him; if it does not seek to know how it can and ought to possess charity without which it does not seek these things; if it does not strive to acquire the six virtues set forth above; [Col. 1145A] if it does not recognize faith, hope, and charity as things now to be possessed, as the Apostle says, and trust that through them it can attain eternity; if it does not despise the body’s corruptibility and prepare itself for incorruption through the four virtues named above; if it does not consider how far charity ought to extend and be enlarged; if it does not desire unchangeable blessedness, weigh in the balance of equity what it must do in order to deserve to attain it, and make its meditation steadfast in all these things?

27. Since, therefore, these things are necessary for the justification of minds, they are rightly signified by the number eight. On account of the mystery it contains, this number is called justice by certain wise men. [Col. 1145B] For, in all the divisions into which it can be divided, it is likened to justice through the causes of justice indicated by the quantities themselves. Its first division is into one and seven, because the first part signifies the simplicity of the Godhead and the second the abundance of his goodness, by which the whole universe of existing things subsists and is ordered. We say that the abundance of God’s goodness is shown by seven because the gifts of the Holy Spirit, by whom the world is filled, are sevenfold; and because, when three and four—the parts of the same number—are multiplied together, twelve, which is the first superabundant number, is manifestly produced.

The second division of the same number eight is into two and six, in which it displays the form of twofold charity and the six virtues previously indicated. In the third division, three and five—the latter a circular number—divide eight; these parts figure faith, hope, charity, and the eternity they confer. The fourth division of the same number is into two fours, by which are signified both the four elements from which we are corruptible and the four principal virtues, by possessing which in this life we hope to become incorruptible. The fifth division of the same number is into four twos, signifying that charity is to be spread among all people of every nation. The same number is also divided by six division into eight units, in which it signifies the one true blessedness and the eight dispositions by which it is acquired. By its very quantity it is a sign of equity, because it is the first to receive [Col. 1145D] the name of an evenly even number. It also signifies firmness of stability, because it is the first to generate the form of the intelligible cube. For when it is called “twice twofold,” eight is shown, and in the mind of one who knows the power of number the form of a cube is generated. A cube is a solid figure, square and equal on every side; therefore, on whichever side it is turned, it lies firm. Hence perhaps a cube is called *cubus* from *cubando* (“lying down”); because of this property, firm stability is denoted by eight.

28. Since, then, the meditations that justify the mind which we have set forth are fittingly signified by eight, and the Lord’s commandments by ten, when these meditations are combined with the commandments in order to stir one to carry them out, ten, as it were, being multiplied by eight, eighty [Col. 1146A] is completed. If we entrust all these things to a memory not erased by forgetfulness, we record in our documents that we owe the Lord precisely eighty measures of wheat. For each of us is in oneself both steward and debtor: steward by reason, debtor by the capacities of bodily action and meditation.

Therefore, brothers, insofar as we are stewards, let us fear the Lord’s threat of removal from stewardship, because we have not preserved his goods as we ought, and let us take precautions lest we fall into reflection upon that threat. While it is permitted, let us render an account of our stewardship in repentance. And, insofar as we are debtors, let us discharge the Lord’s debt by faithfully obeying him: preserving faith in the Trinity, persevering in works of mercy, seeking through unceasing prayers the grace of the Holy Spirit to cleanse the life of the flesh from the filth of vices, and seeking only that blessedness in which there is not a year but eternity of jubilation and joy. Thus let us make excuse for the debts of bodily action which we did not pay to the Lord during the time of our past life.

Let us also make excuse for the debts of meditation, by which we ought to have cleaved solely to God and his commandments, but instead subjected it to vain, filthy, and criminal pleasures and desires: during the remaining span of life, meditating day and night on the law of the Lord (Ps. 1:2); contemplating the simplicity of God’s substance, which contains in itself every true good without diversity and therefore needs nothing; admiring his manifold goodness, by which, though needing none of them, he created all things that subsist and orders them, and lavishly grants us countless goods of body and soul; kindling in ourselves ever more the charity of brotherhood; continually considering that truth of faith, chastity, humility, sobriety, generosity, and concord are to be possessed; embracing every hour the three virtues that now remain, as the Apostle says—faith, hope, and charity (1 Cor. 13:13)—and trusting through them to attain eternity; despising the temporal corruptibility of bodies; judging prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance to be the path to incorruption; extending charity to all; discerning those dispositions which are followed by true blessedness; and contemplating equity with unchangeable [Col. 1146D] love. Let us understand that we are dealt with mercifully if, by leading the remaining life in this way, we deserve to be freed from the damnation which we earned by our former life.

For at every hour that we have lived, as we showed above and reasoned that the hundred signifies, we ought earnestly and zealously to have obeyed the Lord’s will in the duties of body and mind. But because we did not obey, we stand liable for our debts to eternal punishment, not only because we did what we ought not to have done, but also because we failed to do what we ought to have done.

29. These are the debts which we remit from the hundred measures of oil and the same number of measures of wheat, if we spend whatever remains of temporal life according to the signification of fifty and eighty that has been shown. Yet let us not despair of pardon or doubt our reward if we cannot fulfil all the observances of work, action, and meditation as we have shown to be required: let us merely strive, to the extent of our ability, to exercise ourselves in both capacities. For our Lord and Redeemer, who teaches these things and to whom we must render an account, is gracious; he will neither condemn anyone who does what he can for what he cannot do, nor take away that person’s reward.

Let us therefore, beloved, remit the debts for which we deserve punishment, and inscribe upon our bond and documents, as has been explained, that we shall render fifty and eighty to the Lord to the extent that we can, so that we may be praised by him as prudent stewards—that is, rewarded. For when the most merciful [Col. 1147B] Lord and teacher added, “And the master praised the steward of injustice because he had acted prudently,” he wished to give us secure hope of reward, lest we despair of pardon if we too act prudently according to the steward’s pattern in the wrongful management of our stewardship.

30. This steward is called the steward of injustice because of his squandering of his master’s goods; but because, for his own advantage, he remitted his master’s debtors’ debts, he is commended by that same master for his prudence. So too, although we may have been unjust in our former life, if henceforth we live prudently as stated, we shall receive from him who proposed this parable the reward of praise. Because he wishes to confer this reward upon us without measure, the good teacher wished to teach us how vigorous we ought to be in this prudence. For when he had said, “And the master praised the steward of injustice because he had acted prudently,” he added, as though giving the reason why he praised him for prudence: “Because the children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light”; thus he openly showed that we who have been children of this age must strive to surpass the children of light in this prudence if we wish to obtain praise for prudence.

31. We do not accept the interpretation by which some explain that the prudence of the children of this age—that is, the prudence they exercise in secular business—is greater than the prudence by which the children of light seek blessedness. For in that case truth would be said to have compared the reality of what does not exist with the reality of what exists, which is impossible. The children of this age are not prudent when they pursue secular affairs; rather, the vanities they desire and the damnation that follows plainly prove them foolish. But the children of light are always prudent, because they ardently long for goods and, in longing for them, do not cease to seek what they know will never fail. Temporal things, whether possessed or unpossessed, which draw their attention away from these goods, they expel from the mind’s love as being of no use whatever.

32. How then can a comparison in prudence be made from those foolish persons to these prudent ones, unless perhaps someone—something not to be thought of Truth—takes pleasure, according to customary speech, in speaking falsely? But grant that such a comparison can properly be made: could that statement be judged true if all who strive to please God are understood as children of light? What miser, however provident a seeker of temporal goods, was ever so cautious in multiplying them as Peter, Paul, and innumerable thousands of martyrs and confessors of both sexes, every nation, condition, and age, were in obtaining heavenly things? Or what children of this age so cautiously avoided the snares of the envious and hostile as these frustrated every temptation of evil spirits? Many prudent followers of this age often surrendered temporal goods, which they had amassed over a long time by their sharpest precautions, in order to escape imminent danger of death. But these children of light subjected themselves to the dangers of death itself lest they lose anything of the everlasting goods which they sought in hope. [Col. 1148B] They were therefore more prudent than the former, because by dying they preserved both incorruptible life and the unfailing goods they had sought. The others, however, after surrendering the goods for whose multiplication they were thought prudent as the price of their lives, could not retain even life itself.

33. Moreover, even if the statement were true, it would neither be appropriately placed there nor carry any weight of teaching. It remains, therefore, as we began to explain, that it is said for the purpose of showing both why the master praised him for prudence and, through that demonstration, inflaming the mind of the converted sinner toward prudence deserving the Lord’s praise. The meaning, then, is this: that master praised the steward because he had acted prudently, because, though a child of this age, he surpassed many children of light in that very prudence. For many children of light could be found who either would not or would not know how to show mercy to those debtors as he showed mercy.

“The children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light.” That is, the children of this age deserve praise only when they are found more prudent than the children of light; and this naturally happens to them whenever they are generated. Children of light, therefore, are those who, avoiding crimes throughout their whole life in order to attain eternal life, live in harmony with faith. But children of this age are called those who strive to obtain worldly gain and carnal desires by right or wrong.

34. While these pursue such things, they are in corruption and tend toward non-being; but when, by whatever means through divine grace, they recognize their damnation and repent, they are, as it were, generated and proceed toward being. For generation and corruption are and are called contrary motions. Thus, just as lovers of carnal things, while pursuing them, are in their corruption and fall into the deficiency of misery, so, when they begin to hate those same carnal things, withdraw from them, and return in repentance to the Creator, they are in their generation and are recalled toward the increase of blessedness.

[Col. 1149A] 35. Therefore, while existing in this their generation, the children of this age are more prudent than the children of light; for if they are not more prudent, they are not yet in their generation. When, therefore, they are in their generation, they are more prudent, because the latter, already secure concerning the purity of their life and therefore acting moderately, receive support from many; while the former labour to cleanse themselves from the filth which, by living wickedly, they contracted from the world as father, and by every means they can to recover the goods they had lost. Surely one is more prudent who both prudently avoids impending loss and by the same deed vigorously obtains the reward set before many, than one who, exclusively intent upon gaining the reward, eventually grasps it somehow or other.

The children of light are prudent because, preserving their purity, they tend toward the end of blessedness; nevertheless, receiving carnal support from many, they distribute and, as it were, sell the goods by which they ought to become blessed. But the children of this age are more prudent in their generation, because they both cleanse themselves as much as they can and do not cease from the goods by which they may deserve blessedness; caring to receive nothing from others, they willingly spend what they possess upon the poor and upon all whom they judge to be children of light. Therefore, if it is more blessed to give than to receive, they must be called more prudent, because no sound person will hesitate to acknowledge that it is more prudent to do what is more blessed.

The children of light are prudent because they both live well and frequently become intercessors with the Lord on behalf of others; but the children of this age are more prudent in their generation because, lest they fail of the blessedness [Col. 1149C] they desire, they seek to have many helpers. For one to reach it securely, it is safer to be helped by many than to help others.

36. In order that children of this age, established in their generation, may obtain this assistance from many, they strive to give away whatever worldly possessions they have to those whom they judge it necessary and worthy to receive them, without being recalled by any anxiety about tomorrow. Nor are they only more prudent than others: in their generation they surpass even themselves, made children of light, by growing more and more in virtue from day to day. Therefore, in order to exhort his own to this outstanding prudence, the Lord, not content with the example proposed, [Col. 1149D] added his own commands, saying: “And I say to you: Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of injustice,” and so forth.

For when he added this, he both commanded us to imitate the prudence possessed by the children of this age in their generation and, lest we be deceived, plainly showed us in it, as most compassionate teacher, its pattern. For when he said, “And I say to you: Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of injustice,” and so forth, what else does he seem to say, if the matter is rationally examined, than if he had used words more familiar to readers? “This example which I have set before you concerning the steward and the prudence of the children of this age has been set before you so that you may strive to imitate it. And so that you may not be sluggish and have every excuse removed, I say to you—that is, by my command I exhort you to imitation, and in the same exhortation instruct you how you can attain their prudence—make for yourselves friends from the mammon of injustice.”

That is: remove from yourselves the mammon of injustice and distribute it to others who need it; thus prepare them as friends—that is, helpers—for yourselves, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings. That is, when your own justice is not found sufficient for your salvation, you may nevertheless be received into the dwelling of eternal tabernacles through their intercession.

37. But lest you err in understanding his expression “mammon of injustice,” supposing it means money acquired by some unlawful means, know that friends of this kind cannot be procured by money acquired unlawfully. For it is written that to make alms from robbery is as pleasing to God as it would be to a father if he saw an executioner slaughter his son before his eyes (Ecclus. 34:24). But even money acquired lawfully is called mammon of injustice, because, while one is intent on gathering it, the mind is necessarily drawn away from the Creator’s inspiration and from his service, to which it ought always to cleave. Who of sound mind would deny that it is unjust to depart from the Creator, even for a moment, for however slight an advantage? Therefore it is fitting, salutary, and a sure redemption of time to distribute, for love of the Creator, whatever could separate us even for an hour from his sight and desire, to poor children of light. Indeed, the principle of justice, even by the contrary argument, requires that for love of God one despise everything for which the sinner’s conscience remembers having set him aside even for an hour.

[Col. 1150C] 38. Therefore the good Physician, knowing that a medicine contrary to the disease is effective for healing, said: “Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of injustice.” But whom? Certainly children of light above all; but he did not wish to specify them, because he wishes his own, according to the teaching of the Apostle Paul, to share their goods with all, especially with those of the household of faith (Gal. 6:10).

The friends here may also be understood to mean the very fruits of almsgiving. These indeed will be found friends to their makers at that time, because they will pray to God for them, that he may not suffer them to be separated from the outer dwellings. This is suggested to us by that command of the Holy Spirit: “Give alms, and it itself prays to the Lord for you” (Luke 11:41). These friends will truly receive their friends, when they fail, into [Col. 1150D] eternal tabernacles, because, though on account of preceding sins they should rightly be subjected to damnation, these friends will become their advocates and the cause of their salvation.

They are said to receive them into eternal tabernacles because they are the reason why they will possess the blessed life. This life is signified by tabernacles because it has many dwelling places and whoever enters it, like soldiers in tents after the labour of daily military service, is refreshed without end from every labour of temporal life. May he who taught these matters which we have treated as best we could, and proposed them for imitation—Jesus Christ our Lord—bring us into it and refresh us from the miserable labour of this way; to him belongs not only glory, but he also glorifies beyond all comparison in merits those who obey him, unto ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1151]

## B. DIPLOMAS OF ODO

### I. He confirms donations made to the abbey of Jette, now Diligem, of the Premonstratensian order. (A.D. 1106.)

[Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica*, II, 958, from the manuscripts of the archive of the chapter of Anderlecht.]

[Col. 1151A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, ODO, by God’s grace bishop of Cambrai, offer peace and salvation to all Christ’s faithful.

Let it be known to all Christ’s faithful, both future and present, that in our days, at our prompting and exhortation and that of Abbot Walthelm, Everard Rudolph of Tournai, in memory of the soul of his wife Helwilde, by the consent and conveyance of his son Walter, transferred eighteen bonniers of land, with the dwelling-sites belonging to them, and with a meadow of three parts of a *jugerum*, free from every advocacy, to the church of Jette and to Abbot Walthelm and his successors, without anyone’s objection.

Whatever rights Walter the priest and a certain devout widow, Goda, possessed in this benefice, they had previously transferred and relinquished by the rod to the aforesaid Everard Rudolph before their men.

Whoever presumes to violate any of these provisions shall be subject to curse and excommunication. May peace and blessing therefore protect those who preserve them; but may the vengeance of eternal fire strike the destroyers together with the devil.

And in order that this may remain ratified and unshaken, we strengthen this charter by the authority of our seal, with the testimony subscribed below.

Done at Cambrai in the year 1106, the first year of our episcopate.

### II. Privilege for the church of the canons of St John the Baptist in the city of Valenciennes, now an abbey of regulars of the Order of St Augustine. (A.D. 1107.)

[Miraeus, as above, p. 675.]

ODOARDUS, bishop of Cambrai . . . . I willingly resolved to grant the pious request of the canons of the church of St John the Baptist, in which, by God’s authorship, they serve at Valenciennes. They requested from me that the altar of Estruem—especially their fellow canon Tiegerus, who had held that altar—should be transferred free from a personal incumbent to the aforesaid church; and they obtained this.

The mark of Wedric, abbot of the monastery of Hautmont. The mark of Lambert of Crespin. The mark of Alard, abbot of Celles. The mark of Reiner, abbot of Laetitiae. The mark of Ivo, dean.

Done in the year 1107, in the fourth year of my episcopate, in the second indiction.

### III. He confirms to the Abbey of St Peter of the Benedictine Order near Ghent the altars situated in his diocese. (A.D. 1108.)

[Miraeus, as above, vol. III, p. 665, from the archives of the Abbey of St Peter.]

[Col. 1152B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, ODO, by God’s mercy bishop of Cambrai, offer to all Christians salvation and everlasting glory.

If our Saviour Christ Jesus founded the holy Church, as he says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church,” then, following his example, we ought to labour greatly that it may grow through us and always increase toward what is better.

Accordingly, having heard the petitions of Lord Abbot Siger, [Col. 1152C] Prior Gozelin, Lord Provost Ansbold, and the other venerable brothers living the monastic life in the monastery of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, at Blandinium, for the salvation of ourselves and our predecessors we grant that henceforth they may possess forever, canonically and free of personal incumbents, their altars which they had held through such incumbents:

Namely, the altar of Merlebeek [Note: [Col. 1151C] Merlebeek, today a parish of the Diocese of Mechelen, [Col. 1151D] on the river Scheldt, under the deanery of Oirdeghem; a lordship of the Triest family of Ghent.], with its appurtenances; Rothen [Note: [Col. 1151D] Rothen, otherwise Schelde-Rode; today the marquisate of Rhodes, under the deanery of Oirdeghem in the Diocese of Mechelen; formerly an appurtenance of the parish of Merlebeek, but now a separate parish.]; and Bottelaer [Note: [Col. 1151D] Bottelaer, a village under the deanery of Oirdeghem, celebrated for devotion to Blessed Mother Anne, where the Calced Carmelites had also established a convent from the year 1607.]. The altar of Holthem [Note: [Col. 1151D] Holthem, now Letter-Hauthem, distinguished from another neighbouring village called St Lieven’s-Hauthem, [Col. 1152C] under the same deanery.]. The altar of Materna [Note: [Col. 1152D] Materna, commonly Maetere, near Oudenaarde, under the deanery of Ronse in the Diocese of Mechelen. For the acquisition of this altar, see Miraeus, diploma p. 944.]. The altar of Bostut [Note: [Col. 1152D] Bostut, now Bosta, commonly Roobort, a parish of the same diocese under the deanery of Ronse.], with its appurtenance Rosbecca [Note: [Col. 1152D] Roosbeeck, now an appurtenance of the said parish of Bost. There are elsewhere several parishes of the same name, and especially two in this diocese: one under the deanery of Tienen, the other formerly called Rebecque, under the deanery of St Peter at Leeuw.]. The altar of [Col. 1153A] Hillinghem [Note: [Col. 1153C] Hilleghem, a parish of the same diocese under the deanery of Oirdeghem.]. The altar of Dulciac [Note: [Col. 1153C] Dulciacum, commonly Doucy, a parish of Hainaut in the Diocese of Cambrai; Emperor Otto I confirmed it to this abbey in 966, according to Miraeus, vol. I, p. 261.], with its appurtenance of Nigella [Note: [Col. 1153C] Nigella, commonly Noielles, a parish of the Diocese of [Col. 1153D] Cambrai, formerly an appurtenance of the preceding one.].

This is on condition that the abbot or prior of the monastery observe the synods of the bishop of Cambrai and pay annually, without any objection, episcopal dues to the bishop or his officials; while the priests of those altars shall receive the care of souls from the hand of the bishop or one of his officials, and shall not refuse to observe the chapters of their archdeacon or dean.

If anyone therefore attempts to oppose this our decree, by the authority of God, of the same Apostle Peter, and of ourselves, we separate that person from the body of holy Mother Church. And lest it be annulled at any future time on any pretext, we confirm it with the impression of our seal.

[Col. 1153B] Suitable witnesses are summoned to confirm the authority of this privilege.

The mark of Fulgentius, abbot of Affligem. The mark of Tancred, abbot of Ename. The mark of Emellard, abbot of Geraardsbergen. The mark of Rudolph, archdeacon. The mark of Theodoric, archdeacon. The mark of Ansel, archdeacon. The mark of Everard, archdeacon. The mark of Gonfrid, canon of St Mary. The mark of Gerard, likewise canon. The mark of Lambert, canon. The mark of Mazelin, canon. The mark of Segard, dean [Note: [Col. 1153D] This Dean Segard was omitted, under the year 1108, from the succession of deans of the metropolitan church of Cambrai by the Benedictine Fathers who authored the *New Gallia Christiana*. Note also that the dean of this church subscribed only after the archdeacons, who consequently held the place of precedence, as may be seen from another diploma of the same year in Miraeus, p. 82.]. The mark of Libert, subdean. [Col. 1153C] The mark of Albero, canon of Ronse.

This was done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1108, in the first indiction and the third year of the aforesaid bishop. Salvation, honour, and glory to all Christians.

### IV. Confirmation of the collegiate church of the canons of Teneraemonda, founded by Remigius or Ringot the Bald, lord of Teneraemonda, and his wife Adelwide. (A.D. 1108.)

[Miraeus, as above, vol. I, p. 82.]

[Col. 1154A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen.
