Odardus [Note: [Col. 1153D] Odardus, or Odo, formerly first abbot of the monastery of St. Martin at Tournai, became bishop of Cambrai and died in 1113.], by the grace of God bishop of Cambrai, for the salvation of my soul and of my predecessors, out of great devotion to the Church, at the request of Lady Adelwidis, the venerable wife of Remigius [Note: [Col. 1153D] Remigius, otherwise Ringotus, surnamed the Bald, founder of the college of canons and church of Dendermonde, died in 1106, as is recorded in the so-called Obituary Book of that church. Two years later Adelwidis, formerly Remigius’s wife and now his widow, obtained from Bishop Odardus this confirmation of the foundation. [Col. 1154C] After Ringotus, William, advocate of Arras and lord of Béthune and Dendermonde, together with his wife Matilda, bestowed various tithes on the church of Dendermonde. At the request of the widow Matilda, John of Béthune, bishop of Cambrai and brother of William the advocate, confirmed that donation, as is clear from a charter issued in 1217. The same Matilda [Col. 1154D] converted three chaplaincies into as many canonries after her husband’s death. A charter concerning this, issued in 1215, survives. Not long afterward other chaplaincies founded by Matilda were likewise converted into canonries by Robert, apparently her son; and thus the number of prebends was increased to twelve. The right, patronage, and presentation of all these belongs to the count of Flanders as lord of Dendermonde. In 1632, under the most illustrious and most reverend Lord Antonius Triest, bishop of Ghent, with the consent of the chapter and of the king himself, the revenues of all the prebends were united or consolidated. For more, see Lindanus, *Teneramunda*, book I, chapter 6, and book II, chapter 2. See the genealogy of the lords of Dendermonde in the *Belgian Chronicle* under the year 1248.], lady of Dendermonde, and at the most earnest petition of the canons of Dendermonde, emancipates them from every personal dependency and every lay molestation by the authority of God and of ourselves, and grants canonical liberty to the canons of that church. We grant that the dean, who has charge of the canons serving God there, shall have power to excommunicate offenders against the Church. Yet the same church shall, in remembrance of its liberty, pay three solidi of Dendermonde currency annually to the dean of Brussels for our use.

I have freely and canonically granted to the church of Dendermonde the two church altars of Opwijk and Lebbeke, namely those of the Holy Trinity and of St. Christian, solely to be retained for the fabric or ornaments of the church. Subject to the reservation of our episcopal revenues, priests shall be appointed to them by the dean and canons, and they shall be presented to us or to our ministers to receive pastoral care.

We also freely and wholly confirm to the aforesaid church its freeholds at Winsia [Col. 1154C], in fields, woods, and meadows; at Morsel, in fields, woods, and meadows; and at Gheverghem, in fields, woods, and meadows, with all jurisdiction over land and wood, to benefit solely the uses of the canons.

Moreover, whatever has been offered, or may hereafter happen to be offered, by anyone to the aforesaid church in lands, woods, meadows, or other possessions, we decree shall in every way remain and be preserved for the canons’ use. Lest these goods be handed over to oblivion, we mark them with the image of our seal; and lest anyone violate them, we forbid it, under anathema, by the authority of God and our own. The witnesses of this confirmation are:

The sign of Rudolph, archdeacon. The sign of Anselm, archdeacon. The sign of Everard, archdeacon. The sign of Sigard, dean. The sign of Lambert, subdean. The sign of Lambert, canon of St. Mary. The sign of Gerard, canon. The sign of Marcellin, canon.

This was enacted in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1155B] 1108, in the first indiction, in the third year of the aforesaid bishop.

Health and glory to all Christians.

## V. He grants to the abbey of Cortemberghe, of nuns of the Order of St. Benedict near Brussels, the altars of Cartembergh, Noneghem, and Quaederebbe. (1110.)

[Miraeus, as above, vol. II, p. 969, from the manuscript archive of the chapter of Anderlecht.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: Odo, by God’s grace bishop of Cambrai, to all Christ’s faithful, greeting in Christ Jesus.

Let those now living and those to come know that, while I was examining the places in my diocese to learn which were under religious observance and which otherwise, I found at Cortemberghe a place, through the assent and assistance of Duke Godfrey and through the service of the advocates Arnulf and Golterius, already in part adorned by the handmaids of God. At the request of my archdeacons and the faithful, I arranged for its enlargement: namely, by my authority I made that altar free from the annual episcopal provisions due from it, and remitted those dues for the use of those serving God, his holy mother Mary, and St. Amand there.

I also granted to the aforesaid church the altar of Quatrebbe (otherwise Querps) and the altar of Nethengem (otherwise Nosseghem), free of personal incumbents; provided, however, that the episcopal dues shall each year be paid from them to the bishop and his ministers.

I further ordained that the priests of these altars and of the altar mentioned above shall receive the care of souls from the bishop’s hand, observe the chapters of the archdeacon and dean, and that the abbess of that place shall come to the synod at Cambrai on the feast of Luke the Evangelist.

If anyone should attempt to contravene this privilege of our ordinance, let him be guilty and excluded from the sight of the Lord until he comes to repentance.

And, that this may remain fixed, I confirmed it by the testimony of those subscribing below.

The sign of Lord Fulgentius, abbot of Affligem. The sign of Lord Gislebert, abbot of Eham. The sign of Radulf, archdeacon of these same altars. [Col. 1156A] The sign of Lord Gualtelm, abbot of Jette. The sign of Lord Martin, abbot of Bornhem. The sign of Evrard, archdeacon. The sign of Gualbert of Isle. The signs of Bernard, Gerard, and Mozelin, canons. The sign of Gislebert. The sign of Thitbold of Ronnac.

Enacted in the year of the Incarnate Word 1110, the fifth year of my episcopate, the third indiction, the twenty-eighth epact.

## VI. He grants various free churches and other benefices to the abbey of Jette or Diligem, Order of Prémontré. (1112.)

[Miraeus, as above, II, 959.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, Odo, by God’s grace bishop of Cambrai.

On the eighth day before the Kalends of October, with God’s approval, I dedicated to the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ and in honor of the Virgin St. Mary the cell situated in the village called Jette; I blessed its assigned precinct, and confirmed it as free, so that it should look to no lord of any inheritance except the see of the church of Cambrai. And if the land is placed under ban because of anyone’s fault, this church shall sing, all others under ban being excluded.

Since we ought to rejoice in the good will of all members of our household who are most ready to promote the exaltation of holy Church, it is also fitting that, if they ask anything of us, we should not refuse, so that, led by our example, they may always advance toward life.

Therefore I judged not to be rejected the petition of my son Abbot Galtelm, whom I consecrated with my own hands, asking that I endow with liberty the parish church of Jette with its dependency of Ganshoren, and the church of Mosen and the church of Humbeek.

Judging this petition good and accordingly hearing it in a fatherly manner, I free the aforesaid churches from every exaction and from provisions due, and deliver them to the brethren in the church of St. Mary at Jette.

Further, I graciously grant that they may have free election in establishing an abbot; but the person elected shall be presented to the bishop of Cambrai, that he may be consecrated by him without any objection.

Nor shall the abbot himself be compelled to go to the synod unless he has been summoned by the bishop’s sealed letters.

For the use of the brethren serving God in this place and observing the Rule of blessed Augustine, Onulf of Wolvertem, a free man who feared God and founder of the church, for the redemption of his own soul and the souls of his mother Ava, his wife Remudis, his parents, and his children William, Walter, Lambert, Siger, Godescalc, Eustace, Arnold, and his noble daughter Ava, gave to those serving God and his holy Mother in the aforesaid church fourteen bonniers of his freehold; a brewery with its appurtenances, which pays annually ten [units unstated]; six modii of oats by the Brussels measure; the freehold of the mill at Jette; the tithe he held at Wolvertem; and the freehold of the tithe of Melbroek.

After the death of his son Lambert, he gave nine bonniers of land to the same church; for the soul of his son William, he granted six bonniers of land; for the soul of Siger, his brothers and their sister Lady Ava gave nine bonniers of land and, of the tithe of the whole village, which is divided into nine sheaves, two sheaves; they also added a third part of the alder-grove.

Eustace gave six solidi at Rochem (commonly Rossem, a dependency of Wolvertem); Lady Ava and her brother gave to the church a freehold of twelve bonniers beside the village called Selloca.

Two free men, Walter and Arnold, sons of Onulf, attended our dedication rite [Col. 1157B], together with their sister Lady Ava. All of them renewed the gift of the aforesaid benefices and caused them to be lawfully assigned to the altar in my presence.

That this may remain valid for all time and be violated by no malicious presumptuous person, I have publicly excommunicated all destroyers of these benefices, separating them from the bosom of mother Church, unless they come to amendment and satisfaction.

This was enacted in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1112, the seventh year of our episcopate, while Henry V was emperor.

The witnesses of this confirmation are:

The sign of John, archdeacon. The sign of Ancel, archdeacon. The sign of Rudolph, archdeacon. [Col. 1157C] The sign of Theodoric, archdeacon. The sign of Everald, archdeacon. The sign of Erlebald, archdeacon. The sign of Adam, abbot. The sign of Rainer, abbot. The sign of Geoffrey, abbot. The sign of Ernald, abbot. The signs of Mastellin and Livin, chaplains. The sign of Robert, cantor. Gerard. Herevard. I, Gerinbald, have read and recognized [this document].

## VII. Privilege for the church of Nivelles. (1112.)

[Miraeus, as above, I, 676.]

Odo, by God’s grace bishop of Cambrai, to all children of the holy Church of God, forever.

Assenting to the pious petition of Richeta, abbess of the church of St. Gertrude at Nivelles, and also hearing the prayers of the ladies of the monastery and of the canons, I deliver to the Church, wholly free henceforth from personal incumbents, the altars which they had hitherto held through persons in the bishopric of Cambrai.

These are the altars: the altar of Ittre; the altar of Rosbeek, with its dependency of Hainieres; the altar of Meerbeek; [Col. 1158A] the altar of Wambeek, with its dependency Nath’; the altar of Lombek; the altar of Goy; the altar of Altres; the altar of Guislines; and the altar of Luvroila. The witnesses of this grant of ours are:

The sign of Rudolf, archdeacon. The sign of Erlebard, provost. The sign of Erlebard, dean. The sign of Alexander, dean. The sign of Segard, dean. The sign of Machelin, dean. The sign of Walter, abbot of Lobbes. The sign of Guidric, abbot of Hautmont. Fulgentius, abbot of Affligem.

Enacted in the year 1112, in the fifth indiction, the seventh year of the aforesaid bishop. [Col. 1158B]

## VIII. He approves the foundation and endowment of the abbey of Bornhem, made about the year 1100 by Wenemar, castellan of Ghent. (1112.)

[Miraeus, as above, I, 371.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, Odo, by God’s grace bishop of Cambrai, greet all Christ’s faithful.

I wish it to be known to future generations as well as those present that Wenemar [Note: [Col. 1157D] Wenemar: see the foundation charters made by Wenemar, *Diplomata Belgica*, book I, chapters 45 and 46.], castellan of Ghent, providing and taking thought for himself, for the remedy of his soul and of all his faithful departed, scatters earthly things that he may reap heavenly ones.

He gave to the church of Bornhem, of which he himself is founder, land lying in the parish of Bucholt: twenty measures belonging to Everbold the priest; fourteen *admoti* [a term of uncertain meaning]; one half of Fredenod’s holding; one and a half measures belonging to Boltro; and one third of the freehold called Mulnemerholt in the parish of Steens, free from every lay exaction. [Note: [Col. 1157D] Bornhem, a town in the region of Waas, where there formerly stood [Col. 1158D] an abbey of regular canons, later converted into a Benedictine monastery under the abbey of Affligem. See *Diplomata Belgica*, book I, chapters 49 and 50.] This is on the condition that, if any matter of no use arises there which deserves adjudication, Wenemar himself or his heir, with the brethren as their fellow-brother and not with lordship or authority, shall return for discussion of that matter by common and charitable counsel; and at his request, whoever among future generations dares, beyond these provisions, to exercise any lordship or exaction shall be anathematized.

I, Bishop Odo, have also authenticated this for that church and confirmed it by the impress of my seal. I have added that, if anyone plunders the goods of that church or breaks its peace and ordinances, he shall be struck with the sword of anathema. If anyone should presume to enter such a church, the church shall cease from the Lord’s office until he departs. And if the whole district is placed under ban because of some persons’ offences, the church, secular laypeople being excluded, shall not cease but shall sing in silence. [Col. 1159A] I confirmed this by the testimony of those subscribing below.

The sign of Odo the bishop himself. The sign of Radulf, archdeacon of the same altar. The sign of Ansel, archdeacon. The sign of Theodoric, archdeacon. The sign of Everard, archdeacon. The sign of Erlebold, provost. The sign of Elebod, dean.

Signs of abbots:

The sign of Gilbert of Eham. The sign of Snellard of Geraardsbergen. The sign of Ambold of Ghent. [Col. 1160A] The sign of Rainer of the Holy Sepulchre. The sign of Geoffrey of Nieuwkasteel. The sign of Fregdo, dean of the same altar. The sign of Segard of Helles. The sign of Ribert, dean. The sign of Alexander, dean of Halle. The signs of Bernard of Waas and his brother Fulcard. The sign of Conrad, dean of Ghent. The signs of Meinard, Tangrad, and Gomar.

Enacted at Cambrai in synod, on the third Ides of March, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1112, the seventh year of my episcopate.

[Col. 1159]

# APPENDIX TO BLESSED ODO: EXCERPTS

From the book of Godfrey, master of Rheims, entitled *The Dream concerning Odo of Orléans*. (Mabillon, *Annals*, V, Appendix, p. 651.)

[Col. 1159B]

The sinking sun had hidden its swift course in the waters

[lacuna]

Odo appeared, great glory among my friends [lacuna]

He praises his gifts at length, and then continues thus concerning his lineage:

His race, descending from ancestors, and the line of lofty blood,  
Adorns him, wholly derived from freeborn men.

The waters of golden Loire cannot keep silence  
About their deeds, their honors, peace, and fearful wars.

Against him they shattered camps in countless array,  
Wherever such camps had dared harm his own men.

Against him they laid hostile bands low in arms;  
Against him they tamed untamed men.

Born from these forefathers and these ancestors, Odo  
Was rightly to be regarded as close to heaven.

But although the most illustrious rank of lineage should fail,  
And such great honor contribute nothing to praise,

The utterly clear stream of his deep intellect suffices,  
And the fact that Minerva has wholly poured herself into him.

Indeed, his verses are so composed for me  
As though someone drew strings with a skillful thumb:

There is nothing there to burden the heart or weigh down the ear,  
Nothing that could rightly be called superfluous work. [Col. 1160B]

[lacuna]

After praising his verses more fully, he tells how Odo appeared to him in a dream:

At last, having watched me for a short while, he sat down,  
Touched my breast with a silent hand,

And said: “Your Odo has entered your dwelling and sits  
Beside your bed, my Godfrey;

Yet I came neither borne on horse, nor by sail over blue waters,  
Nor on foot, nor in frail wheeled vehicles.

Through empty air, my body suspended upon wings,  
A light breeze bore me from Orléans to Rheims.” [lacuna]

He says much about his desire to see him, impelled by which he came in this manner.

“Thus, trusting myself to the winds for your sake, my friend,  
I did not fear to travel suspended by uncertain paths.

And because my little works are always dear to you  
And are not to be cast aside at your discretion,

I have brought the little book that sings of the Trojan wars,  
Which you so often have me recite to you.” [lacuna]

He asks him to recite the verses he had composed on the Trojan War.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1100: WALTER, BISHOP OF CHALON-SUR-SAÔNE

[Col. 1159]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IV, p. 887.)

[Col. 1159D]

Walter—also called Gualterius or Walterus—after a long vacancy in the episcopal see, was at last elected bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône in 1080 by the wishes and consent of all. Since the charter of his election is valuable both because of its antiquity and because it contains the highest praises of Walter, we judged it worthwhile to include it among the documents. Here we shall relate certain matters most pertinent to our present purpose.

The canons give the grounds of his election as follows: “He is, as is readily apparent, born of a line of noble stock; he is highly learned not only in the knowledge of sacred literature but also in the practical discipline of secular laws; distinguished by fasts, vigils, prayers, and every work of mercy; illustrious for the utmost probity of his moral conduct; most beautifully crowned with discretion, the mother of all virtues; possessed also of most eloquent speech and exceptional fluency. So far as the frailty of human condition allows, he remains conspicuous for every goodness.”

In the same year he attended the synod of Meaux and subscribed the letters by which Count Geoffrey of Maurienne and his wife Beatrice confirmed to the church of St. Denis of Nogy the gift which they had made to the Cluniacs. In 1081, A[—], bishop of Autun; R[—], bishop of Langres; G[—], bishop of Chalon; and L[—], bishop of Mâcon, wrote to all bishops, abbots, and others of the province of Tours. By these letters they summoned to Lyons the count of Anjou, the bishop, and the monks of Marmoutier for trial; if they refused obedience, they suspended the bishop from episcopal and priestly office, and excommunicated Count Fulk and the monks by the authority of St. Peter and of Lord Hugh, primate and legate of the Roman Church.

He wrote this charter in 1087, cited by Pérard: “I, Walter, humble bishop of the holy church of Chalon, have resolved to restore the church of St. Mary situated in the suburb of Chalon, and I restore and grant it to St. Benignus of Dijon and to Abbot Jarenton, with all that pertains to it, to possess in perpetual right, under the reverence and honor of the church of Chalon and of my successors. The sign of Gauslen, dean; of Landric, provost and archdeacon; of Rudolf, treasurer,” etc.

Together with the archbishop of Lyons, he is named as arbiter of the dispute between the canons of the cathedral church of St. Vincent and the regulars of St. Peter at Mâcon concerning burial rights. Perry reports that in 1093, through the efforts of Walter, the archbishop of Aix, and the bishop of Grenoble, the bishop and count of Maguelonne were restored to concord. In 1094 he attended the council of Autun, at which Philip, king of the Franks, was cut off from communion on account of Bertrada.

Godfrey of Vergy, lord of Donzy, about to go to the Holy Land with Godfrey of Bouillon, needed money and was unable to obtain it from his uncle. Through Walter’s mediation, he sold to Bishop Walter and the chapter—whose goods were then held in common—the half share of the county of Chalon which he possessed, for a price of one hundred ounces of pure gold, the greater part of which they had taken from the altar of St. Vincent. We have included the charter among the documents. It appears to have been issued in 1096.

He attended the dedication of the church of St. Stephen at Nevers in 1097 and the consecration of Bérard, archdeacon of Lyons, as bishop of Mâcon; and he was sent to obtain the consent of Jarenton, abbot of St. Benignus, to the election of Hugh, a monk, as abbot of Flavigny.

He contributed greatly to the foundation and expansion of the Cistercian Order. For when St. Robert had departed Molesme with his followers to seek a place where they could observe the Rule of St. Benedict to its strictest points, they finally found Cîteaux, where they resolved to establish themselves. “By the will of the bishop of Chalon and with the consent of him whose land it was, they began to construct a monastery” there in 1098. When it was completed, Robert was elected abbot by the common vote of all the brethren and received the pastoral staff from the same bishop, according to the customary practice of that time.

But the holy man did not bear it long. The monks of Molesme, grievously enduring their father’s absence, begged Pope Urban with most urgent prayers that he be restored to them. For their sake the pope wrote most weighty letters to Hugh, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See. By force of these letters, at a council held at Pierre-Scize, at which Walter was present, it was decreed by unanimous consent in 1099 that Robert should be sent back to Molesme, on this condition: “that before Robert returned there, he should come to Chalon and receive absolution at the hand of the bishop to whom, according to the custom of other abbots, he had made profession; that he should surrender the staff and care of the abbey, and should release the monks of the New Monastery”—for Cîteaux was at first so called—“from the obedience due to him.”

All these things were carried out; indeed Alberic was blessed as abbot, as appears from Walter’s letters to the bishop of Langres. Walter was also the first to request from the Roman Church a privilege confirming Cîteaux, in these words:

“To the venerable Father Pope Paschal, Walter, bishop of the church of Chalon, greeting and due submission … We humbly ask that you approve what has been done concerning those brethren who, out of desire for a stricter life, withdrew from the church of Molesme on the counsel of holy men, and whom divine mercy placed in our bishopric. The bearers of this present letter, sent by them, stand before you. We ask that, by the privilege of your authority, you deign to strengthen the arrangement that that place may remain forever a free abbey, saving nevertheless the canonical reverence due to our person and to our successors. Moreover, the abbot whom we have appointed in that place and the other brethren with all their strength entreat this confirmation from your mercy as a safeguard for their peace.”

In 1100, summoned to the synod of Valence, at which the case of Norgaud, bishop of Autun, accused of many crimes, was to be examined, he refused to attend, allegedly prevented by his metropolitan, Hugh of Lyons. When the matter was referred to the council of Poitiers, he accompanied Norgaud thither, having been sent by the archbishop of Lyons to defend the accused’s cause; but their efforts were fruitless, and they could not prevent his condemnation. In the same year he attended the synod of Anse.

In his presence, and with Hugh of Lyons, in 1103 the same Norgaud confirmed to Lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny, for the monastery of Blessed Mary Magdalene of Quadrella, the churches of that district concerning which Leotbald of Dijon was bringing suit. In 1107, by written charter, he declares that Hugh and Saticher, together with Airard, brothers of Marchia, had bestowed many things at Aluze upon the monastery of St. Marcellus. Jothald, dean, Gauceran, cantor, and others subscribed. In the same year he is named with the metropolitan of Lyons as arbiter of the dispute between the canons of St. Vincent and of the cathedral church of St. Peter at Mâcon.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1111, Walter, bishop of Chalon, and Jarento, abbot of Dijon, entered into the following association: “Whenever notice of the death of a canon of Chalon comes to Dijon, or of a monk of Dijon to Chalon, the full office of the dead—that is, vigil and Mass—shall immediately be performed for him, and he shall have a prebend that day … Furthermore, in the week after Mid-Lent Sunday, a general office and Mass shall be performed by each community for the other. The aforesaid Bishop W. further granted to Abbot J. and all his successors one full daily canonical prebend in the church of St. Vincent; the same abbot granted this to a monk of Dijon residing at St. Mary’s, so that this monk might perform a week’s service at St. Vincent’s, and so that, on account of this alms, the church of Dijon might render service to the church of Chalon, both bodily and spiritually, according to its ability.”

With Bernard’s arrival at the New Monastery and the example of his virtues, the Cistercian community increased so greatly that Abbot Stephen considered founding a new monastery. Walter, the diocesan bishop, knowing of the plan, explored his diocese with him. They found a wooded place near the river Grosne, and there a monastery was founded in 1113. Its church, in honor of Mary, Mother of God, was dedicated by Walter on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the presence of Joceran, bishop of Langres, and Counts Gauderic and William. The new monastery was given the name La Ferté, because it was then that the Cistercian institution first began to be made firm and stable.

He wrote this charter for the benefit of St. Marcellus in the following year: “I, Walter, by God’s grace bishop of Chalon, desiring forgiveness of my sins and the mercy of divine compassion, grant to God … [lacuna] to the place of St. Marcellus at Chalon the church of Boens, with all that pertains to it … This was done in the city of Chalon, in the chapter of the canons, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the year from the Incarnation 1114.”

He attended the synod of Tournus in 1115. In 1117 he granted the canons of St. Stephen at Dijon, as Dom Fiot affirms, the church of St. Martin, situated in the place commonly called Arcs. Pérard also reports his charter, though without a date, by which he confirms and grants anew to the same canons the church of Bussy, which his predecessors Acard and Roclen had already granted, with its tithes, offerings, and all its appurtenances, while reserving to himself synodal service, etc. He does not appear to have died before 1120 or the end of 1121, since Jotsald, who succeeded him in the episcopate, was still dean according to a letter of Callixtus II.

[Col. 1163]

# FORM OF WALTER’S ELECTION

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, IV, Documents, p. 231.)

[Col. 1163C]

The author of our redemption, the Only-Begotten of the most high Father, coeternal and consubstantial with him before the beginning of all time, when, with the fullness of time now come, he descended from the heights of heaven and assumed man on earth, preserving in the humanity assumed the majesty of divinity—after finally fulfilling all that the most noble heralds of the ancient law had truthfully foretold in prophetic utterances concerning the humanity he would assume in time—the condition of the most holy Church immediately began to be renewed throughout the world by the most salutary teaching of the apostles, indeed by the greatness of the powers and excellence of the signs which the grace of divine dispensation worked through them in a wonderful manner.

Their sound, according to the prediction of the prophesying king, has gone out into all the earth; and the whole assembly of Christ’s faithful professes that their words have reached the ends of the world. The distinguished rulers of the Church immediately followed these highest and chosen senators of the heavenly court. Because they led the right way to the palace of the heavenly King, they were deservedly considered worthy to be marked with the title of bishops.

They labored to adorn by word and example the Church entrusted to them by the Shepherd of the fathers, so that, though raised to the venerable summit of the highest pontificate, they chose rather to benefit those subject to them than to rule them, governing them by the most equitable discipline and measured moderation. But whenever zeal for righteousness required them to be stirred to any degree of strictness against the depraved conduct of their subjects, the virtue of gentleness was so preserved in their minds amid the terror of severity that the gentleness of discretion tempered anger, while the same zeal of discretion kindled that gentleness lest it perhaps dissolve into laxity.

Desiring above all to imitate these fathers of such venerable life, admirable guardians of heavenly discipline, we humble children of the most holy mother Church of Chalon, especially because the episcopal chair of our see has long been bereft of its own shepherd and now endures many and innumerable disgraceful assaults from worldly powers, have by common consent and unanimous vote chosen a certain former cleric and archdeacon of the same Church, Walter by name, to govern, Christ the Lord so ordaining, at the summit of the episcopate of the aforesaid see. To his jurisdiction and the yoke of his governance we entrust ourselves and our place to be ordered, according to the canons and the inviolable privilege of the whole Church.

For, as is readily apparent, he is born of a line of noble stock; highly learned not only in sacred letters but also in the practical discipline of secular laws; distinguished by fasts, vigils, prayers, and every work of mercy; illustrious for the utmost integrity of his moral conduct; most beautifully crowned with discretion, mother of all virtues; possessed of most eloquent speech and exceptional fluency; and, so far as the frailty of human condition allows, conspicuous for every goodness.

Therefore, because of such numerous and great gifts of heaven bestowed on him by a heavenly gift, with the grace of the Holy Spirit cooperating, he is chosen to the summit of pastoral office not only by us, the children of the aforesaid Church, but also by the people of every rank living within and outside the walls of our city, followed by an innumerable multitude from the surrounding districts, of different sexes and ages. All alike, from the innermost affection of their hearts and with many earnest prayers, ask that this man elected by us may, Jesus the Lord consenting, be raised by the episcopal mitre to the see of Chalon.

Very many illustrious and most noble rulers of God’s churches are likewise lawful supporters of this election of ours: namely, Lord Gibuinus, eminent archbishop of the most holy see of Lyons; and Lord Agano, venerable bishop of the church of Autun, together with the reverend communities entrusted, by the grace of Christ the Lord providing, to the governance of each. The religious bishop Lord Landric of the church of Mâcon, with the venerable assembly of that clergy, also assents and gives manifold support, hoping in God’s mercy that assistance may come to himself and his church through the celebration of so great an ordination.

To these distinguished bishops already named are joined illustrious fathers of monasteries, favoring this election with all their prayers: among them stand out Lord Hugh, truly most renowned abbot of the sacred monastery of Cluny; Lord Peter, venerable ruler of Tournus; and Lord Raynard, presiding over the abbey of St. Peter in the city of Chalon, together with the reverend congregations of fathers from both places, serving in Christ’s name under the discipline of monastic training. All these, without doubt, are fully qualified promoters and lawful confirmers of the whole election.

The sign of Gauslen, dean of our mother church. The sign of Almaric, dean of Langres. The sign of Gotselm, archdeacon. The sign of Hugh of Port. The sign of Engilbert. The sign of Geoffrey. The sign of Landric, archpriest. The sign of William. The sign of Peter. The sign of Charles. The sign of Bernard. The sign of Robert. The sign of Lambert. The sign of Hugh. The sign of Letard, archpriest. The sign of W. of Vernes and his mother Adelaide. The sign of Walter of Neblensis. The sign of Dalmasius of Gigny. The sign of Bernard of Port. The sign of Gotseran and his brother Idmar. The sign of Duran, archpriest. The sign of Ademar. The sign of Robert. The sign of Jotsald.

This ecclesiastical and general election was held in the year 1080 from the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten Word, while, by divine appointment, the most eminent Pope Gregory presided over the Roman See; while the most noble of kings, Philip, wielded the scepter of the kingdom; and while the consulship of the city of Chalon remained at that time without a temporal prince.

[Col. 1165]

# WALTER’S CHARTERS

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, IV, Documents, p. 231 ff.)

## I. Charter of Walter, bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône, concerning the acquisition from Count Saveric of Chalon of a share of the county of Chalon. (About 1096.)

[Col. 1165D]

In the name of the supreme and indivisible Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen. Since human minds sometimes, through the darkness of their error, lose the marks of truth; since time commonly erases from human memory the sayings and deeds of men; and since nothing unwritten remains known for long: therefore I, Walter, bishop of the Church of Chalon, have taken care [or, have caused] to commit to writing and remembrance the agreement which I and our canons made with Savaric, count of Chalon.

Let it therefore be known to all, present and future, that when Geoffrey of Dunziac wished to set out for Jerusalem [Col. 1166D], he who possessed one half of the county of Chalon, which he had divided with Guy of Tyhaera [otherwise, Thies], resolved to sell his share of the aforesaid county [Latin: *comitatus supradicti*; otherwise, *supradicto*] to his uncle, Lord Savaric. Savaric accordingly came to us with his wife, asking that we should receive from him in pledge the portion of that half which he was purchasing, and assist him with the money which he was paying. Induced by this expectation, we lent Lord Savaric two hundred ounces of the purest gold, each worth forty shillings, from coinage of which one half was silver, which we had gathered from the treasury of Saint Vincent; and we received from him the pledge he offered us, on this condition: that the church of Saint Vincent should peacefully possess one half of the revenues, both lawful and unlawful, belonging to the share of Geoffrey or of Savaric, his successor, within [Col. 1167A] these boundaries: from the crosses erected beyond the village of Saint-Marcel to the port of Luci; as Falieta [Talieta] flows from the bridge of Dirot [Doret] to the bridge of Campiferreol; and as all that land extends to the Forest, called the canonical [otherwise, canonic] Vabria, as far as the aforesaid crosses. Excepted are the dwellings of the knights, the small castle, and the servants whom he holds in lordship; likewise excepted are those seizures which he has lawfully or unlawfully made upon the property of the monks of the church of Saint-Marcel.

Moreover, Savaric entirely renounced and remitted all exactions and lawful or unlawful customary dues which he said he possessed in the village of Saint-Isidore, in Gemula, and in the dependencies of those villages. In the court, however [otherwise, nevertheless], of Saint-Isidore he retained his revenue [Col. 1167B], on the condition that he should not burden the canons or their peasants, and that he should maintain from this source a complete and firm peace with the Church of Chalon. In the presence of Lord Gocerannus [otherwise, Joceranus], bishop of Langres, Falcon of Reione [otherwise, Fulco of Reone], and Hugh of Bajac [Barac], Savaric swore to maintain perpetual peace; and his wife ordered a certain knight named Arbert to swear on her behalf. That this peace might be held more securely, Savaric gave twenty hostages, upon the following terms: if Savaric himself, or any of his men, should take anything from it, and should not restore the principal within forty days after an account had been settled with him [otherwise, after the matter had been settled], he shall not leave the circuit of the walls of the city of Chalon, except by such extension as the bishop of Chalon [Col. 1167C], or the dean of that church together with two other persons, may grant.

If the aforesaid Savaric does not fulfil this agreement, then, after the hostages have been summoned by the canons or the bishop, they shall either restore the principal within forty days or remain captive in the aforesaid city until what was taken has been restored. Savaric also caused his son Simon with his wife, and likewise his other son Arveus, to approve this agreement. Concerning the hostages, this law was established: whenever one has died, another shall immediately be substituted in his place.

The mark of Gaucerannus [otherwise, Jocerandus], bishop of Langres. The mark of Falcon of Reione. The mark of Hugh of Bajac [Barac]. The mark of Humbert of Villiac. The mark of Raymond Gumbad. The mark of Hugh Rodulf. The mark of Guy of Montfaucon.

## II. Notice of the Foundation of Cîteaux (1098)

[Col. 1167D]

Let it be known to all Christians, present and future, that Rainald, viscount of Beaune, and his wife Hodierna, and their sons Hugh, Humbert, Rainard, and Hagan, and their sister Raimundis, for the remission of their own sins and those of their forebears, granted to Lord Robert and the brethren, who desired to observe the Rule of Saint Benedict more strictly and faithfully than they had hitherto done, from their estate, anciently called Cîteaux, whatever should be necessary for those servants of God and their successors: for constructing a monastery and [Col. 1168A] its buildings, for ploughing, indeed for every necessary use.

Accordingly, Rainald himself and his wife, by right of whose inheritance that same freehold had come to them, and their above-named sons, made a lawful gift for the use of those brethren: first to God, and especially to the most blessed Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary, in whose honour the place now called the New Monastery, situated within the territory of the aforesaid freehold of Cîteaux, was consecrated. And because the brethren did not think it worthy to receive from his hand, since he was a layman, the church of that place which he had hitherto held and which belongs solely to divine right, he relinquished it and, renouncing all further possession of it, left it to the aforesaid brethren for the service of God.

As to the remaining portion of that land which the said Rainald wished to retain, Duke Odo of Burgundy, with Rainald’s consent and at his desire, made with him the following exchange and agreement for the use of the same monks: namely, that for that land Rainald and his heirs after him should receive twenty shillings annually at the castle of Beaune. Therefore, in the same exchange, the duke granted to Rainald and his sons as many vineyards as they might plant and cultivate in the district of Beaune on their own demesne. Rainald, however, retained two serfs of the same freehold, Theodoric and Martin, and a female servant named Osanna, together with so much of the land itself as would suffice for their cultivation for their own use. They shall cultivate only that land which the duke [Col. 1168C], the often-mentioned Rainald, and his wife, should she wish to be present, and also the lord abbot, shall divide and assign to them—namely, a part remote from the monks’ cultivation.

Later, when the church of the New Monastery was dedicated, the duke himself and Rainald with his wife again made a gift, in the presence of a large crowd assembled there, into the hand of Lord Walter, bishop of Chalon, for the use of the aforesaid brethren; so that under the protection of their bishop they might be free from lay power and every disturbance of secular affairs, and might devote themselves more peacefully to the service of their Creator. The duke himself also granted those brethren the fullest right of use both in the forest adjoining the aforesaid monastery and throughout all his surrounding demesne.

Hugh, the duke’s son, was present at this above-written exchange [Col. 1168D] and gift and likewise granted it; and his brother Henry later granted the same. The following witnesses were also present: Hugh of Mont-Saint-Jean, Gualo of Salvi, Seguin of Beaune and his son Hugh, Hugh of Grancey, etc.

## III. Letter of Walter, Bishop of Chalon, to Robert, Bishop of Langres, concerning the Reception of Abbot Robert, Formerly of Cîteaux, Returning to His Earlier Monastery of Molesme (1099)

To his dearest brother and fellow bishop ROBERT, bishop of Langres: WALTER, servant of the Church of Chalon, greetings.

Let it be known to you that Brother Robert, to whom we had entrusted the abbacy [Col. 1169A] situated in our bishopric and called the New Monastery, has, according to the judgment of Lord Archbishop Hugh, been released by us from the profession which he made to the Church of Chalon and from the obedience which he promised to us. He himself has released from their obedience and profession those monks who resolved to remain in the aforesaid New Monastery, and has left them free. Therefore do not hesitate henceforth to receive and honourably treat him. Farewell.

## IV. Letter of the Same Walter to Pope Paschal concerning the Monastery of Cîteaux (1100)

[Col. 1169B]

To the venerable Father, Pope PASCHAL: WALTER, servant of the Church of Chalon, greetings and due submission. “As Your Holiness,” etc. See under Paschal II.

## V. Walter, Bishop of Chalon, and Jarento, Abbot of Dijon, Establish a Fellowship between Themselves and the Congregations Entrusted to Them (1111)

In the name of Christ. Since all the goods of believers are generally held in common through unity of faith and the bond of charity, an ancient custom has nevertheless prevailed among religious persons: that they should bind themselves to one another by a special fellowship, so that, in proportion as they know themselves to be more closely united by the bond of charity, they may rejoice more devotedly in one another’s prosperity and grieve in one another’s adversity [Col. 1169C].

We therefore make known to present and future generations by what special intimacy the Churches of Chalon and Dijon have united themselves mutually, so that this bond of affection, which the Church of Chalon entered into with that of Dijon with great devotion, and which that of Dijon received from Chalon with great thanksgiving, may never be erased among posterity by the age of forgetfulness, nor ever broken by any division of discord.

Accordingly, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1111, Lord Walter, bishop of Chalon, and Lord Jarento, abbot of Dijon, entered into the following fellowship between themselves and the congregations committed to them: whenever notice comes to Dijon of a canon of Chalon, or to Chalon of a monk of Dijon [Col. 1169D], a complete office for the dead shall immediately be celebrated for him—that is, a vigil and a Mass—and he shall receive a prebend on that day. Moreover, it was established that, in the week after Mid-Lent Sunday, a general office and Mass should be celebrated by each community for the other.

Furthermore, the aforesaid Lord Walter, bishop, granted to Lord Jarento, abbot, and all his successors one entire daily canonical prebend in the church of Saint Vincent; the same Lord Abbot granted it to a monk of Dijon living at Saint Mary’s. The said monk shall perform a week’s service at Saint Vincent’s; and, on account of this alms, the church of Dijon shall render to the church of Chalon such service, both materially and spiritually, as it is able.

## VI. Charter of Walter, Bishop of Chalon, by Which He Gives the Church of Boens to Saint-Marcel

[Col. 1170A]

To all who live in unity of faith, await Christ’s mercy, and nourish the secret places of their minds with the food of God’s word, the divine utterance proclaims that the Redeemer’s dispensation so provides for the rich that, from their own possessions, which they hold only temporarily, they may acquire a hundredfold return, provided that they use those possessions well and strive to distribute what they have to the poor. And because, as the Apostle says, “we have here no lasting city” (Heb. XIII, 14), and our days vanish daily like a passing shadow; and because it is clearer than light from the voice of Truth that every tree which does not bear good fruit [Col. 1170B] must be cut down and cast into the fire (Matt. VII, 19): we especially, who seem set above others, ought, while we remain in this body, to perform, with God’s help, some work belonging to the worship of God, so that in the future we may deserve to become participants in eternal recompense.

Therefore I, Walter, by God’s grace bishop of the people of Chalon, desiring to obtain forgiveness for my sins and the merciful compassion of divine grace, give and grant to God and to His holy apostles Peter and Paul, for the place of Saint Marcel, martyr of Chalon—over which presides Lord Hugh, surnamed Berald, monk of Saint Peter of Cluny, to whose governance the same place appears to belong—and to the brethren serving God in that place, the church of Boens with all things belonging to it: namely, lands, meadows, woods, and waters. This is on condition that they hold, keep, and possess it forever, and pray for us to Christ’s clemency.

And because that church appears to belong and be subject to the church of Saint Vincent of Chalon, this gift was made and confirmed, on the day of the Invention of Saint Vincent, in the general chapter, with the counsel and consent of the canons of that church: namely, Lord Jotsald the dean, Hugh the cantor, Ansideus the archdeacon, Hugh of Miliac, Robert of Mirmanda, Raymond of Bussiac, Rodulf Sigwin, Stephen Brun the archpriest, and all the others present, greater and lesser; it was made by the gift of my ring into the hand of the aforesaid prior [Col. 1170D].

Since, therefore, that which is not quickly committed to writing quickly slips from memory, we have ordered and caused this charter to be made, for the security of its possessors and against the complaints of the envious; and we have confirmed it by our authority. This gift was thus made in the city of Chalon, in the chapter of the canons, in September, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October [23 September], in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1114, the epact being 23, in the reign of Louis, king of the French.

## VII. Gift of Walter, Bishop of Chalon, under Peter, Abbot of La Ferté

Let it be known to all that Lord Walter, bishop of Chalon, successor to Lord Jotsald, bishop of the aforesaid city, after the death of Lord Jotsald, [Col. 1171A] having become bishop in a chapter before the canons of the church of Chalon, namely on the Invention of Saint Vincent the martyr, granted to the church of Saint Mary of La Ferté, into the hand of Lord Peter, abbot of that church—who [Col. 1172A] afterwards became archbishop of Tarentaise—one half of the *parata* which he held from the church of Saint Ambrose, in perpetuity. Witnesses to this are Raymond the archdeacon, etc.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1115. RAOUL TORTAIRE, MONK OF FLEURY

[Col. 1171]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(Literary History of France, vol. X, p. 88.)*

[Col. 1171B] Raoul, surnamed Tortaire—that is, “of the Tart”—was born at Gien-sur-Loire, in the diocese of Auxerre (MAB., *Ann.*, bk. LXXVIII, no. 45). From childhood he was instructed in the liberal arts, in which he made great progress for his time. Afterwards, disgusted with the world, he embraced the monastic profession at Fleury, or Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire. Studies had flourished there since the learned Abbo had renewed them, and the abbey had never since ceased to produce men of letters, including several celebrated writers. At the time when Raoul increased their number (Gall. Chr. nov., vol. VIII, p. 1555), it included a Christian, a Hugh of Sainte-Marie, and a Clarius: the first celebrated for his great learning, and the other two for their writings.

[Col. 1171C] Raoul thus had every means of cultivating and perfecting his love of letters. He also knew how to profit from them so advantageously that he acquired a great store of ecclesiastical and secular learning. It has even been claimed that he possessed everything written up to that time by ancient and modern authors. He applied himself especially to writing verse and prose, and succeeded in it as well as any writer of his century. Poetry held a singular attraction for him; he cultivated it extensively and with such success that he deserved to be regarded as a poet above the ordinary (BOL., 21 March, p. 301, nos. 9–11; BART., *Adv.*, bk. LII, ch. 7). Yet what most deserves praise in him is that he devoted himself so fully to study without neglecting any duty [Col. 1171D] attached to his profession. On the contrary, he fulfilled them so exactly that he became a model to his brethren, an ornament to his house, and a support of regular observance. His virtue was so favourably known that no one doubted that his death was precious in the sight of the Lord.

It is surprising that, after various writings of Raoul had been published, from which one can discover fairly precisely the period in which he flourished, scholars should have divided on this point into two opinions as far apart from one another as they are contrary to the truth of the matter. Some, such as Barthius and Vossius (BART., ibid.; Voss., *Hist. lat.*, bk. IV, pt. III, ch. 11), supposed that he lived as early as the beginning of the tenth century, almost two hundred years before he became known to the world. Others, notably Oudin and still more celebrated modern writers, maintain that he lived beyond 1144, even to 1160. But the latter fell into this error only because they confused Raoul Tortaire with another poet named Raoul, a monk of Cluny, who composed in verse a eulogy of that illustrious abbey, and who was probably the same man who wrote the Life of Saint Abbot Peter the Venerable after 1156 (OUD., *Scri.*, vol. II, p. 1474; *Supp.*, p. 433; [Col. 1172C] MAB., ibid.; LE BEUF, *Hist. d’Aux.*, vol. II, p. 486).

Yet it was easy to correct, or even avoid, both errors by reading with some attention the collection of Saint Benedict’s miracles made by our writer. Supporters of the first opinion would have seen there that Raoul relates events occurring under Rainier, William, Veran, and Joscerand, all abbots of Fleury in the eleventh century, the last of whom lived into the beginning of the next. They would also have seen that he speaks of the expedition of William IX, count of Poitiers, to the Holy Land, which took place only in 1102, and consequently that he could have written only after that date. Those supporting the contrary opinion would have found that, having been present at a miracle performed in 1095, Raoul presents himself [Col. 1172D] as a grown man when he says that he joined the others in giving thanks to God for it. There is, however, a considerable distance from that description to the year 1160 and beyond.

On these indications Dom Mabillon, and Cave after him, initially judged that Raoul flourished in the early years of the twelfth century; and the author of the still-manuscript history of the abbey of Fleury believes him to have died as early as 1107 (MAB., ibid., bk. XXXVIII, no. 10; *Act.*, vol. VI, p. 347, no. 22; CAVE, [Col. 1173A] p. 559; *Flor. Hist. mss.*, p. 374). The latter’s reason is that Raoul makes no mention in his writings of a translation of Saint Benedict’s relics, carried out with great ceremony in that year or the following, from one shrine to another. This reason, however, is not very decisive, since Raoul did not undertake the history of his house, but only an account of Saint Benedict’s miracles; an event unaccompanied by miracles lay outside his purpose.

The earliest successors of Bollandus succeeded better than all those just mentioned in determining the time when Raoul wrote. But the basis upon which they rely is manifestly unsound. They say that it was in 1117, and maintain that this date is expressed in the second of the following two verses with which our poet ends his long poem on the martyrdom of Saint Maurus and his translation:

> *Mille sui versus, sua demant crimina mille*  
> *Septies et deni cum centum caetera demant.*

> A thousand of my verses, may they take away a thousand of my sins;  
> And seven times ten together with a hundred, may they take away the rest.

[The printed Latin *Septies et deni cum centum* literally gives seven times ten plus one hundred, while the French commentary below interprets the number as one hundred and seventeen. The discrepancy is retained.]

It is clear that there is no chronological calculation here. It is only the poet’s prayer: he wishes that one thousand of his verses might erase a thousand of his faults, and that another hundred and seventeen might erase the rest. We are almost persuaded that Raoul intended thereby to indicate the number of verses composing his poem. Those possessing the manuscript in which it appears entire could easily verify this.

After all, there is no testimony more precise or [Col. 1173C] better able to settle minds concerning the end of Raoul’s life than that of Hugh of Sainte-Marie, his fellow monk and contemporary. We possess his continuation of the history of Saint Benedict’s miracles, which he wrote no later than 1120 and which remains in manuscript only. In the preface at its head he plainly says that Dom Raoul, his venerable brother, whose work he undertakes to continue—these are his own words—was then no longer in the world. Since he relates miracles performed in 1114, it may legitimately be concluded that Raoul died in that same year, or at the latest in the following year.

During his lifetime Raoul used his pen not only to celebrate various saints but also, as will be seen below, to extol the merit of certain learned friends. After his death, there were accordingly men who used theirs to transmit his memory honourably to posterity. Epitaphs were devoted to him, and these are read at the head of the collection of his poems, as the second verse of the one which we shall copy announces. This is the first; it is by one called Francus Beatus, and is somewhat mutilated through the defect of the manuscript.

## EPITAPH

> *RODULPHUS fuit hic decus, ecclesiaeque columna,*  
> *Carmina cujus in hoc corpore, lector, habes.*  
>   
> *Imbutus a puero doctrinis grammaticorum,*  
> *Secli cum vita deseruit studium.*  
>   
> *Inde fuit sacrae vas legis et historiarum*  
> *Novit quippe novum, quidquid avumque fuit.*  
>   
> *Post in hoc monachus fuit et speculum monachorum:*  
> *[lacuna] factis, vestibus, ore Deum*  
>   
> *[lacuna] Dic talo [perhaps Galo; printed *talo*] quod perficit omnia dulce:*  
> *Quodque fide petiit, nunc habeat specie*  
>   
> *Sit cum Rodulpho tua portio, France Beate,*  
> *[Ut similis] fias nocte dieque stude.*

> Rodulf was here an ornament and pillar of the Church,  
> Whose poems, reader, you possess in this volume.  
>   
> Steeped from childhood in the teachings of grammarians,  
> He abandoned the pursuit of the world along with worldly life.  
>   
> Then he became a vessel of sacred law and histories;  
> For he knew whatever was new and whatever was ancient.  
>   
> Afterwards he became a monk here and a mirror to monks:  
> [lacuna] in deeds, clothing, and speech, God.  
>   
> [lacuna] Tell Galo [perhaps “Galo,” printed *talo*], who sweetly brings all things to completion,  
> That what he sought by faith he may now possess by sight.  
>   
> May your portion be with Rodulf, blessed Francus;  
> [that you may become like him,] strive night and day.

Among Raoul’s writings, several have been printed, but most remain in manuscript. We shall begin by discussing those of the first class, then pass to the others.

[Col. 1174B] 1. The best known is his continuation of the history of Saint Benedict’s miracles performed in France, especially at Fleury. As early as the ninth century, Adrevald, a monk of that place, had begun to collect them. After Adrevald, Adelere, Aimon, and Andrew, other monks of Fleury, each in his own time, continued their narration. Then Raoul Tortaire resumed it, and after him Hugh of Sainte-Marie continued it down to 1119. Raoul’s collection begins with the reign of Henry I, king of France, in 1031, and carries the sequence to 1114, when Hugh undertook to continue it, as stated above. Raoul had been an eyewitness of some of the miracles he describes and had good records for the others. This cannot be doubted when one sees how careful he is to name the persons cured by miracles and the places where the events occurred.

Although his collection is extensive and contains forty-nine miracles, he would have enlarged it still further if men of letters or inhabitants of places far from Fleury had taken care to preserve some record of miracles performed there. Such accounts are ordinarily considered of little interest. Yet our writer’s account has merit and usefulness. Besides being written in a very good style for its time, and with much candour and deep sentiments of piety, it can serve to elucidate topography and general history by making known in detail [Col. 1174D] various places and persons of some importance.

Father Jean du Bois, a Celestine, was the first to present it to the public (*Flor. bib.*, pt. I, pp. 149–218). He printed it from an ancient manuscript of Fleury in the first part of the *Library, or Ancient Monuments* of that abbey, published at Lyons in octavo in 1605. But because the copy of the work lacked its author’s name, the editor presented it as the writing of an unknown, though learned, monk.

Later, the successors of Bollandus, having found it in other manuscripts and discovered that it belonged to Raoul Tortaire, republished it [Col. 1175A] with notes of their own, restoring it to its true author.

Finally, Dom Mabillon issued a new edition based upon the two preceding editions and the manuscripts.

2. After Raoul had written this account in prose, he rendered it in verse, as he himself says in the following two lines found at the beginning of his poem:

> *Quae nuper prosa, nunc digero carmine gesta*  
> *Claruerit noster quae faciendo Pater.*

> The deeds lately set forth in prose I now arrange in verse—  
> The deeds by which our Father has become renowned.

He carried his work on Saint Benedict much further, also putting into verse the saint’s Life, the history of his translation into France, and the various accounts of his miracles that had preceded his own. The successors of Bollandus attest that they saw this large work, together with Raoul’s other principal writings, in a very ancient manuscript of Queen Christina of Sweden, then numbered 1640 (MONTF., *Bib.*, p. 44), and, after it passed with the others to the Vatican Library, numbered 1343. In all likelihood it is the same manuscript which M. de la Curne de Sainte-Palaye, in his manuscript memoirs, testifies that he saw on his journey through Italy. This is inferred from the enumeration he gives of the writings contained in it. The author dedicated or addressed this great work on Saint Benedict to one of his friends, Fulk, speaking as follows and identifying himself by name:

> *Accipe, mi Fulco, tibi quae tetrasticha mitto:*  
> *Legislatoris perlege gesta Patris.*  
>   
> *Haec tibi jucundo scripsi Rodulphus amico,*  
> *Ut tua sit nostris mentio facta libris.*

> Receive, my Fulk, these quatrains which I send you;  
> Read through the deeds of the Father who gave the Rule.  
>   
> I, Rodulf, wrote these things for you, my delightful friend,  
> That mention of you might be made in my books.

[Col. 1175C] The work, however, appears to contain nothing historical that is not found in the prose account. This reason, joined to its excessive length, prevented the Bollandists from burdening their collection with it. They wisely confined themselves to publishing forty-six quatrains that contain the account of miracles written by the monk Andrew. All its verses are elegiac and rhyme at the hemistich and at the end, like the four quoted above. Apparently the whole work is composed in the same kind of versification.

3. The Vatican manuscript, formerly Queen Christina’s, mentioned above, also contains the acts of the life and martyrdom of Saint Maurus, who suffered in Africa, together with the history of his translation to Fleury; our poet set the whole in long rhyming verses. At the end of this other work occur the following two lines, in which the author, who identified himself by name in his earlier poems, tells us his surname:

> *Maure sacer meritis, exaudi vota precantis.*  
> *Quod dedit exiguus Tortarius, accipe munus.*

> Holy Maurus, rich in merits, hear the prayers of your suppliant.  
> Receive the small gift which Tortarius has given.

Of this long poem, Father du Bois, who had found it in a manuscript of Fleury, published only what concerns the history of the saint’s translation. He suppressed the part containing the martyrdom and the other events of Maurus’s life, on the pretext that they were sufficiently known to the public. [Col. 1176A] He also omitted the last verse of the printed section (*Flor. Bib.*, ibid., pp. 349–355).

Raoul also composed a hymn in Sapphic verse containing a concise account of the entire history of the same holy martyr. The preceding editor had found it in a Fleury manuscript, but, being unable to decipher it, left it unpublished. In reporting this fact, the manner in which he expresses himself, taken together with the title he gives his printed text, seems to show that he distinguished Raoul, monk of Fleury, from Tortaire—though they are in fact the same person. Moreover, the hymn in question is also found in the Vatican manuscript, after the acts and the history of the translation.

4. Under our poet’s name, the same manuscript further presents [Col. 1176B] another large work in elegiac verse, preceding all the others just described. Another copy is even in the same library among the manuscripts of Alexandre Petau (MONTF., ibid., p. 82), to whom it doubtless came, directly or indirectly, from Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire. This other work, addressed to one of the author’s friends, is divided into nine books and bears the title *On Marvels*, or *On Wonderful Things* (*De mirabilibus*). It contains approximately a thousand distichs, making two thousand verses. Raoul included in it the most memorable things he had read concerning different kingdoms, wars, triumphs, acts of virtue, excesses of vice, ingenious flashes of wit, and other such subjects.

Let us hear the poet himself outline its plan. This will enable one to judge the value of the poetry he employed in it; and, in doing him justice, one will admit that it surpasses that of all his contemporary versifiers. Yet this was his first attempt, as he seems to say clearly enough in the last of the ten verses we shall quote:

> *Dum vacat, et curis mens non agitatur avaris.*  
> *Dum lentis animus fluctibus abstrahitur;*  
>   
> *Flores de vernis metrico decerpere pratis,*  
> *Pollice decrevi, noster amice, tibi.*  
>   
> *Hic portenta tibi, miracula, somnia scripsi,*  
> *Scripsi de rebus hic memorabilibus.*  
>   
> *Recte, perverse, versute dicta vel acta*  
> *Dixi, quae fato contigerint vario.*  
>   
> *Urges ad famam, Clio, quae prima poetam,*  
> *Adsis principiis ex Helicone meis.*

> When the mind has leisure and is not troubled by greedy cares,  
> When the spirit is drawn away by gentle waves,  
>   
> I have resolved, my friend, to pluck for you with metrical thumb  
> Flowers from the springtime meadows.  
>   
> Here I have written for you prodigies, miracles, dreams;  
> Here I have written of memorable things.  
>   
> I have told of words or deeds rightly, wrongly, or cunningly spoken or done,  
> Which befell through changing fate.  
>   
> Clio, you who first urge the poet toward renown,  
> Be present at these first beginnings of mine from Helicon.

5. Following this large work, the same manuscript contains eleven epistles or letters of Raoul in verse, addressed to as many friends. The first is written to one Garnier Bourdon, the very person to whom he addressed the preceding work, and begins thus:

> *Accipe descriptam, Guarneri Burdo, salutem,*  
> *Dirigit a Torta quam tibi, nomen habens.*

> Receive the greeting here set down, Guarnerius Burdo,  
> Which he who bears the name “from the Tart” sends you.

The second is addressed to a man named Bernard, a name then extremely common among men of letters. Here are its first two lines:

> *Pro meritis, Bernarde, tuis tibi verba salutis*  
> *Paucula Rodulphus adnotat ipse tuus.*

> In return for your merits, Bernard, your own Rodulf  
> Writes down for you a few words of greeting.

It is evident that in these two openings of letters our poet expressed his name and surname so plainly that he cannot readily be confused with another.

Nevertheless, this is what happened to the copyist who lent his hand to one of the two copies of Tortaire’s collection of poems held by the Vatican Library (MAB., *Ann.*, bk. LXXVIII, no. 45). Having come upon the epitaph of Peter Abelard, the eulogies of Saint Bernard and Peter the Venerable, and that of the abbey of Cluny—all composed by Raoul, a monk of that house under the same Peter the Venerable—he joined all these pieces to those of Raoul Tortaire. It is true that the two poets bore the same name and that the poetry of both has the same character, rhyming at the hemistich and at the end, with both heroic and elegiac verse. But Tortaire’s surname and the period in which he flourished ought to have given pause and invited closer scrutiny. Yet, aided by this initial confusion, Dom Mabillon (ibid.) and those who followed him (LE BEUF, *Hist. d’Aux.*, vol. II, p. 486) attributed all these poems indiscriminately to Raoul Tortaire, monk of Fleury. It is nevertheless indisputable that a writer dead before 1120—as we have shown Tortaire to have been, on the testimony of one of his brethren before whose eyes he died—could not speak of events which occurred only in 1142, 1144, and later still [Col. 1177C]. Let us resume our discussion of our poet.

In his letter to Bernard, he recounts at some length the story of two friends, Amelius, a native of Auvergne, and Amicus, of Gascony. The latter risked his life in a duel out of attachment to the former; after both had gone to Italy, they died and were buried at Vercelli.

[Col. 1178A] Another letter of Raoul, written to Robert, contains the account of a journey he made while visiting several cities of France; it includes descriptions, specifically, of Blois, Caen, and Bayeux.

Another is addressed to a brother of the author; by calling him *adelphus*, rather than “brother,” it suggests that Raoul knew Greek. It is in this letter that Raoul tells us that he came from Gien or its vicinity.

His other letters are addressed to Udo, Philus, Syncope, and other persons equally little known. Those who have read them do not say whether they contain any noteworthy details; apparently, like almost all the preceding ones, they are merely letters of courtesy and friendship.

[Col. 1178B] 6. The Vatican Library manuscript presents yet another work of Raoul Tortaire: a verse history of the First Crusade, dedicated to Galon, bishop of Paris from 1105 until February 1116, the end of his life. This circumstance removes every ambiguity concerning Raoul of Fleury and Raoul of Cluny, and permits no doubt that the poem belongs to the former. Indeed, the other Raoul, who was still writing after 1156 and even later, was too young before 1116 to undertake a work of this nature.

It is easy to understand from all these details that Ralph Tortaire was an exceedingly industrious writer. [Col. 1178C] His peculiar taste for rhyme in verse cost him much time and labour as well. Moreover, constraint and restriction prevented him from giving himself full scope, and account for the fact that his poetry is not better; although it is true that, such as it is, it still surpasses that of almost all the other versifiers of the same period.

[Col. 1177]

# MIRACLES OF SAINT BENEDICT  
BY RODULFUS TORTARIUS

## ON THE BRINGING-IN OF THE RELICS OF SAINT FATHER BENEDICT,  
together with six books of his miracles performed in Gaul and Italy.

(Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, century IV, part II, p. 343.)

## I

[Col. 1177D]

1. The beginnings of the monastery of Fleury, and the translation into Gaul of the relics of Saints Benedict and Scholastica, have been discussed more fully in the second century, both in the Eulogy of Saint Mummolus and in the History of the Translation of Saint Benedict. The history of the bringing-in is referred to this place, together with the books of miracles which followed the time of that bringing-in.

2. From ancient authors one may recover a twofold cause of this feast, of which one may in some fashion be called primary, [Col. 1179A] the other secondary. The primary cause is put forward by Adalbert, Adrevald, Saint Odo the abbot, and others: namely, the burial of Saint Benedict in the basilica of Saint Mary on 4 December. For when the body of Saint Benedict had been transferred from Monte Cassino to the monastery of Fleury and deposited, on 2 July, in the oratory of Saint Peter, it remained there until a suitable resting-place for the sacred body had been prepared in the church of Saint Mary. There, finally, Adalbert the monk—and after him Aimoin in his little work *On the Translation of Saint Benedict*—reports that it was placed on the day before the Nones of December, that is, 4 December.

Accordingly, from that time onward this day, called the burial or deposition of Saint Benedict, was celebrated both at Fleury and in very many monasteries of Gaul, as Adrevald testifies in book *On the Miracles*, chapter 22:

> “The solemn feast [Col. 1179B] of Benedict, the holy confessor of Christ, was at hand, which by ancient custom is celebrated every year on the day before the Nones of December, when a gathering of many peoples is accustomed to flock to the monastery in memory of so great a Father.”

And Saint Odo the abbot, in his sermon on Saint Benedict, treats of his holy translation and likewise of his burial, saying that many proofs of signs show that these things were divinely ordained.

In the Cartulary of Perrecy, published by Stephen Gerard in the *Collection of Monuments of Burgundy*, this feast is mentioned in charters 29, 32, and 34, where it is called “the Mass of Saint Benedict which is in the month of December.” “Mass” means feast; the feast is found entered in very many ancient martyrologies. In the Corbie Calendar [Col. 1179C] written more than eight hundred years ago, prefixed to Saint Gregory’s *Pastoral Rule*, one finds, on the day before the Nones of December: “The deposition of Benedict, abbot.” Finally, the term “burial” still flourished in the twelfth century, as appears from Rodulfus Tortarius’s book *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chapter 33, in these words:

> “Therefore, at the Father’s burial, which is observed every year with reverence throughout all Gaul during the days of the Lord’s Advent, a woman…”

From this it is clear what the primary institution of this celebration was.

3. The secondary cause is reported by Diederic, a German monk of Hersfeld. He lived for a long time at the monastery of Fleury at the beginning of the eleventh century; after returning to his homeland, he was once asked by Richard, [Col. 1179D] abbot of Amerbach, what was the reason for the feast of the most blessed Father Benedict of monks, which was especially celebrated in Gaul during the days of the Lord’s Advent under the name of the “bringing-in” (*illatio*). He composed a little book on the subject, in which he relates that the reason for this solemnity was the return of Saint Benedict’s body from the city of Orléans after the devastation inflicted on the monastery of Fleury by the Northmen. In this return journey, the Loire—frozen solid—carried back to Fleury, once the ice had melted, a little boat laden with sacred relics through the contrary waters of its channel; and trees burst into bloom, whence the place received the name Fleury. He adds that on that day the sacred relics of Saint Benedict were placed in the monastery—that is, the church—of Saint Peter; and that on the anniversary day of the following year they were brought into their own mausoleum [Col. 1180A] in the church of Blessed Mary, which had for two years lacked the presence of its inhabitant.

The bishops who had witnessed the event therefore decreed that, since the return and the bringing-in had occurred on the same day a year apart, this day should be solemnly celebrated every year throughout all Gaul for all future time. Finally, in the same book the author relates that Caroloman—whom he mistakenly calls Sigebert—was sent into Gaul after this return to reclaim the body of Saint Benedict, but that this undertaking came to nothing because God opposed it.

This is Diederic’s account. The Bollandist Associates diminish its credibility in their March volume, where they omit what Diederic relates about this bringing-in because, they say, it is almost entirely invented and may be read in Jean Bosc. They content themselves with a simple presentation [Col. 1180B] of the double miracle: the ice beneath Saint Benedict’s body melting of its own accord, and trees bursting into flower. Yet in their notes on Adrevald’s book *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, no. 19, they admit that both miracles are suspect to them.

4. Yet a prudent reader will, one may hope, render a fairer judgement if he observes that not only Diederic committed this history of the bringing-in to writing, but also Rodulfus Tortarius, Peter the abbot of Cluny called the Venerable, the chronicler of Fleury printed by Ghesnius at the beginning of the historians of the Northmen, and many others, who report it in precisely the same way. Rodulfus Tortarius, a Cluniac monk, at the beginning of the twelfth century rendered into verse, among other works, the History [Col. 1180C] of the Translation of Saint Benedict’s Body into Gaul, and at the end of his poem adds these lines:

> What the pious patron accomplished after his limbs were buried,  
> I gather here together in this one little page.  
>
> The river Loire, bound fast with ice in wintertime,  
> affords a noble passage to the holy lawgiver.  
>
> They place the master’s body in a boat without a helmsman,  
> which cuts across the opposing stream and the ice.  
>
> Fleury blooms—a village marvellous to behold—  
> at the Father’s entry; darkness had been put to flight.  
>
> From this it took its name; formerly its appellation  
> was Golden Valley, because its soil is rich.

Peter the Venerable, in his hymn on the translation of Saint Benedict—which hymn is mentioned in book IV, letter 30—represents this double miracle of the bringing-in [Col. 1180D] in these verses:

> The vessel floats through the river without a helmsman;  
> with wondrous force it cleaves the ice.  
> Bearing the saint’s limbs against the current,  
> it drives the waters backward.  
>
> When the dry ground perceived him drawn forth from the river,  
> heedless of the cold of that icy season,  
> it immediately clothed all things in fresh flowers,  
> and the soil changed its appearance.

I do not think that so great a man as Peter, like Tortarius, was led to write these things merely by the authority of Diederic, an outsider; rather, they had before their eyes more certain records which are hidden from us. Perhaps there was mention of this event in the book which Blessed Odo is said to have written *On the Arrival of Saint Benedict*. Certainly Aimoin, at the beginning [Col. 1181A] of book II *On the Miracles*, appears to suggest that Fleury acquired its name from the miracle of the flowers:

> “By a favourable sign of heavenly condescension, this monastery in which, by God’s authorisation, we serve God received the name Fleury; in ancient times it was called Golden Valley, with no less a prerogative of grace.”

These words agree entirely with those of Diederic and Tortarius. The latter two append the two miracles just mentioned immediately after the History of the Translation—as Peter the Venerable also does—by anticipation; not because they believed that the miracles occurred immediately after the translation, as seemed to the Bollandist Associates, but because so remarkable a miracle had to be joined to the narrative of the translation, so that from one miracle we might understand the others.

5. Finally, at Orléans there still exists a church [Col. 1181B] of Saint Benedict, now a parish church, popularly called “of the Return” (*de Reditu*) in memory of this event, according to the conviction of the citizens. It had, however, already been built before the bringing-in by Abbot Medo, though perhaps it was restored after the devastation of the Northmen in commemoration of the bringing-in.

The term *illatio*, however, is rarely found in ancient martyrologies and ecclesiastical books. I find it in only one martyrology, that of the abbey of Saint Mary of the Forty [Martyrs] in the diocese of Narbonne, where our Claude Stephanotius read:

> “On the day before the Nones of December, at Orléans, in the place called Fleury: the bringing-in of the body of Benedict, abbot and monk.”

This martyrology was written about the year 1110.

6. We must now weigh the documentary grounds which moved both the Bollandist Associates and others to call into doubt [Col. 1181C] this History of the Bringing-in as first described by Diederic, and must answer them according to our capacity, insofar as the laws of truth and religion allow—religion commanding us to test all things and to give an answer to everyone who asks a reason.

7. The first ground for doubt may be drawn from the silence of domestic authors earlier than Diederic, namely Adrevald, Adelerius, and Aimoin. Although they wrote deliberately, one after another, about matters concerning Saint Benedict and miracles performed through him, none of them makes mention of the bringing-in or of the two miracles which Diederic records.
