Adrevald may perhaps have been unable to see those events because he died before they took place; nevertheless Adelerius could have seen them, since he records the encounter of Abbot Hugh and Girbold, count of Auxerre, with the Northmen over the plundering of Fleury monastery. This Girbold appears to have been none other than Count Gislolf, advocate of that monastery, mentioned in Diederic’s narrative, who at the prompting of Saint Benedict appearing in a dream pursued and defeated the Northmen. The same distinctive features occur in both Adelerius and Diederic: namely, the count saw Saint Benedict, dressed in monastic habit, while fighting; with one hand the saint led the horse of the combatant, while with the other he killed many enemies.

8. Not greatly different is the argument pressed from Diederic’s own writing. Since it comes from a later author and contains many false statements—such as that the name Fleury was obtained through the miracle of the flowers which he reports, and that Caroloman, whom by another error he calls Sigebert, came into Gaul after the devastation of the Northmen—it appears [Col. 1182A] to have weakened authority. For Diederic cannot have been better acquainted with Fleury’s affairs than Aimoin, who wrote shortly before him. Aimoin wrote his books *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict* in the year 1005. Diederic, however, dedicated his little book *On the Bringing-in* to Richard, abbot of Amerbach—wrongly printed in the editions as “Marbeach”—who died in 1039, as Brower testifies in chapter 20 of his *Antiquities of Fulda*.

9. The final difficulty arises from the time when these things are said to have occurred: namely, after the burning and plundering of the monastery of Fleury by the Northmen. [Col. 1182B] In reputable authors only one burning of this monastery by the Northmen is recorded, in the year of Christ 865, of which Adrevald writes in chapter 34 of *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, as do the Annals of Saint-Bertin and the short Chronicle which André Duchesne prefixed to the writers on the Northmen. Yet the bringing-in did not occur in that year: first, because Adrevald, who survived for several years and wrote much about Saint Benedict that occurred after that time, would have mentioned it; secondly, because the body of Saint Benedict was not then brought to Orléans, but carried here and there as the necessity of flight compelled.

Further, Diederic sufficiently identifies the king of the Franks during whose reign the bringing-in occurred as Caroloman, son of Louis the Stammerer; while the anonymous chronicler to be presented below identifies Charles, surnamed the Simple. Yet this event would not have escaped Adelerius, writing in Caroloman’s time, if it had occurred during Caroloman’s reign; and if it occurred while Charles the Simple was king, Aimoin would have known of it, since he was separated from Charles by less than a century.

10. Moreover, one cannot say that the return of Saint Benedict’s body occurred after Adelerius had finished writing, first because in the Northmen’s plundering described by Adelerius no monks of Fleury are said to have been killed, whereas Diederic’s narrative says otherwise; secondly, because the men of Fleury had then fled not to Orléans—which city seems from Adelerius to have been captured at that time—but to the estate of Matriniacum in the district of Wastinensis, [Col. 1182D] whither they had carried all their valuables, and therefore Saint Benedict’s body as well. Even if it was at some time brought to Orléans for refuge, it does not seem to have been deposited in the church of Saint Anianus, as Diederic writes, for that church was then outside the walls. Rather, it was probably placed in the small sacred building that Abbot Medo had constructed in honour of Saint Benedict, as has been said. For the people of Fleury were accustomed to flee there at that time, according to Adrevald in chapter 21 of his book *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*.

11. Finally, although the Northmen may at that time have violated the monastery of Fleury, it is by no means the case that Rollo, their leader, after laying waste Burgundy extensively, wished to profane Saint Benedict’s monastery or permitted that province—namely the territory of Fleury—to be plundered because of Saint Benedict. So writes Dudo, dean of Saint-Quentin, in book II, and William of Jumièges, a monk, confirms this in book II, chapter 14, in the very same words. These are the chief considerations which may be brought against the authority of Diederic’s account. Though we grant that they are not slight, they do not have such force that the things he reports ought without hesitation to be deemed fictitious.

12. First, Diederic’s error in assigning the cause that gave Fleury its name is either no error at all, or at least of the slightest consequence. Aimoin too seems to hold the same opinion, and writers commonly play upon a serious matter when occasion is given. But suppose Diederic is wrong in fixing the time when Caroloman came into Gaul: this does not prevent him from having attained the truth in the substance [Col. 1183B] of the narrative itself. Certainly, the silence of various writers who successively committed Saint Benedict’s miracles to posterity is not so decisive that Diederic’s case should fail on that account.

For apart from the possibility that the history of the bringing-in was perhaps written by some other ancient author whose work has perished, the following point is especially relevant: it is clear from chapter 13 of book III of the *Life of Saint Odo* that neither were all the miracles of Saint Benedict which occurred in that period recorded, nor did Aimoin read everything that had been committed to writing about them. There the monk John recalls a miracle of Saint Benedict omitted by other writers—although Adrevald in chapter 22 and Adelerius report something similar—and also says that the book *On the Arrival of the Body of Saint Benedict*, which Saint Odo is said to have written in the monastery at Orléans, was unknown to Aimoin. Furthermore, Aimoin himself confesses, in chapter 4 of book I *On the Miracles*, that miracles performed in Abbot Odo’s time remained unknown partly through antiquity and partly because they had been consigned to oblivion by the negligence of writers. How much more might those things which happened amid those most turbulent storms of the Northmen have escaped his knowledge?

13. It is somewhat less easy to answer the objection concerning the time when this history of the bringing-in, related by Diederic, is said to have occurred. Perhaps there was another burning of Fleury by the Northmen besides the one mentioned by Adrevald and others, which cannot be fitted to the bringing-in. Certainly Adelerius strongly supports Diederic’s position in that he records a large part of Diederic’s narrative when describing the incursion of the Northmen into Fleury, and recounts Girbold’s victory over them, won under Saint Benedict’s leadership during Caroloman’s reign. Nor does it matter that Adelerius omitted the burning of the monastery and the killing of certain monks, and committed nothing to writing about the bringing-in which Diederic says occurred afterwards. For Adelerius’s book ends with the victory of Hugh and Girbold over the Northmen, after the return of Saint Benedict’s body had taken place; by then Adelerius had already ceased writing, and perhaps living. Besides, how many such particular circumstances do we see omitted daily by some historians in a lengthy account, though they are reported by others?

Nor [Col. 1184A] does Adelerius say that Saint Benedict’s body was taken to Matriniacum, or that the city of Orléans was then captured by the Northmen; he says only that all valuables were carried to the estate of Matriniacum and that the Northmen came into that city. Indeed, even if he said both things, it would not prevent the holy relics from having been brought from Matriniacum to the city of Orléans until the monastery of Fleury had been restored to some extent.

14. From these facts, moreover, we easily understand why Rollo, after later devastating Burgundy, ordered that the monastery and territory of Fleury be spared because of Saint Benedict, whom he revered on account of the miracles performed in Girbold’s victory and in the return of his body. Here is the complete passage from book II of Dudo, dean of Saint-Quentin, and transmitted in the same words by William of Jumièges:

> “Rollo, thinking that because of the security he had given he was regarded as contemptible by the Franks, began fiercely and cruelly, by laying waste the provinces, to tear, afflict, and destroy the people. But his followers, going into Burgundy and sailing by the Yonne into the Saône, devastated on every side the lands adjoining the rivers as far as Clermont. They invaded the province of Sens and, after laying all waste, returned from Saint Benedict against Rollo. But when Rollo saw the monastery of Saint Benedict, he was unwilling to profane it, nor did he permit that province to be plundered because of Saint Benedict.”

Surely religion would not have entered the mind of a fierce man unless through prodigies like those [Col. 1184C] reported by Diederic. And perhaps for the same reason Count Theoderic restored to the monastery of Fleury the monastery of Perrecy, which he had taken away, with a great indication of penitence, as is read in instrument 11 of the Cartulary of Perrecy, dated in April of the year of King Carloman’s death, in the year 885 of the Lord’s Incarnation. For that year was the first after Carloman’s death, he having died in the preceding year of Christ. In that same year he had made a truce with the Northmen, as we read in the Annals of Saint-Bertin—namely, after the attack made by them which Adelerius describes. Finally, in the year 883 the first day of Advent fell on the Kalends of December. All these points agree well with Diederic’s narrative.

15. From this it is apparent that Diederic’s view—that the bringing-in occurred during Caroloman’s reign—must be preferred to the authority of the anonymous chronicler, who refers it to the time of Charles the Simple, Caroloman’s brother, namely about the year 900, shortly after the siege of Chartres. On this anonymous view, however, one would have to say that Rollo did indeed order his men to spare Saint Benedict’s monastery, but that certain foragers and raiders nevertheless plundered it against his command.

In that view, to tell the truth, there is this advantage: Charles the Simple was at Fleury in the year 900, as is clear from a diploma granted to the canons of the monastery of Saint-Evroult—for canons then lived there—confirming their estates. The diploma ends as follows:

> “Given on the day before the Kalends of November, in the third indiction, in the eighth year, [Col. 1185A] renewed the third time, of the reign of the most glorious lord King Charles. Done at the monastery of Saint Benedict.”

We learn incidentally from the heading prefixed in the manuscript codex how this diploma returned to the hands of the monks of Saint-Evroult:

> “Robert, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Evroult, found at Orléans the form of the appended charter of King Charles; and at his command Goscelin, a monk and excellent scribe, swiftly copied it and sent it to the monks of Saint-Evroult in the time of Philip, king of the Franks, so that the great fame which Blessed Evroul had formerly possessed among the Gauls might be made known.”

Therefore, as I have said, it is probable that Charles came to Fleury at that time, drawn by reverence for the place and by remembrance of the victory which Gistolf had recently won from the Northmen through heaven’s aid. Enough concerning that entire controversy; we must now turn [Col. 1185B] to other matters.

## II

16. Besides the authors who committed the life of Saint Benedict to writing, several—especially Gauls—also brought his miracles to light. The first to write the History of the Translation into Gaul and the miracles then performed was Adalbert, monk of Fleury, as Rodulfus Tortarius testifies in his poem on that same translation, which he begins thus:

> Adalbert teaches of the Father’s limbs translated,  
> setting down certain deeds in a polished style.

At one time I thought that Adalbert was none other than Adrevald, led both by Aimoin’s testimony in the prologue to the *Miracles*, where he says that Adrevald had included both the sequence of the translation [Col. 1185C] of the sacred body and the signs performed throughout Gaul, and by the assertions of Sigebert and Trithemius that Adrevald bore two names and was also called Adalbert. But that they were different persons is persuaded to me by a passage in the Chronicle of Fleury, in Chesnius, volume III of the *History of France*, p. 355:

> “In the year 853 Adalbert, a monk of blessed memory, died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January.”

This must without doubt be understood of Adalbert, author of the Translation, and cannot be applied to Adrevald, who lived longer.

17. For Adrevald composed the book *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict* when the Northmen had already ravaged Gaul for nearly thirty years, according to chapter 33, and therefore about the year of Christ 875. In chapter 28 he testifies that he had been a little boy while Emperor Louis Augustus reigned. I have included the books of Adalbert and Adrevald in the second century, together with Adelerius’s appendix.

18. Adelerius, likewise a monk of Fleury, added only two chapters to Adrevald’s book, as Aimoin testifies in his prologue. Those chapters end with the death of Louis the Stammerer, who, Aimoin says, had held the kingdom scarcely two years and died in 879. From this it is understood that Adrevald died shortly before Charles the Bald, and that Adelerius wrote these things during Caroloman’s reign.

19. Aimoin, certainly a monk of Fleury, continued the History of the Miracles of Saint Benedict, publishing two books which he dedicated to Gauzlin, abbot of Fleury, in the year following the death of Abbo, [Col. 1186A] abbot of Fleury, who died in 1004, as is read in book II, chapter 1. Aimoin received the monastic habit from Abbot Amalbert, according to book I, chapter 18. He also wrote four books of the *History of the Franks*, such as those published in volume III of Chesnius; these too he dedicated to the aforesaid Abbot Gauzlin. He also wrote a poem on the translation, a sermon on the holy Father Benedict, a book *On the Life of Abbot Saint Abbo*, and a book *On the Deeds of the Abbots of His Monastery*, which does not survive. That Aimoin was an Aquitanian of noble birth is clear from chapter 18 of the *Life of Saint Abbo*.

20. Diederic, or Theodoric, a monk of Hersfeld in Thuringia, at approximately the same time composed a little book *On the Bringing-in of the Relics of Saint Benedict*, at the urging of Richard, abbot of Amerbach, incorrectly printed in the editions as “Marbeach.” Richard died in 1029, according to Brower, book I, chapter 20 of the *Antiquities of Fulda*. He is called “of Amerbach” because he founded the monastery of Amerbach, dedicated to Saint Simplicius, in a recess of Franconia not far from the Main, as Brower says. Trithemius wrongly attributes Adalbert’s book *On the Translation of Saint Benedict* to Diederic and confuses the History of the Bringing-in with the Life of Saint Benedict.

21. Almost Diederic’s contemporary was Andrew, monk of Fleury, who added one book on the miracles of Saint Benedict to Aimoin’s books. Rodulfus Tortarius rendered it into verse. Andrew’s book remains hidden to this day.

22. Rodulfus, surnamed Tortarius, likewise of Fleury, besides this book also published another *On [Col. 1186C] the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, in prose and verse. Jean Bosc printed the prose work in the *Library of Fleury* without the author’s name, but the Bollandist Associates identified the author’s name. They saw at Rome several little works by this author and others in the library of the Queen of Sweden, which for the most part consists of manuscripts from the library of Fleury. This author wrote at the beginning of the twelfth century, after the death of Abbot Joscerand and the burning of Fleury in 1095, at which he was present, according to chapter 27.

23. I do not yet know when Girald, also a monk of Fleury, wrote. He composed a poem on the translation of Saint Benedict and another in honour of Saint Benedict. The Bollandist Associates were the first to mention both, publishing only their openings. The first begins:

> When the impious race of the Lombards, amid the darkness  
> of the treachery of the reprobate, would not depart from its ways, etc.

The other begins:

> This whole day is now spent in the praise  
> of the King of Heaven and of you, Benedict.  
>
> The pious limbs of the righteous prophet were moved from their place;  
> the Father’s bones were moved from their own place.

24. Besides these monks of Fleury, Italians also made known the miracles performed by the holy Father at Cassino. Chief among them is Abbot Desiderius, later Roman pontiff and called Victor III. He composed four books *On Miracles Performed at Cassino and in Other Places of Italy*, of which only three survive.

[Col. 1187A]

25. To all these are added Leo of Marsi, formerly a monk of Cassino and later cardinal-bishop of Ostia, and Peter the Deacon. In the Chronicle of Cassino they report many miracles of Saint Benedict; Peter likewise records several in the *History of the Discovery of the Body of Saint Benedict*, published in the Bollandist March volume.

26. Of all these, I have selected only four authors, apart from Adalbert, Adrevald, and Adelerius, whose little works are found in the second century together with Aimoin’s poem on the translation. I have selected, I say, Diederic, Aimoin, Rodulfus Tortarius [Note: [Col. 1187] “We publish only the work of Rodulfus Tortarius. The others we have already published.”], and Desiderius, or Victor. I have thought fit to publish only the first part of Diederic, rejecting the second, which concerns Caroloman’s attempted recovery of Saint Benedict’s body and wrongly states, through a gross error, that it occurred after the bringing-in.

[Col. 1187B] To Aimoin’s two books I append the book of Rodulfus Tortarius, published by Jean Bosc under the name of “Anonymous,” omitting Tortarius’s two books in verse. In the first he renders in verse the little book of the monk Andrew; in the second he versifies this work which I here present. Andrew’s work itself has perished. Tortarius’s verse translation survives in the Bollandist March volume, but it is so thin and barren that scarcely any profit can be derived from it beyond the bare cures of the sick. Its poem begins:

> The wondrous deeds which Andrew is said to have written for you  
> concerning the Father’s acts, my reed-pipe records.  
>
> But while the people of Limoges suffered a sacred fire,  
> God striking them, he counsels them  
>
> to carry the venerable relics of the Father into the city.  
> [Col. 1187C] When this was done, the wicked plague ceased.

Below I shall cite certain other matters from it concerning the cell of Barcelona. Rodulfus is followed—though they ought to have preceded him—by the dialogues of Desiderius, or Victor, in order that we may place before our eyes in a continuous sequence the miracles performed in Gaul and those performed in Italy. Jean-Baptiste Marus, a Roman canon, brought Desiderius’s dialogues out of a Vatican manuscript codex. A man truly deserving of the commonwealth of letters and of the Benedictine order, he illustrated them with learned notes. Since these suit our purpose, it has seemed fitting to reproduce them almost entire and word for word.

At the beginning of the dialogue Desiderius promises four books *On Miracles Performed Both through Saint Benedict and through Other Saints, Especially His Disciples*. The first two represent miracles at Cassino; the other two, miracles performed elsewhere in Italy. But whether he did not complete his work, or whether the Vatican codex—formerly belonging to the Library of Cassino—does not transmit it complete, the end of the third book and the whole fourth have by no means reached us.

## III

27. Besides Cassino and Fleury, places which the holy Father adorned with more notable signs of his presence, two other places are celebrated in the following books: namely, the cells of Perrecy and Barcelona, where Saint Benedict was renowned for miracles.

28. Aimoin treats of Perrecy in book II, chapter 15 and following; Tortarius, in chapter 39 and elsewhere. Aimoin says:

> “Perrecy is the name of an estate situated in the territory of Autun, in the region of Burgundy. Eckhard, a very wealthy count of Burgundy, granted it with generous liberality to Saint Benedict and the brothers of the monastery of Fleury, for certain necessary expenses. When he had died and been buried in the monastery of Fleury beside the church of Saint Mary, the brothers established a dwelling for themselves on the aforesaid estate. There, too, relics of Saint Father Benedict having been brought from Fleury, a church was constructed in honour of God and of the glorious Virgin Mary, and likewise of that outstanding confessor. By the merits of his holy Mother and of his beloved servant Benedict, Christ the Lord made that basilica renowned by miracles very often.”

29. Who this Count Eckhard was, and in what time he flourished, is taught us by an excellent monument of antiquity: the Cartulary of Perrecy, recently printed by Stephen Perard in his collection of ancient documents relating to the history of Burgundy. This paper codex contains thirty-nine diplomas. In the first is read the grant of the estate of Perrecy by Heccard as a refuge for the aforementioned monks of Fleury. The following words deserve note:

> “I, Eckhard, count by God’s gift, and my wife Richeldis, fearing the day of our last summons, lest, weighed down by the burden of sins, we be found barren, without the fruit of good work, grant for the remedy of our souls, and as alms for Childebrand, my father, and Donnana, my mother, and also for my own brother Theoderic, and for my wives Albegundis and Richeldis—and we wish it to be granted for ever—our possessions to the monastery of Saint Mary, Saint Peter, and Saint Benedict of Fleury, [Col. 1188C] where Saint Benedict himself rests in due honour, and where the venerable man Abbot Theodbert is known to preside with the great multitude of monks there serving the Lord; which possessions are situated in the district of Autun, in the district of Mâcon, and in that of Chalon, that is, in the estate called Perrecy, with the church consecrated in honour of Saint Peter, etc.”

Given in the month of January, in the first year of the reign of the lord Charles the Younger, namely Charles the Bald, at the beginning of 876. Eckhard had received this estate with its appurtenances as a gift from Louis Augustus by letters given at Poitiers on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in the twenty-seventh year of the emperor’s reign, third indiction—that is, at the end of 839.

30. From these documents we learn several noteworthy matters. First, the lineage of Count Eckhard: his father Childebrand, son, I think, of Count Nibelung; his mother Donnana; his wives Albegundis, or Aldegundis, and Richeldis; and his brother Theoderic. From the will of this same Eckhard, the fifth charter in order, we learn that he had a sister, Adana, a nun in the monastery of Afranum or Afaranum, then governed by Bertradana. This seems to be none other than the monastery of Saint Fara in the Brie district. In the same will [Col. 1189A] he calls Gerbergana his niece, as in subsequent letters he calls Guiniterius his nephew; two charters of this Guiniterius, or Winiterius, occur as nos. 20 and 26. See charters 13, 14, and 15 concerning Count Nibelung, whom I believe to be this Eckhard’s grandfather.

We also learn from the first charter, and likewise from the second, that Abbot Theodbert was presiding over the monastery of Fleury after Bernard from at least the year 876 onward; and that he is the same man who presided there in the year 885, according to charter 11. Charter 27 establishes that Gibert succeeded Theodbert in 890; charter 29, that Lambert did so in 907. More will be said of the location of Perrecy in connection with chapter 46 of Tortarius.

31. Another place distinguished by Benedict’s miracles was a certain cell in the district of Barcelona, consecrated to the holy Father. It is mentioned in the appendix to Rodulfus Tortarius and by Tortarius himself in his metrical rendering of the book of the monk Andrew, in these verses:

> There is a spacious house of the Father, situated in the district of Barcelona,  
> where, often invoked, he performs many marvels.  
>
> [Col. 1190A] There a diligent company serves God in Christ  
> and, secure in your protection, O patron, rejoices.  
>
> A friendly knight came there to pray  
> and, until he should depart, left his horses outside.  
>
> A thief greedily stole them and was drowned in a neighbouring stream;  
> the knight recovered the horses which he had feared to lose.  
>
> The Hagarenes, brought there in fleets, hasten thither  
> in order to consume the place with fire and strip it of its goods.  
>
> They wish to pour out wine, but it congeals hard as ice;  
> and a fire, once applied, dies of its own accord.  
>
> The king judges them weaklings and sends fiercer men;  
> he marvels why the same thing happens to these also.  
>
> One man, wishing to demolish the sacred altar,  
> kills himself while he raises a blow.

[Col. 1190B] This cell, or monastery, is said in the appendix to Tortarius—where this first miracle is recounted—to lie one day’s journey from Barcelona.

### 32. It is now time to introduce the narrative of Diederic, which in the manuscript codex bears this title:

## MIRACLES OF SAINT BENEDICT, BY RADULFUS TORTARIUS

[Col. 1189]

### CHAPTER I.—Odo, who plundered Saint Benedict’s property and the Paschal candle, dies miserably.

[Col. 1189C]

While Henry happily held the sceptre of the Franks, and his brother Robert in some fashion governed the duchy of Burgundy, their brother Odo lived as a private person, raised to no height of rank. Because he had no property of his own, he coveted the theft of that which belonged to others, devoting himself to robbery and plunder. Thus it happened one day that, having gathered a strong force of soldiers, he went to despoil the lands of the people of Sully, near Fleury, and of their neighbours. Returning thence laden with spoil and booty, he happened also to have seized certain goods of the poor belonging to Father Benedict.

Turning aside into an estate of the same Father, called Garminiacum (Germigny), [Col. 1189D] he took up quarters there by force, despite the opposition of the estate’s officers, who told him how severely the Almighty avenged, through the merits of Father Benedict, those who violated that place. Disdaining their words, he ordered the plunder of the poor to be stored about the church there dedicated in honour of the Saviour of the world. This church had a cemetery enclosed by the protection of a rampart.

When the servants of the aforesaid Father demanded back what he had stolen from them, he stubbornly refused to restore anything at all; indeed, he threatened to have them beaten if they did not keep silent, for he was a man of excessive ferocity and arrogance. He therefore ordered a lavish feast to be prepared for himself and his men from the goods of the poor. Since wax was lacking for the lights needed by the diners, he asked whether there were candles in that church. When he was told that there was no wax there except the Paschal candle—offered in the customary solemn manner by the parishioners in honour of the Lord’s Resurrection—he ordered it to be brought at once and an abundant supply of candles to be made from it. He did not fear the affront to the Saviour, to whom both the candle and the church had been consecrated.

Accordingly, after he and his companions had carefully refreshed themselves with wine and various dishes, he went to sleep, sound and unharmed, after idly prolonging his night-watch with tedious conversation. Having passed some hours of the night in light sleep, he was suddenly disturbed by the anguish of illness and cried out for his attendants. As they stood about him, he announced that he was gripped by a mortal sickness. Thus, as the affliction grew worse, he remained in that place through the rest of the night. [Col. 1190D]

When morning came, plainly recognizing that no one, however distinguished by noble blood, could with impunity violate the property of Father Benedict, he mounted a horse as best he could and departed. As the same illness grew worse, he ended his last day—providing sufficient proof of the truth of the saying that there is no respect of persons with God (Rom. 2:11).

### CHAPTER II.—A negligent steward. Punishment for neglecting a church.

There was a steward of that same estate named Vivian, a man barbarous in character and grim in appearance. The care of the aforesaid church, as also of the other affairs of that holding, had been entrusted to him. Considering it superfluous to spend time on such matters, since he did not know how highly one should value the care entrusted to him of holy places, he entirely neglected it, [Col. 1191A] attending rather to exacting an annual profit from the goods of the poor people subject to him.

Thus the enclosure of that oratory, neglected through his carelessness, was protected by no rampart or other barrier; with its doors open, it lay accessible to dogs, swine, and animals of every kind. Vivian was a cultivator of fertile land, rich in possessions and abundant in livestock. Since he was a constant hunter, he kept a pack of dogs skilled in catching small and large wild beasts of various kinds.

One day, therefore, because the entrance lay open and no one opposed it, one of the dogs entered the aforesaid oratory of the Holy Saviour, followed by several others. The first dog to enter saw that a lamp, containing oil poured in to drive away the nighttime darkness of that sacred place, hung low near the pavement. Leaping up, it knocked the lamp down and licked with its tongue the oil that had spilled from the broken lamp. This dog was very dear to its master, since it was of a breed of dogs that overtakes hares by swiftness of foot.

The others rushed in as well, wishing to share this delicacy. Without delay, those which had licked the oil were driven mad. Leaving the oratory—marvellous to relate!—they mingled with other dogs which happened to be in the house or street and made them all rabid. Running about in packs in every direction, they tried to tear with their teeth and rend with their claws every animal they met. Nor was there any respite from their attacks for those dwelling throughout that village until all the dogs [Col. 1191C] had perished by various kinds of death.

### CHAPTER III.—Another punishment. A monk at the end of his life.

Vivian was therefore reproved by friends and by whatever sensible men lived nearby: he was told not to despise the sacred place, but to enclose its precinct and keep his animals from entering it. Yet he gave no heed whatever to their warnings and incurred another, greater loss.

He had a large number of swine—nearly eighty—but refused to appoint a guard lest they enter the sacred place mentioned above. One day, some of them entered the innermost part of the sanctuary and were driven mad. Leaving it, they encountered their whole herd. At once all the pigs, like the dogs above, [Col. 1191D] became insane, so that not one of them ever returned to its accustomed sty in Vivian’s house. You might see them wandering everywhere, their mouths agape, rushing wildly about with the ferocity said to seize that animal when madness comes upon it, defiling with their unclean mouths and trampling underfoot whatever they encountered. Nor did they cease from that frenzy until all were killed by different kinds of death.

The unconquerable patience of the Almighty toward such transgressors deserves reflection: drawing them to repentance, he prefers to exact vengeance from their possessions rather than from themselves. For Vivian afterward became a monk, although only at the end of his life.

### CHAPTER IV.—A thief who wronged the saint pays the penalty.

Now Gaufredus, surnamed Rufus, incited by greed, violently carried off four oxen assigned on that same estate to cultivate newly cleared lands for the revenues belonging to the brethren. When warned to return them, he would by no means consent. Indeed, he threatened to inflict many evils upon those who served Father Benedict.

For as he travelled through the village of the same Father called Bulliacus, he summoned Gauterius, the mayor of that village. Among other mad words which he uttered from his furious mouth, he declared that, as long as he lived, Saint Benedict would never have peace with him. Gauterius, a modest man, answered him thus: “We have endured many threats of this sort, and from all of these the Lord has delivered us through the merit of our most holy lord Benedict; yet no one who vainly uttered such words against him has long rejoiced in having uttered them with impunity.” [Col. 1192B]

Not yet eight days had passed after he had stolen the oxen when, behold, he was surrounded by an enemy of his own, upon whom he too had inflicted very many injuries, and died pierced by a sword. Thereafter he troubled in no respect those who served Father Benedict. “For the wicked,” as Solomon says, “shall be destroyed from the earth, and those who act unjustly shall be taken away from it” (Prov. 2:22).

### CHAPTER V.—The peacock of Abbot Hugh is crippled. A candle made to the peacock’s measure.

While Abbot Hugh [Note: [Col. 1191D] Abbot Hugh is recorded in 1044 in *Gallia Christiana*; he is mentioned again below in chapters 11 and 36.] was still a young man, he did many youthful things because he wished to be considered magnificent. Since he derived his origin from the illustrious stock of the Franks, he thought himself degenerate unless he performed deeds whose manifold renown would strike the ears of the populace. Therefore, among other things, he ordered his servants to gather for him on the above-mentioned estate—namely, Germigny—a great flock of those birds called peacocks.

Obeying their lord’s commands, they ran everywhere, sought out people who kept birds of that kind, and in a short time obtained an abundance of them, by entreaties as well as gifts. Devoting care to their offspring, they gratified their lord’s wishes.

One day, as often happens, one of the males wandered about alone. While roaming here and there, it entered the church of the Holy Saviour mentioned above; walking through it, [Col. 1192D] it suddenly spread its wings and flew up to the altar. As soon as it touched the altar-step, it was immediately crippled in its legs and remained motionless beside the altar.

After several hours, certain persons entering the church found it rolling about beside the altar. Taking it up, they handed it over to those entrusted with feeding the birds. These men received it, reported their bird’s misfortune to their lord, and explained how it had happened. Full of faith, he ordered a wick of tow to be made to the peacock’s measure, from the tip of its beak to the end of its tail, wrapped in wax, lit, and set before the altar at which the injury had occurred.

Fulfilling his commands, they placed the made and lighted lamp before the altar. Before the lamp had burned out, the bird completely recovered its former health. Behold what faith accomplished. Although the Psalm says, “Because thy mercy, O God, is multiplied, saving human beings and beasts” (Ps. 35:7), and blessed Augustine says, “He who saves you also saves your hen,” yet, as the Apostle says, we know that God does not care for such irrational creatures except insofar as the use and necessity of a rational creature require it (1 Cor. 9:9).

### CHAPTER VI.—An evil advocate is punished.

In the district of Porcien is an estate called Arvini Curtis, [Note: [Col. 1193D] Hervini-Curtis, mentioned above in Aimoin, book I, chapter 17. It seems to me to be the village commonly called Harnicourt, in the district of the castle of Porcien, situated on the river Aisne below Regitestum—Rethel—in Champagne. There is there a priory still dependent on Fleury, in the diocese of Reims; the printed editions wrongly give Beauvais.] long possessed by this founder of the monastic order. The advocate of that estate was called Adelard. Although he ought to have protected and defended what had been entrusted to him, [Col. 1193B] he worked more to ruin and destroy it than to rescue it from the violence of others.

With jaws always gaping for the goods of the country people, by lawful means and unlawful he took their possessions and appropriated them for his own use. Nor was it enough for him simply to plunder their goods: he also subjected them to many beatings. Though repeatedly warned by the brethren appointed over that estate that he ought to cease from such great wickedness, he refused to amend and instead flared into still greater cruelty.

He had taken something from a poor woman. She ran to the church, stripped the altar of the linen coverings with which it was covered, and for a long time beat it with rods, reproaching Father Benedict as if he were present in these words: “Benedict, most ancient one, sluggish and lethargic, what are you doing? Why are you asleep? Why do you permit your servants to be subject to such great outrages?” [Note: [Col. 1193D] Is this religion? Such were the practices of those times: when anything had been taken from any church, they stripped the altars, clothed them in haircloth, scourged them, and did other things of this sort. Later this passed into customary use whenever an ecclesiastical interdict was proclaimed. Maurice, archbishop of Rouen, because the property of the church of Rouen had been seized, ordered his entire diocese to be placed under interdict; accordingly, he ordered every image of the Blessed Virgin—indeed, of Christ the Lord as well—throughout his diocese to be set upon a chair or some seat and surrounded with thorns. His letter on this matter is extant in volume II of the *Spicilegium*, p. 521. It is established from p. 821 that this interdict occurred in 1233. Shortly afterward Pope Gregory X abolished this custom, as I showed in the preface to Century II, no. 48.]

Moreover, stirred by the goads of wickedness, he attacked a peasant of great simplicity, named Arnaldus, while the latter was working in his field one day. Seizing the goad with which Arnaldus drove his yoked beasts, he beat him so severely that he left him half dead. Nor, moved by repentance, did he ever wish to appease him with any compensation.

The man who had suffered the beating demanded vengeance upon Adelard from Almighty God, imploring the aid of Benedict, his lord, in this matter. The Lord, who delivers the poor from the powerful, did not delay long in repaying the wicked man according to his wickedness. One day, hearing that his enemies were hastening toward the place [Col. 1193D] where he was, he mounted his horse, armed himself, and hurried to meet them. Put to flight by them, he hastened to leap his horse across a little stream called Minio. Holding the spear which he carried extended far before him and braced upon the ground, he carelessly brought its iron point back toward his own throat. Spurring the horse he rode in his eagerness to cross the stream, he drove the lance into his throat. Immediately dead, he was carried home by his companions, never thereafter to inflict beatings upon the servants of Father Benedict. [Col. 1194A]

### CHAPTER VII.—A perjurious thief is punished.

Another man named Rainerius, one of the collectors on the same estate, likewise proved by the outcome to have been malicious toward the servants of the leader of the monks. Acting often as he ought not, repeatedly oppressing innocent people with false accusations and violently plundering their goods unjustly, he took from a certain widow the one pig she possessed.

When the widow demanded back her pig and repeatedly pleaded, weeping and groaning, that he restore it to her, he would not consent at all. Grieved by this, she continually heaped imprecations upon him. It then happened one day that this same widow unexpectedly entered the house where Rainerius was reclining at table with several others. Since the recollection of her lost animal tormented her with heavy sorrow, she began, as she was accustomed to do, to demand that her pig be restored.

Thinking that what he was about to say could not harm him, he rashly uttered words which he afterward regretted having spoken. He supposed that Father Benedict did not care if someone dared recklessly to violate by words the pledged faith owed to him. “By the oath,” he said, “which I made to Saint Benedict, I have never touched your pig.” [Col. 1194C]

This same Rainerius, in order to obtain the office of collector for the village, had promised by oath, according to the custom of the place, [Note: [Col. 1194D] For the form of the oath sworn by advocates, see the end of the first preface to Century III.] that he would devise nothing unjust against the servants of the Father mentioned above.

After uttering this false oath in perjury, angered, he threw upon the table the knife which he happened to be holding. It rebounded from the table, its point turned upward, struck the perjurer’s eye, and condemned him to permanent blindness. At last the wicked man, after understanding that by divine judgment he had been deprived of sight in one eye, confessed that he had previously spoken falsely, recognizing that the tears of widows, which descend from the cheek to the ground, are by no means to be despised, and that the Almighty Lord is their protector. [Col. 1194D]

### CHAPTER VIII.—The sacred fire is extinguished.

The merciful compassion of the Almighty, who is to be embraced and cultivated with every favour, is one “who corrects whom he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives” (Prov. 3:12). He therefore sometimes permits the spirits of diverse illnesses to rule our bodies, so that, admonished at least by our own suffering, we may remember his merciful patience. If with our whole mind we implore his goodness because of that suffering, he will readily grant our sighs access to himself, unless he foresees that this would harm the growth of our souls. For he rejoices in the salvation of his entire creation.

And if, as Scripture says, people turn to any one of his saints (Job 5:1), he will hear the voice of his faithful one pleading our prayers before him. The wondrous works often shown us through Father Benedict confirm this assertion. [Col. 1195B]

A certain man among the servants of the same Father, named Archembaldus, brother of Hildruardus, steward of Bray—a by no means insignificant possession of the leader of that monastic company—was being consumed by sacred fire. Brought from his village to the most sacred relics of that saint, and with continual groans imploring the aid of the Creator of all things through the merit of his lord, he was restored to the health he desired more swiftly than he had hoped. For when the fire that had already consumed the front part of his foot was extinguished, he returned rejoicing to his home, offering devout tributes of prayer to God the Saviour and extolling with great praises his patron, through whose merits he had obtained healing.

### CHAPTER IX.—A similar case.

Another, a young man from the parts beyond the Loire, afflicted by the same illness, was brought by his mother to Fleury on an ass. He proved to possess a more vigilant faith, for as soon as he knew that he was being burned by the sacred fire, he immediately asked his mother to carry him to Fleury. He believed that through the merit of Father Benedict he could be healed by Almighty God.

Nor did the devotion of his praiseworthy faith deceive him. Brought before the altar of the glorious Mother of God, he was without delay restored, according to his faith, to complete health through the grace of the Ever-Virgin herself and the merit of the pious Father. Thus he returned joyfully with his happy mother, who had accompanied him in grief and deep sorrow. [Col. 1195C]

### CHAPTER X.—A woman who violated the feast is punished and healed.

[Col. 1195D]

The feast of the Purification of Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God—who has always been most pure and most chaste beyond all human purity and chastity—was being celebrated, and it was a Sunday, in the year 1046. A woman named Tescelina, an inhabitant of the village of Fleury, was engaged in spinning wool. As evening was now drawing on, she considered that both the feast itself and Sunday had passed, and wished to gain some small portion of the day for herself. She took up her distaff and, spreading the wool carefully over her knees, moistened it with her dewy saliva and began lightly winding that wool round the distaff.

She took care, however, that her neighbours should not see what she was doing. But the Redeemer of the world, to whose eyes all things are naked and open, severely avenged both the insult to his Mother and the violation of his own Sunday. For when this irreligious woman profaned a day made sacred by this twofold religious observance, her hands were drawn backward and wholly disabled; she experienced in herself the punishment deserved by violators of holy days. Along with the twisting of her hands, she suffered another great torment: she felt an intolerable burning issuing from between her fingers. [Col. 1196A]

As she was tortured by immense sufferings, at the urging of neighbouring women she entered the monastery two days later. Standing before the altar of the Mother of God, she humbly implored the Mother of Mercy with continual sobs to have pity on her. She also frequently called upon Father Benedict to intercede for her. After several hours of the day had passed, her hands returned to their former condition and the burning was extinguished. She gave thanks to God, creator of all things, and to the glorious ever-virgin Mary, not at all forgetting Benedict, lawgiver of the monks. [Col. 1196B]

### CHAPTER XI.—The condition of former serfs. A serf’s flight. A dispute over a serf settled by duel. The rite of the duel.

The aforesaid Abbot Hugh granted to Tescelinus of Pithiviers a man of the household of Father Benedict, named Letardus, so that both he and his descendants should serve Tescelinus forever in servile subjection. Tescelinus, having become his lord, held him for many years.

After a long time, the same nobleman was asked by one of his knights, named Ingrannus, to grant him the aforesaid serf as a benefice; he consented. Ingrannus died and left him to be possessed by his son Isembardus. The aforesaid Letardus fathered a son named Rotbertus, whom Isembardus, as his own household-born serf, fed and raised in his house.

When Rotbertus had grown older, he learned from his parents that he sprang from the household of Father Benedict, but had been sold by the aforesaid abbot as though he were worthless chattel. He grieved and could not long conceal the pain in his heart. Therefore he fled and withdrew himself from Isembardus’s presence.

Unable to remain hidden for long, he was brought home by Isembardus and suffered the penalties customary for a fugitive. In addition, Isembardus bound him by oath not henceforth to refuse to bear the yoke of servitude. Because he had not yet passed beyond the years of adolescence, Rotbertus kept silent for the time, until advancing age gave him strength enough to resist his unjust lord. [Col. 1196D]

When the flower of youth had clothed his cheeks and the years of adolescence had passed, he sought Abbot William (see chapter 25), who was then head of the community at Fleury. Pouring out before him the anguish of his heart with anxious sighs, he complained of the injustice inflicted upon himself and his family.

William was an energetic man, always desiring with all his heart to increase his commonwealth. He replied that he wished to have pity on Rotbertus’s troubles, to lay his just complaints openly before prudent men, and, if possible, to be his support. When Isembardus learned that Rotbertus, whom he believed to be his perpetual serf, had fled to the asylum of his former lords, [Col. 1197A] he ordered the named abbot to restore his own slave to him, otherwise declaring himself thereafter the abbot’s enemy.

William sent messengers to convey his reply: the man whom Isembardus unjustly claimed was a household serf of Father Benedict, and Isembardus had unlawfully possessed him too long. Therefore, if he wished henceforth to hold him as a serf, it was necessary for him to come to court.

When Isembardus heard this, reflecting that he neither ought nor could unjustly resist the abbot, he appointed a day upon which the dispute would be ended. On the appointed day, with many noble and shrewd men gathered on each side, the parties argued long and much; but the claim did not reach a conclusion that day. At length, after many assemblies had first been held, it was adjudged that the matter should be settled by single combat. [Note: [Col. 1197D] In the eleventh century, trial by duel was still in force in cases involving monks, as is evident both from this passage and from several others. André Duchesne provides some examples in his notes to the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, and our Acherius likewise provides some in his notes to Guibert. Memorable in this connection is the diploma granted in 1118 by Louis VI, king of the Franks, to Theobald, abbot of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés: the serfs of that monastery were to have free licence, against all persons, free as well as servile, to give testimony and to fight in every lawsuit. Pope Gregory IX later prohibited this by letters addressed to the abbot and monks of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés.]

A day was appointed for the single combat. They met in the designated place: Rotbertus, who was claimed, and a certain man named Airicus, whom Isembardus put forward in his place, strong in body and a knight by profession. Airicus was tall of stature, but Rotbertus small. Although Rotbertus feared the bulk of the man fighting him, he nevertheless had confidence, as he later related, in Father Benedict, his rightful lord. He kept saying to the hostile man: “I do not fight against you, but my lord Benedict, whose serf I profess myself to be, fights against you.”

Airicus, who attacked him, dealt the first blows, as was customary. Protected by the grace of God, Rotbertus endured them steadfastly [Col. 1197C] and remained unharmed. Attempting in return to strike his enemy, and with the power of the Father—whose name he held in his mind—guiding his hand, he struck forcefully the buckle (*bucula*) of the shield with which his adversary covered himself. [Note: [Col. 1198D] The boss of a shield, where the hand is inserted; commonly *boucle*, whence the French name for a shield, *bouclier*, according to the Bollandist annotation.]

The buckle, torn from the nails fastening it, sprang far away; immediately his adversary’s hand was exposed. There had been an opening in the shield, covered by the buckle, which was fastened inside to a half-foot piece of wood. Holding this in his hand, Rotbertus’s powerful adversary could turn the heavy shield more easily.

Seeing his opponent’s hand exposed, Rotbertus repeated his blow and struck it with all his strength. Unable to bear the pain, the other let go of the shield. Since the hand with which he controlled his defence was disabled, he had no means of protecting himself; worn down by Rotbertus’s incessant blows, [Col. 1197D] he declared himself defeated.

Then, disarmed by the victor, he returned home in confusion with Isembardus, for whom he had entered that shameful contest. Rotbertus thereafter had no doubt that Father Benedict would not fail his own people in adversity. This victory brought no small rejoicing to the people of Fleury, but the greatest confusion to their enemies. In this event the holy Father showed that no one could in any way alienate his household serfs. Let those beware who wickedly distribute to lay persons, or to persons of whatever kind, servants, rents, or estates bestowed upon holy places in order that praise may be rendered to Almighty God. [Col. 1198A]

### CHAPTER XII.—The feast of Saint Benedict’s Translation. Its violator is chastised. The injury remitted after a vow.

The wretched race of people dwelling in the countryside scarcely ever desires to submit its iron neck to Christ’s light yoke. Rather, like a fierce bull, first sensing that the yoke is to be laid upon its untamed neck, kicks against the goad and ploughs crooked furrows; so this race of people, always resisting sacred religion, scarcely ever consents to walk in the way of uprightness.

Thus a certain peasant heard the priest, according to custom, proclaiming the celebrated solemnity of the Translation of Father Benedict, which every year is solemnly commemorated among many nations in July. Disregarding the priest’s command that all his parishioners should keep holiday, he determined to perform agricultural work that day.

He lived on a small estate of Father Benedict called Vinoilum. Rising at dawn, while all his neighbours abstained from manual labour, he alone yoked oxen and went to the field he wished to till. He desired to break up again the field which he had ploughed in winter, so that, softened by summer heat and winter cold, and reduced to dust when its clods were broken by the toothed harrow at sowing-time, it might, after receiving seed, yield a more abundant crop to its cultivator at harvest. [Col. 1198C]

While he performed this desired work, behold, a man in monastic dress stood before him. Seizing both his hands, he bound them so tightly to the forked wood by which the plough is covered that blood issued from every nail, and the peasant could in no way tear his hands from that wood. After doing this, the monk who had appeared was no longer seen by him.

The man, distressed alike by intense pain and shame, was uncertain what to do. When people gathered and marvelled at so great a prodigy—for through the ploughman, who had told them in unrestrained agitation, they had learned what he had seen—they openly observed what had happened to him. Those who had come running inferred from the circumstances, namely the appearance in a monk’s form and the violation of that feast-day, that the leader of the monks had inflicted this punishment on one who had presumed to commit so great an offence.

They urged him to make a vow to the same Father: that as long as he lived he would never violate the saint’s feasts, that he would visit his monastery, and that he would do penance for so great a sin. When he made this vow, and when all whom amazement at so unprecedented an event had drawn together prayed Almighty God for him and repeatedly invoked Father Benedict in a tearful voice [Col. 1199A] to have pity on the wretch, his hands were released. He began to stand free, though a little earlier he had been held bound by invisible cords.

Filled with inexpressible joy, he diligently endeavoured to fulfil the vow he had made. Going to Fleury, he presented himself to Abbot Rainerius [Note: [Col. 1199D] Abbot Rainerius is recorded as having attended the coronation of King Philip in 1059.] and the brethren on the octave of that feast, while Mass was being celebrated, and related what mighty works Almighty God had shown in him through the merits of Benedict, his faithful servant.

They rejoiced with great gladness and proclaimed praises to the Saviour with all earnestness of heart, extolling the great Father with great praises. Having corrected the man with salutary chastisements, they granted him leave to return home. For he had learned that he must by no means despise the warnings of his priest, since the Saviour says of such matters: “Whoever despises you despises me, and whoever hears you hears me” (Luke 10:16). [Col. 1199B]

### CHAPTER XIII.—A bent woman is made upright.

In the district of Troyes there is an estate belonging to the same Father, upon the river Seine. Because an oratory had been built there in his honour, it is called Saint Benedict on the Seine. A woman named Maria lived there. Held by a long illness, her backbone had become contracted, and she was bent so that she could in no way raise her face toward heaven.

She was a native of that estate and sprang from the household of the same Father. Having remained bent in this way for many years, she had already despaired of her recovery and did not dare hope that she could ever again be raised upright.

One Sunday, while standing with the others in that oratory and hearing the celebration of Mass, the Gospel was read. The joints of her spine, long displaced from their proper position, returned to their former state; her back contracted to a shorter form, while her belly, which for a long time had been more tightly contracted, was lengthened. Suddenly she began to stand upright, though for a long time she had walked bent over.

All who were present, and who had known her from childhood and were aware of her infirmity, marvelled at so unexpected a cure. They raised their hands to heaven, praising through Saint Benedict the supreme Maker, who deigns to grant his aid to those who venerate him. [Col. 1199C]

That woman, therefore, extolling the merit of the same Father with much praise, remained in the health she had received until the end of her life. [Col. 1199D]

### CHAPTER XIV.—Speech restored to a monk for confession. The office of provost. Confession, including venial sins. The penalty for delayed confession. Excellent counsel. Viaticum.

Since the remaining matters we record are works of mercy, mercifully bestowed by the almighty Lord through Father Benedict, we have nevertheless judged it worthy to relate one [Col. 1200A] that may properly be called a work of mercy—both because of its own importance and because, should the need ever arise, it ought likewise to be imitated; and so that the compassionate mercy of Father Benedict may be made clearer, which, prompted by his teaching, he more readily bestows upon those who hasten to submit their necks to Christ’s light yoke.

There was a monk of our congregation named Humbald. While still a young man, and apparently energetic in his affairs, he had obtained charge of certain estates subject to the monastery of Fleury—namely Almericourt and its dependencies. Having remained provost there for nearly three years [Note: [Col. 1199D] Provostships were instituted for the purpose that a provost, assisted by one or two companions, might administer an estate, as will elsewhere, God willing, be discussed more fully. Meanwhile, see Brower, *Antiquities of Fulda*, book I, chapter 7.], he decided one day, as was his custom, to revisit Fleury, eager to learn whether all was going well among his fellow citizens.

While undertaking the journey [Col. 1200B], he happened to fall seriously ill on the road. Yet he yielded in no way to his suffering; though his sickness grew worse daily, he at last, nearly dying and exhausted by extreme fatigue, brought his body to Fleury, having at last achieved the desire he had long cherished. There, as his strength was broken by illness and he lay in bed, the brothers visited him and admonished him, mindful of himself at the end, to confess his own sins to the abbot or to any of the elders he chose.

But, imitating the raven’s cry, he began to promise that on the morrow he would do what he was urged to do. I wonder indeed what forgetfulness had settled upon his mind, when this ought above all to be every Christian’s concern—especially a monk’s—if he has sinned, as is human, that he should immediately hasten to the remedy, namely by confessing his own [Col. 1200C] sin to some religious man. Even if, by the gift of the Almighty, he is held free from harmful crimes, it is nevertheless the safeguard of humility to believe oneself guilty and to confess at every hour, according to the ordinances of his Rule (*Rule of St Benedict*, chapter 4); especially when even a slight illness strikes, so that he may always consider himself more secure in regard to himself.

Thus this sick man of whom we began to speak, urged again and again about the same matter even by his closest friends, continually put it off until tomorrow, as he did with other promises. By no means could they draw from him any consent to apply to himself the remedies of confession. He continued to answer thus until, having lost his voice, he immediately ceased to speak.

When the brothers then discovered that he had become mute, they were dismayed in spirit and did not know where to turn, fearing that the conscience of that brother was stained by some very great crime [Col. 1200D], which he had not dared to reveal even at the last. Accordingly, when the question was raised in chapter what ought to be done in this matter, all fearing for the brother’s salvation, one of them, named Gauzbertus [Note: [Col. 1200D] “Gaurbertus” in the printed editions, incorrectly. He had been, if I am not mistaken, abbot of Ferrières, and is mentioned above in the Life of St Aldric, bishop of Sens. If this is so, he is placed far out of sequence in the printed editions, where he is counted sixteenth. That regular discipline was especially relaxed in his time is clear from the said Life. This accords sufficiently with the present passage.], a God-fearing man who had also exercised the office of abbot, but, unable to reform the habits of those subject to him, had resigned a title he held to no purpose and sought Fleury out of love for Father Benedict, spoke as follows [Col. 1201A]:

“I am astonished, brothers, that you, wise men, should be so uncertain about this matter, when you have present with you so great a patron, the author of your Rule, illustrious in the prerogative of miracles. If therefore my counsel pleases you, let us enter the monastery [Note: [Col. 1201D] That is, the church, as is evident from the course of the context.], prostrate ourselves upon the ground before him, and through him appease the wrath of the supreme Judge by chanting a litany with seven psalms.”

Having heard the exhortation of this wise man, the brothers cried out that what he suggested should be done. Therefore, prostrate on the pavement before the Father’s tomb, they chanted the litany with seven psalms. When these had been completed, they sent to the sick brother a certain man of sound mind, named Milo. When he called him by his own name, the sick man, as though awakened from the sleep of death, opened his eyes and immediately, his speech restored, answered him. Then [Col. 1201B], when admonished, he confessed his sins. When this had been done, he received the provision for his salvation—that is, the body and blood of the Lord—and departed this life. The brothers, greatly rejoicing, gave thanks to almighty God, who through the merit of Father Benedict had deigned so wonderfully to help their brother who was about to perish.

## CHAPTER XV.—A robber excommunicated. Despising excommunication, he perishes miserably.

Alberic, one of the leading men of the castle of Châtillon [Note: [Col. 1201D] Commonly Châtillon-sur-Loing, above the town of Montargis, on the river Loing, in the district of Gâtinais in Burgundy.], which stands upon the little river Loing, driven by the goads of madness, repeatedly ravaged by frequent plundering the estates of the often-mentioned Father, especially those adjoining the estate of La Cour Marigny [Note: [Col. 1201D] The estate of Marigny below, commonly *la Cour Marigny*, [Col. 1202D] in the diocese of Sens, in the deanery of Gâtinais; Bordelles also belongs to it, which, if I am not mistaken, the author below calls Malumtalentum, “Evil Counsel,” on account of its indecent secular name. Adrevald mentions Marigny more than once.].

For this reason Abbot Rainerius [Col. 1201C], together with the brothers dwelling under him, sent word that he should correct what he had done and take care in future not to commit such acts against Father Benedict. He treated their commands as nothing and added worse deeds to his evil ones. The brothers grieved that the Father, so often to be named, should be held in contempt and that his servants should be abused. Having taken counsel together, they punished that robber and those sharing with him in this crime with the sword of anathema, unless he should desist and repair what he had neglected [Note: [Col. 1202D] On the rite of excommunication observed at that time, see the preface to this Century.].

But he persisted in evil and despised their excommunication as some trifling matter. Hardened in mind, he refused to repair what he had neglected and would not cease from his perversity. Therefore the Almighty, who does not despise the cries of the humble and who looks down from on high upon the groans of widows and orphans, deigned to console his servants in [Col. 1201D] this distress.

It happened that the aforesaid robber was leading Count Theobald’s army against the inhabitants of a castle which secular men call by an indecent name, but which we, to whom foul speech is forbidden, call Malumtalentum, “Evil Counsel.” As he was advancing as leader in the first division, by the aforesaid estate of Marigny, its frightened inhabitants, seeing a man hostile to them approaching with so great a multitude of soldiers, came out armed to meet him [Col. 1202A] at suitable positions in that village, lest, having open access, he might inflict some danger upon them.

Angered by this, the wicked man swore solemnly that, after completing the business toward which he was proceeding, he would carry them all away as captives and moreover burn the whole village. The men replied:

“It is clear that you have great power and desire to harm us. But God, through the merits of our lord Benedict, whose servants we are, has power to deliver us mightily from the calamities with which you threaten us.”

With a threatening cry, that wretched man spurred his horse and continued toward his destination. Whereas he ought to have implored Father Benedict in a suppliant voice to aid him, lest he perish in such danger, he instead declared that he would threaten the Father’s servants with plunder [Col. 1202B], seize their goods, and burn their dwellings with fire.

When he reached the castle mentioned above, he attacked it with the first troop that he commanded—for the rest of the army, together with the count, was following far behind—and began to harass those inside with arrows and various missiles. But the armed inhabitants of the castle came out through its gates and proved stoutly resistant in what followed. A man of the opposing side drew his bow and shot an arrow at Alberic. Struck by it, he immediately fell from the horse he rode, collapsing forward over one of his knees so that his helmet struck the ground. He died and was permitted to perish with the threats he had vainly uttered against our Father; indeed, after receiving the wound, he was unable to say anything [Col. 1202C].

Such recompense did the God of vengeance render to the proud (*Psalm* 93).

## CHAPTER XVI.—An excommunicated man is absolved after death. Another robber will perish miserably.

Seguinus, likewise a brother of this Alberic of whom we have spoken, both in flesh and in malice, was in no way frightened by the terrible death of his brother. Indeed, he became more wicked than his brother, daring greater things against our Father and assailing his servants with manifold cruelty. After his brother’s killing, he came to Fleury to obtain absolution for him; and, having obtained it, promised that thereafter he would be faithful and would give much from his own property. But he lied in everything: instead of faithful he became faithless; instead of a giver, a robber.

Following then in his brother’s crooked path, he too began to commit robberies [Col. 1202D] upon Father Benedict’s possessions, taking such of his servants as he could and plundering their goods, as though he sought vengeance for his brother from Father Benedict’s servants. Though repeatedly admonished to desist from his wickedness, he would not comply in any way.

At last, one day, while he was driving off a herd of swine as plunder from land adjoining the estate of Marigny, men were sent to demand back what was theirs and urge him to make restitution. When they departed, they found him in [Col. 1203A] his house. This house was a wooden tower, for he was a powerful man, one of the nobler inhabitants of the same castle to which Alberic had belonged.

The tower had an upper story, a *solarium* [Note: [Col. 1203D] That *solarium* means an upper chamber is established by countless examples. An excellent one occurs in King Guntram’s charter concerning the endowment of the monastery of St Marcellus at Chalon, where it is ordered that they make for it a *solarium* with a heated chamber from Gergy and Alciat.], where Seguinus lived with his household, conversed, dined, and slept at night. In its lower part was a cellar containing storerooms of various kinds, suitable for receiving and preserving the necessities of human sustenance. The floor of the upper chamber, as is customary, was formed of hewn beams: rather slight in thickness, somewhat broad in width, but very great in length.

Those who had been sent found the man in this upper chamber. Approaching him, they began gently [Col. 1203B] to recount what had been charged to them. But he paid no attention whatever to their message. Savage in spirit, he answered furiously, declaring with dreadful oaths that he intended to set upon the monastery of St Benedict a fire of such force that it would burn its towers and consume every building adjoining them.

He spoke these words while standing upon the end of one of the beams which, as we said, formed the floor of the upper chamber. He had scarcely vomited them from his poisoned mouth when the end of the beam on which he stood gave way, while its other end was lifted aloft. He fell headfirst below with such a fall that his head was driven between two chests in the cellar—which, as we said, lay beneath the upper chamber—like a wedge driven into wood; the rest of his body was thrown back over one of those chests [Col. 1203C].

A cry arose, and the household servants rushed into the cellar. They found their lord had breathed out his life with his neck broken. Carrying him back upstairs, they shed the bitterest tears for his sudden death. By this end, “the mouth speaking iniquity was stopped” (*Psalm* 62:12). In this faithless man the ancient power of the same Father was renewed: when Florentius fell, the whole structure of the house remained unharmed except for the upper chamber upon which Florentius stood (*Gregory*, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 8). So too when this man fell, the entire tower remained intact; only the beam upon which he stood suffered collapse.

## CHAPTER XVII.—The immunity of St Benedict’s cemetery. Punishment for stolen grain.

There is a small estate in the district of Le Mans called Alsonia [Note: [Col. 1204D] Alsonia, Ausson, is a village in the diocese of Sens, in the deanery of St Florentin; the church of this village belongs to the monastery of Fleury. Therefore the district of Le Mans must be located here, unless the printer has erred; more correctly, it is the district of Leomans.], long ago granted to Father Benedict by the worthy man Leotbert. There the same Father, through grace given him by God, displayed such a multitude of miracles that all the people of that region honour the place with the greatest devotional reverence.

They set up rather tall crosses around the cemetery, which no one pursuing an enemy, however deadly the hatred holding him, dares cross if that enemy has fled for refuge to [Col. 1204A] the church built there. Fugitives, murderers, and anyone else compelled by the distress of some guilt to seek refuge in that place remain immune so long as they keep themselves within the bounds of the cemetery. No one dares steal anything or perpetrate any fraud upon anyone in that precinct.

It happened one day that hunters of a certain nobleman named Adelard, the advocate of that estate, were returning from hunting and rested there with their tired dogs. Since they had nothing with which to feed their dogs, they brought their complaint to a prudent man named Isaac, whom the brothers of Fleury had placed in charge of the property. When he answered that he did not know what they could do, they said that they would take one sextarius of Father Benedict’s grain [Col. 1204B], which was stored in that place, so that food might be prepared from it for the dogs.

He replied that they could not do this with impunity; he absolutely did not consent to such rashness and feared that, should it occur, the punishment soon to follow their presumption would fall back upon him. They treated his words as nothing, took as much grain as seemed good to them, ground it into flour by the turning of millstones, and made food from it for their beasts. When these had been filled with such food, as night approached they shut them together in a small building.

At dawn they arose from their beds, wishing to resume their customary pursuit of hunting. Approaching the room where they had shut in their dogs, they opened its door [Col. 1204C]. Looking inside, they saw that the dogs had died: some lay stretched full-length upon the floor; others lay dead with their mouths turned upward; still others clung to the wall of the building with their forefeet, their heads bent back over their shoulders.

Seeing this, some raised a cry and beat their thighs with their palms; others clasped their hands together and uttered a loud sound with mournful voices. For they feared that their lord would justly impose punishment on them for the loss of the dogs. Having long remained in bewildered astonishment and lamentation, they finally departed, intending to report to their lord the misfortune that had befallen them and how severe an avenger Father Benedict had shown himself against them.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—A similar occurrence concerning a meadow.

At another time [Col. 1204D], as knights were passing by the same village at the hour of their midday meal, they turned aside there. While some were preparing food and all things suitable for those about to eat, one of them said to his squire:

“Why, most worthless of men, has such laziness overcome you that you do not provide some fodder for your horses while the necessities for our meal are being prepared?”

He replied that he did not know from whom he might ask for hay or straw. “Go,” said his master, “to St Benedict’s meadow adjoining this [Col. 1205A] village. Gather a bundle of grass as large as you alone can lay upon a horse’s neck, bring it back, and set it before your animals.”

Obeying his master’s commands, he borrowed a scythe from someone and hurried into the meadow. With all his strength he cut the grass, that he might return as quickly as possible and not be deprived of his companions’ meal. Meanwhile, while he persisted in this unlawful work, one of the villagers saw him and quickly ran to report it to the aforementioned Isaac, the village’s steward; for that meadow adjoined Isaac’s house.

When Isaac saw the squire cutting the meadow’s grass with a scythe, he shouted from afar in a loud voice: “Who are you, wicked man, who have rashly entered St Benedict’s meadow in violation of right? Leave, pestilent fellow, quickly, lest divine vengeance more swiftly destroy you.”

But despising the warning voice, he burst out in these profit-seeking words [Col. 1205B]: “St Benedict,” he said, “will pardon me this small offence on this occasion.” Having made a bundle of grass, he returned to his lodging and gave fodder to his animals. Then he hurried to the house where his companions were feasting and feasted with them.

When the food had been consumed and breakfast ended, each mounted his own horse and they hastened to proceed where they had intended. But the despiser of Father Benedict was the last of all to leave the village. I believe that some grass was still left which he was waiting for his horse to consume. At length, in order to join his companions, who were already some distance away, he spurred his horse and tried to catch them. But before he had left the village, the horse fell headlong to the ground and died with its neck broken. The rider [Col. 1205C] also fell; his thigh was broken, and he could not rise from the ground except when lifted by others’ arms.

A crowd gathered at this sudden vengeance of divine judgment, and Isaac too was present. Rebuking the wretch, he said: “Did I not tell you, miserable man, that Blessed Benedict does not long leave his injuries unavenged? But because you refused to believe me, behold: you lie helpless, your limbs broken.”

## CHAPTER XIX.—A penitent bound with iron is loosed at Fleury.

A certain man, fearing the day of final judgment because of crimes he had committed, had his arms bound in iron [Note: [Col. 1205D] We have seen several examples of this kind of penance, which still flourished in the eleventh century, in the preface to Century II, no. 41, and above in book III of *The Deeds of St Conwoion, Abbot*.]. To appease for himself the fear of the supreme Judge, he travelled through very many regions and sought the shrines of many saints, beseeching them with frequent groans that the crimes for which his conscience reproached him might be blotted out [Col. 1205D].

Though he diligently continued this course for several years, and though it must faithfully be believed that the blessed ones whose commemorations he had visited prayed to the Almighty for absolution of his sins, he appeared to have experienced no manifest aid from any of them. For this was his belief: once his sin had been remitted by the merciful Judge, the release of his arms would immediately follow.

As he travelled about in every direction, trusting that Father Benedict’s aid would benefit him, he reached Fleury. Entering the greater church [Col. 1206A], where the most sacred bones of that Father rest, he made devout offerings of prayer to God before each altar as he went round them. When he came to the altar of the Mother of God [Note: [Col. 1206D] They call it the morning altar; it is still seen behind the altar of St Benedict.], behind which stood the altar of the often-named Father, he stretched his hands to heaven and earnestly prayed to almighty God that his debts might be forgiven him, frequently invoking the Mother of God together with that Father.

While intent upon that prayer, suddenly the nail by which the iron bond was fastened broke, and the iron sprang onto the pavement with a clatter. Seeing himself released, and understanding that in this visible release the invisible bonds of his sins had been loosed, he rejoiced exceedingly with unspeakable joy, proclaiming praise to almighty God and [Col. 1206B] rendering countless thanksgivings to the Mother of God and Father Benedict.

## CHAPTER XX.—The pestilence is remitted when the relics of St Maurus are carried barefoot.
