Because of the weight of sins, it once happened that an extremely intense drought continued for several months, while the sun’s star, by its heat, scorched all things more fiercely than usual. Consequently, the people of Fleury were grievously afflicted by a most severe pestilence raging among them for some time.

You might see houses empty, after the master of the household suddenly perished with his children and his entire household; you might see storehouses overflowing with wine and chests filled with wheat, yet no one dared touch them, as all people withered away in fear of the plague that had come upon them. The very person with whom you had just been speaking, you would immediately see or hear had died [Col. 1206C] by an unheard-of manner of death. Someone would feel himself pierced by a sudden stabbing pain—in the shoulders, arms, thigh, breast, or belly—and immediately fall to the ground and die.

This unremitting plague had held Fleury for several monthly cycles. Therefore both the brothers and all the people of the place resolved to carry in litany the sacred body of the most renowned martyr Maurus to the mother church of the borough. This church had been consecrated to Christ in honour of Sebastian, Christ’s witness. They trusted that the Saviour, appeased by the merits of his faithful servant whose relics they carried and by the prayers of Father Benedict, would have mercy upon his people.

On the appointed day, barefoot and bathed in tears, the sacred order and the people, including children and women [Col. 1206D], came with litany to the aforesaid church. Two clergy, as was customary, carried the blessed martyr’s body on their shoulders. How many groans were then poured out from the depths of hearts, how many tears shed, and how many vows of prayer offered to almighty God is exceedingly difficult to recount.

When the celebration of Mass had been completed according to custom, each returned home, awaiting the immeasurable mercy of almighty God; and it was not long absent. For immediately, when the dry north wind had been driven out, the moist south wind, flying freely over the fields of Fleury, moistened with dewy wings all things that the heat of the sun had made dry [Col. 1207A], watering the parched ground with abundant rain. It also refreshed the bodies of people and of all other animals with its welcome moderation and entirely extinguished their heat.

When the excessive heat of the sun ceased, the hateful plague too ceased; thereafter, beyond the usual course, no one died in that place at that time. Those delivered from so great a calamity rendered due praise to almighty God with all their hearts, giving fitting thanks to Blessed Maurus the martyr and to Father Benedict.

## CHAPTER XXI.—A similar event. The shrine washed with wine.

After a few days had passed, the same pestilential plague invaded the inhabitants [Col. 1207B] of the castle called Gordanicum, situated in the district of Bourges. The sun exerted greater force than usual and scorched the land of Gaul with such heat that springs which had flowed through almost all the preceding age dried up and could no longer furnish their accustomed drink to the inhabitants. The earth, split everywhere by gaping cracks, opened innumerable chasms deeper than usual.

Accordingly, broad rivers which, like a great abyss, had been accustomed to carry laden ships, had their channels dried up; navigation was lost, and they afforded a crossing to a twelve-year-old boy, should he need to pass over on foot. What need is there to recount the burning of the meadows? In summer these are normally clothed in grasses beautiful in green colour, emulating the appearance of an emerald; but, scorched by the sun’s heat, they were so dry as though they had never possessed any [Col. 1207C] moisture.

A deadly plague accompanied calamities so many and so great as our age had not experienced. It daily produced innumerable deaths among human bodies, and it afflicted especially the inhabitants of the aforesaid castle, while the other disasters held sway over almost the whole Gallic world. In that castle appeared nothing but the image of death: all was full of grief, full of mourning, full of pain. There was no laughter, no joy of heart, no cheerfulness of face; everyone walked with eyes cast down to the ground. No voices of those rejoicing were heard there; no clear songs of women leading dances rang out. There were no crowds in the streets; and, strangely, in so populous a town, with fear of death running through all, you would see scarcely any gatherings, or none at all [Col. 1207D].

Women’s finery, children’s playfulness, youths’ high spirits, and the varied ornament of clothing had been changed into black garments. Nor without reason: scarcely a house there could be found free of a corpse. The person with whom you were then discussing something became a corpse shortly afterward. When someone dies, we normally seek gravediggers to arrange burial for the dead; but there, before it was known who would be laid in them, very many graves were dug by those who performed that office, quite certain that they could not be cheated of payment for their labour.

Pressed by these and even greater evils, the townspeople of the castle just mentioned finally recalled how almighty God, through the blessed martyr Maurus and with the merits of Father Benedict accompanying him, had delivered the people of Fleury from a most bloody plague in earlier years [Col. 1208A]. Having taken counsel, they decided to send prudent men to Fleury to communicate the people’s common prayers to the brothers of Fleury, asking that the worshippers of Christ should not delay in aiding a people perishing in crowds, by bringing to them the body of the aforesaid martyr together with relics of Father Benedict.

When the envoys came to Fleury and set forth in order the matter for which they had come, it seemed hard to the brothers to remove the glorious martyr from Fleury and separate him from it by even a small distance, since after their most holy Father their greatest hope rested in him. Yet it seemed harsher to all whose counsel was sound that they should allow so great a people—especially one devoted to Father Benedict—to perish [Col. 1208B], particularly as they were certain that help could quickly be given them and retained confidence in the faith of those making the request.

Accordingly, some devout brothers took the most renowned martyr with the most sacred pledges of Father Benedict, surrounded by an honourable company of both clerics and laypeople, as befitted so great a martyr, and came to their intended destination. When the people of Gordanicum, to whom they were travelling, learned of their arrival, persons of every sex and age rushed to meet them: decrepit old men supporting their bent limbs with staffs, and little children whom age had only recently made able to take part in public gatherings. With every word they could, they begged for swift help.

For immeasurable joy filled their hearts because they beheld the relics of most blessed Maurus [Col. 1208C], which they had desired with their whole mind to see, now confident of salvation through him whom they had heard had such power with almighty God. The canons of St Satyrus also came in procession with the greatest rejoicing, clothed in white vestments and overlaid with silken copes, with crosses, candles, and censers steaming with incense carried before them.

The most blessed martyr was led by this multitude of people to the upper part of the castle, which, as those who saw it remember, stood on the height of a steep hill. Barrels were set out on the plain of the town, and wine was brought competitively in amphorae and other vessels suited to carrying wine, and poured into them, so that the shrine containing the blessed martyr’s body might be washed. From this drink—*saint vinage*, “holy wine”—as though it had been infused with the sacred body itself, or were some medicinal preparation, all might drink [Col. 1208D].

You could see crowds of both sexes and every age converging, carrying goblets, cups, bowls, and vessels of every kind to receive the drink. Each person, having received a draught of that remedy in his own cup, carried none of it home to those who remained there before he himself had been sufficiently refreshed. For he feared that if even a short delay intervened after he had received it, the sudden plague might destroy him. Indeed, whoever could drink more of it hoped to obtain greater health.

When all had been abundantly refreshed by it—the castle, moreover, abounds above others in wine, and everyone rejoiced who could provide it—they urgently begged [Col. 1209A] that the blessed martyr be carried through the streets and lanes of the town, so that the pestilential plague, fleeing from his presence, might be driven from all its quarters. When this was done, the wind immediately began with a gentle breath to gather the air into clouds, and then the sky grew dark with their thickness. Without delay, as rain commonly falls in April with the soft murmur of breezes, most welcome rain poured down in a gentle fall into the bosom of the thirsty earth, driving away the harmful heat of the sun which had long held sway over the world in mourning.

The deadly calamity was immediately expelled. As the blessed martyr traversed those regions, the plague, which had wrought many deaths there in an unprecedented manner, thereafter dared touch no one there in an unusual manner. Delivered from their dreadful danger, they rejoiced with such joy as cannot readily be expressed [Col. 1209B], rendering songs of praise to almighty God, who through his most faithful witness had deigned to rescue them from the peril of sudden death.

Nevertheless, bound by love of our lawgiver, they extolled his merit in lofty proclamation, since he had merited to have so great a companion, through whom, with the Father’s prayers joined, they had escaped their imminent death. Therefore anyone can judge how great were the offerings of gifts, when each hastened to offer his chief possessions lest another appear more devout than he. For three days they kept their health-bringing guest, so that, made more certain of the granted salvation, no fear of the plague might remain in their minds.

Finally, on the fourth day, with hymns and songs worthy of so great a martyr [Col. 1209C], they escorted his shrine for a considerable distance along the road; bidding him farewell, they returned home. The brothers, returning to Fleury, told those who remained what great deeds almighty God had performed through the merits of his faithful servants. Rejoicing, they then rendered praise to the Creator of all, earnestly commending themselves to the prayers of the blessed martyr and their Father.

## CHAPTER XXII.—Where the arms of St Maurus are kept. A perjurer punished. Oaths upon relics.

Let no one consider it burdensome if we append two chapters in praise of this most holy martyr now under discussion, relating the wondrous works which almighty God deigned to show through him in two regions far [Col. 1209D] removed from Fleury, where his most sacred pledges are kept. But first the matter must briefly be made known to those ignorant of it.

When his venerable relics had been translated to Fleury, the brothers of Fleury placed two venerable bones of his arms in two possessions under their jurisdiction, namely for their aid and protection. One of these is called Diacus, Die, situated in Burgundy, in the territory of Tonnerre; the name of the other, although it is less fitting to record it in writing [Col. 1210A], because it is barbarous, we have nevertheless written down in its barbarous form as it is pronounced: it is called Pontons, situated in Gascony.

At Die there was a steward of that place named Joscelin. Since in many matters he acted improperly—concealing his lords’ dues, fraudulently appropriating the revenues of the fields, and stealing the goods of peasants entrusted to him—he was repeatedly rebuked and warned to correct his wicked conduct. Since he was not corrected, he was compelled by Rainerius, then provost of that estate and later abbot, to render account of certain matters he had managed dishonestly.

After the question concerning these matters had been examined in judicial fashion, it was decided that he must refute by oath the accusations made against him, since he denied everything of which he was charged [Col. 1210B]. He answered that he would readily swear the oath. Without further delay, the aforesaid provost ordered the relics of the blessed martyr mentioned above to be brought before them.

But miserable Joscelin, although his own conscience reproached him, compelled by fear of his provost, rashly presumed to lay his hand upon the sacred pledges. When the oath had been completed as those who had adjudged it to be made prescribed, the wicked perjurer, now confident because divine vengeance had not immediately struck him, cheerfully and with insolent words seized the long beard that reached down to his chin and said: “By this beard I have safely sworn the oath.”

When he had said this, the entire beard followed the hand with which he had grasped it [Col. 1210C], and for the remainder of his life his chin remained wholly deprived of a beard. Thus, when his faithlessness was made clearer than daylight, he rightly lost his stewardship; thereafter neither he nor his descendants could serve as steward. He learned that the blessed martyr possessed wondrous power, whom before he had not honoured with due reverence.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—A violator of a church is punished. The audacity of the Poitevins.

Moreover, while the count of Poitiers [Note: [Col. 1209D] Namely William, eighth of that name—ninth according to others—who set out for the Holy Land in 1101, and whose banner, according to Orderic Vitalis, *History*, book X, was said to have been followed by thirty thousand armed men. William’s wife was Philippa-Matilda, as the Bollandist editors observed.] was leading many thousands of armed men on the Jerusalem expedition, his wife was administering the provinces subject to her authority. Thus it happened that, while travelling through Gascony, she crossed the Garonne and reached the borders of that region, in which lies the place mentioned above, Pontons [Note: [Col. 1210D] Commonly Saint-Maur de Pontons, described in printed books as a priory of the diocese of Agen; more correctly, here, of Auch (*d’Auch*), since it is said to lie upon the river Adour, vernacularly *l’Adour*.], that is, in the district of Auch, on the river Adour, subject to the jurisdiction of the brothers of Fleury, where, as we have said, the relics of the already-mentioned most renowned martyr are kept. Necessity of travel accordingly inviting her, the countess, surrounded by a company of soldiers, took lodging there.

When the arrival of the Poitevins three days beforehand became known, the inhabitants of those places, fearing them—for they held their lordship in especial hatred—brought in all their possessions that could be carried into the church, and piled them up in the chapel of that estate: various kinds of clothing, provisions, and other things suitable for human use [Col. 1211A]. The Poitevins, once lodged there, heard that the country people had, as stated, placed all their goods in the church. Although that nation was headlong enough in attempting every unlawful act, the rest nevertheless feared to violate the holy place. One of them, bolder than the others, rushed into the church, put a sack full of grain upon his shoulders, and, burdened with sacrilege, returned to his lodging—not, however, to rejoice long in such a deed.

For as soon as he crossed the threshold of his quarters, all his limbs began to shake like those of persons afflicted with quartan fever; an intolerable chill spreading through his whole body bound all his limbs in icy rigidity [Col. 1211B]. The inhabitants of that place, who knew more certainly why so sudden a sickness had come upon him—for they were fully aware of the great powers of the blessed martyr—urged the wretch to restore the grain which he had violently taken from the church. They obtained with difficulty the fulfilment of what they urged; but the blessed martyr was in no way appeased by his unwilling repentance.

Therefore, when the Poitevins departed from that place with their lady on the next day, the wretched man, fearing to remain there, proceeded with them as best he could. But as he went along the road with his companions, gradually seized by a dreadful madness, he began, with an insatiable dog-like bite, to tear his own arms. Those wishing to restrain him were wholly unable to do so. While he persisted in such madness, they came to a river. As the others crossed the ford, the wretch voluntarily threw himself into the river and perished, drowned in the water [Col. 1211C], striking great terror into his companions and making them thereafter cautious not to presume further to become violators of holy places.

There were indeed many more things that might be said concerning this most excellent martyr. But lest some opponent should wish to frame an accusation against us, saying that we have exceeded our purpose because, when we ought to relate the wonderful deeds of Father Benedict, we have narrated certain acts of blessed Maurus, let us return to what was omitted above. Yet we do not fail to know that Father Benedict shared in those things which we have singularly attributed to blessed Maurus: for they rest in the same church [Col. 1211D] and have received the same places to protect; and the same estates in which we have said that the blessed martyr performed the reported miracles are subject to Fleury itself. By the gift of almighty God, each became patron of that place.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—Historical Matters. Soldiers Who Violated a Church Are Punished.

When Queen Matilda passed the bounds of life, King Henry took in marriage Anna, daughter of the king of the Rusʹ, Ladislaus. She bore him three sons: Philip, Robert, and Hugh. Robert died while still a little boy; Hugh afterwards obtained the county of Vermandois [Col. 1212A]; but Philip, upon his father’s death, acquired the governance of the whole kingdom of the Franks. He was seven years old when his father died. [Note: [Col. 1211D] Philip was therefore born in 1053, for Henry his father died in 1040.] The most illustrious Baldwin, Count of Flanders, called Baldwin V of Lille, accordingly received his guardianship. Administering the affairs of the kingdom most prudently until Philip reached years of understanding, he subdued, by counsel and arms alike, the tyrants springing up throughout all France, and caused a profound peace to prevail.

Accordingly, when Philip had become a young man, Baldwin restored the kingdom entire, without the loss of a single hamlet; and he himself not long afterward ended his life. Philip, indeed, performed many deeds vigorously in his early years; but as age advanced and the weight of his flesh burdened him, he devoted greater attention to food and sleep than to warfare. He married Bertha, daughter of the duke [Col. 1212B] of Frisia, who bore him Louis.

Certain nobles of the Franks rebelled against him, trusting in the wealth and strength of William, king of the English. Among them Hugh of Le Puiset took up arms against him, gathering many helpers to himself. The king, wishing to restrain his audacity, assembled a force of soldiers from every side. Among the other auxiliaries, he ordered an army to come from Burgundy. Having received the command, they hastened into France: namely Odo, duke of Burgundy; William, count of Nevers; Geoffrey, bishop of Auxerre; and very many others whom we have judged it too lengthy to enumerate. Setting out upon their intended route, they took lodging at an estate of Father Benedict called Evera [Note: [Col. 1211D] Evera: Yèvre-le-Châtel, in the diocese of Orléans, [Col. 1212D] where there was a priory subject to Fleury.], [Col. 1212C].

Now, as country people customarily fear, cry out, flee in every direction, and hide their possessions in safer places at the arrival of soldiers, so, especially amid so great a tumult, the peasants of the aforesaid district carried all their goods to the church, both grain and assorted household goods. After the companies of soldiers had refreshed bodies weary from the journey with food, they sought provisions for their horses and discovered that the villagers had hidden their entire supply of grain in the church. Dejected, they reported the entire matter in order to the leaders of the army: the peasants had moved the hope of their subsistence to a safer harbour—the church, that is—and were wholly unwilling either to give or sell them provisions necessary for their mounts.

The leaders, at a loss for counsel, did not know what to do. For they neither wished nor presumed to become violators of holy places [Col. 1212D]. Then the bishop, who ought to have been more cautious than the rest, driven by youthful rashness, asked in a mocking tone whether the people had carried that grain into the church. When he was answered, “Yes,” he said, “Then let men take it out.” He therefore ordered the swift men [Note: [Col. 1212D] Thus in the Bollandists. Boscius has *perpetuos*, which he thought the name of a military office.] to go and provide their horses with as much barley as necessity required. They hurried to the church, violently removed the barley from it, and supplied it as fodder to the horses.

On the next day they proceeded toward their destination, believing that they had incurred no injury from Father Benedict for the violation of that place and the wrong done to his people [Col. 1213A]. But while the king, with the remaining legions of soldiers, hastened toward Le Puiset, they too joined him. Both they and the king pitched camp around the castle itself. After the castle had been besieged, many assaults made, and several days spent there, on a certain day those who seemed shut in—Hugh, namely, with his men—opened the gates and unexpectedly came upon the besiegers, resounding with every tumult of war, while trumpeters likewise sounded with a terrifying blast.

Those in the camp, terrified by the enemy’s sudden boldness, believed that the military cohorts of all France had entered that castle by night, and that Hugh had therefore ventured upon so great an exploit. What more need be said? They turned their backs and entrusted themselves to the protection of flight, leaving tents of different kinds full of varied equipment [Col. 1213B], and everything else which they had brought for so great an expedition. Seeing them flee—something they had never before presumed even to conceive, that so great a multitude could be routed by so few—the enemy pursued more fiercely.

Very many noblemen were captured in that flight, especially men of the Burgundian army, who had dared to wrong Father Benedict by plundering his estate. Finally, the bishop who had impelled the others to commit this wicked act by his mocking words was captured together with the count of Nevers, his father, and was forced to ransom himself for no small sum of money. At last released from captivity, he went to Fleury and confessed that he had acted foolishly and that what had happened to him had happened justly [Col. 1213C]. He asked forgiveness and obtained it.

In that flight one might have seen fulfilled what is read at the end of Deuteronomy among the curses which Moses, the man of God, pronounced upon the people of Israel if they should ever depart from the law of their God: “By one road you shall go out against your enemies, and by seven you shall flee” (Deut. 28:25); and in Leviticus: “You shall flee, with no one pursuing” (Lev. 26:17).

## CHAPTER XXV.—The Relics of St Benedict Are Placed in Another Shrine. Pieces of the Shrine Bring Healing to the Sick.

The basilica of Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God, in which the body of blessed Father Benedict rests, having been partly ruined by age and partly by fire, Abbot William [Note: [Col. 1213D] Abbot William is recorded for the years 1062 and 1075 in the more extensive *Gallia Christiana*.], with the assistance of the worthy man Odilo, keeper of that basilica, resolved to demolish the old structure and raise a new work in its place [Col. 1213D]. It was therefore decided that the venerable remains of that Father, stored in a wooden chest enclosed on the inside by a bronze casing for durability, had to be removed from the chest and placed elsewhere in another receptacle.

From the remains of that chest many remedies are granted to the sick through the merits of the Father whose venerable bones it enclosed. Indeed, whoever is held by fever—daily, tertian, or quartan—if he washes any small piece of the wood of that chest in water or wine and drinks that potion with the aid of faith, immediately escapes healed, the fever having died [Col. 1214A]. We have proved this very often by repeated experience. Many people from different regions also carried to their own homes pieces of the wood from which that chest had been made, for the sake of their health; afterwards they testified that these had been of great benefit against various kinds of illnesses.

Passing over the many signs displayed through these pieces, let us relate only one, by whose example we may show that many similar things could have occurred. Veranus [Note: [Col. 1213D] No Veranus appears in the commonly printed lists of abbots of Fleury. This Veranus seems not to have been an abbot but the ruler or parish priest, as they call him, of the people of Fleury.], who for several years held the governance of Fleury, was severely afflicted with quartan fevers for nearly six months. Though he earnestly applied the care of very many physicians, learned, as he thought, he gained nothing. He merely spent a considerable amount of money [Col. 1214B] in purchasing remedies and in fees for men who, unless paid, refused even the small labour of applying their art in vain. He too, since he claimed to possess some little knowledge of medicine, tried many things upon himself, but nothing helped him.

Deprived, therefore, of every aid and robbed of hope in medicine, he remembered that many persons oppressed by the burden of this illness had been restored to their former health through relics of that chest. At dawn on a certain day, rising from his bed and carried by the hands of his chamber attendants, he entered the church. Before the altar where the aforesaid relics had been deposited, he threw himself upon the floor, asking with tears and groans that the prayers of the blessed Father might bring him aid. Finally lifted from the hardness of the ground [Col. 1214C] and supported by the arms of his bearers, he asked the keeper of the aforesaid sacred bones to bring him a small piece of the chest, wash it in unmixed wine, and give it to him.

When he had obtained this, he drank the potion; then, his strength failing, he fell from the hands of his bearers to the ground. Vomiting up for nearly an hour the entire excess of humours which had brought him that sickness, he lay prostrate on the ground in a faint. Then, recovering a little strength and raising himself, he was carried back to his bed. After sleeping a little in peaceful rest, he felt thereafter no distress from his illness. He thus learned that, in sickness, it is better to seek the mercy of almighty God as medicine than to trust in the juices and powers of precious herbs [Col. 1214D].

## CHAPTER XXVI.—Fundraising Preaching. A Man with a Disabled Hand Is Healed.

One of the brethren, surnamed Gallebertus, who had been placed over the masons working on the aforementioned project, sometimes lacked sufficient money. He went about many places, taking with him half-trained preachers, by whose exhortation the hearts of men and women, entangled in worldly business, might be stirred to relieve his want by some contribution, however small. As he travelled about, he came to Vitry [Note: [Col. 1214D] Vitry in the forest of Orléans, where there was a priory subject to Fleury.], a place adorned in our time with the distinction of a royal palace [Col. 1215A].

Entering the church, he admonished the people in an exhortatory sermon to flee the mutability of this present life and to seek with ardent desire of heart the permanence of the life to come. Among other things, he gently urged them—for this was the origin of the whole exhortation—to provide some assistance for the work entrusted to him, or at least to give a few coins.

Among the people present was a certain peasant named Marcus. His left hand was disabled, so that he could perform no work with it. Its sinews were contracted, the tips of the fingers driven into the middle of the palm, and the thumb bound over them, so that it represented, in some fashion, the form of a fist capable of striking when closed. He had been afflicted with this disability for nearly five years and could receive no help from physicians [Col. 1215B]. His fellow villagers knew that he had long been burdened by that very infirmity.

Therefore, when he heard the preacher frequently extolling Father Benedict’s powers among his other praises, and saw before him certain relics of saints enclosed in gold, which the aforesaid brother had brought with him in order to stir the devotion of the people, I believe that by the inspiration of the grace of almighty God, who had determined to show him mercy on this occasion, he turned to the brother mentioned above and said:

“I hope, my lord—and my faith holds this as certain within itself—that if, with these sacred relics which I see here before me, you trace around my disabled hand the outward sign of the cross, invoking the name of Saint Benedict [Col. 1215C], the Father whose servants you are, then, when the disability is driven away, it will be restored to its former soundness.”

Those present heard his request and, astonished at his faith, urged that what he requested should be done. The brother himself, likewise full of faith and trusting in the power of the holy relics and in the merits of the Father, took the sacred relics and traced around the disabled hand, as requested, the outward sign of the cross. Immediately, with a great cracking sound from the sinews, it received complete health, all the fingers straightening themselves. Thus the peasant who had long possessed only a useless fist began to have a free hand.

Seeing in himself so great a mercy of almighty God, he offered thanksgiving according to his ability and understanding for his restoration, also giving thanks to Father Benedict, through whose merits he declared that he had obtained health [Col. 1215D]. Nor did all who had assembled in that church do less: for a very long time they continued in the praises of the Redeemer, exalting as best they could the mighty works of him “who is wonderful everywhere in his saints” (Ps. 67:36).

## CHAPTER XXVII.—The Fire at Fleury in 1095. The Library and Charters Are Saved. Christ’s Shroud and Other Relics Set Against the Flames. The Fire Is Checked.

In the year 1095 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the flame of a devouring fire consumed the greater part of the borough of Fleury [Col. 1216A]. It is unknown whether the fire was accidental or deliberately set. On the night following the most sacred Sunday of Easter, a violent fire seized one of the houses lying on the northern side outside the enclosure of the borough. Since it was a cattle-shed, it contained much hay and straw. Although these are at every time exceedingly ready fuel for fire, they were then far more so because, all other winds having been shut out, the north wind alone blew freely over Gaul. Burning all things in its accustomed manner, it had made them dry, while not a single drop of rain had fallen for some time.

Therefore, at the beginning of the third watch of the night, called *canticinium*, those who first saw the fire raised an alarm [Col. 1216B], and the rest of the people, awakened, answered that fearful cry with dreadful wailing: “To the fire! To the fire!” Awakened by the noise, the brothers left their beds and rushed into the basilica. For the Paschal celebration that basilica had been very splendidly adorned with silk hangings. The younger brethren eagerly set themselves to take these down and place them in the treasury, since that building was protected by a stone vault. The work was completed very quickly: some set up ladders; others flew up their steps to the heights of the hall and took down the decorations; others received them upon shoulders and arms and carried them to the aforementioned safe place.

Likewise fearing that the violence of the fire would destroy the indispensable abundance of books, we gathered them there together with the mass of our charters and privileges [Col. 1216C]. For we feared that the little tower in which they were stored, succumbing to the force of the flames, might be reduced to ashes, since it was full of cracks after having been consumed by an earlier fire which ruined the monastery of Fleury in the time of Lord Abbot Gauzlin [Note: [Col. 1215D] This should be read thus, or *Gauzlin*, in whose abbacy the fire occurred which Aimoin described above in book II, chapter 19.].

While the younger brethren were occupied with the matters just mentioned, those who were more devout and advanced in age carried the sacred body of the Father—more precious not merely than these things but than all treasures a thousand times over—into the aforesaid treasury, together with the relics of the other saints resting in that church. Others took out the remains of the most sacred martyr Maurus and the golden right hand [Note: [Col. 1215D] This is why, as the insignia of the monastery of Fleury, a right hand extended in the manner of blessing is depicted with [Col. 1216D] this inscription: “THE RIGHT HAND OF THE LORD,” as Jean du Bois noted.], in which a part [Col. 1216D] of the Lord’s shroud is enclosed, and set them against the fire.

But, unable to endure the smell of the fire, they withdrew within the circuit of the castle. Mounting the wall, they implored the Lord’s help, while nevertheless holding the sacred relics against the flames. Joscerandus, a man of blessed memory, who at that time vigorously performed the office of abbot [Note: [Col. 1216D] Simon succeeded him not long afterward; Tortarius was writing during Simon’s abbacy. Read the notes at the end of this book.] at Fleury, took with him a few brothers and boys who were still kept under stricter discipline. Walking around the dwellings [Col. 1217A] of the monastery until dawn, he conducted litanies with hands stretched to heaven, repeatedly crying, “Kyrie eleison”—“Lord, have mercy.”

Meanwhile the fire gradually increased its strength. Having consumed the buildings outside the town on the northern side, which it had first begun to devour, it was driven by the violently blowing north wind and seized the church of Saint Denis [Note: [Col. 1217D] Concerning this church, read the book *On the Life of King Robert* by the monk Helgaud, who made it first of wood and, after the fire, of stone. This church [Col. 1218D] no longer exists, perhaps from the time of this later fire.], situated almost in the middle of the town. From there, as though released from a higher position into freer bounds, it spread in every direction, even burning wine-presses in vineyards nearly one hundred paces away.

Its roar was so great that all who heard it were terrified in heart and could scarcely stand, their knees shaken by excessive trembling [Col. 1217B]. At last a great fear seized all the brothers when they saw embers mingled with burning sparks falling upon the monastery, which was roofed with thatch. They feared that in a single moment all their dwellings would be consumed by that fire. The monastery which, as we said above, had begun to be rebuilt was still unfinished and was roofed with thatch.

At length, the Saviour, appeased, as we believe, by the merits of his glorious Mother, of Father Benedict, and of the religious man mentioned above, caused a strong south-west wind (*Africus*) to rise. Blowing crosswise, it wholly excluded the north wind from the precinct of the monastery and entirely drove away the fiery vapours which the latter was propelling by its blasts. Seeing this mercy of the Almighty, we rendered, according to our ability, thanks to his immeasurable clemency [Col. 1217C], for he had delivered us from so terrible a danger. Indeed, that same wind did not cease to blow strongly until the entire fire was quenched.

The fire continued raging and destroying the houses of Fleury, together with the food, clothing, and various household goods which it found in them, from the third hour of the night until the first hour of the following day. It devastated everything from the northern gate eastward as far as the southern gate, leaving only a few houses toward sunrise that stood outside the town.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—A Blind Woman Receives Sight.

A certain poor old woman, coming from regions unknown to us, happened by chance to reach Fleury while going from door to door seeking food. Long afflicted by blindness, she had completely lost hope of recovering sight [Col. 1217D]. Holding a little boy’s hand in her left hand, and carrying a staff in her right for support, she made her way along.

Entering the church of the Mother of God, she stood, guided by her guide, before an image of our Saviour clothed in shining silver and beautifully adorned with golden brilliance. There, at that time, the venerable remains of the most blessed Father had been moved because the church was being rebuilt. Mindful of her own poverty, the old woman prayed to the holy Father that he would aid her need by supplying necessities of food and clothing [Col. 1218A]. She did not presume to offer a prayer concerning the restoration of her eyes, for she had already despaired of it.

But the kindly Father, who could grant both, gave what was better; for, once her sight was restored, she could more easily procure the other things for herself. Thus, unexpectedly freed from blindness, she began clearly to behold the light of heaven. Rejoicing greatly, she extolled with all the praises of her heart the merits of the most holy Father, through whom her eyes had received the gift of light. She reported that someone had stood beside her and cut with a sharp razor the thin membrane which had covered her pupils; once it was cut, she immediately received sight.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—A Demoniac Is Delivered.

A man of middle age, possessed by the adversary of the human race, had become deprived of reason and lost the keenness of all perception [Col. 1218B]. Bound by his closest blood-relations with tight straps, he was brought to the most renowned tomb of the Father. He spent an entire day there, joining to that day the following night. Though he kept vigil all night, when dawn broke on the next day, no sign of the health he sought appeared in him, as the demon that had possessed him continued incessantly to torment him.

Indeed, fixing a terrible gaze upon anyone who approached, he would, if permitted, have torn them with his teeth like a dog, gnashing and charging at them as far as he could. But, as we have said, bound by dreadful bonds, he could do no harm either to himself or to anyone approaching him. He uttered horrible and incoherent sounds from his mouth [Col. 1218C], speaking also impious and abominable words.

Because this possessed man, powerless over himself, did not at all remember to pray for his own salvation, not only those who had brought him but everyone entering the church in which he was offered suitable prayer to almighty God on his behalf. Thus it happened that, midway through the second hour of the day, he gave a terrible cry and, as though struck by a mighty blow, fell backward to the ground. Immediately purged of the expelled demon, he became sound in mind and magnified almighty God, who through the most blessed Father had made him free after he had been captive to the most evil enemy.

The brethren who were present hurried to announce in the chapter-house, where the others were sitting, this miracle performed through the venerable Father in his deliverance [Col. 1218D]. They immediately rose, entered the chapel, and with all devotion of mind sang joyfully the festive psalmody which we customarily chant in a louder voice in praise of almighty God—namely, “We praise thee, O God”—and joyfully magnified Father Benedict as well.

The man who had been healed reported that at the hour when he was freed after the demon’s flight, he had seen a man of striking appearance enter through the eastern apse of the basilica, holding in his hand a staff bent at its head. When he hastened up to him [Col. 1219A] and struck him on the head with the staff he carried, he immediately fell to the ground from the blow and recovered sobriety of mind.

## CHAPTER XXX.—A Workman Falls and Is Unhurt.

Recently, while masons were hastening to raise a vault of remarkable height on the right side of the church, carpenters had placed beams high upon the firm structure of the walls. These were intended to support the timbers made in the form of a hemisphere, upon which the mass of stone and mortar was to rest. One morning, as the beams were damp with a light rain and the workmen walked upon them above, preparing what had been ordered, one of them, named Otgerius, walked less cautiously. Striving hard to plant his foot firmly upon one beam, he slipped [Col. 1219B] and fell headlong from that height through the timbers joined together for him, through the manifold pile of wood, and amid heaps of stones to the ground.

Nearly the whole area of ground was covered with piled wood and stones; only a small space, equal to a human body’s length, remained clear of them. To the astonishment of those present, the young man fell into it as though deliberately thrown there. Yet his head was bruised by the hardness of the ground, his eyes nearly forced out, his tongue protruding from his mouth, and his face covered in a stream of blood; he lay on the ground as if dead.

A crowd of laypeople and monks immediately ran together. Although we had not seen the fall, we had heard the affection and lamentation of the workmen. With groaning and tearful voices, we all began to implore [Col. 1219C] the aid of the glorious Mother of God and the intercession of Father Benedict, that they might help the wretch and that the few remaining traces of life might not immediately depart.

For we feared that, if he breathed his last, the work would be interrupted because the courage of the entire populace—who were eagerly devoting both money and bodily strength to completing it—would be broken. Since the populace is fickle and bends like a reed stirred by the wind toward whatever direction the lightness of its mind impels it, it might perhaps murmur that Father Benedict exercised no providence over that place and did not care if adversity befell the work.

They therefore lifted the weakened young man and laid him before the nearby altar of the Mother of God [Col. 1219D], awaiting help from her and from our Father. Nor was this in vain. After a short while, he who was thought about to die immediately recovered breath, opened his eyes, began to speak to those standing around him, and reassured them of his soundness, to their amazement and to the glory of the Lord. He was then carried to his own home and, after not many days, restored to complete health.

Asked what he had experienced when he fell from such a height, he answered that the earth had received him as though he had fallen upon many mattresses, and that he had not felt the ground’s hardness at all.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—A Man Bereft of Mind Recovers.

Stephen, also one of the household, a man of knightly rank, worn down by a long illness, finally completely lost his reason [Col. 1220A]. Like someone in a frenzy, he had to be bound with strong straps and could scarcely be restrained from leaping from his bed and, in his headlong staggering, wandering in every direction.

His friends and kinsmen, worn down by great distress, could find no remedy to oppose his most grievous lethargy. Discouraged, they had already despaired of his recovery. At last, through the favourable providence of God, who had determined to restore his health, they conceived the idea of carrying him into the church and placing him before the altar of the Mother of God, so that they might implore her and Father Benedict’s unfailing mercy to hasten to aid the sick man through their merits.

They resolved to do this only when the dusk of night was approaching, for they were ashamed to bring him out of his house by day because of his continual frenzy, lest he offend the eyes of those who looked upon him [Col. 1220B]. Placed before the aforesaid altar of the Mother of God, he spent the night there, wholly unaware that he was in that place. But while dawn’s circle still gave the world an uncertain light, as darkness was already thinning, his friends carried him back to his own dwelling, and he knew nothing whatsoever of having been taken from it.

Thereafter, as memory gradually returned, the oblivion of mind that had possessed him for many days left him; and shortly afterward he fully recovered the understanding which he had lost. His neighbours and relatives rejoiced with him and, for his recovery, praised almighty God.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—A Violator of the Feast of the Translation Is Punished. She Is Better after Making a Vow.

A certain estate of our holy Father, called Boson’s-village [Col. 1220C], lies near the castle called Petveris [Pithiviers, in the Beauce], and in it, through the grace which that Father deserved from the Lord, the three signs set down below were performed.

In July, the Translation of that glorious Father is celebrated solemnly not only among the Gauls but also among many nations. A certain girl lived on the aforesaid estate. Since she did not derive her origin from the Father’s household, she thought she could violate so great a solemnity with impunity. She took distaff and spindle and began to run about the village spinning, as though taking a walk.

Other women, belonging to the Father’s household, saw this and rebuked her because she presumed, while dwelling upon his estate [Col. 1220D], to violate his most eminent feast. Angrily she answered them: “You who are his maidservants, keep holiday and zealously observe this celebration; but since I am bound to him in no respect, allow me by the labour of my hands to earn the food which I shall eat today.”

Having given this reply, she pursued the work she had begun with still greater obstinacy. Suddenly, as divine vengeance invisibly pursued her, she was struck on the jaw and received a bloody blow. As abundant blood flowed from her teeth, terrified both by the pain of the stroke and by fear of her striker, she fled to the church of that village.

No small gathering of country people assembled in that church, drawn there by the woman’s cries and by report of so great a miracle. Offering her sound advice [Col. 1221A], they urged her to give herself as a handmaid to the holy Father and promise henceforth to observe reverently, as was fitting, all his feasts. Trusting their worthy counsel, she complied with their just advice; and immediately she was freed both from the pain in her teeth and from fear.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—A Similar Case. The Feast of the Burial.

In the same district there had arrived another poor woman, who worked as a weaver. Hired for wages by a certain man named Rodulf, a Breton by birth, she had as a fellow-worker another woman of the same trade; but this latter was descended from the household of Father Benedict, whereas the former was not. The Breton himself, however, was of free birth. Having come from his own country, he lived on the estate of the same Father [Col. 1221B], with a dwelling in that district; and he was a hard-working farmer, strong enough to endure labor.

At the commemoration of the Father’s burial, which is annually observed with reverence throughout all Gaul during the days of the Lord’s Advent, the woman, swollen with the pride of bodily freedom, said to the other, who rejoiced that she too belonged among the Father’s servants: “Come, my dear; let us hurry to finish the work that we began together.” For they had undertaken to weave linen cloth, which was the Breton’s web.

The other replied: “Far be it from me, sister, to presume today to undertake any work and thereby profane the solemn celebration of my lord, whose servant I am.”

But the former answered in turn: “You, if you have leisure, keep the holiday; for I am going to work today in order to have food to eat. You, meanwhile, celebrate the feast of your lord.”

The Breton himself intervened in this dispute. Asking what sort of conversation they were having with one another, and learning the cause, he compelled both women, by his exhortations, to undertake the work they had begun. The Father’s servant therefore sat anxiously at the loom, waiting to see what her companion would do. The latter took hold of the weft; and when she had first passed the thread through the warp, she took up the wooden comb and beat the same thread into the rest of the woven fabric. Immediately, by the ensuing vengeance of righteous judgment, the comb stuck fast to her hand. When she perceived this, she began in terror to cry aloud, repeatedly trying whether she might somehow shake the comb from her own hand. But, seeing that she did so in vain, she abandoned the attempt.

Very many inhabitants of the village, roused by her cries, ran together [Col. 1221D], and the Breton was among them. He, showing no reverence whatever for the most righteous judgments of the Almighty—which, although at times hidden, are nevertheless always just—seized the right hand of the woman to which the comb adhered and violently pulled it away.

### CHAPTER XXXIV.—A Translation Called a Burial-Commemoration. A Vow of a Candle.

The vengeance of the heavenly Judge immediately struck that Breton, as he deserved for his proud presumption. His right hand, namely, which had violently wrenched the comb from the woman’s hand [Col. 1222A], was at once withered, so that, rendered useless, it could perform no work. With that very withering there grew another affliction of an unusual kind: as though he were accused by some fear of his guilt, he was shaken by trembling convulsions and could not be kept in one place even when bound with chains, but, with unprecedented restlessness, leapt about without any repose.

Then, as the force of the illness gradually increased, that peasant was struck with grievous paralysis and lost the use of half his body, so that he became incapable of every kind of labor. Yet the wretch was possessed by such madness and hardened obstinacy of mind that he would not consent to confess that he had incurred so great an illness because of the aforesaid presumption, until, worn down by the long-established severity of the disease, he reluctantly declared in his own voice how this had happened to him [Col. 1222B].

At the urging of his fellow inhabitants of the village, he went to Fleury at the Father’s Translation—the feast in which, leaving Cassino, the Father chose the region of Gaul as the resting-place for his sacred remains. There he professed henceforth to be a servant of Peter, and, after the night of the Father’s most holy burial-commemoration, he kept vigil through the night which followed the feast day, beseeching the mercy of him whose vengeance he had provoked against himself. This we ourselves saw. But because his sin arose from the swelling pride of arrogance, he obtained no forgiveness for which he prayed; rather, accompanied by the hidden judgment of the Almighty, he remained uncured until the end of his life.

The woman, therefore, who had experienced in herself the Lord’s severe vengeance, terrified also by that peasant’s dreadful sufferings [Col. 1222C], professed herself a servant of Father Benedict. She promised that, at that solemnity, she would offer a candle every year for as long as she lived, and that she would observe that feast and all his other feasts with due devotion.

### CHAPTER XXXV.—One Incapacitated in His Limbs Is Healed. At Castellio (Châtillon-sur-Loire).

On a considerable estate belonging to the Father, where the blessed confessor Posennius rests—

> **Note [Col. 1221D].** Posennius is so called in the metrical version of Andrew’s book by Tortarius, who thus sings of this saint’s miracle and discovery:
>
> “Constantius, twice warned, you are chastised a third time by scourges on account of sacred Posennius’ body. Compelled to disclose what the vision taught, you disclose it; when found, he is placed in a sacred tomb.”

—concerning whom Andrew—

> **Note [Col. 1222D].** Andrew, a monk of Fleury, wrote a book *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, from which material is cited in no. 20 of the Preliminary Observations.

—reported many things in his writings, the mercy of the Almighty often displays great works to the praise of His name through the merits of both Fathers. We too shall relate some of them.

A little man named Herbert fell into an illness so severe that, with all his limbs relaxed [Col. 1222D], he could use none of them, except his tongue, which retained, though only very faintly, its power of speech. His want was sustained by the food supplied by God-fearing men, who had also built for him a little hut in the portico of the basilica of that place. There, for many years, he lay curled up like a ball, scarcely able even to lap thin liquid sips with his mouth, and wholly unable to move from place to place for the need of relieving his bowels.

But through the pitying omnipotence of the merciful Savior, aided by the prayers of our Father and of the blessed confessor of Christ Posennius [Col. 1223A], his limbs gradually recovered their lost health, and he was made whole. He gave thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ according to the measure of his understanding, and to both His faithful servants. He remained in the same place for many years, devoted to the service of the church, supplying water, lights, and whatever was suitable for the service of the altar. We ourselves saw him faithfully performing that duty for many years.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.—A Plunderer Punished by Death. Damage Restituted by His Parents. A Golden Chalice Offered in the Dead Man’s Hand.

In the territory of Nevers there stands a certain castle called Huben, on the summit of a steep hill. Its lord was named Hugh, a man of advanced age. He had begotten a son named Gautier [Col. 1223B], who, puffed up by the arrogance of youth and giving too little thought to the commandments of Almighty God, avidly desired to seize by plunder the property of churches and the poor, and to spend it for his own needs.

Thinking, therefore, that he could carry off rich booty from the estate already mentioned because of the multitude of various animals there—for it was suitable for raising livestock owing to the richness of its pasture—he gathered companies of horsemen and foot soldiers and came there, fearing neither offense against God nor the merit of our Father. The inhabitants of that place and of the surrounding countryside, learning of his mad greed and fearing the large number of raiders, called to their assistance the lord of the castle called Saint-Brice, a man named Robert [Col. 1223C], truly valiant both in arms and in counsel. Surrounded by a band of his own men, he hastened there in a ready spirit, prepared with them to suffer whatever loss might threaten, for the sake of obtaining the Father’s aid and for the benefit of the neighbors who had called upon him.

Gautier, having attacked the people of Castellio, strove to carry out in deed what he had conceived in mind: namely, to carry off with him the country people, their livestock, and their goods. But Robert advanced to meet him with his men, joined also by the cultivators of the neighboring places. Unable to engage him because he feared his forces, Robert turned his back. Gautier therefore urged on his followers with loud cries and, spurring the horse he rode, swiftly pursued him.

When Robert saw him now drawing very near, he did what fleeing men commonly do: he cast his spear back over his shoulder and presented its iron point to his pursuer. Gautier, not foreseeing his enemy’s intention, eagerly sought to reach him on horseback and rushed heedlessly onto the iron [Col. 1223D]. The point pierced his throat and immediately deprived him of life.

When his retainers saw their lord lifeless, they filled the air with wailing and their cheeks with tears; placing his body upon their shoulders, they hastened away. Through the mercy of the very man by whose spear he had perished, and with the consent of those whom he had come to plunder, they were freely allowed to flee. The inhabitants proclaimed praises to Almighty God and gave thanks to Father Benedict and to the holy confessor Posennius for so swift a punishment of their enemy.

When the dead man’s father and mother saw their son extinguished—the only son they possessed, upon whom all their hope depended [Col. 1224A]—it is not easy to say what groans they uttered or how many tears they shed, mourning in inconsolable sorrow the one whom they embraced with singular love. Yet, fearing the future examination of the just Judge, God—for they were devout persons—and because all hope of their son’s bodily life had been removed, they considered how they might provide for his soul, so that one who had brought his final end upon himself so wretchedly might find pardon.

They therefore took with them the bishop of Auxerre, a man worthy of reverence, and, with a great funeral procession and their son’s lifeless body, hastened to Fleury. Falling at the knees of Hugh—see above, chapter 5—who was then serving as abbot there, and of the whole community [Col. 1224B], they begged that the bonds of the dead man’s guilt might be loosed through their prayers. They held it certain that his sin would be forgiven before the supreme Judge if those to whom injury had been done first remitted it here and now with all their heart.

Accordingly, they placed in their son’s right hand a chalice of the purest gold, weighing one pound, and offered it as a pledge, so that he might deserve to obtain more readily the pardon of his sin if they made some recompense for his presumption. They believed that whenever sacrifice was offered in it to the supreme Godhead, he would not be excluded from that sacrifice.

The brothers, moved by pious compassion, offered sacrifice to Almighty God for him collectively, asking that his offenses be forgiven. They themselves, according to the power granted by Christ to His faithful servants, forgave what he had sinned against them. When the funeral offices had been completed with fitting honor [Col. 1224C], they dismissed the parents, together with the noblemen whom they had brought in their company, to their own homes, carrying back no small consolation concerning their son’s salvation.

### CHAPTER XXXVII.—Plunderers Drowned in the Waters of the Loire.

After some years had passed, certain raiders from neighboring parts of Burgundy, allied against these same people of Castellio, gathered a considerable force of retainers, horsemen, and foot soldiers. Having crossed the Loire, they spread through the fields belonging to that estate. So great was their security, trusting in their numbers [Col. 1224D], and such their arrogance in the strength and vigor of their youth, that they had a buffoon go before them, playing a musical instrument and singing beforehand of brave deeds and the battles of earlier men, in order that they might be more keenly stirred to accomplish what they had conceived in their malicious hearts.

At that time the brothers had appointed as overseer of the estate a worthy man named Aimeric. Having abandoned the pomp of the world and assumed the monastic habit, he served Almighty God with faithful devotion and remained continually faithful to Father Benedict in the matters entrusted to him. Before changing his clothing, he had held the office of priest; his neighbors and those who knew him bore witness that he had lived lawfully for as long as he remained in the clerical state.

The bands of plunderers broke open the houses of the country people [Col. 1225A], loaded themselves with spoils, and drove before them herds of cattle which they had found grazing in the adjacent meadows beside streams or on the bank of the Loire. The peasants, who had known in advance of the raiders’ arrival, had concealed a great number of their animals in woods and rugged valleys.

Then, with their singer leading the way and fearing nothing, they hurried to the riverbank, where they had posted several of their men to guard the boats in which they had crossed the river. The farmers of the said estate had now gathered together and followed them at a distance, for they did not dare approach. The aforementioned overseer, deeply grieved in heart, was greatly troubled, not knowing what he should chiefly do. He saw that it would not be safe for himself or his men to attack the enemy, nor to seize their vessels in advance, since those assembled with him were few in number and not sufficiently resolute in spirit [Col. 1225B].

Since human strength was lacking and he was deprived of earthly power, he turned with all his being to divine aid. Prostrating his whole body upon the ground, he prayed that help might come to his people from heaven. Then, turning toward the enemy, he cursed them in the name of the Lord and ordered his own men, with the loudest possible shout, to pursue from a distance the backs of the evildoers. The raiders, descending the slope of the hill, were hastening to board their boats and return home, supposing that no one would dare oppose their exploits.

Hearing behind them the uproar of those shouting and the cries as though they were urging one another on, such fear entered their hearts [Col. 1225C] that they all gave themselves over to headlong flight and raced competitively toward the river. No one attempted to restrain them from fleeing, as is usual in such a situation; for those who had been leaders in wickedness were first in flight.

Then one might have seen fulfilled, though in another sense, the saying of blessed Job: “The harp is turned to mourning, and the organ into the voice of those who weep” (Job 30:31). They hurriedly entered the boats; but as each one hastened to cross the river, the vessels, weighed down by the mass of people, split apart and sank when they had reached deep water. The banks resounded with the groaning and cries of the wretched and with the wails of the dying; the hollow valleys and dense woods echoed in answer.

One might see bows with arrows, and spears with shields, floating beneath the surface in the channel of the Loire [Col. 1225D], carried downstream by the river’s swift current. It is said that no small number of those who were drowned and suffocated in the blind whirlpools of that river perished. A considerable multitude was captured who had been unable to reach the boats or, terrified by the river, had remained on the bank. By command of the abbot and the other brothers, all these were released, and they spread abroad everywhere the Father’s power. Blessed in all things is God [Col. 1226A], who cast down their obstinacy and shattered their strength.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.—A Madman Recovers His Mind.

At the estate of Matrigniacus mentioned above, there was a certain young man, proud in the bloom of youth, named Waldo. Unable to endure the itch of his flesh, he had formed a habit of fornication with a certain woman. Often reproved by his friends, he dismissed her and took a wife. But the former woman, grieving and wholly intent on revenge, sought the means by which she might avenge her injury. Applying herself diligently to magical practices, she prevailed so far as to derange the young man’s mind and utterly extinguish in him, by her poisons, the power of reason.

Having lost his mind, he left his home, while his own household did not know what he intended to do. Taking a bow and arrows—for he practiced that art [Col. 1226B]—he went into the woods of Calvus Mons and hid in them without food for several days. At length he left them and came to Fleury on the vigil of the blessed John the Baptist. Going to the greater church, he stood before the altar which has behind it a silver image commemorating the Lord, while the brothers sang hymns to the Lord according to their solemn custom.

There he remained, stupidly turning lights this way and that among the candlesticks and grinding the pavement with his heels. The brothers who knew him watched in suspense to see what he intended to do. When they finally learned that he had gone out of his mind, he was expelled from his place in the church. Moving swiftly onward, he made his way to the altar of the Mother of God. There he spent that entire night in tireless vigil and, as he himself later confessed to many people, was restored to his former health by a saving vision [Col. 1226C]. For he saw the Mother of God, Father Benedict, and the holy martyr Maurus standing before him. Of these, the holy martyr spoke first to Father Benedict: “Free this your servant.”

### CHAPTER XXXIX.—Miracles Performed at Patriciacus. A Cripple Restored.

It seems fitting that we should also record some of the wonders which Almighty God works through the same Father at Patriciacus and in places subject to it. For he is known to shine with no smaller abundance of miracles there than at Fleury, where he rests in body. Thus the same place is held in the highest honor by its neighbors and is thronged by many peoples [Col. 1226D], both by those who come running to this Father’s solemnities and by those who, when afflicted by various calamities, come to make supplication.

We have scarcely touched upon a few of the works which the glorious Father performed there: some have been consigned to oblivion through the carelessness of the inhabitants, and some through the negligence of our predecessors, who, though skilled in writing, neglected to record them.

A certain peasant, named Durand, a servant of Saint Gratus of Paray—

> **Note [Col. 1225D].** Read: “Saint Gratus of Paray,” commonly Paray-le-Monial, in the diocese of Autun, on the river Bourbince, which flows into the Loire a little below. Count Lambert of Chalon built this monastery; his son Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, subjected it to Cluny in the year 1000, with the approval of King Robert.
>
> The monastery is said in letters of Hugh, bishop of Autun, printed by Pérard in *Monuments of Burgundy*, p. 167, to have been originally dedicated to Blessed Mary and Saint John the Baptist, where it is called the Golden Valley. But in the cartulary of that place, a copy of which was supplied to me by the very learned Antoine Héroval, Saint Gratus is shown to have been one of its patrons. It is now a priory united to Cluny. Paray is mentioned in the *Life of Saint Hugh, Abbot of Cluny*, in the *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*, ch. 49, and in Glaber, book III, ch. 2.

—had suffered a contraction of his lower limbs: namely, his thighs [Col. 1227A], shins, and feet. Because, through the disability of his limbs, he had no means by which to supply the lack of his livelihood, he had a portable little bed made for himself. Carried in it through the homes of faithful men, he might receive from them a daily alms for the remission of their sins.

His neighbors and kinsmen, however, being thoroughly wearied by the continual support of his poverty, it happened that he left his own home and was carried on his bed to Patriciacus. There, for some time, by begging he received the *agape*, charitable food provided by those who supported him.

On the solemn day of the Translation of the aforementioned Father, which is celebrated there more splendidly in July, crowds not only of common people but also distinguished clergy and nobles gathered. While the brothers were keeping the night vigils [Col. 1227B], he asked to be carried to the monastery, wishing to take part in the vigils, and his request was granted. As the fourth responsory was sung, through the inspiration, I think, of divine mercy—which had decreed to show him pity through the merits of the glorious Father—he earnestly requested to be carried beneath the shrine containing the relics.

Two men from among the people therefore took his bed, on which he was customarily carried, and bore him beneath the place he had requested. Once he had passed beneath it, his sinews at once stretched out and the knots by which they had been held tight were loosened; he regained the use of all his limbs. His legs, calves, and the other parts which had long been afflicted were freed from their former pain. Released from every distress, he began, according to the measure of his understanding [Col. 1227C], to render many thanks to God, Savior of all, and to exalt Father Benedict with great praises, through whom he had obtained health.

When the brothers saw this, they and the entire people who had assembled for the feast devoted themselves to like work, spending a long time in the praises of the Almighty, who grants benefits to His servants through the merits of the aforesaid Father.

### CHAPTER XL.—Another Such Healing. A Fornicator Punished. Collection for the Poor.

Another man named Belin, of the household of the same Father and himself one of the estate’s cultivators, worn out by an excessive affliction of his limbs, took to his bed. Lying there for a prolonged period, the excessive force of his illness constricted his veins and impeded the course of his blood; his sinews dried up [Col. 1227D], deprived of the moisture that nourished them. Since he could not work with his hands to obtain food for himself, he began to suffer no small lack of necessities.

For this reason he had a bed made like the implement by which livestock manure is carried out from stalls when they are cleaned, so that his kinsmen might carry him in it through villages and fields and he might receive food from merciful people. Thus, while he visited various places to sustain his life, though miserably, he was at last carried to Patriciacus [Col. 1228A]. There too, as in the other places where he had lived, he obtained a daily ration for some time by begging.

But hearing that Father Benedict, his lord also in a bodily sense, granted many benefits of healing to others, he began to reason with himself:

> “If my lord so magnificently aids strangers that, even though they are very far away, he cures them of every kind of disease when they come to him in humble-minded supplication, how much more ought he to restore health to my own limbs, which are subject to his service! For although I am his servant in body, in mind also I am most devoted to him.”

Turning these and similar thoughts over in his mind, he asked to be carried to the monastery. Within not many days, according to his faith [Col. 1228B], he received perfectly complete health and recovered all his limbs.

Greatly rejoicing, he remained in that place, sleeping at night in a stable adjoining the house prepared there for guests. But, thinking that he was now free to do whatever he wished, one night—yielding to his heart’s lust, while an evil spirit tempted him—he fell into fornication. The blessed Father did not take this matter lightly: both because, after receiving health, he ought to have preserved the strength of chastity, and because he had not hesitated to commit so great a crime in holy places. For the house in which he committed the fornication stood before the monastery gate.

Because he had despised the salvation of his soul by yielding to shameful pleasure, he immediately lost the health of body which he had obtained. Yet when his mouth was afflicted with pains [Col. 1228C], he was again pierced in heart and prayed to the merciful Father to spare him. The merciful Father, pitying his sufferings, again restored him to complete health.

For a time he restrained himself out of fear of the earlier danger. But because, burning with lust, he did not take care to tame the itch of his flesh, he again entered into illicit intercourse, joining himself to one of the shameful women and wholly forgetting his former peril. Therefore swift vengeance followed his disgraceful deed: the harmful illness which he had already escaped twice returned.

He returned to the remedy which he had already experienced twice and prayed with much groaning to be helped again. But Father Benedict, wishing to check his folly [Col. 1228D], did not restore him to whole health as before. Rather, having healed him in part, he allowed him to remain partly weak, so that, even in this way, afflicted by the scourge of the flesh, he might keep more vigilant guard over his soul.

He thereafter remained in the health which he had later obtained, supporting his weakened limbs with two crutches. Since he was poor and unable to procure necessities for himself, the brothers appointed him as one of those who receive there the daily alms for the welfare of the benefactors of that place [Col. 1229A]. They hung his bed in the wooden tower in which the bells hang, where it remained hanging for a long time as a memorial of so great a wonder.

### CHAPTER XLI.—Speech Restored to a Mute Man.

At another time, a young man who had for a long time lost the use of his tongue, remaining mute, came to Patriciacus. He wished, once the bond upon his mouth had been loosened, to resume the lost office of his tongue’s plectrum—that is, speech. One day, when the brothers, at the invitation of the ninth hour, were rendering the appointed course of psalms to Almighty God, he was present among them in the choir as they sang psalms. Led by them as far as the altar of the Mother of God, he stood before it.

Since he could not at all do so with his mouth, he poured out with attentive heart the vows of his prayers to the Savior and Lord. He prayed that the Lord would have mercy on him through the merits of Father Benedict, presenting his prayer to the Lord through that same Father, whom he wished to be his intercessor. Very soon he experienced the help for which he had faithfully asked [Col. 1229B].

For the barriers of his mouth were opened, and his tongue began to attempt, through various movements, to recover the intricate modes of speech. It had lain as though dead for a very long time in the tomb of his teeth; now, in restored speech, it sounded forth its first words like the first sprouting shoots. For several moments he naturally remained uncertain whether he was permitted continually to enjoy the gift newly granted to him, until experience itself taught him that he had fully recovered the use of speech.

Dancing with joy at the lavish generosity of Father Benedict shown to him, he did not delay gratefully to render such recompense as he could [Col. 1229C]. For a very great part of the stone vaulting of that church on the northern side had collapsed. Since its foundation had been entirely undermined because it lacked sufficient strength, the brothers determined to rebuild it more securely, so that the vault, set upon a stronger foundation, might itself stand more firmly. In building this structure, the young man persevered as an energetic and diligent worker until it was fully completed. Afterwards, having rendered thanks to Father Benedict and received leave from the brothers, he joyfully returned home.

### CHAPTER XLII.—Light Restored to a Blind Woman.

A certain girl had become blind, deprived by habitual loss of both eyes’ light. As is customary for the minds of those deprived of this world’s sunlight to be more clearly illumined by the light of livelier intelligence, she became more God-fearing and more fervent in the love of the Lord; for although, because of the limitations of her age, she had possessed too little of the right fear of Almighty God, those burdened by bodily weakness are often stronger in mind [Col. 1229D].

Made more diligent in the worship of the Lord, she frequently attended church, begging His unfailing mercy to deign to relieve her sufferings. Yet, perceiving that she could not attain this at all through her own prayers [Col. 1230A] unless she had some of His faithful servants as intermediaries to present her petition more acceptably, she visited the memorials of many saints. Hearing that some were nearer to Almighty God through more illustrious merits, she enlisted them as advocates and repeatedly invoked them by name in her prayers.

Having visited many places but not obtained, through the mercy of the saints she had sought, the brightness of sight for which she longed, she came to Patriciacus and sought the holy Father, whom she had heard was made illustrious by continual miracles. Asking his protection, while standing in his oratory she devoutly begged him that, through his intervention, her eyes’ lights might be rekindled by the divine gift.

The Almighty Lord, moved by the Father’s prayers, heard the poor woman’s petition [Col. 1230B]. He kindled her pupils with renewed light and, expelling the shadows of blindness, granted her clearly to behold the radiance of the gleaming sun. Greatly rejoicing at the sight restored to her, it is not easy to explain with what gladness of heart she joyfully rendered praises to the Creator of all things. To Father Benedict, through whom she had obtained such great benefits, she remained a faithful servant all the days of her life.

### CHAPTER XLIII.—A Man Bereft of His Mind Healed. Relics Washed with Wine.

A certain nobleman, Gaufred by name, a very powerful man and lord of the castle called Sinemurus—

> **Note [Col. 1229D].** There are two castles or towns of that name in Burgundy. One is in the district of Auxois, commonly Semur-en-Auxois, on the little river Armançon. The other is not far from the Loire above Patriciacus, vernacularly Semur-en-Brionnais; this passage seems to refer to the latter [Col. 1130D].

—was oppressed by a severe illness of the head, became deprived of reason, and wholly lost his memory [Col. 1230C]. Therefore all his household, a considerable number of whom served in his attendance, were dismayed over their lord; bereft of counsel, they devoted all their effort to grief and lamentation. The distinguished men who seemed connected with him by kinship, friendship, or benefaction were likewise deeply distressed by his misfortune and gripped by no small anguish of heart.

Having therefore taken common counsel, they resolved that he ought to visit the shrines of eminent saints: namely, of the apostle Peter in the monastery of Cluny, of blessed Philibert at Tournus—

> **Note [Col. 1230D].** Turnucum, or Tornutium—Tournus—is a town of Burgundy on the Saône, distinguished by its abbey, to which the relics of Saint Philibert were brought; the history of that translation was published above.

—and of other saints whose names were widely proclaimed by resplendent merits in that region. His servants set themselves competitively, with a great retinue, to fulfill this resolution [Col. 1230D]. Accompanied by no contemptible company of attendants, he travelled through the places of the great saints. These, reserving this work for the venerable Father, were altogether unwilling to restore him to his former health.

At last, those who guided him remembered that the great Father was accustomed to work great things at Patriciacus, and they directed their course there.
