When they arrived with their lord, the brothers received them in the guesthouse; and, as the Father himself says (*Rule of Saint Benedict*, chapter 53), “the very fear inspired by the rich demands honor for itself” [Col. 1231A]. For nearly three weeks that he stayed among them, he and his companions were treated honorably.

During the whole time that he lived with them, prayer was directed for him to the ears of Almighty God. The sacred pledges—that is, the relics—were washed with unmixed wine, and this was given to him to drink; thus he obtained the health he sought. Giving thanks to the Creator of all and to Father Benedict, through whom he had deserved to be healed, he returned rejoicing to his own home, with all his well-wishers rejoicing with him.

### CHAPTER XLIV.—The Feast of the Translation. Candles Offered. Ornaments Untouched by Flames.

The translation of the same Father was being celebrated, a feast observed every year throughout all Gaul in summertime. It is customary for those who rejoice that they trace their descent from the Father’s household, wherever they live near Patriciacum, to come to the same feast and, out of devotion, bring lamps to be lit before the altar of their lord. Among the rest, therefore, a certain man named Robert, an inhabitant of the castle called Luciacus, hastening to come, offered a lamp of no negligible size, declaring his affection of heart toward the same Father. Having had it lit on the vigil of the solemnity, he asked the custodians of the sacred basilica that his lamp not be extinguished throughout the entire feast-day, but that, with its flames gleaming, it should endure until the following morning. This he readily obtained from them.

Thus, lit together with many others likewise offered by persons of both sexes, it burned throughout that holy night and feast-day, until the celebration of the solemn Mass was completed. When this was over, the brothers, intending to refresh their bodies—wearied by the labor of watching and chanting—more generously than usual entered the refectory.

Moreover, the *apocrisiarius* of that sacred place [Note: In monasteries the *apocrisiarius* was the custodian of the basilica, as is clear here; elsewhere he is called *archarius*, in the *Book of the Miracles of Saint Maurus the Abbot*, no. 22, above.], a truly modest man named Iterius, said to a certain layman named Dagobert, who customarily kept watch in that basilica under his supervision: “My brother, since I have decided to dine with the others who are about to dine, you, as a watchful guardian, take care that we incur no negligence during this interval. Investigate whether any person of malicious intent has entered this basilica, wishing to inflict some harm upon us. Take care lest any of the blazing lamps fall from the altar and cause even slight damage. And, that we may be more certain, let us inspect those lamps and see how they are fastened to the candlesticks.”

Having said this, they did what they had proposed. The lamp of which the account began was placed beside the altar of the glorious Mother of God, which holds the foremost place in that church. They pressed it more firmly onto the point of the candlestick, trusting in its thickness. When this had been done, the aforesaid brother went with the others to dine. But the layman left on guard, being less occupied with the duties assigned to him than he ought to have been, acted otherwise.

That lamp, which we said had been placed beside the altar of the Mother of God, fell upon the same altar, its wax softened by the summer heat. The altar itself, because of the solemn day, was covered with more ornate veils. Thus, during the whole interval in which the brothers sat down to dine, that lamp burned with gleaming flames upon the altar, while the coverings with which it had been draped remained uninjured, except that traces of ashes could be seen.

Then the brothers, having dined, went to church, offering thanks to Almighty God.

[Note: From this passage and many others it is clear that among our forebears it was customary, after eating, to go to church to give thanks, not to the chapter-house. This is evident from chapter 22 of the *Chapters of the Monks of Saint Gall* and elsewhere.]

Seeing the lamp upon the altar, they ran up, thinking that all its linens had been consumed by fire. But when they found them uninjured, they gave thanks to Almighty God, who deigned to display such benefits to them through the merits of their Father.

## Chapter XLV.—A Thief Preserved Unharmed on the Gallows

A certain old woman of the household of the above-mentioned Father, destitute of every necessity, had as the sole staff of her widowhood and old age a son. Since he had no means to support his mother’s need and could not, by the labor of his hands, provide food and clothing necessary for either her or himself, he resolved to make up the deficiency by theft. Persisting in this wickedness, he first stole very small things, then gradually broke out into daring greater crimes. Everything that he stole he brought to his mother; with it he fed and clothed her and sustained all her poverty.

After he had for some time, with an accomplice joined to him, been enticed by this abominable vice and caused much loss to his neighbors, they discovered that this young man—the son of their neighboring widow—was making so great a reduction in their possessions. One day, while he was stealing in his usual manner, they seized him with his companion and brought them before the judicial authority, charging them with the crimes they had committed. The young men, being convicted, were condemned to die by hanging.

But the old woman, whom we have said was the mother of one of the young men, heard that her son was being led to the gallows. She hastened with breathless speed to the monastery and, entering it, addressed Father Benedict in these words:

“My lord Benedict, what is this wretched handmaid of yours to do? As you know better than anyone, I had no other support than this son of mine, who is now being led to punishment. You know, lord, that necessity compelled him to commit these thefts. Restore to me, my lord, my son—your servant—now corrected for the future, who consoles my hardships, lest this handmaid of yours perish through hunger. Show your customary mercy toward me, a poor woman; let my complaint touch your compassionate heart.”

With these and other lamenting groans, her cheeks drenched in tears, she poured forth prayers. The compassionate Father, moved to mercy by the pitiful lament of this poor old woman, displayed in our times an unheard-of miracle.

Both young men were led to the place appointed for such punishment and were hanged from the gallows. One of them—the companion of the widow’s son—immediately died. But the other, though hanging from sunrise until the third hour, could not die, because his mother’s prayers stood in the way. Shepherds, hurrying as usual to see those who had been hanged, came to the place and saw that one had died while the other lived. Astonished at so great a miracle, they hurried off to report what they had seen both to the soldiers and to the mixed crowd of people.

The hearers, not believing their words, sent men to report back whether what they had heard was true or false. Those who had been sent hastened to the place of execution and, discovering that matters were as the shepherds had said, reported to those who had sent them. All were astonished. They sent men to release the young man and bring him before them, intending to learn the whole matter from him more fully.

They learned that Almighty God had preserved the son’s life through the tears and prayers of that widow, whom they had seen, drenched in tears, hurry to the church and devoutly entreat Father Benedict. They magnified the mercy of the Almighty over this deed.

Finally, when questioned, the young man declared that he had felt no injury during the entire time of his hanging. From this it may be inferred that he had committed theft from need rather than malice.

## Chapter XLVI.—A Demoniac Set Free

Gauterius of Capriacum, on a night preceding Saturday, was hastening to the castle called Mons Sancti Vincentii. He wished to be present at the gathering customarily held for assembling merchandise. Hence both the place of such a gathering and the business conducted there are commonly called a market. It is held in that place on Saturday.

As he rode alone past the little river Wldraca, at a place called Planchia-Guillelmi, he was first shaken by enormous terror and sensed that demons were present. Forgetting to make upon himself the sign of the cross, he was surrounded by them, protected by no defense. Seizing him and the horse on which he sat, and carrying them through the air, they finally attempted to plunge him into a whirlpool.

[Note: The Wldraca, or Wldraga, is called in the cartulary of Patriciacum *l’Oudrac* in the vernacular. It flows into the Loire above Bourbon-l’Ancy, as it is called, in the territory of the Aedui. Count Eccardus defines the site of Patriciacum in charter 6 as follows: “This place, then, situated in the district of Autun, is bounded on the east by these streams, namely the Parrula and the Burbuncia; then on the south by the same Burbuncia, descending into the river Isara as far as the church of Saint John,” etc.]

But, with God favorable to him, Gauterius recalled the name of the glorious Father Benedict. When he was already close to being submerged by the demons in the depths of the river, he began repeatedly to cry aloud: “Saint Benedict! Saint Benedict!” Terrified by the invocation of this name, the demons immediately left him and vanished according to their custom.

Seeing himself rescued through the power of that name, he returned by the road he had come to Patriciacum, not daring in any way to continue the journey he had begun. Upon returning, because of the extreme terror which the demons had instilled in him, he lost his mind. But on the following day his people brought him to the monastery; after he had remained there for some time and prayers had been poured out to Almighty God for him, he recovered the sound sobriety of his mind through the merits of the Father whom he had invoked.

## Chapter XLVII.—A Servant Vindicated

Hugh, surnamed Bidulfus, one of the knights living at Patriciacum, was hostile to that place in many respects. On account of a disturbance that had arisen in the same town among the mounted men, he one day attacked a peasant named Guarinus, called “of the Combes,” one born of the Father’s household. Although there was no cause for any just complaint, he beat him so cruelly that he shattered his arm.

Since this peasant could find no avenger of his injuries, and had no one whom he could especially make the advocate of his complaint—for the man who had struck him was proud and showed reverence to no one—he fled in great distress to the aid of his lord Benedict. Entering the church of the same Father, he approached the altar, laid his broken arm upon it, and poured forth these words from a contrite heart with much groaning:

“Saint Benedict, my lord, I acknowledge myself to be your servant and you, by right, to be my lord. You see this broken arm: it was yours, and no one except you ought to have exercised dominion over it. If you had broken it, I would have had no complaint against you, for it belongs to your jurisdiction. But, my lord, why did you allow Hugh Bidulfus, to whom it owes obedience in nothing, to break it? Know that from this day I shall in no way serve yours or you, unless you exact just vengeance from his arm and body.”

The brothers present, who heard these and similar words, were moved to tears. They wept with him and, joining their groans to his, asked the same thing. When he had finished, the peasant left the church and returned with great sorrow to his dwelling.

The holy Father did not at all forget his complaint, but exacted most just vengeance upon the wicked man. The arm on the same side on which he had destroyed the peasant’s arm with blows, together with the whole shoulder, was seized by such force of illness that it became entirely useless and fit for no service whatever. The wretched man was long tormented by this pain and could be cured by no physician. His distress increased; the same disease spread through all his limbs; and, worn out by dreadful pains, he miserably gave up his unhappy spirit.

## Chapter XLVIII.—Two Crippled Men Restored

Two men, both of rural birth, were disabled in their limbs by an old, wasting contraction of the sinews and lay for a very long time helpless on their beds because of this illness. One was an inhabitant of the village called Saint Bonitus of Vetulavinea; the other is said to have come from the village called Palingias.

At the beginning of their illness, too credulous beyond reason of old women’s tales, they for many days allowed themselves to be deceived by the false incantations of little women, encouraged by false hopes. They also tried the mad help of popular healers, who commonly deceive the vulgar crowd with the juices of mugwort, vervain, beets, and other herbs which the earth produces everywhere, or with the fats of various animals. But they made no progress whatever. Discouraged, they ceased to hope that they could obtain the cure they had so eagerly sought.

Persisting long in that despair, they thought nothing of their recovery. But the immeasurable mercy of Almighty God, who had decreed to have pity on them, put it into their hearts to have themselves carried to Patriciacum and to entreat Father Benedict to deign to intercede for their health. They did so, though not at the same time but at different times. After they had spent several days and nights in prayer at the monastery of that place, they received complete health. Then, with joyful hearts, giving thanks to the holy Father, they returned home, proclaiming to all the mighty works which Almighty God had displayed in them.

## Chapter XLIX.—A Thief Punished Through His Son; Upon Repentance, He Obtains His Son’s Health

An estate called Sulmeriacus lay under the authority of the men of Patriciacum and annually supplied them with no negligible aid in provisions.

[Note: This estate was situated in the district of Mâcon and was assigned to Fleury by Winiterius, nephew of Count Eccardus, according to charters 20 and 22 of the Patriciacum codex.]

Very recently the brothers had placed one of their own men in charge of it, to protect the place, ward off robbers, and gather annually the fruits of the customary payment. His name was Odo, and from his report I learned what I write.

A certain Archembaldus, surnamed Albus, a powerful man, exercised the right of ancestral lordship not only over the peasants of that estate but also over those living nearby. His wife, while traveling through the neighboring countryside on an occasion of base profit, came with a proud retinue, as matrons of that kind are accustomed to proceed, to the aforesaid place.

It was autumn, when wine pressed in the winepress is customarily stored in prepared storerooms for preservation in the future. At that time, a considerable quantity of wine was there. The lady ordered the monk to provide a prompt meal for her and her followers. Hearing the command, the monk, a spirited man, was stirred by great indignation and replied that he had not been sent to expend the resources of that estate on women’s banquets, but to transmit them faithfully, once collected, to those who had sent him; nor was he willing to impose upon the place a custom which he had not found there.

The woman thought herself despised by this reply and departed in fury. She ordered Ansegisus Brutnio, who had received authority over those places from her, to load onto carts whatever wine he found belonging by right to the monks, carry it off, and store it in her cellar. He promptly obeyed his lady’s command, loaded the wine onto wagons, and hurried to convey it into his storehouses. But he did not rejoice long.

For as soon as the carts reached the doors of his house, his very little son, whom he loved uniquely, began to be afflicted with such violent fevers that he almost breathed out his soul. The man, not at all doubting that this misfortune had befallen him because he had obeyed his mistress’s wicked orders, restored the wine. Acknowledging that he had acted foolishly, he made satisfaction for his offense and prayed to Father Benedict for the boy’s health. The compassionate Father accepted his repentance, heard him, and restored the child to his former health.

[Note: The author does not reach the year 1107, when the translation of the relics of the holy Father Benedict into a new shrine took place on 21 March, in the presence of King Louis, John, bishop of Orléans, and Humbald, bishop of Auxerre. Christian, likewise a monk of that place, who committed the event to writing, says that at that time Boso, the second abbot of that name, was elected in place of Simon, who had died a few days earlier.]

# Appendix A  
## Added at Greater Length by the Bollandists from a Manuscript Codex of Patriciacum

### 1

In the time of the most glorious Father Gauzlin, archbishop of Bourges, many nobles, renouncing the trifles of worldly life, submitted themselves to the rule of God and our Lord in the arena of this place, under the profession of holy religion. No less did others come from the furthest retreats of Spain: some reared from childhood in divine observance; others raised to the summit of pastoral care. Renouncing homeland and possessions, they sought the presence of this prince of God, counting it a great thing if they might be allowed to enjoy the sight of one by whose teaching and instruction they had been formed.

You might have seen crowds of people streaming together from every direction and, as if with one voice, proclaiming that noble prophecy of Isaiah: “From the ends of the earth we have heard praises: glory to the righteous” (Isaiah 24:16); and the Psalmist’s words: “For the lawgiver shall give blessing” (Psalm 83:8).

That they might deserve a share in this blessing, two brothers, touched by the nectar of heavenly inspiration, set out from the city of Barcelona and with one purpose sought the most holy tomb of our common protector. One of them, named John, had been trained in sacred letters from childhood in the monastery of the Mother of God called Rivipollensis.

[Note: The monastery of Ripoll, of the Order of Saint Benedict in Catalonia, still stands. Enneco was its abbot during the reign of Louis Augustus, as appears from the charter of Countess Ava:

“I, Ava countess, and my sons, namely Count Juniofrecus, Count Wifredus, Count Ooliba, and Miro the levite, together give to the house of Saint Mary, situated in the county of Ausona, in the place called Riopullo, to the aforesaid house founded in honor of Saint Mary, Mother of God and perpetual Virgin, and to Abbot Ennego and the monks who serve God there,” etc.

Written on 20 June, in the sixth year of the reign of King Louis, son of Charles.]

John had received the pastoral charge—that is, the abbacy—of Saint Cecilia, virgin and martyr, situated upon the summit of a mountain. The other brother, Bernard by name, had been trained in secular knighthood under certain nobles, though subject to God insofar as was possible for a layman. Having cast aside the delights of flourishing military life and, what is marvelous, having despised marriage torches, he overcame the fires of his heart by the fire of heavenly contemplation. With his own brother he came to Fleury, as was said above, humbly sought the habit of holy religion there, and reverently received it.

On his trustworthy report we learned that in those regions there was a certain monastery dedicated in honor of this friend of God, one day’s journey from the aforesaid city; there innumerable miracles take place, to the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ, through the merits of our most blessed Father Benedict. From these it pleased us to touch briefly upon the following few.

### 2

A young man of distinguished character was traveling beside the aforesaid basilica and turned aside there with his own squire in order to pray. Leaving his horses outside the church doors, he said: “Saint Benedict, meanwhile I entrust these to your protection,” and gave himself to prayer before the sacred altar.

While he was attentively pouring out prayers with frequent sobs, it happened that another man was passing by on the same road, though engaged in a very different work. Finding no guard, the wretch employed force against the invisible charioteer; he seized the animals with their equipment and made for the ford of a little stream called Lubrigatus. But the madman, blinded by the darkness of his own faithlessness, attempted to swim across the middle of the whirlpool, fell headlong into the waters, and was never seen again.

When the young man came out of the church and turned his eyes here and there, he was not unreasonably distressed by his loss. As soon as he noticed the enemy’s treachery, he rushed in agitation into the basilica of the one who owed him restitution, crying out in a complaining voice:

“Come now, most holy Benedict, how will you commend to Christ the prayers of one who entreats you, when you were unable to guard a single four-footed beast? I swear that I shall not leave this place until you restore what I know I have lost through your negligence.”

As he persistently made these and similar complaints, the robber’s booty immediately returned; without any driver’s skill it stood in the place from which it had unjustly been taken. At once a crowd of people gathered, and great rejoicing took place, etc.

# Miracles of Saint Benedict from the History of the Monk Andrew, Rendered in Verse by Rodulfus Tortarius

*(Bollandists, Acta Sanctorum, 21 March, from a manuscript of the Queen of Sweden.)*

## Notice

Boscus calls the following book of miracles “the work of an ancient anonymous author, a learned author, a monk of Fleury.” He found the book without its author’s name in a very ancient parchment codex of the monastery of Fleury. Yet at the head of book II, chapter 22, he adds that some conjecture Aimoin to have been the author of the same book. This cannot stand in any way, since no. 22 of the said book IV recounts the expedition to Jerusalem of the count of Poitou, undertaken in 1101, and no. 27 narrates the fire at Fleury in 1095, whereas Aimoin had already been dead seventy or eighty years.

But Rodulfus Tortarius, monk of Fleury, reveals himself to be the author of this book in his poem *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, where he has all these same matters with this proem:

> What was recently set forth in prose, I arrange in verse—  
> the deeds by which our Father has shone forth.

We found this poem and various other works of his in a very ancient manuscript of the Queen of Sweden, numbered 1640. There were proposed nine books of marvels, composed in several thousand distichs, concerning kingdoms, wars, triumphs, examples of virtues and vices, prudent sayings and deeds, and similar matters. We give the prologue of them all:

> When there is leisure, and the mind is not troubled by greedy cares,  
> when the spirit is carried away on gentle waves,  
> I have resolved, dear friend, to pluck for you flowers  
> from spring meadows in metrical form.  
>
> Here I have written for you portents, miracles, dreams;  
> here I have written of memorable things.  
> I have told of sayings and deeds, right, perverse, or cunning,  
> which occurred in diverse events.  
>
> You urge me toward renown, Clio, who first inspire the poet:  
> be present from Helicon at my beginnings.

There followed eleven letters to various persons. The first, to Guarnerius Burdo, begins:

> Receive, Guarnerius Burdo, the greeting here described,  
> which one whose name derives from “crooked” sends you.

The second is to Bernard and begins:

> For your merits, Bernard, Rodulfus himself, your own,  
> writes down these few words of greeting for you.

Third were read the acts of the life and martyrdom of Saint Maurus the African, whose final part, concerning the translation of his body to the monastery of Fleury, Boscus published from page 349, with this conclusion indicating the year 1117 in which these things were written:

> Holy Maurus, hear through your merits the vows of one who prays;  
> receive the small gift given by Tortarius:  
> a thousand verses of his—may they remove a thousand sins of his;  
> may seven times ten together with a hundred wipe away the rest.

There was also added a hymn in Sapphic verse concerning the same Saint Maurus, which Boscus confesses at page 355 that he could not read in the Fleury manuscript because of the thinness and age of its parchment. There he makes Rodulfus of Fleury the hymn’s author, mistakenly supposing him different from Torta or Tortarius, under whose name he had already published the aforementioned translation of Saint Maurus.

Finally there were the acts, translation, and miracles of Saint Benedict. Their excessive bulk prevents us from giving them here. Their prologue begins:

> Receive, my Fulco, these quatrains which I send you;  
> read through the deeds of the Father, the Lawgiver.  
> Rodulfus wrote these for you, his pleasant friend,  
> that mention of you might occur in my books.

From this poem we give the fourth book, containing forty-six miracles, which the monk Andrew had previously composed in prose and which hitherto we have found nowhere. Rodulfus Tortarius mentions this Andrew in book V, chapter 35, in these words:

> “In no small part of that same Father’s castle-territory, where the blessed confessor Possennus (of whom Andrew also related many things in his writings) [lacuna], the mercy of the Almighty displays many miracles.”

There follows the fifth book of miracles, written by the same Rodulfus.

# Miracles of Saint Benedict

> Andrew is said to have written for you, Father,  
> wondrous things concerning the Father’s deeds; our pipe records them.  
>
> When the people of Limoges suffered sacred fire by God’s stroke,  
> they took counsel to carry the venerable relics  
> of the Father through the city; when they had done so,  
> the cruel plague disappeared.  
>
> A little woman saw the sacred bier being carried;  
> crippled, she could not walk upon her feet.  
> “Holy Father,” she said, “if I could, I would accompany you”;  
> and she obtained completely what she requested.  
>
> A rider of perverse mind is kindled with jealous fire:  
> he lets his horse loose through his brother’s fields.  
> Hurrying beside a pond, he is swallowed up all at once;  
> the rider barely escapes, but the steed perishes.  
>
> A certain girl had been granted to a shameless spirit;  
> he rages, hurling insults at the Father.  
> He swears the possessed girl will not leave him;  
> yet groaning as he flees, and fleeing as he groans, he departs.  
>
> Ranulf greedily desired to seize frequent prey;  
> one day he did as he habitually did.  
> He prepared a lavish meal from widows’ tears;  
> the first morsel choked his savage throat.  
>
> Gauterius, because you seize estates, you see the troops  
> of the black demon present at your funeral.  
> You have become a monk, you once called by a surname;  
> and you swiftly meet life’s end.  
>
> Why, Gerald, do you support the Father’s enemies for profit?  
> The Virgin Mother of God appears to you.  
> She reproves you for defending her enemies;  
> your wife Eva dies with your children.  
>
> There is a spacious house of the Father in the district of Barcelona,  
> where, often invoked, he works many marvels.  
> There a diligent company serves God and Christ  
> and rejoices, patron, in your protection.  
>
> A friendly knight came there to pray,  
> leaving his horses outside until he returned.  
> A thief greedily seized them, then drowned in a neighboring stream;  
> the knight recovered the horses he feared lost.  
>
> Saracens arrive there in fleets, intending  
> to burn it with fire and despoil it of its goods.  
> They wish to pour out the wines, but they freeze hard as ice;  
> fire thrown upon them dies of itself.  
>
> He points out these effeminate men and sends three more savage ones;  
> he wonders why the same happens to them.  
> One, wishing to destroy the sacred altar,  
> raises his blow and kills himself by striking.  
>
> A cleric, standing upright, utters wicked curses in his own house,  
> when a sparrow flying above him defecates in his mouth.  
> He swears himself angered against the Father and thirsts for vengeance;  
> soon the bird falls, its entrails spilled out.  
>
> In you, Alaricus, the true saying is fulfilled:  
> “The false witness shall not go unpunished.”  
> While, with you as witness, a count asserts the wood to be his own,  
> an oak trunk gouges out your weeping eye.  
>
> Constantius, bring forth Possennus from the holy ground;  
> twice warned, the third time you are chastised with whips.  
> Compelled, you reveal what the vision taught;  
> what is found is placed in a sacred tomb.  
>
> Dust from the tomb gives you healing, Tetberga;  
> a spirit pressed you with harsh goads.  
> When the dust is drunk, the wicked guest is driven out;  
> the Holy Spirit has His own dwelling.  
>
> Before the church doors another woman lay for no short time,  
> stretched prone with contracted knees.  
> As the priest sang Mass and urged the brothers to pray,  
> at that moment she was healed without delay.  
>
> A knight charges that the saints are sleepy,  
> since he carried off their goods without loss.  
> He is handed over to Satan; though free, he becomes the enemy’s slave.  
> He believed them snoring; he discovers them wakeful.  
>
> Albericus, when you deny that you are hereditary serf,  
> you are rebuked from heaven with threats.  
> With fingers fixed into the palm together with the right thumb,  
> you appease the offended lord by lawfully acknowledging him.  
>
> While all else is devoured by fire, an image of Christ’s Mother,  
> though carved of wood, remains unharmed.  
> Those who remove the sacred objects complain that they have suffered cold,  
> while the robes and varied vestments remain uninjured.  
>
> Peasant, when you drive a cart loaded with hay,  
> counting the Father’s famous feast-day as nothing,  
> fire reduces your carts to a few ashes;  
> you and your oxen lose your feet.  
>
> Constantius, there is no need to distinguish truth by heated iron:  
> you are entirely exposed as a false witness.  
> The shameful noise from your burst belly  
> bears witness to the Lawgiver’s *decimam* (“tenth”; the reading or referent is uncertain).  
>
> When you break your vow, you lose your sight again—  
> you had vowed that your female servant would remain forever.  
> Yet you recover it again, and thereafter lose your sight no more,  
> keeping your vow by retaining your servant.  
>
> Landricus presses from behind with a great troop;  
> Geilo enters the Father’s lands from the castle.  
> He orders a soldier to cry out “Benedict!” as a signal;  
> he captures Landricus and scatters the column.  
>
> The niece of Gallaicus seizes the Father’s sacred halls,  
> which her uncle had acquired by serving him.  
> Thus on an appointed day there is much dispute,  
> beneath which she, miserable woman, is struck with paralysis.  
>
> He calls himself freeborn and refuses servitude;  
> *Stabilis*, you betray this with shield and staff.  
> He ties a penny in his sleeves as though it were a poll-tax;  
> it drops out, enormous as a shield.  
>
> A demon suffocates you, Robert; at first he had filled you.  
> The earth casts you down, and three times does the same.  
> There the power of a document sent from Fleury was made clear:  
> when it was placed upon you, the ground held you fast.  
>
> Gauterius, you drag an enemy away from a church sacred in Benedict’s name,  
> and are handed over to a demon.  
> When you repent, you are purified of the crime again:  
> for you release a captive and give a small estate as well.  
>
> Guisbert drives a cart loaded with sheaves  
> stolen, leader Benedict, from your land.  
> The ox feels neither goad, blow, nor sound:  
> it cannot go forward, retreats, and carries the burden back.  
>
> The priest of the aforesaid church drives a two-yoked team;  
> proud young men arrive with carts.  
> They drive away the team; holy Benedict is entreated.  
> At once their cart stands rigid as a mountain.  
>
> While you write to destroy their worthless hereditary title,  
> you tremble when exposed upon the hostile shore.  
> Given over to demonic whips, you are tortured by them;  
> deprived of mind, you are never cured, but die.  
>
> Gauterius, you incur a deadly illness  
> when you dare to give away entrusted relics.  
> Having confessed your offense, you are healed; yet you do not pass  
> through that same year, but die within it.  
>
> You mock the Father and labor to cut down the harvest;  
> peasant, you cut your hand in two with the sickle.  
> They say that fire, falling upon all—animals and cart—  
> consumed the rest, but not the house.  
>
> Gauterius too is reckoned among such men:  
> a vision warned him to abandon what he does.  
> He is beaten with immense blows, because he feels nothing;  
> neighbors carry him back from his own field.  
>
> A squire sees a goose feeding on a pond’s banks;  
> urged by appetite, he hastens vainly.  
> He savagely spurs his hoofed horse in headlong pursuit,  
> and is drowned and buried in the waters.  
>
> Monk, when you secretly remove an offered lamp,  
> warned in a dream, trembling you restore it.  
> Then for three days you suffer fevers for your crime,  
> so that thereafter you may commit nothing similar.  
>
> As he sits at table, eating food obtained through the tears of the poor,  
> he is suddenly roused by the sound of a resounding trumpet.  
> Archembaldus rushes up swiftly with weapons snatched up;  
> his temples are struck by a deadly missile.  
>
> A strange thing: though a vessel has been pierced by countless holes,  
> no wine flows out, whether it be frozen rigid with cold.  
> The impious enemy burns it and pierces it with heated spits;  
> although he does this, he achieves nothing.  
>
> A boy reports what he has seen and urges his parents to believe;  
> they mock him, thinking the dreams false.  
> But the boy, crawling humbly on his accustomed little benches,  
> sought Fleury and returned from there whole.  
>
> Another comes, seeking the use of nimble speech—  
> mute from his mother’s breasts.  
> He sees himself address a snow-white dove;  
> he says what it wishes him to say, and receives it.  
>
> When a third little boy heard what two miracles  
> the Father had performed in saving two boys,  
> this little household servant asked that his own steps be restored to him;  
> and immediately he obtained it.  
>
> A voice at night warned Radulfus, son of Disesia,  
> to seek Fleury that he might be made well.  
> Believing the words, he drags himself on his knees;  
> on the day when Christ ascends, he recovers his feet.  
>
> When the potter William stretches out both hands,  
> swearing, in an uncertain phrase (*quassa*; reading uncertain), that the patron is merciful,  
> his elbow and hand wither in one instant;  
> but wood placed beneath the elbow helps him.  
>
> Roaldus the Breton, possessed by a raging demon,  
> crosses swiftly rivers and pools, rocky places and open expanses,  
> wilderness and cultivated fields. The fierce spirit, pretending to be a dog,  
> leaves the man.  
>
> But when he wishes to visit his densely settled native land,  
> the pestilential guest enters his familiar lodging.  
> Like a black bird it enters his mouth while the wretch trembles;  
> then it is discharged through excessive urination.  
>
> It grieves at being driven out; having assumed the voice of a raven,  
> it terrifies any timid persons it finds.  
> It attacks the brother who had adjured Odo;  
> upon hearing the Father’s name, it falls silent.  
>
> Captured by his enemy, he is bound in a prison-cell,  
> tightened with chains, fetters, and handcuffs.  
> In vain he calls aloud on many patrons;  
> our Father, whom he invokes, rescues him.  
>
> A woman asks a maidservant for her finest clothing  
> so that, more richly dressed, she may hurry to the great church.  
> Unable to find it, the maid, overcome by fear, goes mad.  
> She recovers her senses—but at the Father’s tomb.  
>
> Loose-tongued custodians, yielding to unlawful talk at night,  
> break the established ordinances of the holy rule.  
> First a divine blow chastises them;  
> it teaches them to act more cautiously in holy places.  
>
> A nocturnal vision warns one man to rise from his bed.  
> He scorns what he has seen and lazily turns to the other side.  
> The bed-covering falls upon the sluggish man;  
> immediately the ceiling collapses, yet does him no harm.
